title: Security Deposit: Holding, Notice and Interest
bodyText: Landlord will hold the Security Deposit in trust for Tenant and will not mingle it with Landlord's own property. Landlord will deposit or invest it in an interest-bearing account or fund of the kind New Jersey law requires, located in New Jersey. Within 30 days after receiving the Security Deposit, Landlord will notify Tenant in writing of the name and address of the institution or fund holding it, the type of account, the current interest rate, and the amount deposited. Landlord will give the same notice within 30 days after moving the deposit to another institution, fund or account, within 30 days after any transfer of ownership or control of the property, and with each annual interest payment. The interest earned belongs to Tenant and will be paid to Tenant in cash each year, or credited toward Rent due on the renewal or anniversary of this Lease or, if Landlord has given Tenant written notice, on January 31 of each year. If Landlord fails to hold the deposit, give a required notice, or pay interest as described here, Tenant may give Landlord written notice to apply the Security Deposit, plus interest at 7 percent per year, toward Rent due, after which Landlord may not demand a further security deposit; for a missed annual payment or annual notice alone, Tenant must first give written notice and allow Landlord 30 days to comply.

DORMANT ROW REWRITTEN AND ACTIVATED (instruction 21). Controlling text: N.J.S.A. 46:8-19 (L.1967,c.265,s.1; last amended 2003, c.188, s.1). Pre-rigor row had the topic and 'annual interest' right; it missed: (1) the 30-day written notice with institution, account type, rate and amount, repeated on transfer, account change and each annual payment (46:8-19(c)); (2) the account-type split - 10+ units: insured NJ money-market fund or variable-rate NJ bank account (46:8-19(a)); fewer than 10 units: interest-bearing NJ bank account at the time/savings rate (46:8-19(b)); (3) cash payment or rent credit on anniversary/renewal or Jan 31 by election; (4) the tenant's 7%-interest rent-offset remedy and permanent loss of further deposits, with a 30-day cure only for annual-payment/notice failures; (5) scope: the Act excludes owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units unless the tenant gives 30 days' written notice invoking it (46:8-26) - builder should suppress this row for that case only if no invocation notice; (6) seasonal (<=125 days) rentals exempt from the investment requirement (46:8-19(d)). Trust and anti-commingling: 46:8-19 first paragraph; diversion is a disorderly persons offense (46:8-25); waiver void (46:8-24). Transfer on sale/foreclosure: 46:8-20, 46:8-21 (buyer responsible). Interest-computation rules may exist under 46:8-19.1 (Commissioner of Banking) - not read. title: Security Deposit Interest
bodyText: If the Security Deposit exceeds fifty dollars or one month's Rent, whichever is greater, the portion of the Security Deposit in excess of that amount will bear interest at the rate of five per cent per annum for any period during which Tenant remains in possession of the property for six months or more. Landlord will compute and pay that interest to Tenant annually. No interest is owed on the portion of the Security Deposit at or below fifty dollars or one month's Rent, whichever is greater.

The prior text had five defects: (1) promised interest on the WHOLE deposit when the statute reaches only the excess over the greater of $50 or one month's rent - landlord-adverse, and zero interest is owed where deposit = one month's rent; (2) keyed to lease TERM rather than duration of POSSESSION; (3) said 'exceeds 6 months' against the statutory 'six months or more'; (4) deferred to 'the rate required by Ohio law' without stating 5%; (5) omitted the annual computation-and-payment duty. title: Smoking Policy
bodyText: Smoking of any kind, including tobacco, marijuana, and vaping, is not permitted anywhere on the property, including inside the dwelling, on porches, balconies, or in any common area. Tenant will be responsible for any cost Landlord incurs to remediate odor, staining, or damage caused by smoking by Tenant, an occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant in violation of this Section, and a violation may be treated as a default under this Lease.

title: Utilities Paid by Tenant
bodyText: Except for any utility Landlord agrees in this Lease to provide, Tenant is responsible for arranging and paying directly to the service provider for all other utilities and services to the property, including electricity, gas, telephone, cable, and internet, as applicable.

title: Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness
bodyText: Tenant will keep and maintain the property in a clean, safe, and sanitary condition, and will regularly dispose of garbage and waste in a clean and safe manner. Tenant will use all appliances, fixtures, and equipment in a safe and reasonable manner consistent with their intended purpose, will not obstruct access to doors and windows, and will maintain the property in the same condition as it was delivered to Tenant, except for ordinary wear and tear and any condition that applicable law requires Landlord to repair or remedy.

title: No Subletting or Assignment
bodyText: Tenant will not sublease or assign all or any portion of the property or this Lease without the prior written consent of Landlord, in Landlord's sole discretion. Tenant will not rent the property, or any portion of the property, through any short-term rental program such as Airbnb, VRBO, or similar service, and doing so will be cause for termination of this Lease by Landlord. Any attempted sublease or assignment without such consent will be void and cause for termination of this Lease. No sublease will release Tenant from any obligation under this Lease.

title: No Alterations
bodyText: Tenant will not perform any alterations or improvements to the property, including adding, changing, or removing appliances, fixtures, shelving, wallpaper, or paint, without the prior written consent of Landlord. If Landlord approves an alteration, Tenant understands it will remain part of the property at the end of the Term unless Landlord requires its removal. This Section does not limit any repair, installation, rekeying, or reasonable modification that applicable law entitles Tenant to perform, and does not change who owns an installation that applicable law makes Tenant's property.

title: Joint & Several Liability
bodyText: If more than one individual signs this Lease as Tenant, all such individuals are jointly and severally liable for the performance of all agreements, covenants, and obligations of Tenant under this Lease. Rent is due in full regardless of how Tenant chooses to divide payment among themselves.

This clause contains an exculpatory liability-waiver sentence ('Tenant waives all liability of Landlord for any interruption...') matching the pattern KS and NE found PROHIBITED under their general prohibited-lease-provisions statutes (§ 58-2547, § 76-1415), and which WY only confirmed safe after directly reading all 11 sections of its own Article 12. Minnesota's statute walk this session did NOT find a single consolidated 'prohibited lease provisions' statute like CO/KS/NE — instead MN has scattered per-section non-waiver rules — but that is not the same as a confirmed absence of a general exculpatory-clause prohibition, which may exist elsewhere in MN law (consumer protection statutes, case law) outside Chapter 504B. Leaving MN untagged until checked directly, consistent with WY's methodology rather than assuming safety from silence. | NE RE-AUDIT 2026-08-31 — REWORDED, and the diagnosis differs from the one flagged going in. §76-1415(1)(d) read from primary source (nebraskalegislature.gov): it bars exculpation or limitation of landlord liability 'arising due to ACTIVE AND ACTIONABLE NEGLIGENCE of the landlord.' This clause is already self-limited to 'causes beyond Landlord's reasonable control,' and a cause beyond the landlord's reasonable control is by definition not the landlord's active and actionable negligence — so the ORIGINAL NE SESSION'S REASONING ON (d) WAS CORRECT and no gross-negligence carve-out is needed here. That is why this clause differs from tenants-property-insurance-ne, parking-ne, and storage-space-ne: those three carried BLANKET disclaimers with no limiting qualifier, so they genuinely needed the carve-out. The apparent 'fixed four of five' asymmetry is not an oversight; the fifth clause needed a different and smaller fix. THE REAL EXPOSURE IS §76-1415(1)(a), NOT (d): the phrase 'TENANT WAIVES all liability of Landlord' is a tenant-side waiver, and (a) bars a rental agreement providing that the tenant 'agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.' Even where the practical scope is narrow, waiver-framed language invites the (a) argument for free. Recast as an allocation ('Landlord is not liable') rather than a tenant waiver. Substance unchanged; exposure removed. §5a.1 PROPAGATION JUDGMENT — UNIFORM, not state-driven. Applied to all three tagged states (CO;WY;NE). CO: §38-12-801(3) voids waivers of quiet enjoyment and of good faith and fair dealing, so waiver-framed phrasing is mildly worse there too — the reword is beneficial. title: Maintenance & Repairs
bodyText: Subject to Tenant's own maintenance obligations under this Lease, Landlord will maintain the property, including its structural elements, roof, and systems, in good order and repair, and will be responsible for repairing the appliances, fixtures, and equipment located at the property, except where repair is necessary due to improper use by Tenant or a guest of Tenant. Tenant will notify Landlord promptly in writing of any condition requiring repair or maintenance, and Landlord will undertake required repairs within a reasonable time, consistent with applicable law.

title: Repair Notices: Tenant's 7-Day Remedies
bodyText: Florida does not set a deadline for starting repairs. Instead, a tenant's remedies start with a written notice. If Landlord materially fails to comply with the building, housing and health codes (or, where there are none, the structural and plumbing duties in Fla. Stat. §83.51(1)) or with material lease provisions, the tenant may deliver written notice specifying the problem and stating that the tenant intends to terminate. If Landlord has not complied within 7 days after delivery, the tenant may terminate the lease. Promises Landlord makes in the lease beyond the statute, such as maintaining appliances, providing utilities or services, or broader repair duties, count as lease provisions for this purpose, so a material failure to keep them can also let the tenant end the lease, and the tenant may sue for damages for any lease breach. Only for a failure to comply with the codes or the Fla. Stat. §83.51(1) duties (not for other lease promises), a tenant may instead give written notice specifying the problem and stating that the tenant intends to withhold rent; 7 days after delivery, the tenant may raise the material noncompliance as a complete defense to an eviction for nonpayment, and the court decides how much the rent is reduced for the lost value. This notice may go to Landlord, the person designated to receive notices, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent. If the failure is due to causes beyond Landlord's control and Landlord keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it, the lease may be ended or altered: a tenant who vacates an untenantable unit owes no rent while it stays uninhabitable, and a tenant who stays in a unit that is not untenantable gets a proportional rent reduction. Failures of the additional duties for apartment buildings and similar units (pest extermination, locks and keys, common areas, garbage removal, heat, running water and hot water, Fla. Stat. §83.51(2)) cannot be raised as a defense to an eviction for possession.

What the pre-rigor row got right: the 7-day written-notice period. What it got wrong: Florida imposes no duty to 'begin remedial action within 7 days'; the 7 days is the cure window after which TENANT remedies open, and it covers only §83.51(1) (codes or, absent codes, structural components and plumbing) and material lease provisions, not a health-or-safety test. Controlling text: Fla. Stat. §83.56(1)(a)-(b) (termination; beyond-control rules; last amended s. 2, ch. 2026-143, which amended (2)(a)); §83.60(1)(a)-(b) (withholding defense; notice recipients; s. 12, ch. 2013-136); §83.51(2)(c) (noncompliance with (2) is not a defense to possession); §83.60(2) (tenant raising any defense other than payment must deposit accrued rent into the court registry). title: Repair Notices: Tenant's Remedies and Deadlines
bodyText: Arizona law does not set a deadline for a landlord to begin repairs. The day counts come from the tenant's remedies. If the landlord materially fails to comply with the lease, the tenant may give written notice that the lease will end on a date at least 10 days after the landlord receives it unless the breach is remedied within 10 days. If the landlord's failure to maintain the property materially affects health and safety, the period is 5 days. If the landlord remedies the breach in time, the lease does not end, and the tenant cannot terminate over a condition the tenant, a family member or a guest caused. For a repair costing less than $300 or half the monthly rent, whichever is greater, the tenant may give written notice and, if the landlord does not comply within 10 days (or as promptly as an emergency requires), have a licensed contractor do the work and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent after giving the landlord an itemized statement and a lien waiver. If the landlord deliberately or negligently fails to supply running water, gas or electric service, hot water, heat, air-conditioning or cooling where installed, or other essential services, the tenant may give reasonable notice and then buy the service and deduct its cost from rent, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing and stop paying rent for that period (with limited recovery of any extra cost). The tenant may also recover damages and obtain a court order for the landlord's noncompliance, and in an eviction for nonpayment may counterclaim, in which case the court may order rent paid into court.

WRONG: Arizona imposes no duty to BEGIN remedial action by any deadline; 5 and 10 days are the tenant's termination-notice cure windows (A.R.S. §33-1361(A)), and 10 days is also the repair-and-deduct window (§33-1363(A)). For any other essential-service repair Landlord is responsible for under this Lease, Landlord will begin remedial action within 10 days, as required by Arizona law."

title: Repairs — Tenant's Statutory Remedies
bodyText:
[This entire Section must be printed in bold or underlined type. Tex. Prop. Code §92.056(g).]
REPAIRS AND TENANT'S STATUTORY REMEDIES. If Landlord fails to repair or remedy a condition that materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant, Tenant may have remedies under Sections 92.056 and 92.0561 of the Texas Property Code. In general, Tenant must give notice of the condition to the person to whom, or at the place where, Rent is normally paid, and must not be delinquent in Rent when any required notice is given. Unless Tenant sends the first notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, by registered mail, or by another form of mail that allows tracking of delivery by the United States Postal Service or a private delivery service, Tenant must give Landlord a subsequent written notice after Landlord has had a reasonable time to repair. Seven days is presumed to be a reasonable time to repair; that presumption may be rebutted based on the date Landlord received the notice, the severity and nature of the condition, and the reasonable availability of materials, labor, and utilities. If Landlord is liable under Section 92.056, Tenant may: (1) terminate this Lease; (2) have the condition repaired or remedied and deduct the cost from Rent as provided by Section 92.0561; and (3) obtain judicial remedies under Section 92.0563. Repair and deduct is available only under the conditions in Section 92.0561, which include limits on the amount that may be deducted (in any one month, not more than one month's Rent or $500, whichever is greater), a requirement that the repair be made by an independent contractor or repairman who is licensed where the city requires it and in compliance with building codes, and a requirement that Tenant give Landlord a copy of the repair bill and receipt with the balance of the Rent.

title: Landlord's Right of Entry
bodyText: Tenant will not unreasonably withhold consent to Landlord's entry into the property to inspect it, make necessary or agreed repairs, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or show it to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors. Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable to do so, Landlord will give Tenant at least two days' written notice of its intent to enter, or at least one day's written notice of its intent to enter to show the property to prospective or actual purchasers or tenants, and will enter only at reasonable times. Each notice will state the exact time and date or dates of entry, or a period during that date or dates in which entry will occur together with the earliest and latest possible times of entry, and the telephone number to which Tenant may communicate any objection or request to reschedule. Landlord may enter without Tenant's consent in an emergency or if Tenant has abandoned the property. Landlord will not abuse its right of entry, use it to harass Tenant, or unreasonably interfere with Tenant's enjoyment of the property by showing it excessively, and has no other right of entry except by court order, arbitrator or Tenant's consent.

'the landlord shall give the tenant at least two days' written notice of his or her intent to enter and shall enter only at reasonable times' (RCW 59.18.150(6)); the notice 'must state the exact time and date or dates of entry or specify a period of time during that date or dates in which the entry will occur, in which case the notice must specify the earliest and latest possible times of entry' and 'must also specify the telephone number to which the tenant may communicate any objection or request to reschedule the entry' (RCW 59.18.150(6)). One day for showings: 'where the landlord has given at least one day's notice of intent to enter to exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers or tenants' (the statute does not say 'written' for the one-day notice; the clause requires writing, a stricter floor). Purposes track RCW 59.18.150(1); emergency and abandonment, RCW 59.18.150(5); 'The landlord has no other right of access except by court order, arbitrator or by consent of the tenant' (RCW 59.18.150(7)). title: Default by Tenant
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and does not cure the failure within the time period specified by applicable law after receiving written notice from Landlord. Tenant will also be in default if Tenant fails to comply with any other obligation under this Lease and does not cure the failure after receiving written notice. Landlord need not give Tenant an opportunity to cure any breach, including a failure to pay Rent, where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without one. Except as required by applicable law, Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise all rights and remedies available under applicable law, including terminating this Lease, regaining possession of the property, and recovering unpaid Rent, late fees, and reasonable costs and expenses, less amounts obtained from the Security Deposit. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to mitigate damages resulting from Tenant's default to the extent required by applicable law. To the extent permitted under applicable law, the prevailing party may recover from the other party court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in connection with any legal proceedings related to this Lease.

This resolves ND's piece of the standing fee-shifting-mutuality question (though the broader cross-state consolidation across CO/WY/KS/NE/MN remains a separate open item). | 5a.1 RETROACTIVE CLASSIFICATION 2026-08-28: the prevailing-party attorney-fee rewrite here was STATE-DRIVEN (forced by C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(II)), not uniform, and was inherited by WY/MN/ND/SD without classification - the exact failure mode 5a.1 exists to prevent. The standing open item -- 'is this clause's fee language genuinely mutual, and does it work in every tagged state?' -- is resolved. Operative sentence: 'To the extent permitted under applicable law, the prevailing party may recover from the other party court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in connection with any legal proceedings related to this Lease.' FIVE DISTINCT STATE ARCHITECTURES, not one question: (1) CO -- a landlord-only fee clause is VOID and the lease must be drafted mutual; 'prevailing party' SATISFIES this. (2) MN -- fee clauses are made mutual BY OPERATION OF LAW regardless of lease text; consistent, no conflict. (3) KS (K.S.A. 58-2547) and NE (§ 76-1415(1)(c)) -- attorney-fee clauses are BANNED OUTRIGHT in either direction; this clause is correctly NOT tagged to either, and a library-wide check confirmed ZERO LEASE_CLAUSE rows tagged KS or NE contain attorney-fee language. (4) ND -- § 47-16-13.6 awards fees to 'the prevailing party' by statute; clause language matches exactly. (5) WY -- American Rule, no reciprocity statute, contract governs. OPEN FLAG FOR WYOMING, surfaced not resolved: per edu-no-fee-reciprocity-wy the Wyoming Supreme Court requires a contract to 'unequivocally provide' for fee recovery before fees may be awarded. This clause hedges twice -- 'TO THE EXTENT PERMITTED UNDER APPLICABLE LAW' makes the entitlement conditional on an external referent, and 'MAY recover' is permissive rather than mandatory. Under a strict unequivocal-provision standard that phrasing may not suffice, which would leave a WY landlord with NO fee recovery in a state whose default is that each side bears its own. No Wyoming case applying the standard to comparable hedged language was located, and no edit is made on that basis -- flagged for Taylor. Note the hedge exists for a reason: it is what makes the clause safe to share with CO and MN. Any WY fix should be a WY-specific override, NOT an edit to the shared text. | WYOMING FLAG RETRACTED 2026-09-06 after reading the actual case law rather than this library's characterisation of it. NO WY-SPECIFIC OVERRIDE IS NEEDED. The Wyoming standard is EXPRESS CONTRACTUAL AUTHORISATION, not a heightened magic-words test: Cowardin v. Finnerty (Wyo. 1999) -- 'absent statutory or contract language expressly authorizing recovery of attorney fees, parties are responsible for payment of their own attorney fees'; Emken, 2006 WY 112, ¶ 8 -- 'a prevailing party may be reimbursed for its attorney fees when express statutory or contractual authorization exists'; Thorkildsen v. Belden, 2012 WY 8; Circle Resources v. Hassler, 2023 WY 22, ¶ 8 -- 'A prevailing party may, however, be reimbursed for attorneys' fees when provided for by contract or statute.' The Wyoming failure cases are ones where the contract said NOTHING about fees. Cowardin is explicit: 'Given the absence of any reference to attorney fees in the purchase agreement, Sellers were not entitled to recover attorney fees.' THIS CLAUSE EXPRESSLY REFERS TO ATTORNEY FEES, NAMES THE PREVAILING PARTY, AND USES THE COURT'S OWN FORMULATION. The supposed defect -- 'may recover' being permissive -- is the verb the Wyoming Supreme Court itself uses in stating the rule. 'To the extent permitted under applicable law' is a savings clause; no Wyoming authority was located suggesting a savings clause defeats otherwise-express authorisation, and the circularity concern raised earlier in this session was speculative. The cases say 'expressly authorizing' / 'express... authorization'. title: Default by Tenant
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and does not cure the failure within the time period specified by applicable law after receiving written notice from Landlord. Tenant will also be in default if Tenant fails to comply with any other obligation under this Lease and does not cure the failure after receiving written notice. Landlord need not give Tenant an opportunity to cure any breach, including a failure to pay Rent, where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without one. Except as required by applicable law, Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise all rights and remedies available under applicable law, including terminating this Lease, regaining possession of the property, and recovering unpaid Rent and late fees, less amounts obtained from the Security Deposit. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to mitigate damages resulting from Tenant's default to the extent required by applicable law. To the extent permitted under applicable law, the prevailing party may recover from the other party court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in connection with any legal proceedings related to this Lease.

title: Surrender at End of Term
bodyText: Upon the expiration or earlier termination of this Lease, Tenant will surrender possession of the property and return all keys to Landlord immediately, unless applicable law entitles Tenant to remain. The property will be left in the same condition as at the start of the Term, except for ordinary wear and tear, and free of all personal property of Tenant and any occupants. Personal property left at the property after Tenant vacates may, to the extent permitted by applicable law, be treated as abandoned and disposed of at Tenant's cost.

title: Early Termination
bodyText: Tenant may terminate this Lease before the end of the Term by providing Landlord at least 30 days' written notice. Tenant will pay an early termination fee equal to one month's Rent ({{monthly_rent}}) or 30% of the remaining Rent due under the Term, whichever is greater, and remains responsible for Rent and other obligations up to the termination date. Landlord may terminate this Lease early by providing Tenant at least 30 days' written notice if Tenant breaches a material term of this Lease and fails to cure the breach within 10 days of receiving written notice, or on such shorter notice and cure period as applicable law permits, or if Tenant vacates or abandons the property without notifying Landlord. Nothing in this Section limits any right either party has under applicable law. This includes a Tenant's right to terminate without penalty due to active military service under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, due to the property becoming uninhabitable through no fault of Tenant, or — except as prohibited by law in the case of a Tenant's death — any other termination right or limitation provided by applicable law.
notes: CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself EDITED this session WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | UNIFORM EDIT 2026-10-03 (rule 62, WY's proposal of 2026-10-01): the landlord limb now adds 'or on such shorter notice and cure period as applicable law permits', so the 30-day notice and 10-day cure no longer give up a shorter statutory route. Vetted and supported by every tagged state (CO, WY, MN, ND, SD, OH); GA, NC, NV and TX also found it lawful before moving to `early-termination-ks`. Noted in each tagged state's log. | MN extended (Minnesota session, CO;WY-scoping resolution): the clause's '10 days to cure' for landlord-initiated termination is more generous than Minnesota law requires (MN has no general statutory cure period for material lease violations, confirmed absent this session) — unlike KS/NE, where a real statutory cure period (14 days) made this clause's shorter figure a rights-shortening conflict. No conflict for MN. | Cross-state plain-language cleanup (Minnesota session, follow-up to MN's plain-language audit): long compound sentence split into shorter ones, no substantive change. Not a legal requirement for this clause's other tagged states (only MN's Plain Language Contract Act, Minn. Stat. §325G.31, was confirmed to apply this project) — done as a general readability improvement since the pattern was found library-wide, not MN-specific. | ND extended (North Dakota session 1, same scoping review): no numeric conflict with N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-16/17's landlord/tenant termination rights, neither of which specifies a notice period or cure timeline that would contradict this clause's 30-day/10-day figures. | SD extended (South Dakota session 1, Title 21-16 review): generic mechanics (30-day notice + 1 month's rent fee) are not statutorily mandated for SD but not prohibited either; no conflicting SD statute found (SDCL 43-32-19's tenant-termination causes are different grounds, not a fee framework). | NJ: added 2026-09-26 (tag-first screen, instruction 26). Tagged as lawful-but-exposed (same posture as KS/NE/OH/NV/TX): fee enforceability against a mitigation duty is case law, not read. Statutory tenant terminations it preserves: death (N.J.S.A. 46:8-9.1 - note it yields to a lease that 'explicitly provide[s] otherwise'; this clause does not), disability/assisted living/low-income housing (46:8-9.2), domestic violence (46:8-9.6, non-waivable 46:8-9.9), flood non-disclosure (46:8-50(e)). Landlord early termination for breach still requires an Anti-Eviction ground and court process. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | NJ: REMOVED 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12 retro, rules 37 and 43). Two defects in NJ: (1) its landlord-termination sentence promises a 10-day cure for any material breach, which can give away New Jersey's no-cure grounds (willful or grossly negligent damage and the criminal-activity grounds, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(c), (n)-(r), on three days' notice, 2A:18-61.2(a)), and its 30-day notice does not track the one month's notice 2A:18-61.2(b) sets for lease-breach removal; (2) the fee measured on "the remaining Rent due under the Term" assumes a fixed Term. NJ now uses early-termination-ks. Not a re-audit. | AZ: Applies as written. No early-termination fee statute in ch. 10 (full read). "Nothing in this Section limits any right" preserves the A.R.S. §33-1318 domestic-violence and sexual-assault termination (no early termination penalties or fees) and §33-1318.01 law-enforcement officer release. The landlord's 10-day cure tracks §33-1368(A); the statutory no-cure grounds remain available. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | AZ: REMOVED 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.13 retro, rules 37 and 43). Two defects in AZ: (1) the fee measured on 'the remaining Rent due under the Term' and the option to end 'before the end of the Term' read as reaching a month-to-month tenancy, which either party may end on 30 days' written notice under A.R.S. §33-1375(B) with no fee (a fee on that statutory right risks §33-1315(A)(1) and the (B) penalty); (2) its landlord-termination sentence promises a 10-day cure for any material breach, which can give away §33-1368(A)'s no-cure grounds (material and irreparable breach; a second breach of the same or similar nature; falsified criminal or eviction record). AZ now uses early-termination-ks. Not a re-audit. | GA: Applies as written. No Georgia cap on early-termination fees located; a fee is liquidated damages, binding 'unless the agreement violates some principle of law' (O.C.G.A. § 13-6-7; penalty case law not relied on). 'Any other termination right' preserves the non-waivable military (O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-22, 44-7-37) and family-violence (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-23) rights. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | GA: REMOVED 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 37; rule 43 and fix 23 screened). The fee measured on 'the remaining Rent due under the Term' and the option to end 'before the end of the Term' read as reaching a Georgia tenancy at will (any tenancy with no time set for it to end, O.C.G.A. § 44-7-6), which the tenant may end on 30 days' notice with no fee (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-7). GA now uses `early-termination-ks`, whose fixed-Term limb answers this and whose landlord limb defers to the default provisions. Rule 43: the landlord limb's 30-day notice plus 10-day cure was lawful in Georgia (no statutory cure or no-cure grounds; O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50(a) and (c)), so no defect there. Not a re-audit. s5a.1: states-only change. | NC: Applies as written. No North Carolina statute regulates contractual early-termination fees (the N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-46 fee list governs late fees, eviction administrative fees, litigation costs and insurance, not early termination); enforceability as liquidated damages is case law, not relied on. The savings sentence preserves the military-technician (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-45), N.C. Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (Chapter 127B, Article 4), domestic-violence (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-45.1) and foreclosure (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-45.2) termination rights. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | NC: REMOVED 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.21 retro, rule 37; rule 43 and fix 25 screened). The fee measured on 'the remaining Rent due under the Term' and the option to end 'before the end of the Term' read as reaching a North Carolina periodic tenancy, including the month-to-month tenancy `holdover-ca` creates 'on the same terms', which either party may end on seven days' notice (two days week to week) with no fee (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-14). NC now uses `early-termination-ks`, whose fixed-Term limb answers this and whose landlord limb defers to the default provisions. Rule 43: the landlord limb's 30-day notice and 10-day cure gave up no statutory North Carolina route (none exists for non-rent breaches; Article 7 and N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-3 were preserved by the savings sentence). Not a re-audit. s5a.1: states-only change. | NV: Read in full 2026-09-24 against NRS 118A (revisor text Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated). Applies as written. Equal 30-day notice both ways satisfies 118A.220(1)(e). Fee is lawful-but-exposed under NRS 118A.230 unconscionability (same posture as KS/NE/OH, CA s5.41); no per se liquidated-damages bar located in 118A. Savings sentence preserves 118A.340 and 118A.345 rights. | NV (text batch 2, 2026-09-24): NRS 118.175 (read): on abandonment the landlord must make reasonable efforts to re-rent at fair rental, and the former tenant owes actual damages. The contractual early-termination fee is an agreed option, not abandonment; OH's warning applies - never pair the fee with a waiver of that mitigation duty. | NV (retro SOP 1.27, 2026-10-02): NV REMOVED from this row (rule 37). Its fee is measured on 'the remaining Rent due under the Term', which only makes sense in a fixed Term, and NRS 118A.210(2) makes any tenancy without a definite term week-to-week or month-to-month, so the row read literally gives a periodic tenant a fee with no base. NV now uses early-termination-ks, whose option and fee apply only to a fixed Term and whose landlord limb defers to the default and notice provisions. This NV segment and the earlier NV segments are history. | TX: Read in full 2026-09-25 against Tex. Prop. Code chs. 24, 54, 91, 92 and 301 (official statutes.capitol.texas.gov text for chs. 24/54/91/301). Applies as written. Contractual option. Tex. Prop. Code s91.006: landlord's duty to mitigate on abandonment is non-waivable, and the clause does not purport to waive it. Fee is lawful-but-exposed (no per se liquidated-damages bar in chs. 24/91/92) - same posture recorded for KS/NE/OH/NV. Statutory termination rights (ss92.016, .0161, .017, .0162) preserved by the clause's savings sentence; the REQUIRED Texas statement is early-termination-rights-statement-tx. s92.1031 (failure to occupy + replacement tenant) caps retention at an agreed cancellation fee or actual re-letting costs in that narrow case. | TX: REMOVED 2026-10-03 (SOP 1.29 retro, rule 37; rule 43 and fix 22 screened). The fee measured on 'the remaining Rent due under the Term' and the option to end 'before the end of the Term' read as reaching a Texas month-to-month tenancy, including the one `holdover-ca` creates 'on the same terms', which either party may end on one month's notice with no fee (Tex. Prop. Code §91.001(a)-(b)). The landlord limb also promises 30 days' notice and a 10-day cure for any material breach, which a court could read as displacing the Tenant Default route (§24.005(a): three days' notice to vacate, or a shorter or longer period the lease sets, and no cure for a non-rent breach); the closing 'Nothing in this Section limits any right ... under applicable law' does not clearly save a contractual remedy (contract-construction case law not read). TX now uses `early-termination-ks`. This TX segment and the earlier TX segment are history. | OH: no Ohio conflict, but the greater-of-one-month-or-30% fee carries real §5321.14 unconscionability exposure, and Ohio's mitigation duty (Lemstone, commercial holding) is waivable — do NOT stack a waiver with this fee. CROSS-STATE FLAG RAISED AND NOT RESOLVED 2026-09-19 - it is wider than first recorded. The fee of 'one month's Rent or 30% OF THE REMAINING RENT, whichever is greater' appears IDENTICALLY in this row and its KS and NE variants, i.e. across EIGHT states (CO, WY, KS, NE, MN, ND, SD, OH). California is the only state where it was removed, because Civ. Code s1671(d) makes a liquidated-damages provision in a DWELLING lease void unless fixing actual damages would be impracticable, with s1951.5 confirming s1671 reaches leases of real property. Every state applies some liquidated-damages or penalty doctrine, and a percentage-of-remaining-rent charge is its classic target. The identical figure in all eight suggests it was INHERITED rather than verified state by state. UNLIKE the setoff flag, this CANNOT be fixed by a savings clause - where such a term is void it is the AMOUNT that offends, and 'as permitted by law' does not cure it. Needs a per-state read of liquidated-damages law before the next lease goes out. CA: early-termination-ca. FLAG DOWNGRADED AND CLOSED 2026-09-19 — MY ESCALATION WAS OVERSTATED. I recorded the 30%-of-remaining-rent fee as an unresolved eight-state risk needing a fresh per-state read. The library already answered it: each state's own session screened this clause (MN Plain Language Act check; ND - no conflict with N.D.C.C. ss47-16-16/17; SD - not mandated but not prohibited, no conflicting statute; OH - no conflict but real s5321.14 unconscionability exposure and do NOT stack with a mitigation waiver; KS and NE - the cure-period figure was corrected and the tenant's voluntary 30-day-plus-fee right expressly left intact). THE ACTUAL POSITION: CALIFORNIA IS THE OUTLIER, not the other eight. Civ. Code s1671(d) is a PER SE statutory bar on liquidated damages in a dwelling lease; no other state in the library has one. Everywhere else the ceiling is CASE-BY-CASE UNCONSCIONABILITY - statutory in KS, NE and OH (s5321.14), general doctrine in SD (53-9-3) and by common law in WY and MN, with CO's express liquidated-damages prohibition confined to the death-of-tenant context (edu-death-of-tenant-co). So the fee is NOT void per se outside CA; it is lawful-but-exposed, and the exposure rises with the size of the figure. PRODUCT GUIDANCE: keep the fee configurable, set it defensibly against actual re-letting loss, and in OH never combine it with a waiver of the mitigation duty. No further statute reading is required. | OH UNTAGGED 2026-10-03 (SOP 1.48 targeted fix 2, rule 37). Ohio now uses early-termination-ks, whose fixed-Term limb answers the periodic-tenancy problem I raised in the 2026-10-02 OH retro - 'one month's Rent or 30% of the remaining Rent due under the Term, whichever is greater' has no referent in a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy under R.C. 5321.17(A) and (B), where the greater-of silently collapses to one month's rent - and whose landlord limb defers to the Tenant Default and notice provisions instead of promising 30 days plus a 10-day cure. Same move as GA, NC, NV and TX. Ohio's substantive findings on this clause are carried forward into early-termination-ks's OH segment, not lost here. Not a re-audit; nothing else in Ohio was reviewed. | WY (Claude Code, 2026-10-04 backfill, rule 79): basis is the 2026-08-21 full-library cross-check that tagged WY (generic mechanics, no Wyoming-specific statute or figure; GENERIC in the WY citations file). No section was read for this row; the cross-check is recorded in the first state's segment above.

title: Holdover Tenancy
bodyText: If Tenant does not vacate the property by the end of the Term, Landlord may pursue any remedy allowed by applicable law to recover possession. Landlord will also be entitled to recover from Tenant holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law for each day Tenant remains in possession after the end of the Term. Alternatively, Landlord may accept Tenant's continued payment of Rent, in which case this Lease will be deemed to continue on a month-to-month basis on the same terms and conditions, terminable by either party upon the written notice required by applicable law or, where applicable law sets no notice period, by this Lease.
notes: CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself unchanged WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | NE added (session 1): Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1437(3) allows up to 3x periodic rent or 3x actual damages for willful bad-faith holdover — higher than this clause's double-rent figure, so the clause still holds up in NE without an override (per Taylor's read, Flag 6). See edu-holdover-ne for the full NE figure and a note to revisit the double-rent baseline once more states are surveyed. | MN extended (Minnesota session, whole-library audit): generic mechanics, already vetted against KS/NE's prohibited-lease-provisions statutes (the strictest bar found in this project to date) since this clause was already tagged KS;NE; no MN-specific statutory language or number identified in this session's statute walk that conflicts. No exculpatory/liability-waiver language present. | Cross-state plain-language cleanup (Minnesota session, follow-up to MN's plain-language audit): long compound sentence split into shorter ones, no substantive change. Not a legal requirement for this clause's other tagged states (only MN's Plain Language Contract Act, Minn. Stat. §325G.31, was confirmed to apply this project) — done as a general readability improvement since the pattern was found library-wide, not MN-specific. | SHARED-CLAUSE PASS 2026-09-03 (§5a.1). EDIT: removed the hardcoded 'double the Monthly Rent ... or the maximum amount allowed under applicable law, if less' and replaced it with a pure deferral to the statutory maximum. §5a.1 JUDGMENT: **STATE-DRIVEN** — the holdover figure genuinely differs per state — but the EDIT itself is uniform-safe and no per-state override is required, because each state's figure is already carried by its own education row. WHY THE OLD TEXT WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, which is why leaving it was not an option: (1) OVER-PROMISED in MN — Minnesota has NO holdover multiplier at all (§504B.141 and the eviction chapter, confirmed at MN re-audit), so 'double the Monthly Rent' described a remedy that does not exist; the self-limiting tail made it lawful but misleading. (2) UNDER-CLAIMED in NE — Nebraska allows three months' periodic rent or threefold actual damages, whichever is greater, PLUS statutory attorney fees (§76-1437(3)), all of which EXCEED double monthly rent. The old 'or the maximum allowed ... if less' language could only ever cap DOWNWARD, so a Nebraska landlord relying on the clause would recover materially less than the statute allows. A ceiling-only formulation silently forfeits recovery in any state whose statutory figure is higher than the hardcoded one. KS is unaffected either way (1.5x cap under K.S.A. 58-2570(c), already below double, per edu-holdover-ks). GAP SURFACED, NOT CLOSED: CO and WY have NO holdover-damages education row and their statutory figures have never been verified in this project. The 'double' figure appears to have originated as Colorado's, but that has not been confirmed against C.R.S. Recommend verifying CO and WY holdover figures and adding edu-holdover-co / edu-holdover-wy, matching KS/NE/MN. | FOLLOW-UP 2026-09-03: the gap flagged in the shared-clause pass is now closed, and the answer is worse than expected. THE 'DOUBLE THE MONTHLY RENT' FIGURE HAD NO STATUTORY BASIS IN ANY OF THE FIVE TAGGED STATES. CO: no multiplier, damages = reasonable rental value (§13-40-123, Behr v. Burge). WY: no multiplier, actual damages plus 10% interest (§1-21-1211(b), provisional). KS: 1.5x cap, BELOW double (K.S.A. 58-2570(c)). NE: three months' periodic rent or threefold actual plus attorney fees, ABOVE double (§76-1437(3)). MN: no multiplier at all. So the number was wrong in every direction simultaneously — too high in three states, too low in one, and baseless in the two where it was assumed to have originated. The shared-clause pass hypothesized it 'appears to have originated as Colorado's'; that hypothesis is now DISPROVED. It appears to be generic template boilerplate that entered the library before any state research and was never questioned, and it survived four state re-audits. Removing it was correct. Recording the provenance because it is the clearest example in the project of an unsourced number propagating through a shared clause: nothing in the library ever asserted where 'double' came from, and every state's own research quietly contradicted it. |  SHARED EDIT 2026-09-28 (Taylor's decision, gap-discovery backfill): the month-to-month notice now falls back to this Lease where the law sets no period. Wyoming has none, and `periodic-tenancy-notice-wy` supplies it. Raised by the WY backfill. Uniform under §5a.1: the words are self-limiting, so no state needs an override. | AZ: Applies as written. The referent exists: A.R.S. §33-1375(C) - if the holdover is willful and not in good faith, the landlord may recover up to the greater of two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages; if the landlord consents in writing to continued occupancy, §33-1314(D) makes it month-to-month. holdover-ca NOT tagged: its actual-damages measure would give up the statutory recovery (K.3). The "for each day" wording does not match Arizona's lump-sum measure but does not cap it. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | AZ: REMOVED 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.13 retro, rules 53 and 37); superseded for AZ by holdover-az. A.R.S. §33-1375(C) gives a one-time measure ('an amount equal to not more than two months' periodic rent or twice the actual damages sustained by the landlord, whichever is greater') only for a holdover that is willful and not in good faith, triggered by remaining in possession after expiration of the term or its termination (so also after a notice ending a periodic tenancy). This row's 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law for each day ... after the end of the Term' misstates that shape and trigger, and its acceptance-of-Rent month-to-month sentence differs from §33-1375(C), which applies §33-1314(D) on the landlord's written consent (acceptance of rent with knowledge of a default also waives termination for that breach, §33-1371(C)). Not a re-audit. | FL: Applies as written (tag-first screen, instruction 26). The referent exists: Fla. Stat. §83.58 lets the landlord recover double the rent for the period a tenant holds over without permission (last amended s. 10, ch. 2013-136). holdover-ca NOT tagged: it would give up the double-rent recovery (K.3, ceiling-only). §83.575(3): a tenant who stays with permission after termination without §83.57(3) notice owes one additional month's rent; statutory, no lease text needed. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | FL: FL retro 2026-10-03 (SOP 1.30) - rule 37 / rule 53: Fla. Stat. §83.58's double rent runs 'after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord', for 'the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession'; in a month-to-month tenancy the agreement expires on the date set by a §83.57 notice. The clause's 'after the end of the Term' and 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' do not start earlier than the statute. Once the tenancy continues month to month, early-termination-fl and end-of-term-notice-fl now switch themselves off. Rule 79 basis: Part II read whole in the FL pass; §§83.57, 83.575(3) and 83.58 re-read section-open on Online Sunshine 2026-10-03. | WY (Claude Code, 2026-10-04 backfill, rule 79): basis is the 2026-08-21 full-library cross-check that tagged WY (generic mechanics, no Wyoming-specific statute or figure; GENERIC in the WY citations file). No section was read for this row; the cross-check is recorded in the first state's segment above.

title: Month-to-Month Termination Notice
bodyText: Either party may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice served as provided in Code of Civil Procedure section 1162 or by certified or registered mail. Tenant will give at least [state the notice period: at least 30] days' notice. Landlord will give at least [state the notice period] days' notice, or any longer notice California law requires, together with any statement California law requires in the notice.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 from primary text of Civ. Code s1946.1. The pre-existing dormant row was defective in four ways: (1) it applied the 30/60 split to BOTH parties - s1946.1(b) imposes 60 days on the OWNER only; a tenant's notice is one tenancy period regardless of occupancy length, so the old text bound a long-term tenant to a 60-day duty CA law does not impose, while reciting 'as required by California law'; (2) it omitted the s1946.1(d) bona-fide-purchaser 30-day path entirely; (3) it omitted the s1946.1(h) abandoned-property statement the owner's notice must contain; (4) it was silent on the s1946.2 just-cause overlay, so for a covered unit it told the tenant the tenancy could be ended on notice alone, which is false. title: Notices
bodyText: Any notice of termination, notice of default, or other notice required to be given in writing under this Lease or applicable law will be delivered to the addresses specified in this Lease, or to any updated address either party provides in writing to the other. Where applicable law requires a particular method, form, timing, or content for a notice, that requirement will control over this Section, and nothing in this Lease designates an alternative method of delivery for any notice governed by law.

title: Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance
bodyText: Landlord's insurance does not cover loss or damage to Tenant's personal property, and Landlord is not liable for any such loss or damage. Tenant will obtain and maintain renter's insurance covering Tenant's personal property and liability throughout the Term, with liability coverage of at least {{tenant_insurance_minimum}}, and will provide Landlord with evidence of coverage upon request.

title: Entire Agreement
bodyText: This Lease, along with any attached addenda and legal disclosures, contains the entire agreement between Landlord and Tenant and may not be changed except in writing signed by all parties, or as applicable law permits Landlord to change it by written notice to Tenant. This Lease is binding on and inures to the benefit of the permitted heirs, legal representatives, and assigns of the parties.

Rule 15: written section-open. | MA: Tagged as written (tag-first screen, rules 26-28, MA log §2.1). Ordinary integration clause; written-change exception defers to applicable law. No Massachusetts conflict found. A landlord must give the tenant a signed copy within 30 days (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15D; 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(3)(c)), a separate duty (`edu-lease-copy-ma`). Rule 15: written section-open. | CT: Tagged as written (tag-first screen, rules 26-28, CT log §2.1). Consistent with Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-9(b) (a later rule that substantially modifies the agreement needs the tenant's written consent). Rule 15: written section-open. | RI: Tagged as written (tag-first screen, rules 26-28, RI log §2.1). Consistent with § 34-18-25(b) (a later rule that 'works a substantial modification' of the bargain needs the tenant's written consent) and the 60-day rent increase notice (§ 34-18-16.1). title: Addendum Precedence
bodyText: Tenant acknowledges that the legal disclosures and addenda attached to this Lease are part of this legal agreement. The terms of this Lease will control in the event of any conflict between the terms of an Addendum and the terms of this Lease, except that any disclosure, notice, or addendum that applicable law requires, or that applicable law says controls over this Lease, will control over any conflicting term of this Lease.

title: Electronic Signatures
bodyText: All individuals indicated in the Basic Terms as comprising Tenant will sign this Lease and related attached Addenda where indicated. Each of Landlord and Tenant consents to the other party's execution of this Lease by electronic signature. Delivery of this Lease containing the electronic signature of a party or otherwise by facsimile through electronic means or as a digital copy will have the same full force and effect as a manually executed original version.

title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord. Tenant will pay Landlord a pet deposit, if applicable, and pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor, and disturbance caused by a pet, and will indemnify Landlord from claims arising from Tenant's pet(s). Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and may enter the property and remove a pet, without liability to Tenant to the extent applicable law permits, if the pet becomes vicious or displays symptoms of severe illness, or if Tenant dies, becomes incapacitated, or is otherwise unable to care for the pet and Landlord believes in good faith that the pet is being abused or neglected.

title: Pet Insurance Requirement
bodyText: If Tenant keeps an approved pet at the property, Tenant will maintain renter's insurance that includes coverage for pet-related liability, and will name Landlord as an interested party on the policy upon Landlord's request. This requirement does not apply to an assistance animal, and Tenant will not be required to carry liability insurance in connection with an assistance animal.

title: Parking & Vehicle Requirements
bodyText: Only operable, currently registered passenger vehicles may be parked at the property; commercial vehicles, recreational vehicles, trailers, and oversized vehicles are not permitted without Landlord's prior written consent. Landlord may require Tenant to provide vehicle registration information and may issue parking tags, decals, or access cards, the cost of which may be charged to Tenant. Landlord may, in accordance with applicable law, have a vehicle towed at the vehicle owner's expense if it is illegally parked, abandoned, inoperable, or has expired registration. Vehicle repairs are not permitted at the property except minor emergency repairs necessary to move the vehicle, and vehicles may be washed only in areas Landlord designates, if any.

title: Guest Policy
bodyText: Guests are welcome for reasonable, non-continuous stays. A guest who stays beyond the period specified by Landlord within a given time frame will be considered an unauthorized occupant and subject to Landlord's prior written consent under this Lease's occupancy terms.

title: Use of Property & Common Areas
bodyText: Tenant will not, without Landlord's written consent, drill holes, use nails, hooks, or screws on the property, or fasten anything to its fixtures, appliances, or interior or exterior surfaces. Tenant will comply with any weight restrictions on balconies or porches and will not use them to store personal belongings without Landlord's consent. Tenant will not keep a waterbed or other water-filled furniture at the property, or any item (such as a piano or safe) whose weight Landlord has not agreed is reasonable for the floor, without Landlord's prior written consent. Tenant will not burn wax candles at the property. Tenant will not post or display any sign, banner, or advertisement visible from outside the property without Landlord's consent. Nothing in this Section restricts any display that applicable law entitles Tenant to make, such as the display of the flag of the United States or of religious or cultural items, subject to any lawful limits on its size, placement, and manner.

title: Lead-Based Paint Disclosure
bodyText: LEAD WARNING STATEMENT. Housing built before 1978 may contain lead-based paint. Lead from paint, paint chips, and dust can pose health hazards if not managed properly. Lead exposure is especially harmful to young children and pregnant women. Before renting pre-1978 housing, lessors must disclose the presence of known lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards in the dwelling. Lessees must also receive a federally approved pamphlet on lead poisoning prevention. Landlord's disclosure: [state either that Landlord has no knowledge of lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards in the dwelling, or describe all known lead-based paint and lead-based paint hazards]. Records and reports: [state either that Landlord has no reports or records pertaining to lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards in the dwelling, or list all available records and reports and confirm they have been provided to Tenant]. Tenant acknowledges receipt of the information above and of the federally approved pamphlet Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home. Landlord and Tenant each certify, to the best of their knowledge, that the information they have provided is true and accurate.

title: Bed Bug Disclosure
bodyText: Information about Bed Bugs. Bed bug Appearance: Bed bugs have six legs. Adult bed bugs have flat bodies about 1/4 of an inch in length. Their color can vary from red and brown to copper colored. Young bed bugs are very small. Their bodies are about 1/16 of an inch in length. They have almost no color. When a bed bug feeds, its body swells, may lengthen, and becomes bright red, sometimes making it appear to be a different insect. Bed bugs do not fly. They can either crawl or be carried from place to place on objects, people, or animals. Bed bugs can be hard to find and identify because they are tiny and try to stay hidden. Life Cycle and Reproduction: An average bed bug lives for about 10 months. Female bed bugs lay one to five eggs per day. Bed bugs grow to full adulthood in about 21 days. Bed bugs can survive for months without feeding. Bed bug Bites: Because bed bugs usually feed at night, most people are bitten in their sleep and do not realize they were bitten. A person's reaction to insect bites is an immune response and so varies from person to person. Sometimes the red welts caused by the bites will not be noticed until many days after a person was bitten, if at all. Common signs and symptoms of a possible bed bug infestation: • Small red to reddish brown fecal spots on mattresses, box springs, bed frames, mattresses, linens, upholstery, or walls. • Molted bed bug skins, white, sticky eggs, or empty eggshells. • Very heavily infested areas may have a characteristically sweet odor. • Red, itchy bite marks, especially on the legs, arms, and other body parts exposed while sleeping. However, some people do not show bed bug lesions on their bodies even though bed bugs may have fed on them. For more information, see the Internet Web sites of the United States Environmental Protection Agency and the National Pest Management Association. Tenant shall report any suspected bed bug infestation to Landlord promptly and in writing, using the following procedure: {{bed_bug_reporting_procedure}}.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against Civ. Code s1954.603 (primary text supplied by Taylor). Statute requires the information 'in substantially the following form' and in AT LEAST 10-POINT TYPE - shipped effectively verbatim because 'substantially' is not a licence to compress. THIRD type-size floor found in CA (8-point at s2079.10a, 10-point here, 12-point at s1946.2(f)(3)); the schema still cannot express any of them. The prior dormant row was a four-line paraphrase and had two substantive defects beyond omitting the entire prescribed block: (1) it promised 'Landlord's process for investigating a suspected infestation' - s1954.603(b) requires the opposite, the procedure for the TENANT TO REPORT to the landlord, which is why this row now carries a landlord-supplied {{bed_bug_reporting_procedure}} field; (2) it asserted the notice covers 'the danger of self-treating with pesticides' - NO SUCH ELEMENT EXISTS in s1954.603. That element appears in other states' bed-bug statutes, so this is the Instruction 18 error shape (another state's architecture imported as fact) sitting inside a shipped CA row. Timing: duty attaches on and after 2017-07-01 prior to creating a NEW tenancy. The separate one-time catch-up duty to notify all existing tenants by 2018-01-01 is spent and is deliberately not modelled. s1954.601 defines 'pest control operator' as a Branch 2 licensee of the Structural Pest Control Board. bodyText: Methamphetamine or Fentanyl Contamination Disclosure. [If a local health officer has issued a remediation order affecting this property and no notice requiring no further action has since been received, state that fact here and attach a copy of the order to this Lease; otherwise state 'Landlord has received no remediation order affecting this property under Health and Safety Code section 25400.22 or 25400.25.'] Tenant acknowledges in writing receipt of this notice and of a copy of any pending order. notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against H&S s25400.28 (primary text supplied by Taylor; Chapter 6.9.1, amended by Stats. 2019 ch. 691 (AB 1596), eff. 2020-01-01). The chapter is 6.9.1, not 6.9.2 as I guessed. Five defects in the prior dormant row. (1) TRIGGER WRONG: the row keyed off 'an order prohibiting occupancy due to methamphetamine contamination that has not been satisfied'. The statute keys off a REMEDIATION ORDER under ss25400.22/25400.25, and the duty runs until the owner receives a s25400.27 notice that the property requires NO FURTHER ACTION. An occupancy prohibition is not the trigger. (2) FENTANYL OMITTED: the chapter has covered methamphetamine OR FENTANYL since AB 1596 took effect 2020-01-01. The row was meth-only and is retitled - six years stale. (3) TIMING: s25400.28(b) attaches the duty to all prospective tenants WHO HAVE COMPLETED A RENTAL APPLICATION, earlier than lease signing. The row modelled it purely as a lease disclosure, so the duty could be missed entirely for an applicant who never reaches signature. (4) FREE TEXT IS NOT COMPLIANCE: the statute requires four mechanical things - written notice, A COPY OF THE ORDER provided, the tenant's WRITTEN ACKNOWLEDGMENT before signing, and the notice ATTACHED to the rental agreement. The old '[describe any known contamination order]' bracket satisfies none of them. This is document assembly, not clause text - same class of problem as the s1632 translation duty. (5) REMEDY OMITTED: if the owner does not comply with (b), THE PROSPECTIVE TENANT MAY VOID THE RENTAL AGREEMENT. Severe, and absent from the old row. OUT OF SCOPE, flagged not resolved: s25400.28(c) is a separate stricter regime for a mobilehome, manufactured home or recreational vehicle subject to an order - it may not be sold, rented OR OCCUPIED until notice of all meth or fentanyl laboratory activities and any remediation is given, with notice and order attached to the rental agreement, and (c)(4) gives the same void right. Consistent with the standing mobilehome-park deprioritization. Subdivision (a) is the sale-side duty and is not our concern. | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): optional (Taylor's pattern 3): the disclosure is owed before signing; the clause records it. notes: CA: STILL INACTIVE after reading H&S s26147 (primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19). The row asserts a live disclosure duty; the statute's own commencement clause may mean no such duty has ever taken effect. s26147(e): 'The requirements of this section shall not apply until the first January 1 or July 1 that occurs at least six months after the department adopts standards pursuant to Sections 26103 and 26105 AND develops guidelines pursuant to Section 26130.' The operative trigger in (a) is likewise defined by reference to the s26103 permissible exposure limits or the s26105 health-threat guidelines. VERIFIED FROM TEXT: the duty is contingent and self-suspending. NOT VERIFIED: whether the department ever adopted those standards and guidelines - that is a factual question outside the section text and is the single thing needed to close this row. It is widely reported that the PELs were never adopted, but this project has been burned by widely reported, so it stays open. This is a NEW ERROR SHAPE for the checklist, adjacent to the s2924.85 repeal: a statute that is on the books, correctly cited, and still not in force. Other limbs read and captured for whenever it does commence: (b) no duty to conduct air or surface testing; (c)(1) disclosure to prospective tenants before entering the agreement and (c)(2) to current tenants in affected units as soon as reasonably practical; (d) exemption where the mold was remediated per the s26130 guidelines. NOTE the (a) trigger reaches mold 'both visible and invisible or hidden'. SEPARATE AND UNREAD: Civ. Code s1941.1(a)(7) is reported to place visible mold in the habitability list, which would make mold actionable in CA regardless of s26147's status. Not read this pass - pull it before concluding CA has no mold obligation. CORRECTION 2026-09-19: my earlier pointer to Civ. Code s1941.1(a)(7) as the mold limb was WRONG - (a)(7) is garbage and rubbish receptacles. The real route is the OPENING WORDS of s1941.1(a), read section-open: a dwelling is untenantable if it substantially lacks the listed characteristics OR IS A RESIDENTIAL UNIT DESCRIBED IN H&S s17920.3 OR s17920.10. That incorporation is confirmed from the text. Whether s17920.3 actually lists visible mold growth as a substandard condition is NOT confirmed - s17920.3 has not been read. NEEDED: H&S s17920.3. The supplied s1941.1 text also stopped at (a)(7), so (a)(8) onward is unread. RESOLVED 2026-09-19 on the habitability limb: H&S s17920.3(a)(13) (read section-open; amended by Stats. 2024 ch. 487 (SB 1465), eff. 2025-01-01) DOES list 'Visible mold growth' as a substandard condition, and Civ. Code s1941.1(a) incorporates s17920.3 by reference. So California DOES have a live mold obligation - it is a HABITABILITY duty, not a disclosure duty. This row is a disclosure clause and stays INACTIVE: the s26147 disclosure duty remains contingent under s26147(e) and the only question left on it is factual, whether the department ever adopted the s26103/s26105 standards and s26130 guidelines. Two limits on the habitability route that matter and are easy to overstate: (1) visible mold growth must be 'as determined by a health officer or a code enforcement officer, as defined in Section 829.5 of the Penal Code' - it is NOT self-executing on a tenant's or landlord's own assessment; (2) it EXCLUDES mold that is minor and found on surfaces that can accumulate moisture as part of their properly functioning and intended use (shower surrounds and the like). The s17920.3 preamble adds a further threshold: the condition must exist to an extent that endangers life, limb, health, property, safety or welfare. s17920.10, the OTHER s1941.1(a) incorporation, READ 2026-09-19 - it governs lead hazards, not mold, so it does not affect this row. See edu-lead-hazards-ca. FACTUAL QUESTION RESOLVED 2026-09-19: the s26147(e) predicate standards were NEVER ADOPTED. Primary source: CDPH's own 2005 Report to the Legislature on implementing the Toxic Mold Protection Act concluded that science-based permissible exposure limits for indoor mold could not be established, and CDPH's 2017 Statement on Indoor Dampness and Mold confirms the scientific basis for that conclusion had not changed as of 2015 and that no federal or state policy sets safe exposure limits. The SB 655 (2015) Senate floor analysis quotes the same CDPH position. Consistent secondary sources through 2026 report no PELs adopted. So s26147 has NEVER COMMENCED and this row correctly stays INACTIVE - now VERIFIED as not in force, the same posture as foreclosure-disclosure-ca. WORTH NOTING: at least one 2026 secondary source describes s26147 as operative with a 'practical trigger' of visible mold - the exact misreading s26147(e) forecloses. Another secondary-source error of the kind this project was built to catch. Residual limit: CDPH's primary statements run to 2017; post-2017 status rests on consistent secondary reporting and the absence of any contrary source.

title: Mold Disclosure in the Move-In Report
bodyText: As part of the move-in inspection report, Landlord will state in writing whether there is any visible evidence of mold in areas readily accessible within the interior of the property. A statement that there is no visible evidence of mold will be considered correct unless Tenant objects in writing within five days after receiving the report. If the report states that there is visible evidence of mold, Tenant may choose to terminate this Lease and not take possession or not remain in possession. If Tenant chooses to take or remain in possession, Landlord will promptly remediate the mold condition, no later than five business days after Tenant's choice, reinspect the property, and give Tenant a new report stating that there is no visible evidence of mold.
notes: VA: VA-SCOPE: STATEWIDE. Read section-open 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser on the official Code of Virginia (law.lis.virginia.gov; Title 55.1 Chapter 12 read whole from the vacodefull page, which prints the 2026-session amendments and every delayed-effective version with its history line); 2024-2026 amending chapters read in enrolled text on lis.virginia.gov with their effective-date clauses (VA log §1). Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1215 (history ends 2019, c. 712), read with the § 55.1-1200 definitions of 'visible evidence of mold', 'readily accessible' and 'interior of the dwelling unit'. Continuing duties: prevent moisture and mold, remediate per Va. Code Ann. § 8.01-226.12(E), give the tenant a summary of remediation information (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1220(A)(5)); tenant's moisture and mold duties (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1227(A)(10)); relocation for remediation up to 30 days (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1231) - edu-mold-rules-va. DORMANT ROW REWRITTEN AND ACTIVATED (kickoff): the pre-project text had the landlord 'disclose any visible evidence of mold observed' in the lease itself ('[describe ... or state none observed]'), which is the wrong document and the wrong time: the statute puts the statement in the written move-in report delivered within five days after occupancy, gives it deemed-correct effect only after a five-day objection window, and attaches the tenant's termination or five-business-day remediation option. Now REQUIRED (the statute uses 'shall'), verified and active.

title: Flood Disclosure
bodyText: Flood Hazard Disclosure. [If Landlord has actual knowledge that the property is located in a special flood hazard area or an area of potential flooding, state that fact here; otherwise state 'Landlord has no actual knowledge that the property is located in a special flood hazard area or an area of potential flooding.'] Tenant may obtain information about hazards, including flood hazards, that may affect the property from the Internet Web site of the Office of Emergency Services, including the MyHazards tool at {{myhazards_url}}. Landlord's insurance does not cover the loss of Tenant's personal possessions, and it is recommended that Tenant consider purchasing renter's insurance and flood insurance to insure Tenant's possessions from loss due to fire, flood, or other risk of loss. Landlord is not required to provide additional information concerning the flood hazards to the property, and the information provided pursuant to Government Code section 8589.45 is deemed adequate to inform Tenant.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against Gov. Code s8589.45 (primary text supplied by Taylor, current as of 2026-01-01). STRUCTURAL DEFECT CORRECTED - rule_type moved CONDITIONAL -> REQUIRED. The prior dormant row treated the WHOLE disclosure as conditional on the property being in a flood zone. It is not: s8589.45(a) requires the disclosure in EVERY residential lease entered into on or after 2018-07-01, and only element (a)(1) carries the 'if the owner has actual knowledge' qualifier. Elements (a)(2), (3) and (4) are unconditional. As previously modelled, a non-flood-zone CA property would have received NO disclosure at all. Four further defects in the old text: (1) it omitted element (a)(2) entirely, including the statutory requirement that the disclosure CONTAIN the MyHazards Internet Web site address; (2) it omitted element (a)(4), the landlord safe harbour; (3) it narrowed element (a)(3) to 'renter's insurance covering flood damage' - the statute requires stating that the owner's insurance does not cover the tenant's possessions AND recommending both renter's and flood insurance against fire, flood or other risk of loss; (4) it glossed the trigger as a 'special flood hazard area as designated by the Federal Emergency Management Agency' - the statute says 'special flood hazard area OR AN AREA OF POTENTIAL FLOODING' and never mentions FEMA, so the row imported a narrower federal definition the statute does not use. ACTUAL KNOWLEDGE is defined, not left at large - s8589.45(a)(1)(A)-(C): written notice from any public agency, the mortgage holder requiring flood insurance, or THE OWNER CURRENTLY CARRYING FLOOD INSURANCE. The third is the one landlords overlook: carrying the policy is itself actual knowledge. This belongs in the builder as a question, not as landlord free text. Prescribed floor: NO SMALLER THAN EIGHT-POINT TYPE. s8589.45(b) subjects the disclosure to Civ. Code s1632 - SECOND statute in CA carrying the translation duty after s1946.2(f)(3). OPEN: {{myhazards_url}} is an app-config value, not landlord input. The statute requires the address to appear; the current CalOES MyHazards address has NOT been verified from primary source this pass and must be confirmed and maintained at sync - a hardcoded URL is exactly the kind of value that rots silently.

title: Flood Disclosure
bodyText:
[Separate document. Required for a rental agreement with a term of 1 year or longer; give it to the prospective tenant at or before execution of the rental agreement.]

FLOOD DISCLOSURE

Flood Insurance: Renters' insurance policies do not include coverage for damage resulting from floods. Tenant is encouraged to discuss the need to purchase separate flood insurance coverage with Tenant's insurance agent.

1. Landlord has ☐ has no ☐ knowledge of any flooding that has damaged the dwelling unit during Landlord's ownership of the dwelling unit.

2. Landlord has ☐ has not ☐ filed a claim with an insurance provider relating to flood damage in the dwelling unit, including, but not limited to, a claim with the National Flood Insurance Program.

3. Landlord has ☐ has not ☐ received assistance for flood damage to the dwelling unit, including, but not limited to, assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

4. For the purposes of this disclosure, the term "flooding" means a general or temporary condition of partial or complete inundation of the dwelling unit caused by any of the following:
a. The overflow of inland or tidal waters.
b. The unusual and rapid accumulation of runoff or surface waters from any established water source, such as a river, stream, or drainage ditch.
c. Sustained periods of standing water resulting from rainfall.
notes: FL: DORMANT ROW REWRITTEN AND ACTIVATED 2026-09-26 (instruction 21).
