title: Foreclosure Disclosure
bodyText: Foreclosure Disclosure. Before Tenant entered into this Lease, Landlord disclosed to Tenant in writing whether the property is the subject of any foreclosure proceedings. Landlord's disclosure: [state that the property is the subject of foreclosure proceedings and describe them, or state that the property is not the subject of any foreclosure proceedings].
notes: NV: REWRITTEN AND ACTIVATED 2026-09-24 from the dormant, UNVERIFIED Aug-2026 row (instruction 21). Section-open read of revisor text (leg.state.nv.us, Rev. 4/15/2026). NRS 118A.275 (Added 2009, 2791; no amendment in the source line). (1) duty runs to a PROSPECTIVE tenant - so disclosure must precede the lease; (2) a WILLFUL violation is a deceptive trade practice for purposes of NRS 598.0903-598.0999 - NOT itself a stated misdemeanor, confirming the old note that the penalty had been overstated. Remedies under ch. 598 not read and not stated. DEFECTS IN THE OLD ROW: (a) "pending foreclosure proceeding" narrowed the statute's "any foreclosure proceedings"; (b) "none known" inserted a knowledge qualifier the duty lacks (willfulness only gates the DTPA consequence); (c) framed as disclosure at signing rather than to a prospective tenant; (d) "as required by Nevada law" named the state in body text. rule_type CONDITIONAL -> REQUIRED (the either/or statement is always included). OPEN INTERPRETIVE POINT: whether a recorded notice of default in a nonjudicial trustee sale (NRS ch. 107, not read) is a "foreclosure proceeding" - the clause does not decide it. Topic key aligned with foreclosure-disclosure-mn (different statute, not shareable). Previous notes: UNCHANGED - pre-existing tag from before this project, not touched this session | NV (text batch 2, 2026-09-24): Related duty now read: NRS 40.255(2)-(5) - after a foreclosure sale of a single-family residence (up to 4 units), a tenant in actual occupation may be removed only after a change-of-ownership notice and 60 days (monthly or longer) or one rental period (shorter), the new owner is bound by the lease during that period, and no eviction record may be entered for a tenant who vacates within it. See edu-foreclosure-sale-tenants-nv. | NV: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): optional (Taylor's pattern 3): the written foreclosure disclosure is owed before the tenant enters the lease; the clause records it. Companion: edu-foreclosure-disclosure-nv. | NV (retro SOP 1.47, 2026-10-03): Targeted fix 2 (rule 78 as amended in SOP 1.35): the scrub's demotion to RECOMMENDED / SERVES_LANDLORD is KEPT. NRS 118A.275(1) reads in full: 'A landlord shall disclose in writing to a prospective tenant if the property to be leased or rented is the subject of any foreclosure proceedings.' It has no vehicle words: it does not say 'in the rental agreement', 'with the rental agreement' or 'in the lease' (contrast A.R.S. 33-1331(A), 'with the rental agreement'). The duty is a written disclosure to a PROSPECTIVE tenant, so it must be made before the tenant signs, by any writing; the lease is not its required vehicle. This clause only records that the disclosure was made. Keeping it optional is correct; the duty itself is stated in edu-foreclosure-disclosure-nv. Also noted: the duty arises only IF the property is the subject of foreclosure proceedings; the clause's 'or state that the property is not' alternative is a voluntary record, not a statutory requirement. title: Sex Offender Registry Notice
bodyText: Notice: Pursuant to Section 290.46 of the Penal Code, information about specified registered sex offenders is made available to the public via an Internet Web site maintained by the Department of Justice at www.meganslaw.ca.gov. Depending on an offender's criminal history, this information will include either the address at which the offender resides or the community of residence and ZIP Code in which the offender resides.
notes: CA: VERBATIM STATUTORY TEXT - Civ. Code s2079.10a(a)(3), primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (Amended by Stats. 2018, ch. 907 (AB 1289), eff. 2019-01-01). Prescribed floor: NOT LESS THAN 8-POINT TYPE. Do not add a preamble, reword, or drop the URL. The prior dormant row was a PARAPHRASE and dropped four operative elements: the 'Notice:' opener, the Penal Code s290.46 citation, the www.meganslaw.ca.gov address (the only actionable content in the notice), and the precise 'address at which the offender resides' / 'community of residence and ZIP Code in which the offender resides' phrasing. It also prepended 'As required by California law, Landlord provides Tenant the following notice:' to prescribed text. Same failure shape as the federal Lead Warning Statement correction in the CO re-audit. SCOPE - rule_type set to CONDITIONAL, not REQUIRED, and this is a judgment call to overturn if you disagree: s2079.10a(a) reaches leases of SINGLE-FAMILY residential real property and leaseholds in multiunit property with MORE THAN FOUR dwelling units. A lease of a unit in a 2-4 unit building falls between the two limbs and is NOT covered. The old row was REQUIRED with no scope condition, so it rendered on duplex/triplex/fourplex leases as legally mandated when it is not. Shipping the bare statutory notice on an uncovered property is harmless surplusage; reciting that it is required is not. Paragraphs (a)(1) and (a)(2) are historical - the (a)(1) form governs contracts entered 1999-07-01 to 2005-08-31 and references the repealed Penal Code s290.4 database and a '900' line; (a)(2) is the transition window. Only (a)(3) applies to contracts entered on or after 2006-04-01. Do not ship (a)(1). LANDLORD SAFE HARBOUR, not yet its own row: s2079.10a(b) provides that delivery of the notice discharges any duty to supply further information about the proximity of registered offenders, and gives a registered offender no cause of action against the disclosing party; s2079.10a(c) preserves all other existing duties. CROSS-CHAPTER: this section sits in Title 6, ch. 3, art. 2 ('Duty to Prospective Purchaser of Real Property') - entirely outside the Civ. Code s1940 et seq. landlord-tenant provisions. Instruction 7 pattern confirmed for CA. SECOND type-size floor found in CA after s1946.2(f)(3)'s 12-point requirement. COUNTERPART, added 2026-09-19: Pen. Code s290.46(j) PROHIBITS using the website's information for housing decisions except to protect a person at risk - so the landlord must tell tenants about the site but must not use it to choose them. See edu-megans-law-housing-use-ca.

title: Termination Notice (Property Exempt from For-Cause Requirements)
bodyText: Either Landlord or Tenant may terminate a periodic tenancy under this Lease at the end of a tenancy period, or elect not to renew a fixed-term tenancy at the end of the term, by giving the other written notice at least [state the notice period in days] days before that date, or any longer notice Colorado law requires for the length of the tenancy. This Section applies only for so long as this tenancy is exempt from Colorado's for-cause eviction requirements under C.R.S. section 38-12-1302(1). The exemption Landlord relies on is: [describe the applicable exemption - see C.R.S. section 38-12-1302(1)(a), (1)(b), (1)(d), (1)(e) or (1)(f)]. If that exemption ceases to apply at any time - in particular, the exemption for a tenant who has not been a tenant of the premises for at least twelve months ends once Tenant has been a tenant for twelve months - Landlord may terminate or decline to renew only on a ground and with the notice that C.R.S. section 38-12-1301 et seq. then requires.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 13-40-107(1), (2), (3); amended by HB24-1098 (ch. 113, § 5, eff. 2024-04-19); references § 38-12-1302(1)(a), (b), (d), (e), (f). Corrected 2026-09-06: replaced a flat 21-day figure with the real 5-tier notice scheme (3/21/28/91 days by tenancy length, all floors not fixed periods, per HB24-1098's 'at least' language). (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.) | CO: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): Taylor's pattern 2: the notice is the landlord's chosen period, with the statutory tiers and notice-content rules moved to edu-termination-notice-periods-co and a builder check (Addendum M.13). Exemption statement kept. | CO: CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, targeted fix 19 (rule 78) and rule 37. RESTORED a condition the 2026-09-29 scrub left out, and fixed a defect the scrub did not cause. C.R.S. § 38-12-1302(1)(e) exempts "a residential tenant who has not been a tenant of a residential premises for at least twelve months" - an exemption that EXPIRES during the tenancy. A landlord who filled the bracket with (1)(e) at signing had a clause that was true in month one and false from month thirteen, at which point acting on it means serving a no-cause termination that § 38-12-1303(1) forbids, and § 38-12-1306 makes non-compliance an affirmative defense on which "the court shall dismiss the eviction proceeding". No number check can catch that; per fix 19 the condition belongs in the clause, so the clause now self-limits to the period the exemption actually applies. This also resolves the UNRESOLVED FLAG carried on month-to-month-notice-co-covered: there is no gap in months 0-12, because the tenancy is exempt under § 38-12-1302(1)(e) for exactly that period and the exempt variant governs it; from month twelve the covered regime applies and the landlord needs cause under § 38-12-1303(2) or a no-fault ground under § 38-12-1303(3) with 90 days' notice (45 where the landlord is on active military duty or is such a person's spouse). title: Early Termination - Victim of Unlawful Sexual Behavior, Stalking, or Domestic Violence
bodyText: A Tenant who is a victim of unlawful sexual behavior, stalking, domestic violence, or domestic abuse may terminate this Lease and vacate the property without further obligation, upon providing Landlord written notice and the documentation required under Colorado law (a police report written within the preceding 60 days, a valid protective or restraining order, or a qualifying advocate's written statement). Notwithstanding this Lease's Early Termination Section, Landlord's compensation for actual damages resulting from a termination under this Section is limited to no more than one month's Rent ({{monthly_rent}}), and Landlord must provide Tenant a written statement of those damages within 30 days of the termination date.

title: Radon Disclosure Acknowledgment
bodyText: Before signing this Lease, Tenant received from Landlord a separate written radon disclosure document, signed by Tenant to acknowledge receipt, which contained the radon warning statement Colorado law prescribes, all of Landlord's knowledge of radon testing, concentrations, records, reports, mitigation and any radon mitigation system at the property, and a copy of the most recent radon brochure published by the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment. Tenant acknowledges receipt of that document and of the brochure.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-803. Confirmed (Claude Browser follow-up, 2026-09-13). The companion 180-day/one-year-lease remedy (edu-radon-lease-length-co) is at (3)(b) per an earlier pass, not independently re-confirmed this round. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.) | CO: CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 48 (also rules 40, 46, 79). FIXED - a lease clause cannot be the vehicle for this disclosure. C.R.S. § 38-12-803(2)(a) requires the landlord, "Before signing a lease agreement", to "disclose and provide in writing to the tenant the following information in a document that the tenant signs to acknowledge receipt of the disclosure", comprising (I) a warning statement "in bold-faced type that is clearly legible in substantially the same form as is specified", (II) all of the landlord's radon knowledge including current records and reports and any mitigation-system description and documentation, and (III) a copy of the most recent CDPHE brochure under § 25-11-114(2)(a); (2)(b) requires the tenant to acknowledge receipt by signing the disclosure. Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). Three defects in the prior clause: it was the disclosure rather than an acknowledgment of a separate pre-signing document; it paraphrased a warning statement the statute prescribes in substantially fixed form and in bold-faced type (rule 59); and it collected only "testing results, concentrations, or mitigation systems" where (2)(a)(II) also requires the current records and reports and the mitigation-system documentation. Rewritten as an acknowledgment, which is lawful and gives the landlord written proof. PRODUCT ITEM for Taylor and the builder: Steinoak must generate the separate signed radon disclosure document (prescribed warning text, landlord knowledge fields, brochure attachment) - the lease clause alone does not discharge § 38-12-803(2). Remedy for failure: § 38-12-803(3)(a)(I) lets the tenant void the lease and vacate under § 38-12-507.

title: Service and Assistance Animals
bodyText: A service animal or other assistance animal that Tenant or an Occupant needs as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is not considered a pet under this Lease, regardless of any pet policy, breed, weight, or size restriction stated elsewhere in this Lease. Landlord will not charge a pet deposit, pet rent, or other pet-related fee for an assistance animal. If the disability and the disability-related need for the animal are not readily apparent, Landlord may request reliable documentation confirming the need for the accommodation, to the extent permitted by applicable law; if the disability and need are readily apparent, Landlord will not require such documentation. Tenant remains responsible for any damage to the property caused by an assistance animal. Landlord may deny or withdraw this accommodation if the specific animal poses a direct threat to the health or safety of others, or would cause substantial physical damage to the property, that cannot be reduced or eliminated by another reasonable accommodation.
notes: NEW - universal/federal baseline (Fair Housing Act), CO tag added since the CO-specific override below was verified against it this session WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | NE extended (session 2, whole-library generic-clause audit): generic mechanics, no NE-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with NE findings from this project. | Display-collision bug fixed (session 7, full-library supersedes audit): CO,WY removed — already covered by a state-specific override that supersedes this row; both versions were displaying simultaneously before this fix. | AUDIT 2026-08-27 (Opus/high/research re-audit): FEDERAL CURRENCY FLAG - HUD withdrew FHEO-2020-01 (the assistance-animal guidance) effective 2025-09-17 (Fed. Reg. Docket FR-6571-N-01); HUD states it 'should not be relied upon.' The clause text does not cite FHEO-2020-01 and rests on the Fair Housing Act itself (42 U.S.C. 3601 et seq.; 24 CFR 100.204), which is unchanged - so the operative language still stands. Flagged NEEDS_REVIEW rather than corrected because the federal posture is in flux (including post-Loper Bright litigation over the ESA no-fee rule) and any HUD replacement guidance should be picked up. CO-specific layer (documentation limits, misrepresentation warning) is unaffected. | ESA/FEDERAL-DIVERGENCE RESOLUTION 2026-08-27: REMAINS NEEDS_REVIEW - deliberately, and now for a sharper reason. This is the generic/universal version resting on the federal FHA baseline alone, with no state overlay. On May 22 2026 HUD's FHEO rescinded the 2020 assistance-animal notice and adopted a new enforcement posture: it will find reasonable cause only for animals individually trained to provide disability-related assistance (the ADA service-animal standard), and will no longer expect housing providers to categorically grant accommodations or fee waivers for untrained assistance animals (ESAs). HUD has stated it intends notice-and-comment rulemaking. Clause text UNCHANGED and should stay unchanged: this is an enforcement posture, not a change to 42 U.S.C. 3601 et seq. or 24 CFR 100.204, it does not bind courts, private FHA plaintiffs, or DOJ, and narrowing the clause would create asymmetric risk (an uncollected pet fee vs. a discrimination claim). Holding NEEDS_REVIEW because any state adopting this clause without its own ESA protection inherits a genuinely unsettled federal picture - each new state must confirm its own basis the way CO just did. | 5a.1 PROPAGATION NOTE -> KS (recorded 2026-08-29, KS re-audit), covering the earlier move to NEEDS_REVIEW following HUD's guidance withdrawal. RULE GAP FLAGGED, NOT AMENDED: 5a.1 triggers on edits to bodyText, rule_type or content_type. A verification_status change is NOT on that list, so this propagation note is owed by instruction and practice, not by the rule as written. Same species as the row-vs-text gap flagged at WY log 3. | KS DETERMINATION COMPLETE, ROW DOES NOT MOVE. Kansas splits by animal type: trained service animals have a strong independent state basis (K.S.A. 39-1102/1107/1108, statutory no-fee rule, criminal backing at 39-1103, class C misdemeanor); ESAs are expressly excluded from that statute by 39-1113(f), leaving only the generic KAAD duty at 44-1016(h)(3)(B), which is textually independent of federal law but judicially untested in housing. See edu-kaad-accommodation-duty-ks and edu-service-animal-denial-penalty-ks. | TWO INDEPENDENT REASONS THE ROW STAYS NEEDS_REVIEW: (1) the row is tagged KS;NE and NEBRASKA HAS NOT BEEN CHECKED - a KS-only answer cannot resolve a shared row; (2) even for KS alone the answer is split, with an untested generic basis running against an adverse express exclusion in a neighboring statute. | DRAFTING ISSUE FOR A FUTURE PASS, not resolved here: the row's documentation sentence says Landlord may request reliable documentation "to the extent permitted by applicable law." Kansas's statutory verification procedure (K.S.A. 39-1111) does NOT reach housing, so for KS that phrase resolves against federal law alone. | UNRESOLVED DATE CONFLICT: project records treat 2025-09-17 (guidance withdrawal) and 2026-05-22 (narrowed enforcement) as two sequential events; secondary sources located during the KS re-audit treat them as conflicting accounts of one event. This row's NEEDS_REVIEW rationale cites both. Must be reconciled against HUD primary documents before this row is resolved for any state. | NE RE-AUDIT 2026-08-31: NE removed — Nebraska has its own express service-animal HOUSING statute (Neb. Rev. Stat. §§20-131.01 to 20-131.04, read from primary source) with a no-additional-deposit rule this generic does not state, so NE now takes assistance-animal-accommodation-ne. Both blockers on this row's NEEDS_REVIEW are now resolved: (1) the NE state-law basis is determined; (2) the HUD question is resolved as TWO SEQUENTIAL EVENTS, not conflicting accounts of one — 2025-09-17 withdrawal of FHEO-2020-01 and FHEO 2013-01 (later formalized at Fed. Reg. Docket FR-6571-N-01), then a separate 2026-05-22 FHEO enforcement memo narrowing enforcement to individually-trained animals. Neither touched the FHA statute itself. Row flipped to VERIFIED for Kansas. §5a.1: states-field change only, bodyText untouched — no propagation note owed on clause text, but a note IS owed in the KS log recording the status flip. | NV: Text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-24 from the Justia 2025 NRS reproduction (host, with source lines) - one notch below revisor text, same basis CA accepted. INSTRUCTION 24 FAMILY CLOSED FOR NV. Applies as written. NV has an INDEPENDENT STATE BASIS the federal-only rows lack: NRS 118.105 bars refusing to rent a 118A dwelling to a person with a disability solely because an animal that "assists, supports or provides service" will live there - support animals expressly included, so the HUD-guidance uncertainty recorded above does not reach NV's core rule. title: Service and Assistance Animals
bodyText: A service animal or other assistance animal that Tenant or an Occupant needs as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is not considered a pet under this Lease, regardless of any pet policy, breed, weight, or size restriction stated elsewhere in this Lease. Landlord will not charge a pet deposit, pet rent, or other pet-related fee for an assistance animal. If the disability and the disability-related need for the animal are not readily apparent, Landlord may request reliable documentation confirming the need for the accommodation, but will not require details about the nature or severity of Tenant's disability beyond what is necessary to verify the need for the accommodation, as required by Colorado law. If the disability and need are readily apparent, Landlord will not require such documentation. Tenant remains responsible for any damage to the property caused by an assistance animal. Landlord may deny or withdraw this accommodation if the specific animal poses a direct threat to the health or safety of others, or would cause substantial physical damage to the property, that cannot be reduced or eliminated by another reasonable accommodation. Tenant is hereby warned, as required for enforcement under Colorado law, that intentionally misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or assistance animal to obtain a right or privilege under this Section is unlawful under C.R.S. sections 18-13-107.3 and 18-13-107.7, punishable by escalating fines.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 24-34-502 (CADA); § 18-13-107.3; § 18-13-107.7; HB 16-1426 (eff. 2017-01-01); HB 21-1271. CADA (not HUD/FHA) is CO's independent basis, unaffected by HUD's 2025-09-17 ESA guidance withdrawal or its 2026-05-22 enforcement narrowing. Corrected 2026-08-28: misrepresentation mischaracterized as always criminal - 18-13-107.3 (housing) is a civil infraction; only 18-13-107.7 (public accommodations) remains a petty offense. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Security Deposit Maximum (Landlord Reference)
bodyText: Colorado law caps the security deposit you can charge at two months' rent (C.R.S. section 38-12-102.5). This is a ceiling on what you're allowed to collect - it's not something your lease needs to tell the tenant, since stating the legal maximum only gives them a number to hold you to. The actual deposit amount you're charging this specific tenant is already captured in your lease through the Security Deposit clause. Use this as a guardrail when entering the deposit amount for a Colorado lease: if you type in more than two months' rent, that number is not enforceable.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-102.5 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited
bodyText: Colorado law prohibits taking action against a tenant - raising rent, cutting services, declining to renew, or starting an eviction - because they reported an unsafe condition, exercised a right under the lease, or joined a tenant organization (C.R.S. section 38-12-509). This applies whether or not your lease mentions it, so there's no need to include it in tenant-facing text. What matters practically: if you have an independent, legitimate reason to raise rent or not renew (the lease naturally ending, a real violation, etc.), document that reason - having a clear paper trail is what protects you if a tenant later claims a decision was retaliatory.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-509 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Rent Can't Be Raised More Than Once a Year
bodyText: No matter what your lease says, you cannot raise a tenant's rent more than once every 12 months in Colorado (C.R.S. section 38-12-702). This applies to month-to-month tenancies as much as fixed terms. Keep this in mind if you ever build a rent-escalation or annual-increase clause - the 12-month floor overrides anything the lease tries to specify.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-702 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: For-Cause Eviction Rules (After 12 Months)
bodyText: Once a tenant has lived in a property for 12 months or more, Colorado generally requires you to have a specific legal reason - 'cause' (like nonpayment or a lease violation) or a defined 'no-fault' reason (such as selling the property or doing major renovations, with 90 days' notice) - before you can end the tenancy or decline to renew (C.R.S. section 38-12-1301 et seq.). This does NOT apply if the property is your own primary residence or directly adjacent to it, a short-term rental, a mobile home lot, or employer-provided housing. Check which of your properties fall into an exempt category - this determines which version of the month-to-month termination clause applies.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-1301 et seq. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Never Waive a Tenant's Right to Call Police
bodyText: Colorado law makes it void for any lease to contain language that waives, discourages, or penalizes a tenant for calling police or emergency services (C.R.S. section 38-12-402). This mainly matters if you're ever tempted to add a 'crime-free housing' or repeated-nuisance-call type clause - that pattern is exactly what this law targets, and any such clause would be unenforceable.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-402 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Confidentiality Duty for a Tenant Who Is a DV/Stalking Victim
bodyText: If a tenant qualifies for early termination as a victim of domestic violence, stalking, or sexual assault, you have a legal duty not to disclose their status or new address to anyone without their consent, except where the law specifically requires it (C.R.S. section 38-12-401/402). This obligation exists regardless of whether the lease mentions it.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-401 / § 38-12-402 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Never Ask About Immigration or Citizenship Status
bodyText: Colorado's Immigrant Tenant Protection Act prohibits asking a tenant about their immigration or citizenship status, disclosing or threatening to disclose it, or using it to harass, intimidate, or deny housing (C.R.S. section 38-12-1201 et seq.). Violations carry real penalties - up to $2,000 per violation plus attorney's fees. Any lease provision attempting to waive these protections is void, even if the tenant agrees to it in writing.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-1201 et seq. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Attorney Fee Clauses Must Work Both Ways
bodyText: Two Colorado rules work together here, and between them they decide whether you ever see a dollar of attorney fees. First, a clause that only lets the landlord recover attorney fees and court costs - but not the tenant, if the tenant wins - is void under C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(II), and any fee-shifting clause must award fees to the prevailing party once the court finds the party prevailed and the fee is reasonable. Second, and less well known: under 13-40-123 a prevailing residential landlord or tenant is not entitled to recover attorney fees at all "unless the residential rental agreement between the parties contains a provision for either party to obtain attorney fees". So silence costs you the fees, and a landlord-only clause costs you the fees too, because it is void. The only version that works is a mutual prevailing-party clause - which is why the Default by Tenant clause has one, and why it is worth checking any clause you write yourself for the same thing.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3)(a)(II) (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.) | CO: CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 79 and rule 54. EXTENDED - C.R.S. § 13-40-123 added. Found by reading that section section-open for edu-holdover-co (read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00), title 13): a prevailing residential party gets no attorney fees unless the lease contains a fee provision. That makes the mutual fee clause a rule 54 optional clause of the "right that exists only if the lease invokes it" kind - a right the lease is silent on is lost - and the library already offers it inside the shared default-by-tenant row, so it is OFFERED, not declined. Citation now: § 38-12-801(3)(a)(II); § 13-40-123.

title: If a Tenant Dies During the Lease
bodyText: Colorado's 'Letty's Act' (C.R.S. section 38-12-801(3.5)) prohibits charging liquidated damages, accelerating rent beyond the end of the month (or 10 business days after the unit is vacated, whichever is later), clawing back move-in concessions, or any other early-termination penalty when a lease ends because a tenant died. You can retain enough of the security deposit to cover any damage related to the death, and you can take possession without filing an eviction once the estate's representative surrenders the unit, or automatically 30 days after death if rent is unpaid or the unit has been cleared out.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3.5) ("Letty's Act") (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Notify Tenants If Your Identity or Agent Changes
bodyText: If you (or your authorized agent) change - for example, a property changes management companies, or ownership transfers - Colorado law requires the new landlord or agent to notify each tenant within 1 business day, either in writing/electronically or by posting the new information conspicuously at the property (C.R.S. section 38-12-801(2)). This is an ongoing operational duty, not something that needs to be in the lease itself.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-801(2) (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Don't Charge for a Service You Don't Actually Provide
bodyText: Colorado's Honest Pricing law prohibits charging a fee for any service you don't actually provide (C.R.S. section 6-1-737). This is a good general check for any fee-based clause you write yourself: make sure the fee corresponds to something real.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 6-1-737 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Offer at Least One Fee-Free Way to Pay Rent
bodyText: You can't charge a rent payment processing fee unless you also offer at least one payment method with no fee attached (C.R.S. section 6-1-737). When you list your accepted payment methods in the lease, make sure at least one of them is genuinely free to the tenant.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 6-1-737 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Advertised Rent Must Show the Full Price
bodyText: When you advertise or list a property, Colorado's Honest Pricing law requires showing a single all-in price including mandatory fees, displayed more prominently than any broken-out fee amounts - not itemized separately (C.R.S. section 6-1-737). This applies to marketing and listings, not lease text, and becomes relevant if Steinoak ever adds a listing/marketing feature.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 6-1-737 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Utility Billing Rules Are Still Being Clarified
bodyText: If you use a shared or master utility meter and allocate costs among tenants by formula (RUBS), Colorado now has a statutory safe harbor (C.R.S. 6-1-737(4.5), added by HB26-1013). You may allocate utility costs this way if: the total you bill across all tenants does not exceed what the utility provider charged for the whole premises; you add no markup, surcharge, or administrative fee beyond what C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(VI) allows (either 2% of the billed amount or a flat $10 per month, not both); common-area and shared-facility costs are excluded from the allocation; and the allocation method is clearly disclosed in the lease or an addendum. This replaces the interim Attorney General enforcement guidance issued in late 2025.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 6-1-737(4.5) (HB26-1013); § 38-12-801(3)(a)(VI). Status moved NEEDS_REVIEW -> VERIFIED 2026-08-27 once HB26-1013 passed, codifying the safe harbor. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Radon Disclosure Risk Changes With Lease Length
bodyText: The radon disclosure itself is required before every lease is signed, whatever its length. What changes with length is the tenant's escape hatch. Under C.R.S. 38-12-803(3)(a) a tenant may void the lease and vacate under 38-12-507 if you fail to give the required written disclosures, or if you fail to make a reasonable effort to mitigate within 180 days after being notified that a radon measurement professional found 4 picocuries per liter or more (3)(a)(II). From January 1, 2026 that whole subsection (3) stops applying to a lease of one year or less (3)(b). Read the line carefully: a standard 12-month lease is "one year or less", so it escapes; a 13-month lease or a longer renewal does not. If you offer a term over a year, the void-and-vacate remedy is live, and the 180-day mitigation clock is the thing to diary.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-803(3)(b). Citation supplied this round (Claude Browser follow-up, 2026-09-13) via the earlier pass that located radon-disclosure-co's § 38-12-803 - not independently re-confirmed at the (3)(b) pinpoint this round. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.) | CO: CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 79. CITATION CORRECTED - the row cited § 38-12-803(3)(b) for the 180-day/void-the-lease rule. (3)(b) is not that rule: it is the carve-out, "On or after January 1, 2026, this subsection (3) does not apply to a lease agreement that is one year or less in duration." The void-and-vacate remedy is § 38-12-803(3)(a), and the 180-day reasonable-effort limb is § 38-12-803(3)(a)(II). Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00); previously the pinpoint rested on an earlier pass, not an official read. Substance also sharpened: the carve-out is "one year or less", so an ordinary 12-month lease falls outside subsection (3) entirely - the prior wording ("longer than one year" / "one year or less") was right but the consequence for the common 12-month term was not stated. Citation now: § 38-12-803(3)(a), (3)(a)(I), (3)(a)(II), (3)(b).

title: You Must Accept Housing Vouchers
bodyText: Colorado law requires every residential landlord to accept applicants using a housing voucher - there is no exemption for small landlords anymore (HB25-1240 removed it). Refusing an applicant solely because they use a voucher is source-of-income discrimination and can carry penalties of $5,000 to $50,000 per violation. You can still decline a voucher applicant for legitimate, consistently-applied reasons - credit, income, rental history - just never because of the voucher itself. You also can't refuse to cooperate with the approval process (inspection, paperwork) as a way of avoiding this duty.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 24-34-502 (HB25-1240 removed the small-landlord exemption, eff. 2025-05-29) (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: How the Voucher Approval Process Actually Works
bodyText: A voucher applicant doesn't move in until the unit is inspected and the Housing Assistance Payment contract is signed - you're not required to let someone occupy the unit before that happens. If a tenant does move in early anyway, standard guidance puts them on the hook for full, unsubsidized rent until the contract is finalized - you're not left holding the shortfall. The multi-year wait some landlords worry about is the tenant's wait to be issued a voucher in the first place; once a voucher holder actually applies to your specific unit, the approval process itself typically takes days to a few weeks, not years.
notes: CO: NOT_STATUTE. Operational/practical guidance, not itself citing a statute. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Security Deposit Rights Can Never Be Waived
bodyText: A tenant cannot waive their rights regarding return of the security deposit, whether orally or in writing - any lease provision attempting this is unenforceable (C.R.S. section 38-12-103(7)). Keep this in mind for any custom security deposit language you write yourself.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-103(7) (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Alternate Housing May Be Required During Major Repairs
bodyText: This is triggered by the TENANT'S REQUEST, not automatically. If a condition materially interferes with a tenant's life, health, or safety (or is a condition under C.R.S. 38-12-505(4)(l)), and the tenant requests it, you must provide - within 24 hours of that request, at no cost to the tenant - either a comparable dwelling unit or a hotel room, your choice which. Requirements: at least as many beds as the tenant uses; habitable; accessible if the tenant has a disability; within 5 miles of the unit unless the tenant consents otherwise (you may go 5-10 miles if substantially cheaper, and if nothing is available within 10 miles, the nearest available). If the stay runs past 48 hours, the place must have a refrigerator with a freezer and a range stove or oven - OR you pay each tenant a per diem for meals and incidentals at least equal to the Colorado state employee intrastate travel per diem, paid when you first reasonably expect the stay to exceed 48 hours and every 24 hours after. Beyond the per diem, you pay only reasonable relocation costs such as storage and transportation. Two things that protect you: the tenant still owes rent during the relocation and for the rest of the term; and if you put a tenant in a hotel and the condition cannot be fixed within 60 consecutive days for reasons outside your reasonable control, you can cap the hotel at 60 consecutive days - but only if you give written notice at the earliest opportunity stating that it cannot be fixed in 60 days, the end date for hotel coverage (no earlier than 60 days in), and that the tenant may terminate the lease with no liability or penalty, AND you return the tenant's full security deposit on or before you give that notice.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-503(4)(a)(II), (4)(c); referencing (505)(4)(l) (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Pet Deposit and Pet Rent Limits
bodyText: Colorado caps what you can charge for a pet: the pet security deposit can't exceed $300 and must be fully refundable - you can no longer charge a non-refundable 'pet fee.' Pet rent can't exceed $35 per month or 1.5% of the monthly rent, whichever is greater (C.R.S. section 38-12-106, HB 23-1068). The actual amounts you charge a specific tenant are entered in your lease's Pets clause - use these numbers as the ceiling when entering them for a Colorado property.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-106 (HB 23-1068) (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Carpet Damage Has a Special Rule
bodyText: You can't deduct from a security deposit for carpet being "substantially and irreparably damaged" unless the carpet has not been replaced with new carpet within the ten years preceding the end of the lease or surrender of the premises (C.R.S. 38-12-103(11)(c), as amended by HB25-1249, effective January 1, 2026). Even then, you may retain only the minimum amount necessary to replace the carpet - or to repaint - in the specific area that is damaged, not the full room or unit and not the full replacement cost (C.R.S. 38-12-103(11)(a)-(b)). Keep this in mind at move-out before assuming worn or stained carpet justifies a deduction.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-103(11)(c) (ten-year carpet rule); § 38-12-103(11)(a)-(b) (minimum-necessary/damaged-area/repaint rule); amended by HB25-1249, eff. 2026-01-01. Corrected 2026-08-27: lookback was written as 5 years (from a superseded reengrossed draft), corrected to the enrolled texts 10 years. CORRECTED AGAIN 2026-09-13 (Claude Browser follow-up): the minimum-necessary/damaged-area/repaint rule was miscited as C.R.S. 38-12-104 (a different section entirely) - actual citation is 38-12-103(11)(a)-(b), with (11)(c) being the ten-year carpet rule. Also surfaced, not yet added anywhere: 38-12-103(12) exempts mobile-home-park rental agreements from both this rule and the walkthrough right (1.5). (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: What Counts as "Bad Faith" When Withholding a Deposit
bodyText: If you retain 125% or more of a tenant's actual documented damages from their security deposit, Colorado law presumes you did so in bad faith (HB 25-1249). Bad-faith withholding also includes retaining a deposit without cause, or for an unlawful, retaliatory, or discriminatory reason. Bad-faith withholding exposes you to treble damages - document your actual costs carefully before making a deduction.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-103(3.5)(b); bad faith generally at (3.5)(a)(I)-(IV). Read verbatim (Claude Browser follow-up, 2026-09-13): '...if the amount retained is one hundred twenty-five percent or greater than the actual damages incurred.' (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Either Party Can Request a Move-Out Walkthrough
bodyText: Either you or the tenant can request a walkthrough inspection near the end of the lease (in person or by video) to identify anything beyond normal wear and tear before move-out (HB 25-1249). Doing a walkthrough does not legally lock you out of charging for genuine damage discovered afterward - the law's definition of 'wrongfully withheld' doesn't reference walkthrough completeness at all. That said, missing something during a walkthrough could still work against you if a dispute goes to court, since a tenant could argue you'd have caught it if it were real damage.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-103(1.5). Confirmed (Claude Browser follow-up, 2026-09-13): covers the mutual walkthrough request right, in person or by telecommunication, before termination and after furniture removal. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Never Charge a Tenant for Normal Wear and Tear or Preexisting Issues
bodyText: Any lease provision assigning a tenant a fee or charge for repairs, cleaning, or other work due to normal wear and tear, or for damage/defective conditions that existed before their tenancy began, is void under Colorado law (HB 25-1249). This was actually the reason the Use of Security Deposit clause got corrected during this review - worth keeping in mind for any custom deposit-related language you write yourself.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-103(7)(b). Confirmed (Claude Browser follow-up, 2026-09-13). Related, not yet its own row: (7)(a) is broader - voids any provision waiving or modifying a Part 1 tenant benefit generally, not just the wear-and-tear charge. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Domestic Abuse / Sexual Violence — Rent Liability After Vacating
bodyText: Wyoming's Safe Homes Act provides Tenant a defense against a claim for unpaid rent under certain circumstances. If Tenant or a member of Tenant's household vacates the property because of a credible imminent threat of domestic abuse or sexual violence at the property, or because Tenant or a household member was a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence occurring at the property within the preceding 60 days, Tenant will not be liable for rent accruing after the date Tenant vacates. If hospitalization, or seeking shelter or counseling related to the abuse or violence, prevented Tenant from giving notice within that 60-day window, Tenant may still give notice as soon as practicable afterward. To use this protection, Tenant must provide Landlord written notice at least 7 days before vacating, stating the reason for vacating and, where applicable, the date of the incident along with supporting medical, court, or police evidence. This Section does not excuse rent owed for any period before Tenant vacated and gave the required notice, and does not limit Landlord's other lawful remedies for nonpayment of rent accruing before that date.
notes: WY added 2026-08-21. Citation: W.S. 1-21-1303(a),(b),(d). Statutorily-accurate/defense-framed version — SELECTED variant per Taylor's decision 2026-08-21 (chose over the proactive-grant alternative, see dv-safe-homes-proactive-wy). Not a legal requirement for this clause's other tagged states (only MN's Plain Language Contract Act, Minn. Stat. §325G.31, was confirmed to apply this project) — done as a general readability improvement since the pattern was found library-wide, not MN-specific. | WY: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-safe-homes-rent-defense-wy). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Domestic Abuse / Sexual Violence — Early Termination Right (alternate posture, not selected)
bodyText: If Tenant or a member of Tenant's household experiences a credible imminent threat of domestic abuse or sexual violence at the property, or was a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence at the property within the preceding 60 days, Tenant may terminate this Lease and vacate the property. If hospitalization, or seeking shelter or counseling related to the abuse or violence, prevented Tenant from acting within that 60-day window, Tenant may still act as soon as practicable afterward. To do so, Tenant must provide Landlord written notice at least 7 days before vacating, stating the reason and, where applicable, the date of the incident along with supporting medical, court, or police evidence. Upon proper notice and vacating, Tenant owes no further rent for any period after the date Tenant vacates.
notes: WY added 2026-08-21, is_active FALSE by design — NOT the selected variant. Goes beyond W.S. 1-21-1303's actual mechanic (a court-tested affirmative defense) by proactively granting an unconditional lease-level termination right on notice+evidence alone, without preserving Landlord's ability to contest weak evidence in court first. Kept drafted and logged (not deleted) in case a future 'per-property posture setting' feature makes this selectable. Citation basis same as dv-safe-homes-wy: W.S. 1-21-1303(a),(b). | Cross-state plain-language cleanup (Minnesota session, follow-up to MN's plain-language audit): long compound sentence split into shorter ones, no substantive change. Not a legal requirement for this clause's other tagged states (only MN's Plain Language Contract Act, Minn. Stat. §325G.31, was confirmed to apply this project) — done as a general readability improvement since the pattern was found library-wide, not MN-specific.

title: Can't Terminate a Tenancy Solely for Domestic Abuse / Sexual Violence Victim Status
bodyText: Wyoming law prohibits terminating a tenancy based solely on a tenant's, applicant's, or household member's status as a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence (W.S. 1-21-1303(c)). This does not prevent an adverse housing decision based on other lawful factors you're otherwise aware of — it specifically targets using victim status itself as the reason. Also logged as a standing cross-check: any future WY clause or custom termination language should be checked against this rule before use.
notes: WY added 2026-08-21. Citation: W.S. 1-21-1303(c). Dual-logged as both content and a standing validation check, same pattern as CO's Part 4 police-call rule. Source: law.justia.com/codes/wyoming/title-1/chapter-21/article-13/section-1-21-1303/. | WY: RETRO 2026-10-04 (SOP 1.56, rule 79). BASIS: section-open, official Wyoming Legislature NXT gateway, 2026 Wyoming Statutes, read 2026-10-04 (Art. 12 at /1/53/65, Art. 13 at /1/53/66). Both articles' live text is character-identical to the 2026-09-30 read, so no amendment intervened and no history-line discrepancy arises. VERDICT: confirmed, including the qualifier. W.S. 1-21-1303(c) is two sentences: the status-based termination ban, then 'This subsection does not prohibit adverse housing decisions based upon other lawful factors within the landlord's knowledge.' The row carries both, correctly attached. Was a host copy; now primary.

title: Safe Homes Act Rights Can Never Be Waived or Modified
bodyText: The protections in Wyoming's Safe Homes Act (W.S. 1-21-1301 through 1304) cannot be waived or modified by a lease or any separate agreement between landlord and tenant (W.S. 1-21-1304). Keep this in mind for any custom termination or waiver language you write yourself — attempting to contract around these protections would be unenforceable. Also logged as a standing cross-check, same pattern as CO's deposit-nonwaiver rule.
notes: WY added 2026-08-21. Citation: W.S. 1-21-1304. Source: law.justia.com/codes/wyoming/title-1/chapter-21/article-13/section-1-21-1304/. Note absence flagged separately: unlike CO's version of this protection, WY's Safe Homes Act (W.S. 1-21-1301–1304, read in full) contains no landlord confidentiality duty regarding victim status/new address — treated as a genuine state difference, not a research gap, pending any future correction. | WY: RETRO 2026-10-04 (SOP 1.56, rule 79). BASIS: section-open, official Wyoming Legislature NXT gateway, 2026 Wyoming Statutes, read 2026-10-04 (Art. 12 at /1/53/65, Art. 13 at /1/53/66). Both articles' live text is character-identical to the 2026-09-30 read, so no amendment intervened and no history-line discrepancy arises. VERDICT: confirmed. W.S. 1-21-1304 bars waiver or modification 'in any lease or separate agreement', and the recorded WY-versus-CO difference holds: Art. 13 read whole contains no landlord confidentiality duty.

title: You May Refuse an Uneconomical Repair and Terminate Instead
bodyText: If a tenant notifies you of a habitability issue and the cost to fix it would be unreasonable relative to the rent charged and the nature of the property, Wyoming law lets you refuse the repair and terminate the rental agreement instead (W.S. 1-21-1203(d)). You must notify the tenant in writing and give them no less than 10 and no more than 20 days to find substitute housing. Rent is prorated to the tenant's move-out date, and any balance plus the deposit gets refunded per the standard deposit-return rules. This is a real option worth knowing about for a low-rent unit facing a major, disproportionate repair cost — not something to state to the tenant in the lease itself, since it only becomes relevant if you choose to invoke it.
notes: WY added 2026-08-21. Citation: W.S. 1-21-1203(d). Classified LANDLORD_EDUCATION per Taylor's 2026-08-21 call (overrode initial LEASE_CLAUSE recommendation). Source: law.justia.com/codes/wyoming/title-1/chapter-21/article-12/section-1-21-1203/. | WY: RETRO 2026-10-04 (SOP 1.56, rule 79). BASIS: section-open, official Wyoming Legislature NXT gateway, 2026 Wyoming Statutes, read 2026-10-04 (Art. 12 at /1/53/65, Art. 13 at /1/53/66). Both articles' live text is character-identical to the 2026-09-30 read, so no amendment intervened and no history-line discrepancy arises. VERDICT: confirmed. W.S. 1-21-1203(d) is the subdivision that carries the owner's right to refuse an unreasonably costly repair and terminate, and the 10-to-20-day substitute-housing window. title: Habitability Baseline
bodyText: Landlord will maintain the property in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation, including operational electrical, heating, and plumbing systems, with hot and cold running water, unless otherwise agreed in writing by both parties. Tenant will cooperate in maintaining the property consistent with this Section.
notes: WY added 2026-08-21. Citation: W.S. 1-21-1202(a),(b). Source: law.justia.com/codes/wyoming/title-1/chapter-21/article-12/section-1-21-1202/. Note: (d) of this section allows duties to be reassigned/modified by explicit written agreement — logged separately as edu-habitability-modifiable-wy rather than folded into this clause, since most leases won't modify the baseline. (a) also carries a seasonal-rental-unit carve-out (e.g. summer cabins without utilities) — N/A for typical Steinoak use case, not drafted. | WY: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-habitability-baseline-wy). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Tenant's Duties
bodyText: Tenant will keep the property clean and safe and not unreasonably burden any common area; dispose of all garbage and waste in a clean and safe manner; keep all plumbing fixtures as sanitary as their condition permits; and use all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, and other facilities and appliances in a reasonable manner. Tenant will also occupy the property only in the manner for which it was designed, not increase the number of occupants above what this Lease specifies without Landlord's prior written permission, remain current on all payments required under this Lease, and comply with all lawful requirements of this Lease. Before vacating, Tenant will remove all property and garbage belonging to Tenant or Tenant's guests and clean the property to the condition it was in at the start of this Lease.
notes: WY added 2026-08-21. Citation: W.S. 1-21-1204(a)(i)-(viii). title: Prohibited Acts by Tenant
bodyText: Tenant will not intentionally or negligently destroy, deface, damage, or impair any part of the property, or knowingly permit any other person to do so; interfere with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the property; or unreasonably deny access to, refuse entry to, or withhold consent to enter the property to Landlord or Landlord's agent for the purpose of making repairs, inspecting the property, or showing it for rent or sale.
notes: WY added 2026-08-21. Citation: W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(i)-(iii). Source: law.justia.com/codes/wyoming/title-1/chapter-21/article-12/section-1-21-1205/. Note absence: WY has no statutory advance-notice-for-entry requirement — this clause only bars the tenant from unreasonably refusing entry, it does not itself establish a landlord notice obligation. Flagged in decision log §2 as an open absence to verify. | WY: RETRO 2026-10-04 (SOP 1.56, rule 79). title: Nonrefundable Portion of Deposit
bodyText: Of Tenant's total security deposit of {{security_deposit}}, the nonrefundable portion is {{nonrefundable_deposit_amount}}. Any nonrefundable portion will not be returned to Tenant at the end of this Lease regardless of the condition of the property. If the nonrefundable portion is $0, no part of the Security Deposit is nonrefundable.
notes: WY added 2026-08-21. Citation: W.S. 1-21-1207. Source: law.justia.com/codes/wyoming/title-1/chapter-21/article-12/section-1-21-1207/. Genuine REQUIRED disclosure — satisfies bucket-test criterion #1. Note: statute requires this be stated in the agreement AND separately, in writing, at the time the deposit is collected — this clause satisfies the first prong only; the second is a process step, logged separately as edu-nonrefundable-deposit-separate-notice-wy so it isn't lost. | WY: RETRO 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.15, rule 42). W.S. 1-21-1207 read section-open 2026-09-30: 'Any rental agreement shall state WHETHER any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable'. The duty runs on every Wyoming rental agreement that takes a deposit, including one with no nonrefundable portion, so the row stays REQUIRED rather than CONDITIONAL. Text rewritten because the old wording asserted that '$0 ... is nonrefundable and will not be returned to Tenant regardless of the condition of the property', which reads as a nonsense assertion in the (common) $0 case and left the statutory 'whether' answered only by a parenthetical aside. New wording states the answer affirmatively either way. Rule 40 note: the section prescribes no type size, bold, underline or placement, and no sanction attaches to omitting it -- W.S. 1-21-1208(c)'s penalty reaches only subsections (a) and (b) of 1-21-1208, not 1-21-1207. W.S. 1-21-1207 is a single sentence with two prongs; this clause carries the in-agreement prong. Re-confirmed on the live text.

title: Give Separate Written Notice of Nonrefundable Deposit at Collection Time
bodyText: Wyoming law requires you to give the tenant separate written notice that a portion of their deposit is nonrefundable at the time you actually collect the deposit — not just state it in the lease itself (W.S. 1-21-1207). Stating it in the lease satisfies one part of the requirement; you should also hand or send the tenant a standalone written notice when you take the deposit, to be safe.
notes: WY added 2026-08-21. Citation: W.S. 1-21-1207. Companion item to nonrefundable-deposit-notice-wy — covers the process/timing half of the same statutory requirement. | WY: RETRO 2026-10-04 (SOP 1.56, rule 79). The separate-notice prong is the second half of the same single sentence in W.S. 1-21-1207: written notice 'at the time the deposit is taken'. Subdivision correct (the section has no subsections). title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant will notify Landlord in writing, within 30 days after termination of this Lease, of the address where the balance of the Security Deposit and any notice about it should be sent. The address Tenant gives under this Section, or the address stated for Tenant in this Lease if Tenant gives no other, is also furnished to Landlord in writing specifically for the purpose of any notice about personal property Tenant leaves behind, and Landlord may send that notice to it by certified mail.
notes: WY added 2026-08-21. Citation: W.S. 1-21-1208(a). Source: law.justia.com/codes/wyoming/title-1/chapter-21/article-12/section-1-21-1208/. Mechanics differ materially from CO's security-deposit-use clause (different timelines, different extension trigger) — drafted independently rather than adapted from the CO version. | BODYTEXT EDIT 2026-08-28 (deposit split): removed deposit-application sentence, now carried by the generic security-deposit-use clause (WY newly tagged). Return mechanics only; all elements still sourced to Wyo. Stat. 1-21-1208(a). | WY: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): kept the tenant's forwarding-address duty; the restated return deadline and itemization duty moved to edu-security-deposit-return-wy. | WY: RETRO 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.15, targeted fix 17 with rules 46 and 50). The 2026-09-29 scrub left this clause carrying only the W.S. 1-21-1208(a) forwarding-address duty, scoped to the deposit. No landlord figure can break a statutory limit here (the clause carries no fillable number), so the number-check half of fix 17 is clean. The condition a number check cannot catch: W.S. 1-21-1210(a)(i)(A) deems an abandoned-property notice served on the date it is mailed by certified mail only to 'an address furnished to the owner by the renter in writing specifically for this purpose', and no WY row furnished one -- leaving personal service under W.S. 1-21-1210(a)(i)(B) (W.R.C.P. Rule 4) or newspaper publication under (C) as the only routes. Second sentence added so the lease is itself that writing. Both sections read section-open 2026-09-30.
