title: Holdover
bodyText: If Tenant does not vacate the property by the end of the Term, Landlord may pursue any remedy allowed by applicable law to recover possession. If Tenant remains in possession and Landlord accepts Rent, this Lease will be presumed renewed on the same terms and for the same period as the original Term, not exceeding one year. Where the renewed term is one the parties did not specify, either party may terminate it by giving the other notice at least as long before its expiration as the length of the term itself, not exceeding one month.
notes: SD re-audit 2026-09-07 (Tier B resolved). Supersedes generic `holdover`, withheld from SD because it promises 'holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law for each day Tenant remains in possession'. SD HAS NO HOLDOVER DAMAGES MULTIPLIER - no double rent, no per-diem penalty (see edu-holdover-mechanics-sd). In SD that phrase resolves to zero, so the generic would promise the landlord a remedy that does not exist - the inverse of the usual defect: not a misstated rule but a clause whose operative term is NULL in this jurisdiction. Replaced with SDCL 43-32-14's actual mechanic: 'If a lessee of real property remains in possession thereof after the expiration of the hiring and the lessor accepts rent from him, the parties are presumed to have renewed the hiring on the same terms and for the same time, not exceeding one year.' The generic's 'month-to-month basis' fallback was also wrong for SD - 43-32-14 renews for the SAME TIME as the original term, not monthly. Final sentence carries 43-32-15's scaling so the renewed term is terminable. ND is excluded from the generic and has no override; SD gets one rather than an exclusion because leaving SD clause-less would reproduce the omission failure mode this session exists to correct. [Source-integrity: full ch.43-32 text via consumer.sd.gov/docs/LLTen_Statutes43-32.pdf, CONFIRMED STALE as to 43-32-24 (prints 'two weeks', source line omits SL 2026 ch 179). All other sections used carry source lines ending 1939-2022 and were unamended 2024-2026. See Addendum L.8.] TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Holdover (South Dakota)' -> 'Holdover' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO). | Retro checks (SOP 1.51) 2026-10-04. GROUND CORRECTED; THE OVERRIDE ITSELF STANDS. These notes justified withholding the generic `holdover` from SD on the reasoning that 'SD HAS NO HOLDOVER DAMAGES MULTIPLIER - no double rent, no per-diem penalty', so the generic's promise of 'holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' would 'resolve to zero' in South Dakota. That reasoning is wrong: SDCL 21-3-8 (double the yearly value, on conditions) and SDCL 21-3-7 (double the rent, on different conditions) are multipliers, SDCL 21-3-5 supplies a residual value-of-use measure, and SDCL 21-16-10 channels 21-3-8 into the FED judgment - so the generic's phrase would have resolved to a real figure, not to zero. The override is still correct for the reason the notes give second and should have given first: SDCL 43-32-14 renews the hiring for the SAME TIME as the original term on acceptance of rent, not month-to-month, so the generic's month-to-month fallback was wrong for SD on its own terms. No change to bodyText - 'any remedy allowed by applicable law to recover possession' is accurate and now points at a real damages family, and the stipulated alternative is offered separately as `holdover-rate-sd`. See `edu-holdover-mechanics-sd` for the corrected statement of the measures. SDCL ch. 21-3 parsed and proved complete against the site's own chapter index: 16 of 16 sections, no extras. Decoded as UTF-16LE per the encoding fix recorded in the 1.24 retro.

title: Repair Requests
bodyText: Tenant will notify Landlord promptly in writing of any condition requiring repair or maintenance. A request for written notice does not limit Landlord's repair and habitability duty, which South Dakota law imposes whether or not Tenant's notice is in writing, and does not affect any remedy South Dakota law gives Tenant after Tenant has given notice of a condition requiring repair.
notes: SD re-audit 2026-09-07 (Tier B resolved). Supersedes generic `landlord-maintenance` (tagged CO only), which opens 'Subject to Tenant's own maintenance obligations under this Lease, Landlord will maintain...'. That subordination is the problem in SD: SDCL 43-32-8 allocates the repair duty to the lessor and states expressly 'The parties to a lease or hiring of residential premises may not waive or modify the requirements imposed by this section'. A clause making the lessor's duty subject to the tenant's obligations is arguably a modification and void pro tanto. Drafted to track 43-32-8's own language and to state the non-waiver and the repairs-in-lieu-of-rent exception on the face of the clause. Closing sentence preserves the 43-32-9 remedies (repair-and-deduct, vacate-and-discharge, rent escrow where repair cost exceeds one month's rent) without restating them. CROSS-STATE BACKLOG: the CO;WY-only scoping of the generic maintenance pair has been open since the MN session; this resolves SD's instance only, by override rather than extension. Why the generic is CO-only remains open for CO/WY. [Source-integrity: full ch.43-32 text via consumer.sd.gov/docs/LLTen_Statutes43-32.pdf, CONFIRMED STALE as to 43-32-24 (prints 'two weeks', source line omits SL 2026 ch 179). All other sections used carry source lines ending 1939-2022 and were unamended 2024-2026. See Addendum L.8.] TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Landlord Maintenance and Repair (South Dakota)' -> 'Landlord Maintenance and Repair' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO). | SD: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): kept only the tenant's written repair-notice duty; the restated landlord duties are in the existing edu-habitability-duty-sd. It still supersedes the shared landlord-maintenance. | Retro checks (SOP 1.24) 2026-10-02. TARGETED FIX 20 (SOP rule 78 with rule 47): the 2026-09-29 scrub cut this clause to the tenant's written repair-notice duty alone. CONDITION RESTORED, because a number check could not catch it. SDCL 43-32-9, read section-open this pass, conditions the tenant's repair-and-deduct and vacate-and-discharge remedies on 'notice to the lessor' with NO writing requirement; only the third remedy, the rent-escrow route, requires 'written notice stating the specific reason for the withholding'. The trimmed clause flattened that into writing for every repair notice, so a landlord could argue an orally-notified tenant never triggered the duty. SDCL 43-32-19(1) separately does require a 'written request' for the tenant's termination right, so the statute is genuinely mixed and the clause may ask for writing - it may not make writing a precondition. The added sentence restores only that. SEPARATELY CHECKED AND NOT RESTORED: no South Dakota statute requires any text in the lease itself. The rule 40 and rule 42 batteries across the whole code returned ZERO residential hits for 'underlined', boldface, type size, capital letters, 'separate document', 'substantially equivalent', or a must-include-in-the-lease pattern, so the CO retro shape (a bold statement hiding in the habitability part) does not exist in South Dakota. SDCL 43-32-8's non-waiver sentence and its repairs-in-lieu-of-rent exception remain correctly stated in edu-habitability-duty-sd. title: Tenant Belongings After an Eviction
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no post-writ inventory, storage, notice, or care-standard duty specific to eviction. The general abandoned-property rules govern instead, and they are triggered by the tenant having quit the premises rather than by service of a writ. Property with a total reasonable value of five hundred dollars or less, left for ten days after the tenant has quit, is presumed abandoned and may be disposed of. Property worth more than five hundred dollars must be stored, and Landlord has a lien on it to the extent of the costs of handling and storing the property; after storing it for thirty days or more, Landlord may treat it as abandoned and dispose of it. Because the trigger is the tenant quitting rather than the writ, the same timeline applies whether the tenant leaves voluntarily or is removed.
notes: SD re-audit 2026-09-07, eviction-duty screen (item 7, never run against SD before). The screen found CO and KS carrying ZERO self-help rows despite substantial remedies; against SD it found self-help/ouster covered, willful utility shutoff covered by the same row via 43-32-6's 'willfully diminishes services' limb, and writ-execution timing covered - but NO row on post-writ property duties and none on post-writ animal duties. Primary text: SDCL 43-32-25 and 43-32-26. CROSS-STATE COMPARISON recorded as comparison not inheritance (Dakota-ancestry rule): ND's equivalent describes a materially similar structure, but ND's lien is expressly subordinated to a prior perfected security interest and SD's 43-32-26 contains NO such priority carve-out. Similar architecture, non-identical text. CONFIDENCE CAVEAT: the ch.43-32 half is primary-verified (43-32-25/26 read in full; source lines end SL 2008 ch 227, unaffected by the L.8 staleness). The TITLE 21-16 half - that SD's eviction chapter imposes no post-writ duty of its own - now rests on the full 21-16 text supplied by Taylor, which contains no post-writ property or animal provision across 21-16-1 to 21-16-12. title: No Rules for Tenant Animals After an Eviction
bodyText: South Dakota law says nothing about what happens to a tenant's animals after an eviction. There is no animal-control notification route, no notice-posting requirement, no unattended-animal rule, and no duty assigned to Landlord or to the sheriff. The abandoned-property provisions are written for property and are a poor fit for a live animal, so a landlord facing this situation has no statutory procedure to follow and should contact local animal control.
notes: SD re-audit 2026-09-07, eviction-duty screen. Confirmed absence, given its own row per the standing rule that a log-only absence is invisible to every future canvass. Coverage: the full ch.43-32 was read section-by-section this session and contains no animal provision outside the service-animal group at 43-32-33 to -36, which concerns accommodation and fraudulent-claim damages, not post-eviction custody. Matches ND's edu-no-post-writ-animal-duty-nd; CO is the outlier with an affirmative duty, so the absence is the regional norm. The closing practical note is guidance, not a statement of law, because no law exists to state. title: Pet Policy
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord. Tenant will pay Landlord a pet deposit, if applicable, and pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor, and disturbance caused by a pet, and will indemnify Landlord from claims arising from Tenant's pet(s). Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern. If the pet becomes vicious or displays symptoms of severe illness, or if Tenant dies, becomes incapacitated, or is otherwise unable to care for the pet and Landlord believes in good faith that the pet is being abused or neglected, Landlord may enter the property and remove the pet. Any such entry will be made in accordance with the Access and Entry section of this Lease, except that in an emergency, or where giving notice is impracticable, Landlord may enter without prior notice.
notes: SD re-audit 2026-09-07. Supersedes the generic `pet-policy` (CO;WY;ND), which was the last Tier B item held back from the L.2 generic-clause audit. Option C of three presented to Taylor and approved by him. TWO CHANGES from the generic, both narrow: (1) The phrase 'without liability to Tenant' is STRUCK. SDCL 53-9-3 voids any contract term whose object is to exempt a party from responsibility for 'violation of law whether willful or negligent'. A blanket no-liability exemption attached to an entry-and-remove right reaches the tail cases where the entry is not clearly lawful - tenant incapacitated but the animal in no distress, or a good-faith belief that turns out wrong - and in SD an unlawful entry is expensive: SDCL 43-32-6 gives the tenant two months' rent plus return of any advance rent and deposit. Striking the phrase costs the landlord nothing they actually had, because the exemption would not have been enforced that far anyway. (2) Entry is now tied to the lease's Access and Entry section, with the statutory emergency/impracticability exception stated on the face of the clause. This closes an internal inconsistency created earlier in the same session: `landlords-access-sd` was written to carry SDCL 43-32-32's four mandatory notice elements (date(s), a period during normal business hours, purpose, and a means to request rescheduling), while the generic pet-policy granted a separate entry right that mentioned none of them. Two entry rights in one lease on different terms is a drafting defect independent of any statute. ASSESSMENT CORRECTED IN THE OPEN: this row was originally flagged as a clear 53-9-3 third-prong violation. On re-reading, the enumerated entry grounds - a vicious animal, a severely ill animal - are mostly genuine emergencies, and 43-32-32 expressly excepts emergencies from the notice requirement, so the entry itself is usually lawful. The risk is narrower than first stated and is confined to the non-emergency tail. Recorded because the earlier framing overstated it and the overstatement is part of the record. DOWNSIDE OF THE ALTERNATIVE, for the record: SD has no enumerated prohibited-terms statute (edu-no-prohibited-terms-list-sd), so an overbroad exculpatory phrase is not unlawful in SD - it simply would not be enforced to that extent. Tagging the generic as-is was a defensible option; the override was chosen for the entry-consistency reason as much as the 53-9-3 one. CROSS-STATE CANDIDATE, not acted on: ND is tagged on the generic and has N.D.C.C. 9-08-02, the direct counterpart to 53-9-3, so the same 'without liability' phrase plausibly has the same limit in ND. Per L.4 and the Dakota-ancestry rule this is recorded as a candidate for ND's next pass, NOT an inherited conclusion, and no ND row was touched. CO and WY unexamined for this point. S5a.1: this is a new override row, not an edit to the shared generic - the generic's text and its CO;WY;ND tags are unchanged, so no other state's rendering is affected and no propagation is owed. TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Pet Policy (South Dakota)' -> 'Pet Policy' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO).

title: Reasonable Accommodation of Disabled Tenants
bodyText: South Dakota imposes its own reasonable-accommodation duty in housing, separate from federal fair housing law. SDCL 20-13-23.7 provides that for purposes of employment, public accommodation, public service, and education or housing, good faith efforts shall be made to reasonably accommodate a disabled person unless the accommodation would impose undue hardship. The standard is framed as good faith efforts subject to an undue-hardship limit, and the statute does not define either term or set out a request-and-response procedure, so in practice a landlord should document what was requested, what was considered, and why any accommodation was or was not made. Two limits sitting in the same chapter qualify that duty and are easy to miss. SDCL 20-13-21.1 provides that nothing in chapter 20-13 requires a person selling, renting or leasing property, or anyone acting for the owner, to modify the property in any way, to incur any additional expense, or to exercise a higher degree of care for a person having a disability than for a person who does not have one. It further provides that the chapter does not relieve any person of the obligations generally imposed on all persons, regardless of disability, in a written lease or rental agreement, and does not forbid distinctions based on an inability to fulfil the terms and conditions of the lease, including its financial obligations. So South Dakota's own good-faith accommodation duty carries no state-law obligation to pay for or carry out physical modifications, and it does not excuse a tenant from rent. Federal fair housing law is a separate and generally more demanding source - it requires you to permit reasonable modifications made at the tenant's expense and to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services - and SDCL 20-13-21.1, which limits only what chapter 20-13 requires, does not cut it down. One more provision in the same chapter cuts the other way and should be read with SDCL 20-13-21.1, not instead of it. SDCL 20-13-20(4) makes it an unfair or discriminatory housing practice to refuse to permit, AT THE EXPENSE OF THE DISABLED PERSON, reasonable modifications of existing property that may be necessary to afford full enjoyment of the property - and it lets the landlord, where reasonable, condition permission on the renter agreeing to restore the premises to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. So South Dakota does impose a state-law duty to PERMIT modifications; what SDCL 20-13-21.1 denies is any duty to PAY for them or to carry them out. The two fit together. Note also that the owner-occupied exemption in SDCL 20-13-20 reaches subdivision (4) as well as (1) and (2), so in a dwelling with living quarters for no more than two families where the owner occupies one of them, the modification duty does not apply either - though the advertising prohibition in subdivision (3) still does.
notes: SD re-audit 2026-09-07. SDCL 20-13-23.7 verbatim: 'For purposes of employment, public accommodation, public service, and education or housing, good faith efforts shall be made to reasonably accommodate the disabled person unless the accommodation would impose undue hardship.' Source: SL 1986 ch 170 S4, unamended. Primary text supplied by Taylor. GENUINELY NEW - nothing in the library recorded a STATE-level reasonable-accommodation duty for SD; the assistance-animal rows carry SD's animal-specific documentation rules (43-32-33 to -36) and the fair-housing row carries the protected classes, but neither reaches accommodation generally. Found only because the chapter index was finally swept after the third L.12 failure - i.e. the sweep that was overdue produced a second finding beyond the one it was run for. SCOPE NOTE: the section is a general Title 20 human-rights provision covering five contexts at once, of which housing is one. Recorded as LANDLORD_EDUCATION rather than a lease clause because it states a standard of conduct, not a term the parties agree to - and because a lease clause purporting to define 'undue hardship' in the landlord's favour would be a poor idea in a state whose only limit on such terms is the general 53-9-3 / unconscionability backstop. RELATIONSHIP TO FEDERAL LAW: the FHA's reasonable-accommodation requirement is broader and better developed; this row records that SD ALSO has one at state level, not that it displaces or narrows the federal duty. No attempt is made here to map where the two diverge - that is a real question and is NOT answered by this row. TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Reasonable Accommodation of Disabled Tenants (South Dakota)' -> 'Reasonable Accommodation of Disabled Tenants' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO). | BODY ADDITION 2026-09-28 (SD scenario screen, gap-discovery source 3): SDCL 20-13-21.1 added. Found by the L.12 adjacent-provision sweep across ch. 20-13 while re-verifying this row's authority - the section sits two subsections away from 20-13-21 and had never been read, and it is the express limit on the very duty this row states. Primary text read section-open and verbatim on law.justia.com's current SD codification; source line 'SL 1986 ch 170 S14; SL 1991 ch 179 S16', unamended since 1991. THIS IS A MATERIAL OMISSION BEING FIXED, NOT A REFINEMENT: the row previously stated SD's good-faith accommodation duty with none of its statutory qualifications, which reads as a broader state-law obligation than ch. 20-13 actually imposes - in particular it left a landlord to infer a duty to fund modifications that 20-13-21.1 expressly disclaims. The federal-law sentence is included so the limit is not over-read in the other direction; the FHA's reasonable-modification (at tenant expense) and reasonable-accommodation duties are separate and unaffected. ALSO RE-CONFIRMED: SDCL 20-13-23.7 is unamended, source line SL 1986 ch 170 S4. NOT READ, FLAGGED: SDCL 20-13-21.2 (design and construction of multifamily dwellings - access for disabled persons and wheelchairs), which is adjacent and may bear on new construction but was not opened, and is therefore not characterised anywhere in this row. | Retro checks (SOP 1.24) 2026-10-02. RULE 79 / L.12 ADDITION. SDCL 20-13-20 read section-open and end-to-end this pass. The 2026-09-28 pass added SDCL 20-13-21.1's limits to this row but never paired them with SDCL 20-13-20(4), which is the affirmative state-law reasonable-MODIFICATION duty - at the disabled person's expense, with a restoration condition the landlord may impose where reasonable. Left as it stood, the row read as though South Dakota imposed no modification duty at all, which is wrong. ALSO CONFIRMED from the same read: the exemption sentence is 'The provisions of subdivisions (1), (2), and (4) do not apply to rooms or units in dwellings that contain living quarters for no more than two families living independently of each other, if the owner maintains and occupies one of the living quarters as the owner's residence' - so it reaches the modification duty, which the library did not record, while subdivision (3)'s advertising ban stays live. The shared no-alterations clause already saves 'any repair, installation, rekeying, or reasonable modification that applicable law entitles Tenant to perform', so no clause change is needed. SDCL 20-13-21.2 (design and construction access in multifamily dwellings) remains unread and is still not characterised anywhere in this row.

title: Deposit Documentation on Tenant Request
bodyText: From January 1, 2026, a Colorado tenant may make a written request for the documentation behind any amount you retained from a security deposit, and you must provide it within 14 days. The duty covers documentation in your possession relevant to the retention - photographs, inspection forms or reports, receipts, invoices, and estimates. Keep this material as you go rather than assembling it after a dispute starts: the same statute deems a withholding wrongful where your written statement fails to list exact reasons, and the landlord carries the burden of proving both that a retention was not wrongful and what the actual damages were.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-103(8); added by HB 25-1249, eff. 2026-01-01 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.) title: Signed Condition Statement Required at Move-In
bodyText: North Dakota requires you to provide the tenant, at the time the rental agreement is entered into, a statement describing the condition of the facilities in and about the premises to be rented. The statement must be agreed to and signed by both you and the tenant. **It then constitutes prima facie proof of the condition of the facilities and the premises at the beginning of the rental agreement** — which makes it the single most useful document you will have in any later dispute about damage, because without it you are arguing about the starting condition from memory while the tenant does the same. The statute fixes no form, no itemisation standard, and no penalty for skipping it; the consequence of omission is evidentiary, and it falls on you. Complete it carefully and specifically rather than treating it as a formality, keep a signed copy with the lease, and give the tenant one.
notes: Added 2026-09-07 (cross-state core-obligations canvass, run during the SD re-audit). N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.2, read in full from the official chapter PDF at ndlegis.gov/cencode/t47c16.pdf. **NOT A CORRECTNESS FIX - A FINDABILITY FIX, and recorded as such.** The duty was already in the library, but as the closing sentence of `edu-no-lease-copy-duty-nd`, a row titled 'No Duty to Give a Lease Copy'. That row is accurate and is unchanged. The problem is that a REQUIRED affirmative duty, whose output is PRIMA FACIE PROOF in exactly the deposit and damage disputes where it matters, was filed under a heading announcing the ABSENCE of a different duty. A landlord reading ND guidance on deposits or move-in would not reach it. ND's own decision log records this failure shape from the ND re-audit - an entire escheat regime under ch. 47-30.2 that 'existed in the library as one trailing sentence of clause text'. Same shape, smaller scale. WHY IT MATTERS EVIDENTIALLY: the prima facie effect shifts who has to prove what. ND's deposit remedy is TREBLE damages for withholding without reasonable justification (47-16-07.1(4)), so a landlord without a signed condition statement faces the worst combination available - a high penalty and no presumption. CROSS-STATE CONTEXT from the canvass: three of seven states mandate a move-in document - ND 47-16-07.2, MN 504B.182 (initial and final inspections, with a deposit-DOUBLING penalty attached to the notice failure), KS 58-2548 (joint five-day inventory). SD and WY have none; CO's 38-12-103(1.5) walkthrough right is on-request rather than mandatory. S5a.1: new ND-only row; no shared clause touched; no propagation owed. ALSO CHECKED THIS PASS AND FOUND ALREADY COVERED - no action taken: N.D.C.C. 47-16-20.1's payment-method fee ban is fully carried by edu-payment-method-fee-ban-nd and cross-cited in returned-payments and acceptable-payment-methods. That flag from the canvass was a FALSE POSITIVE, raised because the canvass looked for a dedicated row and reasoned from its absence. Recorded so the flag is not re-raised. TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Signed Condition Statement Required at Move-In (North Dakota)' -> 'Signed Condition Statement Required at Move-In' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO). | CHANGED 2026-09-27 (gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36). PRECISION FIX, two overstatements of the statute removed. (1) The body said the statement must describe 'the condition of the facilities in and about the premises to be rented **and of any furnishings or appliances you supply**'. § 47-16-07.2 says 'the condition of the facilities in and about the premises to be rented' and nothing about furnishings or appliances. Reasonable as a gloss on 'facilities', but it was stated as statutory text in a REQUIRED row. (2) The body said '**each of you keeps a copy**'. The statute imposes no copy-keeping or copy-delivery duty at all — that is practice, and it is now phrased as advice in the closing sentence rather than as a requirement. Added instead: what the statute genuinely does not supply (no form, no itemisation standard, no penalty) and where the consequence of omission actually lands. WHY IT MATTERS: this is the citation-described-wrongly failure mode (instruction 11(b)) — the citation is correct and the screen cannot see the error. Found by mapping a real North Dakota lease's condition/inventory provision against this row (gap-discovery source 2). Corroborated independently by a research pass on 2026-09-27: 'a document-delivery/signature duty tied to lease inception ... no penalty for omission is specified (its consequence is evidentiary).'

title: You Must Give the Tenant a Signed Copy Within Seven Days
bodyText: If there is a written rental agreement, you must give the tenant a copy signed by both you and the tenant no later than the seventh day after the tenant signs. An electronic copy is sufficient unless the tenant asks for a paper copy, in which case you must provide one on paper. The agreement must also state the name and address of the landlord or the landlord's authorized agent.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-801(1), (2) (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.) TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'You Must Give the Tenant a Signed Copy Within Seven Days (Colorado)' -> 'You Must Give the Tenant a Signed Copy Within Seven Days' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO).

title: No Penalty Clause Tied to an Eviction
bodyText: A Colorado written rental agreement must not include a clause that assigns a penalty to a party stemming from an eviction notice or an eviction action resulting from a violation of the rental agreement. Any provision included in violation of this rule is void and unenforceable. This is separate from the rent and damages a court may award in an eviction proceeding - what is prohibited is a lease term imposing its own penalty because a notice was served or an action was filed.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3)(a)(I), (3)(b) (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.) TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'No Penalty Clause Tied to an Eviction (Colorado)' -> 'No Penalty Clause Tied to an Eviction' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO).

title: Mobile-Home-Park Leases Are Exempt From the Walkthrough and Carpet/Paint Rules
bodyText: If the property is a mobile-home-park rental agreement, two specific security-deposit rules do not apply: the move-out walkthrough right, and the special carpet/paint deduction rules (the ten-year carpet lookback and the minimum-necessary, damaged-area-only repaint rule). Ordinary security-deposit rules still apply to a mobile-home-park agreement - only these two specific rules are carved out.
notes: Surfaced 2026-09-13 (Claude Browser follow-up) while correcting edu-carpet-damage-co's citation - confirmed via primary text of C.R.S. 38-12-103(12) alongside that correction. Not linked to any mobile-home-specific product logic since mobile-home-park leases aren't deeply modeled in this app yet; flag for any future mobile-home-lot handling.

title: Service-Animal Misrepresentation Penalty Is Conviction-Gated
bodyText: North Dakota makes it an infraction to knowingly claim a pet is a service or assistance animal, or to knowingly submit fraudulent supporting documentation, in order to obtain a reasonable accommodation (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.6(1)). The penalty that actually matters practically is separate and conditional: only where the tenant pleads guilty to, or is convicted of, that infraction may the landlord evict the tenant and recover a damage fee of up to $1,000 (§ 47-16-07.6(2)) -- a landlord cannot simply assess this fee based on their own belief that a claim is fraudulent; a criminal disposition has to happen first. Read narrowly, subsection (2)'s fee is tied to a tenant who "provides fraudulent disability documentation" specifically, which is narrower than subsection (1)'s two grounds (a false claim OR fraudulent documentation) -- on the statute's own words, the $1,000 fee may not be available for a bare false claim that isn't accompanied by fraudulent paperwork. No North Dakota authority resolves that gap; treat it as an open drafting question rather than a settled one.
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.6(1)-(2), confirmed via Claude Browser primary-source verification 2026-09-17, closing out a PARTIAL item from this project's ND citation-extraction pass (see assistance-animal-accommodation-nd, which intentionally left this penalty unstated as a specific number pending verification). Genuinely new to the library -- no prior ND row recorded these mechanics. Also resolves the same session's other open question: a 2025 bill, SB 2222, was believed to have amended §§ 47-16-07.5/-07.6 via corroborating secondary sources -- WRONG. SB 2222 failed on second reading in the ND Senate, 2025-02-17 (yeas 1, nays 44), and never amended anything; both sections are unchanged from what assistance-animal-accommodation-nd already cites.

title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant will provide Landlord with Tenant's forwarding address in writing. If Tenant does not, Tenant remains entitled to the return of any balance due, but is not entitled to damages or attorneys' fees for Landlord's failure to comply with the rules for returning the Security Deposit.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.16(B), read from primary text 2026-09-18. Two triggers, conjunctive - termination AND delivery of possession - unlike MN/SD which key the clock to receipt of the tenant's address. The final sentence states the statute's own landlord protection: 5321.16(B) provides that a tenant who fails to furnish a forwarding address in writing forfeits (C) damages and attorneys' fees, while keeping the deposit itself. 5321.16(C) remedy = the money due PLUS damages equal to the amount wrongfully withheld PLUS reasonable attorneys' fees - nets to double, but the statute never says 'double' and provides no treble damages. TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Return of Security Deposit (Ohio)' -> 'Return of Security Deposit' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO). | OH: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): kept the tenant's forwarding-address duty and its landlord-favorable consequence; the restated 30-day return and itemization duty moved to edu-security-deposit-return-oh.

title: Holdover
bodyText: If Tenant does not vacate the property by the end of the Term, Landlord may pursue any remedy allowed by applicable law to recover possession, and may join in that action a claim for Rent and other amounts due under this Lease. For each day Tenant remains in possession after the end of the Term, Tenant will pay holdover rent at the daily rate of {{holdover_daily_rate}}, which the parties agree is a reasonable estimate of Landlord's loss and not a penalty.
notes: OH: parent clause withheld - it promises 'holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law', and OHIO HAS NO HOLDOVER DAMAGES FORMULA AT ALL. Confirmed absent on full-chapter primary reads of both R.C. ch. 5321 and ch. 1923 (2026-09-18). 1923.02(A)(1) makes holding over a ground for possession; 1923.081 permits joining rent and damages claims 'under a rental agreement'. Holdover damages in Ohio are therefore PURELY CONTRACTUAL, so the rate must be stated or the clause promises nothing - same failure mode as SD (see holdover-sd), different cause. 5321.14 unconscionability is the only ceiling; set {{holdover_daily_rate}} defensibly. CAUTION: no 'acceptance does not create a new tenancy' sentence is included, because accepting rent for a FUTURE period after a 1923.04 notice waives the notice as a matter of law regardless of lease language (King v. Dolton, 2003-Ohio-2423; N. Face Props. v. Lin, 2013-Ohio-2281) - a contract term cannot preserve a jurisdictional notice. TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Holdover (Ohio)' -> 'Holdover' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO).

title: Owner and Agent Identity
bodyText: The name and address of the owner of the property, and of any person authorized to manage the property or to act as the owner's agent, are stated in this Lease. Landlord will notify Tenant in writing of any change to that information.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.18 - every WRITTEN rental agreement shall contain the name and address of the owner and of the owner's agent. For an oral tenancy the same information must be given in writing at commencement. FOURTH sanction architecture in this library: Ohio does not make the non-discloser an implied agent (KS), or the landlord (NE), or impose a maintenance bar (MN) - under 5321.18(C) failure WAIVES the landlord's right to receive the tenant's 5321.07 and 5321.08 notices, so the tenant may proceed to rent escrow without giving the landlord the 30-day cure window. Entity-specific rules about principal place of business in the county were read at chapter level; verify section-open before relying on them in the builder's field validation. TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Owner and Agent Identity (Ohio)' -> 'Owner and Agent Identity' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO).

title: Flag Display
bodyText: Nothing in this Lease restricts Tenant's right to display the flag of the United States, the National League of Families POW/MIA flag, the flag of the State of Ohio, or a service flag approved by the United States Secretary of Defense, where the flag is displayed in accordance with applicable federal, state, or local law and the applicable patriotic customs. Before installing a flag pole, or a bracket to be permanently affixed to the unit, for display of the flag of the United States or the POW/MIA flag, Tenant will contact Landlord with reasonable notice to discuss placement and size. Tenant remains obligated to return the property at the end of the Term in the same condition as when Tenant took possession.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.131, verified section-open 2026-09-18 (was UNVERIFIED on a chapter-level read). NEW TOPIC - no other state in this library has a flag-display row. (A) bars any rental-agreement restriction on the four flags. SCOPE CORRECTION from the first draft: the (B) notice-and-consultation duty applies ONLY to a flag POLE or a permanently affixed BRACKET, and only for the US and POW/MIA flags - it does not attach to the state flag or service flag limbs, and not to ordinary display. (B)(1)(a) requires discussion of local zoning and underground utility service requests (OUPS); (B)(1)(e) requires flag and pole size consistent with the size and character of the building. (C) SHIELDS THE LANDLORD: a landlord who does not receive the (B) notifications is not liable for damages, fines or costs arising from the tenant's placement of the pole or bracket. (D) any violating provision is unconscionable under 5321.14 and the violation is against public policy and unenforceable. (E) expressly preserves a lease covenant to return the premises in their original condition - carried into the clause text. LEGAL WATCH: SB 202 of the 136th GA would amend 5321.131 (and 4781.40); PASSED THE SENATE, NOT ENACTED as of 2026-09-18 - do not cite it, monitor it. TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Flag Display (Ohio)' -> 'Flag Display' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO). | OH: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-flag-display-oh). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Three-or-Fewer-Units Notice
bodyText: Landlord is a party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units, and Landlord gives Tenant notice of that fact. Tenant's remedies under Ohio Revised Code section 5321.07 do not apply to Landlord.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.07(C). TWO-LIMB CONJUNCTIVE exemption - the landlord must both (a) be party to agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units and (b) GIVE WRITTEN NOTICE OF THAT FACT. The disclosure is a condition precedent, so the exemption simply fails without this clause. INCLUDE ONLY where limb (a) is actually true; it is a factual representation. Ohio has FOUR different portfolio thresholds across four provisions - none (ch. 4112 fair housing), three or fewer (5321.07(C)), fewer than four (1923.062(C) active-duty stay), four or more (5321.04(A)(5) waste receptacles) - so never reuse a size-keyed clause across provisions. 5321.07(D) separately excludes student tenants. TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Three-or-Fewer-Units Notice (Ohio)' -> 'Three-or-Fewer-Units Notice' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO).

title: Occupancy by a Registered Offender
bodyText: If the property is located within one thousand feet of any school premises, preschool or child care center premises, children's crisis care facility premises, or residential infant care center premises, Tenant will not allow any person to occupy the property if both of the following apply to that person: the person's name appears on the state registry of sex offenders and child-victim offenders, and the registry indicates the person was convicted of or pleaded guilty to a sexually oriented offense that is not registration-exempt, or to a child-victim oriented offense, and was not sentenced to a serious youthful offender dispositional sentence. If Tenant allows occupancy in violation of this Section, Landlord may terminate this Lease as to Tenant and all other occupants.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.051(A)(1),(A)(2),(B), verified section-open 2026-09-18 (was UNVERIFIED on a chapter-level read). CONJUNCTIVE two-part test - registry listing AND a qualifying offence - both limbs required; a bare registry hit is not enough. Registry is the one maintained under R.C. 2950.13. Termination under (A)(2) reaches THE TENANT AND ALL OTHER OCCUPANTS, and is also triggered where a person establishes residence in violation of R.C. 2950.031. (B) SHIELDS THE LANDLORD: a landlord authorised to terminate who chooses NOT to is not liable in tort or other civil action for injury, death or loss allegedly resulting from that decision - the shield is at 5321.051(B) (an earlier draft mis-attributed it to 1923.02(C)(2)). The premises list has broadened over time: the 2006 text reached only school premises. RESOLVED 2026-09-18 - THE INCONSISTENCY IS REAL: 1923.02(A)(14) and (A)(15) both reach premises within 1,000 feet of 'school premises, PRESCHOOL OR CHILD CARE CENTER premises, children's crisis care facility premises, or residential infant care center premises', but 1923.02(C)(1) lists only 'school premises, children's crisis care facility premises, or residential infant care center premises' - preschool and child care are OMITTED. Confirmed identical across codes.ohio.gov, Justia (2025), FindLaw and LawServer. PRACTICAL GUIDANCE: rely on 5321.051, which does include preschool and child care premises, for both the tenant duty and the termination right; treat the 1923.02(C)(1) route as narrower and do not assume it covers a preschool-proximity case. TITLE NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Occupancy by a Registered Offender (Ohio)' -> 'Occupancy by a Registered Offender' (state name in the title was a per-session convention used only by SD, OH, ND and CO).

title: Ohio Duty-Shifting Runs One Direction Only
bodyText: You can agree to take on your tenant's obligations. Your tenant cannot agree to take on yours. R.C. 5321.13(A) makes the whole of Chapter 5321 non-waivable except through division (F), and (F) permits only one move: the landlord assuming the tenant's 5321.05 duties. There is no route in the other direction. So a clause making the tenant responsible for a duty Chapter 5321 assigns to you is void, however it is worded and whatever the tenant agreed to. R.C. 5321.13(E) closes the obvious workaround by barring any agreement that lets you receive rent free of the obligation to comply with 5321.04.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.13(A),(E),(F). INVERSE of the KS/ND/NE structured-delegation architecture, where duty-shifting runs toward the tenant under conditions. Do not import those states' delegation clauses into Ohio. Answers Core Obligations row 'is that duty waivable' for OH: no, and uniquely one-directional.

title: Drug Activity Is a Duty to Act, Not an Option - And Ignoring It Is a Crime
bodyText: In most situations Ohio leaves eviction to your discretion. Drug activity is the exception. Under R.C. 5321.04(A)(9), once you have actual knowledge of - or reasonable cause to believe - that the tenant, a household member, or a guest has used, sold, or manufactured a controlled substance on the premises, you SHALL give the three-day termination notice under 5321.17(C) and SHALL promptly bring an eviction action. This is framed as a landlord obligation, not a landlord right, and the matching eviction ground sits at 1923.02(A)(6). Serving the 5321.17(C) notice also satisfies the ordinary three-day notice requirement under 1923.04(B), so no second notice is needed. R.C. 1923.051 puts this track on an accelerated schedule. Note what you do NOT need: the notice may be given whether or not the tenant or other person has been charged with, has pleaded guilty to, or has been convicted of anything. Reasonable cause to believe is the trigger, and once you have it the statute says you SHALL act. There is a second, sharper reason to act. Under R.C. 2925.13 an owner, lessee, occupant, or person having custody, control, or supervision of premises who KNOWINGLY PERMITS them to be used for the commission of a felony drug abuse offence commits permitting drug abuse - a first-degree misdemeanour, and a fifth-degree felony where the underlying offence is trafficking or manufacturing, or where you had actual knowledge that Schedule I or II manufacturing chemicals were involved. So the same facts that trigger your Chapter 5321 duty can also expose you personally to criminal charges if you sit on them. Watch the asymmetry in the two standards. Chapter 5321 turns on 'reasonable cause to believe', which is a lower bar and fires earlier; R.C. 2925.13 turns on 'knowingly permits', which requires more. That means there is a window where you must act civilly but are not yet criminally exposed - and acting in that window is what keeps you out of the second statute.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.04(A)(9); 5321.17(C); 1923.02(A)(6); 1923.04(B); 1923.051; 2925.13. CHANGED 2026-09-27 BY THE GAP-DISCOVERY BACKFILL (source 4, outside-title search): added the R.C. 2925.13 criminal exposure and the knowledge-standard asymmetry. WHY: the original row stated the civil duty and stopped there, which understates the stake - a landlord reading it would learn eviction is mandatory but not that inaction is separately chargeable. 2925.13 sits in Title 29 (CRIMES), outside the landlord-tenant title, which is exactly the class of provision source 4 exists to catch. READ SECTION-OPEN 2026-09-27: current version effective 2025-04-09, H.B. 29 (135th G.A.); 'premises or real estate, including vacant land'; (A) knowingly permit use for felony drug abuse offence; penalties at (C). UNCHANGED AND STILL VERIFIED FROM 2026-09-18: 5321.05(A)(9) is the tenant duty; 5321.05(A)(2) directs that the landlord 'promptly shall give' the 5321.17(C) notice; 5321.17(C) states the tenancy terminates three days after the notice is given and that it may be given regardless of charge, plea or conviction; if the tenant does not vacate within three days the landlord 'promptly shall comply with' 5321.04(A)(9). The accelerated service and trial deadlines in 1923.051 remain chapter-level - verify section-open before stating specific day counts to a landlord. The DUTY framing remains the finding: no other state in this library makes eviction mandatory. The asymmetry sentence is an interpretive reading of the two statutory standards side by side, not a quotation from either and not a case holding - no Ohio case applying 2925.13 to a landlord who failed the 5321.04(A)(9) duty was searched. Flagged, not resolved. CROSS-REFERENCE: edu-no-meth-disclosure-oh carries the same statute from the disclosure angle.

title: Never Name a Minor on an Ohio Eviction Complaint
bodyText: If you list a minor tenant as a defendant on an eviction complaint alongside a parent or adult guardian, the court SHALL dismiss the action without prejudice and SHALL order you to pay the minor tenant's reasonable attorneys' fees. Naming every occupant is ordinary practice in most states; in Ohio it costs you the filing and the other side's legal bill. A 'minor tenant' is a tenant under eighteen who is not emancipated. Note that this fee award is statutory, so Ohio's general ban on attorney-fee agreements does not protect you from it.
notes: OH: R.C. 1923.05(B),(C) with the 'minor tenant' definition at 1923.01(C)(15). ADDED BY SB 237 (135th GA), effective 2025-04-09 - recent, and unlikely to be reflected in older Ohio landlord guidance. Same act added the two-year limitations period for FED actions at 1923.01(B). If Steinoak ever generates eviction filings or occupant lists, this is a hard validation rule, not an education note.

title: Ohio Prescribes the Words of Your Notice
bodyText: Most states tell you how long to wait. Ohio also tells you what to say. Every notice you give to recover residential premises must contain, printed or written in a conspicuous manner, the following statement verbatim: "You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance." Serve it at least three days before you file, by certified mail return receipt requested, by personal delivery, or by leaving it at the tenant's usual place of abode or at the premises. A notice missing this exact language will not support the action.
notes: OH: R.C. 1923.04(A). VERBATIM TEXT ADDED 2026-09-19, replacing the earlier paraphrase: confirmed via two independent official Ohio state sources (codes.ohio.gov and legislature.ohio.gov), fetched separately and returning byte-identical quoted language both times: "You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance." This is a step below this project's usual primary-text-read standard (a fetch-and-summarize tool, not a direct read of the codified text) -- reasonably reliable given two independent official sources agreed exactly, but re-verify directly against the primary text before this exact wording is ever baked into a real notice-generator feature that ships to users, not just an internal reference row. Local practice glosses 'three or more days' variously as three BUSINESS days excluding the posting date, or a full 72 hours excluding weekends and holidays; the statute itself says only 'three or more days'. R.C. 1923.06(B) prescribes a second script for the summons, but that one is court-issued. | 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.23 rule 79 retro): BASIS UPGRADED AND THE ROW'S OWN OPEN FLAG IS CLOSED. R.C. 1923.04(A) was read section-open on codes.ohio.gov in the built-in browser on 2026-10-02 (effective 2007-10-18, H.B. 56, 127th G.A.). The quoted notice language matches the codified text verbatim, and the surrounding requirements were read with it: the language must be 'printed or written in a conspicuous manner'; the notice must be given three or more days before the action begins; service is by certified mail return receipt requested, by handing a written copy to the defendant in person, or by leaving it at the defendant's usual place of abode or at the premises; and under (B) service of the R.C. 5321.17(C) notice constitutes compliance. The row's note asking for 'one more direct read before this exact wording is ever used in a real notice-generator feature' is satisfied. The prescribed wording is also now carried in edu-statutory-forms-oh as Ohio's answer to the rule 27 'statutory-forms' topic.

title: Electing Out of the Civil Rights Commission Can Cost You More
bodyText: If the Ohio Civil Rights Commission issues a housing discrimination complaint against you, you - not just the complainant - may elect to move the matter into common pleas court. Think before you do. In the administrative track the commission MAY award damages and fees, and the civil penalty is capped ($10,000, rising to $25,000 with one prior violation in five years and $50,000 with two or more in seven). In court, R.C. 4112.055(D) says the court SHALL award actual damages, reasonable attorneys' fees, court costs, expert witness fees and other litigation expenses, and MAY add punitive damages - with no cap and a right to a jury. Electing out trades a capped penalty for uncapped exposure. The election must be mailed certified, return receipt requested, within thirty days of the notice.
notes: OH: R.C. 4112.055(A)(2),(D) and 4112.05(B)(5),(G)(1)(b); OAC 4112-3-05(C)(2). Current 4112.055 effective 2025-09-30, amended by HB 96 (136th GA) - the biennial BUDGET bill, which is how Ohio has repeatedly moved this body of law. Filing windows: one year for a commission charge (4112.05(B)(1)) AND one year for a private civil action (4112.055(A)(1)); the two-year figure in circulation is the EMPLOYMENT window at 4112.051 and does not apply to housing.

title: Ohio's Alarm Duty Comes From Code - Except in a High-Rise
bodyText: For an ordinary Ohio rental there is no smoke-alarm or carbon-monoxide-alarm statute telling you what to install. The duty reaches you indirectly: R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) requires you to comply with the building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety, and R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) preserves local codes from Chapter 5321's preemption - so the answer for any given property is in the applicable building and fire code and the local ordinance, not in the landlord-tenant chapter. There is one direct statute, and it is narrow. R.C. 3781.104 requires an automatic smoke detection system in an existing apartment or condominium building over seventy-five feet tall that lacked one: a board-approved detector in each dwelling unit just outside every sleeping room, with alarms clearly audible in all bedrooms with the doors closed, plus detector spacing rules for the parts of the building outside the units. For that statute an apartment building is one where at least seventy-five per cent of the units are residential and let on other than a transient basis, which excludes a hotel but expressly includes a college or university dormitory. Below seventy-five feet, R.C. 3781.104 does not apply and you are back to the codes.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.04(A)(1); 5321.19(B)(1); 3781.104. CHANGED 2026-10-02 BY THE SOP 1.23 RULE 79 RETRO, AND THIS IS THE RETRO'S MAIN CORRECTION. The row previously said flatly that 'there is no direct Ohio smoke- or carbon-monoxide-alarm statute for rentals' and carried citation_status CONFIRMED_ABSENT on a basis of 'a full-chapter read of ch. 5321 plus secondary-source agreement for the rest of the Code'. That is exactly the basis rule 79 exists to distrust, and the code-wide search it requires found what secondary agreement had missed: R.C. 3781.104, a DIRECT statute naming apartment buildings, in Title 37 ch. 3781 (Building Standards) outside both ch. 5321 and the fire code. R.C. 3781.104 READ SECTION-OPEN 2026-10-02; effective 1981-11-15, H.B. 694, 114th G.A., never amended. THE CONCLUSION SURVIVES, THE TEXT AND THE BASIS DID NOT: 3781.104 reaches only buildings 'that exceed seventy-five feet in height', so for ordinary rentals the row's original answer was right. But a landlord with a high-rise had a direct statutory duty the row denied existed. Status moves from a flat confirmed absence to present-for-high-rises / absent-otherwise. Instrument: the official Ohio Revised Code keyword search at codes.ohio.gov, driven in the built-in browser with Taylor's approval 2026-10-02 (quoted phrases; control 'zqxvbnmwt' 0 hits, 'radon' 23 hits, so validated both ways). Terms run: 'smoke detector' (1 hit, 3781.104 - the find), 'smoke alarm' (0), 'carbon monoxide' (7 hits: 5.2321 powerboat safety month, 3701.82 burners and heaters, 959.06 destruction of domestic animals, 1561.25 mine rescue stations, 3704.011 and 3704.141 emissions, 3745.11 fees - none residential-rental, so the CO limb IS confirmed absent code-wide). THE 75-FOOT RULE IS A SIZE THRESHOLD OUTSIDE ch. 5321, measured by HEIGHT rather than unit count - a different axis from the five portfolio tests in edu-portfolio-thresholds-oh, which is deliberately not edited again here (it was changed on 2026-09-27 and rule 1 bars re-scrubbing); the cross-reference is recorded in the log instead. 3781.104's 'apartment building' definition INCLUDES a college or university dormitory, which pairs with R.C. 5321.01(C) excluding institutional occupancy from 'residential premises' and with R.C. 5321.031 on student tenants - a dormitory can be outside ch. 5321 and inside 3781.104 at once. TRAP RETAINED FROM 2026-09-18: OAC 3701-33-13 looks on point but is ch. 3701-33 AGRICULTURAL LABOR CAMPS under R.C. 3733.42, units excluded from ch. 5321 by 5321.01(C)(7). STILL DIFFERENT ARCHITECTURE from NE (Neb. Rev. Stat. 81-5,144) and ND (N.D.C.C. 23-13-15), which impose direct duties on all rentals - do not adapt those rows to Ohio. NOT READ: the Ohio Building Code and Fire Code themselves (OAC 4101 and 1301:7-7), and the board of building standards rules 3781.104(C) directs. Flagged - this row points at them rather than stating their content.

title: Ohio Voids Attorney-Fee Clauses Both Ways
bodyText: A prevailing-party or fee-shifting clause does nothing for you in Ohio. R.C. 5321.13(C) provides that no agreement to pay the landlord's OR the tenant's attorney's fees shall be recognised in any residential rental agreement, or in any other agreement between a landlord and tenant. Making the clause mutual does not rescue it - mutuality is the fix in some states, and it is irrelevant here. Hedging it with 'to the extent permitted by applicable law' does not rescue it either; the statute says such an agreement is not recognised, so the sentence is inoperative at best and misleading to a tenant at worst. Fees are still available to either side where a STATUTE awards them - 5321.15(C), 5321.04(B), 5321.16(C) and 4112.055(D) all do - because those are statutory awards, not agreements.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.13(C). BROADER than K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(3) and Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1415(1)(c) because of the final limb reaching any OTHER agreement between landlord and tenant, not just the lease. Drives the decision to withhold the generic default-by-tenant from OH and use default-by-tenant-ks-ne instead.

title: Two Cure Windows Before a Bounced Payment Costs Anything
bodyText: Ohio gives you no statutory returned-check fee cap - the $30-or-10% figure you will find quoted in Ohio lease templates is R.C. 1319.16, which caps what a COLLECTION AGENCY may charge, and 1319.12(A)(2) excludes a landlord collecting its own account. Your fee rides on the lease. As for going after the tenant: recovery under R.C. 2307.61 requires a THEFT OFFENCE, which means purpose to defraud plus knowledge - insufficient funds alone is not one. On top of that the tenant has two cure windows you cannot contract away: paying within ten days of notice of dishonour defeats the presumption of knowledge (2913.11(C)(2)), and paying within thirty days of your written demand bars the civil action outright (2307.61(D)). And 2307.61(B) cuts back at you - if you pursue costs and fees and the tenant wins, you pay the tenant's fees and defence costs.
notes: OH: R.C. 1319.16; 1319.12(A)(2); 2913.11(B),(C)(2); 2307.61(A),(B),(C),(D),(H)(2)(b). 2307.61(H)(2)(b) includes the bank's charges in the 'value' that gets trebled. 2307.61(C) prescribes required notice content for the written demand - re-read section-open before building a demand-letter generator. 2913.11(A)(1)(b) defines 'check' to include ACH and card transactions, so a failed electronic rent payment is inside this framework. 2913.11 measures from 'the time of issue OR THE STATED DATE, whichever is later' - Ohio accommodates postdated checks rather than penalising them, the inverse of the ND-derived checklist row.

title: Taking Rent After Your Notice Can Void It
bodyText: The line is about WHICH PERIOD the money covers. Accepting rent for obligations already incurred at the time of your three-day notice does not waive it. Accepting rent for a FUTURE period after serving the notice waives the notice as a matter of law, and you cannot proceed on it - you start over. Holding the payment is not a safe middle ground: a landlord who sits on checks without telling the tenant they are not being accepted has accepted them. If you do not want the money, say so in writing and return it. Two further cautions: a pattern of quietly accepting late or partial rent can waive the due date in your lease, and accepting the current month's rent BEFORE you serve the notice can jeopardise the action too. A 'no waiver' clause in your lease will not save you here, because the three-day notice is jurisdictional and parties cannot confer jurisdiction by contract.
notes: OH: King v. Dolton, 9th Dist. No. 02CA0041, 2003-Ohio-2423, para 12; Bristol Court v. Jones, 4th Dist. 1994; N. Face Properties v. Lin, 2013-Ohio-2281 (12th Dist.) (holding checks silently then cashing = acceptance), citing Associated Estates v. Bartell, 24 Ohio App.3d 6; OZ Property Mgt. v. Williams, 2025-Ohio-318 (12th Dist.) (pre-notice acceptance of current month); Premiere Mgt. v. Nutt, 2010-Ohio-1255 (3d Dist.). CASE LAW, not statute (Instructions item 16). 2d, 3d, 4th, 9th and 12th Districts agree - statewide consensus, not district variation. Holdings confirmed as quoted verbatim in published opinions; individual opinions not read end to end.

title: Selling the Property Does Not Get You Off the Deposit
bodyText: Ohio has no statute transferring deposit liability to a buyer, and no safe harbour for doing it properly - unlike states where handing the deposit over plus notifying the tenant relieves you. Ohio treats a security deposit as a personal obligation in the nature of a PLEDGE between you and your tenant. The liability to return it does not run with the property. It stays with you unless the buyer either assumes the obligation or receives a credit on the purchase price for the deposits. So the thing that protects you is not moving the money - it is what the purchase and sale agreement says. Get the deposits itemised in the PSA and on the rent roll, name them, and confirm assumption or a price credit in writing. Pet and other deposits count, and get missed.
notes: OH: Castlebrook, Ltd. v. Dayton Properties Ltd. Partnership, 78 Ohio App.3d 340, 348 (2d Dist. 1992), citing Tuteur v. P. & F. Enterprises, Inc., 21 Ohio App.2d 122, 133 (8th Dist. 1970); applied in Grisham v. Meadow Ridge Cincinnati Assocs. (12th Dist.), which turned on whether a PET deposit fell inside the PSA's 'Tenant Deposit' definition and appeared on the rent roll. CASE LAW, not statute (Instructions item 16). Tuteur adopted the New Jersey pledge rule because no Ohio law existed in 1970. PRODUCT NOTE: this belongs in the ownership-transfer workflow, not only the lease. Secondary sources conflict and at least one asserts the successor is automatically liable - the statutory silence does not support that. | 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.23 rule 79 retro): BASIS STATED HONESTLY. Rule 79's method is to re-read the cited SECTION, and this row cites no section - it rests on three appellate opinions (Castlebrook, Tuteur, Grisham). NONE OF THE THREE OPINIONS HAS BEEN READ IN FULL; the holdings are taken from quoted passages, which is a weaker basis than this project's standard and is flagged as unread authority per rule 76. What WAS confirmed this pass is the statutory half: an official code-wide search found no Ohio provision transferring security-deposit liability on a sale and no safe harbour for doing it properly. Instrument: the official Ohio Revised Code keyword search at codes.ohio.gov, driven in the built-in browser with Taylor's approval 2026-10-02 (quoted phrases; control 'zqxvbnmwt' 0 hits, 'radon' 23 hits, so validated both ways). So the row's statement that Ohio has no statute is now primary-verified; its statement of what the common law requires is not. A landlord relying on the pledge analysis to get out of deposit liability should take advice.

title: Ohio Gives You No Way to Deal With Left-Behind Belongings
bodyText: If a tenant leaves possessions behind, Ohio hands you nothing. There is no notice-and-disposal procedure for an ordinary residential tenancy - the detailed machinery of notice, valuation affidavit, county auditor sign-off and sale in R.C. 1923.12 to 1923.14 applies only to manufactured home parks. Meanwhile R.C. 5321.15(B) forbids you from seizing a tenant's furnishings or possessions for rent except under a court order, and 5321.15(C) exposes you to actual damages plus reasonable attorneys' fees if you do. The practical consequence is that there is no statutory step you can follow that makes disposal safe, so get a court order, or get the property out through the writ process rather than on your own initiative.
notes: OH: confirmed absent on FULL-CHAPTER primary reads of both R.C. ch. 5321 and ch. 1923 (2026-09-18). 5321.15(B),(C). 1923.12-.14 are park-only. There is also no post-writ duty regarding a tenant's PET left at the property - a gap worth noting separately. A commercial form vendor states 'No statute' for Ohio on this; that happens to be right, but it was confirmed here from the chapters rather than adopted from the vendor. | 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.23 rule 79 retro): BASIS CLARIFIED, no change to the conclusion. The row's notes mentioned a commercial form vendor stating 'No statute', which made it look like a secondary-source row on a keyword screen. It is not: the absence was established by full primary reads of ch. 5321 and ch. 1923 on 2026-09-18, and the vendor is corroboration only. Recorded here explicitly so the next rule 79 screen does not re-flag it. The post-writ PET gap the row notes is confirmed again by the 2026-09-18 eviction-duty screen (log rows 103 and 104, both ABS-full x2) and remains Ohio's most notable eviction-duty absence.

title: Ohio Has Five Different Small-Landlord Thresholds
bodyText: There is no general 'small landlord' concept in Ohio law. Five separate provisions use five different portfolio tests, so you have to check the one attached to the duty in front of you. Fair housing under Chapter 4112 has NO small landlord exemption at all - every landlord is covered regardless of size. The rent-escrow remedy at R.C. 5321.07(C) does not reach a landlord party to agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units WHO GIVES WRITTEN NOTICE OF THAT FACT. The active-duty stay at R.C. 1923.062(C) does not apply to a landlord operating fewer than four residential premises. The waste receptacle duty at R.C. 5321.04(A)(5) applies only where you are party to agreements covering four or more dwelling units in the same structure. And the nuisance receivership scheme at R.C. 3767.41 - under which a court can put a receiver in possession of your building, let the receiver collect the rents, and make the receiver's spending a first lien ahead of your mortgage - reaches every residential property EXCEPT one that is owner-occupied and contains three or fewer units. Read those five tests carefully: they are not variations on one rule. One counts dwelling units, one counts premises, one counts units in the same structure, one adds a written-notice condition you can fail, one turns on whether you live there yourself, and one does not exist. Never reuse a size-keyed clause across provisions.
notes: OH: R.C. 4112.024 (exemption list contains no portfolio test; 4112.01(A)(1) 'person' sweeps in any owner, lessor, manager or agent); 5321.07(C); 1923.062(C); 5321.04(A)(5); 3767.41. CHANGED 2026-09-27 BY THE GAP-DISCOVERY BACKFILL (source 4, outside-title search): added R.C. 3767.41's owner-occupied-three-or-fewer-units carve-out as the FIFTH threshold and retitled from 'Four' to 'Five'. WHY: the row's whole point is that a landlord must not carry one size test across provisions, so a missing fifth test is a defect in the row's own thesis, not a footnote. 3767.41 sits in Title 37 (HEALTH - SAFETY - MORALS), outside the landlord-tenant title, which is why the 2026-09-18 pass did not see it. READ SECTION-OPEN 2026-09-27. Also added a sentence naming what each test actually counts, because the four original tests count four different things and the original body did not say so. UNCHANGED AND STILL VERIFIED FROM 2026-09-18: CONTRAST WITH KANSAS, which exempts the small landlord from fair housing entirely (K.S.A. 44-1018(b)) - Ohio does not. Caveat still standing: 4112.01 and 4112.024 were read in full, the rest of ch. 4112 was not, so an exemption elsewhere in the chapter has not been ruled out. CROSS-REFERENCE: edu-nuisance-receivership-oh in this same delta carries 3767.41 as its own row, from the receivership-exposure angle rather than the threshold angle.

title: Most Ohio Limits You Expect Do Not Exist
bodyText: Ohio is a thin-statute state on money terms. There is no security deposit cap, no late fee cap, no returned check fee cap that binds a landlord, no holdover damages formula, and no required mold, radon, bed bug, meth, asbestos or flood disclosure. Mandated lease content is almost as thin: R.C. 5321.18 requires every written rental agreement to contain the name and address of the owner and of the owner's agent, and federal law requires the lead paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing. There is one more, and it applies only if you are an institution: R.C. 5321.031 requires a college or university letting to a student tenant to specify in the written agreement the conditions under which it may be terminated and the institution's notice and hearing procedures. That freedom is real but it is not unlimited: R.C. 5321.14 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable clause or limit its application, and it is the only ceiling on every one of these terms. Set numbers you could defend to a judge, because nothing else will do it for you.
notes: OH: absences confirmed on a full-chapter read of ch. 5321 plus secondary agreement across the Code; 5321.16 has no cap (the $50-or-one-month figure is the INTEREST THRESHOLD, widely misreported as a cap); 5321.18; 5321.14. R.C. 5302.30 is a SALES disclosure form and does not apply to rentals - the likeliest trap on an 'Ohio disclosure' search. Pending but NOT enacted: HB 841 (introduced 2026-04-30) would create a mold/lead/radon/CO awareness program; it would not create a disclosure duty even if passed. | CHANGED 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.23 rules 42 and 79 retro). TWO FIXES. (1) The row said 'Your only mandated lease disclosure is the owner and agent identity under R.C. 5321.18, plus the federal lead paint requirement'. R.C. 5321.031, READ SECTION-OPEN 2026-10-02, is a second mandated lease-content provision: 'The written rental agreement must specify the conditions under which the rental agreement may be terminated and specify the college's or university's notice and hearing procedures.' Narrow - it binds only a college or university landlord - but the row stated the 'only' without the qualifier. Found by the rule 41 screen, not by a disclosure search, which is why four prior passes missed it. This also corrects the named-topic checklist's CORE OBLIGATIONS row 130 ('Required state disclosures (full list) | One | 5321.18 ... Nothing else'). (2) BASIS UPGRADED from 'a full-chapter read of ch. 5321 plus secondary agreement across the Code' - the rule 79 basis - to a code-wide official search. Instrument: the official Ohio Revised Code keyword search at codes.ohio.gov, driven in the built-in browser with Taylor's approval 2026-10-02 (quoted phrases; control 'zqxvbnmwt' 0 hits, 'radon' 23 hits, so validated both ways). Terms run this pass: 'late fee' (21 hits; the residential-rental count is zero - 5322.05 is self-service storage, 1345.031 is the CSPA, which R.C. 1345.01(A) does not extend to a lease of real property), 'flood plain' (10 hits, none in ch. 5321, 5301 or 5302), 'capital letters', 'point type', 'boldface', 'conspicuous'. The mold, radon, bed bug and meth limbs were searched on 2026-09-27 and each has its own row. ASBESTOS NOT SEARCHED THIS PASS and not searched on 2026-09-27 either - that limb of the sentence still rests on the 2026-09-18 chapter read plus secondary agreement. Flagged rather than silently carried.

title: Ohio Sets No Rent-Increase Notice Period
bodyText: Chapter 5321 contains no rent-increase notice provision at all. The '30 days' you will see quoted everywhere is R.C. 5321.17(B), which is the notice required to TERMINATE a month-to-month tenancy - a different thing. For a periodic tenancy the practical route to a higher rent is to terminate on the statutory notice and offer new terms. For a fixed-term written lease, the rent is whatever the lease says for the term, and a mid-term increase needs the tenant's agreement. If you want a defined mid-term or renewal increase mechanic, it has to be in the lease, because the statute will not supply one.
notes: OH: confirmed absent on a full-chapter read of ch. 5321; 5321.17(B). SAME ERROR SHAPE as the Nebraska row - a widely-cited notice period that is actually the termination rule being reported as a rent-increase rule.

title: Two Ohio Defaults You Are Allowed to Contract Around
bodyText: Most of Ohio's landlord-tenant rules cannot be waived - R.C. 5321.13(A) makes the whole of Chapter 5321 non-waivable except in one narrow direction. But two rules that matter to you sit OUTSIDE Chapter 5321, and both are default rules you may contract around. R.C. 5301.11 says a tenant whose building is destroyed or made unfit for occupancy through no fault of their own stops owing rent - 'unless otherwise expressly provided by written agreement or covenant' - and the tenant must surrender possession to get the benefit. And Ohio's duty to re-rent after a tenant abandons comes from case law that applies 'barring contrary contract provisions'. Because neither lives in Chapter 5321, 5321.13(A) does not protect them. R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability still does. Under the default, rent already owed before the damage stays due, and the tenant stops owing rent only by surrendering possession of all of what remains; they can't stop paying while leaving belongings there or otherwise keeping possession. One practical consequence is worth planning for: under the R.C. 5301.11 default on its own, the tenant stops owing rent and surrenders, but a fixed Term keeps running, so the tenant may claim a right to move back in once you have repaired. The library offers an optional clause that lets you end a fixed-term lease where the home is destroyed or cannot reasonably be repaired within a period you set, while leaving the tenant's R.C. 5301.11 rights untouched and stopping rent from the date the home became unfit. What the library does not offer is the other thing R.C. 5301.11 appears to permit - a term keeping rent running after the home becomes unfit. On its face the statute lets a written agreement do that, but R.C. 5321.13(E) bars any agreement letting a landlord receive rent free of the R.C. 5321.04 duties, and R.C. 5321.04 cannot be waived at all, so such a term would collide with Chapter 5321 even though R.C. 5301.11 sits outside it. A landlord who wants that term should write their own clause and take advice first.
notes: OH: R.C. 5301.11 (Title 53 ch. 5301 Conveyances - an ADJACENT-TITLE find, invisible to a ch. 5321 read; effective 1953-10-01, sole version, unamended); Frenchtown Square Partnership v. Lemstone, 99 Ohio St.3d 254, 2003-Ohio-3648. IMPORTANT: Lemstone's holding is expressly limited to a COMMERCIAL lease - the Court said so in framing the issue - and every decision upholding a mitigation waiver is commercial. Whether a RESIDENTIAL mitigation waiver survives 5321.14 is untested. DECISION 2026-09-18 (Taylor): no mitigation waiver in the default Ohio lease; surface it here as available-but-untested. Failure to mitigate is an affirmative defence, burden on the tenant. Surrender under 5301.11 means yielding all that remains - a tenant cannot stop paying and leave belongings in place. | OH: Sentence added by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29) from fire-casualty-termination-oh (switched off); content unchanged: R.C. 5301.11. | CHANGED 2026-10-03 (SOP 1.48 targeted fix 1). Two sentences added to point at the new optional clause casualty-landlord-termination-oh and to record what the library declines to offer and why, following the pattern of edu-casualty-mi, which does the same for Michigan. R.C. 5301.11 RE-READ SECTION-OPEN 2026-10-03 and quoted verbatim in the new clause's notes; nothing in this row's existing text changed. The 'rent keeps running' term is the option I recorded as barred in substance in the 2026-10-02 retro (rule 54 verdict (a)); it is now stated in the row rather than only in the log, because rule 54 requires a lawful option the library declines to offer to be recorded in an education row, never left to the log, which landlords never see. The R.C. 5321.13(E) reading is from the section text read 2026-09-27, not from case law - no Ohio decision testing a rent-continuation term after casualty was searched. Flagged.

title: Assistance Animal Accommodation
bodyText: A service animal or other assistance animal that Tenant or an Occupant needs as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is not considered a pet under this Lease, regardless of any pet policy, breed, weight, or size restriction stated elsewhere in this Lease. Landlord will not charge a pet deposit, pet rent, additional deposit, or any other pet-related fee for an assistance animal. If the disability and the disability-related need for the animal are not readily apparent, Landlord may request reliable documentation confirming the need for the accommodation, to the extent permitted by applicable law; if the disability and need are readily apparent, Landlord will not require such documentation. Tenant remains responsible for any damage to the property caused by the animal, and for keeping the animal under control and cared for. Landlord may deny or withdraw this accommodation if the specific animal poses a direct threat to the health or safety of others, or would cause substantial physical damage to the property, that cannot be reduced or eliminated by another reasonable accommodation.
notes: R.C. §4112.02(H)(19) (general reasonable-accommodation duty); OAC 4112-5-07(C) (no extra charge for an assistance animal, tenant remains liable for damage it causes), (D) (accommodation duty), (E) (burden on landlord to establish the basis for refusal), (F) (direct-threat/undue-burden exception); OAC 4112-5-02(C) (Ohio's own definition of 'animal assistant' is unusually broad -- 'any animal which aids' a person with a disability, species-neutral and not conditioned on formal training, and is state-administrative rather than tied to the federal HUD definition, so it survives a federal HUD narrowing). Grounded doubly: this is both a federal Fair Housing Act duty (42 U.S.C. §3604(f)(3)(B); 24 C.F.R. §100.204, the same regulation this project's Kansas legal-watch already monitors) and an independently-confirmed Ohio state-regulatory duty. Deliberately drafted WITHOUT a Colorado-style criminal-misrepresentation-penalty warning sentence: Ohio's own §§955.011/955.43 were each read in full and confirmed to contain no such offense reaching private residential housing (canvass items #39/#69/#73/#75) -- unlike Colorado, which has a real statutory penalty to warn about. Also deliberately does not add a documentation-verification-procedure requirement beyond 'to the extent permitted by applicable law': Ohio has no documentation standard or verification procedure in either the ORC or the OAC (canvass items #74/#127) -- this is a right without a stated verification mechanism, so the clause's existing self-limiting language is the correct level of specificity, not an omission.
