title: Holding deposits and money taken before the lease
bodyText: California has no holding-deposit statute, which is exactly why this is a trap. If you take money from an applicant to hold a unit, it is almost certainly security: the deposit statute defines security as any payment, fee, deposit or charge imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to reimburse you for processing a new tenant or as an advance payment of rent, used for any purpose, however denominated. Security counts toward the one-month cap and is refundable, so calling money a non-refundable holding fee does not make it one. The single exception is the application screening fee, which the statute expressly says is not security and not an advance fee, and which has its own cap, receipt and refund rules. Practical consequence: keep the screening fee separate and documented, and treat anything else you collect before move-in as refundable deposit money, or as first month's rent if that is what it is. Whether a true pre-tenancy holding deposit can be forfeited when an applicant backs out is unsettled in the statutes; the safest course is a short written agreement signed before the money changes hands that says what happens if either side walks away.
notes: CA: NEW 2026-09-28, gap-discovery sources 2 and 3. CONFIRMED ABSENT CODE-WIDE by the official leginfo full-text search across all codes, run 2026-09-28: 'holding deposit' returns 4 sections, none landlord-tenant (SHC 31151, MVC 490.5, MVC 1006.6, WAT 11706); 'application deposit' 0; 'reservation deposit' 1 (FIN 17312, not landlord-tenant). Arizona's screen produced the same shape (edu-holding-deposit-az), which is why this was screened for CA. The substantive content rests on sections already read in the CA pass: Civ. title: Tenant Improvements and Construction Liens
bodyText: In Florida, when a tenant makes improvements under an agreement with the landlord, a contractor's lien can reach the landlord's interest in the property. A lease can prevent this, but only if the lease expressly says the landlord's interest is not subject to liens for the tenant's improvements and the landlord also records, in the county's official records before the contractor records a notice of commencement, either the lease (or a short form or memorandum containing that language) or a notice covering the parcel that states the lease language and that all or most leases on the parcel contain it. The tenant must tell its contractors about the provision. If a contractor sends the landlord a written demand for a copy of the lease provision, the landlord must serve a verified copy within 30 days; failing to respond, or sending a false copy, exposes the property to the contractor's lien.

title: Condominium and HOA Rules for Renting
bodyText: Florida condominium and homeowners' associations can affect a rental in three ways. First, approval: if the association's documents require it to approve leases, a condominium association may charge an approval fee only if its documents provide for one, capped at $150 per applicant (adjusted for inflation every 5 years) and not charged for a renewal with the same tenant; it may also require the tenant to put up a deposit of up to one month's rent to protect the common areas, handled like a landlord's deposit. Second, rental restrictions: a homeowners' association rule adopted after July 1, 2021 that prohibits or regulates rentals binds only owners who buy after it is adopted or who consent to it, except that any association may regulate leases shorter than 6 months and limit rentals to three times a year. Third, rent demands: if the owner of a condominium unit or of a home in a homeowners' association falls behind on association charges, the association can demand in writing, using a notice form set by statute, that the tenant pay the rent to the association until the owner's debt is paid. The tenant must then pay the association and is immune from the landlord's claim for the rent paid to it. The tenant also gets credit against the rent owed to the landlord, and the association can serve Chapter 83 notices and evict the tenant for not paying it. A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant for paying rent to an association on its demand.

title: Removing Squatters (Unauthorized Occupants)
bodyText: A Florida property owner can ask the sheriff to remove squatters from a residential property without going to court if all of these are true: the owner or the owner's agent makes the request; the property includes a dwelling; the people entered unlawfully and are still there; the property was not open to the public when they entered; the owner told them to leave; they are not current or former tenants under a written or oral rental agreement the owner authorized; they are not the owner's immediate family; and there is no pending lawsuit about the property between the owner and them. The owner files a sworn complaint with the sheriff, who then serves a notice to vacate immediately and puts the owner back in possession; the sheriff may charge for standing by while locks are changed and belongings removed. A person wrongly removed can be restored to possession and recover actual damages, statutory damages of three times the fair market rent, costs and attorney's fees. This procedure cannot be used against a tenant or a former tenant, including one who stays after the lease ends; that requires an eviction.

title: Sales Tax on Short Rentals
bodyText: Florida charges a 6 percent state tax on rent for living quarters in a hotel, apartment house, rooming house, tourist or trailer camp, mobile home park, recreational vehicle park, condominium or timeshare resort. The tax does not apply to a tenant with a bona fide written lease longer than 6 months for continuous residence, to a tenant who has lived continuously in the same place for more than 6 months and has already paid the tax for the first 6 months, or to rentals in buildings intended primarily as people's permanent residence. Full-time postsecondary students and active-duty military are also exempt. A lease of 6 months or less, and a month-to-month tenancy during its first 6 months, can therefore carry sales tax, and county tourist taxes may apply as well. Whether the tax reaches a single-family house is not settled by this statute's list of facility types.

title: Uncashed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: If a tenant never cashes a Florida landlord's deposit refund, the money does not become the landlord's. Under Florida's unclaimed property law, intangible property a business holds or owes is presumed abandoned after a dormancy period, generally 5 years from when it became payable unless another period is specified by law, and must then be reported and delivered to the state. A landlord should keep records of the refund and the tenant's last known address.

title: Towing Tenants' and Guests' Vehicles
bodyText: A Florida property owner, a tenant of the property, or someone either authorizes (including a condominium association's representative) may have a vehicle parked without permission towed by a regular towing business, without paying for the tow. Except for property that is part of a single-family residence, or when the vehicle's owner is told in person that the space is reserved, the owner must first post permanent signs at each driveway entrance: within 10 feet of the road, with light-reflective letters at least 2 inches high stating that unauthorized vehicles will be towed at the owner's expense, the words "tow-away zone" in letters at least 4 inches high, the tower's name and phone number, mounted 3 to 6 feet above the ground, and in place at least 24 hours before any tow. The tower must store the vehicle nearby, notify the police within 30 minutes, release it within 1 hour of request, and stop and release it for half the posted rate if the owner arrives during the tow. A person who improperly causes a tow is liable for the removal and storage costs, damages, attorney's fees and court costs. Counties and cities may add rules and set maximum towing rates.

title: Removing a Squatter Without an Eviction Action (2026 Act)
bodyText: Kansas enacted a removal of squatters act in 2026 (L. 2026, ch. 56; H.B. 2378). It lets the owner of a dwelling unit, or the owner's agent, have a squatter removed by law enforcement instead of filing an eviction case. A squatter is a person occupying a dwelling who is not entitled to occupy it under a lease or rental agreement and is not authorized to occupy it by a tenant. The owner submits a notarized affidavit to local law enforcement stating six things: that the affiant is the owner or the owner's agent; that the person entered and remains unlawfully; that the person was not authorized to enter; that the person is not a tenant or a holdover tenant; that the affiant asked the person to leave and the person refused; and that the person is not an immediate family member. Law enforcement verifies the affiant's ownership and apparent entitlement to relief, and no sooner than 24 hours after receiving the affidavit an officer serves a notice to vacate immediately, either by hand or by posting it on the front door or entrance. Occupancy by a squatter is excluded from the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and removing a squatter does not require an eviction action under that Act. Three limits make this a poor tool to reach for casually. A current or former tenant is not a squatter, and a holdover tenant is expressly excluded, so a tenant who overstays still goes through the Chapter 61 eviction process. An immediate family member cannot be removed this way; the act's list runs to spouse, child, grandchild of any degree, parent, mother-in-law, father-in-law and grandparent, among others. And the downside is severe: a false affidavit is a class A nonperson misdemeanor, and a person wrongly removed may recover possession, actual costs and damages, treble the fair market rent as punitive damages, court costs and attorney fees. Use this only where you are certain there is no tenancy and no family relationship. Anything short of that belongs in an eviction action.

title: Abandonment Ends the Lease Unless You Try to Re-Rent
bodyText: If a Kansas tenant abandons the dwelling unit, you must make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental (K.S.A. 58-2565(c)). This is not only a duty to mitigate damages — the statute attaches a consequence that ends the lease. If you re-rent for a term beginning before the original rental agreement would have expired, the agreement is deemed terminated as of the date the new tenancy begins. And if you fail to use reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the rental agreement is deemed terminated by you as of the date you had notice of the abandonment. Either way rent stops accruing from that date, so a landlord who leaves an abandoned unit sitting and later sues for the balance of the term will find the claim cut off at the notice date rather than running to the end of the lease. Two practical consequences. Document the re-letting effort — when it was listed, at what rent, showings, applications, why any applicant was turned down — because that record is what preserves a rent claim past the abandonment date. And note that the statute deems the termination to be by the landlord, which matters anywhere your rights or a tenant's turn on which party ended the tenancy.

title: What You Can Sue For When the Lease Ends
bodyText: On termination of the rental agreement, K.S.A. 58-2568 gives you a claim and lets you file an action for possession, for rent, or for both. It also gives you a separate claim for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement, and that damages action may be filed before the rental agreement's termination date — you do not have to wait for the term to run out to sue on a breach. Two things follow. Possession and money are not alternatives in Kansas: suing for possession does not make you give up the rent claim, and you can combine them. And because the damages claim is for actual damages, it is bounded by the other Kansas limits already in this library — the re-letting duty on abandonment, which cuts rent off at the notice date (K.S.A. 58-2565(c)), and the holdover cap of one and one-half times periodic rent or actual damages (K.S.A. 58-2570(c)). Kansas gives you no statutory right to accelerate the remaining rent, and no right to recover attorney fees, because K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(3) voids a lease fee-shifting provision outright.

title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In a Kansas action for possession based on nonpayment of rent, or an action for rent where the tenant still occupies the premises, the tenant must raise any counterclaim for amounts recoverable under the rental agreement or the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act in that action or forfeit the right to bring it (K.S.A. 58-2561(a)). The court may order the tenant to pay accrued and future rent into court and then determine each party's net obligation; the party owed money is paid first out of the funds on deposit, with any remainder paid by the other party. Where no rent remains due after that netting, the tenant may prevail in the possession action. If the tenant has already vacated and you are suing only for rent, the tenant may still counterclaim but is not required to deposit rent into court (58-2561(b)). What this means in practice is that a habitability counterclaim normally lands inside your own eviction case rather than arriving as a separate suit later. A security-deposit claim is different: the Kansas Court of Appeals held that a claim for the deposit plus damages is not a compulsory counterclaim under this section (Asbury v. Mauk, 9 Kan. App. 2d 699 (1984)), so a tenant can bring it separately. Either way, the rent on deposit is the fund your judgment gets paid from — so expect the case to turn on the net number, not on possession alone.

title: Remedies When Entry Is Refused — and When You Enter Wrongly
bodyText: Kansas attaches remedies to entry in both directions (K.S.A. 58-2571). If the tenant refuses to allow lawful access to the dwelling unit, you may obtain injunctive relief to compel access or terminate the rental agreement, and in either case recover actual damages. If you make an unlawful entry, or a lawful entry in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated demands for entry that are otherwise lawful but have the effect of unreasonably harassing the tenant, the tenant may obtain injunctive relief or terminate the rental agreement, and recover actual damages. Read this with the entry standard itself: Kansas requires only reasonable notice at reasonable hours, with no fixed number of hours, so what counts as a lawful entry is judged against that standard rather than against a statutory clock. The practical point for a landlord is that refusal of access is a remedy you have to go get — Kansas gives you an injunction or termination, not a right to let yourself in — and that a pattern of entry demands can itself be the violation even when each individual entry would have been lawful.

title: The Kansas Eviction Process, Step by Step
bodyText: A Kansas eviction runs as a limited-actions case under Chapter 61, Article 38, and it is separate from the notice the lease and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act require. Before filing, you must give a notice to leave the premises at least three days before starting the lawsuit (K.S.A. 61-3803). That three-day period is counted as three consecutive 24-hour periods, intermediate weekends, legal holidays and days the clerk's office is closed are included in the count, and if you mail the notice you add two days. It may be delivered to the other party, left with a person over 12 years of age at the premises, posted in a conspicuous place, or mailed to the premises. The statute allows this notice to be combined with a notice under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so one properly drafted notice can serve both purposes rather than requiring two. You then file a petition, and the court sets the appearance date in the summons: not less than three nor more than 14 days after the summons issues (K.S.A. 61-3805). After a judgment for possession the court issues a writ of restitution at your request, and the writ must be executed within 14 days after the person named in it receives it (K.S.A. 61-3808). If an appeal stay is entered, execution stops immediately, and if possession has already been restored to you it goes back to the tenant. Nothing in this process lets you shortcut the Act's own notice-and-cure periods, which run first. Two things sit outside Chapter 61 and still bite. Kansas has no court rule making a federal notice a condition of filing, but the federal CARES Act's 30-day notice to vacate still applies on its own terms to a 'covered dwelling' — one with a federally backed mortgage or in a federally assisted programme — so check whether the property is covered before relying on the three-day notice alone. And for an eviction under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act the court must consider mediation unless it finds mediation would not materially aid both parties or is impracticable; see the eviction-record row for that and for the expungement rules that follow a judgment.

title: When a Tenant's Unpaid City Utility Bill Can Become a Lien on Your Property
bodyText: In Kansas, unpaid fees for utility service supplied by a municipally owned utility can become a lien on the property served, certified to the county clerk and collected on the tax roll with the usual tax penalties (K.S.A. 12-808c). One subsection decides who carries that risk in a rental: "A lien shall not attach to property for unpaid utility fees or charges, when the utility service has been contracted for by a tenant and not by the landlord or owner of the property to which such service is provided." So whose name is on the utility account is not an administrative detail — it determines whether the city can put the tenant's unpaid water, sewer, trash, gas or electric bill on your tax bill. If the tenant contracts for the service, no lien attaches to your property. If you keep the account in your own name for convenience, for a master-metered building, or because the tenant could not get service, the exception does not apply and the lien can attach. The practical rule is to require tenant-name accounts wherever the service is separately metered, and to treat any account you hold yourself as your own credit exposure rather than the tenant's. Note the limit: this concerns municipally owned utilities. Investor-owned utilities and rural water districts are outside it, and a rural water district's own collection remedies are a separate question.

title: A Deposit Refund the Tenant Never Cashes Is Not Yours
bodyText: When you mail a security deposit refund and the tenant never cashes it, the money does not revert to you. Under the Kansas Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act it becomes presumed abandoned and has to be reported and delivered to the state. A refund owed to a former tenant falls in the Act's catch-all category, "all other property, five years after the owner's right to demand the property or after the obligation to pay or distribute the property arises, whichever first occurs" (K.S.A. 58-3935(a)(16)). A holder of property presumed abandoned reports it to the state administrator before November 1 each year, covering the 12 months ending the preceding July 1 (K.S.A. 58-3950). There is a small-holder exemption: no report is required if you have no individual item over $100 and your aggregated total is under $250, unless the administrator requires otherwise — which will not cover most deposit refunds, since a typical Kansas deposit is capped at a month's rent and exceeds $100. Two practical points. Keep the unclaimed refund in a form you can still deliver five years later rather than writing it back into income. And this is separate from the deposit return rules themselves: complying with K.S.A. 58-2550's 14-day and 30-day deadlines is what avoids the 1.5-times penalty, while this Act governs what happens to the money afterwards.

title: Holding Deposits Sit Outside the Deposit Cap — Until the Lease Names Them
bodyText: Kansas defines a security deposit as "any sum of money specified in a rental agreement, however denominated, to be deposited with a landlord by a tenant as a condition precedent to the occupancy of a dwelling unit" (K.S.A. 58-2543(m)). Two limits in that sentence matter. It is denomination-blind, so calling money a fee, a reservation charge or a last-month payment does not keep it out — if the lease specifies it and occupancy depends on it, it is a security deposit and the K.S.A. 58-2550 cap, retention rules and return deadlines apply. But it is also agreement-scoped: money taken at application, before any rental agreement exists, is not specified in a rental agreement. A true pre-lease holding deposit therefore sits outside the deposit statute — which also means the tenant does not get 58-2550's remedies for it, and Kansas does not otherwise regulate the rental application process. The trap is the handoff. The moment the signed lease recites the holding money, or credits it toward the deposit or first month's rent, it becomes money specified in a rental agreement, counts against the cap, and starts the return clock. Decide up front which of the two you are taking, say so in writing to the applicant, and if you intend it to become part of the deposit, count it against the cap from the start.

title: Nobody Can Collect the Rent Free of the Habitability Duties
bodyText: Kansas law provides that "A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with subsection (a) of K.S.A. 58-2553" (K.S.A. 58-2549). Subsection (a) of 58-2553 is the landlord's habitability duty — codes materially affecting health and safety, common areas, the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems, trash removal, running water and reasonable hot water and heat. What the section does is close the gap between who takes the rent and who owes the duties. An assignment of rents to a lender, a deed, a trust deed or a security instrument cannot be drafted so that the party receiving rent escapes the habitability obligation, and neither can the lease itself. This matters in three ordinary situations: financing that assigns rents as collateral, a receiver or lender collecting rents during a default, and a sale where rent is directed to a new party. In each case the duty travels with the rent. Check any rent-assignment language in your loan documents against this section rather than assuming the lease is the only place the problem could arise.

title: No Kansas Foreclosure Notice or Lease-Survival Statute for Tenants
bodyText: Kansas has no state statute requiring a landlord to disclose a pending foreclosure to a tenant or applicant, and no state statute governing whether a lease survives a foreclosure sale. Several states in this library do have one; Kansas does not. What governs instead is Kansas's judicial foreclosure process, including the redemption period in K.S.A. 60-2414, and the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, which requires a successor in interest to honor an existing bona fide lease and to give a bona fide tenant at least 90 days' notice to vacate. Two practical consequences. If you are selling or losing a tenanted property, Kansas law gives you no disclosure obligation to the tenant, but the tenancy is not yours to terminate merely because the property is in foreclosure. And if you are buying at a Kansas foreclosure sale, expect to inherit the tenancy rather than an empty unit, and expect the federal 90-day floor to apply before you can require the tenant to leave.

title: No Foreign-Adversary Property Ownership Restriction in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas has no statute restricting the ownership of real property by foreign adversaries or by entities tied to designated countries. The legislature passed one in 2024 — House Substitute for Senate Bill 172 — and the Governor vetoed it on May 10, 2024. The veto was not overridden: the bill appears in the 2024 session laws only as a governor's veto message, with no session-law chapter number, and no Kansas enactment on the subject followed in 2025 or 2026. So a Kansas landlord selling to, buying from, or leasing to an entity with foreign ownership faces no state-law ownership restriction or registration duty of this kind. Federal rules still apply on their own terms, including CFIUS review of certain real estate transactions near sensitive sites and the federal agricultural foreign-investment reporting requirement, neither of which this Kansas absence affects.

title: No State Towing Rules for Your Parking Lot
bodyText: Kansas does not regulate towing from private rental property the way some states do. There is no state statute requiring signs at the entrances to your lot, no requirement that you sign a written authorization for each tow, and no state cap on what a towing carrier may charge the vehicle's owner. What Kansas does have is an abandoned-vehicle route and a tower's lien. Under K.S.A. 8-1102, where a vehicle is abandoned on private property the public agency for that jurisdiction may remove and dispose of it "upon request of the owner or occupant of such real property" — a request, not a written authorization — and whoever removes the vehicle at that agency's request has a possessory lien on it for the costs of removing, towing and storing it. K.S.A. 8-1103 carries the related lien provisions. The practical upshot is that the lease clause and your own arrangement with the towing company are doing most of the work here, because no state signage or authorization statute backs them up. Two cautions: Kansas cities have home-rule authority and many do regulate towing by ordinance, and the Kansas Corporation Commission regulates motor carriers — neither was researched, so check the ordinance for each property's city before relying on this.

title: No State Pool Barrier Requirement for Rental Property
bodyText: Kansas has no state statute imposing a pool fence, barrier, gate or safety-notice requirement on a residential landlord. The Kansas pool rules that do exist sit in the Department of Health and Environment's child care regulations — K.A.R. 28-4-129 for child care centers and K.A.R. 28-4-594 for family child care homes — and they apply because of the licensed child care activity, not because the property is rented. Pool barrier requirements in Kansas therefore come from whichever building or pool code the city or county has adopted, which varies from place to place. Two things follow for a landlord. Check the local adopted code for each property with a pool rather than assuming a statewide rule exists, since the absence of a state statute is not the absence of a requirement. And note the overlap with the residential-use clause: if a tenant runs a licensed child care operation out of the home, the K.A.R. 28-4 pool and fencing rules start applying to your property through the tenant's license, which is one more reason the residential-use-only restriction is worth enforcing.

title: Taking Money to Hold a Unit: Minnesota's Prelease Deposit Rules
bodyText: If you take money from a prospective tenant before a lease is signed, Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.175) lets you accept it only under a conspicuous WRITTEN agreement that states the circumstances in which you will return it, and states that you must return it within seven days of one of those circumstances occurring. 'Return' means postmarked within seven days, though the applicant may instead ask you to destroy the payment or hold it for pickup. If the applicant does sign a lease, you must apply the money to their security deposit or rent -- you cannot keep it as a fee. Get the return conditions in writing before you take the money: the penalty is the full amount of the deposit plus another one-half of it, and there is no cure once you have taken money with no written agreement. A reasonable applicant screening fee is NOT a prelease deposit and is governed separately.

Subd. 2(b) defines 'return' as postmarked within seven days, with an applicant-requested alternative of destruction or retrieval. Subd. 4: liability is the deposit plus one-half as a penalty, 'in addition to any other remedies'. History: 1999 c 97 s 1; 1999 c 199 art 1 s 174 -- no recent amendment (Recent History block empty). title: Submetering and Separate Utility Billing: The Rules Outside Chapter 504B
bodyText: If you submeter electricity or natural gas, or apportion gas, in a shared-metered residential building, Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 216B.022 to 216B.024 impose a compliance regime separate from Sec. 504B.216, and it puts you under the Public Utilities Commission's authority. The main duties: submeters installed on or after January 1, 2025 must meet ANSI standards, and every submeter, whenever installed, must measure accurately. You may not apportion electricity at all -- electricity may only be submetered. Charge only for what the tenant's own unit used, never for common areas or space you use yourself; divide fixed and non-usage charges equally among the units; and pass through each unit's equal share of any bill credit. Every submetered bill must show the present and previous readings, the reading date, your rate and the utility's rate to you, the tenant's share of taxes and surcharges, any credit, any administrative billing charge, the total, and the due date and late-fee date and amount. If you overcharge, refund promptly; if you undercharge, you may bill back only six months, and you must offer a no-interest, no-fee payment plan where the tenant was not at fault. You must offer a payment plan for any overdue utility bill, and if you cannot agree, tell the tenant they can go to the Commission's consumer affairs office and give them its current phone number and email. When a tenant moves out before the real bill arrives, you may issue an ESTIMATED final bill based on the previous billing period, prorated to the move-out date, with no extra charges beyond the administrative billing charge and a late fee limited to the prior period.
notes: MN added (gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27, checklist instruction 36 -- sources 2, 3 and 4 only; not a re-audit). Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Sec. 216B.023: subd. 1(b) lease/at-outset notice of billing timing (see utility-billing-schedule-mn) and the no-less-frequent rule; subd. 1(c) the eight mandatory bill-content items; subd. 2(a)(1) electricity may NOT be apportioned; subd. 2(b) the charging methodology (no common areas, equal division of non-usage charges, pro-rata credits); subd. 4 administrative billing charge per Sec. 504B.216 subd. 8 and no other fees; subd. 5 overcharge refund and six-month undercharge limit; subd. 6 late charge per Sec. 504B.216 subd. 9; subd. 7 payment plans plus the consumer-affairs referral; subd. 8 undercharge payment plans with no interest or delinquency fee. title: You Must Hand Over Outstanding Inspection and Condemnation Orders
bodyText: Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195) makes you give out copies of certain code-enforcement paperwork, and the duty runs to APPLICANTS as well as tenants. If a citation has been issued on an inspection order that the housing inspector marks as threatening a tenant's health or safety, or if there is an outstanding condemnation order or declaration that the premises are unfit for human habitation, you must deliver or mail a copy: to an existing tenant within 72 hours of the citation; to any person BEFORE they sign a lease or pay rent or a security deposit for a new tenancy; and to anyone before they take over ownership. If the order does not involve a health-or-safety violation, you instead post a summary in a conspicuous place in each affected building, together with notice that you will make the order available for review on request by a tenant or prospective tenant, and you must actually provide it when asked. You are not in violation if you have only an initial repair order, if the repair deadline and any extension have not expired, if fewer than 60 days have passed since the deadline expired with no citation issued, or if you finish the repairs in time. Proving you disclosed is an affirmative defense. The tenant's remedy runs through the private attorney general statute, so damages, costs and attorney fees are available, and the duty cannot be waived by the lease.

Subd. 1(a) the three recipients and the 72-hour clock; note (2) is triggered by signing OR paying rent OR paying a security deposit, whichever comes first. Subd. 1(b) the conspicuous-posting alternative for non-health/safety orders plus the on-request production duty. Subd. 2 remedies via Sec. 8.31 subd. 3a plus equitable relief. Subd. 3 the four exceptions. Subd. 4 affirmative defense. Subd. 5 remedies are additional and any lease waiver is 'contrary to public policy and void'. Sec. 504B.195 and 504B.204 both sit in that gap and both are non-waivable landlord duties. title: Never Accept Rent or a Deposit After a Condemnation or Vacate Order
bodyText: Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.204) flatly bars you from accepting rent or a security deposit once the premises have been condemned or declared unfit for human habitation, ordered vacated for violating a housing, health or fire code or a rental licensing ordinance, or ordered vacated under a government taking. If you take money anyway you owe the tenant actual damages PLUS three times everything you collected after the date of the order, plus costs and attorney fees -- and the violation also breaches the statutory habitability covenant, which opens up the tenant-remedies machinery on top. The statute says it must be construed liberally in the tenant's favour, and no lease term can waive it. Practically: the moment a vacate or condemnation order lands, stop collecting, and do not accept a payment a tenant offers voluntarily.

Sec. 504B.385 and 504B.395. Paragraph (b): remedies are additional and any lease waiver is void. title: Cold Weather Notice Before Vacating
bodyText: Between November 15 and April 15, if Tenant removes from, abandons, or vacates the property or any part of it while the Term is still running, Tenant will first give Landlord at least three days' written notice of Tenant's intention to do so. This Section does not apply where the tenancy is ending. Tenant understands that the property contains plumbing and other pipes that can be damaged by freezing, and that Minnesota law makes failure to give this notice a criminal offense.
notes: MN added (gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27, checklist instruction 36 -- sources 2, 3 and 4 only; not a re-audit). Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.155 (TENANT MUST GIVE COLD WEATHER NOTICE BEFORE VACATION OF BUILDING), read section-open in full -- it is a single sentence: 'Except upon the termination of the tenancy, a tenant who, between November 15 and April 15, removes from, abandons, or vacates a building or any part thereof that contains plumbing, water, steam, or other pipes liable to injury from freezing, without first giving to the landlord three days' notice of intention so to remove is guilty of a misdemeanor.' PROOF-OF-ABSENCE VIOLATION, AND THE THIRD OF THIS EXACT SHAPE FOR MINNESOTA. Sec. 504B.155 appeared in the library in exactly one place before this pass: the notes of the shared tenant-maintenance row, which asserted that the 'cold-weather-notice-before-vacating duty (Sec. 504B.155)' was 'already reflected elsewhere in the library.' It was not -- no row existed. That is precisely instruction 19's scenario ('asserted covered, no row ever built'), and precisely what happened to MN with Sec. 504B.206 (domestic violence) and Sec. 504B.212 subd. 2 (retaliation). A false 'already covered' note is worse than an honest absence because no later canvass re-flags it. Found here by the source-3 scenario screen (tenant leaves mid-winter and the pipes freeze), not by any keyword probe. DRAFTING NOTES: the statute says 'notice', not 'written notice' -- the clause requires writing as a contract term, which is permissible and evidentially sensible, and the clause does not purport to create the criminal liability, only to state that the law does. The statute's own carve-out ('Except upon the termination of the tenancy') is carried across, so the clause does not collide with surrender-end-of-term-mn-nd or with a lawful Sec. 504B.147 termination notice. Currency: no amendment since 1999 c 199 art 1 s 12. CROSS-STATE: no other state in the library has a cold-weather vacate-notice row; ND, SD and WY share Minnesota's climate and should be asked. Recommended as a new named-topic checklist row.

title: The Unlawful-Activities Covenant Is in Every Minnesota Lease Whether You Write It or Not
bodyText: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.171 writes a covenant into every Minnesota residential lease, oral or written, so you do not need a crime-free clause to have one. Both you AND the tenant covenant not to allow controlled substances in violation of the criminal drug chapter, prostitution or prostitution-related activity, unlawful use or possession of a firearm, or stolen or robbery-obtained property -- and the covenant reaches the common area and curtilage, not just the unit. The covenant is not broken by a third party's conduct unless you or the tenant knew or had reason to know of it, so what matters in practice is what you did once you found out. The tenant separately covenants not to commit domestic-abuse-type acts against another tenant or authorized occupant. A breach voids the tenant's right to possession. Two limits worth knowing: you cannot prohibit a tenant from legally possessing cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles or hemp-derived consumer products, and the tenant cannot waive that right -- but smoking or vaping them is outside the protection, so a smoke-free policy is still enforceable. And because the covenant binds you too, allowing the conduct is your own breach, not merely a ground against the tenant.

title: A Nuisance Notice Can Close Your Building for a Year, and Evicting the Tenant Is the Way Out
bodyText: This is the largest landlord-side risk in Minnesota law that has nothing to do with Chapter 504B. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 617.80 to 617.87, a prosecuting attorney who believes a nuisance is being maintained in your building must first serve written notice on ALL owners, by personal service or certified mail. A nuisance can be established by a single incident of prostitution-related activity, or by two or more incidents of certain other offences within the previous 12 months, anywhere within the building. The notice tells you what kind of nuisance is alleged, summarises the evidence and dates, and warns that if you do not abate it or otherwise resolve matters with the prosecutor within 30 DAYS, a district court complaint may follow that can enjoin the use of your building FOR ANY PURPOSE FOR ONE YEAR. Your way out is Sec. 617.85: as the owner you may file a motion in that same abatement proceeding to cancel the offending tenant's lease and recover the premises, and maintaining a nuisance is an additional ground for eviction beyond the ordinary grounds. Two features make this genuinely protective. It is no defence that your lease does not list this ground, so a thin lease does not cost you the remedy. And the court must not order abatement of the premises where it cancels that tenant's lease and grants you restitution AND finds both that the acts were committed by that tenant and that the tenant was NOT acting in conjunction with you or under your control. Read that second condition carefully: evicting the tenant protects the building only if you were not party to the conduct, so a landlord who knew and did nothing cannot evict his way out of an abatement order. Do not let the 30 days run.
notes: MN added (gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27, checklist instruction 36 -- sources 2, 3 and 4 only; not a re-audit). Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Minn. Stat. Sec. 617.81 and Sec. 617.85, both read section-open. Sec. 617.81 subd. 2(a): a public nuisance exists on proof of one incident of the items at (i), (v), (viii) or (ix), or two or more of (ii), (iii), (iv), (vi), (vii) or (x), committed within the previous 12 months within the building. Subd. 4(a): the prosecuting attorney SHALL serve written notice on all owners and interested parties by personal service or certified mail, return receipt requested. Subd. 4(b)(3): failure to abate or resolve within 30 days of service may lead to a complaint that 'could, among other remedies, result in enjoining the use of the building for any purpose for one year or, in the case of a tenant, lessee, or occupant, could result in cancellation of the lease'. Subd. 4(b)(4): the notice must inform the owner of the Sec. 617.85 options. Sec. 617.85: the owner may move to cancel the lease in the abatement proceeding and may assign that right to the prosecuting attorney; nuisance under Sec. 617.81 subd. 2 is 'an additional ground authorized by law' beyond Sec. Sec. 504B.281 to 504B.371; 'It is no defense ... that the lease or other agreement controlling the tenancy or leasehold does not provide for eviction or cancellation of the lease upon the ground provided in this section'; on a finding the court SHALL cancel and grant restitution; and the court 'must not order abatement of the premises' where it cancels the lease, grants restitution of that portion, and finds the acts were committed by that tenant. NOT READ: Sec. Sec. 617.80 (definitions), 617.82, 617.83, 617.84, 617.86 and 617.87, and the full item list in Sec. 617.81 subd. 2(a) -- the row states the notice, the 30-day clock, the one-year remedy and the Sec. 617.85 safe harbour, and does not enumerate the qualifying offences. Sec. 504B.171 gives the covenant and Sec. 504B.321 the expedited procedure, but the abatement exposure and the owner's motion under Sec. 617.85 are in a different title entirely -- instruction 7 again. title: Minnesota's Expedited Eviction Track Changed on August 1, 2026
bodyText: Minnesota has a fast eviction track, and Laws 2026, ch. 81 widened it as of August 1, 2026. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.321 subd. 2 you may seek an expedited hearing where the case is brought on the unlawful-activities covenant, or where the tenant seriously endangers other residents' safety, intentionally and seriously damages property -- and now also where the tenant ASSAULTS you, your employees or your contractors, using the criminal code's definition of assault. You must file an affidavit stating specific facts and instances explaining why expedition is required; a referee or judge screens it, and the hearing is set no less than five and no more than seven days from issuance of the summons, which must be served within 24 hours unless the court orders otherwise. Two cautions. The penalty for seeking expedition without sufficient basis rose from $500 to $750 in the same 2026 act. And -- this part is not new, it has been in the statute since 2023 -- the court may consider ONLY the expedited allegations and may NOT consolidate them with anything else, including breach of lease, holdover, or nonpayment of rent. So if you want unpaid rent as well, that is a separate action; do not bundle it in and expect the court to hear it.

The court may not consolidate claims heard under the expedited procedure with any additional claims, including but not limited to breach of lease, holding over under section 504B.285, or nonpayment of rent under section 504B.291.' Sec. 504B.281-.371).| *** CORRECTED BEFORE SHIPPING, AND THE ERROR IS WORTH RECORDING. *** My first draft of this row stated that paragraph (e) -- the no-consolidation rule -- was NEW in Laws 2026, ch. 81. THAT WAS WRONG. The court may not consolidate claims heard under the expedited procedure with any additional claims, including but not limited to breach of lease, holding over under section 504B.285, or nonpayment of rent under section 504B.291.' What ch. 81 s 5 ACTUALLY changed is exactly two things: paragraph (a) gains 'assaults the landlord or the landlord's employees or contractors' with the Sec. 609.02 subd. 10 assault definition, and paragraph (d)'s civil penalty goes from $500 to $750. title: If Your Online Rent Portal Goes Down, Minnesota Law Is Now Against You
bodyText: Laws 2026, ch. 81 rewrote Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.118 -- now titled PAYMENT OF RENT -- and added digital-payment rules effective August 1, 2026. A 'digital payment platform' is any electronic application or system under your direct control, or run by a vendor under contract with you, that lets a user conduct financial transactions. If you require or permit tenants to pay through one, then whenever it is not functioning you must offer an alternative way to pay, and you may NOT charge any fee for using that alternative. If you know the platform is down you must either restore access or offer an alternative as soon as practicable. And if a tenant fails to pay because BOTH the platform and the alternative you provided are not working for them, you may not take any adverse action -- the statute names filing an eviction and assessing late fees specifically. The teeth are in the next subdivision: the tenant has an affirmative defence to a nonpayment eviction if you violated the section, and on a showing that you did, the eviction action MUST BE DISMISSED and the tenant gets reasonable attorney fees plus any other equitable relief. Keep dated records of outages and of the alternative you offered. The cash-receipt duty is unchanged and is now subdivision 2.

The section is RETITLED from 'RECEIPT FOR RENT PAID IN CASH' to 'PAYMENT OF RENT' and restructured into four subdivisions: subd. 1 defines 'digital payment platform'; subd. 2 carries the cash-receipt duty forward verbatim; subd. 3(a)-(c) the alternative-payment duty, the no-fee rule, the restore-or-offer duty and the adverse-action bar; subd. 4 the affirmative defence, mandatory dismissal, attorney fees and equitable relief. title: Never Name a Tenant's Child as a Defendant in an Eviction
bodyText: New Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.2136, effective August 1, 2026, says a residential landlord shall not list the minor child of a residential tenant as a defendant in an eviction action complaint against that tenant. The only exception is where a minor is the only person renting the unit from you -- then you may name the minor. The rule cannot be waived or modified by the parties, and any lease provision purporting to waive it is contrary to public policy and void. The tenant recovers actual damages or $300, whichever is greater, for a violation. This is easy to breach by accident: if your process is to name every occupant on the complaint, change it now. It applies to eviction actions filed on or after August 1, 2026.
notes: MN added (gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27, checklist instruction 36 -- sources 2, 3 and 4 only; not a re-audit). Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Laws 2026, ch. 81 (S.F. 4171), s 3, read from the session-law text: 'proposing coding for new law in Minnesota Statutes, chapter 504B' at [504B.2136] MINORS AS DEFENDANTS PROHIBITED. Paragraph (a) the prohibition and the sole-minor-tenant exception; paragraph (b) non-waivable, any waiver 'contrary to public policy and void'; paragraph (c) 'actual damages or $300, whichever is greater'. EFFECTIVE DATE clause read in full: 'This section is effective August 1, 2026, and applies to eviction actions filed on or after that date.' Signed 2026-05-12; in force as of this pass. NOT A NEW TOPIC LIBRARY-WIDE -- CORRECTED BEFORE SHIPPING. My first draft of this row asserted that no state had a row on who may be named as an eviction defendant. That was wrong, and the topic_key alignment check caught it: Ohio already carries edu-minor-tenant-filing-oh on topic_key 'minor-tenant-filing'. Ohio's rule is stronger in remedy and narrower in target -- naming a minor TENANT alongside a parent or adult guardian means the court SHALL dismiss without prejudice AND SHALL order the landlord to pay the minor tenant's reasonable attorney fees, and Ohio defines 'minor tenant' as an unemancipated tenant under 18. Minnesota's Sec. 504B.2136 instead bars naming the minor CHILD of a tenant (whether or not the child is a tenant), is expressly non-waivable, and fixes damages at actual or $300, whichever is greater. So the two are genuinely different rules on the same topic and both belong. This row shares Ohio's topic_key. The topic IS still missing from the named-topic checklist, which is a real gap -- two of fourteen states now have a rule and no canvass row asks about it. Because the section is brand new it will not appear in the 2025 compilation's chapter index at all, which is instruction 35's trap running in the opposite direction (a section IN FORCE but MISSING from the compilation). Recommended as a new named-topic checklist row: every future state should be asked whether it restricts who may be named as a defendant. Practically this is a process/UI matter rather than lease text -- flagged for the eviction-filing side of the product if it ever generates complaints, alongside MN's other product-level items (Sec. 504B.120 page-1 placement, the Sec. 504B.216 subd. 10 attachment).

title: Towing From Your Lot: Posting Is What Makes It Lawful
bodyText: Minnesota's towing rules live in Minn. Stat. ch. 168B, not in the landlord-tenant chapter, and the timeframes turn on what kind of property you have. A vehicle left unattended may be impounded from private property IMMEDIATELY where the property is single-family or duplex residential, and immediately from ANY residential property that is properly posted. Non-residential private property gets immediate removal if properly posted and 24 hours if not. Read that list carefully: the 24-hour fallback is non-residential ONLY, so a multi-unit residential lot that is NOT posted has no timeframe available to it under that provision. If you manage anything larger than a duplex, post the lot. Two further points. Sec. 168B.035 is about towing by government towing authorities from public property, and it expressly preserves a private property owner's authority to authorize a tow under ch. 168B -- so that section's rules are not your rules. And the statutory lien that a tow operator gets for towing and storage arises on a tow requested by a LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICER, so a tow you order yourself does not create it; settle who pays with your towing company in your contract. Chapter 168B does not define 'properly posted', so follow your city's sign requirements.
notes: MN added (gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27, checklist instruction 36 -- sources 2, 3 and 4 only; not a re-audit). Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 168B.04, 168B.011, 168B.035 and 168B.045, all read section-open. Sec. 168B.04 subd. 2(b)(2) is the operative list for private property: '(i) that is single-family or duplex residential property, immediately; (ii) that is private, nonresidential property, properly posted, immediately; (iii) that is private, nonresidential property, not posted, 24 hours; (iv) [vehicle service establishments, five business days after certified-mail notice]; or (v) that is any residential property, properly posted, immediately.' The asymmetry is in the statute, not a paraphrase: clause (iii)'s 24-hour rule is expressly limited to nonresidential property, and there is no unposted-multifamily-residential clause. Sec. 168B.011 subd. 4 defines 'unauthorized vehicle' as one subject to removal under Sec. 168B.035 or Sec. 168B.04 subd. 2 that is not a junk or abandoned vehicle -- so an operable but wrongly parked tenant or guest car is an 'unauthorized vehicle', while the 'abandoned vehicle' definition at subd. 2 additionally requires that the vehicle lack vital component parts or be inoperable. Sec. 168B.035 subd. 5: 'This section does not restrict the authority of the owner of private property to authorize under chapter 168B the towing of a motor vehicle unlawfully parked on the private property.' Sec. 168B.045: the towing and storage lien attaches to a person 'who tows and stores a motor vehicle at the request of a law enforcement officer'. Sec. 168B.011 and 168B.04 but has no definition in Sec. 168B.011 -- checked by reading the definitions section; the row says to follow local sign rules rather than inventing a standard. title: Methamphetamine Contamination: No Disclosure Duty, but an Occupancy Ban and a Recorded Affidavit
bodyText: Minnesota has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose that a property was once a clandestine drug lab. What it has instead is Minn. Stat. Sec. 152.0275 subd. 2, and the practical consequences are bigger than a disclosure duty. A county or local health department or sheriff SHALL order that any property found to be a clandestine lab site and contaminated be prohibited from being occupied or used until it has been assessed and remediated under the Department of Health's cleanup guidelines, and the remediation must be done by a contractor who then verifies the work to you and to the authority within five days; the authority vacates its order after that. If a contractor certifies work that did not meet the guidelines, the contractor is liable to you for the extra remediation cost and your attorney fees, with a six-year limit. Public-health nuisance abatement procedures apply on top. The disclosure happens without you: the authority records an affidavit with the county recorder or registrar of titles naming the owner, describing the property and mapping the contaminated area, expressly to disclose the history 'to any potential transferee', and the recorder must record it so it turns up in an ordinary title search. Affidavits can be filed to show remediation and to vacate the order, after which they stop being notice. Local community health services administrators also keep records of affected properties. So: check the title and the local administrator before you buy, and expect an occupancy prohibition rather than a disclosure form if it happens to you.

title: A Deposit Refund the Tenant Never Cashed Is Not Yours to Keep
bodyText: When you send a security-deposit refund and the former tenant never cashes it, the money does not become yours after a while. Under Minnesota's unclaimed property act (Minn. Stat. Sec. 345.39 subd. 1) intangible personal property held in the ordinary course of your business that stays unclaimed by the owner for more than THREE YEARS after it became payable is presumed abandoned, and the listed examples include customer overpayments, credit balances and miscellaneous outstanding checks. A stale refund check or an uncollected credit balance sits squarely in that category. Do not write it back to income: track it, and when the dormancy period runs, report and remit it to the state. Charges you may lawfully withhold are excluded from the calculation, so what is at issue is the net amount you actually owed the tenant.

Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Minn. Stat. Sec. 345.39 subd. 1, read section-open: 'All intangible personal property, not otherwise covered by sections 345.31 to 345.60, including any income or increment thereon, but excluding any charges that may lawfully be withheld, that is held or owing in this state in the ordinary course of the holder's business and has remained unclaimed by the owner for more than three years after it became payable or distributable is presumed abandoned', with the enumerated examples at (b) 'deposits or payments for repair or purchase of goods or services', (c) 'customer overpayments', and (g) 'credit balances, accounts receivable and miscellaneous outstanding checks'. Currency: Recent History shows only subd. 1 amended 2000 c 488 art 2 s 24. The three-year residual period is therefore the applicable one by category, not by a section naming deposits. NOT READ: the holder reporting and remittance mechanics at Sec. Sec. 345.41 to 345.43, and the penalties at Sec. 345.55 -- the row states dormancy and the duty to report, not the filing procedure; flagged if Taylor wants the mechanics. title: Renting Storage Lockers Separately Can Pull You Into the Self-Service Storage Act
bodyText: If you rent storage space to tenants, check whether Minnesota's self-service storage facility act (Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 514.970 to 514.979) applies before you rely on your storage clause. A 'self-service storage facility' is real property designed and used for renting or leasing individual storage space to occupants who have access to store and remove personal property; the only exclusions are financial-institution vaults, warehouses that issue documents of title, and commercial short-term parking. There is NO exclusion for storage lockers in an apartment building. If the act applies, Sec. 514.975 imposes real requirements on the rental agreement: it must disclose your lien rights including the right to deny access, and the extent and limits of your insurance on the occupant's property; it must let the occupant name an optional alternate contact person, with a space they initial if they decline; any cap on the value of stored property is effective ONLY if printed in bold type or underlined, and may not be set below $1,000; and there is a uniformed-services disclosure. Most importantly, a rental agreement 'may not exempt an owner from liability for damages to an occupant's personal property caused by the owner's negligence' -- so a negligence disclaimer is void where the act applies. The safer reading is that a locker thrown in with a dwelling at no separate charge is not a self-service storage facility, because the property is not designed and used for renting storage space. But if you rent lockers for a separate fee, to your tenants or to the public, assume the act applies and drop the disclaimer.

Subd. 3 'owner' includes a lessor; subd. 5 'rental agreement' is a written agreement for use of storage space at such a facility. Sec. 514.975 subd. 1: the lien-rights and insurance-limits disclosure, the alternate-contact provision and the initial box, and 'A rental agreement may not exempt an owner from liability for damages to an occupant's personal property caused by the owner's negligence.' Subd. 2: a value limit binds only if 'printed in bold type or underlined' and may not be less than $1,000. Subd. 3: uniformed-services disclosure. title: No Rekeying or Lock-Hardware Duty in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota imposes no statutory duty to rekey or change locks between tenancies, and no deadbolt or lock-hardware requirement for rental housing. Locks are a matter for your lease and any local housing code. The one statutory lock rule runs the other way and is already covered in the library: a tenant who is a victim of violence has a right to have the locks changed. Rekeying at turnover is good practice, not a legal obligation, so if you want it as an obligation on the tenant's side, put it in the lease.

title: No Fire-Sprinkler Duty for Private Rental Housing
bodyText: Minnesota's only retrofit sprinkler mandate does not reach private landlords. Minn. Stat. Sec. 299F.48 requires automatic sprinkler systems in existing PUBLIC HOUSING buildings, and the section defines that term narrowly: housing for low-income persons and households financed by the federal government and owned and operated by the public housing authorities and agencies formed by cities and counties, in which at least one story used for human occupancy is 75 feet or more above the lowest level of fire department vehicle access. Compliance is due by August 1, 2033. If you are a private owner, none of that applies to you. New construction and remodelling are still governed by the State Building Code and State Fire Code, which Sec. 299F.48 expressly does not supersede.

title: Selling With a Tenant in Place: No Minnesota Statute Beyond the Deposit Handover
bodyText: Minnesota has no general statute governing what you owe a tenant when you sell a tenanted property, and no release-on-sale provision of the kind some states have. What Minnesota does regulate is the money: the security-deposit transfer and successor-liability rules, which are covered separately in the library. Beyond that, selling with a tenant in place is governed by your lease, by common-law rules about whether the buyer takes subject to the tenancy, and by the ordinary entry-notice rules when you show the unit. There is also no statutory requirement to notify tenants that you have sold, and no statutory right of first refusal for residential tenants. So put what you need into the lease and the purchase agreement, because the statute will not supply it.

title: What North Dakota Law Will Not Let the Lease Do
bodyText: North Dakota has no list of prohibited residential lease terms inside its landlord-tenant chapter, and it is easy to conclude from that the lease can say whatever you want. That is wrong. Five sections of Chapter 9-08 void whole categories of contract term, and a lease is a contract like any other. A provision is unlawful if it is contrary to an express provision of law, contrary to the policy of express law though not expressly prohibited, or otherwise contrary to good morals (§ 9-08-01). A provision whose object is, directly or indirectly, to exempt anyone from responsibility for their own fraud, for willful injury to another person or their property, or for violation of law -- whether the violation is willful or negligent -- is against the policy of the law (§ 9-08-02). Penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void outright (§ 9-08-03). A clause fixing damages in advance is void to that extent, unless it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage (§ 9-08-04). And a clause that restricts a party from enforcing its rights by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or that shortens the time in which it may enforce them, is void unless a North Dakota statute specifically permits it (§ 9-08-05). What this means in practice: a flat "Landlord is not liable" sentence will not protect you where the loss came from your own violation of a statute or building code; a flat early-termination, short-notice, or administrative fee is exposed as a contractual penalty rather than a damages estimate; and Chapter 47-16's own unconscionability section (§ 47-16-13.3) sits on top of all of it as a case-by-case backstop.
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 9-08-01, 9-08-02, 9-08-03, 9-08-04, 9-08-05. The exculpation exposure that forced fixes to this clause family in KS and NE therefore does not arise for ND'. § 9-08-02 IS an enumerated statutory ban; it is simply in Title 9 (Contracts) rather than Title 47. The checklist's own topic row L642 'Lease-content restrictions (state-wide, not just the LT chapter)' recorded ND as 'Outside the chapter: NOT CANVASSED' -- this row is that canvass. A disclaimer is therefore exposed where the loss traces to the landlord's breach of a statute or code (§§ 47-16-13.1, 23-13-15, fair housing), not merely to carelessness. title: The Tenant Can Repair and Deduct, or Just Leave
bodyText: North Dakota gives a tenant three routes when you do not repair, and none of them requires going to court first. If, within a reasonable time after the tenant's notice of dilapidations that you ought to repair, you neglect to do so, the tenant may repair the premises and deduct the expense of the repair from rent; recover that expense from you in any other lawful manner; or vacate the premises -- and a tenant who vacates on that ground is discharged from further payment of rent and from performing the lease's other conditions (§ 47-16-13). There is no escrow mechanism, no statutory dollar cap on the deduction, no requirement that the tenant get your approval of the repair or the contractor, and no notice period fixed in days. Two consequences to plan around. First, a deduction properly made under this section is not unpaid rent, so treating it as a nonpayment default and filing on it is a real risk. Second, on any claim under §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 the court may award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party (§ 47-16-13.6), so a small repair dispute can carry your opponent's fees. Answering a written repair request promptly, in writing, with a date, is the only reliable way to keep this section from being used against you.
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13, with § 47-16-13.6 on fees. Plus § 47-16-13.6' -- and no CSV row existed for it. This is exactly the shape instruction 19 and Addendum L.1 were written for: the checklist asserts coverage, the library has none, and the assertion stops any later canvass from re-flagging it. title: Selling a Property With a Tenant in It
bodyText: North Dakota imposes no duty to tell your tenant you are selling, and no statutory notice period before a sale -- but four other things bind you. The security deposit and accrued interest must be transferred to the buyer; you are not released from liability until that transfer actually happens, and the buyer is bound by North Dakota's deposit rules even though the buyer never received the deposit (§ 47-16-07.1(5)). The buyer steps into your rent remedies (§ 47-16-28), your tenant's remedies under the lease run against the buyer (§ 47-16-29), and your remedies run against anyone the tenant assigned to, for claims accruing while they held the assignment -- except where the assignment was security for a loan and was not accompanied by possession (§ 47-16-30). Separately, selling triggers seller-disclosure duties in Chapter 47-10 that have nothing to do with the lease. For a residential dwelling of four or fewer units you must give the buyer a written disclosure of all material facts you are aware could adversely and significantly affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment, before final acceptance of the purchase agreement -- and that applies whether or not a real estate licensee is involved, subject to nine exemptions including foreclosure, fiduciary and immediate-family transfers (§ 47-10-02.1). Since 2025 you must also disclose in writing any knowledge you have of radon concentrations, give the buyer the prescribed radon warning to acknowledge by signature, and hand over any prior test results and evidence of mitigation reasonably available to you; comply and you are immune from radon-based claims (§ 47-10-02.2). And if the property sits in a homeowners' association or condominium project, you have ten days from executing the agreement to deliver the association's governing documents, budgets, assessments, litigation and violation history -- and if you do not, the buyer may void the purchase contract until they are delivered and for five days afterwards (§ 47-10-02.3).
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-07.1(5), 47-16-28, 47-16-29, 47-16-30 (complete Chapter 47-16 primary text); §§ 47-10-02.1, 47-10-02.2, 47-10-02.3 read from the official compilation ndlegis.gov/cencode/t47c10.pdf on 2026-09-27. | NEW STATUTE CONFIRMED ENACTED, not assumed: § 47-10-02.2 was created by 2025 SB 2204 (69th LA), enrolled 25.0456.03000, Senate 45-0 / House 87-3. The enrolled PDF's governor and Secretary of State date lines are blank, so the enrolled document alone would not have supported a VERIFIED. title: No Radon Disclosure Duty When You Rent -- But There Is One When You Sell
bodyText: North Dakota requires no radon disclosure, testing, or warning from a landlord to a tenant, even though the EPA places the whole state in its highest-risk zone. The one mandatory disclosure at the start of a North Dakota tenancy is the signed condition statement (§ 47-16-07.2), and it says nothing about radon. The picture changes the moment you sell rather than rent: since 2025 a seller of residential real property must disclose any knowledge of radon concentrations in writing, give the buyer a prescribed radon warning to acknowledge by signature, and provide any prior test results and evidence of mitigation (§ 47-10-02.2). Testing and disclosing voluntarily to a tenant is still worth considering, since a habitability claim under § 47-16-13.1 does not require a disclosure statute to exist.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT for leases; PRESENT for sellers. Recorded as a row per the standing rule that log-only absences are invisible to future canvasses. | EVIDENTIARY BASIS UPGRADED. The checklist's ND cell previously read 'Confirmed absent -- Nolo: "North Dakota law requires only one disclosure" (§ 47-16-07.2)' -- a secondary source, and the cited section is the condition statement, not a radon rule. Replaced with: (a) the complete Chapter 47-16 primary text, which contains no radon provision; and (b) an official full-text search of ndlegis.gov for "radon" on 2026-09-27, which returned no Century Code hit at all in its top results -- every hit was a bill, committee minute or testimony. | LEGISLATIVE HISTORY worth knowing, because it shows the rental question was actually put and not answered: 2017 HB 1186 (65th LA) proposed a new chapter of title 47 for seller radon disclosure AND to 'amend and reenact section 47-16-07.2' -- that is, to put radon into the landlord-tenant condition statement. § 47-16-07.2 as it now reads contains no radon language. 2017 HB 1188 covered the same ground. Only the seller half ever became law, via 2025 SB 2204 (§ 47-10-02.2, enactment verified against the current compilation of ch. 47-10). | See edu-selling-rented-property-nd for the seller duty.

title: No Mold Disclosure Duty
bodyText: North Dakota has no mold disclosure requirement, no statutory mold standard, and no remediation timeline. Mold is not therefore risk-free: visible mold or the water intrusion behind it can put you in breach of the duty to keep the premises fit and habitable and to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (§ 47-16-13.1(1)(a)-(b)), and a tenant who gives you notice and gets no repair in a reasonable time can repair and deduct, or vacate and stop paying rent (§ 47-16-13). Treat a moisture complaint as a habitability matter on a clock rather than a disclosure question.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT, recorded as a row per the standing rule on log-only absences. | EVIDENTIARY BASIS UPGRADED. Now resting on the complete Chapter 47-16 primary text (no mold provision) plus an official ndlegis.gov full-text search on 2026-09-27. | SEARCH CAVEAT stated honestly: "mold" is a poor search term in this corpus -- 471 hits, dominated by manufacturing molds, the verb, and unrelated testimony -- so absence here is established primarily by the full-chapter read rather than by the search. A targeted 'landlord mold' search surfaced no Century Code section. | NEAR MISS, not law: 2023 SB 2303 amendments would have required a DEVELOPER to disclose toxic black mold risk in a basement built below the ordinary high water mark, to a PURCHASER. That is a sale-side developer duty in a proposed amendment, not a landlord duty, and it is not in the current code. title: No Bed Bug Disclosure or Treatment Rule
bodyText: North Dakota imposes no bed bug disclosure duty, no treatment timeline, and no allocation of treatment cost between landlord and tenant. An infestation is handled under the general duties instead: your obligation to keep the premises fit and habitable and to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (§ 47-16-13.1(1)(a)-(b)), against the tenant's obligation to keep the occupied part of the premises as clean and safe as its condition permits (§ 47-16-13.2(2)). Because nothing divides the cost by statute, whatever your lease says about pest treatment is what will govern -- so say it.

title: No Duty to Change the Locks for a Domestic Violence Victim
bodyText: North Dakota's domestic violence tenancy statute gives a victim one thing: the right to terminate the lease early on written notice, without penalty, paying the month of termination plus one additional month's rent subject to your duty to mitigate (§ 47-16-17.1). It does not give the tenant a right to require you to change the locks, and it does not give you a deadline, a cost allocation, or any immunity for doing so. If a tenant asks, you are deciding under the lease and under your own judgment, not under a statute -- and you still owe every remaining tenant on that lease quiet possession (§ 47-16-08) and the confidentiality duty in § 47-16-17.1(4), which bars you from disclosing the documentation the tenant gave you and carries statutory damages of $1,000 plus actual damages, fees and costs.

Committee minutes record senators questioning the 48-hour turnaround and the cost. The enacted § 47-16-17.1 has the notice structure and no lock provision. | CROSS-STATE CONTRAST that produced the search: NE has dv-lockchange-ne as a REQUIRED lease clause. ND has no counterpart, so the NE row must not be extended to ND. Found by the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen. | Other hits reviewed: 2019 SB 2205 (enrolled) concerns affidavits about locks changed on foreclosed mortgaged premises, not tenancies. | POINTER CORRECTED 2026-10-02 (retro, SOP rule 78, found by the full ND pointer sweep). title: No Late Fee Cap -- But Do Not Read That as No Limit
bodyText: North Dakota sets no dollar or percentage cap on late fees, and no statutory grace period. It has also declined to set one three times: bills to cap late rent fees were introduced in 2021 (HB 1440, HB 1442) and again in 2025 (SB 2236, which would have amended § 47-16-20 to cap a late fee at eight percent of the overdue rent). None became law. The absence of a cap is not the absence of a limit. Two general contract sections reach a late fee directly: penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void outright (§ 9-08-03), and a clause fixing damages in advance is void unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (§ 9-08-04). A late fee set at a level that looks punitive rather than like a genuine estimate of what a late payment actually costs you is therefore attackable in North Dakota on grounds that have nothing to do with a cap -- and § 47-16-13.3 unconscionability sits behind that. Keep the figure defensible and keep a reason for it. Separately, North Dakota has no statute setting the order in which you must apply a tenant's payment, so whether a payment goes to rent first or to fees first is a contract question here, not a statutory one.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT as to a cap; the operative limits are elsewhere. | Basis: complete Chapter 47-16 read from the official compilation (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t47c16.pdf) on 2026-09-27 -- confirmed directly that no section in the chapter mentions a late fee, a late charge, a cap, or an order of applying payments; plus an official ndlegis.gov full-text search for "late fee" on 2026-09-27 (792 hits, NO Century Code hit). This closes a gap in how the absence had been supported: late-fee's ND note said 'confirmed: full read of ch. 47-16 contains no late-fee provision', which does not exclude a cap living outside the chapter (instruction 7's failure mode). It has now been excluded statewide. | TWO FAILED 2025 BILLS, both confirmed not enacted against the current compilation rather than by reading the bill history: SB 2236 would have amended § 47-16-20 to add an eight percent cap -- § 47-16-20 as it now reads is the unchanged 'Rents - When payable' section.
