title: Stating the Purpose of the Lease Gives You Two Extra Remedies
bodyText: North Dakota attaches a specific consequence to a lease that states what the property is leased for. When real property is leased for a particular purpose the tenant must not use it for any other purpose, and if the tenant does, you may either hold the tenant responsible for the safety of the property during that use in all events, or treat the contract as rescinded (§ 47-16-11). The first of those is unusual and worth understanding: it is not a negligence standard. During a use outside the stated purpose the tenant answers for the property's safety whatever the cause, which shifts a category of loss you would otherwise carry. The second lets you treat the lease as at an end without waiting on the eviction chapter's grounds. Both depend on the lease actually stating a purpose -- which the residential-use clause does -- so this is a right you either capture in the drafting or forfeit silently.
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-11, complete Chapter 47-16 primary text. | ZERO rows in the library cited § 47-16-11 before this one. Found by the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen ('tenant runs a business from the unit', 'tenant lists the unit on Airbnb'), which reached it by walking the core chapter section by section against the ND-active rows -- the section is not something a keyword probe for short-term rentals or business use would return. | OPT-IN LANDLORD RIGHT (instruction 30): the remedy is conditioned on the lease stating a particular purpose. residential-use-only (tagged ND) supplies that condition, so ND leases built from this library do capture it; the point of the row is that a landlord who deletes or waters down that clause loses § 47-16-11 as well, which is not obvious from the clause text. | RELATIONSHIP TO THE EVICTION CHAPTER: § 47-32-01(8) makes violating a material term of a written lease an eviction ground on three days' notice of intention to evict. § 47-16-11's rescission route is a separate, direct contractual remedy under ch. 47-16 -- the same distinction edu-early-termination-grounds-nd draws for §§ 47-16-16 and 47-16-17, and this row belongs with those two. | NOT DETERMINED: whether 'treat the contract as rescinded' permits retaking possession without an eviction action. It almost certainly does not -- § 32-03-29's treble damages for forcible exclusion apply regardless of who is right about the lease (see edu-self-help-eviction-ban-nd) -- and the body deliberately does not suggest otherwise. No ND case law read.

title: Notice of Claims Against the Property
bodyText: If Tenant receives notice of any proceeding to recover the property or its possession -- including a foreclosure action, a tax proceeding, or a claim by any person other than Landlord -- Tenant will inform Landlord immediately and deliver the notice to Landlord. Tenant is responsible to Landlord for all damages Landlord sustains because Tenant failed to inform Landlord of a written notice or failed to deliver it. Tenant will not recognize or attorn to any person other than Landlord as the owner or landlord of the property without Landlord's consent or a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction.
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-25, complete Chapter 47-16 primary text: 'Every tenant who receives notice of any proceeding to recover the real property occupied by the tenant, or the possession thereof, must: 1. Inform the tenant's landlord immediately of the notice; and 2. Deliver the notice to the landlord. The tenant shall be responsible to the landlord for all damages which the landlord may sustain by reason of any omission by the tenant to inform the landlord of the notice or to deliver it to the landlord, if such notice is in writing. The attornment to a stranger is void unless made with the consent of the landlord or in consequence of a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction.' | ZERO rows in the library cited § 47-16-25 before this one. Found by the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen ('lender forecloses', 'a third party claims the property'). | WHY A LEASE CLAUSE AND NOT ONLY EDUCATION: the duty and the damages consequence exist by statute whatever the lease says, but they are worthless in practice if the tenant does not know them -- and the statute conditions the damages liability on the notice being 'in writing', which the clause does not restate because a landlord is better served by the broader contractual duty. RECOMMENDED rather than REQUIRED: North Dakota does not require the lease to contain this. | THE ATTORNMENT SENTENCE is the operative protection in a foreclosure or a disputed sale -- it stops a purported new owner from establishing a tenancy relationship directly with your tenant. Tied to edu-selling-rented-property-nd (§§ 47-16-28, 47-16-29, 47-16-30). | NOT PROPAGATED to any other state: § 47-16-25 is ND law. SD's Field Code ancestry makes an analog likely there but that is a candidate for SD's own session, never an inheritance. | No display collision: new topic_key, no supersedes relationship, and no existing ND-tagged row covers this subject.

title: When a Tenant Leaves Early: What You Can Collect and What You Must Do
bodyText: North Dakota's rules here are narrower than they look, and they differ depending on how the tenancy ended. If you evict, the tenant stays liable for rent for the remainder of the term, and that section expressly does not relieve you of the duty to mitigate damages (§ 47-16-13.7). If the lease is terminated, you have a claim for possession and for rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach (§ 47-16-13.4). If a lease ends before the time originally agreed, the tenant must pay the due proportion for the use actually made, unless that use was merely nominal and of no benefit to the tenant (§ 47-16-21). What North Dakota does not have is a general statutory duty to mitigate covering every tenant who simply leaves: the mitigation section is written into the habitability group, applying to a party aggrieved under §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 (§ 47-16-13.5), and the duty otherwise appears only in § 47-16-13.7 for an evicted tenant and § 47-16-17.1(5) for a domestic violence termination. Do not treat that as licence to sit on an empty unit and bill the departed tenant: your own lease promises reasonable mitigation efforts, common law may supply the rest, and a flat early-termination or lease-break fee is separately exposed as a contractual penalty under § 9-08-03 or as liquidated damages under § 9-08-04. Re-rent, document the effort, and charge actual loss.
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-13.4, 47-16-13.5, 47-16-13.7, 47-16-21, with §§ 9-08-03 and 9-08-04. Complete Chapter 47-16 primary text; ch. 9-08 read from the official compilation on 2026-09-27. | §§ 47-16-13.4 and 47-16-21 had ZERO rows in the library before this one; § 47-16-13.5 appeared only inside edu-holdover-damages-nd's notes. Found by the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen ('tenant wants out early', 'tenant abandons mid-term'). | DISAGREEMENT RECORDED RATHER THAN RECONCILED, per the standing rule. A research pass run for this project on 2026-09-27 characterised § 47-16-13.5's mitigation duty as 'Present -- general'. The primary text does not read that way: the section opens 'Any party aggrieved under sections 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 may recover appropriate damages. However, the aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages.' On its face the mitigation sentence attaches to the aggrieved party that the first sentence defines, which is scoped to the habitability group. This row states the narrower, text-bound reading and flags the difference; it does not adopt the broader one, and it does not rely on the narrower one to tell a landlord it is safe not to mitigate. title: Fire or Casualty Damage
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty to an extent that enjoyment of the property is substantially impaired, Tenant may either (a) immediately vacate the property and notify Landlord in writing within fourteen days afterward of Tenant's intention to terminate this Lease, in which case this Lease terminates as of the date Tenant vacated, or (b) if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate only the part of the property made unusable by the casualty, in which case Tenant's Rent obligation is reduced in proportion to the loss in fair rental value of the property. If this Lease terminates under this Section, Landlord will return all prepaid Rent and the Security Deposit that Tenant is entitled to recover, accounting for Rent as of the date of the casualty. Tenant remains responsible for damage caused by Tenant's own negligence. Nothing in this Section limits any right Tenant has under applicable law.

(1)(a) tenant may immediately vacate and give WRITTEN notice of intent to terminate within FOURTEEN days thereafter, and the agreement then terminates as of the date of vacating -- not the date of notice. (1)(b) if continued occupancy is lawful, tenant may vacate the unusable part and rent liability is reduced in proportion to the diminution in FAIR RENTAL VALUE. (2) on termination the landlord 'shall return all prepaid rent and security recoverable under section 76-1416'; accounting occurs as of the DATE OF THE CASUALTY; and the tenant remains responsible for damage caused by his own negligence. The 14-day figure and the vacate-then-notify order were both taken from the primary text. title: Fire or Casualty - What You Owe Back, and When the Clock Starts
bodyText: If fire or casualty damages the property enough to substantially impair the tenant's enjoyment of it, the tenant may move out immediately and notify you in writing within 14 days that they are ending the lease, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate only the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the loss in fair rental value (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1429). Three details of Nebraska's fire-and-casualty rule catch landlords out. FIRST, the termination date is the date the tenant VACATED, not the date you received their notice: the tenant vacates first and then has fourteen days to notify you in writing, so a notice that arrives two weeks later still ends the tenancy as of the earlier move-out date, and rent is accounted for as of the date of the casualty itself (§76-1429). SECOND, you owe back all prepaid rent plus the security deposit the tenant can recover under §76-1416 - the casualty does not convert the deposit into damages, and the §76-1416 return deadline and penalty still apply. THIRD, a tenant who stays but loses part of the unit owes proportionally less rent, measured by the drop in FAIR RENTAL VALUE, not by floor area. The one thing that stays with the tenant is damage caused by their own negligence. You cannot contract around any of this: §76-1415(1)(a) voids a lease term waiving the tenant's rights under the Act. And if the tenancy ends, §76-1405 puts a duty to mitigate damages on the aggrieved party, so re-letting effort is expected rather than optional.

title: Meth Labs: You Must Report, You Must Not Re-Rent, and You Can Terminate in Three Days
bodyText: Nebraska has a four-section scheme for methamphetamine-contaminated rentals that sits outside the landlord-tenant act entirely, and it imposes real duties on you. YOU MUST REPORT: a property owner with knowledge of a clandestine drug lab on their property must report it as soon as practicable to local law enforcement or the Nebraska State Patrol (§71-2433). YOU MUST NOT RE-RENT: you may not permit human habitation or use of contaminated property until rehabilitation is complete and the local public health department has released the property, and knowingly violating that carries a civil penalty of up to $1,000 enforced by the Department of Health and Human Services (§71-2434(3)). YOU PAY FOR THE OVERSIGHT: the local public health department may charge you for the costs of monitoring the rehabilitation (§71-2434(2)). YOU CAN GET THE TENANT OUT FAST: notwithstanding any other provision of law, if leased property contains a clandestine drug lab you may terminate the lease on THREE DAYS' written notice for the purpose of rehabilitating it (§71-2435) - no cure period, and it overrides the usual 14-day and 7-day notice mechanics. 'Contaminated property' reaches any enclosed area intended for human habitation that has been contaminated by methamphetamine, its residue, or other substances from such a lab (§71-2432(2)).

title: Selling the Property, or Changing Managers - How You Actually Get Off the Hook
bodyText: Nebraska releases a selling landlord from future liability, but only if you do two specific things. FIRST, give the tenant WRITTEN NOTICE of the conveyance: a landlord who conveys the premises in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the lease and the Act only as to events occurring AFTER that written notice (§76-1420(1)). Events before it stay yours. SECOND, deal with the deposit separately: the release does NOT cover money and property the tenant is entitled to under §76-1416, so you remain personally liable for the security deposit and prepaid rent unless you ASSIGN them to the purchaser and give the tenant written notice of the assignment - which then does release you. Selling without assigning the deposit leaves you exposed for it after you no longer hold it. The same structure covers a manager: a manager is relieved of liability as to events after written notice to the tenant that their management has ended (§76-1420(2)). Two cautions. The section opens 'Unless otherwise agreed', so a lease or purchase agreement can change this allocation - check what yours says. And a change of owner or manager also restarts your §76-1417 disclosure duty, since the tenant is entitled to the current owner's and manager's name and address.

(1) releases the conveying landlord 'as to events occurring subsequent to written notice to the tenant of the conveyance', conditioned on a 'good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser', but 'the landlord remains liable to the tenant for any property and money to which the tenant is entitled under section 76-1416, except that assignment of any security deposits or prepaid rents to a bona fide purchaser with written notice to the tenant shall serve to relieve the conveying landlord of any further liability under section 76-1416.' (2) is the manager analog. Both open 'Unless otherwise agreed', which is why the row says the allocation is alterable. Source: Laws 1974, LB 293, s20; Laws 2001, LB 7, s15. *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: §76-1420 was cited NOWHERE in the Nebraska library, and Nebraska had no row of any kind for selling a tenanted property or changing managers, while WY, KS, ND, MN, OH, NV and AZ all do. title: Your House Rules Are Enforceable Only If They Clear Six Tests
bodyText: Nebraska lets you adopt rules about the tenant's use and occupancy of the premises, but a rule is enforceable against the tenant only if ALL SIX of these hold (§76-1422): its purpose is to promote the appearance, convenience, safety or welfare of the tenants, to preserve your property from abusive use, or to distribute services and facilities fairly; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner; it is explicit enough to fairly inform the tenant what they must or must not do; it is not a device for evading your own obligations; and the tenant had notice of it when they entered into the lease. ADDING A RULE MID-TENANCY is allowed on different terms: a rule adopted after the lease is signed binds the tenant if you give reasonable notice of its adoption AND it 'does not work a substantial modification of his bargain'. So a new quiet-hours rule will usually stick; a new rule that effectively re-prices the tenancy or strips away something they bargained for will not. Enforcement runs through the ordinary noncompliance route at §76-1431, which means a rule violation is handled as a lease breach with the notice and cure mechanics that go with it - not as an independent ground for immediate termination.
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. The six conditions in the row are subdivisions (1) through (6) in order, compressed but not reordered or generalized. Closing paragraph quotes the statute's final sentence: 'A rule or regulation adopted after the tenant enters into the rental agreement is enforceable against the tenant if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the tenant and it does not work a substantial modification of his bargain.' The §76-1431 enforcement hook is express in the statute's opening ('It is enforceable as provided in section 76-1431'). Source: Laws 1974, LB 293, s22 -- never amended. *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: §76-1422 was cited NOWHERE in the Nebraska library, even though the NE-active set carries at least five clauses that ARE house rules within the meaning of the section -- common-area-use, no-disturbance, guest-policy, guest-policy-day-limit, parking-ne and smoking-policy -- and the library already has the analogous row for Kansas (edu-rules-regulations-enforceability-ks) and for NV and AZ. title: Towing From Your Lot - No Signs, No Lawful Tow, and No Kickbacks
bodyText: Nebraska conditions a private tow on posted signs, and the rule splits by city size. OUTSIDE Omaha and Lincoln, parking in a PROPERLY POSTED restricted lot without the consent of the owner or tenant authorized to give permission is an infraction, and the vehicle may be towed at the lot owner's or tenant's request (§60-2401.01). IN Omaha (metropolitan class) and Lincoln (primary class), unless the city has adopted a conforming ordinance, vehicles parked without consent are subject to towing 'if the lot is properly posted' (§60-2401). Either way the signs carry the whole thing, and §60-2402 sets what they must say: they must be readily visible and must state the purpose or purposes for parking on the lot, the hours of restricted parking, and WHO TO CONTACT for information about a towed vehicle. A lot with no signs, or signs missing any of those three items, gives you no lawful tow. DO NOT TAKE A KICKBACK: an owner or tenant causing a vehicle to be towed 'shall not solicit or accept therefor a commission, gift, gratuity, or any form of compensation or wealth' from the towing business (§60-2411). Free towing arrangements and per-tow payments from the operator are exactly what this prohibits. The rest is on the tower, not you, but it affects your tenants: the tower must verify that whoever ordered the tow is really the lot's owner or tenant (§60-2409), notify law enforcement of the plate within 24 hours (§60-2403), and send the vehicle's owner and any lienholder a certified-mail notice within 15 business days (§60-2410(2)). Towing and storage become a lien on the vehicle but never on its contents, and the vehicle can be disposed of after 90 days (§60-2410(1)).

CLASS-OF-CITY SCOPE IS REAL, NOT DECORATIVE: §60-2401 applies to 'cities of the metropolitan or primary class' and §60-2401.01 applies 'Except in cities of the metropolitan or primary class' -- Nebraska's metropolitan class is Omaha and its primary class is Lincoln. The city identifications are from general knowledge of Nebraska's statutory city classes and were NOT read from the classification statute today; the statutory text supports the metropolitan/primary split itself, which is what the row turns on. §60-2401 also carries an 'ordinance conforming to section 60-2401.01' escape that a city may have used, so an Omaha or Lincoln landlord should check the local ordinance -- flagged per instruction 20, not resolved. *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: the whole Chapter 60 scheme was cited NOWHERE in the Nebraska library. title: Nebraska Does Regulate Radon - In New Construction, Not in Disclosure
bodyText: Nebraska requires no radon disclosure to tenants, but it does regulate radon in new buildings, and that reaches you if you build or bought new. New construction built after September 1, 2019 that is intended to be regularly occupied by people must be built using radon resistant new construction (§76-3504). The required minimum standards are specific: sealed or gasketed sump lids; a passive subslab depressurization system with a vent pipe of at least three inches running up through the building and terminating at least twelve inches above the roof and at least ten feet from any window or opening; separate vent pipes where interior footings divide the subslab material; visible interior vent pipes labelled 'Radon Reduction System' on each floor and in accessible attics; and an electrical circuit terminated in an approved box near the anticipated fan location so an active system can be added later. THERE ARE ONLY TWO EXEMPTIONS THAT APPLY TO A DWELLING (§76-3505): the project used the design of a licensed architect or professional engineer, or the county's average radon concentration is below 2.7 picocuries per liter as determined by the state. The third exemption - a local building official deciding it is unnecessary - is expressly unavailable 'other than for any residential dwelling unit', so it does not help a rental. Converting the passive system to an active one later is expressly permitted (§76-3506). Nebraska is among the highest-radon states in the country, so a passive system that was never activated is a live habitability and marketing question even though no statute makes you test or disclose.

title: Medical Cannabis Is Now Legal in Nebraska - Your Smoking Ban Still Works, Your Crime Clause Does Not
bodyText: Nebraska voters legalized medical cannabis in 2024, and the practical effect on a lease is narrower than most landlords expect. What changed: it is no longer an offense under state OR local law for a qualified patient to use, possess and acquire an allowable amount of cannabis for a medical condition, or for a caregiver to obtain and deliver it for them, and that conduct is removed from the Uniform Controlled Substances Act (§71-24,105). What did NOT change: nothing in the act requires you to permit cannabis on your property, so a contractual no-smoking clause remains enforceable against a qualified patient as an ordinary lease term. What you should stop relying on: any lease or statutory hook keyed to ILLEGAL or CRIMINAL drug activity. A registered patient's medical use is no longer illegal under state law, so it cannot support Nebraska's fast-track eviction for drug-related criminal activity under §76-1431, and treating it as criminal conduct is a real risk. Enforce it as a breach of your smoking or house-rules term instead, on the ordinary notice-and-cure track. Two further cautions: cannabis remains illegal under federal law, which still matters for federally assisted housing; and a request to use a non-smoked form as a disability accommodation is a fair-housing question under §20-319(2)(b), not a cannabis question.

title: No Duty to Pay Interest on a Security Deposit
bodyText: Nebraska imposes no duty to hold a security deposit in an interest-bearing account, to pay the tenant interest on it, or to keep it in a separate or escrow account. You may hold it with your own funds and keep any interest it earns. What Nebraska does regulate is the amount (one month's rent, plus up to one quarter of a month's rent as a pet deposit) and the return: a written itemized accounting and refund within fourteen days of demand after the tenancy ends, with a penalty for wrongful retention (§76-1416). If you operate in other states, do not carry this one across - deposit-interest duties are one of the most common state divergences in this area, and several states in this library do impose them.

title: How a Nebraska Eviction Runs - and the Second Statute Nobody Reads
bodyText: Nebraska has TWO possession procedures, and which one you are in matters. The landlord-tenant act's own route is an action for possession: you file a complaint for restitution of the premises (§§76-1440, 76-1441), the case is tried on a short statutory timetable, and on a judgment for you the court issues a writ of restitution (§76-1446), with appeal governed by §76-1447. Separately, Nebraska's older forcible entry and detainer statutes, §§25-21,219 to 25-21,235, supply a parallel route with their own jurisdiction, notice-to-leave, trial, restitution and appeal-bond mechanics, and §25-21,220 says expressly that those provisions are not exclusive. Three things to keep straight. First, you cannot take possession yourself: self-help lockouts, removals and service shutoffs give the tenant remedies under §76-1430, and §76-1436 limits recovery of possession to the statutory process. Second, the tenant can turn the nonpayment case into a money fight - in an action for possession based on nonpayment, or an action for rent where the tenant is still in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the Act, and the court may order rent paid into court and net the two sides off (§76-1428). If no rent remains due after that netting, judgment on possession goes to the TENANT. Third, that cuts your way too: if the tenant's defense or counterclaim is without merit and not raised in good faith, you may recover reasonable attorney's fees (§76-1428(1)).
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. Gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36 sources 3 and 4. CONTROLLING TEXT: Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1428 read verbatim section-open, both subsections -- the counterclaim, pay-into-court and netting mechanics and the bad-faith attorney-fee award are all quoted from it. The Chapter 25 forcible entry and detainer sections are identified by section number and title from the official search (§§25-21,219 jurisdiction, 25-21,220 against whom / not exclusive, 25-21,221 notice to leave, 25-21,226 trial and judgment, 25-21,230 writ of execution form, 25-21,234 and 25-21,235 appeal and supersedeas) and were NOT read in full today. The 'not exclusive' statement rests on §25-21,220's title, which is a title-level claim and is flagged as such -- the row says the route exists and is parallel, and deliberately states no Chapter 25 notice period or bond figure, because those were not read. §§76-1440, 76-1441, 76-1446, 76-1430 and 76-1436 are carried from the original NE pass. *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: Nebraska had no eviction-procedure row at all, while SD, TX, FL and AZ each have one, and §76-1428 was cited NOWHERE in the library -- it is one of the two sections (with §76-1429) that the NE citation inventory skipped between 76-1427 and 76-1430. *** THE §76-1428 FEE AWARD IS A LANDLORD-FAVOURABLE OMISSION, not just a gap: edu-statutory-attorney-fee-actions-ne told Nebraska landlords which statutory fee awards exist and did not list this one. That row is amended today to add it. NOT RESEARCHED: the actual Chapter 25 timetables and bond amounts, when a landlord would choose the FED route over the Act's route, and whether the two can be pleaded in the alternative. This row is a map, not a procedure manual, and says so by omission.

title: Things Nebraska Has No Statute For - Checked Across the Whole Code
bodyText: Seven things landlords ask about that Nebraska has no statute on anywhere in its code, not merely nothing in the landlord-tenant act. (1) NO TENANT PROTECTION ON FORECLOSURE: Nebraska has no statute requiring notice to tenants of a pending foreclosure and none giving a tenant the right to stay after a foreclosure sale. The federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act is what governs, and it is federal law that does not depend on Nebraska adopting anything. (2) NO CASH-RENT RECEIPT DUTY: nothing requires you to give a written receipt for rent paid in cash. Give one anyway - it is your proof of payment as much as theirs. (3) NO HOLDING-DEPOSIT RULES: nothing regulates a pre-lease holding or reservation deposit, what it may be used for, or whether it is refundable if the applicant backs out. Your written agreement is the only thing governing it, so put the terms in writing. (4) NO STATE RENTAL REGISTRATION OR LICENCE: there is no statewide rental registry or landlord licence. Omaha and Lincoln run their own programmes and are not resolved here. (5) NO SQUATTER-SPECIFIC REMEDY: Nebraska has no separate unauthorized-occupant or squatter-removal statute; an occupant with no right to be there is removed through the ordinary possession and forcible-entry routes. (6) NO MOLD RULES: no mold disclosure duty, no remediation standard, no mold-specific habitability provision. (7) NO TYPOGRAPHY REQUIREMENTS: no Nebraska statute makes any residential lease term depend on being bold, underlined, capitalised, in a minimum type size, or in a separate document. Nothing in your lease is void for how it is formatted.

Quoting does not force a phrase ('"convenience fee"' returned MORE results than the bare terms), and multi-word input is matched loosely across the words, so 'holding deposit' returned 58 banking-deposit sections and 'application fee' 648. A nonsense control term ('zzzqqqxyzzy') returned 0, so a 0-hit result IS meaningful. Method therefore used the most DISTINCTIVE SINGLE WORD per topic and reviewed every hit across all result pages (pagination is the 'start' POST parameter; 25 per page). Absences below are statutes-only: the Nebraska Administrative Code, municipal codes and case law were not searched. CONFIRMED ABSENT x7, STATUTE-WIDE, each with the terms run. (1) FORECLOSURE: 'foreclosure tenant' (11 results, all reviewed: §§25-202, 25-1104, 25-328, 76-238, 76-301, 77-203, 40-101, 71-15,113, 25-1533, 36-105 -- none a tenant protection). The statute-wide 'landlord' sweep returned no foreclosure section. Several other states in this library DO have one (NV, CA, MN, NJ, FL, AZ), so this is a real divergence, not an untested guess. The PTFA reference is general knowledge, NOT read from primary source -- flagged per instruction 16 as federal and outside any state bill-tracking watch. (2) CASH RECEIPT: 'written receipt' (508 results -- heavy false-positive load from the loose word matching, top pages reviewed and all insurance, tax, lien and licensing provisions; no landlord-tenant hit). Corroborated by the 'landlord' sweep returning no receipt section. WEAKEST of the seven because the result set was too large to review exhaustively -- recorded honestly as such rather than as a clean absence. (3) HOLDING DEPOSIT: 'holding deposit' (58 results, all banking), 'holding fee' (101, all licensing and permit fees); no hit regulates a pre-lease deposit. (4) RENTAL REGISTRATION: 'rental registration' (17 results, all tax, vehicle and gaming). Omaha and Lincoln programmes flagged, not resolved, per instruction 20. (5) SQUATTER: 'unauthorized occupant' (1 result, §25-21,277, diversion of utility services -- not a removal remedy). (6) MOLD: 'mold' (6 results: §§79-10,110, 79-10,110.02, 77-2701.47, 44-5004, 2-3991, 2-2624 -- school health-and-safety levies, manufacturing equipment, health insurance and dairy packaging), 'mildew' (1, §2-2624), 'fungus' (6, all pesticide, nail-technology and plant-pest definitions). This is the cleanest absence in the set. (7) TYPOGRAPHY (instruction 28): 'underlined' (3 results: §§21-214, 25-2602.02, 45-808 -- co-operative definitions, an arbitration-contract statement and a consumer contract; none landlord-tenant), 'boldface' (25 results, all reviewed -- the Chapter 76 hits are §76-2110 condominium and time-share disclosure, §§76-2719, 76-2720, 76-2722 equity-purchase contracts, §76-2713 foreclosure consulting and §76-3112 private transfer fees, none of which reaches a residential lease), 'conspicuous' and 'separate writing' (143 and 123 results; no §76-14xx hit on the pages reviewed). CONCLUSION: NO bold, underline, capitalisation, type-size or separate-document rule conditions any Nebraska residential lease term -- the sharpest contrast in the library with Texas, where 17 terms are void or ineffective without specific formatting. *** BOUNDARY, stated plainly: statutes only. The Nebraska Administrative Code, municipal codes and case law were NOT searched, so each item above is 'no Nebraska STATUTE', which is what the row claims and no more.

title: Steam Radiator Cover Notice
bodyText: [BUILDER: attach as a rider to the lease wherever the property has uncovered steam radiators; Landlord must also give this notice in writing at least once a year and post it in the common area where tenant notices are posted.] Steam Radiator Covers. Tenant may ask Landlord in writing to cover each steam radiator in Tenant's unit with an insulating material or cover that protects tenants, occupants and others from burns caused by contact with the radiator. Landlord will install the covers within 90 days after receiving Tenant's written request.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 2 (real-lease comparison) lead: NJ Realtors Form 125-10/2022 carries a steam-radiator rider. Verified against the chapter law on the Legislature's site: P.L.2021, c.259 (approved 2021-11-08; effective the first day of the third month after enactment), codified N.J.S.A. 52:27D-198.20. 1.a: within 90 days of a tenant's written request, 'an owner of a residential rental property shall cover each steam radiator in the tenant's unit' with insulating material or a cover protecting against burns. 1.b: owner must notify tenants of the right to request covers 'as a rider to any written residential lease agreement and in writing at least annually', and post in common areas where tenant notices are displayed. 1.c: fine up to $500 by the enforcing agency; 1.d: injured tenant, occupant or other person has a private action. The act does not define 'residential rental property' (so no unit-count threshold stated) - builder should include this rider for any unit with steam radiators. No prescribed wording; body tracks the statute. Relation to case law: J.H. v. R&M Tagliareni, LLC (N.J. 2019) held no landlord duty where the tenant controlled the radiator heat - the statute now imposes the duty on request. LAYOUT: lease RIDER (instruction 28); annual written notice and common-area posting are outside the lease. CONDITIONAL on steam radiators. | NJ: Retro check 2026-10-03 (SOP 1.46), rule 79. Basis was the chapter law (official); re-read compiled N.J.S.A. 52:27D-198.20. Qualifier fixed: the rider duty in subsection b. applies to "residential rental property that contains uncovered steam radiators"; the builder note said any unit with steam radiators. Subsection c. fine applies to an owner "who leases any property ... in violation". title: Private Well Water Test Results
bodyText: The property's drinking water comes from a private well. Tenant acknowledges receiving a written copy of the most recent water test results for the property under the New Jersey Private Well Testing Act.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 2 lead: NJ Realtors Form 125-10/2022 §42 (Private Well Testing). Controlling text read on the FindLaw host copy (current as of 2024-01-01; not compared with the official site): N.J.S.A. 58:12A-32 (Private Well Testing Act, N.J.S.A. 58:12A-26 to -37): a lessor of property whose potable water supply is a private well must test within 18 months after 2002-09-14 and at least once every five years thereafter; give a written copy of results to each rental unit within 30 days after receipt; give a new lessee a written copy of the most recent results; seasonal rentals may instead post the results inside the unit. title: Fire and Other Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire without the fault of Tenant, Landlord will repair it as quickly as possible, and Rent will stop until the property has been fully repaired. If the building is totally destroyed by fire or otherwise without the fault of Tenant, Rent will be paid up to the date of destruction, and this Lease will then end.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 2 lead: NJ Realtors Form 125-10/2022 §21 (Fire and Other Casualty). NJ had no casualty row. Controlling text read section-open 2026-09-26 (official N.J.S.A. text pasted by Taylor): N.J.S.A. 46:8-6 (fire injury without lessee's fault: landlord repairs 'as speedily as possible'; in default of repair 'the rent shall cease' until complete repair) and 46:8-7 (total destruction 'by fire or otherwise' without lessee's fault: rent paid to the time of destruction, then the lease ends). Both apply only where the lease does not 'otherwise stipulate', so this clause restates the statutory defaults rather than varying them - a deliberate choice (tenant-neutral; no waiver risk under N.J.S.A. 46:8-48). Form 125 departs from the defaults (90-day repair window / cancellation); not adopted. Partial-destruction-by-other-casualty (non-fire) is not addressed by either section; the clause is silent on it. Checklist row 63 already cited these sections without a row. | NJ: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-casualty-nj). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Owners Must Carry Liability Insurance
bodyText: New Jersey requires the owner of a rental unit to carry liability insurance of at least $500,000 for combined property damage and bodily injury, or at least $300,000 for an owner-occupied multifamily home of four or fewer units. Owners must register the certificate of insurance with the municipality each year. A municipality can fine a noncompliant owner $500 to $5,000.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 2 lead: NJ Realtors Form 125-10/2022 §22 cites the insurance minimums. Verified against the chapter law on the Legislature's site: P.L.2022, c.92 (signed 2022-08-05), codified N.J.S.A. 40A:10A-1 (coverage: $500,000; $300,000 for owner-occupied multifamily of four or fewer units) and 40A:10A-2 (annual registration of the certificate with the municipality; fine $500-$5,000 by summary proceeding). Effective: 90 days (new policies) / 180 days (renewals and the multifamily provision) after enactment; DCA Local Finance Notice 2022-23 gives 2022-11-03 and 2023-02-01. title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText: A New Jersey landlord cannot simply have a tenant's or visitor's car towed because the lease allows it. On most rental properties, a tow without the vehicle owner's consent is lawful only if the landlord has a private-property towing contract with the tow company, has authorized removal of that particular vehicle, and has posted a sign at least 36 by 36 inches at every vehicle entrance stating when and for what parking is allowed, that violators will be towed at the owner's expense, and the tow company's name, contact details, charges and storage address; the car must go to secure storage within a reasonable distance. In a residential community with clearly marked assigned spaces, a simpler entrance sign is allowed, but the landlord must still document approval of each tow. These rules do not apply to a single-family home, an owner-occupied building of six or fewer units, or a car blocking a driveway or garage entrance.

Source 3 (scenario screen) gap: 'car towed from the lot' - parking-vehicle-rules defers to law (NJ note added 2026-09-26); an education row makes the preconditions visible, as AZ did (edu-towing-az). title: Occupancy by Children
bodyText: Children who are members of Tenant's household may live at the property. Each child who will live at the property is to be listed with the other occupants under this Lease's occupancy terms. Landlord places no restriction on occupancy by children other than those occupancy terms, which apply to every occupant regardless of age. [If the property is housing for older persons that qualifies for the fair-housing exemption for such housing, replace this Section with a statement of the property's age requirements for occupancy.]
notes: NV: NRS 118A.200(3)(c), Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked): every written rental agreement must contain provisions relating to "occupancy by children or pets"; 118A.200(9) makes a nonconforming agreement unlawful to use and a contravening provision void. pet-policy-nv covers pets; no NV row covered children until this pass. Surfaced by gap-discovery source 2 (NV log backfill section, Part 1): the GLVAR lease's occupant clause is silent on children too, and mapping it against the (3) list exposed the gap. 118A.200(5)(a) presumes no restriction on children absent a written agreement. Familial status is a protected class (NRS 118.100, edu-fair-housing-nv), so the clause states no child-specific limit; neutral occupancy limits stay in permitted-occupants. BUILDER: offer the age-restricted-housing bracket only on the landlord's say-so; the federal and state exemption texts for housing for older persons were not read. (3)(c) text is unchanged by AB 121 and SB 201 (2025) per the session-law check recorded on edu-lease-content-requirements-nv; effective_from blank (long-standing).

title: Required Fees
bodyText: In addition to the Monthly Rent and any deposit stated in this Lease, Tenant is required to pay the following fees, for the purposes stated: [list each required fee - its amount, when it is due and the purpose for which it is required, e.g. "a nonrefundable cleaning charge of $___, due at signing, to pay for cleaning the premises after Tenant vacates" - or state "None"]. Any required fee that is payable every rental period is included in the Monthly Rent and is not charged in addition to it, except a utility fee that this Lease identifies with the Monthly Rent as the law allows. No charge applies to a late or partial payment of Rent, or to a dishonored check or other returned payment, except a late fee or returned-payment charge stated in this Lease.
notes: NV: NRS 118A.200(3)(e) and (3)(g), Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked): the lease must contain provisions relating to "fees which are required and the purposes for which they are required" and "charges which may be required for late or partial payment of rent or for return of any dishonored check". Before this row no NV clause listed required fees with their purposes, and late-fee-nv and returned-payments-nv are optional rows, so a lease without them said nothing on (3)(g). The last sentence closes (3)(g) whether or not those rows are used, and covers partial payments, which no NV row mentioned (118A.200(5)(c)'s no-charge presumption applies only where there is no written agreement). Periodic fees: 118A.200(6)-(8) (rent-single-figure-nv). BUILDER: a payment whose purpose is to remedy a rent default, repair damage or clean is a security deposit whatever it is called (118A.240). It counts toward the three-month cap (security-deposit-cap-nv) and must be refundable, except a reasonable nonrefundable cleaning charge (118A.242(8)). Don't let a user list a "nonrefundable pet fee" or "damage fee" here. This row gives security-deposit-return-nv's "nonrefundable cleaning charge ... stated in this Lease" a place in the lease. Surfaced by gap-discovery source 2: the GLVAR lease's summary-of-monies section lists each fee by name, the library had no counterpart. (3)(e) and (3)(g) are unchanged by the 2025 bills per the session-law check on edu-lease-content-requirements-nv; effective_from blank (long-standing).

title: Tenant-Performed Repairs and Maintenance
bodyText: [Optional. Include only if Landlord and Tenant agree that Tenant will perform specified tasks.] Tenant agrees to perform the following specified repairs, maintenance tasks or minor remodeling: [list each task specifically, e.g. replace heating and air-conditioning filters every [number] months with filters Landlord provides; replace light bulbs; keep the pool clean and its water balanced]. Landlord and Tenant make this agreement in good faith. Tenant is not entering into it because Landlord or Landlord's agent refused to perform any repair, maintenance task or remodeling that Landlord is required by law to perform, and it does not reduce Landlord's obligations to any other tenant. Landlord remains responsible for keeping the property habitable as applicable law requires, and nothing in this Section requires Tenant to pay any fee or charge for work that is Landlord's duty, except work needed because of a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, a member of Tenant's household, or another person on the premises with Tenant's consent.
notes: NV: NRS 118A.290(2)-(5), Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked) (A. 1999, 2007, 2023). (2): landlord and tenant "may agree that the tenant is to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling only if" the agreement is in good faith and does not diminish the landlord's obligations to other tenants. (3): not in good faith if the landlord owes the work under (1) and the tenant agrees because the landlord refused it. (4): no fee or charge for work that is the landlord's (1) duty (the 2023 home-warranty deductible ban, edu-habitability-duty-nv). (5): charges allowed for tenant-caused conditions. OPT-IN LANDLORD RIGHT (instruction 30): without a written list the tasks stay with the landlord. The recital cannot make the agreement good faith; it records the facts the statute tests. Drafted conservatively: tasks are listed specifically, habitability stays with Landlord, and there is no charge for landlord-duty work. Whether (2) lets a (1) repair itself be shifted is not settled by the text and is not relied on. Surfaced by gap-discovery source 2: the GLVAR lease's maintenance section assigns minor repairs, filters, yard and pool care to the tenant. landscaping-irrigation and snow-removal already allocate those tasks; the builder should not list them twice. Not shareable with tenant-repair-agreement-tx (TX's bold/underline and cost-shifting rules).

title: Designated Repairer for Tenant Repairs
bodyText: [Optional. Include only if Landlord wants to designate who performs this work.] If applicable law permits Tenant to have work done at Landlord's expense because Landlord failed to make a repair or to supply an essential service after notice, that work must be performed by [name the person or firm, or describe a class of persons or firms qualified to do the work, e.g. "a contractor holding a Nevada license for that type of work"], and Tenant will comply with this specification. If that person or firm is unavailable or unable to perform the repairs, Tenant will use another qualified person who performs repairs. This Section does not otherwise limit any remedy applicable law gives Tenant.
notes: NV: NRS 118A.360(2), Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked) (added 1977, no amendment): "The landlord may specify in the rental agreement or otherwise that work done under this section and NRS 118A.380 must be performed by a named person or firm or class of persons or firms qualified to do the work and the tenant must comply with the specifications." title: Political Signs in HOA and Condo Communities
bodyText: If the rental is in a common-interest community (a homeowners' or condominium association), the association may not prohibit a unit's owner or an occupant - which includes your tenant - from displaying political signs in the part of the property the owner or occupant has the right to use exclusively. Protected signs are those supporting or opposing a candidate, political party or ballot question in a federal, state, local or association election. Each may be no larger than 24 by 36 inches, only one sign per candidate, party or ballot question is protected, and signs must follow any law on posting political signs. While a tenant occupies the unit, you as the owner may not display a political sign there unless the tenant consents in writing. The rule binds the association and its governing documents; it does not address what your lease may say about signs.

(2): minimum rights. (3): definition. Found by gap-discovery source 2 (the GLVAR lease cites NRS 116 for political signs). title: Removing a Squatter or Unauthorized Occupant
bodyText: A person who enters your property without the authority of you, your representative or your tenant and does not leave after a written notice to surrender is guilty of forcible detainer, as is anyone who holds possession by force or threats. For a squatter there is a fast court process. Serve a written notice to surrender the way eviction notices are served. It must name the court and tell the occupant: that they may contest by filing an affidavit before the court closes on the fourth judicial day after service; that the court may order the sheriff or constable to remove them within 24 hours; and that property left behind will be stored safely and may be disposed of after 14 calendar days, with inventory, moving and storage costs payable before release. When the notice expires, file an affidavit of complaint with a copy of the notice and proof of service. If the occupant did not contest, or the contest raises no legal defense, the court must order removal within 24 hours; if it raises a defense, a hearing is held within 7 judicial days. An occupant who entered peaceably under an invalid lease or someone else's fraud may be given up to 20 days to leave. Keep property left behind in safe storage for 21 days after the removal or surrender before disposing of it: the notice says 14 days, but the removal section separately requires 21 days' storage. Vehicles go through the abandoned-vehicle law. If every unauthorized adult occupant has been arrested for housebreaking or unlawful occupancy, you may instead retake possession and change the locks, posting a notice with the court and contest details for at least 21 days and filing a copy with the court within 1 day. You may recover three times your actual damage to real and personal property from a person guilty of forcible entry or forcible detainer. Your tenant, as an occupant you authorized, may use the same process. For a tenant or former tenant, use the eviction procedures for tenants instead.
notes: NV: NRS 40.230, 40.240, 40.412 and 40.414, Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked) (40.230 and 40.240 A. 2015; 40.412 and 40.414 added 2015, no later amendment). 40.414 was supplied by Taylor in text batch 2, but no row cited it. STATUTE INCONSISTENCY: 40.414(3)(b)(3) tells the occupant property may be disposed of after 14 calendar days, while 40.414(7)(a)-(b) requires 21 days' safe storage before disposal and gives the occupant 14 days to move to dispute costs. The body tells landlords to wait 21 days. GUESTS: 40.240(1)(b) reaches only a person who entered WITHOUT authority. A guest who came in with the tenant's permission fits (1)(a) only if holding "by force or threats of violence", so the body does not promise this process for an ordinary overstaying guest. 40.412(4): the lock-change route is unavailable if any unauthorized occupant is still in the dwelling. title: Lease Translation When You Advertise in Another Language
bodyText: If, in your business, you advertise a rental in a language other than English and negotiate the lease in that language - orally or in writing, yourself or through an employee or agent - you must give a translation of the lease in that language to the tenant, and to anyone else who may sign it, before it is signed. This applies to a lease or rental agreement of at least one month for a dwelling used as a residence. The translation must include every term and condition; names, addresses, numbers, dollar amounts, dates and words with no accepted translation may stay in English. A later document that substantially changes the parties' rights needs a translation too; routine house rules and furniture inventories do not. If you don't comply, the tenant may cancel (rescind) the lease, and a knowing violation is a deceptive trade practice.

(3)(b): "a lease, sublease, rental contract or agreement or other contract or agreement containing a term of tenancy" of at least 1 month for a dwelling, apartment, mobile home or other dwelling unit used as a residence. title: Repair Orders and Receivership for Multifamily Rentals
bodyText: If you rent out two or more units on one parcel, your county (outside cities) or city must act when it finds that the property violates a habitability standard, a housing or building code, or a habitability, building-safety or fire-safety law badly enough to substantially endanger the health and safety of residents or the public. It must order you to repair, rehabilitate or abate the condition by a deadline. The notice and order is posted on the property and sent by certified mail to you and each affected resident, and it states that you may not retaliate against any tenant. If you don't comply, the county or city can sue to have the property declared substandard and obtain a repair order and civil penalties, and the local government or a nonprofit representing tenants can ask the court to appoint a receiver after 30 days' posted and mailed notice. Once a receiver is appointed you may not collect rent, interfere with the receiver, or encumber or transfer the property; the receiver collects the rents, makes the repairs and may borrow against the property. The court will order you to pay the local government's costs and attorney's fees. If tenants cannot safely stay, it will also order moving costs and up to 120 days of rent differential as relocation benefits, plus a first right to return; a tenant who caused the conditions gets no relocation benefits.

title: Health District Rules for Rental Units
bodyText: In a county served by a district board of health, the board may adopt and enforce regulations on health hazards in rental dwelling units - any biological, physical or chemical exposure, condition or public nuisance that may harm health - and recover its enforcement costs. If it has adopted regulations on the condition of rental units, you must give a copy to a tenant who asks for one. A tenant who gave you written notice of a habitability failure that you did not fix, or reasonably try to fix, within the statutory time may send a copy of that notice to the district board of health. If an inspection finds that you or the tenant failed to keep the unit habitable, the board may take enforcement action or refer the matter to its administrative hearing process.

title: Former Drug-Lab Properties
bodyText: A building that was used to manufacture a controlled substance illegally, such as methamphetamine, is a public nuisance if it has not been deemed safe for habitation by the board of health and the owner either lets it be used for any purpose before a certified or licensed entity has removed or remediated the contamination, or fails to have that done within 180 days after the manufacturing stops. Maintaining a public nuisance is a misdemeanor, so do not rent such a property until it has been remediated and deemed safe. The statutes set no separate duty to disclose a former drug lab to a tenant. The statute that makes certain facts immaterial in a sale deliberately leaves methamphetamine manufacture off that list, so disclosure is the safer course.

bodyText: Nevada statutes do not require a residential landlord to disclose mold, and they set no separate mold-remediation duty. Mold is handled through your general duty to keep the unit habitable and to comply with housing and health codes. In a county with a district board of health, the board can also regulate health hazards in rental units.

bodyText: The state Housing Division may run a free, voluntary program for reporting tenants' rent payments to a credit reporting agency. You may not require a tenant to take part in that program, and you may not impose any penalty or other consequence on a tenant for not taking part.

title: Ohio Private Tow-Away Zones Have Hard Sign Rules
bodyText: Before a towing service may remove a vehicle from your rental property without the vehicle owner's permission, the property must be a valid private tow-away zone. Ohio sets the signs by statute: at least eighteen inches by twenty-four inches, visible from every entrance to the property, and stating that it is a tow-away zone, who may park there (for residential property, tenants and their guests), the property address or business name, the hours of enforcement if it is not around the clock, a telephone number and the address where a towed vehicle can be recovered, and a warning that an unclaimed vehicle may lose its title. You may modify existing signs with stickers or addenda rather than replacing them. Only the property owner or an authorized agent may order a tow, and the towing service must hold a written contract with you. If the vehicle owner arrives before the vehicle is actually removed, they may reclaim it for no more than half the removal fee. Get the signs wrong and the tow is unlawful: the vehicle owner may sue under R.C. 4513.611.
notes: OH: R.C. 4513.601, private tow-away zones, read section-open 2026-09-27; effective 2023-04-07, H.B. 507 (134th G.A.). FOUND BY THE OUTSIDE-TITLE SEARCH (source 4) and the landlord-scenario screen (source 3) - Title 45 Motor Vehicles, invisible to a ch. 5321 read. Division (K) defines 'owner of private property' to include title holders, LESSEES, SUBLESSEES, MANAGERS and their agents, so a property manager is directly covered. Other duties fall on the towing service, not the landlord: notice to the sheriff or municipal police within two hours (division E); certified or express mail notice to the vehicle owner and lienholder within five business days, with a second notice if the vehicle is unclaimed 30 days later (division F); storage within 25 linear miles where practicable, well-lit and near public transit. Violation of division (H) is a minor misdemeanor for the carrier. PUCO sets the fee schedule. NOT READ: R.C. 4513.60, 4513.602, 4513.611 in full, and municipal towing licensing. Same gap shape as Arizona's edu-towing-az (AZ log 18.2).

title: If Utilities Are In Your Name, A Tenant Can Redirect Your Rent
bodyText: Where you are the utility customer of record - master-metered buildings, or any unit where you include utilities in the rent - an unpaid bill is not just your problem with the utility. Before disconnecting, the utility gives you fourteen days' notice and then attempts a separate ten-day notice to each tenant unit and posts notice conspicuously on the building. That ten-day notice tells your tenants their options, and two of them cost you money. A tenant may stop the disconnection by paying an amount equal to the current month's bill, which the utility credits to your account. Or a tenant may use the rent-deposit remedy under R.C. 5321.07 to deposit rent with the court and ask the court to spend it on the utility bill - so the rent you were owed pays the utility instead. If you are the one asking for disconnection, you get ten days' notice and you are liable for everything consumed in that period. Separately, between November 15 and April 15 the utility must give your occupants five days' notice before shutting off, and must tell them about state and federal bill-payment aid.
notes: OH: R.C. 4933.121 (effective 2005-05-18, H.B. 426, 125th G.A.) and OAC 4901:1-18-08 'Landlord-tenant provisions' (effective 2015-04-15), both read section-open 2026-09-27. FOUND BY THE OUTSIDE-TITLE SEARCH (source 4): Title 49 Public Utilities plus the PUCO administrative code - neither reachable from a ch. 5321 read. INSTRUCTION 16 FLAG: OAC 4901:1-18-08 is ADMINISTRATIVE CODE, changed by PUCO rulemaking with no bill and no legislative-tracking signal, the same monitoring problem as Ohio's assistance-animal rule (OAC 4112-5-07). The rule carries a model tenant ten-day notice as its appendix A, supplied by the utility, not drafted by the landlord. The rule read is the ELECTRIC chapter (4901:1-18); parallel gas and water rules were NOT read and may differ - flagged. The R.C. 5321.07 link matters: this is the same escrow mechanism as repair-escrow-exemption-notice-oh, and the 4901:1-18-08 route is NOT subject to 5321.07(C)'s three-or-fewer-units exemption on its face - not determined, flagged.

title: A No-Firearms Clause Does Not Bind a Licensed Ohio Tenant
bodyText: Do not put a handgun ban in an Ohio residential lease expecting it to work. R.C. 2923.126(C)(3)(b) provides that a landlord may not prohibit or restrict a tenant who holds a concealed handgun license, or the tenant's guest while the tenant is present, from lawfully carrying or possessing a handgun on the residential premises, for any rental agreement entered into on or after September 9, 2008. The restriction runs against you, not the tenant, so a lease term to the contrary is simply unenforceable against a licensee. It is narrower than it first looks: the protection is written for a licensee and for that licensee's guest while the licensee is present, and it covers lawful carrying and possession of a handgun.
notes: OH: R.C. 2923.126(C)(3)(b), read section-open 2026-09-27; section effective 2025-04-09, amended by H.B. 452, S.B. 98 and H.B. 33 (135th G.A.). FOUND BY THE OUTSIDE-TITLE SEARCH (source 4) - Title 29 Crimes, concealed-carry article; no ch. 5321 read reaches it. This is an OHIO LEASE-CONTENT RESTRICTION sitting entirely outside 5321.13, so Ohio's prohibited-terms coverage (edu-bilateral-fee-ban-oh for 5321.13(C), edu-one-way-delegation-oh for 5321.13(A),(E),(F)) did not include it. Also not researched: long guns, and whether a landlord may restrict discharge or storage as distinct from carrying or possession.

title: A Tenant Or Neighbor Can Put Your Building Into Receivership
bodyText: Ohio's habitability remedies are not the only exposure for a building in poor condition. Under R.C. 3767.41 a municipal corporation, a township, a neighbor, a tenant, or a nonprofit housing organization may bring a civil action alleging that the building is a public nuisance on grounds of structural safety, habitability, fire hazard or inadequate maintenance. If you have refused or failed to abate, the court may appoint a receiver who takes possession and control of the building, collects the rents and income, pays operating expenses and liens, hires managing agents and carries out rehabilitation work. Approved receiver expenditures and fees become a first lien on the building, superior to all prior and subsequent liens including tax liens, and the property can be sold to satisfy them. Owner-occupied buildings with three or fewer units are excluded.
notes: OH: R.C. 3767.41, read section-open 2026-09-27; effective 2023-10-03. FOUND BY THE OUTSIDE-TITLE SEARCH (source 4) - Title 37 Health-Safety-Morals, nuisance chapter. Surfaced as a landlord-relevant hit in the official code search for 'landlord' (54 results). Distinct from the R.C. 5321.07 escrow route in kind, not just degree: escrow redirects rent temporarily; a 3767.41 receiver takes possession and its lien outranks the mortgage. FIFTH OHIO PORTFOLIO THRESHOLD: owner-occupied with three or fewer units - see edu-portfolio-thresholds-oh, updated in the same delta. NOT READ: the procedural detail of 3767.41 (notice, hearing, who may be appointed, how the receivership ends) and the related nuisance sections in ch. 3767. Arizona's nearest analogue is edu-crime-nuisance-abatement-az, which is a criminal-activity statute, not a condition-based receivership - do not treat them as the same topic.

title: Ohio Requires No Radon Disclosure To A Tenant
bodyText: Ohio imposes no radon testing, mitigation or disclosure duty on a residential landlord toward a tenant. Ohio does regulate radon, but only the professionals: R.C. Chapter 3723 licenses radon testers, mitigation specialists, mitigation contractors and laboratories. Nothing in it reaches the landlord-tenant relationship. Do not be misled by R.C. 5302.30: that is the residential property disclosure form for SALES, and it does not apply to a lease.

Bed bugs in an Ohio rental are handled through the general habitability duty in R.C. 5321.04(A)(1)-(2) and the tenant's own duties in R.C. 5321.05, not through a dedicated statute. Ohio's bed bug provisions sit in the hotel chapter and do not reach a residential tenancy.

title: Ohio Has No Mold Disclosure Or Remediation Statute

A mold complaint is handled under the general habitability duty in R.C. 5321.04(A)(1)-(2), with the tenant's rent-escrow remedy under R.C. 5321.07 as the enforcement route. There is no Ohio mold-professional licensing scheme and no mold chapter.

title: Ohio Gives A Tenant No Right To Install EV Charging
bodyText: Ohio has no right-to-charge law. A residential tenant has no statutory right to install an electric vehicle charging station, and a landlord has no statutory duty to permit or accommodate one. Whether a tenant may install or use charging equipment is a matter for the lease and for R.C. 5321.06, which lets the parties agree to any term not inconsistent with Chapter 5321 or other law. Local zoning and building codes may still govern the installation itself.

title: Ohio Gives A Domestic Violence Victim No Statutory Way Out
bodyText: Ohio has no statewide domestic violence lease-termination right, no DV anti-termination protection, and no DV lock-change duty. A survivor who leaves early remains liable on the lease under ordinary contract principles, and a landlord may pursue the remaining rent, subject only to the common-law duty to mitigate. Seven other states in this library give the survivor a statutory release; Ohio does not. Tenants in federally subsidised housing are covered by the federal Violence Against Women Act instead, which is a separate regime.

title: Ohio Has No Right-To-Call-Emergency-Services Statute
bodyText: Ohio gives a tenant no statutory, non-waivable right to summon police or emergency services. R.C. 5321.02's retaliation protection is close but narrower, and its trigger list is closed: complaining to a governmental agency about a code violation materially affecting health and safety, complaining to the landlord about a R.C. 5321.04 violation, or joining with other tenants to bargain collectively. Calling 911 is on none of those. So a landlord who penalises a tenant for repeated emergency calls faces no specific statutory bar in Ohio - and because Ohio also has no domestic violence tenancy protection, a survivor making repeated calls has no state-law shield either.

title: No Ohio Source-Of-Income Rule, With One Disability Exception
bodyText: Ohio's fair housing statute, R.C. 4112.02(H), does not list source of income or receipt of housing assistance as a protected class, and Ohio has no statewide voucher-acceptance mandate. There is one exception worth knowing, and it is easy to trip over. OAC 4112-5-07(A)(1)(c) makes it unlawful disability discrimination to refuse to consider the sources of a DISABLED applicant's income, or to subject that applicant's source of income or ability to generate income to automatic discounting in whole or in part, because of the disability. So a blanket 'no vouchers' or 'wages only' screening rule applied to an applicant whose income is disability-related benefits can become a disability claim even though Ohio has no general source-of-income protection. Several Ohio cities do protect source of income by ordinance.

title: Ohio Has No Servicemember Residential Lease Termination
bodyText: Ohio gives a servicemember no state-law right to terminate a residential lease on military orders. Two Ohio provisions come close and neither does it. R.C. 1349.02 lets a deployed servicemember or spouse terminate a lease, but it is confined to MOTOR VEHICLE leases - read the definition before relying on it. R.C. 1923.062 gives a deployed tenant a stay or adjustment of an eviction action, not a termination, it runs 90 days unless justice requires otherwise, it reaches only rental agreements entered on or after May 18 2005, and it does not apply to a landlord operating fewer than four residential premises. A servicemember's actual termination right in Ohio is the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which R.C. 5321.04(A)(10) separately requires you to comply with.

title: Ohio Does Not Regulate Immigration-Status Inquiries By Landlords
bodyText: Ohio has no statute prohibiting a landlord from asking about immigration or citizenship status, and no immigrant tenant protection act. R.C. 4112.02(H) protects national origin and ancestry, and R.C. 4112.02(H)(8) bars making inquiries, eliciting information, keeping records or using application forms concerning national origin or ancestry in connection with a lease - so an inquiry framed around national origin is already unlawful. But Ohio has nothing like the immigration-status-specific prohibitions some states have enacted, and nothing barring disclosure of status to third parties.

title: Ohio Requires No Meth-Contamination Disclosure - But Permitting Drug Abuse Is A Crime
bodyText: Ohio imposes no duty to disclose to a prospective tenant that a property was used to manufacture methamphetamine or was otherwise drug-contaminated, and sets no decontamination standard for residential rental property. Four states in this library have such a disclosure; Ohio does not. What Ohio has instead runs the other way, against you: under R.C. 2925.13 an owner, lessee, occupant or person having custody, control or supervision of premises or real estate, including vacant land, who KNOWINGLY PERMITS it to be used for the commission of a felony drug abuse offence commits permitting drug abuse, a first-degree misdemeanour, rising to a fifth-degree felony where the underlying offence is manufacturing or trafficking or involves Schedule I or II manufacturing chemicals with actual knowledge.

title: Two Ohio Lease Terms That Are Never Recognised
bodyText: Two clauses that appear in ordinary lease forms have no effect at all in Ohio, and no amount of careful drafting saves them. R.C. 5321.13(D): no agreement by a tenant to the exculpation or limitation of ANY liability of the landlord arising under law, or to indemnify the landlord, shall be recognised in any rental agreement or other agreement. That reaches the whole familiar family - 'Landlord shall not be liable for', 'Tenant releases Landlord from', 'Tenant agrees to indemnify, defend and hold Landlord harmless', and a hold-harmless buried in a pet, parking, storage or utilities clause. Making it mutual does not help. Narrowing it to a specific risk does not help. Hedging it with 'to the extent permitted by law' does not help either, because the statute does not limit such a clause, it declines to recognise it. R.C. 5321.13(B): no warrant of attorney to confess judgment is recognised in any rental agreement, or in any other landlord-tenant agreement for the recovery of rent or damages. A cognovit provision in an Ohio residential lease is dead on arrival. What you use instead is insurance, not drafting: require the tenant's renter's insurance, carry your own liability cover, and rely on the statutory allocation of duties in R.C. 5321.04 and 5321.05 rather than trying to contract out of it.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.13(B),(D), READ SECTION-OPEN 2026-09-27 (effective 1990-08-22, S.B. 258, 118th G.A.). FOUND BY THE REAL-LEASE COMPARISON (source 2) - see the log's Part 1. The OHFA lease's section 15 is a sweeping exculpation-plus-indemnity clause of exactly the kind (D) refuses to recognise, and its sections 9 and 17 add 'no liability' and 'relieved of all liability' language. A document published by an Ohio state agency carries it, which is the proof that a landlord will write one unless told not to. WHY THIS ROW EXISTS AFTER A DECISION NOT TO WRITE IT: on 2026-09-18 I judged that edu-bilateral-fee-ban-oh, edu-one-way-delegation-oh and edu-no-statutory-caps-oh together covered 5321.13, so a general prohibited-terms row would duplicate them (instruction 26 consolidation). That was right for (A), (C), (E) and (F) and WRONG for (B) and (D): nothing in the Ohio set mentioned confession of judgment, and nothing told a landlord that exculpation and indemnity clauses are void. 5321.13(D) was already applied as a SCREEN across the Ohio lease clauses - four rows cite it (services-utilities-provided-ks-oh, parking-ks-oh-ca, storage-space-ks-oh-ca, tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca, plus pet-policy) - but a screen on the library's own text is not the same as telling the landlord the rule. topic_key reuses prohibited-lease-terms, which KS, NE, NV and TX already carry; Ohio had no row in the family. Ohio's (D) is BROADER than Kansas's K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(4), which carves out a landlord's liability for fire, theft or breakage in common areas - Ohio has NO such carve-out. Do not import the Kansas clause. NOT RESEARCHED: whether an Ohio court has severed a void exculpation clause or voided a whole lease; whether (D) reaches a waiver of subrogation in a tenant's insurance clause. Flagged.

title: Ohio Has Two Cure Tracks, and Picking the Wrong One Loses the Case
bodyText: Before you terminate for a tenant breach, work out which track the breach is on, because Ohio has two and they carry different notice periods. TRACK ONE - the tenant broke a duty R.C. 5321.05 imposes, and the breach materially affects health and safety. R.C. 5321.11 requires written notice specifying the act or omission and stating a termination date NOT LESS THAN THIRTY DAYS after the tenant receives it, and the tenant may cure within that window. This is not advisory: R.C. 1923.02(A)(8) says that before commencing an action on that ground, notice shall be given and compliance secured with 5321.11. It is a condition precedent to filing, so a shorter notice does not merely weaken your case, it defeats it. TRACK TWO - the tenant broke an obligation your written lease imposes, with no health-and-safety dimension. R.C. 1923.02(A)(9) carries no 5321.11 requirement, so whatever period your lease sets is the period that governs. Then, on either track, the separate three-day notice to leave the premises under R.C. 1923.04(B) still has to be served before you file, in the words the statute prescribes. Two exceptions run on their own clocks: nonpayment of rent needs no cure period, and drug activity under 5321.05(A)(9) is carved out of 5321.11 entirely and goes to the mandatory three-day notice under 5321.17(C). The practical trap: many breaches sit in both buckets at once, and if a court reads yours as Track One after you noticed it as Track Two, you filed on a defective notice. When it is genuinely arguable, give thirty days.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.11 and 1923.02(A)(8),(A)(9), BOTH READ SECTION-OPEN 2026-09-27. 5321.11 effective 1990-08-22; 1923.02 effective 2023-10-03, H.B. 33 (135th G.A.) - the same budget bill already on Ohio's legal watch. FOUND BY THE REAL-LEASE COMPARISON (source 2). The OHFA lease's section 16 gives SEVEN days for material noncompliance. That is operative under 1923.02(A)(9) for a written-lease breach and UNENFORCEABLE under (A)(8) for a 5321.05 health-and-safety breach, where 5321.11's thirty days is a condition precedent to filing. A landlord relying on the form would file on a bad notice. WHY IT WAS MISSING: default-by-tenant-ks-ne (Ohio's default clause) defers to 'the time period specified by applicable law' and points to edu-tenant-noncompliance-notice-ks for the figures - a KANSAS row, not tagged OH - so an Ohio landlord got no number from anywhere in the library. The checklist recorded the R.C. 5321.11 30-day cure and the R.C. 1923.02(A)(8) condition precedent on 2026-09-18 and no row was ever written: the same Present-in-the-checklist-absent-from-the-CSV failure as landlord-maintenance and retaliation. topic_key reuses notice-and-cure, previously SD-only. 5321.11's carve-out of 5321.05(A)(9) matches 5321.13(F)'s - the drug duty is the one obligation a landlord may neither assume nor give extra time on; see edu-mandatory-drug-termination-oh. NOT RESEARCHED: which breaches Ohio courts have held to 'materially affect health and safety', and whether a lease may lawfully set MORE than thirty days. No case law searched. Flagged.

title: Towing From Private Property
bodyText:
South Dakota regulates towing from private property through its abandoned-vehicle chapter, and the duties fall on the tow company rather than on you. A vehicle counts as an abandoned motor vehicle on private property only if it was left there without the permission of the landowner or tenant (SDCL 32-36-2(1)). No removal agency may remove an abandoned motor vehicle from private property without the written permission of the landowner or tenant, and a violation is a Class 2 misdemeanor (SDCL 32-36-4.1); once it has that authorization the agency may enter the land to make the removal (SDCL 32-36-4). Removal agency includes an ordinary tow business, and motor vehicle reaches boats, house trailers, trailers, campers, snowmobiles and off-road vehicles as well as cars (SDCL 32-36-2(4), (5)). After a removal the agency must mail certified notice to the registered owner and to all readily identifiable lienholders within forty-five days on a form provided by the Department of Revenue, and if it does not mail that notice within ten days of the removal it may charge no storage beyond the ten-day period until the notice goes out (SDCL 32-36-8). The agency holds a possessory lien for the reasonable costs of taking custody and storage, but no more than five hundred dollars against the contents of the vehicle, and no lien at all against the tools a person keeps for their trade or business, or against clothing or food (SDCL 32-30-18).

Two consequences matter in practice. First, a tenant's own vehicle parked with your permission is not an abandoned motor vehicle, so this chapter gives you no authority to tow it for breaking a parking rule - that is a lease-compliance matter to take up with the tenant, not a towing matter. Second, South Dakota imposes no signage requirement for towing from private property; your written authorization is what makes the tow lawful. The statute does not say whether that authorization must be a per-tow order or may be a standing written contract, so it does not settle which form to use.
