title: Removing Someone Who Is Not a Tenant
bodyText:
When someone who is not your tenant will not leave, South Dakota's criminal trespass statute is the usual tool and it moves faster than an eviction. Under SDCL 22-35-6 a person who enters or remains anywhere knowing they are not privileged to do so, where notice against trespass has been given by actual communication to that person, by posting in a manner reasonably likely to come to a trespasser's attention, or by a fence or other enclosure a reasonable person would recognise as designed to exclude trespassers, is guilty of a Class 2 misdemeanor. If that person then defies an order to leave communicated personally by the owner of the premises or by any other authorized person, the offence becomes criminal trespass, a Class 1 misdemeanor.

Two limits decide whether this is actually available to you. A tenant is privileged to be on the property under the lease, so trespass is never the route against a tenant - use the forcible entry and detainer process instead. And SDCL 22-35-7 makes it an affirmative defence that the person reasonably believed the owner, or another person permitted to license access, would have permitted them to enter or remain. Your tenant is such a person, so a guest your tenant still welcomes has that defence available. A guest who overstays with the tenant's blessing is therefore a lease-violation problem to take up with the tenant under the guest and default provisions, not a trespass problem. Where someone took possession by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth against your prior actual possession, or holds possession by force, threats or menacing conduct, forcible entry and detainer is independently available under SDCL 21-16-1(1) to (3) without regard to trespass.

title: Medical Cannabis Cardholders
bodyText:
South Dakota's medical cannabis law limits how you may treat a registered cardholder. Under SDCL 34-20G-19 a cardholder may not be refused a lease by a landlord, or otherwise be penalized by a landlord, solely for the person's status as a cardholder - unless failing to do so would violate federal law or regulations, or would cause you to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law or regulation. That carve-out is what matters for federally subsidized housing. The same section then provides that it does not prevent a landlord from imposing reasonable restrictions on the medical use of cannabis by a cardholder who resides at the landlord's property.

Two things you may clearly do. SDCL 34-20G-27(3) provides that nothing in the chapter requires a landlord to allow the cultivation of cannabis on the rental property, so a cultivation ban is squarely permitted. SDCL 34-20G-27(2) provides that nothing requires a person in lawful possession of property to allow a guest, client, customer or other visitor to smoke or vape cannabis there. Read that second one carefully: it is written about visitors, not about your resident tenants, so it is not the authority for restricting a tenant's own use. The reasonable-restrictions sentence in 34-20G-19 is.

Steinoak's Smoking Policy clause prohibits smoking and vaping of any kind, including of marijuana, rather than prohibiting possession or non-combusted use, and it applies to every tenant rather than to cardholders as such. That is the shape most likely to qualify as a reasonable restriction: it leaves other methods of medical use available and it is not a penalty imposed for cardholder status. But reasonable is not defined anywhere in the chapter and no South Dakota decision applying it was located, so treat the margin as argued rather than settled. Do not screen out an applicant, raise their rent, refuse a renewal or threaten them because they hold a card, and note that the clause as written says nothing about cultivation even though South Dakota would let you prohibit it.

title: Selling the Property With a Tenant in Place
bodyText:
South Dakota has no statute moving security deposit liability to a buyer when a rented property is sold, and none releasing the selling landlord. Several states do: Kansas, Nebraska, North Dakota, Minnesota, California, Nevada, Texas, New Jersey, Florida and Arizona all have an express successor-liability or transfer-or-return provision. South Dakota does not, and nothing in chapter 43-32 - read in full - requires you to notify a tenant that the property is for sale or has been sold, or imposes a landlord-identity or identity-change disclosure duty.

So in South Dakota the question is answered by your purchase agreement and by ordinary property and contract law rather than by statute. A buyer takes the property subject to an existing lease as a general matter, but no South Dakota statute makes the buyer answerable for a deposit the seller is holding, and none discharges the seller's own obligation under SDCL 43-32-24 to account for that deposit. The practical consequence is that the deposit obligation stays with whoever took the money unless your sale documents move it. Transfer the deposit at closing against a written acknowledgment that the buyer has assumed the accounting duty, keep a copy of the accounting you would have owed, and tell the tenant in writing who now holds the deposit and where to send the mailing address or delivery instructions that start the twenty-one-day clock. If you sell without doing any of that, you remain the person the tenant can pursue.

title: An Uncashed Deposit Refund Is Unclaimed Property
bodyText:
A deposit refund your former tenant never cashes does not become yours. South Dakota's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act presumes all intangible property abandoned when it has remained unclaimed by the owner for more than three years after it became payable or distributable, less any lawful charges, and the owner's failure to make demand or to present the instrument does not stop that clock (SDCL 43-41B-2(a), (b)). Expiry of any limitation period does not prevent the property from being presumed abandoned or affect your duty to report it (SDCL 43-41B-18).

Before you file, you must communicate with the owner and exercise due diligence to find them, and for property worth fifty dollars or more you must mail notice to each person entitled to it - unless your records indicate the address is inaccurate - stating that you hold property that appears to be theirs and that it will escheat to the state (SDCL 43-41B-18). The report goes to the administrator, must be verified, and is due before November 1 each year as of the preceding June 30. It must give the owner's name and last known address for property worth ten dollars or more, the nature and amount of the property, the date it became payable, and the date of your last transaction with the apparent owner; items worth under ten dollars each may be reported in the aggregate. If you took over the property from a previous holder, or your own name has changed while you held it, the report must list every previous holder's name and address.

One practical point: reissuing a stale cheque does not restart the three years, because the period runs from when the refund first became payable rather than from the date of any replacement instrument. For a South Dakota deposit that is when your accounting was due under SDCL 43-32-24 - though the Act does not say so in those terms, so treat it as the better reading rather than a stated rule.

title: Winter Utility Disconnection
bodyText:
South Dakota does not impose a winter moratorium on utility disconnection, but it does lengthen the notice. Under ARSD 20:10:20:10, from November 1 through March 31 a utility may not disconnect residential service without adding thirty days to the time periods in ARSD 20:10:20:03(2), and it must notify the customer before the normal disconnection date that the customer has that additional thirty days. The underlying periods are a payment period of not less than twenty days from the billing transmittal date to the due date, plus a further notice period of not less than ten days during which the bill has been owing. So the runway before a nonpayment disconnection is roughly thirty days outside the winter window and roughly sixty days inside it.

Scope matters more than the numbers here. These are Public Utilities Commission rules made under SDCL 49-34A, and they reach the gas and electric utilities subject to that chapter. Whether a municipal utility or a rural electric cooperative is bound by them was not determined, and water and sewer service is not covered by this rule at all. Two consequences for you. If the tenant is the customer of record, a winter shutoff takes considerably longer than you might assume, which changes how quickly an unpaid utility becomes a habitability or lease-compliance problem rather than a private matter between the tenant and the utility. If you are the customer of record - a master-metered building, or a lease where you pay a utility - the extension and the notice are yours, and the notice will come to you rather than to the tenant.

None of this touches SDCL 43-32-6, which separately prohibits you from willfully diminishing services by interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service in order to force a tenant out, and gives the tenant damages of two months' rent plus return of advance rent and deposit.

title: Service-Animal Misrepresentation Reaches Public Accommodations, Not Housing
bodyText:
South Dakota now has a criminal penalty for misrepresenting a service animal, and it does not reach housing. SDCL 22-35-9, added in 2026, makes it a Class 2 misdemeanor for an individual to misrepresent an animal in that individual's possession as a service animal, directly or indirectly through statements or conduct, intentionally and in any place of public accommodation, in order to obtain rights or privileges available to someone who qualifies for a service animal under state or federal law, knowing they are not entitled to them. For that section service animal means a dog trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability as set out in 28 C.F.R. 36.104 (January 1, 2026), and the section states expressly that a dog's crime-deterrent effect and the provision of emotional support, well-being, comfort or companionship do not constitute work or tasks.

A leased dwelling is not a place of public accommodation, so do not expect this offence to cover a tenant or applicant who misrepresents a pet as a service or support animal, and do not threaten anyone with it. Your remedy in housing remains civil: SDCL 43-32-36 permits eviction and a damage fee of up to one thousand dollars where a tenant knowingly makes a false claim of disability requiring a service or assistance animal or knowingly supplies fraudulent documentation, which is what the Assistance Animal clause states.

One trap follows from this. South Dakota now carries three different service-animal standards in three places: the civil housing framework in SDCL 43-32-33 to 43-32-36; the criminal prohibition in SDCL 20-13-23.4 on a landlord barring a service animal, which covers only tenants who are totally or partially physically disabled, blind or deaf; and this public-accommodations definition, limited to dogs performing trained tasks and expressly excluding emotional support. Do not carry one section's definition into another, and in particular do not use this section's exclusion of emotional-support animals to deny an assistance-animal accommodation in housing, where federal fair housing law and the chapter 43-32 framework govern and both reach support animals.

title: Residential Rent Is Exempt From Sales Tax
bodyText:
Residential rent is not subject to South Dakota sales tax. The Department of Revenue's Lease and Rental guidance states that the lease or rental of real property is exempt from sales tax, and lists the lease or rental of real property among the transactions exempt from sales and use tax. So you do not collect or remit state sales tax on rent under an ordinary residential lease, and you should not add a tax line to the rent or describe part of the rent as tax.

Two boundaries were not resolved and they matter if you operate outside ordinary residential leasing. Short-term lodging is taxed under a different regime, alongside South Dakota's tourism tax and municipal gross receipts tax, and the point at which a stay stops being an exempt rental of real property and becomes taxable lodging was not researched here - so do not read this as covering a short-term or vacation rental. It is also unresolved whether separately stated charges for furnishings, equipment or services supplied with the dwelling fall outside the real-property exemption, since the exemption is written about real property. If you charge separately for anything other than the dwelling itself, get that specific question answered before deciding not to collect tax on it.

title: When a Tenant Abandons the Unit
bodyText: Texas has no statute that defines when a residential tenant has abandoned a unit, and no notice-and-storage procedure for belongings a living tenant leaves behind. The Property Code lets you exclude a tenant in order to remove the contents of premises the tenant has abandoned, and lets you remove the contents of an abandoned residence. If the tenant had not in fact abandoned, the exclusion is an unlawful lockout: the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover one month's rent plus $1,000, actual damages, court costs and attorney's fees (less any rent owed), and can get an ex parte writ of reentry. Because 'abandoned' is undefined, a lease definition is your main protection; the optional abandonment Section of this lease supplies one, and Texas's standard apartment-association lease also defines it. Before you treat a unit as abandoned, document the signs and give written notice with time to respond. Different rules apply when a sole tenant dies (the certified-mail and 30-day procedure unless the lease sets another) and after an eviction (the officer places belongings outside under the writ). Once the tenant has surrendered, the 30-day deposit refund clock runs, and you must try to re-let to limit your damages.

title: Abandonment and Property Left Behind
bodyText:
[Optional. Texas law does not define when a residential tenant has abandoned the dwelling; this Section supplies the definition. Tex. Prop. Code §§92.0081(b)(2), 54.044(d).]
ABANDONMENT. The dwelling is abandoned only when all of the following have occurred: (a) Landlord reasonably believes that all occupants have moved out, based on facts such as the removal of substantially all of Tenant's belongings or the disconnection of utility service in Tenant's name; (b) Rent is delinquent; and (c) Landlord has posted a written notice on the inside of the main entry door, and mailed a copy to Tenant at the dwelling and to any other address Tenant has given Landlord (and e-mailed a copy if Tenant has given Landlord an e-mail address), stating that Landlord considers the dwelling abandoned, and Tenant has not responded in writing or in person within 5 days after the notice was posted. Once the dwelling is abandoned, Landlord may enter, take possession, change the locks, and remove any personal property left in the dwelling. Landlord will store that property for at least 30 days after the dwelling is abandoned and will release it to Tenant, or to a person Tenant designates in writing, on request during that period. Landlord may charge Tenant the reasonable cost of removing and storing the property but will not refuse to release the property because that cost is unpaid. After the 30-day period, Landlord may donate the property to a charitable organization or discard it. Landlord may discard trash, perishable food, and items that pose a health or safety hazard at any time. Nothing in this Section allows Landlord to exclude Tenant from the dwelling except as Section 92.0081 of the Texas Property Code permits. If Tenant is the sole occupant and dies, Section 92.014 of the Texas Property Code and the provisions of this Lease on the death of Tenant apply instead of this Section.

title: Pools at Multiunit Rentals
bodyText: If you own a multiunit rental complex (two or more units under common ownership and management on the same or adjacent lots, including a condominium project, but not a stand-alone single-family home) with a pool, or a rental unit in a condominium, cooperative or town-home project with a pool, Health and Safety Code chapter 757 applies. A pool includes a permanent swimming pool, wading pool, hot tub or spa more than 18 inches deep. The pool yard must be fully enclosed at least 48 inches high, with limits on openings (no chain link on enclosures built after January 1, 1994); gates must self-close and self-latch, open outward, be lockable, and generally have the latch at least 60 inches high. Unit doors may not open directly into the pool yard where the building or pool first got electrical service on or after January 1, 1994; older doors and windows that do must have specified latches and bolts. You must use reasonable care to inspect, maintain and repair the enclosure, gates and self-closing latches, and inspect them at least once every 31 days, and repair pool-yard window and sliding-door latches, pins and bars after a tenant reports a problem. These duties cannot be waived. A tenant may report those problems orally unless the lease requires written notice in a provision printed in capital letters and underlined, or in 10-point bold type. A tenant or anyone else can sue for a compliance order, actual damages, punitive damages for intentional, malicious or grossly negligent failures, and a civil penalty of up to $5,000 if you do not comply within a reasonable time after a tenant's written notice; the attorney general, a city, a county or a local health department can also enforce. Cities generally may not require a different enclosure than the chapter allows. Your security-device duties under the Property Code still apply.

title: Removing a Squatter Without an Eviction
bodyText: Since September 1, 2025, the owner of residential property, or the owner's agent, can ask the sheriff or a constable to remove immediately a person who unlawfully entered and is living in a dwelling without the owner's consent, without filing an eviction suit. It is available only if the property was not open to the public when the person entered, there is no pending lawsuit between you and the person, you have told the person to leave and they have not, and the person is not your current or former tenant under any oral or written lease and not an immediate family member. You submit a sworn complaint in the statutory form, with a copy of your government-issued ID (and, for an agent, proof of authority). The officer verifies that you are the record owner or agent, then without delay serves a notice to vacate immediately (by hand or by posting on the front door) and puts you in possession; the officer may arrest occupants for trespass or other offenses. You pay the same fee as for executing a writ of possession, plus an hourly rate if you ask the officer to stay while you change the locks and move the occupants' belongings to your property line. You are not liable for damage to belongings removed under this procedure, but a person wrongfully removed can sue to recover possession plus actual damages, three times the fair market rent, court costs and attorney's fees, and a false complaint is perjury. Anyone who was ever your tenant, including a holdover or a tenant whose lease has ended, must be removed through an eviction suit.
notes: TX gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36, scenario screen: 'stranger moves into a vacant unit'). Primary text: Tex. Prop. title: Crime at Your Property: Nuisance Suits
bodyText: Under Texas's common-nuisance law, a person who maintains a place where people habitually go to commit listed crimes, knowingly tolerates it, and fails to make reasonable attempts to stop it maintains a common nuisance. The list includes drug dealing, manufacture or possession, prostitution and human trafficking, gambling, reckless or public gunfire, aggravated assault, robbery, sexual assault, murder, criminal trespass, disorderly conduct, arson, graffiti and serious criminal mischief. A specific rule covers multiunit residential property (three or more units, not a single-family home or duplex). The attorney general, a district, county or city attorney, or a private individual can sue the owner. Frequent crime at the property is prima facie evidence that you tolerated it, and arrests there can be used to show you knew. A court can order you to abate the nuisance, require a bond of $5,000 to $10,000, and order the property closed for one year; if you violate the order it can cut off utilities, revoke the certificate of occupancy, or order you to end a tenant's lease. For multiunit property found to be a nuisance, it can also appoint a receiver to run it for up to a year. Contempt fines run $1,000 to $10,000 plus jail, and the prevailing party may recover attorney's fees. Your protection is acting promptly: calling the police cannot be used as evidence that you tolerated the activity, anyone deciding whether to sue must consider whether you promptly report crime and cooperate with police, while refusing to cooperate can be used against you, and posting a sign alone does not prove you did not tolerate it. Enforcing the lease against a tenant engaged in the activity is the usual reasonable step.
notes: TX gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36, scenario screen: 'drugs, violence or other crime at the unit'). Primary text: Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code ch. 125, Subchs. A and C (and D, gang public nuisance, read), official statutes.capitol.texas.gov text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-27, read in full section-open. s125.001(3) (multiunit residential property: at least three units; excludes a single-family home or duplex), s125.0015(a)-(b) (listed activities; knowingly tolerates and fails to make reasonable attempts to abate), s125.002 (who may sue; in rem; one-year closure on judgment (e); (h) prosecutors consider prompt reporting and cooperation; contempt $1,000-$10,000 and 10-30 days), s125.004 (frequency = prima facie knowledge; arrests admissible; (d) calls for police inadmissible to show toleration; refusal to cooperate admissible; a sign is not conclusive; prior judgment admissible), s125.005 (fees), s125.045 (temporary injunction bond $5,000-$10,000; on violation: utilities, certificate of occupancy, order a landlord to terminate a tenant's lease where both are parties), s125.046 (receiver for multiunit residential property, max one year). CURRENCY: latest amendments shown 2021 (H.B. 1540, S.B. 315, H.B. 375, S.B. 766) and 2023 (S.B. 1900, Subch. D only). title: No Eviction Record Sealing in Texas
bodyText: Texas has no statute that seals or expunges eviction records, including under the 2026 eviction overhaul. The court rules add none: the eviction rule (Texas Rule of Civil Procedure 510, rewritten for 2026) has no sealing provision, and the general sealing rule (Rule 76a) never allows a judgment or order to be sealed and allows other court records to be sealed only if the person asking shows a specific, serious and substantial interest that clearly outweighs the presumption that court records are open, after posted public notice and a hearing. A tenant has no statutory right to have an eviction case sealed, and nothing in Texas landlord-tenant law limits your considering a past eviction when you screen, beyond fair-housing law.
notes: TX gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36, scenario screen: 'tenant asks to seal an eviction record'). CONFIRMED ABSENT (statutes). Evidentiary basis: official full-text search run by Taylor 2026-09-27 for 'eviction record' (the tool ran it as separate words, a broader query than the phrase): 8 hits - Gov't Code chs. 25 and 26 (statutory and constitutional county courts), Loc. Gov't Code chs. 86 (constables) and 154 (officer compensation), Prop. Code chs. 24, 92, 93 (commercial) and 94 (manufactured homes). Chs. 24 and 92 were read in full (ch. 24 as amended by S.B. 38, eff. Jan. 1, 2026): no sealing or expunction provision. The other six hits were reviewed by chapter title only; none is a records-sealing chapter. Previously 'Not located' in the checklist's 'Eviction record sealing' row. Federal screening-report law (FCRA) is out of scope and not researched; fair housing: edu-fair-housing-tx. | TX retro 2026-10-03 (SOP 1.29, rule 39 - public-access rules): Texas Rules of Civil Procedure (txcourts.gov, 'last amended October 1, 2026'; PDF saved, sha256 bd9d874a...e178a) and Texas Rules of Judicial Administration (as of July 1, 2026; sha256 0894acf2...a529b) read for sealing and public access. Rule 510 (eviction cases, rewritten 2026) read in full: no sealing or confidentiality provision; 510.17(e) lets a judge close a remote hearing only on written findings. Rule 76a(1): 'No court order or opinion issued in the adjudication of a case may be sealed'; other court records are presumed open and may be sealed only on a showing of a specific, serious and substantial interest clearly outweighing the presumption and any adverse effect on public health or safety, with no less restrictive means, on written motion and posted public notice (76a(1), (3)). Rule 510.1(b) says the other civil rules do not apply to eviction cases unless specifically provided, so whether Rule 76a reaches a justice-court eviction record at all is doubtful; either way no sealing route exists. TRJA Rule 12 (public access to judicial records) excludes records filed in a case (12.2(d)) and records controlled by Rule 76a (12.3(a)). title: Notice to End a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText: If this Lease continues as a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, either Landlord or Tenant may end it by giving the other at least 30 days' written notice, with the termination taking effect on the last day of a rental period. If notice is given fewer than 30 days before the end of a rental period, the tenancy ends at the close of the following rental period instead. Rent remains payable through the termination date. This Section does not limit either party's right to end this Lease earlier where this Lease or applicable law allows it.
notes: WY added 2026-09-27, gap-discovery source 2 (real-lease comparison, WY log section 20.1). GAP FOUND: Wyoming sets no statutory notice period for ending a periodic tenancy (see edu-no-statutory-termination-notice-wy, which tells the landlord to 'state the notice period in writing rather than relying on a default that does not exist') -- but no WY lease clause did so. This is instruction 19's failure shape: the education row asserted the lease must supply the term, and no row supplied it. Found because the ASUW Approved Lease (Univ. of Wyoming, off-campus) carries exactly this as its Option A. Contract term only: no Wyoming statute supplies or constrains it, so the 30 days and the end-of-rental-period mechanic are the common-law expectation reduced to writing, not a statutory figure. CONDITIONAL because it operates only once the tenancy is or becomes periodic. Interacts with holdover, which says a continued tenancy is 'terminable by either party upon written notice as required by applicable law' -- for WY that phrase points at no statute, and this row is what it now points to. No display collision: holdover is topic_key=holdover, this is topic_key=termination-notice.

title: Agent Not Authorized to Receive Notices
bodyText: Any managing agent, leasing agent, or resident manager identified in this Lease is not authorized to receive notices or other communications on Landlord's behalf. All notices and demands under this Lease, or under Wyoming's Residential Rental Property Act, must be directed to Landlord at the address stated in this Lease.
notes: WY added 2026-09-27, gap-discovery source 2 (WY log section 20.1). Opt-out clause under W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(i), verified section-open: "'Owner' means the owner, lessor or sublessor of a residential rental unit and for purposes of notice and other communication required or allowed under this article, 'owner' includes a managing agent, leasing agent or resident manager UNLESS THE AGENT OR MANAGER SPECIFIES OTHERWISE IN WRITING IN THE RENTAL AGREEMENT." The statutory default is that the agent IS the owner for notice purposes; the only way to vary it is lease text, so this is an instruction 30 opt-in/opt-out right that a silent lease forfeits. CONDITIONAL: include only where an agent or manager is involved AND the landlord wants notices delivered to the landlord directly. Omit it and the agent remains a valid recipient of every notice and demand under Article 12. Surfaced by the ASUW Approved Lease's signature block, which asks the lessor to identify capacity (owner, agent, or holder of a leasehold). Companion education row: edu-agent-capacity-notice-wy. | WY: RETRO 2026-10-04 (SOP 1.56, rule 79). BASIS: section-open, official Wyoming Legislature NXT gateway, 2026 Wyoming Statutes, read 2026-10-04 (Art. 12 at /1/53/65, Art. 13 at /1/53/66). Both articles' live text is character-identical to the 2026-09-30 read, so no amendment intervened and no history-line discrepancy arises. VERDICT: confirmed. The opt-out is the trailing clause of W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(i): 'unless the agent or manager specifies otherwise in writing in the rental agreement'. It attaches to the notice-and-communication sentence, which is the whole of (a)(i). Re-confirmed on the live text.

title: Your Property Manager Is You, for Notice Purposes
bodyText: Under W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(i), a managing agent, leasing agent, or resident manager counts as the "owner" for every notice and communication required or allowed under Wyoming's Residential Rental Property Act -- unless the agent or manager says otherwise in writing in the rental agreement itself. Two practical consequences. If you use a property manager and the lease is silent, a tenant's written notice of a habitability problem, a deposit demand, or a forwarding address is effective when it reaches the manager, and your statutory clocks start running then, whether or not the manager has passed it along to you. And if you want notices to come to you directly, the lease is the only place you can say so -- a side agreement with the manager will not do it, because the statute requires the designation to be in the rental agreement.
notes: WY added 2026-09-27, gap-discovery source 2 (WY log section 20.1). Verified section-open against W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(i) on law.justia.com. No prior WY row covered this: the only two rows citing 1-21-1201 (edu-no-entry-notice-statute-wy, edu-no-prohibited-lease-provisions-statute-wy) cite it for unrelated absences. Distinct from edu-successor-owner-bound-wy (deposit duties following the property on transfer, 1-21-1207/1208) and edu-no-broad-identity-change-notice-wy (no duty to notify tenants of a management change). title: Fire or Other Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty through no fault of Tenant, and the damage makes the property uninhabitable or substantially impairs Tenant's use of it, either Landlord or Tenant may terminate this Lease by written notice to the other, effective on the date Tenant vacates. Rent will be prorated to that date, any prepaid Rent refunded, and the Security Deposit returned as this Lease and Wyoming law provide. If the casualty makes only part of the property unusable and Tenant stays in possession, Rent will be reduced in proportion to the part of the property Tenant cannot use until Landlord completes repairs.
notes: WY added 2026-09-27, gap-discovery source 3 (landlord-scenario screen, WY log section 20.2). GAP FOUND: ten states in this library carry a casualty row (KS, ND, SD, MN, OH, CA, NV, TX, FL, AZ) and Wyoming carried none, so a WY lease had no answer at all to 'the unit burned.' CONTRACT TERM ONLY -- and that is the finding. Wyoming supplies no statutory casualty regime: Article 12 (all 11 sections, read in full in the original WY statute walk) has none, and Title 34 ch. 2 (leases generally) has only 34-2-128 through 34-2-130 (implied tenancy, renewal, mineral leases), index read 2026-09-27 -- no destruction, untenantability or rent-abatement section. The nearest statutory neighbour runs the other way: W.S. 1-21-1203(d) lets the OWNER refuse an unreasonably costly repair and terminate (edu-repair-cost-termination-wy). Because no statute supplies a default, every casualty term here is doing real work; it cannot be inherited from another state's row, each of which is statute-driven. CONDITIONAL per the AZ classification rule (widely used, not legally required). Cross-state note for Taylor: casualty is currently ten separate single-state rows with no shared base -- a consolidation candidate, his call, not actioned here.

title: Towing and Disposing of a Vehicle Left on Your Property
bodyText: Wyoming's rules for a vehicle abandoned on a rental property sit in the motor-vehicle title, not the landlord-tenant title, and they are more procedural than most landlords expect. To have an abandoned vehicle removed by law enforcement, you make a written request on a form the department prescribes; a police officer then places a notice of intent to impound on the vehicle, and on private property that notice must stay there at least five days before removal (W.S. 31-13-104). The towing service has its own duty to notify the registered owner and lienholders by certified mail within three business days of identifying their latest known addresses. If instead you want to clear title by selling the vehicle yourself, W.S. 31-13-109 sets the track: wait 30 days from when you knew the vehicle was left unattended or unclaimed, give written notice to the sheriff of the county of sale and to the owner and any lienholder by certified mail with return receipt, publish notice once a week for two consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation, and hold the public auction no sooner than ten days after notice. Your total recoverable expenses for removal, towing, storage and sale are capped at $1,000. A court action is available but not required.
notes: WY added 2026-09-27, gap-discovery source 3 (WY log section 20.2), and a source-4 finding by nature -- both sections live in Title 31 (Motor Vehicles), outside the landlord-tenant title. Verified section-open on law.justia.com: W.S. 31-13-104 (abandonment on highway or property; removal; notice of intent to impound; notice of towing) and W.S. 31-13-109 (disposition of vehicles left unattended or unclaimed on private property, sold by the property owner or through a court action under 31-13-112(e)). GAP FOUND: parking-vehicle-rules (tagged WY) says Landlord may have a vehicle towed 'in accordance with applicable law' and no WY row said what that law is; four other states (NV, TX x2, AZ) carry a towing row. No clause conflict -- parking-vehicle-rules already defers. NOT READ: 31-13-112(e) (the court route) and the rest of ch. 13; municipal towing ordinances are flagged, not resolved, consistent with WY's state-level-only scope.

title: If the Property Is Foreclosed, Federal Law Protects Your Tenant
bodyText: Wyoming's foreclosure statutes say nothing about tenants. The foreclosure-by-advertisement chapter (W.S. 34-4-101 through 34-4-113) covers notice by publication and service, the sale, and the proceeds, with no tenant-notice step and no provision on what happens to an existing lease. The protection that does apply is federal: the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, which lapsed in 2014 and was restored permanently in 2018, requires whoever takes title at foreclosure to honor a bona fide tenant's existing lease through the end of its term, and to give at least 90 days' written notice to vacate. The main exception is a purchaser who will occupy the property as a primary residence, who may end the lease early but still owes the 90 days' notice. Practically: a Wyoming lease does not evaporate at the foreclosure sale, and neither you nor a buyer can treat the tenant as a holdover on the strength of the sale alone.
notes: WY added 2026-09-27, gap-discovery source 3 (WY log section 20.2). GAP FOUND: seven states carry a foreclosure row (MN, NV x2, CA x2, NJ, FL, AZ x2) and WY carried none. CONFIRMED ABSENT (state law): Title 34 ch. 4 section index read 2026-09-27 -- 34-4-101 through 34-4-113, no section mentioning tenants, leases, occupants or possession by a non-mortgagor. Evidentiary basis is an INDEX read plus Article 12's full read, not an official full-text search of the Wyoming code; an official search would upgrade this. FEDERAL CITATION, flagged per instruction 16: the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act (Pub. L. 111-22 div. A tit. VII, as restored by Pub. L. 115-174 sec. 304, eff. 2018-06-23) is federal and will not appear in any Wyoming bill-tracking watch. The 90-day and bona-fide-lease terms are stated from the federal act as commonly summarized; the act's own text was NOT read section-open in this pass -- worth confirming before relying on the detail.

title: No Statute Bans Lockouts -- and That Is Not Permission
bodyText: Wyoming gives you a court route to recover possession: a notice to quit under W.S. 1-21-1003, a forcible entry and detainer action under W.S. 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017, and a writ of restitution the sheriff executes. W.S. 1-21-1211(a) is explicit that it is the sheriff, acting on a court order, who removes a renter's possessions and prevents reentry. What Wyoming does not have is the express statutory ban on landlord self-help that thirteen other states in this library carry: no located statute prohibits changing the locks, removing a door, or cutting off utilities to force a tenant out, and none sets a penalty for it. Do not read that silence as permission. The FED process is the route the statutes actually provide, and a landlord who locks a tenant out instead is exposed to ordinary civil claims -- wrongful eviction, trespass, and conversion of the tenant's belongings -- none of which carries a statutory cap on what a court may award. The cheap, fast-looking option is the one with the open-ended downside.
notes: WY added 2026-09-27, gap-discovery source 3 (WY log section 20.2). GAP FOUND: 13 of 14 states carry a self-help/lockout/utility-shutoff row (CO, KS, NE, MN, ND, SD, CA, NV, TX x3, NJ, FL, AZ) -- WY was the only one without, on what is among the most consequential questions a landlord asks. ABSENCE CLAIM, evidentiary basis stated per instruction 15: FED article index (titles only), Article 12 full read, Title 34 ch. 2 index, plus consistent secondary-source agreement -- NOT an official full-text search of the Wyoming code, and 1-21-1016 ('Ejectment Not Barred') was not read section-open. This is the weaker-evidence tier, same caveat as edu-no-right-to-call-police-statute-wy. FLAGGED FOR TAYLOR: an official wyoleg.gov full-text search on lockout/utility-shutoff terms is the one step that would move this to the strong tier. | WY: RETRO 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.15). EVIDENCE UPGRADED, conclusion unchanged. The open flag in the note above is now partly closed: all seventeen sections of Title 1 ch. 21 art. 10 were read in full, section-open, on 2026-09-30 -- not the index only -- including W.S. 1-21-1016 ('Ejectment Not Barred'), which the earlier note recorded as unread. 1-21-1016 says only that a pending forcible entry or detainer action does not bar an action of ejectment; it creates no self-help right and bans nothing. Article 13 was also read in full the same day. No express prohibition on lockouts or utility shutoffs, and no penalty for either, appears anywhere in Articles 10, 12 or 13. Remaining boundary, unchanged and still honest: this is three articles read whole plus the Title 34 ch. 2 index, NOT a full-text search of the whole Wyoming code, which the shell could not reach (the organization's egress policy returns 403 for every statute host) and which the official site offers no loadable bulk text for. title: Landlord's Maintenance Obligations
bodyText: Landlord will: comply with all applicable building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety; make all repairs and do whatever is reasonably necessary to put and keep the property in a fit and habitable condition; keep all common areas of the property in a safe and sanitary condition; maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air conditioning fixtures and appliances, and elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by Landlord; and supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water and reasonable heat at all times, except where the building is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose or where the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within Tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection. Where Landlord is a party to rental agreements covering four or more dwelling units in the same structure, Landlord will also provide and maintain appropriate receptacles for ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste and arrange for their removal.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.04(A)(1)-(6), re-read section-open 2026-09-27 for this row. FOUND BY THE LANDLORD-SCENARIO SCREEN (source 3): the 'furnace fails in January' and 'tenant withholds rent over repairs' scenarios had NO Ohio row to answer them. This is a COVERAGE GAP, not newly found law - 13 states carry a landlord-maintenance row and Ohio did not, so an Ohio lease generated from the library had no landlord repair clause at all. Same failure mode as California's (checklist instruction 26, CA log 5.32-5.38). The waste-receptacle duty is stated with its four-or-more-units condition because 5321.04(A)(5) is written that way - one of Ohio's five portfolio thresholds. NOT WAIVABLE: 5321.13(A) makes ch. 5321 non-waivable except through (F), and 5321.13(E) bars any agreement letting the landlord receive rent free of the obligation to comply with 5321.04 - see edu-one-way-delegation-oh. | OH: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-landlord-duties-oh). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: How An Ohio Tenant Forces Repairs: Rent Escrow
bodyText: Ohio does not give tenants a repair-and-deduct right. It gives them the courthouse. If you fail an obligation under R.C. 5321.04 or under the lease, the tenant may give you written notice specifying the acts, omissions or code violations, sent to the person or place where rent is normally paid. If you then fail to remedy within a reasonable time considering the severity, or within thirty days, whichever is sooner - and the tenant is current on rent - the tenant may do one of three things: deposit all rent due and thereafter becoming due with the clerk of the municipal or county court; apply to the court for an order that you remedy the condition, which can include an order reducing the rent until you do or an order spending the deposited rent on the repair; or terminate the rental agreement. Two carve-outs work in your favour. The remedy does not reach a landlord who is party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units and who gives written notice of that fact, and it does not apply to a dwelling occupied by a student tenant.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.07(A)-(D), re-read section-open 2026-09-27. FOUND BY THE LANDLORD-SCENARIO SCREEN (source 3) - Ohio had no row stating the escrow mechanism, only repair-escrow-exemption-notice-oh, which is the EXEMPTION NOTICE and presupposes the reader already knows the remedy it escapes. Pairs with landlord-maintenance-oh in the same delta. 5321.09 and 5321.10 (landlord application for release of rent, partial release) were NOT read section-open in this pass - flagged, and they are what a landlord actually needs to get the money out. Note the 5321.07(C) exemption is conditioned on giving the notice, so it fails silently if the lease omits it: that is why repair-escrow-exemption-notice-oh exists as a CONDITIONAL clause.

title: Ohio Retaliation: The Three Triggers And What It Costs
bodyText: An Ohio landlord may not retaliate against a tenant by raising the rent, decreasing services, or bringing or threatening to bring an action for possession, because the tenant did any of three things: complained to an appropriate governmental agency about a violation of a building, housing, health or safety code that materially affects health and safety; complained to you about a violation of R.C. 5321.04; or joined with other tenants to negotiate or deal collectively with you about the terms and conditions of the tenancy. If you retaliate, the tenant may use it as a defence to your possession action, recover possession, or terminate the rental agreement - and may recover actual damages together with reasonable attorney's fees. What you may still do: R.C. 5321.02(C) expressly preserves a rent increase that reflects the cost of improvements you installed or an increase in your other costs of operating the property. Document that basis before you raise the rent of a tenant who has just complained.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.02(A),(B),(C), re-read section-open 2026-09-27; effective 1974-11-04, S.B. 103 (110th G.A.), unamended. FOUND BY THE LANDLORD-SCENARIO SCREEN (source 3): 'tenant called the city inspector, now I want to raise the rent' had no Ohio row. COVERAGE GAP - 10 states carry a retaliation row and Ohio did not. The attorney-fee award here is STATUTORY, so 5321.13(C)'s ban on fee agreements does not shield a landlord from it (edu-bilateral-fee-ban-oh). Note the trigger list is CLOSED and narrower than it looks: a tenant summoning police or emergency services is not on it, and Ohio has no separate right-to-call-emergency-services statute (edu-no-emergency-assistance-right-oh, same delta). R.C. 5321.03 lets a landlord still bring a possession action on the grounds listed there notwithstanding 5321.02 - NOT read section-open in this pass, flagged.

title: Never Shut Off Utilities Or Change The Locks In Ohio
bodyText: Ohio bans self-help recovery of possession outright, and the ban is written broadly. Under R.C. 5321.15(A) no landlord may initiate ANY act - the statute names terminating utilities or services, excluding the tenant from the premises, and threatening any unlawful act - for the purpose of recovering possession, other than through the procedures in R.C. Chapters 1923, 5303 and 5321. Under division (B) you may not seize a tenant's furnishings or possessions to recover rent except under a court order. This applies to a tenant whose right to possession has already ended, not just a current tenant. Division (C) makes you liable in a civil action for ALL damages caused, together with reasonable attorney's fees. There is no de minimis version of this: turning off the water on a holdover tenant is the conduct the section was written to stop.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.15(A),(B),(C), re-read section-open 2026-09-27; effective 1974-11-04, S.B. 103 (110th G.A.). FOUND BY THE LANDLORD-SCENARIO SCREEN (source 3): 'tenant stopped paying and I want them out fast' and 'tenant changed the locks' had no Ohio row for the ban itself. COVERAGE GAP - 7 states carry a self-help row; Ohio's only mention of 5321.15(B) was inside edu-no-abandoned-property-safe-harbor-oh, which is about belongings, not about exclusion or utility shutoff. The statutory fee award again defeats 5321.13(C). Note the express reach to 'a tenant whose right to possession has terminated' - the period after a judgment but before the writ executes is exactly when landlords self-help, and it is covered.

title: Damage or Destruction by Fire or Casualty
bodyText: If the property is destroyed or so injured by fire or other casualty as to be unfit for occupancy, and the destruction or injury was not caused by Tenant's fault or neglect, Tenant is not liable to pay Rent accruing after that destruction or injury, and Tenant will thereupon surrender possession of the property to Landlord. Rent already accrued and unpaid before the destruction or injury remains payable. To be relieved of Rent under this Section, Tenant must surrender possession of all of the property that remains; Tenant may not stop paying Rent while leaving personal property at the property or otherwise retaining possession.
notes: OH: R.C. 5301.11, verified from official text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-18; effective 1953-10-01, H.B. 1 (100th G.A.), sole version, never amended. FOUND BY THE LANDLORD-SCENARIO SCREEN (source 3): 'the unit burns' had an Ohio education row (edu-casualty-and-mitigation-waivable-oh) but NO LEASE CLAUSE, while 9 states carry a casualty clause. That matters more in Ohio than elsewhere because 5301.11 sits in Title 53 ch. 5301 (Conveyances), OUTSIDE ch. 5321, so 5321.13(A)'s non-waiver does not protect it and the statute itself says 'unless otherwise expressly provided by written agreement or covenant'. This clause therefore states the statutory default rather than contracting around it - a deliberate choice, since Taylor's 2026-09-18 decision was to surface the contract-around option in education only, not to take it in the default lease. The surrender condition is stated because Ohio case law going back to 1890 requires the tenant to yield all that remains to get the benefit. Pairs with edu-casualty-and-mitigation-waivable-oh. | OH: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-casualty-and-mitigation-waivable-oh). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Notice to Terminate a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: Either Landlord or Tenant may end a month-to-month tenancy by giving the other notice at least [state the notice period: at least 30] days before the periodic rental date, or a week-to-week tenancy by notice at least [state the notice period: at least 7] days before the termination date stated in the notice. This Section does not apply to a termination based on a breach of this Lease or of a duty imposed by law.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.17(A),(B),(D), re-read section-open 2026-09-27; effective 1990-08-22, S.B. 258 (118th G.A.). FOUND BY THE LANDLORD-SCENARIO SCREEN (source 3): 'ending a month-to-month either way' had no Ohio clause, though 5 states carry a termination-notice clause. Same gap shape the CROSS-STATE TENANCY-TYPE SENSITIVITY SCREEN (checklist, 2026-09-06) found for WY and MN. 5321.17(D) is carried into the clause text because it is the limit a landlord most often gets wrong - this notice is NOT the route for a breach-based termination, which runs on 5321.11 (30-day cure) or 1923.04's three-day notice. The drug-activity carve-out points at 5321.17(C), already covered by edu-mandatory-drug-termination-oh. Ohio has NO rent-increase notice statute, so this notice is also the practical route to new terms - see edu-rent-increase-notice-gap-oh. | OH: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): Taylor's pattern 2: the notice is the landlord's chosen period; the statutory minimums and the R.C. 5321.05(A)(9) exception moved to edu-termination-notice-periods-oh.

title: Ohio Preempts Local Rent Control, With Findings Attached
bodyText: Ohio forecloses local rent control about as firmly as any state in this library. R.C. 5321.19 bars a political subdivision from enacting, adopting, renewing, maintaining, enforcing or continuing any charter provision, ordinance, resolution, rule or other measure that conflicts with Chapter 5321, or that regulates the rights and obligations of parties to a rental agreement that the chapter regulates, including by imposing or requiring rent control or rent stabilization. R.C. 5321.20 then adds a legislative-findings section devoted to the subject, declaring rent control a matter of overriding statewide interest requiring uniform statewide regulation. What survives preemption matters as much as what does not: 5321.19(B) expressly preserves local housing, building, health and safety codes, any ordinance of the kind described in 5321.04(A)(9), local regulation of rent for premises the subdivision itself owns or operates, and voluntary-incentive programs such as tax abatements or bond financing.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.19 and 5321.20, from the full-chapter read 2026-09-18 (definitions of 'rent control', 'rent stabilization' and 'political subdivision' at 5321.01(O),(P),(Q)); H.B. 430 (134th G.A.), effective 2022-09-23. FOUND BY THE LANDLORD-SCENARIO SCREEN (source 3): 'my city is talking about rent control' had no Ohio row, though 4 states carry a preemption row and Ohio's is the strongest in the library. The 5321.19(B)(1) carve-out for local housing, building, health and safety codes is the same carve-out that makes Ohio's smoke and carbon monoxide alarm duty local rather than statutory - see edu-alarm-duty-fire-code-oh. OUT OF SCOPE BY DECISION 2026-09-18: Ohio's municipal layer is flagged, not resolved, and it is wider than the four largest cities (Newburgh Heights, population c. 2,000, has a full DV lease-termination ordinance).

title: Security Deposit: Move-Out List and Deductions
bodyText: If Tenant is present at the move-out inspection, Landlord and Tenant will both sign the damage list, and the signed list is conclusive evidence of its accuracy; if Tenant disagrees with any item, Tenant must state in writing the specific items Tenant disputes and sign that statement. The list will include written notice of Tenant's duty to sign it or to dissent from it. Landlord may keep from the Security Deposit amounts for unpaid Rent or late fees, abandonment of the property, unpaid utility charges, repair work or cleaning Tenant contracted for with third parties, unpaid pet fees, and actual damages caused by Tenant's breach, which Landlord will attempt to mitigate. Tenant should give Landlord a forwarding address in writing.
notes: GA: Read section-open 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser from Justia's '2025 Code of Georgia', a host copy of the official O.C.G.A. that already prints the 2026 session (history lines cite Ga. L. 2026, pp. 278, 988 and 1069), with each section's history line and editor's notes. Instruction 24 family closed for GA: supersedes the blank-states parent `security-deposit-return` (M.11). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-33(b)(1)-(2) (3 business days after termination and vacation, or surrender and acceptance, whichever first; tenant inspection on request within 5 business days; sign or dissent specifically; unannounced vacancy: reasonable time) (Ga. L. 2018, p. 969/HB 834); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-33(c) (a tenant present who signs or fails to dissent specifically cannot recover 'provided that the lists ... contain written notice of the tenant's duty to sign or to dissent'); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34(a) (30 days after obtaining possession; exact reasons; damage list; first-class mail to last known address deemed compliance; undelivered payment becomes the landlord's 90 days after mailing; wear and tear; retention categories; mitigation); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-35(b) (lists and statements late = forfeiture of the right to withhold AND to sue for damage to the premises); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-35(c) (three times the sum improperly withheld plus reasonable fees; bona fide error defense). SMALL-LANDLORD EXEMPTION (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-36): O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-31, 44-7-32, 44-7-33 and 44-7-35 do not apply to units owned by a natural person who, with spouse and minor children, owns ten or fewer rental units, unless a third party manages them for a fee; O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34 (30-day return and statement) applies to everyone. The clause applies the list procedure to every landlord, which the exempt landlord may follow voluntarily and which keeps the text correct for all. LAYOUT (instruction 28 / M.12): the notice of the duty to sign or dissent must be printed ON the damage lists themselves; this clause only promises it (GA log §4). Waiver barred: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2(b)(6). | GA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): kept the tenant's sign-or-dissent duty, the landlord's permitted deductions and the forwarding-address request; the restated inspection timing, 30-day return, wear-and-tear and mailing rules are in edu-security-deposit-rules-ga. | GA: RETRO 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18, fix 21; rule 78). RESTORED the sentence the 2026-09-29 scrub trimmed: 'The list will include written notice of Tenant's duty to sign it or to dissent from it.' O.C.G.A. § 44-7-33(c) bars a tenant who signs or fails to dissent only 'provided that the lists ... contain written notice of the tenant's duty to sign or to dissent', so the landlord's sign-or-dissent protection in this clause depends on that notice; a number check (cap, days) cannot catch its absence. The move-in list already promises the same notice (`move-in-damage-list-ga`). Required-content search: no other Georgia statute requires text in the lease itself beyond what `landlord-disclosure-ga` (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-3) and `security-deposit-escrow-ga` (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-31) carry; § 44-7-20 (flood) is a separate notice (GA log §4). Deposit cap: moved to education by the scrub (`edu-security-deposit-rules-ga`); the builder check (deposit + pet deposit + last-month amount at most two months' Rent, decision 1) is builder backlog M.13. Read section-open 2026-10-01 in the built-in browser from the official O.C.G.A. on advance.lexis.com (the General Assembly's free LexisNexis public access, 'Current through the 2026 Special Session of the General Assembly'); section text saved and SHA-256 matched to the browser copy (GA retro sources).

title: Where the Security Deposit Is Held
bodyText: Landlord will hold the Security Deposit in trust for Tenant [choose one: in an escrow account used only for security deposits at {{deposit_bank_name}}, {{deposit_bank_address}} / by maintaining a surety bond that Landlord has posted with the clerk of the Superior Court of {{county}} County, Georgia, in place of an escrow account].
notes: GA: Read section-open 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser from Justia's '2025 Code of Georgia', a host copy of the official O.C.G.A. that already prints the 2026 session (history lines cite Ga. L. 2026, pp. 278, 988 and 1069), with each section's history line and editor's notes. Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-31 (except as O.C.G.A. § 44-7-32 provides, a deposit held by a landlord or agent 'shall be deposited in an escrow account established only for that purpose in any bank or lending institution subject to regulation by this state or any agency of the United States government', held in trust; 'Tenants shall be informed in writing of the location of the escrow account'); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-32(a)-(c) (surety bond with the superior court clerk for the lesser of total deposits held or $50,000, conditioned on O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34 compliance and return on bankruptcy or foreclosure); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-35(a)(1) (no escrow or bond is one limb of the no-retention rule). CONDITIONAL: required unless the O.C.G.A. § 44-7-36 exemption applies (natural person who, with spouse and minor children, owns ten or fewer rental units, not managed by a third party for a fee); builder shows it when the landlord is not exempt. A real estate broker holding deposits is governed by O.C.G.A. § 43-40-20 trust-account rules (NOT READ; seen only in a 1976 Attorney General opinion annotated to O.C.G.A. § 44-7-32, instruction 16 flag), and brokers may not use the bond (1984 Op. Att'y Gen. 84-80, annotation, not relied on). No duty to pay interest (`edu-no-deposit-interest-ga`). LAYOUT: written notice of the account location (GA log §4).

title: Move-In Damage List
bodyText: Before Tenant pays the Security Deposit, Landlord will give Tenant a comprehensive written list of any existing damage to the property, which Tenant may keep permanently. Tenant may inspect the property to check the accuracy of the list before moving in. Landlord and Tenant will sign the list, and the signed list is conclusive evidence of its accuracy, but not as to latent defects. If Tenant refuses to sign the list, Tenant will state in writing the specific items on the list Tenant disputes and sign that statement. The list will include written notice of Tenant's duty to sign it or to dissent from it.
notes: GA: Read section-open 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser from Justia's '2025 Code of Georgia', a host copy of the official O.C.G.A. that already prints the 2026 session (history lines cite Ga. L. 2026, pp. 278, 988 and 1069), with each section's history line and editor's notes. Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-33(a) (list presented 'prior to tendering a security deposit', 'for the tenant's permanent retention'; inspection before occupancy; signed list conclusive except latent defects; specific written dissent) and O.C.G.A. § 44-7-33(c) (lists must 'contain written notice of the tenant's duty to sign or to dissent'); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-35(a)(2) (a list not made and presented is one limb of the no-retention rule). CONDITIONAL: required for landlords not exempt under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-36 (see `security-deposit-return-ga`); an exempt landlord may use it voluntarily. TIMING AND LAYOUT (instruction 28 / M.12): the list is a separate document presented BEFORE the deposit is tendered, and the duty-to-sign-or-dissent notice must be printed on it (GA log §4). Georgia's list is joint-signed but has no fixed day count at move-in (contrast KS/NV inventories).

title: Owner and Manager Disclosure
bodyText: Landlord discloses to Tenant, as Georgia law requires: the owner of record of the property, or a person authorized to act for and on behalf of the owner for the purposes of serving of process and receiving and receipting for demands and notices, is [name and address]; and the person authorized to manage the property is [name and address]. If any of these names or addresses changes, Landlord will advise Tenant of the change within 30 days, either in writing or by posting a notice of the change in a conspicuous place.
notes: GA: Read section-open 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser from Justia's '2025 Code of Georgia', a host copy of the official O.C.G.A. that already prints the 2026 session (history lines cite Ga. L. 2026, pp. 278, 988 and 1069), with each section's history line and editor's notes. Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-3(a) (in writing, at or before commencement; owner of record or service agent, and manager; changes within 30 days in writing or by conspicuous posting) and (b) (a person who signs for the owner without making the disclosure becomes the owner's agent for service, for the landlord's obligations, and for applying rent to them). Distinct duty for NON-RESIDENT owners of single-family or duplex rentals: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-25 (Ga. L. 2025, p. 882, § 2/HB 399, effective 2025-07-01) requires a Georgia-licensed broker and, for an out-of-state broker, an in-state person to handle tenant communications; it requires no disclosure to the tenant, so it is education only (`edu-nonresident-landlord-broker-ga`). TIMING (instruction 28): at or before commencement of the tenancy; 'conspicuous place' is a posting option for later changes, not a typography rule.

title: Flooding Notice
bodyText: [Separate written notice. Required only if flooding has damaged any part of the living space covered by this Lease at least three times during the five years immediately before the date of this Lease. Give it to the prospective tenant BEFORE the written lease is signed.] FLOODING NOTICE: The property has a propensity to flood. Flooding has damaged part of the living space covered by this Lease at least three times during the five-year period immediately before the date of this Lease. In this notice, 'flooding' means the inundation of a portion of the living space covered by the lease which was caused by an increased water level in an established water source such as a river, stream, or drainage ditch or as a ponding of water at or near the point where heavy or excessive rain fell. Tenant acknowledges receiving this notice before signing the Lease.
notes: GA: Read section-open 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser from Justia's '2025 Code of Georgia', a host copy of the official O.C.G.A. that already prints the 2026 session (history lines cite Ga. L. 2026, pp. 278, 988 and 1069), with each section's history line and editor's notes. Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-20 (Ga. L. 1995, p. 266; Ga. L. 2026, p. 1069, § 44(19)/HB 1268, effective 2026-07-01, stylistic only: the definition now opens 'As used in this Code section, the term flooding means'). Duty: before entering a written lease for residential occupancy, the owner (directly or through an agent) notifies the prospective tenant in writing of the property's 'propensity of flooding' if flooding damaged any portion of the living space (or attachments) the tenant has sole and exclusive use of at least three times in the five years before the lease date. Sanction: tort liability to the tenant and family for damage to personal property proximately caused by flooding during the term. Applies to leaseholds entered on or after 1995-07-01. No statutory form; the heading and body use the statute's own words. CONDITIONAL (only when the three-in-five history exists). LAYOUT/TIMING (instruction 28 / M.12): a writing delivered BEFORE the written agreement is entered; the builder must deliver it as a separate pre-signing document, not only inside the lease (GA log §4). Kickoff lead confirmed. | GA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): optional (Taylor's pattern 3): the flooding notice is owed as a separate writing before the lease is signed; the clause records it. Companion: edu-flood-disclosure-ga.

title: Service Dogs and Other Assistance Animals
bodyText: A service dog or other assistance animal that Tenant or an Occupant with a disability needs is not a pet under this Lease, regardless of any pet policy, breed, weight or size restriction stated elsewhere in this Lease, and Landlord will not charge a pet deposit, pet rent, pet fee or any other extra compensation for it. Tenant remains liable for any damage the animal does to the property. A service dog, meaning a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks that directly assist a person with a physical or mental impairment and directly relate to that person's disability (or a dog still in training that is operating under a trainer's guidance), is entitled to full and equal access to the property; Landlord is not required to modify the property or to provide a higher degree of care because of it. Any other assistance animal, including an emotional support animal, may be kept at Tenant's request as a reasonable accommodation for a disability. If the disability or the disability-related need for that animal is not readily apparent, Landlord may request reliable documentation of the disability and of the need, to the extent permitted by applicable law. Landlord may deny or withdraw that accommodation if the specific animal poses a direct threat to the health or safety of others, or would cause substantial physical damage to the property of others, that cannot be reduced or eliminated by another reasonable accommodation.
notes: GA: Read section-open 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser from Justia's '2025 Code of Georgia', a host copy of the official O.C.G.A. that already prints the 2026 session (history lines cite Ga. L. 2026, pp. 278, 988 and 1069), with each section's history line and editor's notes. Instruction 24 family closed for GA: supersedes `assistance-animal-accommodation` (base tagged KS;NV;TX;AZ, not GA). WHY AN OVERRIDE: the base lets the landlord deny or withdraw ANY assistance animal for a direct threat or substantial damage; Georgia's service-dog housing rule has no such limit. O.C.G.A. § 30-4-3(b) (Ga. L. 2026, p. 278, § 6/HB 668, the 'Mara Jade Act', effective 2026-07-01): every physically or mentally impaired person who has or obtains a service dog, and every trainer, 'shall be entitled to full and equal access to all housing accommodations' and 'shall not be required to pay extra compensation for such service dog', but is 'liable for any damage done to the premises'; O.C.G.A. § 30-4-3(c): no duty to modify the property or give a higher degree of care; O.C.G.A. § 30-4-3(a) rights are 'subject to the conditions and limitations established by law and applicable alike to all persons'. Definitions (O.C.G.A. § 30-4-1, same act): 'service dog' = individually trained to do work or perform tasks that directly assist and directly relate to the person's disability, or in training under a trainer; it 'shall not include a dog ... that solely provides comfort, companionship, or emotional support'; 'physically or mentally impaired person' = substantially limited in one or more activities of daily living over an extended period; 'housing accommodations' EXCLUDES a single-family residence whose occupants rent not more than one room. Penalties (O.C.G.A. § 30-4-4, same act): denial or interference is a misdemeanor of a high and aggravated nature (fine up to $2,000, up to 30 days); deliberate misrepresentation as qualified to use a service dog is the same grade (`edu-service-dog-law-ga`). EMOTIONAL SUPPORT AND OTHER ANIMALS: no Georgia animal-specific ESA statute (official full-text search 2026-09-28: 'emotional support', 'assistance animal(s)', 'support animal', 'comfort animal' hit only O.C.G.A. §§ 30-4-1, 30-4-4 and the Fair Housing Act sections); the state basis is the general reasonable-accommodation duty in the Georgia Fair Housing Act, O.C.G.A. § 8-3-202(a)(7)(B)(ii) (category: general, not animal-specific), with its direct-threat limit in O.C.G.A. § 8-3-202(d), plus the federal FHA (42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B); HUD guidance withdrawn 2025-09-17 and enforcement narrowed 2026-05-22, per the architecture log; instruction 16 federal flag). CURRENCY (instruction 34): HB 668's O.C.G.A. § 30-4 amendments took effect 2026-07-01 (Justia history lines; the act has no separate effective-date section, so the July 1 general date applies); signed version on gov.georgia.gov 2026 signed legislation.

title: Early Termination: Family Violence or Stalking Order
bodyText: Tenant may terminate this Lease effective 30 days after giving Landlord written notice of termination if a civil family violence order, civil stalking order, criminal family violence order or criminal stalking order, as Georgia law defines those terms, has been issued protecting Tenant or Tenant's minor child, including where Tenant is a joint tenant, even if the protected Tenant had no obligation to pay rent to Landlord. The notice must be accompanied by a copy of the order and, if the order is an ex parte temporary protective order, a copy of the police report. Tenant may occupy the property until the termination is effective. Tenant will be liable for the Rent due under this Lease prorated to the effective date of termination, payable when it would otherwise have been due, and for any delinquent or unpaid Rent or other sums owed to Landlord before termination, but not for any other fees, Rent or damages because of the early termination. If Tenant terminates under this Section 14 or more days before occupancy, no damages or penalties of any kind will be assessed. This Section may not be waived or modified by agreement.
notes: GA: Read section-open 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser from Justia's '2025 Code of Georgia', a host copy of the official O.C.G.A. that already prints the 2026 session (history lines cite Ga. L. 2026, pp. 278, 988 and 1069), with each section's history line and editor's notes. Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-23(a)-(e) (Ga. L. 2018, p. 969, § 2/HB 834; Ga. L. 2021, p. 513, § 1/SB 75; SB 75 § 2 applies the 2021 version to agreements entered into, renewed, modified or extended on or after 2021-07-01). Qualifying orders ((a)(1)-(4)): civil family violence order (protective order under Title 19 ch. 13 art. 1 with respondent present or noticed, or ex parte order with a police report); civil stalking order (O.C.G.A. § 16-5-94, same conditions); criminal family violence order and criminal stalking order (pretrial-release or probation orders). L.5 DEPENDENCIES NOT READ: Title 19 ch. 13 art. 1 ('family violence' definition, O.C.G.A. § 19-13-1) and O.C.G.A. §§ 16-5-90 to 16-5-94 (stalking). Because the definition of 'family violence' limits the perpetrator class (L.5), the clause uses 'as Georgia law defines those terms' rather than a broader 'victim of domestic violence'. No lock-change right in the statute (official full-text search 2026-09-28: no lock or rekey statute). RECOMMENDED, not REQUIRED (Taylor's classification rule, AZ session 2026-09-27): the statute gives the right regardless of lease text and requires none. STATUTE WATCH: flag for the Claude CLI legal-watch in case Georgia later requires lease text. | GA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-dv-lease-termination-ga). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Rent Escalation for Utilities, Taxes or Insurance
bodyText: Monthly Rent may increase during the Term by the amount of any increase, after the Start Date, in [choose one or more: utility charges Landlord pays for the property / real estate taxes on the property / Landlord's insurance premiums for the property], allocated to the property as follows: [describe the calculation]. Landlord will give Tenant at least {{escalation_notice_days}} days' written notice before an increase takes effect, with a statement showing how it was calculated.
notes: GA: Read section-open 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser from Justia's '2025 Code of Georgia', a host copy of the official O.C.G.A. that already prints the 2026 session (history lines cite Ga. L. 2026, pp. 278, 988 and 1069), with each section's history line and editor's notes. OPT-IN LANDLORD RIGHT (instruction 30). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-24(d)(1)(A) (Ga. L. 2019, p. 1026/HB 346): a landlord 'shall not be liable for retaliation' for increasing rent 'Under an escalation clause in a written lease for utilities, taxes, or insurance'. Without such a clause, a rent increase within three months after protected tenant action is an element of a prima-facie retaliation case (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-24(c)(4)); remedies O.C.G.A. § 44-7-24(e). The statute creates the safe harbour only; the escalation mechanism itself is contract. No Georgia rent-increase notice statute (`edu-no-rent-increase-notice-ga`) and rent control is preempted (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-19). CONDITIONAL: offered, not defaulted; the notice period is a product default for the landlord to set.

title: No Criminal Acts or Serious Misconduct
bodyText: Tenant, members of Tenant's household, and Tenant's guests and invitees will not commit criminal acts or other serious misconduct at the property or in any common area, including threatening by word or conduct the personal safety of Landlord, Landlord's employees or another tenant, and intentionally damaging property. A violation of this Section is a material breach of this Lease, for which Landlord may terminate this Lease and pursue the remedies this Lease and applicable law provide.

Limb (C) turns on WRITTEN lease provisions, so a lease without one gives it up; limb (B) needs no lease text. The Georgia REALTORS lease makes an arrest or indictment for unlawful activity a default (GA log §15); this clause is conduct-based on purpose, because an arrest-based trigger raises fair-housing risk (federal disparate-impact doctrine, not relied on; instruction 16). Overlaps `residential-use-only` (illegal purpose) and `no-disturbance` (safety threats); kept separate because (C) rewards explicit wording. CONDITIONAL: offered, not defaulted.

title: Holdover Charge
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession after this Lease ends, whether at the end of the Term or on an earlier termination under this Lease or applicable law (other than a termination for nonpayment of Rent), and Landlord has not agreed in writing to a continued tenancy or accepted Rent for one, then, in place of any actual damages for Tenant's continued possession (including the actual damages and reasonable rental value described in the Holdover section of this Lease), Tenant will pay Landlord a holdover charge of {{holdover_daily_rate}} for each day Tenant remains in possession. Landlord and Tenant agree that Landlord's loss from a holdover, including delay in making the property available to a new tenant, is difficult to estimate accurately in advance, that this charge is a reasonable estimate of that loss, and that it is not a penalty. Landlord's acceptance of a holdover charge is not acceptance of Rent for a continued tenancy. This Section does not limit Landlord's right to recover possession, unpaid Rent and other amounts due for the period before this Lease ended, or damages for harm to the property.
