Every non-optional fee Tenant must pay under this Lease, one-time or recurring, is listed here with its amount and when it is due: [list each non-optional fee, e.g. application fee, pet rent, required parking or amenity fee, utility charges billed by Landlord, or write 'None']. Charges that apply only if a stated event occurs: late fee of {{late_fee_amount}} if Monthly Rent is not paid in full within {{late_fee_grace_days}} days after it is due; returned-payment fee of [amount]; [list any other conditional charge, or write 'None']. Utilities included in Monthly Rent: [list each utility included in rent, or write 'No utilities are included in Monthly Rent']. Tenant is not required to pay any non-optional fee that is not listed on this page.
notes: IL: 765 ILCS 705/35(b) (added by P.A. 104-479): 'All non-optional fees, regardless of whether they are one-time fees or recurring fees, shall be explicitly contained on the first page of a lease agreement. If a fee is not explicitly contained on the first page of a lease agreement, a tenant shall not be liable for payment of such fee.' (b)(2): 'In a lease agreement disclosure or unit listing, the landlord must disclose whether utilities are included in rent.' The Act does not define 'non-optional fee'; the box also lists the late fee and returned-payment fee so a court reading them as non-optional finds them on page 1 (a landlord-protective choice, IL log §6.2). (b)(1) listing disclosure is outside the lease (edu-rental-fee-law-il). (c) banned fees: none may be listed (edu-rental-fee-law-il); a 'move-in fee' (as in the MainStreet form) is lawful only if it does not pay for a banned item such as a walk-through or routine maintenance, and renaming does not help (765 ILCS 705/35(c)(9), (c)(11), (e); builder note). Exempt: leases for units in owner-occupied premises of 6 units or fewer (765 ILCS 705/35(e)); the box is harmless there. Effective date: P.A. 104-479 Section 99 says July 1, 2026; the Public Act page, bill status and the ILCS source note say January 1, 2027; applied now on Taylor's decision, 2026-09-30 (IL log §1.2, §6.1). title: Flood Disclosure
bodyText:
[BUILDER: give Tenant this disclosure in writing BEFORE the Lease or renewal is signed; it must also appear in the signed Lease or renewal lease, signed by both parties.] Landlord ({{landlord_name}}) [is / is not] aware that the rental property is located in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area ("100-year floodplain"). The property has experienced flooding [number] times in the last 10 years. Even if the rental property is not in a Special Flood Hazard Area ("100-year floodplain"), the dwelling may still be susceptible to flooding. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) maintains a flood map on its Internet website that is searchable by address, at no cost, to determine if a dwelling is located in a flood hazard area.
Landlord ({{landlord_name}}) [is / is not] aware that the rental property you are renting has flooded at least once in the last 10 years. The rental property has flooded [number] times in the last 10 years. Even if the dwelling has not flooded in the last 10 years, the dwelling may still be susceptible to flooding.
Most tenant insurance policies do not cover damage or loss incurred in a flood. You are encouraged to examine your policy to determine whether you are covered. If you are not, flood insurance may be available through FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program to cover your personal property in the event of a flood. Information regarding flood risks can be found at the dnr.illinois.gov (Illinois Department of Natural Resources), fema.gov (FEMA), and ready.gov/flood (U.S. National public service).
Landlords are required to disclose the above information pursuant to Section 25 of the Landlord and Tenant Act. A landlord's failure to comply with Section 25 of the Landlord and Tenant Act shall entitle the tenant to remedies as defined in that Section.
Tenant signature and date: ____________________ Landlord signature and date: ____________________
notes: IL: 765 ILCS 705/25 (P.A. 103-754, eff. 1-1-25; P.A. 104-417, eff. 8-15-25). (b): every landlord must disclose in writing before signing whether the property is in the FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area and any actual knowledge of flooding of the property or its parking areas and its frequency; 'Such disclosure shall also be included in the written lease or the written renewal lease and shall be signed by both parties.' (c): the same for a lower-level unit (garden, basement or first floor) as to flooding in the last 10 years. (d): the written disclosure 'shall look substantially similar to' the prescribed form, reproduced verbatim here, with its paragraph breaks, except for these changes (rule 59): '(Landlord)' becomes 'Landlord ({{landlord_name}})'; each '[ ] is or [ ] is not' becomes a hand-filled '[is / is not]'; each '[ ] times' becomes '[number] times'; and the dotted '(Tenant Signature) (Date)' and '(Landlord Signature) (Date)' lines become 'Tenant signature and date' and 'Landlord signature and date' blanks. Remedies for non-compliance (tenant termination within 30 days, refund of prepaid rent and fees within 15 days, damages for flooded personal property) are in (e). Exempt: farm leases, concession leases, property owned or managed by the Department of Natural Resources ((e), second subsection so lettered). A statewide REQUIRED row: the form also covers the 'not aware / 0 times' case, so every non-exempt lease carries it. The form is a statutory form and a separate pre-signing writing; the clause cannot replace the pre-signing delivery (rule 48; builder note). title: Radon Disclosure
bodyText: [BUILDER: use for every dwelling unit except one on the third story or higher above ground level. Give Tenant this form, the pamphlet 'Radon Guide for Tenants' from the Illinois Emergency Management Agency (or an equivalent pamphlet it approves) and copies of any records or reports showing a radon hazard in the unit at the time of application or before this Lease is signed.] DISCLOSURE OF INFORMATION ON RADON HAZARDS TO TENANTS. Radon Warning Statement. Each tenant in this residence or dwelling unit is notified that the property may present exposure to levels of indoor radon gas that may place the occupants at risk of developing radon-induced lung cancer. Radon, a Class-A human carcinogen, is the leading cause of death in private homes and the leading cause of lung cancer in nonsmokers. The lessor of any residence is required to provide each tenant with any information on radon test results of the dwelling unit that present a radon hazard to the tenant. The Illinois Emergency Management Agency (IEMA) strongly recommends that ALL rental properties have a radon test performed and radon hazards mitigated if elevated levels are found in a dwelling unit or a routinely occupied area of a multiple family residence. Elevated radon concentrations can easily be reduced by a radon contractor. Dwelling Unit Address: {{property_address}} Lessor's Disclosure (initial each of the following that apply) ____ Lessor has no knowledge of elevated radon concentrations (or records or reports pertaining to elevated radon concentrations) in the dwelling unit. ____ Radon concentrations (at or above the IEMA recommended Radon Action Level 4.0 pCi/L) are known to be present within the dwelling unit. ____ Lessor has provided the tenant with copies of all available records and reports, if any, pertaining to radon concentrations within the dwelling unit. Tenant's Acknowledgment (initial each of the following that apply) ____ Tenant has received copies of all information listed above. ____ Tenant has received the pamphlet "Radon Guide for Tenants". Certification of Accuracy The following parties have reviewed the information above and each party certifies, to the best of his or her knowledge, that the information he or she provided is true and accurate. Lessor ____________________ Date ________ Tenant ____________________ Date ________
notes: IL: 420 ILCS 46/26 (P.A. 103-298, eff. 1-1-24; leases entered on or after that date, (g)). (a): at application, before a lease is entered into, or on request during the term, the lessor provides the IEMA pamphlet, copies of records or reports indicating a radon hazard, and the Disclosure of Information on Radon Hazards to Tenants form in (f). (f): the form, reproduced verbatim except that the dotted blanks become lines, the unit address is filled from {{property_address}}, and a period follows the two headings when run into one field (rule 59). CONDITIONAL: 420 ILCS 46/20(9) excludes 'Transfers of any residential dwelling unit located on the third story or higher above ground level', and 'transfers' includes leases. Tenant rights (90-day test and termination, (b)-(c), (e); no deposit deduction for testing or mitigation, 420 ILCS 46/30(c)) are in edu-radon-tenant-rights-il. P.A. 104-852 (general revisory act, eff. 8-21-2026, not yet compiled) makes only technical changes to 420 ILCS 46/26(b) and leaves the (f) form unchanged (IL log §1.2). 420 ILCS 46/15 still says the Act applies to leased properties 'to the extent specified in Section 25', a repealed section (stale cross-reference, IL log §10; rule 77). title: Use of the Property for Crimes
bodyText: If any lessee or occupant, on one or more occasions, uses or permits the use of the leased premises for the commission of a felony or Class A misdemeanor under the laws of the State of Illinois, Landlord shall have the right to void this Lease and recover the leased premises.
notes: IL: 735 ILCS 5/9-120(a) (P.A. 100-173): 'A written lease shall notify the lessee that if any lessee or occupant, on one or more occasions, uses or permits the use of the leased premises for the commission of a felony or Class A misdemeanor under the laws of this State, the lessor shall have the right to void the lease and recover the leased premises.' The clause follows the statutory sentence with only these changes: 'the lessor' becomes 'Landlord', 'the lease' becomes 'this Lease', and 'this State' becomes 'the State of Illinois' (rule 59). Omission does not waive the lessor's right (same subsection), so the clause is required text rather than a condition of the right. The procedure (5 days' written notice to vacate after voiding, (d); 7-day stay limit, (f); deposit not forfeited except sheriff fees, (c)) is in edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-il. Controls over any cure promise in default-by-tenant: the statute voids the lease at the lessor's option without a cure (Step D rule 43, IL log §19). title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: If Landlord keeps any part of the Security Deposit for damage to the property, Landlord will, within 30 days after the later of the date Tenant vacates the property and the date Tenant's right of possession ends, give Tenant an itemized statement of the damage and the estimated or actual cost of repairing or replacing each item, with the paid receipts or copies. The statement will be delivered in person, by postmarked mail to Tenant's last known address, or by email to a verified email address Tenant has provided. If the statement gives an estimated cost, Landlord will deliver the paid receipts or copies within 30 days after giving the statement. If Landlord does not give the statement and receipts as required, Landlord will return the full Security Deposit within 45 days after Tenant vacates. Landlord will return the Security Deposit, less any lawful deductions, no later than 45 days after Tenant vacates, in person or by postmarked mail to Tenant's last known address or another address Tenant has provided. When Tenant vacates, Tenant will give Landlord in writing a forwarding mailing address and, if Tenant wishes to receive the statement by email, a verified email address.
notes: IL: Supersedes security-deposit-return for IL. 765 ILCS 710/1(a) (P.A. 103-224, eff. 1-1-24): no withholding for property damage unless, within 30 days of the date the lessee vacated or the date the lessee's right of possession ends, whichever is later, the lessor furnishes by personal delivery, postmarked mail to the last known address or email to a verified email address provided by the lessee, an itemized statement with estimated or actual costs and paid receipts; receipts within 30 days after an estimate; otherwise return in full within 45 days of vacating, in person or by postmarked mail. Lessor's own labor may be charged at reasonable cost. No liability if the lessee gives no mailing or email address (the forwarding-address sentence serves the landlord). 765 ILCS 710/1(b): verified statement where receipts cannot be produced through no fault of the lessor. 765 ILCS 710/1(c): refusal or bad faith plus failure to return makes the lessor liable for twice the deposit due, costs and attorney's fees (edu-deposit-return-rules-il). The statute has no unit-count threshold since P.A. 103-224. The 45-day outer limit for a balance after deductions is a lease promise the statute does not state for that case; it matches the statute's full-return deadline (IL log §6). Deposit interest for 25+ unit properties: edu-deposit-interest-il. title: Specified Cleaning, Repair and Replacement Costs
bodyText: The following costs for cleaning, repairing or replacing components of the property, the building or its common areas apply to damage beyond normal wear and tear, and Landlord may withhold the amount stated from the Security Deposit for that damage: [list each component or amenity and the dollar amount for cleaning, repair or replacement, e.g. carpet cleaning $___; interior door replacement $___; or write 'None']. Each amount is a reasonable cost to restore the property to its condition at the start of this Lease. If Landlord withholds an amount listed here, the itemized statement will refer to it and include a copy of this Section. Any other deduction will follow the itemized-statement and receipt requirements in this Lease and Illinois law.
notes: IL: Optional clause (rule 54, statute lets the lease decide). 765 ILCS 710/1(a) (P.A. 103-224, eff. 1-1-24): 'If a written lease specifies the cost for cleaning, repair, or replacement of any component of the leased premises or any component of the building or common areas that, if damaged, will not be replaced, the lessor may withhold the dollar amount specified in the lease. Costs specified in a written lease shall be for damage beyond normal wear and tear and reasonable to restore the leased premises to the same condition as at the time the lease began. The itemized statement shall reference the dollar amount specified in the written lease associated with the specific building component or amenity and include a copy of the applicable portion of the lease.' The statute's 'that, if damaged, will not be replaced' qualifier is ambiguous as to which components it limits (the clause does not rely on it); case law not read. A companion to security-deposit-use, hence a new topic_key (rule 58). Not a default. title: Returned Checks / Dishonored Payments
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds, a closed or nonexistent account, or a stop-payment order, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount; for a dishonored check, Illinois law makes the writer liable for $25 or Landlord's costs of collection, whichever is greater; to recover more than $25 in a collection without a lawsuit, Landlord must first mail a written demand by certified mail, return receipt requested, demanding payment within 30 days and stating the liability], and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are returned or fail, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check or money order, and Tenant may still use any payment method Illinois law entitles Tenant to use.
notes: IL: Supersedes returned-payments for IL: its 'not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' states only a ceiling (rule 53), and 765 ILCS 705/35(b) makes the fee unrecoverable unless stated on the lease's first page, so it must be a stated figure (carried into fee-disclosure-first-page-il). 810 ILCS 5/3-806: a person who issues a check dishonored for no account, insufficient funds or insufficient credit is liable for $25 or all costs and expenses of collection including reasonable attorney's fees, whichever is greater, plus interest under 815 ILCS 205/4(1); costs above $25 in a nonlitigated collection need a written demand by certified mail, return receipt requested, demanding payment within 30 days and stating the liability. The section does not reach stop-payment orders or failed electronic transfers, which are contract only. Whether a lease may set a higher fixed fee for a dishonored check is not settled by the statute (not read in case law). The last clause preserves 765 ILCS 705/4 (no required electronic payment) and 765 ILCS 705/3.5 (portal fee alternative); a demand for certified funds is not an electronic transfer. title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord: [list approved pets, or state that no pets are permitted]. Any pet deposit ({{pet_deposit}}, if applicable) is part of the Security Deposit and will be held, applied and returned with it under this Lease and Illinois law. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, if applicable. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet, and will reimburse Landlord for claims caused by Tenant's pet, except to the extent a claim arises from the negligence of Landlord or Landlord's agents or employees. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern. Landlord may enter the property in connection with a pet only as this Lease's Access & Entry terms permit, or without notice in an emergency, and will not seize or remove a pet except with the help of animal control or law enforcement or through a court process. This Section does not apply to a service animal or assistance animal.
notes: IL: Supersedes pet-policy for IL: the base clause's indemnity 'from claims arising from Tenant's pet(s)' and entry and removal 'without liability to Tenant' can exempt the landlord from liability for its own negligence, which 765 ILCS 705/1(a) makes void for residential leases ('every covenant ... exempting the lessor from liability for damages for injuries to person or property caused by or resulting from the negligence of the lessor, his or her agents, servants or employees ... shall be deemed to be void'; (b) saves only non-residential property-damage waivers). Wording follows pet-policy-pa without its Pennsylvania deposit-cap sentence (Illinois has no deposit cap). A pet deposit secures damage, so it is a security deposit under 765 ILCS 710/1(a). Pet rent is a recurring non-optional fee once a pet is approved, listed on page 1 (fee-disclosure-first-page-il). Assistance animals: no pet deposit, fee or special insurance (310 ILCS 120/10(f)); covered by assistance-animal-accommodation. No Illinois statute on pets in house or apartment leases (whole-code battery 24: only 765 ILCS 745/9, mobile homes). title: Handling of Property Left Behind
bodyText: Personal property Tenant leaves at the property after Tenant has moved out and returned possession to Landlord, or after Tenant has abandoned the property, may be treated as abandoned. Before disposing of it, Landlord will send Tenant a written notice by first-class mail to Tenant's forwarding address (or, if Tenant has not given one, to the property address) and by email to any email address Tenant has given, describing the property and stating where and when Tenant may collect it. If Tenant does not collect it within [number, at least 10] days after the notice is sent, Landlord may sell, donate or otherwise dispose of it, and will apply any sale proceeds first to the reasonable costs of removing, storing and selling it and then to amounts Tenant owes under this Lease, holding any balance for Tenant. Landlord need not store, and may dispose of right away, garbage, perishable items and anything hazardous. This Section does not apply to property removed when a court's eviction order is carried out, which is handled as the court and Illinois law direct, to motor vehicles, which are handled under Illinois vehicle law, or to the property of a Tenant who has died, which is handled under Illinois estate law.
notes: IL: No Illinois statute sets a procedure for a residential tenant's property left behind in a house or apartment: whole-code battery 19 (abandon near landlord/lessee/tenant terms) found only 735 ILCS 5/9-318 (crops on abandoned premises), 765 ILCS 745/9.5 (mobile homes, out of scope) and unrelated hits; batteries 67 and 87 found no deposit rule. The shared surrender-end-of-term-ks-ne clause, tagged IL, points to this Section, so a contract procedure is supplied (as abandoned-property-pa and -ut do on statute). Distress for rent (735 ILCS 5/9-301 to 5/9-321) is a separate court-supervised remedy not used by this Section. Case law on conversion and on when a tenancy is abandoned was not read; the notice period is a landlord choice with a floor of 10 days as a caution, not a statutory figure (IL log §6). Unauthorized occupants: 735 ILCS 5/9-102(e) (edu-unauthorized-occupants-il). Towing: 625 ILCS 5/4-203(f). Chicago's ordinance has its own rules (flag, not read). title: Notice to End a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText: If this Lease continues as a month-to-month tenancy, either Landlord or Tenant may end it by giving the other written notice at least 30 days before the last day of a rental month, and the tenancy will end on that last day. Landlord's notice will be served in a manner Illinois law allows for a notice to terminate a tenancy. Rent remains payable through the date the tenancy ends. This Section does not limit either party's right to end this Lease earlier where this Lease or Illinois law allows it.
notes: IL: 735 ILCS 5/9-207(b) (P.A. 100-173): in a tenancy for any term less than one year other than week to week, 'where the tenant holds over without special agreement, the landlord may terminate the tenancy by 30 days' notice, in writing'; (a) week to week: 7 days. 735 ILCS 5/9-205: year to year, 60 days' written notice ending at the end of the year. Illinois sets no notice for the tenant; the lease supplies 30 days (fixed text, so no new variable). Ending on the last day of a rental month is a landlord choice at least as generous as 735 ILCS 5/9-207(b); whether Illinois case law requires it was not read. Service: 735 ILCS 5/9-211 (delivery, a person 13 or older residing on or in possession of the premises, certified or registered mail with a returned receipt, or posting if no one is in possession). Reads with holdover-ca, which makes a holdover month-to-month on acceptance of rent. Rule 37 tenancy types are set out in edu-notices-to-quit-il. Foreclosure successors: 90 days (735 ILCS 5/9-207.5). title: Building Manager and Insurer Notice
bodyText: [Use only if the building has more than 4 living units and neither the owner nor a manager or agent employed by the owner lives or keeps an office in the building. This notice in the Lease takes the place of the notice Illinois law otherwise requires to be posted near the mailboxes; if the fire or explosion insurance is later cancelled, Landlord must post or mail a notice of the cancellation within 24 hours after learning of it.] Building management and insurance. The person responsible for managing the building is [name, address and telephone number]. The building is insured against loss or damage by fire or explosion by [name, address and telephone number of each insurance company, or state that the building is not insured against fire or explosion].
notes: IL: 735 ILCS 5/9-320(a) (P.A. 83-707): an owner of residential real property containing more than 4 living units who does not reside or maintain an office there and does not employ a resident or on-site manager or agent must post, near the mailboxes or inside in a place visible to all residents, a notice of at least 20 square inches with the name, address and telephone number of the person responsible for managing the building and of the company or companies insuring it against fire or explosion (or that it is uninsured), and post notice of cancellation within 24 hours of being notified. (b): 'In lieu of the requirement for posting the notices ... the owner's managing agent may include such notice in a written rental or lease agreement or may give such notice by first class mail'. (c): petty offense, fine up to $100 per day. The lease is one permitted vehicle for a required notice, so the basis is a required disclosure. Illinois has no general statewide owner-identity disclosure for other landlords (whole-code; local ordinances such as Chicago's not read). title: Fire or Other Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty not caused by Tenant, members of Tenant's household or Tenant's guests, and the damage makes the property unfit to live in or substantially impairs Tenant's use of it, either Landlord or Tenant may end this Lease by written notice to the other, effective on the date Tenant moves out. Rent will be prorated to that date, any prepaid Rent refunded, and the Security Deposit returned as this Lease and Illinois law provide. If the casualty makes only part of the property unusable and Tenant stays in possession, Rent will be reduced in proportion to the part of the property Tenant cannot use until Landlord completes repairs. This Section does not limit any other right Tenant has under Illinois law.
notes: IL: Opt-in (standing GA decision; rule 54). No Illinois statute governs casualty to a leased dwelling: whole-code batteries 89 (destroyed by fire, fire or other casualty, untenantable, unfit for occupancy, damaged by fire near lease terms: 0 hits), 97 (untenantable, uninhabitable: 765 ILCS 605/14, condominium property, and 765 ILCS 745/21, mobile homes, out of scope, among unrelated hits) and 98 (destruction or casualty near lease terms: unrelated hits only) found no residential casualty statute. title: Keys
bodyText: At the start of the Term, Tenant will receive the keys specified by Landlord and will sign a receipt acknowledging the number and type of keys provided. Tenant will return all keys to Landlord at the end of the Term. If Tenant fails to return all keys or requires a replacement during the Term, Landlord may re-key the applicable locks and charge the cost to Tenant, except for any lock change Illinois law requires Landlord to make between tenancies. Tenant may not duplicate keys without Landlord's consent.
notes: IL: Supersedes keys for IL. 765 ILCS 705/15(b) (P.A. 97-470): in counties of more than 3,000,000 (Cook County; population derived from secondary knowledge, census not read, IL log §7), after a unit is vacated and on or before the day a new lessee takes possession, the lessor must change or rekey the lock; (c) liability for theft attributable to failure; (d) not applicable where the lessee obtained the right to rekey under a written lease; (e) exempt: owner-occupied buildings of 4 units or fewer, rooms in owner-occupied homes. title: Electric Vehicle Charging System Requirements
bodyText: [Use only if the property is a single-family home or multifamily building that has parking spaces.] Tenant may install, at Tenant's expense and for Tenant's own use, a level 1 or level 2 receptacle or outlet or a level 2 electric vehicle charging system at the property, if Tenant first agrees in writing to: comply with Landlord's design specifications for the installation [describe, or attach]; use a duly licensed and registered electrical contractor familiar with the installation and code requirements of electric vehicle charging systems; and, within 14 days after receiving Landlord's consent to the installation, give Landlord a certificate of insurance naming Landlord as an additional insured on Tenant's renter's insurance policy for any claim related to the installation, maintenance or use of the system, or, if Landlord so chooses, reimburse Landlord within 14 days after receiving Landlord's invoice for the actual increase in Landlord's insurance premium attributable to the system. Tenant will register the system with Landlord within 30 days after installation and will comply with Landlord's bona fide safety requirements consistent with applicable building codes or recognized safety standards and Landlord's reasonable requirements for the system's dimensions, placement and external appearance: [describe, or write 'None']. Landlord may require Tenant to reimburse the actual cost of electricity Landlord provides that the system uses (including any network fee), may charge a reasonable fee for access, and may require a security deposit to cover restoring the property if Tenant removes the system. If Landlord installs the system at Tenant's request, Tenant will reimburse the cost of installation, including wiring upgrades directly attributable to the system.
notes: IL: 765 ILCS 1085/35 (P.A. 103-53, eff. 1-1-24; P.A. 103-605, eff. 7-1-24), Electric Vehicle Charging Act; applies to existing and new single-family homes and multifamily residential buildings that have parking spaces (765 ILCS 1085/10(b)). (a)(1): notwithstanding the lease, a tenant may install, at the tenant's expense for its own use, a level 1 or level 2 receptacle or outlet or a level 2 system; (a)(2): no fee except electricity reimbursement (including network fee), a reasonable access fee, a restoration security deposit, installation cost where the landlord installs at the tenant's request, and a reasonable fee to reserve a space in an area accessible to other tenants ((a)(2)(C), carried by ev-charging-shared-area-co); (b): landlord may require bona fide safety requirements, registration within 30 days after installation, and reasonable aesthetic provisions; (c): the tenant may place a system if it complies and agrees in writing to design specifications, a licensed and registered electrical contractor, and a certificate of insurance within 14 days after consent (or, at the landlord's option, premium reimbursement within 14 days after invoice). A tenant whose landlord is a unit owner in an association goes through the landlord under the association provisions ((h), not read). Fees charged under this Section are optional and need not be on page 1. title: Rental Fee Transparency and Junk-Fee Ban
bodyText: For residential leases entered into after the law's effective date (official records give January 1, 2027; the Act's own text says July 1, 2026), every non-optional fee, one-time or recurring, must appear explicitly on the first page of the lease, or the tenant is not liable for it. A listing must disclose non-optional fees clearly and conspicuously (or through an accompanying web link), and the lease or listing must say whether utilities are included in rent. No landlord or lease may require: an application fee, including background checks, over $50 (a landlord may charge the actual cost of a third-party background check above $50 only if it paid the cost up front and bills the applicant with receipts within 14 days, or the fee is waived, and the fee can never be a basis for eviction in the first lease year); a fee at application that duplicates screening costs or covers costs unrelated to screening; a fee for modifying or renewing a lease; a fee for an eviction notice or for filing an eviction before the court grants an eviction order (court costs and filing fees remain recoverable); a fee for after-hours maintenance requests; a fee for contacting the owner or manager about maintenance, the lease or the tenancy; a maintenance travel fee; a maintenance-hotline fee; a fee for routine maintenance and upkeep; a pest-abatement fee where the tenant in no way contributed to the infestation; or a fee for a move-in or move-out walk-through. Renaming a fee does not avoid the law. Leases for units in owner-occupied premises of 6 units or fewer are exempt. Local governments may regulate fees, but only in a way at least as restrictive. A tenant may sue for injunctive and monetary relief, attorney's fees and costs.
notes: IL: 765 ILCS 705/35(a)-(f) (added by P.A. 104-479). Applies to 'all lease agreements for residential rental property entered into after the effective date' (765 ILCS 705/35(e)). title: Application Fees and Reusable Screening Reports
bodyText: Under the rental-fee law (for leases entered into after its effective date, January 1, 2027 in official records; the Act's own text says July 1, 2026), an application fee, including background checks, may not exceed $50, subject to the third-party background check exception described in the rental-fee law, and no additional fee at application may duplicate screening costs. If a prospective tenant offers a reusable tenant screening report that a consumer reporting agency prepared at the tenant's request and expense within the previous 30 days, that is available to the landlord at no cost, and that includes all the criteria the landlord consistently uses in screening (at least the applicant's name, contact information, verification of source of income, last known address and eviction history), the landlord may not charge a fee to access the report or an application screening fee. The landlord may require the applicant to state that there has been no material change in the report's information, and may still collect and process an application of its own as long as it charges no screening fee for it. A local rule that protects prospective tenants more controls.

title: Rent Payment Methods
bodyText: For leases and agreements executed after January 1, 2024, a landlord may not require a tenant or applicant to pay any amount due under a residential lease, renewal or extension by electronic funds transfer, including automatic recurring transfers; beginning 90 days after that date, a violation is an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act. For leases executed after January 1, 2025, a landlord that collects rent through a third-party payment portal that charges a transaction fee must let the tenant pay by paper check or cash delivered to the landlord or its business office, or by another means that carries no fee. A landlord of a building or complex of 100 or more units with an on-site business office that keeps regular hours must accept rent there during those hours without any penalty, fee or charge for paying that way (it may refuse cash), and a conflicting lease term is void.

title: Rent Control Preemption
bodyText: No Illinois unit of local government, including a home rule unit, may enact, maintain or enforce an ordinance or resolution that would have the effect of controlling the amount of rent charged for leasing private residential or commercial property. title: Rent Increases
bodyText: No Illinois statute sets a notice period or a cap for residential rent increases. During a fixed term rent changes only as the lease provides; in a month-to-month tenancy the landlord can end the tenancy on 30 days' written notice and offer new terms. A rent increase made because a tenant complained, organized or used a legal right in good faith is retaliation. A landlord may not raise rent to recover utility payments a tenant lawfully deducted after the landlord failed to pay a landlord-paid utility.

title: Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Any time after rent is due, the landlord may serve a written demand for the rent stating that unless payment is made within a stated time, not less than 5 days after service, the lease will be terminated. If the tenant does not pay within that time, the landlord may treat the lease as ended and file an eviction without further notice or demand, and may join a claim for the rent due. Partial payments of the amount demanded do not invalidate the notice if the notice prominently states: "Only FULL PAYMENT of the rent demanded in this notice will waive the landlord's right to terminate the lease under this notice, unless the landlord agrees in writing to continue the lease in exchange for receiving partial payment." The landlord may agree in writing to continue the lease for a partial payment. Collecting past-due rent after the eviction is filed does not invalidate the suit.

title: Security Deposit Return Rules and Penalties
bodyText: A landlord who keeps any part of a residential security deposit for damage must, within 30 days after the tenant vacates or the tenant's right of possession ends, whichever is later, give the tenant an itemized statement of the damage and the estimated or actual cost of each repair or replacement, with paid receipts (or copies), by personal delivery, postmarked mail to the last known address, or email to a verified email address the tenant provided. If costs are estimated, the paid receipts follow within 30 days after the statement. The landlord may charge the reasonable cost of its own labor. Costs the written lease specifies for cleaning, repair or replacement may be withheld if they are for damage beyond normal wear and tear and reasonable; the statement must reference the amount and include a copy of that part of the lease. If receipts cannot be produced through no fault of the landlord, a verified statement with other evidence of cost may be used. Without a proper statement and receipts, the whole deposit must be returned within 45 days of the tenant vacating. A landlord is not liable where the tenant gave no mailing or email address. A court that finds the landlord refused to give the statement, or gave it in bad faith, and failed to return the deposit on time, awards twice the deposit due plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees. A tenant does not forfeit a deposit solely because of an eviction for criminal activity or drug use, although the deposit may pay the sheriff's eviction fees in a criminal-activity eviction.

title: Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: A landlord of residential property with 25 or more units, in one building or a complex on contiguous parcels, must pay interest on any security deposit held more than 6 months. The rate is the rate the largest commercial bank (by total assets) with its main banking premises in Illinois paid on minimum-deposit passbook savings accounts as of December 31 of the year before the rental agreement began, computed from the date of the deposit. Within 30 days after the end of each 12-month rental period the landlord must pay accumulated interest of $5 or more, in cash or as a credit against rent, unless the tenant is in default; all unpaid interest is due when the tenancy ends. A landlord who willfully fails or refuses to pay is liable for an amount equal to the deposit, plus court costs and attorney's fees. The Act does not apply to public housing. Some local ordinances, including Chicago's, have their own interest rules (not covered).

title: Security Deposits When the Property Is Sold or Foreclosed
bodyText: When a landlord sells, leases, transfers or otherwise disposes of residential property (other than to a lienholder), the new owner becomes liable to the tenant for any security deposit, including statutory interest, and prepaid rent the tenant paid, and the former owner remains jointly and severally liable. When a deposit is actually transferred to the holder of a foreclosure certificate of sale or deed, or to the purchaser at a foreclosure sale, that holder or purchaser is liable for it and must, within 21 days after receiving the deposits and the tenants' names and addresses, post a written notice on the main entrance of each affected unit stating that it has acquired the deposit.

bodyText: Under Illinois' Revised Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, a security deposit is 'property'. bodyText: Illinois has no general statute that sets a residential landlord's repair or habitability duty; Illinois courts recognize an implied warranty of habitability in residential leases (case law, not reviewed here), and local building and housing codes apply. title: Tenant Repair and Deduct
bodyText: If a repair is required by the lease or by a law, rule or local ordinance and its reasonable cost is no more than the lesser of $500 or half a month's rent, the tenant may notify the landlord in writing, by registered or certified mail or other restricted delivery, at the landlord's or agent's address shown in the lease (or the last known address), of the tenant's intention to have the repair made at the landlord's expense. If the landlord does not make the repair within 14 days after notice, or sooner in an emergency, the tenant may have it made in a workmanlike manner by a licensed and insured tradesperson and, after giving the landlord a paid bill from an unrelated tradesperson or supplier, deduct the cost (up to those limits and the customary price) from rent. The right does not apply if the tenant, family or a guest caused the condition. The tenant is responsible for damage caused by its contractor. The Act does not apply to public housing, condominiums, cooperative housing corporations, owner-occupied rental property of 6 or fewer units, or mobile homes. Home rule units may not diminish these rights.

title: Heating and Cooling in 55-and-Older Housing
bodyText: In residential rental property limited to people 55 or older, where a heating or cooling system serves the whole premises, the landlord must: run the cooling system from June 1 through September 30 whenever the heat index exceeds 80 degrees Fahrenheit; and, from October 1 through May 31, keep heat at no less than 68 degrees between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m. when the outside temperature falls below 55 degrees, and no less than 62 degrees between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. If there is no premises-wide cooling system, the landlord must provide at least one cooled indoor common gathering space, free to all tenants, when the heat index exceeds 80 degrees (a property with no such space is exempt).

title: Rekeying Between Tenants (Cook County)
bodyText: In counties of more than 3,000,000 people (Cook County), after a unit with a written lease is vacated and on or before the day a new tenant takes possession, the landlord must change or rekey the lock (replace the lock or cylinder, change a combination or electronic code, or otherwise change the means of access). A landlord who fails to do so is liable for damages from a theft attributable to the failure. The duty does not apply if the written lease gives the tenant the right to change or rekey the lock, to an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units, or to a room in an owner-occupied home. Statewide, the owner of a rental building of 5 or more units whose construction began after the peephole statute took effect (enacted in 1967) must provide and maintain a peephole in each unit's entrance door; a tenant may sue to compel it, and each violation is a petty offense ($25 to $100 per unit, each day a separate offense). Hotels, motels, dormitories and similar buildings are excluded.

title: Landlord-Paid Utilities
bodyText: Where an agreement requires the landlord to pay for water, gas or electric service, the landlord must pay on time so service continues through the lease. If the landlord does not pay, the tenant (or all tenants served by a common meter) may end the lease, or pay the utility if nonpayment jeopardizes service and deduct the payment from rent; the landlord may not raise rent to recover lawful deductions. A utility must give tenants of buildings with 3 or more apartments notice before shutting off service for the landlord's nonpayment, and must restore service to a tenant who pays the past-due amount, or who puts the account in the tenant's own name, meets the utility's credit or deposit rules and agrees to pay future bills. Tenants who receive a utility's termination notice, or the utility, may also ask a court to appoint a receiver to collect rents and pay current utility bills. A tenant billed for service outside the unit because of the landlord's violation may recover it (trebled if knowing or intentional, plus attorney's fees if the utility award exceeds $3,000).

title: Tenant-Paid Utilities on a Shared Meter
bodyText: A landlord may not rent a unit where the tenant pays the utility company directly for service that also serves common areas or other units, unless, before offering a lease or renewal, taking a deposit or otherwise agreeing to rent: the landlord gives a written statement of the areas and uses served by the tenant's meter (including foreseeable ones); gives copies of the unit's utility bills for the previous 12 months, unless the tenant waives them in writing; does not ask the tenant to collect from neighbors; and states in writing any rent reduction offered for usage outside the unit. A landlord may not switch from landlord-paid to tenant-paid utilities, or from master-metered to individually metered tenant-paid utilities, during a lease term; it must give at least 30 days' notice, and for tenants under a lease the notice must come at least 30 days before the lease expires, unless both sign a written amendment. Inconsistent lease terms are void.

title: Disability Modifications and Accommodations
bodyText: A landlord must permit, at the expense of a person with a disability, reasonable modifications of the premises needed for full enjoyment of them, and must make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services. Where reasonable, the landlord may condition a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior at the end of the tenancy (reasonable wear and tear excepted), on a reasonable description of the work, and on assurances that it will be done in a workmanlike manner with required permits. The landlord may not increase the customary security deposit for a person with a disability, but where necessary to ensure restoration funds it may negotiate payments into an interest-bearing escrow account, over a reasonable period, of a reasonable amount not exceeding the restoration cost, with the interest going to the tenant. Refusing to rent to, or discriminating against, a blind, hearing-impaired or physically disabled person because of a guide, hearing or support dog is also a civil rights violation.

title: Illinois Rules That Depend on Property Size or Type
bodyText: Several Illinois rules turn on the size or type of the property, not the landlord's whole portfolio: the rental-fee law exempts leases in owner-occupied premises of 6 units or fewer; the repair-and-deduct law exempts owner-occupied property of 6 or fewer units, condominiums, cooperatives and public housing; the Human Rights Act's housing exemptions cover an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units and rooms in an owner-occupied home (but never discriminatory advertising), and an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units may decide on sexual orientation (these exemptions reach only the general prohibitions in Section 3-102, not the disability provisions); the Cook County rekey duty exempts owner-occupied buildings of 4 or fewer units; the posted manager-and-insurer notice applies to buildings of more than 4 units with no resident or on-site owner or manager; deposit interest applies to properties of 25 or more units; the on-site rent-payment rule applies to 100 or more units with an on-site office; the Safe Homes Act excludes public housing except Housing Choice Vouchers; and the radon disclosure excludes units on the third story or higher. Each rule is described in its own row.

title: Ending a Tenancy: Notices by Tenancy Type
bodyText: Illinois notice rules depend on the kind of tenancy. Fixed term: no notice is needed; the tenant must leave when the term ends. Year to year: 60 days' written notice ending at the end of the year, which may be given at any time in the 4 months before the last 60 days. Week to week, where the tenant holds over without special agreement: 7 days' written notice. Any other term of less than a year, including month to month: 30 days' written notice. Unpaid rent: a written demand giving at least 5 days to pay. Breach of any other lease term: a 10-day written notice to quit, which the statute does not require to offer a chance to cure and gives a suggested form for. Use of the premises for a felony or Class A misdemeanor, or drug activity: the landlord may void the lease and give 5 days' written notice to vacate. After a foreclosure, a new owner may end a bona fide lease only at the end of its term, and a month-to-month or week-to-week lease, with at least 90 days' written notice, except on the ordinary grounds such as nonpayment, breach or criminal activity. Demands and notices are served by delivering a copy to the tenant, leaving it with a person 13 or older residing on or in possession of the premises, certified or registered mail with a returned receipt, or, if no one is in actual possession, posting it on the premises. Once a tenancy is ended by one of these notices, no further demand is needed before filing.

title: How Legal Notices Are Delivered
bodyText: Eviction demands and termination notices must be served by one of the methods in the Code of Civil Procedure: personal delivery; leaving a copy with a person 13 or older residing on or in possession of the premises; certified or registered mail with a returned receipt from the addressee; or, if no one is in actual possession, posting on the premises. The statute does not list email. The deposit statement may be emailed to a verified email address the tenant provided. Illinois' Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lists no exclusion for landlord-tenant notices; its other provisions, including when the parties must have agreed to deal electronically, are not covered here. The repair-and-deduct notice goes by registered or certified mail or other restricted delivery.

title: The Eviction Process
bodyText: An Illinois eviction is a court action under Article IX of the Code of Civil Procedure; the complaint states that the landlord is entitled to possession and the defendant unlawfully withholds it. Under Illinois Supreme Court Rule 139, the landlord must attach to the complaint the notice or demand the case rests on, with proof of service, and, for a case based on breach of a written lease under the 10-day notice statute, a copy of the lease or its relevant portions (or, if unavailable, an affidavit on the Supreme Court's standardized form). Under Rule 99.2 (effective March 1, 2026), circuits may run residential eviction mediation or diversion programs, which must give litigants reasonable time to reach counsel and mediation before a default or eviction judgment. A claim for rent may be joined; unrelated claims may not. Either party may demand a jury despite any lease waiver. An eviction order may not be enforced more than 120 days after it is entered unless the court extends it on the landlord's motion, which must include a statutory notice to the tenant. Tenants may raise defenses including domestic or sexual violence, immigration status, retaliation and servicemember protections, described in their own rows.

title: Minors May Not Be Named in an Eviction
bodyText: An eviction complaint may not name a minor (a person under 18 who has not been emancipated) as a defendant. A complaint that names a minor must be dismissed in its entirety against all defendants and immediately sealed, although the landlord may refile against defendants who can properly be named (the court may not waive the refiling fees). A minor willfully and wantonly named may recover reasonable attorney's fees, actual damages and $1,000 in liquidated damages.

title: Sealing of Eviction Court Files
bodyText: A court may seal an eviction court file if it finds the landlord's case sufficiently without basis in fact or law (including lack of jurisdiction) that sealing is clearly in the interests of justice and not outweighed by the public's interest in the record. title: Criminal Activity: Voiding the Lease and Expedited Eviction
bodyText: If a tenant or occupant uses or permits use of the premises for a felony or Class A misdemeanor, the lease becomes void at the landlord's option; if the tenant does not leave within 5 days after written notice to vacate, the landlord may file an eviction (or, with consent, assign the right to file to the State's Attorney or corporation counsel), and a resulting eviction order may be stayed no more than 7 days unless all parties agree. A separate emergency procedure lets a landlord of privately owned or housing-authority property seek possession on a verified complaint alleging direct evidence of drug activity, an unlawful firearm, or listed violent or sex crimes on the premises with the knowledge or consent of those named: no predicate notice is required, the hearing is held after 14 days' notice, and continuances and stays are limited to 7 days. Where the landlord and tenant signed HUD's drug-free housing addendum or a similar document, a Class X felony charge on the premises followed by a probable-cause finding or indictment lets the landlord void the lease on 5 days' posted notice. A tenant does not forfeit the security deposit solely because of these evictions (in a criminal-activity eviction it may pay the sheriff's fees).

title: Drug Use on the Premises
bodyText: If a tenant or occupant uses the leased premises, or permits them to be used, for unlawfully possessing, storing, making, growing, delivering, using, selling or giving away controlled substances, the lease becomes void at the landlord's option. The landlord may post a written notice (on circuit clerk forms) requiring the occupants to vacate within 5 days, then file an eviction or assign the right to file to the State's Attorney. If a controlled substance is found or used anywhere in an apartment, there is a rebuttable presumption that a tenant or occupant used or possessed it or permitted its use. The tenant does not forfeit the security deposit solely because of this eviction.

title: No Self-Help Evictions or Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: Illinois law prohibits entering land or buildings except where the law allows entry, and then only peaceably, not by force. A landlord recovers possession through the court eviction process. A landlord may not cause or request utility service to tenants in an occupied building to be interrupted, discontinued or terminated, whether by not paying utility bills it is responsible for or by tampering with equipment or lines, except temporary shutoffs for emergencies such as gas leaks or fire, or, on 7 days' written notice to each affected tenant, for building repairs or rehabilitation. A tenant whose service is cut off in violation recovers a full rent abatement for the period plus consequential damages, and where the landlord acted deliberately, recklessly or in bad faith, statutory damages up to $300 per tenant (or $5,000 divided among affected tenants, if less).

title: Holding Over After the Lease Ends
bodyText: A tenant who willfully holds over after the term ends and after the landlord's written demand for possession owes the landlord, for the time the landlord is kept out, double the yearly value of the premises, recoverable in a civil action. A tenant who gives notice of intent to leave on a date when the lease allows it, and then does not leave, owes double the rent that would otherwise be due. The landlord may instead accept rent and continue the tenancy. These double amounts apply only in those two cases. No statute sets an amount for any other holdover, such as a tenant who stays on before any written demand for possession or without acting willfully; the landlord then recovers its actual damages, such as the reasonable rental value, unless the lease sets a measure. The library offers an optional daily holdover charge for those cases; it does not apply after a termination for nonpayment of rent, and it cannot be collected for the same days as either double amount.

title: Distress for Rent (Landlord's Statutory Seizure Remedy)
bodyText: Illinois still allows distress for rent: a landlord may seize a tenant's personal property found in the county where the tenant lives for rent due, but only the tenant's own property, and must immediately file the distress warrant and an inventory with the circuit clerk, after which a court case follows. The right continues for 6 months after the term ends. Property exempt from judgment enforcement is exempt from distress (except crops on the leased premises). Landlords also have a statutory lien on crops grown on leased land. The procedure is technical and court-supervised; a lease clause is not needed to use it.

title: Tenants in Foreclosure and Receivership
bodyText: After a foreclosure, the mortgagee, receiver, certificate or deed holder, or foreclosure-sale purchaser who takes control may end a bona fide lease only at the end of its term, and a month-to-month or week-to-week lease, with at least 90 days' written notice; an individual who buys at the judicial sale and will live in the unit as a primary residence may end the lease on at least 90 days' written notice. The successor keeps the ordinary grounds to end a tenancy, including nonpayment, breach of the lease, holding over and criminal activity. Eviction files against tenants under this rule are sealed. A holder or purchaser who receives tenants' security deposits is liable for them and must post a notice on each unit within 21 days. A court-appointed receiver may not reject an unexpired lease where the tenant occupies the premises as the tenant's primary residence.

title: Unauthorized Occupants and Squatters
bodyText: Nothing in Illinois' eviction Article prevents law enforcement from enforcing criminal trespass, or from removing persons or property from premises when there is a criminal trespass. title: No Statewide Just-Cause Requirement
bodyText: Illinois has no statewide law requiring a landlord to have good cause to end or not renew a residential tenancy. A fixed-term lease ends when the term expires, and a periodic tenancy can be ended with the statutory notice, as long as the landlord's reason is not retaliatory, discriminatory, based on domestic or sexual violence or immigration status, or otherwise unlawful. Some local ordinances may add protections (not covered).

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: Illinois has no statute that ends a residential lease when a tenant dies or gives an estate a special right to terminate; the lease continues against the estate under general law, and the landlord's duty to mitigate applies. A tenant's belongings are handled under Illinois estate law.

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited
bodyText: A landlord may not knowingly end a tenancy, raise rent, decrease services, sue or threaten to sue for possession, or refuse to renew because the tenant in good faith: complained of code violations to a government agency, elected representative or official; complained of code violations or illegal landlord practices to a community organization, or sought its help; asked the landlord for repairs required by a code, ordinance, regulation or the lease; organized or joined a tenants' union or similar group; testified about the premises' condition; or exercised any right or remedy provided by law. A retaliating landlord faces the tenant's defense to its action and a civil action in which the tenant may end the lease and recover the deposit, interest and prepaid rent, recover possession, and recover the greater of 2 months' rent or twice the damages, plus attorney's fees. Evidence of protected activity within one year before the landlord's action creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation, unless the activity began after the landlord's action. The landlord's action is not retaliatory if it had a legitimate non-retaliatory basis or began before the protected activity.

title: Safe Homes Act: Leaving Because of Domestic or Sexual Violence
bodyText: A tenant who leaves the premises is not liable for rent for the period after leaving if a court finds either that, when the tenant left, the tenant or a household member was under a credible imminent threat of domestic or sexual violence at the premises and the tenant gave written notice of that reason before or within 3 days after leaving; or that the tenant or a household member was a victim of sexual violence on premises the landlord owns or controls, the tenant left as a result, and the tenant gave written notice before or within 3 days after leaving, stating the reason and the date and providing medical, court or police evidence or a statement from a victim services or rape crisis organization, with the violence having occurred within 60 days before the notice (or as soon as practicable if the tenant could not reasonably give notice sooner). Rent owed before the tenant left remains owed. The Act's rights cannot be waived or modified in any lease or separate agreement. It does not apply to public housing, except the Housing Choice Voucher program. In an eviction, it is also a defense that the landlord's demand for possession is based solely on the tenant's or a household member's status as a victim, or on an incident of violence against them, with supporting evidence; the landlord may still seek possession against the perpetrator.

title: Safe Homes Act: Lock Changes
bodyText: All tenants on a written lease may give the landlord written notice asking for a lock change if one of them reasonably believes a tenant or household member is under a credible imminent threat of domestic or sexual violence at the premises. If the threat comes from someone not on the lease, the notice must include medical, court or police evidence or a statement from a victim services, domestic violence or rape crisis organization; if it comes from a person on the lease, it must include a plenary order of protection or plenary civil no contact order granting the tenant exclusive possession (and that person's signature is not needed). Within 48 hours after receiving the notice and evidence, the landlord must change the locks or give permission to change them, and must make a good-faith effort to give the tenant a key within 48 hours. The landlord may charge a fee no more than the reasonable price customarily charged for changing a lock. If the landlord does not act within 48 hours, the tenant may change the locks in a workmanlike manner with locks of similar or better quality and must try to give the landlord a key within 48 hours. The landlord is not liable to third parties who cannot enter because of the change. The tenant may get an injunction if the landlord interferes.

title: Safe Homes Act: Confidentiality
bodyText: A landlord may not disclose to a prospective landlord that a tenant or household member exercised rights under the Safe Homes Act, or any information the tenant provided in doing so, unless the disclosure is required by law, occurs in a civil proceeding under the Act, or the victim (or the victim's parent or guardian) consents in writing. Giving the landlord evidence of violence does not waive any confidentiality or privilege the victim has with a third party. A landlord who discloses in violation is liable for actual damages up to $2,000, and a successful tenant may be awarded attorney's fees and costs.

title: Calling Police or Emergency Services
bodyText: No Illinois municipality or county may enact or enforce an ordinance or regulation that penalizes tenants or landlords (through fines, license action, subsidy termination, or termination or nonrenewal of a lease) because of a contact to police or emergency services made to prevent or respond to domestic or sexual violence, or made by or about a person with a disability for a disability-related purpose, or because of domestic or sexual violence, or related criminal activity, against a tenant, household member or guest. In an eviction, it is a defense that the demand for possession is based solely on a tenant's or household member's status as a victim of domestic violence, sexual violence, dating violence or stalking, or on an incident of such violence. A landlord may bar a person who is not a tenant or household member by a written notice to the tenant that says the person is no longer allowed on the premises and that inviting the person onto the premises may be treated as a breach of the lease, whether or not the lease says so; it is a defense to an eviction on that ground if the tenant or household member who was a victim of domestic violence, sexual violence, stalking or dating violence did not knowingly consent to the entry, or a valid court order permitted it.

title: Immigration Status
bodyText: Unless required by law or court order, a landlord may not threaten to disclose, or disclose, information about a tenant's immigration or citizenship status to anyone, including immigration or law enforcement agencies, to harass or intimidate the tenant, retaliate for the exercise of rights, or influence the tenant to leave, and may not bring an action for possession based solely or in part on the tenant's immigration or citizenship status. A tenant may recover actual damages, a civil penalty of up to $2,000 for each violation, attorney's fees and costs. A waiver of these rights is void. It is also a defense to an eviction that the demand for possession is based solely or in part on the tenant's immigration status, or, after the lease has begun and the tenant has taken possession, on the tenant's failure to provide a Social Security number, credit-report information or a form of identification the landlord accepts. Landlords may still comply with legal obligations (including rental-assistance programs and court orders), verify a prospective tenant's financial qualifications, give notices about lease violations, and collect rent. Immigration status is also a protected class under the Human Rights Act; inquiry or use is allowed only in compliance with State or federal law.

title: Servicemember Rights
bodyText: An Illinois resident servicemember (any component of the U.S. Armed Forces or any state's National Guard) who enters military service of more than 29 consecutive days after signing a lease, or who while in service receives orders for a permanent change of station or to deploy for at least 90 days, may terminate a residential lease, as may a family member living with the servicemember, by giving the landlord copies of the orders. Termination takes effect 30 days after notice, or, if rent is paid monthly, 30 days after the next rent due date after the notice; the landlord must refund unearned prepaid rent and the security deposit, less actual damages the lease allows it to deduct. A landlord's refusal to accept a proper termination is a civil rights violation. In a residential eviction, if military service materially affects a servicemember tenant's ability to pay, the court may, and on the tenant's motion must, stay the case for 90 days or adjust the rental obligation. Federal law (the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act) gives additional protections.

title: Illinois Human Rights Act: Housing
bodyText: The Illinois Human Rights Act makes it a civil rights violation, in renting, to refuse to rent, alter terms, refuse offers or negotiation, misrepresent availability, publish or use an application, notice, advertisement, record or inquiry indicating a preference, or use criteria or methods with a discriminatory effect not necessary to a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest, because of actual or perceived race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, age, sex, marital status, order of protection status, disability, military status, sexual orientation (which includes gender-related identity), pregnancy, reproductive health decisions or unfavorable military discharge, or because of familial status, immigration status, source of income or arrest record. Exemptions include rental in a building of 4 or fewer units where the owner lives in one, rental of rooms in a private home where the owner or family lives, reasonable occupancy limits, religious organizations, single-sex rooms, conduct toward persons convicted of illegal manufacture or distribution of controlled substances, housing for older persons (familial status only), an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units deciding on sexual orientation, and inquiry into arrest records or immigration status authorized by or in compliance with State or federal law. The owner-occupied and private-room exemptions never permit discriminatory advertising or inquiries. These exemptions apply only to the general prohibitions in Section 3-102; they do not excuse disability discrimination, refusals of reasonable modifications or accommodations, or discrimination over guide, hearing or support dogs. Separately, the Illinois Constitution gives all persons the right to be free from discrimination on the basis of race, color, creed, national ancestry and sex in the rental of property, enforceable without any statute (the General Assembly may set reasonable exemptions and add remedies), and says that persons with a physical or mental handicap shall be free from discrimination in the rental of property. How courts apply these sections to private landlords alongside the Human Rights Act and its exemptions is case law not reviewed here.

bodyText: Source of income, defined as the lawful manner by which a person supports themselves and their dependents, is a protected class in Illinois housing; it is generally read to include housing vouchers and other lawful assistance. The Human Rights Act's owner-occupied (4 or fewer units) and private-room exemptions apply, but not to advertising.

title: Assistance Animals
bodyText: A housing provider asked to make an exception to a pet policy for an assistance animal may require reliable documentation of the disability and disability-related need only if they are not readily apparent or known. Documentation must be in writing, from a person with whom the requester has a therapeutic relationship, and describe the disability-related need; the provider may offer a form but may not deny a request for not using it. The provider may deny or rescind the accommodation for undue financial and administrative burden, fundamental alteration, or, after an individualized assessment with reliable objective evidence, if the specific animal poses a direct threat to others' health or safety, or causes substantial physical damage to others' property, that another reasonable accommodation cannot reduce or eliminate, or has shown a pattern of uncontrolled behavior the handler has not effectively corrected. The resident pays for damage the animal causes beyond reasonable wear and tear, as for any other resident, but may not be charged a pet deposit or pet fee or required to carry special insurance. The housing provider is not liable for injuries caused by an assistance animal permitted as a reasonable accommodation. A guide, hearing or support dog may not be refused or subjected to different terms.

bodyText: No Illinois statute penalizes a person for misrepresenting an animal as an assistance or service animal in order to obtain housing. title: Radon: Tenant Testing and Termination Rights
bodyText: For leases entered into on or after January 1, 2024, of units below the third story, a tenant has 90 days from the start of the lease to conduct a radon test and must give the landlord copies of the results within 10 days. If the result exceeds the Illinois Emergency Management Agency's Radon Action Level and the landlord chooses not to mitigate, the tenant may terminate the lease; the landlord may hire a radon contractor to retest within 30 days of learning the results, and a contractor's result may disprove the hazard (results are valid 2 years unless the building is renovated). If the landlord never provided the pamphlet, records and disclosure form, the tenant may test at any time during the lease and, if a hazard is shown and the landlord does not dispute it or mitigate, may within 60 days either have a radon contractor mitigate with the landlord's express consent or terminate the lease. Mitigation must be done by a licensed radon contractor; a tenant who mitigates with the landlord's express consent may deduct the cost from rent in equal parts over the rest of the lease. A landlord may not withhold the deposit for radon testing or mitigation after a tenant terminates for lack of the disclosure, except for an improper installation the tenant made without consent. Neither side is required to test or mitigate.

title: Illinois Lead Rules for Rentals
bodyText: In addition to the federal lead disclosure, before entering into a residential lease an owner of a residential building with units built before 1978 must give the prospective tenant the Illinois Department of Public Health's lead information brochure. title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText: Before a building is submitted to the Condominium Property Act as a conversion condominium, every tenant must receive a notice of intent at least 30 days and not more than a year before the declaration is recorded, together with a schedule of selling prices and an offer to sell the tenant's unit, open at least 30 days (except units to be vacated for rehabilitation). Tenants whose leases would expire within 120 days after the notice may extend on the same terms until the 120 days end by written notice within 30 days. The developer must tell each tenant whether the tenancy will be renewed and on what terms. For 120 days the tenant has a right of first refusal to buy the unit on substantially the same terms as a signed contract, exercisable within 30 days after notice of the contract. Occupied units may be shown only a reasonable number of times, at appropriate hours, and only in the last 90 days of an expiring tenancy. An owner who converts without the notice is liable to a tenant who moves out because of non-renewal for moving expenses up to $1,500, 3 months' rent and attorney's fees. Lease terms contrary to or waiving these rights are void.

title: Tenant Right to Install EV Charging
bodyText: In a single-family home or multifamily building that has parking spaces, and notwithstanding the lease, an Illinois tenant may install, at the tenant's expense and for the tenant's own use, a level 1 or level 2 receptacle or outlet or a level 2 electric vehicle charging system, subject to the landlord's bona fide safety requirements, registration within 30 days, reasonable aesthetic rules, and the tenant's written agreement to the landlord's design specifications, a licensed electrical contractor and insurance. The landlord may charge only for electricity used (including network fees), a reasonable access fee, a restoration security deposit, installation costs where the landlord installs at the tenant's request, and a reasonable fee to reserve a shared-area space. A tenant-installed system remains the tenant's property. A landlord who willfully violates the statute owes actual damages and a civil penalty up to $1,000, and a prevailing tenant plaintiff recovers attorney's fees.

title: Cannabis in Rentals
bodyText: A landlord may prohibit a tenant from cultivating cannabis, may prohibit smoking cannabis on the premises, and is not required to allow a tenant to use cannabis on the property. A landlord may not refuse to lease to or penalize a person solely for being a registered medical cannabis patient or caregiver, unless required to avoid violating federal law or losing a federal monetary or licensing benefit, and a landlord is not penalized under State law for leasing to a cardholder or a lawful adult user.

title: Lease Terms Illinois Law Voids or Limits
bodyText: Illinois voids or overrides several kinds of residential lease terms: a clause exempting the landlord from liability for injury or property damage caused by the negligence of the landlord or its agents or employees in operating or maintaining the property; a jury-trial waiver in an eviction case; a requirement to pay by electronic funds transfer; for leases the rental-fee law covers, the fees it bans and any non-optional fee not listed on the lease's first page; a waiver or modification of Safe Homes Act rights; a waiver of Immigrant Tenant Protection Act rights; a utility term inconsistent with the Rental Property Utility Service Act's shared-meter and payment-arrangement rules; a term conflicting with the right of large complexes' tenants to pay at the on-site office; a lease term blocking a tenant's electric vehicle charger that complies with the statute; and a term contrary to or waiving condominium-conversion rights. A power to confess judgment in a lease is doubtful: the confession-of-judgment ban covers consumer transactions involving goods, services or intangibles, and its application to real-property leases was not confirmed.

title: Attorney's Fees
bodyText: Illinois has no general statute on attorney's-fee clauses in residential leases; a lease may provide for fees, and the shared default clause awards them to the prevailing party to the extent the law permits. title: What This Illinois Research Covers
bodyText: The Illinois rows cover state statutes and the Illinois Supreme Court rules named in them for residential leases of houses and apartments. They do not cover mobile home lots (the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Rights Act), farm leases, hotels and short stays, public housing rules, federal law beyond the lead disclosure, or local ordinances. A landlord renting in one of those places must also follow the local ordinance.

title: Landlords Who Are Child Sex Offenders
bodyText: If a landlord who lives in the building is a child sex offender and rents to a person who did not tell the landlord that they are a parent or guardian of a child under 18, the tenant may not terminate the lease on later discovering the landlord's status. Such a landlord may also refuse to rent a unit in the building where they live to a parent or guardian of a minor child without violating the Human Rights Act. Illinois does not require landlords to disclose sex offenders living nearby.

bodyText: Illinois' concealed carry law lets the owner of private real property of any type prohibit carrying concealed firearms on property under the owner's control, with the statutory sign posted unless the property is a private residence; a licensee may still keep a firearm in a locked vehicle in a prohibited parking area. title: No General Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Pennsylvania state law has no general just-cause or good-cause rule for residential tenancies: when a lease term ends and the landlord gives the required notice to quit, the landlord does not need a reason. A few statutes limit this in specific situations. A landlord may not end or refuse to renew a lease because the tenant or a family member takes part in a tenants' organization. In cities covered by the Rent Withholding Act, a tenant may not be evicted for any reason while rent is paid into escrow for a unit certified unfit. When a building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or planned community, tenants cannot be required to move out during the notice year except for nonpayment, waste or disturbing conduct. Manufactured-home community lots have their own good-cause rules, and some cities, including Philadelphia, have local good-cause rules this library does not cover.
