title: No Statute Treating Fees as Rent
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute says whether late fees, utility charges or other fees count as rent, so it depends on the lease. Many Pennsylvania leases call such charges 'additional rent'; whether an eviction for nonpayment can rest on unpaid fees is a question for the courts. One limit is written into the statute: in a building with three or more households, a landlord may not charge any fee, service charge or additional rent for the tenant's right to have guests, workers, delivery people and suppliers. This library's clauses do not label fees as rent.

title: Forms Pennsylvania Law Supplies
bodyText: Pennsylvania's landlord-tenant statute supplies one form: the notice to a tenant about property left behind, which must be sent by first class mail to the rental address and to any forwarding or emergency address the tenant gave, in substantially this form: "Personal property remaining at (address) is now considered to have been abandoned. Within ten days of the postmark date of this notice, you must retrieve any items you wish to keep or contact your landlord at (telephone number and address) to request that the property be retained or stored. If requested, storage will be provided for up to thirty days from the postmark date of this notice at a place of your landlord's choosing, and you will be responsible for costs of storage." Note that the form counts storage from the postmark date, while the statute's own rule counts the 30 days from the date of the notice; dating and mailing the notice the same day avoids the gap. Eviction filings before a magisterial district judge use court forms prescribed by the courts. Pennsylvania does not supply a statutory lease form or notice-to-quit form.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Tennessee has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule in either the 17 Act counties or the other 78: a landlord may decline to renew a fixed-term lease, or end a periodic tenancy with the required notice, without giving a reason. Limits that apply only in particular situations: in the Act counties a landlord may not retaliate against a tenant for a complaint about a violation of the deposit section or for using the Act's remedies; in every county a tenant may not be evicted solely because they are a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking, and a federally assisted 55-and-over elderly facility must give a paid-up tenant 60 days' notice before evicting for redevelopment; in Class 1 and Class 2 counties an owner converting an occupied unit to a condominium must give two months' notice at the same rent; and fair housing law applies everywhere. Tennessee has no rent-escrow bar on eviction and no statute protecting tenants' associations.

title: Tenant's Belongings and Animals After an Eviction
bodyText: When the officer removes the tenant under a detainer judgment, you or your representative must place the tenant's personal property on the premises, in an area clear of the entrance and a reasonable distance from any road, and must not disturb it for 48 hours; after that you may discard what remains. Local government action on the property is suspended during those 48 hours. If you follow this procedure you are not liable for damage to the property unless it is shown by clear and convincing evidence that the damage came from your malicious act or omission. Tennessee has no separate rule for animals left behind after an eviction. A person removed by a detainer who again illegally takes possession commits a Class C misdemeanor. In the 17 Act counties, belongings left after an abandonment (not an eviction) follow the separate abandonment procedure instead.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage.
notes: TN: TN-SCOPE: STATEWIDE TEXT. Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.4) (arose from the rule 50 screen). TAYLOR'S DECISION (2026-09-30): the tenant who causes damage keeps paying; broadened on his question from fire to any damage the tenant causes (frozen pipes, a car through the wall). OTHER COUNTIES: Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-7-102(a) lets a lessee surrender rent-free after the building becomes untenantable only 'if the destruction or injury occurred without fault or neglect by the lessee' and absent an express written agreement to the contrary (text visible in the LexisNexis result list 2026-09-30; read section-open 2026-09-28 (Justia host copy with history line; TN log §1)), so a tenant at fault has no statutory walk-away right and Rent keeps running under the Lease. ACT COUNTIES: Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-503(a) lets the tenant vacate and terminate after fire or casualty substantially impairs use, with no fault exception, and that right cannot be waived (Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 66-28-201(a), 66-28-203(b)); the clause does not try to: part (1) applies only while the Lease continues, and part (2) recovers the landlord's actual damages (Tenn. title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: Landlord will refund the Security Deposit, less any amounts lawfully retained under this Lease, within 30 days after Tenant surrenders the property. If Landlord retains any part of the Security Deposit, the refund will be accompanied by a signed statement itemizing the amounts retained, the purpose of each, and a detailed list of the expenditures made from the Security Deposit. Landlord will not retain any part of the Security Deposit to cover normal wear and tear. When Tenant vacates, Tenant will give Landlord in writing a forwarding address to which the refund and statement should be sent.
notes: ID: Instruction 24 family. Idaho Code § 6-321(2): refunds within 21 days 'if no time is fixed by agreement and, in any event, within thirty (30) days after surrender'; a partial refund must be accompanied by 'a signed statement itemizing the amounts lawfully retained by the landlord, the purpose for the amounts retained, and a detailed list of expenditures made from the deposit'. Rule 50 choice, made on purpose: the clause fixes 30 days, the outer limit the statute allows by agreement; a lease silent on timing gets 21 days. Idaho Code § 6-321(1): no retention for normal wear and tear (defined there). Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(4) lets the tenant sue for failure to return a deposit as required, Idaho Code § 6-317 allows treble damages in that action, and Idaho Code § 6-324 awards the prevailing party attorney fees except where treble damages are awarded (edu-security-deposit-rules-id). The forwarding-address sentence is a tenant duty the statute does not impose; it does not extend the deadline. title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds or a closed account, or because of a stop-payment order that was not legally justified, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount; for a dishonored check, Idaho law limits a set fee agreed in writing to $20], and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are returned or fail, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check or money order.
notes: ID: Replaces the base returned-payments row, whose 'not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' is ceiling-only wording (rule 53) and states no agreed amount. Idaho Code § 55-305(2)(a)-(b): an owner may not charge a fee in an amount greater than that agreed in the rental agreement, or one not included in it (written agreements), so the fee must be stated; Idaho Code § 55-305(1): it must be reasonable. Idaho Code § 28-22-105: for a dishonored check, a holder with the right to a set fee 'under a written agreement' need not send the statutory notice of dishonor and may assess the set fee, which 'may not exceed twenty dollars ($20.00)'; the section does not apply to a check dishonored because of a justifiable stop-payment order. Without a written set fee, if the check is not paid within 15 days after the holder sends notice of dishonor under Idaho Code § 28-22-106 (read in context), the drawer owes 12% interest from dishonor and collection costs up to the lesser of $20 or the check amount, plus court-awarded attorney fees if sued. Whether an electronic (ACH) return is a 'check' (Idaho Code § 28-3-104, not read) is not settled here; for electronic returns the fee rests on Idaho Code § 55-305. title: Vehicle Rules
bodyText: Only operable, currently registered passenger vehicles may be parked at the property; commercial vehicles, recreational vehicles, trailers, and oversized vehicles are not permitted without Landlord's prior written consent. Landlord may require Tenant to provide vehicle registration information and may issue parking tags, decals, or access cards, the cost of which may be charged to Tenant. Landlord may, in accordance with applicable law, have a vehicle towed or booted at the vehicle owner's expense if it is parked without authorization or abandoned, but will not have a vehicle towed or booted solely because its registration is expired or improper. Vehicle repairs are not permitted at the property except minor emergency repairs necessary to move the vehicle, and vehicles may be washed only in areas Landlord designates, if any.
notes: ID: Replaces the base parking-vehicle-rules row for Idaho (state-driven, not a shared edit; rule 62). The base lets Landlord tow a vehicle that 'has expired registration'. Idaho Code § 49-1806(3) (added by 2025 Idaho Sess. Laws ch. 218, effective January 1, 2026): 'No vehicle shall be considered unauthorized and subject to removal or booting ... solely on the basis of the vehicle having expired or improper vehicle registration.' The base's 'in accordance with applicable law' would hide that conflict (rule 53). Idaho Code § 49-1806(1): a person in possession or control of real property 'is permitted to have' an unauthorized vehicle removed or booted if a conspicuous large-print sign says unauthorized vehicles will be removed or booted at the owner's expense and names the towing firm; Idaho Code § 49-1806(2): an abandoned vehicle on non-commercial property may be removed without a sign if the person signs the tow company's release. Idaho Code § 49-122(1) (read in context): an 'unauthorized vehicle' is one parked without the consent of the person owning or controlling the property. The registration requirement stays as a lease rule enforceable as a breach, not as a towing ground. 'Illegally parked' and 'inoperable' dropped as towing grounds: Idaho Code § 49-1806 reaches unauthorized and abandoned vehicles, and a tenant's car parked with consent is neither. See edu-towing-id. title: Smoke Detectors
bodyText: Landlord has verified that approved smoke detectors are installed and in good working order in the dwelling unit at the start of this Lease. Tenant will maintain the smoke detectors in good working order during the tenancy, including testing them and replacing batteries as needed, and will not disable, disconnect or remove any smoke detector. Tenant will promptly notify Landlord in writing if a smoke detector is missing or does not work.
notes: ID: Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(6): the landlord must install approved smoke detectors in each dwelling unit and, 'upon commencement of a rental agreement', verify they are installed and in good working order; 'The tenant shall maintain the smoke detectors in good working order during the tenant's rental period.' An approved detector is a battery-operated device bearing an approved testing agency's label. If the landlord fails to install working detectors, the tenant may send written notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, and, if working detectors are not installed within 72 hours of receipt of the letter, install them and deduct the cost from the next month's rent; the detectors then belong to the landlord (education in edu-landlord-duties-id). Restating the tenant's statutory maintenance duty serves the landlord (rule 55). Carbon monoxide: no Idaho statute requires CO alarms in rentals (whole-code search 'carbon monoxide': 4 sections, none a rental duty, each read in context: Idaho Code § 39-1211B foster homes, Idaho Code § 54-1016 electrical licensing exemptions, Idaho Code § 67-6539 short-term rentals, Idaho Code § 72-438 occupational disease). title: Reasonable Modifications for Disability
bodyText: If Tenant or an Occupant has a disability, Landlord will permit reasonable modifications of the property, at Tenant's expense, that may be necessary to afford that person full enjoyment of the property. Where it is reasonable to do so, Landlord may condition permission for a modification on Tenant agreeing to restore the interior, exterior, or both, of the property to the condition that existed before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted.
notes: ID: Idaho Code § 67-5909(8)(h) makes it a prohibited act 'to refuse to permit, at the expense of a person with a disability, reasonable modifications of existing premises ... if the modifications may be necessary to afford such person full enjoyment of the premises', and provides that 'in the case of a rental, the landlord may, where it is reasonable to do so, condition permission for a modification on the renter agreeing to restore the interior, exterior, or both, of the premises, to the condition that existed before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted. The provision for restoration shall be included in any lease or rental agreement.' The clause carries the statute's own words. title: Handling of Property Left Behind
bodyText: When this Lease ends or Tenant gives up possession, Tenant will remove all of Tenant's personal property from the property. If Tenant leaves personal property at the property after Tenant has moved out and returned possession to Landlord, or after Tenant has abandoned the property, Landlord will send Tenant a written notice, by mail to Tenant's forwarding address (or, if Tenant has not given one, to the property address) and by email to any email address Tenant has given, describing the property and stating where and by what date Tenant may collect it. If Tenant does not collect it within [number, at least 10] days after the notice is sent, Landlord may sell, donate or otherwise dispose of it, and will apply any sale proceeds first to the reasonable costs of removing, storing and selling it and then to amounts Tenant owes under this Lease, holding any balance for Tenant. Landlord need not store, and may dispose of right away, garbage, perishable items and anything hazardous. This Section does not apply to property left after a court enters judgment for possession, which Idaho law allows Landlord to remove and dispose of once the time the law gives Tenant to remove belongings has passed, or to motor vehicles, which are handled under Idaho vehicle law.
notes: ID: CONFIRMED ABSENT: Idaho has no statute on personal property left after a tenant moves out or abandons outside an eviction (whole-code search 'abandon' near tenant, lessee, renter, leased premises or rental: 16 sections, only the floating homes act (Idaho Code §§ 55-2707, 55-2713) and unrelated titles; mobile home act not relied on). The only statutory rule is post-judgment: Idaho Code § 6-316(2) gives a residential tenant 72 hours after the finding for possession to remove belongings, after which, and 3 days after the finding, the sheriff restores possession and the landlord may, subject to security interests under Title 28, Chapter 9, remove and dispose of remaining property, including a vehicle removable under Idaho Code § 49-1806, without compensation (edu-post-eviction-property-id). Rule 54: a measure the statute does not set, which the lease can set; the notice-and-wait procedure is modelled on abandoned-property-il. Common-law conversion and bailment risk if property is disposed of without consent is case law, not read; the tenant's advance agreement here is the protection. title: Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText: If this Lease continues as a month-to-month or other tenancy at will, either Landlord or Tenant may end it by giving the other written notice at least one month before the date stated in the notice on which the tenancy will end. Landlord's notice will be served in a manner Idaho law allows for notices to a tenant. Rent remains payable through the date the tenancy ends. This Section does not limit either party's right to end this Lease earlier where this Lease or Idaho law allows it.
notes: ID: Idaho Code § 55-208: a tenancy 'or other estate at will, however created' may be ended (1) by the landlord's written notice, served 'in the manner prescribed by the code of civil procedure', to remove within a period of not less than one month specified in the notice, or (2) by the tenant's written notice of a vacating date not less than one month from the date of notice. Idaho Code § 55-209: the landlord may re-enter or proceed to recover possession only after the period expires. Idaho Code § 6-303(1): a tenancy at will must be ended by that notice before the tenant holds over unlawfully; service methods are Idaho Code § 6-304. Rule 37: the one-month minimum applies to every tenancy at will, weekly or monthly alike; the statute does not tie the end date to the end of a rental period (case law on periodic tenancies not read). title: Fire or Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty not caused by Tenant, members of Tenant's household, or Tenant's guests, and the damage makes the property unfit to live in or substantially impairs Tenant's use of it, either Landlord or Tenant may end this Lease by written notice to the other, effective on the date Tenant moves out. Rent will be prorated to that date, any prepaid Rent refunded, and the Security Deposit returned as this Lease and Idaho law provide. If the casualty makes only part of the property unusable and Tenant stays in possession, Rent will be reduced in proportion to the part of the property Tenant cannot use until Landlord completes repairs. This Section does not limit any other right Tenant has under Idaho law.

title: Notice-Service Fee
bodyText: If Tenant's default requires Landlord to prepare and serve a notice that Idaho law requires before an eviction, such as a three-day notice to pay Rent or give up possession, Tenant will pay Landlord a notice-service fee of [amount], which Landlord and Tenant agree is a reasonable estimate of Landlord's cost of preparing and serving the notice. The fee will not be charged for a notice whose service costs a court awards to Landlord. Tenant's failure to pay this fee, by itself, will not entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction.

title: Collection Fee
bodyText: If Tenant does not pay an amount owed under this Lease and Landlord assigns the debt for collection to a collection agency licensed under Idaho law, Tenant will pay a collection fee equal to the amount the agency charges Landlord for collecting it, not to exceed [percentage]% of the amount owed. The agreement is the ground a lease can supply; the section's other grounds are a statute, a court ruling or judicial determination, a director-approved form agreement signed by the debtor and the agency, and the cost of processing an electronic payment the debtor preauthorized (Idaho Code § 26-2229A(4)(a)-(b), (d)-(f)). title: Idaho Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: Idaho treats any money a tenant deposits for a purpose other than rent as a security deposit. At the end of the tenancy it must be refunded, except amounts needed for the contingencies the deposit arrangement specifies; nothing may be kept for normal wear and tear. The refund is due within 21 days, or within the time the lease fixes, never later than 30 days after the tenant surrenders the property, with a signed, itemized statement and a detailed list of expenditures for anything kept. After first giving the landlord three days' written notice demanding its return, a tenant may sue over a deposit not returned as required; the court may award three times the actual damages, and the winning party recovers attorney fees unless treble damages are awarded.
notes: ID: Idaho Code § 6-321(1)-(2); Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(4) (tenant's action for failure to return a security deposit 'as and when required by law'); Idaho Code § 6-320(d) (3 days' written notice to the landlord first, served under Idaho Code § 6-323); Idaho Code § 6-317 ('may be entered for three (3) times the amount at which the actual damages are assessed' in a Idaho Code § 6-320 action); Idaho Code § 6-324 (prevailing-party attorney fees in any Chapter 3 action 'except in those cases where treble damages are awarded'). Section 6-321 (read whole) states no forfeiture of the landlord's claim for a late or missing statement; consequences beyond Idaho Code §§ 6-317 and 6-324 are case law, not read. title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: If a rental property changes ownership during a tenancy, the new owner becomes liable for refunding the security deposits made for that property. title: Nonrefundable Fees and Deposits
bodyText: Idaho has no statute allowing a 'nonrefundable deposit'. title: Pet Deposits Are Security Deposits
bodyText: In Idaho a pet deposit is a security deposit. It is refundable at the end of the tenancy except for the contingencies the deposit arrangement specifies, on the same deadline and with the same itemized statement as any other deposit. Monthly pet rent should be stated in the lease; whether Idaho treats it as rent (which the fee statute does not limit) or as a fee that must be reasonable is unsettled. title: Fees Must Be in the Lease
bodyText: For rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023, an owner may not charge a tenant a fee, fine, assessment, interest or other cost larger than the amount the rental agreement states. Under a written rental agreement, a charge the agreement does not include may be imposed only after the owner gives the tenant 30 days' written notice of the change. Every fee must also be reasonable. The rule does not limit the amount of rent.

title: Changing Month-to-Month Terms
bodyText: For a month-to-month lease, an Idaho landlord may change the lease terms by written notice given at least 15 days before the end of a month. The change takes effect at the end of the month, and becomes part of the lease if the tenant stays on. Rent increases need 30 days' written notice instead, and a fee change under a written lease needs 30 days' written notice.

title: Three-Day Notice to Pay Rent
bodyText: To evict for unpaid rent, an Idaho landlord must first serve a written three-day notice requiring payment of the amount due, stated in the notice, or possession of the property. The notice must also tell the tenant that if a court enters judgment against the tenant, a residential tenant will have 72 hours to remove belongings before the landlord may remove and dispose of them. It may be served any time within one year after the rent became due. For the landlord to recover attorney fees, the notice must also tell the tenant that attorney fees will be awarded to the prevailing party. Notices are served by personal delivery; or, if the tenant is away from home and work, by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion there and mailing a copy; or, failing that, by posting a copy on the property, delivering a copy to a resident if one can be found, and mailing a copy. A subtenant in actual occupation must be served too.
notes: ID: Idaho Code § 6-303(2); Idaho Code § 6-324 (for fees in cases requiring the Idaho Code § 6-303(2) notice, 'it shall be necessary that the three (3) days' notice advise the tenant that attorney fees shall be awarded to the prevailing party'); Idaho Code § 6-304 (service); Idaho Code § 6-316(2) (72 hours residential; 7 days commercial or 5+ acres). Rule 37: the 3-day period is the same for every tenancy type; agricultural tenants holding over 60 days without demand are held to renew for a year (Idaho Code § 6-303(2)). No statutory form of notice (Title 6, Chapter 3 read whole); the Idaho courts' self-help forms were not read. No Idaho statute lets the lease waive or shorten this notice (not offered, ID log s6). title: Notice for Other Lease Breaches
bodyText: For a breach other than unpaid rent, an Idaho landlord must serve a written three-day notice requiring the tenant to perform the lease term or give up possession; the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the lease or another interested person can save the lease by performing within the three days. No notice is needed if the breached term cannot afterward be performed. A tenant who assigns, sublets or commits waste contrary to the lease ends the lease by doing so, and the landlord may recover possession after a three-day notice to quit. Because the statute also lists covenants not to assign or sublet among those enforced by the three-day notice to perform, which notice fits an unapproved sublet is unsettled. A lease can also reserve a right of reentry: Idaho Code § 55-210 allows reentry on three days' notice, and § 55-212 then allows an ordinary district-court action for possession, without notice, once the right has accrued. The library does not offer a separate reentry clause. Its default clause already lets you end the lease and recover possession, but only after written notice and a chance to cure, and a clause making reentry accrue without notice would give up that standard to gain only a slower ordinary action; how § 55-212 fits with the three-day notices is case law not reviewed here. A landlord who wants it can add a custom clause, after taking advice.
notes: ID: Idaho Code § 6-303(3) (including 'any covenant not to assign or sublet'; proviso: 'if the covenants and conditions of the lease, violated by the lessee, cannot afterward be performed, then no notice ... need be given'); Idaho Code § 6-303(4); Idaho Code § 6-304 (service). Which breaches 'cannot afterward be performed' is case law, not read. Idaho Code § 55-210: a lease's right of reentry may be exercised on three days' notice. Idaho Code § 55-212: an ordinary action for possession in the district court, of property leased with a right of reentry, may be brought after the right to reenter has accrued, without notice. The library's default-by-tenant makes default depend on written notice and a chance to cure where the law requires one, so under the Idaho lease the right accrues only after that notice; how Idaho Code § 55-212 fits with the Idaho Code § 6-303 notices for the summary unlawful-detainer track is case law, not read (ID log s6.1). title: Drug Activity Evictions
bodyText: A tenant is in unlawful detainer if anyone is or has been engaged in the unlawful delivery, production or use of a controlled substance on the leased premises during the lease term; the statute states no notice or cure period for this ground. In an action only for possession of a tract of five acres or less, a landlord with reasonable grounds to believe that someone is or has been engaged in that activity may use the fast possession track: the court sets trial within 12 days of filing, continuances are limited to two days without a rent bond, and the case is tried to the judge without a jury. Joining a damages claim gives up the early trial.

Whether a notice is nonetheless required is not stated in the statute (case law not read); the 2024 bill to change this ground (H0641) died in committee. title: Idaho Eviction Process
bodyText: Idaho evictions are unlawful detainer actions in the district court of the county where the property is. In an action only for possession, for nonpayment of rent or drug activity, on a tract of five acres or less, the court sets trial within 12 days of filing (not if a damages claim is joined), the summons must be served at least five days before trial, continuances beyond two days need a rent bond, and the judge decides without a jury. Other evictions follow ordinary timing, and factual issues are tried to a jury unless waived. Complaints and answers must be verified. A judgment for the landlord after a breach, nonpayment or drug activity declares the lease forfeited, and the court assesses damages and any rent due; an appeal does not stop enforcement unless the court orders it, and a tenant who appeals must post an extra bond for the rental value.

Tracts larger than five acres: five-day post-judgment redemption for nonpayment where the lease has not expired (Idaho Code § 6-316(1)). title: Belongings After an Eviction Judgment
bodyText: After a court rules for the landlord, a residential tenant has 72 hours to remove belongings (commercial tenants and tenants of five acres or more have seven days). The landlord may deliver the writ of restitution or ask the sheriff to deliver it. After that time, and three days after the court's finding, the sheriff removes the tenant, and the landlord may remove and dispose of the tenant's remaining property, including a vehicle removable under Idaho towing law, without compensating the tenant, subject to any security interests under Idaho's secured-transactions law. The court may award the landlord reasonable costs of removal and restoration for good cause.
notes: ID: Idaho Code § 6-316(2); Idaho Code § 6-311C (writ form authorizing removal under Idaho Code § 6-316(2)); Idaho Code § 49-1806 (vehicles); security interests under Idaho Code Title 28, Chapter 9 (not read). No statutory duty to store or inventory property after the writ, and no animal-specific rule (Title 6, Chapter 3 read whole; rule 39). title: Eviction Record Shielding
bodyText: For unlawful detainer cases filed on or after January 1, 2025, all court records are automatically shielded from public view if the whole case was dismissed, no appeal is pending, and either three years have passed since filing or the parties have filed a stipulation to shield. The parties can still see the records, and any party may petition to seal eviction records under the Idaho Supreme Court's administrative rules. Shielded cases are removed from public court records, so landlords searching those records will not see them.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: An Idaho landlord may not remove a tenant by force, threats or intimidation, or by breaking in; that is a forcible entry or detainer, and the court may enter judgment for three times the tenant's actual damages. The landlord must use the court's unlawful detainer process. Idaho has no statute specifically addressing lockouts or utility shutoffs by a landlord; both carry the same risk.
notes: ID: Idaho Code § 6-301 (forcible entry: breaking open doors or windows, or turning out the party in possession by force, threats or menacing conduct); Idaho Code § 6-302; Idaho Code § 6-317 (treble damages for forcible or unlawful entry or detention). Whole-code search for a landlord interrupting or shutting off utilities: 2 hits (Idaho Code §§ 42-248, 50-1810), neither a landlord rule. Whether a lockout without force is actionable is case law, not read. Narrow statutory exceptions: Idaho Code § 52-414 (lewd use; edu-lewd-use-lease-void-id) and Idaho Code § 6-310A (non-tenant squatters; edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-id). title: Removing Squatters
bodyText: An owner may ask the county sheriff to remove people unlawfully occupying a residential dwelling who are not current or former tenants under a rental agreement the owner authorized, are not immediate family, entered property not open to the public, refused to leave when told, and are not in pending litigation with the owner. The owner submits a verified complaint in the statutory form; the sheriff serves a notice to vacate immediately and restores possession, and may stand by while the owner changes locks. A wrongful use of this remedy exposes the owner to actual damages, statutory damages of three times the fair market rent, costs and attorney fees. This remedy cannot be used against a current or former tenant; for those the landlord must use an eviction. A separate court track for forcible detainer by people who never had a lease with the owner sets trial within 72 hours, excluding weekends and holidays.

title: Lease Void for Lewd Use
bodyText: If a tenant or occupant uses the premises for lewdness, assignation or prostitution, Idaho law makes the lease void at the owner's option; possession reverts to the owner, who may re-enter without court process. Because re-entry without process carries forcible-entry risk if the facts are disputed, landlords should get legal advice before relying on it. The state, a prosecutor or a county resident can also sue to abate a moral nuisance, which can close the building for a year.

title: Holdover Damages
bodyText: A tenant who stays after the lease ends without the landlord's permission is in unlawful detainer. In the eviction case the court assesses the landlord's damages and may enter judgment for three times the actual damages. Idaho has no statute fixing holdover rent or a double-rent penalty. No Idaho statute bars a lease from setting a daily holdover rate either, but the library does not offer one: the statutory measure already reaches every holdover the landlord sues over, as the actual damages (normally the rental value for the time the tenant stays) that the court may treble, and a contract rate would sit inside that trebled figure. A landlord who wants a set holdover rate can add their own clause and should take legal advice first. For agricultural land, a tenant who holds over for more than 60 days without a demand for possession is treated as renewing for another year.

title: Attorney Fees in Landlord-Tenant Cases
bodyText: In any eviction or other action under Idaho's landlord-tenant chapter, the prevailing party, landlord or tenant, is entitled to attorney fees, except where treble damages are awarded. For a nonpayment eviction, the landlord gets fees only if the three-day notice told the tenant that fees would be awarded to the prevailing party. Outside that chapter, Idaho awards fees to the prevailing party where the amount pleaded is $35,000 or less; a plaintiff must have made a written demand at least 10 days before suit and gets no fees if the defendant tendered at least 95% of the award before suit. Fees may also be awarded against a party who sues or defends frivolously.
notes: ID: Idaho Code § 6-324; Idaho Code § 12-120(1), (3) (a 'commercial transaction' excludes transactions for personal or household purposes); Idaho Code § 12-121. The default-by-tenant fee sentence is mutual and consistent. title: Tenant Remedies for Repairs
bodyText: An Idaho tenant's remedy for a landlord's failure to maintain the property is a lawsuit for damages and specific performance, not rent withholding or repair-and-deduct. Before suing, the tenant must give the landlord three days' written notice listing each failure and demanding cure, delivered personally, to an employee at the landlord's place of business, or by certified mail. If the landlord does not cure within three days, the tenant may sue; a suit only for specific performance gets a trial within 12 days, and the court may award three times the actual damages. The one statutory repair-and-deduct right is for missing smoke detectors.
notes: ID: Idaho Code § 6-320(a)-(d); Idaho Code § 6-323; Idaho Code § 6-317; Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(6) (smoke detectors: certified-mail notice, 72 hours, install and deduct from the next month's rent). Not applicable to tracts of five acres or more used for agriculture (Idaho Code § 6-320(e)). No rent-escrow or rent-withholding statute (whole-code search; 'habitab' 4 sections, none a rental rule). title: Landlord Maintenance Duties
bodyText: Idaho has no general habitability code for rentals, but a tenant may sue a landlord who fails to provide reasonable waterproofing and weather protection; fails to keep in good working order the electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling or sanitary facilities the landlord supplies; maintains the premises in a way hazardous to the tenant's health or safety; fails to return a security deposit as required; breaches a lease term materially affecting health and safety; or fails to install approved smoke detectors. The landlord must verify at the start of each rental agreement that the smoke detectors work; the tenant maintains them after that.
notes: ID: Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(1)-(6), (e). Rule 44: Idaho Code § 6-320(a)(5) turns lease promises materially affecting health and safety into enforceable duties (landlord-maintenance tag note). title: Idaho Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Idaho's Human Rights Act makes it unlawful, in renting or leasing, to discriminate because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin or disability; to refuse to rent or negotiate; to set different terms; to misrepresent availability; or to advertise, use application forms or ask questions indicating a discriminatory preference. title: Service Dogs in Rental Housing
bodyText: In Idaho a person with a disability may not be denied housing for rent because they are accompanied by a service dog, and may not be charged anything extra for it, though the person is liable for damage the dog causes. Intentionally violating this is a misdemeanor, and the person harmed can sue for damages plus punitive damages equal to the other damages, at least $500. Idaho's definition of a service dog covers only dogs individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the disability; emotional support animals are not service dogs under Idaho law, but federal fair housing law may still require accommodating them.

title: How Statutory Notices Are Served
bodyText: Idaho eviction notices to a tenant must be served in person; or, if the tenant is away from home and work, by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at either place and mailing a copy to the residence; or, if those fail, by posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the property, delivering a copy to a person living there if one can be found, and mailing a copy to the property. A tenant's three-day notice before suing over repairs or a deposit goes to the landlord or agent in person, to an employee at the usual place of business, or by certified mail. No statute authorizes email service of these notices; Idaho's electronic transactions act does not exclude leases but does not change these service rules.

title: Tenant Waste and Damage
bodyText: An Idaho tenant who commits waste on the property can be sued for it, and the court may award three times the damages. Waste contrary to the lease also ends the lease, and the landlord can recover possession after a three-day notice to quit. The tenant must also keep the smoke detectors in good working order.

title: Consumer Protection Act Reaches Leasing
bodyText: Idaho's Consumer Protection Act covers leasing and renting real property, so the Act's rules against unfair, deceptive and unconscionable practices apply to advertising rentals, renting and collecting rent. In judging unconscionability, a court considers whether the landlord took advantage of a tenant unable to protect their interests, charged a price grossly above similar rentals, or induced an excessively one-sided transaction. The Act's list of unlawful practices also includes getting a signature on a contract that has blank spaces to be filled in after signing, and failing to give the consumer a legible copy of the contract when they sign. Those two items are worded for buyers and sellers, and whether they reach a residential lease is unsettled, so the safe practice is to fill in every blank before the tenant signs and hand the tenant a legible copy at signing.

title: Tenants When the Landlord Is Foreclosed
bodyText: Under Idaho's trust deed law, the buyer at a trustee's sale is entitled to possession on the tenth day after the sale, and anyone still in possession under an interest that came after the deed of trust becomes a tenant at sufferance, who can be removed on the fast eviction track without a notice. Federal law (the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act) gives bona fide tenants at least 90 days' notice and lets many finish their lease.

title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText: A person in possession or control of property is permitted to have an unauthorized vehicle towed or booted if a clearly conspicuous, large-print sign on or near the property says unauthorized vehicles will be removed or booted at the owner's expense and names the towing company. title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule. A landlord may decline to renew a fixed-term lease, or end a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy with the required notice, without giving a reason; the Act says a landlord may terminate 'for any other reason not prohibited by law' unless a court finds the reason was retaliation. Limits that apply only in particular situations: no rent increase, cut in services, eviction or threat of eviction, or termination in retaliation for a housing-code complaint, a complaint or suit under the Act, organizing or joining a tenants' organization, or testifying against the landlord (from January 1, 2027 also media and fair housing complaints, and refusing to renew a voucher holder); a family-abuse victim's lease does not end solely because of the abuse where the abuser has been barred from the home by the landlord or by a court order the tenant has provided; an owner who declines to renew the greater of 20 or 50 percent of the month-to-month tenancies in a multifamily property within 30 days must give each of them 60 days' notice; ending leases to rehabilitate or change the use of a building with four or more units takes 120 days' notice in a separate writing (30 days for month-to-month), and a lease cannot waive that or a condominium or cooperative conversion notice; no suit for a lease violation until the tenant has the state's statement of tenant rights; and a public housing authority that gives notice that it will apply to demolish or dispose of a project may not evict, except for lease violations, for 12 months. Fair housing law applies everywhere.

title: Tenant's Belongings and Animals After an Eviction
bodyText: When the sheriff executes a writ of eviction, the sheriff oversees moving the tenant's belongings into the public way or, at your request, into a storage area you designate, which may be the unit itself. The tenant may take them from the public way during the 24 hours after the eviction, and from your storage area at reasonable times during those 24 hours and afterwards until you dispose of them; if you refuse reasonable access, the tenant can go to court. After 24 hours you must remove or dispose of anything left in the public way, and you may dispose of anything left in your storage area as you see fit. During the 24 hours and until you dispose of the belongings, neither you nor the sheriff is liable for the risk of loss. If you sell anything, pay the money to the tenant's account and apply it to what the tenant owes, including your reasonable eviction, storage and sale costs; treat any balance as a security deposit. The sheriff's 72-hour notice must explain these rights and attach the statute. The writ binds the named tenants, their authorized occupants, guests and invitees, and any trespassers. Virginia has no separate rule for animals left behind after an eviction.

title: A Landlord's Duties During and After an Eviction Case
bodyText: Duties a Virginia landlord has in an eviction case: tell the court of any payments by or for the tenant that reduce what is owed. To raise the amount at the hearing when the summons did not ask for all amounts due as of the hearing, give the tenant a separate written notice of the added amounts and of your intent to amend; once the amount is requested or amended that way, you may not file later suits for amounts that could have been included. If the case is continued to decide final rent and damages, mail the tenant notice of the continuance date and the amounts at least 15 days before it and file a copy with the court. If you get judgment for the whole month's rent and re-rent the home before the month ends, mark that part of the judgment satisfied. When a judgment is paid, have it marked satisfied within 30 days; failing to do so can bring a $100 fine and an order to pay the tenant's costs and attorney fees. When a tenant redeems by paying all amounts at least 48 hours before the scheduled eviction, promptly tell the sheriff to cancel it. A writ of eviction must be issued within 180 days of the judgment for possession and is void if not executed within 30 days of issue, and none may issue if you signed a new written lease with the tenant after the judgment. When the summons is served by posting, it must also be mailed at least 10 days before a default judgment. A business landlord may file eviction papers through an officer, an employee or its managing agent without a lawyer. On an appeal, the tenant (unless indigent) pays the amounts owed into court and then pays you the rent by the fifth of each month; if not, you may ask the court for judgment and possession without a hearing. An owner renting a one- to four-family home whose tenant is unpaid in a federal shutdown can get a 60-day stay of a foreclosure on it by asking the lender, with proof, within 90 days.

title: Virginia Consumer Protection Act and Rentals
bodyText: The Virginia Consumer Protection Act does not reach any part of a rental covered by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act unless the landlord's act is a misrepresentation or fraudulent practice the Consumer Protection Act prohibits. One listed practice bears directly on leases: using in a lease a liquidated damages clause, penalty clause or waiver of defense that is void or unenforceable under Virginia or federal law, or trying to collect under one. A tenant who suffers a loss may recover actual damages or $500, whichever is greater (up to three times actual damages or $1,000 if the violation is willful), plus attorney fees and court costs. The Consumer Protection Act prescribes no lease wording, no statement of waivers and no readability standard.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: If the tenant, an occupant or a guest damages the home, Virginia law gives you these remedies. The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or let anyone else do so, and is responsible for guests' conduct. If the damage materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, you may give written notice, do the work and send an itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost, which is due as rent on the next rent due date, or at once if the lease has ended. You may recover damages for the breach and apply the security deposit to damage from the tenant's breach of duties, less reasonable wear and tear. If fire or casualty makes the home unlivable, the tenant may still end the lease even if the tenant's side caused the damage; you then give a written statement accounting for the deposit and prepaid rent based on the damage and may recover your actual damages, including rent until the term ends or a new tenancy starts, whichever comes first, with a duty to mitigate and no accelerated rent. From January 1, 2027, you may end the lease on 21 days' notice without first meeting the tenant or offering another unit if you determine the tenant's breach of duties caused the damage. If the tenant stays, rent is reduced during repairs only where the damage happened without the tenant's fault or negligence. Because a lease cannot make the tenant give up a right under the Act, no clause can keep the lease and rent running after the tenant ends it for casualty damage.

title: Fees Count as Rent
bodyText: In Virginia, 'rent' means all money other than a security deposit owed or paid to the landlord under the lease, including rent paid more than one month ahead, so charges the lease imposes are rent unless a section says otherwise. The Act says so expressly for damage-insurance and renter's-insurance premiums the landlord charges, ratio-billed utility charges and allocated local government fees with their administrative charges, the utility late charge where ratio billing is used, and the bill for repairs the landlord makes after a tenant's breach. Every deposit and rent charge must appear in the first-page fee disclosure or in a later addendum.

Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1200 ('Rent'), 55.1-1206(A)-(B) (premiums 'shall not be deemed a security deposit, but shall be rent'), 55.1-1212 (late charge and local government fees 'deemed rent'), 55.1-1248 (repair bill 'due as rent'), 55.1-1204.1 (fee disclosure sentence), all read whole. title: Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Breach
bodyText: If a tenant's breach of the lease or of the tenant's statutory duties materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement of a damaged item or cleaning, you may send a written notice specifying the breach and stating that you will enter, do the work in a workmanlike manner and send an itemized bill. The actual and reasonable cost is due as rent on the next rent due date, or at once if the lease has ended. In an emergency you may enter and do the work as promptly as conditions require. You may do the work yourself or hire someone. The right exists by law whatever the lease says.
notes: VA: VA-SCOPE: STATEWIDE. Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.6), rule 27. PRESENT: Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1248 (1974, c. 680; 2019, c. 712; read whole). Unlike Tennessee's Act-county rule, the statute sets no waiting period after the notice. No clause: the right exists by statute for every Virginia landlord, so a lease clause would only restate it; access for it is preserved by § 55.1-1229(C) (landlords-access-va). title: Quiet Enjoyment in Virginia Law
bodyText: Virginia has no statute that writes a covenant of quiet enjoyment into every residential lease. If a lease uses the short phrase that the landlord covenants 'for the lessee's quiet enjoyment of his term', Virginia law gives it a set meaning: a tenant who pays the rent and keeps the lease may peaceably possess the home for the term without interruption or disturbance from anyone. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act protects the same interest in other ways: it limits the landlord's entry, bars lockouts and cutting off essential services, and makes each tenant responsible for keeping guests from disturbing the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment.

title: Tenant-Installed Security Systems and Cameras
bodyText: A Virginia tenant may install new security systems the tenant believes necessary for safety, including chain latches the landlord approves and fire detection devices, if the installation does no permanent damage, the tenant gives the landlord a duplicate of all keys and the operating instructions for every device, and the tenant pays the reasonable cost of removing the devices and repairing any damage when the tenancy ends. The statute does not mention cameras or video doorbells; a camera installed as a security system falls under the same conditions, and the lease's alteration and rules terms cannot take the right away.

title: After the Eviction Judgment
bodyText: After an Alabama eviction judgment for the landlord, the writ of possession issues on the landlord's application once the automatic seven-day stay ends. A sheriff or constable who neglects or refuses to execute the writ owes the landlord $200. A tenant who comes back in without just cause after being removed can be held in contempt, and further writs may issue; going back into possession after being put out under court process is also a crime, punished by a fine of $200 to $1,000 (half paid to the landlord) and at least six months in jail. No Alabama statute sets duties for a tenant's belongings or animals when the writ is executed, or gives landlords immunity for it. The Act lets a landlord dispose of property left in the unit more than 14 days after a lawful termination, with no duty to store or protect it. Removing belongings or changing the locks before the writ is executed is self-help the Act forbids.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Requirement
bodyText: Alabama has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule. A landlord may end a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy by written notice (at least 7 or 30 days) and may decline to renew a fixed-term lease when it ends, without giving a reason, however long the tenant has lived there. Situational limits still apply: a landlord may not bring or threaten an eviction in retaliation for a tenant's code complaint to a government agency, a repair complaint to the landlord, or organizing or joining a tenants' union; a declarant converting a building to condominiums must give tenants at least 60 days' notice and may not require them to leave sooner except for nonpayment of rent, waste or disturbing other tenants; and in a possession case the tenant may counterclaim, paying rent into court, and wins possession if no rent remains due. Federal rules for subsidized housing are not covered here.

title: Consumer Protection Act and Rentals
bodyText: Alabama's Deceptive Trade Practices Act defines 'goods' to include real property and 'sale' and 'buying' to include leasing and renting, so on its face it reaches a residential lease with a tenant renting for personal, family or household use. Its list of unlawful practices includes misrepresenting what is offered (its characteristics, benefits, standard or quality), advertising with intent not to rent as advertised, and false statements about the need for repairs, plus a catch-all for any other unconscionable, false, misleading or deceptive act. The list does not name leaving blanks to be filled in after signing or failing to give a copy at signing. A consumer may recover actual damages or $100, whichever is greater, up to three times actual damages at the court's discretion, and attorney's fees, after a written demand at least 15 days before suing; consumers may not sue as a class. Whether the Landlord and Tenant Act's statement that it is the exclusive remedy for rights under a rental agreement limits these claims is not settled by statute.

title: Returned Payments (Alabama)
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds, a closed or nonexistent account, a stop-payment order or any other reason, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount; for a dishonored check, Alabama law lets a lender, creditor or merchant charge up to $30 or the bank's actual return charge, whichever is greater; whether that limit reaches a landlord collecting rent is not settled, so stay within it], and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are returned or fail, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check or money order.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term (for a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, up to the earliest date the tenancy could have been ended by notice), less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property, although Landlord may first rent other vacant units it has. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage. Part (1) does not apply, and Tenant keeps any right Alabama law gives Tenant to end this Lease or pay reduced Rent, after a fire or casualty that Tenant did not personally cause, such as one caused by a guest.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: If an Alabama tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or someone on the property with the tenant's consent deliberately or negligently causes a condition, the tenant's repair, termination and essential-service remedies do not arise for it. A fire or casualty caused by the tenant gives the tenant no right to end the lease or pay reduced rent; that exception names only 'the tenant', so a fire caused by a guest may still give the tenant those rights. The tenant must not damage the property, or knowingly, recklessly or negligently let anyone else do so. The landlord may recover actual damages and apply the deposit, and for a health or safety problem that repair, replacement or cleaning can fix, may do the work after seven days' written notice and bill it as rent. The tenant may not withhold rent. If the landlord ends the lease for the breach, the landlord has a claim for rent and actual damages, subject to a duty to mitigate. How Alabama courts measure lost future rent is case law not read here. The library offers an optional clause (`tenant-caused-damage-al`).

title: Fees Count as Rent
bodyText: Under Alabama's Act, 'rent' means all payments the tenant is to make to or for the landlord under the rental agreement, so late fees and other lease charges count as rent without any special wording. The nonpayment notice may include late fees, and the cost of repairs the landlord makes after the tenant fails to fix a health or safety problem is billed as rent. This library's default clause still says an unpaid late fee alone will not support ending the lease; that is a library choice, not a legal limit.

title: Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Breach
bodyText: If an Alabama tenant breaks the tenant's statutory upkeep duties in a way that materially affects health and safety, and the problem can be fixed by repair, replacing a damaged item or cleaning, the landlord may give written notice describing it and asking the tenant to fix it within seven days (or as promptly as conditions require in an emergency). If the tenant does not, the landlord may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner, and bill the tenant for the actual and reasonable cost (or its fair and reasonable value) as rent on the next rent due date, or for immediate payment if the lease has ended. No lease clause is needed for this right, and because the bill is rent it can go in a nonpayment notice once it is due.
notes: AL retro 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.8, rule 27). title: No Just-Cause Eviction Requirement
bodyText: South Carolina has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule. A landlord may decline to renew a fixed-term lease when it ends, or end a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 7 or 30 days before the termination date, without giving a reason, however long the tenant has lived there; the end of the term is itself a ground for ejectment. Situational limits still apply: a landlord may not raise rent above fair-market value, cut essential services or sue for possession in retaliation for a tenant's code complaint to a government agency or a complaint to the landlord about a violation of the Act, and a retaliatory refusal to renew can delay recovery of possession for 75 days; a protected domestic-violence tenant may not be made to leave before 60 days after the incident or be retaliated against for ending the lease; and an owner converting a building to condominiums must give tenants written notice and let them stay until the lease expires or for 120 days (90 if under 60), whichever is longer, except for a lease violation. Paying rent into court lets a tenant keep defending a possession case but does not bar eviction. No statute protects tenants' associations. Fair housing law applies everywhere; federal rules for subsidized housing are not covered here.

title: Which Charges Count as Rent
bodyText: Under South Carolina's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, 'rent' means the payment for use of the property and includes late charges, but excludes security deposits and other charges. So an unpaid late fee is unpaid rent under the Act, while other fees the lease imposes (for example a returned-payment fee or a bill for repairs) are not rent under the Act's definition, whatever the lease calls them. Whether a particular charge, such as pet rent, is payment for use of the property or an 'other charge' is not settled by the statute. This library's default clause says an unpaid late fee alone will not support ending the lease; that is a library choice, not a legal limit.
notes: SC: SC retro 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.9, rule 27). PRESENT: S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-210(11) ('"rent" means the consideration payable for use of the premises including late charges whether payable in lump sum or periodic payments, excluding security deposits or other charges'). title: Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Breach
bodyText: If a South Carolina tenant breaks the tenant's statutory upkeep duties in a way that materially affects health and safety, and the problem can be fixed by repair, replacing a damaged item or cleaning, the landlord may give written notice specifying the breach and asking the tenant to fix it within 14 days (or as promptly as conditions require in an emergency). If the tenant does not, the landlord may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner, and the tenant must reimburse the cost; the landlord also keeps the Act's other remedies. No lease clause is needed for this right. The statute calls the payment reimbursement, not rent, and the Act's definition of rent excludes charges other than late charges, so whether an unpaid repair bill can support a nonpayment eviction is not settled by the statute. For a health-and-safety breach that repair, replacement or cleaning cannot fix, the landlord may instead end the lease if the tenant does not comply within 14 days after written notice.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: If a South Carolina tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or someone on the property with the tenant's permission deliberately or negligently causes a condition, the tenant cannot end the lease over it as a landlord breach or use the essential-services remedies for it, and rent paid into court during an eviction case is not reduced for it. Fire or casualty is different: if a fire or casualty substantially impairs use of the home, the tenant may still move out and end the lease by written notice within 7 days, or stay in the usable part at reduced rent, even if the tenant caused it. The tenant's fault there only lets you keep the security deposit and prepaid rent, and you must still send the itemized written notice. The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the property or knowingly let others do so. You may deduct the damage from the deposit and recover actual damages for the breach. For a health or safety problem that repair, replacement or cleaning can fix, you may do the work after 14 days' written notice (sooner in an emergency) and have the tenant reimburse the cost. If the lease ends, you have a claim for actual damages, with a duty to mitigate. No statute says whether those damages include rent lost until the term would have ended; the library offers an optional clause (`tenant-caused-damage-sc`) that sets that measure. A lease cannot keep the full rent running while a tenant-caused casualty is repaired, because that would waive the tenant's statutory right to reduced rent.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, and this Lease ends because of the damage, including because Tenant ends it under South Carolina's fire or casualty law, then Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term (for a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, up to the earliest date the tenancy could have been ended by notice), less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage. It does not limit Tenant's right under South Carolina law to end this Lease or pay reduced Rent after a fire or casualty, or any other right South Carolina law gives Tenant.

title: Use of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit) prior to occupancy. Landlord will hold the Security Deposit in a bank, credit union or other depository institution insured by an agency of the federal government, and any interest earned on it belongs to Landlord. Landlord may withhold from the Security Deposit only the amounts reasonably necessary to: (1) remedy Tenant's default in paying Rent due under this Lease; (2) restore the property to its condition at the start of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted; and (3) compensate Landlord for actual damages caused by Tenant's failure to give the notice required by law or this Lease to end the tenancy, after Landlord makes reasonable efforts to reduce those damages. Landlord will not apply the Security Deposit to ordinary wear and tear or to any damage or defective condition that existed before the tenancy. Tenant may not apply or deduct any part of the Security Deposit in place of paying Rent at any time, including the last month's Rent. The Security Deposit does not limit Landlord's right to recover damages greater than the Security Deposit.

title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, Landlord will either return the full Security Deposit to Tenant or give Tenant a written itemized list of the damages for which any part of the Security Deposit is withheld, together with the balance. Landlord may do so by mailing the list and any payment to Tenant's last known address. Before the inspection to determine any amount to be withheld, Landlord will give Tenant reasonable written notice, at Tenant's last known address or in person, of the date and time of the inspection, which will be held at a reasonable time, and Tenant may be present. When Tenant vacates, Tenant will give Landlord in writing a forwarding address to which the Security Deposit and any itemized list should be sent.
notes: MO: Instruction 24 family. Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.300(3): within 30 days after the date of termination of the tenancy the landlord shall return the full deposit or furnish a written itemized list of the damages for which any portion is withheld, along with the balance; mailing the statement and payment to the tenant's last known address complies. Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.300(5): reasonable written notice of the date and time of the move-out inspection, at the last known address or in person; inspection at a reasonable time; tenant's right to be present. Penalty for wrongful withholding: twice the amount wrongfully withheld (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.300(6); edu-security-deposit-rules-mo). The 30 days run from the end of the tenancy, not from move-out or the tenant's demand; the statute does not let the lease fix another period (rule 50). The forwarding-address sentence is a tenant step the statute does not impose; it does not extend the deadline. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Handling of Property Left Behind
bodyText: When this Lease ends or Tenant gives up possession, Tenant will remove all of Tenant's personal property from the property. (1) If Tenant has moved out, returned the keys and given up possession to Landlord but left personal property behind, Landlord will send Tenant a written notice by mail to Tenant's forwarding address (or, if Tenant has not given one, to the property address) describing the property and stating where and by what date Tenant may collect it; if Tenant does not collect it within [number, at least 10] days after the notice is sent, Landlord may dispose of it, and need not store garbage, perishable items or anything hazardous. (2) If Landlord reasonably believes Tenant has moved out and does not intend to return, but Tenant has not given up possession, and Rent has been due and unpaid for 30 days, Landlord may post on the property, and mail to Tenant's last known address by both first-class mail and certified mail, return receipt requested, the notice of belief of abandonment that Missouri law prescribes. If Tenant does not pay the Rent or respond in writing stating that Tenant has not abandoned the property within 10 days after the notice has been both posted and mailed, the property is considered abandoned, and Landlord may remove and dispose of any personal property remaining there without liability to Tenant. (3) Property left after a court's judgment for possession is carried out will be handled as the court and Missouri law direct. While Tenant remains in possession, Landlord will not remove Tenant's personal property, remove or change the locks, or interrupt essential utilities to force Tenant out, except as this Section or a court order permits. This Section does not apply to motor vehicles, which are handled under Missouri vehicle law.
notes: MO: Part (2) follows Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.065: premises are deemed abandoned if (1) the landlord reasonably believes the tenant has vacated and intends not to return, (2) rent is due and has been unpaid for thirty days, (3) the landlord posts written notice on the premises and mails it to the tenant's last known address by both first-class and certified mail, return receipt requested, with the statute's notice text, and (4) the tenant fails to pay rent or respond in writing within ten days after both the posting and the mailing; the landlord may then remove or dispose of property without liability. The builder should generate the statutory notice verbatim from Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.065(3), inserting the landlord's name and street address (MO log §4). Part (3): after a judgment, the officer delivers possession within five days of receiving the execution (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.040(1)); the landlord is not liable for removing property under a court-ordered execution except for willful, wanton or malicious acts, but must give third-party owners of conspicuously labelled property certified-mail notice and five business days to recover it (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.040(2)-(3)); if the officer has not delivered possession within seven days, the landlord may, within 60 days of the judgment and with a law enforcement officer present, take possession and remove property (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.060(5)-(6)) (edu-post-eviction-property-mo). Part (1) is a contractual procedure: no Missouri statute governs property left after a voluntary surrender, and removing a tenant's property without judicial process except under Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.065 is forcible entry and detainer (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.233(1)); whether a person who has surrendered possession is still a 'tenant' (one who 'occupies the premises with the landlord's consent', Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.005(6)) for that rule is case law, not read, so part (1) applies only after the tenant has given up possession and returned the keys. Vehicles: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 304.157 (edu-towing-mo). title: Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText: If this Lease continues as a month-to-month tenancy, either Landlord or Tenant may end it by giving the other a written notice stating that the tenancy will end on a day Rent is due that is at least one month after the other party receives the notice. Rent remains payable through the date the tenancy ends. This Section does not limit either party's right to end this Lease earlier where this Lease or Missouri law allows it.
notes: MO: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.060(4)(1): the landlord or the tenant may terminate a month-to-month tenancy by written notice stating that the tenancy shall terminate 'upon a periodic rent-paying date not less than one month after the receipt of the notice'. Other tenancy types (rule 37): a tenancy at will, by sufferance or 'for less than one year' (which includes week-to-week) may be ended by the person entitled to possession on one month's written notice (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.060(1)); year-to-year tenancies need written notice not less than 60 days before the end of the year (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.050); a fixed term ends without notice to quit (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.070); a tenancy under an unwritten agreement is month to month (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.060(3)); a mobile-home lot tenancy follows Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.060(4)(2). See edu-notice-to-quit-mo. Holdover with accepted rent becomes month to month under holdover-ca. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds, a closed or nonexistent account or a stop-payment order, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount; for a check that a financial institution dishonors or returns unpaid, Missouri law limits the charge to a reasonable service charge of not more than $25 plus the amount Landlord's bank actually charges for the returned item], and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. Stat. § 570.120(6)(2): if a dishonored or returned check is not referred to the prosecuting or circuit attorney, the party to whom it was issued, or a holder, 'may collect from the issuer, in addition to the face amount of the check, a reasonable service charge, not to exceed twenty-five dollars, plus an amount equal to the actual charge by the depository institution for the return of each unpaid or dishonored instrument'. The cap is stated for checks; the section's offense provisions also reach 'any other form of presentment involving the transmission of account information', but subdivision (6)(2) speaks only of a 'check'; whether it caps fees on failed electronic payments is not settled by the text. The bracket states the landlord's figure (rule 55); the builder should cap a check fee at $25 plus the bank's actual charge (MO log §10). Section read whole and saved (outside-title, source 4). title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord: [list approved pets, or state that no pets are permitted]. Tenant will pay a pet deposit of {{pet_deposit}}, if applicable, which is separate from the Security Deposit; Landlord may apply it to damage, cleaning or waste removal caused by a pet and will return any balance with the Security Deposit. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, if applicable. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet, and will reimburse Landlord for claims caused by Tenant's pet, except to the extent a claim arises from the negligence of Landlord or Landlord's agents or employees. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and Tenant will then remove the pet within [number] days after Landlord's written notice; failure to do so is a default under this Lease. Landlord may enter the property in connection with a pet only as this Lease's Access & Entry terms permit, or without notice in an emergency, and will not seize or remove a pet without a court order. This Section does not limit animal control or law enforcement acting under their own authority. This Section does not apply to a service animal or assistance animal.
notes: MO: Overrides pet-policy, whose term letting the landlord 'enter the property and remove a pet, without liability to Tenant to the extent applicable law permits' risks forcible entry and detainer: a landlord who removes a tenant's personal property without judicial process (except under Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.065) is guilty of forcible entry and detainer (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.233(1)), and the self-limiting phrase would hide that conflict (rule 53). Pet deposit: Missouri's 'security deposit' 'does not include any money or property denominated as a deposit for a pet on the premises' (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.300(8)), so a pet deposit is outside the two-month cap and the 30-day return rule; the clause sets its own return term, and a servicemember who ends the lease under Mo. Rev. Stat. § 41.944 gets the pet deposit back in full if the lease was otherwise complied with (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 41.944(3)) (edu-pet-deposit-mo). Stat. § 441.233(1) also reaches a landlord who 'causes' a removal without judicial process and court order (corrected after the independent check, MO log §13). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Smoking Policy
bodyText: Smoking of any kind, including smoking tobacco or marijuana, and vaping tobacco or nicotine products with an electronic cigarette or similar device, is not permitted anywhere on the property, including inside the dwelling, on porches or balconies, or in any common area. Tenant will be responsible for any cost Landlord incurs to remediate odor, staining or damage caused by smoking or vaping in violation of this Section, and a violation may be treated as a default under this Lease. As the Missouri Constitution requires, this Section does not prohibit Tenant from lawfully possessing marijuana or consuming it by means other than smoking.
notes: MO: Overrides smoking-policy, whose ban on 'smoking of any kind, including tobacco, marijuana, and vaping' would bar consuming marijuana by vaporization. Mo. Const. art. XIV, § 2.3(4) (effective 12/8/2022) lets an entity prohibit or limit marijuana consumption, cultivation and the like on property it leases, 'except that a lease agreement executed after the effective date of this section may not prohibit a tenant from lawfully possessing and consuming marijuana by means other than smoking'. The Constitution's medical-marijuana definition of 'administer' lists 'Vaporization or smoking' as one method beside ingestion (Mo. Const. art. XIV, § 1.2(1)(b), read as an excerpt), so whether vaporizing marijuana is a 'means other than smoking' under Mo. Const. art. XIV, § 2.3(4) is unsettled (case law not read). This clause therefore bans smoking of anything and vaping of tobacco or nicotine, and leaves marijuana consumption by non-smoking means, including vaping marijuana, alone. Applies to leases executed after 12/8/2022, which is every lease the builder makes. No Missouri smoke-drift or smoke-free-housing statute (MO batteries 36, 76) (edu-cannabis-mo).
