title: Fire or Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire, tornado or other casualty not caused by Tenant, members of Tenant's household or Tenant's guests, and the damage makes the property unfit to live in or substantially impairs Tenant's use of it, either Landlord or Tenant may end this Lease by written notice to the other, effective on the date Tenant moves out. Rent will be prorated to that date, any prepaid Rent refunded, and the Security Deposit returned as this Lease and Missouri law provide. If the casualty makes only part of the property unusable and Tenant stays in possession, Rent will be reduced in proportion to the part of the property Tenant cannot use until Landlord completes repairs. This Section does not limit any other right Tenant has under Missouri law, including the rule that a tenant who did not cause a disaster that destroys the residence owes no Rent for the rest of the Term.
notes: MO: Optional clause (rule 54; standing GA decision: offer landlord casualty termination where no statute controls it). Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.645 (2010): if a residence is destroyed by an act of God, including fire, tornado or other natural or man-made disaster, 'so long as the tenant was not the person who caused the disaster', the tenant is not liable for rent for the remainder of the term; it gives neither party a termination right and says nothing about partial damage. Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.010: a covenant to repair does not oblige a tenant to rebuild after a fire not caused by the tenant's 'procurement, connivance or neglect' unless the tenant specially covenants to do so. No statute gives the landlord a termination right (whole-code search; battery 70 missed Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.645's 'destroyed by an act of God' wording, so this answer rests on the whole read of Chapter 441; MO log §17). The clause's last sentence preserves Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.645. Same structure as casualty-termination-il and casualty-termination-id with Missouri named (edu-casualty-mo). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage. This Section does not make Tenant liable for damage from a fire that begins accidentally at the property where Missouri law protects a tenant from that liability, and it is not an agreement by Tenant to rebuild after a fire. If the residence is destroyed by a disaster that Tenant did not cause, and Missouri law releases Tenant from Rent for the rest of the Term, this Section does not make Tenant liable for that Rent or for lost Rent as damages.
notes: MO: Optional clause (rule 54, tenant-caused damage). Model: tenant-caused-damage-tn, with a Missouri carve-out. Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.645 releases rent for the rest of the term where a residence is destroyed 'so long as the tenant was not the person who caused the disaster', so a tenant who causes destruction gets no statutory release; the clause fills that lost-rent gap. Where an Occupant, guest or invitee (not a tenant) causes the destruction, the statute's text still releases the tenant's rent, so the last sentence keeps the clause from charging that rent or lost rent as damages; the tenant's liability for repair costs caused by household members and guests is not affected by Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.645. Corrected after the independent check (MO log §13). Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.010: no action may be maintained against a tenant 'in whose house or apartment any fire shall accidentally begin', and a repair covenant does not oblige a tenant to rebuild after a fire not caused by the tenant's 'procurement, connivance or neglect' unless the tenant specially covenants to rebuild. Whether a negligently caused fire 'accidentally' begins under that section is case law, not read, so the last sentence defers to it rather than drawing the line; the clause is not a special covenant to rebuild. A tenant for years who commits waste without written licence owes treble damages (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.420), and a tenant may not commit waste (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.030) (edu-tenant-caused-damage-mo). Rule 15: written section-open. title: No Criminal Activity
bodyText: Tenant, members of Tenant's household and Tenant's guests will not engage in criminal activity on or in the immediate vicinity of the property that threatens the health, safety or right of peaceful enjoyment of the premises by other residents, neighbors or Landlord's employees, and will not allow the illegal possession, sale or distribution of controlled substances on the property. A breach of this Section is a breach of a condition of this Lease, for which Landlord may end Tenant's right of possession by giving Tenant the notice to vacate that Missouri law requires, without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure. This Section controls over any other provision of this Lease that would require notice and an opportunity to cure. This Section does not apply to the possession or use of marijuana that Missouri law permits, although this Lease's smoking and cultivation terms still apply, or to criminal activity of which Tenant or a member of Tenant's household is the victim.
notes: MO: Optional clause (rule 54; crime-free / criminal-activity family, model criminal-activity-nc). Missouri law: a tenant may not 'violate any of the conditions of his written lease' (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.030), and on a violation the landlord may re-enter 'after giving ten days' notice to vacate the premises ... by the procedure specified by law' (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.040); no cure right is stated. Allowing illegal possession, sale or distribution of controlled substances on the premises makes the lease void (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.020); drug-related criminal activity also supports the expedited eviction track (Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 441.710 to 441.880; edu-expedited-drug-eviction-mo). The clause adds non-drug criminal activity that threatens safety, which no statute makes a ground, as a lease condition. Carve-outs: (1) Mo. Const. art. XIV, § 2.3(4) bars a post-12/8/2022 lease from prohibiting lawful possession and non-smoking consumption of marijuana (edu-cannabis-mo); (2) Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.920(2): no tenant may be evicted or found in violation of a lease because the tenant is, has been or is in imminent danger of becoming a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking (subject to the section's exceptions; edu-dv-protections-mo). title: Missouri Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: Missouri limits a security deposit to two months' rent and requires you to keep it in a federally insured bank, credit union or depository institution (any interest is yours). Within 30 days after the tenancy ends you must return the full deposit or give the tenant a written itemized list of damages with the balance; mailing to the tenant's last known address is enough. You may withhold only for unpaid rent, restoring the unit to its move-in condition beyond ordinary wear and tear, and actual damages from the tenant's failure to give proper notice to end the tenancy (after trying to reduce them). Before the move-out inspection, give the tenant reasonable written notice of its date and time; the tenant may attend. If you wrongfully withhold any part, the tenant recovers twice the amount wrongfully withheld. A pet deposit is not a security deposit under this law.
notes: MO: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.300(1)-(8) (2018 S.B. 581 is the latest amendment; version date 8/28/2018). Government landlords, including housing authorities, are exempt only from the holding rule in Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.300(2). The revisor prints an annotation that the double-damages provision does not apply to commercial tenants (PDQ Tower Services, Inc. v. Adams, 213 S.W.3d 697 (Mo. App. W.D. 2007)); case not read. No deposit anti-waiver section (MO battery 91). Local deposit caps are preempted (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.043(2)(3)). Clauses: security-deposit-use-mo, security-deposit-return-mo. title: Security Deposit Cap
bodyText: You may not demand or receive a security deposit of more than two months' rent. The limit covers any deposit of money or property, however you label it, that secures the tenant's performance of the lease, so be careful about extra 'deposits' that push the total over two months' rent. A deposit labelled as a pet deposit does not count. Cities and counties may not impose a lower cap.

title: Tenant Repair and Deduct
bodyText: A Missouri tenant may repair and deduct only if all of these apply: the tenant has lawfully lived there six consecutive months, paid all rent and charges, and had no uncured written lease or rule violation notice in that time; the condition violates a local housing or building code and harms habitability, sanitation or security; it costs less than $300 or half the periodic rent, whichever is greater, and no more than one month's rent; and you fail to fix it within 14 days of the tenant's written notice (or sooner in an emergency). If you dispute the need in writing within that period, the tenant must first get written certification from the local government that the condition violates the code. The tenant must use workmanlike repairs and give you an itemized statement with receipts. The remedy is unavailable for conditions the tenant's household or guests caused, and is limited to one month's rent in any 12 months. No lease may waive it.

title: Housing Code Receivership
bodyText: If a building violates building or housing codes in a way that threatens health or safety, a county, city, local housing corporation or neighborhood association may, after 60 days' written notice to interested parties, ask a court to appoint a receiver who collects the rents and fixes the property. Rent a tenant pays to the receiver under the court's order is a defense to an eviction for nonpayment. A lease term waiving a tenant's protections under these sections is void. Occupants have their own duties under this law (paying rent, keeping the unit sanitary, not damaging it, and not taking in extra occupants without the owner's consent).

title: Unpaid Heat Utilities in Master-Metered Buildings
bodyText: In a building of two or more units where the owner pays for gas or electric heat service, if the owner falls behind and the utility gives notice of termination, the utility must tell tenants at least five days before shutoff, and any tenant or the utility may ask the associate circuit court to appoint a receiver to collect rents and pay for heat. The utility may not cut off heat while a receivership exists, or while a petition is pending (if a tenant filed it, once the utility has had at least 24 hours' prior written notice of the filing). An owner who collects rent while a receiver is appointed is in contempt of court.
notes: MO: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.650 (1985 S.B. 294). Stale cross-reference: subsection 3(3) appoints receivers 'in accordance with sections 515.240 to 515.260', which the revisor notes were repealed by S.B. 578 (2016) (MO log §10, rule 77). title: Water and Sewer Bills
bodyText: Municipal and district water and sewer service is treated as furnished to both the occupant and the owner, so the provider may sue either or both for unpaid bills. Once the occupant is 30 days behind, the provider must try in good faith to tell the owner; the owner is not liable for more than 90 days of service, and any termination notice must go to both. Where several residences share a water or sewer line, the property owner is liable. Services billed directly to the owner under an owner's account are the owner's responsibility.
notes: MO: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 250.140(1)-(5) (2005). Applies to cities, towns, villages and sewer or water districts organized under Chapter 247; private utilities not covered by this section. The 120-day rule for some large cities expired after January 1, 2007 by its own terms. title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: You may not remove or exclude a tenant or the tenant's belongings, or remove or change the locks, without judicial process and a court order, except under Missouri's abandonment procedure. You may not willfully interrupt essential services such as electricity, gas, water or sewer to force a tenant out, unless you do so for health or safety reasons. A landlord who does either is guilty of forcible entry and detainer, and the tenant may sue to get back in, with double the damages found.

Abandonment exception: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.065 (abandoned-property-mo). title: No Retaliation Statute
bodyText: Missouri has no general statute barring a landlord from retaliating against a tenant for complaining about conditions or using legal rights. Specific protections still apply: you may not evict because a resident has an elevated blood lead level or because of lead enforcement, or deny or evict a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. Federal fair housing law bars retaliation for exercising fair housing rights.

title: Notice to End a Tenancy
bodyText: How much notice Missouri requires depends on the kind of tenancy. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date with no notice to quit. A month-to-month tenancy ends by written notice from either party ending it on a rent-paying date at least one month after the other party receives it. A tenancy at will, by sufferance or for less than a year (such as week-to-week) may be ended by the landlord on one month's written notice. A year-to-year tenancy needs written notice at least 60 days before the end of the year. A lease that is not in writing and signed is treated as month-to-month. These notices are not needed before a rent-and-possession case for unpaid rent. A mobile-home lot tenancy has a longer 60-day rule. Missouri also lets the parties dispense with the notice to quit by special agreement (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.070). The library does not offer a clause that does this: it would remove the one-month notice from a month-to-month tenancy, how far a court lets such an agreement reach has not been reviewed, and a term like this is read strictly against the landlord who drafted it. It is lawful, so a landlord who still wants it can add a custom clause, after taking advice.
notes: MO: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.070 (no notice to quit for a term ending at a certain time, or when 'by special agreement, notice is dispensed with'); Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.060(1), (3), (4)(1), (4)(2); Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.050; Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.020 (giving the notice provided in Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.060 is not required before a rent-and-possession case). title: Demand for Rent Before Filing
bodyText: Missouri has no pay-or-quit notice period for unpaid rent. Before filing a rent-and-possession case, you must demand the rent that is due from the tenant or the person occupying the property; the demand is valid any time after the rent is due, and in a suit for possession when one month's rent or more is in arrears and you have a right by law to re-enter for the nonpayment, serving the complaint and summons counts as the demand. If your written lease declares the lease forfeited for nonpayment 'for a specified time', you cannot start the case until that time has passed, so avoid building a grace period into a forfeiture clause unless you mean it.
notes: MO: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.020 (statement verified by affidavit that rent has been demanded and not paid); Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.060 (demand good when made any time after the rent becomes due); Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.120, Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.140 (action when one month's rent or more is in arrears and the landlord has a subsisting right to re-enter; service of complaint and summons is a sufficient demand); Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.050 (forfeiture clause with a specified time delays process). The revisor's annotation to Mo. Rev. Stat. § 534.330 reports New Brentwood Realty v. Strad, Inc. (Mo. App. 1974) on demanding the exact amount due on the due day; case law, not read. No prescribed demand form (MO batteries 86-87). title: Missouri Eviction Process
bodyText: Missouri has two main eviction tracks. A rent-and-possession case (for unpaid rent) is filed with an associate circuit judge after a demand for rent; the court date must be within 21 business days of the summons unless you agree to later, the tenant may stop the case by paying all rent and costs on the judgment date, and the officer must deliver possession within 5 days of receiving the execution. An unlawful detainer case covers a tenant who holds over after the lease ends and refuses to leave after a written demand for possession; execution for possession may issue no sooner than 10 days after judgment, and the judgment awards double damages and double monthly rent until possession is restored. In a rent-and-possession case the tenant has 10 days from the judgment to move to set it aside or apply for a trial de novo, and in either track an appeal stays execution only with a sufficient bond (in rent cases, one covering rent). If service is only by posting and mailing and the tenant defaults, no money judgment is entered. Self-help eviction is prohibited, and local governments may not impose eviction moratoriums.

title: Lease Violations and Illegal Use
bodyText: Missouri gives no cure period for lease violations. If a tenant violates a condition of a written lease, assigns or sublets without your written consent (for terms of two years or less, at will or by sufferance), or commits waste, you may give 10 days' notice to vacate (in writing, to be safe) and then recover possession through the courts. If a tenant allows illegal gaming, a bawdyhouse or the illegal possession, sale or distribution of controlled substances on the premises, the lease becomes void and you have the same remedies as against a tenant holding over. You are not liable for relying on a written notice from law enforcement that the premises are being used for illegal drug activity.
notes: MO: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.030, Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.040 (re-entry 'after giving ten days' notice to vacate the premises ... by the procedure specified by law'; landlord's burden to prove drug use; reliance on written law enforcement notification), Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.020. Whether a particular lease term is a 'condition' and whether accepting rent after notice waives the violation are case law, not read. The library's default-by-tenant cure promise carries an exception for breaches the law lets the landlord act on without a cure (rule 43). Clause: criminal-activity-mo. title: Expedited Eviction for Drug Activity and Emergencies
bodyText: A landlord or prosecutor may bring an expedited eviction in the associate circuit court, heard within 15 days of service, where drug-related criminal activity occurred on or near the property or the tenant's household or guests engaged in it, or where an emergency makes ordinary eviction too slow to prevent physical injury or major property damage (only after first trying to abate it through police or mental health services). No notice to vacate is needed first, except that if someone other than the tenant committed the activity, you must give the tenant 5 days' written notice and a chance to seek a protective order or report it to police. An innocent tenant who did not know of the activity can defend, and the court may then remove only the person responsible. On eviction the tenant has 24 hours to vacate. Rent continues to accrue during the case.
notes: MO: Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 441.710 to 441.880: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.710 (standing), Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.720 (15-day hearing; Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 535.030 and 535.110 apply), Mo. Rev. title: Property Left After an Eviction
bodyText: When a judgment for possession is carried out, you are not liable for loss of or damage to the tenant's belongings you remove or dispose of under the court-ordered execution, except for willful, wanton or malicious acts. But if property left behind is conspicuously and permanently labelled as belonging to a third party, you must notify that person by certified mail, return receipt requested, and give them five business days after receiving the notice to recover it. If the officer has not delivered possession within seven days after receiving the writ, you may, within 60 days of the judgment and with a local law enforcement officer present, remove the locks, take possession and remove belongings, after showing the officer the judgment and execution and filing the officer's written acknowledgment with the court within five days.
notes: MO: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.040(2)-(3) (2009 S.B. 231); Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.060(5)-(6) (landlord liable only for negligent, willful or wanton acts or for failing to obtain and file the acknowledgment); Mo. Rev. Stat. § 534.355. No statutory storage, inventory or animal-care duty (Chapters 441, 534 and 535 read whole). Clause: abandoned-property-mo. title: Removing Squatters
bodyText: Since August 28, 2024, a property owner may file a verified petition to remove people unlawfully occupying a residential property who were never tenants. The court issues an ex parte removal order immediately on good cause, with a hearing within 48 hours, and the sheriff enforces it. This fast track is available only if, among other things, the property had not been leased to anyone for three consecutive months, the occupants are not current or former tenants or immediate family, and there is no pending litigation with them. A person wrongly removed may recover $1,000 in statutory damages plus actual damages. For current or former tenants, use the ordinary eviction process.

title: Holdover Damages
bodyText: Missouri sets several double measures for tenants who stay too long. A tenant for life or years who willfully holds over after the term ends, and after you make a demand and give written notice requiring possession, owes double the yearly value of the property for the time you are kept out. A tenant who gives written notice of intent to leave on a date and does not leave owes double the rent for as long as the tenant stays. In an unlawful detainer judgment, the court awards double the damages found and double the monthly rent found until possession is restored. After a written lease ends, oral evidence that it was renewed or extended is not admissible in a possession suit. Each of these measures needs a willful holdover, your written demand, the tenant's own notice to quit or a court judgment; for other holdover days you recover your actual damages, or the daily holdover charge in your lease if you choose to include one.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Missouri does not require a reason to end a tenancy at the end of a fixed term or on proper notice for a periodic tenancy. Specific limits still apply: you may not end or refuse a tenancy for a discriminatory reason, because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or because a resident has an elevated blood lead level or because of lead enforcement, and a condominium conversion requires 120 days' notice with added rights for some elderly and disabled tenants. The expedited drug-eviction law expressly preserves a landlord's right to refuse to renew.

title: Domestic Violence, Sexual Assault and Stalking Protections
bodyText: You may not deny tenancy to, evict, or find a lease violation against an applicant or tenant because the person is, has been, or is in imminent danger of becoming a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, if the person otherwise qualifies. The protection does not apply if the person let the named abuser into the premises, or if you reasonably believe the named abuser threatens other occupants or the property. A tenant who vacates has a defense to rent for the period after leaving if a court finds the tenant was a victim or in imminent danger and the tenant notified you and gave any documentation you asked for (a signed statement from a victim-service provider or health professional, or a police, court or agency record). You may charge a reasonable termination fee when a tenant ends a lease early under this law. False information may be grounds to deny or evict. Missouri has no domestic-violence lock-change statute.
notes: MO: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.920(1)-(7) (2019 H.B. 243 & 544); definitions incorporated from Mo. Rev. Stat. § 455.010 (not read; rule 77 check: the pointer is current). title: Military Lease Termination
bodyText: A member of the U.S. Armed Forces on active duty, or a Missouri Army or Air National Guard member on full-time duty or serving as a civil service technician, may end a residential lease after receiving permanent change of station orders, temporary duty orders of more than 90 days at least 25 miles away, discharge or release from that duty, or orders to live in government quarters. The member gives written notice of termination effective on a stated date at least 15 days after service, and gives you a copy of the orders or a signed letter from the commanding officer before that date. The final payment is due by the termination date, and the member is entitled to the full return of the security deposit and any pet deposit if the lease and the deposit law were otherwise followed. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act gives additional rights.
notes: MO: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 41.944 (1991 S.B. 358, effective 6/12/1991). Federal SCRA (50 U.S.C. § 3955) not read (rule 21). title: Occupancy Limits
bodyText: Missouri presumes an occupancy limit of two persons per bedroom to be reasonable. Children born to the tenants during the lease do not count against that limit. title: Assignment and Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: A tenant for a term of two years or less, at will or by sufferance, may not assign or transfer the lease without the landlord's written consent. In a rent or possession case, if the tenant let another person come into sole possession without the landlord's permission, the court may award damages of up to twice the rent due, in addition to the rent. Assignments of leases must be in writing.

title: When the Tenant Causes Damage
bodyText: If a tenant causes damage, Missouri law gives you these points. The rule that a tenant owes no rent after a disaster destroys the residence does not apply if the tenant caused the disaster. A tenant who commits waste owes treble damages, and waste is a ground for 10 days' notice to vacate. But no action may be brought against a tenant in whose home a fire accidentally begins, and a repair promise in a lease does not require a tenant to rebuild after a fire the tenant did not cause through procurement, connivance or neglect unless the tenant specially agreed to rebuild. Whether a careless fire counts as 'accidental' under that rule is unsettled.

title: Missouri Fair Housing Law
bodyText: The Missouri Human Rights Act bars refusing to rent, setting different terms, misrepresenting availability, or advertising a preference because of race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, sex, disability or familial status. You must allow reasonable disability modifications at the tenant's expense (and may, where reasonable, require restoration of the interior) and make reasonable accommodations in rules and policies. Exempt, except from the advertising ban: a private owner renting a single-family house without a broker or advertising who owns no more than three such houses, and rooms or units in an owner-occupied building for four or fewer families. Missouri does not protect source of income or age in housing; federal law adds its own rules and exemptions.

title: Lead Hazards
bodyText: Besides the federal lead disclosure, Missouri requires an owner who receives written notification of a lead hazard to abate it or establish interim controls in a way the state health department allows, within the applicable time; an owner of a rental may instead take it off the rental market. title: Delivering Notices
bodyText: Missouri sets delivery rules for particular notices rather than one general method. Notices ending a tenancy must be in writing. title: County Habitability Rules (Boone County)

title: When the Tenant Causes the Damage - You Can Charge Them, But You Cannot Stop Them Leaving
bodyText: If a tenant, occupant or guest causes damage that makes the home uninhabitable, Nebraska splits the answer in a way that catches landlords out. WHAT YOU CAN RECOVER: the tenant is liable for the damage. §76-1429(2) says that notwithstanding the rest of the casualty rule 'the tenant is responsible for damage caused by his negligence', and the Nebraska Supreme Court has gone further - because a specific statute holds a tenant responsible for negligent fire damage, a lease provision doing the same cannot be struck down as void against public policy or unconscionable (SFI Ltd. Partnership 8 v. Carroll). Your Tenant Maintenance clause already carries that liability. If the tenancy ends you may also pursue possession, a claim for rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach (§76-1435), which can include rent lost while the property is repaired - subject to §76-1405's duty to mitigate, so re-letting effort is expected. WHAT YOU CANNOT DO: stop the tenant leaving, or switch off the rent reduction. Nebraska's landlord-noncompliance and essential-services remedies each carry an express tenant-fault exception - the tenant may not terminate or claim for a condition caused by their own or their household's deliberate or negligent act (§§76-1425, 76-1427). The casualty section has NO such exception. §76-1429 makes the tenant pay for the damage but still lets them vacate and end the lease on 14 days' written notice, or stay and pay proportionally reduced rent, even where they caused the fire. A lease term saying rent will not abate or that a tenant at fault cannot terminate would take away a right the Act gives them, which §76-1415(1)(a) voids - and if you used it knowing it was prohibited, §76-1415(2) adds the tenant's actual damages and attorney's fees. Charge for the damage; do not try to trap the tenant in the lease.

title: Converting to Condominiums: 60 Days, a For-Cause-Only Window, and a Right of First Refusal
bodyText: If you are converting a building to condominiums, Nebraska gives the sitting residential tenants and subtenants a set of rights that override your ordinary notice position (§76-886). NOTICE: you must give each residential tenant and any subtenant in possession notice of the conversion, with the public-offering statement if there is one, no later than 60 days before they are required to vacate, hand delivered to the unit or sent by prepaid US mail, and the notice must set out generally the rights this section gives them. FOR THOSE 60 DAYS YOU ARE IN A FOR-CAUSE-ONLY WINDOW: no tenant or subtenant may be required to vacate on less than 60 days' notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste, or conduct that disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment - and you may not alter the terms of the tenancy during that period. If you skip the notice, that failure is a defense to your action for possession. RIGHT OF FIRST REFUSAL: for 60 days after the notice you may offer to sell each unit occupied for residential use to the tenant who leases it; if you make the offer and they do not buy within those 60 days, you may not offer that unit to anyone else on better price or terms for the next 30 days. That does not apply to a unit that will be restricted to non-residential use, or where the converted unit's boundaries do not substantially match the residential unit. TWO MORE POINTS: a conversion notice that specifies a date by which the unit must be vacated counts as a notice to vacate, and nothing in the section lets you terminate a lease in breach of its own terms. A tenant can waive these protections, but only by a written instrument signed AFTER the date of the notice - so your lease cannot do it in advance.

title: In Nebraska Every Payment Under the Lease Is "Rent" - Which Cuts Both Ways
bodyText: Nebraska defines rent broadly by statute: 'Rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement' (§76-1410(13)). You do not need a lease sentence designating fees as additional rent - the definition already does it. The consequence runs both ways. In your favour, an unpaid fee that the lease requires the tenant to pay to you is on its face 'rent', which matters because §76-1431(2) lets you terminate when rent is unpaid and the tenant does not pay within seven calendar days of your written notice. Against you, anything the lease makes payable to you is swept into every other rule that turns on 'rent' - including the deposit cap, which is measured in rent, and the holdover and damages measures. Note that the standard Tenant Default clause says that failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying rent, will not by itself support termination or eviction. That is a choice to ask for less than Nebraska law allows, not a legal requirement.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix the Tenant's Breach and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Nebraska did not adopt the URLTA provision that lets a landlord remedy a tenant's breach and charge the cost as rent. If the tenant fails to do something the lease or §76-1421 requires, your statutory routes are the notice-and-cure termination at §76-1431(1), damages and injunctive relief under §76-1431(3) - with attorney's fees if the noncompliance was willful - and, for a tenant who breaches the duty to maintain, the ordinary measures. There is no statutory self-help-and-bill mechanism, so doing the work yourself and adding it to the next rent demand is a contract claim, not a statutory one, and treating it as rent risks a defective nonpayment notice.

Note the interaction with the new edu-fees-as-rent-ne row: because §76-1410(13) defines rent as all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement, a lease that purported to make self-cure costs payable as rent might arguably bring them inside 'rent' by contract — that is a drafting theory, NOT a statutory right, and it was not researched. BOUNDARY: URLTA plus the statute-wide 'landlord' sweep run on 2026-09-27 (153 results, all reviewed), neither of which surfaced a self-cure provision.

title: No Rule Against Blank Spaces, and No Duty to Give the Tenant a Copy
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute requiring a written lease to have every blank space completed, and no statute making an incomplete lease a material noncompliance. It also imposes no duty to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and no consequence for failing to - unlike states where that failure is a defense to enforcement. Fill in the blanks and hand over a copy anyway: both are ordinary evidence of what was agreed, and Nebraska's broad deceptive-practices standard is a live backstop even without a specific rule.
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-30 from nebraskalegislature.gov in the built-in browser. The whole URLTA (§§76-1401 to 76-1449, 54 sections, 78,605 chars, SHA-256 73533d60a357f1a7f89f4dd8da75b8f2) was loaded via display_html.php and pattern-screened in page; named sections were then read individually. Retro checks, SOP 1.10. RULE 27 and RULE 51 (SOP 1.10) — CONFIRMED ABSENT. Pattern run against the full URLTA text: 'blank' returned one hit and it is a case name (Blankenau v. Landess, annotated under §76-1437) — a useful illustration of why rule 19 requires reviewing hits rather than counting them. No lease-copy delivery duty appears anywhere in the act. CONSUMER-STATUTE LEG (rule 51, ID 3): the Idaho retro added the question whether a consumer protection act lists blank spaces filled after signing, or failing to give a copy at signing, as unlawful practices. Nebraska's two candidates were read: §87-302 (Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act, 'Deceptive trade practices; enumerated') lists fifteen-plus practices, all concerned with passing off, confusion, geographic origin, false representations about goods or services, advertising, pyramid schemes and referral sales — NEITHER a blank-space nor a copy-at-signing practice; and §59-1602 (Consumer Protection Act) is a general standard with no enumerated list at all ('Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce shall be unlawful'). NOT RESOLVED, and flagged as doctrine not read (rule 76): whether either act reaches a residential lease at all. Nebraska's CPA has a public-interest requirement in the case law, and no case was read, so the row claims only that no SPECIFIC rule exists and describes the general standard as a backstop rather than asserting it applies.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession in a Lease
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute writing a covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession into a residential lease. The one statutory provision on quiet enjoyment, §76-207, is about covenants in CONVEYANCES of real property - deed warranties broken by actual or constructive eviction by someone with paramount title - and does not reach a landlord and tenant. What Nebraska does give the tenant instead is specific and narrower: the habitability duties at §76-1419, the remedies for an unlawful ouster or a cut-off of services at §76-1430, and the bar on recovering possession except through the Act at §76-1436. A common-law implied covenant may still exist; that is case law, not statute.
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-30 from nebraskalegislature.gov in the built-in browser. The whole URLTA (§§76-1401 to 76-1449, 54 sections, 78,605 chars, SHA-256 73533d60a357f1a7f89f4dd8da75b8f2) was loaded via display_html.php and pattern-screened in page; named sections were then read individually. Retro checks, SOP 1.10. RULE 27 (SOP 1.10) — CONFIRMED ABSENT as a landlord-tenant covenant. Pattern 'quiet (enjoyment|possession)' against the full URLTA text: NO HIT. Statute-wide search 'quiet enjoyment' returned 7 results, the only relevant being §76-207 (Covenants; breach; constructive eviction; acts constituting), read section-open: it governs 'Covenants of quiet enjoyment and covenants of warranty in conveyances of real property' breached 'by reason of the hostile assertion of a paramount title holder', and lists three constructive-eviction situations all framed around a paramount title holder. That is a conveyancing provision, not a lease term, and must not be cited as a tenant's quiet-enjoyment right. EXPRESSLY LEFT OPEN and labelled as such in the row: whether Nebraska recognises a common-law implied covenant of quiet enjoyment in a lease. That is doctrine I have NOT read (rule 76), so the row says a covenant 'may still exist' rather than denying one. Note `no-disturbance` already obliges the tenant not to disturb other tenants, and §76-1419(1)(c) and §76-1421 carry the statutory analogues.

title: Nebraska Prescribes No Lease or Notice Forms
bodyText: Nebraska prescribes no form for a residential lease and no wording you must copy into one. Your lease-side notices generally need only contain what the relevant section requires - for example a termination notice specifying the acts constituting the breach and the termination date under §76-1431(1), or 30 days to the periodic rental date under §76-1437(2). ONE IMPORTANT EXCEPTION, outside the landlord-tenant act: if a tenant leaves property behind, the notice you must send under Nebraska's Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act has to contain one of two statements set out WORD FOR WORD in the statute, and which one you use depends on whether you believe the property is worth less than two thousand dollars (§69-2304). That is prescribed statutory text in the strict sense, and a notice missing it is not a compliant notice - see the Handling of Property Left Behind guidance. The other places Nebraska prescribes contents are court documents rather than anything you draft: the complaint for restitution (§76-1441) and the summons (§76-1442).
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-30 from nebraskalegislature.gov in the built-in browser. The whole URLTA (§§76-1401 to 76-1449, 54 sections, 78,605 chars, SHA-256 73533d60a357f1a7f89f4dd8da75b8f2) was loaded via display_html.php and pattern-screened in page; named sections were then read individually. Patterns run against the full URLTA text, including the forms-specific phrasings rule 19 requires ('following form', 'substantially as follows', 'as follows:'): NO HIT. The 'shall contain / shall state / shall be included / must state' battery returned exactly two hits and both are court process — §76-1441 (the complaint 'shall contain' the statutory authority, the facts with particularity, and a description) and §76-1442 (the summons 'shall state' the cause, the time and place of trial, the answer day and the default warning). NOTHING in the act prescribes text for a lease or a landlord's notice, which also answers rule 42 for Nebraska: no statute forces a sentence into a fee, deposit or other clause. Consistent with the 2026-09-27 typography screen, which found no bold, underline, capitalisation, type-size or separate-document rule conditioning any Nebraska residential lease term. BOUNDARY: statutes only; Nebraska Supreme Court rules and county court forms were NOT read, and eviction forms in particular may exist as court forms — flagged, since rule 39 treats court rules as governing eviction procedure. | NE: Read 2026-10-03 from nebraskalegislature.gov in the built-in browser. BASIS: section-open. *** ERROR CORRECTED 2026-10-03, in a row this chat created on 2026-09-30 and shipped VERIFIED. *** The row said Nebraska 'supplies no statutory form for a residential lease, a disclosure, or any notice a landlord gives a tenant' and that 'There is no prescribed wording you must copy'. That is WRONG as to notices. §69-2304 ('Notice; statement required'), read section-open today, provides that a notice given under §69-2303 'shall contain one of the following statements, as appropriate', and then sets out two statements verbatim — one for property going to public sale with the surplus to the State Treasurer, one for property believed worth less than two thousand dollars that may be kept, sold or destroyed. That is prescribed statutory text a landlord must copy. HOW THE ERROR HAPPENED, because the shape matters more than the fix: the row's own notes recorded the boundary honestly — 'Patterns run against the full URLTA text' for 'following form', 'substantially as follows' and 'as follows:' — but the landlord-facing sentence was written as an unbounded statewide claim. §69-2304 sits in CHAPTER 69, outside the URLTA, so a correctly-scoped search produced a correctly-scoped note and an over-broad claim. A bounded battery does not license an unbounded sentence, and the note stating the boundary did not stop the body from overreaching. Found by rule 79's re-read of abandoned-property-ne's cited sections, not by any forms search. The §76-1441 and §76-1442 observations are unchanged and still correct.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute giving a tenant the right to install a security camera or video doorbell, and none restricting one. So it is governed by your lease: the No Alterations clause already requires your written consent before the tenant attaches anything to the property, and the Use of Property & Common Areas clause covers fixing things to exterior surfaces. Two cautions that are not lease questions. A camera that records audio can raise wiretapping issues, and one that overlooks another tenant's unit can raise privacy ones; neither is answered by the landlord-tenant act. Treat a request from a tenant with a disability as a reasonable-accommodation question instead.
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-30 from nebraskalegislature.gov in the built-in browser. The whole URLTA (§§76-1401 to 76-1449, 54 sections, 78,605 chars, SHA-256 73533d60a357f1a7f89f4dd8da75b8f2) was loaded via display_html.php and pattern-screened in page; named sections were then read individually. Retro checks, SOP 1.10. RULE 27 (SOP 1.10) — CONFIRMED ABSENT. Patterns 'camera|surveillance|recording device' against the full URLTA text: NO HIT. Statute-wide searches: 'camera' returned 25 results, all criminal procedure and remote-computing provisions (§§29-1926 child-witness in camera testimony, 86-2,107, 29-1917) — note the term of art 'in camera' is the dominant false positive, which is why every hit was reviewed; 'surveillance' returned 36, the nearest being §§54-2949, 25-21,284 and 86-293, none landlord-tenant. No tenant installation right and no landlord restriction exists. The clauses the row points at (`no-alterations`, `common-area-use`) were read and do cover attachment to the property. NOT RESEARCHED and flagged as unread doctrine (rule 76): Nebraska's wiretapping and eavesdropping provisions, and any privacy tort — the row raises both as cautions without stating a rule.

title: Good-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: New Jersey is a good-cause state. In most residential rentals a landlord may remove a tenant, or refuse to renew a lease, only for one of the causes the Anti-Eviction Act lists, proven in court; the end of a lease term is not a cause. The Act does not cover owner-occupied buildings with no more than two rental units or transient and seasonal rentals. The full rules are in the Anti-Eviction Act entry.
notes: NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rule 41b. PRESENT. Pointer row: the rule itself is stated in edu-anti-eviction-act-nj (topic eviction-process), not moved. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 (grounds a-r; exclusions (1)-(3)), 2A:18-61.3 (no removal or non-renewal except for good cause). title: Eviction Court Rules: Landlord Duties
bodyText: New Jersey court rules add duties to an eviction case. A default judgment for possession needs the landlord's affidavit stating the facts that give good cause and that every charge claimed as rent, other than base rent, is allowed to be charged as rent by the lease and by law; a landlord's attorney must certify the same, and any required notice to quit must be attached with a statement that it was served and is true. A business entity other than a sole proprietor, or a partner in a general partnership, must appear through an attorney. A consent judgment for possession against an unrepresented tenant must be reviewed and signed by a judge that day. When the landlord believes service at the rental may fail, the landlord must also ask for service by mail at another address. A warrant of removal cannot issue until three business days after judgment (two days for a seasonal tenancy) and cannot be executed before the third business day after it is served; if the landlord does not apply for it within 30 days of judgment, or it is not executed within 30 days of issuance, the landlord must apply to the court with seven days' written notice to the tenant. A court may stay a warrant for up to seven days for an orderly move. A levy on belongings inside a home may be made only between 6:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m.
notes: NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rule 39. Rules Governing the Courts of the State of New Jersey, read whole for Part VI (6:1 to 6:7, 6:10, 6:12; 36 rules) from njcourts.gov, amendments effective on or before 2026-09-01: R. 6:6-3(b) (default judgment for possession affidavit and attorney certification), R. 6:10 with R. 1:21-1(c) (entity landlords), R. 6:6-4 (consent judgments), R. 6:2-3 (alternate-address service), R. 6:7-1(d) (warrant timing, 30-day lapse), R. 6:6-6(b) (orderly removal stay), R. 6:7-4(a) (levy hours). Court rules, not statutes (monitor separately, rule 21). Not located in Part VI or the statutes read: any post-writ animal duty (pattern animal|pet 0 hits in Part VI) or landlord immunity for writ execution. Post-writ property is edu-property-left-behind-nj; lockout ban is edu-self-help-eviction-ban-nj.

title: Eviction Records Kept From Public Access
bodyText: New Jersey court records of a landlord-tenant case are not public if the case ended without a judgment for possession, or if the judgment for possession was entered seven or more years ago. Eviction records for nonpayment during the COVID-19 emergency period are also shielded and may not be used in screening. No statute gives a landlord a right to object.
notes: NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rule 39. PRESENT by court rule: R. 1:38-3 (court records excluded from public access: records of landlord tenant cases in which no judgment for possession was ever entered, and cases in which a judgment for possession was entered seven years ago or longer), read from njcourts.gov, amendments effective on or before 2026-09-01. COVID-period records: N.J.S.A. 46:8-51 (edu-screening-rules-nj). General statutory sealing bills (S402, A2589, 2026-2027 session) are introduced only, not law (rule 18). Court rule, not statute (rule 21).

title: Electronic Notices
bodyText: New Jersey's electronic-transactions law applies only when both sides have agreed to do business electronically, and either side may later refuse further electronic dealings. It does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of someone's home, so those must go by the methods the eviction statutes require (personal delivery, leaving a copy at the home with a family member over 14, or certified mail, with regular mail if certified mail is not claimed). An electronic record the sender stops the tenant from printing or saving cannot be enforced against the tenant.
notes: NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rule 45. N.J.S.A. 12A:12-3(c)(1)-(2) (exclusions, including (2)(b) notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for a primary residence), 12A:12-5(b)-(c) (agreement required; right to refuse not waivable), 12A:12-8(a), (c), (d) (retention; unenforceable if printing or storing is inhibited; not variable by agreement); 2A:18-61.2 (service methods). No NJ clause relies on electronic delivery of an excluded notice (notices, electronic-signatures checked). Federal E-SIGN not read. title: Plain Language Rules for New Jersey Leases
bodyText: New Jersey's plain-language law applies to residential leases: a lease must be written in a simple, clear, understandable and easily readable way, judged as a whole. Courts and the Attorney General look at guidelines such as confusing cross-references, needlessly long sentences, double negatives and exceptions to exceptions, and illogical order, and whether sections are logically divided and captioned, a lease over 3,000 words has a table of contents or index, and conditions and exceptions get the same prominence as the main promise in at least 10-point type. Technical terms alone are not a violation, and wording a law or agency requires or approves is protected. A landlord who violates the law owes the tenant actual damages if the tenant was substantially confused, plus up to $50 and attorney's fees up to $2,500, but not if both sides performed, the landlord tried in good faith to comply, the contract follows an Attorney General opinion, or the tenant supplied the wording. The Attorney General will certify a form on request for a fee of up to $50.
notes: NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rule 51. PRESENT. N.J.S.A. 56:12-1 ("consumer contract" includes a written agreement in which an individual "Leases or licenses real or personal property" for personal, family or household purposes), 56:12-2, 56:12-3, 56:12-4 (class-action caps, host copy only), 56:12-5, 56:12-6, 56:12-8 (AG certification, host copy only), 56:12-10 (guidelines). No dollar exclusion found in the sections read. Builder backlog (flag, not fixed): section captions, a table of contents above 3,000 words, and a 10-point floor for conditions and exceptions. The separate Truth-in-Consumer Contract, Warranty and Notice Act does not apply to residential leases (56:12-15). Case law applying the Act to leases not read. title: Consumer Fraud Act and Leases
bodyText: New Jersey's Consumer Fraud Act makes it unlawful to use any unconscionable commercial practice, deception, fraud, misrepresentation, or knowing omission of a material fact in connection with the sale or advertisement of merchandise or real estate, and the Act defines a sale to include a rental. It is also unlawful to ask a consumer to sign a document evidencing a transaction without giving a full and accurate copy at the same time, so give each tenant a complete copy of the signed lease when they sign. A person who loses money or property because of an unlawful practice recovers three times the damages plus attorney's fees and costs. The Act lists no rule about blank spaces in a lease.
notes: NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rule 51. N.J.S.A. 56:8-1(c), (e) ("Sale" includes "rentals"), 56:8-2, 56:8-2.22 (copy at signing, stated for a "sale of merchandise"), 56:8-19 (treble damages, mandatory fees). Whether 56:8-2.22 reaches a lease of real property, and how far courts apply the Act to residential landlords, is case law, not read (labelled unread doctrine). Blank spaces: Folio search "blank spaces" 9 hits, none on residential leases. title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: If a New Jersey tenant, occupant or guest causes damage, the statutory protections tied to damage do not help the tenant: rent stops after a fire only if the damage happened without the tenant's fault, the lease ends on total destruction only if it happened without the tenant's fault, and a rent-into-court case fails if the condition was caused maliciously or by abnormal or unusual use by the petitioning tenant or family. Willful or grossly negligent damage is a cause for removal on three days' notice, with no notice to cease first. You may apply the security deposit to damage after the tenancy ends, never while the tenant stays, and you may sue for the cost of repair. Lost rent after the tenancy ends is recoverable as damages, subject to your duty to try to re-rent.
notes: NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rule 54t. Each provision checked separately for its own fault exception: casualty abatement N.J.S.A. 46:8-6 ("without the fault of the lessee"), total destruction 46:8-7 (same), rent into court 2A:42-91(b) (narrower: "maliciously or by abnormal or unusual use"; mere negligence is not a defense), removal ground 2A:18-61.1(c) with 2A:18-61.2(a) notice. Deposit: 46:8-21.1 (no deduction in possession; edu-security-deposit-rules-nj). Essential-services withholding and constructive eviction rest on case law (Marini v. Ireland), not read; damages and mitigation (Sommer v. Kridel) also case law, not read. Optional clause offered: tenant-caused-damage-nj. title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, and Tenant's tenancy ends because of the damage, then Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term (for a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, up to the earliest date Tenant could have ended the tenancy by notice), less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage, and it does not limit any proceeding New Jersey law allows Tenant to bring to deposit Rent with a court.
notes: NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rule 54t. OPTIONAL clause (not a default), state version of tenant-caused-damage-tn (read; TN row not tagged), following tenant-caused-damage-sc: only TN part (2) is used. Part (1) (no abatement while the lease continues) is left out because N.J.S.A. 46:8-6 already denies abatement where the tenant is at fault, and a broad no-abatement promise could be read to waive the rent-into-court remedy, whose tenant-fault defense covers only malicious or abnormal use (2A:42-91(b)); waiver of that remedy is barred (edu-truth-in-renting-lease-provisions-nj). Lawful stipulation: 46:8-6 and 46:8-7 yield to the lease, and the clause only restates damages for the tenant's own fault, with mitigation (Sommer v. Kridel, case law, not read). Periodic-tenancy measure (rule 37). Gap it fills: lost rent after the tenancy ends, which otherwise rests on case law. Rule 47: no clearly established right is limited. title: Fees Treated as Rent
bodyText: In New Jersey, late fees, attorney's fees and other charges count as rent in an eviction for nonpayment only if the lease expressly says so, and never for Section 8 or public-housing tenants. This library's lease does not call any fee rent, so an unpaid fee cannot support an eviction for nonpayment; collect it another way. In a default judgment for possession, the landlord must swear, and a landlord's attorney must certify, that every charge claimed as rent other than base rent may be charged as rent under the lease and the law.
notes: NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rule 27. PRESENT. Court rule R. 6:6-3(b) read (njcourts.gov, through 2026-09-01). Case law: Community Realty Mgmt. v. Harris, 155 N.J. 212 (1998); Hodges v. Sasil Corp., 189 N.J. 210 (2007), from the 2026-09-26 research pass, not read section-open. Library decision: Taylor, 2026-09-26 (NJ log §11), no fee labeled rent; default-by-tenant-nj and application-of-payments (rent first) carry it.

title: Algorithmic Rent-Setting Ban
bodyText: From July 1, 2027, New Jersey's FAIR Act makes it a violation of the state antitrust law for a rental property owner, or its agent, to pay for or use the services of a "coordinator": software or a device that sets or recommends rents, material lease terms or occupancy levels using competitively sensitive, nonpublic information from two or more owners, or that recommends the same pricing to competing owners. Tacit or express price coordination between owners is also barred. Publicly available free rent estimates, research that is not used to set rents, equal-access brokerage listing databases and government affordability controls are excluded, as are spreadsheets without artificial intelligence that need human analysis.
notes: NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rule 27. PRESENT (future effective). Text read from S451, Second Reprint (as amended by the Senate 2026-06-18), pub.njleg.gov/bills/2026/S0500/451_R2.HTM, supplementing N.J.S.A. 56:9-1 et seq.: s.3 definitions, s.4 unlawful acts, s.6(b) municipal preemption, s.9 effective "the first day of the twelfth month next following the date of enactment". title: Forms and Wording New Jersey Supplies
bodyText: New Jersey prescribes the exact wording or form of several lease items: the Department of Community Affairs Flood Risk Notice, the renter's flood-insurance sentence every lease must contain, the window-guard notice for buildings of three or more units, the Truth in Renting statement, the condominium or cooperative conversion statement, the bold tenant attorney-fee sentence, and the foreclosure notice to tenants. The library's entries for each carry the required text. Eviction complaints must use the court's form.

PRESENT; pointer row. flood-risk-disclosure-nj (N.J.S.A. 46:8-50, DCA model form), flood-insurance-lease-notice-nj (46:8-50(c)), window-guard-notice-nj (N.J.A.C. 5:10-27.1(c), App. 27A), truth-in-renting-statement-nj (46:8-45, -46), conversion-statement-nj (2A:18-61.9), default-by-tenant-nj (2A:18-61.67), edu-foreclosure-tenant-rights-nj (2A:50-70); R. 6:3-4(c) (Appendix XI-X complaint form, read from njcourts.gov).

title: Cannabis in Rentals
bodyText: Adult cannabis use is legal in New Jersey, but a landlord may still limit it. The owner of a building with three or more units may prohibit or regulate smoking, vaping or aerosolizing cannabis there; the owner of other property may prohibit or regulate eating or otherwise consuming cannabis on the property, but that power is not given for multi-unit buildings. A landlord may not refuse to rent to someone, or penalize a tenant, because cannabis metabolites are found in the person's body from lawful use, unless that would break a federal contract or cost federal funding. The cannabis law does not change landlord-tenant law otherwise.
notes: NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rule 35c. Constitution Art. IV, s. VII, para. 13 (lawful and "subject to regulation"); N.J.S.A. 2C:35-10a(c) (L.2021, c.16, s.46; amended 2021, c.25, s.11), 24:6I-51(b)(1), 24:6I-55(b). Not located: whether a 1-2 family landlord may ban smoking cannabis is not addressed expressly; the library treats it as permitted (see smoking-policy NJ note). Medical cannabis (24:6I-1 et seq.) not read. title: Use of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit) prior to occupancy. Landlord may use the Security Deposit only to: (1) reimburse Landlord for actual damages to the property or any ancillary facility that are not the result of ordinary wear and tear; (2) pay Rent in arrears under this Lease, and Rent due because Tenant ends this Lease before the end of the Term; (3) reimburse Landlord for utility or sewer charges that are Tenant's obligation under this Lease, that Landlord paid and that Tenant did not pay; and (4) pay the Rent for the last payment period, but only if Landlord and Tenant have agreed in writing that the Security Deposit will serve as the last payment of Rent due. Unless Landlord has so agreed in writing, Tenant may not apply the Security Deposit to Rent. Landlord will not apply the Security Deposit to ordinary wear and tear or to any damage or defective condition that existed before the tenancy. The Security Deposit does not limit Landlord's right to recover other damages to which Landlord is entitled.

Code § 32-31-3-13). 'Unless otherwise agreed, a tenant is not entitled to apply a security deposit to rent' (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-12(a)); rule 50: the default here is no application, and item (4) lets the landlord agree in writing. The base row's cleaning sentence is dropped: whether cleaning cost is 'actual damages' under Ind. Code § 32-31-3-13(1) is case law, not read. 'Security deposit' includes prepaid rent beyond the first full rental period, a sum above the average rent, and any other amount returnable on the unit's return in the required condition (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-9(b)), so a refundable pet deposit is part of it (pet-policy-in). No cap and no interest or holding rule (whole read of Ind. Code ch. 32-31-3; IN batteries 40, 76); local deposit regulation is preempted (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-20(c)(2)). A landlord may accept but not require a lien on the tenant's motor vehicle as security (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-13.5); not offered. Waiver of the chapter is void (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-17). title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: Not more than 45 days after Tenant's occupancy of the property ends, Landlord will return the Security Deposit to Tenant, less any amounts applied as this Lease and Indiana law allow, with a written itemized list of the amounts applied. For each item of damage claimed, the list will state the estimated cost of repair. Landlord will mail the list, with a check or money order for the balance, to the mailing address Tenant gives Landlord in writing. Tenant will give Landlord that mailing address in writing when Tenant moves out.
notes: IN: Ind. Code § 32-31-3-12(a): on termination the landlord returns the deposit minus accrued rent, damages from the tenant's noncompliance and unpaid utility or sewer charges, all itemized in a written notice delivered not more than 45 days after termination of the rental agreement and delivery of possession; the landlord is not liable under the chapter until the tenant supplies a mailing address in writing. Ind. Code § 32-31-3-14: not more than 45 days after the termination of occupancy, the landlord mails an itemized list of damages with the estimated cost of repair for each damaged item, with a check or money order for the balance. Failure to give the list is agreement that no damages are due, and the full deposit must be remitted at once (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-15); the landlord is liable for the amount withheld plus reasonable attorney's fees and costs (Ind. Code §§ 32-31-3-12(b), 32-31-3-16). The two sections count the 45 days from different events (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-14: termination of occupancy; Ind. Code § 32-31-3-12(a): termination of the rental agreement and delivery of possession); the clause runs from the end of occupancy, which is never later than either, so a landlord who follows it meets both (IN log §10). A protected individual who ends the lease under Ind. Code § 32-31-9-12 is entitled to deposits as if the tenancy expired (Ind. Code § 32-31-9-12(e)), but where other tenants remain the landlord need not account until 45 days after all tenancies end (Ind. Code § 32-31-9-13); the statute does not reconcile the two (IN log §10). The owner at termination is bound (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-12(d)); on a sale see edu-deposit-on-sale-in. The statute does not let the lease fix another period (rule 50). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds, a closed or nonexistent account, a stop-payment order or any other reason, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount; for a check, draft, order or similar instrument that is dishonored or returned unpaid, Indiana law limits the charge to $20 plus the amount Landlord's bank actually charges for the returned item], and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are returned or fail, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check or money order.
notes: IN: Overrides returned-payments, whose 'not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' states only a ceiling (rule 53). Ind. Code § 26-1-3.1-502.5(a): a person to whom a check, draft, order or like instrument is tendered may, if it is dishonored or returned unpaid for any reason, charge the maker or drawer 'an amount not to exceed twenty dollars ($20) plus an amount equal to the actual charge by the depository institution for each returned or dishonored instrument'; the charge is not interest or a finance charge. Whether a failed electronic (ACH) payment is a 'like instrument' is not settled by the text. Separate statutory remedies are in Ind. Code ch. 26-2-7: 18% interest and collection costs (Ind. Code § 26-2-7-5), and, after certified-mail notice and 30 days, three times the face amount if $250 or less or the face amount plus $500 (Ind. Code § 26-2-7-6(b)) (edu-dishonored-check-remedies-in). The bracket states the landlord's figure (rule 55); the builder should cap a check fee at $20 plus the bank's actual charge (IN log §10). Real-lease lead: the CRM lease's $25 fee cites Ind. Code § 24-4.5-7-202, a small-loan section repealed and revised into Ind. Code art. 37-3 in 2026 (IN battery 92; IN log §15). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord: [list approved pets, or state that no pets are permitted]. Tenant will pay a pet deposit of {{pet_deposit}}, if applicable. Under Indiana law a refundable pet deposit is part of the Security Deposit, so Landlord will hold, use and return it under this Lease's Security Deposit terms. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, if applicable. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet, and will reimburse Landlord for claims caused by Tenant's pet, except to the extent a claim arises from the negligence of Landlord or Landlord's agents or employees. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and Tenant will then remove the pet within [number] days after Landlord's written notice; failure to do so is a default under this Lease. Landlord may enter the property in connection with a pet only as this Lease's Access & Entry terms permit, or without notice in an emergency, and will not seize, remove or dispose of a pet without a court order. This Section does not limit animal control or law enforcement acting under their own authority. This Section does not apply to a service animal or assistance animal.
notes: IN: Overrides pet-policy, whose term letting the landlord 'enter the property and remove a pet, without liability to Tenant to the extent applicable law permits' conflicts with Ind. Code § 32-31-5-5(a): except as provided in Ind. Code § 16-41-27-29 (mobile home community liens), Ind. Code ch. 32-31-3 or Ind. Code ch. 32-31-4, a landlord may not take possession of, remove, deny access to or dispose of a tenant's personal property to enforce an obligation under the rental agreement; a waiver is void (Ind. Code § 32-31-5-1(c)). The self-limiting phrase would hide that conflict (rule 53). Pet deposit: 'security deposit' includes 'any other amount of money or property returnable to the tenant on condition of return of the rental unit' in the required condition (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-9(b)(3)), so a refundable pet deposit follows the deposit rules (closed uses, 45-day itemized return; security-deposit-use-in, security-deposit-return-in); a nonrefundable pet fee or pet rent is not returnable and so not a deposit (edu-pet-deposit-in). No fee may be required to keep an emotional support animal (Ind. Code § 22-9-7-13). Model: pet-policy-mo with the Indiana deposit rule. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Handling of Property Left Behind
bodyText: When this Lease ends or Tenant gives up possession, Tenant will remove all of Tenant's personal property from the property. (1) If Tenant has vacated the property and a reasonable person would conclude that Tenant has surrendered possession of personal property left there, that property is considered abandoned, and Landlord may remove, store or dispose of it and is not liable for its loss or damage. [Optional: Before disposing of abandoned property that appears to have value, Landlord will mail Tenant a notice at Tenant's forwarding address (or, if none, the property address) and hold the property for [number] days.] (2) If a court awards Landlord possession of the property, Landlord may ask the court for an order allowing removal of Tenant's personal property; property Tenant does not remove by the date in the order may be removed and delivered to a warehouse or a storage facility approved by the court, after the order and the warehouse's or facility's name and location are personally served on Tenant. Medically necessary items, items Tenant uses for a trade or business, and a week's supply of seasonal clothing, blankets and items needed for the care and schooling of a minor child will be released to Tenant without payment; other property may be sold if not claimed within 45 days after Tenant receives notice. (3) While Tenant remains in possession, Landlord will not take, remove, deny Tenant access to or dispose of Tenant's personal property to enforce Tenant's obligations, change or add locks to exclude Tenant, or interrupt essential utilities to force Tenant out, except as this Section or a court order permits. This Section does not apply to motor vehicles, which are handled under Indiana vehicle law.
notes: IN: Part (1) follows Ind. Code § 32-31-4-2(a)-(b): a landlord has no liability for loss or damage to a tenant's personal property if it has been abandoned, and property is abandoned 'if a reasonable person would conclude that the tenant has vacated the premises and has surrendered possession of the personal property'; a rental agreement 'may not define abandonment differently' (Ind. Code § 32-31-4-2(c)), so the clause uses the statutory test word for word and adds only an optional courtesy notice. A dwelling unit is abandoned for the lockout rule if the tenants failed to pay or offer rent and a reasonable person would conclude they surrendered possession (Ind. Code § 32-31-5-6(b)). Whether the statute authorizes disposal, as distinct from relieving liability, is not stated; case law not read. Part (2): Ind. Code §§ 32-31-4-2(d)-(e), 32-31-4-3 (personal service of the removal order and the warehouse identity; exempt property released free; waiver void), 32-31-4-1 (exempt property), 32-31-4-4 (warehouse lien), 32-31-4-5 (sale after 45 days, cut from 90 by P.L. 154-2025, effective July 1, 2025; IN log §1.2). Part (3): Ind. Code §§ 32-31-5-5, 32-31-5-6(c). A tenant's representative on death or incapacity has the tenant's Ind. Code ch. 32-31-4 rights (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-23(h)). Vehicles: Ind. Code §§ 9-22-1-15, 9-22-1-16 (edu-towing-in). Real-lease lead: the CRM lease defines abandonment by its own terms and lets the landlord remove property 'left on the street'; Ind. Code § 32-31-4-2(c) bars the first (IN log §15). See edu-post-eviction-property-in. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Property Manager and Agent for Notices
bodyText: Management and notices. The person residing in Indiana who is authorized to manage the property is: [name and address]. The person residing in Indiana who is reasonably accessible to Tenant and is authorized to act as agent for the owner for service of process and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands is: [name and address]. notes: IN: Ind. The duty binds successor landlords, owners and managers (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-18(b)); a person who fails to disclose becomes the landlord's agent for service and notices and for performing the landlord's obligations (Ind. title: Smoke Detectors
bodyText: [Tenant to complete when Landlord delivers the property:] Tenant acknowledges that the property is equipped with a functional smoke detector. Tenant's initials: ______ Date: ______. During the tenancy, Tenant will ensure that each smoke detector installed in the property remains functional and is not disabled, will test each smoke detector at least once every six months, and will replace the batteries in any battery-operated smoke detector as necessary. Tenant will give Landlord written notice if a smoke detector needs to be repaired or replaced, including a hard-wired smoke detector Tenant believes is not functional (for a hard-wired detector Tenant may send the notice by certified mail, return receipt requested), and Landlord will repair or replace it within seven days after receiving the notice. Tenant will not tamper with or remove a smoke detector except when necessary for maintenance.
notes: IN: Ind. Code § 32-31-5-7(a): 'At the time a landlord delivers a rental unit to a tenant, the landlord shall require the tenant to acknowledge in writing that the rental unit is equipped with a functional smoke detector.' Ind. Code § 32-31-5-7(b): the smoke-detector requirements of Ind. Code § 22-11-18-3.5 cannot be waived in a rental agreement or separate writing. Tenant duties: keep each detector functional and not disabled, replace batteries, and give notice under Ind. Code § 22-11-18-3.5(e)(2) for a hard-wired unit believed not functional (Ind. Code § 32-31-7-5(6)); detectors must be tested by the occupant at least every six months (Ind. Code § 22-11-18-3.5(d)(3)); no tampering or removal except for maintenance (Ind. Code § 22-11-18-3.5(f)). Owner duties: install, and repair or replace within seven working days after written notice (Ind. Code § 22-11-18-3.5(e)). A landlord commits a Class B infraction (Class A for a repeat) for a violation at delivery or for failing to fix a hard-wired detector within seven days after certified-mail notice (Ind. Code § 22-11-18-5.5); others commit a Class D infraction (Ind. Code § 22-11-18-5(c)). The clause promises repair within seven days, the shorter of the seven working days in Ind. Code § 22-11-18-3.5(e)(2) and the seven days that trigger the infraction in Ind. Code § 22-11-18-5.5(2). Ind. Code § 22-11-18-2(b) exempts a totally sprinkled building from Ind. Code ch. 22-11-18, but Ind. Code § 32-31-5-7(a) has no such exception, so the acknowledgment stays REQUIRED. The acknowledgment is owed at delivery, so the bracket tells the builder to collect it then (IN log §4). Restating the tenant's statutory duties serves the landlord; the acknowledgment is the required text (rule 55). Real-lease lead: the CRM lease has the acknowledgment (IN log §15). See edu-alarm-duties-in. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText: If this Lease continues as a month-to-month tenancy, either Landlord or Tenant may end it by giving the other written notice at least one month before the end of a monthly rental period, and the tenancy will end at the end of that rental period. Rent remains payable through the date the tenancy ends. This Section does not limit either party's right to end this Lease earlier where this Lease or Indiana law allows it.
notes: IN: Ind. Code § 32-31-1-4: for a tenancy of not more than three months that extends from one period to another by express or implied agreement, 'Notice to the tenant equal to the interval between the periods is sufficient' to end it; a general tenancy by the landlord's express or constructive consent is month to month (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-2). The statute speaks only of notice to the tenant and sets no form; the clause makes the notice written and mutual and ends it at a period boundary, which is at least the statutory interval. Other tenancy types (rule 37): a tenancy at will ends on one month's written notice delivered to the tenant and cannot arise without an express contract (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-1); a week-to-week tenancy ends on a week's notice under Ind. Code § 32-31-1-4; a year-to-year tenancy ends on notice not less than three months before the end of the year (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-3; form in Ind. Code § 32-31-1-5); a fixed term ends without notice (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-8(1)-(2)). Service: Ind. Code § 32-31-1-9. See edu-notice-to-quit-in. Holdover with accepted rent becomes month to month under holdover-ca. Rule 15: written section-open.
