title: Holdover Charge
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession after the end of the Term, and Landlord has not agreed in writing to a continued tenancy or accepted Rent for one under the Holdover section of this Lease, then, in place of the actual damages and reasonable rental value described in that section, Tenant will pay Landlord a holdover charge of {{holdover_daily_rate}} for each day Tenant remains in possession. Landlord and Tenant agree that Landlord's loss from a holdover, including delay in making the property available to a new tenant, is difficult to estimate accurately in advance, that this charge is a reasonable estimate of that loss, and that it is not a penalty. Landlord's acceptance of a holdover charge is not acceptance of Rent for a continued tenancy. This Section does not limit Landlord's right to recover possession, unpaid Rent and other amounts due for the period before the Term ended, or damages for harm to the property.
notes: IN: Optional clause (rule 54; standing GA decision: offer an opt-in holdover rate where no statutory measure exists). title: Fire or Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire, storm or other casualty not caused by Tenant, members of Tenant's household or Tenant's guests, and the damage makes the property unfit to live in or substantially impairs Tenant's use of it, either Landlord or Tenant may end this Lease by written notice to the other, effective on the date Tenant moves out. Rent will be prorated to that date, any prepaid Rent refunded, and the Security Deposit returned as this Lease and Indiana law provide. If the casualty makes only part of the property unusable and Tenant stays in possession, Rent will be reduced in proportion to the part of the property Tenant cannot use until Landlord completes repairs. This Section does not limit any other right Tenant has under Indiana law.
notes: IN: Optional clause (rule 54; standing GA decision: offer landlord casualty termination where no statute controls it). No Indiana statute addresses fire or casualty damage to leased residential premises, rent abatement or termination (IN battery 121: 41 sections, none a residential casualty rule; known-positive passed; whole read of Ind. Code art. 32-31). The landlord's duties to deliver and keep the premises habitable and to maintain systems cannot be waived (Ind. Code §§ 32-31-8-4, 32-31-8-5), and the clause does not waive them. title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage.
notes: IN: Optional clause (rule 54, tenant-caused damage). Model: tenant-caused-damage-tn. Indiana law: a tenant must not deface, damage, destroy, impair or remove any part of the rental premises (Ind. Code § 32-31-7-5(4)); the landlord may sue for actual damages and attorney's fees after notice and a reasonable time to remedy, or without notice once occupancy has ended, and must document repairs it made (Ind. Code § 32-31-7-7); waste supports an emergency possessory order (Ind. Code §§ 32-31-6-3(a)(2), 32-31-6-7). No casualty, abatement or rent-withholding statute exists to carve around (IN batteries 121, 122), so no Indiana statutory right is waived by the no-abatement term; the landlord's non-waivable repair duties (Ind. Code § 32-31-8-5) still apply, and the clause does not excuse them. Whether lost-rent damages are recoverable beyond the statute is case law, not read (edu-tenant-caused-damage-in). title: No Criminal Activity
bodyText: Tenant, members of Tenant's household and Tenant's guests will not commit a crime on or near the property that affects the health or safety of another tenant, Landlord or Landlord's agents, and will not allow the illegal possession, manufacture, sale or distribution of a controlled substance on the property. A breach of this Section is a material breach of this Lease, for which Landlord may end this Lease and seek possession, including by a petition for an emergency possessory order where Indiana law allows, without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure. This Section controls over any other provision of this Lease that would require notice and an opportunity to cure. This Section does not apply to criminal activity of which Tenant or a member of Tenant's household is the victim.
notes: IN: Optional clause (rule 54; crime-free / criminal-activity family, model criminal-activity-mo). Since July 1, 2025, a landlord may petition for an emergency possessory order if a tenant or the tenant's guest 'has committed a crime that affects the health and safety of another tenant, the landlord, or an agent of the landlord', and on finding immediate and serious injury, loss or damage the court orders possession returned within 7 days of the hearing (Ind. Code §§ 32-31-6-3(a)(3)(A), 32-31-6-7.1, P.L. 157-2025, effective date read in the act; IN log §1.2). The clause's first sentence uses that wording. A tenant who creates a drug nuisance may be ordered to vacate within 72 hours (Ind. Code § 32-30-8-11; edu-drug-nuisance-in). Carve-out: a landlord may not terminate, refuse to renew or retaliate solely because a tenant or household member is a protected individual (victim with a protective or no-contact order) (Ind. Code § 32-31-9-8), and the emergency-order chapter preserves the rights of a crime victim under Ind. Code ch. 32-31-9 (Ind. Code § 32-31-6-3(b)). Whether Indiana courts enforce a no-cure termination for a lease-term breach outside the statutory procedures is case law, not read. Not a default. No crime-free statute (IN battery 38: 0 hits). title: Tenant's Representative on Death or Incapacity
bodyText: If Tenant is the sole occupant of the property and dies, or Landlord believes that Tenant is incapacitated and absent from the property, Landlord will notify Tenant's representative, give the representative access to the property at a reasonable time to remove Tenant's personal property, may require the representative to prepare and sign an inventory of the property removed, and will pay the representative the Security Deposit and unearned Rent to which Tenant would otherwise be entitled. Tenant designates the following person as Tenant's representative: [name, address and telephone number]. The representative accepts the appointment by giving Landlord written notice. A person Tenant later designates in a separate written document delivered to Landlord takes priority over this designation. Tenant will tell Landlord in writing if this information changes.
notes: IN: Optional clause (rule 54). Ind. Code § 32-31-1-23 (P.L. 184-2021): if the landlord knows of the death of a tenant who was the sole occupant under a lease, or believes a sole-occupant tenant is incapacitated and absent, the landlord shall notify a tenant's representative, give access at a reasonable time to remove personal property, may require a signed inventory, and shall pay the security deposit and unearned rent due under Ind. Code § 32-31-3-12 ((a), (b)). Representatives in decreasing priority: (1) a person designated by the tenant in a written document delivered to the landlord; (2) 'A person designated, in writing, by the tenant in a written lease between the tenant and the landlord'; then an attorney in fact, guardian, heir, or a probate-court appointee ((c)); the representative accepts by written notice to the landlord ((d)). A complying landlord is not liable to the tenant, the estate or other claimants; a willful violation makes it liable for actual damages ((f), (g)). The representative also has the tenant's Ind. Code ch. 32-31-4 rights ((h)). A named representative is what lets the landlord comply quickly and earn the immunity, so the clause serves the landlord; it states that a separate later designation outranks it, matching (c)(1)-(2). The statute does not end the lease on death; whether it ends is case law, not read (edu-tenant-death-in). Same topic as emergency-contact-va and deceased-tenant-contact-tx. title: Mid-Term Rent Increase
bodyText: During the Term, Landlord may increase Monthly Rent to the rent charged for comparable market rentals by giving Tenant at least 30 days' written notice stating the new Monthly Rent and the date it takes effect. Tenant may instead end this Lease, effective the day before the increase takes effect, by giving Landlord written notice before that date, and will owe Rent only through that date.
notes: IN: Optional clause (rule 54). Taylor decided to offer it, with this text, no frequency limit and no cap (IN log §6.2). Ind. Code § 32-31-8.5-5(b)(2): the retaliation ban does not prohibit 'Increasing a tenant's rent to that which is charged for comparable market rentals, regardless of whether the increase is effective: (A) at the conclusion of the term of the rental agreement; or (B) if provided for in the rental agreement, during the term of the rental agreement.' The clause is the 'provided for in the rental agreement' term, worded to the statute's market measure: an increase above comparable market rent loses the safe harbour if the tenant has engaged in a protected activity (Ind. bodyText: Indiana limits local rental programs. A penalty for a code violation requires notice and a stated reasonable time to cure first. A political subdivision whose rental registration or inspection program was created before July 1, 1984 is exempt from the permit, inspection and registration-fee limits. title: Rent Increases
bodyText: Indiana has no statute aimed specifically at rent increases. In a fixed-term lease the rent is set for the term unless the lease provides for a change (see the optional Mid-Term Rent Increase clause). A change to a rental agreement needs at least 30 days' written notice unless the written lease sets a different procedure. In a month-to-month tenancy, a landlord who wants more rent can also end the tenancy on notice equal to the rental period and offer a new one. Raising rent in response to a tenant's protected activity is retaliation, except an increase to comparable market rent at the end of the term, or during it if the lease provides for that.

title: Mid-Term Rent Increases
bodyText: An Indiana fixed-term lease can allow rent increases during the term, but only if the lease says so. Without the optional Mid-Term Rent Increase clause, the rent stays fixed until the term ends. If you include it: (1) Retaliation: you may not raise rent because a tenant did something the statute protects, such as complaining to a code-enforcement agency, complaining to you in writing about repairs, a lockout or entry, or joining a tenant organization; but raising rent to what comparable market rentals charge is not retaliation, and an increase during the term is covered only when the lease provides for it. An increase above comparable market rent loses that protection, which is why the clause ties the new rent to market rent instead of a number. (2) Notice: Indiana requires at least 30 days' written notice before changing a rental agreement, unless the written agreement sets something different; the clause uses 30 days. (3) Tenant's choice: the tenant may end the lease instead of paying the increase. That exit keeps the clause from locking the tenant into the term at a price you set alone. (4) Leasing impact: tenants usually expect a fixed rent for a fixed term, so a mid-term increase clause may affect how readily applicants sign.
notes: IN: Linked to midterm-rent-increase-in by topic key, at Taylor's request (IN log §6.2). Ind. Code §§ 32-31-8.5-2, 32-31-8.5-4, 32-31-8.5-5(b)(2); Ind. Code § 32-31-5-4. Indiana case law on clauses that let one side change the rent was not read; neither was case law applying the consumer-protection unconscionability standard (Ind. Code § 24-5-0.5-10(b)) to leases. Point (4) is information, not a legal rule. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Retaliation
bodyText: Indiana bars a landlord from retaliating because a tenant complained to a code-enforcement agency about a violation materially affecting health or safety, complained to the landlord in writing about a lockout, utility shutoff or improper entry or about the landlord's repair duties, sued under the emergency-possession or landlord-duty laws, organized or joined a tenant organization, or testified against the landlord. Retaliation means raising rent, cutting or interfering with services, or bringing or threatening a possession, eviction or early-termination action. You may still decline to renew at the end of the term, raise rent to comparable market rent at the end of the term (or during it if the lease provides for it), cut services for all tenants equally, and bring a possession action where the problem was caused by the tenant or the tenant's household or guests, rent is unpaid after the cure time, code compliance requires work that displaces the tenant, the tenant's breach materially affects health or safety, the tenant holds over after a fixed term, the action was begun in good faith before the protected activity, or you in good faith want the unit back at the end of the term to live in, to renovate in a way that displaces the household, or to take off the rental market for at least six months. The rule cannot be waived.

title: Indiana Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: An Indiana security deposit includes prepaid rent beyond the first full rental period and any other amount returnable when the unit is returned in the required condition. You may use it only for actual damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, rent owed (including rent due because the tenant ended the lease early), unpaid utility or sewer charges the tenant owed and you paid, and the last period's rent if agreed in writing. Within 45 days after the tenant's occupancy ends you must mail an itemized list of damages, with the estimated repair cost of each item, and a check or money order for the balance; you are not liable under the deposit law until the tenant gives you a mailing address in writing. If you do not send the list, you are treated as agreeing that no damages are due and must return the whole deposit at once, and the tenant can recover the amount withheld plus attorney's fees and court costs. These rules cannot be waived. Deposit cases may be filed in small claims.

title: Smoke Detectors
bodyText: Every Indiana dwelling must have at least one functional smoke detector outside each sleeping area and on each additional story, including basements, installed as the statute describes; a totally sprinkled building that met building code standards when built is exempt from the smoke detector chapter. The owner, or its manager or rental agent, must install the required detectors and repair or replace one within seven working days after written notice. When you deliver the unit you must get the tenant's written acknowledgment that it has a functional smoke detector, and the occupant must test detectors at least every six months. A landlord who violates the rule at delivery, or does not fix a hard-wired detector within seven days after certified-mail notice, commits a Class B infraction (Class A for a repeat). These requirements cannot be waived, and local codes may be stricter. Indiana has no statute requiring carbon monoxide alarms in rentals.

title: Entering the Unit
bodyText: In Indiana you must give the tenant reasonable written or oral notice before entering, may enter only at reasonable times, and may not abuse the right of entry or use it to harass. You may enter without notice in an emergency that threatens the occupants' safety or your property, and without consent under a court order or after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit. A tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply services, or show the unit to buyers, lenders, tenants, workers or contractors. These rules cannot be waived.

title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: Except under a court order, an Indiana landlord may not deny or interfere with a tenant's access to or possession of the unit, including by changing locks or adding a device to exclude the tenant, removing doors, windows, fixtures or appliances, or interrupting electricity, gas, water or other essential services (except for an emergency, good-faith repairs or necessary construction). You also may not take, remove, withhold or dispose of a tenant's belongings to enforce the lease. A tenant may get an emergency possessory order returning possession, heard within three business days. The lockout and utility rules do not apply to a unit the tenants have abandoned (rent unpaid and circumstances showing a reasonable person they surrendered possession); belongings left behind are handled under the abandoned-property rules.

title: Emotional Support Animals
bodyText: Under Indiana's emotional support animal law, if a person's disability is not readily apparent you may require written verification from a health service provider who treats the person (not one who only sells verification letters) that the person has a disability, has a disability-related need for the animal, and is helped by it; a person who moves from another state may provide documentation from a physician, psychiatrist, social worker or other mental health professional licensed there with whom the person has an ongoing treatment relationship. You may evaluate the documents, but may not charge any fee to keep an emotional support animal. You may require the tenant to follow the lease and rules like other residents, pay for damage the animal causes as other pet owners would, and sign an addendum setting out the owner's responsibilities. A landlord who allows an emotional support animal as a reasonable accommodation is not liable for injuries it causes to others, subject to any other federal, state or local law. The law does not apply to dwellings exempt from Indiana's fair housing act.

title: Lead-Safe Work in Older Rentals
bodyText: If you renovate, remodel or maintain target housing built before 1960 that is occupied by someone other than you or your immediate family, and the work disturbs more than 20 square feet of exterior paint, more than 2 square feet in any one room, or more than 10% of the painted surface area, Indiana bans open-flame burning, machine sanding, grinding or abrasive blasting without HEPA exhaust control, heat guns above 1,100 degrees or that char paint, and most dry scraping and dry sanding; bars volatile chemical strippers in unventilated spaces; and requires visible exterior paint chips to be cleaned up within 48 hours. title: Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: In Indiana you may end a lease for unpaid rent on at least 10 days' notice, unless the parties agreed otherwise or the tenant pays the rent in full before the notice period expires. The statute supplies a form notice to vacate within 10 days unless the rent is paid. No notice is needed where the lease expressly requires rent in advance and the tenant does not pay it. The library's lease requires rent in advance, so it does not require you to give notice before ending the lease for unpaid rent that was due in advance. You may still give the 10-day notice first; if you do, the statute does not let you end the lease on that notice if the tenant pays the rent in full before it expires. A notice may be served on the tenant; if the tenant cannot be found, on a person living at the premises (who must have it explained); and if no one is found, by attaching it to a conspicuous part of the premises. Because of the 'unless the parties agreed otherwise' wording, a lease could also shorten or waive the 10-day notice where it applies, but the library does not offer that clause: how courts read the phrase has not been reviewed. It is lawful, so a landlord who still wants it can add a custom clause, after taking advice.

title: Ending a Tenancy
bodyText: Indiana notice rules depend on the tenancy. A fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term without notice. A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy of three months or less ends on notice equal to the rental period (a week for week-to-week, a month for month-to-month); occupancy by the landlord's consent without other terms is month to month. A tenancy at will ends on one month's written notice and cannot exist without an express contract. A year-to-year tenancy ends on notice at least three months before the end of the year. No notice is needed for a tenant at sufferance or a tenant at will who commits waste. Indiana supplies form notices for year-to-year tenancies and unpaid rent.

title: Eviction Court Process
bodyText: Indiana evictions are court cases. A possession case where the rent due when filed is $10,000 or less may be filed on a small claims docket, and filing there waives your right to a jury; the tenant may request a jury within 10 days after receiving the notice of claim. Attach a copy of a written lease to the claim. Small claims venue between landlord and tenant cannot be changed by contract. An order of possession may not be issued more than 30 days after judgment, and it lasts no more than 30 days. Before final judgment, a court may order possession only after you post a court-approved bond, and the officer may not remove occupants until 48 hours after the order is served. If the case settles before final judgment, you must move to dismiss it unless you are still seeking damages, including keeping the deposit; eviction diversion programs must be voluntary.

title: Emergency Possessory Orders
bodyText: Indiana has a fast court track. A landlord may petition the small claims docket for an emergency possessory order if the tenant has committed or threatens waste, if the tenant or a guest committed a crime affecting the health and safety of another tenant, the landlord or the landlord's agent, or if the tenant gave materially false information to get the lease. The court must hold a hearing within three business days, and a continuance is allowed only on clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would otherwise result. On a crime or false-application finding, the tenant must return possession within 7 days of the hearing. Tenants may use the same track against lockouts and utility shutoffs. The track does not override the rights of a tenant who is a crime victim.

title: Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: Indiana courts must, on their own, seal the records of an eviction case that is dismissed (including when the landlord settles or stops prosecuting), that ends in the tenant's favor, or whose judgment against the tenant is overturned on appeal. If a judgment was entered against the tenant, the tenant may move to seal the records once any money judgment is paid, or after seven years if there was no money judgment. Sealed records are open only under a court order, to law enforcement, or as the law requires. If you file an eviction and then settle, you must dismiss the case unless you still seek damages, and a case you leave idle for 180 days may be dismissed and sealed.

title: Tenant Property After Eviction
bodyText: After a court awards you possession, you may ask the court for an order allowing removal of the tenant's property. Property not removed by the date in the order may be delivered to a warehouse or a court-approved storage facility, but only after the order and the facility's name and location are personally served on the tenant. title: Domestic Violence, Sexual Offense and Stalking Protections
bodyText: Indiana protects a tenant or applicant who is a victim (or alleged victim) of domestic or family violence, a sex offense or stalking and who has a civil protection order or criminal no-contact order. You may not terminate, refuse to renew, refuse to enter into a lease, or retaliate solely because the person or a household member is protected, or because the person ended a lease under this law. A protected tenant may end the lease with written notice at least 30 days before the termination date, with a copy of the order and, for domestic violence or sexual assault, a safety plan from an accredited program, dated within 30 days, recommending relocation. The tenant owes rent prorated to the termination date and no early-termination rent or fees, and owes nothing if the notice comes at least 14 days before the right to occupy begins. Other adult tenants stay bound, and you need not account for the deposit until 45 days after all tenancies end. These rights cannot be waived.

title: When a Tenant Dies or Is Incapacitated
bodyText: If you know that a tenant who was the sole occupant has died, or believe a sole-occupant tenant is incapacitated and absent, Indiana law requires you to notify the tenant's representative, give the representative reasonable access to remove the tenant's belongings, and pay the representative the deposit and unearned rent the tenant would have received; you may require a signed inventory. The representative is, in order of priority, a person the tenant named in a separate written document delivered to you, a person named in the lease, an attorney in fact, a guardian, an heir, or a person the probate court appoints, and accepts by written notice to you. If you comply you are not liable to the tenant, the estate or others; a willful violation makes you liable for actual damages. The statute does not say whether the lease ends.

title: Drug Nuisance Actions
bodyText: Using a leased house, apartment or building to commit a controlled-substance offense is a nuisance under Indiana law. The prosecutor, a city or county attorney, the Attorney General or the property owner may sue to abate it; anyone other than the owner must give each tenant and the owner 45 days' notice first. An owner who knew of the nuisance may be ordered to submit a plan to prevent it; other relief needs no proof that a defendant knew.

title: Consumer Protection Act
bodyText: Indiana's Deceptive Consumer Sales Act covers leases of real property for personal or household purposes, so a landlord who regularly leases is a 'supplier'. Soliciting a tenant to sign terms that are oppressively one-sided, unduly limit remedies or set an unduly excessive price, where unequal bargaining power led the tenant to sign unwillingly or unknowingly, is an unconscionable act treated as a deceptive act; signing a written lease creates a rebuttable presumption that the tenant knew its terms. A tenant's private damages and class actions under the Act do not apply to consumer transactions in real property; how the Act is otherwise enforced was not reviewed here. The Act's list of deceptive acts has no item on leaving blanks at signing or giving a copy at signing.

title: Indiana Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Indiana's fair housing act bars refusing to rent, setting different terms, misrepresenting availability, or advertising a preference because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, disability or national origin, and requires reasonable disability modifications and accommodations. The act does not apply to an owner of no more than three single-family houses who rents one without a broker and without discriminatory advertising (one such rental in 24 months if the owner was not the last resident), or to rooms or units in an owner-occupied building for four or fewer families; federal law, not reviewed here, may still apply, including to advertising. The act does not bar discrimination based on a conviction for illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance. Indiana's civil rights law also names ancestry and status as a veteran among protected traits.

title: Eviction Court Rules: Landlord Duties
bodyText: Arizona's Rules of Procedure for Eviction Actions put several duties on a landlord who files an eviction. The complaint must state the specific reason for the eviction and when and how the notice was served, attach the notice, and be verified. A money claim must state the rent, the due dates, how late fees are calculated, the amounts due and any rent concession claimed. A nonpayment complaint must tell the tenant how to reinstate before judgment, and the landlord must serve the lease provisions the eviction relies on and, in a nonpayment case, the last six months of the tenant's charges and payments. A landlord who accepted a partial payment must show the court the partial-payment agreement the tenant signed, or the case is dismissed. The court awards late fees and other periodic fees only if a written lease specifies them, and attorney fees only where a statute or written contract provides for them, never more than the landlord paid or agreed to pay. A property manager may not represent the owner in court unless the manager is a lawyer. After a default judgment the landlord must mail or deliver a copy to the tenant. The landlord has 45 days after a judgment for possession to apply for a writ without explaining the delay. If the landlord later concludes the eviction was not valid, it must promptly move to set the judgment aside. Once a judgment is paid in full, the landlord must file a satisfaction of judgment within 30 days under the court rule (the statutes say 40 days) and serve a copy on the tenant; a landlord who does not answer a tenant's motion to compel satisfaction within 15 days risks having the case sealed.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Arizona has no just-cause eviction rule for houses and apartments. Either party may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date (10 days' notice for a week-to-week tenancy), with no reason required, and a fixed-term lease ends on its expiration date; no length of tenancy changes this. The limits are situational: a landlord may not raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction in retaliation for a tenant's code complaint, repair complaint, or joining or organizing a tenants' union or similar organization (a complaint within the prior six months creates a presumption of retaliation); fair housing law applies; and the domestic-violence statute preserves eviction of a victim for actions unrelated to the violence. Arizona has no condominium-conversion notice for apartments and no rule barring eviction while rent is paid into court. Mobile home parks have their own termination rules.

title: Electronic Notices and Signatures
bodyText: Arizona's Electronic Transactions Act lets an electronic record or signature satisfy a law that requires a writing or a signature, but only between parties who have agreed to do business electronically, and either party may refuse to do a later transaction electronically. A notice the law requires in writing can be sent electronically only in a form the recipient can print and store; a record the sender keeps the recipient from printing or storing cannot be enforced against the recipient. Where a law sets a delivery method, the electronic record must still go by that method: an abandonment notice, for example, must be sent by certified mail and posted. Arizona's landlord-tenant act treats a notice as received when it comes to the tenant's attention or is delivered in hand or mailed by registered or certified mail; email is not one of the listed methods, so an emailed notice rests on proof that it reached the tenant. A lease signed on paper may authorize doing business electronically only through the tenant's separate and express agreement that says which parts will be electronic and how, gives an email address, and promises to report a change. The Act has no special exclusion for eviction, default or cure notices.

title: Tenant-Caused Damage
bodyText: If a tenant, a family member or a guest damages the property, Arizona law makes the tenant responsible. The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or knowingly let anyone else do so, and the landlord may recover all reasonable damages from the breach and all quantifiable damage the tenant caused to the premises, plus court costs and reasonable attorney fees. Where the damage materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, the landlord may give 14 days' written notice, then do the work and bill it as rent on the next rent due date, or for immediate payment if the lease has ended. The tenant's own repair remedies do not apply to a condition the tenant, a family member or a guest caused: no termination for the landlord's breach, no repair-and-deduct, and no essential-services remedies. The fire and casualty section is different. It lets a tenant leave, or pay reduced rent for the part that can't be used, after damage that substantially impairs enjoyment, and it states no exception for damage the tenant caused; a lease cannot take that right away. Whether rent lost after a tenant leaves under that section counts as damages the landlord can recover is not settled by statute.

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: Arizona's landlord-tenant act defines rent as the payments made to the landlord in full consideration for the rented premises, so late fees and other charges are not rent unless a statute treats them that way. One does: if a tenant doesn't fix a maintenance problem after the landlord's 14-day notice, the landlord's repair cost can be billed as rent on the next rent due date. The 5-day nonpayment notice covers rent only, but to reinstate before an eviction is filed the tenant must also pay a reasonable late fee set out in a written lease. In an eviction, the court awards late charges only if a written lease specifies them, and other periodic charges (such as extra-person, pet, storage, signage or common-area fees) only if a written lease specifies them and they are collected periodically with rent; anything else must be sued for separately. A partial payment of rent or other charges keeps the landlord's eviction rights only with the tenant's contemporaneous signed agreement.

title: Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Neglect
bodyText: If a tenant's failure to keep up the unit materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacing a damaged item or cleaning, an Arizona landlord may give written notice that describes the problem and asks the tenant to fix it within 14 days, or as promptly as an emergency requires. If the tenant does not, the landlord may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner, and bill the actual and reasonable cost, or the fair and reasonable value, as rent on the next rent due date, or for immediate payment if the lease has ended. This is one of the few entries the access statute allows without the tenant's consent. No lease clause is needed for this right.

title: Complete, Signed Lease Copies
bodyText: A written Arizona lease must have every blank space completed, and the landlord must give the tenant a signed copy, with the tenant returning one fully signed copy, within a reasonable time after it is signed. Failing to do either is a material noncompliance with the lease by whichever party failed. Before signing, make sure every blank, bracket and placeholder in the lease is filled in or struck.

title: No Statutory Quiet-Enjoyment Covenant
bodyText: Arizona's landlord-tenant act has no express covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession. It protects possession in other ways: a landlord may not lock out a tenant, remove belongings or cut essential services, and owes the greater of two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages for an unlawful ouster; an unlawful or harassing entry costs actual damages of at least one month's rent. Whether a covenant of quiet enjoyment is implied in an Arizona lease is a question of case law, which was not reviewed.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Arizona prescribes few forms for residential landlords. The one lease form is the foreclosure notice: a lease signed after a foreclosure action has started must include a notice substantially in the statute's words, and the same notice goes to existing tenants within five business days after the owner receives a first notice of trustee's sale (not for buildings of four or more connected units). The pool safety notice is a Department of Health Services document, not statutory text. No form is required for eviction notices: courts and agencies may not require a mandatory or technical form, and a notice that meets the statute's content requirements is enough. In court, the eviction summons must include the Arizona Supreme Court's Residential Eviction Information Sheet on a separate page.

title: Consumer Fraud Act and Leases
bodyText: Arizona's Consumer Fraud Act makes deception, false promises, misrepresentation and concealment of material facts in the sale or advertisement of merchandise unlawful. Merchandise includes real estate, and a sale expressly includes leases and rentals of real estate subject to a deed restriction imposed in an earlier sale; whether the Act reaches other residential leases depends on case law, which was not reviewed. The Act has no list of specific lease practices such as blanks filled in after signing. Arizona's landlord-tenant act covers those directly by requiring a completed lease and a signed copy. Arizona has no plain-language statute for leases.

title: Holdover Charge
bodyText: [Optional.] If Tenant remains in possession after this Lease ends and Landlord has not consented in writing to a continued tenancy, Tenant will pay Landlord a holdover charge of {{holdover_daily_rate}} for each day Tenant remains in possession, in place of Rent and actual damages for the use of the property during that time. Landlord and Tenant agree that Landlord's loss from a holdover, including delay in making the property available to a new tenant, is difficult to estimate accurately in advance, that this charge is a reasonable estimate of that loss, and that it is not a penalty. Landlord's acceptance of a holdover charge is not consent to a continued tenancy and is not acceptance of Rent. This Section does not limit Landlord's right to recover possession, unpaid Rent and other amounts due for the period before this Lease ended, damages for harm to the property, or any amount Arizona law allows for a holdover that is willful and not in good faith.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 54t / rule 54). Modelled on tenant-caused-damage-tn, which was read, not tagged. OFFERED BECAUSE THE LAW LEAVES THE GAP OPEN: Wyoming has no casualty or untenantability statute at all (Article 12 read in full 2026-09-30; Title 34 ch. 2 index read 2026-09-27 -- no destruction, untenantability or rent-abatement section), so there is no statutory tenant exit or abatement right for this clause to waive, which is what bars the equivalent clause in several other states. Each Wyoming abatement or exit route was checked separately for its own tenant-fault exception and all three already carry one: W.S. 1-21-1203(c) (owner need not correct a condition caused by the renter, the renter's family or guests by inappropriate use or misuse), W.S. 1-21-1206(a) (the renter's repair remedies are available only to a renter in compliance with 1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205), and the library's own casualty-termination-wy, which is a contract term and is already limited to casualty 'through no fault of Tenant'. There is no rent-into-court or repair-escrow statute in Wyoming, so that limb does not arise. CONDITIONAL, offered not defaulted, per rule 54. Companion education row: edu-tenant-caused-damage-wy. title: When Your Tenant Causes the Damage
bodyText: Wyoming law is unusually good to the landlord here, and it works without any lease clause. A renter must not intentionally or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the unit, or knowingly let anyone else do so (W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(i)). If the renter damages the property you may apply the deposit to the damage, and the renter stays liable for whatever the deposit does not cover, plus interest at ten percent a year on the unpaid balance, and you may take any legal action available to recover it (W.S. 1-21-1211(b)). Two defences the tenant would otherwise have are switched off. You are not required to correct any condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, guests or invitees through inappropriate use or misuse (W.S. 1-21-1203(c)). And the renter's repair remedies -- the notice-to-repair ladder, the civil action, the court-ordered termination -- are available only to a renter who is in compliance with the renter-duty and prohibited-act sections (W.S. 1-21-1206(a)), so a renter who caused the damage is generally outside them. What Wyoming does not give you is a rule about rent. There is no casualty or untenantability statute in Wyoming at all, so nothing in the statutes says whether rent keeps running while a unit the tenant wrecked is repaired, or whether you can recover the rent you lose if the lease ends. That is left entirely to the lease, which is why the optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause exists. Without it you are arguing common-law damages and mitigation from scratch.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 54t). Every cited section read section-open 2026-09-30. Companion to the optional clause tenant-caused-damage-wy. The 10% figure in W.S. 1-21-1211(b) is the statute's, already carried as a CONSTRAINED term by unpaid-damages-interest-wy; repeated here as context, not as a second source of truth. title: Utility Deposit Identified Separately
bodyText: Of the amounts Tenant pays Landlord before occupancy, {{utility_deposit}} is held separately as a utility deposit, identified apart from the Security Deposit, and is held to cover utility charges Tenant incurs during this Lease. Landlord will refund it as Wyoming law provides once Tenant shows that all utility charges Tenant incurred have been paid.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, targeted fix 18 with rules 50 and 54). The 2026-09-29 scrub switched off utility-deposit-return-wy and moved its content to edu-utility-deposit-return-wy. Fix 18's question -- did that clause carry a written notice or disclosure a statute requires? -- answers NO: W.S. 1-21-1208(b), read section-open 2026-09-30, imposes refund duties on the owner and requires nothing to appear in the lease, so the switched-off clause only restated a duty the law imposes anyway and is correctly left off. But reading 1-21-1208(b) for that question surfaced a separate point the scrub did not touch: the subsection applies only to 'property or money held and SEPARATELY IDENTIFIED as a utilities deposit'. The separate identification is the trigger for the whole regime, including the landlord-favourable limb that lets the owner apply the deposit to the tenant's outstanding utility debt after 45 days. Nothing in the library identified one, so a Wyoming landlord taking a utility deposit fell outside 1-21-1208(b) and the money was treated as ordinary deposit under 1-21-1208(a). This clause supplies the identification. CONDITIONAL: include only where a utility deposit is actually taken. Note W.S. 1-21-1207 separately requires the rental agreement to state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable, which reaches a utility deposit too -- carried by nonrefundable-deposit-notice-wy. title: What You List, You Must Maintain
bodyText: Wyoming turns part of your own lease into a statutory duty. W.S. 1-21-1203(a)(iv) requires an owner to 'maintain other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted in the rental agreement' -- so whatever you list in the lease stops being a courtesy and becomes an obligation under the Residential Rental Property Act, enforceable through the renter's remedy ladder in W.S. 1-21-1206: written notice, then a formal notice to repair, then a civil action in circuit court that can award the renter costs, damages, rent improperly retained, an order to repair, or termination of the lease. List the window air conditioner and you have to keep it running. Two related levers run the other way. The baseline in W.S. 1-21-1202(a) -- operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water -- applies 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties'. And W.S. 1-21-1202(d) lets any duty or obligation in the article be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties. Wyoming is unusually permissive on this; most states make habitability non-waivable. Both are real, and both are blunt instruments: a lease that contracts away heat or hot water is a lease you will have to defend. The practical rule is to list appliances deliberately rather than generously, and to treat any shifting of a core duty as a decision to take advice on, not a form field.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 44 -- terms the statute turns into landlord duties). W.S. 1-21-1202 and 1-21-1203 read section-open 2026-09-30. The rule-44 wording screen found five 'as agreed in the rental agreement' hooks in Article 12: 1-21-1201(a)(i) (agent as owner for notice unless the agreement says otherwise -- already carried by agent-capacity-designation-wy), 1-21-1202(a) (habitability baseline 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing'), 1-21-1202(d) (any duty assignable by explicit signed written agreement -- already carried by edu-habitability-modifiable-wy), 1-21-1203(a)(iv) (appliances and facilities 'as specifically contracted') and 1-21-1204(a)(v) (occupancy above the number 'specified in the rental agreement' -- already carried by permitted-occupants). 1-21-1203(a)(iv) was the one with no row: the shared appliances-included clause, tagged WY among 26 states, silently creates a statutory maintenance duty in Wyoming. RULE 78 POINTER NOTED, NOT FIXED HERE: appliances-included tells the tenant Landlord will maintain the listed items 'as described in this Lease's Maintenance & Repairs Section', but the 2026-09-29 scrub switched off habitability-baseline-wy and did not restore the shared landlord-maintenance clause, so a Wyoming lease has no landlord-repair clause and that pointer resolves to a section containing only tenant duties. The legal outcome is unaffected because 1-21-1203(a)(iv) supplies the duty directly, but the lease reads as promising something it does not contain. appliances-included is shared across 26 states, so under rule 62 this is flagged in the log's propagation section rather than edited. title: Which Notices You Cannot Send by Email
bodyText: Wyoming's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (W.S. 40-21-101 through 40-21-119) is broad: it excludes only wills, codicils and testamentary trusts, most of the Uniform Commercial Code, and the Uniform Computer Information Transactions Act (W.S. 40-21-103(b)). Unlike some states, it carves out nothing for eviction, default or cure notices, and nothing for residential leases. That does not make email safe for the notices that matter, because the landlord-tenant statutes prescribe their own service. The three-day notice to quit that must precede any forcible entry and detainer action is served 'by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business' (W.S. 1-21-1003) -- a physical delivery. The habitability notices under W.S. 1-21-1203(b) and the renter's notice to repair under W.S. 1-21-1206(b) must go by certified mail or in the manner W.S. 1-21-1003 specifies. The abandoned-property notice under W.S. 1-21-1210(a)(i) is deemed served only by certified mail to an address the renter furnished in writing for that purpose, by personal service under Rule 4, or by newspaper publication. UETA itself says a transaction it covers is still subject to other applicable substantive law (W.S. 40-21-103(d)), so these methods control. Two further limits. The act applies only between parties who have each agreed to conduct transactions electronically, judged from the context and the parties' conduct (W.S. 40-21-105(b)). And a party who has agreed may still refuse to conduct other transactions electronically -- a right the statute says in terms 'may not be waived by agreement' (W.S. 40-21-105(c)). A blanket lease clause consenting to electronic notice for everything cannot take that away.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 45 -- the electronic-transactions act read itself, not only the landlord-tenant section that refers to it). W.S. 40-21-103 and 40-21-105 read 2026-09-30 on law.justia.com (current edition); W.S. 1-21-1003, 1-21-1203(b), 1-21-1206(b) and 1-21-1210(a)(i) read section-open the same day on the official wyoleg.gov 2026 text. NO CLAUSE DEFECT FOUND: the shared notices clause is self-limiting ('Where applicable law requires a particular method, form, timing, or content for a notice, that requirement will control over this Section, and nothing in this Lease designates an alternative method of delivery for any notice governed by law'), and electronic-signatures reaches execution of the lease, not notices under it -- and UETA does not exclude leases, so that clause is sound. This row exists because the screen produced a real landlord-facing answer, not because a clause failed. CITATION FLAG (rule 21): W.R.C.P. Rule 4, cited through W.S. 1-21-1210(a)(i)(B), is a court rule, not a code section, and needs separate monitoring.

title: Does Consumer Law Reach Your Lease?
bodyText: Wyoming has no plain-language statute for consumer contracts, so there is no readability test to meet and no required statement of the rights a tenant is giving up. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act (W.S. 40-12-101 and following) is the only general consumer statute in play, and whether it reaches a residential lease is genuinely unsettled on the words. It defines 'merchandise' to include 'any service or any property, tangible or intangible, real, personal or mixed' -- real property is expressly in. But it reaches only a 'consumer transaction', defined as the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of merchandise to an individual for primarily personal, family or household purposes. Renting a home is plainly for household purposes; whether letting it is a 'sale or distribution' is the open question, and the statute does not answer it. No Wyoming case law on the point was reviewed. What the Act does not contain is worth knowing, because other states do have these: there is no provision making it unlawful to leave blank spaces in a contract to be filled in after signing, and none requiring that the consumer be given a copy at signing. The unlawful-practice list in W.S. 40-12-105 runs to misrepresentation, false pricing, bait-and-switch and the like, with a catch-all at (a)(xv) for 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices'. If the Act does reach leases, that catch-all is the realistic exposure -- a lease term or a rental advertisement that misleads -- rather than anything about formatting. Practical reading: draft honestly and fill in every blank before signing, but do not expect a Wyoming consumer-law formatting rule, because there is not one.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 51). W.S. 40-12-102 (definitions) and 40-12-105 (unlawful practices) read 2026-09-30 on law.justia.com, current edition; the definitions were read as rule 51 requires, not only the practice list. Checked for and NOT found: a plain-language consumer-contract statute, an express residential-lease exclusion, a blank-spaces-filled-after-signing practice, and a copy-at-signing practice. The reach question is left open rather than resolved because the text does not resolve it and no case law was read -- stated that way in the body. Overlaps but does not duplicate edu-no-rental-fee-transparency-law-wy, which answers the narrower fee-transparency question from the same section; that row keeps topic_key fee-transparency and this one takes consumer-protection-act. Rule 40 note: no type-size, bold, underline, conspicuousness or placement requirement appears in the WCPA either.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: Wyoming statutes do not regulate the use of algorithmic or software pricing tools to set residential rents. Wyoming regulates rent lightly in general: there is no rent control, no rent-increase notice period and no cap. Federal antitrust law and any city ordinance may still apply.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 27). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT. Basis: Title 1 ch. 21 articles 10, 12 and 13 read in full section-open 2026-09-30 -- Wyoming's entire residential landlord-tenant code -- plus the existing primary-verified absence in edu-no-rent-increase-statute-wy. Search boundary stated per rule 19: this is three articles read whole, not a full-text search of the Wyoming code; the shell could not reach any statute host (organization egress policy, 403) and the official site publishes no loadable bulk text, so no code-wide battery with a nonsense control was possible. Municipal ordinances not checked, per the state-law-only scope.

title: Fees Are Not Rent in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming's Residential Rental Property Act never defines 'rent', and no statute converts a fee into rent. That matters most at the eviction door. A forcible entry and detainer action for nonpayment is available only 'after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due' (W.S. 1-21-1002(a)(i)); unpaid late fees, pet fees or utility charges are not rent, and calling them 'additional rent' in the lease does not make them the thing the statute names. Trying to evict on unpaid fees alone is how a Wyoming nonpayment case gets dismissed. The statutes keep the two apart elsewhere too: a deposit may be applied to 'accrued rent' and separately to 'other costs provided by any contract' (W.S. 1-21-1208(a)), and in an FED judgment the court finds 'the amount of rent due and payable' and adds costs and attorney's fees as the lease provides (W.S. 1-21-1008(b)). You can still collect fees -- sue for them, deduct them from the deposit, or treat them as a lease breach. What you cannot do is run them through the three-day nonpayment route.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 27). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT (no statute makes fees rent), with the affirmative consequence stated. W.S. 1-21-1002(a)(i), 1-21-1008(b) and 1-21-1208(a) read section-open 2026-09-30; Article 12's definition section (1-21-1201(a)) read in full and contains no definition of 'rent'. Consistent with the shared default-by-tenant clause, which already says Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent, does not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate or pursue eviction -- that sentence is correct for Wyoming and this row explains why. title: No Right to Fix It and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Some states let a landlord give notice, do work the tenant should have done, and add the cost to the next rent payment. Wyoming does not. Nothing in the Residential Rental Property Act gives an owner a self-cure right, a notice period for one, or a way to bill the cost as rent. What you do have: the renter owes the statutory duties in W.S. 1-21-1204 and must not commit the prohibited acts in W.S. 1-21-1205, and may not unreasonably refuse you entry to make repairs or inspect (W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(iii)). Breach of either section is a ground for a forcible entry and detainer action in its own right (W.S. 1-21-1002(a)(vi)). If the renter damages the property you may apply the deposit and sue for the rest plus ten percent interest (W.S. 1-21-1211(b)). So the Wyoming route is entry, then damages or possession -- not self-help repair billed forward as rent. A lease clause purporting to make repair costs 'additional rent' would also run into the point that Wyoming's three-day nonpayment eviction reaches rent only.

title: No Blank-Space or Lease-Copy Rule
bodyText: Wyoming imposes no statutory requirement that a written lease have every blank space completed, and none that the landlord give the tenant a signed copy. Neither failure is a statutory breach the way it is in some states. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act does not list either one among its unlawful practices. Two things still bite. Wyoming recognises oral rental agreements -- the Act's definition of 'rental agreement' covers 'any agreement, written or oral' (W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(ii)) -- so an incomplete written lease does not leave you with no lease; it leaves you arguing about terms. And several Wyoming rights turn on something being in the rental agreement in writing: the nonrefundable-deposit statement (W.S. 1-21-1207), the agent notice opt-out (W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(i)), appliances you must maintain (W.S. 1-21-1203(a)(iv)), the occupancy number (W.S. 1-21-1204(a)(v)) and any reassignment of duties (W.S. 1-21-1202(d)). A blank left in one of those is a right left on the table. Fill in every blank, bracket and placeholder before signing, and give the tenant a copy -- not because a statute says so, but because the statutes that matter all point back at the document.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rules 27 and 51). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT. Basis: Article 12 read in full section-open 2026-09-30; W.S. 40-12-105 (WCPA unlawful practices, all seventeen paragraphs) and 40-12-102 (definitions) read 2026-09-30 and checked specifically for a blank-spaces practice and a copy-at-signing practice -- neither is present. The affirmative half of this row (which Wyoming rights depend on written lease text) comes from sections read section-open the same day. title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: Wyoming's Residential Rental Property Act contains no covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession running from the landlord to the tenant. The Act's only 'peaceful enjoyment' language runs the other way: it is a renter's duty not to 'interfere with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property' (W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(ii)), which protects neighbouring tenants from this one, not this tenant from you. Possession is protected instead by the shape of the eviction process: the three-day notice to quit, the court action, and a sheriff acting on a court order (W.S. 1-21-1003, 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017, 1-21-1211(a)). Wyoming attaches no statutory damages to an unlawful ouster, which is the gap covered separately in the self-help row. Whether a covenant of quiet enjoyment is implied in a Wyoming lease as a matter of common law was not researched and is not answered here.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 27). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT as a statute; case law explicitly NOT LOCATED and the boundary stated in the body per rule 19. Basis: Articles 10, 12 and 13 read in full section-open 2026-09-30. The W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(ii) point -- that Wyoming's only peaceful-enjoyment provision is a tenant duty, not a landlord covenant -- was read directly and is the substantive finding here. title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Wyoming prescribes no form for a residential lease, no form for an eviction notice and no agency-issued tenant-rights document that has to be attached to anything. There is no 'substantially in the following form' language anywhere in the residential rental statutes. What the statutes prescribe is content, not form, and in two places only. The abandoned-property notice must describe the property claimed to be abandoned and state that it will be disposed of seven days after service unless the renter acts (W.S. 1-21-1210(a)(i)), and it is deemed served only by certified mail to an address the renter furnished in writing for that purpose, by personal service under Rule 4, or by newspaper publication. The renter's own 'notice to repair or correct condition' has five prescribed contents under W.S. 1-21-1206(b) -- that one is the tenant's to draft, but knowing its required elements tells you whether a notice you received is effective. Outside the landlord-tenant title, the bad-check demand under W.S. 1-1-115(a) has prescribed content too: it must state that the drawer has to pay the value of the check and the collection fee, and state the amount of that fee.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 27). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT for forms; PRESENT for three content-prescribed notices, each read section-open 2026-09-30. Rule 19 form-search terms applied to the read text: 'following form', 'substantially as follows', 'as follows:' and 'substantially in the form' -- the only 'as follows' hits are W.S. 1-21-1210(a) ('disposed of as follows') and W.S. 1-21-1206(b) ('This notice shall:'), both introducing content requirements rather than a form. Boundary: three articles plus W.S. 1-1-115 read whole, not a code-wide full-text search; Wyoming Supreme Court forms and circuit-court eviction forms are court-rule material and were not reviewed (rule 21 flag). bodyText: Wyoming statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras, video doorbells or similar devices. The lease's alteration and installation terms govern -- in this library, the Alterations section, which requires your written consent before a tenant adds or changes a fixture. Wyoming's recording and surveillance laws, and any homeowners-association rules, were not reviewed and may apply to what a camera records rather than to its installation.

title: Specific Maintenance Duties Assigned to Tenant
bodyText: Landlord and Tenant expressly agree, as an explicit written agreement under Wyoming Statutes section 1-21-1202(d), that responsibility for the following specific items is assigned to Tenant rather than Landlord: {{reassigned_duties}}. For each item listed, Tenant will keep it in good working order, arrange and pay for its routine servicing and its repair, and promptly tell Landlord in writing of any condition affecting it that Tenant cannot correct. This assignment is limited to the items listed. It does not reach, and Landlord remains responsible for, the property's electrical, heating and plumbing systems and its hot and cold running water; the safe and sanitary condition of the property as a whole and its fitness for human habitation; and the common areas. Nothing in this Section assigns to Tenant any duty that applicable law does not permit to be assigned. If Tenant does not maintain an item assigned under this Section, Landlord may, after written notice to Tenant and a reasonable opportunity to correct it, have the work done and recover the reasonable cost from Tenant as a debt under this Lease, which is not Rent.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rules 50 and 54). TAYLOR'S DECISION, 2026-09-30: asked in chat whether to offer this and answered yes; scope as recommended -- named non-core items only, core baseline expressly excluded. W.S. 1-21-1202(d), read section-open 2026-09-30: 'Any duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties.' Wyoming is an outlier in permitting this; most states make habitability non-waivable, which is why this clause exists for WY and must not be inherited by any other state. The signed lease is the explicit written agreement the subsection requires, so no separate document is needed (rule 48 checked: 1-21-1202(d) imposes no separate-document requirement, unlike 1-21-1207). DELIBERATE SCOPE LIMIT: the carve-out tracks W.S. 1-21-1202(a) (operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water) and W.S. 1-21-1203(a)(i)-(iii) (not renting unless reasonably safe, sanitary and fit; common areas; electrical, plumbing, heating, hot and cold water). What remains assignable in practice is the 1-21-1203(a)(iv) category -- 'other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted' -- plus discrete site items such as a well pump, a septic system, a propane tank or an outbuilding, which is the real rural-Wyoming use case. A separate decision was made NOT to offer any clause under 1-21-1202(a)'s 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties', which would let a lease contract away heat or hot water: lawful in Wyoming, declined as a product. UNREAD RISK, LABELLED (rule 76): no Wyoming case law construing 1-21-1202(d) was read, so how far a court would enforce a reassignment against the 1-21-1203(a) owner duties -- which the statute states without an express 'unless agreed' qualifier -- is unknown. The narrow scope and the final savings sentence are the response to that uncertainty, not a resolution of it. CONDITIONAL: include only where the landlord is actually assigning a named item. The cost-recovery sentence is contractual and deliberately says the cost is NOT Rent, keeping it consistent with edu-no-landlord-self-cure-wy (Wyoming gives no statutory fix-and-bill-as-rent right) and edu-fees-as-rent-wy (the three-day nonpayment route reaches rent only). Shares topic_key habitability-modifiable with its education companion edu-habitability-modifiable-wy, per rule 58; no display collision, that row is LANDLORD_EDUCATION. New {{variable}} for the builder backlog: {{reassigned_duties}}. title: The Utilities Waiver -- Legal in Wyoming, and Still a Bad Idea
bodyText: Wyoming lets a lease do something almost no other state allows. The sentence in W.S. 1-21-1202(a) requiring operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water ends with 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties'. Read plainly, a signed lease can remove the requirement itself -- not shift who maintains the water heater, but agree there need not be hot water. Keep that separate from the other flexibility in the same section. W.S. 1-21-1202(d) lets you assign a specific duty to the tenant: the unit still has to have a working well pump, the tenant just looks after it. That one is in the lease library as an optional clause. The (a) waiver removes the amenity from the deal altogether, and it is not offered as a clause -- deliberately. Three reasons to leave it alone. The habitability duty in the first sentence of 1-21-1202(a) -- safe, sanitary, fit for human habitation -- carries no such escape, so a unit with no heat in a Wyoming winter may well fail that duty whatever the lease says, and you would be arguing the point in front of a judge. No Wyoming case law on this sentence was reviewed for this library, so how far a court would let it stretch is unknown. And a tenant's agreement to go without heat is exactly the kind of term that invites an unconscionability argument and reads badly to everyone who later looks at it. If what you actually have is a cabin, you may not need the waiver at all: the same subsection says it 'shall not prevent the rental of seasonal rental units such as summer cabins which are not intended to have such amenities'. A genuinely seasonal property sits outside the utilities requirement by statute. If after all that you still want the term, it is lawful and you can add it as your own custom clause. Put the specific amenity and the reason in writing, keep it off anything that touches safety, and get advice first.
notes: WY added 2026-10-01, RETRO follow-up (SOP 1.15, rules 50 and 54). TAYLOR'S DECISION, 2026-10-01: having declined the clause, he asked whether an education row covered the point, reasoning that a landlord who wants the term after reading it can write their own. It did not -- W.S. 1-21-1202(a)'s waiver appeared only as nine unexplained words inside edu-habitability-baseline-wy (and that row attached them to the wrong sentence; fixed in the same delta). This row is the result and is the better design: the library explains the lawful option without shipping it. W.S. 1-21-1202(a) read section-open. Three sentences, and the distinction matters: (1) safe and sanitary, fit for human habitation -- NO waiver language; (2) operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water -- 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties'; (3) 'Provided, however, this section shall not prevent the rental of seasonal rental units such as summer cabins which are not intended to have such amenities'. The waiver reaches sentence (2) only. NEW topic_key habitability-waiver, no other state has one. Rule 58 weighed: this could have shared habitability-modifiable with edu-habitability-modifiable-wy and duty-reassignment-wy, but waiving a requirement and reassigning a duty are different mechanisms with opposite risk profiles, and conflating them is precisely what went wrong in the baseline row. A separate key also makes the cross-state check ask every other state whether its habitability duty is waivable -- in most the answer is 'no, void', which is worth recording per state. Collapse it at sync if Taylor prefers one key. UNREAD RISK, LABELLED (rule 76): no Wyoming case law construes 1-21-1202(a), and the unconscionability point is doctrinal, not read from a Wyoming decision. Stated in the body as untested rather than as a prediction. Overlaps in passing with edu-contracted-appliances-duty-wy, which mentions the same waiver accurately while explaining a different subject (1-21-1203(a)(iv)); that row is left unchanged. W.S. 1-21-1202 read section-open from the official Wyoming Legislature NXT gateway, 2026 Wyoming Statutes; text confirmed identical in the 2024 and 2026 editions.

title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: When this Lease ends, Tenant must ask for the Security Deposit back by written demand to Landlord, and should include in the demand the address to which the refund should be sent. Landlord may apply the Security Deposit to accrued Rent and to damages Landlord has suffered because Tenant did not comply with this Lease or the Oklahoma Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, as itemized in a written statement that Landlord will deliver to Tenant by mail, return receipt requested, or in person. Within 45 days after the tenancy ends, Tenant has delivered possession of the property and Landlord has received Tenant's written demand, Landlord will return the balance of the Security Deposit, without interest. IMPORTANT: If Tenant does not make a written demand for the Security Deposit within six months after the tenancy ends, the Security Deposit becomes Landlord's property and Tenant's interest in it ends.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 115(B): the deposit may be applied to accrued rent and damages from the tenant's noncompliance with the act and the rental agreement, itemized in a written statement delivered by mail, return receipt requested, to be signed for by any person of statutory service age at the address, or in person; the balance is returned without interest within forty-five (45) days after termination of tenancy, delivery of possession and written demand by the tenant; if the tenant makes no written demand within six (6) months after termination, the deposit reverts to the landlord and the tenant's interest terminates. Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 115(E): a landlord who fails to comply lets the tenant recover the deposit and any prepaid rent. The six-month reversion is the landlord-serving reason for the clause (the statute does not require the warning in the lease; it is stated so the tenant cannot say he was unaware). Rule 37: the 45 days run from termination of the tenancy, which for a periodic tenancy is the date set by the termination notice (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111). title: Flooding Disclosure
bodyText: [Use if the property has been flooded within the past five years and Landlord knows it.] FLOODING DISCLOSURE: The premises have been flooded within the past five years: [describe what Landlord knows, including when and which areas were affected]. For this disclosure, 'flooded' means general and temporary conditions of partial or complete inundation of normally dry land areas and structures on those areas from the overflow of lakes, ponds, streams, rivers, creeks or other inland waters.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 113a(A): if the premises have been flooded within the past five (5) years and the landlord knows it, the landlord 'shall include such information prominently and in writing as part of any written rental agreements'; failure lets a tenant who is a party sue and recover the personal property damages the tenant sustains from flooding of the premises. title: Handling of Property Left Behind
bodyText: When this Lease ends or Tenant gives up possession, Tenant will remove all of Tenant's personal property from the property. If Tenant abandons or surrenders possession of the property, or is lawfully removed through eviction proceedings, and leaves household goods, furnishings, fixtures or other personal property behind, Landlord may take possession of it. (1) If, in Landlord's judgment, the property has no ascertainable or apparent value, Landlord may dispose of it without any duty of accounting or liability, and may dispose of perishable property in any manner Landlord considers fit. (2) If, in Landlord's judgment, the property has an ascertainable or apparent value, Landlord will send Tenant a written notice by certified mail to Tenant's last known address stating that property not removed within the time specified in the notice will be deemed abandoned. Property left with Landlord for 30 days or longer is conclusively abandoned, and Landlord may then dispose of it in any manner Landlord deems reasonable and proper without liability to Tenant or anyone else. (3) While Landlord holds the property, Landlord will store it in a place of safekeeping and exercise reasonable care, and is responsible only for loss caused by Landlord's deliberate or negligent act. If Landlord stores it in the property, the storage cost will not exceed the fair rental value of the property; if it is moved to a commercial storage company, the storage cost includes the actual charge for storage and moving it there. If Tenant removes the property within the time allowed, Tenant will pay the storage cost for the time Landlord held it plus all other costs that accrued under this Lease.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130(A)-(E), followed closely: no-value property may be disposed of without accounting or liability; perishables in any manner; valuable property: written notice by certified mail to the last-known address that property not removed within the time specified will be deemed abandoned, and property left thirty (30) days or longer is conclusively determined to be abandoned; storage in a place of safekeeping with reasonable care, liability only for deliberate or negligent loss; storage in the unit capped at fair rental value; commercial storage includes actual charges; a tenant who removes the property within the time pays storage and accrued costs; compliance shields the landlord, but a deliberate or negligent violation makes the landlord liable for actual damages (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130(E)). The statute sets no minimum time for the notice beyond the 30-day conclusive rule; the clause does not invent one. The procedure is the act's; Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 103(B) makes a conflicting agreement unenforceable, so the clause mirrors the statute rather than shortening it. Separate procedure for a deceased sole tenant: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130.1 (tenant-death-contact-ok, edu-tenant-death-ok). Pointed to by surrender-end-of-term-ks-ne ('Handling of Property Left Behind Section'). Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130 read whole. title: Contact Person if Tenant Dies
bodyText: Tenant names the following person to contact if Tenant dies: [name, address and telephone number]. Tenant will tell Landlord in writing if this information changes. If Tenant dies while Tenant is the sole occupant of the property, Tenant authorizes Landlord to: (1) give this person access to the property at a reasonable time and in the presence of Landlord or Landlord's agent; (2) allow this person to remove any of Tenant's property found at the property, after signing an inventory of the property removed; and (3) refund the Security Deposit, less lawful deductions (including the cost of removing and storing Tenant's property), to this person. Landlord may remove and store all property found in the property. If this person does not remove the property by the thirtieth day after the postmark date of Landlord's written request sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, and no one has contacted Landlord claiming the property before Landlord discards it, Landlord may discard it.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130.1(A): on the landlord's written request the tenant shall provide the name, address and telephone number of a person to contact on the tenant's death and sign a statement authorizing the landlord to grant that person access at a reasonable time in the landlord's presence, allow removal of the tenant's property, and refund the deposit less lawful deductions to that person; (C): on the death of a sole occupant the landlord may remove and store all property, shall turn it over to the designee or anyone lawfully entitled who asks before it is discarded, shall refund the deposit less lawful deductions including removal and storage costs, the remover signs an inventory, and the landlord may discard the property if the certified-mail request (return receipt requested) goes unanswered by the thirtieth day after the postmark and no one has claimed it; (D): a written lease may set a different procedure; (E): a tenant who knowingly fails to provide the information after a notice of request relieves the landlord of responsibility for the property; (F): a landlord who knowingly violates (C) after being furnished the section is liable to the estate for actual damages. The clause is the Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130.1(A) statement placed in the lease (rule 54: a right the lease can invoke) and follows the (C) procedure rather than using (D) to vary it.
