title: Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy
bodyText: If this Lease continues as a month-to-month tenancy, either Landlord or Tenant may end it by giving the other written notice at least 30 days before the date the tenancy is to end, counted from the day the notice is served. If the tenancy is shorter than month-to-month, such as week-to-week, either party may end it by written notice served at least seven days before the date the tenancy is to end. Notices will be served in the way Oklahoma law requires. Rent remains payable through the date the tenancy ends. This Section does not limit either party's right to end this Lease earlier where this Lease or Oklahoma law allows it.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111(A): month-to-month or at will, written notice at least thirty (30) days before the termination date, the period running from service under subsection E; Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111(B): less than month-to-month, written notice served at least seven (7) days before; Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111(C): a definite term expires without notice unless otherwise agreed; Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111(E): personal service, else delivery to a family member over twelve (12) residing with the tenant, else posting plus certified mail (or the Firm Mailing Book); a landlord who cannot be served personally is served by certified mail to the Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 116 person. Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 110: without a written definite term, a weekly-paying roomer or boarder is week-to-week and every other tenancy month-to-month. The older general rules (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, §§ 4, 5, 9: thirty days, three months for year-to-year, a ten-day floor for posted notices) sit outside the act; the act controls residential tenancies (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 103(A)). Tenancy type (rule 37): monthly 30 days, shorter periods 7 days, fixed term none. Okla. Stat. tit. 41, §§ 110, 111 read whole. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds, a closed or nonexistent account, a stop-payment order or any other reason, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount], and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. title: Smoke Detectors
bodyText: Landlord has explained to Tenant how to test the smoke detector(s) in the property. Tenant is responsible for checking the smoke detector(s) regularly to make sure they are in working order, and will promptly notify Landlord in writing if a smoke detector is missing, damaged or not working. Tenant will not tamper with, remove, destroy or disconnect any smoke detector or remove its power source, except to replace a battery or as Landlord directs; Oklahoma law makes doing so a misdemeanor.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 74, § 324.11a(C): a lessor of residential rental property 'shall explain to the lessee or tenant the method of testing the smoke detector'; the responsibility for checking whether a detector is in working order is with the tenant leasing a one- or two-family dwelling, including an apartment in each apartment house, and not with the lessor. Okla. Stat. tit. 74, § 324.11a(E): tampering with, removing, destroying, disconnecting or removing power from an installed detector, except in inspection, maintenance or replacement, is a misdemeanor ($50-$100). Okla. Stat. tit. 74, § 324.11a(A): owners of buildings used as apartment houses, rooming houses and other listed buildings install detectors under the State Fire Marshal Commission's adopted codes; Okla. title: Fire or Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty not caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, a member of Tenant's family, Tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with Tenant's consent, and the damage substantially impairs Tenant's use and enjoyment of the property, Landlord may end this Lease by written notice to Tenant, effective on the date stated in the notice or, if earlier, the date Tenant vacates. Rent will be accounted for as of the date of the fire or casualty, and Landlord will return all prepaid and unearned Rent and the Security Deposit as this Lease and Oklahoma law provide. This Section does not limit Tenant's own right under Oklahoma law to vacate and end this Lease, or to vacate the unusable part of the property with a proportionate reduction in Rent, after such a casualty.
notes: OK: Rule 54 (landlord rights left to contract). Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 122(A): if a fire or casualty substantially impairs enjoyment, unless caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a family member, the tenant's animal or pet or another person or animal on the premises with consent, the tenant may vacate and notify the landlord in writing within one (1) week of intent to terminate (termination as of vacating), or vacate the unusable part with rent reduced in proportion; Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 122(B): on termination the landlord returns deposits recoverable under 'Section 15 of this act' (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 115) and all prepaid and unearned rent, accounting as of the date of the casualty. The statute gives the landlord no termination right and does not bar one; the clause adds it for the landlord and keeps the tenant's statutory rights (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 113(A)(1) bars waiving them). Tenant-caused casualty: tenant-caused-damage-ok. Optional (CONDITIONAL), the standing GA decision. Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 122 read whole. title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, a member of Tenant's family or household, Tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with Tenant's consent, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage.
notes: OK: Rule 54, tenant-caused damage (always asked). Each Oklahoma abatement or exit provision carries its own tenant-fault exception: casualty, Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 122(A) ('unless the impairment is caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of his family, his animal or pet or other person or animal on the premises with his consent'); repair-and-deduct, essential services and habitability termination, Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 121(E) (the tenant's rights 'do not arise ... if the condition complained of was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of his or her family, his or her animal or pet or other person or animal on the premises with his or her consent'); the FED cure for a minimum-services claim (Okla. Stat. tit. 12, § 1148.10B) rests on Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 121(C), so it inherits Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 121(E). So a no-abatement term for tenant-caused damage waives no statutory right (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 113(A)(1)). The tenant's duty not to destroy, damage or impair the premises or permit any person, animal or pet to do so: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 127(5). Mitigation: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 105(A), Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 129(B). The fault group in the clause follows the statute's words (it adds 'household' alongside 'family'). title: No Criminal Activity
bodyText: Tenant, members of Tenant's household, Tenant's guests and other persons under Tenant's control will not engage in criminal activity that threatens the health, safety or right of peaceful enjoyment of the premises by other tenants or is a danger to the premises, and will not engage in any drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises. Under Oklahoma law, such activity is grounds for immediate termination of this Lease, and Landlord may end this Lease and seek possession without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure. This Section controls over any other provision of this Lease that would require notice and an opportunity to cure. This Section does not apply to domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking of which Tenant or a member of Tenant's household is the victim.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 127(8) (tenant duty) and Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 132(D): any criminal activity that threatens the health, safety or right of peaceful enjoyment of the premises by other tenants, committed by the tenant, a household member, a guest or other person under the tenant's control, or that is a danger to the premises, and any drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises by any of them 'shall be grounds for immediate termination of the lease'. The clause uses the statute's own words. Victim carve-out: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 113.3 (no denial, nonrenewal or termination because a household member is a victim or alleged victim of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking). The statute does not define 'drug-related criminal activity'; a licensed patient's or caregiver's medical use of marijuana in accordance with the medical marijuana laws is not subject to arrest, prosecution or penalty under state law (Okla. Stat. tit. 63, § 427.8(F)), and a landlord may not penalize a licensed patient solely for that status (Okla. Stat. tit. 63, § 425(A); edu-medical-marijuana-ok). How a court applies 'immediate termination' procedurally (notice to quit, FED filing) is case law, unread; the shared default clause already carves out no-cure grounds (default-by-tenant-ks-ne). title: Rules and Changes to Rules
bodyText: Tenant will comply with the rules and regulations for the property in effect when this Lease is signed: [attach or describe the rules, or state that there are none]. Landlord may adopt new rules or regulations, or amend existing ones, during the Term by giving Tenant written notice. A rule binds Tenant only if its purpose is to promote the convenience, peace, safety or welfare of the tenants, preserve the property from abusive use, or make a fair distribution of services and facilities; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner; it is explicit enough to tell Tenant what to do or not do; and it is not for the purpose of evading Landlord's obligations. A new or amended rule that works a substantial modification of Tenant's bargain under this Lease binds Tenant only if Tenant consents to it in writing.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 126(A): a landlord may adopt rules 'from time to time', enforceable only if they meet six conditions (purpose; reasonable relation; fair application to all tenants; sufficiently explicit; not to evade the landlord's obligations; the tenant has notice at signing or when adopted); Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 126(B): a rule adopted after the tenant enters the rental agreement that works a substantial modification of the bargain is not valid against the tenant unless he consents in writing. Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 127(7): the tenant must comply with rules in accordance with Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 126. 'Rental agreement' includes valid rules adopted under Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 126 (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 102(12)). The clause states the statute's conditions (it cannot loosen them, Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 103(B)) and gives the written notice Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 126(A)(6) requires. Model rules-amendment-in (Taylor approved that kind of clause for IN, 2026-09-30); unlike Indiana, Oklahoma itself lets the landlord adopt rules mid-term, so the clause adds the documentation and binds the tenant to the notice method rather than creating the right. Optional (CONDITIONAL). Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 126 read whole. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Chores and Repairs by the Tenant Need a Separate Writing
bodyText: In Oklahoma, if you want the tenant to take on specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling (yard work, snow removal, filter changes and the like), put it in a conspicuous writing independent of the lease, signed separately; a chore clause inside the lease or an attached addendum risks being unenforceable. Use the optional Tenant Maintenance Agreement, printed as its own document.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 118(A)-(B); Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 127 (tenant duties); Okla. Stat. tit. 41, §§ 103(B), 113(A)(1). title: No Marijuana Cultivation
bodyText: Tenant will not grow or cultivate marijuana anywhere on the property, and will not permit any occupant or guest to do so. Tenant will not operate marijuana extraction equipment or use any marijuana extraction process at the property.
notes: OK: Optional clause (rule 54). A licensed patient or caregiver may grow medical marijuana only on real property the patient owns or 'for which the patient license holder has the property owner's written permission to grow marijuana on the property' (Okla. Stat. tit. 63, § 427.12(A)); the clause confirms that no permission is given by the lease, so a landlord who wants to allow growing would say so in writing instead. Extraction using butane, propane, carbon dioxide or any potentially hazardous material is prohibited in a residential property (Okla. Stat. tit. 63, § 427.12(C)); the clause's broader ban on any extraction process is a lease term the landlord may choose. A landlord may not refuse to lease to or penalize a person solely for patient status (Okla. Stat. tit. 63, § 425(A)); this clause restricts conduct, not status, and leaves non-smoked consumption alone (Okla. Stat. tit. 63, § 427.8(C); smoking-policy tagged). The OREC 2026 Residential Lease bars growing and cultivation (OK log §15). Recreational marijuana is not legal in Oklahoma. edu-medical-marijuana-ok. CONDITIONAL: offered, not a default. title: Registered Sex Offenders Living Together
bodyText: Tenant will not allow any person who is required to register under the Oklahoma Sex Offenders Registration Act to live at the property if another person who is required to register also lives at the property, unless Oklahoma law permits them to live together (for example, because they are married to each other or are blood relatives).
notes: OK: Optional clause (rule 54). It is unlawful for two or more persons required to register as sex offenders to reside together in any individual dwelling, except married persons and blood relatives, and except separate dwellings in a properly zoned multi-unit structure (Okla. Stat. tit. 57, § 590.1(A)(1)-(4)); 'No person or entity shall knowingly establish, lease, operate, or own any structure or portion of a structure where persons required to register ... are allowed to reside together in violation of this section', a misdemeanor rising to a felony (Okla. Stat. tit. 57, § 590.1(E)-(F)) (read whole; amended by 2025 Okla. Sess. Laws ch. 486, eff. Jan. 1, 2026, per the history line; current text read). The clause restates the statutory prohibition as a tenant duty so the landlord does not 'allow' a violation. Registrants are not a protected class (Okla. title: Oklahoma Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: Any damage or security deposit you require must be kept in an escrow account for the tenant at a federally insured financial institution in Oklahoma; misappropriating it is a crime punishable by up to six months in county jail and a fine of up to twice the amount taken. When the tenancy ends you may apply the deposit to accrued rent and to damages caused by the tenant's noncompliance with the lease or the Landlord and Tenant Act, itemized in a written statement delivered by mail, return receipt requested, or in person. You must return the balance, without interest, within 45 days after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession and the tenant makes a written demand. If the tenant makes no written demand within six months after the tenancy ends, the deposit becomes yours. If you do not follow these rules, or do not return prepaid rent the Act requires you to return, the tenant may recover the deposit and the prepaid rent. Unless the lease allows it, the tenant may not use the deposit as the last month's rent. When you sell or otherwise lose your interest in the property, you must within a reasonable time either transfer the deposits to your successor and tell the tenants in writing who holds them, or return them.

title: Tenant Remedies for Repairs
bodyText: If you materially fail to comply with the lease or with your repair duties in a way that materially affects health or safety, the tenant may give written notice that the lease will end on a date at least 30 days after you receive it unless you fix the problem within 14 days. If the problem materially affects health and can be fixed for no more than one month's rent, the tenant may give written notice and, if you do not fix it within 14 days (or as promptly as an emergency requires), have the work done in a workmanlike manner and deduct the actual, reasonable cost from rent after giving you an itemized statement. If you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may, after written notice, end the lease immediately, buy the service and deduct the cost, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing and pay no rent for the period. If the unit becomes uninhabitable or poses an imminent threat to health and safety and you do not fix it promptly, the tenant may end the lease immediately by written notice. None of these rights arises until the tenant gives you written notice, or if the tenant, a family member, a pet or a person or animal there with the tenant's consent caused the problem. A tenant evicted for rent withheld over a good-faith essential-services claim, who gave you written notice within 10 days after the rent was due, may cure within 72 hours of judgment by paying the judgment, costs and fees.

title: Nonpayment of Rent
bodyText: If rent is unpaid when due you may sue for it at any time, or wait out the cure period first. To end the lease for nonpayment, give the tenant written notice demanding payment; if the tenant does not pay within five days after the notice, you may terminate. The notice may be given before or after you file suit, and a demand for past-due rent counts as a demand for possession, so no separate notice to quit is needed. The notice must be served as the Landlord and Tenant Act requires: personally; if the tenant cannot be located, by delivery to a family member over 12 living with the tenant; otherwise by posting it conspicuously on the unit and mailing a copy by certified mail.

title: Other Lease Violations
bodyText: For a breach other than nonpayment, your remedy depends on the breach. If it can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning and the tenant does not fix it within 10 days after written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires), you may enter, have the work done and bill the reasonable cost as rent due on the next rent date (you may not then terminate for that breach). For a material breach, you may serve written notice that the lease will end on a date at least 15 days after the tenant receives it unless the tenant remedies the breach within 10 days; if the tenant remedies it, the lease continues, but any later breach allows immediate termination on written notice. If the breach causes or threatens imminent and irremediable harm to the premises or any person and is not remedied promptly, you may terminate by immediately filing an eviction. Criminal activity that threatens other tenants' health, safety or peaceful enjoyment or endangers the premises, and drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises, by the tenant, a household member, a guest or another person under the tenant's control, are grounds for immediate termination. Notices are served as the Act requires (personally, to a family member over 12, or by posting plus certified mail).

bodyText: If the tenant's breach can be remedied by repair, replacement of a damaged item or cleaning, and the tenant does not remedy it within 10 days after your written notice (served as the Act requires) or as promptly as an emergency requires, you may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner, and submit an itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost as rent due on the next rent date, or for immediate payment if the lease has ended. title: No Lockouts
bodyText: You may not remove or exclude a tenant from the unit except through the court eviction process. If you wrongfully remove or exclude a tenant, the tenant may recover possession in court or end the lease, and in either case recover up to twice the average monthly rent or twice the tenant's actual damages, whichever is greater; if the lease ends you must return the deposit and all prepaid and unearned rent. Using force or violence to enter or keep possession of another's property, except as the law allows, is a misdemeanor.

title: The Eviction Case
bodyText: An eviction (forcible entry and detainer) is filed in district court by an affidavit on a form the Oklahoma Bar Association develops, and for cases on the small claims docket the court clerk prepares the affidavit and summons and assists unrepresented plaintiffs. Claims for rent, damage to the premises and Landlord and Tenant Act claims may be joined, but no others. Cases within the small claims limit go on the small claims docket, and a court may assign any eviction there to decide possession. The summons sets trial not less than five nor more than ten days after it issues and must be served at least three days before trial; if the tenant cannot be served personally or through a resident over 15, it may be served by certified mail, or (for possession only) posted and mailed at least five days before trial. Possession is tried without a jury; a jury may be requested only on the money claims, which are then severed. A reasonable attorney fee goes to the prevailing party. After judgment the writ of execution issues; you, your agent or an officer must give notice that you will return in 48 hours to restore possession, and may ask the sheriff or city police for help. A motion for new trial must be filed within three days and does not stay the writ. The tenant may post a supersedeas bond within two days after judgment (a judge may extend this to seven days); while an appeal is pending the tenant must keep paying current rent into the court clerk's office, and failing to pay is treated as abandoning the appeal.

title: Property Left After an Eviction
bodyText: After a tenant is lawfully removed through an eviction, the Landlord and Tenant Act's abandoned-property procedure applies to belongings left in or around the unit: property with no apparent value may be disposed of; property of apparent value requires written notice by certified mail, and property left 30 days or longer is conclusively abandoned. Store it with reasonable care in the meantime. Executing a writ in the lawful manner does not expose you to an unlawful-entry claim. A person who returns to live on the property without authority after being removed by court process commits a misdemeanor, as does anyone who wrongfully refuses to surrender possession when the writ is served.

title: Tenant Who Stays After the Lease Ends
bodyText: If a tenant stays without your consent after the lease ends or is terminated, you may sue at once for possession and damages. If the holdover is willful and not in good faith, you may also recover up to twice the average monthly rent, prorated daily, for each month or part of a month the tenant stays. If you consent to the tenant staying, a month-to-month tenancy is created unless you agree otherwise. Separately, an older statute makes double rent the measure of damages when a tenant who gave notice of intent to leave fails to give up the premises. If you accept rent after the term ends without any agreement, an older presumption of renewal on the same terms (for up to a year) may be argued; say in the lease what happens instead.

title: Domestic Violence, Sexual Violence and Stalking
bodyText: You may not deny, refuse to renew or terminate a tenancy because an applicant, tenant or household member is a victim or alleged victim of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking, whether or not there is a current protective order, and you may not deny a tenancy to or retaliate against someone because they previously ended a rental agreement as a victim. A victim may end the lease without penalty by giving you written notice and a protective order within 30 days of the incident, unless you waive that time limit. The lease cannot waive a tenant's right to call the police or other emergency help.

title: Removing Unauthorized Occupants and Squatters
bodyText: Someone who never had a rental agreement with you and whom you never accepted as a tenant is not protected by the Landlord and Tenant Act's termination rules: you may demand that the person leave without filing an eviction, and refusing within a reasonable time is a trespass (fine up to $500). An occupant living with a tenant who breaches the lease must leave on your written request (trespass, fine up to $500 or 30 days in jail). For squatters, an owner or authorized agent may file a verified complaint on the statutory form asking the sheriff for immediate removal, if the property was not open to the public, the occupants were told to leave, they are not current or former tenants, cannot show a lease signed by the owner or government mail at the address in the last 12 months, are not the owner's immediate family, and no litigation is pending. The sheriff serves a notice to vacate and puts the owner in possession. A person wrongfully removed this way can recover actual damages, three times the fair market rent, costs and fees. The squatter law does not override the Landlord and Tenant Act.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111(G) (2021 Okla. Sess. Laws ch. 410), Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 117(B); Okla. title: Tenant Who Abandons During the Lease
bodyText: Every party to a lease must mitigate damages. If a tenant wrongfully abandons during the term, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent. If you re-rent for a term starting before the old lease ends, the old lease ends when the new tenancy starts. If you do not make reasonable efforts, or accept the abandonment as a surrender, the lease is treated as ended by you on the date you learned of the abandonment. If you make reasonable efforts but cannot re-rent at a fair rent, the tenant owes the rent (or the shortfall) for the rest of the term; for a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy the 'term' is one month or one week.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, §§ 105(A), 129(B). Belongings left behind: abandoned-property-ok. Rule 37: periodic term measured as one period (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 129(B)). title: Fire or Casualty
bodyText: If fire or another casualty substantially impairs the tenant's use of the unit, the tenant may move out and notify you in writing within one week of an intent to end the lease (the lease ends on the date of moving out), or, if the unit can still be partly used, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion. These rights do not apply if the tenant, a family member, a pet or a person or animal there with the tenant's consent caused the damage deliberately or negligently. If the lease ends, return the deposit and all prepaid and unearned rent, accounting as of the date of the casualty. The statute gives you no termination right of your own; the lease can add one.

title: Damage the Tenant Causes
bodyText: The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or let anyone, or any animal, do so. Oklahoma's casualty, repair-and-deduct, essential-service and habitability remedies are each unavailable when the tenant, a family member, a pet or a person or animal there with the tenant's consent caused the condition, so a tenant who causes a fire cannot use the casualty statute to walk away rent-free or reduce the rent. You can recover the repair cost and your other damages, subject to your duty to mitigate. The optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause states in the lease that rent does not abate and that the tenant owes lost rent if the lease ends because of the damage.

title: Tenant Duties
bodyText: Oklahoma law requires the tenant to: keep the part of the premises the tenant uses as safe, clean and sanitary as its condition permits; dispose of garbage and waste safely; keep plumbing fixtures as clean as their condition permits; use electrical, plumbing, heating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances safely; not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or let any person or pet do so; not disturb other tenants' quiet enjoyment or let others do so; follow valid rules; and not engage in threatening criminal activity or drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises, personally or through household members or guests. The tenant must also report defects the tenant has reason to believe you do not know about as soon as practicable, and must promptly tell you about any legal proceeding to recover the property.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: You may ask each tenant in writing for the name, address and phone number of a person to contact if the tenant dies, and for a signed statement authorizing you to let that person in (with you present), let them remove the tenant's belongings and refund the deposit to them. If a sole occupant dies, you may remove and store the belongings; you must hand them over to the designated person, or anyone else lawfully entitled, who asks before they are discarded; refund the deposit less lawful deductions (including removal and storage costs); and have anyone who removes property sign an inventory. You may discard the property if you mailed the designee a certified-mail request, return receipt requested, the property was not removed by the 30th day after the postmark, and no one has claimed it. A lease may set a different procedure. A tenant who knowingly refuses to provide the information after your request relieves you of responsibility for the belongings; a landlord who knowingly violates the procedure after receiving a copy of the statute is liable to the estate for actual damages.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130.1 (2006 Okla. Sess. Laws ch. 23) read whole. The act does not say whether the lease itself ends at the tenant's death (case law and probate law unread). title: Landlord's Lien on Tenant Property
bodyText: Oklahoma gives a residential landlord a lien on the tenant's property in the unit, in an amount reasonably related to the debt, for proper charges owed and the cost of enforcing the lien, with a right to possession until paid. The lien is secondary to a prior chattel mortgage or conditional seller, and does not reach tools, instruments and books used in a trade, family portraits, clothing, medical and health aids and appliances, bedding, washers, refrigerators, food, cooking and eating utensils, baby beds and baby-care items, among others. It is enforced like any other general lien under the lien statutes. A lease may not create any other lien on the tenant's property.

title: Who the Landlord and Tenant Act Covers
bodyText: The Oklahoma Residential Landlord and Tenant Act governs rental agreements for dwelling units in Oklahoma, including lots leased for manufactured or mobile homes. It does not govern (unless the arrangement was created to avoid the Act): residence in an institution incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counseling or religious services; occupancy under a contract for deed by the buyer; fraternal or social organization housing for members; transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or similar lodging, however long the stay; occupancy by a condominium owner or cooperative proprietary lessee; and occupancy of premises used primarily for agricultural purposes. Nonresidential property left behind is governed by a separate procedure.

title: How to Serve Notices
bodyText: A written notice to end a tenancy under the Landlord and Tenant Act must be served on the tenant personally unless the law says otherwise. If the tenant cannot be located, deliver it to a family member over 12 living with the tenant. If neither can be served, post it in a conspicuous place on the unit and mail a copy by certified mail (or through the Postal Service's Firm Mailing Book for Accountable Mail). A tenant serves you personally or, if you cannot be served personally, by certified mail to the person named to accept service. Times are counted by excluding the first day and including the last, and a last day that is a legal holiday is skipped.

title: Oklahoma Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Oklahoma's Discrimination in Housing Act makes it unlawful to refuse to rent, to set different terms, to advertise a preference, or to falsely say a unit is unavailable because of race, color, religion, gender, national origin, age, familial status or disability. 'Familial status' covers a person who is pregnant, lives with a child under 18 as parent, legal custodian or with the parent's written permission, or is getting custody of a child; 'age' protects adults 18 and older. You may not refuse to consider a verified source of income such as public assistance, alimony or court-awarded child support where the refusal is because of one of those protected classes. You must allow reasonable modifications for a person with a disability at that person's expense (the person may be required to provide a surety bond guaranteeing restoration), and make reasonable accommodations in rules and policies. The Act does not protect any other class, and it does not prohibit refusing a person convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. It does not apply to a single-family house rented by an owner of no more than three such houses without a broker or discriminatory advertising (if the owner was not the most recent resident, only one such sale or rental every 24 months), to rooms or units in a building of up to four families where the owner lives in one of them, to certain religious and private-club housing, or (for familial status) to qualifying housing for older persons. A complaint to the Attorney General may be filed within one year; a court may award actual and punitive damages and attorney fees. Federal fair housing law applies separately and its exemptions differ.

title: Assistance Animals and Service Dogs
bodyText: A person with a disability may ask for a reasonable accommodation to keep an assistance animal (a service animal or an emotional support animal). Unless the disability or the need is readily apparent, you may ask for reliable supporting documentation that verifies the disability under the Fair Housing Act, describes the accommodation needed and shows how it relates to the disability, and you may independently verify it. Documentation that was bought is presumed fraudulent. You are not liable for injuries caused by an assistance animal you allowed as an accommodation. If a tenant got the accommodation by knowingly making a false claim or giving fraudulent documentation, you may use the ordinary lease-breach notice procedure, and in an eviction you may be awarded court costs, fees and up to $1,000 in damages. You may not refuse to rent to a blind, deaf or disabled person because of a properly trained guide, signal or service dog, or charge an extra nonrefundable fee or an unreasonable deposit for one, but the tenant may be liable for damage the dog does.

title: Foreign Ownership and Leasing of Land
bodyText: Oklahoma's Constitution and statutes bar an alien who is not a bona fide resident of Oklahoma from acquiring title to or owning land, and require an affidavit with each recorded deed. Starting November 1, 2026, the statute also says that such a person, a designated foreign terrorist organization, a Specially Designated National, or a foreign government adversary may not lease land in Oklahoma. The ban does not apply to an alien who is or becomes a bona fide resident of Oklahoma. Whether an ordinary residential lease of a home is 'leasing land' under this statute has not been decided in anything read here. Starting July 1, 2027, a foreign principal from a foreign adversary country (including an individual domiciled there who is not a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident) may not rent or otherwise control real property within ten miles of a military base or installation, a military operating area or other critical infrastructure, and conflicting rental agreements are invalid; a landlord who is not such a foreign principal is not required to inquire and has no civil or criminal liability under that section. Asking applicants about citizenship carries fair housing risk (national origin).

title: Registered Sex Offenders
bodyText: Two or more people required to register as sex offenders may not live together in the same individual dwelling (a house, an apartment, a room in a boarding house, or a unit in a multi-unit building), unless they are married to each other or are blood relatives; separate units in a properly zoned apartment building are allowed. A person or entity that knowingly leases or owns a structure where registrants are allowed to live together in violation of this rule commits a crime (a misdemeanor, rising to a felony on a third conviction). Renting rooms to registrants as a boarding house or group home is unlawful unless treatment services are provided. A registrant also may not live within 2,000 feet of a school, child care facility, qualifying park or playground or the victim's home, and a registrant whose victim was a minor may not live with a minor child except his or her own child, stepchild or grandchild who was not the victim; those duties fall on the registrant. Oklahoma's fair housing law does not protect people because of a criminal record.

bodyText: Oklahoma has no general statute on tenant screening, application fees or criminal-history policies for private landlords. title: Medical Marijuana Patients
bodyText: Oklahoma allows medical marijuana for licensed patients; recreational marijuana is not legal. You may not refuse to lease to, or otherwise penalize, a person solely because he or she is a licensed medical marijuana patient, unless leasing to that person would put you at risk of losing a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law. You may prohibit smoking or vaporizing marijuana on the premises, inside its structures and within ten feet of the entry, but a patient may not be denied other lawful, non-smoked products. A patient or caregiver may grow marijuana only on property he or she owns or with the property owner's written permission, and the plants must not be accessible to the public or visible from the street. Extraction using butane, propane, carbon dioxide or another hazardous material is prohibited in a residential property.

title: Penalties and Fixed Damages in a Lease
bodyText: Oklahoma voids contract penalties for non-performance. A lease term fixing in advance the amount owed for a breach is valid only when, from the nature of the case, it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage; otherwise it is void to that extent. title: Consumer Protection Act
bodyText: Oklahoma's Consumer Protection Act prohibits deceptive and unfair trade practices in 'consumer transactions', defined as advertising, offering, selling, purchasing or distributing services or property, including real property, for personal, household or business purposes. title: Electronic Leases, Signatures and Notices

title: Two Habitability Statements Your Colorado Lease Must Carry
bodyText: Since January 1, 2025 every Colorado residential lease must carry two separate statements, both in at least twelve-point bold-faced type (C.R.S. 38-12-505(3)(c) and (3)(d)). The first says the tenant is entitled to safe and healthy housing under the warranty of habitability and that you may not retaliate for reporting unsafe conditions, requesting repairs or asserting that right. The second must appear in both English and Spanish, and must give an address where the tenant can mail or hand-deliver written notice of an uninhabitable condition and an email address or online tenant portal for the same notice - both, not either. Two practical points. If you offer an online tenant portal, the same English-and-Spanish statement must also be posted conspicuously inside the portal (38-12-505(3)(e)). And whatever channels your lease names become channels that count: a tenant notice is sufficient if it uses any method the rental agreement permits (38-12-503(3)(f)(I)), so you have to actually monitor the mailbox, the inbox and the portal. Never name a phone number or any verbal method - a lease that lets the tenant give habitability notice verbally waives your right to written notice entirely (38-12-503(3)(f)(II)).

title: Surrender at End of Term
bodyText: When Tenant's right to possess the property ends - because the Term expires and applicable law does not entitle Tenant to remain, because Landlord lawfully terminates this Lease, because Tenant gives notice and vacates, because Landlord and Tenant agree to end the tenancy, or because a court enters and lawfully executes a judgment for possession - Tenant will surrender possession of the property and return all keys to Landlord immediately. The property will be left in the same condition as at the start of the Term, except for ordinary wear and tear, and free of all personal property of Tenant and any occupants. Personal property left at the property after Tenant vacates may, to the extent permitted by applicable law, be treated as abandoned and disposed of at Tenant's cost.
notes: CO: CITED - C.R.S. § 38-12-1303(1), (2)(c); § 38-12-1305; § 13-40-104(1)(c). NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 41. Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). Supersedes the shared surrender-end-of-term, whose unqualified "upon the expiration or earlier termination ... Tenant will surrender possession" is wrong for a covered Colorado tenancy: expiration alone is not cause (§ 38-12-1303(2)(c) limits the holdover ground to nonresidential premises and the § 38-12-1302(1)(a), (b), (d), (e), (f) exemptions), and § 38-12-1305 voids a lease provision that modifies part 13. This wording works for both covered and exempt Colorado tenancies: for an exempt tenancy the first limb operates on expiration, and for a covered one it operates only once a no-fault ground under § 38-12-1303(3) or a cause ground has been used. title: Landlord and Authorized Agent Identity
bodyText: As Colorado law requires, Landlord states that the name and address of the person who is the Landlord, or the Landlord's authorized agent, is: [insert the name and address of the landlord or the landlord's authorized agent].

(Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). Verbatim duty: "A written rental agreement must include a statement indicating to the tenant the name and address of the person who is the landlord or the landlord's authorized agent." Colorado had NO row on the owner-identity-disclosure topic before this retro, although 24 of the other 25 states do and § 38-12-801(2) plainly makes it required lease content. The separate one-business-day duty to notify or conspicuously post on a change of landlord or agent (§ 38-12-801(2)(a), (2)(b)) is an operational duty and stays in edu-identity-change-notice-co. No exemption: unlike § 38-12-801(2.5), subsection (2) carries no small-landlord carve-out, and the § 38-12-801(4) and (8) carve-outs reach only subsection (3).

title: Only the Monthly Occupancy Payment Is Rent
bodyText: For the purpose of any remedy to collect Rent, including eviction, "Rent" under this Lease means only the set monthly payment for occupancy of the property. No other amount or fee set out in this Lease - including any pet fee, pet rent, late fee, returned-payment charge, utility or service charge, or other charge - is Rent for that purpose, and Landlord will not pursue eviction or any other remedy for the collection of Rent on the basis of Tenant's failure to pay such an amount. Landlord may pursue any other remedy applicable law allows for those amounts. This Section controls over any contrary provision of this Lease.
notes: CO: CITED - C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3)(a)(V), (3)(b), (7)(c); § 38-12-105(7). NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 27 (topic fees-as-rent) and rule 42. Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). Verbatim prohibition: a written rental agreement must not include "A provision that characterizes any amount or fee set forth in the rental agreement, with the sole exception of the set monthly payment for occupancy of the premises, as 'rent' for which all remedies to collect rent, including eviction, are available. Such amounts and fees include any fees for utilities or services and any other charge that is not rent." § 38-12-801(3)(b): any provision included in violation of subsection (3) "is void and unenforceable". § 38-12-105(7) says the same for late fees specifically and cross-refers § 13-40-104(1)(d). Why a lease clause and not education only: the library uses an undefined capitalised "Rent" across rent-payment, due-at-signing, application-of-payments and default-by-tenant, while pet-policy charges "pet rent" - so without this clause a Colorado tenant can argue the lease characterises fees as Rent with eviction available, which voids the offending provision under (3)(b). Stating the narrow definition protects the landlord's remedies rather than conceding anything, so it is a SERVES_LANDLORD lease clause under the rule 55 three-bucket test. SCOPE (rule 32): § 38-12-801(4) exempts a mobile home in a mobile home park and § 38-12-801(8) exempts an owner-occupied duplex, triplex or ADU from (3)(a)(V); the clause is lawful and harmless for those landlords too, so it is offered to all. Chosen over forking the shared pet-policy row (rule 62): one CO clause cures the characterisation for the whole lease. Companion: edu-fees-not-rent-co.

title: In Colorado, Only the Monthly Rent Is Evictable Rent
bodyText: Colorado bars you from writing a lease that treats anything except the set monthly payment for occupancy as "rent" with all the rent-collection remedies, eviction included (C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(V)). Utility and service charges are named in the statute, and so is "any other charge that is not rent". A provision that breaks this rule is void and unenforceable (38-12-801(3)(b)), and a late fee gets the same treatment in its own section (38-12-105(7)). The practical consequence is the part landlords most often get wrong: you can charge pet rent in Colorado, up to the 38-12-106(2) cap, but you cannot evict for it. Online guidance that says unpaid pet rent is grounds for a 10-day demand and an eviction is wrong here. Same for unpaid utility charges, late fees and returned-payment charges: they are real debts you can sue for, but not a basis for a possession action. Two carve-outs: subsection (3)(a)(V) does not apply to a mobile home in a mobile home park (38-12-801(4)) or to a duplex, triplex or accessory dwelling unit where you live in one of the units or on the same lot (38-12-801(8)).
notes: CO: CITED - C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3)(a)(V), (3)(b), (4), (8); § 38-12-105(7); § 38-12-106(2). NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 27 (topic fees-as-rent). Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). Resolves an open question carried in this project: the widely-copied claim that Colorado pet rent is rent and supports an eviction is wrong on the enacted text. § 38-12-106(2) permits "additional rent" for a pet up to the greater of $35/month or 1.5% of monthly rent, so the charge is lawful; § 38-12-801(3)(a)(V) separately forbids making it evictable. Pet caps: edu-pet-caps-co. Clause: rent-definition-fees-not-rent-co.

title: Electronic Notices: What Colorado Will Not Let You Email
bodyText: Colorado's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act carves residential landlords out of exactly the notices that matter most. It does not apply to any notice of default, acceleration, repossession, foreclosure or eviction, or of the right to cure, under a rental agreement for an individual's primary residence (C.R.S. 24-71.3-103(3)(b)(II)), nor to a notice cancelling or terminating utility service including water, heat and power (3)(b)(I). So a 10-day demand for payment or compliance, a notice to terminate and a notice of default get no help from the electronic-records statute: email or portal delivery of one of those rests on ordinary proof that it actually reached the tenant, not on a statutory rule that electronic counts as writing. Three more limits. The Act only applies between parties who have each agreed to transact electronically, and a party who agrees once may refuse the next transaction - a right that cannot be waived by agreement (24-71.3-105(2), (3)). An electronic record satisfies a writing requirement only if the recipient can retain it at the time of receipt, and if your system stops the tenant printing or storing it the record is not enforceable against them (24-71.3-108(1), (3)). And those requirements cannot be varied by agreement (24-71.3-108(4)), so no lease clause fixes any of this. Send default, cure, termination and eviction notices the way article 40 of title 13 requires, and keep habitability notices separate - those the law positively requires you to accept by email or portal.

The electronic-transactions act itself was read, not only the landlord-tenant notice sections that refer to it: read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00) (title 24). Colorado had no row on the notice-delivery-methods topic before this retro. Clause screen result: no CO-tagged clause relies on electronic delivery of an excluded notice. The shared notices row is what protects the library - its closing sentence ("nothing in this Lease designates an alternative method of delivery for any notice governed by law") is load-bearing in Colorado and should not be trimmed. landlords-access-co's "written or electronic" bed-bug entry notice is NOT an excluded notice and is expressly authorised by § 38-12-1004(1)(a). Habitability notice runs the other way: § 38-12-505(3)(d) requires an email or portal channel in the lease. Contrast with edu-written-notice-strictly-required-co, which is about the landlord's right to receive written notice.

title: Mandatory Mediation Before Filing, and the Waiver You Cannot Put in the Lease
bodyText: Before filing an eviction against a residential tenant who receives SSI, Social Security disability insurance under Title II, or Colorado Works cash assistance, you must have gone through mandatory mediation and had it fail, and your complaint must carry an affidavit saying so (C.R.S. 13-40-110(1)(a)). You are exempt if you are a 501(c)(3) that offers tenants mediation, or a landlord with five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five total rental units including any single-family homes. The tenant can also take you out of it by not disclosing, or declining to disclose in writing, that they receive one of those benefits in response to your written inquiry - which is a good reason to make that written inquiry. Mediation is free to the tenant; you pay only your share; the Office of Dispute Resolution must schedule it within 14 days of your request. Getting this wrong is fatal to the case: non-compliance is an affirmative defense and the court "shall dismiss the case without prejudice" (13-40-110(1)(d)). The part that touches your lease: a tenant may voluntarily waive mandatory mediation, "but a waiver must not be in any lease agreement or other agreement" (13-40-110(1)(b)), and 38-12-801(3)(a)(III)(E) separately voids a lease waiver of it. A lease clause also may not let you recoup mediation costs from the tenant (38-12-801(3)(a)(VII)). So the waiver has to be a separate, later, voluntary document - never a lease term.

NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 48 (also rules 47, 50). Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). This is Colorado's separate-document answer: the mediation waiver is a thing the statute allows the tenant to do but expressly forbids the lease to carry. Note for rule 21: § 38-12-801(3)(a) contains TWO subsections numbered (VII), a single-session double-amendment artifact in the official 2026 compilation - the first is the voucher-provider utility-nonpayment ban, the second the mediation-cost recoupment ban. Flagged for the legal watch; cite by the act where the number matters.

title: When the Tenant Causes the Damage
bodyText: Colorado handles this in one place rather than remedy by remedy, and it handles it in your favour. If a condition is substantially caused by the misconduct of the tenant, a member of the tenant's household, a guest or invitee, or someone under the tenant's direction or control, that condition "does not constitute a basis for a breach of the warranty of habitability" (C.R.S. 38-12-503(9)). Because every tenant remedy in 38-12-507 - the 10-to-60 day termination right, the recurrence termination right, repair-and-deduct, appliance replace-and-deduct, the damages claim including any reduction in fair rental value, and injunctive relief - is predicated on a breach of that warranty, tenant-caused damage switches all of them off at once. You also stop being the one who pays: 38-12-503(7) makes the landlord responsible for remedying at the landlord's own expense "except as described in subsection (9)". There is one exception to the exception: it is not misconduct if the condition resulted from domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking against the tenant and you have notice of it. Colorado has no casualty or untenantability statute in article 12 giving a tenant a separate right to walk away after a fire, so there is no second door for them to leave by; the only casualty termination is yours, under 38-12-503(11), and it needs your lease to permit it. Recovering the money runs through ordinary channels - the tenant's maintenance obligations, the deposit (38-12-103(1)(b) allows retention for repair of damage beyond normal wear and tear) and a contract claim for lost rent. No special Colorado clause is needed or offered, and a clause purporting to strip abatement rights more broadly than 38-12-503(9) does would be void under 38-12-503(10).
notes: CO: CITED - C.R.S. § 38-12-503(7), (9), (10), (11); § 38-12-507(1)(a)-(e); § 38-12-103(1)(b). NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 54t. Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). Rule 54t asks for each abatement or exit provision to be checked separately for its own tenant-fault exception: in Colorado there is a single gate at § 38-12-503(9) that conditions the whole of part 5, so every § 38-12-507 remedy inherits it and no per-remedy check diverges. Casualty: "casualty", "damaged by fire" and "fire or other" return zero hits across article 12 of title 38 in the official 2026 text (control term returns zero), consistent with the confirmed absence already recorded in edu-casualty-habitability-co. VERDICT on a state version of tenant-caused-damage-tn (read, not tagged): NOT OFFERED - the law already allocates repair cost and abatement, and a clause going further risks § 38-12-503(10) and the § 38-12-801(3)(a)(I) eviction-penalty ban. Boundary: common-law measures for lost rent were not researched.

title: Colorado Regulates AI That Prices or Screens Housing
bodyText: Colorado has no rent-setting-cartel statute of the kind some states have passed, but it does have something broader that reaches the same software. The Colorado Artificial Intelligence Act (C.R.S. 6-1-1701 et seq.) regulates systems that make, or substantially contribute to, a "consequential decision" - and housing is one of the listed domains (6-1-1701(3)(f)). If you deploy an AI or algorithmic tool to set rents, score applicants or decide renewals, you are a deployer, with duties to avoid algorithmic discrimination, run a risk-management programme, disclose the system to the consumer and report discovered discrimination (6-1-1702 to 6-1-1705). Violating part 17 is itself a deceptive trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act (6-1-105(1)(hhhh)), which carries treble damages, so the exposure is not theoretical. Watch the date: SB 26-189 repealed and reenacted part 17, and the new version applies to consequential decisions made on or after January 1, 2027, with a narrower "covered domain" structure and express carve-outs for low-stakes and routine decisions. Until then the 2024 version governs. Separately, the Colorado Privacy Act gives consumers an opt-out of profiling in decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects, which it defines to include the provision or denial of housing.

(Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00) (title 6). title: No Statutory Right to Fix a Tenant's Neglect and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Colorado gives a landlord no statutory self-cure right of the kind several states have - there is no provision letting you notice a tenant's neglect, do the work yourself and add the cost to the next rent payment. Two Colorado rules get in the way of writing one into the lease. Entry for repairs is governed by the habitability sections rather than a general access statute, so a self-cure entry has no statutory authorisation to rest on. And you could not bill the cost "as rent" even if you did the work: 38-12-801(3)(a)(V) reserves rent, and the remedies that go with it, to the set monthly payment for occupancy. The routes that do work are the ordinary ones - a 10-day demand for compliance or possession under 13-40-104(1)(e), the tenant's maintenance obligations, the security deposit for damage beyond normal wear and tear, and a money claim. Nothing stops you contracting for the right to do the work and recover the cost as a debt rather than as rent, but you would be drafting that from scratch and should take advice first.

title: No Blank-Space Rule, But a Real Copy Duty
bodyText: Colorado has no statute of the kind some states have requiring every blank space in a written lease to be completed, and no consumer-protection provision making a blank-filled-after-signing lease an unlawful practice. What Colorado does have is a copy duty with a deadline: you must give the tenant a copy of the written agreement signed by both of you no later than the seventh day after the tenant signs, and it may be electronic unless the tenant asks for paper (C.R.S. 38-12-801(1)). Colorado also prescribes specific content the agreement must contain - the landlord or agent name and address (38-12-801(2)), the source-of-income statement for a non-exempt landlord (38-12-801(2.5)), and the two bold-faced habitability statements (38-12-505(3)(c) and (3)(d)). So the discipline still applies even without a blank-space statute: fill or strike every bracket and placeholder before anyone signs, because an unfilled habitability-notice address or a missing identity statement is a missing required disclosure, not just an untidy lease.

title: Quiet Enjoyment Is Non-Waivable, With One Carve-Out You May Use
bodyText: Colorado does not spell out a covenant of quiet enjoyment, but it does something more useful to know about: it makes a lease waiver of the implied covenant void. A written rental agreement must not include a waiver of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment, or of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and any provision included in breach of that is void and unenforceable (C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(III)(C), (D) and (3)(b)). The same subsection then hands you a narrow permission: "a written rental agreement may provide that the landlord is not responsible for any violation of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment that is committed by a third party acting beyond the reasonable control of the landlord". That is worth using, and it is the only quiet-enjoyment disclaimer Colorado allows - a broader one is void. Two carve-outs from the prohibition itself: it does not reach a mobile home in a mobile home park (38-12-801(4)) or an owner-occupied duplex, triplex or accessory dwelling unit (38-12-801(8)). Quiet enjoyment also shows up as a limit on entry, which is why the Colorado access clause ties the notice period to it.

Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). PRESENT, not absent: Colorado has no express statutory covenant but it has a non-waivability rule plus an express optional disclaimer, which is the operative content for a landlord. RULE 54 OPTIONAL CLAUSE: the third-party quiet-enjoyment disclaimer is a lawful option and the library already carries its substance in the shared services-utilities-provided clause ("Landlord is not liable for any interruption or insufficiency of a service or utility resulting from causes beyond Landlord's reasonable control"); a broader stand-alone disclaimer is NOT offered because (3)(a)(III)(D) would void it. title: Statutory Forms in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado prescribes no form of lease, but it does prescribe text and forms you have to use. The radon warning statement is given in the statute's own words and must appear in bold-faced type "in substantially the same form" (C.R.S. 38-12-803(2)(a)(I)), inside a separate document the tenant signs. The source-of-income statement is set out in 38-12-801(2.5)(a) and the two habitability statements in 38-12-505(3)(c) and (3)(d) are prescribed by content, language and type size. On the court side, an eviction is commenced "using the standard form of eviction complaint and affidavit for a residential tenancy that is available online through the judicial department's website" (13-40-110(1)(a)), though the court must accept a different form that meets the section's requirements (13-40-110(1)(f)). The Judicial Branch also publishes the JDF demand, notice, summons, answer and writ forms; those are court forms, not statutory text, and are worth using because they are kept current. No form is prescribed for the 10-day demand itself - what matters is that its content matches 13-40-104.

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: Colorado statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells. The lease governs, through its alteration and installation terms and its rules on fixing things to the building. If you do allow one, remember that a doorbell camera is an alteration to the property for which the no-alterations clause requires your written consent, and that Colorado's wiretap, eavesdropping and privacy-tort law was not reviewed here and is the place any recording question gets answered.

title: The Radon Disclosure Cannot Live in the Lease
bodyText: Colorado does not let the lease carry this one. Before the lease is signed, you must give the tenant a separate written radon disclosure "in a document that the tenant signs to acknowledge receipt" (C.R.S. 38-12-803(2)(a)), and that document has to contain three things: the radon warning statement in bold-faced type, clearly legible and in substantially the form the statute sets out; everything you know about radon at the property - whether a test has been done, the current records and reports, any concentrations detected, any mitigation or remediation performed, and a description and documentation of any mitigation system; and a copy of the most recent radon brochure the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment publishes. The tenant acknowledges receipt by signing that document, not the lease (38-12-803(2)(b)). Your lease's Radon Disclosure Acknowledgment says the tenant received all of that - so if you never produced the separate document, you have had the tenant sign a statement that is not true, which helps them and not you. Produce the document first, get it signed, then sign the lease. One thing to watch: the statute says "a copy of" the brochure, so emailing a link may not be enough; attach the brochure itself.
notes: CO: CITED - C.R.S. § 38-12-803(2)(a)(I)-(III), (2)(b); § 25-11-114(2)(a) (the CDPHE brochure). NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 48, added on Taylor's decision 2026-10-01 ("Acknowledgment + warning now, builder later"). Companion to the rewritten radon-disclosure-co, which is now an acknowledgment rather than the disclosure. Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). BUILDER BACKLOG (Taylor, 2026-10-01): Steinoak is to generate the separate pre-signing radon disclosure document - prescribed bold-faced warning text, landlord-knowledge fields, brochure attached. Until it exists this row is what stops the acknowledgment clause becoming evidence against the landlord. OPEN/UNREAD: whether providing a link rather than "a copy of" the brochure discharges (2)(a)(III) - no authority found either way, stated as a caution not a conclusion. Remedy for failure: § 38-12-803(3)(a)(I), tenant may void the lease and vacate under § 38-12-507, except that from 2026-01-01 subsection (3) does not apply to a lease of one year or less (§ 38-12-803(3)(b)) - see edu-radon-lease-length-co.

title: Jury Waiver for a Possession Hearing
bodyText: Landlord and Tenant each waive the right to a jury trial in any hearing to determine possession of the property, to the extent Colorado law permits that waiver. This waiver applies only to a hearing to determine possession. It does not waive either party's right to a jury trial on any claim for damages or on any other issue, and it does not waive any other right either party has under applicable law. This Section does not apply to a rental agreement concerning the occupancy of a mobile home in a mobile home park.
notes: CO: CITED - C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3)(a)(III)(A). NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 54, added on Taylor's decision 2026-10-01. Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). Verbatim basis: a written rental agreement must not include a waiver of "The right to a jury trial; except that the parties may agree to a waiver of a jury trial in a hearing to determine possession of a dwelling unit." The clause is drafted to the carve-out and no further: a waiver reaching damages or any other issue falls back inside the prohibition and is void under § 38-12-801(3)(b). Mutual rather than one-sided, because the statute speaks of "the parties" agreeing and a mutual waiver gives no unconscionability handle. OPTIONAL BY DESIGN - offered per lease, never auto-included: no choice_group and no is_default, so nothing marks it as a library default; the builder's "add my default clauses" feature runs off flags the USER sets at runtime, so no library field change is needed to honour this (Taylor, 2026-10-01). SCOPE (rule 32): one clause, not two variants. § 38-12-801(8) (owner-occupied duplex/triplex/ADU) and § 38-12-801(4) (mobile home in a mobile home park) exempt those properties FROM the (3)(a)(III) prohibition, so they would permit a BROADER waiver - the narrow possession-hearing waiver is lawful for every Colorado residential property type, and a broader owner-occupied variant is deliberately not offered because it would go void the moment the property stopped being owner-occupied. The clause is scoped away from mobile-home-park tenancies because those run under the Mobile Home Park Act (part 2 of this article; § 38-12-801(5) preserves MHPA rights), which was NOT read this pass. UNREAD: Colorado's jury-demand rules and practice for FED proceedings - how often a tenant actually demands a jury was not researched, so the practical value of the clause is not established. Related: edu-mandatory-mediation-co (§ 38-12-801(3)(a)(III)(E) mediation waiver, which by contrast may NOT be in the lease).

title: The Repayment Plan You Must Offer a Victim-Survivor
bodyText: This one is a three-business-day clock that can end your eviction case, and it is easy to miss because it sits in the eviction statute rather than the domestic-violence part. If a tenant tells you they are a victim-survivor of domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking and backs it with any one of the accepted documents - a police report, a valid protection or restraining order, a self-attestation affidavit, or a letter from a qualified third party such as a victim-service worker, attorney, social worker, medical professional, faith leader or mental health provider - then you shall offer a repayment plan no later than three business days after you serve a demand for unpaid rent, or three business days after you receive the documentation, whichever is later (C.R.S. 13-40-104(4)(e)(I)(A)). Not offering one is an affirmative defense to your unlawful-detainer action. The plan is structured at the tenant's discretion, must require full repayment of all lawfully owed rent in monthly payments of at least $25, and cannot run more than nine months. You may not charge any fees, interest or penalties connected to it (4)(e)(I)(C). The protections cannot be waived in the lease or any other agreement (4)(c). Two things that run in your favour: the tenant waives the affirmative defense if they neither accept your plan nor propose a conforming alternative within seven days of receiving yours; and if they miss a payment or make three or more late ones, you can serve a notice of default demanding all remaining rent and then move for judgment. None of this stops you seeking possession against a different tenant who is the one responsible for the abuse (4)(d).
notes: CO: CITED - C.R.S. § 13-40-104(4)(a), (4)(c), (4)(d), (4)(e)(I)(A), (4)(e)(I)(B), (4)(e)(I)(C), (4)(e)(II). NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01. Flagged rather than added under rule 1, then ADDED ON TAYLOR'S EXPRESS DECISION 2026-10-01 ("Add it now"). Sits beside edu-dv-lease-termination-co, edu-dv-confidentiality-co and edu-police-call-waiver-co, none of which covered § 13-40-104(4). Non-waivable, so no lease clause is offered or possible. Documentation routes are § 13-40-104(4)(a)(I)-(IV). STILL UNREACHED (rule 79, unchanged): the subparagraph of § 38-12-402(2)(a.5) carrying the 60-day police-report window - Taylor chose "Add it now" rather than the option that also chased that pinpoint, so edu-dv-lease-termination-co stands as it is and remains marked.

title: The Terms Colorado Will Not Let Your Lease Contain
bodyText: Colorado gives you a closed list of terms a written rental agreement "must not include", and anything on it that ends up in your lease is void and unenforceable (C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a) and (3)(b)). The list, in the statute's order: a penalty on either party stemming from an eviction notice or an eviction action that results from a lease violation; a one-way fee-shifting clause - any fee-shifting provision must award attorney fees to the prevailing party once the court finds they prevailed and the fee is reasonable; a waiver of the right to a jury trial, except that the parties may agree to waive a jury in a hearing to determine possession; a waiver of the ability to pursue, bring, join, litigate or support any joint, class or collective claim arising from the tenancy; a waiver of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; a waiver of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment, except that the lease may say you are not responsible for a third party's violation of it beyond your reasonable control; a waiver of the mandatory mediation required by 13-40-110(1); a fee, damages or penalty for a tenant failing to give notice of nonrenewal before the end of the agreement, except your actual losses from the missing notice; characterising any amount other than the set monthly payment for occupancy as "rent" with rent remedies including eviction; requiring the tenant to pay a markup or fee on a service a third party bills you, beyond either 2% of what you were billed or $10 a month, but not both; letting a voucher or subsidy provider pursue possession based solely on unpaid utilities; and recouping the cost of mandatory mediation from the tenant. Two practical warnings. The class-action waiver is the one most often imported by accident - it is boilerplate in form leases from other states, and in Colorado it is simply void, so do not paste a lease in from elsewhere without checking. And the nonrenewal item is narrow rather than absent: you cannot charge a fee or a set amount for a missing nonrenewal notice, but your actual losses are still recoverable, so there is nothing to gain from a fee clause and something to lose. Who is exempt: 38-12-801(4) switches off the jury, good-faith, quiet-enjoyment, nonrenewal, fees-as-rent, markup and voucher items for a mobile home in a mobile home park, and 38-12-801(8) switches off the whole waiver group and those same items for a duplex, triplex or accessory dwelling unit where you live in one of the units or on the same lot. The eviction-penalty and fee-shifting items have no exemption and apply to everyone.
notes: CO: CITED - C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3)(a)(I), (3)(a)(II), (3)(a)(III)(A)-(E), (3)(a)(IV), (3)(a)(V), (3)(a)(VI), both subsections numbered (3)(a)(VII), (3)(b), (4), (8); § 13-40-110(1). NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, resolving Q4 on Taylor's decision 2026-10-01 ("One edu-prohibited-lease-terms-co row"). Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: Colorado had NO row on the prohibited-lease-terms topic although 20 of the other 25 states do, and Colorado has one of the longest such statutes - the list was covered piecemeal across edu-eviction-penalty-clause-ban-co, edu-fee-shifting-co, edu-quiet-possession-co, edu-fees-not-rent-co, edu-rubs-uncertainty-co, edu-mandatory-mediation-co and jury-waiver-possession-co, with no row stating the list as a list. Two subsections had no CO row at all and are now covered: (3)(a)(III)(B) the joint/class/collective-action waiver, and (3)(a)(IV) the nonrenewal-notice fee. ON (3)(a)(IV) - THE Q4 QUESTION: Taylor's call was that the content is education, not a lease clause, and he was right on the rule 55 three-bucket test. It is not a required disclosure (the statute requires no lease text), not a constrained term (no landlord figure to state), and it does not serve the landlord: "responsible only for actual losses" plus a list of charges that do not apply is a restatement of a statutory CEILING in the tenant's favour, which the restatement check and this project's own statutory-ceiling rule both send to education. My earlier argument for a clause rested on creating the carve-out's "notice required pursuant to the rental agreement" hook, but that hook already exists in month-to-month-notice-co-exempt and month-to-month-notice-co-covered, and a sentence capping the tenant's exposure deters nothing. No lease clause offered. RULE 21 FLAG: § 38-12-801(3)(a) contains TWO subsections numbered (VII) in the official 2026 compilation, a single-session double-amendment artifact - shown here rather than silently renumbered; cite by the act where the number matters. Rule 47: the sanction is voidness under (3)(b), not conditioned on knowing use. Detail rows as listed above; fee-shifting also interacts with § 13-40-123 (no fees for a prevailing residential party unless the lease provides for them) - see edu-fee-shifting-co.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no just-cause eviction rule for houses and apartments. A fixed-term lease ends on its last day, and a tenancy with no end date (a tenancy at will, including month-to-month) ends on 60 days' notice from the landlord or 30 days' notice from the tenant, with no reason required; no length of tenancy changes this. The limits are situational. Within three months after a tenant in good faith exercises a legal or lease right, gives a notice to repair, complains to a code-enforcement agency or utility, or forms or joins a tenant organization about habitability, a landlord who files a dispossessory action, ends the lease or raises the rent faces a retaliation claim, unless the action rests on unpaid rent, intentional damage or threats, a breach of written lease rules against serious misconduct or criminal acts, or a holdover after notice ending the lease at the end of its term as the written lease provides. When an apartment building is converted to condominiums, the developer must give each qualifying tenant at least 120 days' notice and may not require the tenant to leave during that time except for nonpayment of rent, waste, or conduct that disturbs other tenants. Georgia has no repair rent-escrow procedure that bars eviction; the only rent paid into court is rent the tenant pays into the court registry while a dispossessory case is pending. Fair housing law applies.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 41b; rule 41). CONFIRMED ABSENT (statutes) of a just-cause rule for dwellings, with situational limits, so rules 27 and 41 give the same answer. Controlling text: O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-6, 44-7-7 (tenancy at will; notice); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-24(b)(1)-(4), (c), (d)(2)(A)-(E) (retaliation, three months, tenant organization; holdover after the landlord's end-of-term notice 'as agreed upon in the written lease' is a safe harbour, offered as `end-of-term-notice-ga`); O.C.G.A. § 44-3-87(a), (d), (g), (j) (conversion condominiums created after 1980-07-01: 120-day notice; tenants not in default and in residential occupancy; a notice naming a vacate date is also a demand for possession); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-54 (registry payments during a dispossessory only). Official O.C.G.A. full-text search 2026-10-01 (nonsense control 0 hits; GA retro battery B1-B4): 'good cause' near eviction or termination words, 30 hits, none for dwellings; 'just cause' or 'for cause' near tenant or eviction words, 3 hits (innkeepers, O.C.G.A. §§ 43-21-1, 43-21-3.1; estates, O.C.G.A. § 53-2-7); conversion near tenant near condominium or apartment, 3 hits (O.C.G.A. § 44-3-87); tenant-organization and rent-escrow patterns, 6 hits, known positives O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-24 and 44-7-54 returned, no repair rent-escrow statute. Rule 41 wording screen: no just-cause rule, so no wording that converts the end of the term into a for-cause event. Model: `edu-no-for-cause-eviction-az` (read, not tagged). Fair housing: `edu-fair-housing-ga`. Case law and local ordinances not searched.
