title: Notice That This Lease Ends at the End of the Term (Optional)
bodyText: This Lease ends at the end of the Term whether or not Landlord gives notice. Landlord may also give Tenant written notice, at least {{end_of_term_notice_days}} days before the last day of the Term, that this Lease will end at the end of the Term and will not be renewed or extended. If Landlord gives that notice, Tenant will vacate the property by the end of the Term.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rules 50 and 54). OPTIONAL clause (CONDITIONAL, not a default). The lease choice it makes: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-24(d)(2)(E) says a landlord is not liable for retaliation for a dispossessory action or termination when 'The tenant holds over after the landlord gives notice of termination at the end of the rental term as agreed upon in the written lease'. Without an agreed end-of-term notice in the written lease, that safe harbour has nothing to point to, and a landlord who declines to renew within three months of a tenant's repair notice, code complaint or tenant-organization activity relies on the other exceptions only (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-24(c)(4) lists terminating the lease). The first sentence keeps the notice optional, so the Term still ends on its own (a fixed term needs no notice; only a tenancy at will does, O.C.G.A. § 44-7-7). It does not replace the demand for possession a dispossessory needs (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50(a), (d)), and it sits beside `holdover-ca`, whose continued-tenancy limb still applies if Landlord later accepts Rent. Same family as the GA pass's other safe-harbour clauses, `rent-escalation-ga` ((d)(1)(A)) and `serious-misconduct-prohibition-ga` ((d)(2)(C)). Whether a court requires more than the statute's words for the safe harbour is case law, not read. BUILDER: show only when the lease has a fixed Term and the landlord opts in; require {{end_of_term_notice_days}} (same placeholder as `end-of-term-notice-fl`); no statute sets the number; a landlord who wants the tenant to have time to move might use 30 to 60 days (judgment, not statute). Basis: SERVES_LANDLORD (the landlord's own notice right). title: Waiver of Exemptions (Optional)
bodyText: Tenant waives and renounces Tenant's right to the benefit of the exemption from levy and sale provided by Article 1 of Chapter 13 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, as to any amount Tenant owes under this Lease. This waiver does not apply to wearing apparel or to $300.00 worth of household and kitchen furniture and provisions, which Georgia law protects despite any waiver.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 54: a waiver the statute lets a tenant give in the contract). OPTIONAL clause (CONDITIONAL, off by default), same treatment as `exemption-waiver-al` (Taylor's AL decision 4: offer it for consistency, never default). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-13-40 ('Any debtor may, except as to wearing apparel and $300.00 worth of household and kitchen furniture and provisions, waive or renounce his right to the benefit of the exemption provided for by this article by a waiver, either general or specific, in writing simply stating that he does so waive or renounce such right, which waiver may be stated in the contract of indebtedness'); 'this article' is Article 1 ('Constitutional Exemptions') of Title 44 ch. 13, whose O.C.G.A. § 44-13-1 exempts $5,000.00, or $21,500.00 for property that is the debtor's primary residence. After a levy the debtor sets apart the $300 by schedule and affidavit (O.C.G.A. §§ 44-13-41, 44-13-42); a levy made to harass can cost the creditor up to 25% of the value levied (O.C.G.A. § 44-13-41). The clause uses the statute's own words ('waives and renounces', the two excepted items) per rule 59. Not barred by O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2(b) (its list does not include exemptions). UNREAD: whether a residential lease is a 'contract of indebtedness' and how courts treat such waivers (case law); the bankruptcy exemptions (O.C.G.A. § 44-13-100) are a separate article and not addressed. Education: `edu-exemption-waiver-ga`. Basis: SERVES_LANDLORD. title: Waiver of Collection Exemptions
bodyText: Georgia exempts from levy and sale a debtor's property worth up to $5,000, or up to $21,500 for property that is the debtor's primary residence. A debtor may waive that exemption in writing, including in the contract that creates the debt, except as to wearing apparel and $300 worth of household and kitchen furniture and provisions; after a levy the debtor can claim that $300 of property back by filing a schedule. The library offers an optional waiver clause (`exemption-waiver-ga`), off by default. Whether a residential lease counts as a 'contract of indebtedness' for this purpose, and how courts treat such waivers, is case law this library has not reviewed. It is a collection term aimed at the tenant that many residential leases leave out, so use it only as a deliberate choice.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 54). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. §§ 44-13-1, 44-13-40, 44-13-41, 44-13-42 (see `exemption-waiver-ga` notes). Found by GA retro battery B11 (waive or renounce near homestead or exemption, 77 hits; the rest were tax, licensing, insurance and bankruptcy exemptions). Model: `edu-exemption-waiver-al` (read, not tagged). title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term (for a tenancy with no fixed Term, up to the earliest date Tenant could have ended the tenancy by notice), less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will make repairs as Georgia law requires and will use reasonable efforts to re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 54t). OPTIONAL clause (CONDITIONAL, not a default), state version of `tenant-caused-damage-tn` (read; TN row not tagged). Each abatement or exit route checked for a tenant-fault exception: (i) casualty: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-15 ('The destruction of a tenement by fire or the loss of possession by any casualty not caused by the landlord or from a defect of his title shall not abate the rent contracted to be paid') gives no abatement and no exit, so part (1) waives no statutory right; the opt-in `casualty-termination-ga` already excludes damage caused by Tenant, household members, guests or invitees; (ii) essential services and landlord-breach termination: no Georgia statute (ch. 7 read whole); (iii) rent into court: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-54 is registry rent during a dispossessory only. Repair duty: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-13(a) has no tenant-fault carve-out in its text and cannot be waived or avoided (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2(b)(1)); whether courts relieve a landlord for tenant-caused damage is case law, not read. So TN's 'Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair' became 'Landlord will make repairs as Georgia law requires', which cannot be read as softening that duty. Part (2) fills a gap: no Georgia statute measures lost rent when the lease ends because of tenant-caused damage. Tenancy-type limb (rule 37) from `tenant-caused-damage-al`: a tenancy at will ends on the tenant's 30 days' notice (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-7). Deposit: damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, including from negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, household members, invitees or guests, may be kept from the deposit (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34(a)). Education: `edu-tenant-caused-damage-ga`. Basis: SERVES_LANDLORD. title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: Georgia law leaves much of the cost of tenant-caused damage with the tenant. Destruction by fire, or loss of possession through a casualty the landlord did not cause, does not reduce the rent unless the lease says otherwise, and the library's optional casualty clause (`casualty-termination-ga`) gives no termination or rent reduction for damage caused by the tenant, household members, guests or invitees. The landlord may keep from the security deposit the cost of damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, including damage from negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, household members, invitees or guests, and may sue for the rest. The landlord's statutory duty to keep the premises in repair has no stated exception for damage the tenant caused and cannot be waived; whether courts relieve a landlord of it in that case is case law, not reviewed here. No Georgia statute measures the landlord's lost rent if the lease ends because of tenant-caused damage; the library offers an optional clause that does (`tenant-caused-damage-ga`).
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 54t). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-15, 44-7-34(a), 44-7-13(a), 44-7-2(b)(1); see `tenant-caused-damage-ga` notes. title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: Georgia law makes rent bear interest from the time it is due. Where the lease states no rate, the legal rate is 7% a year simple interest. Parties may set a different rate by written contract, but where the principal amount involved is $3,000 or less, the rate on a forbearance to enforce the collection of a sum of money may not exceed 16% a year simple interest, and Georgia defines interest broadly, as a charge for the use of money computed in any way or form. How those limits apply to unpaid rent, and whether a late fee counts toward them, were not reviewed, so the library offers no interest clause. A landlord who wants a contract rate can add one, and should take advice first.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 54: a measure the lease can set). DECLINED OPTION, education row per rule 54 (lawful, not offered, why). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-16 ('All contracts for rent shall bear interest from the time the rent is due'); O.C.G.A. § 7-4-2(a)(1)(A) (7 percent simple 'where the rate percent is not established by written contract'; written contract may set any rate where the principal is more than $3,000.00 and less than $250,000.00), (a)(2) ('Where the principal amount involved is $3,000.00 or less, such rate shall not exceed 16 percent per annum simple interest on any loan, advance, or forbearance to enforce the collection of any sum of money'), (a)(3) (interest 'computed in any other way or any other form'). Why not offered: one month's rent is usually under $3,000, so a contract rate meets the 16% ceiling, and whether a late fee is 'interest' under (a)(3), and whether a lease arrearage is a 'forbearance', are usury questions not reviewed (case law and O.C.G.A. § 7-4-18 not read); MO took the same course (`edu-legal-interest-mo`). `edu-landlord-remedies-ga` keeps the one-line interest statement. title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: Georgia statutes do not regulate the use of algorithmic or software pricing tools to set residential rents. Georgia also has no rent control and bars cities and counties from regulating the amount of rent on private rental property (`edu-local-preemption-ga`). Federal antitrust law may still apply.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 27). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT. title: Fees and the Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: Georgia's eviction statute names fees alongside rent rather than treating them as rent. For leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2024, when a tenant fails to pay the rent, late fees, utilities or other charges owed to the landlord, the landlord may give a notice to vacate or pay all of them within three business days and then file a dispossessory action. Other steps still turn on rent: a tenant can stop a nonpayment case by tendering all rents claimed plus the cost of the dispossessory warrant within seven days of service (the landlord must accept that only once in any 12 months), and while a case is pending the tenant pays into the court registry the rent and utility payments the lease makes the tenant's responsibility. The library's shared Default clause gives up one part of this on purpose: except where the law requires otherwise, an unpaid late fee alone, apart from the Rent itself, does not let the landlord end the lease or evict. Other unpaid charges are not covered by that sentence.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 27). Verdict: PRESENT (by statute; no statute converts fees into rent, the eviction statute names them directly). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50(c) ('fails to pay the rent, late fees, utilities, or other charges owed to the landlord'; three business days; HB 404 § 6, leases entered into or renewed on or after 2024-07-01; older tenancies at will: `edu-eviction-process-ga`); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-52(a) ('all rents allegedly owed plus the cost of the dispossessory warrant'; 'only once in any 12 month period'); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-54(a) ('All rent and utility payments which are the responsibility of the tenant payable to the landlord under terms of the lease'). Library choice: `default-by-tenant` ('Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction'), kept as the library default. title: No Statutory Right to Fix It and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Some states let a landlord give notice, do work the tenant failed to do, and add the cost to the rent. No provision of Georgia's landlord-tenant chapter gives a landlord that right, sets a notice period for it, or makes the cost rent. What Georgia law does give: the landlord may keep from the security deposit the cost of damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, may sue for the rest, and for unpaid charges owed to the landlord may use the three-business-day notice to vacate or pay. Whether a repair cost the lease makes the tenant's responsibility is such a charge is not settled by the statute's text.

title: No Blank-Space or Lease-Copy Rule
bodyText: Georgia imposes no statutory requirement that a written residential lease have every blank completed, and none that the landlord give the tenant a signed copy. Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act reaches residential leases, but its list of unlawful practices has no blank-space or copy-at-signing item for an ordinary lease. Several Georgia rules still turn on what the lease says: the owner and agent disclosure, the statement of where the deposit is held, and any delivery methods for the three-day notice and demand for possession that the lease adds to posting on the door. A blank left in one of those is a right or a duty left unclear. Fill in every blank before signing and give the tenant a copy, as good practice rather than a statutory duty.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: Georgia's statutes contain no covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession running from the landlord to the tenant. Possession is protected instead by the dispossessory process: a landlord recovers possession through a court action and a writ executed by an officer, not by self-help (`edu-prohibited-practices-ga`). Whether Georgia implies a covenant of quiet enjoyment in a lease is case law; case notes in the official code refer to one, but the cases were not read and this row does not rely on them.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Georgia prescribes no form for a residential lease, and none for the three-day notice to vacate or pay or the demand for possession; the statute prescribes how those notices are delivered (posted in a sealed envelope on the door, plus any method the lease adds), not their wording. Two prescribed forms can reach a landlord: the written demand sent before suing on a dishonored check, which must be in substantially the statutory form (`edu-dishonored-payment-remedies-ga`), and, for a property covered by the federal CARES Act, the CARES Act affidavit form in the Uniform Magistrate Court Rules (`edu-eviction-process-ga`). Magistrate courts' own dispossessory filing forms were not reviewed.

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: Georgia statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras, video doorbells or similar devices. The lease's alteration terms govern; in this library that is the Alterations section, which requires the landlord's written consent before a tenant adds or changes a fixture. Georgia's eavesdropping and surveillance laws, and any homeowners' association rules, were not reviewed and may limit what a camera records rather than its installation.

bodyText: "NOTICE: Michigan law establishes rights and obligations for parties to rental agreements. This agreement is required to comply with the Truth in Renting Act. title: Use of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit) prior to occupancy. Landlord may use the Security Deposit only to: (1) reimburse Landlord for actual damages to the rental unit or any ancillary facility that are the direct result of conduct not reasonably expected in the normal course of habitation of a dwelling; and (2) pay Landlord for Rent in arrears under this Lease, Rent due because Tenant ended this Lease early, and utility bills Tenant did not pay. Landlord will not apply the Security Deposit to ordinary wear and tear or to any damage or condition that existed before the tenancy. Tenant may not apply the Security Deposit to Rent, including the last month's Rent, without Landlord's written consent. The Security Deposit does not limit Tenant's liability for amounts greater than the Security Deposit.
notes: MI: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.607: a security deposit 'may be used only for' (a) actual damages to the rental unit or any ancillary facility that are the direct result of conduct not reasonably expected in the normal course of habitation, and (b) all rent in arrearage, rent due for premature termination by the tenant, and utility bills not paid by the tenant; items (1)-(2) track it (rule 59). The base's 'remedy a Tenant default' and cleaning sentence are broader, and the act may not be waived (Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 554.606, 554.633(1)(b)); this row supersedes security-deposit-use for MI. title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: Within 4 days after Tenant's occupancy ends, Tenant will give Landlord a forwarding address in writing, at the address in the Security Deposit Notice, where Tenant can receive mail. Within 30 days after Tenant's occupancy ends, Landlord will either return the full Security Deposit or mail Tenant a notice of damages that itemizes each charge against the Security Deposit, with the estimated cost of repair of each damaged item, and returns the balance by check or money order with the notice or by electronic transfer to Tenant's account within 10 days after mailing the notice. Tenant must respond to a notice of damages by ordinary mail, at the address in the Security Deposit Notice, within 7 days after receiving it, stating in detail whether Tenant agrees or disagrees with each charge. If Tenant does not respond in time, Tenant forfeits the amount claimed. If Tenant disputes a charge in time, Landlord will, within 45 days after Tenant's occupancy ends, either return the disputed amount, agree with Tenant in writing on how it will be handled, or start a court action for it.

Laws § 554.611 (tenant's written forwarding address within 4 days; failure relieves the landlord of the notice of damages but does not prejudice the tenant's later claim); Mich. Comp. title: Tenant Default
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due or fails to comply with any other obligation under this Lease. If Tenant fails to pay Rent, Landlord may serve Tenant a written demand for possession for nonpayment, and Tenant may cure by paying the Rent due within 7 days after the demand is served, or as Michigan law otherwise allows. For any other breach that can be corrected, Landlord will give Tenant written notice describing the breach, and Landlord may end this Lease if Tenant does not correct the breach within [number] days after the notice. No opportunity to cure applies to a breach of this Lease's criminal activity terms, or where Michigan law lets Landlord end the tenancy without one, including when Tenant, a member of Tenant's household or a person under Tenant's control causes or threatens physical injury to an individual, other than Tenant or a member of Tenant's household, on real property Landlord owns or operates and the police have been notified. Except as required by applicable law, Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to end this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise all remedies available under Michigan law, including ending this Lease, recovering possession through the courts, and recovering unpaid Rent, late fees, and court costs as allowed by statute, less amounts properly applied from the Security Deposit. Landlord will mitigate its damages as Michigan law requires.
notes: MI: Supersedes default-by-tenant for MI (default-by-tenant-ks-ne is not tagged either). (1) Fees: a rental agreement may not make a party liable for 'legal costs or attorney fees incurred by another party, in connection with a dispute arising under the rental agreement, in excess of costs or fees specifically permitted by statute' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(g)); the base's prevailing-party sentence and the ks-ne variant's 'reasonable costs and expenses' are replaced by 'court costs as allowed by statute' (summary-proceeding costs, Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5759; MCR 4.201(L)(4)) (rules 49, 53). (2) Rent limb: Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(a) (holding over 7 days after service of a written demand for possession for nonpayment; rent due excludes accelerated amounts), demand form and service Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 600.5716, 600.5718; the 7 days is the statute's period, not an added notice (rule 43). Payment of the judgment amount and costs also prevents the writ (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5744(7)). (3) Other breaches: possession after termination 'pursuant to a power to terminate provided in the lease' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(c)(i)); the cure period is the landlord's figure (hand-filled bracket). Case law: the notice and demand of possession operates as the landlord's assertion of its intention to forfeit (Gurunian v Grossman, 331 Mich 412, 418 (1951)); accepting rent for a period after the date in the notice, when the tenant has not received notice that summary proceedings have begun, waives the notice, and a landlord who has habitually accepted late payments must give notice that strict compliance will be required before forfeiting for lateness (Park Forest of Blackman v Smith, 112 Mich App 421, 425-428 (1982); edu-acceptance-of-payment-mi); case law on a minimum cure period was not searched (MI log §1.4). No agreement can take away the tenant's statutory right to cure by paying the judgment amount (Birznieks v Cooper, 405 Mich 319 (1979)); the clause does not try to. (4) No-cure carve-out in its own sentence reaching both limbs (rule 43): the drug ground runs on 24 hours' notice under a lease clause (Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 554.134(4), 600.5714(1)(b); criminal-activity-mi), and the threatened-injury ground on a 7-day notice to quit with no cure, only if the police department with jurisdiction has been notified, and not where the person injured or threatened is the tenant or a household member or where it would violate federal housing regulations (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(e)); the clause states the police and household conditions and relies on 'where Michigan law lets Landlord' for the federal-regulation exception. (5) Mitigation may not be released (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(k)); summary-proceeding rights may not be waived (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(j)). Chapter 57 of the Revised Judicature Act, Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 600.5701-600.5759, read whole. Court rule: MCR 4.201 read whole from the Michigan Court Rules PDF updated Sept. 2, 2026 (courts.michigan.gov) (MI log §1). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Landlord's Entry
bodyText: Landlord, its agents and contractors may enter the property at reasonable times to inspect it, make repairs or perform maintenance, and show it to prospective tenants, purchasers or lenders. Except in an emergency, Landlord will give Tenant at least 24 hours' notice and will request and obtain Tenant's permission before entering, and Tenant will not unreasonably refuse permission. In an emergency, including fire, flood, or another threat of serious injury or death, Landlord may enter at any time.
notes: MI: Supersedes landlords-access for MI. Where the Housing Law of Michigan applies, 'Before entering a leasehold regulated by this act, the owner of the leasehold shall request and obtain permission to enter the leasehold. However, in the case of an emergency, including, but not limited to, fire, flood, or other threat of serious injury or death, the owner may enter at any time.' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 125.526(11)). The Housing Law covers cities, villages and townships of 10,000 or more by the last federal census, and private and 2-family dwellings only in those of 100,000 or more unless the local body adopts it (Mich. Comp. Laws § 125.401(2)). Rule 32: the clause is drafted to the stricter rule so it is lawful everywhere, so no municipality list was built. Outside Housing Law places no Michigan statute sets entry notice (MI batteries 11, 12); the 24-hour figure is the landlord's. Entry may not become unlawful interference with possession (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.2918(2)-(3)(b)). No published case construing Mich. Comp. Laws § 125.526(11), including whether a lease term can itself supply the permission it requires, was found (MI log §1.4), so the clause asks for permission each time. edu-entry-mi. Rule 15: written section-open. Pub. Acts 102 and 103, eff. Sept. 21, 2026) (MI log §1, MI log §17). | IA: Applies as written (tagged instead of the base `landlords-access`, independent check round 1). Iowa Code § 562A.19: tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for listed purposes, including to inspect, repair and show the unit to purchasers, mortgagees and prospective tenants (1); entry without consent in an emergency (2); except in an emergency or where impracticable, at least 24 hours' notice and entry only at reasonable times (3); no other right of access except court order, Iowa Code §§ 562A.28, 562A.29, abandonment or surrender (4). This variant's 'request and obtain Tenant's permission ... Tenant will not unreasonably refuse permission' matches Iowa Code § 562A.19(1); its notice duty is stricter than Iowa's (no impracticability exception), which is lawful. The base `landlords-access` grants a 'right of reasonable access' on notice without the consent framing; an entry without consent is a common law trespass (Butter v Midwest Property Management IC, LLC, ___ N.W.3d ___ (Iowa 2025) (No. 24-1752, filed Dec. 31, 2025, amended Jan. 6, 2026): the lease there was 'subject to Resident's consent, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld', and consent is judged by what the tenant's conduct led the landlord to believe), so the base is not tagged for Iowa. Remedies, Iowa Code § 562A.35; see `edu-landlord-entry-ia`. | CT: Tagged as written (tag-first screen, rules 26-28, CT log §2.1). Connecticut entry requires the tenant's consent, which the tenant 'shall not unreasonably withhold' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16(a), (d)), with 'reasonable written or oral notice' and entry 'only at reasonable times, except in case of emergency' (§ 47a-16(c)); this variant (notice, request and obtain permission, not unreasonably refused, emergency entry) fits. The base `landlords-access` grants a "right of reasonable access" without consent and is not tagged. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Smoking Policy
bodyText: Smoking of any kind, including smoking tobacco or marihuana, and vaping tobacco or nicotine products with an electronic cigarette or similar device, is not permitted anywhere on the property, including inside the dwelling, on porches or balconies, or in any common area. Tenant will be responsible for any cost Landlord incurs to remediate odor, staining or damage caused by smoking or vaping in violation of this Section, and a violation may be treated as a default under this Lease. As Michigan law requires, this Section does not prohibit Tenant from lawfully possessing marihuana or consuming it by means other than smoking.
notes: MI: Supersedes smoking-policy for MI. Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act (Initiated Law 1 of 2018), Mich. Comp. Laws § 333.27954(4): a person may prohibit or regulate the consumption and cultivation of marihuana on property the person owns, occupies or manages, 'except that a lease agreement may not prohibit a tenant from lawfully possessing and consuming marihuana by means other than smoking'; smoking where prohibited by the person who owns, occupies or manages the property is not authorized (Mich. Comp. Laws § 333.27954(1)(e)). The act does not define 'smoking' (MI battery 40), and no Michigan appellate decision on whether vaping marihuana is smoking was found (MI log §1.4); the clause bans vaping of tobacco and nicotine only and keeps the base's smoking ban (model smoking-policy-mo). Medical marihuana: an owner need not lease to a person who smokes or cultivates marihuana on the premises 'if the prohibition against smoking or cultivating marihuana is in the written lease' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 333.26427(c)(3)); this clause is that written prohibition for smoking; cultivation is cannabis-cultivation-mi. A lease term contrary to the act would be void (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(2)-(3)). edu-cannabis-mi. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord: [list approved pets, or state that no pets are permitted]. Tenant will pay a pet deposit of {{pet_deposit}}, if applicable. Any refundable pet deposit is part of the Security Deposit for all purposes of Michigan law, including the limit on the total Security Deposit, and will be held, used and returned under this Lease's Security Deposit terms. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, if applicable. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet, and will reimburse Landlord for claims caused by Tenant's pet, except to the extent a claim arises from Landlord's failure to perform, or negligent performance of, a duty imposed by law. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and Tenant will then remove the pet within [number] days after Landlord's written notice; failure to do so is a default under this Lease. Landlord may enter the property in connection with a pet only as this Lease's Access & Entry terms permit, and will not seize or remove a pet without a court order. This Section does not limit animal control or law enforcement acting under their own authority. This Section does not apply to a service animal or assistance animal.
notes: MI: Supersedes pet-policy for MI (model pet-policy-mo). (1) A security deposit is 'a deposit, in any amount, paid by the tenant ... to be held for the term' and includes 'any other amount of money or property returnable to the tenant on condition of return of the rental unit' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.601(d)), so a refundable pet deposit is a security deposit and counts toward the 1 1/2-month cap (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.602) and the act's uses and return rules (Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 554.607-554.613); a nonrefundable pet fee or pet rent is not (edu-pet-deposit-mi). (2) The reimbursement sentence carves out the lessor's failure to perform or negligent performance of a duty imposed by law (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(e)). (3) Removal of a tenant's property is unlawful interference with possession (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.2918(2)(b)); entry follows landlords-access-mi (Mich. Comp. Laws § 125.526(11)). Reasonable accommodation for an assistance animal: Mich. Comp. Laws § 37.1506a(1)(b). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Parking & Vehicle Requirements
bodyText: Only operable, currently registered passenger vehicles may be parked at the property; commercial vehicles, recreational vehicles, trailers, and oversized vehicles are not permitted without Landlord's prior written consent. Landlord may require Tenant to provide vehicle registration information and may issue parking tags, decals, or access cards, the cost of which may be charged to Tenant. A vehicle parked or kept in violation of this Section is a breach of this Lease. Landlord may have a vehicle that remains on the property without Landlord's consent removed as Michigan law allows, but Landlord will not remove a vehicle of Tenant or an Occupant without a court order. Vehicle repairs are not permitted at the property except minor emergency repairs necessary to move the vehicle, and vehicles may be washed only in areas Landlord designates, if any.
notes: MI: Supersedes parking-vehicle-rules for MI (independent check, MI log §13). The shared clause's towing sentence ('illegally parked, abandoned, inoperable, or has expired registration') reaches further than Michigan's private-property route, which covers a vehicle that 'has remained on private property without the consent of the property owner' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.252a(10)); a tenant's or occupant's vehicle parked with the lease's permission is not such a vehicle, and removing it is 'Removal, retention, or destruction of personal property of the possessor', an unlawful interference with possession (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.2918(2)(b)), for actual damages or $200.00, whichever is greater, for each occurrence. The replacement keeps towing for vehicles on the property without consent, makes a violation a lease breach, and routes removal of a tenant's or occupant's vehicle through court. title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds, a closed or nonexistent account, a stop-payment order or any other reason, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount], and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are returned or fail, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check or money order; Landlord will not charge an additional fee for paying by at least one of those methods.
notes: MI: Supersedes returned-payments for MI (model returned-payments-ok). The base's 'not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' points at no general Michigan cap (rule 53): Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.2952 fixes a $25 processing fee (paid within 7 days, excluding weekends and holidays, after its statutory written demand is mailed) or $35 (within 30 days), with civil damages and costs only through that demand procedure (edu-dishonored-check-mi). The fee is a hand-filled landlord figure. Penalty test: Michigan courts enforce an agreed sum that is reasonable with relation to the possible injury suffered and not unconscionable or excessive, and decide enforceability as a question of law (Curran v Williams, 352 Mich 278, 282 (1958); UAW-GM Human Resource Ctr v KSL Recreation Corp, 228 Mich App 486, 508 (1998)); no published Michigan case applying the test to a residential lease fee was found (MI log §1.4). The certified-funds requirement is a contingency agreed at signing, not a later change by the lessor (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(l)); acceptable-payment-methods-mi defers to it expressly so the two do not conflict, and the last clause keeps a fee-free method as Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(o) requires (2026 Mich. Pub. Acts 103). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Controlled Substances and Criminal Activity
bodyText: Tenant, members of Tenant's household and other persons under Tenant's control will not unlawfully manufacture, deliver, possess with intent to deliver, or possess a controlled substance on the property, and will not engage in other criminal activity on the property that threatens the health, safety or peaceful enjoyment of other residents, neighbors, Landlord or Landlord's agents. If any of them unlawfully manufactures, delivers, possesses with intent to deliver, or possesses a controlled substance on the property, Landlord may terminate this Lease, and if a formal police report has been filed alleging that conduct, Landlord may give Tenant a written 24-hour notice to quit. A breach of this Section is a material breach for which Landlord may end this Lease without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure, and this Section controls over any other provision of this Lease that would require one. This Section does not apply to the possession or use of marihuana that Michigan law permits, although this Lease's smoking and cultivation terms still apply, or to criminal activity of which Tenant or a member of Tenant's household is the victim or threatened victim.
notes: MI: Optional (rule 54, identification trigger). Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.134(4) and Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(b) give a 24-hour notice to quit or demand for possession only where the lease is terminated 'pursuant to a clause in the lease providing for termination because a tenant, a member of the tenant's household, or other person under the tenant's control has unlawfully manufactured, delivered, possessed with intent to deliver, or possessed a controlled substance on the leased premises' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(b); Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.134(4) reads 'because the tenant' and omits 'unlawfully'), and only if a formal police report has been filed; 'controlled substance' means a schedule 1, 2 or 3 substance under Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 333.7211-333.7216. Without this clause the 24-hour route is unavailable. Such a case is heard at the first appearance (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5735(7)) and a writ may issue immediately (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5744(3)(f)). The statute speaks of 'unlawfully' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(b)); lawful marihuana use under Mich. Comp. Laws § 333.27954 is carved out. The other-crime sentence is a lease covenant; ending the lease for it runs through the power-to-terminate route (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(c)(i)); the threatened-injury ground is statutory (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(e)). Models criminal-activity-mo / -in; the RPOA lease has a crime-free policy and a drug clause (MI log §15). Federal subsidized housing: 24 C.F.R. § 966.4(l) (public housing lease grounds) and 24 C.F.R. § 982.310 (voucher owner grounds) read; in a covered housing program a tenant may not lose tenancy solely for criminal activity directly relating to domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking where the activity is engaged in by a household member, guest or other person under the tenant's control and the tenant or an affiliated individual is the victim or threatened victim (24 C.F.R. § 5.2005(b)(2)); the clause's carve-out covers victims and threatened victims in Tenant's household. title: Consent to Electronic Service of a Demand for Possession
bodyText: Tenant may, but is not required to, consent to receive a demand for possession or payment by electronic service. Landlord will not refuse to enter into this Lease because Tenant declines. If Tenant consents by initialing here [Tenant's initials] and providing the following e-mail address: [e-mail address], the consent takes effect only after Landlord or Tenant sends this consent, or a confirmation of it, to the other by e-mail and the other affirmatively replies by e-mail. The e-mail address remains Tenant's electronic service address until Tenant notifies Landlord in writing that Tenant no longer has an electronic service address, or the parties repeat this process with a different address.
notes: MI: Optional (rule 54). Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5718(1)(d): a demand for possession or payment may be served 'by electronic service, if the person in possession has in writing specifically consented to electronic service of the demand and if the consent or confirmation of the consent has been sent by 1 party and affirmatively replied to, by electronic transmission, by the other party'; Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5718(2): the address remains in effect until the process is repeated or the party gives written notice it no longer has one, and 'A landlord shall not refuse to enter a lease because the prospective tenant declines to consent to electronic service under this section.' Other methods remain (personal delivery, delivery to a household member, first-class mail, Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5718(1)(a)-(c)). Michigan's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act applies only between parties who agreed to transact electronically, and a party may refuse further electronic transactions (Mich. Comp. Laws § 450.835(2)-(3)). Builder: the e-mail confirmation and reply is a step after signing (MI log §10). The RPOA lease has an e-service consent paragraph (MI log §15). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Water and Sewer Bills
bodyText: Tenant will pay all water and sewage system charges for the property directly to the provider, with the service in Tenant's name where the provider allows. Landlord is the lessor for purposes of the following sentence. The lessor shall not be liable for payment of water or sewage system bills accruing subsequent to the filing of the affidavit provided by Mich. Comp. Laws § 123.165.
notes: MI: Optional (rule 54, identification trigger). Municipal water and sewer charges are a lien on the premises supplied, with priority over all other liens except taxes and special assessments (Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 123.162, 123.165), enforceable by shutoff or suit (Mich. Comp. Laws § 123.166). The Municipal Water Liens act 'shall not apply if a lease has been legally executed, containing a provision that the lessor shall not be liable for payment of water or sewage system bills accruing subsequent to the filing of the affidavit provided by this section' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 123.165); the second sentence quotes that provision verbatim except that 'this section' is replaced by its citation, since the lease is not that section (rule 59); the affidavit is filed 'with the board, commission, or other official in charge of the water works system or sewage system, or both'. The landlord must then file the affidavit (with the lease's expiration date) and give 20 days' notice of any cancellation, change or termination of the lease (edu-municipal-water-lien-mi). Where a municipality's charges run under a revenue-bond ordinance instead, written notice with a copy of the lease stops the lien and the municipality must then receive a cash deposit before giving further service (Mich. Comp. Laws § 141.121(3)). The RPOA 2024 lease cites Mich. Comp. Laws § 123.165 (MI log §15). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Rules and Changes to Rules
bodyText: Tenant will comply with the rules and regulations for the property in effect when this Lease is signed: [attach or describe the rules, or state that there are none]. During the Term, Landlord may change the rules only with Tenant's written consent, or by giving Tenant at least 30 days' written notice of a change that is required by federal, state or local law, rule or regulation, or that is required to protect the physical health, safety or peaceful enjoyment of tenants and guests.
notes: MI: Optional (rule 54, 'the lease controls'). Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(l): a lessor may not alter a provision after commencement without the tenant's written consent, 'except that an agreement may provide for the following types of adjustments to be made on written notice of not less than 30 days: (i) Changes required by federal, state, or local law or rule or regulation. (ii) Changes in rules relating to the property that are required to protect the physical health, safety, or peaceful enjoyment of tenants and guests.' A lease silent on this leaves only consent. Model rules-ok / rules-amendment-in. The RPOA lease's 'any rules ... published by Landlord become part of this Agreement' goes further than (l) allows (MI log §15). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Rent Adjustment for Increased Operating Costs
bodyText: During the Term, Landlord may increase Monthly Rent to cover additional costs of operating the property that Landlord incurs because of increases in ad valorem property taxes, increases in charges for electricity, heating fuel, water or sanitary sewer services consumed at the property, or increases in premiums Landlord pays for liability, fire or worker's compensation insurance. Landlord will give Tenant at least 30 days' written notice stating the new Monthly Rent, the date it takes effect, and how the increase was calculated. An increase may not exceed the increase in those costs allocated to the property.
notes: MI: Optional (rule 54, 'the lease controls'). Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(l)(iii) lets a rental agreement provide for 'Changes in the amount of rental payments to cover additional costs in operating the rental premises incurred by the lessor because of increases in ad valorem property taxes, charges for the electricity, heating fuel, water, or sanitary sewer services consumed at the property, or increases in premiums paid for liability, fire, or worker compensation insurance' on written notice of not less than 30 days. Without the clause, rent may not rise mid-term without written consent. The calculation statement and the allocation limit keep the increase to the statute's 'to cover additional costs'. title: Acceleration of Rent After Breach
bodyText: If Tenant breaches this Lease and Landlord ends Tenant's right of possession, Landlord may declare the Rent for the remainder of the Term due at once. As Michigan law requires, this Section includes a statement that the tenant may not be liable for the total accelerated amount because of the landlord's obligation to minimize damages, and that either party may have a court determine the actual amount owed, if any.
notes: MI: Optional (rule 54, statute wording that lets the lease decide). Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(i): a rental agreement must not provide that rental payments may be accelerated on breach 'unless the provision also includes a statement that the tenant may not be liable for the total accelerated amount because of the landlord's obligation to minimize damages, and that either party may have a court determine the actual amount owed, if any.' The second sentence quotes that statement verbatim (rule 59). Accelerated rent is not 'rent due' for a nonpayment demand (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(a)), and mitigation may not be released (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(k)). Fixed-term leases only (rule 37): a periodic tenancy has no remaining Term to accelerate. Offered as an option the statute expressly contemplates; it adds little beyond actual damages (MI log §6.1). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Holdover Charge
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession after the end of the Term, and Landlord has not agreed in writing to a continued tenancy or accepted Rent for one under the Holdover section of this Lease, then, in place of the actual damages and reasonable rental value described in that section, Tenant will pay Landlord a holdover charge of {{holdover_daily_rate}} for each day Tenant remains in possession. Landlord and Tenant agree that Landlord's loss from a holdover, including delay in making the property available to a new tenant, is difficult to estimate accurately in advance, that this charge is a reasonable estimate of that loss, and that it is not a penalty. Landlord's acceptance of a holdover charge is not acceptance of Rent for a continued tenancy. This Section does not limit Landlord's right to recover possession, unpaid Rent and other amounts due for the period before the Term ended, or damages for harm to the property.
notes: MI: Optional (rule 54, a measure the statute does not set). Michigan has no statutory holdover multiplier (MI battery 63: 0 relevant hits); a landlord who obtains possession may sue for damages from the notice to quit or demand for possession (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5750). Rule 54 shape question: no statutory measure exists for any holdover case, so the clause fills the whole gap. Penalty test: Michigan courts enforce an agreed sum that is reasonable with relation to the possible injury suffered and not unconscionable or excessive, and decide enforceability as a question of law (Curran v Williams, 352 Mich 278, 282 (1958); UAW-GM Human Resource Ctr v KSL Recreation Corp, 228 Mich App 486, 508 (1998)); no published Michigan case applying the test to a residential lease fee was found (MI log §1.4). The clause's reasonable-estimate sentence records the parties' basis; a court still decides enforceability. Text is holdover-rate-in's; it points to holdover-ca (tagged MI, titled 'Holdover'). Variable {{holdover_daily_rate}} is the IN one (not in the kickoff list; already used by holdover-rate-in, so not new; MI log §10). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Fire or Casualty: Landlord Termination (Lease of 1 Year or More)
bodyText: This Section applies only if the Term of this Lease is at least one year, and does not apply to any month-to-month or other periodic continuation of this Lease. If the property is destroyed by fire, storm or other casualty, or is damaged by one so that it is unfit to live in and the repairs cannot reasonably be completed within [number] days after the casualty, Landlord may end this Lease by written notice to Tenant. If this Lease ends under this Section, Rent stops as of the date the property became unfit to live in, any Rent Tenant prepaid for the period after that date will be refunded, and the Security Deposit will be returned as this Lease and Michigan law provide. Tenant keeps any claim Tenant has for Landlord's failure to make repairs before this Lease ends. If the damage was caused by the wilful or irresponsible conduct, or lack of conduct, of Tenant, ending this Lease does not release Tenant from liability for the damage or for Landlord's resulting losses. Nothing in this Section limits Tenant's right under Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.201 to quit and surrender possession, and owe no Rent after surrender, if the damage occurred without Tenant's fault or neglect, or any other right Tenant has under Michigan law.
notes: MI: Optional, never a default (rule 54). Taylor, 2026-10-01 (MI log §6.2): narrow clause, for a Term of at least one year only, with the tenant's statutory surrender right expressly preserved, rent stopping from the date the home became unfit, no release for tenant-caused damage. Basis: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.201 gives the tenant, not the landlord, a surrender right where a building is destroyed or made untenantable without the tenant's fault or neglect 'and no express agreement to the contrary has been made in writing'; the preservation sentence keeps this clause from being read as such an agreement. The landlord's covenant to keep the premises in reasonable repair runs 'during the term of the lease' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(1)(b)) and may be modified only where the lease has a current term of at least 1 year (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(2)), hence the one-year condition written into the clause; a provision that 'Waives or alters a remedy available to the parties when the premises are in a condition that violates the covenants of fitness and habitability' is void (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(a)), which is why the tenant keeps any claim for the landlord's failure to repair before termination. No published Michigan case construing Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 554.201 and 554.633(1)(a), or a landlord casualty-termination clause, was found (MI log §1.4); Taylor's reading, recorded at his direction: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(e)'s carve-out for a release from liability for fire or other casualty covered by insurance shows the Legislature expected leases to address casualty (an inference from the text, not from a source read). Tenant fault: the repair covenant excepts disrepair 'caused by the tenants wilful or irresponsible conduct or lack of conduct' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(1)(b)); rule 54 tenant-caused-damage point. Shorter tenancies: edu-casualty-short-term-mi. The repair period is a hand-filled landlord figure. Model casualty-termination-in / -mo, narrowed. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant or an Occupant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. Items (1) and (2) do not apply where Michigan law releases Tenant from Rent because the damage occurred without Tenant's fault or neglect. Tenant will be liable to Landlord for any damage to the property, including fire damage, caused by the deliberate, negligent or irresponsible acts or omissions of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, other than ordinary wear and tear, including the cost of repairing it.
notes: MI: Optional (rule 54, tenant-caused damage, always asked). Each Michigan abatement or exit provision has its own fault exception, so a no-abatement term for tenant-caused damage waives nothing: casualty surrender only if the destruction 'occurred without his fault or neglect' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.201); the repair covenant excepts disrepair 'caused by the tenants wilful or irresponsible conduct or lack of conduct' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(1)(b)); Housing Law rent escrow does not apply where the owner shows the conditions 'were caused by the occupant or occupants' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 125.530(3)), and a court may let the owner correct a violation the occupant caused and assess the cost against the occupant or the security deposit (Mich. Comp. Laws § 125.534(5)). Landlord's own repair labor is recoverable in a possession case (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5739(2)); a tenant who willfully or negligently causes a serious continuing health hazard or extensive continuing injury may be removed if, for 7 days after a demand, the tenant neither delivers possession nor substantially restores or repairs the premises (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(d)). Mitigation kept (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(k)). Items (1) and (2) are limited to Tenant and Occupants, with a saving sentence, because the statutory exceptions speak of 'the tenants' conduct and of the occupants (Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 554.139(1)(b), 125.530(3)) and Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.201 turns on 'his fault or neglect'; no published case deciding whether a guest's act is the tenant's fault was found (MI log §1.4; independent check, MI log §13). Liability sentence (closeout round, rule 76): absent an express and unequivocal agreement, a tenant is not liable to the lessor or its fire insurer in tort for negligently caused fire damage (New Hampshire Ins Group v Labombard, 155 Mich App 369, 377 (1986)); a lease term making the tenant 'liable for any damage to the Premises ... that is caused by the acts or omissions of Tenant or Tenant's guests' was held clear and unambiguous, covering fire damage and supporting a breach-of-contract claim that Labombard does not bar (Laurel Woods Apts v Roumayah, 274 Mich App 631 (2007)). The sentence follows that wording and names fire damage expressly; it reaches guests (as the enforced term did) and invitees; it is limited to deliberate, negligent or irresponsible conduct and excludes ordinary wear and tear (independent check round 4) so it uses the fault standard of items (1) and (2) plus 'irresponsible' from the repair covenant's exception, the wear-and-tear exceptions in security-deposit-use-mi and the shared surrender and maintenance clauses, and the repair covenant's exception for disrepair 'caused by the tenants wilful or irresponsible conduct or lack of conduct' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(1)(b)); charging a tenant for a guest's negligent damage in a lease under 1 year rests on Laurel Woods, which did not consider Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(2) (risk recorded, MI log §6.1); the saving sentence is scoped to items (1) and (2) so it does not cut back the liability sentence. It is not an exculpation of the landlord (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(e)) and adds no fee or legal cost (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(g)). edu-tenant-caused-damage-mi. Model tenant-caused-damage-in. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Handling of Property Left Behind
bodyText: When this Lease ends or Tenant gives up possession, Tenant will remove all of Tenant's personal property from the property. (1) While Tenant remains in possession, Landlord will not remove, keep or destroy Tenant's personal property, change or add locks without immediately giving Tenant keys, board up or remove doors, windows or locks, or interrupt essential services to force Tenant out. (2) If Landlord believes in good faith that Tenant has abandoned the property, and after diligent inquiry has reason to believe Tenant does not intend to return, and current Rent is not paid, Landlord may retake possession and remove personal property left at the property. [Optional: Before disposing of property that appears to have value, Landlord will mail Tenant a notice at Tenant's forwarding address (or, if none, the property address) and hold the property for [number] days.] (3) Property left at the property when a court officer carries out an order of eviction will be handled by that officer as Michigan law provides. (4) If Tenant dies while the sole Tenant, Landlord will follow the procedure Michigan law sets before retaking possession.
notes: MI: Michigan has no general abandoned-property disposal statute for residential tenants (MI battery 30); the controlling text is the unlawful-interference statute. Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.2918(2): a tenant whose possessory interest is unlawfully interfered with recovers actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, per occurrence; interference includes removal, retention or destruction of personal property, lock changes without immediately providing keys, boarding, removal of doors, windows or locks, and interruption of essential services. Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.2918(3)(c): no unlawful interference where the owner 'believes in good faith that the tenant has abandoned the premises, and after diligent inquiry has reason to believe the tenant does not intend to return, and current rent is not paid' (item 2 tracks it); (3)(d) deceased tenant procedure (item 4, edu-tenant-death-mi); the section may not be waived (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.2918(7)). After a judgment, the officer executing the writ removes occupants and personal property to an area open to the public or the right-of-way, or delivers it to the sheriff, and determines abandonment (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5744(1)-(2)). The optional hold-and-notice step is the landlord's choice. The RPOA lease's 'dispose of any and all ... abandoned personal property' at the landlord's 'sole discretion' is broader (MI log §15). Model abandoned-property-in; surrender-end-of-term-ks-ne points here. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Tenant Repair Agreement (Lease of 1 Year or More)
bodyText: Landlord and Tenant agree that, during the Term, Tenant will make the following specified repairs or perform the following specified maintenance at the property, and Landlord's obligation to do so is modified to that extent: [list each repair or maintenance item specifically]. Landlord remains responsible for every other obligation Michigan law places on Landlord, including keeping the property and all common areas fit for the use intended, keeping the property in reasonable repair except for the items listed above, and complying with the applicable health and safety laws of the state and of the local unit of government. This Section does not change any remedy Tenant has if the property is in a condition that violates the covenants of fitness and habitability. This Section ends if this Lease continues on a month-to-month or other periodic basis, or if this Lease no longer has a current term of at least 1 year.
notes: MI: Optional (rule 54, statute lets the lease decide; offered narrowly, rule 54 outlier wording). Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(2): 'The parties to the lease or license may modify the obligations imposed by this section where the lease or license has a current term of at least 1 year.' Builder: show only for a fixed Term of at least 1 year (MI log §10). Narrowed: named items only; the health and safety law compliance in Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(1)(b), fitness of premises and common areas in Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(1)(a) kept with the landlord; no remedy altered, since a provision that 'Waives or alters a remedy available to the parties when the premises are in a condition that violates the covenants of fitness and habitability' is void (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(a)). The covenants are 'liberally construed' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(3)); no published case on how far a Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(2) modification reaches was found (MI log §1.4). The repair covenant in Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(1)(b) does not apply to common areas, which fall under the fitness covenant in (1)(a) (Allison v AEW Capital Mgt, LLP, 481 Mich 419 (2008)), so the clause leaves common areas entirely with the landlord. Decided by Claude under Taylor's stance that a lawful option is the landlord's call (methodology memory; MI log §6.1). Model tenant-repair-agreement-tn / -ok. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Michigan's Prohibited Lease Terms (Truth in Renting Act)
bodyText: Michigan's Truth in Renting Act voids any lease term that: waives or alters a remedy available to either party when the premises violate the covenants of fitness and habitability; waives security deposit rights; discriminates in violation of Michigan's civil rights acts; provides for a confession of judgment; exculpates you for failing to perform, or negligently performing, a duty imposed by law (a mutual release limited to insured fire or casualty losses, with subrogation waived, is allowed); waives a jury trial or any notice or procedure required in court; makes a party pay the other's legal costs or attorney fees beyond what a statute specifically allows; gives you a security interest in the tenant's personal property, except as the law allows; accelerates rent on breach, unless it also states that the tenant may not owe the full accelerated amount because you must minimize damages and that either party may have a court decide the amount; waives rights under the lockout statute or the summary eviction chapter; releases either party from the duty to mitigate damages; lets you change the lease after it starts without the tenant's written consent, except changes on 30 days' written notice that are required by law, rule changes needed for health, safety or peaceful enjoyment, or rent changes to cover increases in property taxes, listed utility charges or insurance premiums; violates the Michigan Consumer Protection Act; requires a power of attorney; or, from September 21, 2026, charges a fee on every allowed method of paying rent (if more than one method is allowed, one must be fee-free). A term that a statute or a published Michigan Supreme Court or U.S. Supreme Court decision on Michigan law declared unenforceable at least 90 days before the lease was signed is also barred. You may cure a void term by written notice to every current tenant. If you do not cure within 20 days after a tenant's written notice, the tenant may sue to void the lease and end the tenancy, for an injunction, and for $250 per action (or $500 for an explicitly prohibited term or a missing required statement) or actual damages if greater, plus costs and statutory attorney fees; no prior notice is needed where you knew the term was unlawful. These rules cannot be waived.
notes: MI: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(a)-(o), (2), (3) (as amended by 2026 Mich. Pub. Acts 103, eff. Sept. 21, 2026, adding (1)(o)); cure Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.635; remedies Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.636(1)-(7); remedies cumulative Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.637; printed forms Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.638; no waiver Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.639. 'Rental agreement' is a written agreement beyond bare terms (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.632(a)). Each Michigan clause in the library was screened against every subdivision (MI log §19). The Truth in Renting Act, Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 554.631-554.641, read whole. Rule 47: knowing use removes the tenant's notice step and the cure defense (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.636(3)), so 'nothing in this lease limits your rights' does not make a void term safe. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Statements Every Michigan Lease Must Contain
bodyText: A Michigan lease must state the name and address at which notices under the Truth in Renting Act are to be given to you, and must print, in a prominent place in type at least 12-point (or legible print with letters at least 1/8 inch), the notice that Michigan law establishes rights and obligations for parties to rental agreements and that the tenant may want to seek legal help with questions. The library includes both. If a lease omits either one, you may cure it by giving every current tenant a written notice containing the statement; if you do not cure within 20 days after a tenant's written notice, the tenant may sue to void the lease and for $500 or actual damages. Other statements Michigan requires: a lease must give a tenant who has lived in the unit more than 13 months a right to end it on 60 days' notice when the tenant qualifies for subsidized senior housing or can no longer live independently; a condominium lease must state that the tenant will comply with the condominium documents; and if you take a security deposit you must give the tenant, within 14 days after move-in, a written notice of where it is held and of the 4-day forwarding-address rule, with a statement in 12-point boldface type at least 4 points larger than the rest of the notice.
notes: MI: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.634(1)-(2); cure Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.635(2)-(3); remedy Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.636(2)(d). Other required statements: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.601a(1) (early-termination-senior-infirmity-mi), Mich. Comp. Laws § 559.212(3) (hoa-compliance-mi), Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.603 (security-deposit-notice-mi). The domestic violence statement is optional in the lease but must otherwise be posted or delivered (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.601b(1); dv-release-notice-mi). title: No Exculpation of the Landlord
bodyText: A Michigan lease may not excuse you from liability for failing to perform, or negligently performing, a duty imposed by law. The one exception is a release from liability for loss, damage or injury caused by fire or other casualty for which the other party carries insurance under a policy that permits waiver of liability and waives the insurer's subrogation rights, and only to the extent the insured party recovers under the policy. For that reason the library's Michigan parking, storage, renter's insurance and services clauses do not say that you are 'not liable', and the pet clause's reimbursement promise excludes losses from your own failure to perform a legal duty.
notes: MI: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(e), (3). Rule 52: parking-ks-oh-ca, storage-space-ks-oh-ca, tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca and services-utilities-provided-ks-oh tagged instead of the bases; pet-policy-mi carve-out. The insurance-and-subrogation exception is quoted closely because a mutual waiver clause is the one exculpation a Michigan lease may carry; the library does not offer one (MI log §6.1). No published Michigan case deciding whether a broad tenant indemnity (as in the RPOA lease ¶ 26) is an exculpation under Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(e) was found (MI log §1.4). title: Attorney Fees and Court Costs
bodyText: A Michigan lease may not make a party pay the other party's legal costs or attorney fees in a dispute under the lease beyond what a statute specifically allows. In an eviction case the court may award costs as allowed in other civil actions in that court, plus limited extra amounts ($75 for a motion that results in dismissal or judgment or a default or consent judgment, and $150 for a trial), and only those costs. A party who wins a Truth in Renting Act action recovers court costs plus statutory attorney fees, and a tenant who proves discrimination may recover damages including attorney fees under the Elliott-Larsen and Persons with Disabilities civil rights acts. A prevailing-party attorney-fee clause in the lease would be void, so the library's Michigan default clause claims only court costs allowed by statute.
notes: MI: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(g); summary-proceeding costs Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5759(1)-(2) and MCR 4.201(L)(4) ('Only those costs permitted by MCL 600.5759 may be awarded'); Truth in Renting Act Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.636(4); civil rights Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 37.2801(3), 37.2802, 37.1606(1), (3); source-of-income actions Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.601d(1). Clause: default-by-tenant-mi. The RPOA lease's ¶ 57 ('taxable court costs and reasonable attorney fees') goes beyond the statute (MI log §15). title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText: In Michigan the total security deposit for a rental unit may not exceed 1 1/2 months' rent. Anything you collect that is returnable to the tenant when the unit is returned in the required condition counts toward the limit, including a refundable pet deposit, any required prepayment of rent other than the first full rental period, and any rent charged in a period above the average rent for the term. A nonrefundable fee is not a security deposit. The limit is the same for every kind of tenancy because it is measured against the deposit held, not a lease year.
notes: MI: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.602 ('shall not exceed 1 1/2 months' rent'); definition Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.601(d) (excludes an option-to-purchase payment unless intended to evade the act, and a cooperative membership). title: Holding the Security Deposit
bodyText: You must deposit a Michigan security deposit in a regulated financial institution. You may use the deposited money for any purpose only if you have deposited with the Michigan Secretary of State a cash bond or surety bond, acceptable to the Attorney General, securing all deposits up to $50,000 and 25% of any amount above $50,000. title: Move-In and Move-Out Inventory Checklists
bodyText: If you take a security deposit in Michigan, you must use inventory checklists at the start and end of every tenancy. At the start of the lease, give the tenant 2 blank copies of a commencement inventory checklist, identical to the form you will use at move-out, listing every item you own in the unit (carpeting, draperies, appliances, windows, furniture, walls, closets, shelves, paint, doors, plumbing fixtures and electrical fixtures). Unless you agree on a shorter time, the tenant returns one copy within 7 days after receiving possession. At move-out, complete a termination inventory checklist listing all damages you claim the tenant caused. You may not charge a tenant for damage claimed on a previous tenant's termination checklist.

title: Michigan Security Deposit Return Rules and Penalties
bodyText: Within 30 days after the tenant's occupancy ends, you must mail any notice of damages, itemizing each damaged item with its estimated repair cost and the amounts you intend to charge, with a check or money order for the balance, or, from September 21, 2026, instead transfer the balance electronically to the tenant's bank or payment account within 10 days after mailing the notice. The notice must state, in 12-point boldface type at least 4 points larger than the rest: 'You must respond to this notice by mail within 7 days after receipt of the notice of damages, otherwise you will forfeit the amount claimed for damages.' If you miss the 30 days you are treated as agreeing that no damages are due and must return the full deposit immediately. If the tenant disputes your claim in time, you may keep the disputed amount only if you start a court action for it within 45 days after occupancy ends and obtain a judgment, or the tenant agrees in writing; you need no judgment where the tenant gave no forwarding address, did not respond, agreed in writing, or the claim is entirely unpaid rent. If you do not comply fully, you waive all claimed damages and owe the tenant double the amount you retained. The tenant or the Attorney General may sue to enforce the act.

bodyText: A security deposit refund you cannot deliver is 'intangible property' under Michigan's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act. title: Michigan Covenants of Fitness and Repair
bodyText: In every Michigan residential lease you promise that the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended, that you will keep the premises in reasonable repair during the term, and that you will comply with the state and local health and safety laws, except where disrepair or a violation was caused by the tenant's wilful or irresponsible conduct or lack of conduct. A tenant's chance to inspect before signing does not defeat these promises, and they are liberally construed. The parties may modify them only in a lease with a current term of at least 1 year, and no lease may waive or alter the tenant's remedies when the premises violate them. In cities, villages and townships covered by the Housing Law of Michigan you must also keep every dwelling, including plumbing, heating, ventilating and electrical wiring, in good repair, keep the roof from leaking, and keep the building free from vermin, while tenants keep the parts they occupy and control clean. Common areas such as parking lots, sidewalks and stairways are covered by the fitness promise, which can require you to remove ice from a shared sidewalk; the repair promise does not apply to common areas, and fitness is judged with the tenants the property is meant for in mind. To evict a residential tenant you must allege in the complaint that you have performed these covenants or that the parties modified them.

Remedies protected by Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(a). Common areas: (1)(b) does not apply to common areas, a parking lot is a common area, and natural snow and ice make it unfit only in much more exigent circumstances than inconvenient access (Allison v AEW Capital Mgt, LLP, 481 Mich 419 (2008)); an interior sidewalk covered with ice is not fit for walking, and open-and-obvious does not bar the statutory claim (Benton v Dart Props, Inc, 270 Mich App 437 (2006)); Allison's principles apply to all common areas, including stairways (Hadden v McDermitt Apts, LLC, 287 Mich App 124 (2010)); Allison not overruled, and fitness is judged in light of the tenants the property holds itself out to (Bowerman v Red Oak Mgt Co, Inc, ___ Mich ___ (2026) (Docket No. 167718)). title: Modifying the Repair Covenant in a Lease of 1 Year or More
bodyText: Michigan lets the parties to a lease with a current term of at least 1 year modify the landlord's covenants of fitness and repair, for example by making the tenant responsible for specified repairs. A month-to-month or other lease without a current term of 1 year cannot do so, and no lease may take away the tenant's remedies when the premises are unfit. The library offers a narrow optional clause for fixed terms of 1 year or more that shifts only named repair or maintenance items and keeps fitness of the premises and common areas and health and safety law compliance with you. How far a court will let a modification reach is not settled by the statute or by a published case, so get advice before shifting more.

title: Tenant Remedies When Repairs Are Not Made
bodyText: Michigan tenants have several statutory remedies when a rental is not kept fit or in repair. In an eviction for nonpayment, the court deducts any rent excused by your breach of the lease or of the covenants of fitness and repair, and no possession judgment enters for nonpayment if your breach excused the rent. Where the Housing Law applies and a certificate of compliance is withheld or suspended, rent is suspended and paid into an escrow account to fund repairs, unless the tenant caused the hazard. An occupant may sue in the occupant's own name to enforce the Housing Law, a court may let the occupant correct a violation the occupant did not cause and deduct the cost from rent, and an occupant may recover actual damages after notice to you and a failure to correct unsafe, unsanitary or unhealthful conditions. A tenant's own repair labor is compensated at a reasonable rate when the court awards repair costs for your breach.

title: The Housing Law of Michigan: Where It Applies
bodyText: The Housing Law of Michigan applies in every city, village and township with a population of 10,000 or more under the last federal census; it reaches private (single-family) and 2-family dwellings only in places with 100,000 or more, unless the local governing body adopts it by resolution. Where it applies, the local enforcing agency may keep an owner registry (owners of multiple dwellings and rooming houses offered for rent more than 6 months a year must register within 60 days), inspect rental dwellings and charge reasonable inspection fees, and issue certificates of compliance. Inspectors need the tenant's consent to enter unless the lease authorizes inspector entry, the tenant complained, the unit is vacant or an administrative warrant issues; you must notify the tenant of a requested inspection and make a good-faith effort to obtain consent. You must request and obtain the tenant's permission before entering yourself, except in an emergency. Units in multiple dwellings and rooming houses may not be occupied until the enforcing agency issues a certificate of compliance, ordinarily after inspection. An owner who does not live in a multiple dwelling of more than 8 families must designate a responsible person. You provide covered garbage receptacles in a multiple dwelling; in single-family and 2-family homes the occupants do. Many Michigan cities, including Detroit, Ann Arbor, Grand Rapids and Lansing, run their own rental registration and inspection ordinances; this library does not cover local ordinances.
