Note Sec. 504B.204's treble remedy and Sec. 504B.195's Sec. 8.31 route are remedies for landlord conduct, not for drafting.

title: No Just-Cause Rule — the End of the Term Does End Possession
bodyText: North Dakota has no just-cause or good-cause eviction regime. Holding over after the termination of the lease or the expiration of the term is itself a ground for eviction (N.D.C.C. § 47-32-01(4)), so a lease that says possession ends when the term ends states North Dakota law rather than contradicting it, and you do not need a reason beyond the expiry. Four situational limits are worth knowing. The material-breach ground applies only to “a material term of the WRITTEN lease agreement” (§ 47-32-01(8)), so an oral North Dakota tenancy gives you no material-breach ground at all — you are left with nonpayment, holdover, or the disturbance ground. A tenant in a mobile home park may defend an eviction by showing you violated § 47-10-28, and the court may then refuse to order eviction (§ 47-32-01.1). On a showing that immediate restitution would work a substantial hardship on the tenant or the tenant's family, the court may stay the special execution for up to five days — except where the judgment rests wholly or partly on a disturbance of the peace (§ 47-32-04). And a tenant who exercised the domestic violence termination right is protected from retaliation in the rental of a dwelling (§ 47-16-17.1(10)).
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 47-32-01, 47-32-01.1, 47-32-02, 47-32-04; § 47-16-17.1(10). §§ 47-32-01 and 47-32-02 transcribed verbatim from the official compilation (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t47c32.pdf) on 2026-10-02; the chapter has six sections and no section 47-32-06. | RULE 41b. The verdict already existed in this log (§§ at lines recording 'For-cause eviction protection after 12 months: confirmed absent' and 'no statewide just-cause framework'), but no row carried it and no row used the for-cause-eviction topic_key, so rules 27 and 41 did not give the same answer. This row is that answer; nothing was re-opened. | RULE 41 SCREEN RESULT: no ND-tagged clause needed a change. surrender-end-of-term-mn-nd, early-termination, security-deposit-use, no-alterations and keys were all read for end-of-term-ends-possession wording; § 47-32-01(4) makes that wording correct in North Dakota, which is the opposite of the New Jersey problem (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.3(a)) that prompted the rule. | CONFIRMED ABSENT, with the boundary stated: no conversion-notice year, no rent-escrow bar and no tenants'-association protection located anywhere in ch. 47-32 or ch. 47-16. ND has no URLTA adoption, so there is no act-wide non-waiver section to generate one. | THE WRITTEN-LEASE LIMIT IN § 47-32-01(8) IS NEW TO THIS LIBRARY and is a real product point: it is an argument for always papering an ND tenancy.

title: Does North Dakota’s Consumer Fraud Law Reach a Lease? Unsettled
bodyText: North Dakota's consumer fraud statute (N.D.C.C. ch. 51-15) has no list of unfair practices — nothing about leaving blank spaces to be filled in after signing, nothing about giving the tenant a copy at signing, and no plain-language requirement. What it does have is a broad general standard: § 51-15-02 makes unlawful any deceptive act, fraud, false pretense, false promise or misrepresentation, with the intent that others rely on it, and separately any act or practice “which is unconscionable or which causes or is likely to cause substantial injury” — in both cases “in connection with the sale or advertisement of any merchandise,” and whether or not anyone was in fact misled. Whether that reaches renting a home is genuinely open. “Merchandise” is defined to include “real estate.” But “sale” is defined as a sale, offer for sale, or attempt to sell merchandise for consideration, and the definition never mentions a lease, a rental or leasing. So the act plainly covers selling a house and plainly does not list renting one; nothing in the chapter mentions a lease or rental of a dwelling anywhere. Treat it as a live risk rather than a settled exposure: the attorney general enforces this chapter, civil penalties are available, and the unconscionable limb needs no intent. North Dakota's own lease-specific unconscionability rule (§ 47-16-13.3) applies regardless.
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 51-15-01, 51-15-02; chapter section list and the definitions of 'merchandise' and 'sale' read from the official compilation (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t51c15.pdf) on 2026-10-02. | RULE 51, asked as its two separate questions. (a) ENUMERATED LIST: CONFIRMED ABSENT. ch. 51-15 has no enumerated unfair-practices list; §§ 51-15-02.1 (check endorsements), 51-15-02.2 (solicitation by bill or invoice) and 51-15-02.3 (facilitating and assisting) are the only specific practices named, and none touches a lease. (b) GENERAL STANDARD: NOT LOCATED / UNSETTLED, boundary stated. The text pulls both ways — 'merchandise' includes real estate, 'sale' does not mention leasing — and no North Dakota case law was read. Labelled unread rather than resolved (rule 76). | PLAIN LANGUAGE: CONFIRMED ABSENT. An official full-text search for "plain language" with 'contract' returned one Century Code chapter, ch. 23-17.4 (Title 23, Health), and no consumer-contract plain-language act. North Dakota has no analogue to Pennsylvania's Plain Language Consumer Contract Act, which drove a shared-row edit propagated into this log on 2026-09-29. | NO BLANK-SPACES RULE: confirmed absent here and separately at edu-no-lease-completeness-rule-nd. | METHOD LIMIT (rule 12): the official site serves the Century Code only as PDF and the browser pane cannot extract PDF text, so these sections were read through a fetch tool against the official PDF, with the operative wording taken as short verbatim fragments rather than a summary. Recorded rather than implied.

title: No Plain-Language Requirement for a Lease
bodyText: North Dakota has no plain-language statute for consumer contracts, and none for residential leases. There is no readability standard, no required type size, no rule about defined terms, and no sanction for a lease a tenant finds hard to read. Writing plainly is still worth doing — § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease provision, and how a term was presented is part of what a court looks at — but nothing requires it.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT, recorded as a row per the standing rule that log-only absences are invisible to future canvasses. | Basis: official ndlegis.gov full-text search for "plain language" together with 'contract', 2026-10-02 — one Century Code hit, ch. 23-17.4 (Title 23, Health), not a consumer-contract statute. ch. 47-16 read whole and contains no readability or type-size provision (see also the rule 40 layout table in this section). | RULE 51. Separated from edu-consumer-protection-act-nd deliberately: the consumer-fraud reach question is unsettled, this one is a clean absence, and merging them would let the uncertainty in one contaminate the other.

title: Shifting Your Repair Duties to the Tenant Needs More Than a Lease Clause
bodyText: North Dakota lets you move some of your own maintenance duties onto the tenant, but the route differs by property type and one of the two cannot be done in the lease at all. For a single-family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant performs your waste-receptacle and water-and-heat duties, and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodelling — but only if the transaction is entered into in good faith (§ 47-16-13.1(4)). For any other dwelling unit, the tenant may agree to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodelling only if all four of these hold: the agreement is in good faith; it is set forth in a SEPARATE WRITING signed by the parties and supported by ADEQUATE CONSIDERATION; the work is not needed to cure a failure of your waste-receptacle duty; and the agreement does not diminish or affect your obligations to other tenants (§ 47-16-13.1(5)). Because the statute requires a separate signed writing supported by its own consideration, a paragraph inside the lease cannot supply it. And you may not treat the tenant's performance of a single-family agreement as a condition of any obligation under the rental agreement (§ 47-16-13.1(6)) — so it cannot be a condition of renting. Your building-and-housing-code duty is never shiftable: where it is greater than any other duty in the list, it governs (§ 47-16-13.1(3)).
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(3)-(6), complete chapter text read from the official compilation (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t47c16.pdf) on 2026-10-02. | RULE 48, and the rule 40 keyword battery MISSED IT. The full-code battery for "separate document" returned six Century Code chapters, none reaching a residential lease (the Title 47 hit, ch. 47-33, expressly excludes 'any rent, reimbursement, charge, fee, or other amount payable by a lessee to a lessor under a lease' from its definition of a private transfer fee). The statute here says 'separate WRITING'. The requirement was found by reading the chapter section by section, not by the battery. Proposed as an SOP change: add 'separate writing' and 'separate instrument' to the rule 40/48 battery. | AFFECTS TWO SHARED CLAUSES: landscaping-irrigation and snow-removal shift maintenance tasks inside the lease, so in ND they bind only for a single-family residence (§ 47-16-13.1(4)); each carries an ND note segment saying so, and maintenance-allocation-nd covers every other dwelling. | This is also the rule 50 answer for § 47-16-13.1(4): the single-family duty-shift IS available in the lease, and is offered through the same optional agreement, maintenance-allocation-nd, which the bracketed scope instruction routes by property type. The non-single-family route is a SEPARATE SIGNED DOCUMENT, offered as maintenance-allocation-nd and printed outside the lease, per Taylor's decision 2026-10-02 following the AZ, NE and OK precedent. | NOT DETERMINED: what counts as 'adequate consideration' for § 47-16-13.1(5) — whether a rent reduction is required or a recited nominal sum suffices. No North Dakota case law read (rule 76 label).

title: Tenant Maintenance Agreement
bodyText: [Optional. Use for a property that is NOT a single-family residence; this agreement must be a separate writing signed by Landlord and Tenant, printed as its own document and not a section of the Lease. For a single-family residence, landscaping and snow removal are covered by the Lease’s Landscaping & Irrigation and Snow Removal sections, and this agreement may be used for other tasks.] Landlord and Tenant agree, in good faith and not to evade Landlord’s obligations, that Tenant will perform the following tasks: {{tenant_maintained_items}} [check each that applies: ☐ lawn and landscaping care, keeping to any irrigation schedule Landlord sets, and promptly reporting irrigation leaks or watering problems; ☐ prompt, reasonable removal of snow and ice from walkways, driveways, porches and entrances Tenant uses; ☐ replacing heating and air-conditioning filters; ☐ replacing light bulbs; ☐ taking garbage and other waste to the collection point; ☐ other: ______]. In consideration of Tenant performing these tasks, Landlord will {{maintenance_agreement_consideration}} [state what Landlord gives in return, for example a stated monthly rent reduction]. Landlord will not treat Tenant’s performance of this agreement as a condition of any obligation under the Lease, and will not withhold any right under the Lease because Tenant has not performed it. This agreement does not reduce any duty Landlord owes to other tenants of the premises, does not cover work needed because Landlord failed to provide receptacles or arrange removal of ashes, garbage, rubbish or other waste, and does not shift Landlord’s duty to comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety.
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(3)-(6); complete ch. 47-16 text read from the official compilation (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t47c16.pdf) on 2026-10-02. | RULE 54 OPTIONAL CLAUSE, built on TAYLOR’S DECISION 2026-10-02 to follow the AZ, NE and OK precedent (maintenance-allocation-az; edu-tenant-maintenance-agreement-ok plus tenant-repair-agreement-ok) rather than fork landscaping-irrigation and snow-removal for ND. | WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: § 47-16-13.1(5) makes an agreement that the tenant perform ‘specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling’ in a dwelling unit OTHER THAN a single-family residence effective only if it is in good faith, ‘set forth in a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration’, not needed to cure a § 47-16-13.1(1)(e) waste failure, and does not diminish or affect the landlord’s obligations to other tenants. A paragraph inside the lease cannot satisfy that, so landscaping-irrigation and snow-removal bind in ND only for a single-family residence under § 47-16-13.1(4). | EVERY ELEMENT OF § 47-16-13.1(5) IS IN THE TEXT, deliberately: good faith and not-to-evade; a separate signed document; a consideration blank, because ‘adequate consideration’ is a statutory condition and a recited nominal sum is the thing most likely to fail it; the no-condition sentence from § 47-16-13.1(6); the other-tenants limit; the waste-removal carve-out; and the § 47-16-13.1(3) code floor, which is never shiftable. | SNOW AND SHARED AREAS: snow-removal was rewritten on 2026-10-02 (MI sync) to exclude ‘areas shared with other residents’, which keeps it clear of § 47-16-13.1(1)(c) (landlord keeps common areas clean and safe). The checkbox here is scoped the same way, to areas Tenant uses. | BUILDER GAP, recorded for ND as AZ and NE recorded it: the builder cannot hide or show a clause by property type, so nothing stops a landlord printing this agreement for a single-family home or printing landscaping-irrigation for a duplex. The bracketed scope instruction is the only guard available until that gap is closed. | NOT DETERMINED: what counts as ‘adequate consideration’ — whether a rent reduction is required or a recited nominal sum suffices. No North Dakota case law read (rule 76 label).

title: Holdover
bodyText: If Tenant does not vacate the property when this Lease ends, whether at the end of the Term or on an earlier termination, Landlord may pursue any remedy allowed by law to recover possession and may recover the actual damages caused by Tenant's continued possession, including the reasonable rental value of the property for the period Tenant remains. Alternatively, Landlord may accept Tenant's continued payment of Rent, in which case this Lease will continue as a month-to-month tenancy on the same terms, terminable as provided by law. Nothing in this Section limits any statutory damages measure applicable law provides for a holdover.
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-06, 47-16-13.7, 32-03-27, 32-03-28, with §§ 9-08-03 and 9-08-04 as the constraint on a stated figure. BASIS (rule 79, recorded because every new CITED row records its basis): §§ 47-16-06 and 47-16-13.7 from the complete ch. 47-16 text read from the official compilation (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t47c16.pdf), re-read 2026-10-02; §§ 32-03-27 and 32-03-28 read from primary text at the ND re-audit 2026-09-06 (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t32c03.pdf, whole chapter) and carried on edu-holdover-damages-nd, NOT re-read today; §§ 9-08-03 and 9-08-04 transcribed verbatim from the official compilation (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t09c08.pdf) on 2026-09-27 and recorded on edu-prohibited-lease-terms-nd. | RULE 54 OPTIONAL CLAUSE, filling a real gap: North Dakota was the ONLY state in the library with no holdover lease clause at all. ND is untagged on the shared `holdover` (the provenance finding removed its baseless 'double the Monthly Rent' figure), and `edu-holdover-damages-nd` is education, which a tenant never reads. | WHY THERE IS NO STATED PER-DAY FIGURE, and this is the whole drafting decision: ND has two statutory double-damages measures but each has a narrow trigger — § 32-03-27 needs the tenant to have GIVEN NOTICE of intent to leave and then stayed, and § 32-03-28 needs a WILFUL holdover after notice of intention to evict AND demand for possession. The ordinary case (tenant stays, gave no notice, no demand yet) falls outside both, which is the 'for which cases and in what shape' question rule 54 asks. The lease may fill that gap — but a stipulated figure is liquidated damages, void under § 9-08-04 absent an impracticability showing, and void outright as a penalty under § 9-08-03 if it looks punitive. North Dakota is therefore in the same double bind as California: no statute to point at for the ordinary case, and a stated figure exposed to a per se rule. Body claims actual damages and reasonable rental value only. Modelled on holdover-ca for exactly that reason. | THE MONTH-TO-MONTH LIMB STATES § 47-16-06: where a residential lessee stays after expiration and the lessor accepts rent, the parties are presumed to have renewed as a month-to-month tenancy (and the section's own 'Except in the case of a lease with an automatic renewal clause' opening is why automatic-renewal-nd exists). 'Terminable as provided by law' rather than a figure, because § 47-16-15 then governs. | LAST SENTENCE preserves §§ 32-03-27 and 32-03-28 rather than displacing them — a clause claiming only actual damages must not be read as a waiver of the statutory multipliers.

title: Automatic Renewal
bodyText: This Lease will renew automatically for a further term of [state the renewal term] unless either party gives the other written notice of non-renewal at least [state the notice period] before the end of the then-current Term. Landlord will notify Tenant in writing of this automatic renewal provision, delivered personally or by first-class mail, not less than thirty days before the expiration date of the then-current Term. If Landlord does not give that notice, this Lease expires at the end of the Term and its terms convert to a month-to-month tenancy.
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-06, 47-16-06.1; complete chapter text read from the official compilation 2026-10-02. | RULE 54 OPTIONAL CLAUSE. An automatic renewal clause is a term North Dakota law expressly contemplates and conditions rather than bans, and ND had an education row for the notice duty (edu-automatic-renewal-notice-nd) and no clause to attach it to. | THE CLAUSE CARRIES ITS OWN DEFEAT CONDITION DELIBERATELY. § 47-16-06.1 applies to any residential lease 'of a specified term of two months or more' and makes the renewal clause UNENFORCEABLE unless the lessor gave written notice of the automatic renewal provision not less than thirty days before expiry; if that notice was not given, 'the lease expires, and the terms of the latest lease convert to a month-to-month tenancy'. Stating the condition and the consequence in the clause itself is the only way a landlord reading the lease learns that the renewal they are relying on is conditional. | DELIVERY IS CLOSED, NOT OPEN: § 47-16-06.1 says 'delivered personally or by first-class mail'. Email does not satisfy it, and ch. 9-16 does not cure that — § 9-16-07(2)(b) requires a record to be sent by the method the other law specifies, and § 9-16-07(4)(b)'s variation carve-out reaches only a first-class-mail requirement 'to the extent permitted by the other law', which § 47-16-06.1 does not permit. See edu-no-electronic-notice-regime-nd. | INTERACTION WITH HOLDOVER: § 47-16-06's month-to-month presumption on accepting rent after expiry is expressly subject to 'Except in the case of a lease with an automatic renewal clause', so a lease with this Section renews on its own terms instead of converting — provided the thirty-day notice was given. | TWO-MONTH FLOOR NOT STATED in the body because the builder cannot condition on term length yet; a lease of a term under two months is outside § 47-16-06.1 and the notice duty does not arise. Recorded here rather than guessed at in the text.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, freezing, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's obligation to repair deteriorations or injuries to the property caused by Tenant's ordinary negligence.
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-10, 47-16-14(4), 47-16-17(2), 47-16-13.4, 47-16-13.5, 47-16-13.7; complete chapter text read from the official compilation 2026-10-02. tenant-caused-damage-tn read as the model and NOT tagged. | RULE 54t, run as the rule directs — each exit or abatement provision checked SEPARATELY for its own tenant-fault exception. § 47-16-17(2) (tenant may terminate when the greater part, or the part that was the material inducement, perishes) HAS one: 'from any cause other than the ordinary negligence of the lessee'. § 47-16-14(4) (the leasing terminates 'by the destruction of the property leased') has NONE — so a total loss the tenant caused still ends the lease automatically, and the landlord is left with a damages claim rather than a continuing tenancy. That asymmetry is the reason part (2) of this clause exists. | NOTHING TO WAIVE ON THE ABATEMENT SIDE: North Dakota has no statutory rent-abatement provision at all — no essential-services abatement, no rent-into-court, no proportional reduction (its casualty right is all-or-nothing). Part (1) therefore does not contract around a tenant protection, because there is no abatement right to contract around. Checked rather than assumed. | WHAT THE LAW ALREADY GIVES, so the clause does not duplicate it: § 47-16-10 obliges the lessee to 'repair all deteriorations or injuries thereto occasioned by the lessee's ordinary negligence' (the statutory phrase is 'ordinary negligence' and the closing sentence uses it rather than paraphrasing to 'negligence'); § 47-16-13.4 gives a separate claim for actual damages for breach. The GAP the lease fills is lost rent during repairs and after an early end, for which ND supplies no measure. | MITIGATION: § 47-16-13.5's duty is scoped by its own first sentence to parties aggrieved under §§ 47-16-13.1 through 13.6, and § 47-16-13.7's applies to an evicted lessee, so neither squarely covers this case — the mitigation sentence here is contractual, and is included because § 9-08-04 would otherwise leave part (2) looking like an unbounded stipulated loss. See edu-early-departure-mitigation-nd for the scoping disagreement on record. | UNREAD RISK (rule 76 label): whether a North Dakota court measures the landlord's damages as lost rent through the end of the Term rests on case law not read.

title: Where North Dakota Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: North Dakota's leasing chapter leaves six things to the lease, and a lease that is silent takes the statutory default instead of the choice. (1) The products of the property during the term belong to the tenant “in the absence of any agreement to the contrary” (§ 47-16-04), so if a garden, fruit trees or standing hay matter to you, say so. (2) A lease with an automatic renewal clause escapes the holdover-converts-to-month-to-month presumption (§ 47-16-06) — see automatic-renewal-nd. (3) A single-family residence may shift some of your maintenance duties to the tenant (§ 47-16-13.1(4)) — see tenant-duty-shift-single-family-nd. (4) Any other dwelling unit may do so only in a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration (§ 47-16-13.1(5)), which the lease cannot be. (5) A month-to-month tenancy takes one calendar month's notice “unless the parties have otherwise agreed in writing to a longer notice period or a different notice time” (§ 47-16-15(2)) — and a longer period binds the tenant only if initialled (§ 47-16-15(4)). (6) Double-letting of a room cannot be agreed around at all: the first tenant takes the whole room “notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary” (§ 47-16-26). Two further terms are lawful but not offered in this library. A landlord's own right to terminate after a fire or casualty: North Dakota gives you none, and nothing bars the lease from creating one, but it has to be drafted against § 47-16-14(4), which already ends the lease on destruction, and against § 47-16-17(2), which is the tenant's right and cannot be taken away. A clause reserving the products of the property: lawful under § 47-16-04, but it belongs in an agricultural or rural lease rather than a dwelling lease. If you want either, add your own clause and take advice first.
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-04, 47-16-06, 47-16-13.1(4)-(6), 47-16-15(2), 47-16-15(4), 47-16-26, 47-16-14(4), 47-16-17(2); complete chapter text read from the official compilation 2026-10-02. | RULE 50, run as an inventory: every place the chapter lets the lease or the parties decide, each with a deliberate choice rather than a default. The six are the complete set found in ch. 47-16; the phrases are 'in the absence of any agreement to the contrary' (§ 47-16-04), 'Except in the case of a lease with an automatic renewal clause' (§ 47-16-06), 'may agree in writing' / 'may agree' (§ 47-16-13.1(4),(5)), 'unless the parties have otherwise agreed in writing' (§ 47-16-15(2)) and 'notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary' (§ 47-16-26, which runs the other way and forbids agreement). | RULE 54 — THE TWO DECLINED OPTIONS GET THIS ROW RATHER THAN SILENCE, per the rule's requirement that a lawful option the library declines still gets an education row saying so, because landlords never see the log. | Landlord casualty termination: offered in GA, NC, SC, AL and PA; declined for ND because § 47-16-14(4) already terminates the leasing on destruction, so the clause would add value only for PARTIAL damage, where it would sit directly against the tenant's § 47-16-17(2) right and risk reading as a waiver of it. A narrow version is possible and is a product decision rather than a legal bar. | Products reservation: lawful, declined as out of scope for a dwelling lease (SOP agricultural scope). | OPTIONS OFFERED by this retro instead: automatic-renewal-nd, tenant-duty-shift-single-family-nd, holdover-nd, tenant-caused-damage-nd.

title: North Dakota Writes a Covenant of Quiet Possession Into Every Lease
bodyText: North Dakota does not leave quiet possession to the lease's wording. An agreement to lease real property binds the lessor to secure to the lessee the quiet possession of the property during the term, against all persons lawfully claiming the same (§ 47-16-08). The duty runs against lawful claims — a mortgagee, a buyer, a co-owner, a superior title — rather than against a trespasser or a noisy neighbour, and it is yours whether or not the lease mentions it. Two consequences for you. A tenant whose possession you fail to secure may terminate if you do not fulfil the obligation within a reasonable time after a request (§ 47-16-17(1)). And it is the reason the tenant must pass on any notice of a proceeding against the property and may not recognise anyone else as landlord without your consent or a court judgment (§ 47-16-25) — your duty and that one are two halves of the same arrangement.
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-08, with §§ 47-16-17(1) and 47-16-25; complete chapter text read from the official compilation 2026-10-02. | RULE 27 topic quiet-possession: PRESENT, with a row. ND had none. | CORRECTS THE FRAMING OF A PRIOR FINDING IN THIS LOG. The 2026-09-27 gap-discovery backfill (§ 43.7(D)) recorded that no state had a quiet-possession LEASE CLAUSE and left ND's statutory covenant as a cross-state product question. The clause question is still Taylor's; the statutory duty was ND's to row and is rowed here. A library-wide clause gap and a missing state row are different defects and the first should not have absorbed the second. | WHY EDUCATION AND NOT A CLAUSE: § 47-16-08 binds the lessor by operation of the leasing agreement itself, so a clause restating it adds nothing a tenant could enforce that they cannot enforce already, and the three-bucket scrub's own test (2026-09-29) puts a landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says in education. | SCOPE PRECISION: the statute's words are 'against all persons lawfully claiming the same'. The row says so rather than implying a general quiet-enjoyment warranty against any disturbance, which is the commoner but wrong reading.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent Setting
bodyText: North Dakota has no statute addressing algorithmic or software-assisted rent setting, and no ban on using a third-party pricing service or on sharing rent data with one. Federal antitrust law still applies to agreements among competing landlords, and § 47-16-02.1 separately bars a political subdivision from controlling what you may charge — so neither a local rent cap nor a state rule stands in the way, and the exposure such a service creates is a federal one rather than a North Dakota one.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT, recorded as a row per the standing rule on log-only absences. | RULE 27 topic algorithmic-rent-setting — one of the seven topics no state had a row for when the SOP was written; 13 states now do and ND did not. | Basis: official ndlegis.gov full-text search 2026-10-02; ch. 47-16 read whole from the official compilation and contains no rent-setting provision of any kind beyond § 47-16-02.1's preemption of political subdivisions. | Federal antitrust exposure named but NOT researched — outside this project's state-law scope (SOP rule 4). Boundary stated rather than implied.

title: No Rule on Calling Fees “Rent”
bodyText: North Dakota has no statute that lets you designate fees as additional rent, and none that stops you. Nothing in the leasing chapter defines rent, and no provision restricts what a lease may treat as rent. That silence matters most at eviction: the nonpayment ground is “fails to pay rent for three days after the rent is due” (§ 47-32-01(4)), and whether an unpaid fee the lease calls rent supports that ground has not been settled in North Dakota. Treat it as unsettled rather than available. This library's shared payment clause applies each payment to rent first and only then to other charges, which keeps an unpaid fee from turning into an apparent rent shortfall — the practical protection, whatever the label question turns out to be.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT as to any statute, with the eviction-ground question flagged as unsettled. | RULE 27 topic fees-as-rent; 16 states have a row and ND did not. | Basis: official ndlegis.gov full-text search for "additional rent" 2026-10-02 — the only Century Code hit is ch. 53-06.1 (gaming), nothing in landlord-tenant law. ch. 47-16 read whole: no definition of rent. § 47-32-01(4) transcribed verbatim from the official compilation. | NO ND CASE LAW READ on whether a lease-designated fee is 'rent' for § 47-32-01(4) (rule 76 label). Stated as unsettled rather than resolved in either direction, because the landlord-favourable reading would put an eviction at risk and the tenant-favourable reading would give up a remedy. | Cross-reference to application-of-payments is deliberate: it is the reason the unsettled point is survivable in practice.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix the Tenant’s Breach and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: North Dakota gives you no URLTA-style right to remedy a tenant's breach yourself and recover the cost as rent. What the chapter gives you instead is a termination right: you may terminate the lease and reclaim the property before the end of the term if the tenant uses it contrary to the agreement, or does not make the repairs the tenant is bound to make within a reasonable time after a request (§ 47-16-16). You may also sue for the cost — the tenant must repair deteriorations or injuries caused by the tenant's ordinary negligence (§ 47-16-10), and a terminated lease leaves you a separate claim for actual damages (§ 47-16-13.4). What you cannot do is treat the repair cost as rent and evict for nonpayment of it; that route does not exist in North Dakota, and trying it risks the eviction.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT, recorded as a row. | RULE 27 topic landlord-self-cure (URLTA § 4.105-style); 13 states have a row and ND did not. | Basis: ch. 47-16 and ch. 47-32 read whole from the official compilation 2026-10-02. ND has not adopted URLTA, which is why the right is missing — the architectural reason, not just the absence. | The remedies named as substitutes are each primary-confirmed: § 47-16-16 (termination for contrary use or failure to repair after request), § 47-16-10 ('repair all deteriorations or injuries thereto occasioned by the lessee's ordinary negligence'), § 47-16-13.4 (separate claim for actual damages). | The closing warning connects to edu-no-fees-as-rent-rule-nd: both failure modes are the same move — relabelling something as rent to reach the § 47-32-01(4) ground.

title: No Rule Against Blank Spaces in the Lease
bodyText: North Dakota has no statute requiring a written lease to have every blank space completed, and no provision making an incomplete lease a breach or unenforceable. Leaving blanks is still a bad idea — § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision, and a term filled in after signing invites exactly that argument — but there is no North Dakota rule to point at, and no consumer-protection list of unfair practices that names it.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT, recorded as a row. | RULE 27 topic lease-completeness; 12 states have a row and ND did not. | Basis: ch. 47-16 read whole from the official compilation 2026-10-02 — no completeness or blank-space provision; and ch. 51-15 read for an enumerated unfair-practices list, which it does not have (see edu-consumer-protection-act-nd). AZ's analogue is A.R.S. § 33-1322(E); ND has no counterpart. | The § 47-16-13.3 route is stated as an argument a tenant could make, not as a rule, because that is what it is.

title: Statutory Forms North Dakota Supplies
bodyText: North Dakota supplies no form for a residential lease and no form for an eviction notice — the three days' written notice of intention to evict has no prescribed wording (§ 47-32-02). Two forms are set out verbatim in statute, and only one is likely to touch you. If a tenant's cheque is dishonoured and you want the civil penalty rather than just the collection fee, § 6-08-16(4) prints the notice of dishonour you must mail, including its demand that the tenant pay within ten days; the notice itself is optional, but the penalty depends on it. The other, § 47-16-36, prints a notice for cancelling a forfeited oil, gas or mineral lease and has nothing to do with a dwelling. The move-in condition statement § 47-16-07.2 requires is a mandatory document with no prescribed form — the statute says what it must describe and who must sign, and leaves the layout to you.
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 6-08-16(4), 47-16-36, 47-16-07.2, 47-32-02. §§ 47-16-36 and 47-16-07.2 from the complete chapter text read from the official compilation 2026-10-02; § 47-32-02 transcribed verbatim the same day; § 6-08-16(4) already primary-confirmed on edu-returned-check-fee-cap-nd. | RULE 27 topic statutory-forms; 14 states have a row and ND did not. | THE DISTINCTION THIS ROW EXISTS TO DRAW: a form the statute PRINTS (§§ 6-08-16(4), 47-16-36) is not the same as a document the statute REQUIRES without prescribing its shape (§ 47-16-07.2). Conflating the two is how a landlord ends up hunting for an official condition-statement form that does not exist. | § 6-08-16(4)'s notice is permissive ('may be mailed') but conditions the § 6-08-16(2)(c) civil penalty — the point already recorded on edu-returned-check-fee-cap-nd and corroborated by State v. Ohnstad, 392 N.W.2d 389, 390 (N.D. 1986), which is cited there and NOT independently read here (rule 76 label).

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: North Dakota has no statute about a tenant installing a security camera, a video doorbell or a monitoring device at a rented home — nothing permitting it, nothing banning it, and no rule about recording common areas or a neighbour's door. So the lease governs. Two limits are worth knowing anyway: a camera or doorbell that is screwed, drilled or wired into the property is an alteration under this library's alterations clause and needs your written consent, while a device that simply sits on a shelf or plugs in is not; and a request to install one as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is a fair housing question rather than an alterations question, which North Dakota law does reach.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT, recorded as a row. | RULE 27 topic tenant-security-cameras; 12 states have a row and ND did not. | Basis: official ndlegis.gov full-text search for "security cameras" 2026-10-02 — no Century Code hit; ch. 47-16 read whole, no device or installation provision. VA's analogue (tenant security systems) has no ND counterpart. | The alterations distinction is a reading of this library's own `no-alterations` clause applied to ND facts, not a statutory holding, and is phrased so it cannot be read as one. The accommodation route is edu-disability-modification-nd.

title: Medical Cannabis and Your Smoking Ban
bodyText: North Dakota allows medical marijuana for registered qualifying patients and has not legalised recreational use. Its medical chapter says almost nothing about renting. It expressly does not require “a landlord to allow production or processing on rental property” (§ 19-24.1-34(1)(c)) — production and processing only, not possession or use by a patient. It bans consumption on school, correctional and child-care grounds, and where the smoke or vapour would be inhaled by a minor who is not the patient (§ 19-24.1-33), but not in a rented home. And it protects a registered qualifying patient from “arrest or prosecution or the denial of any right or privilege” (§ 19-24.1-32(1)) without saying whether housing is among those privileges. The result is an untested gap: your flat lease ban on smoking marijuana is not void — nothing in North Dakota law voids it, and there is no constitutional cannabis provision here — but whether it can be enforced against a registered qualifying patient's medical use has not been decided. A ban on smoking of any kind, applied to every tenant alike and justified by odour, damage and fire risk, is the stronger ground than one aimed at marijuana; and a patient who asks to use a non-smoked form is making a request worth considering on its own.
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 19-24.1-32(1), 19-24.1-33, 19-24.1-34(1)(c), read from the official compilation (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t19c24-1.pdf) on 2026-10-02. | RULE 35c, and the constitution limb came out clean: the ND Constitution has sixteen articles and Article XIV is the ETHICS COMMISSION, not cannabis. Article I (Declaration of Rights) read in full from the official PDF (ndlegis.gov/constit/a01.pdf), all twenty-five sections: § 1 (arms, 'for the defense of their person, family, property, and the state, and for lawful hunting'), § 4 (speech), § 8 (searches, 'persons, houses, papers and effects'), §§ 16 and 18 (takings; 'law impairing the obligations of contracts'). All bind the state, none regulates a private contract or protects tenant conduct against a private landlord. So the Missouri problem — Article XIV voiding the shared smoking-policy's ban on vaping marijuana — DOES NOT ARISE in North Dakota, and no clause needed an override. | METHOD FINDING worth an SOP note: the official ndlegis.gov full-text search corpus does NOT include the state constitution. A search for "keep and bear arms" returns only session documents, with no CONSTITUTION document type anywhere in the results. Rule 35c's instruction to 'load the state constitution into your full-text search' cannot be satisfied on this state's official search; the constitution has to be read article by article instead, and the rule should say so. | WHY THIS ROW AND NOT A CLAUSE CHANGE: the asymmetry in § 19-24.1-34(1)(c) — production and processing expressly preserved to the landlord, possession and use not mentioned — is what makes the question live rather than settled. ND is one of twenty-six states on the shared smoking-policy row, and proposing a shared edit on an untested theory would be worse than recording it. No ND case law read (rule 76 label).

title: Property Manager and Agent for Notices
bodyText: Management and notices. The person authorized to manage the property is: [name and address]. An owner of the property, or a person authorized to act for and on behalf of the owner for the purpose of service of process and for the purpose of receiving and receipting for notices and demands, is: [name and address]. Landlord will keep this information current and will tell Tenant in writing if it changes.
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 562A.13(1): the landlord or a person authorized to enter into a rental agreement for the landlord 'shall disclose to the tenant in writing at or before the commencement of the tenancy' the name and address of (a) the person authorized to manage the premises and (b) an owner or a person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands. Kept current and binding on a successor landlord, owner or manager (Iowa Code § 562A.13(2)); a person who fails to disclose becomes the landlord's agent for service and for performing the landlord's obligations, including spending rent collected (Iowa Code § 562A.13(3)); a manager who fails to disclose is a 'landlord' (Iowa Code § 562A.6(5)). Tenant notices may be served on the agent designated here (Iowa Code § 562A.8(1)(b)(1)-(2)). The lease is the writing; the statute prescribes no wording or format (IA log §4). title: Late Fee
bodyText: If Tenant does not pay Monthly Rent in full within {{late_fee_grace_days}} days after it is due, Tenant will owe a late fee of {{late_fee_daily_amount}} for each day after that period until the Rent is paid in full, but the late fees for any one month will not total more than {{late_fee_monthly_max}}. Acceptance of a late payment does not waive Landlord's right to require full and timely payment of Rent in the future, to charge a late fee for any later late payment, or to pursue any remedy for a different breach.
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 562A.9(4): where rent does not exceed $700 per month, a rental agreement 'shall not provide for a late fee that exceeds twelve dollars per day or a total amount of sixty dollars per month'; where rent is greater than $700 per month, not more than $20 per day or $100 per month (2013 Iowa Acts ch. 97, § 3). BUILDER (backlog M.13): cap {{late_fee_daily_amount}} at $12 and {{late_fee_monthly_max}} at $60 when {{monthly_rent}} is $700 or less, and at $20 and $100 when it is more; the clause states the landlord's figures, never the statutory limits (rule 55). A flat one-time fee is not used because a single charge above the daily ceiling could exceed 'per day' (IA log §6.3). The non-waiver sentence is drawn narrowly because accepting performance that varies from the agreement waives the right to terminate for that breach (Iowa Code § 562A.30(1)); a temporary waiver needs notice under Iowa Code § 562A.30(2). Late fees are 'rent' under Iowa Code § 562A.6(10) (`edu-fees-as-rent-ia`). No grace period is required by Iowa law. Supersedes the base `late-fee` (flat fee and broad non-waiver). title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If a check, draft or order Tenant gives Landlord is dishonored, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-check charge of {{nsf_fee}}, except where the reason for the dishonor is that Tenant stopped payment. Landlord will also post a clear and conspicuous notice of this charge and its amount at the usual place of payment or in Tenant's billing statement. If any payment of Rent is dishonored or otherwise fails, Landlord may require that it be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order, and if more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term fail, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by one of those methods.
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 554.3512(1): the holder of a dishonored check, draft or order may assess a surcharge 'not to exceed thirty dollars'; (2): not assessable unless the holder 'clearly and conspicuously posts a notice at the usual place of payment, or in the billing statement of the holder, stating that a surcharge will be assessed and the amount', and never where the dishonor is because the maker stopped payment under Iowa Code § 554.4403. BUILDER: cap {{nsf_fee}} at $30 (§10). Whether the lease itself counts as the posting is not settled, so the clause commits to the statutory posting (IA log §4). The statute covers checks, drafts and orders only; no fee is charged for a failed electronic payment. Supersedes the base `returned-payments`, whose 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' wording states only a ceiling (rule 53). title: Tenant Default
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and does not pay it within three days after Landlord's written notice of nonpayment and of Landlord's intention to terminate this Lease if the Rent is not paid within that time. Tenant will also be in default if Tenant materially fails to comply with this Lease, or fails to comply with Tenant's statutory maintenance duties in a way that materially affects health and safety, and does not adequately remedy the failure within seven days after receiving Landlord's written notice specifying the breach and stating that this Lease will terminate on a date not less than seven days after receipt of the notice if the breach is not remedied. Neither of these opportunities to pay or remedy applies where Iowa law permits Landlord to terminate without one, including a recurrence within six months of substantially the same breach for which notice was given, and conduct creating a clear and present danger to the health or safety of others. Except as required by applicable law, Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise all rights and remedies available under applicable law, including terminating this Lease, regaining possession of the property through the courts, and recovering unpaid Rent and actual damages, less amounts lawfully withheld from the Security Deposit. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to mitigate damages resulting from Tenant's default to the extent required by applicable law.
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 562A.27(2) (rent: three days after written notice of nonpayment and of the intention to terminate if not paid); Iowa Code § 562A.27(1) (material noncompliance with the rental agreement or a noncompliance with Iowa Code § 562A.17 materially affecting health and safety: written notice specifying the breach and a termination date not less than seven days after receipt; no termination if the breach is remediable and adequately remedied before that date; recurrence of substantially the same act within six months: termination on at least seven days' written notice without a cure); Iowa Code § 562A.27A (clear and present danger: single three days' notice of termination and notice to quit, no cure; `edu-clear-present-danger-ia`); Iowa Code § 562A.27(5) (a municipal housing agency established under ch. 403A may give a 30-day notice citing a federal regulation, no cure). Rule 43: the no-cure carve-out is its own sentence and reaches both limbs; the rent limb adds no pre-suit notice beyond the statute's own three-day notice. Termination notices are served under Iowa Code § 562A.29A. Damages: Iowa Code § 562A.27(3), Iowa Code § 562A.32; mitigation Iowa Code § 562A.4(1), Iowa Code § 562A.29(3). NOT TAGGED `default-by-tenant`: its prevailing-party attorney-fee sentence is a term Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(c) prohibits ('agrees to pay the other party's attorney fees'), and willful use of a known prohibited term exposes the landlord to actual damages, plus up to three months' periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(3)). NOT TAGGED `default-by-tenant-ks-ne`: its 'reasonable costs and expenses' could be read as collection or attorney costs the tenant agrees to pay (rule 49; cross-state flag OK log §10), so this variant recovers only unpaid Rent and actual damages; statutory fee awards (Iowa Code §§ 562A.27(3), 562A.34(4)) need no lease term. title: Use of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit) prior to occupancy. Landlord will hold the Security Deposit for Tenant in a bank, savings and loan association or credit union insured by an agency of the federal government, and will not commingle it with Landlord's personal funds. Any interest earned on the Security Deposit during the first five years of the tenancy belongs to Landlord. Landlord may withhold from the Security Deposit only the amounts reasonably necessary to: (1) remedy Tenant's default in paying Rent or other funds due to Landlord under this Lease; (2) restore the property to its condition at the commencement of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted; and (3) recover expenses Landlord incurs in acquiring possession of the property from a Tenant who does not act in good faith in failing to surrender and vacate it after a noncompliance with this Lease and Landlord's notice of that noncompliance under Iowa law. The Security Deposit does not relieve Tenant of any obligation to pay Rent, and Tenant may not apply it to Rent without Landlord's written consent.
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 562A.12(1) (not more than two months' rent as a security deposit; BUILDER: cap {{security_deposit}} plus any {{pet_deposit}} at two times {{monthly_rent}}, §10); Iowa Code § 562A.12(2) (held for the tenant in a federally insured bank, savings and loan association or credit union; not commingled with the landlord's personal funds; may be in a common or interest-bearing trust account; 'Any interest earned on a rental deposit during the first five years of a tenancy shall be the property of the landlord'; the statute is silent on later interest, `edu-deposit-interest-ia`); Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a)(1)-(3) (the only withholding grounds, quoted closely); Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(b) (landlord's burden of proof). A 'rental deposit' excludes a deposit exclusively in advance payment of rent (Iowa Code § 562A.6(12)). NOT TAGGED `security-deposit-use`: its 'any Tenant default under this Lease' and cleaning standard are broader than Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a), and a lease cannot enlarge the statutory grounds (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)). Rule 37: the cap is a flat two months' rent for every tenancy type. title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: When this tenancy ends, Tenant will give Landlord in writing a mailing address or delivery instructions for the return of the Security Deposit. Within 30 days after the later of the end of the tenancy and Landlord's receipt of Tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions, in writing or otherwise, Landlord will return the Security Deposit or give Tenant a written statement showing the specific reason for withholding any part of it, and, for any amount withheld to restore the property, the nature of the damage, returning any balance with the statement. If Tenant gives Landlord no mailing address or delivery instructions within one year after the tenancy ends, the Security Deposit reverts to Landlord and Tenant forfeits all rights to it.
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 562A.12(3)(a) (within thirty days from the date of termination of the tenancy and receipt of the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions, return the deposit or furnish a written statement showing the specific reason for withholding; if withheld for restoration, the statement specifies the nature of the damages); Iowa Code § 562A.12(4) (a landlord who fails to provide the statement within thirty days forfeits all rights to withhold any portion; if no mailing address or instructions are provided within one year from termination, the deposit reverts to the landlord and the tenant is deemed to have forfeited it); Iowa Code § 562A.12(7) (bad-faith retention: punitive damages up to twice the monthly rental payment plus actual damages); Iowa Code § 562A.12(8) (fees to the prevailing party in a deposit dispute; limited to rental deposit disputes, Butter v Midwest Property Management IC, LLC, ___ N.W.3d ___ (Iowa 2025) (No. 24-1752, filed Dec. 31, 2025, amended Jan. 6, 2026)). 'Later of' reflects that both events must occur before the 30 days run (Claude's reading of 'and'); the clock runs from receipt of the address in any form, as the statute does, though the clause asks for it in writing (independent check round 1). The tenant's written address is the landlord-serving reason for the clause. Rule 37: runs from termination of the tenancy for every tenancy type. Supersedes the blank-states parent (rule 25 family). title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord: [list approved pets, or state that no pets are permitted]. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, if applicable, which is Rent under this Lease. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and Tenant will then remove the pet within [number] days after Landlord's written notice. Landlord may enter the property in connection with a pet only as this Lease's Access & Entry terms and Iowa law permit, including without consent in an emergency. This Section does not apply to a service animal or other assistance animal.

title: Holdover
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession without Landlord's consent after this Lease ends, whether at the end of the Term or after a termination, Landlord may bring an action for possession. Landlord and Tenant agree that the fair rental value of the property for each day Tenant remains in possession is the Monthly Rent apportioned daily, and Tenant will pay it. If Tenant's holdover is willful and not in good faith, Landlord may also recover the actual damages Landlord sustains, as Iowa law provides. If Landlord consents to Tenant's continued occupancy, the tenancy continues from month to month on the terms of this Lease (week to week if Tenant is a roomer who pays weekly rent), and either party may end it by written notice given at least 30 days before the periodic rental date specified in the notice (for a week-to-week tenancy, at least 10 days before the termination date specified).
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 562A.34(4): if the tenant remains without the landlord's consent after expiration or termination, the landlord may bring an action for possession and, if the holdover is willful and not in good faith, may in addition recover actual damages and reasonable attorney fees; if the landlord consents, Iowa Code § 562A.9(5) applies (week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly rent, otherwise month-to-month); Iowa Code § 562A.34(1) (week-to-week: 10 days before the termination date), Iowa Code § 562A.34(2) (month-to-month: 30 days before the periodic rental date). Fair rental value for use and occupancy: Iowa Code § 562A.9(2)-(3) (rent apportionable day to day). NOT TAGGED `holdover-ca`: it gives actual damages for any holdover, while Iowa gives actual damages only for a willful, bad-faith holdover (rule 53, trigger). NOT TAGGED base `holdover`: 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' states only a ceiling. The clause does not mention attorney fees (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(c)); the statutory award needs no lease term. Iowa Code § 562.2 (double rental value after notice to quit) is described in `edu-holdover-ia`; no stipulated holdover rate is offered (`edu-holdover-rate-ia`). title: Handling of Property Left Behind
bodyText: When this Lease ends or Tenant gives up possession, Tenant will remove all of Tenant's personal property from the property. While Tenant remains in possession, Landlord will not remove, hold or dispose of Tenant's personal property, and Landlord will never hold Tenant's property to secure or collect Rent or any other amount. If Tenant has surrendered or abandoned the property, or a court has restored possession to Landlord, and personal property remains, Landlord will send Tenant a written notice, by mail to Tenant's forwarding address (or, if Tenant has not given one, to the property address) and by e-mail to any e-mail address Tenant has given, describing the property and stating where and by what date Tenant may collect it. If Tenant does not collect it within [number, at least 10] days after the notice is sent, Landlord may sell, donate or otherwise dispose of it, and will apply any sale proceeds only to the reasonable costs of removing, storing and selling it, holding any balance for Tenant. Landlord need not store, and may dispose of right away, garbage, perishable items and anything hazardous. Motor vehicles will be handled under Iowa's abandoned-vehicle law instead of this Section.
notes: IA: CONFIRMED ABSENT: Iowa has no statute on a residential tenant's personal property left after surrender, abandonment or eviction, outside mobile home parks (Iowa Code ch. 555B and ch. 555C reach only mobile, manufactured and modular homes in parks and personal property associated with them, Iowa Code § 555B.1(5)-(6), Iowa Code § 555C.1) (IA battery 35: 5 hits, Iowa Code §§ 321.89, 555B.2, 555B.4, 578A.8, 657A.6, none for residential tenants; known positives passed; battery 23 too broad, rerun as 35). Related law read: Iowa Code § 562A.31 (a landlord's lien on household goods is unenforceable; distraint for rent abolished), which is why the clause never holds property for rent and applies proceeds only to handling costs; Iowa Code § 562A.19(4) and Iowa Code § 562A.33 (access and possession after abandonment or surrender); Iowa Code § 562A.29(3) (abandonment of the dwelling and mitigation); Iowa Code § 648.22 (removal on execution, no property procedure); Iowa Code § 321.89 (abandoned vehicles). Claude's drafting choices, not statutory: the notice and the 10-day minimum. Disposal of a tenant's property without a statute carries conversion risk; Iowa case law on it was not searched (IA log §1.4). Model: `abandoned-property-id`. title: Landlord's Option to End the Lease After a Fire or Casualty
bodyText: [Optional.] If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty to an extent that Tenant's enjoyment of it is substantially impaired, and continued lawful occupancy of any part of the property is not possible while it is repaired, Landlord may terminate this Lease by written notice to Tenant given within 30 days after the casualty, effective on the date stated in the notice, which will be at least [number, at least 14] days after the notice is given. Rent will be accounted for as of the date of the casualty, and Landlord will return all prepaid rent and the Security Deposit as Iowa law requires. This Section does not limit Tenant's own right under Iowa law to vacate and terminate this Lease after a fire or casualty, or, where continued occupancy of part of the property is lawful, to occupy the usable part at reduced Rent, and it does not relieve Tenant of liability for damage caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant or anyone on the property with Tenant's consent.
notes: IA: Optional (rule 54, landlord rights left to contract). Iowa Code § 562A.25 gives only the tenant a casualty right: if enjoyment is substantially impaired, the tenant may immediately vacate and notify the landlord in writing within fourteen days of the intention to terminate (terminating as of the vacating date), or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part with rent reduced in proportion to the diminution in fair rental value; on termination the landlord returns all prepaid rent and recoverable security, and rent is accounted for as of the date of the casualty (Iowa Code § 562A.25(2)). No Iowa statute gives or bars a landlord casualty termination (IA log §6.1); Iowa Code § 562A.9(1) allows terms 'not prohibited by this chapter or other rule of law'. Claude's narrowing (rule 76): substantial impairment plus no lawful continued occupancy of any part (so the clause never cuts off the tenant's Iowa Code § 562A.25(1)(b) right, which exists only 'If continued occupancy is lawful'; independent check rounds 1-2), a 30-day window and a 14-day minimum notice, the tenant's Iowa Code § 562A.25 rights preserved. Residual risk, recorded not resolved: termination also ends the landlord's Iowa Code § 562A.15 repair duty for the rest of the term, which a court could weigh under Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a); no Iowa case searched (IA log §6.1). Iowa Code § 562A.25 has no tenant-fault exception (`tenant-caused-damage-ia`). title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, Tenant will be liable to Landlord for the reasonable cost of repairing the damage and for Landlord's other actual damages caused by it, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, for no longer than the remaining Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from Tenant or from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section does not take away any right Iowa law gives Tenant after a fire or casualty, including the right to vacate and terminate this Lease or to a reduction in Rent, but Tenant's use of that right does not release Tenant from liability under this Section.
notes: IA: Rule 54 (tenant-caused damage, always asked). Each Iowa abatement or exit provision was checked for a tenant-fault exception: tenant termination for landlord noncompliance excludes a condition caused by the tenant, family or a person on the premises with consent (Iowa Code § 562A.21(1)(c)); essential-services remedies do not arise for a condition so caused (Iowa Code § 562A.23(3)); retaliation protection does not bar possession where a code violation was caused primarily by the tenant's household or guests (Iowa Code § 562A.36(3)(a)); but the fire or casualty section has NO fault exception (Iowa Code § 562A.25(1)), so a no-abatement or no-termination term would waive a ch. 562A right (Iowa Code § 562A.11(1)(a)) and the shared `tenant-caused-damage-tn` model is not used. Tenant liability: Iowa Code § 562A.17(6) (not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or knowingly permit a person to do so) and Iowa Code § 562A.27(3) (damages for noncompliance); liability for a guest's or invitee's negligence without the tenant's knowledge is a contractual extension beyond Iowa Code § 562A.17(6). Recovering lost rent as damages while the tenant keeps the Iowa Code § 562A.25 right is Claude's reading; no Iowa case on it was searched (IA log §1.4). title: Smoke Detectors and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: Tenant will not tamper with or otherwise make inoperable any smoke detector or carbon monoxide alarm at the property, and will notify Landlord in writing if any detector or alarm is not working. [Optional: After Tenant has lived at the property for longer than 30 days, Tenant will provide the batteries for any battery-operated smoke detector or carbon monoxide alarm.] Landlord will correct an inoperable detector or alarm within 30 days after receiving Tenant's written notice.
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 10A.518(7): if a smoke detector or carbon monoxide alarm is found inoperable, the owner or manager of a multiple-unit residential building or single-family rental unit corrects it within thirty days after written notification by the tenant (or officials); if not, the tenant may repair or install one and deduct the cost from the next rent; 'a lessor or owner may require a lessee, tenant, guest, or roomer who has a residency of longer than thirty days to provide the battery'. Iowa Code § 10A.518(8): no person may render a required detector or alarm inoperable by tampering (simple misdemeanor, (9)). Installation duties for existing single-family rental units and multiple-unit buildings are in rules the director adopts (Iowa Code § 10A.518(2)(b), (3)(b), (5); rules not read, IA log §7; (2)(b) and (3)(b) amended by 2026 Iowa Acts ch. 1115, §§ 121-122, homestead wording only, effective July 1, 2026); light-emitting devices on request for a tenant who is deaf or hard of hearing (Iowa Code § 10A.518(2)(c), (3)(c)); `edu-alarm-duties-ia`. title: Rules and Changes to Rules
bodyText: Tenant will comply with the written rules for the property in effect when this Lease is signed: [attach or describe the rules, or state that there are none]. Landlord may adopt new written rules during the Term by giving Tenant reasonable notice of their adoption. A rule binds Tenant only if its purpose is to promote the convenience, safety or welfare of the tenants in the premises, preserve Landlord's property from abusive use, or make a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for the tenants generally; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner; it is explicit enough to tell Tenant what Tenant must or must not do to comply; and it is not for the purpose of evading Landlord's obligations. A rule adopted after this Lease is signed does not bind Tenant if it works a substantial modification of this Lease, unless Tenant agrees to it in writing.
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 562A.18(1) (a rule is enforceable only if written and if (a)-(f) are met, including notice at the time the tenant enters the rental agreement); Iowa Code § 562A.18(2) (a later rule is enforceable 'if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the tenant and it does not work a substantial modification of the rental agreement'). A valid rule is part of the 'rental agreement' (Iowa Code § 562A.6(11)). Accepting performance that varies from a later rule waives termination for that breach (Iowa Code § 562A.30(1)). The written-consent route for a substantial modification is an agreement, not an Iowa Code § 562A.18 rule. Not tagged `rules-ok`: Oklahoma's purposes include 'peace' and its later-rule test differs. title: E-mail Notices (Optional for Tenant)
bodyText: [Optional for Tenant.] Landlord and Tenant agree that either may send the other any notice under this Lease that Iowa law does not require to be served by a particular method, by e-mail to the address the other provides for that purpose: Tenant: [e-mail address]; Landlord: [e-mail address]. An e-mailed notice counts only when it is actually received, and the sender will not send it in a form that keeps the recipient from printing or storing it. This Section does not apply to a notice of termination, a notice to quit, or any other notice that Iowa law requires to be served by delivery with a signed acknowledgment, personal service, or posting and mailing; those will be served only as Iowa law requires. Either party may stop receiving notices by e-mail at any time by written notice to the other.
notes: IA: Rule 45 (the electronic transactions act read itself). Iowa Code § 562A.8(1)(a)(6), (b)(6): a notice under ch. 562A may be served by 'a method of providing notice that results in the notice actually being received'; Iowa Code § 562A.8 does not reach the notices in Iowa Code § 562A.29A. Iowa Code § 562A.29A(1) and Iowa Code § 648.3(2): termination notices under Iowa Code §§ 562A.27(1), (2), (5), 562A.27A, 562A.34(1)-(3) and notices to quit must be served by signed acknowledgment of delivery by a resident at least eighteen, personal service under Iowa R. Civ. P. 1.305, or posting on the primary entrance door plus regular and certified mail. Iowa Code § 554D.106(2)-(3): the act applies only between parties who agreed to transact electronically; a party may refuse further electronic transactions and that right 'may not be waived by agreement'; Iowa Code § 554D.110(2)(b): where other law requires a record to be sent by a specified method, it must be sent by that method; Iowa Code § 554D.110(1), (3): a record whose printing or storage is inhibited is not 'capable of retention' and is unenforceable against the recipient. So no e-mail method satisfies Iowa Code § 562A.29A or Iowa Code § 648.3. title: Landlord May Fix Tenant-Caused Conditions
bodyText: If Tenant fails to comply with Tenant's statutory maintenance duties in a way that materially affects health and safety and can be remedied by repair, replacement of a damaged item or cleaning, and Tenant does not remedy it as promptly as conditions require in an emergency, or within seven days after Landlord gives Tenant written notice specifying the breach and requesting that Tenant remedy it within that time, Landlord may enter the property and have the work done in a competent manner. Tenant will pay the actual and reasonable cost, or the fair and reasonable value, of the work, as shown on Landlord's itemized bill, as Rent on the next date periodic Rent is due, or immediately if this Lease has ended.
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 562A.28 (noncompliance with Iowa Code § 562A.17 materially affecting health and safety, remediable by repair, replacement of a damaged item or cleaning; the tenant fails to comply as promptly as conditions require in an emergency or 'within seven days after written notice by the landlord specifying the breach and requesting that the tenant remedy it'; the landlord may enter and cause the work to be done 'in a competent manner' and submit an itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost or the fair and reasonable value as rent on the next date periodic rent is due, or for immediate payment if the rental agreement has terminated). Entry under Iowa Code § 562A.28 is an authorized access (Iowa Code § 562A.19(4)). The right exists without a lease term; restating it serves the landlord (rule 55). title: No Criminal Activity
bodyText: Tenant, members of Tenant's household, and Tenant's guests and invitees will not engage in criminal activity at the property or in any common area, including physical assault or the threat of physical assault, illegal use or threatened illegal use of a firearm or other weapon, and illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance; illegal possession of a controlled substance by Tenant, or by anyone else on the property with Tenant's consent where Tenant knew of it, is also a violation. A violation of this Section is a material noncompliance with this Lease. Where the activity creates a clear and present danger to the health or safety of others, Landlord may terminate this Lease by a single three days' written notice of termination and notice to quit as Iowa law provides, subject to the exemptions Iowa law gives Tenant; otherwise Landlord may proceed as this Lease's Tenant Default section provides. This Section does not restrict Tenant's lawful possession or storage of a firearm in the dwelling unit, and it does not apply to Tenant or a household member who is the victim of the criminal activity or who summons law enforcement or emergency assistance.
notes: IA: Optional (rule 54; crime-free clause precedents AZ, NC, GA, MO). Iowa Code § 562A.27A(1)-(2): a clear and present danger (including physical assault or its threat; illegal use or threatened illegal use of a firearm or weapon or possession of an illegal firearm; possession of a controlled substance without a valid prescription, by the tenant or a person on the premises with consent, the latter only if the tenant knew) allows a single three days' written notice of termination and notice to quit stating the specific activity and setting forth the language of Iowa Code § 562A.27A(3); 'The mere possession or storage of a firearm by a tenant in the dwelling unit that the tenant rents does not constitute a clear and present danger' (Iowa Code § 562A.27A(2)(b)). Iowa Code § 562A.27A(3): exemption where another person conducted the activity and the tenant sought a protective order, reported to law enforcement or the county attorney, or wrote the trespass letter, with written proof before suit. Iowa Code § 562A.27B(1): no penalty or eviction for summoning law enforcement or emergency assistance for a victim or an emergency; waiver void; civil penalty of one month's rent (Iowa Code § 562A.27B(3)). Drug possession by anyone other than Tenant (household members, guests, invitees) counts only where Tenant knew of it, matching Iowa Code § 562A.27A(2)(c) (independent check rounds 1-2). Other criminal activity is a 'material noncompliance' under Iowa Code § 562A.27(1) (seven-day notice; whether a crime is 'remediable' is not settled, case law not searched). Federally assisted housing: the clause does not restrict lawful firearm possession in the unit (Iowa Code § 562A.11(2)). title: Iowa Late Fee Cap
bodyText: Iowa caps any late fee a lease provides by the size of the monthly rent. If rent is $700 a month or less, the fee may not exceed $12 per day or $60 in total for a month; if rent is more than $700, it may not exceed $20 per day or $100 in total for a month. Iowa requires no grace period. Accepting a late payment can cost you the right to end the lease for that late payment, so if you want to rely on strict deadlines later, say so in writing before the tenant relies on your leniency.
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 562A.9(4) (2013 Iowa Acts ch. 97, § 3); waiver: Iowa Code § 562A.30(1)-(2). Late fees are 'rent' (Iowa Code § 562A.6(10)); in a HUD-assisted tenancy, a notice that demanded late fees barred by HUD rules was nullified (Seldin Co v Calabro, 702 N.W.2d 504 (Iowa Ct. App. 2005)). Clause: `late-fee-ia`. Rule 37: the cap is per month of rent, the same for every tenancy type. title: Fees Count as Rent in Iowa
bodyText: In Iowa, 'rent' means any payment the tenant must make to you under the rental agreement, so on the statute's plain reading pet rent, utility charges, late fees and other required fees are rent for the three-day nonpayment notice; no reported Iowa case read for this library decides that, and the library's default clause does not end a lease for unpaid late fees alone. Demand only amounts the lease and the law actually allow: an Iowa court threw out an eviction because the nonpayment notice demanded charges the landlord could not lawfully collect, and you must prove any amount you claim.
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 562A.6(10) ('Rent' means a payment to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement); Iowa Code § 562A.27(2). Seldin Co v Calabro, 702 N.W.2d 504 (Iowa Ct. title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: You must tell each tenant in writing about a rent increase at least 30 days before it takes effect, and the increase cannot take effect before the original lease, or a renewal or extension of it, expires. So you cannot raise rent in the middle of a fixed term. Whether a rent step written into the original lease counts as an 'increase' under this rule has not been decided in any case read for this library; if a court treats such a step as an increase, it could not take effect before the term ends even with notice, so a step that takes effect at a renewal is the safer course, with the 30 days' written notice. In a month-to-month tenancy each month is a new period, so give the written notice at least 30 days before the rental date on which the increase starts. An increase made because the tenant complained about conditions, or because the tenant became eligible for Iowa's rent reimbursement credit, can be challenged.
notes: IA: Iowa Code § 562A.13(5) ('Each tenant shall be notified, in writing, of any rent increase at least thirty days before the effective date. Such effective date shall not be sooner than the expiration date of original rental agreement or any renewal or extension thereof.'); retaliation, Iowa Code § 562A.36(1)-(2) (presumption within one year of a good-faith complaint; rising costs a defense); Iowa Code § 425.35 (affirmative defense if the landlord increased rent primarily because the tenant received or was eligible for rent reimbursement). bodyText: You may not demand or receive more than two months' rent as a security deposit. Every deposit that secures the tenant's performance counts toward that limit, including a pet deposit. title: Three-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: If rent is unpaid, serve a written notice of nonpayment stating that the lease will terminate if the rent is not paid within three days. If the rent is not paid, you may file for eviction without a separate notice to quit. The Iowa Supreme Court has held that the federal CARES Act's 30-day notice applies only to rent defaults that arose during the 2020 moratorium.

title: Notice for Other Lease Violations

title: Clear and Present Danger: Three-Day Termination
bodyText: If a tenant, or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent, creates a clear and present danger to the health or safety of other tenants, you, your staff, or others on or within 1,000 feet of the property (for example, assault or threats, illegal use or threatened use of a weapon, or illegal possession of a controlled substance; drug possession by someone other than the tenant counts only if the tenant knew of it), you may serve a single three days' notice of termination and notice to quit and then file for eviction. The notice must state the specific activity and set out the statute's exemption language word for word. A tenant is exempt where someone else did it and the tenant sought a protective order, reported it to police or the county attorney, or sent the statutory trespass letter, and gave you written proof before you sued. Simply keeping a firearm in the unit is never a clear and present danger.

title: How Eviction Works in Iowa
bodyText: Iowa evictions are 'forcible entry and detainer' actions, usually filed in small claims court in the county where the property is. Give a three days' written notice to quit before filing, except after a three-day nonpayment notice has already ended the tenancy or where the occupant entered by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth. The court sets a hearing within 8 days of filing (up to 15 if you ask or agree), and the tenant must be served at least three days before the hearing. If you win, the order directs removal within three days, carried out in the daytime by the sheriff. Only a claim for rent, or for other recovery the statute lists (such as your damages after the lease is terminated), may be joined with the case. An employee of an individual owner, or an officer or employee of the property manager, may bring the small claims case without a lawyer. Waiting 30 days of peaceable possession after the cause arises, with your knowledge, bars the action.
