title: Ending a Fixed-Term Lease
bodyText: Two Iowa statutes touch the end of a fixed term. A general statute says a written agreement fixing the date a tenancy ends terminates it on that date without notice. The landlord-tenant act also lets either party end a tenancy longer than month-to-month by written notice at least 30 days before the end of the term. Because no Iowa decision reconciling the two was found, serve a written notice at least 30 days before the last day of the term whenever you want the unit back, using a method the termination-notice statute allows. If the tenant stays after the term without your consent, give a three days' notice to quit before filing for eviction. If you accept rent and let the tenant stay, the tenancy becomes month-to-month.

title: When a Tenant Abandons
bodyText: If a tenant abandons the unit, you must make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental. If you re-rent for a term beginning before the lease would have ended, the lease ends when the new tenancy begins. If you make no reasonable effort, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the lease is treated as ended when you learned of the abandonment. Iowa's landlord-tenant act does not define 'abandonment'; during an absence of more than 14 days you may enter at reasonably necessary times.

title: Fire or Casualty Damage
bodyText: If fire or another casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may move out immediately and, within 14 days, notify you in writing of the intent to end the lease, which then ends on the move-out date; or, if staying is lawful, the tenant may stop using the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value. If the lease ends, return all prepaid rent and the recoverable deposit, accounting for rent as of the date of the casualty. Iowa's statute has no exception for damage the tenant caused, and it gives you no termination right; an optional clause adds one.

title: Servicemember Lease Rights
bodyText: A tenant who enters military service during a lease, or who receives orders for a permanent change of station or a deployment of at least 90 days, may end the lease by written notice with a copy of the orders. For a monthly lease the termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date; prepaid rent must be refunded within 30 days. You may not end the lease of a servicemember or dependents for nonpayment during military service where the rent is under $1,200 a month, except through a court, which may stay the case for up to three months. If the tenant signed before entering service, a court may also grant relief or a stay; whether a residential lease is an 'installment contract' for those purposes is not settled. Federal law also applies.

title: No Retaliation

title: Tenant Remedies for Repairs
bodyText: If you materially fail to comply with the lease or your maintenance duties, the tenant may give a written seven-day notice and end the lease if you do not fix it, and may recover damages. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water or essential services, the tenant may, after written notice, buy them and deduct the cost from rent, or recover reduced rental value. In an eviction for unpaid rent, a tenant who told you at least seven days before rent was due, and then in good faith fixed a condition costing no more than one month's rent before receiving your termination notice, can deduct the cost. In a rent case the tenant may counterclaim, and the court may order rent paid into court. A tenant may also repair or replace a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm you did not fix within 30 days of written notice and deduct the cost.

title: Lease Terms Iowa Prohibits
bodyText: An Iowa lease may not make the tenant (or landlord) waive rights under the landlord-tenant act, authorize a confession of judgment, agree to pay the other party's attorney fees, or exculpate, limit the liability of, or indemnify the other party for liability arising under law. The waiver ban does not apply to a single family residence on agricultural land in an unincorporated area. In federally assisted housing (USDA rural rental assistance and HUD voucher and listed project programs) a lease may not bar lawful firearms in the tenant's own unit.

title: How to Serve Notices in Iowa
bodyText: Most landlord notices may be served by hand delivery, delivery with a signed and dated acknowledgment from a resident at least 18, personal service, regular plus certified mail, posting on the main entrance door (dated, within the notice period), or any method that results in the tenant actually receiving it. E-mail is never enough for a termination notice or notice to quit, and works for other notices only if the tenant agreed to e-mail and actually receives it.

title: Landlord's Duty to Keep the Unit Fit
bodyText: You must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety; make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable; keep common areas clean and safe; keep supplied electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, in good and safe working order; provide and arrange removal from garbage receptacles; and supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat (unless the tenant controls a unit-only system on a direct utility connection). A lease cannot waive these duties. In a single family residence you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant handles garbage, water and heat supply and specified repairs or tasks; for any other unit only by a separate signed writing with adequate consideration that does not affect other tenants. You are not liable for injuries caused by things a tenant put in the common areas.

title: Landlord's Right of Entry
bodyText: The tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs or improvements, supply services, or show the unit to buyers, lenders, prospective tenants, workers or contractors. Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give at least 24 hours' notice and enter only at reasonable times. You may enter without consent in an emergency, to fix a health-and-safety condition the tenant failed to remedy, during an absence of more than 14 days, or after abandonment or surrender; otherwise only with a court order. Abusing entry lets the tenant get an injunction or end the lease and recover actual damages of at least one month's rent plus attorney fees; a tenant's refusal of lawful entry lets you get an injunction or end the lease and recover your actual damages and attorney fees. An entry without consent can also be a trespass: the Iowa Supreme Court upheld per-entry damages, judging consent by what the tenant's conduct led the landlord to believe.

title: City Utility Bills and Liens
bodyText: Unpaid city utility charges (water, sewer, storm water, solid waste and some others) can become a lien on the rental property. You can protect the property from a lien for charges a tenant pays directly (for water, only if the unit's water is separately metered) by giving the city utility written notice that the property is a rental and the tenant is liable, with the tenant's name, the address and the date occupancy begins; the utility may require a deposit of up to 90 days of usual charges (60 days for gas and electric). Give a new notice within 30 business days after each change of tenant or owner. Repair charges are not covered. If you ask in writing, the utility must also send you its disconnection and lien notices for your tenant's account.

title: Smoke Detectors and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: Iowa requires smoke detectors in single-family rental units and multiple-unit residential buildings, and carbon monoxide alarms where there is a fuel-fired heater or appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage, installed under the rules the director adopts under the statute. On request, supply light-emitting devices for a tenant who is deaf or hard of hearing. Fix an inoperable detector or alarm within 30 days after written notice, or the tenant may repair or install one and deduct the cost from rent. You may require a tenant who has lived there longer than 30 days to provide batteries. Tampering with a required device is a misdemeanor.

title: Towing Vehicles From a Rental Property
bodyText: A vehicle unlawfully parked on private property, or placed there without the owner's consent, for more than 24 hours is an 'abandoned vehicle'. Police may take it into custody, or you may hire a garagekeeper to take custody and dispose of it after the certified-mail notice to the owner and lienholders. Since July 1, 2026, that notice must go out within 10 days of custody, the owner has 20 days to reclaim the vehicle (and may retrieve listed personal items once during that time), the tower must post its storage and impound fees, and the statute preempts county and city ordinances on towing abandoned vehicles. Iowa gives no separate authority to tow a tenant's authorized vehicle for expired registration or because it does not run; handle that through your parking rules and the lease.

title: Iowa Fair Housing Law
bodyText: The Iowa Civil Rights Act bars housing discrimination because of race, color, creed, sex, sexual orientation, religion, national origin, disability or familial status, including in advertising and in the terms of a rental, and bars discrimination against a tenant because of the race, color, creed, religion, sex, sexual orientation, disability, age or national origin of the tenant's guests. Gender identity was removed from the Act effective July 1, 2025. Exemptions include an owner-occupied building with two units, rental of fewer than four rooms in an owner-occupied dwelling, an owner-occupied building of up to four units where the owner qualifies for the homestead credit or exemption, housing for older persons, and shared living areas by sex; the small-building exemptions never cover advertising. Federal fair housing law applies separately.

title: Assistance and Service Animals in Iowa
bodyText: A tenant with a disability and a disability-related need may ask to keep an assistance or service animal; evaluate and respond within a reasonable time, and give a written determination. If the disability or need is not readily apparent, you may ask for information that reasonably supports the need for that particular animal. Iowa sets out a written finding a listed licensed professional can provide, which must state, among other things, whether the provider has known the person for at least 30 days, and is valid for 12 months or the lease term, whichever is longer; other reliable proof is still allowed. An online registration or certificate is not enough. Do not ask for a diagnosis, severity or medical records. You may require proof of licensing and vaccination, and you may deny the request for undue financial and administrative hardship, a fundamental alteration of your operations, a direct threat or substantial damage that cannot be reduced by a reasonable accommodation, or because the accommodation is not otherwise reasonable. The tenant is liable for damage the animal causes.

title: Firearms
bodyText: In most Iowa rentals the lease may restrict firearms, but not in federally assisted housing: if you receive USDA rural rental assistance or HUD voucher or listed project-based payments, the lease may not prohibit or restrict lawful firearms, components or ammunition in the tenant's own unit, though you may reasonably restrict them in common areas and the tenant must store them with reasonable care. Where the law requires you to allow firearms, you are not liable for resulting harm except for willful, reckless or grossly negligent conduct. Merely keeping a firearm in the unit is never a clear and present danger. Iowa's constitutional right to keep and bear arms binds the government; whether it limits a private landlord was not decided in any case read for this library.

title: Statutory Forms and Prescribed Wording
bodyText: Iowa prescribes no form of residential lease and no form for the ordinary notices to tenants; the 3-day nonpayment notice and the 7-day notice to remedy a breach must say what the statute requires, in your own words. One notice must quote the statute: a 3-day notice of termination and notice to quit for conduct creating a clear and present danger must state the specific activity and set out, in full, the subsection that exempts a tenant who acts against the person causing the danger. Small claims court forms exist for filing an eviction, but they are court forms, not lease or notice forms.

title: No Separate Quiet-Enjoyment Statute
bodyText: Iowa's landlord-tenant act has no separate quiet-enjoyment covenant, but it protects the tenant's possession directly. You may not take possession except after abandonment, surrender or as the act permits, and cutting off electric, gas, water or another essential service counts as taking possession. If you remove or exclude the tenant unlawfully or willfully cut a service, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover actual damages, punitive damages up to twice the monthly rent and attorney fees, and on termination you must return all prepaid rent and the deposit. An unlawful entry, a lawful entry made unreasonably, or repeated demands for entry that harass the tenant let the tenant get an injunction or end the lease and recover at least one month's rent and attorney fees.

title: Tenant Default
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and does not pay all past-due Rent within 10 days after Landlord's written demand for it, or fails to comply with any other obligation under this Lease and does not cure the failure after receiving written notice. Landlord need not give Tenant an opportunity to cure before seeking possession for criminal activity, or in any other case where North Carolina law permits Landlord to proceed without one. Except as required by applicable law, Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise all rights and remedies available under applicable law, including terminating this Lease, regaining possession of the property, and recovering unpaid Rent, late fees and Landlord's actual damages, less amounts obtained from the Security Deposit. Landlord will not charge Tenant any administrative fee, out-of-pocket expense or litigation cost for filing a complaint for summary ejectment or money owed except those N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-46 allows. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to mitigate damages resulting from Tenant's default to the extent required by applicable law.
notes: NC: NEW 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.21 retro, rules 49, 43 and 47; replaces `default-by-tenant-ks-ne` for NC, which is untagged). Text is `default-by-tenant-ks-ne`'s with three North Carolina changes. (1) RULE 49: 'recovering unpaid Rent, late fees, and reasonable costs and expenses' became 'unpaid Rent, late fees and Landlord's actual damages', plus a sentence limiting eviction filing charges to those N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-46 allows. It is 'contrary to public policy ... for a lease to provide for the payment of, any out-of-pocket expenses or litigation costs for filing a complaint for summary ejectment and/or money owed other than those expressly authorized under subsection (i)' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-46(h)(3a)); administrative fees other than (e)-(g) likewise ((h)(3)); contrary provisions are void ((h)(4)). The shared 'reasonable costs and expenses', read literally, provides for litigation costs beyond (i), and 'available under applicable law' is self-limiting wording that hides the conflict (rule 53). Collecting a charge the landlord is not 'legally entitled to' also risks N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 75-55(2), 75-56(b) (rule 47). What (i) allows: court filing fees, service costs, and, under a written lease, attorneys' fees capped at 15% (the opt-in `eviction-fees-nc`, on by default per Taylor's 2026-09-28 decision). Damages that are not eviction filing costs (re-renting costs, repairs) remain recoverable as actual damages and from the deposit (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-51(a)(2), (5)). (2) RULE 43, RENT LIMB: summary ejectment always needs a 'demand made for its surrender' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-26(a)), but no statute sets a cure period for nonpayment where the lease itself provides the forfeiture (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-26(a)(2)). The 10 days come from the forfeiture North Carolina implies where a lease does not: 'upon failure to pay the rent within 10 days after a demand is made by the lessor or his agent ... for all past-due rent' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-3). The shared clause's 'time period specified by applicable law after receiving written notice' is written out as that implied period, with the demand in writing. That is a 10-day written cure the clause gives by contract (rule 43): a deliberate choice that keeps the library default of a cure promise for rent and matches the period North Carolina implies anyway. Tender of rent and costs before judgment still ends a nonpayment case (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-33). (3) RULE 43, CARVE-OUT: the no-cure carve-out is now its own sentence reaching both limbs, not a tail on the non-rent limb. It waives only the cure, not the demand for surrender summary ejectment needs (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-26(a)) or the written notice N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-43(b) requires for maintenance breaches; it was narrowed from 'notice or an opportunity to cure' after the independent check. North Carolina's no-cure route is Article 7 (expedited eviction for criminal activity, N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 42-59 to 42-76, 'deemed to apply to all residential rental agreements', N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-59.1), named expressly, and the opt-in `criminal-activity-nc` makes criminal activity a no-cure lease breach. Non-rent limb unchanged: North Carolina sets no statutory cure period for other breaches; the lease's stipulations govern forfeiture (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-26(a)(2)); the landlord must give written notice of breaches of the tenant's maintenance duties except in emergencies (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-43(b)). Default and cure notices for a primary residence are outside the UETA (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 66-313(e)(2); `edu-electronic-notices-nc`). Late-fee sentence: library default, kept (an administrative fee is never a default ground, N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-46(h)(2)). Mitigation: case law, not read. Tenant-side fee recovery: none (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 6-21.6 excludes consumer contracts; read 2026-09-28). Basis: SERVES_LANDLORD | CONSTRAINED_TERM (the clause now states a statutory cost limit). title: Returned Payments (North Carolina)
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds, because Tenant has no account, or for any other reason, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount; North Carolina caps the processing fee for a check refused for insufficient funds or no account at $35.00 where the statute applies (checks taken in payment for goods or services), and no statute sets a fee for a failed electronic payment, so $35.00 or less is the safe figure for any returned payment], and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. If more than two of Tenant's payments during any 12-month period are returned or fail, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check or money order.
notes: NC: NEW 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.21 retro, rule 53; fix 24; rule 37). Replaces the shared `returned-payments` for NC (untagged). The shared clause states only a ceiling ('not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law'). North Carolina's figure is a processing fee 'not to exceed thirty-five dollars ($35.00)' that 'A person who accepts a check in payment for goods or services' may charge for a check refused for insufficient funds or no account (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 25-3-506). Whether rent is 'payment for goods or services' is not settled by the text, so the ceiling may have no referent at all; for failed ACH or card payments no statute exists (full-text search 2026-09-28). The clause therefore states a fee with the statutory figure shown, the pattern of `returned-payments-tn`, `-sc` and `-al`, and recommends $35.00 or less for any returned payment (rule 47: collecting a fee the landlord is not 'legally entitled to' risks N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 75-55(2), 75-56(b)). Rule 37 and fix 24: 'during the Term' became 'during any 12-month period' (AZ's proposed shared wording), because a month-to-month tenancy has no Term; no North Carolina statute limits how many returned payments a landlord may count or when it may require certified funds, so the wording is lawful here. Civil remedy for a knowingly bad check, with statutory-form demand letters: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 6-21.3 (`edu-dishonored-payment-remedies-nc`). The fee is not a N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-46 late fee; a late fee on the same payment is charged separately and only once. title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule for private houses and apartments. A fixed-term lease ends on its last day, and a periodic tenancy ends on the notice North Carolina law sets (seven days for month-to-month, two days for week-to-week, one month before the end of the year for year-to-year), with no reason required. The limits are situational. A tenant may defend an eviction as retaliatory if it is substantially in response to protected activity in the 12 months before filing, such as a good-faith repair request or code complaint, an attempt to enforce lease or legal rights, or involvement with a tenants' rights organization; the landlord still wins in listed cases, including a breach of the rent covenant or another substantial covenant, a holdover after a fixed term with no option to renew, a good-faith notice to quit given before the protected activity, and a good-faith recovery at the end of the term to live in the unit, to demolish it or make major alterations that require the household to move out completely, or to stop renting it for at least six months. A landlord may not end or refuse to renew a tenancy based substantially on a tenant's or household member's status as a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. When a building is converted to condominiums, tenants cannot be required to leave on less than 90 days' notice except for nonpayment, waste, disturbing other tenants or another breach giving a right to repossess, and the tenancy terms cannot change during that period. Public housing authorities and manufactured home communities have their own rules, which this library does not cover. North Carolina has no rent-escrow procedure that bars eviction: rent paid to the clerk during an appeal only stays the eviction while the appeal is pending. Fair housing law applies.

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: No North Carolina statute says whether late fees, utility charges or other fees count as rent; that depends on the lease. Several statutes keep fees apart from rent. Unpaid landlord-billed water, sewer or electric charges can never be a ground to end the lease, and payments go to rent first unless the tenant directs otherwise. An eviction administrative fee cannot be deducted from a later rent payment or made a ground for a later eviction, and a late fee for one payment cannot be deducted from a later payment to put it in default. The eviction filing costs and fees the law allows may be included in the amount needed to cure a default. This library's clauses do not label fees as rent, and its default clause does not let an unpaid late fee alone end the lease.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix It and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Some states let a landlord give notice, do work the tenant failed to do, and add the cost to the rent. North Carolina has no such statute. Two narrower rules exist: after repairing an imminently dangerous condition that is the tenant's fault, the landlord may recover the actual and reasonable cost of the repair from the tenant; and a tenant who disables or damages a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm must reimburse the reasonable and actual cost of repairing or replacing it within 30 days of the landlord's written notice. Otherwise the landlord recovers the cost of tenant-caused damage as damages or from the security deposit. The landlord must give the tenant written notice of breaches of the tenant's maintenance duties, except in emergencies.

title: No Blank-Space or Lease-Copy Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be completed, treating a blank as a breach, or requiring the landlord to give the tenant a signed copy. Several North Carolina rules still turn on what the lease says: where the security deposit is held (the landlord must tell the tenant within 30 days after the term begins, and naming the bank or bond company in the lease is the simplest way), the late fee and the eviction fees and attorneys' fees (allowed only if the lease provides for them), and the emergency contact a landlord names in a tenant-death affidavit. A blank in one of those leaves a right lost or a duty unclear. Fill in every blank before signing and give the tenant a copy, as good practice rather than a statutory duty.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: No North Carolina statute states a landlord's covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession for residential leases. The closest statute is the policy statement behind the expedited criminal-activity eviction procedure, which recognizes residents' right to the peaceful, safe and quiet enjoyment of their homes and applies that procedure to every residential rental agreement. Possession is otherwise protected by the ban on self-help eviction: a residential tenant can be removed only through a court eviction. Whether a lease carries an implied covenant of quiet enjoyment is a question of case law that this library has not reviewed.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: North Carolina prescribes no form for a residential lease or for a landlord's demand for rent or notice to quit. The statutes do supply a few forms a landlord may meet. The small claims statute sets out a sufficient form of complaint in summary ejectment. A court form published by the Administrative Office of the Courts may not be modified in a way that keeps its official appearance, and anyone who modifies one must clearly note that it was modified and say what changed. A tenant who appeals an eviction may stay it with a bond and undertaking substantially in a statutory form. A landlord who sues on a knowingly bad check must first send demand letters substantially in the statutory forms. The notice to the State Bar about an attorney tenant's files has statutory contents but no set form.

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: North Carolina statutes do not address whether a tenant may install security cameras, video doorbells or similar devices. The lease's alteration terms govern; in this library that is the Alterations section, which requires the landlord's written consent before a tenant adds or changes a fixture. North Carolina's eavesdropping, electronic surveillance and privacy laws were not reviewed and may limit what a camera records rather than its installation.

title: Unfair Trade Practices Act and Rentals
bodyText: North Carolina's Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act declares unlawful unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce, and defines commerce to include all business activities. How far it reaches residential leasing is settled by court decisions this library has not reviewed, but several landlord-tenant statutes assume it can apply (for example, the statute allowing a partial-payment non-waiver clause says using one is not a violation of the Act). The Act has no list of unfair practices for leases, and nothing on blank spaces filled in after signing or on giving the tenant a copy. A person injured by a violation may recover three times their damages, and a court may award attorney's fees where the violation was willful and there was an unwarranted refusal to resolve the matter. Separately, the Act's debt-collection article bars anyone collecting a consumer debt from collecting any fee, charge or expense incidental to the debt unless legally entitled to it, or from falsely representing that the debt may be increased by attorney's fees or other fees; a violation carries actual damages plus a civil penalty of $500 to $4,000 for each violation. So collecting a fee that a void lease term provides for, such as a late fee above North Carolina's cap or an eviction cost the law does not allow, can create liability, not just an unenforceable term. A knowing violation of the North Carolina Servicemembers Civil Relief Act is also an unfair trade practice.

Stat. § 75-1.1(a)-(b) ('all business activities, however denominated'). Its reach to residential leases is case law, NOT read (rule 76 label). The statutes presuppose it: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 75-16 (treble damages), N.C. Gen. Stat. § 75-16.1 (attorney fee for a willful violation with an unwarranted refusal to resolve). Rule 47 (penalties for using a prohibited term): North Carolina's contrary-term statutes void the term only (N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 42-25.8, 42-46(h)(4)), but collecting under it engages N.C. Gen. Stat. § 75-55(2) ('collecting or attempting to collect any interest or other charge, fee or expense incidental to the principal debt unless legally entitled to such fee or charge'; court costs actually incurred excepted) and N.C. Gen. Stat. § 75-54(6), with a civil penalty of $500 to $4,000 per violation under N.C. Gen. Stat. § 75-56(b). 'Debt collector' means 'any person engaging, directly or indirectly, in debt collection from a consumer' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 75-50(3)); whether a landlord collecting its own rent is one is case law, NOT read. Consequence for the library: a 'nothing in this lease limits your rights' sentence does not make a void fee term safe, which is why `late-fee-limit-nc` keeps its once-only and subsidy conditions and `default-by-tenant-nc` limits eviction costs to N.C. title: No Plain-Language Lease Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no plain-language or readability statute for residential leases, no type-size or bold-print rule for them, and no statute requiring a lease to list the rights a tenant gives up. title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) as long as Landlord makes the repairs within a reasonable time, Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term (for a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, up to the earliest date Tenant could have ended the tenancy by notice), less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will make repairs as North Carolina law requires and will use reasonable efforts to re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage.
notes: NC: NEW 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.21 retro, rule 54t). OPTIONAL clause (CONDITIONAL, not a default), state version of `tenant-caused-damage-tn` (read; TN row not tagged), wording as `tenant-caused-damage-ga`. Each abatement or exit route checked for a tenant-fault exception. (i) Casualty: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-12 gives a surrender right only where the damage occurred 'without negligence on the part of the lessee or his agents or servants', and only if 'there is no agreement in the lease respecting repairs, or providing for such a case'; 'This section shall not apply if a contrary intention appear from the lease.' The right is displaceable, so part (1) waives no non-waivable right, and the opt-in `casualty-termination-nc` already excludes damage caused by Tenant, household members, guests or invitees. (ii) Essential services and landlord-breach termination: no North Carolina statute; the tenant's rent duty and the landlord's fitness duty are 'mutually dependent' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-41), and rent abatement for a landlord's breach is case law, NOT read (rule 76 label: whether a court would abate rent for a condition the tenant caused while the landlord repairs within a reasonable time). (iii) Rent into court: only the appeal stay bond (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-34(b)), not an abatement route. Repair duty: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-42(a)(2) has no tenant-fault exception and cannot be waived (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-42(b)); for imminently dangerous conditions the landlord must repair even when the tenant is at fault and then 'may recover from the tenant the actual and reasonable costs of repairs that are the fault of the tenant' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-42(a)(8)). Hence 'Landlord will make repairs as North Carolina law requires', which cannot be read as softening that duty. Part (1) is also NARROWED (rule 76, a drafting call; prompted by the independent check) to apply only 'as long as Landlord makes the repairs within a reasonable time', so it bars abatement only while the landlord is itself complying; any abatement claim for the landlord's own delay is untouched (N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 42-41, 42-42(b)). This narrowing departs from `tenant-caused-damage-ga` on purpose. Tenant duties: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-43(a)(4), (6); retaliation defense unavailable where the tenant's household or guests caused the condition (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-37.1(c)(3)). Part (2) fills a gap: no North Carolina statute measures lost rent when the lease ends because of tenant-caused damage. Periodic limb (rule 37): N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-14 notice periods. Deposit: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-51(a)(2), (3), (5). Accidental damage despite reasonable diligence is outside the clause (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-10; `edu-tenant-caused-damage-nc`). UNREAD RISK (rule 76 label): whether a North Carolina court measures damages as lost Rent to the end of the Term, and the mitigation standard, rest on case law not read. title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: North Carolina law leaves much of the cost of tenant-caused damage with the tenant. A tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or knowingly let anyone else do so, and is responsible for damage inside the unit under the tenant's exclusive control except ordinary wear and tear, acts of the landlord, defective products or repairs the landlord authorized, acts of third parties who are not the tenant's invitees, and natural forces. The landlord must still make the repairs needed to keep the home fit and habitable, and must fix an imminently dangerous condition within a reasonable time even when the tenant caused it, but may then recover the actual and reasonable repair cost from the tenant; the security deposit may also be applied to damage. The statutory right to surrender the lease after a fire or other casualty does not apply if the tenant's (or the tenant's agents' or servants') negligence caused the damage, or if the lease provides for repairs or casualty; the library's optional casualty clause excludes damage caused by the tenant, household members, guests or invitees. No North Carolina statute addresses rent during repairs or the landlord's lost rent if the lease ends because of tenant-caused damage; the library offers an optional clause for that. A tenant is not liable for damage that happens accidentally despite reasonable diligence unless the tenant agreed to be. That agreement is lawful, but the library does not offer it, because it would sit uneasily with the landlord's repair duty, which cannot be waived, and with the statute's list of damage the tenant is not responsible for; a landlord who wants one can add their own clause after taking legal advice. Willfully damaging the rented house is also a misdemeanor.

title: No General Just-Cause Rule in Ohio, With Three Situational Limits
bodyText: Ohio has no general just-cause or good-cause requirement for ending a residential tenancy. Under R.C. 5321.17 either party may end a month-to-month tenancy on at least 30 days' notice before the periodic rental date, or a week-to-week tenancy on at least 7 days' notice, and the landlord needs no reason; holding over after a term ends is itself a ground for a possession action under R.C. 1923.02(A)(1). Three situations narrow that. FIRST, retaliation. R.C. 5321.02(A) bars you from raising the rent, cutting services, or bringing or even threatening a possession action because the tenant complained to a government agency about a code violation materially affecting health and safety, complained to you about an R.C. 5321.04 violation, or joined with other tenants to bargain collectively. The tenant can use that as a defence, recover possession, or terminate, plus actual damages and attorney's fees. But the bar is expressly 'subject to section 5321.03', and R.C. 5321.03(A) then lets you bring the action anyway on four enumerated grounds: the tenant is in default in rent; the violation the tenant complained of was primarily caused by the tenant, the tenant's household, or someone there with the tenant's consent; compliance would need alteration, remodelling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit; or the tenant is holding over. So once a tenant has done something R.C. 5321.02 protects, those four grounds are in practice the only ones available - a for-cause rule in that situation, even though Ohio has none in general. R.C. 5321.02(C) separately lets you raise rent to reflect the cost of improvements or an increase in operating costs. SECOND, student tenants of a college or university. R.C. 5321.031 lets a college or university end a student tenant's agreement early only after a hearing at which it determined the student broke a lease term or the institution's code of conduct, preceded by written notice and a right to be heard. R.C. 5321.03 does not apply to a unit occupied by a student tenant at all. THIRD, the registered-offender ground runs the other way, adding a cause: R.C. 5321.03(A)(5) and R.C. 5321.051 let you terminate where the premises are within 1,000 feet of school, preschool, child care, children's crisis care or residential infant care premises and a tenant or occupant is on the R.C. 2950.13 registry for a qualifying offence.

title: Ohio Has No Rule on Algorithmic Rent Pricing
bodyText: Ohio has no statute on setting rents with algorithmic or revenue-management pricing software, and none on sharing rent or occupancy data with other landlords or with a pricing vendor. Federal and state antitrust law and the general law on unfair competition still apply, and Ohio's rent-control preemption (R.C. 5321.19 and 5321.20) says nothing either way.

title: No Ohio Rule on Whether Fees Count as Rent
bodyText: No Ohio statute says whether a late fee, a utility charge or any other fee counts as 'rent', so nothing in Ohio law stops a lease from calling such a charge additional rent - and nothing confirms that an eviction for nonpayment can rest on unpaid fees alone. Two things bear on it. The notice that starts an Ohio eviction is a notice to leave the premises under R.C. 1923.04, not a pay-or-quit notice, so there is no statutory text tying the amount demanded to 'rent'. And R.C. 5321.14 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, which is the only real ceiling. This library's clauses do not label fees as rent, and the shared Application of Payments clause applies each payment to rent first and only then to fees, so a tenant who pays in full cannot be left owing rent because a fee absorbed the payment.

title: Ohio Has No Landlord Self-Cure Statute
bodyText: Ohio gives you no statutory right to fix a tenant's breach yourself - repairing damage, cutting the grass, hauling away rubbish - and bill the cost back as rent. Some states have one; Ohio does not. What you have instead is the ordinary route: recover the cost as damages, or apply the security deposit at the end of the tenancy under R.C. 5321.16(B), which reaches past due rent and damage from the tenant's noncompliance. The lease can give you a self-cure right by contract, but take care with two Ohio rules: R.C. 5321.13(C) means you cannot add your attorney's fees to the bill, and a self-cure clause must not become a way to charge the tenant for something R.C. 5321.04 makes your own duty, which R.C. 5321.13(A) and (E) would void.

title: No Ohio Rule Requiring Every Blank to Be Filled
bodyText: Ohio has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be completed, and no statute making a blank a breach or a ground to void the lease. Fill them in anyway. A blank leaves the term unsettled, and in Ohio the practical risk lands on you twice over: R.C. 5321.14 lets a court refuse to enforce a term it finds unconscionable, and several of the figures this library leaves for you to set - the holdover daily rate, the late fee, the returned-payment fee - have no statutory cap in Ohio, so an unfilled or indefensible number is the whole of your protection.

title: No Ohio Quiet-Enjoyment Statute - the Duty Comes From Elsewhere
bodyText: No Ohio statute states a covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession for a residential lease. The protection a tenant actually has in Ohio comes from two other places. R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) to (6) sets out your repair and habitability duties and R.C. 5321.13(A) makes them non-waivable, and R.C. 5321.15 bars you from excluding the tenant from the premises, cutting off utilities, or threatening either, outside a court process. Ohio courts also treat a lease as carrying an implied covenant of quiet enjoyment as a matter of common law rather than statute. So a clause promising quiet enjoyment adds little in Ohio, and leaving it out takes nothing away.

title: Ohio Prescribes One Form of Words, and It Is the Eviction Notice
bodyText: Ohio supplies no statutory residential lease form and no statutory notice-to-terminate form. It prescribes exactly one piece of wording, and it is the notice that starts an eviction. Under R.C. 1923.04(A) every notice a landlord gives to recover residential premises must contain this language, printed or written in a conspicuous manner: "You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance." The notice must be given three or more days before the action begins, by certified mail with return receipt requested, by handing a written copy to the tenant, or by leaving it at the tenant's usual place of abode or at the premises. Serving the three-day drug-activity notice under R.C. 5321.17(C) counts as compliance with that requirement. One other provision dictates lease content rather than a form: R.C. 5321.031 requires a college or university letting to a student tenant to specify in the written agreement the conditions for termination and the institution's notice and hearing procedures.

title: No Ohio Rule on Tenant Cameras - and Ohio Is One-Party Consent
bodyText: No Ohio statute says whether a tenant may install a security camera or a video doorbell, so the lease controls, together with its rules on alterations. Audio is where Ohio differs from several other states, and it differs in the permissive direction: under R.C. 2933.52(B)(4) a person who is not a law enforcement officer may lawfully intercept a communication if that person is a party to it, or if any one party consented, provided the recording is not made to commit a crime, a tort, or another injurious act. Ohio is a one-party-consent state, so a tenant recording a conversation they are part of - a doorstep exchange with you, for instance - is generally lawful. A device left running to capture conversations between other people, where no participant consented, is not.

title: Your Ohio Lease Is the Switch for Cannabis Home Grow
bodyText: Ohio adult-use cannabis law makes your lease the deciding document on home growing, and if the lease says nothing the tenant may grow. Under R.C. 3796.04(A)(1) an adult-use consumer may cultivate up to six plants at their primary residence, and up to twelve at a single residence, inside a secured enclosed area not visible by normal unaided vision from a public space and not accessible to anyone under 21. But that authority does not apply at "a residential premises occupied pursuant to a rental agreement that prohibits the activities otherwise authorized by this section" - R.C. 3796.04(A)(1)(d)(iii). So a lease term prohibiting cultivation removes the right, and a silent lease leaves it in place. If you do not want plants grown at your property, the prohibition has to be in the lease. Use and possession work differently. R.C. 3796.221 lets an adult-use consumer use and possess cannabis and gives no lease-prohibition hook, but its protection is framed as freedom from arrest and prosecution, not as a contract right against a landlord - and R.C. 3796.04(C)(2) separately bars consuming in a public place. A lease ban on smoking or vaping cannabis therefore rests on ordinary freedom of contract under R.C. 5321.06, and the shared smoking clause in this library is lawful in Ohio. Watch the citations: this chapter was Chapter 3780 when adult use began and was amended and renumbered into Chapter 3796 by S.B. 56, effective March 20 2026. Older Ohio guidance still cites 3780.

title: No Cannabis Cultivation
bodyText: Tenant will not cultivate, grow or process cannabis or marijuana anywhere on the property, including inside the dwelling, in any enclosed or secured area, and anywhere on the grounds, and will not permit any occupant or guest to do so. This Section is intended to prohibit the activities that would otherwise be authorized at the property by Ohio's home grow provisions. Nothing in this Section restricts any use or possession that applicable law entitles Tenant to, or affects any accommodation Tenant is entitled to for medical use under applicable law.
notes: OH: OPTIONAL CLAUSE (rule 54: a landlord right that exists only if the lease invokes it). R.C. 3796.04(A)(1)(d)(iii), READ SECTION-OPEN 2026-10-02; effective 2026-03-20, S.B. 56, 136th G.A. WHY IT IS A CLAUSE AND NOT JUST EDUCATION: 3796.04(A)(1)(d)(iii) withholds the home-grow authority at 'a residential premises occupied pursuant to a rental agreement that prohibits the activities otherwise authorized by this section'. The statute makes the lease the trigger, so without a clause the regime does not apply and the tenant may grow up to six plants (twelve per residence). This is the same shape as WY's utility-deposit and abandoned-property identifications recorded under rule 54. MODELLED ON cannabis-cultivation-il (read, not tagged) and extended in three ways Ohio needs: it names growing and processing as well as cultivating, because 3796.04(A)(2) authorises processing separately; it reaches the grounds and enclosed areas, because 3796.04(A)(1)(c) locates the authority in 'a secured closet, room, greenhouse, or other enclosed area in or on the grounds'; and it tracks the statute's own words ('the activities otherwise authorized by this section') so the clause plainly engages (d)(iii) rather than leaving a court to infer it. THE SAVING SENTENCE IS DELIBERATE: the clause does not purport to bar use or possession, because 3796.04's lease hook is attached only to home grow and a broader prohibition would overstate what the statute lets the lease switch off; a use ban rests on R.C. 5321.06 and lives in smoking-policy instead. The medical limb is there because R.C. 3796.22 (rights of a registered patient) and the reasonable-accommodation duty in R.C. 4112.02(H)(19) were NOT researched for this row - the sentence preserves the position rather than resolving it. title: Electronic Notices Work in Ohio, But Consent Is Not Something You Can Take Once
bodyText: Ohio's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, R.C. Chapter 1306, applies to landlord-tenant records. Its list of exclusions in R.C. 1306.02(B) covers only wills, codicils and testamentary trusts and specified UCC chapters - unlike some states it carves out nothing for eviction, default or cure notices. Two conditions matter to you. R.C. 1306.04(B) applies the Act only between parties who have each agreed to conduct transactions by electronic means, and whether they agreed is judged from the context, the surrounding circumstances and the parties' conduct, so a signature block is not the end of the question. And R.C. 1306.04(C) says a party who agrees to conduct one transaction electronically may refuse to conduct others that way, and that right may not be waived by agreement - so a lease term committing the tenant to accept every future notice electronically is unenforceable to that extent. Separately, R.C. 1923.04(A) sets its own service methods for the notice to leave the premises: certified mail with return receipt requested, personal delivery, or leaving it at the premises or the tenant's usual place of abode. Email is not on that list. Do not serve an eviction notice electronically.
notes: OH: CITED, SOP 1.23 rule 45 retro 2026-10-02. topic_key reuses notice-delivery-methods, which 24 other states already carry and Ohio did not - the family holds NE's and ND's electronic-notice rows, so id follows their convention (edu-no-electronic-notice-regime-nd). R.C. 1306.02 and 1306.04 BOTH READ SECTION-OPEN 2026-10-02 - the Act itself, not only a landlord-tenant section referring to it, as rule 45 requires. 1306.02 effective 2011-06-29 (H.B. 9, 129th G.A.); 1306.04 effective 2000-09-14 (H.B. 488, 123rd G.A.). 1306.04 READ IN FULL including its exceptions: (A) nothing requires electronic form; (B) consent, judged from conduct; (C) the unwaivable right to refuse OTHER transactions; (D) other provisions MAY be varied by agreement, and the presence of 'unless otherwise agreed' in some provisions does not imply the rest are fixed. So (C) is the only unwaivable condition, and the row says that rather than implying the Act as a whole is unwaivable. R.C. 1923.04(A) read section-open the same day for the service-method point. WHICH CLAUSES THIS BEARS ON: electronic-signatures (shared) consents to electronic EXECUTION of the lease only and does not purport to waive the 1306.04(C) right, so it is lawful in Ohio as written and needs no override; notices (shared) expressly defers to any method applicable law requires and states that nothing in the lease designates an alternative method for a notice governed by law, which is exactly what 1923.04(A) needs. Neither clause was changed. NOT RESEARCHED: whether a residential lease is a 'transaction' within R.C. 1306.01's definition - the definition was not read section-open, and if it excluded real-property leases the first sentence of this row would narrow. Flagged as the row's weakest link.

title: A Void Term Costs You Nothing Extra in Ohio
bodyText: Ohio attaches no penalty to using a lease term the law prohibits. R.C. 5321.13 lists the terms that are not recognised - confession of judgment, attorney's fees either way, exculpation or indemnity of the landlord, and any waiver of Chapter 5321 - but it provides no damages, no civil penalty and no fee award for having used one. The term simply has no effect, and R.C. 5321.14 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable term or limit how it is applied. That is a real difference from some states: Kansas, for example, gives the tenant actual damages where a landlord deliberately uses an agreement containing terms it knows are prohibited. Ohio's consumer protection act does not fill the gap either, because R.C. 1345.01(A) defines a consumer transaction by reference to goods, services, a franchise or an intangible, and a residential lease of real property is none of those. None of this makes a prohibited term safe. It is unenforceable the moment you need it, a tenant can raise it as a defence, and a lease built on terms that fail is worse than one drafted to Ohio law in the first place.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Requirement
bodyText: South Dakota has no just-cause or good-cause eviction statute. The end of the term ends the right to possession, and a landlord may decline to renew without giving a reason. SDCL 43-32-14 and 43-32-15 presume renewal where a lessee holds over and the lessor accepts rent, or where the term was never specified and neither party gives the scaling notice - so the way to end an unspecified-term tenancy is to give that notice, not to show cause. For a tenancy at will, SDCL 43-8-8 requires 15 days' written notice, or two months where the tenant or an immediate family member is on active military service. SDCL 43-32-27 is the one place a reason matters: a notice to vacate not based on a breach of the lease can support a retaliation claim if it follows a protected event, and the statute says expressly that failing to renew a written lease before or upon its expiration is not retaliation. No conversion-notice year, no rent-escrow filing bar, and no tenants'-association protection beyond SDCL 43-32-27's union-organising limb were found.

Battery run against the whole South Dakota code loaded from the official sdlegislature.gov API (71 title endpoints) plus all 30 constitution articles, section-parsed, with the pattern tested against a known positive first and a nonsense control returning 0. Positives for both patterns passed on synthetic text in the statute's own idiom. Sections read section-open for the affirmative statements above: SDCL 43-32-14, 43-32-15, 43-8-8, 43-8-9, 43-32-27. The situational limits rule 41 names were each searched and none exists in South Dakota. Matches the WY/KS/NE/ND/PA/TN posture, not the CO/NJ/MN/OH/MI/IA/OK one.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent Setting
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute addressing algorithmic or software-assisted rent setting, revenue-management pricing, or the sharing of rent data among landlords. Nothing requires disclosure that software set the rent, and nothing prohibits using it. SDCL 43-32-6.1 caps the security deposit and SDCL 43-32-13 governs how a month-to-month rent change is noticed, but neither speaks to how the figure is arrived at, and South Dakota separately preempts local rent control. Federal and state antitrust law still applies to agreements among competitors, and that is a different question from the lease.

Synthetic positive ('the use of an algorithm to set rent is prohibited') passed. Not searched: antitrust case law and any Attorney General enforcement position.

title: Whether Fees Count as Rent
bodyText: No South Dakota statute deems a non-rent charge to be rent, and none forbids a lease from defining rent to include other charges. Two places make the distinction matter anyway. SDCL 21-16-1(4) gives a forcible entry and detainer ground where a lessee 'fails to pay his rent for three days after the same shall be due' - that ground is written about RENT, so a lease that sweeps late fees, utilities and other charges into the defined term risks an eviction built on unpaid fees rather than unpaid rent, which is a weaker filing. SDCL 43-32-24 separately lets a landlord withhold from the security deposit both rent defaults and 'other funds due to the landlord pursuant to an agreement', so for deposit purposes the lease's own definition of what is owed does the work and no relabelling is needed. The practical course is to keep rent meaning the monthly payment for occupancy and to pursue other charges as other charges.

SDCL 21-16-1(4) and 43-32-24 read section-open this pass; the FED-ground point is a reading of the statute's word 'rent', recorded as a drafting caution rather than a holding - no South Dakota case on whether a lease may define rent to include fees for FED purposes was searched.

title: No Landlord Self-Cure and Bill-Back Right
bodyText: South Dakota gives a landlord no statutory right to perform a tenant's obligation, cure a tenant's breach, and bill the cost back as rent. The statutory traffic runs the other way: SDCL 43-32-9 lets the TENANT repair and deduct from rent when the landlord fails to repair within a reasonable time after notice, and SDCL 43-32-8 permits the parties to agree that the tenant performs specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent. SDCL 43-32-10 makes the tenant liable to repair deterioration or damage caused by the tenant's own negligent, willful or malicious conduct, which is a liability rule, not a self-help mechanism. So a landlord who wants to fix something the tenant should have fixed and recover the cost is relying on the lease and on ordinary damages, not on a statute, and should expect to prove the cost was reasonable and actually caused by the tenant.

SDCL 43-32-8, 43-32-9 and 43-32-10 all read section-open this pass. Distinguish the tenant-side repair-and-deduct right in edu-habitability-duty-sd, which is the converse and is statutory.

title: No Lease-Completeness or Copy Requirement
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no statutory requirements about the physical completeness of a residential lease. There is no rule against leaving blank spaces to be filled in after signing, no requirement to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, no deadline for delivering one, and no requirement that the lease identify the landlord or an agent for service. The lease also need not be in writing at all: SDCL 43-32-8 and 43-32-10 both apply to a hiring of residential premises 'whether in writing or parol'. None of that makes blanks or a missing copy a good idea - a landlord who cannot produce a complete signed lease has trouble proving the term, the rent and any lease-defined eviction ground under SDCL 21-16-1(7), which depends entirely on what the lease says.

title: Quiet Possession and Quiet Enjoyment
bodyText: South Dakota puts the covenant of quiet enjoyment in statute rather than leaving it to common law. SDCL 43-32-6 requires a lessor to deliver the leased premises to the lessee and to secure the lessee's quiet enjoyment against all lawful claimants. The same section supplies the remedy when the landlord is the one interfering: if the landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant, or willfully diminishes services by interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service, the tenant may sue for an injunction, recover possession by suit, or terminate the rental agreement, and in any case recover damages equal to two months' rent plus the return of any advance rent and deposit. SDCL 43-32-19(1) adds a termination right where the landlord does not, within a reasonable time after the tenant's WRITTEN request, put or keep the tenant in quiet possession. Two practical consequences: the duty runs against lawful claimants - a title or lien claim - rather than against every nuisance a neighbour creates; and because it is statutory and tied to SDCL 43-32-6's remedy, a lease cannot usefully disclaim it.

Battery run against the whole South Dakota code loaded from the official sdlegislature.gov API (71 title endpoints) plus all 30 constitution articles, section-parsed, with the pattern tested against a known positive first and a nonsense control returning 0. Pattern 'quiet (enjoyment|possession)' returned exactly 2 residential hits, SDCL 43-32-6 and 43-32-19, both read section-open this pass and both quoted above. South Dakota joins VA, CO and the other 'Present' states rather than the PA/TN/AL/SC/NE/AZ/WY 'no statute' group. The 'written request' qualifier on 43-32-19(1) is attached to the sentence the statute attaches it to - contrast SDCL 43-32-9, where the repair-and-deduct and vacate remedies need only 'notice'. No exculpation analysis beyond edu-exculpatory-clause-limit-sd; whether a lease could waive 43-32-6 was not litigated here, though SDCL 53-9-3 reaches an exemption from a violation of law.

title: No Statutory Lease or Notice Forms
bodyText: South Dakota prescribes no form for a residential lease or for any landlord notice. There is no statutory lease form, no prescribed notice-to-quit or termination form, and no 'substantially the following form' language anywhere in the landlord-tenant statutes. What the statutes prescribe is content and service, not layout: SDCL 43-32-13 requires the month-to-month modification notice to be in writing and given 30 days before the end of the month; SDCL 43-8-9 requires a notice ending a tenancy at will to be in writing and served by delivery to the tenant or to a person of discretion residing on the premises, or, if neither can be found with reasonable diligence, by affixing it to a conspicuous part of the premises where it can conveniently be read; and SDCL 43-32-32 requires an entry notice to specify the date or dates of entry, a period during normal business hours, the purpose, and a means for the tenant to ask to reschedule. Meet those and the wording is yours.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute about a tenant installing a security camera, video doorbell or other recording device at a rented home, and none about a landlord doing so. Nothing gives a tenant a right to install one over the landlord's objection, and nothing prohibits a landlord from allowing or refusing it. In practice the question is answered by the lease: a camera screwed to a door frame or wired into the building is an alteration, so the no-alterations clause governs, and a device a tenant can hang and remove without damage usually is not. Two outside limits are worth knowing. A camera a tenant aims at a neighbour's windows or a shared bathroom can reach South Dakota's criminal invasion-of-privacy provisions, which are not a landlord-tenant matter but are a reason to write the rule down. And a tenant whose disability makes a monitoring device necessary may be entitled to install one as a reasonable modification at the tenant's expense under SDCL 20-13-20(4).

title: Electronic Notices and Delivery
bodyText: South Dakota's landlord-tenant statutes say nothing about delivering notices electronically, so the rules come from the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act in SDCL chapter 53-12, and three of its provisions cannot be contracted around. First, the Act applies only between parties who have each agreed to conduct transactions by electronic means, judged from the context and the parties' conduct (SDCL 53-12-8) - a clause reciting consent helps, but conduct can establish or undercut it. Second, a party who agrees to one electronic transaction may refuse to conduct others, and SDCL 53-12-9 says that right 'may not be waived by agreement' - so a lease cannot bind a tenant to accept every future notice electronically. Third, where a law requires information in writing, an electronic record satisfies it only if the record is capable of retention by the recipient, and a record is not capable of retention if the sender or its system inhibits the recipient's ability to print or store it (SDCL 53-12-17); if the sender does inhibit that, the record 'is not enforceable against the recipient' (SDCL 53-12-19). SDCL 53-12-20 makes those requirements unvariable by agreement, with two narrow exceptions - where the other law's writing requirement is itself variable by agreement, and where the other law's first-class-mail requirement is variable. The Act also does not reach transactions under SDCL chapter 15-6 or other transactions involving the Unified Judicial System (SDCL 53-12-3), so court filings and service in an eviction action are outside it. Practical upshot: use a portal the tenant can download and print from, keep paper available for any notice that ends the tenancy, and do not treat a consent clause as permanent.
notes: Retro checks (SOP 1.24) 2026-10-02. RULE 45 - the electronic-transactions act itself read, not just a landlord-tenant section referring to it, which is what rule 45 requires. SDCL 53-12-2, 53-12-3, 53-12-4, 53-12-8, 53-12-9, 53-12-10, 53-12-17, 53-12-18, 53-12-19 and 53-12-20 all read section-open from the official sdlegislature.gov endpoint. GENUINELY NEW: no South Dakota row recorded any of this. The variation-by-agreement sections were read in full per rule 45: SDCL 53-12-10 is the general 'may be varied by agreement' opening, and SDCL 53-12-20 is the carve-out that takes 53-12-17 to -19 back out of it, with its own two exceptions - stating either alone would misdescribe both the tenant's protection and the lease's freedom. CLAUSE SCREEN: no SD-tagged clause relies on electronic delivery of an eviction, default or cure notice. The shared notices clause is already correctly deferential ('Where applicable law requires a particular method, form, timing, or content for a notice, that requirement will control over this Section, and nothing in this Lease designates an alternative method of delivery'), and electronic-signatures goes to execution rather than notice and supplies the mutual consent SDCL 53-12-8 needs. No clause change proposed. The whole-code battery for 'electronic (record|signature|notice|transmission|communication)' returned 8 residential hits, none in a landlord-tenant chapter, which is why the Act itself had to be read directly.

title: Tenant-Caused Damage
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the negligent or willful act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not be reduced or abated while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's obligation under South Dakota law to repair deterioration or damage caused by Tenant's own negligent, willful or malicious conduct, or that of persons acting under Tenant's direction or control. Nothing in this Section limits any right South Dakota law gives Tenant to terminate this Lease after the property is destroyed.
notes: Retro checks (SOP 1.24) 2026-10-02. RULE 54t - the always-ask question, answered for South Dakota, and the lease may lawfully fill part of the gap. WHAT SOUTH DAKOTA LAW ALREADY GIVES THE LANDLORD, all read section-open this pass: SDCL 43-32-10 makes the lessee liable to preserve the premises and 'repair all deteriorations or damage thereto occasioned by his negligent, willful or malicious conduct or such conduct of persons acting under his direction or control' - so the REPAIR COST is statutory; and SDCL 43-32-8 carves disrepair 'caused by the negligent, willful or malicious conduct of the lessee' out of the landlord's own repair duty. WHAT IT DOES NOT GIVE: rent during repairs, and lost rent if the lease ends. That is the gap this clause fills. EACH ABATEMENT AND EXIT PROVISION CHECKED SEPARATELY for its own tenant-fault exception, per rule 54t: SDCL 43-32-19(2) (tenant's casualty termination) excludes destruction caused by 'the ordinary negligence of the tenant' but, read literally, not the tenant's willful act, so this clause does NOT purport to remove that statutory right and says so expressly; SDCL 43-32-6 (essential-services remedy) and SDCL 43-32-9 (repair remedies) carry no tenant-fault exception at all and are untouched by this clause; SDCL 43-32-9's rent-escrow route is likewise untouched. LAWFULNESS: South Dakota has no enumerated prohibited-lease-terms statute (edu-no-prohibited-terms-list-sd), and this clause measures ACTUAL damages with a mitigation duty rather than fixing a sum, which keeps it clear of SDCL 53-9-4 (penalties for nonperformance void) and SDCL 53-9-5 (anticipated-damages terms void outside the impracticability exception) - both read section-open this pass. CONDITIONAL and offered, never a default, per rule 54. Modelled on tenant-caused-damage-tn, which was read and NOT tagged; the TN row rests on Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-102 and 66-28-503 and its county-split architecture does not transfer. Paired with fire-casualty-rent-abatement-sd, whose exit limb was given a matching tenant-fault carve-out in this same pass.

title: Management and Notices
bodyText: Management and notices. The person authorized to manage the property is: [name, address and telephone number]. An owner of the property, or a person authorized to act for and on behalf of the owner for the purpose of service of process and for the purpose of receiving and receipting for notices and demands, is: [name, address and telephone number]. Landlord will keep this information current and will tell Tenant in writing if it changes.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-19(A): the owner 'shall disclose to the resident in writing at or before the commencement of the residency the name, address and telephone number of: (1) the person authorized to manage the premises; and (2) an owner of the premises or a person authorized to act for and on behalf of the owner for the purpose of service of process and for the purpose of receiving and receipting for notices and demands.' The lease is the writing. NMSA 1978, § 47-8-19(B): kept current and enforceable against any successor owner or manager; (C): each person named becomes the owner's agent for those purposes; (D): failure to comply relieves the resident of any obligation to give the owner notice required by the act. Written for New Mexico rather than tagging `landlord-disclosure-ia` or `landlord-disclosure-mo`, whose bases rest on their own states' statutes and which omit the telephone number New Mexico requires (rule 26). A nonresident owner may also designate an in-state agent for service of process with the secretary of state (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-10(B); `edu-nonresident-owner-agent-nm`). title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds, a closed account, a stop-payment order or any other reason, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of {{nsf_fee}}, and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are returned or fail, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check or money order.
notes: NM: No New Mexico statute caps a returned-payment fee for residential rent (NM battery 10 (dishonored check / insufficient funds service charge): 86 hits, control 0; known positives passed; hits are banking, tax, public-body and Uniform Commercial Code sections, and the civil worthless-check statute). The fee must be stated: it is an unfair or deceptive trade practice for an owner 'to charge fees that are not included in the rental agreement' (NMSA 1978, § 57-12-27(C)), and the published listing must describe all fees that will be assessed during the residency (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-19.1); a fee the rental agreement provides may be increased only on 60 days' written notice (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-19.4). The base `returned-payments` is not used because it names no amount ('not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law'), and New Mexico has no maximum, so the fee would be neither stated nor capped (rules 53, 42). A returned-payment fee is not rent (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-3(P)) and is not part of the rent on which a late fee is calculated (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-15(D)). Separately, the civil worthless-check statute allows the greater of $100 or triple the check amount, capped at $500 over the check, only for a check drawn with intent to defraud and only after a written demand sent by certified mail at least ten days before suit (NMSA 1978, § 56-14-1; `edu-dishonored-check-nm`). BUILDER: {{nsf_fee}} has no statutory cap in New Mexico (NM log §10). title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: When this tenancy ends, Tenant will give Landlord in writing a forwarding address for the return of the Security Deposit. Within 30 days after the later of the date this Lease terminates and the date Tenant moves out, Landlord will return the Security Deposit to Tenant or, if Landlord keeps any part of it, give Tenant an itemized written list of the deductions and the balance, if any, together with that balance. Landlord may mail the list and any payment to Tenant's last known address. Landlord will not keep any part of the Security Deposit to cover normal wear and tear.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-18(C): no deposit 'shall be retained to cover normal wear and tear'; where actual cause exists for retaining any portion, the owner 'shall provide the resident with an itemized written list of the deductions from the deposit and the balance of the deposit, if any, within thirty days of the date of termination of the rental agreement or resident departure, whichever is later', and 'is deemed to have complied with this section by mailing the statement and any payment required to the last known address of the resident'. NMSA 1978, § 47-8-18(D): an owner who fails to provide the statement and the balance within thirty days forfeits the right to withhold any portion, the right to counterclaim in an action to recover the deposit, and the right to an independent action for damages to the property, and is liable for court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees; (E): bad-faith retention, $250 civil penalty (`edu-deposit-return-penalty-nm`). Where a mailed notice under the act comes back undeliverable, or the last known address is the vacated unit, the owner must serve at least one more notice at any alternative address the resident gave (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-13(F)); the forwarding-address sentence is the landlord-serving reason for the clause. Rule 37: the thirty days run from the later of termination or departure for every tenancy type. Supersedes the blank-states parent (rule 25 family). rule_type RECOMMENDED, not the parent's REQUIRED: no New Mexico statute requires this text in the lease (rule 56; library-wide point flagged in NM log §10). title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord: [list approved pets, or state that no pets are permitted]. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, if applicable, and a refundable pet deposit of {{pet_deposit}}, if applicable. Any pet deposit counts toward the limits applicable law places on deposits and will be held, applied and returned with the Security Deposit. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and Tenant will then remove the pet within [number] days after Landlord's written notice. Landlord may enter the property in connection with a pet only as this Lease's Access & Entry terms and applicable law permit. This Section does not apply to a service animal or other assistance animal.
notes: NM: Replaces the base `pet-policy`, which allows entry to remove a pet beyond New Mexico's entry rules (the owner 'has no other right of access except by court order' or as NMSA 1978, § 47-8-24 and NMSA 1978, § 47-8-34 permit, NMSA 1978, § 47-8-24(D)) and does so 'without liability to Tenant', a waiver of the resident's remedies that no rental agreement may contain (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-16; rule 52). A refundable pet deposit is a 'deposit' (an amount delivered 'as a pledge to abide by terms and conditions of the rental agreement', NMSA 1978, § 47-8-3(F)) and counts toward the one-month limit for an agreement shorter than a year and the interest threshold for an annual agreement (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-18(A); `edu-pet-deposit-nm`). Pet rent is a fee the rental agreement must include (NMSA 1978, § 57-12-27(C)) and the listing must describe (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-19.1); it is not part of the rent on which a late fee is calculated if it is an additional fee (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-15(D)). Failing to remove a pet after revocation is a material noncompliance handled under NMSA 1978, § 47-8-33(A)-(B). No New Mexico statute limits pet rules in ordinary private rentals (NM battery 103 (pet deposit / pets in rental housing): 2 hits, control 0; known positives passed (hits: NMSA 1978, §§ 17-2-31, 17-11-2)); the Mobile Home Park Act's pet provision (NMSA 1978, § 47-10-15.1) applies only to parks, which are out of scope. Not tagged: `pet-policy-mo`, `pet-policy-nc` and the others rest on their own states' statutes (rule 26).
