title: Landlord's Entry
bodyText: Tenant will consent to Landlord, its agents and contractors entering the property to inspect it, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or show it to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, prospective tenants, workers or contractors. Before entering for any of these purposes, Landlord will give Tenant at least 24 hours' written notice of Landlord's intent to enter, stating the purpose of the entry and the date and a reasonable estimate of the time frame of the entry. If Tenant gives reasonable prior notice of an alternate time or date for the entry, Landlord will try to reasonably accommodate it where that is practicable or will not cause Landlord economic detriment. Advance notice is not required when Landlord enters to perform repairs or services within seven days after Tenant requests them, or is accompanied by a public official conducting an inspection or by a cable television, electric, gas or telephone company representative. Landlord may enter without Tenant's consent in an emergency, if Tenant has abandoned or surrendered the property, and during any absence of Tenant of more than seven days at times reasonably necessary. Landlord will not abuse this right of access.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-24(A): the resident 'shall, in accordance with provisions of the rental agreement and notice provisions as provided in this section, consent to the owner to enter into the dwelling unit in order to inspect the premises, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, prospective residents, workmen or contractors'; (A)(1): 'unless otherwise agreed upon by the owner and resident', only after 'twenty-four hours written notification of his intent to enter, the purpose for entry and the date and reasonable estimate of the time frame of the entry'; (A)(2): the subsection does not apply to repairs or services within seven days of the resident's request or when the owner is accompanied by a public official or a cable television, electric, gas or telephone company representative; (A)(3): reasonable accommodation of alternate times where practicable or 'will not result in economic detriment to the owner'; (B): emergency entry without consent; (C): no abuse of access; (D): no other right of access except by court order, on abandonment or surrender, or during an absence of more than seven days (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-34(B)). Not the base `landlords-access` (its 'right of reasonable access' on '24 hours' notice' omits the written form and contents New Mexico requires, and could be read as an agreement 'otherwise' under (A)(1)) and not `landlords-access-mi` (consent 'not unreasonably' refused, oral notice); written for New Mexico (rule 53; the Iowa consent flag, IA log §10.5). A written entry notice is a written notice to the resident, so it must be hand-delivered or mailed, or posted and also mailed or hand-delivered (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-13(D); `edu-landlord-entry-nm`, `edu-notice-service-nm`). Remedies: NMSA 1978, §§ 47-8-24(E)-(F), 47-8-38. title: Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy
bodyText: If this Lease is, or continues as, a month-to-month tenancy, Landlord may end it by written notice given to Tenant at least [state Landlord's notice period: at least 30] days before the periodic rental date specified in the notice as the termination date, and Tenant may end it by written notice given to Landlord at least 30 days before the periodic rental date specified in the notice. If it is, or continues as, a week-to-week tenancy, Landlord may end it by written notice given at least [state Landlord's notice period: at least 7] days before the termination date specified in the notice, and Tenant may end it by written notice given at least 7 days before the termination date specified in the notice. Rent remains payable through the termination date. This Section does not limit either party's right to end this Lease earlier where this Lease or applicable law allows it.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-37(A): a week-to-week residency ends by written notice 'at least seven days prior to the termination date specified in the notice'; (B): a month-to-month residency ends by written notice 'at least thirty days prior to the periodic rental date specified in the notice'. NMSA 1978, § 47-8-15(C): unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the residency is week-to-week for a weekly payer and otherwise month-to-month. The bracketed period is the landlord's own notice figure, at least the statutory minimum (rule 55); Tenant's period is fixed at the statutory minimum, because a longer period binding the resident would make the resident forgo the statute's seven- or thirty-day right, which no rental agreement may do (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-16) (independent check round 1). A notice that gives fewer than thirty days before the stated date is effective for the next rental date, and a notice coupled with an option to stay at a higher rent does not terminate (T.W.I.W., Inc. v. Rhudy, 1981-NMSC-062, as summarized in the compilation's annotation to NMSA 1978, § 47-8-37; opinion not read, NM log §1.4). Written for New Mexico rather than tagging `periodic-tenancy-notice-tn`, whose basis is Tennessee's statute and whose week-to-week figure (10 days) differs (rule 26). Notice service: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-13(D) (`edu-notice-service-nm`); Supreme Court form: Form 4-903 NMRA (thirty-day notice to terminate). Retaliation limits: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-39 (`edu-retaliation-nm`). title: Holdover
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession without Landlord's consent after this Lease ends, whether at the end of the Term or after a termination, Landlord may bring an action for possession. Landlord and Tenant agree that the rental value of the property for each day Tenant remains in possession is the Monthly Rent apportioned daily, and Tenant will pay it. If Tenant's holdover is willful and not in good faith, Landlord may also recover the damages Landlord sustains and reasonable attorney's fees, as applicable law provides. If Landlord consents to Tenant's continued occupancy, the tenancy continues from week to week if Tenant pays Rent weekly and otherwise from month to month, on the terms of this Lease, and either party may end it by the written notice applicable law requires.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-37(C): 'If the resident remains in possession without the owner's consent after expiration of the term of the rental agreement or its termination, the owner may bring an action for possession and if the resident's holdover is willful and not in good faith the owner, in addition, may recover the damages sustained by him and reasonable attorney's fees. If the owner consents to the resident's continued occupancy, Subsection C of Section 15 [47-8-15 NMSA 1978] ... applies' (week-to-week for a weekly payer, otherwise month-to-month, NMSA 1978, § 47-8-15(C)). Supersedes `holdover-ca`, whose 'actual damages caused by Tenant's continued possession' for any holdover is a measure New Mexico allows only for a willful, bad-faith holdover (rule 53 trigger; the IA log §10.6 flag); the clause fixes only the daily rental value for every holdover, which is not a penalty and not a late charge, so the nonpayment-termination exclusion in rule 53 is not needed. The forcible-entry double-rent measure on appeal (NMSA 1978, § 35-10-5) does not apply to a residential tenancy under the act (NMSA 1978, § 35-10-2). During an appeal the resident must pay rent into escrow to stay the writ (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-47(A)). A stipulated holdover rate above the rent is lawful to consider but not offered (`edu-holdover-rate-nm`). title: Handling of Property Left Behind
bodyText: When this Lease ends or Tenant gives up possession, Tenant will remove all of Tenant's personal property from the property. Personal property left on the premises will be handled as follows. (1) If this Lease ends because Tenant abandons the property (an absence of more than seven continuous days without notice to Landlord, after Rent has become delinquent), Landlord will store the property for at least 30 days and will give Tenant written notice, personally delivered or sent by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to Tenant's last known address, stating Landlord's intent to dispose of the property on a date at least 30 days after the date of the notice and giving a telephone number and address where Tenant can reasonably contact Landlord to retrieve it. If the notice is returned undeliverable, or Tenant's last known address is the property, Landlord will also send at least one notice to any other address Tenant has given Landlord, including Tenant's place of employment or a family member or emergency contact on Landlord's records. Tenant may retrieve the property at any time before the disposal date, and Landlord will give Tenant reasonable access and adequate opportunities to do so. (2) If this Lease ends because Tenant voluntarily surrenders the property, Landlord will store the property for at least 14 days after the surrender and give Tenant reasonable access to retrieve it. (3) If this Lease ends by a writ of restitution, Landlord has no obligation to store property left more than three days after the writ is executed, and will give Tenant a reasonable opportunity to retrieve it within those three days. (4) After the applicable period, Landlord may dispose of property Tenant has not retrieved. Property with a market value of less than $100 may be disposed of in any manner. For property worth $100 or more, Landlord will either sell it, or keep it and credit Tenant's account with its fair market value, and within 15 days will mail to Tenant's last known address an itemized statement and any amount exceeding what Tenant owes Landlord; if that address is the property, Landlord will also mail a copy to any other address Tenant has given. (5) Tenant will pay reasonable storage fees for the time Landlord stores the property and moving fees at the prevailing rate, and Landlord may require payment of them before releasing the property. Landlord will not hold the property for any other debt.
notes: NM: Mirrors NMSA 1978, § 47-8-34.1: (A) abandonment (store at least thirty days; written notice of intent to dispose on a date at least thirty days after the notice, with a telephone number and address; personal delivery or first-class mail; second notice to another address the resident gave, including employment, family member or emergency contact; retrieval any time before the date; reasonable access); (B) voluntary surrender (store at least fourteen days, reasonable access); (C) writ of restitution (no obligation to store after three days following execution, 'unless otherwise agreed'); (D) market value under $100, any manner; (E) over $100, sell or retain, mailing the excess with an itemized statement within fifteen days; (F) second mailing where the last known address is the unit; (G) reasonable storage fees and the prevailing rate of moving fees, payable before release; (H) no holding for other debts or unexecuted judgments, and no retention of exempt property. 'Abandonment' is the statutory definition (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-3(A)). The statute is silent on property worth exactly $100; the clause treats it under the stricter $100-or-more procedure. Owners must give a reasonable opportunity to recover property within three days after a writ is executed (White v. Farris, 2021-NMCA-014, as summarized in the compilation's annotation to NMSA 1978, § 47-8-34.1; opinion not read, NM log §1.4). No landlord's lien exists for a dwelling unit (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-36.1(A); NMSA 1978, § 48-3-5(A)), so the clause applies proceeds only as the statute allows. Title matches the pointer in `surrender-end-of-term-ks-ne`. A deceased sole resident's property follows NMSA 1978, § 47-8-34.2 (`deceased-resident-contact-nm`). title: Tenant Maintenance Agreement
bodyText: [Optional. Use for a property that is NOT a single family residence; this agreement must be a separate writing signed by Landlord and Tenant, not a section of the Lease. For a single family residence, landscaping and snow removal are covered by the Lease's Landscaping & Irrigation and Snow Removal sections, and this agreement may be used for other tasks.] Landlord and Tenant agree, in good faith and not for the purpose of evading Landlord's obligations, that Tenant will perform the following specified repairs or maintenance tasks: [check each that applies: ☐ lawn and landscaping care, keeping to any irrigation schedule Landlord sets, and promptly reporting irrigation leaks or watering problems; ☐ prompt, reasonable removal of snow and ice from walkways, driveways, porches and entrances that only Tenant uses; ☐ pool or spa care; ☐ replacing heating and air-conditioning filters; ☐ replacing light bulbs; ☐ other specified task: ____]. In exchange for these tasks, Tenant will receive the following consideration: [state the consideration, e.g. a Monthly Rent reduction of $__]. This agreement does not diminish or affect Landlord's obligations to any other resident, and it does not make Tenant responsible for keeping the property in compliance with housing codes materially affecting health and safety, in a safe condition, or supplied with running water, hot water and heat, which remain Landlord's responsibility. Tenant's failure to perform a task under this agreement that is one of Landlord's obligations under applicable law will not be a basis for eviction and will not be treated as a material breach of the Lease.
notes: NM: Settled by SOP rule 48 (Taylor, 2026-09-30 and 2026-10-02; not re-asked); modeled on `maintenance-allocation-az` and `maintenance-allocation-ia`. NMSA 1978, § 47-8-20(D): the owner and resident of a dwelling unit other than a single family residence 'may agree that the resident is to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling only if: (1) the agreement of the parties is entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the owner and is set forth in a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by consideration; and (2) the agreement does not diminish or affect the obligation of the owner to other residents in the premises.' NMSA 1978, § 47-8-20(E): any arrangement for the resident to perform the owner's obligations does not diminish them, 'nor shall the failure of the resident to perform the obligations of the owner serve as a basis for eviction or in any way be considered a material breach'. NMSA 1978, § 47-8-20(C): for a single family residence (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-3(U)) the agreement may be in the lease and may also cover the owner's waste-removal and water and heat duties in (A)(5)-(6); this separate form does not shift those for other units. The snow checkbox is limited to areas only Tenant uses because common areas are the owner's (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-20(A)(3)). Rule 48: separate document. Tasks and consideration are hand-filled brackets, not variables, so no bracket prints beside a filled variable (rule 60). Builder property-type gate: gap (NM log §10). title: E-mail Communications (Optional)
bodyText: [Optional.] Landlord and Tenant agree that either may send the other routine communications, and any notice that neither this Lease nor applicable law requires to be delivered in a particular way, by e-mail to the address the other provides for that purpose: Tenant: [e-mail address]; Landlord: [e-mail address]. Tenant may also send Landlord any notice under this Lease or applicable law by e-mail to Landlord's address above. The sender will not send an e-mail in a form that keeps the recipient from printing or storing it. This Section does not apply to any notice to Tenant of nonpayment, default, termination, eviction or the right to cure, or to any other written notice to Tenant that applicable law requires to be hand-delivered, mailed or posted; Landlord will deliver those as applicable law requires and may also send an e-mail copy. Either party may stop using e-mail under this Section at any time by written notice to the other.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 14-16-5(b): the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act applies only to transactions between parties each of which has agreed to conduct transactions electronically; (c): a party may refuse further electronic transactions and that right 'may not be waived by agreement'. NMSA 1978, § 14-16-3(B)(2)(b): the act does not apply to a notice concerning 'default, acceleration, repossession, foreclosure, eviction or the right to cure, under ... a rental agreement for a primary residence of an individual'. NMSA 1978, § 14-16-8(b)(2), (d)(2): where other law requires a record to be sent by a specified method, it must be sent that way, except that a first-class-mail requirement may be varied by agreement only to the extent the other law permits; (c): a record the sender keeps the recipient from printing or storing is not enforceable against the recipient. NMSA 1978, § 47-8-13(D): a nonpayment notice is effective only when hand-delivered, mailed or posted, and any other written notice to the resident, even if posted, must also be mailed by first-class mail or hand-delivered. Because no New Mexico provision clearly permits an agreement to replace that mailing or hand delivery, the clause keeps every written notice the act requires to the resident on paper and uses e-mail only for routine communications and for notices from Tenant, which the owner receives when delivered at 'any place held out by him as the place for receipt of the communication' (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-13(C)(2)) (Claude's reading; no case law searched, NM log §1.4). title: Rules and Regulations
bodyText: Tenant will comply with the written rules and regulations for the property in effect when this Lease is signed, a copy of which Landlord has given Tenant: [attach or describe the rules, or state that there are none]. Landlord may adopt or amend rules during the Term by giving Tenant reasonable notice of the new or amended rule. A rule binds Tenant only if its purpose is to promote the appearance, convenience, safety or welfare of the residents in the premises, preserve Landlord's property from abusive use or make a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for the residents generally; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies to all residents in the premises in a fair manner; it is explicit enough to tell Tenant fairly what Tenant must or must not do to comply; and it is not for the purpose of evading Landlord's obligations. A rule adopted after this Lease is signed does not bind Tenant if it works a substantial modification of Tenant's bargain under this Lease.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-23: an owner 'may adopt rules or regulations, however described, concerning the resident's use and occupancy of the premises', enforceable under NMSA 1978, § 47-8-33 only if (A) their purpose is to promote the appearance, convenience, safety or welfare of the residents, preserve the owner's property from abusive use or make a fair distribution of services and facilities; (B) reasonably related to that purpose; (C) applied to all residents fairly; (D) sufficiently explicit; (E) not to evade the owner's obligations; and (F) the resident 'is presented with copies of existing rules and regulations at the time he enters into the rental agreement' and with notice of later amendments; a later rule binds 'if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the resident and it does not work a substantial modification of his bargain'. Valid rules are part of the 'rental agreement' (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-3(Q)). Written for New Mexico rather than tagging `rules-ia` or `rules-ok` (different purpose lists and bases, rule 26). NMSA 1978, § 47-8-23(F) requires only 'reasonable notice' of a new rule; serving it as a written notice under NMSA 1978, § 47-8-13(D) is Claude's conservative reading. title: Contact Person if Tenant Dies
bodyText: [Optional.] Tenant names the following contact person, to be contacted and to receive Tenant's property if Tenant dies: [name, address and telephone number]. Tenant will tell Landlord in writing if this information changes. By signing here, Tenant authorizes Landlord, in the event of Tenant's death, to: (a) grant the contact person access to the property at a reasonable time and in the presence of Landlord or Landlord's agent; (b) allow the contact person to remove Tenant's property from the property; and (c) refund Tenant's Security Deposit, less lawful deductions, to the contact person. Tenant's signature: ______ Date: ______
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-34.2(B): the owner 'may request in writing, including by a requirement in the rental agreement', that the resident (1) provide the name, address and telephone number of a contact person and (2) 'sign a statement authorizing the owner in the event of the resident's death to: (a) grant the contact person access to the dwelling unit at a reasonable time and in the presence of the owner or the owner's agent; (b) allow the contact person to remove the resident's property from the dwelling unit; and (c) refund the resident's security deposit, less lawful deductions, to the contact person.' The clause is that written request and the signed statement (rule 54: a right that exists only if the lease invokes it). NMSA 1978, § 47-8-34.2(F): if, after a written request, the resident provides no contact person, the owner has no responsibility after the resident's death for the property in the dwelling. When a sole occupant dies, the owner turns over property and refunds the deposit (less lawful deductions, including removal and storage costs) to the contact person or another person lawfully entitled, may require an inventory, and may discard property only after a certified-mail request to the contact person and thirty days without removal or any claim (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-34.2(D)); violating (D) makes the owner liable to the estate for actual damages (G). A different procedure may be agreed in writing (E); not offered (`edu-tenant-death-nm`). Written for New Mexico rather than tagging `deceased-tenant-contact-tx` or `tenant-death-contact-ok` (their bases are Texas and Oklahoma statutes, rule 26). title: Landlord's Option to End the Lease After a Fire or Casualty
bodyText: [Optional.] If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty to an extent that Tenant's enjoyment of it is substantially impaired, and continued lawful occupancy of any part of the property is not possible while it is repaired, Landlord may terminate this Lease by written notice to Tenant given within 30 days after the casualty, effective on the date stated in the notice, which will be at least [number, at least 14] days after the notice is given. Rent will be accounted for as of the date Tenant vacates, and Landlord will return the balance of any prepaid Rent and the Security Deposit as applicable law requires. This Section does not limit Tenant's own right under applicable law to vacate and terminate this Lease after a fire or casualty, or, where continued occupancy of part of the property is lawful, to occupy the usable part at reduced Rent, and it does not relieve Tenant of responsibility for damage caused by Tenant's negligence.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-31(A): if the dwelling unit or premises are damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty 'to an extent that enjoyment of the dwelling unit is substantially impaired', the resident may (1) vacate and notify the owner in writing within seven days, terminating as of the date of vacating, or (2) if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part with rent reduced in proportion to the diminished fair rental value; (B): on termination the owner returns the balance of prepaid rent and deposits recoverable under NMSA 1978, § 47-8-18, accounting as of the date of vacating, and 'the resident is responsible for damage caused by his negligence'. The act gives the owner no casualty termination right; a lease may include terms not prohibited by the act (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-14). Offered narrowly (rule 54): only where no part can lawfully be occupied, so it never cuts off the resident's partial-occupancy remedy, and the resident's own statutory rights are preserved (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-16). Modeled on `casualty-termination-ia`. Whether a court would read a landlord casualty termination as inequitable was not searched (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-12; NM log §1.4). Education: `edu-casualty-nm`. title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: [Optional.] If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, a member of Tenant's household, or another person on the premises with Tenant's consent, Tenant will be liable to Landlord for the reasonable cost of repairing the damage and for Landlord's other actual damages caused by it, including, to the extent applicable law allows, the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, for no longer than the remaining Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from Tenant or from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section does not take away any right applicable law gives Tenant after a fire or casualty, including the right to vacate and terminate this Lease or to a reduction in Rent, but Tenant's use of that right does not release Tenant from liability under this Section.
notes: NM: Rule 54 (tenant-caused damage), provision by provision: the resident's repair-based remedies (termination on seven days' notice and rent abatement) 'do not arise if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the resident, a member of his family or other person on the premises with his consent' (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-27.1(B)); abatement runs through the same section (NMSA 1978, §§ 47-8-27.1(A)(2), 47-8-27.2). The fire-or-casualty section has no fault exception: the resident may still vacate and terminate or take a proportional rent reduction, but 'the resident is responsible for damage caused by his negligence' (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-31). So a no-abatement term would waive a statutory right, which no rental agreement may do (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-16), and the clause has none (the `tenant-caused-damage-tn` model's term (1) is left out, as in `tenant-caused-damage-ia`). The resident must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-22(F)); intentional damage carries liability of two times the monthly rent (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-48(D)); the owner recovers damages for noncompliance (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-33(F)) and must mitigate (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-6(A)). Lost-rent damages alongside the casualty exit: no case law searched (NM log §1.4), so the lost-rent limb is limited 'to the extent applicable law allows' (independent check round 1). title: No Criminal Activity
bodyText: [Optional.] Tenant, members of Tenant's household, and Tenant's guests and other persons on the premises with Tenant's consent will not engage in criminal activity on the premises. A violation of this Section is a material noncompliance with this Lease, for which Landlord may give the written notices and pursue the remedies this Lease's Default by Tenant section and applicable law provide. Where the conduct is a substantial violation as applicable law defines it and Tenant knowingly committed or consented to it, Landlord may instead terminate this Lease on the shorter written notice applicable law allows for a substantial violation, subject to the defenses applicable law gives Tenant. This Section does not apply to Tenant or a household member who is the victim of the criminal activity.
notes: NM: New Mexico's three-day, no-cure route is limited to a 'substantial violation': the conduct listed in NMSA 1978, § 47-8-3(V)(1)-(7) (controlled substances other than misdemeanor possession and use; unlawful use of a deadly weapon; unlawful action causing serious physical harm; sexual assault or molestation; entry into another's dwelling or vehicle to commit theft or assault; robbery-type theft; intentional or reckless property damage over $1,000) occurring in the unit, on the premises or within 300 feet, which 'shall be the sole grounds for a substantial violation'; the resident must knowingly commit or consent to it (NMSA 1978, §§ 47-8-22(I), 47-8-33(I)). A lease cannot add grounds to that list. Other criminal activity becomes a lease breach only by a term like this one, and then follows the seven-day notice and second-noncompliance route (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-33(A)-(C)). Defenses to a substantial-violation action: the resident is a victim of domestic violence (J); the resident did not know of and could not have prevented another person's violation (K); reasonable and lawful self-defense (L); a frivolous or bad-faith action costs the petitioner two times the monthly rent plus damages and costs (M). A lessor may also void a lease when the lessee is convicted of using the property as a house of prostitution or a gambling place (NMSA 1978, §§ 30-9-9, 30-19-11; `edu-nuisance-nm`). Rule 54 (crime-free clause): offered. Education: `edu-substantial-violation-nm`. title: Landlord's Right to Remedy Tenant's Failure
bodyText: [Optional.] If Tenant fails to keep the property as clean and safe as its condition permits, to dispose of waste in a clean and safe manner, or to avoid damaging the property, and the failure can be remedied by repair, replacement of a damaged item or cleaning, and Tenant does not remedy it within seven days after Landlord delivers written notice specifying the failure and requesting that Tenant remedy it, Landlord may have the work done in a workmanlike manner, entering the property as this Lease's Access & Entry terms permit. Tenant will reimburse Landlord the reasonable cost of the work, as shown on Landlord's itemized bill, within 30 days after receiving the bill. This amount is not Rent.
notes: NM: New Mexico's act has no owner self-help remedy for a resident's maintenance failure (NM battery 111 (landlord self-cure: owner remedies resident's breach and charges cost): 2 hits, control 0; known positives passed (hits: NMSA 1978, §§ 47-8-6, 47-10-9); hits: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-6 and the Mobile Home Park Act). The owner may recover damages for the resident's noncompliance with the rental agreement or NMSA 1978, § 47-8-22 (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-33(F)), and a lease may add terms the act does not prohibit (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-14). The resident duties named track NMSA 1978, § 47-8-22(B), (C), (F). Entry for repairs requires the 24-hour written notice (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-24(A)(1); `landlords-access-nm`). The charge is stated not to be rent so it is never the basis of a three-day nonpayment notice (NMSA 1978, §§ 47-8-3(P), 47-8-33(D)), and is not a late fee. The seven-day notice here is a contract step, separate from the act's seven-day notice of noncompliance used to terminate (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-33(A)). Offered as an option (rule 54), modeled on `landlord-self-cure-ia` without billing the cost as rent. title: Early Termination
bodyText: Tenant may terminate this Lease before the end of the Term by providing Landlord at least 30 days' written notice. Tenant will pay an early termination fee equal to one month's Rent ({{monthly_rent}}) or 30% of the remaining Rent due under the Term, whichever is greater, and remains responsible for Rent and other obligations up to the termination date. This early-termination option and fee apply only if this Lease has a fixed Term; a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy ends on the notice that applicable law and this Lease provide, without an early termination fee. Landlord may terminate this Lease early only in accordance with this Lease's Default by Tenant and notice provisions and applicable law. If Tenant abandons the property (an absence of more than seven continuous days without notice to Landlord, after Rent has become delinquent), Landlord may take possession of it and re-rent it as applicable law provides. Nothing in this Section limits any right either party has under applicable law, including a Tenant's right to terminate without penalty due to active military service under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, due to the property becoming uninhabitable through no fault of Tenant, or any other termination right or limitation provided by applicable law.
notes: NM: Supersedes `early-termination-ks` for New Mexico because its landlord limb lets Landlord terminate 'if Tenant vacates or abandons the property without notifying Landlord'. In New Mexico an owner may terminate for a resident's breach only on the written notices in NMSA 1978, § 47-8-33 (seven days to remedy; a second noncompliance within six months; three days for nonpayment or a substantial violation), which no rental agreement may waive (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-16), and may take immediate possession without them only on statutory 'abandonment', an absence 'without notice to the owner, in excess of seven continuous days; providing such absence occurs only after rent for the dwelling unit is delinquent' (NMSA 1978, §§ 47-8-3(A), 47-8-34(C)); vacating while rent is paid is neither. On abandonment the owner may re-rent at a fair rental, and the rental agreement 'is deemed to be terminated as of the date the new tenancy begins' (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-34(C)). Tenant option and fee unchanged (fixed Term only). No New Mexico statute regulates a tenant-elected early termination fee (NM battery 124 (early termination fee / liquidated damages / lease break (tenancy context, whole code)): 4 hits, control 0; known positives passed (hits: NMSA 1978, §§ 55-2A-103, 55-2A-504, 55-2A-523, 57-27-2): hits are goods-lease liquidated-damages sections and a definitions section outside housing); a court may limit a provision it finds was inequitable when made (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-12) and the aggrieved party must mitigate (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-6(A)); penalty case law not searched (NM log §1.4). The fee is a fee the rental agreement includes (NMSA 1978, § 57-12-27(C)) and the listing should describe (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-19.1). New Mexico has no statutory lease-termination right for domestic violence or for death (`edu-no-dv-termination-nm`, `edu-tenant-death-nm`); the base text's death carve-out is dropped as inapplicable. Flagged as a possible issue for other states whose acts define abandonment narrowly (NM log §10). title: Fees and Charges
bodyText: Fees and charges. In addition to Monthly Rent and any deposit stated in this Lease, the following are all of the fees and charges Tenant may be required to pay during the tenancy, with the amount of each and when or why it is due: [list each fee or charge, one-time or recurring, e.g. pet rent, parking or amenity fee, utility charges billed by Landlord, returned-payment fee, late fee, rekeying charge, early termination fee; or write 'None']. Landlord will not charge Tenant any fee that is not included in this Lease. Landlord may increase a fee listed in this Lease only by written notice given at least 60 days before the periodic rental date specified in this Lease; if this Lease has a fixed Term, an increase will not take effect before the end of the Term and requires written notice at least 60 days before the end of the Term. For a periodic tenancy of less than one month, the notice will be given at least one rental period before the first fee payment to be increased.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 57-12-27(C) (2025 N.M. Laws ch. 122, § 9, effective June 20, 2025): 'It is an unfair or deceptive trade practice for an owner to charge fees that are not included in the rental agreement in violation of the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act.' The rental agreement is the required vehicle for every fee (rule 42), so the clause is REQUIRED; 'None' covers a lease with no fees. NMSA 1978, § 47-8-19.4 (2025 N.M. Laws ch. 122, § 5): an owner may increase a fee provided by the rental agreement only on written notice at least sixty days before the periodic rental date or at least sixty days before the end of a fixed term, and for a periodic residency of less than a month at least one rental period before the first increased payment; the clause reads the fixed-term limb as an increase effective at the end of the term (Claude's reading of 'prior to the end of the term'). NMSA 1978, § 47-8-19.1: the published listing must disclose 'in plain language all costs of a rental agreement', including base rent and 'a description of all fees or charges that will be assessed during the residency, which shall be itemized and readily identifiable' (`edu-fee-transparency-nm`). Remedies under the Unfair Practices Act: actual damages or $100, whichever is greater, up to treble or $300 for willful violations, and attorney fees (NMSA 1978, § 57-12-10(B)-(C)). A fee is not rent (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-3(P)), and late fees are calculated only on rent (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-15(D)). Topic shared with VA, IL and NV fee statements; written for New Mexico (rule 26). title: Utility Bills and Allocation
bodyText: [Use only if the property is in multi-unit housing with separate utility metering, submetering or apportioned common-area utility costs.] On request, Landlord will give Tenant a copy of the utility bill for Tenant's unit, the apartment's utility bill if the unit is submetered, any common-area utility bills whose costs are apportioned to Tenant, and the calculations used to apportion common-area and submetered costs. Landlord may charge an administrative fee of {{utility_bill_copy_fee}} for each monthly request.

title: Late Fee
bodyText: If Tenant fails to pay Monthly Rent in full within {{late_fee_grace_days}} days after it is due, Tenant will owe a late fee of {{late_fee_amount}} for that rental period. Landlord will give Tenant notice of any late fee charged no later than the last day of the rental period immediately following the one in which the Rent was late, and will not collect a late fee for which that notice was not given. The late fee is not Rent. Acceptance of a late payment does not waive Landlord's right to require full payment of Rent on the date it is due or to pursue any other remedy available under this Lease.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-15(D), as amended by 2025 N.M. Laws ch. 122, § 6 (effective June 20, 2025): a late fee may be charged only 'If the rental agreement provides for the charging of a late fee', may not exceed 'five percent of the rent for each rental period that the resident is in default', is 'calculated only based on rent' (not deposits, additional fees or utilities), and 'To assess a late fee, the owner shall provide notice of the late fee charged no later than the last day of the next rental period immediately following the period in which the default occurred.' Landlords who gave no notice could not collect late fees (Hedicke v. Gunville, 2003-NMCA-032, as summarized in the compilation's annotation to NMSA 1978, § 47-8-15; opinion not read, NM log §1.4). Supersedes the base `late-fee` for New Mexico because its 'a late fee ... will be assessed' reads as automatic, while New Mexico conditions assessment on the owner's notice (rule 42; independent check round 1). The clause is the rental agreement's provision the statute requires before any late fee may be charged (rule 54). The late fee is not rent (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-3(P)) and cannot support a three-day nonpayment notice by itself (`edu-fees-as-rent-nm`). Its non-waiver sentence preserves the owner's own rights and waives no tenant right (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-16 not engaged). title: Maintenance & Repairs
bodyText: Subject to Tenant's own maintenance obligations under this Lease, Landlord will maintain the property, including its structural elements, roof, and systems, in good order and repair, and will repair the appliances, fixtures, and equipment Landlord supplies at the property. Where a repair is necessary because of the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an occupant or a guest of Tenant, Tenant will reimburse Landlord the reasonable cost of the repair. Tenant will notify Landlord promptly in writing of any condition requiring repair or maintenance, and Landlord will undertake required repairs within a reasonable time, consistent with applicable law.

title: New Mexico Late Fee Rules
bodyText: New Mexico allows a late fee only if the lease provides for one. The fee may not exceed 5% of the rent for each rental period the tenant is in default, and it is calculated only on rent, not on deposits, other fees or utilities. To charge it, you must give the tenant notice of the late fee no later than the last day of the next rental period after the one in which the rent was late. There is no required grace period. The 5% cap took effect June 20, 2025; leases written for the earlier 10% cap must not charge more than 5%.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-15(D), as amended by 2025 N.M. Laws ch. 122, § 6 (effective June 20, 2025; 'ten' changed to 'five' and the rent-only sentences added, per the enrolled act and the compilation's annotation): 'If the rental agreement provides for the charging of a late fee and if the resident does not pay rent in accordance with the rental agreement, the owner may charge the resident a late fee in an amount not to exceed five percent of the rent for each rental period that the resident is in default. Late fees shall be calculated only based on rent. Rent calculations to determine late fees shall not include deposits, additional fees or utilities. To assess a late fee, the owner shall provide notice of the late fee charged no later than the last day of the next rental period immediately following the period in which the default occurred.' Landlords who never gave notice of late fees could not collect them (Hedicke v. title: Fees Are Not Rent in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico defines rent as the payments the lease requires for use of the home, not including deposits, and the three-day nonpayment notice is for unpaid rent. Late fees are calculated only on rent, and the act treats other fees and utilities separately. To be safe, put only unpaid rent in a three-day notice and collect fees and other charges as separate debts.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-3(P): '"rent" means payments in currency or in-kind pursuant to terms and conditions of the rental agreement for use of a dwelling unit or premises, to be made to the owner by the resident, but does not include deposits'. NMSA 1978, § 47-8-33(D): the three-day notice applies '[i]f rent is unpaid when due'. NMSA 1978, § 47-8-15(D): late fees 'shall be calculated only based on rent', and 'Rent calculations to determine late fees shall not include deposits, additional fees or utilities'. NMSA 1978, § 47-8-33(E) refers to an action 'for nonpayment of rent or other charges' only to give a resident who disputes the amount three days after judgment to pay. title: Rent Increase Notice in New Mexico
bodyText: To raise rent in a month-to-month tenancy, give the tenant written notice at least 30 days before the rental date on which the increase starts. In a fixed-term lease, give written notice at least 30 days before the end of the term; the increase takes effect for the period after the term. For a tenancy shorter than month-to-month, give notice at least one rental period before the first increased payment. An increase may not be made in retaliation for protected tenant activity, though a uniform increase for similar units, given with proper notice, is allowed.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-15(F): 'An owner may increase the rent payable by the resident in a month-to-month residency by providing written notice to the resident of the proposed increase at least thirty days prior to the periodic rental date specified in the rental agreement or, in the case of a fixed term residency, at least thirty days prior to the end of the term. In the case of a periodic residency of less than one month, written notice shall be provided at least one rental period in advance of the first rental payment to be increased.' A mid-term increase in a fixed term is not authorized by the section (Claude's reading; a rent step written into the original lease is not an 'increase' by notice, not decided by any case found; case law not searched, NM log §1.4), so no mid-term escalation clause is offered (NM log §6.1). title: Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico

title: Fee Disclosure in Listings and Leases
bodyText: Since June 20, 2025, a New Mexico rental listing must disclose, in plain language, the base rent and an itemized description of every fee or charge that will be assessed during the tenancy. Charging an applicant any fee other than a screening fee or a deposit, or a fee not published in the listing, and charging a tenant any fee not included in the lease, are unfair or deceptive trade practices under the Unfair Practices Act. Tenants can recover actual damages or $100 (up to triple or $300 for willful violations) plus attorney fees. You are not liable for a third-party website's failure to show all the costs you provided.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-19.1 (2025 N.M. Laws ch. 122, § 2): 'An owner shall disclose to applicants in plain language all costs of a rental agreement in a published listing of the dwelling unit, including the base rent that will be assessed and a description of all fees or charges that will be assessed during the residency, which shall be itemized and readily identifiable in the listing. An owner shall not be liable for violating the provisions of the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act for a third-party website's failure to represent all costs provided by the owner.' title: Application Screening Fees in New Mexico
bodyText: Since June 20, 2025, a New Mexico landlord may charge an applicant (including a guarantor or cosigner) a screening fee of no more than $50, and no other fee to process an application. You must give written or digital notice of the fee, get the applicant's written agreement to pay it, and give a receipt. You may not charge it when you know the unit is not available, and you must hold card payments or wait to deposit cash or checks until earlier applicants have been screened and rejected or have declined. Return the fee within 30 days if an earlier applicant takes the unit or you do not actually screen the applicant. Do not charge the same applicant twice within 90 days for properties under the same ownership. An unauthorized screening fee costs $250 plus a refund of all fees paid.

bodyText: New Mexico law bars cities, counties and other political subdivisions, including home-rule cities, from enacting rent control for privately owned property. title: Returned Checks in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico does not cap a returned-payment fee in a residential lease, but you may charge one only if the lease states it and your listing described it. title: Applying Rent Payments in New Mexico
bodyText: Unless you and the tenant agree in writing, you may not apply a rent payment to deposits or damages. title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts in New Mexico

title: New Mexico Security Deposit Limits
bodyText: A deposit must be reasonable. If the lease runs less than one year (including a month-to-month tenancy), the deposit may not exceed one month's rent. Under an annual lease, a deposit larger than one month's rent is allowed, but you must pay the tenant interest on it every year, and that larger deposit may not be treated as prepaid rent. A refundable pet deposit counts toward these limits; last month's rent paid in advance under the lease does not.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-18(A): 'An owner is permitted to demand from the resident a reasonable deposit to be applied by the owner to recover damages, if any, caused to the premises by the resident during his term of residency. (1) Under the terms of an annual rental agreement, if the owner demands or receives of the resident such a deposit in an amount greater than one month's rent, the owner shall be required to pay to the resident annually an interest ... (2) Under the terms of a rental agreement of a duration less than one year, an owner shall not demand or receive from the resident such a deposit in an amount in excess of one month's rent.' NMSA 1978, § 47-8-18(B): the section does not include 'the last month's prepaid rent, which may be required by the rental agreement', and a deposit 'shall not be construed as prepaid rent'. title: Penalties for Mishandling a Deposit in New Mexico
bodyText: If you do not give the tenant an itemized written list of deductions and the balance due within 30 days, you lose the right to keep any part of the deposit, the right to counterclaim in the tenant's suit for it, and the right to sue separately for damage to the property, and you must pay the tenant's court costs and reasonable attorney fees. If you do send a timely list, a 2025 Court of Appeals decision held that a landlord who complied could still bring a claim for damage not included on the list.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold in New Mexico
bodyText: When you sell or otherwise transfer the property, the new owner becomes liable for all obligations under the lease and the act, including the deposit. You are relieved of liability only for events after you give the tenant written notice that your interest has ended, unless the lease says otherwise. After receiving that notice, the tenant pays rent to the new owner.

The successor in interest to the owner shall be liable for all obligations under the rental agreement or under the [act]. Upon receipt by the resident of written notice ..., the resident shall pay all future rental payments, when due, to the successor in interest'; (B): a manager is relieved after written notice of the end of management. title: Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico landlords must substantially comply with minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety; make repairs and keep the premises safe; keep common areas safe; keep supplied electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances in good and safe working order; provide garbage receptacles and arrange removal; and supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat (unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or heat or hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control supplied by a direct utility connection). A lease cannot waive these duties. Only for a single family residence may the lease itself shift garbage, water and heat duties and specified repairs to the tenant; for other units, specified repairs or maintenance tasks may be shifted only by a separate signed writing supported by consideration.

title: Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico
bodyText: If you fail to meet your repair duties, the tenant must give you written notice. For a material breach of the lease, or a violation of the act materially affecting health and safety, the tenant may give notice that the lease ends in at least 7 days unless you make a reasonable attempt to fix it. Or, if you do not fix a covered condition within 7 days of written notice, the tenant may withhold one-third of the daily rent from the notice date until it is fixed, or all of the rent if the home is uninhabitable and the tenant does not live there. The tenant may also sue for damages. These remedies do not apply to conditions the tenant or the tenant's household or guests caused, or to amenities. New Mexico does not let tenants repair and deduct.

title: Entry Rules in New Mexico
bodyText: The tenant must consent to entry to inspect, repair, supply services or show the unit, but you must first give 24 hours' written notice stating the purpose, the date and a reasonable estimate of the time frame. A written notice to a tenant must be hand-delivered or mailed (or posted and also mailed or hand-delivered). No notice is needed to make repairs within 7 days of the tenant's request or when accompanied by an inspector or utility or cable representative. Try to accommodate a tenant's reasonable request for another time. You may enter without consent in an emergency, after abandonment or surrender, or at reasonably necessary times during an absence of more than 7 days. A tenant who refuses lawful access can be made to allow it or have the lease terminated, with damages and fees; abusive or unlawful entry gives the tenant the same remedies. The statute lets the lease set different entry terms, but the library keeps the statutory notice; take advice before changing it.

title: Three-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: If rent is unpaid when due, you may give the tenant written notice of nonpayment and of your intention to terminate. If the tenant does not pay within 3 days after the notice, you may terminate and seek possession; but if the tenant tenders the full amount due, in the way the notice states, before the 3 days run out, you cannot sue for that nonpayment. A 2023 Court of Appeals decision held that the petition may be filed no earlier than the day after the third day. The notice is effective only if hand-delivered, mailed, or posted on an exterior door, and must show the posting date. If the last day falls on a weekend or federal holiday, the period runs to the next day that is not a weekend or federal holiday. The Supreme Court's Form 4-901 is the standard notice.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-33(D): 'If rent is unpaid when due and the resident fails to pay rent within three days after written notice from the owner of nonpayment and his intention to terminate the rental agreement, the owner may terminate the rental agreement and the resident shall immediately deliver possession of the dwelling unit; provided that tender of the full amount due, in the manner stated in the notice, prior to the expiration of the three-day notice shall bar any action for nonpayment of rent.' NMSA 1978, § 47-8-33(H) (weekend or federal holiday extension of the remedy period). NMSA 1978, § 47-8-13(D) (service by hand delivery, mail or posting on an exterior door; date of posting stated and is the effective date; posting by taping all sides or in a receptacle). A petition filed on the third day was premature: the owner may file only on the day following the third day (Cheng v. Rabey, 2023-NMCA-013, as summarized in the compilation's annotation to NMSA 1978, § 47-8-33; opinion not read, NM log §1.4). Form 4-901 NMRA (as amended by Supreme Court Order No. 20-8300-018, effective December 31, 2020) tells the resident they cannot be evicted without a court order and states the accepted payment methods. title: Seven-Day Notice for Other Lease Breaches
bodyText: For a first material breach other than rent (or a breach of the tenant's statutory duties materially affecting health and safety), give written notice describing the breach, with dates and specific facts, stating that the lease will end on a date at least 7 days after the tenant receives it unless the breach is remedied in 7 days, and stating that the lease will end on a second material breach within 6 months. Give it within 30 days of the breach or of learning of it. For a second material breach within 6 months, give a written notice with the same detail stating that the lease will end at least 7 days after receipt; no cure is allowed. A court can grant relief only on the grounds stated in the notice.

title: Three-Day Notice for a Substantial Violation
bodyText: If a tenant knowingly commits, or consents to another person in the unit or on the premises knowingly committing, a 'substantial violation', you may give a written notice specifying the time, place and nature of the act and stating that the lease will end at least 3 days after receipt. Only the conduct listed in the statute counts: controlled-substance offenses other than misdemeanor possession and use; unlawful use of a deadly weapon; unlawful action causing serious physical harm; sexual assault or molestation; entering another's home or vehicle to commit theft or assault; theft by force or threat of force; and intentional or reckless property damage over $1,000, in the unit, on the premises or within 300 feet. The tenant has defenses for domestic violence victims, for lack of knowledge, and for reasonable self-defense, and a frivolous or bad-faith action costs the landlord two times the monthly rent plus damages and costs.

title: Domestic Violence and Substantial-Violation Evictions
bodyText: In an eviction based on a substantial violation, it is a defense that the tenant is a victim of domestic violence. If the tenant has filed for or obtained a temporary domestic violence restraining order because of the incident behind the notice, or an earlier incident, the court may not issue a writ of restitution. In other cases where domestic violence is raised, the court has discretion to evict only the resident accused while letting the other residents' tenancy continue.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no just-cause or good-cause eviction statute: a fixed term ends on its end date, and a periodic tenancy can be ended by the required written notice without stating a reason. Limits still apply: you may not end a tenancy, raise rent or cut services in retaliation for protected tenant activity within the last 6 months; a condominium conversion requires 60 days' notice and an offer to sell the unit to the tenant; a lease term letting a converting declarant end the lease early is unenforceable; and terminations for breach must follow the statutory notices.

title: When a Fixed-Term Lease Ends in New Mexico
bodyText: A New Mexico fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term. If the tenant stays without your consent after the term expires, you may bring an action for possession; no statute requires a notice to end a fixed term, but giving written notice that you will not renew avoids disputes. If you consent to the tenant staying, the tenancy becomes month-to-month (week-to-week if rent is paid weekly), which then needs 30 days' (or 7 days') written notice to end. Rent and fee increases for the next term need notice before the term ends.

title: Holdover Tenants in New Mexico
bodyText: If a tenant stays after the lease ends without your consent, you may bring an action for possession. Only if the holdover is willful and not in good faith may you also recover the damages you suffer and reasonable attorney fees. If you consent to the tenant staying, the tenancy continues month to month (week to week for weekly rent). If the tenant appeals an eviction judgment, the writ is stayed only if the tenant pays the rent into escrow or to you within 5 days of the appeal and keeps paying monthly.

title: Stipulated Holdover Rates in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico sets a damages measure only for a willful, bad-faith holdover (actual damages and attorney fees). A lease may fix a daily rate for holding over, and the library's holdover clause sets it at the Monthly Rent apportioned daily. A higher stipulated rate, such as one and a half or double rent, is not offered: a court may refuse to enforce a term it finds inequitable or a penalty. If you want one, take advice first.

title: Abandonment and Re-renting in New Mexico
bodyText: A tenant has 'abandoned' the unit only if absent, without notice to you, for more than 7 continuous days after rent became delinquent. Then you may take possession immediately, must store the tenant's property as the law requires, and may make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental; if you re-rent for a term starting before the lease would have ended, the lease ends when the new tenancy begins. Any party claiming damages must mitigate them.

The owner shall, in such cases, be responsible for the removing and storing of the personal property ... Upon abandonment, the owner may make reasonable efforts to rent the dwelling unit and premises at a fair rental. If the owner rents the dwelling unit for a term beginning prior to the expiration of the rental agreement, it is deemed to be terminated as of the date the new tenancy begins'); NMSA 1978, § 47-8-6(A) ('The aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages'). title: Property Left After an Eviction in New Mexico
bodyText: After a writ of restitution is executed, you have no obligation to store property left more than 3 days, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise, and may then dispose of it in any manner. Within those 3 days the tenant has a right to a reasonable opportunity to recover it, on paying reasonable moving and storage fees if you require them. You may not hold the tenant's property for other debts, and New Mexico gives landlords no lien on a residential tenant's belongings.

title: Fire or Casualty Damage in New Mexico
bodyText: If fire or another casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the home, the tenant may move out and give written notice within 7 days ending the lease as of the move-out date, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stop using the unusable part and pay rent reduced by the lost rental value. If the lease ends, you must return the balance of prepaid rent and the deposit as the deposit law provides. The tenant remains responsible for damage caused by the tenant's negligence. The statute gives the landlord no termination right; an optional lease clause can add a narrow one.

title: Damage a Tenant Causes in New Mexico
bodyText: A tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises, and a tenant who intentionally damages the premises is liable for two times the monthly rent; you may also recover damages for the tenant's noncompliance (whether both may be recovered for the same damage is not settled here). When the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused a condition, the tenant cannot use it to end the lease or withhold rent under the repair remedies. But after a fire or casualty the tenant may still end the lease or reduce the rent even if the tenant was negligent, while remaining liable for the damage. A lease cannot take that casualty right away.

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited in New Mexico
bodyText: You may not raise rent, decrease services, or bring or threaten an eviction because, within the previous 6 months, a tenant who is in compliance with the lease complained to a housing-code agency, joined or organized a tenants' union, exercised rights under the act in good faith (including a written repair request), filed a fair housing complaint, won or has pending a lawsuit against you about the tenancy, testified for another tenant, or lawfully abated rent. A violation makes you liable for two times the monthly rent and other remedies, and is a defense to eviction. Increases or service changes that are uniform for similar units and given with proper notice at the end of the term are allowed, and you may still evict for nonpayment, material noncompliance, a substantial violation or a code violation the tenant caused.

title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico
bodyText: Except after abandonment or surrender, you may not exclude or remove a tenant without a court order by fraud, changing or adding locks, blocking an entrance, interfering with utilities or services, removing the tenant's belongings, removing appliances or fixtures (except for legitimate repairs), or making the unit inaccessible or uninhabitable. A judgment for possession is not a court order permitting a utility shutoff before the writ is executed. You need not pay a tenant's own utility bills, but you may not direct a utility to cut service. The tenant may abate all rent for each affected day, recover two times the monthly rent and damages, and regain possession or end the lease.

title: How Evictions Work in New Mexico
bodyText: After the required notice expires, an owner files a petition for restitution in magistrate or metropolitan court (a metropolitan court has the magistrate courts' jurisdiction) or district court, stating the facts, describing the premises and showing the notice was given. Trial is set 7 to 10 days after the summons is served, and the court may continue it up to 7 days for good cause. If the owner wins, the court issues a writ directing the sheriff to restore possession on a date 3 to 7 days after judgment. An owner or the property manager may appear without a lawyer in magistrate and metropolitan court. The Supreme Court's eviction prevention and diversion program was withdrawn for new cases in January 2023, but some of its forms remain in the rules.

title: Removing Unauthorized Occupants in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no special squatter-removal statute. A person who entered and occupied property without the owner's consent and refused to leave after notice can be removed by a forcible entry or unlawful detainer action, and knowingly remaining on property after consent is denied can be criminal trespass. Anyone who is a resident under a rental agreement, including an occupant the tenant allowed in, must be removed through the act's notice and court process, never by lockout.

title: When a Tenant Dies in New Mexico
bodyText: If a tenant who is the sole occupant dies, you must turn the property in the home over to the tenant's named contact person, or another person lawfully entitled, if they ask before it is discarded, and refund the deposit less lawful deductions (including removal and storage costs). You may remove and store the property, require an inventory signature, and discard it only after a certified-mail request to the contact person and 30 days without removal or any claim. If you asked in writing for a contact person and the tenant gave none, you have no responsibility for the property. The death does not end the lease by statute. A lease may set a different procedure, but the library uses the statutory one; take advice before changing it.

title: Sale of the Property or a New Manager in New Mexico
bodyText: When the property is sold or management changes, give the tenant written notice and keep the required owner and manager disclosures current; they bind any successor owner or manager. title: Prohibited Lease Terms in New Mexico
bodyText: A New Mexico lease may not make the tenant (or the landlord) waive or give up rights or remedies under the law, so 'landlord is not liable' clauses, waivers of notice and similar terms are void. A landlord who deliberately uses a lease containing terms known to be prohibited owes the tenant the resulting damages and reasonable attorney fees. A confession-of-judgment clause signed before a claim arises is void, there is no landlord's lien on a tenant's belongings, and a court may limit any term it finds was inequitable when made.

title: Attorney Fees in New Mexico Landlord-Tenant Cases
bodyText: In a suit by an applicant or a party to enforce the lease or the Owner-Resident Relations Act, the winning side is entitled to reasonable attorney fees and court costs. Fees also follow from specific violations, such as failing to return a deposit properly, a willful holdover, refusing or abusing access, a bad-faith counterclaim, or knowingly using prohibited lease terms. A lease may provide for prevailing-party fees, which matches the statute.

title: What the New Mexico Owner-Resident Act Covers
bodyText: The Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act governs rental agreements for dwelling units in New Mexico, wherever the agreement was made. It does not apply, unless an arrangement was created to avoid it, to residence at an institution incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, counseling, religious or educational services; occupancy under a contract of sale by the purchaser; fraternal or social organization housing; transient occupancy in a hotel or motel; employee housing under a written agreement conditioning occupancy on employment; or agricultural rentals. title: How to Serve Notices in New Mexico
bodyText: A notice of nonpayment of rent is effective only if handed to the tenant, mailed, or posted on an exterior door of the unit. Any other written notice to a tenant may be posted only if it is also mailed first class or handed to the tenant. Every notice must state the posting date, which is its effective date; a posted notice must be taped on all sides or placed in a mail or notice receptacle. If a mailed notice comes back or the tenant's last known address is the vacated unit, serve one more notice at any other address the tenant gave you. E-mail does not replace these methods: New Mexico's electronic transactions law does not apply to default, eviction or right-to-cure notices for a primary residence.
notes: NM: NMSA 1978, § 47-8-13(A)-(F); NMSA 1978, § 14-16-3(B)(2)(b); NMSA 1978, §§ 14-16-5(b)-(c), 14-16-8(b)-(d). If the owner fails to give the NMSA 1978, § 47-8-19 disclosure, the resident is relieved of the obligation to give the owner notice (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-19(D)). title: Fair Housing Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act
bodyText: The New Mexico Human Rights Act bars refusing to rent, discriminating in rental terms, conditions, privileges or services, and advertising or inquiring in a way that shows a preference, because of race, religion, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, sexual orientation, gender, gender identity, pregnancy, childbirth or a related condition, spousal affiliation, physical or mental disability, or military status. The Act does not list familial status or age for housing; the federal Fair Housing Act protects families with children. Narrow exemptions cover some single-family homes rented by an owner of no more than three without discriminatory advertising, owner-occupied buildings of up to four units, and some religious organizations.

bodyText: Treat a request to keep an assistance animal for a disability as a reasonable-accommodation request under fair housing law; do not charge pet fees for it. title: Cannabis in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: Adults 21 and older may lawfully use and grow limited amounts of cannabis at home in New Mexico (up to six mature and six immature plants per person, and no more than twelve mature plants per household). The act does not restrict a person's ability to prohibit cannabis conduct on the person's privately owned property, which the library reads as letting a rental owner ban it in the lease. title: No Statute Treating Fees as Rent
bodyText: No Kansas statute says whether a late fee, a utility charge or any other fee counts as rent, so the lease decides, and the courts decide what the lease means. That matters because Kansas's three-day pay-or-quit notice runs on unpaid rent (K.S.A. 58-2564(b)): calling fees 'additional rent' is how some leases try to reach them, and an eviction resting on unpaid fees rather than unpaid rent is untested in Kansas. This library's clauses do not label fees as rent, and the Tenant Default clause says plainly that failing to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the rent itself, is not by itself a ground to terminate or evict.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: No Kansas statute gives a residential tenant a covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment. Kansas's one statutory use of the phrase runs the other way: K.S.A. 58-2555 makes it the tenant's duty not to engage in, or allow any person or pet on the premises to engage in, conduct that will disturb the quiet and peaceful enjoyment of the premises by other tenants. So the statutory right belongs to the neighbours, not to the tenant complaining about you. A tenant's protection against your interference comes instead from the habitability duty (K.S.A. 58-2553), the lockout and utility-shutoff remedy (K.S.A. 58-2563), the entry limits (K.S.A. 58-2557) and Kansas common law, not from a statutory covenant.

title: No Statutory Right to Cure a Tenant's Breach and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Kansas gives you no statute letting you fix a tenant's breach — damage, a maintenance failure, an unremoved hazard — and add the cost to the next month's rent as rent. Several URLTA states have that right; Kansas did not adopt it. What you have instead is the notice-and-cure route in K.S.A. 58-2564(a), your claim for actual damages under K.S.A. 58-2568, and the security deposit under K.S.A. 58-2550. The practical difference matters: a cost you bill as rent can support a three-day pay-or-quit notice, while the same cost as damages cannot, so doing the work yourself and charging it does not give you an eviction route for nonpayment.

NAMING TRAP: the one hit in Article 25's range is K.S.A. 58-2531, in the pre-1975 block, which is a preamble about FARM land leases adding unpaid taxes to money rent — not a residential self-cure right, and deprioritized by product decision. title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Kansas has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in before signing, and no statute making a blank a breach or a deceptive practice. Fill them in anyway. Two Kansas rules bite on an incomplete lease from different directions: a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease or term (K.S.A. 58-2544), and where a lease is never signed and delivered but the parties act on it, K.S.A. 58-2546 gives it effect for no longer than one year whatever term the document states. A blank left for later also invites the K.S.A. 58-2570(e) problem, where a document you hand the tenant to sign adds terms the lease does not contain.

title: The One Form of Words Kansas Puts in Your Hands
bodyText: Kansas prescribes one piece of verbatim text a landlord may have to use, and it is not in the lease. Under K.S.A. 58-2570(e), if you give a tenant a document which, signed, would be the tenant's written notice that they intend to vacate, and that document contains any additional terms not contained in the rental agreement, the document must include this statement in no less than ten-point boldface type: 'YOUR SIGNATURE ON THIS DOCUMENT MAY BIND YOU TO ADDITIONAL TERMS NOT IN YOUR ORIGINAL LEASE AGREEMENT. IF YOUR LEASE REQUIRES YOU TO GIVE WRITTEN NOTICE OF YOUR INTENT TO VACATE, YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO DECLINE TO SIGN THIS DOCUMENT AND TO PROVIDE WRITTEN NOTICE IN ANOTHER FORM.' Leave it out and the tenant's signature does not bind them to any of those additional terms. The way to avoid the problem is to put your move-out terms in the lease itself, because then they are not additional terms and no statement is needed. Kansas supplies no statutory lease form, no notice-to-quit form and no deposit-accounting form; the three-day notice content comes from K.S.A. 61-3803 and 58-2564(b), not from a form.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: No Kansas statute says whether a tenant may install a security camera or a video doorbell, so the lease controls, including its alterations terms where mounting hardware is involved. Two Kansas points are worth knowing. A device that records sound is a different question from one that only records pictures, and Kansas's eavesdropping statute reaches recording a private conversation without the consent of a party to it, so a doorbell capturing audio in a shared hallway or a neighbour's doorway can raise an issue a video-only device does not. And nothing here limits your own entry rules: you still owe reasonable notice at reasonable hours under K.S.A. 58-2557, and a tenant's camera does not change that.

title: Landlord Termination After Fire or Casualty
bodyText: [Optional.] If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty to an extent that the use and habitability of the property is substantially impaired, and the fire or casualty was not caused by Landlord's deliberate or negligent act, Landlord may terminate this Lease by written notice to Tenant, effective on the date stated in the notice or, if Tenant has already vacated, on the date Tenant vacated. Rent will be accounted for as of the date Tenant vacates all or part of the property, and Landlord will return the portion of the Security Deposit Tenant is entitled to under Kansas law. Landlord may recover possession only as Kansas law permits. This Section is in addition to the rights Kansas law gives Tenant after a fire or casualty and does not reduce or condition them.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: [Optional.] If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, Tenant is liable to Landlord for Landlord's actual damages. Those damages include the cost of repairing the damage and, to the extent Kansas law allows, the Rent Landlord loses while the property is being repaired and after this Lease ends, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair the property and to re-rent it. Nothing in this Section reduces, conditions or waives any right Kansas law gives Tenant after a fire or casualty, including the right to vacate and terminate or to have Rent reduced for a part of the property rendered unusable, and Tenant's liability under this Section is separate from and additional to those rights.

THE FINDING, from reading each abatement and exit provision separately for its own tenant-fault exception: K.S.A. 58-2559(a)(2) HAS one — a tenant 'may not terminate for a condition caused by an act or omission of, or which is or can be properly attributable or applicable to, the tenant or any person or animal or pet on the premises at any time with the tenant's express or implied permission or consent' — but K.S.A. 58-2562, the fire-and-casualty section, HAS NONE. Neither its immediate-vacate termination in (a)(1) nor its proportional rent reduction in (a)(2) is conditioned on the casualty not being the tenant's fault. So in Kansas a tenant whose own negligence starts the fire can still terminate, and can still have rent reduced for the unusable part.
