title: Use of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant will pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit) before occupancy. Under Montana law, any deposit Tenant must provide or keep in effect for part or all of the Term, and any fee or charge for cleaning and damages however it is named, is a security deposit. Landlord may deduct from the Security Deposit only: the damage Landlord shows was caused by Tenant or Tenant's family, licensees or invitees; unpaid Rent, late charges, utilities, penalties due under this Lease and other money Tenant owes Landlord at the time of the deduction; and actual cleaning expenses, including a reasonable charge for Landlord's labor, for cleaning needed to bring the property back to its condition at the start of the tenancy, beyond normal wear. Before deducting any cleaning charge, Landlord will give Tenant written notice of the cleaning Tenant has not done and the additional amount and type of cleaning needed to bring the property back to its condition at the start of the tenancy, and Tenant will have 24 hours after the notice is delivered to complete it, except where applicable law excuses the notice (for example, if Tenant vacates without notifying Landlord). Landlord notes that it performs the following normal maintenance on a cyclical basis: [list, e.g. carpet cleaning or repainting at set intervals, or state none]; Landlord will not impose cleaning charges for that maintenance unless Landlord must perform it because of Tenant's negligence. At the request of either party, the property may be inspected within 1 week before the tenancy ends. The Security Deposit does not relieve Tenant of the obligation to pay Rent when due.
notes: MT: Replaces the base `security-deposit-use`, which lets Landlord apply the deposit to cleaning costs without the written notice and 24-hour opportunity Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-201(3) requires before a cleaning charge is deducted (rule 53: a fee clause is checked for a statutory notice step as well as its figure). Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-101(4): 'If a leasehold agreement or an agreement incident to a leasehold agreement requires the tenant or prospective tenant to provide or maintain in effect any deposit to the landlord for part or all of the term of the leasehold agreement, the deposit must be presumed to be a security deposit. A fee or charge for cleaning and damages, no matter how designated, is presumed to be a security deposit.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-201(1): the landlord 'may deduct from the security deposit a sum equal to the damage alleged to have been caused by the tenant, together with a sum equal to the unpaid rent, late charges, utilities, penalties due under lease provisions, and other money owing to the landlord at the time of deduction, including rent owed under 70-24-441(3), and a sum for actual cleaning expenses, including a reasonable charge for the landlord's labor'; Mont. title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: When this tenancy ends, Tenant will give Landlord a forwarding address in writing. Within 30 days after this tenancy terminates, or after Tenant surrenders the property and Landlord accepts the surrender, whichever happens first, Landlord will give Tenant a written list of any Rent due and any damage and cleaning charges Landlord claims are Tenant's responsibility, together with payment of the balance of the Security Deposit, if any. If, after inspection, there is no damage, no cleaning is required, no Rent is unpaid and Tenant shows that no utilities are unpaid, Landlord will return the Security Deposit within 10 days. Landlord may make the refund by electronic funds transfer, cash, check or another form of payment, or by mailing it to the forwarding address Tenant provides or, if none is provided, to Tenant's last known address, and will deliver the written list by a method applicable law allows for notices. These time limits do not apply if this Lease has terminated, Landlord has brought an action for possession, and Landlord has a pending claim for actual damages filed in court.
notes: MT: Replaces the blank-states parent `security-deposit-return` (rule 25 family). rule_type is RECOMMENDED: Montana requires the list and refund but no lease text about them (rule 56). Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-202(1)(a)(i): 'Each landlord, within 30 days subsequent to the termination of a tenancy or within 30 days subsequent to a surrender and acceptance of the leasehold premises, whichever occurs first, shall provide the departing tenant with a written list of any rent due and any damage and cleaning charges, brought after the provisions of 70-25-201 have been followed ... Delivery of the list must be accompanied by payment of the difference, if any, between the security deposit and the permitted charges set forth in 70-25-201.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-202(1)(a)(ii) and (b)(ii): refund 'by different forms of payment that include electronic fund transfers, cash, check, or other forms of refund, or by mailing the security deposit to the new address provided by the tenant or, if a new address is not provided, to the tenant's last-known address'; the list must be noticed under Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-108. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-202(1)(b)(i): no damage, cleaning, unpaid rent or unpaid utilities: return 'within 10 days'. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-202(1)(c): mailing to the last-known address of a tenant who gave no new address is not a wrongful withholding, but the landlord remains liable for the amount. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-202(2): 'This section does not apply if a rental agreement is terminated pursuant to 70-24-427 or 70-33-427 and the landlord has a pending claim filed in court.' The enrolled text of 2025 Mont. Laws ch. 656, § 2 as extracted (pdf.js drops strike-through) reads 'a pending claim for actual damages filed in court'; the compiled 2025 code omits 'for actual damages', consistent with those words being struck (the same extraction runs struck and new words together in Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-202(1)(a)(ii)); not confirmed from the PDF's drawing marks (MT log §1.2, weaker method). The clause uses the narrower 'claim for actual damages', so it never excuses the deadlines where the compiled text would not (flagged for the legal watch, MT log §10). Consequences: forfeiture of the right to withhold for damage or cleaning (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-203); liability for the sum wrongfully withheld and discretionary attorney fees (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-204(1)); `edu-deposit-penalty-mt`. A tenant's failure to give a new address does not bar recovery (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-205). Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-202 was amended by 2025 Mont. Laws ch. 656, § 2 (effective May 12, 2025, MT log §1.2). title: Existing Condition of Property
bodyText: When this Lease was signed, Landlord gave Tenant a separate written statement, signed by Landlord, of the present condition of the property (Condition Statement). Tenant has examined the property and agrees that, except as noted in the Condition Statement, it is in the condition the Condition Statement describes (Existing Condition). Landlord will deliver possession of the property to Tenant on the Start Date in the same or better condition as the Existing Condition, except for ordinary wear and tear. At Tenant's written request, Landlord will give Tenant a copy of the written list of damage and cleaning charges, if any, given to the previous tenant of the property.
notes: MT: Replaces the base `existing-condition`, whose acknowledgment that the property is 'in good order and repair' would stand in for the separate condition statement Montana requires of every landlord who takes a security deposit (rule 48: no lease clause can supply a separate document). Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-206(1): 'Any person engaged in the rental of property for residential purposes who requires a security deposit shall furnish to each tenant, in conjunction with execution of a lease or creation of a tenancy, a separate written statement as to the present condition of the premises intended to be let. At the written request of the tenant, a copy of the written list of damage and cleaning charges, if any, provided to the tenant of the immediately preceding leasehold agreement for the premises in question must be provided to the tenant.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-206(2): the statement must contain 'a clear and concise statement of the present condition of the premises known to the landlord or the landlord's agent or which should have been known upon reasonable inspection', a statement that the premises have never been let if so, and the signature of the landlord or agent. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-206(3): without the statement (and, on written request, the prior tenant's list), the landlord 'is barred from recovering any sum for damage to or cleaning of the leasehold premises unless the person can establish by clear and convincing evidence' that the damage occurred during the tenancy and was caused by the tenant or the tenant's family, licensees or invitees. The clause records delivery of the statement; the statement itself is a separate document (`edu-condition-statement-mt`; layout table, MT log §4). title: Landlord's Entry
bodyText: Tenant will not unreasonably withhold consent to Landlord or Landlord's agent entering the property to inspect it, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or show it to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors. Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable to do so, Landlord will give Tenant at least 24 hours' notice of Landlord's intent to enter and will enter only at reasonable times; Landlord may give that notice by any method this Lease's notice terms allow or by conspicuously posting it on the main entry door of the property. Landlord may also enter without Tenant's consent in an emergency, under a court order, during any absence of Tenant of more than 7 days at times reasonably necessary, to do work applicable law allows Landlord to do after Tenant fails to maintain the property, and when Tenant has abandoned or surrendered the property. Landlord will not abuse this right of access or use it to harass Tenant. Tenant will not remove a lock or replace or add a lock not supplied by Landlord without Landlord's written permission, and if Tenant does, Tenant will give Landlord a key.
notes: MT: Replaces the base `landlords-access`, whose 'during normal business hours' and maintenance-and-showing purposes do not track Montana's statutory purposes and its exclusive list of other access rights (rule 53). Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-312(1): 'A tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to the landlord or the landlord's agent to enter into the dwelling unit in order to inspect the premises, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers, or contractors.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-312(2): entry without consent in an emergency. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-312(3)(a): 'A landlord may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant. Except in the case of an emergency or unless it is impracticable to do so, the landlord shall give the tenant at least 24 hours' notice of the intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-312(3)(b): posting on the main entry door is notice, in addition to Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-108. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-312(4): 'A landlord has no other right of access except: (a) pursuant to court order; (b) as permitted by 70-24-425 and 70-24-426(2); or (c) when the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises.' (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-425: entry to remedy the tenant's health-and-safety noncompliance after 14 days' notice; Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-426(2): entry during an absence over 7 days at times reasonably necessary.) Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-312(5): no lock removal, replacement or addition without written permission; a tenant who does so must provide a key. Remedies: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-424 (refused access or a lock without a key: 24-hour notice to correct, then a 3-day notice to terminate; amended by 2023 Mont. Laws ch. 715) and Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-410 (tenant's remedies for unlawful or harassing entry). The Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-312(4) list is exclusive, so the clause adds no access right beyond it (MT battery 136 (landlord access / entry notice): 18 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 0 synthetic)). title: Early Termination
bodyText: Tenant may end this Lease before the end of the Term by giving Landlord at least 30 days' written notice and paying Landlord, on or before the termination date stated in the notice, an early termination fee of [state the fee, not more than one month's Rent]. Tenant remains responsible for Rent and other obligations up to the termination date stated in the notice. If Tenant ends this Lease early without using this option, Landlord may recover the damages applicable law allows, including Rent until a new tenancy of the property begins or the Term ends, whichever comes first, and Landlord will make reasonable efforts to re-rent the property at a fair rental. This early-termination option and fee apply only if this Lease has a fixed Term; a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy ends on the notice applicable law and this Lease provide, without an early termination fee. Landlord may end this Lease early only under this Lease's Default by Tenant provisions and applicable law. Nothing in this Section limits any right either party has under applicable law, including a servicemember's right to end this Lease after being ordered to a new permanent duty station without paying an early termination fee or other damages, or Tenant's right to end this Lease because the property has become uninhabitable through no fault of Tenant.
notes: MT: Replaces `early-termination-ks`, whose fee ('one month's Rent ... or 30% of the remaining Rent due under the Term, whichever is greater') can exceed Montana's cap, and whose landlord limb ends the lease if Tenant 'vacates or abandons the property without notifying Landlord' (rules 37, 53). The base `early-termination` has the same fee and a 10-day cure promise for any breach (rule 43). Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-201(2)(f), as amended by 2021 Mont. Laws ch. 536, § 3: 'if either party terminates the rental agreement without cause prior to the expiration date of the lease term, the aggrieved party is entitled to monetary damages up to 1 month's rent or an amount that is agreed on in the rental agreement, which may not exceed 1 month's rent. Landlords shall follow 70-24-426(3) and are entitled to rent from defaulting tenants up to the date a new tenancy starts or the date the rental agreement term expires.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-426(3): the landlord 'shall make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental'. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-422(6): 'Treble damages may not be recovered for the tenant's early termination of the tenancy.' Servicemembers: Mont. Code Ann. § 10-1-905(1), (3), (4) (a 'service member on active duty' ordered to a permanent duty station more than 60 miles away; written notice with a copy of the orders; effective 45 days after delivery; 'not liable for early termination fees or other damages arising from early termination'); in that part 'service member' means a member of the Montana army or air national guard serving on active duty (Mont. Code Ann. § 10-1-902(1), (5)); the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act was not read (MT log §1.4); `edu-servicemember-mt`. Uninhabitable premises: Mont. Code Ann. §§ 70-24-406, 70-24-409. The option is drafted so that the agreed fee (the 'amount that is agreed on in the rental agreement') and Rent to the notice's termination date are all a tenant who uses it owes; the rent-until-re-let recovery is reserved for a tenant who leaves without using the option, because Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-201(2)(f)'s second sentence speaks of 'defaulting tenants' and a court could read the first sentence as capping recovery at one month's rent where the option is used (Claude's drafting call, rule 76, MT log §6.3; independent check round 1; no Montana case construing the two sentences was found, web search, MT log §1.4). The fee is the landlord's own figure, entered by hand, not more than one month's Rent (MT battery 135 (early termination damages / without cause before expiration): 6 hits, control 0; known positives passed (3 real sections, 0 synthetic)). title: Holdover
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession without Landlord's consent after this Lease ends, whether at the end of the Term or after a termination, Landlord may bring an action for possession. Tenant will pay Rent for each day Tenant remains in possession, at the Monthly Rent apportioned daily. Where applicable law allows, Landlord may also recover more: for example, if Landlord ends a month-to-month tenancy without cause by a lawful 30-day notice and Tenant remains after the termination date, or if Landlord ends a tenancy longer than month-to-month for cause and Tenant's holdover is purposeful and not in good faith, Landlord may recover an amount not more than three months' periodic rent or treble damages, whichever is greater. If Landlord consents to Tenant's continued occupancy, the tenancy continues from week to week if Tenant is a roomer who pays Rent weekly and otherwise from month to month, on the terms of this Lease.
notes: MT: Replaces the base `holdover`, which claims 'holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' for every day after the Term ends, a ceiling-only figure (rule 53); Montana's enhanced measure applies only in two cases. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-429(1): action for possession if the tenant remains without consent after expiration or termination. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-429(2): 'If the term is longer than month-to-month and the landlord terminates the rental agreement with cause and the tenant's holdover is purposeful and not in good faith, the landlord may recover an amount not more than 3 months' periodic rent or treble damages, whichever is greater.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-429(3): 'If the term of the rental is month-to-month and the landlord terminates the rental agreement without cause and issues a lawful 30-day notice and the tenant remains in the rental unit after the termination date, then the holdover is purposeful and the landlord may recover an amount not more than 3 months' periodic rent or treble damages, whichever is greater.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-429(5): if the landlord consents to continued occupancy, Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-201(2)(e) applies (week to week for a roomer who pays weekly, otherwise month to month). Rent is uniformly apportionable from day to day (Mont. Code Ann. §§ 70-24-201(2)(d), 70-24-441(3)). The daily-rent sentence states the rental value Tenant already owes, not a premium; a stipulated premium rate is declined (`edu-holdover-rate-mt`; Mont. Code Ann. § 28-2-721). The general treble-rent holdover statutes (Mont. Code Ann. §§ 70-27-207, 70-27-208) do not apply to ch. 24 tenancies except for forcible entry and detainer (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-27-101(1)). Answer time in a holdover action: 5 business days (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-429(4), amended by 2023 Mont. Laws ch. 715) (MT battery 98 (holdover / holding over / treble rent): 13 hits, control 0; known positives passed (2 real sections, 0 synthetic)). title: End of Term and Extension
bodyText: This Lease ends on {{end_date}} unless it is extended as this Section provides. If neither Landlord nor Tenant gives the other written notice of termination at least 30 days before that date, the tenancy will continue after that date on the terms of this Lease [choose one: ☐ on a month-to-month basis; ☐ for a further term of ___ months, and then for further terms of the same length until either party gives the other written notice of termination at least 30 days before the end of a term]. A month-to-month tenancy may be ended by either party by at least 30 days' written notice, as applicable law provides.
notes: MT: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-205: 'If the landlord and tenant fail to establish a default extension period for the lease in the rental agreement and neither party gives a 30-day written notice to the other to terminate the tenancy before the rental agreement's original termination date, the tenancy continues on a month-to-month basis.' The statute lets the rental agreement set a 'default extension period' (rule 50); this clause makes the choice on purpose, with month-to-month (the statutory default) as the first option. A written fixed-term lease therefore does not simply end on its last day unless a party gives the 30-day written notice; `edu-end-of-term-mt`. Month-to-month termination: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-441(2). No Montana statute requires a pre-renewal reminder notice or special formatting for an extension term (MT battery 113 (extension or renewal at end of term / default extension period): 8 hits, control 0; known positives passed (2 real sections, 0 synthetic); layout table, MT log §4). Hand-fill: the extension length; the bracket is not next to a variable (rule 60). title: Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy
bodyText: If this Lease is, or continues as, a month-to-month tenancy, Landlord may end it by written notice given to Tenant at least [state Landlord's notice period: at least 30] days before the termination date stated in the notice, and Tenant may end it by written notice given to Landlord at least 30 days before the termination date stated in the notice. If it is, or continues as, a week-to-week tenancy, Landlord may end it by written notice given at least [state Landlord's notice period: at least 7] days before the termination date stated in the notice, and Tenant may end it by written notice given at least 7 days before that date. The tenancy ends on the date stated in the notice, whether or not that date is the end of a rental period, and Rent is apportioned from day to day. This Section does not limit either party's right to end this Lease earlier where this Lease or applicable law allows it.
notes: MT: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-441(1): 'The landlord or the tenant may terminate a week-to-week tenancy by a written notice given to the other at least 7 days before the termination date specified in the notice.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-441(2): 'The landlord or the tenant may terminate a month-to-month tenancy by giving to the other at any time during the tenancy at least 30 days' notice in writing prior to the date designated in the notice for the termination of the tenancy.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-441(3): 'The tenancy terminates on the date designated and without regard to the expiration of the period for which, by the terms of the tenancy, rents are to be paid. Unless otherwise agreed, rent is uniformly apportionable from day to day.' No reason is required (`edu-for-cause-eviction-mt`). The landlord may choose a longer notice (a floor, rule 53); the tenant's period is the statute's. A landlord who ends a month-to-month tenancy this way and is met by a holdover may recover under Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-429(3) (`holdover-mt`). Written for Montana rather than tagging another state's periodic-tenancy-notice row, whose basis rests on that state's statute (rule 26). title: Handling of Property Left Behind
bodyText: When this Lease ends, Tenant will remove all of Tenant's personal property from the property. Personal property left behind will be handled as follows. (1) If the tenancy ends by court order, the property is considered abandoned and Landlord may dispose of it as the law allows. (2) If the tenancy ends in any other way, Landlord will treat property as abandoned only when Landlord has clear and convincing evidence that Tenant has abandoned all personal property Tenant left at the property and at least 48 hours have passed since Landlord obtained that evidence; Landlord may then remove it and immediately dispose of trash and of any item that is hazardous, perishable or valueless as the law defines those terms (personal photos, jewelry and other small irreplaceable items are not valueless). An item clearly labelled 'rent to own' or 'leased' will be discarded only with the lessor's confirmation that it has no lien, after a reasonable effort to contact the lessor. (3) Landlord will inventory and store, with reasonable care, property Landlord reasonably believes is valuable, and may charge a reasonable storage and labor charge plus the cost of moving it to storage, or the actual charge of a commercial storage company plus that cost. (4) Landlord will then make a reasonable attempt to notify Tenant in writing, by certified mail or with a certificate of mailing to Tenant's last known address, that the property must be removed by a stated time at least 10 days after mailing or it will be disposed of. If Tenant responds in writing by that day that Tenant will remove it, Tenant must do so within 7 days after delivering the response, and must pay the allowed storage costs before removing it. (5) After that, Landlord may sell the property at a public or private sale conducted as the law requires, or destroy or otherwise dispose of property whose value Landlord reasonably believes is less than the cost of storing or selling it. Landlord may deduct from the sale proceeds the reasonable costs of notice, storage, labor and sale and any delinquent Rent or damages owed, and will send Tenant the remainder with an itemized accounting or, if Tenant cannot be found after due diligence, deposit it with the county treasurer. When this Lease terminates, Landlord will also give Tenant a plain-language notification of these terms.
notes: MT: Mirrors Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-430: (1)(a) termination by court order, property 'considered abandoned' and may be disposed of immediately 'as allowed by law'; (1)(b) other terminations: 'clear and convincing evidence that the tenant has abandoned all personal property that the tenant has left on the premises and a period of time of at least 48 hours has elapsed since the landlord obtained that evidence', then immediate removal and disposal of 'any trash or personal property that is hazardous, perishable, or valueless'; (1)(c) items labelled 'rent to own' or 'leased'; (1)(d) definitions ('valueless' excludes 'personal photos, jewelry, or other small items that are irreplaceable'); (2) inventory, safekeeping, reasonable care, storage and labor charges, commercial storage; (3) written notice 'with a certificate of mailing or by certified mail to the last-known address of the tenant, stating that at a specified time, not less than 10 days after mailing the notice, the property will be disposed of if not removed'; (4) sale or disposal; (5) the tenant's written response and 7 days to remove, storage costs payable before removal; (6) liability only for purposeful or negligent loss; (7) sale under Mont. Code Ann. § 30-9A-610 or the sheriff's sale provisions of Title 25, ch. 13, part 7; (8) deductions, remittance with an itemized accounting, county treasurer deposit, reversion after 3 years; (9) 'The landlord shall ensure that the terms of this section are included in plain and understandable language as a notification upon termination of the lease or rental agreement.' The last sentence promises that notification; the clause does not replace it (rule 46; `edu-abandoned-property-notice-mt`). Titled to match `surrender-end-of-term-ks-ne`'s pointer ('Handling of Property Left Behind'). Last amended by 2021 Mont. Laws ch. 536, § 8. title: Tenant Maintenance Agreement
bodyText: [Optional. Under the safest reading of Montana law, this agreement must be a separate writing signed by Landlord and Tenant, not a section of the Lease, and supported by adequate consideration, for every kind of dwelling, including a single-family house.] Landlord and Tenant agree, in good faith and not for the purpose of evading Landlord's obligations, that Tenant will perform the following specified repairs or maintenance tasks: [check each that applies: ☐ lawn and landscaping care, keeping to any irrigation schedule Landlord sets, and promptly reporting irrigation leaks or watering problems; ☐ prompt, reasonable removal of snow and ice from walkways, driveways, porches and entrances that only Tenant uses; ☐ replacing heating and air-conditioning filters; ☐ replacing light bulbs; ☐ taking garbage and recycling to the collection point; ☐ other specified task: ____]. In exchange for these tasks, Tenant will receive the following consideration: [state the consideration, e.g. a Monthly Rent reduction of $__]. This agreement does not make Tenant responsible for any work needed to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, which remains Landlord's responsibility, and it does not diminish Landlord's obligations to any other tenant of the premises.
notes: MT: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-303(4): 'A landlord and tenant may agree that the tenant is to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling only if: (a) the agreement of the parties is entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord and is set forth in a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration; (b) the work is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subsection (1)(a); and (c) the agreement does not diminish the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-303(3) separately allows a written good-faith agreement that the tenant perform the Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-303(1)(e) and (1)(f) duties (garbage receptacles and removal; running water, hot water and heat) and 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alteration, and remodeling'. Unlike the uniform act's split, neither subsection is limited to a single-family residence: every past edition read (1997, 2001, 2007, 2013, 2015, 2017 and 2019, saved as mt-70-24-303-editions.json, MT log §1.1) limited both (3) and (4) to 'a landlord and tenant of a one-, two-, or three-family residence', and the 2023 edition, after the 2021 amendments (2021 Mont. Laws ch. 2, § 10 and 2021 Mont. Laws ch. 536, § 4), has the phrase in neither. Reading Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-303 to give effect to every provision (Mont. Code Ann. § 1-2-101), subsection (4)'s separate-writing condition governs any specified repair or maintenance task in every dwelling, so this is the Oklahoma treatment under rule 48 (subsection (3) alone would allow an in-lease writing for the (1)(e) and (1)(f) duties, and (1)(e) yields to the rental agreement for garbage; the clause follows (4), the stricter subsection, for every task, and the row's instruction says it is the safest reading, independent check round 1): `landscaping-irrigation` and `snow-removal` are not tagged for Montana and this agreement is offered instead (MT log §6.3; Claude's legal call, rule 76; no Montana case reconciling (3) and (4) was found, web search, MT log §1.4). Modeled on `maintenance-allocation-az` and `maintenance-allocation-nm` (rule 48), and like them a LEASE_CLAUSE row whose instruction says it is a separate signed writing; whether the builder prints it as a separate addendum is an app question for Claude Code (rule 10; MT log §10). title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If any check, draft, electronic funds transfer or order for payment Tenant gives Landlord is dishonored for lack of funds or credit or because Tenant does not have an account with the bank, Tenant will pay Landlord a service charge of {{nsf_fee}}, and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. Landlord will demand the service charge in writing, mailed to the address shown on the check or to Tenant's last known address, stating that Tenant must pay the value of the dishonored payment and the service charge, and stating the amount of the service charge. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are dishonored, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check or money order.
notes: MT: Replaces the base `returned-payments`, whose fee is ceiling-only ('not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law', rule 53) and which omits the written demand Montana requires before a service charge is owed (rule 53, NM 4). Mont. Code Ann. § 27-1-717(1)(a), (2): a person who issues a check, draft, converted check, electronic funds transfer or order that is 'dishonored for lack of funds or credit or because the issuer does not have an account with the drawee' is liable 'for a service charge in an amount not greater than $30 ... Demand for the service charge must be made in writing by the payee or the payee's assignee and mailed to the address shown on the check, draft, converted check, or order or to the issuer's last-known address. The demand must state that the issuer is required to pay the value of the check, draft, converted check, electronic funds transfer, or order and service charge and must state the service charge provided for in this section.' Mont. Code Ann. § 27-1-717(3)-(4): civil damages (the service charge plus the greater of $100 or three times the amount, not more than $500 above the value) only after a demand at least 10 days before suit. The landlord's figure {{nsf_fee}} must not exceed $30 (builder cap, MT log §10). A dishonor charge is not a fee 'based on rent payment type' (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-201(4)) (MT battery 20 (dishonored check / service charge): 19 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 1 synthetic)). title: Residential Use Only
bodyText: Tenant will occupy the property only as a dwelling and will not use or permit the use of the property for any illegal purpose. Tenant may operate a limited business or cottage industry at the property, subject to state and local laws, only with Landlord's written consent, which Landlord will not unreasonably withhold if the business is operated within Landlord's reasonable rules: [state any rules for a home business, or state none].
notes: MT: Replaces the base `residential-use-only`, whose flat ban on 'any commercial purpose' conflicts with the tenant's statutory right to a limited home business. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-322(1): 'Unless otherwise agreed, a tenant shall occupy the tenant's dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-321(1)(g): 'This section does not preclude the right of the tenant to operate a limited business or cottage industry on the premises, subject to state and local laws, if the landlord has consented in writing. The landlord may not unreasonably withhold consent if the limited business or cottage industry is operated within reasonable rules of the landlord.' A lease term waiving that right would be void (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-202(1)) (MT battery 75 (tenant business / cottage industry / home occupation): 2 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 0 synthetic)). title: Smoking Policy
bodyText: Smoking of any kind, including smoking tobacco or marijuana, and vaping tobacco or nicotine products with an electronic cigarette or similar device, is not permitted anywhere on the property, including inside the dwelling, on porches or balconies, or in any common area. Tenant will be responsible for any cost Landlord incurs to remediate odor, staining or damage caused by smoking or vaping in violation of this Section, and a violation may be treated as a default under this Lease. As Montana law requires, this Section does not prohibit Tenant from lawfully possessing marijuana or consuming it by means other than smoking.
notes: MT: Replaces the base `smoking-policy`, whose ban on 'vaping' of any kind reaches marijuana vaporized rather than smoked. Mont. Code Ann. § 16-12-108(6): 'Nothing in this chapter may be construed to prohibit a person from prohibiting or otherwise regulating the consumption, cultivation, distribution, processing, sale, or display of marijuana, marijuana products, and marijuana paraphernalia on private property the person owns, leases, occupies, or manages, except that a lease agreement executed after January 1, 2021, may not prohibit a tenant from lawfully possessing and consuming marijuana by means other than smoking unless required by federal law or to obtain federal funding.' Chapter 16-12 treats vaping separately from smoking (Mont. Code Ann. § 16-12-102(24), 'concentrates intended for use by smoking or vaping'), while the Clean Indoor Air Act defines smoking to include 'an electronic smoking device' for its own purposes (Mont. Code Ann. § 50-40-103(3), (9)); because a ban on vaping marijuana may be a ban on consuming it 'by means other than smoking', the clause bans only vaping tobacco or nicotine (Claude's legal call, rule 76; MT log §6.3; the `smoking-policy-mo` model). A landlord of federally assisted housing that must ban marijuana should take advice (`edu-cannabis-mt`). Last amended by 2025 Mont. Laws ch. 100, § 3 (subsection (6) unchanged in substance, MT log §1.2) (MT battery 58 (marijuana / cannabis on private or leased property): 3 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 0 synthetic)). title: No Marijuana Cultivation
bodyText: [Optional.] Tenant will not cultivate marijuana anywhere on the property, and will not permit any occupant or guest to do so.
notes: MT: Mont. Code Ann. § 16-12-108(6) lets a person prohibit 'the consumption, cultivation, distribution, processing, sale, or display of marijuana' on private property the person owns or manages; the lease limit reaches only possession and consumption by means other than smoking. A tenant who is not the owner may cultivate for personal use only with 'written permission to cultivate and store marijuana from the owner of the private residence' (Mont. Code Ann. § 16-12-106(1)(c)(iii)), and cultivation may not be visible from the street or other public area (Mont. Code Ann. § 16-12-108(3)). Without this clause and without written permission, a tenant still may not grow; the clause makes the bar express and binds occupants and guests (rule 27: the statute keys the right to the owner's writing). title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord: [list approved pets, or state that no pets are permitted]. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, if applicable, and a refundable pet deposit of {{pet_deposit}}, if applicable. Any pet deposit is a security deposit under Montana law and will be held, applied and returned with the Security Deposit. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern by written notice to Tenant, and Tenant will remove the pet within [number] days after the notice. Landlord may enter the property in connection with a pet only as this Lease's Access & Entry terms and applicable law permit. This Section does not apply to a service animal or an emotional support animal Landlord has approved as a reasonable accommodation.
notes: MT: Replaces the base `pet-policy`, which lets Landlord 'enter the property and remove a pet, without liability to Tenant', an entry outside Montana's exclusive access list (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-312(4)) and an exculpation for the landlord's own negligence (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-202(3)), and whose indemnity reaches liability for Landlord's own negligence (same subsection). A pet deposit is a security deposit: 'If a leasehold agreement ... requires the tenant ... to provide or maintain in effect any deposit to the landlord for part or all of the term ... the deposit must be presumed to be a security deposit' (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-101(4)). Pet rent agreed in the rental agreement is 'rent' (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-103(14)). An unauthorized pet is a 3-day curable noncompliance (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-422(1)(a)-(b)). Service animals: no extra compensation, but the person is liable for damage (Mont. Code Ann. § 49-4-214(2)); emotional support animals: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-114 (`edu-assistance-animals-mt`). The `pet-policy-nm` model, with Montana's deposit sentence. title: Maintenance & Repairs
bodyText: Subject to the maintenance duties applicable law places on Tenant and to any separate repair agreement that meets applicable law, Landlord will maintain the property, including its structural elements, roof, and systems, in good order and repair, and will maintain in good and safe working order the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems and the appliances Landlord supplies. Where a repair is necessary because of the purposeful or negligent act or omission of Tenant, a member of Tenant's family or another person on the premises with Tenant's consent, Tenant will reimburse Landlord the reasonable cost of the repair. Tenant will notify Landlord promptly in writing of any condition requiring repair or maintenance, and Landlord will undertake required repairs within a reasonable time, consistent with applicable law.
notes: MT: Replaces the base `landlord-maintenance`, whose 'except where repair is necessary due to improper use by Tenant or a guest of Tenant' would excuse Landlord from repairs the statute requires without a fault exception. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-303(1)(d): the landlord 'shall maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord'. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-303(1)(b) (fit and habitable 'except when it is the tenant's responsibility to maintain the dwelling unit pursuant to 70-24-321'). The tenant's duty not to damage: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-321(2); the landlord's damages: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-422(5) (actual damages; treble for purposeful noncompliance). The tenant's termination, essential-services and casualty rights exclude conditions the tenant, a family member or a person on the premises with consent caused (Mont. Code Ann. §§ 70-24-406(1)(a)(iii), 70-24-408(3), 70-24-409(2)); repair-and-deduct and damages (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-406(1)(b), (2)) have no fault exception. Shifting a task to the tenant needs a writing that meets Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-303(3)-(4) (`maintenance-allocation-mt`). A rental-agreement responsibility that the landlord maintain the premises under Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-303 cannot be found unconscionable (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-404(2)(b)). The `landlord-maintenance-nm` model. title: E-mail Notices (Optional)
bodyText: [Optional. Landlord may not require Tenant to provide an e-mail address as a condition of this Lease; complete this Section only if Tenant chooses to.] Tenant elects to receive notices under this Lease and applicable law by e-mail at: [Tenant's e-mail address]. Landlord's e-mail address for notices is: [Landlord's e-mail address]. A notice sent by e-mail to an address in this Section is complete when the sender receives a read receipt generated by an e-mail system or an e-mail reply other than an automatically generated reply; until then it is not complete, and the sender may deliver the notice by another method this Lease and applicable law allow. The sender will not send an e-mail in a form that keeps the recipient from printing or storing it. Either party may stop receiving notices by e-mail at any time by written notice to the other, and notices will then be delivered by another method. This Section does not apply to a notice that applicable law requires to be sent by a particular method, such as certified mail or mail with a certificate of mailing; that notice will be sent by the required method and may also be sent by e-mail. This Section controls over any contrary statement in this Lease's Notices section.
notes: MT: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-202(4), as amended by 2017 Mont. Laws ch. 290, § 2: a rental agreement may not provide that a party 'must provide an electronic mail address as a condition of entering into the agreement. However, a party may voluntarily provide an electronic mail address if the agreement contains a provision allowing a party to elect to receive notice by electronic mail.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-108(1)(c): a person has notice if 'it is transmitted to an electronic mail address provided by the tenant or the landlord in the rental agreement. Notice by electronic mail is complete on receipt of a read receipt generated by an electronic mail system or an electronic mail reply other than an automatically generated electronic mail reply.' Montana's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act has no exclusion for eviction, default or cure notices (MT battery 118 (electronic transactions act exclusions (eviction, default, termination), scoped to 30-18-): 0 hits, control 0; known positives passed (0 real sections, 1 synthetic)); it applies only between parties who have agreed to transact electronically, and 'A party that agrees to conduct a transaction by electronic means may refuse to conduct other transactions by electronic means. The right granted by this subsection may not be waived by agreement' (Mont. Code Ann. § 30-18-104(2)-(3)); an electronic record whose sender inhibits printing or storing it is 'not enforceable against the recipient' (Mont. Code Ann. § 30-18-107(1), (3)). Rule 45: read the act itself. The statute turns the election into the trigger (rule 54); without this Section, e-mail is not a notice method. A notice applicable law requires by a specified method (for example the abandoned-property notice by certified mail or certificate of mailing, Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-430(3)) must still go by that method (Mont. Code Ann. § 30-18-107(2)(b)). title: Rules and Regulations
bodyText: Tenant will comply with Landlord's written rules for the property in effect when this Lease is signed, a copy of which Landlord has given Tenant: [attach or describe the rules, or state that there are none]. Landlord may adopt new rules concerning Tenant's use and occupancy of the property by giving them to Tenant in writing. A rule is enforceable against Tenant only if its purpose is to promote the convenience, safety or welfare of the occupants of the premises, preserve Landlord's property from abusive use or make a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for the tenants generally; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies to all occupants in the premises in a fair manner; it is explicit enough to inform Tenant fairly of what Tenant must or must not do to comply; it is not for the purpose of evading Landlord's obligations; and Tenant had notice of it when Tenant entered into this Lease or when it was adopted. A rule adopted after this Lease is signed that works a substantial modification of Tenant's bargain is not valid until 30 days after written notice to Tenant in a month-to-month tenancy or 7 days after written notice in a week-to-week tenancy, and during a fixed Term it does not bind Tenant unless Tenant agrees to it in writing.
notes: MT: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-311(1): a landlord may adopt a rule concerning the tenant's use and occupancy, enforceable only if (a) 'its purpose is to promote the convenience, safety, or welfare of the occupants in the premises, preserve the landlord's property from abusive use, or make a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for the tenants generally'; (b) reasonably related to that purpose; (c) 'it applies to all occupants in the premises in a fair manner'; (d) sufficiently explicit; (e) not for the purpose of evading the landlord's obligations; and (f) 'the tenant has notice of it at the time that the tenant enters into the rental agreement or when it is adopted.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-311(2): rules 'must be in writing and must be given to each tenant residing on the premises and to each new tenant upon arrival.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-311(3): 'If a rule is adopted after a tenant enters into a rental agreement that works a substantial modification of the tenant's bargain, it is not valid until 7 days after written notice to the tenant in the case of a week to week tenancy or 30 days' written notice in the case of tenancies from month to month.' Valid rules are part of the 'rental agreement' (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-103(16)) and must be uniformly and fairly applied and enforced (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-401(3)). Subsection (3) is silent on a fixed term; the clause conditions a substantial mid-term change on the tenant's written agreement (Claude's drafting call, rule 76; MT log §6.3). title: Mold Disclosure
bodyText: Mold disclosure. Known mold and testing [check each that applies: ☐ Landlord has no knowledge that mold is present in the building and does not know that the building has been tested for mold. ☐ Landlord knows that mold is present in the building, as follows: ____. ☐ Landlord knows that the building has been tested for mold; a copy of the results, if available to Landlord, and evidence of any later mitigation or treatment are attached.] Furnishing test results and evidence of mitigation or treatment is not a promise, warranty or representation that the results are accurate or the mitigation or treatment effective. [Optional statement; if used, it must appear exactly as follows, and Tenant signs below to acknowledge receipt:] "MOLD DISCLOSURE: There are many types of mold. Inhabitable properties are not, and cannot be, constructed to exclude mold. Moisture is one of the most significant factors contributing to mold growth. Information about controlling mold growth may be available from your county extension agent or health department. Certain strains of mold may cause damage to property and may adversely affect the health of susceptible persons, including allergic reactions that may include skin, eye, nose, and throat irritation. Certain strains of mold may cause infections, particularly in individuals with suppressed immune systems. Some experts contend that certain strains of mold may cause serious and even life-threatening diseases. However, experts do not agree about the nature and extent of the health problems caused by mold or about the level of mold exposure that may cause health problems. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is studying the link between mold and serious health conditions. The seller, landlord, seller's agent, buyer's agent, or property manager cannot and does not represent or warrant the absence of mold. It is the buyer's or tenant's obligation to determine whether a mold problem is present. To do so, the buyer or tenant should hire a qualified inspector and make any contract to purchase, rent, or lease contingent upon the results of that inspection. A seller, landlord, seller's agent, buyer's agent, or property manager who provides this mold disclosure statement, provides for the disclosure of any prior testing and any subsequent mitigation or treatment for mold, and discloses any knowledge of mold is not liable in any action based on the presence of or propensity for mold in a building that is subject to any contract to purchase, rent, or lease." Tenant acknowledges receipt of this mold disclosure statement: ____ (Tenant's signature).
notes: MT: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-16-703(2): 'Whenever a seller or landlord or an agent of either has knowledge that a building has mold present, the seller, landlord, or agent of either shall, prior to or upon entry into a contract for the purchase, rent, or lease, disclose to the buyer or renter the presence of the mold. Whenever a seller or landlord knows that a building has been tested for mold, the seller or landlord, prior to or upon entry into a contract for the purchase, rent, or lease of that building, shall advise the buyer or tenant that testing has occurred and shall provide to the buyer or tenant a copy of the results of that test, if available to the seller or landlord, and evidence of any subsequent mitigation or treatment.' It adds: 'The furnishing of test results and evidence of mitigation or treatment is not to be construed as a promise, warranty, or representation of any sort ...'. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-16-703(1): the landlord 'may provide the following disclosure statement' on a document executed before or with the lease, and the tenant 'shall acknowledge receipt of this disclosure statement by signing a copy of the disclosure statement'; the statement is quoted verbatim (rule 59). Mont. Code Ann. § 70-16-703(3): a landlord who provides the (1) statement and complies with (2) 'is not liable in any action based on the presence of or propensity for mold in the building.' CONDITIONAL: the (2) disclosure is required only when the landlord knows of mold or testing, and the (1) statement is optional but is the condition of the immunity. The verbatim statement has no type-size or bold rule (MT battery 5 (prescribed statement in quotation marks (disclosure text)): 3 hits, control 0; known positives passed (2 real sections, 0 synthetic); layout table, MT log §4) (MT battery 36 (mold disclosure): 11 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 0 synthetic)). title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: [Optional.] If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the purposeful or negligent act or omission of Tenant, a member of Tenant's family, or a guest or other person on the premises with Tenant's consent, then: (1) Rent will not abate while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) Tenant will be liable to Landlord for the reasonable cost of repairing the damage and for Landlord's other actual damages caused by it, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, for no longer than the remaining Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from Tenant or from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property.
notes: MT: Rule 54 tenant-caused damage, answered provision by provision. Fire or casualty: the tenant's right to vacate and terminate, or to occupy the usable part at reduced rent, 'does not apply when the fire and casualty damage was caused by the purposeful or negligent act of the tenant or the tenant's family or guests' (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-409(2)). Essential services: the tenant's rights 'do not arise ... if the conditions were caused by the act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or any other person on the premises with the tenant's consent' (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-408(3)). Landlord breach: 'the tenant may not terminate for a condition caused by the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other persons on the premises with the tenant's consent' (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-406(1)(a)(iii)). Rent into court (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-421) has no separate fault exception but turns on what the tenant 'may recover under the rental agreement or this chapter'. Damages: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-422(5) (actual damages, treble if purposeful); destroying or damaging the premises is a 3-day no-cure termination ground (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-422(3)); the aggrieved party must mitigate (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-401(1)). The abatement and exit rights the clause touches (casualty, essential services, termination for breach) each exclude tenant-caused conditions, so the no-abatement term waives no statutory right (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-202(1)); repair-and-deduct and damages for the landlord's own breach (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-406(1)(b), (2)) have no fault exception, and the clause does not touch them. The `tenant-caused-damage-tn` and `tenant-caused-damage-nm` models, with Montana's 'purposeful or negligent' and family wording. Offered as an option (MT log §6.1). title: Landlord's Option to End the Lease After a Fire or Casualty
bodyText: [Optional.] If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty to an extent that Tenant's enjoyment of it is substantially impaired, Landlord may terminate this Lease by written notice to Tenant given within 30 days after the fire or casualty, effective on the date stated in the notice, which will be at least [number, at least 14] days after the notice is given. For the period after the fire or casualty, Tenant will owe Rent only for any part of the property Tenant lawfully continues to occupy, reduced in proportion to the loss in its fair rental value (unless the damage was caused by the purposeful or negligent act of Tenant or Tenant's family or guests), and Landlord will return the balance of any prepaid Rent and the Security Deposit as applicable law requires. This Section does not limit Tenant's own right under applicable law to vacate and terminate this Lease after a fire or casualty, or to occupy the usable part of the property at reduced Rent, and it does not relieve Tenant of responsibility for damage caused by the purposeful or negligent act of Tenant or Tenant's family or guests.
notes: MT: Montana's casualty statute gives rights to the tenant only: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-409(1) (if enjoyment is 'substantially impaired', the tenant may 'immediately vacate the premises and notify the landlord in writing within 14 days of the tenant's intention to terminate', or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part with rent 'reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value'); (2) (no application where the tenant, family or guests caused the damage purposefully or negligently); (3) (return of security and prepaid rent; 'Accounting for rent in the event of termination or apportionment must be made as of the date of the fire or casualty'). No statute gives or bars a landlord's termination right (MT battery 108 (fire or casualty damage (tenancy)): 3 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 0 synthetic)), so it is left to contract (rule 54). The clause preserves the tenant's Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-409 rights (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-202(1)) and keeps the abatement for the period after the casualty. The `casualty-termination-nm` model. Offered as an option (MT log §6.1). title: No Dangerous or Criminal Activity
bodyText: [Optional.] Tenant will not engage in, or knowingly allow any person to engage in, any activity on the premises that creates a reasonable potential that the premises may be damaged or destroyed or that neighboring tenants may be injured, including criminal production or manufacture of dangerous drugs, operation of an unlawful clandestine laboratory, gang-related activities, or unlawful possession of a firearm, explosive, or hazardous or toxic substance. If Tenant does, Landlord may terminate this Lease by giving Tenant 3 days' written notice specifying the violation, as applicable law allows. Tenant, members of Tenant's household and Tenant's guests also will not engage in other criminal activity on the premises; that is a noncompliance with this Lease, for which Landlord may give the written notices and pursue the remedies this Lease's Default by Tenant section and applicable law provide. Landlord will not treat Tenant as violating this Section because Tenant or a member of Tenant's household is the victim of the activity.
notes: MT: Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-321(3): 'A tenant may not engage or knowingly allow any person to engage in any activity on the premises that creates a reasonable potential that the premises may be damaged or destroyed or that neighboring tenants may be injured, including but not limited to any of the following activities: (a) criminal production or manufacture of dangerous drugs as prohibited by 45-9-110; (b) operation of an unlawful clandestine laboratory as prohibited by 45-9-132; (c) gang-related activities as prohibited by Title 45, chapter 8, part 4; (d) unlawful possession of a firearm, explosive, or hazardous or toxic substance; or (e) any activity that is otherwise prohibited by law.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-422(4): the landlord 'may terminate the rental agreement upon giving 3 days' written notice specifying the violation', with no cure. Subsection (3)(e) is read as an example of an activity that creates the reasonable potential of damage or injury, not as making every unlawful act a 3-day ground (Claude's reading; no case searched, MT log §1.4), so other criminal activity is a 14-day curable noncompliance under Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-422(1)(a), (d). Hearing within 5 business days for a Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-321(3) termination (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-427(2)(a)). The victim sentence is not required by Montana law (no domestic-violence eviction protection was found, `edu-no-dv-termination-mt`). Offered as an option (MT log §6.1) (MT battery 110 (criminal / drug / gang activity on premises (tenancy)): 6 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 0 synthetic)). title: Emergency and Death Contact (Optional)
bodyText: [Optional.] Tenant names the following person for Landlord to contact if Tenant dies or has an emergency: [name, address and telephone number]. title: Rent Increases and Term Changes in Montana
bodyText: In a month-to-month tenancy, Montana lets a landlord change the rent or other terms by written notice served at least 15 days before the end of the month; the change takes effect at the end of the month if the tenant stays. A fixed-term lease's rent can't be raised during the term unless the lease itself provides for it. Montana has no rent control, but you may not raise rent in retaliation for a tenant's protected complaint or union activity.

The notice, when served upon the tenant, shall of itself operate and be effectual to create and establish as a part of the lease the terms, rent, and conditions specified in the notice if the tenant shall continue to hold the premises after the expiration of the month.' Chapter 26 (general landlord-tenant law) has no exclusion for ch. 24 tenancies (contrast Mont. title: Application Fees in Montana
bodyText: Montana sets no cap on application fees. Since October 1, 2025, a property manager of four or more dwelling units who requires an application fee must refund it within a reasonable time if the applicant does not become a party to the rental agreement, keeping only the out-of-pocket costs of services actually performed that were itemized in writing when the fee was collected (such as a credit check). The manager's own time can't be kept as a cost. Wrongful withholding makes the manager liable for the amount withheld, and attorney fees may be awarded. 'Property manager' is defined broadly, so owners who manage four or more units themselves should follow this rule too.

title: Penalties for Mishandling a Deposit in Montana
bodyText: If you don't give the departing tenant the written list of damage and cleaning charges on time, you forfeit the right to withhold any part of the deposit for damage or cleaning. A landlord who wrongfully withholds any part of a deposit is liable for the amount wrongfully withheld, and the court may award attorney fees to the winning party. You bear the burden of proving damage. If you take a deposit without giving the tenant a separate signed condition statement at move-in, you can't recover for damage or cleaning unless you prove by clear and convincing evidence that the tenant caused it.

Code Ann. § 70-25-203: a landlord 'who fails to provide the departing tenant with a written list of damage and cleaning charges as required by 70-25-202 shall forfeit all rights to withhold any portion of the security deposit for the damages or cleaning charges.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-204(1): liability 'for an amount equal to the sum determined to have been wrongfully withheld or deducted. The attorney fees may be awarded the prevailing party at the discretion of the court. The burden of proof of damages caused by the tenant to the leasehold premises is on the landlord.' Mont. Code Ann. § 70-25-204(2): the tenant may not sue before a written denial, or before 30 days after termination or surrender, or 10 days after the landlord indicated no deductions. Mont. title: Pet Deposits and Pet Rent in Montana
bodyText: A pet deposit is presumed to be a security deposit under Montana law: it must be refundable and handled, accounted for and returned under the deposit rules, though Montana sets no cap on it. A one-time 'pet fee' for cleaning or damage is also presumed to be a security deposit, however it is labelled. Monthly pet rent agreed in the lease counts as rent. You may not charge extra for a service animal.

Code Ann. § 70-25-101(4) (any required deposit presumed a security deposit; 'A fee or charge for cleaning and damages, no matter how designated, is presumed to be a security deposit'). Mont. title: Landlord's Entry in Montana
bodyText: Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give the tenant at least 24 hours' notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times. Posting the notice conspicuously on the main entry door counts. The tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to inspect, repair, supply services or show the unit. Beyond that, you may enter only in an emergency, under a court order, to do health-and-safety repairs or cleaning the tenant fails to do after 14 days' written notice, during an absence of more than 7 days, or after abandonment or surrender. Don't abuse the right or use it to harass. A tenant who refuses lawful access can be given a 24-hour notice to correct and then a 3-day notice to terminate; a tenant facing unlawful or harassing entry may end the lease or get an injunction, plus damages.

title: Notice for Unpaid Rent in Montana
bodyText: If rent is unpaid when due, give the tenant written notice of the nonpayment and of your intention to terminate the lease if the rent isn't paid within 3 days. title: Holdover Charges in Montana
bodyText: Montana lets you recover up to the greater of three months' periodic rent or treble damages when a tenant purposefully holds over after you end a month-to-month tenancy without cause by a lawful 30-day notice, or after you end a longer tenancy for cause and the holdover is purposeful and not in good faith. Outside those cases you recover actual damages, including the rental value for each day of holdover. A lease can lawfully set a holdover rate, but the library doesn't offer a premium daily rate: Montana voids damages fixed in advance unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and holdover loss usually isn't. title: Abandonment and Re-Renting in Montana
bodyText: If a tenant abandons the unit, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent it at a fair rental. If you re-rent for a term starting before the lease ends, the old lease terminates when the new tenancy begins. If you don't make reasonable efforts, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the lease is treated as terminated by you on the date you had notice of the abandonment. You may enter during an absence of more than 7 days at reasonably necessary times, and if the lease requires notice of an extended absence and the tenant doesn't give it, you may recover actual damages. Every party has a duty to mitigate damages.

title: Fire and Casualty Damage in Montana
bodyText: If fire or casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may immediately vacate and give written notice within 14 days of intent to terminate (the lease ends on the date of vacating), or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value. If the lease ends, you must return the security deposit and all prepaid rent, accounting for rent as of the date of the fire. These rights don't apply when the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused the damage purposefully or negligently. Montana gives the landlord no statutory right to end the lease after a casualty; the library offers an optional clause.

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited in Montana
bodyText: You may not retaliate by raising rent, decreasing services, or bringing or threatening a possession action after a tenant has complained to a government agency about a code violation materially affecting health and safety, complained to you in writing about a maintenance violation, or organized or joined a tenants' union. A complaint within 6 months before your action creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation (not if the complaint came after notice of the rent increase or service cut). The tenant may recover possession or terminate and recover up to the greater of three months' periodic rent or treble damages. You may still bring a possession action if the tenant caused the code violation, is in default in rent, or compliance requires work that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit.

title: The Montana Eviction Process
bodyText: After a lawful termination, file an action for possession in district court or in a justice's, city or municipal court (small claims court hears only money and personal-property claims). The tenant has 5 business days after service of the summons and complaint to answer. The court must hear the case within 10 business days after the tenant's appearance or answer date (5 business days for dangerous-activity terminations) and rule within 5 days after the hearing; a damages hearing must be held within 45 days after possession and rent are decided. If you win possession, the court issues writs of possession and assistance immediately, and the sheriff executes the writ within 5 business days. Either side may demand a jury.

title: Unauthorized Occupants and Squatters in Montana
bodyText: A person who can't produce authorization to occupy (a written rental agreement, or written or verified verbal permission from you, or from a tenant for a guest) is an unauthorized person or trespasser and may be removed immediately by law enforcement at your request; law enforcement may stand by while you change locks and remove the occupant's belongings. title: Foreclosure of a Montana Rental
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to tell tenants or applicants about a pending foreclosure. After a trustee's sale, the purchaser is entitled to possession on the 10th day after the sale, and anyone remaining in possession under an interest that came after the trust indenture (which generally includes a tenant whose lease postdates the loan) is treated as a tenant at will. After a sheriff's sale, the purchaser is entitled to collect rent from the tenant in possession until redemption. A tenant who is served with notice of a proceeding to recover the property must promptly tell you and deliver any written notice to you. Federal law on tenants after foreclosure is not covered here.

title: Montana Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Montana's Human Rights Act makes it unlawful to refuse to rent, set different terms, make discriminatory inquiries, misrepresent availability or publish discriminatory notices or ads because of sex, marital status, race, creed, religion, color, age, familial status, physical or mental disability or national origin. Disability discrimination includes refusing reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense (you may, where reasonable, require restoration of the interior) and refusing reasonable accommodations in rules and policies. Renting up to three sleeping rooms in an owner-occupied single-family home is exempt from these rules. The age and familial-status rules do not apply to qualifying housing for older persons, or to a dwelling for no more than two families where the owner lives in one of the units. Montana's Constitution also says no person, firm or corporation shall discriminate against anyone in the exercise of civil or political rights because of race, color, sex, culture, social origin or condition, or political or religious ideas; how far that reaches private rental decisions is unsettled. Federal fair housing law also applies.

title: Service and Emotional Support Animals in Montana
bodyText: A tenant with a disability may ask to keep an emotional support animal as a reasonable accommodation. Unless federal law says otherwise, you may deny an animal that poses a direct threat to others' health or safety, or of physical damage to the property, that another accommodation can't reduce or eliminate. If the need isn't readily apparent, you may ask for supporting information from a Montana-licensed mental health practitioner who has known the tenant at least 30 days and has done a clinical evaluation (including the practitioner's license type, number and effective date), or from another source you find reliable under fair housing law, and you may require proof of licensing and vaccinations. You may not ask for a diagnosis, its severity or medical records, and an online registration or certificate alone isn't enough. You must issue a written determination by a notice method the Act allows. The tenant is liable for damage the animal does. A person with a service animal is entitled to full and equal access to housing and can't be charged extra, but is liable for damage.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Nevada has no just-cause eviction rule for houses and apartments. A fixed-term lease ends at its expiration without notice, and a periodic tenancy can be ended without a reason on written notice of at least 7 days (week to week) or 30 days (other periodic tenancies); no length of tenancy changes this. The limits are situational: you may not end or refuse to renew a tenancy, raise rent, cut services or bring or threaten an eviction in retaliation for protected acts such as a good-faith code or landlord-tenant complaint, joining or organizing a tenants' union, raising habitability in a proceeding, or exercising fair-housing or domestic-violence rights (a termination for cause is not retaliation); a tenant who is 60 or older or has a disability (except in a week-to-week tenancy) can ask for 30 more days, and a qualifying government worker can stay until 30 days after a shutdown ends; fair housing law applies, and a violation is a defense to eviction; the domestic-violence termination statute keeps your right to end a tenancy for unrelated reasons; after a foreclosure sale of a building of up to four units the tenant gets a change-of-ownership notice and at least 60 days (one rental period if rent is due more often than monthly); and when apartments are converted to condominiums, tenants get 120 days' notice and a first offer to buy. Mobile home parks have their own termination rules.

title: Eviction Court Rules: Landlord Duties
bodyText: Court rules add duties for a landlord who brings an eviction. Statewide, a summary-eviction notice must be specific about the ground it alleges. In a formal unlawful-detainer case the court may not shorten the tenant's time to answer below 10 days, the trial can't be held sooner than 21 days after service, and, except in extraordinary circumstances, a hearing on a temporary writ of restitution can't be held sooner than 14 days after service; the writ also needs a court-approved bond. The justice courts' local rules add more. In the Las Vegas, Henderson, North Las Vegas and Pahrump justice courts, the notice must name that justice court specifically (a reference to the justice of the peace or a county courthouse is not valid), and the complaint must be filed with the notice and proof of service. Henderson, North Las Vegas and Pahrump also require notices to be typed or clearly legible and unaltered, bar filing the complaint before the notice period ends, and require a postmarked certificate of mailing where mailing is required. Henderson, North Las Vegas and Pahrump treat a notice as expired if the complaint is not filed within 30 days after the notice period ends. Las Vegas allows 45 days, but requires the court-approved notice and complaint forms, and a surrender notice there lapses unless the eviction notice is served within 30 days after the time to comply ends. By statute, the court file is sealed if you have not filed your complaint within 30 days after the tenant files a contest affidavit, so file within 30 days of the tenant's affidavit and in any case within 30 days after the notice period ends. Under these courts' local rules, an order for summary eviction that is not executed expires after 30 days unless the court orders otherwise. These courts hold rent a tenant withholds for a habitability failure in escrow, and a tenant who does not deposit it loses that defense.

title: Electronic Leases, Signatures and Notices
bodyText: Nevada's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lets a lease, a signature or a written record be electronic, but only between parties who have agreed to do business electronically, and a party who agreed may refuse to do later transactions electronically (that right cannot be waived). If the sender prevents the recipient from storing or printing an electronic record, the record is not enforceable against the recipient, and a lease that must be in writing can be denied effect if the electronic copy can't be kept and accurately reproduced by everyone entitled to it. Where another law requires a notice to be sent by a specified method, it must still be sent that way: written notices to a tenant under the landlord-tenant act are served as the eviction statutes prescribe. A notice of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of a tenant's primary residence never satisfies a writing requirement if it is given electronically, and the parties cannot agree otherwise.

title: Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Neglect
bodyText: If a tenant's failure to meet the tenant's basic obligations can be fixed by repair, replacing a damaged item or cleaning, you may give written notice specifying the problem and asking the tenant to fix it within 14 days (or sooner in an emergency). If the tenant doesn't use best efforts to comply, you may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner and give the tenant an itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost or the fair and reasonable value of the work. The bill is payable as rent on the next rent due date, or, if the lease has ended, immediately or out of the security deposit. This is one of the few entries the access statute allows without the tenant's consent. No lease clause is needed for this right.

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: Nevada defines rent as all periodic payments to you for occupancy, including reasonable and actual late fees set forth in the lease, and every mandatory periodic fee must be included in the single rent figure the lease states (a qualifying utility charge is the one exception). A bill for repair or cleaning you did after the tenant failed to fix a problem is payable as rent on the next rent date. A one-time fee is not a periodic payment, so it is not rent. After you serve a pay-or-quit notice, you may not refuse rent because collection fees, attorney's fees, other non-rent costs, a late or dishonored-check charge or a deposit is unpaid, and this lease does not let an unpaid late fee alone end the tenancy. Whether an unpaid late fee alone can support a pay-or-quit notice is not settled here; base a nonpayment notice on unpaid periodic rent.
