title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Nevada prescribes few forms for residential landlords. A tenant ending the lease because of domestic violence may use an affidavit from a qualified third party in substantially the statute's form. A single-family lease not signed by a licensed property manager must carry the statutory disclosure about occupancy presumptions at the top of the first page, in type at least twice the size of any other text. Summary-eviction notices must contain the statements the eviction statute lists (the court with jurisdiction, how to contest, what happens if the court rules against the tenant, and the lockout remedies), but no statewide form is prescribed; the Las Vegas Justice Court requires its court-approved notice and complaint forms. A lender collecting rents after an assignment may notify tenants on a statutory form, and a trustee's or execution sale of an occupied home requires a separate notice posted and mailed to the tenants.

title: No Separate Quiet-Enjoyment Statute
bodyText: Nevada's landlord-tenant act has no separate quiet-enjoyment covenant, but it protects the tenant's possession directly. You may recover possession only through a court proceeding or after surrender or abandonment; locking the tenant out, removing them or willfully interrupting an essential service lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover actual damages plus up to $2,500. You may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant, and an unlawful or unreasonable entry, or repeated demands for entry that harass the tenant, let the tenant get an injunction or end the lease and recover actual damages. Retaliation against a tenant's protected acts is also barred.

title: No Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Nevada has no statute barring a landlord from having a tenant sign a residential lease with blank spaces, or requiring the lease to be complete at signing. The landlord-tenant act lists what a written lease must contain, and you must give the tenant a free copy of the signed lease when it is signed. Fill in every blank before anyone signs: a blank filled later invites a dispute over what was agreed.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: [Optional.] If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, a member of Tenant's household, or another person on the premises with Tenant's consent, Tenant will be liable to Landlord for the reasonable cost of repairing the damage and for Landlord's other actual damages caused by it. If the damage results from a deliberate or negligent act of any of those persons, Rent will not abate while the damage is repaired, and the damage does not give Tenant a right to end this Lease. If this Lease ends because of the damage, Landlord's damages include the Rent Landlord loses for no longer than the remaining Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property, and Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section does not take away any right applicable law gives Tenant.
notes: NV: NEW 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.27 retro, rule 54t; model tenant-caused-damage-nm, re-drafted for NV). Provision by provision, each abatement or exit right has its own tenant-fault exception (tenant, household member or person on the premises with consent), but the wording differs: landlord-breach termination, 118A.350(2) (termination only), habitability remedies including withholding into escrow, 118A.355(2)(a), repair and deduct, 118A.360(3), and essential services including full abatement, 118A.380(5), all say 'deliberate or negligent act or omission'; casualty termination and rent reduction, NRS 118A.400(3), say only 'if it is determined that the fire or casualty were caused by deliberate or negligent acts' (no omissions). So the no-abatement and no-exit sentence is limited to damage from a deliberate or negligent ACT, the narrowest exception, and waives no chapter right (118A.220(1)(a)); liability for repair cost and damages still reaches acts and omissions (118A.310(1)(f), 118A.420). The clause keeps a savings sentence for any right outside those sections and for a disputed cause, which a court determines. Caught by the independent check before delivery (NV retro log, rule 54t). Liability: 118A.310(1)(f), 118A.420, 118A.290(5); lost rent on termination is actual damages (118A.420; no NV statute on rent during repairs); mitigation follows 118.175. title: Damage a Tenant Causes
bodyText: A tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or knowingly let anyone else do so. For a tenant's breach you may recover your actual damages and get a court order; end the lease on a 5-day notice if the tenant doesn't fix a fixable breach (or at once if it can't be fixed, unless a tenant unable to fix it lets you enter and fix it and pays the reasonable cost); or, after 14 days' written notice, have the repair or cleaning done yourself and bill the reasonable cost as rent on the next rent date (or deduct it from the deposit after the lease ends). Committing or permitting waste is a ground for a 3-day notice to surrender with no cure. You may charge the tenant for repairs of a condition the tenant, a household member or a guest caused deliberately or negligently. When they caused the condition, the tenant cannot use it to end the lease, to repair and deduct, to withhold rent, or for the essential-services remedies, and if it is determined that their deliberate or negligent acts caused a fire or casualty, the casualty rules (ending the lease or reducing the rent) don't apply. No Nevada statute addresses rent lost while repairs are made; claim it as damages, and the lease's optional tenant-caused-damage clause provides for it.

title: Tenant Default
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and does not pay it within the time stated in any notice to pay Rent or vacate that applicable law requires Landlord to give, or fails to comply with any other obligation under this Lease and does not cure the failure after receiving written notice. No opportunity to pay or cure applies, whether the default is nonpayment of Rent or any other breach, to: (a) nonpayment of Rent by a Tenant who was late or delinquent in paying Rent before the month in which Landlord gives notice, where Texas law permits a notice to vacate instead of a notice to pay Rent or vacate; (b) Tenant, a member of Tenant's family, or a guest or invitee of Tenant intentionally damaging property on the premises or by word or conduct threatening the personal safety of Landlord, Landlord's employees, or another tenant; or (c) a termination under Section 91.003 of the Texas Property Code. Except as required by applicable law, Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise all rights and remedies available under applicable law, including terminating this Lease, regaining possession of the property, and recovering unpaid Rent, late fees, and reasonable costs and expenses, less amounts obtained from the Security Deposit. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to mitigate damages resulting from Tenant's default to the extent required by applicable law. To the extent permitted under applicable law, the prevailing party may recover from the other party court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in connection with any legal proceedings related to this Lease.
notes: TX: NEW 2026-10-03 (SOP 1.29 retro, rule 43; fix 23 screened). Supersedes `default-by-tenant` for TX. Base text kept except the default sentences. WHY: Texas has a no-cure route for rent - a tenant who was late or delinquent before the month of the notice may be given a notice to vacate rather than a notice to pay rent or vacate (Tex. Prop. Code §24.005(a), as amended by S.B. 38, eff. Jan. 1, 2026) - and the base row's carve-out reached only the non-rent sentence, while its rent limb ('does not cure ... within the time period specified by applicable law') could be read to give every tenant a payment window. The rent limb now runs only from a notice to pay rent or vacate that the law requires; the no-cure sentence stands alone and reaches both limbs (rule 43), and lists its cases rather than saying 'where Texas law permits Landlord to proceed without one' (the base wording; in Texas, which requires no cure for any non-rent breach, that phrase would cancel the cure promise it qualifies - independent check, 2026-10-03). The cases: (a) the §24.005(a) notice to vacate for a previously late tenant; (b) intentional damage or threats to safety, in the words of §92.332(b)(2), which the Legislature lists among grounds 'valid ... in any event' (narrowing the voluntary cure promise is a drafting judgment, rule 76); (c) §91.003 (termination after a final Penal Code ch. 43 conviction for use of the property; 'applies regardless of a term of the lease to the contrary'). The rent limb adds no contractual notice: §24.005(a) itself requires written notice before filing. The voluntary cure promise for non-rent breaches stays (Texas requires none). `edu-eviction-notice-tx` still advises always using a notice to pay rent or vacate for nonpayment; the clause keeps the landlord's choice. COSTS (rule 49, fix 23): no Texas statute bars a lease from recovering collection or eviction costs (battery 'collection cost|cost(s) of collection|expenses of collection': 0 hits in Prop. Code chs. 24, 54, 91, 92; none in the Bus. & Com. or Finance Codes). §24.006(b)-(c): a lease fee clause entitles a prevailing landlord to fees and makes them reciprocal for a prevailing tenant; (d) the prevailing party recovers all costs of court by statute; Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §38.001(b)(8) allows fees on a written-contract claim without a lease term. 'Reasonable costs and expenses' is KEPT: Tex. Fin. title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Texas has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date, and either side may end a month-to-month tenancy without giving a reason on the notice Texas law sets (for a monthly rent period, at least one month, unless both of you signed an agreement setting a different period), however long the tenant has lived there. Cities and counties cannot add a cause requirement: Texas voids local rules that regulate evictions or restrict or delay notices to vacate or eviction filings. The limits are situational. Within six months after a tenant in good faith uses a legal right or remedy, gives a repair notice, makes a good-faith code or utility complaint, or establishes or takes part in a tenant organization, you may not retaliate by filing an eviction, ending the lease, raising the rent or cutting services; retaliation is a defense to an eviction. Some grounds are always valid, including rent delinquency, intentional damage or threats, a material breach other than holding over, and a holdover after your end-of-term termination notice given before the tenant's protected act. After a foreclosure sale, a buyer who will not continue the lease must give a tenant who is current at least 30 days' notice to vacate. Fair-housing law bars ending a tenancy for a discriminatory reason. Federally assisted housing may carry its own cause and notice rules, which this library has not reviewed; a federal notice period does not delay your filing but does delay service of the writ.

title: Sending Notices by E-mail
bodyText: Texas's electronic-transactions law covers landlord-tenant records and, unlike some states, carves out nothing for eviction, default or cure notices. Three of its rules matter to you. It applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, judged from the context and their conduct. A tenant who agreed to deal electronically on one matter may still refuse to deal electronically on other matters, and a lease cannot take that right away. And an e-mailed notice that the law requires in writing counts only if the tenant can keep it: if you send it in a form, or through a portal, that stops the tenant from printing or saving it, it cannot be enforced against the tenant, whatever the lease says. Texas landlord-tenant law adds its own conditions: a notice to vacate or to pay rent or vacate may go by e-mail only if the tenant agreed in writing (the lease's optional e-mail consent clause), though a notice the tenant actually receives counts however it was sent, deposit notices may go by e-mail once you and the tenant have e-mailed each other, and a copy of the lease may be e-mailed if you have e-mailed about the lease. Because a tenant may argue that a later notice is another matter the tenant can refuse to handle electronically, and a disputed e-mail is hard to prove, also deliver eviction notices by one of the paper methods.

title: Deceptive Trade Practices Act and Rentals
bodyText: Texas's Deceptive Trade Practices Act reaches residential leasing: it defines goods to include real property leased for use, so a tenant is a consumer. Two parts matter. Its list of unlawful practices includes representing that an agreement gives rights, remedies or obligations it does not have or that the law prohibits, and failing to disclose known information to induce a transaction the consumer would otherwise have refused; the list has nothing on blank spaces or on giving the tenant a copy (Texas's lease-copy rule is in the Property Code). Separately, the act lets a consumer sue for any unconscionable action, meaning taking advantage of a consumer's lack of knowledge, ability, experience or capacity to a grossly unfair degree. A consumer who wins recovers economic damages, court costs and attorney's fees, and up to three times the damages if you acted knowingly. A tenant cannot waive the act in a lease unless the tenant is not in a significantly disparate bargaining position, is represented by a lawyer the tenant chose, and signs a waiver in the statute's bold-face form. Separately, Texas's debt-collection act bars collecting a fee or expense incidental to a debt unless the agreement expressly authorizes it or the law otherwise allows it, and makes a violation a deceptive trade practice; whether that act reaches a landlord collecting its own rent is unsettled. So a lease term the law voids is not merely unenforceable: using it can create liability.
notes: TX: NEW 2026-10-03 (SOP 1.29 retro, rules 51 and 47; topic `consumer-protection-act`, which 17 states carry and TX did not). Rule 51 asked two questions. (1) Enumerated list: YES, and it reaches leases. Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §17.45(1) 'Goods' means tangible chattels or real property purchased or leased for use; (4) consumer; (6) trade and commerce include lease. §17.46(b)(12) 'representing that an agreement confers or involves rights, remedies, or obligations which it does not have or involve, or which are prohibited by law'; (b)(24) failure to disclose known information to induce a transaction. No blank-space or copy-at-signing item in §17.46(b) (searched). title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: [Optional.] If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the negligence or fault of Tenant, a member of Tenant's family, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, and not from normal wear and tear, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; (2) if the damage makes the property as a practical matter totally unusable for residential purposes, Landlord may terminate this Lease by written notice to Tenant; and (3) Tenant will be liable for the reasonable cost of repairing the damage and, if this Lease ends because of the damage, for the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term or, in a month-to-month tenancy, up to the earliest date Tenant could have ended the tenancy by notice, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property.

Each Texas abatement and exit provision checked separately for a tenant-fault exception: casualty termination (Tex. Prop. Code §92.054(b)) and casualty rent reduction (§92.054(c)) both apply only if the casualty 'is not caused by the negligence or fault of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or a guest or invitee of the tenant'; the repair duty and so the termination and repair-and-deduct remedies (§§92.052(b), 92.056, 92.0561) do not reach a condition caused by the tenant, a lawful occupant, family or a guest, other than normal wear and tear. So a no-abatement term waives no statutory right, provided the clause's fault group is no wider than §92.054's: it names the tenant, family members and guests or invitees only, and leaves out 'an Occupant' (in the TN model and in §92.052(b) but not in §92.054(b)-(c)); with it, a casualty caused by an occupant who is neither family nor a guest would leave the tenant a §92.054(b) termination right that item (3) would penalize (independent check, 2026-10-03). GAP the clause fills: §92.054(b)'s termination right is denied to BOTH parties when the tenant caused the casualty, and no Texas statute sets the landlord's damages for tenant-caused damage (chs. 24, 54, 91, 92 read; common law of waste and damages not read), so the clause gives the landlord a termination option and states the damages measure. Lawful: §92.006 bars waiving the landlord's repair duty, and §92.052(b) says there is none for tenant-caused conditions; the clause excludes normal wear and tear and the landlord's own negligence, so it is not a §92.006(f) tenant-repair agreement. Mitigation: §91.006 (abandonment) and the clause's own reasonable-efforts promise. Damage-measure end date covers a periodic tenancy (rule 37; §91.001). title: When the Tenant Causes Damage
bodyText: Texas law leaves the cost of tenant-caused damage with the tenant in several places. If a fire or other casualty caused by the negligence or fault of the tenant, the tenant's family or a guest makes the home unusable, the tenant cannot end the lease and gets no rent reduction under the casualty statute; but the same statute's termination right is not available to you either. You have no statutory duty to repair a condition the tenant, an occupant, family or a guest caused (normal wear and tear excepted), so the tenant's repair, repair-and-deduct and termination remedies do not apply to it. You may deduct the damage from the security deposit, never for normal wear and tear, with an itemized list. Charging for security-device repairs needs an underlined lease term and is limited to misuse or damage by the tenant, family, an occupant or a guest. A specific bold or underlined agreement is needed only to make the tenant pay, whoever caused them (other than your negligence), for drain stoppages from foreign or improper objects in lines serving only the unit, damage to doors, windows or screens, and damage from windows or doors left open. No Texas statute says what you can recover beyond that, so the library offers an optional clause: no rent reduction while you repair, your right to end the lease if the damage makes the home unusable, and the tenant's liability for repair costs and lost rent less what you get from re-renting. Try to re-rent; Texas requires a landlord to mitigate when a tenant abandons.

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: Texas statutes do not define rent or say whether a fee can be treated as rent, and none lets a lease turn fees into rent. Texas does treat late fees separately: the late-fee statute governs only the fee and does not change your right to end the lease for unpaid rent. The library's lease applies each payment to rent first and does not call any fee rent. When you give a notice to pay rent or vacate, demand only the unpaid rent, so the notice cannot be attacked for including amounts that are not rent.

title: No Statute on Fixing a Tenant's Neglect
bodyText: Texas has no statute letting a landlord fix a tenant's failure to maintain the property and bill the cost as rent. Any such right comes from the lease. Keep two Texas limits in mind: you have no duty to repair conditions the tenant, an occupant, family or a guest caused (other than normal wear and tear), but a lease can make the tenant pay for repairs you would otherwise owe only through the narrow bold or underlined agreements the statute allows. Entering to do the work is governed by the lease, since Texas has no entry-notice statute.

title: No Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Texas has no statute barring a landlord from having a tenant sign a residential lease with blank spaces, or requiring the lease to be complete at signing, and the Deceptive Trade Practices Act's list of unlawful practices has no blank-space item. title: No Separate Quiet-Enjoyment Statute
bodyText: Texas's landlord-tenant statutes have no separate quiet-enjoyment covenant; any covenant comes from the common law and the lease. The statutes protect the tenant's possession directly instead: you may change the locks only in the narrow cases the statute allows, may interrupt utilities only as it allows, and may not, in retaliation for a protected act, engage in bad faith in a course of conduct that materially interferes with the tenant's rights under the lease. Each carries money penalties.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Texas prescribes only a few forms a residential landlord uses. The floodplain notice, and the prior-flooding notice where you know of flood damage in the last five years, must be substantially in the statute's words, with its check boxes, and signed by you and the tenant (the library's flood disclosure clause). The lease must contain language substantially equivalent to the statute's statement on the tenant's special rights to end the lease early for family violence, certain sex offenses or stalking, or military service, or you lose the right to collect unpaid rent from a tenant who leaves under those rights (the library's statement clause). A homeowner removing an unauthorized occupant uses the complaint the statute sets out. Other notices (the electricity termination notice, the smoke-alarm notice, the repair-remedies statement) have required content and print, not a fixed text.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Florida has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date, and either party may end a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy without giving a reason, on the written notice the statute sets (at least 7 days before the end of a weekly period, 30 days before the end of a monthly or quarterly period, or 60 days before the end of a yearly period). Cities and counties cannot add a cause requirement: state law preempts local regulation of residential tenancies, including notice requirements and the terms of rental agreements. The limits are situational. A landlord may not raise rent, cut services or bring or threaten an eviction mainly to retaliate against a tenant who in good faith complained to a code agency, joined a tenant organization, gave a 7-day repair notice, ended a lease as a servicemember, paid rent to an association on its demand or used fair-housing rights, though an eviction for good cause such as nonpayment or a lease violation is not retaliation. Fair-housing law bars ending a tenancy for a discriminatory reason. After a foreclosure, federal law requires a buyer to honor a bona fide lease and give 90 days' notice. A developer converting a building to condominiums must let existing tenants extend their leases. An eviction against a servicemember on state active duty can be stayed.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: [Optional.] If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the wrongful or negligent act of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term or, in a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, up to the earliest date Tenant could have ended the tenancy by notice, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use good-faith efforts to repair and re-rent the property. Separately, Tenant will pay the reasonable cost of repairing damage, other than normal wear and tear, caused by the wrongful or negligent act of Tenant, a member of Tenant's family, or another person on the property with Tenant's consent.

title: When the Tenant Causes Damage
bodyText: Florida law leaves the cost of damage a tenant causes with the tenant. A tenant may end the lease or pay reduced rent after a fire or other casualty only if the damage was not caused by the tenant's own wrongful or negligent act. A landlord is not responsible under the maintenance statute for conditions caused by the negligent or wrongful act of the tenant, the tenant's family or another person on the property with the tenant's consent, so the tenant's 7-day repair notice, termination and rent-withholding remedies do not reach them. The tenant must not damage the property or let anyone else do so. Intentional destruction or damage lets the landlord end the lease on a 7-day notice without a chance to cure; other damage is a breach the tenant must be given 7 days to cure. The landlord may claim repair costs against the deposit, following the deposit claim-notice rules, and sue for the rest. If the tenant leaves or is evicted, the landlord chooses among the statutory remedies, including holding the tenant liable for rent through the end of the lease less what good-faith re-renting brings in. The optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause states the rent consequences in the lease.

title: Florida Consumer Protection Law and Leases
bodyText: Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act declares unfair or deceptive acts and unconscionable practices in trade or commerce unlawful, and trade or commerce expressly includes renting property. The Act carries no list of specific unfair lease practices (such as blank spaces filled in after signing or not giving the tenant a copy); it relies on general standards read in light of federal trade law. It also says it does not affect the remedies for residential tenancies under the landlord-tenant act. Florida has no plain-language statute for consumer contracts or leases. Separately, the consumer collection law bars anyone collecting a consumer debt from enforcing a debt they know is not legitimate. Fill in every blank before the tenant signs and give the tenant a signed copy.

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: In Florida, rent includes any other payment the written lease designates as rent, so a lease can turn a fee into rent. The library's lease does not call late fees or other charges rent, applies each payment to rent first, and labels only pet rent as rent. When you deliver a 3-day notice for unpaid rent, demand only the rent: a notice that also demands charges the lease does not designate as rent can be attacked as defective.

title: No Statute on Fixing a Tenant's Neglect
bodyText: Florida has no statute letting a landlord fix a tenant's failure to maintain the property and bill the cost as rent. A landlord may enter on at least 24 hours' notice, between 7:30 a.m. and 8 p.m., to make repairs, and is not responsible for conditions the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused. The cost of damage the tenant caused can be claimed against the deposit or recovered as damages, but it is not rent unless the lease designates it as rent, and the library's lease does not.

title: No Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Florida has no statute barring a landlord from having a tenant sign a residential lease with blank spaces, or requiring the landlord to give the tenant a copy, and Florida's consumer protection act has no list of specific unfair lease practices. title: No Separate Quiet-Enjoyment Statute
bodyText: Florida's residential landlord-tenant act has no separate quiet-enjoyment covenant; any covenant comes from the common law and the lease. The act protects the tenant's possession directly instead: a landlord may not cut off utilities, lock the tenant out, remove doors, windows or the tenant's belongings except as the statute allows, or abuse the right of entry to harass the tenant. These violations cost the landlord actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees.

bodyText: Florida prescribes many forms a residential landlord uses, most of them 'in substantially the following form'. In or with the lease: the security deposit disclosure (landlords with five or more units), the fee-in-lieu-of-deposit disclosure, the e-mail notice addendum, the flood disclosure (separate document, leases of a year or more), the early termination fee addendum (separate, signed at signing), the abandoned-property legend, and the radon notice (exact words). Others concern associations and squatters: a condominium or homeowners' association's demand that the tenant pay rent to it, and an owner's sworn complaint to have the sheriff remove unauthorized occupants. title: Just Cause Is Required After 12 Months
bodyText: California has one of the strongest just-cause rules in the country, and it is the single thing most likely to catch out a landlord who has rented elsewhere. Once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied the home for 12 months, you may not end the tenancy without a just cause, and the cause must be stated in the written notice. If you added another adult to the lease before the original tenant reached 24 months, the rule applies once all tenants have reached 12 months or any one tenant has reached 24. The end of a fixed term is not itself a reason to recover possession: a covered tenancy continues, and a tenant's refusal to sign a renewal on similar terms is itself one of the listed at-fault causes. At-fault causes include nonpayment, breach of a material lease term, nuisance, waste, criminal activity, unlawful subletting and refusing lawful entry. No-fault causes include an owner or close relative moving in, withdrawing the home from the rental market, complying with a government order, and demolition or substantial remodel; a no-fault termination requires relocation assistance or a waiver of the final month's rent, and getting that wrong voids the notice. Several kinds of property are exempt, and a local just-cause ordinance can displace the state scheme entirely.

title: California Has an Algorithmic Pricing Statute
bodyText: California is one of the few states with a statute aimed at algorithmic pricing, and it took effect on January 1, 2026. It is antitrust law rather than landlord-tenant law, and it does not ban revenue-management software. Two things are unlawful: using or distributing a common pricing algorithm as part of an agreement or conspiracy to restrain trade, and using or distributing one to coerce someone else into adopting a price or commercial term the algorithm recommends for the same or similar product or service. A common pricing algorithm is any method, including software, used by two or more people that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilise, set or otherwise influence a price or term, and 'price' is defined broadly. The practical reading for a landlord: using pricing software on your own data is not what this targets; feeding or drawing on competitors' non-public rent data through a shared tool, or pressing another owner to follow its numbers, is where the risk sits. Federal and California antitrust and unfair-competition law apply as well.

title: When a Fee Counts as Rent
bodyText: California has no general statute saying whether late fees, utility charges or other fees count as rent for a dwelling, so the lease and the courts decide - with two important exceptions that run in opposite directions. Submetered water is expressly NOT rent: the statute says so, which is why an unpaid water bill can never support a three-day pay-or-quit notice and instead has its own route (180 days overdue or $200 unpaid, then a notice to perform covenants or quit). An unpaid separately-leased parking fee likewise cannot support an eviction on a qualifying property. Practical consequence: do not label fees 'additional rent' in a California lease to make them evictable. A three-day notice that demands rent plus non-rent charges risks being defective for overstating the rent due, and this library's clauses keep fees separate from Rent for that reason. Fees still remain collectible as contract debts, and the deposit may be applied only to the four purposes the deposit statute lists.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix a Breach and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: California gives a landlord no statutory right to step in, fix a tenant's breach and add the cost to rent. What California does give you is better than nothing and differently shaped: a tenant must use ordinary care to keep the home safe and in good condition, and must repair any deterioration or injury caused by the tenant's own want of ordinary care. That is a statutory repair duty you can enforce as a debt or as damages, and the deposit may be applied to repairing damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. The lease may also give you a contractual right to do the work and recover the cost. Two cautions. Do not treat such a charge as rent - see the note on when a fee counts as rent - because a three-day notice that demands repair costs as rent risks being defective. And entry to do the work still needs a lawful entry ground and the required notice.

title: No Rule on Blank Spaces, but You Must Give a Copy
bodyText: California has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in, and no statute making a blank a breach. One related duty is real and often missed: you must give the tenant a copy of the signed lease within 15 days of the tenant signing it, and once each year after that you must give another copy if the tenant asks. If you do not have the lease or a copy, you must instead give a written statement saying so, with the owner and manager details, where rent is paid and the forms of payment you accept. Fill in every blank before signing anyway. California prescribes the exact words for several lease statements and sets minimum type sizes for some of them, and a blank left in a statement whose wording the statute dictates is a compliance problem rather than just an unclear term.

title: California Has a Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: Unlike most states, where quiet enjoyment is a court-made implied promise, California puts a covenant in the statute: an agreement to let binds the landlord to secure the tenant's quiet possession of the home during the term, against everyone lawfully claiming it. Read it for what it says - it is a promise about superior claims to the property, such as a lender, a co-owner or a prior tenant, rather than a general promise of peace and quiet. The broader protection comes from elsewhere: it is unlawful for a landlord to interfere with a tenant's quiet enjoyment of the home for the purpose of influencing the tenant to vacate, and that provision carries real penalties. The practical point is that you cannot contract out of either one by saying the lease is the whole of your obligations, and a title problem you knew about is your risk, not the tenant's.

(Enacted 1872.) It sits in Title 5 Chapter 1 (Hiring in General), which the original pass read end to end, so this is a topic-coverage gap rather than a reading gap - the `quiet-possession` topic_key did not exist when California was done. title: Wording California Dictates Word for Word
bodyText: California prescribes the exact words for more lease statements and notices than any other state in this library, and in several places the type size too. In the lease itself: the rent-cap and just-cause notice, or instead the exemption statement for an exempt property, both quoted verbatim and the first in at least 12-point type; the tenant acknowledgment where the tenant supplies their own refrigerator; and the owner, manager and rent-payment details. Delivered with or before the lease: the flood-hazard disclosure in at least 8-point type, the bed-bug notice in at least 10-point type, the water-submeter disclosure in at least 10-point type, and the mould booklet the Department of Public Health publishes. In the automatic-renewal clause, the renewal terms must be in at least 8-point boldface. Notices during and after the tenancy have their own prescribed wording: the pesticide caution statement, the abandoned-property statement that must appear in your termination notice, the third-party rent acknowledgment, the abandoned-property claim notice, and the statements a tenant uses to end a tenancy after abuse or violence. Use the statute's words, not a paraphrase.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: No California statute says whether a tenant may install a security camera or a video doorbell, so the lease controls, through its rules on alterations and on attaching things to the building. Two things make this more sensitive in California than almost anywhere else. Privacy is an inalienable right under the state constitution, and California courts apply it to private conduct, not only to the government - so a camera covering a shared hallway, a neighbour's door or a yard is a live issue even between neighbours. And California requires the consent of everyone involved before a confidential conversation is recorded, so a device that captures audio outside the tenant's own space raises a criminal-law question, not just a lease one. A reasonable approach is to allow a device that views only the tenant's own entry and requires no drilling, and to ask for written consent otherwise.

title: Damage the Tenant Causes: What You Can Recover
bodyText: California law already answers most of this, which is why this library offers no separate tenant-caused-damage clause for California. Repair costs: a tenant must use ordinary care and must repair any deterioration or injury caused by the tenant's own want of ordinary care, so the claim is statutory, and the deposit may be applied to repairing damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. Rent while the home is repaired: the tenant's right to end the lease after destruction or serious damage applies only where the damage was not the tenant's fault, the repair-and-deduct remedy is unavailable to a tenant who has breached their own upkeep duties, and the rule barring you from demanding rent for a substandard home does not apply where the tenant caused the condition. So rent generally continues to run where the tenant is at fault. Lost rent if the lease ends: if the tenant breaches and abandons, or you lawfully terminate for breach, the statutory damages measure covers the rent for the balance of the term less what the tenant proves you could reasonably have avoided - the lease's Early Termination clause states it. Adding a no-abatement sentence is not worth the risk here, because the habitability rights it sits next to cannot be waived.
notes: CA: PRESENT - the law covers it, so no lease clause is offered. SOP 1.31 rule 54t retro 2026-10-03, and this is the eighth topic California had no row for: `tenant-caused-damage` is active in 25 states and was missing here. `tenant-caused-damage-tn` WAS READ for comparison and deliberately NOT tagged. Each abatement or exit provision was checked separately for its own tenant-fault exception, as rule 54t requires, and California has one in every one checked: Civ. Code s1932(2) tenant termination on destruction or serious damage turns on the damage occurring without the lessee's fault; s1942(c) with s1941.2 withholds the repair-and-deduct remedy from a tenant in breach of their own upkeep duties; s1942.4's bar on demanding rent for a substandard dwelling does not apply where the tenant's violation of s1941.2 caused the condition. Repair-cost limb: Civ. Code ss1928 and 1929, read section-open on leginfo 2026-10-03; deposit limb s1950.5(b)(2) (security-deposit-use-ca). Lost-rent limb: s1951.2, already stated in early-termination-ca. LEGAL CALL, rule 76, made here and recorded: a no-abatement sentence of the kind tenant-caused-damage-tn carries would add little in California - rent already continues where the tenant is at fault - while sitting next to s1942.1, which voids any agreement waiving s1941 or s1942 rights, so a clause drafted even slightly too wide risks being void rather than merely narrowed. NOT READ: no case law on apportioning fault, and s1933 was not re-read at this retro.

title: Good Cause Eviction Law Notice
notes: NY: Prescribed statutory text, quoted verbatim from N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 231-c(1) (rule 59); the landlord fills in the blanks and marks the answers. 'A landlord as defined in subdivision two of section two hundred eleven of this chapter shall append to or incorporate into any initial lease, renewal lease, notice required pursuant to paragraph (a) of subdivision one of section two hundred twenty-six-c of this article, notice required pursuant to subdivision two of section seven hundred eleven of the real property actions and proceedings law, or petition pursuant to section seven hundred forty one of the real property actions and proceedings law, the following notice' (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 231-c(1)). 'Landlord' is 'any fee owner, lessor, sublessor, assignor, court appointed receiver, or any other person or entity receiving or entitled to receive rent for the occupancy of any housing accommodation or an agent of any of the foregoing' (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 211(2)), so the notice goes in every New York residential lease and renewal, including leases of units the Good Cause Eviction Law does not cover (answer 2.A covers a place outside New York City that has not opted in). Added by L. 2024, ch. 56, part HH, § 3; L. 2024, ch. 56, part HH, § 7(a): 'sections two, three, four, and five of this act shall take effect on the one hundred twentieth day after this act shall have become a law' (August 18, 2024, the date the compiled N.Y. title: Flood History and Risk Notice
bodyText:
Flood history and risk of the leased premises:
(a) The leased premises [are / are not / are partially] located in a Federal Emergency Management Agency ("FEMA") designated floodplain.
(b) The leased premises [are / are not / are partially] located in the Special Flood Hazard Area ("SFHA"; "100-year floodplain") according to FEMA's current Flood Insurance Rate Maps for the leased premises' area.
(c) The leased premises [are / are not / are partially] located in a Moderate Risk Flood Hazard Area ("500-year floodplain") according to FEMA's current Flood Insurance Rate Maps for the leased premises' area.
(d) Prior flood damage to the leased premises due to a natural flood event, such as heavy rainfall, coastal storm surge, tidal inundation, or river overflow, that Landlord knows or reasonably should know has occurred: [state 'none known' or describe each event and the nature of the damage].
"Flood insurance is available to renters through the Federal Emergency Management Agency's (FEMA's) National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) to cover your personal property and contents in the event of a flood. A standard renter's insurance policy does not typically cover flood damage. You are encouraged to examine your policy to determine whether you are covered."

title: Returned Checks / Dishonored Payments
bodyText: If a check, draft or similar instrument (other than a money order, bank cashier's check or certified check) Tenant gives Landlord for Rent is dishonored by Tenant's financial institution for insufficient funds or another cause not attributable to Landlord, Tenant will pay Landlord a dishonored check fee of {{nsf_fee}}, but not more than the greater of $20 or Landlord's actual costs, charges or fees for the return of that check. If that fee is more than $20, Landlord will give Tenant, on request, evidence that the fee equals Landlord's actual costs, charges or fees for the return of the dishonored check. Landlord may require that the dishonored payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are dishonored, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check or money order.
notes: NY: Replaces the base `returned-payments`, whose fee is ceiling-only ('not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law', rule 53) and so does not provide for a fee in the lease, as the statute's 'provided for in the lease' requires. N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 238-a(2-a)(a)-(b): no payment, fee or charge 'for the delivery of a check, draft or like instrument that was given in payment for rent and subsequently dishonored by the tenant's financial institution for insufficient funds', except that a landlord 'may demand any payment, fee, or charge from a tenant for the delivery of a dishonored check only if such payment, fee, or charge was provided for in the lease', and the fee may not exceed 'the actual costs, charges or fees incurred by landlord ... for the return of such dishonored check or the amount set forth in subdivision three of section 5-328 of the general obligations law, whichever is greater'; above that amount the landlord must 'provide to the tenant upon request evidence substantiating the equivalence'. N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 5-328(3)(a) sets 'the amount of twenty dollars'; N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 5-328(3)(b) repeats the rent rule and requires the charge to have been 'contracted for in the lease agreement ... in accordance with the requirements of subdivision two-a of section two hundred thirty-eight-a of the real property law'. 'Dishonored check' (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 238-a(2-a)(c); N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 5-328(1)(b)): 'not paid or is dishonored or is returned by such institution due to insufficient funds or other cause not attributable to the holder'. N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 238-a(2-a) was added, and N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 5-328(3) amended to add paragraph (b), by L. 2025, ch. 431 (A. 56-B), whose effective-date clause is in NY log §1.2; nysenate.gov prints the compiled text as current from 2025-10-17. Waiver void (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 238-a(3)). Builder cap (NY log §10): {{nsf_fee}} at most the greater of $20 or the landlord's actual returned-check costs. Requiring certified funds after a dishonored payment does not make electronic payment the only method (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-g). title: Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant will pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit), which is not more than one month's Rent. When Tenant moves out, Landlord may keep only the reasonable and itemized costs of: unpaid Rent; damage caused by Tenant beyond normal wear and tear; unpaid utility charges that this Lease makes payable directly to Landlord; and moving and storing Tenant's belongings. Landlord will not keep any part of the Security Deposit for ordinary wear and tear, for damage caused by a prior tenant, or for any condition, defect or damage noted in a move-in inspection agreement signed under this Lease. The Security Deposit does not relieve Tenant of the obligation to pay Rent when due.
notes: NY: Replaces the base `security-deposit-use`, which lets the deposit cover any 'Tenant default' and cleaning costs; New York's list of permitted retentions is closed (rule 53). N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a)(a): 'No deposit or advance shall exceed the amount of one month's rent', except a registered seasonal-use unit or an owner-occupied cooperative apartment (N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(4)-(6)). N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a)(b): 'The entire amount of the deposit or advance shall be refundable to the tenant upon the tenant's vacating of the premises except for an amount lawfully retained for the reasonable and itemized costs due to non-payment of rent, damage caused by the tenant beyond normal wear and tear, non-payment of utility charges payable directly to the landlord under the terms of the lease or tenancy, and moving and storage of the tenant's belongings. The landlord may not retain any amount of the deposit for costs relating to ordinary wear and tear of occupancy or damage caused by a prior tenant.' N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a)(c): no retention for 'any condition, defect, or damage noted in such agreement' (the move-in inspection agreement, `existing-condition-ny`). The deposit stays the tenant's money held in trust (N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-103(1); `edu-deposit-rules-ny`). Waiver void (N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law §§ 7-103(3), 7-108(3)). Cleaning is not a listed retention; dirt that amounts to damage beyond normal wear and tear falls under the damage item (Claude's reading; no case searched, NY log §1.4). N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a) does not apply in rent-controlled units, CCRCs, assisted living and the other facilities named in N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a); rent-stabilized units follow the parallel N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-107 (out of scope, `edu-scope-ny`). Builder cap (NY log §10): {{security_deposit}} plus any {{pet_deposit}} and any other deposit or advance (including prepaid last month's rent) at most {{monthly_rent}}. title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: Within 14 days after Tenant vacates the property, Landlord will give Tenant an itemized statement showing the basis for any amount of the Security Deposit Landlord keeps, and will return the rest of the Security Deposit, with any interest owed to Tenant. Tenant will give Landlord a forwarding address in writing when Tenant vacates. After either party gives notice of its intention to end the tenancy, Landlord will notify Tenant in writing, within a reasonable time, of Tenant's right to request an inspection before moving out and to be present at it, unless Tenant ends the tenancy on less than two weeks' notice.
notes: NY: Replaces the blank-states parent `security-deposit-return` (rule 25 family) and resolves the dormant lead `security-deposit-return-ny-hi` (left switched off; NY log §5). rule_type RECOMMENDED: New York requires the statement, refund and inspection notice but no lease text about them (rule 56). N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a)(e): 'Within fourteen days after the tenant has vacated the premises, the landlord shall provide the tenant with an itemized statement indicating the basis for the amount of the deposit retained, if any, and shall return any remaining portion of the deposit to the tenant. If a landlord fails to provide the tenant with the statement and deposit within fourteen days, the landlord shall forfeit any right to retain any portion of the deposit.' N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a)(d): 'Within a reasonable time after notification of either party's intention to terminate the tenancy, unless the tenant terminates the tenancy with less than two weeks' notice, the landlord shall notify the tenant in writing of the tenant's right to request an inspection before vacating the premises and of the tenant's right to be present at the inspection', with the inspection one to two weeks before the end, 48 hours' written notice, an itemized statement of proposed deductions and a chance to cure. The statute names no delivery method or forwarding-address rule; the forwarding-address request is the landlord-serving reason for the clause. Interest: N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-103(2), (2-a) (`deposit-bank-notice-ny`). Burden of proof on the landlord; willful violation, punitive damages up to twice the deposit (N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a)(f)-(g); `edu-deposit-penalty-ny`). Landlord may keep, as administration expenses, a sum equal to one percent per year on the Security Deposit; the rest of the interest belongs to Tenant and will be [paid to Tenant once a year / held in trust and paid when the Security Deposit is returned or applied].]
notes: NY: Use when the deposit is put in a bank, which is mandatory for a building with six or more family dwelling units. N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-103(2): 'Whenever the person receiving money so deposited or advanced shall deposit such money in a banking organization, such person shall thereupon notify in writing each of the persons making such security deposit or advance, giving the name and address of the banking organization in which the deposit of security money is made, and the amount of such deposit. Deposits in a banking organization pursuant to the provisions of this subdivision shall be made in a banking organization having a place of business within the state. If the person depositing such security money in a banking organization shall deposit same in an interest bearing account, he shall be entitled to receive, as administration expenses, a sum equivalent to one per cent per annum upon the security money so deposited, which shall be in lieu of all other administrative and custodial expenses. The balance of the interest ... shall either be held in trust ... until repaid or applied for the use or rental of the leased premises, or annually paid to the person making the deposit of security money.' N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-103(2-a): for 'property containing six or more family dwelling units', the deposit must be in 'an interest bearing account in a banking organization within the state which account shall earn interest at a rate which shall be the prevailing rate'. N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-103(2-b): interest collectible at a lease termination between interest dates is paid over. The written notice can be the lease section when the bank is chosen before signing (rule 46); if Landlord deposits later or moves the money, a separate written notice is still owed. Waiver void (N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-103(3)). A grantee is deemed to know of a deposit placed in a bank under N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-103(2-a) within six months before closing (N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(2)(b)(i)). title: Move-In Inspection and Condition of Property
bodyText: After this Lease is signed and before Tenant moves in, Tenant may inspect the property with Landlord or Landlord's agent. If Tenant asks for the inspection, Landlord and Tenant will sign, before Tenant moves in, a written agreement describing the condition of the property and specifically noting any existing defects or damage. Landlord will not keep any part of the Security Deposit for a condition, defect or damage noted in that agreement. Landlord will deliver possession of the property in the same or better condition than the condition described in that agreement, except for ordinary wear and tear.
notes: NY: Replaces the base `existing-condition`, whose acknowledgment that the property 'is in good order and repair' at signing stands in for the inspection-and-agreement process New York prescribes (rules 42, 53; MT log §10 item 7). N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a)(c): 'After initial lease signing but before the tenant begins occupancy, the landlord shall offer the tenant the opportunity to inspect the premises with the landlord or the landlord's agent to determine the condition of the property. If the tenant requests such inspection, the parties shall execute a written agreement before the tenant begins occupancy of the unit attesting to the condition of the property and specifically noting any existing defects or damages. Upon the tenant's vacating of the premises, the landlord may not retain any amount of the deposit or advance due to any condition, defect, or damage noted in such agreement. The agreement shall be admissible as evidence of the condition of the premises at the beginning of occupancy only in proceedings related to the return or amount of the security deposit.' The clause is the written offer, timed as the statute times it ('After initial lease signing'); it serves the landlord by fixing the move-in baseline for deposit deductions. Waiver void (N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(3)). title: Amounts Due Upfront
bodyText: Before or when this Lease begins, Tenant will pay Landlord only: the first month's Monthly Rent ({{monthly_rent}}); the Security Deposit ({{security_deposit}}) and any other deposit or advance this Lease requires (such as a pet deposit or prepaid rent), which together are not more than one month's Rent; and, if Landlord ran a background or credit check on Tenant, one fee for all background and credit checks of no more than their actual cost or $20, whichever is less, which Landlord will waive if Tenant gave Landlord a copy of a background or credit check conducted within the past 30 days, and which is due only after Landlord gives Tenant a copy of the check and the receipt or invoice from the company that ran it. [specify the due date for each amount]. A deposit or advance (including any prepaid rent) is held, applied, credited and returned as this Lease and applicable law provide.
notes: NY: Replaces the base `due-at-signing`, whose bracketed example lists a pet deposit and last month's rent on top of a full security deposit, which New York's one-month cap and fee ban forbid (rule 53). N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 238-a(1)(a): 'Except in instances where statutes or regulations provide for a payment, fee or charge, no landlord, lessor, sub-lessor or grantor may demand any payment, fee, or charge for the processing, review or acceptance of an application, or demand any other payment, fee or charge before or at the beginning of the tenancy, except background checks and credit checks as provided by paragraph (b) of this subdivision'. The security deposit is a payment a statute provides for (N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a)(a) regulates it; Claude's reading); first month's rent is the rent the lease itself reserves, not a fee for the tenancy's start (Claude's reading; Attorney General guidance not read, NY log §1.4). N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 238-a(1)(b): the check fee is 'no more than the actual cost of the background check and credit check or twenty dollars, whichever is less', waived if the applicant gives a check from the past 30 days, and collectible only if the landlord gives the applicant a copy of the check and the receipt or invoice (`edu-application-fee-ny`). N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a)(a): 'No deposit or advance shall exceed the amount of one month's rent'; the one-month cap applies to all deposits and advances together, and a prepaid last month's rent is an 'advance', while the first month's rent paid at the start is the rent for that month, not money held as security or applied to a later payment (Claude's reading of 'deposit or advance', which N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-103(1) defines as money 'deposited or advanced ... as security for performance of the contract or agreement or to be applied to payments upon such contract or agreement when due'; no case searched, NY log §1.4). Waiver void (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 238-a(3)). Builder cap (NY log §10). title: Occupants
bodyText: The property will be occupied by {{tenant_names}}, members of their immediate families, and {{occupant_names}}. In addition to the persons named above, as New York law allows, if this Lease is signed by one Tenant, Tenant may also share the property with one additional occupant and that occupant's dependent children, so long as Tenant or Tenant's spouse occupies the property as a primary residence; if this Lease is signed by two or more Tenants, the total number of Tenants and occupants (not counting occupants' dependent children) may not exceed the number of Tenants named in this Lease (Landlord's consent to the persons named above is in addition to this allowance), and at least one Tenant or a Tenant's spouse must occupy the property as a primary residence. Tenant will tell Landlord the name of any occupant within 30 days after that person begins living at the property, or within 30 days after Landlord asks. No occupant acquires any right to stay at the property after Tenant leaves, or any other tenancy right, without Landlord's express written permission. Nothing in this Section permits occupancy beyond what federal, state or local occupancy limits allow.
notes: NY: Replaces the base `permitted-occupants`, whose 'will be occupied only by' the named persons restricts occupancy in a way New York voids (rule 53). N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(2): 'It shall be unlawful for a landlord to restrict occupancy of residential premises, by express lease terms or otherwise, to a tenant or tenants or to such tenants and immediate family. Any such restriction in a lease or rental agreement entered into or renewed before or after the effective date of this section shall be unenforceable as against public policy.' N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(3) (one tenant: 'the tenant, immediate family of the tenant, one additional occupant, and dependent children of the occupant provided that the tenant or the tenant's spouse occupies the premises as his primary residence'); N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(4) (two or more tenants: total tenants and occupants, excluding occupants' dependent children, may not exceed 'the number of tenants specified in the current lease or rental agreement', with a tenant or spouse in primary residence); N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(5) (name within 30 days after occupancy begins or after the landlord's request); N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(6) (no right to continued occupancy without 'express written permission of the landlord'); N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(7) (waiver void); N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(8) (landlord may restrict occupancy to comply with federal, state or local occupancy laws). Remedies: injunction, actual damages, costs (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(9)). 'Tenant' includes only parties to the lease and certain statutory tenants (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(1)(a)); 'occupant' is a person other than a tenant or immediate family occupying with the tenant's consent (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(1)(b)). Occupancy limits must not discriminate on familial status (N.Y. Exec. Law § 296(5)(a); N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 237-a). title: Guests
bodyText: Tenant may have guests for reasonable, temporary stays. A guest who begins living at the property is an occupant, and Tenant will tell Landlord that person's name within 30 days, as this Lease's Occupants Section requires. Occupancy by guests and occupants together may not exceed what this Lease's Occupants Section and applicable law allow. Tenant is responsible for the conduct of Tenant's guests at the property.
notes: NY: Replaces the base `guest-policy` (and is the New York answer for `guest-policy-day-limit`, not tagged), whose rule that a guest staying beyond a set period needs 'Landlord's prior written consent' would require consent for the one additional occupant New York lets a sole tenant add without consent (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(3), (5); rule 53). N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(5): 'The tenant shall inform the landlord of the name of any occupant within thirty days following the commencement of occupancy by such person or within thirty days following a request by the landlord.' N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-f(7): a lease provision purporting to waive the section 'is null and void'. No New York statute defines a guest or caps a guest stay (NY battery 35 (guest / visitor definition or limit): 19 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 1 synthetic)); a guest who stays only temporarily is not an occupant (Claude's reading; no case searched, NY log §1.4). Responsibility for guests' conduct: N.Y. Mult. Dwell. Law § 78(1) and N.Y. Mult. Resid. Law § 174 (tenant liable for violations caused by a guest's wilful act or negligence). title: Subletting and Assignment
bodyText: Tenant will not assign this Lease without Landlord's prior written consent. Landlord may withhold consent to an assignment without cause, but if Landlord unreasonably withholds consent, Landlord will release Tenant from this Lease on Tenant's request on 30 days' notice. If the property is in a building with four or more residential units, Tenant may sublet the property with Landlord's prior written consent, which Landlord will not unreasonably withhold; Tenant will request consent by certified mail, return receipt requested, with the information New York Real Property Law section 226-b requires, and Landlord's failure to respond within 30 days after the request, or after the additional information Landlord reasonably asks for within 10 days, whichever is later, is consent. In any other building, Tenant will not sublet without Landlord's prior written consent. A subletting does not release Tenant from any obligation under this Lease. In a building with three or fewer residential units, Tenant will not rent the property, or any part of it, for stays of fewer than 30 consecutive days through a short-term rental service such as Airbnb or VRBO, or otherwise. In a building with four or more residential units, any such rental is a sublet that needs Landlord's consent under this Section. A sublet or assignment that does not follow this Section and New York Real Property Law section 226-b is a substantial breach of this Lease.
notes: NY: Replaces the base `no-sublet-assign`, whose 'sole discretion' for any sublet or assignment contradicts New York's statutory rights (rule 53). N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 226-b(1): 'Unless a greater right to assign is conferred by the lease, a tenant renting a residence may not assign his lease without the written consent of the owner, which consent may be unconditionally withheld without cause provided that the owner shall release the tenant from the lease upon request of the tenant upon thirty days notice if the owner unreasonably withholds consent which release shall be the sole remedy of the tenant.' N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 226-b(2)(a): 'A tenant renting a residence pursuant to an existing lease in a dwelling having four or more residential units shall have the right to sublease his premises subject to the written consent of the landlord in advance of the subletting. Such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.' N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 226-b(2)(b)-(c): certified-mail request with seven listed items; landlord may ask for more information within ten days; 'Landlord's failure to send such a notice shall be deemed to be a consent'; the tenant remains liable. N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 226-b(5): 'Any sublet or assignment which does not comply with the provisions of this section shall constitute a substantial breach of lease or tenancy.' N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 226-b(6): waiver void. N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 226-b(3): not public housing or cooperative proprietary leases; N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 226-b(4): rent-regulated units follow their own laws. The short-term rental sentences are a lease restriction, not a statement of law. In a building of four or more units an outright ban would cut down the N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 226-b(2)(a) sublet right, which N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 226-b(6) makes void to waive, so there a short-term rental is treated as a sublet needing consent; whether a short-term purpose is a reasonable ground to withhold consent is not settled by the statute (case law not searched, NY log §1.4); New York City's short-term rental rules (multiple dwelling occupancy for fewer than 30 days, N.Y. Mult. Dwell. Law § 4(8)) and local registration laws are flagged, not resolved (rule 3). In a building of three or fewer units the sublet right does not apply (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 226-b(2)(a)), so consent may be withheld. title: Holdover
bodyText: If this Lease ends and Tenant remains in possession without a right under applicable law to stay (for example, a right to renewal or to continued occupancy under New York's Good Cause Eviction Law), Landlord may proceed as the law allows to recover possession and may recover the reasonable value of Tenant's use and occupancy of the property for the period Tenant remains, which will be not less than the Monthly Rent apportioned daily. Payments Landlord accepts as use and occupancy, and Rent Landlord accepts after starting a court proceeding to recover possession, do not create a new tenancy. If Landlord otherwise accepts Rent for any period after this Lease ends, Tenant's continued occupancy is a month-to-month tenancy on the same terms, which either party may end only as applicable law provides.
notes: NY: Replaces `holdover-ca` (and the base `holdover`, ceiling-only, rule 53) for New York, whose 'If Tenant does not vacate the property by the end of the Term ... may recover the actual damages caused by Tenant's continued possession' treats every tenant who stays as a wrongdoer, which is untrue where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies: no landlord shall remove a covered tenant 'notwithstanding that the tenant has no written lease or that the lease or other rental agreement has expired or otherwise terminated, except upon order of a court ... in which the petitioner ... has established one of the following grounds as good cause' (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 216(1); rule 41). Use and occupancy: 'The landlord may recover a reasonable compensation for the use and occupation of real property' (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 220); after a summary proceeding the landlord may recover by action 'the reasonable value of the use and occupation to the time when the warrant was issued, for any period of time with respect to which the agreement does not make any provision for payment of rent' (N.Y. Real Prop. Acts. Law § 749(3)). Acceptance of rent: 'if the landlord shall accept rent for any period subsequent to the expiration of such term, then, unless an agreement either express or implied is made providing otherwise, the tenancy created by the acceptance of such rent shall be a tenancy from month to month commencing on the first day after the expiration of such term' (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 232-c); but acceptance of rent after a holdover proceeding is commenced does not end it (N.Y. Real Prop. Acts. Law § 711(1)). Double rent applies by statute where the tenant gave notice of intention to quit and does not leave on that date (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 229; `edu-holdover-ny`); the clause sets no premium rate (rule 54; `edu-holdover-rate-ny`). The 'not less than the Monthly Rent apportioned daily' floor is a measure of use and occupancy the landlord may ask a court to award, not a self-executing charge (Claude's reading; no case searched, NY log §1.4). title: Surrender at End of Term
bodyText: When this Lease ends, unless Tenant has a right under applicable law to remain in possession (for example, a right to continued occupancy under New York's Good Cause Eviction Law), Tenant will surrender possession of the property and return all keys to Landlord. The property will be left in the same condition as at the start of the Term, except for ordinary wear and tear and any condition noted in a move-in inspection agreement, and free of all personal property of Tenant and any occupants. If Tenant leaves personal property at the property after surrendering possession, Landlord will send Tenant written notice at Tenant's forwarding address, or if none, at the property and Tenant's last known address, describing the property and stating that Landlord will dispose of it if Tenant does not claim it within [at least 30] days after the notice; Landlord will hold it safely during that time and may deduct the reasonable cost of moving and storing it as this Lease's Security Deposit terms allow.
notes: NY: Replaces the surrender-at-end-of-term clauses for New York. The base and its `-ks-ne` and `-mn-nd` variants each require surrender 'Upon the expiration ... of this Lease', untrue where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies (N.Y. Real Prop. Law §§ 215, 216(1): removal only on a court order on a listed ground, even after the lease has expired; rule 41); the base's 'to the extent permitted ... be treated as abandoned' sets no New York procedure and the variants point to a property section New York has no statute for. New York has no statute on a departed tenant's abandoned property (NY battery 25 (tenant property left behind (abandoned, technical)): 0 hits, control 0; known positives passed (0 real sections, 2 synthetic)); the notice-and-hold procedure is a lease term the parties may set (rule 54, measures the statute does not set), chosen so a landlord acts as a careful bailee (Claude's drafting; no case searched, NY log §1.4). Moving and storage of belongings is a permitted deposit retention (N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a)(b)). A person who knowingly holds the property of a senior or disabled tenant who lawfully ended the lease under N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 227-a to subject it to a claim for later rent commits a misdemeanor (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 227-a(3)); when a warrant is executed, the officer must give at least 14 days' notice and check for companion animals (N.Y. Real Prop. Acts. Law § 749(2)(a)-(b)), but no New York statute sets what happens to belongings left after execution. The '[at least 30]' bracket is a hand-filled landlord choice with a floor (rule 60). title: Maintenance and Repairs
bodyText: Subject to Tenant's own maintenance obligations under this Lease, Landlord will keep the property, including its structure, roof, systems and the appliances, fixtures and equipment Landlord supplies, fit for human habitation and in good repair, and will make required repairs within a reasonable time after learning of the need. Tenant will notify Landlord promptly in writing of any condition requiring repair. If the need for a repair was caused by the misconduct, wilful act or negligence of Tenant, a member of Tenant's household or Tenant's guest, Landlord will still make the repair and Tenant will reimburse Landlord for its reasonable cost.
notes: NY: Replaces the base `landlord-maintenance`, whose 'except where repair is necessary due to improper use by Tenant' excuses the owner from repairs that a multiple dwelling owner must make whoever caused them (rule 53). N.Y. Mult. Dwell. Law § 78(1): 'Every multiple dwelling ... and every part thereof ... shall be kept in good repair. The owner shall be responsible for compliance with the provisions of this section; but the tenant also shall be liable if a violation is caused by his own wilful act, assistance or negligence or that of any member of his family or household or his guest.' N.Y. Mult. Resid. Law § 174 (same, for multiple dwellings outside the Multiple Dwelling Law's cities). Warranty of habitability: the premises are 'fit for human habitation and for the uses reasonably intended by the parties'; a condition 'caused by the misconduct of the tenant or lessee or persons under his direction or control' is not a breach (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-b(1)); waiver void (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 235-b(2)). Reimbursement for tenant-caused damage rests on the tenant's liability (N.Y. Mult. Dwell. Law § 78(1); N.Y. Mult. Resid. Law § 174) and on damages for breach; the cost is not rent and cannot be sought in a summary proceeding (N.Y. Real Prop. Acts. Law § 702(1)). title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, beginning with the second month of the Term and due with each Monthly Rent payment. Any pet deposit counts toward the one-month limit on all deposits under this Lease's Security Deposit Section. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet, and will indemnify Landlord against claims arising from Tenant's pet, except claims caused by or resulting from the negligence of Landlord or Landlord's agents, servants or employees. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or a danger to people or property, on written notice giving Tenant a reasonable time to remove it. This Section does not apply to an assistance animal, which this Lease's Service and Assistance Animals Section governs.
notes: NY: Replaces the base `pet-policy`, which takes a pet deposit 'if applicable' on top of the security deposit and lets Landlord enter and remove a pet 'without liability to Tenant' (rule 53). N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108(1-a)(a): 'No deposit or advance shall exceed the amount of one month's rent' (all deposits together; `edu-pet-deposit-ny`). An indemnity reaching the landlord's own negligence would be an agreement 'exempting the lessor from liability for damages for injuries to person or property caused by or resulting from the negligence of the lessor', void under N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 5-321; the carve-out keeps the indemnity to the tenant's pet. Removing an occupant's possessions is listed among conduct that prevents lawful occupancy or induces the occupant to vacate (N.Y. Real Prop. Acts. Law § 768(1)(a)(iii)); the clause removes a pet only by the tenant on notice. Pet rent starts with the second month so that nothing for the pet is demanded 'before or at the beginning of the tenancy' (N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 238-a(1)(a)). Pet rent is not 'rent' for a summary proceeding, which covers only 'the monthly or weekly amount charged in consideration for the use and occupation of a dwelling' (N.Y. Real Prop. Acts. Law § 702(1)), so unpaid pet rent is collected by action, not eviction (Claude's reading). New York City's pet law (N.Y.C. Admin. Code § 27-2009.1) and other local rules are flagged, not resolved (rule 3). Assistance animals: N.Y. Exec. Law § 296(18)(2).
