title: Holdover Charge
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession after this Lease ends, whether at the end of the Term or on an earlier termination under this Lease or Missouri law (other than a termination for nonpayment of Rent), and Landlord has not agreed in writing to a continued tenancy or accepted Rent for one, then, in place of any actual damages for Tenant's continued possession (including the actual damages and reasonable rental value described in the Holdover section of this Lease), Tenant will pay Landlord a holdover charge of {{holdover_daily_rate}} for each day Tenant remains in possession. Landlord and Tenant agree that Landlord's loss from a holdover, including delay in making the property available to a new tenant, is difficult to estimate accurately in advance, that this charge is a reasonable estimate of that loss, and that it is not a penalty. For any day for which Landlord recovers a double measure that Missouri law provides for a holdover, Landlord will not also recover this charge for that day. Landlord's acceptance of a holdover charge is not acceptance of Rent for a continued tenancy. This Section does not limit Landlord's right to recover possession, unpaid Rent and other amounts due for the period before this Lease ended, or damages for harm to the property.
notes: MO: Optional clause (rule 54, as amended at the NE sync; MO retro, SOP 1.42). Missouri's three statutory holdover measures are each conditional, so they leave a gap: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.080 (double the yearly value) applies only where a tenant 'for life or years' 'shall willfully hold over' and only 'after demand made and notice in writing given, requiring the possession'; Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.100 and Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.110 (double the rent reserved) apply only after the tenant's own written notice of intent to quit; Mo. Rev. Stat. § 534.330(1) (double the damages found and double the monthly rents from judgment until restitution) applies only in an unlawful detainer judgment, which requires a willful holdover and a written demand for possession (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 534.030(1)). Not covered: a good-faith or non-willful holdover, the days before any written demand or notice, and a holdover that ends without a judgment. For those cases holdover-ca gives actual damages, including the reasonable rental value; this clause lets the landlord fix a daily charge instead. Rule 53: the trigger reaches an earlier termination, so a termination for nonpayment is excluded, because a tenant in a rent-and-possession case can stop the proceedings by tendering all rent in arrears and costs on the judgment date, and can stay execution by satisfying the money judgment before it becomes final (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.160); a daily charge from the termination would raise the price of that statutory right. Non-stacking sentence: where a statutory double measure is recovered for a day, this charge is not also recovered, so the charge cannot be doubled on top of a Mo. Rev. Stat. § 534.330 award. Model: holdover-rate-nc (GA family, nonpayment excluded). Variable: existing {{holdover_daily_rate}}; the builder should prompt for a figure that approximates the landlord's actual daily loss (for example the daily Rent plus re-letting delay costs). Whether Missouri courts enforce a stipulated holdover rate as liquidated damages rather than a penalty is case law, not read. Not a default. title: Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections
bodyText:
NOTICE OF DOMESTIC ABUSE PROTECTIONS
(1) As provided in section 106.50 (5m) (dm) of the Wisconsin statutes, a tenant has a defense to an eviction action if the tenant can prove that the landlord knew, or should have known, the tenant is a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault, or stalking and that the eviction action is based on conduct related to domestic abuse, sexual assault, or stalking committed by either of the following:
(a) A person who was not the tenant’s invited guest.
(b) A person who was the tenant’s invited guest, but the tenant has done either of the following:
1. Sought an injunction barring the person from the premises.
2. Provided a written statement to the landlord stating that the person will no longer be an invited guest of the tenant and the tenant has not subsequently invited the person to be the tenant’s guest.
(2) A tenant who is a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault, or stalking may have the right to terminate the rental agreement in certain limited situations, as provided in section 704.16 of the Wisconsin statutes. If the tenant has safety concerns, the tenant should contact a local victim service provider or law enforcement agency.
(3) A tenant is advised that this notice is only a summary of the tenant’s rights and the specific language of the statutes governs in all instances.
notes: WI: Required in every residential rental agreement: 'A residential rental agreement shall include the following notice in the agreement or in an addendum to the agreement' (Wis. Stat. § 704.14). Body is the statutory notice verbatim, including its own section references and curly apostrophes (rule 59; checked by script). A rental agreement that allows the landlord to terminate the tenancy 'for a crime committed in relation to the rental property' and lacks this notice is void and unenforceable (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(10); Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.08(10)); the court of appeals held void under Wis. Stat. § 704.44(10) a lease that lacked the Wis. Stat. § 704.14 notice and barred knowingly permitting use of the premises for an unlawful purpose, together with a general termination-for-breach term (Koble Investments v. Marquardt, 2024 WI App 26, as the site's annotation and 2026 WI 19, ¶ 23 report), and the supreme court reversed on other grounds without deciding that point: 'We do not need to resolve this issue' (Koble Investments v. Marquardt, 2026 WI 19, ¶¶ 24-25). The question is open. title: Code Violations and Habitability Conditions
bodyText: Before this Lease was signed and before any earnest money or security deposit was accepted, Landlord disclosed to Tenant the following. (1) Building or housing code violations that Landlord actually knows of, that affect the dwelling unit or a common area of the premises, that present a significant threat to Tenant's health or safety, and that have not been corrected: [describe each violation, or state "None"]. (2) Any of the following conditions that Landlord knows of or could know of on the basis of a reasonable inspection: the dwelling unit lacks hot or cold running water; heating facilities serving the dwelling unit are not in safe operating condition or cannot maintain a temperature of at least 67 degrees Fahrenheit (19 degrees Celsius) in all living areas during all seasons of the year in which the unit may be occupied; the dwelling unit is not served by electricity, or its electrical system is not in safe operating condition; structural or other conditions in the dwelling unit or premises constitute a substantial hazard to Tenant's health or safety or create an unreasonable risk of personal injury from reasonably foreseeable use other than negligent use or abuse by Tenant; the dwelling unit is not served by plumbing facilities in good operating condition; or the dwelling unit is not served by sewage disposal facilities in good operating condition: [describe each condition that exists, or state "None"].
notes: WI: The disclosures must be made 'Before entering into a rental agreement or accepting any earnest money or security deposit from the prospective tenant' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)); the code-violation limb is also a statutory duty (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(bm)), and the habitability list in ATCP § 134.04(2)(b)1.-6. is restated condition by condition. The Lease is the vehicle only if it is furnished before signing and before any deposit (ATCP § 134.03(1)); otherwise give the same disclosure separately and earlier. title: Use of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit). When Tenant vacates the property, Landlord may withhold from the Security Deposit only amounts reasonably necessary to pay for: (1) tenant damage, waste, or neglect of the premises; (2) unpaid rent for which Tenant is legally responsible, subject to Landlord's duty to mitigate under Wis. Stat. § 704.29; (3) payment Tenant owes under this Lease for utility service provided by Landlord but not included in the rent; (4) payment Tenant owes for direct utility service provided by a government-owned utility, to the extent Landlord becomes liable for Tenant's nonpayment; (5) unpaid monthly municipal permit fees assessed against Tenant by a local unit of government under Wis. Stat. § 66.0435(3), to the extent Landlord becomes liable for Tenant's nonpayment; and (6) any other payment for a reason provided in a separate written document entitled "NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS" that Landlord specifically identified with Tenant before Tenant entered into this Lease. Landlord will not withhold any amount for normal wear and tear, or for other damages or losses for which Tenant cannot reasonably be held responsible under applicable law. The Security Deposit does not relieve Tenant of the obligation to pay Rent when due.
notes: WI: Replaces the base `security-deposit-use`, which lets Landlord apply the deposit to 'remedy a Tenant default' and to cleaning costs: Wisconsin's withholding list is closed ('may withhold from the full amount of the security deposit only amounts reasonably necessary to pay for any of the following', Wis. Stat. § 704.28(1); Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.06(3)(a)), and anything else needs a nonstandard rental provision 'provided to the tenant in a separate written document entitled “NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS.”' and specifically identified before the tenant enters into the agreement (Wis. title: Returned Checks / Dishonored Payments
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned unpaid or dishonored for any reason, including insufficient funds, a closed account, or a stop-payment order, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of {{nsf_fee}}, and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check, or money order. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are returned unpaid, Landlord may require that all future payments of Rent be made by cashier's check, certified check, or money order.
notes: WI: Replaces the base `returned-payments`, whose fee 'not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' is ceiling-only wording that hides that Wisconsin sets no figure (rule 53): no Wisconsin statute caps a landlord's returned-payment fee for residential rent (WI battery 4 (returned / dishonored payment fee): 26 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 1 synthetic)) (WI battery 5 (returned check civil liability / penalty statute): 18 hits, control 0; known positives passed (0 real sections, 1 synthetic)). The caps found apply to credit: § 422.202(1)(d) ('a charge not to exceed $15 for each check presented for payment to a creditor which is returned unsatisfied' in a consumer credit transaction other than open-end credit; (2m)(a) for open-end plans), payday lenders (§ 138.14) and electric cooperative credit (§ 185.995(2)(b)3., $30). A lease with monthly rent is not an agreement to defer payment (Koble Investments v. Marquardt, 2026 WI 19, ¶¶ 4, 15-16), so on that reasoning the § 422.202 cap does not reach the fee (Claude's reading). The issuer of a worthless check is separately liable under Wis. Stat. § 943.245 (exemplary damages plus attorney fees capped at $500 per violation, § 943.245(3)), which this clause neither invokes nor waives. The fee is not a standard security-deposit withholding (Wis. Stat. § 704.28(1)); deducting it needs `nrp-deposit-withholding-wi`. Collecting the fee under a lease with monthly rent is not governed by Wis. Stat. § 427.104 (Koble Investments v. Marquardt, 2026 WI 19, ¶ 4). Uses the existing variable {{nsf_fee}} (NY). bodyText: Landlord will not store any items of personal property that Tenant leaves behind when Tenant removes from the premises, or if Tenant is evicted from the premises, except that Landlord will hold any prescription medication or prescription medical equipment Tenant leaves behind for 7 days from the date Landlord discovers it and will promptly return it if Tenant asks for it before Landlord disposes of it. title: Automatic Renewal
bodyText: This Lease will be automatically renewed for a further term of [length of renewal term] on the same terms unless Tenant or Landlord gives the other written notice of nonrenewal at least [number] days before the end of the Term. This automatic renewal provision is not enforceable against Tenant unless Landlord gives Tenant separate written notice, in a manner Wis. Stat. § 704.21 allows, calling Tenant's attention to this provision: (1) at least 15 days but not more than 30 days before the last day for Tenant to give notice of nonrenewal; and (2) at least 15 days but not more than 30 days before the renewal takes effect.
notes: WI: Option under rule 54. An automatic renewal provision 'is not enforceable against the tenant unless the lessor, at least 15 days but not more than 30 days prior to the time specified for the giving of such notice to the lessor, gives to the tenant written notice in the same manner as specified in s. 704.21' (Wis. Stat. § 704.15); the DATCP rule bars enforcing one unless 'the tenant was given separate written notice of the pending automatic renewal or extension at least 15 days, but no more than 30 days before its stated effective date' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(3)). Rule 31: the two count from different dates; the clause commits Landlord to both windows, so it complies with either reading. Whether ATCP § 134.09(3) survives Wis. title: Holdover
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession without Landlord's consent after this Lease expires, or after the tenancy is terminated by notice or by agreement, Landlord may proceed in any manner permitted by law to remove Tenant and may recover the damages Landlord suffers because Tenant failed to vacate on time. Unless Landlord proves greater damages, those damages are at least twice the rental value of the property, apportioned on a daily basis, for the time Tenant remains in possession; rental value means the amount for which the property might reasonably have been rented, but not less than the Rent actually paid or payable for the prior rental period. If, before starting proceedings to remove Tenant, Landlord accepts Rent for a period after this Lease expires or otherwise shows an intent to allow Tenant to remain, Tenant becomes a month-to-month tenant (or, if the Rent under this Lease is weekly or daily, a periodic tenant on that basis) on the same terms as this Lease, except any right to renew or extend this Lease, any right to purchase the property, and any right to be offered the property before a sale; that tenancy may be ended by the notice Wis. Stat. § 704.19 requires.
notes: WI: Replaces the base `holdover`, whose 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' is ceiling-only (rule 53), and `holdover-ca`, whose 'actual damages' understates the statute. Damages: 'In absence of proof of greater damages, the landlord shall recover as minimum damages twice the rental value apportioned on a daily basis for the time the tenant remains in possession', with 'rental value' defined (Wis. Stat. § 704.27); the measure applies after expiration, termination by notice from either party, or termination by agreement (same section), so the trigger matches (rule 53). Periodic tenancy on acceptance of rent: Wis. Stat. § 704.25(2)(b)-(c), (3) (the new tenancy does not carry an option to renew or purchase or a restriction on selling without first offering to the tenant); terminable under § 704.19 (§ 704.25(6)). Removal after termination by notice: Wis. Stat. § 704.23. Rule 54 holdover rate: a statutory minimum exists for every holdover, so no stipulated rate is offered (`edu-holdover-rate-wi`). title: Default by Tenant
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and does not pay within the time stated in a written notice Landlord gives as Wisconsin law requires, or if Tenant fails to comply with any other obligation under this Lease and does not remedy the failure after written notice, except where Wisconsin law permits Landlord to end the tenancy without giving Tenant an opportunity to remedy. Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise the rights and remedies available under applicable law, including terminating the tenancy, regaining possession through a judicial eviction under Wis. Stat. ch. 799, and recovering unpaid Rent and damages, less amounts lawfully withheld from the Security Deposit. Landlord will make reasonable efforts to rerent the property to mitigate damages as Wis. Stat. § 704.29 requires. This Lease does not require Tenant to pay Landlord's attorney fees or costs; costs and attorney fees are recoverable only as a court awards them under Wis. Stat. ch. 799 or 814.
notes: WI: Replaces the base `default-by-tenant`, which lets Landlord recover 'reasonable costs and expenses' and lets 'the prevailing party' recover attorneys' fees: a residential rental agreement is void and unenforceable if it 'Requires payment by the tenant of attorney fees or costs incurred by the landlord in any legal action or dispute arising under the rental agreement', except costs or fees under a court order under ch. 799 or 814 (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(4m); Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.08(4)); rule 49. `default-by-tenant-ks-ne` is not tagged for the same reason. Cure (rule 43): nonpayment and breach notices with and without a chance to remedy are in Wis. Stat. § 704.17(1p), (2), (3), (3m); 'provisions in the lease or rental agreement for termination contrary to this section are invalid except in leases for more than one year' (§ 704.17(5)(a)), and the clause promises nothing beyond the statute. Late fees owed for past-due rent are 'rent' for a nonpayment notice (§ 704.17(1g)); the library's late-fee sentence is kept as a uniform choice. Self-help is barred (§ 704.44(2m); ATCP § 134.09(7)); mitigation cannot be waived (§ 704.44(3m)). Collecting rent and damages under a lease with monthly rent is not governed by Wis. Stat. § 427.104 (Koble Investments v. Marquardt, 2026 WI 19, ¶ 4). rule_type RECOMMENDED: Wisconsin requires no default clause (rule 56). title: Early Termination
bodyText: If this Lease has a fixed Term, Tenant may end this Lease before the end of the Term by giving Landlord at least [number] days' written notice and paying Landlord, on or before the termination date stated in the notice, an early termination fee of [fixed dollar amount]. Tenant remains responsible for Rent and other obligations up to that termination date. If Tenant gives the notice and pays the fee as this Section requires, Landlord accepts Tenant's surrender of the property as of the termination date, and Tenant will owe no Rent for any later period. This option does not apply to a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, which ends on the notice Wisconsin law and this Lease provide. Nothing in this Section limits any right either party has under applicable law, including Tenant's rights under Wis. Stat. § 704.16 (domestic abuse, sexual assault, stalking, and threats of serious physical harm), Wis. Stat. § 704.165 (death of a tenant), Wis. Stat. § 321.62 and the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (military service), and Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4) (untenantable premises).
notes: WI: Replaces `early-termination-ks` and the base: their fee of 'one month's Rent ... or 30% of the remaining Rent ... whichever is greater' scales with the remaining term like liquidated damages, and a rental agreement is void if it 'Provides for an acceleration of rent payments in the event of tenant default ... or otherwise waives the landlord’s obligation to mitigate damages' (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(3m)); and their landlord limb for vacating 'without notifying Landlord' sits outside the termination rules of Wis. Stat. § 704.17, which a lease of one year or less cannot vary (§ 704.17(5)(a)). This version is an advance agreement to accept surrender for a fixed fee chosen by the landlord, the route Wis. Stat. § 704.29(1) recognizes ('unless the landlord has expressly agreed to accept a surrender of the premises and end the tenant’s liability'); an agreement to terminate a lease more than one year before its expiration must be in writing signed by both parties (§ 704.03(4)). No Wisconsin statute caps an early-termination fee (WI battery 81 (early termination fee): 5 hits, control 0; known positives passed (0 real sections, 1 synthetic)). Whether a court would treat a fixed fee as a penalty was not searched (WI log §1.4). Landlord-chosen figures are hand-filled brackets (Taylor, IN). title: Maintenance & Repairs
bodyText: Landlord will keep in a reasonable state of repair the portions of the property over which Landlord maintains control, keep in a reasonable state of repair the equipment under Landlord's control that supplies services Landlord has agreed to furnish, make all necessary structural repairs, repair or replace the plumbing, electrical wiring, machinery, appliances, and equipment furnished with the property when they are no longer in reasonable working condition, and comply with any local housing code that applies to the property. Landlord's duty does not include repairs made necessary by the negligence of, or improper use of the property by, Tenant. Tenant will pay the reasonable cost of repairing damage caused by the negligence or improper use of the property by Tenant or Tenant's guests or invitees. Tenant will notify Landlord promptly in writing of any condition requiring repair, and Landlord will make required repairs within a reasonable time.
notes: WI: Replaces the base `landlord-maintenance`, whose exception for repairs needed 'due to improper use by Tenant or a guest of Tenant' would excuse the landlord's repair duty for a guest's misuse; Wisconsin excuses only 'repairs made necessary by the negligence of, or improper use of the premises by, the tenant' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)), the duty cannot be waived (§ 704.07(1)), and a lease that 'Waives any statutory or other legal obligation on the part of the landlord ... to maintain the premises' is void (§ 704.44(8); Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.08(8)). Duties restated from § 704.07(2)(a)1.-5.; the landlord here also takes on the equipment repairs that § 704.07(2)(a)4. and (3)(b) would otherwise leave to a tenant or a local housing code, a choice that serves the tenant and is lawful. Cost recovery for guest damage is allowed: a lease may impose liability for damage caused by 'the tenant or the tenant’s guests or invitees' (§ 704.44(7)(b)); tenant reimbursement: § 704.07(3)(a). The body uses the statute's words 'guests or invitees' rather than 'occupant'. Rule 44: services 'expressly or impliedly agreed' trigger § 704.07(2)(a)2. title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord. Tenant will pay Landlord pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month and, if this Lease states one, a pet deposit of {{pet_deposit}}, which is part of the Security Deposit and will be held, withheld from, and returned only as this Lease's security deposit terms provide. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor, and disturbance caused by Tenant's pet, and will indemnify Landlord against claims arising from Tenant's pet, except claims arising from Landlord's own negligence. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern. If a pet becomes dangerous, or if Tenant dies, becomes incapacitated, or is otherwise unable to care for a pet and Landlord believes in good faith that the pet is being abused or neglected, Landlord may enter the property as Wisconsin law permits, including in a health or safety emergency, and may notify Tenant's emergency contact, animal control, a humane officer, or law enforcement.
notes: WI: Replaces the base `pet-policy`, whose entry and removal 'without liability to Tenant' risks being read as exculpating Landlord's negligence, which voids the whole agreement (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(6); Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.08(6); rule 52); the indemnity excludes Landlord's own negligence for the same reason. A pet deposit is part of the security deposit: 'Security deposit' means 'the total of all payments and deposits given by a tenant to the landlord as security for the performance of the tenant’s obligations' (ATCP § 134.02(11)) (WI battery 33 (pet deposit): 0 hits, control 0; known positives passed (0 real sections, 1 synthetic)). Entry: Wis. Stat. § 704.05(2); ATCP § 134.09(2)(b)2. (health or safety emergency). A pet is the tenant's property, and except under Wis. Stat. §§ 704.05(5), 704.11 and 779.43 'or by express agreement of the parties, a landlord has no right to a lien and is prohibited from seizing or holding a tenant’s property' (ATCP § 134.09(4)(a)); such an agreement must be a signed NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISION (ATCP § 134.09(4)(b)), so the clause does not let Landlord take or board the pet. A humane officer or law enforcement officer may take custody of an animal (Wis. Stat. § 173.13(1)). Assistance animals are not pets (`assistance-animal-accommodation`). title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle, or any other cause, and the damage is caused by the negligence or improper use of the property by Tenant, then Rent will not abate because of the damage and Tenant may not move out and stop paying Rent because of it. If the property is damaged by the acts or inaction of Tenant, or by the negligence or improper use of the property by Tenant's guests or invitees, Landlord may elect to repair the damage, and Tenant will reimburse Landlord's reasonable cost of the repair, or Landlord may allow Tenant to repair it and restore the property's appearance. If the tenancy ends early because of damage Tenant caused, Tenant remains liable for Rent and damages as Wis. Stat. § 704.29 allows, subject to Landlord's duty to mitigate.
notes: WI: Rule 54t. The untenantability remedies (moving out, rent abatement) are 'inapplicable if the damage or condition is caused by negligence or improper use by the tenant' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4), last sentence), so the first sentence restates the statute and is limited to Tenant's own negligence or improper use: extending it to guests would waive a § 704.07 right, which is void (§ 704.07(1)). Repair cost: 'If the premises are damaged ... due to the acts or inaction of the tenant, the landlord may elect to allow the tenant to remediate or repair ... However, the landlord may elect to undertake the remediation ... and in such case the tenant must reimburse the landlord for the reasonable cost thereof' (§ 704.07(3)(a)); liability for damage by guests or invitees is permitted (§ 704.44(7)(b)). Lost rent: § 704.29. Modeled on `tenant-caused-damage-tn`. Read section-open 2026-10-03 from the whole Wisconsin Statutes (2023-24, updated through 2025 Wis. title: Landlord Termination After Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, or other casualty that is not the result of the negligence or intentional act of Landlord, and the damage makes the property untenantable or Landlord reasonably determines that the repairs cannot be completed within [number] days, Landlord may end this Lease by written notice to Tenant, given by a method Wis. Stat. § 704.21 allows, within [number] days after the casualty. The Lease ends on the date stated in the notice, which will be at least [number] days after the notice is given, or on the date the notice is given if the property is untenantable. Rent is apportioned to the date the property became untenantable or the date the Lease ends, whichever is earlier, and Landlord will return any Rent paid in advance for a later period and the Security Deposit as this Lease provides. This Section does not limit Tenant's rights under Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4).
notes: WI: Option under rule 54 (landlord right the statute leaves to contract). For casualty not caused by the landlord, Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2) 'is inapplicable and either sub. (3) or (4) governs' (§ 704.07(2)(c)); § 704.07(4) gives the tenant the right to move out and abates rent, and requires repayment of advance rent if the tenant justifiably moves out. No statute gives or bars a landlord casualty termination (WI battery 76 (casualty / fire damage termination): 26 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 0 synthetic)); it is not a termination for breach under Wis. Stat. § 704.17, so § 704.17(5)(a) does not reach it. Removal of a tenant who stays still requires an eviction under Wis. Stat. ch. 799. title: Criminal Activity
bodyText: Tenant, members of Tenant's household, and guests and other invitees of Tenant or of a member of Tenant's household will not engage in any criminal activity that threatens the health or safety of, or right to peaceful enjoyment of the premises by, other tenants; any criminal activity that threatens the health or safety of, or right to peaceful enjoyment of their residences by, persons residing in the immediate vicinity of the premises; any criminal activity that threatens the health or safety of Landlord or an agent or employee of Landlord; or any drug-related criminal activity, as defined in Wis. Stat. § 704.17(3m)(a), on or near the premises. If this Section is violated, Landlord may terminate the tenancy, without giving Tenant an opportunity to remedy the violation, by a written notice that complies with Wis. Stat. § 704.17(3m) and requires Tenant to vacate on or before a date at least 5 days after the notice is given. This Section does not apply to a Tenant who is the victim of the criminal activity, and Landlord will not terminate a tenancy based solely on a crime of which Tenant, or someone who lawfully resides with Tenant, is the victim.
notes: WI: Option under rule 54 (crime-free clause). Restates the statutory no-cure ground, notice and victim exception in Wis. Stat. § 704.17(3m)(b)1., (c); 'Provisions in any lease or rental agreement for termination contrary to sub. (3m) are invalid' (§ 704.17(5)(b)), so the clause adds no ground beyond the statute. A lease that lets the landlord terminate 'based solely on the commission of a crime ... if the tenant, or someone who lawfully resides with the tenant, is the victim' is void (§ 704.44(9)), and one that allows termination 'for a crime committed in relation to the rental property' without the Wis. Stat. § 704.14 notice is void (§ 704.44(10)) [BUILDER: never print this clause without `dv-protections-notice-wi`]; the court of appeals held void under Wis. Stat. § 704.44(10) a lease that lacked the Wis. Stat. § 704.14 notice and barred knowingly permitting use of the premises for an unlawful purpose, together with a general termination-for-breach term (Koble Investments v. Marquardt, 2024 WI App 26, as the site's annotation and 2026 WI 19, ¶ 23 report), and the supreme court reversed on other grounds without deciding that point: 'We do not need to resolve this issue' (Koble Investments v. Marquardt, 2026 WI 19, ¶¶ 24-25). The question is open. The notice's required contents (basis, description, date, identity, legal-help advice, right to contest) are in § 704.17(3m)(b)1. and `edu-criminal-eviction-wi`. title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors
bodyText: Tenant will maintain the smoke detectors in the dwelling unit, including testing them and replacing batteries as needed, and, if the building has only one or two dwelling units, will maintain any carbon monoxide detectors in the unit the same way. Tenant will not tamper with, remove, destroy, disconnect, or remove batteries from any detector except in the course of inspection, maintenance, or replacement. If a detector is not functional, Tenant will give Landlord written notice, and Landlord will provide any maintenance necessary to make it functional within 5 days after receiving the notice.
notes: WI: Restates tenant duties that serve the landlord. Smoke detectors: in a one- or two-unit dwelling 'The occupant of such a dwelling unit shall maintain any smoke detector in that unit', with owner maintenance 'within 5 days after receipt of that notice' (Wis. Stat. § 101.645(3)); in a building of 3 or more units the occupant maintains detectors in the unit on the same terms (Wis. Stat. § 101.145(3)(c)). Carbon monoxide detectors: in a one- or two-unit dwelling the same structure applies (Wis. Stat. § 101.647(3)(a), (b)), with a tampering ban (§ 101.647(6)) and an owner liability exemption (§ 101.647(5)); in a building of 3 or more units 'The owner of a residential building shall reasonably maintain every carbon monoxide detector' and repairs within 5 days after an occupant's written notice (Wis. Stat. § 101.149(3)(a)-(b)), so the tenant's maintenance duty is limited to one- and two-unit buildings; tampering is barred in either case (§ 101.149(4)). `edu-smoke-co-detectors-wi`. title: Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText: If this Lease is, or continues as, a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, either Landlord or Tenant may end it only by written notice given to the other at least 28 days before the end of a rental period, stating that the tenancy will end and the termination date, which will be the last day of a rental period (for a year-to-year tenancy, the end of the rental year). If Rent is payable more often than monthly, notice of at least one full rental period is enough. Each party will give notice by a method Wis. Stat. § 704.21 allows. Rent remains payable through the termination date. This Section does not limit either party's right to end the tenancy earlier where this Lease or Wisconsin law allows it, including for nonpayment of Rent or breach under Wis. Stat. § 704.17.

(a periodic tenancy 'can be terminated by notice under this section only at the end of a rental period'; for a year-to-year tenancy 'the end of the rental period is the end of the rental year even though rent is payable on a more frequent basis'), (3) ('At least 28 days’ notice must be given except ... title: Late Fees in Wisconsin
bodyText: Wisconsin sets no cap or grace period for late fees, but you may charge one only if the lease specifically provides for it. Before charging a late fee you must apply any rent the tenant prepaid to the rent owed, and you may never charge a fee for not paying a late fee. Keep the fee in line with your real cost of late payment. To be safe, list unpaid late fees in a NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS document if you want to deduct them from the security deposit.

ATCP § 134.09(8)(b): 'Before charging a late rent fee or late rent penalty to a tenant, a landlord shall apply all rent prepayments received from that tenant to offset the amount of rent owed by the tenant.' ATCP § 134.09(8)(c): 'No landlord may charge any tenant a fee or penalty for nonpayment of a late rent fee or late rent penalty.' title: Late Fees in a Nonpayment Notice
bodyText: For a Wisconsin pay-or-vacate notice, rent expressly includes past-due rent and late fees owed on that past-due rent; the statute does not say other charges count, so treat unpaid non-rent charges as a breach under the notice-to-cure rules rather than adding them to a pay-rent notice. State the amount due carefully: a notice with a wrong amount is still valid unless the error was intentional or the tenant paid or offered what the tenant believed was due. Accepting past-due rent after the notice or after filing does not by itself end an eviction case.

title: Application and Screening Charges
bodyText: The only application charge Wisconsin expressly allows is the actual cost of a consumer credit report, up to $25, and for a nonresident applicant the actual cost of a background check, up to $25. Tell the applicant about the charge before ordering the report and give them a copy. You may not charge for a credit report if the applicant gives you a nationwide report less than 30 days old. Any other money taken to have an application considered is an earnest money deposit that must be refunded or credited under DATCP's rules.
notes: WI: Wis. Stat. § 704.085(1)(a): 'a landlord may require a prospective tenant to pay the landlord’s actual cost, up to $25, to obtain a consumer credit report on the prospective tenant from a consumer credit reporting agency that compiles and maintains files on consumers on a nationwide basis. The landlord shall notify the prospective tenant of the charge before requesting the consumer credit report, and shall provide the prospective tenant with a copy of the report.' § 704.085(1)(b): not if the applicant provides a report 'that is less than 30 days old'. § 704.085(2): nonresident background check, 'actual cost, up to $25'. The credit report rule is repeated in Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.05(4); the nonresident background-check charge rests on § 704.085(2) alone. title: Earnest Money (Holding) Deposits
bodyText: Before taking earnest money or a deposit from an applicant, identify the unit or units they are being considered for. If you sign a lease, apply it to rent or the security deposit, or return it. If an approved applicant backs out (and you have not significantly altered the rental terms you disclosed), you may keep only your actual costs and damages, and lost rent only after reasonable efforts to rerent.

title: No Local Rent Control in Wisconsin
bodyText: Wisconsin bars cities, villages, towns and counties from regulating the amount of rent or fees for residential rental units, and from inclusionary zoning. Limits can still come from your own agreements, such as a subsidy contract or a deal with a housing authority, and you may not raise rent in retaliation.

title: Raising Rent in Wisconsin
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute setting a notice period for a rent increase. During a fixed-term lease you can raise rent only as the lease itself provides. For a month-to-month tenancy, the safe course is to give written notice of the new rent at least 28 days before the end of a rental period, the same notice that ends a periodic tenancy. You may not raise rent in retaliation for a tenant's good-faith complaint or for exercising a legal right, and a lease that lets you raise rent because a tenant contacted police, health or safety services is void. (Manufactured home community operators follow separate DATCP rules: no increases during the term (with limited exceptions) and 28 days' written notice of changes at renewal.)

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice
bodyText: In Wisconsin, accepting past-due rent after serving a notice or filing an eviction does not by itself require dismissal, and a past waiver or a custom of accepting late rent is not a defense to eviction or damages. But accepting rent for a period after a lease expires can turn the tenant into a month-to-month (or week-to-week, if rent is weekly) tenant unless you have already started proceedings or the lease provides otherwise. Be clear in writing about what a payment covers.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: Wisconsin's legal rate of interest is 5% a year. A higher contractual rate is possible only within the limits of other statutes and only if clearly stated in writing. title: Penalties for Deposit Violations
bodyText: A security deposit violation is enforced through Wisconsin's consumer-protection law: a tenant can sue for twice the amount of the loss, plus costs and reasonable attorney fees, and DATCP or a district attorney can seek forfeitures of $100 to $10,000 per violation. Missing the 21-day deadline or withholding for items not allowed can therefore cost far more than the deposit.

title: The NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS Document
bodyText: Wisconsin limits what you can deduct from a deposit to tenant damage, unpaid rent, certain unpaid utility charges and municipal permit fees, unless you add other reasons in a separate document titled "NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS." title: Returning the Deposit Within 21 Days
bodyText: Deliver or mail the deposit, less lawful deductions, within 21 days. title: Tenant Duties Under Wisconsin Law
bodyText: Wisconsin tenants may not make physical changes, including decorating, without your consent, may not use the unit for an unlawful purpose or unreasonably interfere with other occupants, and must comply with any local housing code. If the tenant damages the unit, including through a pest infestation the tenant caused, you may let the tenant repair it or do the work yourself and bill the tenant; your cost is presumed reasonable and may include your own time at a reasonable hourly rate. Where no local housing code applies, the tenant also makes minor repairs to furnished equipment when the cost is small relative to rent.

title: Marijuana in Wisconsin Rentals

title: Unpaid Municipal Utility Bills
bodyText: A tenant's unpaid bill to a city, village or town utility (water and sewer, and electric where the statute allows) can become a lien on your property: each October the utility gives notice to the owner or occupant, a 10% penalty is added if not paid by November 1, and unpaid amounts after November 15 go on the tax roll as a special charge. For water or electric service, you can shift collection toward the tenant by notifying the utility in writing of your name and address and the responsible tenant's name and address (and giving it the lease if asked); when the tenant moves out, give the utility the tenant's forwarding address within 21 days. Even then, the utility can still put the arrears on your tax bill if it notifies you within 14 days after the tenant's charges become past due; you may, at least 14 days after that notice, ask it to shut off electric service. You may also ask the utility whether a prospective tenant owes it past-due charges at another address.

bodyText: Each unit in a multi-unit residential building built after March 1, 1980 must have its own electric meter, with limited exceptions in the Public Service Commission's rules. title: Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Wisconsin requires you to keep the parts of the property you control in reasonable repair, maintain equipment for services you agreed to provide, make structural repairs, repair furnished plumbing, wiring and equipment (where no local housing code applies), and comply with any local housing code. These duties cannot be waived, and a lease that waives your duty to deliver or maintain a habitable unit is void in its entirety. One tenant's damage does not excuse repairs owed to other tenants.

title: Tenant Remedies for Untenantable Conditions
bodyText: If the unit becomes untenantable from fire, water or other casualty or a health hazard, or you substantially violate your repair duties in a way that materially affects health or safety, the tenant may move out unless you promptly repair (or even if you do, when the repair would impose undue hardship), owes no rent after the unit became untenantable, and gets back rent paid in advance for that period. A tenant who stays has rent reduced to the extent they lose normal use, but may not withhold all rent. Wisconsin has no repair-and-deduct statute, and these remedies do not apply if the tenant caused the condition.
notes: WI: Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4): the tenant 'may remove from the premises unless the landlord proceeds promptly to repair or rebuild'; 'rent abates to the extent the tenant is deprived of the full normal use of the premises. This section does not authorize rent to be withheld in full, if the tenant remains in possession'; 'This subsection is inapplicable if the damage or condition is caused by negligence or improper use by the tenant.' Undue hardship and repayment of advance rent: same subsection. Local abatement ordinances limited: § 704.07(5). No repair-and-deduct or rent-escrow statute (WI battery 51 (repair and deduct / rent withholding / escrow): 4 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 1 synthetic)). Receivership for public nuisance buildings: Wis. Stat. § 823.23 (not a tenant remedy). Also answers `landlord-breach-remedy` (WI log §18). title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors
bodyText: One- and two-unit buildings: you must install a working smoke detector in the basement and on each floor level of each unit (not the attic or storage area), and a carbon monoxide detector in the same places (not the garage) unless the building has no attached garage, no fireplace and no fuel-burning appliance; the tenant maintains the detectors in the unit, but you must fix one within 5 days after a tenant or inspector gives you written notice that it does not work. Buildings with 3 or more units: you must install and maintain smoke detectors in the basement and at the head of each stairway on each floor, plus one in or within 6 feet of each sleeping area of each unit (not in a kitchen); you maintain common-area detectors and tenants maintain those in their units, subject to the same 5-day repair rule, with forfeitures of up to $50 a day. Carbon monoxide detectors are required near the sleeping areas of units that contain a fuel-burning appliance; of other units in a building that contains one, such as a central boiler or water heater, unless there is no opening between the appliance and the unit or a detector is installed between them or on the ceiling of the appliance room; of units served by a fuel-burning forced-air furnace; and of units near an attached garage (with listed exceptions, and none at all if every fuel-burning appliance in the building is a warrantied sealed-combustion unit), and you must maintain them and repair or replace one within 5 days after a tenant's written notice.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: You must allow a tenant with a disability to make reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense when needed for full enjoyment of the housing, and, where it is reasonable, you may condition interior modifications on the tenant's agreement to restore the unit at the end of the tenancy, other than reasonable wear and tear. You must also make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services unless the accommodation would impose an undue hardship. Assistance animals have their own rules.

title: Wisconsin Disclosure Checklist
bodyText: Before signing and before taking any deposit: give the lease and written rules to review; disclose known uncorrected code violations and listed habitability conditions; disclose if water, heat or electricity is not included in rent and how shared charges are split; tell an applicant about any credit-report or background-check charge before ordering it; disclose non-rent charges with any rent quote; and give the check-in notice before taking a deposit. In the lease or an addendum: the Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections. At move-in: the check-in sheet. If you will not store property left behind: written notice at signing and renewal. title: Notices for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenant, a year-to-year tenant, or a lease of one year or less, you may give a 5-day notice to pay or vacate. A month-to-month tenant in default may instead get a 14-day notice to vacate with no chance to pay. Under a lease of one year or less, or a year-to-year tenancy, if the tenant was given a 5-day notice and then pays late again within one year, a 14-day notice to vacate ends the tenancy. A lease of more than one year needs a 30-day notice to pay. The notice must be in writing and served by a method the statute allows; a wrong amount does not invalidate it unless it was intentionally wrong or the tenant paid or offered what they believed was due.

title: Notices for Other Lease Violations
bodyText: For a breach other than rent, a tenant under a lease of one year or less, or a year-to-year tenant, gets a 5-day notice to remedy the default or vacate; a tenant is complying if they promptly take reasonable steps to fix it or offer to pay adequate damages. A second breach within a year allows a 14-day notice to vacate with no cure. A month-to-month tenant can be given either the 5-day notice to remedy or a 14-day notice to vacate. Leases over one year need a 30-day notice to comply. Criminal activity and law-enforcement nuisance notices have their own 5-day no-cure rules.

title: Ending a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: Unless you both agreed on another method or the tenant surrenders the unit, either side can end a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy only by written notice, at the end of a rental period, given at least 28 days before (or one full rental period if rent is paid more often than monthly). The notice must state the intent to end the tenancy and the termination date. A notice with a wrong date is generally effective on the first date that would have been proper. If a periodic tenant moves out without notice and stops paying, the tenancy ends as if notice had been given on the day you learn they left.

If rent is payable on a basis less than monthly, notice at least equal to the rent-paying period is sufficient'), (4), (5), (6). When notice is given: § 704.19(7) (registered or certified mail within Wisconsin: the 2nd day after mailing; leave-and-mail or post-and-mail: the later of leaving or mailing; personal delivery: that day). Day counting: 'Notice is given on the day specified below, which is counted as the first day of the notice period' (§ 704.19(7)); on that specific rule, Wis. Stat. § 990.001(4) does not govern these notices (Claude's reading; no case searched). Manufactured home community terminations also follow Wis. title: How to Serve a Notice
bodyText: A landlord's notice under Wisconsin's landlord-tenant chapter must be served by one of these methods: personal delivery, or leaving it at the tenant's home with a competent family member at least 14 who is told what it says; leaving it with a competent person in charge of the premises and mailing a copy; posting it conspicuously and mailing a copy, if the first two cannot be done with reasonable diligence; registered or certified mail; or service like a summons. Certified mail is the simplest to prove: the post office's proof of certified mailing is enough in an eviction case. Notice to one cotenant counts as notice to all, and a notice actually received counts even if not served properly, if you can prove receipt by clear and convincing evidence.
notes: WI: Wis. Stat. § 704.21(1)(a)-(e), (4), (5). Wis. Stat. § 799.40(1g): for notices under §§ 704.16, 704.17 or 704.19 sent by certified mail, 'proof of certified mailing from the United States post office shall be sufficient'. Electronic notice does not substitute for termination notices (Wis. Stat. § 137.12(2r)(b); `electronic-delivery-wi`). Also answers `eviction-service-party` (WI log §18). title: No Just-Cause Requirement
bodyText: Wisconsin does not require a reason to end a periodic tenancy with proper notice or to decline to renew a lease (manufactured home community operators are different: they may end or refuse to renew a resident's tenancy only on listed grounds, including other good cause). But you may not end or refuse to renew a tenancy in retaliation or for a discriminatory reason, a lease that lets you do so because the tenant called police, health or safety services is void in its entirety, and a tenant has a defense if you knew or should have known the tenant is a victim and the eviction is based on conduct related to domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking by a non-guest or a guest they have excluded. Cities, villages, towns and counties may not impose eviction moratoriums.

title: The Wisconsin Eviction Process
bodyText: After the notice period ends, you file a small claims eviction. The summons return date is 5 to 25 days after issuance (at least 20 days for a nonresident), and if the tenant appears and contests, a trial must be held within 30 days after the return date. If you win, the court orders judgment and a writ of restitution, which only the sheriff executes; a writ received by the sheriff more than 30 days after issuance cannot be executed. Either side may demand a jury by the time issue is joined, and appeals must be started within 15 days. Accepting rent after filing does not by itself require dismissal. The court must pause the case for up to 10 working days if the tenant applies for emergency assistance before a writ is issued.
notes: WI: Wis. Service members' dependents on state active duty and foreclosed homeowners have separate stays.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: You may not raise rent, cut services, sue for possession, refuse to renew, or threaten any of these because a tenant complained in good faith to an elected official or a local housing code agency (DATCP's rule covers reports to any government agency), complained to you about repairs or code violations, or exercised a legal right; DATCP also protects tenants who join or organize a tenants' union. You may still evict for unpaid rent, the protection does not cover complaints about defects the tenant caused, and the tenant must show the action would not have happened but for the protected conduct. A lease that lets you take these steps because a tenant called police, health or safety services is void.

title: Property After an Eviction
bodyText: When the sheriff executes a writ, the sheriff removes the tenant and, unless you choose otherwise, removes the tenant's property. You may have to advance the removal cost, which is added to the judgment; storage after the sheriff delivers the property to safekeeping is the tenant's expense. As an alternative, when delivering the writ you may tell the sheriff that you will remove and store or dispose of the property yourself under the abandoned-property statute; if you did not give the will-not-store notice, you must then follow the 2009 version of that statute.

bodyText: If a tenant leaves early or is evicted, you can recover rent and damages only after crediting what you could earn by reasonable efforts to rerent, meaning the steps you would normally take under local practice. title: Attorney Fees and Costs
bodyText: A Wisconsin lease may not require the tenant to pay your attorney fees or costs for any dispute; a lease that does is void in its entirety. You can recover only the costs and fees a court awards by statute, which in an eviction is $10 plus the statutory amount on any damages recovered. When suing over a worthless check, a separate statute allows exemplary damages and reasonable attorney fees, together capped at $500 per check.

title: Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease
bodyText: A Wisconsin residential lease is void and unenforceable in its entirety if it: lets you raise rent, cut services, evict or refuse to renew, or threaten to, because the tenant called police, health or safety services; allows eviction without a court; accelerates rent or waives your duty to mitigate; requires the tenant to pay your attorney fees or costs; allows confession of judgment; says you are not liable for your own negligence; makes the tenant liable for injuries beyond their control or for damage from natural disasters or people other than the tenant and the tenant's guests or invitees; waives your duty to keep the unit habitable; allows ending a tenancy based solely on a crime of which the tenant or someone lawfully living with them was the victim; or allows termination for a crime committed in relation to the rental property unless the lease includes the Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections.
notes: WI: Wis. Stat. § 704.44(1m)-(10) ('Notwithstanding s. 704.02, a residential rental agreement is void and unenforceable if it does any of the following'); Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.08(1)-(10) (WI battery 90 (confession of judgment): 10 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 0 synthetic)). (Wis. Stat. § 806.25 separately voids confession-of-judgment authorizations in notes.) On an unlawful-use clause without the notice, the court of appeals held void under Wis. Stat. § 704.44(10) a lease that lacked the Wis. title: DATCP Enforcement and Double Damages
bodyText: DATCP's residential rental rules are orders under Wisconsin's trade-practices law. A tenant who suffers a money loss because you violated them, including the deposit, disclosure and prohibited-term rules, can recover twice the loss plus costs and reasonable attorney fees, and the State can seek forfeitures. The tenant must show the violation actually caused a money loss. In 2026 the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that the Consumer Act's debt-collection prohibitions do not govern a residential lease with rent payable monthly; for other payment arrangements, get advice before collecting arrears.

title: Jury Trials in Evictions
bodyText: In a Wisconsin eviction either side may demand a jury, by filing a written demand and paying the fee at or before joinder of issue; otherwise the right is waived. No Wisconsin statute addresses a lease jury waiver and its enforceability is unsettled, so the clause library does not include one.

bodyText: Status as a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking is a protected class in Wisconsin housing. bodyText: When a residential tenant dies, the tenancy ends 60 days after you learn of the death or at the end of the lease term, whichever is earlier; a periodic tenancy ends 60 days after you learn of it. title: Service Members
bodyText: Besides the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, Wisconsin protects members of the Wisconsin National Guard or state defense force ordered to state active duty for 30 days or more. A member who signed a lease before entering state active duty may end it by written notice delivered personally or by first-class mail; for monthly rent, termination is effective 30 days after the next rent due date. Evicting the family of a member on state active duty from a dwelling whose rent does not exceed the federal limit requires a court order, and on the member's application the court must stay the case for up to 90 days unless the member's ability to pay is not materially affected.

title: Criminal Activity and Nuisance Terminations
bodyText: You may end a tenancy on a 5-day written notice, without a chance to cure, if the tenant, a household member or a guest engages in criminal activity threatening other tenants, neighbors or you and your staff, or in drug manufacturing or distribution on or near the premises. The notice must state its basis, describe the activity, its date and the people involved, tell the tenant they may seek help from a lawyer, a volunteer legal clinic or a tenant resource center, and state their right to contest the allegations in court. No arrest or conviction is needed, but the rule does not apply to a tenant who is the victim. A property owner may also give a 5-day notice to vacate after police or the district attorney give written notice that a drug or criminal-gang nuisance exists in the unit or was caused by the tenant on the owner's property; that notice must state its basis and the tenant's right to contest the termination in an eviction action. A lease that allows termination for a crime committed in relation to the rental property is void in its entirety unless it includes the Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections.

title: Repairing Damage the Tenant Caused, and Being Reimbursed
bodyText: If the tenant's acts or inaction damage the premises, including by an insect or other pest infestation, Wisconsin lets you choose who fixes it: you may let the tenant repair or remediate the damage and redecorate, or do the work yourself and require the tenant to reimburse your reasonable cost (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(3)(a)). Your cost is presumed reasonable unless the tenant proves otherwise, and it can include materials or labor you provide yourself and, at a reasonable hourly rate, your time buying or providing materials, supervising your agent or hiring a contractor. The statute calls this a reimbursement; it does not make the cost rent. When the tenant moves out you may withhold from the security deposit amounts reasonably necessary for tenant damage, waste or neglect, but never for normal wear and tear (Wis. Stat. § 704.28(1)(a), (3)). Entering the unit to do the work follows Wisconsin's ordinary entry rules (`edu-landlord-entry-wi`). These rules apply to every residential tenancy whatever the lease says: an agreement to waive them is void (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(1)).

bodyText: Wisconsin imposes no statutory requirement that a written residential lease have every blank completed. Several Wisconsin rules still turn on what the lease and the papers given at signing say: the domestic abuse protections notice must be in the lease or an addendum (Wis. Stat. § 704.14); the names and addresses of the person who manages the premises and of the owner or person authorized to accept legal papers must be disclosed in writing at or before signing (Wis.
