title: Nebraska's Constitution Protects Gun Ownership - But It Does Not Bind You
bodyText: Nebraska's constitution contains a right to keep and bear arms, and landlords regularly assume it stops them restricting guns in a rental. It does not. Article I-1 lists among the inalienable rights 'the right to keep and bear arms for security or defense of self, family, home, and others, and for lawful common defense, hunting, recreational use, and all other lawful purposes', and then says those rights 'shall not be denied or infringed BY THE STATE OR ANY SUBDIVISION THEREOF'. That last clause is the whole point: it binds government, not a private landlord writing a lease. So a privately owned rental may restrict firearms by lease term, and Nebraska has no statute - unlike several other states in this library - making such a term unenforceable against a permit holder or protecting a tenant's firearms in rental housing. Two places the constitutional limit does bite. A city, village or county is a subdivision, so a local ordinance could not compel landlords to ban firearms, or ban them in rentals outright. And housing owned or operated by a public body is the state or a subdivision acting, so a public housing authority is bound where a private owner is not. Nothing in the standard lease restricts firearms, so this is a decision you can make either way rather than a problem to fix.
notes: NE: Constitution screen 2026-10-03 (rule 35c). The Nebraska Constitution is NOT in the official keyword index — a control term that must hit ('Legislature') returned 2,678 results and every one was a statute section, no constitution article among them — so per rule 35 it was read article by article instead: all 239 sections of the Preamble and Articles I to XVIII fetched individually from /laws/articles.php, 671,243 chars raw and 120,392 chars of operative text once the case annotations were stripped, SHA-256 prefix (normalised, lowercased, whitespace-collapsed) bb04a3c123de07049a580dd743ccb464. Controls inside the corpus: 'Legislature' 207 hits, 'Governor' 76. FOUND, operative text: Neb. Const. art. I-1 (source line: Neb. Const. art. I, sec. 1 (1875); Amended 1988, Initiative Measure No. 403), read in full. The firearms language and the 'by the state or any subdivision thereof' limitation are quoted verbatim. WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: the constitution screen found the provision, and Nebraska had NO row on firearms while fourteen other states in the library do (TX, OH, TN x2, VA, UT, IL, MO, OK, MI, IA, NM, MT x2). No NE-tagged clause restricts firearms, so there was nothing to fix or override — the screen's product is this row, not an edit. STATE-ACTION LIMIT IS THE OPERATIVE POINT and it is read off the text, not inferred: the right runs against the state and its subdivisions, so it does not void a private lease term. NOT RESEARCHED and flagged as unread doctrine (rule 76): whether any Nebraska case has applied art. I-1 to a landlord, and whether any Nebraska statute outside the code (or a municipal ordinance) restricts a landlord's firearm rules — the public-housing point is read off 'subdivision thereof' and is not supported by a case. The statute-wide searches run on 2026-09-27 and today found no Nebraska firearms-in-rentals statute.

title: Holdover Charge
bodyText: [Optional.] If Tenant remains in possession after this Lease ends and Landlord has not consented in writing to a continued tenancy, Tenant will pay Landlord a holdover charge of {{holdover_daily_rate}} for each day Tenant remains in possession, in place of Rent and actual damages for the use of the property during that time. Landlord and Tenant agree that Landlord's loss from a holdover, including delay in making the property available to a new tenant, is difficult to estimate accurately in advance, that this charge is a reasonable estimate of that loss, and that it is not a penalty. Landlord's acceptance of a holdover charge is not consent to a continued tenancy and is not acceptance of Rent. This Section does not limit Landlord's right to recover possession, unpaid Rent and other amounts due for the period before this Lease ended, or damages for harm to the property. Where Tenant's holdover is willful and not in good faith, Landlord may instead recover the amount Nebraska law allows for such a holdover, and will not recover both that amount and a holdover charge under this Section for the same period.
notes: NE: Read 2026-10-03 from nebraskalegislature.gov in the built-in browser. BASIS: section-open. FIX 3(a) (rule 54, optional clause NE's 2026-09-30 retro found but did not draft). Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1437 read section-open again today. THE GAP THIS FILLS: §76-1437(3) lets the landlord recover 'an amount not more than three months' periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees' — but ONLY 'if the tenant's holdover is willful and not in good faith', and as a LUMP measure, not a daily rate. For an ordinary holdover that is neither willful nor in bad faith Nebraska sets no damages measure at all, which is precisely rule 54's 'measures the statute doesn't set, which the lease can set instead'. DRAFTED ON THE HOUSE PATTERN of holdover-rate-az / -ga / -nc / -sc / -tn / -va / -al / -pa / -in / -mi: same CONDITIONAL rule_type, same CONSTRAINED_TERM basis, same liquidated-damages recital, and it reuses the existing {{holdover_daily_rate}} variable rather than creating one (rule 60). ONE NEBRASKA-SPECIFIC CHANGE to that pattern, and it is the reason this clause is safe here: the AZ text closes by preserving 'any amount Arizona law allows for a holdover that is willful and not in good faith' ALONGSIDE the daily charge. Nebraska's §76-1437(3) figure is a ceiling on the total recoverable for a willful holdover, so stacking a contractual daily charge on top of it could exceed the statutory maximum. This row therefore makes the two ALTERNATIVE rather than cumulative for the same period. NO UNTAGGING: shared `holdover` stays tagged NE, as it does in the ten other states that carry a holdover-rate companion; this is a companion clause, not an override, so there is no display collision. NOT READ and flagged as unread doctrine (rule 76): Nebraska's liquidated-damages-versus-penalty case law. The recital follows the house pattern and the clause is offered as OPTIONAL, which is the mitigation; a landlord who sets a daily figure far above actual loss risks it being treated as a penalty, and the row does not promise otherwise.

title: Landlord Termination After Fire or Casualty
bodyText: [Optional.] If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty to an extent that enjoyment of the property is substantially impaired, and the fire or casualty was not caused by Landlord's deliberate or negligent act, Landlord may terminate this Lease by written notice to Tenant, effective on the date stated in the notice or, if Tenant has already vacated, on the date Tenant vacated. Rent will be accounted for as of the date of the casualty, and Landlord will return all prepaid Rent and the Security Deposit Tenant is entitled to recover under Nebraska law. Landlord may recover possession only as Nebraska law permits. This Section is in addition to the rights Nebraska law gives Tenant after a fire or casualty and does not reduce or condition them: Tenant keeps the right to vacate and end this Lease, or to stay and pay reduced Rent, whether or not Landlord terminates and whether or not Tenant caused the damage.
notes: NE: Read 2026-10-03 from nebraskalegislature.gov in the built-in browser. BASIS: section-open. FIX 3(b) (rule 54, the standing GA landlord-casualty-termination rule). Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1429 read section-open again today. WHY IT IS LAWFUL HERE: §76-1429 confers rights on the TENANT only — vacate and terminate on written notice within fourteen days after vacating, or stay and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost fair rental value — and says nothing about the landlord. Nothing in the URLTA gives the landlord a casualty termination, and nothing bars the lease from supplying one, so this is contract territory. Colorado was judged likely void; Nebraska is not Colorado, and the row is drafted so it cannot be read as a waiver. THE ONE THING THAT WOULD MAKE IT VOID, and how the text avoids it: §76-1415(1)(a) voids any provision by which the tenant waives rights or remedies under the Act, and §76-1415(2) adds the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees where a landlord deliberately uses a provision known to be prohibited. So the closing sentence is load-bearing, not boilerplate — it preserves BOTH of §76-1429(1)'s limbs expressly, and it says 'whether or not Tenant caused the damage' because, as edu-tenant-caused-damage-ne records, §76-1429 is the one Nebraska exit route with NO tenant-fault exception (contrast §§76-1425 and 76-1427, which each have one). A landlord-termination clause that quietly cut off a negligent tenant's §76-1429 exit would be exactly the void term rule 47 warns about. ACCOUNTING follows the statute: §76-1429(2) requires the landlord to return all prepaid rent and security recoverable under §76-1416 and fixes the accounting date as the date of the casualty. Drafted on the casualty-landlord-termination-az / -ks pattern, adjusted for that accounting date and the fault point. NO UNTAGGING and no collision: Nebraska's tenant-side casualty content is education (edu-casualty-damage-ne), so this is the only NE casualty LEASE clause.

title: Landlord Termination After Fire or Casualty
bodyText: [Optional.] This Section applies only if this Lease has a fixed Term. It does not apply to a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, which either party may end under this Lease's termination-notice provisions. If the property is destroyed by fire or other casualty, or is so injured by one as to be unfit for occupancy, and the repairs cannot reasonably be completed within [number] days after the casualty, and the casualty was not caused by Landlord's deliberate or negligent act, Landlord may end this Lease by written notice to Tenant, effective on the date stated in the notice or, if Tenant has already surrendered possession, on the date Tenant surrendered. Tenant is not liable for Rent accruing after the date the property became unfit for occupancy. Rent that accrued and was unpaid before that date remains payable, any Rent Tenant prepaid for a period after that date will be refunded, and the Security Deposit will be returned as this Lease and Ohio law provide. Ending this Lease under this Section does not relieve Landlord of any obligation Landlord owed Tenant while this Lease was in force, and does not limit any remedy Tenant has for Landlord's failure to meet one of those obligations before this Lease ends. Ending this Lease under this Section does not release Tenant from liability for a casualty caused by the fault or neglect of Tenant or of anyone on the property with Tenant's consent. Nothing in this Section limits Tenant's right under Ohio law, where a destruction or injury occurs without Tenant's fault or neglect, to owe no Rent after that destruction or injury and to surrender possession, or any other right Tenant has under applicable law. Landlord may recover possession only as Ohio law permits.
notes: OH: NEW ROW 2026-10-03, SOP 1.48 targeted fix 1, under SOP rule 54 (landlord rights the statute leaves to contract - the rule names casualty termination as its example). Decided by Claude Code at the 2026-10-02 OH sync under rule 76; my 2026-10-02 retro had deferred it only to avoid churn after the three-bucket scrub, which rule 54 does not accept as a reason. R.C. 5301.11 READ SECTION-OPEN 2026-10-03 on codes.ohio.gov in the built-in browser; effective 1953-10-01, H.B. 1, 100th G.A., sole version, never amended. Verbatim: 'The lessee of a building which, without fault or neglect on his part, is destroyed or so injured as to be unfit for occupancy, is not liable to pay rent to the lessor or owner thereof, after such destruction or injury, unless otherwise expressly provided by written agreement or covenant. The lessee thereupon must surrender possession of such premises.' WHY THE LEASE IS THE ONLY SOURCE: R.C. 5301.11 gives the TENANT rent relief and imposes a surrender duty, and says nothing about the landlord ending the lease. R.C. 5321.06 lets a rental agreement carry any term not inconsistent with ch. 5321 or any other rule of law, so a landlord termination right is contractual or it does not exist. The gap it fills is specific: under the statutory default alone, rent stops and the tenant surrenders, but the fixed Term keeps running, so the tenant may claim a right to re-occupy once repairs are done. This Section ends that. THE THREE LIMITS THE SYNC REQUIRED, AND HOW EACH IS MET. (1) R.C. 5301.11 LEFT INTACT: the clause does not use the statute's 'unless otherwise expressly provided by written agreement or covenant' hook at all. The penultimate sentence preserves both limbs of the tenant's right - no rent after the destruction or injury, and surrender - in the statute's own terms. (2) RENT STOPS AT THE UNFIT DATE, not at the notice date and not at termination, which tracks the statute's 'after such destruction or injury' rather than improving on it; pre-casualty arrears stay payable and post-casualty prepaid rent is refunded. (3) R.C. 5321.13(E) (read section-open 2026-09-27: no agreement may permit receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with R.C. 5321.04) IS NOT ENGAGED, because no rent runs after the property becomes unfit, and the clause expressly preserves Landlord's obligations owed while the Lease was in force and every tenant remedy for a pre-termination failure to meet them - so the R.C. 5321.07 escrow and damages routes survive. NAMING FOLLOWS KANSAS, BODY FOLLOWS MICHIGAN. The id is casualty-landlord-termination-oh because Ohio's structure is Kansas's: the tenant-side fire-casualty-termination-ks and fire-casualty-termination-oh are both switched off and the live clause is the landlord-side one (same in AZ and AL). The TEXT is modelled on casualty-termination-mi and casualty-termination-ia as the prompt directs, and MI is the right model because Mich. Comp. Laws 554.201 is a near-twin of R.C. 5301.11 - an old-style surrender-and-no-rent provision - whereas KS, AZ, AL and IA are URLTA-style substantial-impairment-plus-rent-reduction states. Both read, neither tagged. DELIBERATE DEPARTURES FROM THE MODELS (rule 19 - do not import another state's architecture). MI limits its clause to a Term of at least one year; Ohio has NO term-length condition anywhere in R.C. 5301.11, so importing 'one year' would invent a threshold. The clause is limited to a FIXED TERM instead, on a different and Ohio-specific ground: for a periodic tenancy the landlord already has a no-cause exit under R.C. 5321.17(A) and (B) (7 and 30 days), so a casualty clause would add nothing and only create confusion. IA's 30-day notice window and 14-day minimum effective date are also not imported - Ohio has no statutory casualty notice period, and for a fixed Term R.C. 5321.17 does not apply at all, since (A) and (B) reach only week-to-week and month-to-month tenancies. 'Landlord may recover possession only as Ohio law permits' is there for R.C. 5321.15(A), which bars exclusion of the tenant outside a court process - a termination right is not a self-help right. OPTIONAL, NEVER A DEFAULT: is_default blank, rule_type CONDITIONAL, body opens '[Optional.]', matching casualty-landlord-termination-ks and -az. NOT RESEARCHED: whether an Ohio court has tested a landlord casualty-termination clause against R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability, and whether the Lemstone mitigation line bears on a casualty termination (Lemstone is commercial - see edu-casualty-and-mitigation-waivable-oh). No case law read. Flagged.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term (for a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, up to the earliest date Tenant could have ended the tenancy by notice), less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will make repairs as this Lease and Pennsylvania law require and will use reasonable efforts to re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage. It does not limit Tenant's right under Pennsylvania law to pay Rent into escrow while a city or county has certified the property unfit for human habitation, or to deduct from Rent a payment Tenant makes to a utility because Landlord did not pay it.
notes: PA: NEW 2026-10-03 (SOP 1.49 retro, rule 54t). OPTIONAL clause (CONDITIONAL, not a default), state version of `tenant-caused-damage-tn` (read; TN row not tagged); periodic-tenancy limb from `tenant-caused-damage-nj`/`-ga` (rule 37). Each abatement or exit route checked separately for a tenant-fault exception: (i) casualty: no Pennsylvania statute (1951 Act read whole; battery t5 0), so part (1) waives no statutory right, and the opt-in `casualty-termination-pa` already excludes tenant-caused damage; (ii) rent into escrow: City Rent Withholding Act § 1 (35 P.S. § 1700-1) suspends rent 'Notwithstanding any other provision of law, or of any agreement' once a city or county department certifies the dwelling unfit, with no tenant-fault exception in its text, so the last sentence preserves it; (iii) essential services: 66 Pa.C.S. § 1529 lets a tenant deduct from rent a payment made to a utility 'on account of nonpayment of charges by the landlord ratepayer'; it turns on the landlord's own failure, has no fault exception, and the last sentence preserves it (retaliation for using it is barred, 66 Pa.C.S. § 1531); (iv) landlord-breach termination: no statute; the implied warranty of habitability (Pugh v. Holmes, 486 Pa. 272 (1979)) and whether it reaches tenant-caused conditions are case law, not read. No statutory repair code exists, so TN's 'reasonable efforts to repair' became 'make repairs as this Lease and Pennsylvania law require', which cannot be read as softening a duty a court finds. Part (2) fills a gap: no Pennsylvania statute measures lost rent when the lease ends because of tenant-caused damage. Repair cost: the deposit may be kept for 'the actual amount of damages to the leasehold premises caused by the tenant' with the 30-day list (68 P.S. § 250.512(a)-(b), Act § 512), and a possession complaint may claim 'damages ... for injury to ... the real property' (Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J. 503(B)(8)). Plain Language Act: the clause waives no statutory right, so nothing is added to `consumer-restrictions-statement-pa`. Rule 47: no Pennsylvania penalty for knowingly using a prohibited term (instruction 49). Education: `edu-tenant-caused-damage-pa`. Read section-open 2026-10-03 in the built-in browser on palegis.us: The Landlord and Tenant Act of 1951 (hash-matched to the live page, 72 of 72 sections), City Rent Withholding Act (1965 P.L. 1534, No. 536) § 1 whole, 66 Pa.C.S. §§ 1527, 1529, 1531; Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J. 503(B)(8) on pacodeandbulletin.gov (court rule, current compilation). Battery: battery_rule54t_2026-10-03.json (Pa.C.S. control 'zqxvbnmwt' 0; unconsolidated control 0).

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: If a Pennsylvania tenant, someone in the household or a guest damages the home, the statutes give you a few tools. You may keep the security deposit for the actual damage the tenant caused, but only if you give the tenant a written list of the damage within 30 days after the lease ends or you accept the tenant's surrender, whichever comes first; missing the list forfeits the right to keep any of the deposit and to sue for damage to the property. In a building with three or more households, the tenant must not wilfully or wantonly damage the property or let guests do so. An eviction complaint before a magisterial district judge can claim damages for injury to the property along with rent. No Pennsylvania statute lets a tenant end the lease or stop paying rent because of a fire or other casualty, so a tenant who caused the damage has no statutory casualty right to use; the library's optional casualty clause covers only damage the tenant did not cause. Two statutory rent remedies have no tenant-fault exception in their text: in cities covered by the Rent Withholding Act, rent is suspended and paid into escrow while the city or county certifies the home unfit for human habitation, and a tenant who pays your unpaid utility bill to keep service on may deduct it from rent. Whether rent continues during repairs and whether you can recover lost rent after the lease ends come from court decisions and the lease; the optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause covers both.
notes: PA: NEW 2026-10-03 (SOP 1.49 retro, rule 54t). Controlling text: 68 P.S. § 250.512(a)-(c) (Act § 512: list within 30 days; forfeiture under (b) of 'all rights to withhold any portion' and to sue for damage to the premises; landlord's burden of proof under (c)); 68 P.S. § 250.503-A(1) (Act § 503-A(1): no wilful or wanton damage, Article V-A buildings, Act § 501-A); Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J. 503(B)(8) (court rule); City Rent Withholding Act § 1 (35 P.S. § 1700-1); 66 Pa.C.S. §§ 1527, 1529. Proof of absence (casualty and abatement): Pa.C.S. battery t1-t6 (fault of tenant 3 hits, all 13 Pa.C.S. goods-lease sections §§ 2A221, 2A404, 2A528; caused by tenant 0; untenantable 2, land-bank sections; rent abatement and rent escrow 1 each, the drug-nuisance remedy 42 Pa.C.S. § 8389; fire near lease 0); unconsolidated: 'untenantable AND tenant' 0, '"destroyed by fire" AND tenant AND lease' 0, '"caused by the tenant"' 3 (the 1951 Act only), '"unfit for human habitation" AND rent' 9 (City Rent Withholding Act and a tax-exemption act). Boundary: Pa. Code regulations, local ordinances and case law not searched; rent during repairs, lost-rent damages, mitigation and the implied warranty's reach are case law, not read (instruction 16). title: Holdover Charge
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession after this Lease ends, whether at the end of the Term or on an earlier termination under this Lease or applicable law (other than a termination for nonpayment of Rent), and Landlord has not agreed in writing to a continued tenancy and has not accepted Rent for one, then, in place of any damages for Tenant's continued possession that Landlord could otherwise recover, Tenant will pay Landlord a holdover charge of {{holdover_daily_rate}} for each day Tenant remains in possession. Landlord and Tenant agree that Landlord's loss from a holdover, including delay in making the property available to a new tenant, is difficult to estimate accurately in advance, that this charge is a reasonable estimate of that loss, and that it is not a penalty. This charge is an alternative to any damages South Dakota law measures for the same period, not an addition to them: Tenant will not pay a holdover charge under this Section for any day for which Landlord recovers statutory holdover damages, and no statutory multiplier applies to the holdover charge. Landlord's acceptance of a holdover charge is not acceptance of Rent for a continued tenancy and does not renew this Lease under the Holdover section. This Section does not limit Landlord's right to recover possession, unpaid Rent and other amounts due for the period before this Lease ended, or damages for harm to the property.
notes: Retro checks (SOP 1.51) 2026-10-04. NEW, per Taylor's decision at the 2026-10-02 SD sync (rule 76) on my own recommendation. Modelled on `holdover-rate-nc`, which is the variant rule 53 cites for excluding a nonpayment termination, rather than on `holdover-rate-ga`, whose trigger reaches one. CONDITIONAL and offered, never a default (rule 54). THE GROUND FOR THIS CLAUSE IS NOT THE ONE THE INSTRUCTION GAVE, and the difference is recorded in the SD log: the instruction said SDCL 43-32-14 and 43-32-15 'give no damages measure for holding over', which is true of chapter 43-32 but not of South Dakota - the measures sit in chapter 21-3, which no SD row had read. SDCL 21-3-8 gives DOUBLE THE YEARLY VALUE of the property for the time of withholding, plus compensation for the detriment, for WILFULLY holding over after the end of the term, after a notice to quit duly given and a demand of possession made; SDCL 21-3-7 gives DOUBLE THE RENT where the tenant gave notice of intention to leave and then failed to give up the premises; SDCL 21-3-5 measures the residual case as the value of the use plus the costs of recovering possession; and SDCL 21-16-10 lets the court award 21-3-8 damages in the FED judgment itself where claimed in the complaint. All read section-open this pass. THE GAP IS THEREFORE NARROWER THAN STATED BUT REAL, which is what rule 54 asks (for which cases, and in what shape): 21-3-8 does not reach a non-wilful holdover, does not reach an EARLIER termination (its words are 'after the end of his term'), and does not reach a holdover where no notice to quit was given - which is now the common case, because South Dakota repealed its statutory notice-to-quit requirement in 2024 (former SDCL 21-16-2, repealed SL 2024 ch 75 S 1). A stipulated daily charge fills those cases. RULE 53 SCREEN, each test run and recorded. (1) JUDGMENT-STAGE MULTIPLIER: PRESENT - SS 21-3-7 and 21-3-8 are both doublers and 21-16-10 channels 21-3-8 into the judgment, so the clause carries the MO-circle-back sentence that the charge is not recovered for any day a statutory multiple is and that no multiplier applies to the stipulated figure. (2) STATUTORY CAP ON WILFUL-HOLDOVER RECOVERY: none - 21-3-8 is a measure, not a ceiling - but it is a statutory measure for the same period, so the NE-circle-back alternative-not-additive framing is carried anyway. (3) LATE-FEE CAP: CONFIRMED ABSENT from primary text, not from the log - batteries for 'late (fee|charge)|delinquent fee' and 'grace period' across chs. 43-32, 43-8, 21-16, 37-24, 57A-3, 54-3 and 54-4 returned no residential hit (the two ch. 54-4 hits, SS 54-4-44.3 and 54-4-45, are consumer lending and money-lender licence renewal and mention no lessor, lessee, landlord or tenant), with a passing positive. (4) TENDER, REDEMPTION OR CURE UNTIL JUDGMENT: CONFIRMED ABSENT - word-boundary batteries for 'cure', 'reinstate', 'redeem|redemption' and a pay-to-retain-possession proximity pattern across chs. 21-16, 43-32, 43-8, 15-6 and 21-3 returned nothing; the single 'redemption' hit is SDCL 21-16-1(5)'s MORTGAGE redemption after a foreclosure sale, read in context, not a tenant's right to redeem a tenancy. An unbounded 'cure' pattern first returned false hits inside the word 'secure', which the word-boundary rerun and its reject-test eliminated. NONPAYMENT TERMINATIONS EXCLUDED ANYWAY, as a drafting judgment under rule 76 and recorded as such: neither of rule 53's two stated triggers fires in South Dakota, but SDCL 53-9-4 voids penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance and SDCL 53-9-5 voids anticipated-damages terms outside the impracticability exception, and SD's late fee is builder-set with NO statutory ceiling - so stacking an uncapped late fee, unpaid Rent and a daily holdover charge over the same days is the classic penalty profile those two sections create. Excluding the case costs the landlord little and removes the argument. BUILDER CONSTRAINT: {{holdover_daily_rate}} must approximate actual loss - daily Rent plus documented re-letting loss - and must not be set as a multiple of Rent, or the 53-9-4/53-9-5 recital in the body stops being true. FITS WITH `holdover-sd`: that clause carries SDCL 43-32-14's renewal-on-acceptance-of-rent presumption, so this clause both conditions itself on Landlord not having accepted Rent for a continued tenancy and says expressly that accepting a holdover charge does not renew the Lease under it. The cross-reference wording used by the GA and NC variants ('the actual damages and reasonable rental value described in the Holdover section') was deliberately NOT copied, because `holdover-sd` describes no damages measure and the pointer would have dangled. Primary text read section-open from the official sdlegislature.gov API through the built-in browser (shell egress to that host is denied by org policy). SDCL ch. 21-3 parsed and proved complete against the site's own chapter index: 16 of 16 sections, no extras. Decoded as UTF-16LE per the encoding fix recorded in the 1.24 retro.

title: Default by Tenant
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and neither pays it nor surrenders the property within the period stated in a written pay-or-vacate notice served as Washington law requires. Tenant will also be in default if Tenant substantially breaches a material term of this Lease, or a tenant obligation imposed by law other than one for monetary damages, and does not adequately remedy the breach by the date stated in Landlord's written notice, which will be at least 10 days after service of the notice. Washington law gives no opportunity to cure, and Landlord may proceed on a three-day written notice to quit, if Tenant commits or permits waste or nuisance on the premises, unlawful activity that affects the use and enjoyment of the premises, or other substantial or repeated and unreasonable interference with the use and enjoyment of the premises by Landlord or neighbors. title: Early Termination
bodyText: This Section applies only while this Lease is for a fixed Term. Tenant may end this Lease before the end of the Term by giving Landlord at least 30 days' written notice and paying Landlord, by the termination date, an early termination fee equal to one month's Rent ({{monthly_rent}}). Tenant remains responsible for Rent and other obligations up to the termination date and owes no Rent for any later period. If Tenant leaves before the end of the Term without using this option, Tenant's liability is governed by Washington law, including Landlord's duty to make a reasonable effort to re-rent the property. Landlord may end this Lease before the end of the Term only for a cause Washington law allows, after the notice and any cure period that law requires. Nothing in this Section limits any termination right Tenant has under applicable law, including on military orders, as a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, unlawful harassment or stalking, because of threatening behavior by Landlord, or because of a defective condition Landlord fails to remedy.

bodyText: Tenant represents that the information Tenant gave Landlord in Tenant's rental application at the start of the tenancy was true, correct and complete, and acknowledges that Landlord relied on it in entering into this Lease. bodyText: PORTABLE COOLING DEVICES. Tenant may install a portable cooling device (an air conditioner or portable heat pump, including one mounted in a window or designed to sit on the floor) of Tenant's choosing, as Washington law allows. title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If Tenant, a member of Tenant's family, an invitee or another person acting under Tenant's control causes damage to the property, including damage that makes the property unfit to live in: (a) Tenant will pay Landlord the reasonable cost of repairing the damage, beyond wear resulting from ordinary use; (b) Landlord has no duty under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act to repair a defective condition caused that way, and Tenant may not use any defense or remedy under that Act, including withholding or reducing Rent or ending this Lease, because of that condition; and (c) Tenant's obligation to pay Rent continues while the condition is repaired, and if the tenancy ends because of the damage, Tenant is liable for Landlord's actual damages, including lost Rent, as Washington law allows, subject to Landlord's duty to mitigate. Before acting under this Section on a condition Tenant has a duty to remedy, Landlord will give Tenant written notice specifying the condition, as Washington law requires.
notes: WA: Rule 54t answer. Washington already removes the tenant's remedies for a tenant-caused condition: 'No duty shall devolve upon the landlord to repair a defective condition under this section, nor shall any defense or remedy be available to the tenant under this chapter, where the defective condition complained of was caused by the conduct of such tenant, his or her family, invitee, or other person acting under his or her control' (RCW 59.18.060). This one exception reaches every chapter 59.18 remedy, including termination for an unremedied defect (RCW 59.18.090(1)), repair-and-deduct (RCW 59.18.100) and court-ordered termination (RCW 59.18.120), so the clause waives nothing (rule 54t asks about each exit separately). Washington has no casualty-termination statute ((WA battery 33 (casualty / fire termination right (statutory)): 1 hit, control 0; known positives passed (0 real sections, 1 synthetic)) (WA battery 34 (casualty everyday rerun (untenantable / uninhabitable)): 11 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 1 synthetic)); `edu-casualty-termination-wa`). Tenant duty: RCW 59.18.130(4) bars damage by the tenant, family, invitee or anyone under the tenant's control. Notice step: RCW 59.18.170(1), 59.18.160; for a health-or-safety condition the tenant can fix by repair, replacement or cleaning, RCW 59.18.180(1) gives the tenant 30 days after written notice and then lets the landlord do the work and bill the actual and reasonable cost (`edu-landlord-self-cure-wa`). The statutory exits that do not turn on the condition (military orders, victim protection, landlord threats) are untouched because the clause reaches only a condition the tenant caused. Lost rent is ordinary contract damages; no Washington statute sets a measure for it beyond RCW 59.18.310 for abandonment (Claude's reading). Tenant-caused-damage clauses for TN were the model. title: Fixed Term That Does Not Continue Month to Month
bodyText: [Optional. Use only if the first rental agreement of this tenancy was for a specified Term of 12 months or more, or if every rental agreement since the tenancy began has been for a specified period of six months or more, and the tenancy has never been month to month or periodic.] This Lease is for the specified Term only and is not written to continue on a month-to-month or periodic basis after the Term ends. title: Service and Assistance Animals
bodyText: A service animal or other assistance animal that Tenant or an Occupant needs as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is not considered a pet under this Lease, regardless of any pet policy, breed, weight, or size restriction stated elsewhere in this Lease. Landlord will not charge a pet deposit, pet rent, or other pet-related fee for an assistance animal, but may require the same cleaning or damage deposit it requires of all tenants. If the disability and the disability-related need for the animal are not readily apparent, Landlord may request reliable documentation confirming the need for the accommodation, to the extent permitted by applicable law; if the disability and need are readily apparent, Landlord will not require such documentation. Tenant remains responsible for any damage to the property caused by an assistance animal. Landlord may deny or withdraw this accommodation only if the specific animal poses a direct threat to the health or safety of others, or would cause substantial physical damage to the property, that cannot be reduced or eliminated by another reasonable accommodation. For a trained dog guide or service animal, Landlord will not require its removal unless its presence, behavior or actions pose an unreasonable risk of injury or harm to property or other persons and a reasonable attempt to eliminate that behavior or those actions has failed, and will not remove it from the entire property because of a risk that arises in only part of the property.
notes: WA: Overrides `assistance-animal-accommodation`, which is not tagged: its withdrawal standard ('cannot be reduced or eliminated by another reasonable accommodation') can be applied as a prediction, while Washington requires, for a dog guide or service animal, that a reasonable attempt has actually failed and bars removal from the whole property for a risk in part of it: 'It is an unfair practice to remove a trained dog guide or service animal from the entire rental property because the animal presents a risk of injury or harm when in part of the rental property' (WAC 162-38-105(1)); the conditions are WAC 162-38-105(1)(a)-(b). Deposits: 'It is not an unfair practice for a landlord to enforce on a tenant with a disability using a dog guide or service animal its standard cleaning or damage deposit if the same cleaning or damage deposit is enforced equally on all tenants' (WAC 162-38-100(4)); no pet deposit WAC 162-38-100(5); no-pet policy inapplicable WAC 162-38-100(3). Otherwise the text is the shared clause's, with two WA changes: the cleaning or damage deposit sentence and the added 'only if' limit on denial. title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: Give each affected tenant at least 90 days' written notice of any rent increase, and do not make an increase effective before the current fixed term ends. Use the state's Rent and Fee Increase Notice form and serve it the way eviction notices are served (personal delivery, or leaving it with a suitable person and mailing, or posting and mailing). 'Rent' here includes every recurring or periodic charge in the lease for use and occupancy, such as pet rent or parking, so a new or higher recurring fee is a rent increase. If rent is set by the tenant's income in a subsidized tenancy, 30 days' notice applies and the form is not required (a tenant paying with a portable voucher still gets the form). New rules other than rent changes take effect only after 30 days' written notice and at the end of the term, unless the tenant agrees sooner.
notes: WA: 'a landlord shall provide a minimum of 90 days' prior written notice of an increase in the amount of rent to each affected tenant, and any increase in the amount of rent may not become effective prior to the completion of the term of the rental agreement' (RCW 59.18.140(3)(a)); subsidized income-based tenancies, 30 days (RCW 59.18.140(3)(b)); a transition rule for fixed terms with 60 to 90 days left on May 7, 2025 (RCW 59.18.140(3)(c), now spent). Form: 'a landlord must provide a tenant with notice of rent increases in a form that is substantially the same as the form provided in subsection (3) of this section' (RCW 59.18.720(1)(a)), served under RCW 59.12.040 (RCW 59.18.720(1)(b)); form not required for income-based subsidized tenancies, but a portable voucher tenancy is not 'subsidized' for this purpose (RCW 59.18.720(2)). Rent definition: 'means recurring and periodic charges identified in the rental agreement for the use and occupancy of the premises, which may include charges for utilities' (RCW 59.18.030). title: Statewide Rent Increase Limit
bodyText: Washington limits rent increases for every type of tenancy, month-to-month or fixed-term: no increase at all during the first 12 months of a tenancy, and in any 12-month period no more than 7% plus the Seattle-area CPI, or 10%, whichever is less. The Department of Commerce publishes each year's maximum. Rent includes recurring fees. You may reset rent freely only after a tenant vacates. Exempt: units whose first certificate of occupancy is 12 years old or less at the date of the notice; units owned by public housing or development authorities or by rent-regulated nonprofits; qualifying tax-credit housing; and, if the owner is not a REIT, a corporation or an LLC with a corporate member, rooms sharing a kitchen or bath with the owner, owner-occupied single-family homes renting up to two units or bedrooms, and owner-occupied duplexes to fourplexes. Claim an exemption by stating its supporting facts in the increase notice. If you overcharge, the tenant must first give you a written demand to cure, and may end the lease on 20 days' written notice before the increase takes effect, owing rent for the full month of moving out but no fee; courts award the excess, up to three months of the unlawful amount, and fees, and the Attorney General may seek civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation. Do not report unpaid unlawful increases to a screening service. No city or county may otherwise regulate the amount of rent, but check local notice and fee ordinances (Seattle, Tacoma, Spokane and others).

title: Same Terms for Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Leases
bodyText: Washington bars terms of payment or other material conditions that are more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant, or the reverse. For any one unit, the rent you offer on different lease types may differ by no more than 5%, and that difference may not push the rent past the statewide increase limit. Offering a lower rent only for a 12-month lease, or a fee only for month-to-month, can therefore break the rule if the gap is larger than 5% or the burden is material.

title: Late Fees in Washington
bodyText: You may not charge a late fee for rent paid within five days after its due date; once rent is more than five days late, the fee may run from the first day after the due date. For these tenancies Washington sets no cap on the late fee itself (mobile home lot agreements have percentage caps), but in an eviction for nonpayment the court's judgment, and the amount the tenant pays to be reinstated, may include late fees only up to $75 in total. A lease term charging a late fee within the five days is void, and knowingly using a lease with that term exposes you to actual damages plus statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees. You may still serve a 14-day pay-or-vacate notice any time after rent is due.

title: What Counts as Rent
bodyText: In Washington, rent means the recurring and periodic charges in the lease for use and occupancy, which can include utilities, pet rent or parking. Late fees, damages, deposits, legal costs and other one-time fees are not rent, and a tenant's right to stay cannot be conditioned on paying them (except the court costs, late fees up to $75 and awarded attorneys' fees a tenant pays to be reinstated in a nonpayment eviction): put only rent in a 14-day pay-or-vacate notice, and collect other charges by other lawful means. The exception: if you gave an installment plan for deposits or nonrefundable fees at the start of the tenancy and the tenant defaults, the missed installment may be treated as rent owing. A fee in lieu of a deposit is never rent. Do not roll a balance from an earlier lease or unit into rent.

The last sentence answers the real lease's prior-balance clause (WA log §15): a balance from another tenancy is not a charge 'identified in the rental agreement for the use and occupancy of the premises' (Claude's reading of RCW 59.18.030). title: Rent Receipts and Accepted Payment Forms
bodyText: You may refuse cash, but if you accept cash you must give a receipt. For any other payment, give a written receipt when the tenant asks. title: Bounced Rent Checks
bodyText: After a tenant's personal check to you is returned for nonsufficient funds or a closed account, you may refuse personal checks from that tenant for nine months, but you must still accept a cashier's check or money order. Washington's dishonored-check law lets the payee collect a reasonable handling fee for each returned check; if the check is still unpaid 15 days after you send the statutory notice of dishonor, interest at 12% and collection costs of up to $40 (or the check amount, if less) may be added, and in a court action on the check further damages and fees apply. Keep your fee reasonable and state it in the lease.

title: Screening Charges for Applicants
bodyText: You may charge an applicant for a tenant screening report, or your own actual screening costs up to what local screening services customarily charge, only if before getting any information you told the applicant in writing (or by posting) what you will check, what criteria can lead to denial, the consumer reporting agency's name and address and the applicant's rights to a free copy and to dispute it, and whether you accept a comprehensive reusable screening report. title: Screening Notices and Adverse Action
bodyText: Before you obtain any information about an applicant, give the screening notice in writing or by posting (types of information, denial criteria, the reporting agency's details and rights, and whether you accept a comprehensive reusable report). If you deny the application or approve it with conditions (a higher deposit, a guarantor, last month's rent or higher rent), give a written adverse action notice stating the reasons, in substantially the statutory format. If you have a website advertising rentals, its home page must say whether you accept comprehensive reusable reports. Do not use a victim's status or a tenant's lawful source of income against them. Screening companies may not report or score an eviction case a court has ordered limited, and treating such a case as unreported is good practice. Don't take adverse action over rent unpaid during the COVID-19 period (March 1, 2020 to six months after the moratorium ended); don't ask about, consider or require medical records or history except to evaluate an accommodation or modification request. A condominium or homeowners association may require owners to screen tenants but may not demand the report.

title: Holding Fees and Deposits
bodyText: After you offer a unit, you may take a fee or deposit to hold it, up to 25% of the first month's rent. Immediately on payment, give a receipt and a written statement of any conditions under which you may keep it. If the applicant moves in, credit it to the first month's rent or the security deposit; if not, you may keep it only as the written statement allows. You may not keep any of it if the unit fails a tenant-based rental assistance inspection; if that inspection doesn't happen within 10 days (or an agreed longer time), you may tell the applicant the unit is no longer held and must then promptly return the money. A screening charge is separate and is not a holding fee.
notes: WA: 'A landlord may not request a fee or deposit to hold a dwelling or secure that the prospective tenant will move into the dwelling unit in excess of twenty-five percent of the first month's rent' (RCW 59.18.253(3)); receipt and written conditions RCW 59.18.253(2); credit or keep RCW 59.18.253(4)(a); screening costs excluded RCW 59.18.253(4)(b); failed inspection RCW 59.18.253(4)(c). title: Source of Income Discrimination
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent to, evict, or set different terms for an applicant or tenant because of a lawful source of income, including housing vouchers, public assistance, emergency rental assistance, veterans benefits, Social Security or SSI. Do not advertise preferences such as 'no Section 8'. If you use an income threshold, subtract the voucher or subsidy from the rent before applying it. A narrow exception lets you refuse where the voucher requires an inspection, the written estimate of repairs to pass is over $1,500, and you have not received landlord mitigation program money for the repairs. Violations cost up to four and one-half times the monthly rent plus fees.

title: Rent Concessions and the Increase Limit
bodyText: Washington has no statute written for rent concessions such as a free month or a move-in discount, but two rules reach them. A lease may not require the tenant to keep the concession, the rent or other offer terms confidential. And because rent includes recurring charges and the statewide limit caps any increase in a 12-month period, a recurring monthly discount that ends can look like a rent increase measured from the discounted rent; the statute does not say. To stay safe, put any concession in the lease as a one-time credit with its amount and timing. Treat the end of a recurring discount as an increase: no increase is allowed in the first 12 months of a tenancy or before a fixed term ends, so don't schedule a discount to end then, and otherwise give the 90-day notice and keep the change within the limit unless an exemption applies.

title: Interest on Money a Tenant Owes
bodyText: No Washington landlord-tenant statute sets interest on unpaid rent or damages. Washington's usury law sets 12% as the interest rate on a loan or forbearance of money when no rate is agreed in writing, and caps any rate at the higher of 12% or a Treasury-bill-based rate, and court judgments carry their own statutory interest (a judgment for unpaid consumer debt bears 9% unless a written contract rate applies). Whether a lease may add contractual interest on unpaid rent is not settled by statute, and a charge that works like a late fee within the first five days is void, so the library offers no interest clause.

bodyText: Washington's retail sales tax reaches lodging for less than a month, not ordinary residential rent: occupancy for a continuous period of one month or more is presumed to be a rental of real property rather than a license to use it. title: Pet Deposits, Fees and Pet Rent
bodyText: For tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act, Washington sets no cap on pet deposits, pet fees or pet rent (mobile home lot agreements entered into on or after May 7, 2025, not renewals of earlier ones, cap move-in fees and deposits at one month's rent, or two months' if the tenant brings pets). A refundable pet deposit is a deposit under the deposit statute (written terms and the move-in checklist); a nonrefundable pet fee must be stated in writing as nonrefundable; monthly pet rent is a recurring charge, so it counts as rent for the increase limit and the increase notice. On written request, tenants may pay deposits and fees in installments unless deposits and nonrefundable fees total no more than 25% of the first full month's rent and no last month's rent is required upfront. Do not charge a pet deposit or pet fee for an assistance animal.

bodyText: If a government or nonprofit emergency rental assistance program gives the tenant a pledge, you must accept it if it arrives before a pay-or-vacate notice expires and covers the full rent owed; after the notice expires, you must accept a written pledge that will contribute to paying the full amount due. title: Deposits When the Property Changes Hands
bodyText: If you sell or otherwise transfer your status as landlord during a tenancy, the deposit money must move at the same time to an equivalent trust account of the new landlord, who must promptly tell the tenant about the transfer and the new depository. bodyText: Miss the 30-day deadline for the itemized statement, documentation and refund, and you owe the tenant the full deposit. title: Installment Payments of Move-In Costs

title: Charging Damage Beyond the Deposit
bodyText: Back every damage deduction with estimates or invoices; for work you or your employees do, include the materials receipt (or a vendor price list for stock on hand) and the time spent and hourly rate. title: Fee in Lieu of a Deposit: Your Duties
bodyText: If you offer a monthly fee instead of a deposit, keep it strictly optional, offer it to every approved applicant and never use the choice in deciding an application; any nonrefundable part must be disclosed in the lease and separately acknowledged by the tenant; the fee is not rent, and nonpayment is not a cause for eviction, though you may sue for it; give the statutory disclosure form with the lease and any renewal; disclose in writing the terms of the insurance you buy with the fees (coverage, exclusions and caps) and, if the insurer requires you to try the tenant first, that the fee doesn't stop you or the insurer pursuing the tenant; use the fee only to buy that insurance, charging no more than its cost and administration; still give the move-in checklist; and let the tenant switch to a deposit at any time. Once the insurer pays a valid claim you may not seek those amounts from the tenant, and if it denies a claim as not a loss under the lease or for insufficient documentation you may not invoice or pursue the tenant for it; wait 60 days after notifying the tenant and sending documentation (and 60 days after filing the claim) before any collection; sue within one year after the tenancy ends. If you stop offering the option, give 60 days' notice before the end of the term, credit the fees paid against the deposit and offer a three-month installment plan.

title: Just Cause: When You May End a Tenancy
bodyText: Washington requires a listed cause to evict, to refuse to continue a tenancy, or to end a month-to-month tenancy. The end of a fixed term does not by itself end possession: unless the lease uses one of two narrow options (a first lease of six to 12 months that rolls to month-to-month, ended with 60 days' notice before the first term ends; or a fixed term that has never been month-to-month, where the first lease was 12 months or more or every lease since the start was for six months or more, ended with 60 days' notice before the term ends), the tenancy becomes month-to-month. The causes are: unpaid rent after a 14-day notice; a material breach not cured within a 10-day notice; waste, nuisance or unlawful activity after a 3-day notice; owner or immediate family move-in (90 days); sale of a single-family home (90 days); demolition, substantial rehabilitation or change of use (120 days); condominium conversion; a unit certified or condemned as uninhabitable (30 days); a shared unit with the owner (20 days); transitional housing ending (30 days); refusing a reasonable new lease offered at least 30 days before a fixed term ends (not for periodic tenancies); intentional, material application misrepresentations (30 days); other legitimate economic or business reasons (60 days); four or more cured violations in 12 months with written warnings (60 days); a sex-offender registration requirement (60 days); and sexual harassment of the owner, staff or another tenant based on race, gender or other protected status in violation of the lease (20 days). Owner move-in, sale, and demolition, substantial rehabilitation or change of use can't end a fixed term early unless you and the tenant agree in writing and the tenant gets at least 60 days to vacate. Each notice must be served as eviction notices are served and state the supporting facts. If you remove a tenant, or cause a tenant to be removed, in violation of this law, you owe the greater of the tenant's economic and noneconomic damages or three months' rent, plus attorneys' fees and court costs. When a tenant permanently leaves other than because you ended the tenancy, give remaining occupants who lived there at least six months a 30-day notice to apply for the tenancy or vacate (not in subsidized housing). Some cities add their own just-cause rules.

Notice periods for (2)(f) come from RCW 59.18.200(2)(c). title: Notice Periods to End a Tenancy
bodyText: A tenant may end a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy with written notice of at least 20 days before the end of a rental period, and a fixed-term tenancy with written notice at least 20 days before the term ends; a servicemember (or spouse or dependent) with permanent change of station or deployment orders that don't allow 20 days' notice may give less, and a servicemember (or spouse or dependent) with permanent change of station or deployment orders meeting the statutory criteria may end a fixed term early on 20 days' written notice with a copy of the orders or a commanding officer's letter. A landlord may end a tenancy only for a just cause, with that cause's notice period, except that a qualifying fixed term may be ended without cause at its end on 60 days' written notice (see the just-cause row and the two optional term clauses); longer periods apply to condominium conversion (120 days) and demolition, substantial rehabilitation or change of use (120 days). A 90-day notice applies before changing to a policy of excluding children, but such a policy is lawful only where an exemption allows it (such as housing for older persons), and the change isn't a listed cause: the tenancy can still end only on a just cause (possibly the 'other good cause' ground, 60 days). Every landlord notice ending a tenancy must be served by personal delivery; or, if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion there and mailing a copy; or, if the tenant's residence isn't known or no such person can be found, by posting a copy conspicuously, delivering a copy to a resident if one can be found, and mailing a copy; it must state the date to vacate or comply; mailing from within Washington completes service, but you must wait five extra days before filing an eviction based on a mailed notice.

Landlord periods: RCW 59.18.200(2)(a)-(c), 59.18.650(2) (other good cause (2)(m)); older-persons exemption RCW 49.60.222(6); fixed terms ended without cause RCW 59.18.650(1)(b)-(c). title: The 14-Day Pay or Vacate Notice
bodyText: For unpaid rent, serve a 14-day notice to pay or vacate in substantially the statutory form, which lists monthly rent, utilities and other recurring charges due (no late fees or other one-time charges), tells the tenant about the Attorney General's translated notices and rental assistance, the right to a lawyer and an interpreter, and mediation, and states where to pay. You may serve it any time after rent is due. Accept payment as the lease allows or by nonelectronic means, including (but not limited to) cashier's check, money order or other certified funds; any payment must go first to the amount on the notice. Serve it the way RCW 59.12.040 requires (personal delivery, or the substitute methods, which include mailing a copy); when a copy is mailed, allow five additional days before filing. State in the notice the date by which the tenant must pay or vacate, which the service statute now requires of every termination notice. You must accept a rental assistance pledge that covers the full rent before the notice expires.

No late fees or one-time charges: rent excludes nonrecurring charges (RCW 59.18.030, applied by RCW 59.12.030(3)). Service and five days: RCW 59.12.040, which also requires a termination notice to specify the date to vacate or comply (Laws of 2026, ch. 144, § 1); the RCW 59.18.057 form has no date field, so add one. title: Cure Periods for Lease Violations
bodyText: For a breach other than unpaid rent or money damages, give a written 10-day notice to comply or vacate that specifies the acts or omissions; the tenant (or a subtenant or mortgagee) may cure within the 10 days and save the tenancy. A breach must be substantial and of a material lease term, a material subsidized-housing requirement, or a tenant duty imposed by law. No cure applies to waste, nuisance, unlawful activity affecting others' use and enjoyment, or other substantial or repeated and unreasonable interference: a 3-day notice to quit. Repeated cured violations can support a 60-day end-of-term notice only after four separate violations in 12 months, each with a written warning containing the statutory statements. For unpaid rent the tenant can still pay and be reinstated up to five court days after judgment.

No cure: RCW 59.18.650(2)(c), 59.12.030(5). Warnings: RCW 59.18.650(2)(n)(ii)(A)-(D). Reinstatement: RCW 59.18.410(2). title: The Eviction Court Process
bodyText: Only a court can evict. After the notice period runs, file an unlawful detainer case in superior court with the statutory Eviction Summons (Residential). You may ask for a show cause hearing 7 to 30 days after service, where the tenant may answer orally or in writing; if you prevail, the court issues a writ of restitution that the sheriff executes. If you can't serve the tenant personally after three attempts over at least two days at different times, you may post and mail (regular and certified) at least nine days before the return date, but then the court can only restore possession, not enter a money judgment. Subject to state funding, the court must appoint a lawyer for an indigent tenant, and hearings may be continued for that. Some superior courts add local rules: for example, requiring a copy of the lease with the complaint, pleading the just-cause basis, serving a local notice with the show cause order, or (in Skagit County) notifying the local legal aid office before filing. Check the county's local court rules.

title: Court Payment Plans and Stays in Nonpayment Cases
bodyText: In a nonpayment eviction, the tenant can end the case by paying the rent due, court costs, up to $75 in late fees and any awarded attorneys' fees before judgment or within five court days after it (longer with a rental assistance pledge letter), plus $50 for each prior post-judgment reinstatement in the last 12 months. Even after judgment the court may stay the writ for up to 90 days on a payment plan, weighing factors such as willfulness, hardship and payment history; the tenant must pay one month's rent within five court days. A tenant served three or more pay-or-vacate notices in the past 12 months generally can't get this stay. If the tenant later defaults on the plan, serve the statutory notice of default; the tenant then has three calendar days before the sheriff may execute the writ. The court may find the tenant eligible for the state landlord mitigation program to pay you.

title: Limited Dissemination of Eviction Records
bodyText: A court may order an eviction case to be of limited dissemination if your case lacked a basis in fact or law, if the tenancy was reinstated, or for other good cause. Once ordered, tenant screening services may not report that case or use it in a score. Expect courts to use this where a tenant paid and was reinstated. Separately, you may not deny or end a tenancy because someone was a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or because they ended a lease under the victim-protection statute.

title: No Lockouts, Utility Shutoffs or Property Seizures
bodyText: Never remove or exclude a tenant without a court order: no lock changes, removal of doors or belongings, or utility shutoffs. A tenant locked out may recover possession or end the lease, plus damages and fees. Intentionally causing termination of water, heat, electricity or gas (other than for a reasonable time to make repairs) costs actual damages plus up to $100 a day. Taking or keeping a tenant's belongings without specific written consent, after a written demand for their return, can cost up to $500 a day (capped at $5,000) if intentional. The police may remove a squatter on the owner's sworn declaration, but never a tenant or a tenant's guest.

title: No Landlord Lien on Tenant Property
bodyText: Washington abolished the landlord's right of distress for rent. A lease clause creating a lien on the tenant's personal property, or authorizing you to seize it for rent, is void. You may take a tenant's property only with the tenant's specific written consent to that taking, after an abandonment, after a writ of restitution, or after a sole tenant's death, each under its own procedure.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: While a tenant complies with the landlord-tenant act, you may not retaliate (by eviction, a rent increase, reduced services or added obligations) for good-faith complaints to a government agency about code violations that may endanger health or safety, or for asserting rights under the act. Acting within 90 days after such a complaint or the resulting inspection creates a presumption of retaliation; a tenant behind on rent or in breach when you give a termination notice gets the opposite presumption; a rent increase notice that states reasonable grounds avoids the presumption; impracticality of repairs with the tenant in place can rebut it for an eviction, and a tenant complaint made within 90 days after your notice of a rent increase is presumed not made in good faith. Do not retaliate against a tenant who lets a code official inspect.

title: Property Left After an Abandonment
bodyText: If a tenant who owes rent has shown by words or actions an intent not to return, you may enter, take any property left, and store it somewhere reasonably secure. Mail a notice by first-class mail to the last known address and any other known address giving your name and address, where the property is, the sale or disposal date, and the tenant's right to get it back first. Return it if the tenant asks in writing before the sale and pays the lesser of actual or reasonable moving and storage costs. You may sell or dispose of it 45 days after the notice (7 days if its total value is $250 or less, except personal papers, family pictures and keepsakes). Apply proceeds to what you're owed and hold any excess for one year. A sole tenant's death follows a separate procedure.

title: Rent Owed After a Tenant Abandons
bodyText: When a tenant in default abandons, make a reasonable effort to re-rent. A month-to-month tenant owes rent for the 30 days after the earlier of the date you learn of the abandonment or the next rent due date. A tenant with a longer term owes the lesser of all rent for the rest of the term, or the rent accrued while re-renting at a fair rental, plus any shortfall in the new rent, plus your actual re-renting costs, statutory court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees. Your deposit statement is due within 30 days after you learn of the abandonment.

title: Tenant Property After a Writ of Restitution
bodyText: When the sheriff executes a writ, take possession of the tenant's property left in the unit. You must store it if the tenant served a written storage request (the sheriff gives the tenant a form you supply) within three days after service of the writ, and, if you know the tenant has a disability that impairs or prevents a request, must presume one unless the tenant objects in writing; if the tenant objects, or makes no request and you choose not to store, the property goes on the nearest public property. Return stored property when the tenant pays the lesser of actual or reasonable moving and storage costs. Before selling property worth over $250, give notice and wait 30 days; for $250 or less, 7 days (personal papers, family pictures and keepsakes may not be sold under the small-value rule). Hold excess sale proceeds for one year, then report them to the Department of Revenue as unclaimed property.

title: When a Sole Tenant Dies
bodyText: You may ask a tenant to designate, in a writing separate from the lease, a person to act on the tenant's death if the tenant lives alone. When a sole occupant dies, promptly mail or hand-deliver (and email if you know an address) a notice to any known personal representative, designated person, emergency contact and likely successor, and to the tenant at the unit, stating the death, rent paid-through date, and that the tenancy ends 15 days after the notice or at the paid-through date, whichever is later, unless a representative arranges to prepay rent for up to 60 days from the death. Release property to a representative who asks in writing, takes an inventory and signs a possession-only acknowledgment. Refund unearned rent and account for the deposit within 30 days after removal. Before selling or disposing of unclaimed property, send a second notice and wait at least 45 days; property worth over $1,000 must be sold in a commercially reasonable manner, and personal papers and photographs may not be sold.

title: Early Termination by Victims
bodyText: A tenant who gives written notice that the tenant or a household member was a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, unlawful harassment or stalking, and provides a protection order or a qualified third party's signed report, may end the lease without further obligation if the request is made within 90 days of the incident. The tenant owes no rent after the month of moving out, and owes that month's rent unless the termination also met the 20-day periodic notice rule, and gets the full deposit back, subject to lawful deductions (documented damage beyond ordinary wear, unpaid rent or charges), whatever the lease says about forfeiture. If you claim damages from the state landlord mitigation program, you may not keep any of that tenant's deposit or pursue the tenant for property damage beyond the deposit. Other co-tenants remain bound unless they are victims. If the tenant or a household member is a victim of sexual assault, stalking or unlawful harassment by the landlord (including the landlord's employees), the tenant may leave first and deliver the order or report within seven days of moving out, owing rent only until the later of moving out or delivering the report and notice, with a pro rata refund of prepaid rent. title: Other Statutory Ways a Tenant May Leave Early
bodyText: Beyond the military and victim rights, a Washington tenant may end the lease without further obligation if: you fail to remedy a defective condition within the statutory period to start repairs after written notice and a reasonable time to finish; a court or arbitrator finds a defect too substantial to fix in time; you threaten the tenant with a firearm or deadly weapon and are arrested; another tenant threatens them with a firearm or deadly weapon, is arrested, the tenant notifies you, and you don't file an eviction within seven calendar days after law enforcement notifies you of the arrest; or you raise rent unlawfully above the statewide limit (after a written cure demand, on at least 20 days' written notice, ending before the increase takes effect, owing rent for the full month of moving out). If you knowingly rent a unit an agency has condemned or declared unlawful to occupy, the tenant recovers the greater of three months' rent or up to three times actual damages, plus costs and attorneys' fees, and, on leaving, all deposits and prepaid rent; relocation assistance is owed where you knew or should have known of the conditions, with exceptions for tenant or third-party illegal conduct you didn't know of, natural disasters and eminent domain.

title: Premium Holdover Rates (Not Offered)
bodyText: Washington sets no statutory holdover measure for residential tenancies (the general double-damages rule for unlawful detainer doesn't apply to them), so a lease could set a stipulated daily charge for a tenant who stays after the tenancy lawfully ends. The library's holdover clause charges daily rent instead. If you want a premium, add your own clause and take advice first.

title: Fire, Casualty and Uninhabitable Units
bodyText: Washington has no statute written for fire or casualty damage to a rental. If the unit becomes defective, the tenant uses the repair-notice remedies: if you don't start repairs within the statutory period after written notice and finish within a reasonable time, the tenant may end the lease, and a court may end it if the defect can't feasibly be fixed in time. You may end a tenancy for a damaged unit only on a just cause, for example a unit certified or condemned as uninhabitable by a local agency where continued occupancy would expose you to civil or criminal penalties (30 days' notice, or as much as the order allows) or demolition or substantial rehabilitation (120 days; not before a fixed term ends unless the tenant agrees in writing and gets at least 60 days). If a code agency condemns the unit and you knew or should have known of the conditions, you owe relocation assistance (not for natural disasters or tenant or third-party illegal conduct you didn't know of). A lease clause letting you end the lease after a casualty isn't offered: it would add a cause the statute doesn't list. If the tenant, family, guest or anyone under the tenant's control caused the damage, you have no repair duty for it and the tenant has no remedy for it under the landlord-tenant act.

title: Criminal Activity and Dangerous Conduct
bodyText: Washington's statute already makes these tenant duties: no drug-related activity at the premises (and not allowing it with the tenant's knowledge or consent); no imminently hazardous activity involving an assault or unlawful use of a firearm or deadly weapon that leads to an arrest; and no gang-related activity endangering two or more households. Waste, nuisance or unlawful activity affecting others' use and enjoyment lets you serve a 3-day notice to quit with no cure. Neighbors in the same building or complex, or within a one-block radius, whose safety or property is endangered by a tenant's gang activity may serve you a 10-day demand to file an eviction, and may petition the court if you don't investigate, if you investigate and find no gang activity, or if your steps don't stop it. The library offers no separate crime-free clause: the statute covers the ground, a broader lease definition could reach conduct the statute protects (victims), and city crime-free programs may not bar renting to someone solely for criminal history.

title: Tenants and Foreclosure
bodyText: If a rental is sold at a foreclosure (trustee's) sale, a tenant in possession must get 60 days' written notice to vacate before removal, except for waste or nuisance; where the trustee elects to foreclose the occupants' interests, it must also post and mail the statutory notice to residents when the sale is noticed. title: Condemned or Unlawful Units and Relocation Assistance
bodyText: Once a code agency notifies you that a unit is condemned or unlawful to occupy, you may not rent it until the conditions are fixed; knowingly doing so costs the greater of three months' rent or up to treble damages, plus all deposits and prepaid rent if the tenant leaves. If you knew or should have known of the conditions, you must pay displaced tenants relocation assistance of the greater of $2,000 per unit or three months' rent, plus deposits and prepaid rent, within seven days of the agency's notice (exceptions: tenant or third-party illegal conduct you didn't know of, natural disasters, eminent domain). From the agency's first notice of violations until relocation assistance is paid or the conditions are fixed, you may not evict, harass or intimidate tenants to avoid or reduce this duty, and may not reduce services, raise rent at all, or materially increase or change other obligations.

title: Your Duty to Keep the Unit Fit
bodyText: Throughout the tenancy keep the premises fit for human habitation: substantially comply with codes where a violation endangers health or safety; keep structural parts usable and the unit weathertight; keep shared areas clean, sanitary and safe; provide pest control at the start of the tenancy and, except in a single-family residence, during it unless the tenant caused the infestation; repair everything except ordinary wear; provide adequate locks and keys and safeguard master keys; keep supplied electrical, plumbing, heating and other facilities and appliances working; provide garbage receptacles and removal except in a single-family residence; and provide facilities for heat, water and hot water. These duties can't be waived in a standard lease. You have no repair duty, and the tenant no remedy, for a condition the tenant or the tenant's family, guests or people under their control caused, or where the tenant unreasonably refuses access for repairs.

title: Fixing a Tenant's Breach Yourself

title: Tenants' Duties Under Washington Law
bodyText: Washington law requires every tenant to pay rent as agreed and obey applicable codes, and to: keep their part of the premises as clean and sanitary as conditions permit; dispose of garbage properly and pay for extermination of infestations they cause; use fixtures and appliances properly; not damage or remove any part of the dwelling or let others do so; not permit a nuisance or waste; not engage in or knowingly allow drug-related activity; maintain the smoke detector, including batteries; not engage in imminently hazardous assaults or unlawful weapon use leading to an arrest; not engage in gang-related activity; and at move-out restore the unit to its initial condition except ordinary wear and conditions you failed to fix. A tenant who paid a nonrefundable cleaning fee may not be charged for normal cleaning.

title: Shifting Repair Duties to a Tenant
bodyText: A landlord and tenant may exempt themselves from the landlord's repair and habitability duties (and the related tenant remedies) only by a written agreement that is not in a standard form lease, between parties of roughly equal bargaining power, that doesn't undercut safe and sanitary housing, and that the county prosecutor, the Attorney General's consumer protection division or the tenant's own attorney has approved in writing. A lease clause shifting those duties is otherwise void. Ordinary upkeep a tenant uses exclusively, such as a single-family home's yard or snow on the tenant's own walkway, is not one of the landlord's statutory duties. The library offers no tenant-repair agreement for Washington: one generated from a template is a standard form, and the approval must come from an official or the tenant's lawyer.

title: Utility Shutoffs and Heat Alerts
bodyText: You may never intentionally cause a tenant's water, heat, electricity or gas to be shut off, except for a reasonable time to make repairs. The landlord-tenant act also contains rules for a landlord-supplied electric or water service disconnected for nonpayment: no involuntary disconnection on any day the National Weather Service has issued or announced a heat-related alert for the area, a disconnection notice that explains how to ask for reconnection, a prompt reconnection attempt on request on such a day, and any payment plan capped at 6% of the tenant's monthly income. Those rules assume such disconnections happen, but they don't authorize them, and the general shutoff ban has no nonpayment exception; don't disconnect a tenant's utilities without advice. Where a city or town utility serves the property and either several units share one account, the billing address differs from the service address, or the city has been told a tenant lives there, the city must make a good-faith effort to give seven days' written notice at the service address before cutting electricity or water for your nonpayment, and a tenant who puts the service in their own name may deduct those charges from rent.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: Install smoke detection devices inside every rental dwelling unit, test them and make them work before each new occupancy, and instruct the occupants on their purpose, operation and maintenance; the tenant maintains them, including batteries. title: Water Heater Temperature
