title: Lease Terms Washington Voids
bodyText: Any lease term waiving a section of the landlord-tenant act is unenforceable (the narrow exemption agreement aside), and a lease may not provide that the tenant: waives rights or remedies under the act; gives up the right to sue or join a class action against you or your agents; signs a nondisclosure agreement about the lease or the offer (rent, deposits, fees, concessions, move-in gifts, specials); authorizes a confession of judgment; agrees to pay your attorneys' fees except as the act allows and a court awards; exculpates or limits your liability under law, or indemnifies you for it; agrees in advance to a particular arbitrator, or to arbitrate unless you pay all its cost and the agreement is notarized; pays late fees on rent paid within five days of its due date; or must pay rent electronically only. A lease term creating a lien on the tenant's belongings is void. Agreements made in an eviction case that make the tenant pay more than the act allows, or waive the tenant's rights, are void too. Knowingly using a lease with a prohibited term exposes you to statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent.

title: Penalty for Using a Prohibited Term
bodyText: A prohibited term is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease containing terms you know are prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages, statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees. title: Attorneys' Fees
bodyText: A lease may not make the tenant pay your attorneys' fees except as the landlord-tenant act authorizes and a court awards. Any lease clause giving one party fees is read to give fees to whichever party prevails, and can't be waived. In an eviction, a court may award you fees, but not after a default judgment, and not where the rent awarded is two months' rent or $1,200 or less, whichever is greater; if the tenant has moved to stay the writ, the court may award you fees only if the tenant is reinstated under the hardship-stay rules, and those fees are then subject to repayment under the stay order. title: Who the Landlord-Tenant Act Covers
bodyText: Washington's Residential Landlord-Tenant Act covers most residential rentals. It doesn't cover: institutional residence incidental to care, detention or education; occupancy under an earnest money agreement or contract of sale by the buyer; a seller staying up to three months after closing under a qualifying written agreement; hotels and transient lodging; certain owner-condemnee, agricultural, seasonal farmworker and state-land rentals; and an employee whose right to occupy depends on employment on the premises, unless any arrangement is set up mainly to avoid the act. Mobile and manufactured home lots have their own act. A lease of a single-family dwelling for a year or more, or with a bona fide purchase option, can opt out of the act only if the tenant's attorney approves the exemption on the face of the lease; the library doesn't offer that opt-out.

title: Washington Fair Housing Classes
bodyText: Washington bars discrimination in renting because of sex, marital status, sexual orientation, race, creed, color, national origin, citizenship or immigration status, families with children status, honorably discharged veteran or military status, any sensory, mental or physical disability, or the use of a trained dog guide or service animal. Local ordinances add more classes.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: You must make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies and services when needed for a person with a disability to use and enjoy the home, and allow reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense, conditioned where reasonable on restoring the interior at move-out. Don't ask an applicant about disability beyond what the tenancy needs, and don't require waivers or hold-harmless agreements because a disabled person will live there. These two duties don't apply to an owner renting a single-family house who owns no more than three, rents without a broker and without discriminatory advertising, or to an owner-occupied building of up to four units (federal law may still apply). title: Ending a Federal Housing Contract
bodyText: If you own federally assisted housing and the assistance contract will expire or you plan to prepay the mortgage or loan, Washington requires (unless an exception applies; Section 8 certificate or voucher contracts are outside the statute, and some long-term use agreements excuse a prepayment notice) written notice at least 12 months ahead, by regular and certified mail, to each tenant household, the city or county clerk, the public housing agency and the Department of Commerce. For 12 months after the notice (or until expiration or prepayment, if later) you may not evict except as the federal program allows, raise rent above the program amount, or change lease terms except as the lease permits; post the notice as the statute requires. title: Evictions for Drugs, Weapons and Gang Activity
bodyText: For drug-related activity, for imminently hazardous assaults or unlawful weapon use that led to the tenant's arrest, and for gang-related activity, the usual 30-day chance to fix a duty breach doesn't apply: you may proceed directly to an unlawful detainer action after a 3-day notice to quit for waste, nuisance or unlawful activity. title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage. This Section does not limit any right Tenant has under the Utah Fit Premises Act or other Utah law, including the right of a victim of domestic violence to end Tenant's future obligations under this Lease.
notes: UT: Added 2026-10-04, RETRO (SOP 1.53, rule 54t / rule 54). Modelled on tenant-caused-damage-tn, which was read, not tagged; text is the TN/WY text plus a Utah saving sentence. OFFERED BECAUSE THE LAW LEAVES A GAP THE LEASE CAN LAWFULLY FILL. What Utah gives the landlord without it: the renter may not intentionally or negligently damage the unit or knowingly permit any person to do so (Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-5(2)(a)); the deposit may be applied to damage beyond reasonable wear and tear (Utah Code Ann. § 57-17-3(1)); waste supports a 3-calendar-day no-cure notice (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-802(1)(d), (2)) and waste damages, if alleged and proved, are trebled in the eviction judgment (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-811(2)(c), (3)); a separate action for waste by a tenant for years may include treble damages (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-1001); after a forfeiture for nonpayment or for a covenant breach not cured after a perform-or-quit notice, the tenant stays liable for payments for the rest of the term, and the statute leaves any duty to mitigate unchanged rather than creating one (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-811(1)(c), (d)); whether a no-cure waste eviction is a forfeiture under (1)(c) is unsettled on the text; an abandoning tenant owes rent as Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-816(1) provides. The gap: no statute says rent keeps running while a tenant-caused loss is repaired, guest damage the renter did not knowingly permit is outside Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-5(2)(a), and lost rent is statutory only on a (1)(c) forfeiture or abandonment (abandonment is presumed only where rent goes unpaid and the tenant gave no notice of absence, Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-815(1)). EACH ABATEMENT OR EXIT ROUTE CHECKED FOR ITS OWN FAULT EXCEPTION (rule 54t): (a) casualty: Utah has no casualty statute (retro battery R2-R8), and casualty-termination-ut is a contract term limited, as edited the same day, to casualty 'not caused by Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant'; (b) essential services and landlord-breach termination: the Fit Premises Act's rent-abatement remedy (which ends the agreement) and repair-and-deduct remedy reach only a 'deficient condition', which excludes a condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, guest or invitee, or by a use violating the agreement or law (Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-6(1)(b)(ii), (4)(a)), and no renter remedy is available to a renter out of compliance with Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-5 (Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-6(4)(b)); heat, water and electricity are habitability standards inside that same regime (Utah Code Ann. §§ 57-22-3(1), 57-22-4(1)(b)(ii)); (c) rent into court: none for residential renters (R12, R12b; the possession bond under Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-808 is not a rent-escrow defence; Utah Code Ann. § 57-16-8 (search hit, read in context only) concerns mobile home park residents, whose lots are outside the Fit Premises Act, Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-2(5)); (d) landlord-paid utility: no utility-specific tenant statute (R13-R15, R14b, R15b; Utah Code Ann. § 10-7-10.5 lets a city cut water or sewer for the owner's nonpayment and itself gives the tenant nothing), but losing heat, water or electricity because the owner did not pay is a deficient condition the tenant did not cause, so the Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-6 remedies apply with no fault exception to engage; the saving sentence keeps them; (e) failure to deliver possession (Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-4.1) arises before possession, so tenant-caused damage is unlikely to trigger it (a tenant given early access could in theory cause it); the statute has no fault exception and the saving sentence preserves it; (f) domestic-violence termination: a victim may end future obligations even while out of compliance with Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-5(2), if the noncompliance occurred less than 30 days before the notice and is due to domestic violence, and stays liable for that noncompliance (Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-5.1(4), (5), (8)(b); unchanged in the version effective 2027-01-01). The route is unavailable after a notice of eviction is served (Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-5.1(7)). It has its own statutory fault rule; no anti-waiver provision was found in Chapter 22 and none is relied on, so the last sentence preserves the route expressly. Part (1) therefore waives no statutory abatement right; where a renter remedy does apply (for example a condition the tenant did not cause), the saving sentence keeps it. 'Occupant' as in tenant-caused-damage-tn and the UT-tagged assistance-animal-accommodation. UNREAD RISK (rule 76 label): whether a Utah court measures lost Rent through the end of the Term this way, and whether contract damages recovered in an eviction case are trebled as 'amounts due under the contract' (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-811(2)(d), (3)), are case-law questions not read. CONDITIONAL: offered, not defaulted (rule 54). Companion education row: edu-tenant-caused-damage-ut. Complements casualty-termination-ut and tenant-maintenance. BUILDER: show on opt-in; place immediately after casualty-termination-ut where both are chosen, otherwise in Default & Termination. title: Damage Caused by Tenant (Utah)
bodyText: Utah law already covers most of what happens when a tenant, a member of the tenant's family or a guest damages the home, even badly enough to make it unlivable. A renter must not intentionally or negligently destroy, damage or impair any part of the unit, or knowingly let anyone else do so. At move-out you may apply the deposit to damage beyond reasonable wear and tear and recover the rest from the tenant. If the damage is waste, or a breach that cannot afterwards be cured, you may serve a 3-calendar-day notice to quit with no chance to cure; in the eviction judgment the court must award three times the damages it assesses, including waste damages you allege and prove. A separate lawsuit for waste may also include treble damages, though that statute names tenants 'for life or years', so a month-to-month tenant may not be covered. The tenant's repair remedies do not apply: a condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, a guest or invitee, or by a use that breaks the lease or the law is not a 'deficient condition', so the renter can neither abate rent and end the lease nor repair and deduct, and a renter who is not meeting the renter's own duties gets neither remedy anyway. No Utah statute lets a tenant walk away after a fire or flood the tenant's side caused, and Utah has no procedure for a renter to pay rent into court. A tenant who abandons owes the rent for the rest of the term or, if less, the rent for the time reasonably needed to re-rent at a fair rental value plus any shortfall, a reasonable leasing commission and restoration costs beyond normal wear and tear, even if you have not re-rented. An eviction judgment for unpaid rent, or for a breach the tenant did not fix after a notice to comply, ends the lease without ending the tenant's liability for rent for the rest of the term; the statute does not say whether the same applies after a no-cure eviction for waste. The statute leaves any duty to mitigate unchanged; how far you must try to re-rent is case law the library has not read. What the statutes do not say is that rent keeps running while you repair, or that you recover lost rent when the lease ends some other way; the optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause says both. One exception: unless an eviction notice has already been served, a domestic violence victim who meets the statute's conditions may end future obligations under the lease even if damage that was due to the domestic violence happened in the 30 days before the notice; the renter stays liable for that damage. The optional Fire or Other Casualty clause already excludes a casualty caused by the tenant, an occupant, or a guest or invitee.
notes: UT: Added 2026-10-04, RETRO (SOP 1.53, rule 54t). Sentence by sentence: renter duty, Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-5(2)(a); deposit, Utah Code Ann. § 57-17-3(1) ('damages to the premises beyond reasonable wear and tear'; recovery of the balance is ordinary damages for breach of that duty); no-cure notice, Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-802(1)(d), (2); treble damages in the eviction judgment, Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-811(2)(c), (3) ('if waste is alleged in the complaint and proved at trial'; 'shall enter the judgment ... for three times the amount of the damages assessed'); separate waste action, Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-1001 ('may include treble damages'; it names a 'tenant for life or years', and whether a periodic tenant is one is case law, not read, so the body says a month-to-month tenant may not be covered); deficient condition, Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-6(1)(b)(ii), (4)(a), (4)(b); no casualty statute and no rent-into-court route for renters, whole-code searches 2026-10-04 (retro battery R2-R8, R12, R12b; Utah Code Ann. § 57-16-8, a search hit read in context, concerns mobile home park residents, whose lots are outside the Fit Premises Act, Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-2(5)); abandonment, Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-816(1) ('notwithstanding that the owner did not rerent'); forfeiture, Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-811(1)(c) (only for 'neglect or failure to perform any condition or covenant' or 'default in the payment of rent', which mirrors the curable notices in Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-802(1)(c), (h); whether a (1)(d) waste eviction counts is unsettled on the text) and (1)(d) ('does not change any obligation on either party to mitigate': it creates no duty, so the body says the duty is unchanged and its extent is case law); domestic violence, Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-5.1(4), (5), (7), (8)(b) (same text in the version effective 2027-01-01). Whether serious negligent damage is 'waste' is case law, not read, so the body says 'if the damage is waste'. Companion to the optional clause tenant-caused-damage-ut; complements edu-renter-remedies-ut (which states the compliance bar but not the deficient-condition exclusion) and edu-abandonment-rent-liability-ut. title: Holdover Charge
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession after the end of the Term, and Landlord has not agreed in writing to a continued tenancy or accepted Rent for one under the Holdover section of this Lease, then Tenant will pay Landlord a holdover charge of {{holdover_daily_rate}} for each day Tenant remains in possession, which, except in an eviction action, is in place of the actual damages and reasonable rental value described in that section. Landlord and Tenant agree that Landlord's loss from a holdover, including delay in making the property available to a new tenant, is difficult to estimate accurately in advance, that this charge is a reasonable estimate of that loss, and that it is not a penalty. Landlord may recover the charge from the Security Deposit or in a separate action, but will not claim it in an eviction action, where Utah law requires the court to award three times the damages it assesses, and will not offer the agreed daily figure as evidence of its damages in an eviction action. The charge is not due for any day for which Landlord recovers damages for Tenant's unlawful detainer, and Landlord will credit any holdover charge already received for a day covered by an eviction judgment against that judgment. Landlord's acceptance of a holdover charge is not acceptance of Rent for a continued tenancy. This Section does not limit Landlord's right to recover possession, unpaid Rent and other amounts due for the period before the Term ended, or damages for harm to the property.
notes: UT: Added 2026-10-04, RETRO targeted fix (rule 54 as amended at the NE sync, 2026-09-30). REVERSES the original pass's decline (UT log s6.1, decided by Claude, not Taylor). SHAPE OF THE STATUTORY MEASURE: Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-811(2)(b), (3) makes the court assess the damages from the unlawful detainer and enter judgment for the rent and three times those damages. Not conditional on its face: no willfulness or bad-faith element in the text (whether Utah courts add one is case law, not read). But a different shape, which leaves a gap: (1) it is a judgment-stage multiplier on court-assessed damages, so it sets no figure for the loss itself; (2) it exists only in an eviction judgment under Part 8, so a tenant who leaves a few days late without a suit leaves the landlord with actual damages only; (3) when it starts is unsettled on the text: a fixed term ends 'without notice' (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-802(1)(a)), but 'unlawful detainer' is defined as remaining after receiving a notice to quit (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-801(10)); case law not read. No other holdover measure: whole-code searches 2026-10-04 for holdover words and phrasings ('held over', 'remains in possession after the expiration', 'after the expiration of the term') and every multiplier phrasing ('treble', 'three times', 'double'/'twice'/'two times'/'1.5 times' the rent, and number-times the monthly or yearly rent or value) found only the eviction trebling, the waste action (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-1001) and the agricultural 60-day renewal (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-803) (retro battery R10, R10b, R11, R11b, R11c; rule 54 outside-title search: the 34 other multiplier sections are liens, theft, trees and similar). The original decline also relied on the trebling sweeping a contract rate in as 'amounts due under the contract' (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-811(2)(d)); the non-stacking sentence answers that (rule 53, MO circle-back 1), in three parts, because a bare 'not due for days the court trebles' would not be enough (independent check 2026-10-04): (a) the landlord promises not to claim the charge in an eviction action, so it is never pleaded as an (2)(d) amount; (b) it is not due for any day for which unlawful-detainer damages are recovered; (c) the landlord will not offer the agreed figure as evidence of damages in an eviction action (a promise by the landlord, since the parties cannot bind what evidence a court weighs), so the agreed-estimate sentence is not used as the (2)(b) measure that is then trebled; in an eviction action the landlord keeps holdover-ca's actual damages, because the charge replaces them only outside one ('except in an eviction action'), so no day is left with neither measure; outside one the charge is recovered from the deposit or in a separate action. UNREAD: whether a separate action for the charge is precluded because it could have been joined in the eviction action (claim preclusion, case law); a charge already taken (for example from the deposit) is credited against an eviction judgment. The charge therefore works only outside an eviction case, which is the gap. TRIGGER TIMING (rule 53's 'after this Lease ends' check): that conflict arises where a statute regulating holdover damages starts them later than the lease does; Utah's statute regulates no contract holdover charge, its own text ends a fixed term without notice (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-802(1)(a)), and the charge never runs on days the statutory measure is recovered; Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-801(10) leaves when the statutory measure starts unsettled, which is part of the gap. RULE 53 SCREEN: trigger is the end of the Term only, as in holdover-rate-in and holdover-rate-tn, so it never follows a nonpayment termination (Utah caps late fees at the greater of 10% of rent or $75, Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-4(5)(a)) and never runs while a tenant can still pay or perform to save the lease (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-802(2)); no statutory cap on holdover recovery; the lease is not kept enforceable for rent after a holdover. A fee 'in an amount greater than the amount agreed to in the rental agreement' or 'not included in the rental agreement' is barred (Utah Code Ann. § 57-22-4(5)(b)); this charge is stated in the lease. It is a cost 'provided for in the contract' that the deposit may be applied to (Utah Code Ann. § 57-17-3(1)). Whether a given rate is enforceable or a penalty is Utah case law, not read; the agreed-estimate sentence is common drafting, not a safe harbour. Whether accepting money after the Term creates a tenancy despite the acceptance sentence is also case law, not read. Text is holdover-rate-in's / holdover-rate-tn's plus the Utah non-stacking and credit sentence; an add-on to holdover-ca (tagged UT). CONDITIONAL: offered, not defaulted (rule 54). BUILDER: show only on opt-in; place immediately after holdover-ca; require {{holdover_daily_rate}}; show the daily equivalent of Monthly Rent. Companion education row: edu-holdover-damages-ut. title: Holdover Damages in Utah
bodyText: Utah's eviction statute says a fixed term ends at its end without any notice, and a tenant who stays on is in unlawful detainer. But the statute's definitions describe unlawful detainer as staying after a notice to quit, so it is unsettled (a question of case law the library has not read) whether you can file, or claim tripled damages, without first serving a written notice to quit; serving one avoids the question. A month-to-month or other periodic tenant is in unlawful detainer after staying past a notice served at least 15 calendar days before the period ends, and a tenant at will after a notice of at least 5 calendar days. In the eviction case the court assesses your damages from the unlawful detainer and any amounts due under the lease, and must enter judgment for the rent plus three times those damages, with reasonable attorney fees and costs to the prevailing party. The statute does not say the holdover must be willful, but it sets no figure for your loss, and the tripling applies only in an eviction case. Outside an eviction case, for example when a tenant leaves a few days late and you do not sue, you recover your actual damages as the lease's Holdover section describes. The optional Holdover Charge clause sets a daily figure for those days. Under it you agree not to claim the charge in an eviction case, so it is never part of what a court triples; because it is a charge set out in the lease you may take it from the deposit or sue for it separately, crediting it if you later win an eviction judgment for the same days. In an eviction case you claim your actual damages instead. Whether a separate suit for the charge is barred once an eviction case has been decided is case law the library has not read. An agricultural tenant who stays more than 60 days after the term without any demand for possession or notice to quit is treated as renewing for another full year.
notes: UT: Added 2026-10-04, RETRO targeted fix (rule 54 holdover shape). Sentence by sentence: Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-802(1)(a), (1)(b)(i)-(ii); Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-811(2)(b), (2)(d), (3), (5)(a); shape and gap as recorded in holdover-rate-ut; Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-801(10) (definition) against Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-802(1)(a), case law not read; actual damages, holdover-ca (tagged UT); deposit, Utah Code Ann. § 57-17-3(1) ('other costs and fees provided for in the contract'); agricultural renewal, Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-803 ('more than 60 days ... without any demand of possession or notice to quit'). Revised after the independent check 2026-10-04: the fixed-term sentence no longer reads as settled, and the clause sentence now matches holdover-rate-ut's no-claim wording. Answers the holdover topic's damages question for UT and supplies the education row rule 54 asks for. title: Amounts Due Upfront
bodyText: Tenant will pay Landlord the following amounts, at the time specified for each: [specify each amount and when it is due, e.g. first month's Monthly Rent ({{monthly_rent}}) payable at signing and held as prepaid rent until the first rental period begins; Security Deposit ({{security_deposit}}) due at signing; any pet deposit ({{pet_deposit}}) due at signing (none for an assistance animal); any last month's rent deposit due at signing]. A pet deposit and a last month's rent deposit are security deposits, held and accounted for as this Lease's Security Deposit terms provide, and Landlord will apply a last month's rent deposit to the Rent for the last month of the tenancy as Oregon law requires. Landlord will not charge any fee at the beginning of the tenancy.
notes: OR: Overrides `due-at-signing`, which is not tagged: its last sentence ('not credited against, Rent due for any other month') contradicts the rule that 'The landlord must apply any last month’s rent deposit to the rent due for the last month of the tenancy' (ORS 90.300(9)) (when either party gives a termination notice other than an ORS 90.394 notice, on agreement, or when a term tenancy ends under its written terms), and its bracket could list a move-in fee: 'A landlord may not charge a fee at the beginning of the tenancy for an anticipated landlord expense' (ORS 90.302(1)). A last month's rent deposit is a security deposit ('security deposit” includes any last month’s rent deposit' (ORS 90.300(1))), and a pet deposit is a refundable deposit securing performance, so a security deposit too (ORS 90.100 definition; `edu-pet-fees-or`). The written agreement must list every security deposit (ORS 90.300(3)); `security-deposit-use-or` lists {{security_deposit}} and this clause lists the others. Rent is not due before the first day of each rental period (ORS 90.220(7)(a)); money paid earlier is 'Prepaid rent' (ORS 90.100(38)), accounted for under ORS 90.300(11)-(12); payment type ORS 90.140(1)(f). No pet deposit for an assistance animal (ORS 90.300(4)). Rule 26 fee screen: ORS 90.140(1) lists the payment types a landlord may require or accept, and ORS 90.302(1) bars any fee the fee statute doesn't list. No deposit cap (`edu-no-security-deposit-cap-or`). title: Application of Payments
bodyText: Landlord will apply each payment Tenant makes in the following order, whatever this Lease or a note on the payment says: first to Rent owed for earlier rental periods; then to Rent for the current rental period; then to utility or service charges; then to late charges; and last to fees and other charges, including charges for damage or other claims. Nothing in this provision limits any statutory right Tenant may have to cure nonpayment of Rent.
notes: OR: Overrides `application-of-payments`, which is not tagged: it lets Tenant direct a payment elsewhere and says 'current or oldest' period, but Oregon fixes the order 'Notwithstanding a provision in a rental agreement regarding the order of application of tenant payments, a landlord shall apply tenant payments in the following order' (ORS 90.220(9)(a)): outstanding rent from prior periods, current rent, utility or service charges, late rent payment charges, then fees or charges under ORS 90.302 or other damage or claim charges (ORS 90.220(9)(a)(A)-(E)). Not for facility tenancies under ORS 90.505 to 90.850 (ORS 90.220(9)(b)), which the library does not cover. The cure sentence keeps the shared clause's saving language (rule 43: a tenant who tenders the amount owed under a nonpayment notice before judgment gets the case dismissed, ORS 90.395(3)(c)). title: Acceptable Forms of Payment
bodyText: Tenant may pay Rent and other amounts due under this Lease by check, or by any other method Landlord accepts: [list any other accepted methods, e.g. money order, electronic payment service, online portal]. Landlord will not require Tenant to pay by debit card, credit card, electronic check, tenant portal or any other form of electronic payment. [Optional: If Tenant chooses to pay by credit card, debit card, tenant portal or other electronic means, Tenant will pay any processing fee the payment processor charges Landlord for that payment, but only if the processor allows the fee to be passed to the payer. Landlord will make records of processing fees charged to Landlord and passed through to Tenant available to Tenant within a reasonable time after Tenant's written request.]
notes: OR: Overrides `acceptable-payment-methods` and `acceptable-payment-methods-nj`, which are not tagged: the first lets Landlord choose and change methods freely, including electronic-only, and the second protects only a non-EFT method. Oregon: 'A landlord shall allow a tenant to make payments by check or other commercially reasonable methods' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 3(1)); 'A landlord may not require a tenant to make payments by debit card, credit card, electronic check, tenant portal or any other form of electronic payment' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 3(2)) (effective June 5, 2026, § 8; for rental agreements entered into before, on or after that date, § 7(1)). Whether 'check or other commercially reasonable methods' obliges a landlord to take a personal check, or only some non-electronic method, is not settled by the text; the clause accepts checks, which satisfies either reading (Claude's drafting choice). Processing fees: the 2026 act rewrote ORS 90.302(7)(d) so that processing fees charged to the landlord for a card, tenant-portal or other electronic payment may be passed through only if 'The payment processing company allows fees to be passed to the payor', the landlord allows nonelectronic payment as § 3(1) requires, and 'Records of fees charged to the landlord and passed through to the tenant are made available to the tenant upon written request within a reasonable time' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 5); the optional bracket follows those conditions. The 2025 compiled ORS 90.302(7)(d) still prints the earlier credit-card-only text (OR log §1.2). Rule 26: a charge for a payment method is otherwise a fee ORS 90.302(1) doesn't allow. title: Place of Payment for Nonpayment Notices
bodyText: A payment to cure a nonpayment of Rent after Landlord serves a termination notice for nonpayment is to be made in person at [specify a location on the premises, or the place where Tenant has made all previous Rent payments in person], which will be available to Tenant throughout the notice period. If Landlord serves the notice by personal delivery, by first class mail and attachment, or by first class mail and electronic mail, and the notice also states this location, a cure payment is not timely merely because it was mailed within the notice period; a payment made in person at this location within the notice period is timely. This paragraph does not limit the forms of payment Tenant may use for Rent at other times.
notes: OR: Optional clause (rule 54: a choice the statute leaves to the written rental agreement). A tenant who receives a nonpayment notice pays on time 'if mailed to the landlord within the period of the notice' (ORS 90.394(4)) unless the notice was served by personal delivery, mail and attachment or mail and electronic mail (ORS 90.394(4)(a)(A)-(C)), 'A written rental agreement and the notice expressly state that payment is to be made at a specified location that is either on the premises or at a place where the tenant has made all previous rent payments in person' (ORS 90.394(4)(b)), and the place 'is available to the tenant for payment throughout the period of the notice' (ORS 90.394(4)(c)). title: Use of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant will pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit) before occupancy, and Landlord will give Tenant a receipt for it. Any pet deposit and any last month's rent deposit Tenant pays are also security deposits under this Section. Landlord may claim from the Security Deposit only the amount reasonably necessary to remedy Tenant's defaults under this Lease, including unpaid Rent, and to repair damage to the property caused by Tenant, not including ordinary wear and tear or damage for which applicable law makes Tenant not responsible. Any labor Landlord charges for cleaning or repairs will be at a reasonable hourly rate. Except as ORS 90.367 or other applicable law provides, the Security Deposit does not relieve Tenant of the obligation to pay Rent when it is due.
notes: OR: Overrides `security-deposit-use`, which is not tagged: it lets Landlord deduct for damage by 'Tenant's guests' without Oregon's exceptions and adds a cleaning test the statute doesn't use. Listing: 'A written rental agreement, if any, must list a security deposit paid by a tenant or required by a landlord' (ORS 90.300(3)) (REQUIRED whenever a deposit is taken; CONDITIONAL because a deposit is optional). Receipt: ORS 90.300(2)(a). Claims: 'The landlord may claim from the security deposit only the amount reasonably necessary' (ORS 90.300(7)(a)) to remedy defaults including unpaid rent and 'To repair damages to the premises caused by the tenant, not including ordinary wear and tear' (ORS 90.300(7)(a)(A)-(B)); labor 'must be based on a reasonable hourly rate' (ORS 90.300(7)(b)). A tenant 'is not responsible for damage that results from' acts of God or 'Conduct by a perpetrator relating to domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking' (ORS 90.325(3)), which the clause carries as 'damage for which applicable law makes Tenant not responsible'. Foreclosure: a tenant with actual notice that the property is in foreclosure may apply the security deposit or prepaid rent to the tenant's obligation to the landlord after notifying the landlord in writing, and that is not grounds for termination (ORS 90.367(1)-(2)); the clause preserves that right. No forfeiture for a month-to-month tenant's failure to stay a minimum number of months (ORS 90.300(8)). Carpet cleaning needs its own lease term (`carpet-cleaning-deduction-or`). No deposit cap (`edu-no-security-deposit-cap-or`); no new or increased deposit in the first year except for a modification such as a pet (ORS 90.300(5)(a); `edu-deposit-installments-or`). title: Carpet Cleaning Deduction
bodyText: Landlord may deduct from the Security Deposit the reasonable cost of cleaning the carpets with a machine specifically designed for cleaning or shampooing carpets, whether or not Tenant cleans the carpets before delivering possession, if the carpets were cleaned or replaced after the previous tenancy or their most recent significant use and before Tenant took possession.

A landlord may recover from the deposit for carpet cleaning 'other than the use of a common vacuum cleaner' only if the cleaning is 'performed by use of a machine specifically designed for cleaning or shampooing carpets' (ORS 90.300(7)(c)(A)(i)), the carpet was cleaned or replaced after the previous tenancy or most recent significant use and before the tenant took possession (ORS 90.300(7)(c)(A)(ii)), and 'The written rental agreement provides that the landlord may deduct the cost of carpet cleaning regardless of whether the tenant cleans the carpet before the tenant delivers possession' (ORS 90.300(7)(c)(A)(iii)). title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: Within 31 days after the tenancy ends and Tenant delivers possession of the property, Landlord will give Tenant a written accounting stating specifically the basis or bases of any claim against the Security Deposit or any prepaid Rent, with a separate accounting for prepaid Rent, and will return any amount Landlord does not claim. Landlord will deliver the accounting and any refund by personal delivery or by first class mail. Tenant will give Landlord a forwarding address in writing.
notes: OR: Replaces the blank-states parent `security-deposit-return` (rule 25 family). RECOMMENDED: Oregon requires no deposit-return text in the lease (rule 56). Deadline and accounting: 'within 31 days after the tenancy terminates and the tenant delivers possession the landlord shall give to the tenant a written accounting that states specifically the basis or bases of the claim' (ORS 90.300(12)); 'The landlord shall give a separate accounting for security deposits and for prepaid rent'; refund of any unclaimed portion 'not later than 31 days after the tenancy terminates and the tenant delivers possession' (ORS 90.300(13)). Delivery: 'by personal delivery or by first class mail' or by e-mail only under an ORS 90.155(1)(d) addendum (ORS 90.300(14)); an electronic refund to a bank account needs an addendum 'executed after the tenancy begins and the tenant has occupied the premises' (ORS 90.300(13)), so the lease itself can't authorize it (rule 48). Prepaid rent is accounted for and refunded the same way (ORS 90.300(11)). Penalty: twice the amount withheld without an accounting or in bad faith (ORS 90.300(16); `edu-security-deposit-penalty-or`). The forwarding-address sentence is a tenant duty, not a condition: the statute's clock doesn't depend on it. title: Late Charges in Oregon
bodyText: You may charge a late charge only if the rent is not received by the fourth day of the weekly or monthly rental period, and only if your written rental agreement states the tenant's obligation to pay it, its type and amount, the date rent is due and the date the late charge becomes due. Oregon allows three structures, and each is a ceiling: a reasonable flat amount (what landlords customarily charge in that rental market), once per rental period; a reasonable daily charge from the fifth day through the end of that rental period, each day's charge no more than 6% of a reasonable flat amount; or 5% of the periodic rent for each five-day period (or part) the rent stays unpaid, from the fifth day through the end of that rental period. In a periodic tenancy you may change the type or amount on 30 days' written notice. You may not deduct an earlier late charge from a later rent payment to make that rent late; unpaid late charges may earn simple interest at the judgment rate. Nonpayment of a late charge alone does not support a nonpayment notice, though it is a cause for a for-cause notice; you may list a late charge on a nonpayment notice only if the notice makes clear the tenant can cure by paying the delinquent rent alone. A discount for paying early counts as a late charge. Since June 5, 2026, you may not charge a late charge if you refused a payment the tenant offered by check or another commercially reasonable method.
notes: OR: ORS 90.260(1) (conditions; 'The rent payment is not received by the fourth day of the weekly or monthly rental period for which rent is payable' (ORS 90.260(1)(a))), (2)(a)-(c) (structures; 'The per-day charge may not exceed six percent of the amount described in paragraph (a)'), (3) (30 days' written notice in periodic tenancies), (4) (no deduction), (5) (interest at the ORS 82.010(2) judgment rate), (6) ('Nonpayment of a late charge alone is not grounds for termination of a rental agreement for nonpayment of rent under ORS 90.394, but is grounds for termination of a rental agreement for cause under ORS 90.392' (ORS 90.260(6))), (7) ('A late charge includes an increase or decrease in the regularly charged periodic rent payment imposed because a tenant does or does not pay that rent by a certain date' (ORS 90.260(7))). Refused payments: Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 3(3). Payment order puts late charges after rent and utility charges (ORS 90.220(9)). The library's clause uses the flat structure (`late-fee-limit-or`). Present or absent (rule 27): the reasonable flat amount is the only cap on the flat charge; no fixed-dollar or percentage cap applies to it (OR battery 200 (late charges and late fees (caps)): 24 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 1 synthetic); scope CONST 383, OAR 40864, ORS 39614, SL2026 142). title: Bounced Rent Checks
bodyText: For a dishonored check you may charge a fee of up to $35 plus whatever your bank charged you for processing it, and only if your written rental agreement describes the fee. The fee covers a check returned for insufficient funds or credit, no account, or a stop payment without good cause; Oregon's fee list has no fee for a failed card or electronic payment (whether a returned electronic check counts as a 'check, draft or order for the payment of money' is not settled by the text). A rent check that bounces is not an acceptance of rent for waiver purposes. If you sue on the check, statutory damages (the greater of $100 or three times the check, but not more than $500 over the check amount) and attorney fees are available only after a written demand at least 30 days before suing and only if the tenant didn't pay the check amount, accrued interest and the fee before you sued; a fee you collected reduces those damages; no statutory damages if the tenant pays the check, interest, fee, costs and your attorney fees after suit but before trial, and a court may waive them for economic hardship. Oregon requires you to let a tenant pay by check or another commercially reasonable method and bars requiring electronic payment; whether you may insist on certified funds after a check bounces is not settled by the statute, so the library's clause doesn't claim that right.

Waiver: a landlord has not accepted rent if 'The rent payment is made in the form of a check that is dishonored' (ORS 90.412(3)(b)). Payment methods: Or. title: Tenant Portals
bodyText: If you take rental applications through a tenant portal (an app, website or platform you provide for applying, setting up, keeping or ending a tenancy, not ordinary e-mail or text), you must either post a printable application on your website or send a printed or printable copy within seven days of a written request, and you must process applications received outside the portal. title: Statewide Rent Increase Limit
bodyText: For tenancies other than week-to-week, you may not raise the rent during the first year of the tenancy, more than once in any 12-month period, or by more than the maximum percentage the Department of Administrative Services publishes each September for the next calendar year: the lesser of 10% or 7% plus the annual West-region CPI change. The cap, and the limit on the next tenancy's rent after a first-year no-cause termination, do not apply if the unit's first certificate of occupancy was issued less than 15 years before the date of the increase notice, or if the unit is regulated or certified affordable housing and the change doesn't increase the tenant's share of the rent or is required by the program or a change in the tenant's income. Notice periods and contents: `edu-rent-increase-notice-or`. Exceeding the cap costs three months' rent plus actual damages. If you end a tenancy without cause in its first year, the next tenancy's rent is held to what you could have charged the tenant you removed. Cities and counties may not control rent, apart from narrow exceptions.

title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: A week-to-week rent increase needs written notice at least seven days before it takes effect. title: Local Rent Control Is Preempted
bodyText: Oregon bars cities and counties from enacting rent control on residential property, with exceptions: rent limits a state agency, city, county or urban renewal agency reserves on property it has contracted to benefit (for example with tax exemptions, financing or subsidies) to provide reduced rents for low-income tenants; condominium conversion ordinances limiting increases during the conversion notice period; temporary controls after a natural or man-made disaster that materially eliminates a significant part of the rental housing supply, removed once supply is substantially normal again; and inclusionary-zoning requirements that set the price of new multiunit housing. title: What Counts as Rent
bodyText: In Oregon, rent does not include security deposits, fees or utility and service charges you bill under the utility statute. Fees, late charges and utility charges are not rent for a nonpayment notice: unpaid, they support only a for-cause notice with its own cure period. The fees you may charge are limited to those the fee statute lists, each described in your written rental agreement. Recurring charges you set as part of the rent (such as pet rent or a parking charge you call rent) are rent and count toward the rent-increase limits.

title: Fees You May Charge
bodyText: Oregon lets you charge only the fees its fee statute lists, and each must be described in your written rental agreement. Per-occurrence fees: late charges (as the late-charge rules allow); a dishonored check (up to $35 plus your bank's charge); removing or tampering with a working smoke or carbon monoxide alarm (up to $250, unless the State Fire Marshal fines the tenant); and, for a tenant who leaves a fixed term early without cause, a fee of no more than one and one-half times the monthly rent (not allowed when the tenant leaves under the victim or servicemember termination rights, or when, after you give a qualifying-reason notice ending a fixed term, the tenant ends the tenancy early with the tenant's own written notice of at least 30 days), in which case you give up rent after the date you knew or reasonably should have known of the departure, and reletting costs. Rule-violation fees: after a written warning notice, for the second violation of the same kind within a year (up to $50) and later ones (up to $50 plus 5% of that period's rent), but only for late utility charges, pet or service-animal waste or garbage left outside the unit, parking violations and improper vehicle use, smoking in a clearly designated nonsmoking area (up to $250, 24 hours after the warning) or an unauthorized pet capable of causing damage (up to $250, 48 hours after the warning). You may not charge a fee at the start of the tenancy for an expected expense, any other liquidated damages, or both a fee and a termination for the same violation. Outside the fee rules: attorney fees awarded by a court, screening charges, charges for improvements or other actions the tenant asks for that the lease or law doesn't require of you (including replacing a lost key), processing fees passed through under the payment rules, renter's insurance requirements and association assessments passed through as the statute allows. A fee not allowed by the statute costs twice your tenant's actual damages or $300, whichever is greater (this penalty doesn't apply to the per-occurrence fees listed above).

title: Fees for Repeated Rule Violations
bodyText: Landlord may charge Tenant a fee for a second or later violation of the same or a similar kind as the violation described in a written warning notice, within one year after Landlord gives Tenant that notice, of a written rule or policy about: [select any that apply: late payment of a utility or service charge Tenant owes Landlord; failing to clean up pet waste, or service or companion animal waste, outside the dwelling; failing to clean up garbage or other waste outside the dwelling; parking violations; improper use of vehicles on the premises; smoking in a clearly designated nonsmoking unit or area; keeping an unauthorized pet capable of causing damage to persons or property]. The warning notice will describe the specific violation and the fees for a second and any later violation. The fee is [amount, not more than $50] for the second same or similar violation within the year and [amount, not more than $50 plus 5% of that rental period's Rent] for each later same or similar violation, except that the fee for a second or later violation for smoking in a designated nonsmoking area or for an unauthorized pet is [amount, not more than $250] and may not be charged until 24 hours (smoking) or 48 hours (pet) after the warning notice. Landlord will give the warning notice or charge the fee within 30 days after the violation, will give written notice describing the violation when charging the fee, will not deduct the fee from a Rent payment, and will not both charge a fee and terminate the tenancy for the same violation.

title: Interest on Money a Tenant Owes
bodyText: Oregon's legal interest rate is 9% a year on money after it becomes due, unless the parties agreed to a different rate, and judgments carry 9% simple interest unless the law or the agreement sets another rate. The landlord-tenant act lets you charge simple interest at the judgment rate on an unpaid late charge, from the date you imposed it. Whether a lease may set its own interest rate on unpaid rent or damages without running into the act's fee and liquidated-damages limits is not settled by the statutes, so the library doesn't offer a contractual rate.

title: Accepting Rent After a Violation or Notice
bodyText: If you accept rent knowing of a tenant's violation during three or more separate rental periods, or accept performance that departs from the lease, you waive the right to end the tenancy for that violation. You avoid waiver by refunding the rent within 10 days, by agreeing otherwise with the tenant after the violation, or by giving a written warning notice before the third period that describes the conduct or the money owed, says the tenant must stop the conduct, correct the violation or pay, and says it may lead to termination; a warning for ongoing conduct lasts 12 months and can be renewed. There is no waiver for a 24-hour termination, a last month's rent deposit, rent released by a court, or rent paid more than one period in advance, and a dishonored check is not accepted rent. Accepting a partial payment waives a nonpayment termination unless you follow the statute: before the notice, on an agreement to pay the balance by a set time, serving the notice no earlier than allowed, and letting the tenant avoid termination by paying the balance within the notice period or by the agreed date, whichever is later; after the notice, only with a written agreement that acceptance is not a waiver. After a termination notice, accepting rent waives it unless the statute's refund or written-notice conditions are met. A lease clause written before the violation does not do this for you.
notes: OR: ORS 90.412(2)-(5) ('During three or more separate rental periods, accepts rent with knowledge of the violation by the tenant' (ORS 90.412(2)(a)); 'The landlord and tenant agree otherwise after the violation has occurred' (ORS 90.412(4)(a))); ORS 90.414 (acceptance after a termination notice) read section-open; ORS 90.412(4)(b)(B), (4)(c)(B); ORS 90.417(2), (4)(a)(A)-(C), (6) (partial rent). Housing assistance payments are not 'rent' for these sections (ORS 90.412(1)). This is why `late-fee-limit-or` leaves out the shared non-waiver sentence. title: Changing Terms During a Tenancy
bodyText: A fixed term lease can't be changed by either party alone during the term. In a periodic tenancy, Oregon sets specific notice periods for some changes: rent increases (seven days week-to-week; 90 days otherwise, and none in the first year); the type or amount of a late charge (30 days); adding a renter's liability insurance requirement to an existing month-to-month tenancy (30 days, with the exceptions summary); requiring a public service charge adopted by a provider or local government within the previous six months, in a month-to-month tenancy (60 days); and a new or increased security deposit (none in the first year except with an agreed change such as a pet; after the first year, at least three months to pay). A new house rule that substantially modifies the bargain needs the tenant's written consent. From January 1, 2027, a landlord may adopt a smoking ban inside units or interior common areas without that consent only under the 2026 act's conditions, including 180 days' written notice.

title: Rent Concessions and Discounts
bodyText: Oregon treats an increase or decrease in the regular rent based on whether the tenant pays by a certain date as a late charge, so an early-payment discount has to meet the late-charge rules. title: No Sales Tax on Rent
bodyText: Oregon has no general sales tax, so long-term residential rent is not taxed. The state transient lodging tax doesn't apply to a dwelling the same person rents for 30 consecutive days or more; shorter stays may be taxed, and vacation and transient occupancies fall outside the landlord-tenant act anyway.

title: Screening Charges for Applicants
bodyText: You may charge an applicant a screening charge only to cover the cost of screening, no more than your average actual cost or the customary charge of a screening company or credit agency for comparable screening, and only after you adopt written screening criteria and give the applicant written notice of the matters the statute lists (the charge, your criteria and process, dispute and appeal rights, nondiscrimination, the rent and deposits, any renter's insurance requirement and refund rights) and an estimate of available units and applications already under consideration. Give a receipt and confirmation of any outside screening; charge only one screening charge in any 60-day period across all your units; don't charge when you know no unit is or will soon be available; and refund within 30 days if you fill the unit before screening or haven't screened before the applicant withdraws in writing. Violations cost twice the screening charge plus $250.

title: Deposits to Secure a Rental Agreement
bodyText: Apart from a screening charge, you may take money from an applicant only as a deposit to secure the execution of a rental agreement, after you approve the application and before you both sign, and only after giving a written statement of the rent, fees and deposits, the terms of the agreement to sign and the conditions for refunding or keeping the deposit. When the agreement is signed, you must apply the deposit to the money due under it or refund it immediately. If the applicant fails to sign as agreed, you may keep the deposit, unless the applicant rejected the agreement because of material habitability defects. If you fail to sign, or the applicant rejects for habitability, you must return the deposit within five business days; the applicant can recover the deposit, and late return (unless caused by an act of God) adds a penalty equal to the greater of the deposit or an amount you agreed on.

title: Screening Rules and Denials

If you deny an applicant after applying your criteria, give a written statement of one or more reasons within 14 days (a $100 remedy if you don't); before denying on criminal history, let the applicant submit supplemental evidence and make an individualized assessment. title: Last Month's Rent Deposits
bodyText: A last month's rent deposit is a security deposit in Oregon. You must apply it to the rent for the last month of the tenancy when either of you gives a termination notice (other than a nonpayment notice), when you agree to end the tenancy, or when a fixed term ends under the written agreement, and account for and refund any part you don't apply. Unless you both agree otherwise, the tenant can't make you apply it to any other month, and it does not cap the rent you may charge unless the written agreement says so. Accepting one collected at the beginning of the tenancy is not acceptance of rent that waives a violation.

title: Deposits When the Property Changes Hands
bodyText: Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is responsible to the tenant for the security deposit and prepaid rent and bound by the deposit rules, so a buyer takes on the deposits of tenants in place; a purchaser at a foreclosure sale has a separate rule. Agree with the buyer on transferring deposits at closing.

title: No Deposit Interest or Trust Account Rule
bodyText: Oregon does not require you to pay interest on security deposits. If you manage your own rental, no statute requires a separate or trust account; a licensed property manager must deposit tenant security deposits in a federally insured security deposits account and keep them there until they are forwarded to the owner, disbursed or refunded under the lease and management agreement (`edu-no-deposit-holding-rule-or`). You hold the deposit for the tenant: the tenant's claim to it comes before your creditors', including a bankruptcy trustee, and the tenant's creditors can't garnish it from you.

title: Where to Keep the Deposit
bodyText: Oregon law doesn't tell a landlord who manages their own rental where to keep a security deposit, require a separate account, or require notice of the bank. You must give the tenant a receipt and hold the deposit for the tenant, and the tenant's claim to it comes ahead of your creditors. If a licensed property manager collects deposits for you, the manager must put them in a federally insured trust account labeled for security deposits (or, where the management agreement and lease say the owner holds the deposit, pass it to you the month it arrives), keep records and not mix the money with the manager's own funds.

title: Move-In Condition Records
bodyText: Oregon does not require a move-in inspection or condition checklist for ordinary tenancies. title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: No Oregon landlord-tenant statute addresses a deposit refund the tenant never cashes or claims. Under Oregon's unclaimed property law, money held or owed in the ordinary course of business and unclaimed for more than three years after it became payable is presumed abandoned, and the holder must report it and pay it to the State Treasurer, after first trying to reach the owner. Don't keep or write off an uncashed refund.

ORS 98.342(1) ('has remained unclaimed by the owner for more than three years after it became payable or distributable is presumed abandoned' (ORS 98.342(1))); ORS 98.352(1), (4)-(5) (report and payment to the State Treasurer, filed October 1 to November 1 for accounts dormant as of June 30; due diligence to reach the owner first). 'Intangible property' includes 'security deposits, refunds' (ORS 98.302(8)(a)); if the money is held in a fiduciary capacity (perhaps by a property manager; Claude's reading), ORS 98.332(1) may apply instead, with the same three-year period. title: Pet Deposits, Fees and Pet Rent
bodyText: A pet deposit is a refundable security deposit in Oregon: list it in the written agreement, and claim from it only as the deposit rules allow. You may not charge a pet deposit for an assistance animal a tenant with a disability needs. Oregon's fee statute has no one-time pet fee for ordinary tenancies, so a nonrefundable pet fee isn't allowed; pet rent you set as part of the rent is rent. For repeat problems you may use the rule-violation fees for pet waste or an unauthorized pet (after a warning).

ORS 90.302(2)(d) is read as a facility fee (`edu-required-fees-or`); facility tenancies may charge no pet rent, deposit or one-time pet charge (ORS 90.530; out of scope). title: Landlord's Right of Entry
bodyText: Landlord or Landlord's agents may enter the dwelling to inspect it, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, perform agreed yard maintenance or grounds keeping, or show it to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors. Except as this Section provides, Landlord will give Tenant at least 24 hours' actual notice of the intended entry and will enter only at reasonable times, and Tenant will not unreasonably withhold consent to entry. If Tenant asks in writing for repairs or maintenance, Landlord may enter to make them without further notice, at the times Tenant's request allows or otherwise at reasonable times, until the repairs are completed, but that permission ends seven days after the request unless the repairs are in progress and Landlord is making a reasonable effort to complete them. In an emergency, Landlord may enter at any time without notice and, if Tenant is absent, will give Tenant actual notice within 24 hours after the entry of the fact, date and time of the entry, the nature of the emergency and the names of the persons who entered. During any absence of Tenant of more than seven days, Landlord may enter at times reasonably necessary.
notes: OR: Overrides `landlords-access` and `landlords-access-mi`, which are not tagged: the first gives a 'right of reasonable access' on 24 hours' notice, but in Oregon 'The landlord or landlord’s agent may not enter if the tenant, after receiving the landlord’s notice, denies consent to enter' (ORS 90.322(1)(f)), subject to 'A tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent from the landlord to enter' (ORS 90.322(2)); the second adds lenders and a stricter consent rule but omits Oregon's after-entry notice. Purposes: ORS 90.322(1); notice: 'at least 24 hours’ actual notice' and 'only at reasonable times' (ORS 90.322(1)(f)); repair requests ORS 90.322(1)(c) ('expires after seven days, unless the repairs are in progress'); emergency ORS 90.322(1)(b) ('the landlord shall give the tenant actual notice within 24 hours after the entry' (ORS 90.322(1)(b))); absence ORS 90.410(2); no other access except court order, absence or abandonment (ORS 90.322(5)). Actual notice methods: ORS 90.150 (`actual-notice-method-or`). Entry without notice to show a buyer needs an agreement 'in a writing separate from the rental agreement' with separate consideration (ORS 90.322(1)(d)), so it is not in this clause (rule 48; `edu-landlord-entry-or`). Refusal of lawful access: injunction or ORS 90.392 termination plus damages (ORS 90.322(7)); unlawful or harassing entry: tenant's remedies and not less than one week's rent in a week-to-week tenancy or one month's rent in any other tenancy (ORS 90.322(8)). title: Entry for Yard Maintenance
bodyText: Landlord will perform the following yard maintenance or grounds keeping for the property: [describe, e.g. mowing, weeding, pruning]. Landlord or Landlord's agent may enter the yard and other parts of the premises under Tenant's exclusive control, but not the dwelling, for that purpose without notice, at reasonable times and with reasonable frequency. Tenant may deny an entry at an unreasonable time or with unreasonable frequency by giving actual notice of the denial before or at the time of the attempted entry.
notes: OR: Optional clause (rule 54: a right that exists only if the written agreement provides for it). If a written agreement requires the landlord to do yard work, the parties 'may agree that the landlord or landlord’s agent may enter for that purpose upon the premises under the tenant’s exclusive control not including the dwelling unit, without notice to the tenant, at reasonable times and with reasonable frequency', and 'The terms of the right of entry must be described in the rental agreement or in a separate written agreement' (ORS 90.322(1)(e)); the tenant may deny entry at an unreasonable time or frequency by actual notice (ORS 90.322(1)(e)(A)(ii)); 'Yard maintenance or grounds keeping' includes 'weeding, mowing grass and pruning trees and shrubs' (ORS 90.322(1)(e)(B)(i)). Without this clause, yard entry needs 24 hours' notice like any other (ORS 90.322(1)(f)). Not for use together with a tenant yard-work agreement (`tenant-maintenance-tasks-or`) for the same tasks. title: Default by Tenant
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and does not pay it within the time applicable law allows after Landlord's written notice, or if Tenant materially violates this Lease or Tenant's duties under applicable law and does not cure the violation within the time applicable law allows after Landlord's written notice, except where applicable law permits Landlord to terminate without an opportunity to cure. Nonpayment of a late charge, fee or utility charge is not nonpayment of Rent. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise the rights and remedies applicable law provides, including terminating the tenancy, recovering possession through the courts, and recovering unpaid Rent, other amounts this Lease lawfully provides and actual damages, less amounts lawfully applied from the Security Deposit. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to mitigate damages as applicable law requires. In any action on this Lease, the prevailing party may recover reasonable attorney fees and costs as applicable law provides.
notes: OR: Overrides `default-by-tenant` and `default-by-tenant-ks-ne`, which are not tagged. Rule 49 and rule 47: their 'reasonable costs and expenses' are not a fee ORS 90.302 lists ('may not require the payment of any fee except as provided in this section', ORS 90.302(1)), and a landlord collecting 'interest or other charges or fees that exceed the actual debt unless the agreement, contract or instrument that creates the debt expressly authorizes, or a law expressly allows' them commits an unlawful collection practice (ORS 646.639(2)(n); creditor collecting its own debt is a 'debt collector' under ORS 646.639(1)(h), Claude's reading). The shared clause is itself an express authorization, so the exposure arises only because ORS 90.302(1) and 90.245 make that generic term unenforceable (Claude's reading); for willful use of an unlawful collection practice the damages are 'actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater' (ORS 646.641(1)); this clause recovers only rent, lawful charges and actual damages (ORS 90.140(1)(i); ORS 90.401). Cure (rule 43): for-cause notices carry a cure date of at least 14 days (4 days week-to-week), or no earlier than delivery for a completed separate act, and no cure for a repeat within six months (ORS 90.392(4)(a), (5)(a), (6)); nonpayment notices run 72 hours (week-to-week) or 10 or 13 days (ORS 90.394); a nonpayment case is dismissed if the tenant 'has tendered or caused to be tendered rental assistance or any other payment covering the nonpayment amount owed under the termination notice' (ORS 90.395(3)(c)), so the clause leaves cure periods to applicable law rather than stating or capping them; 24-hour causes have no cure (ORS 90.396). Late charges, fees and utility charges: ORS 90.260(6), 90.302(6), 90.315(4)(e). Attorney fees: 'reasonable attorney fees at trial and on appeal may be awarded to the prevailing party together with costs and necessary disbursements, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary' (ORS 90.255); mitigation ORS 90.125(1), 90.410(3). After the first year of occupancy the landlord ends a month-to-month tenancy only for cause or a qualifying reason (ORS 90.427(3)(c)), except as ORS 90.427(8) allows for owner-occupied premises with no more than two units; fixed terms: ORS 90.427(4); `edu-for-cause-eviction-or`. title: Early Termination
bodyText: If this Lease has a fixed Term, Tenant may end the tenancy before the end of the Term by giving Landlord at least 30 days' written notice and paying an early termination fee equal to one month's Rent ({{monthly_rent}}). If Landlord charges this fee, Landlord will not recover Rent for any period after the date Landlord knew or reasonably should have known that Tenant abandoned or relinquished the property, or any cost of renting it to a new tenant. Landlord will not charge the fee if Tenant ends the tenancy under Oregon's protections for victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking or for servicemembers, or after Landlord has given notice ending the tenancy at the end of the Term for a landlord's qualifying reason. A month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy ends on the notice applicable law requires, without a fee. Landlord may end the tenancy early only as applicable law allows. Nothing in this Section limits any right either party has under applicable law.
notes: OR: Overrides `early-termination` and `early-termination-ks`, which are not tagged: their fee ('one month's Rent ... or 30% of the remaining Rent due under the Term, whichever is greater') can exceed Oregon's limit, and Oregon bars 'any form of liquidated damages, however designated' (ORS 90.302(5)) except 'The abandonment or relinquishment of a dwelling unit during a fixed term tenancy without cause. The fee may not exceed one and one-half times the monthly rent' (ORS 90.302(2)(e)); if the fee is assessed the landlord 'may not recover unpaid rent for any period of the fixed term tenancy beyond the date that the landlord knew or reasonably should have known of the abandonment or relinquishment' and may not recover reletting costs (ORS 90.302(2)(e)(A)-(C)). No fee for a release under ORS 90.453(2) or a servicemember termination under ORS 90.472 or 90.475 (ORS 90.302(2)(e)); none for a tenant who ends a fixed term after the landlord's ORS 90.427(5) notice (ORS 90.372, as added by Or. Laws 2025, ch. 115, § 2). Their landlord limb ('if Tenant vacates or abandons the property without notifying Landlord') adds a cause ORS 90.427(4)(a) doesn't list. The fee must be described in the written agreement (ORS 90.302(1)); this clause does so. One month's rent stays within the cap whatever the rent (Claude's drafting choice). Periodic tenancies: ORS 90.427(2)-(3). title: Holdover
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession without Landlord's consent after the tenancy has ended under this Lease and applicable law, Landlord may bring an action for possession and may recover actual damages resulting from Tenant's holding over, including the value of Rent accruing from the end of the tenancy until Landlord knows or should know that Tenant has relinquished possession. If Landlord consents to Tenant's continued occupancy, the tenancy continues month to month on the same terms, and Landlord may end it only as applicable law allows. The end of a fixed Term does not by itself end the tenancy where applicable law makes it a month-to-month tenancy.
notes: OR: Overrides `holdover` and `holdover-ca`, which are not tagged: `holdover` promises damages 'in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' (rule 53: a ceiling-only figure) and both treat the end of the Term as the end of the tenancy, but 'if the specified ending date for the fixed term falls after the first year of occupancy, the fixed term tenancy becomes a month-to-month tenancy upon the expiration of the fixed term' (ORS 90.427(4)(c)) unless a new term is agreed, the tenant gives 30 days' notice or the landlord has a qualifying reason, subject to ORS 90.427(7) (three warned violations and 90 days' notice) and (8) (owner-occupied premises with two units or fewer). Measure: 'the landlord may recover from the tenant any actual damages resulting from the tenant holding over, including the value of any rent accruing from the expiration or termination of the rental agreement until the landlord knows or should know that the tenant has relinquished possession to the landlord' (ORS 90.427(11)); 'If the landlord consents to the tenant’s continued occupancy, ORS 90.220 (7) applies' (month-to-month). Rule 54: a premium holdover rate is not offered because Oregon bars liquidated damages (ORS 90.302(5); ORS 90.245(1)(d); `edu-holdover-rate-or`). Rule 53: the clause states actual damages only, so it adds no second charge after a nonpayment termination and nothing a court could multiply. title: Surrender at End of Tenancy
bodyText: When the tenancy ends under this Lease and applicable law, Tenant will surrender possession of the property and return all keys to Landlord. Tenant will leave the property in the same condition as at the start of the tenancy, except for ordinary wear and tear and damage for which applicable law makes Tenant not responsible, and free of all personal property of Tenant and any occupants. Personal property left behind will be handled as Oregon law requires.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If Tenant, or a person on the premises with Tenant's permission or consent, deliberately or negligently damages the property, Tenant will pay the reasonable cost of repair, and Tenant may not end this Lease, withhold or deduct Rent, or recover damages from Landlord because of that damage, except as applicable law provides. Tenant remains responsible for Rent while the damage is repaired, except where applicable law excuses Rent (such as Oregon's natural disaster rules). This Section does not apply to damage from an act of God or from conduct by a perpetrator of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking.
notes: OR: Rule 54t answer, offered as an optional clause modeled on `tenant-caused-damage-tn`. Each exit or abatement route was checked for a tenant-fault exception: ORS 90.360(4) ('The tenant may not terminate or recover damages under this section for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant or other person on the premises with the tenant’s permission or consent' (ORS 90.360(4))); ORS 90.365(6) (essential services); ORS 90.368(5)(d) (minor repairs); ORS 90.380(5)(a) (immediate termination after a posting only for conditions 'not caused by the tenant') and (7) (outset conditions 'not caused by the tenant'); ORS 90.375 (landlord's willful acts; no tenant-fault case arises). The 2026 natural disaster rule (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 108, §§ 20-21, effective June 5, 2026, § 31; § 21 added to ORS 90.100 to 90.465) has no fault exception for rent: 'A tenant does not owe rent while the dwelling unit is inaccessible due to the natural disaster or the destruction of the dwelling unit' (Or. The clause therefore keeps rent running only outside that rule and adds 'except as applicable law provides'. Liability: ORS 90.325(2)(b) (no deliberate or negligent damage), ORS 90.401 (damages); exceptions ORS 90.325(3)(a)-(b). title: Residential Use Only
bodyText: Tenant will use and occupy the property for residential purposes only and will not use or permit the use of the property for any non-residential or illegal purpose, including any commercial purpose, without Landlord's written consent. This Section does not prohibit Tenant from using the dwelling as a family child care home that is certified or registered under Oregon law, after Tenant notifies Landlord of that use, subject to the conditions Oregon law allows a landlord to impose.

title: Family Child Care Home Conditions
bodyText: If Tenant uses the dwelling as a family child care home, Tenant will, as Landlord elects here: [choose one: (a) have the parent of each child in care sign a document, before care begins, in which the parent agrees for the parent and the child that Landlord, the owner and any association are not liable for losses from injuries to the children or their guests connected with the operation of the family child care home, and acknowledges that the provider does not maintain liability coverage for those losses; or (b) in addition to any renter's liability insurance this Lease requires, carry and maintain a reasonable surety bond or liability policy that covers claims for injuries to the children and their guests sustained because of the negligence of Tenant or Tenant's employees and names Landlord, the owner and any association as additional insureds]. Tenant will pay in advance for any modification needed for Tenant's use, certification or registration of the dwelling as a family child care home that Landlord is not required to make.
notes: OR: Optional clause (rule 54): the statute lets a landlord require, 'at the election of the landlord, either' the parents' signed document or a bond or policy naming the landlord as an additional insured (ORS 90.358(5)(a)-(b)), and advance payment for modifications 'that are not required of the landlord under ORS 90.320 or the rental agreement' (ORS 90.358(4)(a)). Not otherwise required: 'This section does not require a family child care home to carry any insurance policy unless required by a landlord under subsection (5)(b) of this section' (ORS 90.358(6)). The additional-insured term here comes from ORS 90.358(5)(b), which applies 'In addition to the requirements of ORS 90.222' (whose own bar on additional-insured status covers the renter's liability policy, ORS 90.222(7)(b)).
