title: Maintenance & Repairs
bodyText: Landlord will maintain the dwelling in a habitable condition at all times during the tenancy as Oregon law requires, including its roof and exterior walls, plumbing, heating and electrical systems, and will repair the appliances, fixtures and equipment Landlord supplies. If a repair is needed because of a deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant or a person on the premises with Tenant's permission or consent, Tenant will pay the reasonable cost of the repair, except for damage from an act of God or from conduct by a perpetrator of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking. Tenant will notify Landlord promptly in writing of any condition requiring repair or maintenance (this does not limit any notice Oregon law otherwise accepts), and Landlord will make required repairs within a reasonable time, consistent with applicable law.
notes: OR: Overrides `landlord-maintenance`, which is not tagged: its carve-out for repairs 'necessary due to improper use by Tenant or a guest of Tenant' would put damage by a guest who is a perpetrator of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking on the tenant, but 'A tenant is not responsible for damage that results from' (ORS 90.325(3)) acts of God or 'Conduct by a perpetrator relating to domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking' (the landlord may ask for verification, ORS 90.325(4)). Duty: 'A landlord shall at all times during the tenancy maintain the dwelling unit in a habitable condition' (ORS 90.320(1)) (items (a)-(n); (m) as amended by Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 6, effective June 5, 2026, § 8); a rental agreement may not permit receiving rent free of that duty (ORS 90.250). The habitability duty itself has no tenant-fault exception; tenant fault removes the tenant's remedies (ORS 90.360(4); ORS 90.365(6)) and makes the tenant liable for damage the tenant deliberately or negligently causes, or knowingly permits any person to cause (ORS 90.325(2)(b)); the clause's wider reach to persons on the premises with the tenant's consent borrows the 'permission or consent' wording of ORS 90.360(4) (ORS 90.365(6): 'with the tenant's consent') (Claude's reading) and is recoverable as damages for breach of the lease (ORS 90.401(2)). Rule 44: a 'material noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement' triggers the tenant's termination remedy (ORS 90.360(1)(a)) and damages for any noncompliance (ORS 90.360(2)), so every repair promise here is a remedy trigger; the clause promises no more than ORS 90.320 plus supplied appliances. Remedies: `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-or`. title: Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness
bodyText: Tenant will keep the parts of the property under Tenant's control clean, sanitary and free of accumulated debris, garbage, rodents and vermin, as the condition of the premises permits and to the extent Tenant is responsible for causing the problem, and will dispose of ashes, garbage and other waste in a clean, safe and legal manner. Tenant will use all appliances, fixtures and facilities in a reasonable manner consistent with their intended purpose, will keep plumbing fixtures as clean as their condition permits, will not obstruct access to doors and windows, will test any smoke and carbon monoxide alarms Landlord provides at least every six months, replace batteries as needed, and notify Landlord in writing of any deficiency, and will maintain the property in the same condition as it was delivered to Tenant, except for ordinary wear and tear, any condition that applicable law requires Landlord to repair, and damage for which applicable law makes Tenant not responsible.
notes: OR: Overrides `tenant-maintenance`, which is not tagged: its duty to 'maintain the property in the same condition as it was delivered' has no exception for damage by acts of God or by a perpetrator of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking, for which a tenant 'is not responsible' (ORS 90.325(3)), and its cleanliness duty omits Oregon's limits, which this clause adds ('as the condition of the premises permits and to the extent that the tenant is responsible for causing the problem', ORS 90.325(1)(b)). Duties: ORS 90.325(1)(a)-(f) ('Test at least once every six months and replace batteries as needed in any smoke alarm, smoke detector or carbon monoxide alarm provided by the landlord and notify the landlord in writing of any operating deficiencies' (ORS 90.325(1)(f))); ORS 479.275. Restating tenant duties serves the landlord (rule 55). title: Tenant Maintenance Tasks Agreement
bodyText: Landlord and Tenant agree in good faith that Tenant will perform the following specified maintenance tasks, repairs or minor remodeling: [describe each task clearly and fully, e.g. mowing and watering the lawn; removing snow and ice from the walkways Tenant uses]. In exchange, Landlord will give Tenant the following consideration: [state the consideration specifically, e.g. a Rent reduction of $___ per month]. This agreement is not made to evade Landlord's obligations and does not reduce Landlord's obligations to other tenants. It does not shift to Tenant any duty to keep the dwelling habitable that Oregon law places on Landlord, and Tenant will not perform electrical or plumbing work unless licensed to do so.
notes: OR: Rule 48 and the shared chore clauses: `landscaping-irrigation` and `snow-removal` are not tagged, because Oregon lets the parties agree 'in writing that the tenant is to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling only if' (ORS 90.320(2)) the agreement is in good faith, does not diminish obligations to other tenants, and 'The terms and conditions of the agreement are clearly and fairly disclosed and adequate consideration for the agreement is specifically stated' (ORS 90.320(2)(c)). The rule reaches every dwelling, not only single-family homes, and asks for a writing, not a separate one, so the agreement can sit in the lease when the consideration is stated (Claude's reading; Oregon's chore rule matches neither the uniform-act single-family split nor the separate-writing branch, so rule 48's settled outcomes don't fit exactly). Built on the `maintenance-allocation-az` pattern. Tenants doing repairs for a rent reduction are not employees, may not do electrical or plumbing work unless licensed, and the arrangement doesn't diminish ORS 90.320 (ORS 90.145). Yard work the landlord keeps: `yard-maintenance-entry-or`. title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only the pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord: [describe each approved pet]. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, which is part of the Rent, and any pet deposit stated in this Lease, which is a security deposit. Tenant is responsible for damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet, and will indemnify Landlord against claims arising from Tenant's pet, except to the extent a claim results from the negligence or willful misconduct of Landlord or Landlord's agents. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or a danger to persons or property by written notice as applicable law requires. An assistance animal that Tenant or an occupant needs because of a disability is not a pet under this Section.
notes: OR: Overrides `pet-policy`, which is not tagged: its indemnity reaches claims caused by the landlord's own negligence, but a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant agrees 'to indemnify the other party for that liability' arising from the other party's 'willful misconduct or negligence' (ORS 90.245(1)(c)); and it lets Landlord 'enter the property and remove a pet', while Oregon allows entry only for the ORS 90.322(1) purposes, including emergencies (ORS 90.322(1)(b)), and otherwise only by court order, during an absence of more than seven days (ORS 90.410(2)) or after abandonment or relinquishment (ORS 90.322(5)(a)-(c)), and a landlord may not take possession of a tenant's property except by the ORS 90.425 procedures or court process (Claude's reading). Pet deposit: a security deposit (ORS 90.100 'Security deposit'; listing ORS 90.300(3); first-year pet deposit ORS 90.300(5)(a); `edu-pet-fees-or`). Pet rent: part of the rent (ORS 90.100 'Rent': payment for the right of 'a tenant and any permitted pet to occupy'), subject to ORS 90.323 increase limits. Unpermitted pets: ORS 90.405(1)-(2): a 10-day notice, curable by removing the pet, only for 'a pet capable of causing damage to persons or property' (ORS 90.405(2)); a repeat within six months allows a 10-day notice with no cure (ORS 90.405(3)). No pet deposit for an assistance animal (ORS 90.300(4); `assistance-animal-accommodation`). bodyText: If Tenant keeps an approved pet and this Lease requires Tenant to carry renter's liability insurance, that insurance will include coverage for liability arising from the pet, up to the coverage amount this Lease requires. title: Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance
bodyText: Landlord's insurance does not cover loss of or damage to Tenant's personal property, and Tenant is encouraged to insure it. [Optional requirement: Tenant will obtain and maintain renter's liability insurance throughout the tenancy with coverage of at least {{tenant_insurance_minimum}} per occurrence. Tenant may choose the insurer. Landlord may require Tenant to name Landlord as an interested party on the policy, so that the insurer will notify Landlord of cancellation or nonrenewal, a reduction in coverage or Landlord's removal as an interested party, and may require reasonable documentation that the coverage is in effect. Oregon law allows Landlord to require this insurance only if Landlord obtains and maintains comparable liability insurance and provides documentation of it to any tenant who asks; Landlord does so. This requirement does not apply if Tenant's household income is at or below 50 percent of the area median income, or if the dwelling has been subsidized with public funds as Oregon law describes.]
notes: OR: Overrides `tenants-property-insurance` and `tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca`, which are not tagged. Rule 52: the base clause says Landlord 'is not liable for any such loss or damage', but a rental agreement may not exculpate or limit liability for 'the other party’s willful misconduct or negligence' (ORS 90.245(1)(c)). Both require insurance outside ORS 90.222: 'A landlord may require a tenant to obtain and maintain renter’s liability insurance in a written rental agreement' (ORS 90.222(1)); coverage 'may not exceed $100,000 per occurrence or the customary amount required by landlords for similar properties with similar rents in the same rental market, whichever is greater' (ORS 90.222(1)), a limit the builder's {{tenant_insurance_minimum}} must meet (OR log §10); 'A written rental agreement that requires a tenant to obtain and maintain renter’s liability insurance must include a description of the requirements of this subsection' (ORS 90.222(5)) (REQUIRED_DISCLOSURE when the optional requirement is used, hence CONDITIONAL); interested party ORS 90.222(4)(a); no particular insurer, no additional insured, no subrogation waiver (ORS 90.222(7)(a)-(c)); exemptions ORS 90.222(8)-(10). title: Use of Property & Common Areas
bodyText: Tenant will not, without Landlord's written consent, drill holes, use nails, hooks or screws on the property, or fasten anything to its fixtures, appliances or interior or exterior surfaces, except as needed to install a portable cooling device as this Lease and Oregon law allow. Tenant will comply with any weight restrictions on balconies or porches and will not use them to store personal belongings without Landlord's consent. Tenant will not keep a waterbed or other water-filled furniture at the property, or any item (such as a piano or safe) whose weight Landlord has not agreed is reasonable for the floor, without Landlord's prior written consent. Tenant will not burn wax candles at the property. Tenant will not post or display any sign, banner or advertisement visible from outside the property without Landlord's consent. Nothing in this Section restricts any display or installation that applicable law entitles Tenant to make.
notes: OR: Overrides `common-area-use`, which is not tagged: its blanket ban on fastening anything to surfaces would restrict window air conditioners, but 'A landlord may not prohibit or restrict a tenant from installing or using a portable cooling device of the tenant’s choosing, unless' (ORS 90.355(2)) one of the listed grounds applies (codes, manufacturer guidelines, damage, amperage, window egress and locks, hardware that would damage the window or puncture the building envelope, drainage, fall risk, landlord installation or inspection, seasonal removal), and a restriction is enforceable only if 'in writing and delivered to the tenant' with the cooling-space statement (ORS 90.355(3); `portable-cooling-device-or`). title: Portable Cooling Devices
bodyText: Tenant may install and use a portable cooling device of Tenant's choosing, such as a window-mounted or floor air conditioner or an evaporative cooler, subject only to these restrictions: [state any restrictions Oregon law allows, e.g. the device must not violate building codes or the manufacturer's safety guidelines, damage the property or draw more power than the circuit can carry; a window unit must not be installed in a window needed for emergency exit, must not stop a window reachable from outside from locking, must not use brackets or hardware that would damage or void the warranty of the window or puncture the building envelope, and must be drained and secured against falling; Landlord or Landlord's agent will install, remove, inspect or service window units; units will be removed from October 1 through April 30]. During an extreme heat event for the forecast zone of the premises, Landlord [does / does not] intend to operate one or more community cooling spaces on or near the premises that are kept at no more than 80 degrees Fahrenheit and available to Tenant: [describe location, if any].

'A landlord may not enforce a restriction on portable cooling devices against a tenant allowed under subsection (2) of this section unless the restrictions are in writing and delivered to the tenant' (ORS 90.355(3)); 'The written restrictions must include whether the landlord intends to operate, whenever there is an extreme heat event for the forecast zone of the premises, one or more community cooling spaces available to the tenant that are located on or near the premises and that maintain a temperature of not higher than 80 degrees Fahrenheit' (ORS 90.355(3)). The bracket lists only the grounds ORS 90.355(2)(a)-(c) allows; 'Portable cooling device' includes window-mounted and floor devices but not devices whose installation or use 'requires alteration to the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.355(1)(c)). Termination notices for a cooling-device violation pause on extreme heat days and must say so (ORS 90.355(6)); the landlord is immune for a tenant-installed device (ORS 90.355(4)) and must prioritize disability needs if amperage is limited (ORS 90.355(5)). title: Parking & Vehicle Requirements
bodyText: Only operable passenger vehicles may be parked at the property; commercial vehicles, recreational vehicles, trailers and oversized vehicles are not permitted without Landlord's prior written consent. Landlord may require Tenant to provide vehicle information and may issue parking tags, decals or access cards at no charge. Landlord will have a vehicle towed only as Oregon law allows; Landlord will not have a vehicle towed because its registration has expired or is invalid, will tow an inoperable vehicle parked under this Lease only after affixing a prominent notice to it at least 72 hours before removal, and will tow a vehicle from a space assigned to Tenant only with Tenant's agreement at the time of the tow. Vehicle repairs are not permitted at the property except minor emergency repairs necessary to move the vehicle, and vehicles may be washed only in areas Landlord designates, if any.
notes: OR: Overrides `parking-vehicle-rules` and `parking-vehicle-rules-id`, which are not tagged: both let Landlord charge for tags, decals or cards (not a fee ORS 90.302 lists; rule 26 fee screen), the base lets Landlord tow a vehicle with 'expired registration', and the Idaho variant adds booting. Oregon: 'A landlord may have a motor vehicle removed from the premises only in compliance with this section and either ORS 98.810 to 98.818 or ORS 98.830 and 98.840' (ORS 90.485(1)); 'A landlord may not have a motor vehicle removed under this section because the vehicle’s registration has expired or is otherwise invalid' (ORS 90.485(7)); inoperable vehicles 72 hours after a prominent notice (ORS 90.485(6)); from an assigned space only with the tenant's agreement at the time of the tow, which the landlord may not require (ORS 90.485(4)). A vehicle tag must not reveal the tenant's residence if not removable (ORS 90.263, read). Booting: no Oregon statute authorizes a landlord to immobilize a vehicle (OR battery 125 (towing from rental premises): 43 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 1 synthetic); scope CONST 383, OAR 40864, ORS 39614, SL2026 142); the clause doesn't. title: Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance
bodyText: If the property is in a homeowners association or condominium association, Tenant will comply with the association's rules and regulations that apply to the property. A violation of those rules by Tenant, an occupant or a guest is a breach of this Lease, and Tenant will reimburse Landlord, as damages for that breach, for any fine or assessment the association imposes on Landlord because of it. If Landlord owns the unit, Tenant will also pay any assessment the association imposes for moving into or out of the unit. Landlord will give Tenant a copy of the association's fine or assessment before or at the time Landlord charges Tenant.
notes: OR: Overrides `hoa-compliance`, which is not tagged: making association 'fines' the 'Tenant's responsibility' is a charge outside ORS 90.302 unless it meets the association-assessment exception, which requires that 'The landlord sets forth the assessment requirement in the written rental agreement at the commencement of the tenancy' (ORS 90.302(7)(f)(C)) and that 'The landlord gives a copy of the assessment the landlord receives from the association to the tenant before or at the time the landlord charges the tenant' (ORS 90.302(7)(f)(D)); 'Assessments' are as defined in ORS 94.550 and 100.005, which reach any charge an association imposes on an owner, fines included (Claude's reading of those definitions). Rule 26 fee screen. The four conditions in ORS 90.302(7)(f)(A)-(D) are joined by 'and', so on the text even a violation pass-through must also be a moving-related assessment ((B)); reading (A) and (B) as alternatives is Claude's reading, so the clause recovers violation fines as damages for the tenant's breach (ORS 90.401(2)) and uses the (7)(f) route only for move-in and move-out assessments, which also requires the term in the written agreement at the commencement of the tenancy ((7)(f)(C)): use this clause in the original lease, not a mid-tenancy addendum. Whether association rules bind a tenant depends on the governing documents (no statute found binding tenants generally; Claude's reading); the landlord may prohibit a family child care use that the association's governing documents do not allow (ORS 90.358(4)(b)). title: No Alterations
bodyText: Tenant will not perform any alterations or improvements to the property, including adding, changing, or removing appliances, fixtures, shelving, wallpaper, or paint, without the prior written consent of Landlord. If Landlord approves an alteration, Tenant understands it will remain part of the property at the end of the tenancy unless Landlord requires its removal or applicable law provides that it remains Tenant's property (for example, an electric vehicle charging station installed under Oregon law). This Section does not limit any repair, installation, rekeying, or reasonable modification that applicable law entitles Tenant to perform.
notes: OR: Overrides `no-alterations`, which is not tagged: its approved-alteration sentence would make an EV charging station installed under ORS 90.462 the landlord's property, but 'Unless a landlord and tenant negotiate a different outcome, a charging station installed under this section is deemed to be the personal property of the tenant' (ORS 90.462(8)); a pre-printed term may not be a negotiated outcome and relying on it risks ORS 90.245(1)(a), (2) (Claude's reading). The rest is the shared text. Its last sentence preserves reasonable disability modifications at the tenant's expense (ORS 659A.145(2)(f)), portable cooling devices (ORS 90.355), victims' lock changes (ORS 90.459), EV charging stations (ORS 90.462) and repairs the tenant may arrange (ORS 90.368). An alternative energy device needs the landlord's written permission (ORS 90.265(3)(a)); the 'remain part of the property' sentence may itself be the written agreement ORS 90.265(1) allows, since a device is a landlord fixture only as 'expressly provided in a written agreement' (Claude's reading). title: Keys
bodyText: At the start of the tenancy, Tenant will receive the keys specified by Landlord and will sign a receipt acknowledging the number and type of keys provided. Tenant may not duplicate keys without Landlord's consent. If Tenant loses a key and asks Landlord to replace it, Tenant will pay Landlord's cost of replacing the key. title: Service of Notices by Mail and Attachment
bodyText: In addition to the other methods Oregon law allows, written notices under this Lease may be served by both first class mail and attachment. Notices from Landlord to Tenant will be mailed by first class mail to Tenant at the property, with a second copy attached in a secure manner to the main entrance of the dwelling. Notices from Tenant to Landlord will be mailed by first class mail to Landlord at [Landlord's mailing address], with a second copy attached in a secure manner to [describe with particularity Landlord's designated location, which must be reasonably located in relation to Tenant and available at all hours]. This Section controls over the Notices Section to the extent they differ.
notes: OR: Optional clause (rule 54; rule 46): written notice may be served 'If allowed under a written rental agreement, both first class mail and attachment to a designated location', and 'In order for a written rental agreement to provide for mail and attachment service of written notices from the landlord to the tenant, the agreement must also provide for such service of written notices from the tenant to the landlord' (ORS 90.155(1)(c)); the tenant's copy goes to the landlord's 'designated location, which shall be described with particularity in the written rental agreement, reasonably located in relation to the tenant and available at all hours' (ORS 90.155(1)(c)(B)). Without this clause, a mailed notice adds three days to the notice period (ORS 90.155(2)); with it, mail-and-attach service does not, and hours for termination notices run from 11:59 p.m. the day both are done (ORS 90.160(2)(b)). The control sentence is needed because the shared `notices` clause says nothing in the lease 'designates an alternative method of delivery for any notice governed by law' (rule 46). title: Smoking Policy (Smoking Prohibited)
bodyText: SMOKING POLICY: Smoking is prohibited on the premises. Smoking of any kind, including tobacco, marijuana and vaping, is not permitted anywhere on the property, including inside the dwelling, on porches or balconies, or in any common area. Tenant will be responsible for any cost Landlord incurs to remediate odor, staining or damage caused by smoking in violation of this Section, and a violation may be treated as a violation of this Lease.
notes: OR: Oregon requires the smoking-policy disclosure in every rental agreement for a chapter 90 dwelling: 'The disclosure must state whether smoking is prohibited on the premises, allowed on the entire premises or allowed in limited areas on the premises' (ORS 479.305(1)); 'If the smoking policy allows smoking in limited areas on the premises, the disclosure must identify the areas on the premises where smoking is allowed' (ORS 479.305(1)); also 'the rental agreement must include a disclosure of the smoking policy for the premises that complies with ORS 479.305' (ORS 90.220(4)). Facility spaces are excepted (ORS 479.305(2)). Numbering: ORS 479.305(1) and (2) as compiled in 2025; from January 1, 2027, Or. Laws 2026, ch. 60, § 2 adds a definition as (1), so the disclosure rule becomes (2) and the facility exception (3). The three versions share choice group `smoking-policy-or` because the policy is a fact about the premises that the disclosure must report (rule 6). From January 1, 2027, ORS 479.305 defines 'smoking' as 'inhaling or possessing a lit tobacco product' as defined in ORS 431A.175 (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 60, § 2 (applies to rental agreements entered into before, on or after the effective date, § 3; effective January 1, 2027 per the enrolled act's filing note; the act has no effective-date section)); a lease may still define its own policy more broadly, as the default version does, but the statutory disclosure categories refer to tobacco smoking (Claude's reading). Mid-tenancy changes: a rule that substantially modifies the bargain needs written consent (ORS 90.262(2)); from January 1, 2027 a landlord may add an indoor smoking ban without consent only under the conditions of Or. Laws 2026, ch. 60, § 1 (`edu-smoking-or`). Smoking-fee rules: ORS 90.302(3)(b)(G). Cannabis: no Oregon statute or constitutional provision protects smoking or vaping cannabis in a rental (OR battery 28 (cannabis or marijuana and rental housing): 48 hits, control 0; known positives passed (0 real sections, 1 synthetic); scope CONST 383, OAR 40864, ORS 39614, SL2026 142) (`edu-cannabis-or`). (OR battery 116 (smoking policy and smoking in rentals): 85 hits, control 0; known positives passed (2 real sections, 1 synthetic); scope CONST 383, OAR 40864, ORS 39614, SL2026 142) Default version: overrides the shared `smoking-policy`, which is not tagged because it is a prohibition only, while Oregon needs whichever disclosure fits the premises; this version keeps its text and adds the statutory statement first. 'Default' is changed to 'violation of this Lease' because a violation leads to Oregon's for-cause notice with a cure period (ORS 90.392), not an immediate default. title: 100-Year Flood Plain Notice
bodyText: FLOOD PLAIN NOTICE: The dwelling unit is located within a 100-year flood plain, meaning the level that flood waters may be expected to equal or exceed once each 100 years as determined by the National Flood Insurance Program of the Federal Emergency Management Agency.
notes: OR: Use only if the dwelling unit is in a 100-year flood plain (CONDITIONAL). 'If a dwelling unit is located in a 100-year flood plain, the landlord shall provide notice in the dwelling unit rental agreement that the dwelling unit is located within the flood plain' (ORS 90.228(2)); definition ORS 90.228(1) (FEMA National Flood Insurance Program). Remedy for a missing notice: 'the lesser of the actual damages for the uninsured loss or two months’ rent' after an uninsured flood loss (ORS 90.228(3)). The lease is the statute's vehicle. Other states' generic flood clauses (`flood-insurance-lease-notice-nj`, `flood-disclosure-wa`, `flood-disclosure-ny`) are not tagged: Oregon needs only this statement; renter's insurance advice is in `edu-flood-disclosure-or`. title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: Landlord has supplied and installed the smoke alarms or smoke detectors the property requires and, if the dwelling contains or is connected to a carbon monoxide source, carbon monoxide alarms, and has made sure they work, with working batteries, as of the start of the tenancy. Testing instructions: [give written instructions for testing each smoke alarm and carbon monoxide alarm, for example from the manufacturer's instructions]. Tenant will test the alarms as the manufacturer recommends and at least once every six months, will replace dead batteries as needed, and will notify Landlord in writing of any deficiency other than dead batteries, which Landlord will then repair or replace. Tenant will not remove or tamper with a properly functioning alarm, including by removing working batteries.
notes: OR: Written testing instructions are required by the time the tenant takes possession: the owner 'shall provide a written notice containing instructions for testing of the devices' and 'The notice shall be given to the tenant at the time the tenant first takes possession of the premises' (ORS 479.270(1)); for carbon monoxide alarms 'The landlord shall provide the tenant of the dwelling unit with a written notice containing instructions for testing of the alarms' (ORS 90.317(2)) no later than when the tenant first takes possession (also ORS 90.316(2)). The lease carries the instructions (Claude's choice of vehicle; a separate sheet also satisfies the statutes). Landlord's maintenance duty arises before each new tenancy and on the tenant's written notice of a deficiency other than dead batteries (ORS 479.270(2); ORS 90.317(3)); CO alarm required before a new tenancy if there is a CO source, with working batteries (ORS 90.316(1), (3)); both are habitability items (ORS 479.270(3); ORS 90.317(4); ORS 90.320(1)(j)-(k)). title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: Every rental dwelling must have approved smoke alarms or detectors, and you must supply, install and maintain them and give written testing instructions when the tenant first takes possession. Your maintenance duty, including working batteries, arises before each new tenancy and during the tenancy only when the tenant gives written notice of a deficiency other than dead batteries; the tenant tests at least every six months and replaces dead batteries. If the unit contains a carbon monoxide source, or is in a structure with one and connected to its room by a door, ductwork or ventilation shaft, you may not start a new tenancy without properly installed, working carbon monoxide alarms, and the same instruction, battery and repair rules apply. Both are habitability items. Removing or tampering with a working alarm is prohibited; you may charge a fee of up to $250 for it if your lease describes the fee, unless the State Fire Marshal has assessed the tenant a civil penalty for the same conduct. Placement and type follow State Fire Marshal rules and the state building code.

title: Drinking Water Wells (from 2027)
bodyText: From January 1, 2027, if a rental's drinking water comes from an exempt well and the unit is in a ground water quality management area, you must have the water sampled from the primary drinking faucet and tested by an accredited laboratory for arsenic, coliform bacteria, lead and nitrates (arsenic within 30 days of installing a new well; otherwise at least yearly, with a four-year break after a passing first test), complete the first round before June 1, 2027, give the tenant the results within 30 days after receiving them, and, before entering into a rental agreement, give written notice of the well, the latest results and the next test date. title: Drug Lab Contamination
bodyText: Oregon bars renting property you know, or have reasonable grounds to believe, was used as an illegal drug manufacturing site unless it has been determined fit for use under the Oregon Health Authority's decontamination process, and a lease made in violation is voidable by the tenant. A property officially determined not fit for use stays that way until it is decontaminated by a licensed contractor (or, with the Authority's approval, by the owner or the owner's agent) and certified, or it is assessed, found not contaminated and issued a Certificate of Fitness, or the determination is reversed on appeal. Oregon has no tenant disclosure form for rentals; the full written disclosure rule applies to sales and transfers. The abandoned property statute has special handling for property left in a unit determined unfit because of a methamphetamine lab.

title: When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause
bodyText: Either side may end a week-to-week tenancy on 10 days' written notice at any time. During the first year of occupancy you may end a month-to-month tenancy without cause on 30 days' written notice, and a fixed term ending within the first year on 30 days' written notice before its end date. The first year of occupancy lasts as long as any tenant has lived in the unit for one year or less. After the first year of occupancy, you may end a month-to-month tenancy only for a tenant cause under the notice statutes or for a qualifying landlord reason, and a fixed term ending after the first year becomes month-to-month unless you agree a new term, the tenant gives 30 days' notice, or you have a qualifying reason. The qualifying reasons, each needing at least 90 days' written notice stating the reason and supporting facts: demolition or conversion to a non-residential use; repairs or renovations within a reasonable time where the premises are unsafe or unfit for occupancy, or the unit will be unsafe or unfit during the work; you or an immediate family member moving in as a primary residence when you have no comparable vacant unit in the same building; or a buyer who will live there and whose accepted offer you document. With a qualifying-reason notice you must also pay the tenant one month's rent, unless you own an interest in four or fewer dwelling units. For the buyer reason you may give 60 days' notice instead of 90 if you pay the tenant one more month's rent with the notice, on top of any payment already required. A fixed term also doesn't convert if the tenant had three violations in 12 months, each with a written warning in the statutory form, and you give 90 days' notice. In a building or property with no more than two units where you live, you may end a month-to-month tenancy after the first year on 60 days' notice without cause (30 days for a documented owner-occupant buyer) and a fixed term at its end on 30 days' notice. Terminating in violation of the qualifying-reason, payment or three-violation rules costs three months' rent plus actual damages and gives the tenant a defense to possession; claims must be brought within one year. Some cities add relocation-payment and notice rules.

title: Notice Periods to End a Tenancy
bodyText: Without cause: week-to-week, 10 days' written notice by either side; month-to-month, the tenant may give 30 days' written notice at any time, and you may give 30 days' notice only in the first year of occupancy (after that, see the for-cause rules); a fixed term ending after the first year continues month to month unless ended as the statute allows, and a tenant who wants it to end must give 30 days' written notice before the end date. For cause: 30 days for a material violation with a cure period of at least 14 days (7 and 4 days in a week-to-week tenancy; the cure date can be the delivery date for a separate, completed act that isn't ongoing), 10 days for a repeat within six months (4 in a week-to-week tenancy), 72 hours or 10 or 13 days for nonpayment, 24 hours for serious threats or violence, intentional substantial damage, certain false application information, or acts outrageous in the extreme, 10 days for an unpermitted pet capable of causing damage to persons or property (curable by removing it; 10 days without cure for a repeat within six months), and the special 24- and 48-hour notices for a household member's violence, a unit posted unsafe, drug and alcohol free housing and group recovery homes. Every termination notice must include the veterans' information the statute requires, a nonpayment notice must come with the court's rental-assistance notice, and a notice served by first class mail alone adds three days.

title: Cure Periods for Lease Violations
bodyText: For a material violation of the lease or of the tenant's statutory duties, your 30-day notice must describe the violation and, if it can be cured, say so, describe at least one way to cure it and set a cure date at least 14 days after delivery; if the tenant cures by that date the tenancy continues. For a separate, completed act that isn't ongoing, the cure date can be the date of delivery, so the act can't be cured by waiting. If substantially the same violation recurs within six months after a notice, a 10-day notice with no right to cure is allowed (its termination date can't be earlier than the one in the earlier notice), but not when the only violation is failing to pay the current month's rent. In a week-to-week tenancy the 30, 14 and 10 days become 7, 4 and 4 days. Nonpayment of a late charge, fee or utility charge is a for-cause matter, not a nonpayment-of-rent matter. A 24-hour notice has no cure, except that a pet-based notice is cured by removing the pet. Accepting rent with knowledge of a violation during three or more separate rental periods, or accepting performance that varies from the lease, waives termination for that violation unless an exception applies, such as a written warning with the statutory content given before the third period; 24-hour causes are not waived.

title: Nonpayment of Rent Notices
bodyText: For week-to-week tenancies, give at least 72 hours' written notice, no sooner than the fifth day of the rental period (counting the day rent is due). For other tenancies, give either at least 10 days' written notice no sooner than the eighth day, or at least 13 days' notice no sooner than the fifth day. The notice must state the amount of rent that must be paid and the date and time by which it must be paid to cure, must include the veterans' information, and must be delivered with a copy of the Oregon Judicial Department's rental assistance notice (also required with any summons for nonpayment). A tenant's payment mailed within the notice period is timely unless you served the notice personally, by mail and attachment or by mail and e-mail, both the written rental agreement and the notice name a payment location on the premises or where the tenant has always paid in person, and that place is available to the tenant throughout the notice period. Since June 5, 2026, you must let tenants pay by check or another commercially reasonable method and may not require electronic payment; if you refuse a payment made that way, you may not charge a late fee or terminate for nonpayment. A court will dismiss a nonpayment case if the rental-assistance notice wasn't delivered, if you caused the tenant not to tender rent (including by not reasonably cooperating with a rental assistance program), or if the tenant tenders rental assistance or other payment covering the amount owed; after a dismissal for tender you may charge the tenant the court filing fees, though paying them isn't a condition of the dismissal. title: 24-Hour Terminations
bodyText: You may end a tenancy on at least 24 hours' written notice, specifying the cause and the date and time of termination, if the tenant, someone in the tenant's control or the tenant's pet seriously threatens or inflicts substantial personal injury on someone other than the tenant on the premises (or injures a neighbor living nearby); the tenant or someone in the tenant's control recklessly endangers others; the tenant or someone in the tenant's control intentionally causes substantial damage (a pet, on more than one occasion); the tenant intentionally gave substantial false information on the application within the past year about the tenant's own criminal conviction that would have been material to your acceptance of the application, and you act within 30 days of discovering it; or there is an act outrageous in the extreme, on the premises or in the immediate vicinity, such as prostitution, unlawful manufacture, delivery or possession of a controlled substance, unlicensed cannabis extract manufacture, a bias crime or burglary. A pet-based notice can be cured by removing the pet. Four more 24-hour notices: (1) to a tenant who commits a criminal act of physical violence related to domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking against a household member who is a tenant (only the perpetrator's tenancy ends); (2) to an unauthorized person in possession after the tenant has vacated, if the rental agreement prohibited subletting or other occupants without your written permission and you haven't knowingly accepted rent from that person; (3) to a tenant after an agency posts the unit unsafe for conditions you didn't cause; and (4) in group recovery homes. Someone is in the tenant's control if the tenant lets them enter or stay after the tenant reasonably knows or should know of their act or likelihood to commit such an act. Drug and alcohol free housing programs have a separate 48-hour rule for tenants there less than two years (curable within 24 hours), with a 24-hour notice and no cure for a repeat within six months.

title: Early Termination by Victims
bodyText: A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking may give you at least 14 days' written notice asking to be released from the rental agreement, naming the release date and any immediate family members to be released, with verification: a protective order, a police report, a conviction, or a statement signed by the tenant and a qualified third party (law enforcement officer, attorney, licensed health professional, Department of Justice victim-services employee or victim's advocate) in the statute's form, showing an incident within the previous 90 days (not counting time the perpetrator was incarcerated or lived more than 100 miles away) or a valid protective order. You must release them. They owe no rent or damages incurred after the release date and no fee solely for the termination, and you may not charge an early termination fee. Other tenants remain bound. title: No Adverse Action Against Victims
bodyText: You may not end or refuse to renew a tenancy, serve a termination notice, sue or threaten to sue for possession, raise rent, cut services or refuse to rent because a tenant or applicant is or was a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking, because of a lease violation that consists of an incident against them, or because of criminal activity or a police or emergency response in which they are the victim; nor may you apply different rules to them. The one exception: after a prior written warning about the perpetrator's conduct, you may end the victim's tenancy if the tenant lets the perpetrator on the premises and the perpetrator is an actual and imminent threat to others, or lets the perpetrator live there as an unauthorized occupant. Violations cost up to two months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, and give the tenant a defense. A tenant isn't responsible for damage caused by the perpetrator, though you may require verification of victim status as ORS 90.453 provides. title: Other Ways a Tenant May Leave Early
bodyText: Besides the victim and servicemember rights, an Oregon tenant may end the tenancy: on written notice ending the tenancy at least 30 days later (7 for week-to-week) if you materially fail to comply with the lease, or fail to comply with the habitability duty, and don't remedy it (within 7 days for an essential service, 30 days otherwise); on 48 hours' notice if a failure to supply an essential service poses an imminent and serious threat; immediately if the unit is posted unsafe for conditions the tenant didn't cause, or if conditions existing at the start that the tenant didn't cause pose an imminent and serious threat within six months; on 72 hours' notice (or immediately before move-in) if a utility the tenant must pay can't be obtained because of a prior tenant's or the owner's debt, or a landlord-paid utility is shut off for nonpayment; after an unlawful lockout or a willful utility shutoff; after an unlawful or unreasonable entry, or repeated harassing demands for entry, through the 30-day notice-and-remedy procedure for landlord noncompliance; during a fixed term, on 30 days' notice after you give a qualifying-reason notice for the end of the term; and during a fixed term after a foreclosure notice, on 60 days' notice unless within 30 days you give written evidence from a lender or trustee that the property is no longer in foreclosure, or written evidence that a court has appointed a receiver. A tenancy in a unit destroyed in a natural disaster (including a disaster resulting in a state of emergency declared under ORS 401.165 or 401.309 for wildfires, floods, tsunamis, earthquakes or similar events) ends immediately unless the parties agree otherwise after the disaster (not for facility space rentals). The lease can't waive these rights.

title: Property Left Behind After a Tenancy
bodyText: When a tenancy has ended and you reasonably believe the tenant left personal property with no intention of claiming it, or the tenant has been absent seven days after an unexecuted court order, or the sheriff has given you possession, you must store, sell or dispose of the property only as the statute provides. First give written notice, personally delivered or by first class mail to the tenant at the premises, any known post office box and any forwarding address, saying the property is considered abandoned and must be claimed by a date at least five days after personal delivery or eight days after mailing (45 days for a manufactured dwelling or floating home), where it is stored and how to arrange removal. Store it with reasonable care in a place of safekeeping; you may require payment of removal and storage charges before releasing it, except where the sheriff gave you possession. If the tenant responds by the date, you must make it available for removal by appointment during the next 15 days (30 for a dwelling or home); otherwise it is conclusively presumed abandoned and you may sell it at a public or private sale, or dispose of it if its reasonable value is $1,000 or less or so low that storage and sale costs would probably exceed what a sale would bring, deducting notice, storage and sale costs and unpaid rent from any proceeds. Special rules apply to a sole tenant's death, drug-lab sites and vehicles. A rental agreement may not waive these rights. If you don't comply, the tenant is relieved of liability for unpaid rent and for damage that wasn't deliberate, intentional or grossly negligent and may recover up to twice actual damages; a deliberate and malicious violation also costs twice actual damages.

title: Rent Owed After a Tenant Abandons
bodyText: If a tenant abandons the unit, you must make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental. Renting it to a new tenant for a term starting before the old agreement would have ended terminates the old agreement as of the new tenancy's start. If you don't make reasonable efforts, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the agreement is treated as ended by you as of the date you knew or should have known of the abandonment. For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, the remaining term is treated as one month or one week. Taking back the keys, or trying to re-rent, is not by itself acceptance of a surrender. If you charge the early-termination fee Oregon allows for a fixed term, these rules don't apply and you can't also recover later rent or re-renting costs.

title: The Eviction Court Process
bodyText: After a valid termination notice expires, you may recover possession only through a court action for possession (forcible entry and detainer). You may not file until the notice period (or fixed term) has run. The complaint and summons follow statutory forms; the summons must include the veterans' information and, for nonpayment, the rental-assistance notice. The clerk sets the first appearance seven days after the judicial day following payment of the filing fee (15 days for nonpayment cases), and may delay it up to seven days; if the tenant contests, trial is usually set within 15 days (15 to 30 days for nonpayment claims), and a continuance of more than two days requires the tenant to give security for or pay accruing rent into court. Until September 28, 2027, a nonpayment trial can be rescheduled to 90 to 104 days out for a tenant who is the parent of a child under 12 months living in the unit, receives medical assistance and has been approved for health-related social needs housing supports. If you win, the sheriff executes a writ after a four-day notice of restitution; the judgment can't be enforced if you later sign a new agreement or accept rent for occupancy after the judgment. The court may award attorney fees to the prevailing party, but not to a landlord whose tenant does not contest. The filing fee is set by statute. Some counties' courts have their own forms and procedures.

title: Tenant Property After a Writ
bodyText: When the sheriff returns possession to you, you must remove, store and dispose of the tenant's personal property under the abandoned property statute, and in that case you may not require payment of storage charges before releasing it. Execution, removal, storage and sale costs you don't recover from sale proceeds are added to the judgment. If you don't let the tenant recover the property, the tenant may recover twice the actual damages or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater.

title: No Lockouts, Utility Shutoffs or Property Seizures
bodyText: You may take possession only after an abandonment or relinquishment or through the court process. Removing or excluding a tenant, or seriously attempting or threatening to, or willfully cutting heat, running water, hot water, electricity or another essential service, lets the tenant get a court order restoring possession or end the tenancy and recover up to two months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater; the tenant can also recover damages without ending the tenancy. Distraint for rent is abolished, and a lien on the tenant's household goods is unenforceable unless perfected before October 5, 1973.

title: No Landlord Lien on Tenant Property
bodyText: A landlord's lien or security interest in a tenant's household goods is unenforceable (unless perfected before October 5, 1973), and distraint for rent is abolished. The possessory liens of ORS 87.152 to 87.212 don't apply to tenancies under the act, and a lease can't create a lien in household goods. Abandoned property is handled under the abandoned property statute, and a storage lien under ORS 87.152 can arise only after property is conclusively presumed abandoned.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: You may not raise rent, decrease services, serve a termination notice or bring or threaten an eviction in retaliation because a tenant complained (or said in writing they would complain) to a government agency about a building, health or housing code violation materially affecting health or safety, or about mail delivery or housing discrimination violations; made a complaint to you in good faith and related to the tenancy; organized or joined a tenants' union; testified against you; successfully defended an eviction in the last six months (other than on a notice-service or notice-period defect); uses a dwelling as a family child care home as the statute allows; or asserted any other right under federal, state or local law. 'Decreasing services' includes unreasonably restricting tenant meetings in common areas. The tenant gets the lockout remedies (up to two months' rent or twice damages) and a defense to eviction. You may still evict if a complaint to you or your agent was made unreasonably or harassingly, the code violation was caused mainly by the tenant's household or guests, the tenant was behind on rent when you served the notice (rent paid into court doesn't count), or compliance requires work that would deprive the tenant of the unit.
notes: OR: ORS 90.385(1)-(7) ('The tenant has organized or become a member of a tenants’ union or similar organization' (ORS 90.385(1)(c))). Also ORS 90.465(4). Present (rule 27). title: Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: If the tenant has moved out and someone else remains without permission, you may give that person at least 24 hours' written notice specifying the cause and the date and time to leave, and then recover possession through the court process, but only if the rental agreement prohibited subletting or letting someone else occupy without your written permission and you haven't knowingly accepted rent from that person. A squatter who never had permission is outside the landlord-tenant act; an owner or landlord may recover possession from a squatter through the court process after 24 hours' written notice stating the vacate date and time and that the cause is the person's status as a squatter. A temporary occupant under a written temporary occupancy agreement can be required to leave as that agreement allows and is treated as a squatter if it stays after the tenancy ends or after the tenant revokes permission by ending the agreement.

title: Fire, Casualty and Uninhabitable Units
bodyText: Oregon has no general casualty-termination statute. If a government agency posts the unit as unsafe and unlawful to occupy after the tenancy begins, a tenant who didn't cause the conditions may end the tenancy immediately, and you may end it on 24 hours' written notice if you and your failure to maintain didn't cause them; you must return deposits and prorated prepaid rent within 14 days. If the unit is destroyed in a declared natural disaster (wildfire, flood, earthquake and similar events, even if begun by negligent or intentional acts), the tenancy ends immediately unless you and the tenant agree otherwise afterward: return deposits and prepaid rent (prorated from the disaster), don't charge the tenant for cleanup unless the tenant was responsible for the disaster, and let the tenant search for valuables after the emergency; no rent is owed while the unit is inaccessible or destroyed. Otherwise, an uninhabitable unit triggers the tenant's repair and essential-service remedies. A lease clause letting you end the tenancy after a casualty would add a cause the termination statute doesn't list, so the library doesn't offer one; repairs that make the unit unsafe are a qualifying landlord reason after the first year, with 90 days' notice and a relocation payment where required.

title: Posted or Unlawful Units
bodyText: If an agency posts a unit as unsafe and unlawful to occupy, you may not continue or start a tenancy there until you correct the conditions; knowingly doing so lets the tenant leave immediately and recover two months' rent or up to twice actual damages, whichever is greater. If an agency notifies you that a unit is unlawful but safe for the existing tenant, you may not start a new tenancy until you correct it; a written pre-tenancy disclosure of the determination (with the agency's notice attached) protects you from the tenant's damages claim but not from the agency's penalties or your habitability duty, and the library doesn't offer it as a clause. You may not take a deposit to secure a rental agreement for a posted or noticed unit without that disclosure; if you knowingly do, or don't correct the conditions before the tenancy is to start, the applicant may end the agreement and recover twice the deposit. A city of more than 300,000 people may recover its tenant relocation costs from an owner whose multiple and material code violations for more than 30 days, through the owner's action or inaction, endanger tenants or the public and cause condemnation; as to a tenant's relocation costs, it is a defense that the condition was caused by that tenant's action or negligence.

title: Tenants and Foreclosure
bodyText: Before signing a lease for premises with four or fewer units, you must disclose in writing any outstanding notice of default or trustee's sale, pending foreclosure suit, pending declaration of forfeiture or suit for specific performance of a contract of sale, or pending tax-lien foreclosure. During a foreclosure, a tenant with actual notice of it may apply the deposit or prepaid rent to its obligation to you after written notice without that being grounds for termination, and a fixed-term tenant may end the tenancy on 60 days' notice unless within 30 days you give written evidence from a lender or trustee that the property is no longer in foreclosure, or that a court has appointed a receiver. After a trustee's sale (nonjudicial foreclosure), the purchaser must give the occupants written notice of the sale containing the information the statute lists (a notice in the statutory form complies) within 30 days after the sale, and before or with any 30-day termination notice; a bona fide tenant may stay for 60 days after a written termination notice under a fixed term lease, or at least 30 days for a periodic tenancy, though a purchaser who will live there may end even a fixed term on 30 days' notice. If the purchaser accepts rent, signs a new agreement or fails to terminate the tenancy as the statute allows within 30 days after the sale, the purchaser becomes the landlord. The purchaser's responsibility for deposits follows the foreclosure statute. After an execution sale on a judgment with priority over the lease, a tenant under an unexpired lease may stay until the redemption period expires by paying the purchaser (or redemptioner) each month the greater of the value of the use and occupancy or the lease payments.

title: Condominium Conversion
bodyText: Converting a rental building to condominiums brings the condominium statutes' notices to tenants. Either violation lets the tenant recover six times the monthly rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. Cities may limit rent increases during the conversion notice period within the state cap.

title: Minors as Tenants
bodyText: A minor can be a tenant in Oregon. An unemancipated, unmarried minor living apart from parents or guardians who is 16 or 17 (or younger and a parent, or pregnant) may contract for a dwelling and utilities without parental consent, and the contract binds the minor; parents aren't liable unless they sign as guarantors. The act's definition of tenant includes such a minor, and a minor tenant may appear in an eviction case.

title: Drug and Alcohol Free Housing Programs
bodyText: Oregon recognizes drug and alcohol free housing run by a nonprofit or housing authority for people in recovery, with a written rental agreement that must contain specified terms. title: Drug, Prostitution and Gambling Nuisance Abatement
bodyText: Oregon's place-nuisance statutes declare places used for prostitution, for-profit gambling, unauthorized controlled-substance or unlawful cannabis activity, and drug-lab sites not decontaminated within 180 days to be nuisances. The Attorney General, a district, county or city attorney, or anyone living or doing business in the county may sue to abate one, and a court may order the place closed for up to a year, award damages, and secure the property at a cost that becomes a lien; violating an order is a crime. A court won't order abatement against an owner it finds in good faith had no knowledge of the nuisance or has been making reasonable efforts to abate it, isn't in contempt, and will make best efforts to abate it immediately. Separately, unlawful manufacture, delivery or possession of a controlled substance by the tenant or someone in the tenant's control, on the premises or in the immediate vicinity, supports a 24-hour termination, and a landlord whose good-faith 24-hour termination on such grounds fails in court is not for that reason in violation of a law requiring the tenant's removal, while it keeps making good-faith efforts.

title: How to Deliver Notices
bodyText: Written notices under the landlord-tenant act must be served by personal delivery, by first class mail (adding three days to the notice period, and the notice must say so), or by first class mail plus attachment to the main entrance if the written rental agreement provides for it both ways. E-mail service is allowed only under a written addendum both parties sign after the tenant has moved in, listing each side's e-mail addresses, letting either side end it or change the address on three days' written notice, and containing the statute's notice about receiving legal notices by e-mail; even then, a termination notice sent by e-mail must also go by first class mail. Other methods may be used only in addition to these. 'Actual notice' (for entry, for example) may be given in person or by voicemail, by a written notice left as the statute describes, or by another method agreed and described in the written rental agreement. Days are counted as consecutive calendar days, excluding the day of service and including the last day until 11:59 p.m. Deposit refunds, utility bills and abandoned-property notices have their own delivery rules. Oregon's electronic transactions act applies only between parties who agreed to transact electronically, doesn't override a statute's required delivery method, and itself doesn't authorize electronic notice of default, eviction or a right to cure under a rental agreement for a primary residence; e-mail service rests only on the landlord-tenant act's addendum rule.

title: Written Leases and Long Terms
bodyText: An agreement to lease real property for longer than one year is void unless it, or a note or memorandum of it expressing the consideration, is in writing and signed by the party to be charged or that party's authorized agent. title: Who the Landlord-Tenant Act Covers
bodyText: Oregon's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (ORS chapter 90) covers most residential rentals. It does not cover: residence at an institution incidental to detention or to medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services (off-campus non-dormitory housing is covered); a buyer's or seller's occupancy of up to 90 days around a sale; fraternal or social organization housing; transient occupancy in a hotel or motel; squatters; vacation occupancies (up to 45 days and not a principal residence, or up to 90 days for a recreational vehicle park space on the statute's conditions); an employee's occupancy conditioned on employment on the premises; condominium owners and cooperative proprietary lessees; agricultural rentals; and licensed treatment and care programs. Rentals of spaces in manufactured dwelling parks and floating home marinas (ORS 90.505 to 90.850) follow special rules that the library's lease does not cover. A tenant may be a minor in the circumstances the minors' housing statute allows. Arrangements created to avoid the act are covered anyway.

title: Entering a Tenant's Home
bodyText: Except in an emergency, a written repair request, an agreed yard-work entry, an agreement with the tenant about a specific entry, a court order, abandonment, or an absence of the tenant of more than seven days (entry then only at times reasonably necessary), you must give at least 24 hours' actual notice and enter only at reasonable times. After receiving your notice, the tenant may deny consent (by actual notice, or by a written notice securely attached to the main entrance), but may not unreasonably withhold it; an unreasonable refusal lets you seek a court order or end the tenancy for cause, plus damages. After an emergency entry in the tenant's absence, give actual notice within 24 hours of the fact, date and time, nature of the emergency and the names of those who entered. Entry without notice to show the unit to a buyer requires a separate signed writing, made while you are actively trying to sell, with separate consideration. You may not abuse entry or use it to harass; unlawful or harassing entry lets the tenant seek an injunction or end the tenancy and recover at least one month's rent (one week's for week-to-week). A good-faith attempt to comply protects you if an agency requires entry and the tenant refuses.

title: Selling or Changing Management

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance
bodyText: You may require renter's liability insurance only in a written rental agreement, only if you carry comparable liability insurance and give documentation to a tenant who asks, and only up to $100,000 per occurrence or the customary amount for similar rentals, whichever is greater. Before a new tenancy, tell the applicant in writing about the requirement, the amount and a summary of the exceptions. You may not require it of a household at or below 50% of area median income or for a unit subsidized with public funds (vouchers don't count as a subsidy). To add it to an existing month-to-month tenancy, give 30 days' written notice with the summary; a tenant who doesn't comply can be given a for-cause notice and cure by getting insurance. You may require only interested-party status, not a particular insurer, additional-insured status or a subrogation waiver, and you may claim against the policy only for damage the tenant is liable for (not wear and tear, acts of God or your conduct), only if the claim is greater than the tenant's security deposit and only with a copy to the tenant. Your written agreement must describe your own insurance requirements. Knowing violations cost actual damages or $250, whichever is greater; a frivolous claim costs actual damages plus $500.

title: Keeping Tenants' Information Confidential

title: Collecting Money From Tenants
bodyText: Oregon's unlawful collection practices statute reaches anyone collecting a debt arising from a consumer transaction, which includes a residential lease, and on Claude's reading it reaches a landlord collecting its own rent and charges. Among other things, it bars collecting interest, fees or charges beyond the actual debt unless the agreement expressly authorizes them or a law expressly allows them, threatening action you can't take, contacting the tenant's employer about the debt, and harassing communications. A willful violation lets the tenant recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus possible punitive damages and attorney fees. Since Oregon's fee statute limits what a lease can authorize, a fee the statute doesn't allow is not 'expressly authorized'.

title: The Unlawful Trade Practices Act

title: Oregon Fair Housing Classes
bodyText: Oregon bars housing discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, marital status, familial status, source of income (including Section 8 and other housing assistance) and disability, in renting, terms, advertising, and coercion or interference. A facially neutral policy with a disparate adverse impact on a protected class can violate the law, considering its business purpose and less discriminatory alternatives. Exemptions are narrow: familial status for qualifying housing for older persons; sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and familial status for renting space in an owner-occupied single-family home with shared common space (but not for advertising a preference); and sex where the property requires shared bath or bedroom facilities by unrelated persons of the opposite sex. Except as a federal rent-subsidy or affordable-rent program requires, Oregon's landlord-tenant act also bars discrimination against an applicant, tenant or household member based on actual or perceived immigration or citizenship status, and asking about that status. Local ordinances may add classes.

title: Occupancy Limits
bodyText: Oregon sets no statewide maximum occupancy for rentals, but an occupancy guideline you adopt may not be more restrictive than two people per bedroom and must be reasonable for the bedroom and unit sizes, without discriminatory impact on a protected class. Local housing codes may set their own standards, but no local government may set or enforce a maximum occupancy limit based on the family or non-family relationships among occupants. title: Temporary Occupancy Agreements
bodyText: Oregon lets you, the tenant and a proposed occupant sign a written temporary occupancy agreement. The temporary occupant is not a tenant and has no tenant's rights; the tenant may end the agreement at any time, and you may end it only for a material violation, without a right to cure. You may screen the occupant for conduct or criminal record, but not credit or income. The agreement must expressly state that the occupant is not a tenant and has no tenant's rights and the termination rules, without a right to cure, may require compliance with the rules and may have an end date. If the occupant doesn't leave when it ends, you may give the tenant a for-cause notice (unless the victim protections apply), and an occupant who stays after the tenancy ends, or after the tenant ends the agreement, is treated as a squatter; no written termination notice to the occupant is required. You may not use it to evade your duties, and every tenancy needs at least one tenant.

title: Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies
bodyText: If you materially fail to comply with the lease or the habitability duty, the tenant may give written notice ending the tenancy on a date at least 30 days later (seven days for week-to-week) unless you remedy the breach within seven days for an essential service or 30 days otherwise; a recurrence within six months allows termination on 14 days' notice. The tenant may also recover damages, but not for a condition you neither knew nor reasonably should have known of, if the tenant knew of it and failed to give you timely actual notice or it was caused after the tenancy began by the deliberate or negligent act of someone other than you or your agent. For an essential service you intentionally or negligently fail to supply, after written notice and a reasonable time the tenant may buy the service and deduct its cost, recover reduced-rental-value damages, or, if the unit is unsafe or unfit, get substitute housing and stop paying rent; if the failure poses an imminent and serious threat, the tenant may give 48 hours' notice ending the tenancy unless you remedy it within those 48 hours. For a minor defect costing $300 or less (not mold, radon, asbestos or lead-based paint), the tenant may give at least seven days' written notice and then have it repaired by someone other than the tenant (you may reasonably specify who) and deduct the cost with a written statement. In an eviction for nonpayment or an action for rent, the tenant may counterclaim if you knew or should have known of the problem before you filed, and the court may order rent paid into court. None of these remedies applies to a condition the tenant or a guest caused.

title: Utilities in Your Name and Tenant Accounts
bodyText: If you're responsible for a utility under the lease and it's shut off for nonpayment, the tenant may pay the balance and deduct it from rent, or end the tenancy on 72 hours' actual notice unless you restore service in that time, and you must then return, within four days, rent prepaid for that month prorated from the later of termination or move-out and any other prepaid rent, and the deposit as the deposit statute requires; the tenant may also recover actual damages from the shutoff. title: Pools and Spas at Rentals
bodyText: Oregon licenses and regulates public pools and spas through the Oregon Health Authority: building one needs plan approval and operating one needs an annual license. title: What an Oregon Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Oregon has no single list of required lease contents, but specific rules require items in a written rental agreement: any security deposit, every fee you may charge, the late-charge terms if you charge one, the smoking policy, a flood plain notice if the unit is in a 100-year flood plain, utility or service charges you will pass through (common-area charges and any cable or internet markup described separately), an association-assessment pass-through, the renter's insurance description if you require it, and the landlord and agent disclosures (in the agreement or another writing). title: Assistance Animals
bodyText: Refusing a reasonable accommodation, including an assistance animal a person with a disability needs, is housing discrimination in Oregon. You may not ask for verification when the disability and the need are obvious or already known; otherwise you may ask only for what's needed to evaluate the disability-related need. You may not charge any deposit or fee for keeping the animal. You may refuse a specific animal only if it poses a direct threat to others' health or safety that can't be eliminated or significantly reduced, based on an individualized assessment of objective evidence. The tenant remains responsible for damage, and the rule-violation fee for not cleaning up an animal's waste outside the unit can apply.

title: Penalties for Refusing an Assistance Animal
bodyText: Oregon has no criminal penalty for a landlord who refuses a tenant's assistance animal; the refusal is an unlawful housing practice enforced through a civil rights complaint to the Bureau of Labor and Industries, which can assess civil penalties of up to $11,000 ($27,500 or $55,000 for repeat violators), or a lawsuit; a tenant may also raise it as a defense to a discriminatory eviction unless the tenant is in default in rent. There is no criminal penalty for the refusal itself, although willfully violating a commissioner's order is a Class A misdemeanor. Separately, it is a Class A misdemeanor to intentionally or knowingly injure, or attempt to injure, an assistance animal in the narrower sense of an individually trained dog or other animal designated by rule, or to interfere with one while it is assisting a person with a disability.

title: Liens From Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText: If a tenant hires someone to work on the property, the contractor's construction lien can reach the tenant's leasehold. Your own interest can be liened too: an improvement built with your knowledge is treated as built at your request unless, within three days after you learn of the work, you post a written notice in a conspicuous place on the land or the improvement saying you won't be responsible for it. Requiring your written consent for alterations doesn't by itself protect you once you know work is under way.

title: Receivership for Dangerous Rental Buildings
bodyText: If a city or county believes residential property violates building or housing codes badly enough to threaten public health, safety or welfare, it may ask the circuit court to appoint a receiver to do the repairs, after at least 60 days' written notice to the owner and other interested parties. The receiver's net losses, once the court approves them, can be recorded as a lien on the property that takes priority over most other liens and mortgages (not property tax or assessment liens, the mining, land-preparation, nursery-stock and irrigation-power liens of ORS 87.352 to 87.362, or a purchase-money interest recorded before the city's or county's notice, unless the notice was given to its holder and the buyer or borrower and the holder hadn't moved to foreclose or take possession before the receiver was appointed).

title: Utility Shutoffs and Tenants
bodyText: When the account holder isn't the occupant, regulated utilities must warn the tenants before shutting off service: an energy utility gives occupants a five-day notice addressed to 'tenant' or 'occupant' and, for a master-metered multifamily building, notifies the Public Utility Commission at least five business days ahead; a regulated water utility sends a duplicate notice to the service address and, for a master-metered building, a seven-day notice to each unit. If you are responsible for a utility under the lease and it is shut off for nonpayment, the tenant may pay it and deduct the amount from rent, or end the tenancy on 72 hours' notice unless you restore service within the 72 hours. A regulated water utility must also tell the Public Utility Commission seven days before shutting off a master-metered building.

title: Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Rent
bodyText: No Oregon statute requires the same rent or terms for month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. The statewide rent increase limit and its notice rules apply to both. title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In an eviction for nonpayment, or an action for rent while the tenant is in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for any amount the tenant could recover under the lease or the landlord-tenant act, if the tenant proves you knew or should have known of the facts, or had actual notice, before you filed. On either side's request the court may order the tenant to pay accrued and accruing rent into court, applies it to whatever each side is owed, and enters judgment for the tenant on possession if no rent remains due. A tenant who doesn't pay rent into court as ordered can't pursue the counterclaim. A continuance of more than two days requires the tenant to pay rent into court (or give a bond), and if the tenant doesn't pay as ordered the case is tried immediately.
notes: OR: ORS 90.370(1)-(5) ('If the tenant does not comply with an order to pay rent into the court as provided in subsection (1) of this section, the tenant shall not be permitted to assert a counterclaim in the action for possession' (ORS 90.370(3))); ORS 105.140(1)-(2). Present (rule 27). Rent paid into court is not a default for retaliation purposes (ORS 90.385(6)). title: Settlements, Continuances and Stays in Eviction Cases
bodyText: Oregon eviction cases often end in a stipulated agreement: if the tenant keeps possession on condition of paying or doing something by set dates, the court enters an order, and if the tenant later complies, the case is dismissed. You can enforce such an order by affidavit of noncompliance only if it covers future conduct and payment of past-due amounts for no more than six months and future rent for no more than the next three months; the order is automatically dismissed 12 months after entry unless you've filed a noncompliance affidavit and won, and the tenant can ask for a hearing that delays the writ. A continuance longer than two days requires the tenant to give security for, or pay into court, the rent that accrues. A court may stay the eviction of a state service member for up to 90 days in the circumstances the statute lists. Until September 28, 2027, a nonpayment trial must be rescheduled to 90 to 104 days out if a tenant who is the parent of a child under 12 months living in the unit, receives medical assistance and has been approved for health-related social needs housing supports moves at least three judicial days before trial and has delivered documentation of the approval to you. Beyond these, there is no general statutory hardship stay.
