title: Criminal Activity
bodyText: [Optional.] Tenant, occupants and guests will not engage in criminal activity on or near the property that threatens the health, safety or right to peaceful enjoyment of the premises by others, or that involves the unlawful manufacture, sale, distribution or possession of a controlled substance on the property. A violation is a breach of a covenant of this Lease that cannot be cured, and Landlord may terminate this Lease and seek possession as applicable law allows. This Section does not apply to criminal activity in which Tenant or a member of Tenant's household is the victim, including conduct that is the subject of a protective order protecting them, or to any request for help from the police or other emergency assistance.
notes: WV: A summary-relief petition may rest on the tenant having 'breached a warranty or a leasehold covenant' (W. Va. Code § 55-3A-1(a)(3)); no West Virginia statute makes criminal or drug activity by a tenant of a private landlord a ground of its own (WV battery b-expedited (expedited or immediate eviction for drug, criminal or violent activity): 0 hits, control 0; known positives passed (0 real sections, 1 synthetic); scope CODE 31329, CONST 205) (WV battery criminal-activity (criminal activity or drugs as grounds against a tenant): 8 hits, control 0; known positives passed (0 real sections, 1 synthetic); scope CODE 31329, CONST 205); the one statute on the subject reaches only housing authorities, which 'may impose and enforce occupancy standards and requirements to prohibit any criminal or other activity which threatens the health, safety or right to peaceful enjoyment of the premises or development by other residents' and may evict only on a finding of the tenant's participation or knowledge, with a rebuttable presumption of knowledge (W. Va. Code § 16-15-17(b)); this clause is not written for housing-authority housing (round 1 independent check). So the covenant is what lets the landlord act on it (rule 54; canvass proposal B-2; `edu-no-expedited-criminal-eviction-wv`, `edu-no-drug-free-addendum-wv`). 'Cannot be cured' ties into `default-by-tenant-wv`, which requires no notice or cure 'on a failure that cannot be cured' (rule 43). Real property used 'to commit or to facilitate the commission of a violation of this chapter punishable by more than one year imprisonment' can be forfeited unless the owner establishes the act or omission was 'without his or her knowledge or consent' (W. Va. Code § 60A-7-703(a)(8); `edu-no-expedited-criminal-eviction-wv`), which is the landlord's reason to act promptly. Victim and emergency-call carve-out: West Virginia has no domestic-violence tenancy statute and no police-call statute (`edu-dv-qualifying-documents-wv`, `edu-no-emergency-assistance-rule-wv`), so the carve-out is a drafting choice carried from `criminal-activity-ky`; it also keeps the clause clear of fair housing claims (W. Va. Code § 16B-18-5(b); Claude's reading). Model: `criminal-activity-ky`. title: Rent Increase During the Term
bodyText: [Optional.] During the Term, Landlord may increase Monthly Rent by giving Tenant written notice at least 30 days before the increase takes effect, stating the new Monthly Rent and its effective date. Tenant may instead end this Lease, without an early termination fee, by giving Landlord written notice before the increase takes effect, effective on the last day before the increase. Landlord will not increase Rent to retaliate against Tenant for any complaint, request or other conduct the law protects.
notes: WV: No West Virginia statute permits, forbids or sets notice for a rent increase during a fixed term (WV battery f-rent-midterm (rent or term changes during a fixed-term lease): 13 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 1 synthetic); scope CODE 31329, CONST 205) (WV battery rent-increase (notice of rent increase): 2 hits, control 0; known positives passed (0 real sections, 2 synthetic); scope CODE 31329, CONST 205) (WV battery rent-increase-nc (notice of rent increase (no context limb)): 2 hits, control 0; known positives passed (0 real sections, 2 synthetic); scope CODE 31329, CONST 205); without a term allowing it, the rent stated for a fixed term stands (`edu-rent-escalation-wv`), so the right exists only if the lease grants it (rule 54; canvass proposal F-2). The 30 days and the tenant's no-fee exit are drafting choices carried from `rent-increase-midterm-ky`, not West Virginia figures. The emergency price limit for month-to-month rentals during a declared state of emergency (W. Va. Code §§ 46A-6J-2, 46A-6J-3; `edu-disaster-rent-limits-wv`) does not reach a fixed term by its definition of housing, but a landlord should not use the clause during an emergency (Claude's reading). Retaliation: no general statute (`edu-retaliation-wv`); the sentence is a drafting choice. Fair housing bars different terms for a protected class (W. Va. Code § 16B-18-5(b)). title: Utilities Billed by Landlord
bodyText: [Optional. Use only if Landlord bills Tenant for a utility.] Landlord will bill Tenant for the following utility services to the property: [list each utility, for example water and sewer]. Tenant's share will be measured or calculated by [state one for each utility: submetering equipment / energy allocation equipment / this ratio utility billing formula: describe the formula, for example the building's bill divided by square footage or by number of occupants]. Landlord will give Tenant a written bill for each billing period showing the amount and how it was calculated, and Tenant will pay it within [number] days after receiving it. Landlord will not add any administrative or service fee to these charges. Unpaid utility charges under this Section are Tenant's obligation under this Lease, and those for utility service Landlord has paid for may be applied against the Security Deposit when the tenancy ends.
notes: WV: 'If the rental agreement so provides, a landlord may use submetering equipment or energy allocation equipment, or a ratio utility billing system' (W. Va. Code § 37-6A-1(17)), and a deposit may be applied to 'unpaid utilities that were billed to and paid by the landlord, are the obligation of the tenant under the rental agreement and unpaid by the tenant' (W. Va. Code § 37-6A-2(b)(3)): a right that exists only if the lease invokes it (rules 27, 50, 54; canvass proposals A-1 and C-2; `edu-utility-apportionment-wv`). The utilities the definition lists are 'electricity, natural gas, propane gas, water, sewer, telephone and cable television' (same subdivision). No statute sets a disclosure, cap or billing procedure (WV battery utility-billing (submetering, allocation or resale of utilities to tenants): 5 hits, control 0; known positives passed (1 real section, 0 synthetic); scope CODE 31329, CONST 205); the itemized bill, the payment window and the no-fee sentence are drafting choices (a billing fee the lease set would be part of the tenant's obligation under the library's reading of W. Va. Code § 46A-2-128(d), but whether a fee for reselling utility service is lawful is a utility-regulation question). Not read: Public Service Commission rules and decisions on whether a landlord who resells or allocates utility service is regulated (the definition of a public utility in W. Va. Code § 24-1-2 was not applied to landlords here); `edu-utility-apportionment-wv` says so. A utility allowance with a tenant-paid overage (`utility-allowance-cap-co`) fits inside this clause as a ratio formula and is not offered separately. CONDITIONAL: used only if the landlord bills utilities. title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If a check Tenant gives Landlord is dishonored for insufficient funds or credit, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount, not more than $25] for each dishonored check, but no fee will be charged or collected once a complaint for a worthless-check warrant has been delivered to magistrate court. If any payment Tenant makes is dishonored, returned or otherwise fails, Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order, except that once a complaint for a worthless-check warrant has been presented to magistrate court, payment of the dishonored check, draft or order may be made only through the court. If more than two of Tenant's payments during any 12-month period are returned or fail, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check or money order.
notes: WV: Overrides `returned-payments`, whose fee is 'not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' and so names no figure (rule 53). 'The payee or holder of any dishonored check may impose a fee of up to $25 a worthless check. This fee may not be imposed or collected after a complaint for warrant has been delivered to magistrate court.' (W. Va. Code § 61-3-39e). The fee sentence speaks of 'any dishonored check', and the section's other sentences of a 'check, draft or order' dishonored 'because of insufficient funds or credit' (same section); whether it reaches a failed electronic payment is not stated. If the debt-collection rules reach rent, an incidental fee needs both the agreement and a statute or regulation (W. Va. Code § 46A-2-128(d)); § 61-3-39e is that statute only for a dishonored check, so the fee is limited to that case and a failed electronic payment carries no fee, only the certified-funds replacement (Claude's reading; canvass proposal F-1; round 1 independent check; `edu-returned-check-fee-wv`). The fee may not be imposed or collected after a complaint for warrant has been delivered to magistrate court, and once a complaint 'has been presented to magistrate court, payment may be made only through the court' and a payee 'unlawfully accepting payment after that time shall be liable for all costs' (same section), so the fee sentence and the replacement sentence both yield at that point. The fee sentence names only a check, so the clause's fee sentence does too, rather than 'payment order', which can be electronic (W. Va. Code § 46-4A-103(a)(1)); a check is a draft, other than a documentary draft, payable on demand and drawn on a bank, or a cashier's or teller's check (W. Va. Code § 46-3-104(f)) (round 2, round 4 and round 5 independent checks). The landlord's figure goes in the bracket (CONSTRAINED_TERM: the landlord's choice within the statutory limit). title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors
bodyText: Landlord has provided and installed the operational smoke detectors, and any carbon monoxide detectors, that West Virginia law requires at the property, and will replace a detector that fails for any reason other than a worn battery. If the property is a one- or two-family dwelling that Landlord does not occupy, Tenant will perform routine maintenance on the smoke detectors in the dwelling, including testing them and replacing batteries as needed. Tenant will not disable, remove or otherwise interfere with any detector, and will promptly tell Landlord in writing if a detector is missing, damaged or not working. If a deaf or hard-of-hearing person lives at the property, Landlord will, on a written request by or for that person, provide and install a smoke detector with a light signal sufficient to warn that person of fire.

title: Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit) before occupancy. When the tenancy ends, Landlord may apply the Security Deposit only to: (1) Rent due, including the reasonable charges for late payment of Rent that this Lease specifies; (2) damages Landlord suffers because Tenant did not comply with this Lease, less reasonable wear and tear; (3) unpaid utility charges that were billed to and paid by Landlord and that this Lease makes Tenant's obligation; (4) reasonable costs of removing and storing Tenant's personal property; and (5) other damages or charges that this Lease provides for, including the cost of a third-party contractor to repair damage to the property caused by Tenant. The Security Deposit is not a payment of Rent, and Tenant may not treat it as a credit against Rent owed.
notes: WV: Overrides `security-deposit-use`, whose uses ('to remedy a Tenant default', cleaning only if 'substantially less clean') are not West Virginia's list. On termination a deposit 'may be applied by the landlord only to' five uses (W. Va. Code § 37-6A-2(b)(1)-(5)); two of them turn on the lease's own words: late charges 'specified in the rental agreement' ((b)(1)) and 'other damages or charges as provided in the rental agreement' ((b)(5)), so the clause states them (rule 50); unpaid utilities count only if they are 'the obligation of the tenant under the rental agreement' ((b)(3)). Nothing in § 37-6A-2 entitles the tenant at termination to an immediate credit of the deposit against delinquent rent (W. Va. Code § 37-6A-2(d)); the last sentence states that as a contract term. A 'security deposit' is any refundable deposit securing performance or damages; it excludes rent and prepaid rent, and excludes a pet fee or application fee only where 'the parties expressly agree, in writing' that the fee is nonrefundable (W. Va. Code § 37-6A-1(14)); `nonrefundable-fees-wv`. A lease may not waive any right under the article (W. Va. Code § 37-6A-4). title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors
bodyText: In a one- or two-family dwelling, including a manufactured home, West Virginia requires an operational smoke detector near each sleeping area. The owner must provide, install and replace it, and where the owner does not live there the tenant must do routine maintenance on it. If a deaf or hard-of-hearing person lives in a dwelling you rent out, you must, on a written request by or for that person, install a smoke detector with a light signal; a sprinkler system installed under the State Fire Code and State Building Code may be provided instead of smoke detectors. An AC-powered carbon monoxide detector with battery backup is required in a newly built residential unit with a fuel-burning heating or cooking source, and in apartment buildings, boarding houses and one- and two-family dwellings intended to be rented, in a common area open to the public or in the sleeping rooms next to, above and below rooms with permanently installed fuel-burning appliances; one is also required in a unit connected to a newly built garage, shed or barn with a fuel-burning source, and in newly built apartment buildings and one- and two-family rentals detectors must be hardwired with battery backup. The statute does not say who maintains a carbon monoxide detector, so plan to do it yourself. A violation is a misdemeanor (fines of $250, then $750, then $2,000), and a city or county may impose greater duties. No statute sets smoke detector rules for apartment buildings or a fee for a tenant who disables a detector, so charge a tenant who damages or removes one only the actual cost of repair or replacement; building-wide rules come from the State Fire Code and State Building Code, legislative rules not read here.

title: Heat and Hot Water
bodyText: If a dwelling unit is supplied by direct public utility connections, you must supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, and reasonable heat from October 1 through the last day of April. The duty does not apply where the unit is built so that its running water, heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control. The statute does not define reasonable heat or set a temperature, and it applies the same way to every kind of residential tenancy. Whether you meet the duty when the tenant holds the utility account for a separately metered unit is not settled by statute, so say clearly in the lease who arranges and pays for heat and hot water.

title: Landlord's Repair Duties
bodyText: For residential property, you must deliver the dwelling unit and surrounding premises in fit and habitable condition at the start of the tenancy and keep them that way; keep the property in line with applicable health, safety, fire and housing codes; make all repairs needed to keep it fit and habitable; and keep in good and safe working order the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, that you supply or must supply by written or oral agreement or by law. In a building with more than one living unit, you must also keep common areas under your control clean, safe and in repair and provide appropriate facilities for removing ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste. The code and repair duties do not cover a code violation caused by the fault of the tenant, the tenant's family or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent, or repairs needed primarily because of that person's lack of reasonable care. You are not required to make repairs while the tenant is behind on rent, but if your lease gives you a greater duty than the statute, the lease controls; the Landlord Maintenance clause this library uses for West Virginia promises repairs without an exception for unpaid rent, so if you use it, do not rely on the unpaid-rent excuse. The statute sets no repair deadline and no reporting procedure, so say in the lease how tenants should report problems.

title: Shifting Repairs to the Tenant
bodyText: No West Virginia statute says whether a lease may shift your statutory repair and habitability duties to the tenant or have the tenant waive them, and none sets a procedure, such as a separate signed agreement, for doing so. The habitability statute excuses you only where the tenant, the tenant's family or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent caused the code violation or the need for repair, and it says a lease that gives you a greater duty controls; it does not say a lease may reduce your duties. Whether a court would enforce a reduction or waiver is a question of case law, which was not searched, so keep tenant maintenance terms to routine tasks and do not use them to take away the statutory duties. A tenant's promise to leave the premises in good repair means returning them in good and substantial repair, reasonable wear and tear excepted, and does not oblige the tenant to rebuild or pay for buildings destroyed by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence unless other words in the lease show that intent.

title: Tenant Remedies for Repairs
bodyText: No West Virginia statute lets a tenant repair and deduct, withhold rent, pay rent into escrow or end the lease because you did not make repairs, and no statute sets a notice procedure or deadline for repair requests. In an eviction for unpaid rent, though, the tenant may answer that you breached a material covenant on which the duty to pay rent depends, and the court must then hold a hearing on that issue; a tenant who asks for and gets a continuance must pay the rent coming due into court. If buildings are destroyed or damaged by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence, rent is reasonably reduced until you rebuild unless the lease provides otherwise, and if you do not rebuild within a reasonable time the tenant may surrender possession and owe no further rent. A tenant who wins an eviction appeal after the lease term has ended gets money damages only, unless the case involves title, retaliatory eviction or breach of warranty. Other remedies for breach of your habitability duty, such as damages or rent abatement, depend on case law, which was not searched; the magistrate court's answer form lets the tenant check a defense that the premises are defective and violate the warranty of habitability. Ask tenants to put repair requests in writing and keep records.

bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires you to provide or pay for substitute housing when the rental becomes unlivable, whether from fire, repairs or code enforcement. title: Rent Limits During a Declared Emergency
bodyText: Once the Governor or the Legislature declares a state of emergency, it is unlawful in the area covered by the declaration to rent or offer rental housing leased on a month-to-month term for more than 10 percent above the price you charged on the 10th day before the declaration, unless the increase comes directly from added costs, and then only up to 10 percent above your cost plus your customary markup. The limit lasts for the whole emergency or 30 days after the declaration, whichever is longer; under a declared state of preparedness it applies only to items the proclamation names, and the Governor reviews the covered goods every 15 days. A violation is an unfair or deceptive act under the consumer protection act and a misdemeanor (fine up to $1,000, jail up to one year, or both). The statute's definition of housing names only month-to-month rentals, not week-to-week or fixed-term leases. No West Virginia statute sets other landlord duties after a disaster, such as debris removal or rent during an evacuation; the lease's casualty terms and the rent-reduction statute govern damage.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: No West Virginia statute generally addresses renting the same unit to two tenants, except the reletting rule below. You must deliver the dwelling unit in fit and habitable condition at the start of the tenancy, so confirm a prior tenant has left before committing the unit to a new one; the lease's possession-delay terms govern if you cannot. After a tenant abandons with rent unpaid and you relet under the statutory abandonment and reletting notice, a new tenant who leased under that notice keeps possession if the new lease was made before the original tenant notified you in writing of the intent to resume possession and paid or tendered what is owed.

title: Which Fire, Building and Housing Codes Apply
bodyText: West Virginia's habitability statute requires you to keep a rental in line with applicable health, safety, fire and housing codes, but the codes themselves are not in the statutes. The State Fire Code, a legislative rule of the State Fire Commission, has the force of law statewide as a minimum standard; a stricter local fire ordinance governs only if the Fire Commission has approved it. The State Building Code applies only in counties and cities that adopt it, and only prospectively. Counties may adopt building and housing codes, cities may regulate construction and unsafe buildings, and local boards of health administer housing sanitation and may adopt local health rules with county or city approval. The State Fire Marshal may order an owner to repair or demolish a hazardous building within 30 days, and the cost can become a lien. Check with your city or county; none of these codes or rules was read here.

title: Small Landlords
bodyText: West Virginia's landlord-tenant statutes do not change your duties based on how many units you own. Some rules turn on the building instead: common-area and garbage duties apply in buildings with more than one living unit, and the statutory smoke detector rule covers one- and two-family dwellings. Fair housing law applies to all dwellings, but the state discrimination rules largely do not reach renting rooms in a rooming house where you live with no more than four rooms rented. For familial status only, there are two exemptions: a single-family house rented by a private individual owner who owns no more than three such houses, without a broker or anyone in the business of renting and without discriminatory advertising; and units in a building for no more than four families where you live in one of them. title: Quiet Enjoyment
bodyText: No West Virginia statute reads a covenant of quiet enjoyment into every lease. If your lease contains one, the statute says it has the effect of a promise that a tenant who pays the rent and keeps the lease's covenants shall peaceably possess and enjoy the premises for the term without any interruption or disturbance from any person whatever; its legal scope is then decided by the rules of law and the parties' intent, which is case law that was not searched. Because those words are broad, think carefully before adding such a covenant. A tenant may enforce the lease's covenants against a later buyer of the property as against you. Whether a covenant of quiet enjoyment is implied without express words is a question of case law, which was not searched. Separately, a person turned out of possession by a forcible or unlawful entry may sue to recover possession within three years.

Va. Code § 36-4-14); scope by the plain intent of the parties: 'The legal scope and effect of the covenants mentioned in this article, and the person or persons by and against whom such covenants may be enforced, shall be determined according to the rules of law applicable to such cases, and the plain intent and meaning of the parties' (W. Va. Code § 36-4-17); so whether the covenant reaches, for example, wrongful acts of strangers is case law, not searched. Against a transferee: W. Va. Code § 37-6-2. Forcible or unlawful entry: W. Va. title: Retaliation
bodyText: West Virginia has no general statute barring a residential landlord from raising rent, cutting services or evicting because a tenant complained about conditions or reported code violations. The eviction statute mentions retaliatory eviction only on appeal: a tenant who wins an appeal after the lease term has ended gets money damages, not possession, unless the case involves title, retaliatory eviction or breach of warranty. Fair housing law makes it unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone for exercising fair housing rights or helping someone else do so. The magistrate court's answer form for these eviction cases lets the tenant check a defense that the action was filed in retaliation for complaints the tenant made about the premises. How courts treat that defense is a question of case law, which was not searched, so document an independent reason for any action you take soon after a tenant complains.

title: Code Enforcement and Receivership
bodyText: Cities and counties may adopt ordinances to make owners repair, close or demolish dwellings that are unsafe, unsanitary or unfit for human habitation, charge the costs to the owner, and record them as a lien on the property. A city's code enforcement officials must give the owner reasonable advance notice and ask permission before inspecting, except in exigent circumstances; if the owner cannot be found or refuses, they may get an administrative search warrant, a copy of which goes to the owner and any tenant in possession five days before entry. A city may let its municipal court place a structure in receivership where the owner cannot be found or refuses entry and the building is salvageable but needs prompt repair, and a city may charge a registration fee on uninhabitable property that violates its building code. No West Virginia statute gives tenants a specific right to have a receiver appointed or to pay rent into escrow for repairs of an occupied rental; the general equity receivership statute is not tenant-specific, and whether tenants could use it is case law that was not searched.

title: Billing Tenants for Shared Utilities
bodyText: West Virginia's deposit law says a landlord may use submetering equipment, energy allocation equipment or a ratio utility billing system if the rental agreement so provides, so put any such arrangement, and how charges are calculated, in the lease. No statute sets how a shared bill must be split, caps administrative fees, or requires a particular disclosure form. At the end of the tenancy you may apply the security deposit to utilities that were billed to and paid by you and that the lease makes the tenant's obligation. Whether a landlord who bills tenants for utilities is regulated by the Public Service Commission depends on commission rules and decisions, which were not read.

title: When the Utility Account Is the Landlord's
bodyText: No West Virginia statute gives tenants notice or a right to pay the utility and deduct it from rent when a utility account in your name is about to be shut off, and no statute requires a utility to notify the owner before disconnecting a tenant's own service. If the dwelling unit is supplied by direct public utility connections, though, you must supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 through the last day of April (unless generated by an installation in the tenant's exclusive control), so keep any account you hold current. If the lease makes the tenant responsible for utilities billed to and paid by you, you may apply the security deposit to the unpaid amount at the end of the tenancy. title: Belongings Left by a Tenant Who Abandons
bodyText: If a tenant who owes rent abandons the property, West Virginia law sets the steps. First post a written notice in a conspicuous place on the property requiring the tenant to pay the rent within one month; if it is not paid, you are entitled to possession and may enter, the tenant's right to the property ends, and you may recover the rent owed up to that time. To dispose of belongings left behind, give a second written notice, posted on the property and sent by first-class mail with a certificate of mailing, in an envelope marked "Please Forward", to the rental, to any post office box of the tenant you know of, and to any forwarding address you have. It must say the property is considered abandoned and that belongings must be removed from the property (or from where you stored them) by a stated date at least 30 days after mailing, or at least 60 days if the tenant has told you they are on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces, or the tenant forfeits them and they become yours. If belongings worth more than $300 are not removed by that date and the tenant or a secured creditor tells you they intend to remove them, you must store them for up to 30 more days, provided they pay your reasonable storage and removal costs. The statute covers only a tenant who abandons while owing rent; no statute sets a procedure for belongings left by a tenant who owed nothing, so following the same notice steps is the safe course. Belongings left after a court-ordered eviction follow separate rules.

title: Abandonment, Reletting and Mitigation
bodyText: When a tenant who owes rent abandons the property, the posted notice requiring payment within one month ends the tenancy if the rent is not paid, and the statute then lets you recover the rent owed up to the time you became entitled to possession. To keep the tenant liable for the rest of the lease, include in that same notice a further notice that, after taking possession, you will lease the property to someone else; the tenant then remains liable for the unexpired term for the difference between the rent you receive from the new tenant and the rent under the old lease, and on the lease's other terms. If you give that notice, the tenant can still recover possession by notifying you in writing that they intend to resume possession and paying, or tendering, all rent arrears and other amounts then owed under the lease, unless you have already leased the property to someone else under the notice. No West Virginia statute says whether a landlord must otherwise mitigate damages by trying to re-rent; that is a question of case law, so making and documenting reasonable efforts to re-rent is the safe course.

Va. Code § 37-6-8 (tenant's right to possession on payment of arrears and other accrued liabilities and written notice of intent to resume, except where another person holds under a lease made under the notice first; no other relief from a forfeiture under § 37-6-6). That the landlord without a reletting notice recovers only rent to the date of possession is Claude's reading of § 37-6-6(a) with the word 'however' in § 37-6-7. title: Attorney Fees
bodyText: No West Virginia statute lets a residential landlord recover attorney fees from a tenant, whether through a lease clause or in an eviction or rent case, and the lease in this library does not ask the tenant to pay them. West Virginia's consumer debt-collection law bars anyone collecting a consumer's obligation from collecting a fee or charge incidental to it unless both the agreement and a statute or regulation expressly authorize it, and from representing that the debt may be increased by attorney fees that cannot legally be added, with a penalty of $1,000 per violation, and the tenant may also be awarded attorney fees. This library reads that law as treating a charge added because of a default or for collection, such as attorney fees, as incidental and needing statutory authority, which no statute gives for a landlord's attorney fees; courts have not been checked on this, so a fee clause carries real risk. Statutes do give tenants attorney fees in some cases: when a landlord sues to enforce a lease term waiving security deposit rights, when a court allows them to a prevailing complainant in a fair housing suit, and in a suit for wrongful removal under the squatter-removal law.

The first `attorney-fees` battery pattern requires the possessive form and misses the plain spelling attorney fees used in W. Va. Code § 55-3C-5(b); the -r2 pattern covers both. Debt collection: 'Claim' covers an obligation 'arising out of a transaction in which the money, property, insurance or service which is the subject of the transaction is primarily for personal, family or household purposes' (W. Va. Code § 46A-2-122(b)); a 'Debt collector' is 'any person or organization engaging directly or indirectly in debt collection' (W. Va. Code § 46A-2-122(d)); prohibited: collecting 'any interest or other charge, fee or expense incidental to the principal obligation unless such interest or incidental fee, charge or expense is expressly authorized by the agreement creating or modifying the obligation and by statute or regulation' (W. Va. Code § 46A-2-128(d)), and representing that an obligation 'may be increased by the addition of attorney's fees' when such fees 'may not legally be added' (W. Va. Code § 46A-2-127(g)); remedy 'a penalty of $1,000 per violation' (W. Va. Code § 46A-5-101(1)); consumer's fees in an action under chapter 46A: the court 'may award reasonable attorney's fees and expenses to the consumer' (W. Va. Code § 46A-5-104(a)); a defendant may get fees only for a chapter 46A claim 'brought in bad faith and for the purposes of harassment' (W. Va. Code § 46A-5-104(b)), not a lease, eviction or rent case. Library-wide reading of § 46A-2-128(d) (Claude's reading, case law not searched): a charge that is itself the tenant's contractual obligation (rent, reimbursement of an actual cost the lease makes the tenant's, the price of an option the tenant chooses such as an early-termination fee) is part of the principal obligation; a charge added because of default or for collection (late fee, returned-check fee, collection costs, attorney fees, a holdover premium, interest beyond the statute) is incidental and needs statutory authority (late fee: 'reasonable charges for late payment of rent specified in the rental agreement', W. Va. Code § 37-6A-2(b)(1); returned check: 'a fee of up to $25 a worthless check', W. Va. Code § 61-3-39e). No statute authorizes a residential landlord's attorney fees, so they fall on the incidental side. That the debt-collection article reaches rent at all is part of the same reading (as in `default-by-tenant-wv`). Tenant fee statutes: W. Va. title: Grounds for Eviction and Cure Periods
bodyText: West Virginia's summary eviction procedure lets you petition to remove a tenant who is behind on rent, has breached a warranty or a covenant of the lease, or has deliberately or negligently damaged the property or knowingly let someone else do so. No statute requires a notice or a chance to cure before you file on any of these grounds, in any kind of tenancy. Two limits come from elsewhere: if the lease sets a time that must pass before you may re-enter, such as a cure period, a statute bars starting an ejectment or unlawful detainer case until that time has passed, so honor any cure or waiting period your lease gives before filing; and a tenant who has abandoned the property owing rent is handled by the one-month posted notice. A tenant who simply stays after the lease ends is not on the summary petition's list of grounds; see the holdover row. This library's lease gives written notice and a cure period for curable breaches other than nonpayment of rent.

title: No Required Notice Before Filing for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires a pay-or-quit notice, or any other notice, before you file to evict for unpaid rent; a summary eviction petition may be filed once the tenant is in arrears. The exceptions: if the tenant has abandoned the property, you use the posted notice requiring payment within one month; the federal CARES Act may require 30 days' notice to vacate for some properties (see that row); and you should honor any notice or waiting period your own lease promises. This library does not offer a clause waiving a nonpayment notice, because there is no statutory notice to waive.

title: How Evictions Work in West Virginia
bodyText: Most West Virginia evictions use the summary procedure for wrongful occupation of residential rental property. The owner or the owner's agent files a verified (sworn) petition in the magistrate court or circuit court of the county where the property is, describing the property and the unpaid rent, lease breach or damage relied on; magistrate court can hear it so long as title to the property is not in dispute. The court sets a hearing 5 to 10 judicial days after filing, and you must immediately have notice of the hearing served on the tenant, under the civil service rule (the court's summons form lists the sheriff, a private process server, or certified mail) or by certified mail, return receipt requested, and then file the petition and proof of service. The tenant may serve a written defense within five days of receiving the notice and may raise any defense available in an ejectment or unlawful detainer case, and either side may elect a jury by giving the court written notice within five days after service. If the tenant has filed nothing by the hearing, the court orders immediate possession; otherwise it hears the case. The court may also enter judgment for rent due, and its order sets the date and time to vacate, after which the sheriff removes the tenant. Either party may appeal a magistrate court judgment to circuit court within 20 days by posting a bond, unless excused as unable to pay. Holding over after the lease ends is not one of the listed grounds for the summary petition; unlawful detainer is the procedure written for it (see the holdover row), and the squatter-removal law cannot be used against a current or former tenant.

title: Delays and Stays of an Eviction
bodyText: No West Virginia statute lets a court postpone an eviction because of the tenant's hardship, the weather or the season. In a summary eviction, though, the court's order sets the time by which the tenant must vacate, taking into account whether the property is furnished or unfurnished, the possible relative harm to the parties and other relevant facts, and only after that time does the sheriff remove the tenant. Continuances are for cause only, and a tenant who gets one must pay into court the rent that comes due meanwhile. A party may appeal a magistrate court judgment to circuit court within 20 days, or ask the magistrate within 20 days to set it aside, and a timely appeal or motion stays enforcement; but the summary eviction statute says a tenant is not entitled to remain in possession during an appeal if the tenancy has otherwise expired. Expect delay when a tenant appeals, and get advice on how the two rules apply.

title: Tenants Who Stay After the Lease Ends
bodyText: A tenant whose lease is for a fixed term must leave when it ends; West Virginia requires no notice from either side to end a tenancy whose term is to end at a set time. A tenant who stays on after their right has expired, without your consent, is in unlawful detainer, and you recover possession through an unlawful detainer case in circuit court or magistrate court, filed within three years, in which you can also recover damages for the detention, including mesne profits (the value of the use) for up to three years and any damage or waste. The summary eviction petition lists unpaid rent, breach of a lease covenant and damage as its grounds; whether a holdover can be brought as a breach of the lease's promise to surrender possession is not settled by statute, and unlawful detainer is the procedure written for it. Do not treat a holdover tenant as a squatter: the squatter-removal law does not apply to a current or former lawful tenant, and a periodic tenant who holds over is not a squatter. Whether accepting rent after the term creates a new periodic tenancy is a question of case law; the lease's Holdover terms address it.

title: No Statutory Holdover Rent
bodyText: West Virginia has no statute setting double rent or any other multiple of rent for a tenant who holds over. In an unlawful detainer case you recover damages for the detention, including mesne profits (the value of the use), special damages and waste, and in an action for rent or for use and occupation interest is allowed as on other contracts. This library does not offer a premium holdover rate clause: no statute authorizes one, whether a stated multiple would be enforced or struck as a penalty is a question of case law, and this library reads West Virginia's consumer debt-collection law as treating a premium charged because the tenant stayed past the end of the lease as an added charge that needs statutory authority, which none gives. The lease's Holdover terms let you recover actual damages, including the reasonable rental value for the time the tenant stays. No statute expressly forbids a holdover premium, but under this library's reading of the debt-collection law, collecting one could expose you to a $1,000 penalty for each violation; get advice before adding one.

title: Paying the Rent to Stop an Eviction
bodyText: In an ejectment or unlawful detainer case to recover the property for unpaid rent, if the tenant, or anyone else with a claim to the property, pays or tenders to you or your attorney, or pays into court, all the rent and arrears with interest and costs at any time before trial, the case must stop. Even after a judgment for possession is carried out, the tenant has twelve months to pay the rent in arrear with interest and costs, or to sue in equity for relief from the forfeiture, before losing all right to be restored, and a mortgagee or trustee of the tenant's interest has the same right. Whether these rules also apply to the summary eviction procedure is not settled by statute, though a tenant there may raise any defense available in ejectment or unlawful detainer. If a tenant offers everything owed, with interest and costs, before the hearing, get legal advice before refusing it.

title: Rent Paid Into Court and Counterclaims
bodyText: In a summary eviction for unpaid rent, the tenant may defend by showing that you breached a material covenant on which the duty to pay rent depends, and the court then holds a hearing on it. West Virginia's statutory repair duties do not require you to make repairs while the tenant is behind on rent, but that excuse applies only if the lease does not promise more, because a greater repair duty in the lease controls; this library's maintenance clause promises repairs with no exception for unpaid rent, so under it you remain responsible for repairs even while rent is owed. If a tenant asks for and gets a continuance, the court must require the tenant to pay into court the rent that comes due during it, and the court may pay out money paid in. A tenant may also file a counterclaim, which is tried with your case if it arises from the same transaction, and a tenant who does not file one can still sue on it later. In an ejectment or unlawful detainer case, a tenant who seeks an injunction against the case through a suit in equity must, within 30 days after your answer, bring into court, or deposit in a bank in the state to the credit of the case, the rent you swear is due and the costs. An appeal to circuit court requires a bond unless the appellant is excused as unable to pay.

title: Lockouts and Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: West Virginia's landlord-tenant statutes do not expressly ban lockouts or utility shutoffs by a residential landlord (its rules for manufactured-home lot rentals do), but the lawful ways to recover possession are a court case or, for a tenant who abandons owing rent, the posted-notice procedure. A court order for possession is carried out by the sheriff, and goods can be seized for rent (distress) only by the sheriff or a deputy sheriff under a magistrate's warrant. A person forcibly or unlawfully turned out of possession may sue within three years to recover it, without having to prove title, and recover damages. For units on direct public utility connections you must supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 through the last day of April, unless the tenant controls the installation. Do not change the locks, remove doors or belongings, or cut off utilities to force a tenant out; what else such conduct may expose you to is a question of case law.

title: Tenant's Belongings After an Eviction Order
bodyText: After a court grants you possession in a summary eviction, if the tenant has not removed all personal property by the date and time the order sets, you may: dispose of it without liability if the tenant tells you in writing that it is abandoned or if it is garbage; remove and store it, and dispose of it without liability after 30 days if the tenant has not paid your reasonable storage and removal costs and taken it back, or if the storage costs equal its value; or leave it on the property and dispose of it after 30 days if the tenant has not paid your reasonable costs of leaving it there and taken it back. If property worth more than $300 was not removed within those 30 days with the costs paid, and the tenant or someone holding a security interest in it tells you they intend to remove it, you must store it for up to 30 more days, provided they pay your reasonable storage and removal costs. You may apply the security deposit to reasonable removal and storage costs. The statute requires no separate notice before these steps and has no rule for pets or other animals left behind, and it does not cover belongings left after an unlawful detainer judgment; giving the tenant written notice and a reasonable chance to collect belongings, and keeping records, is the safe course.

title: No Just-Cause Requirement
bodyText: West Virginia has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule for residential rentals. You may let a fixed-term lease end on its last day without giving notice or a reason, and end a periodic tenancy by giving the required notice, without stating a reason. Limits that apply in particular situations: fair housing law bars refusing, ending or changing a tenancy because of a protected characteristic, and coercing, intimidating, threatening or interfering with a person for exercising fair housing rights; the summary eviction statute lets an appeals court restore a tenant whose lease has expired to possession where retaliatory eviction is at issue, and the court's answer form lists retaliation as a defense, though no statute defines retaliation for these rentals; and manufactured-home lot rentals have their own good-cause rules. title: Criminal Activity and Eviction Speed
bodyText: West Virginia has no separate expedited eviction or no-notice termination for criminal or drug activity by a tenant. The ordinary summary procedure is already quick, with a hearing 5 to 10 judicial days after filing, and is available when a tenant breaches a lease covenant, so a lease term against criminal activity lets you act on it promptly. Know your exposure as an owner: real property used to commit or facilitate a drug offense punishable by more than a year in prison can be forfeited to the state, unless the owner shows the act or omission happened without the owner's knowledge or consent, so act promptly once you learn of drug activity. Nuisance laws that can close a property or require evictions are in the nuisance row.

title: Nuisance Laws and Rental Property
bodyText: West Virginia nuisance laws can reach a property owner whose rental is used for crime. A place where lewdness, assignation or prostitution is conducted or permitted is a nuisance: the owner, agent or lessee can be enjoined as maintaining it, and the court may close the place for a year; an owner may ask the court to release it by paying the costs and posting a bond for the property's full value to abate the nuisance, and the court may release it if satisfied of the owner's good faith, lack of knowledge of the use, and that reasonable care would not have revealed it. A place where alcoholic liquor is unlawfully made, sold or stored is a public nuisance that can be abated or closed. A building used by members of an organized criminal enterprise for qualifying offenses is a nuisance, and a court may order the owner or lessee to evict the persons using it and seal the premises. If law enforcement notifies you that a clandestine drug laboratory was found on your residential property, you must keep it unoccupied until the state certifies the remediation, or demolish it. Outside these proceedings, removing a tenant for criminal activity goes through the ordinary eviction process.

title: Guarantors of a Lease
bodyText: A guaranty of a tenant's lease must be in writing and signed by the guarantor (or the guarantor's agent) to be enforced. Once the tenant is in default, a guarantor may give you written notice to sue; if you do not, within a reasonable time, sue every party to the lease who lives in West Virginia and is not insolvent and pursue the case diligently to judgment and execution, you lose your claim against the guarantor. A judgment against the tenant does not bind a guarantor who was not made a party and served, so name the guarantor in your suit. No West Virginia statute says whether a guaranty covers a renewal or extension of the lease; that depends on the guaranty's own words, so say in it whether renewals are covered. The consumer-credit cosigner notice rules apply to leases of goods, not to dwelling rentals. A guaranty is lawful; this library has no guaranty clause, because a guaranty is the guarantor's own contract, and a landlord who wants one can add their own after taking advice.

title: Waiving Exemptions From Collection
bodyText: A lease cannot make a tenant give up West Virginia's exemptions from collection: any waiver of the personal property exemptions is void and unenforceable, and a waiver of the homestead exemption is void except where it comes with a consensual security interest in the homestead itself that cannot be satisfied without encroaching on the exemption. A resident may hold exempt from execution or other process up to $8,000 in household goods, furniture, toys, animals, appliances, books and clothing held for personal or family use, up to $5,000 in one motor vehicle, up to $3,000 in tools of a trade and up to $1,100 on deposit in a federally insured bank, with a $15,000 total for those items. Rent can be collected by distress only through the sheriff or a deputy sheriff under a magistrate's warrant, within a year after it is due, and the code treats exempt property as protected from distress as well as from levy: it refers to property a debtor has listed and set apart as exempt from distress and levy, so expect a tenant to be able to claim the exemptions against a distress. This library does not offer an exemption-waiver clause, because such a waiver is void.

title: Tenants' Statutory Rights to End a Lease Early
bodyText: West Virginia statutes give a residential tenant, or the tenant's estate, these rights to end a lease early: when a tenant dies, an heir, personal representative, devisee or assignee may end the lease by written notice (see the tenant-death row); if the buildings are destroyed or damaged by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence and you do not rebuild as soon as you reasonably can, the tenant may surrender possession after that reasonable time and owe no further rent; and if the whole property is taken by eminent domain, the tenant's liability for rent ends unless the lease expressly provides otherwise. Federal law adds servicemember rights, which West Virginia extends to Guard members on state active duty for 30 days or more. No West Virginia statute gives tenants an early-termination right for domestic violence, illness, disability or a move to a care facility. The lease's Early Termination terms keep these rights.

title: Illness, Disability or Care-Facility Moves
bodyText: No West Virginia statute lets a tenant end a lease early because of illness, disability, age or a move to a nursing home or assisted living. title: Servicemember Tenants
bodyText: West Virginia has no separate state statute letting servicemembers end a residential lease; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, not reviewed here, governs that. title: Notice to End a Tenancy
bodyText: To end a year-to-year tenancy, either side must give the other written notice at least three months before the end of a year of the tenancy. A periodic tenancy with a period shorter than a year, such as month-to-month or week-to-week, may be ended by the same notice or by notice of at least one full rental period before the end of a rental period: for month-to-month, at least a full rental month before the last day of a rental month; for week-to-week, at least a full week before the end of a rental week. No notice is needed from either side to end a lease whose term ends on a set date. Notice to the tenant may be served on the tenant or on anyone holding the property under the tenant; notice from the tenant may be served on any owner or the owner's agent. These rules do not apply where the lease, by special agreement, fixes a different notice period or provides that no notice is to be given, so check your lease. This library offers an optional clause, as that special agreement, letting either party end a periodic tenancy on a stated number of days' written notice before the end of a rental period; it does not offer a no-notice term, because that would let either side end the tenancy without warning. Give every notice in writing and keep proof of delivery.

title: Tenancies at Will
bodyText: No West Virginia statute defines a tenancy at will or says how much notice ends one. The notice statute covers year-to-year tenancies (written notice at least three months before the end of a year) and periodic tenancies shorter than a year (that notice, or notice of one full rental period before the end of a period), and requires no notice for a term that ends on a set date. Whether an arrangement with no set term or rent period is a tenancy at will, and what notice ends it, is a question of case law; if rent is paid by the week or month, treat it as a periodic tenancy and give at least one full period's written notice.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: When a tenant under a residential lease dies, an heir, personal representative, devisee or assignee of the tenant may end the lease before it expires by notice to you, hand-delivered or mailed postage prepaid. The termination takes effect on the last day of the calendar month that is two months after the notice is hand-delivered or postmarked: for example, notice mailed March 10 ends the lease on May 31. The tenant's estate still owes rent and other sums due before and during that two-month notice period, and the cost of restoring the property to its condition at the start of the tenancy, less ordinary wear and tear. No one can waive this right by contract or otherwise, and a lease term requiring longer notice is void. The statute applies to residential leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2012; it does not say how it reaches a month-to-month tenancy that began earlier, so honor it for every tenancy. Otherwise rent may be recovered from the tenant's heirs or personal representative as with other debts. No statute sets a procedure for a deceased tenant's belongings; work with the personal representative or heirs and keep records.

title: Minors in Eviction Cases
bodyText: No West Virginia statute bars naming a minor (a person under 18) as a defendant in an eviction or unlawful detainer case. A magistrate may not enter a default judgment against a minor unless the minor is represented in the case by a guardian ad litem, guardian or similar fiduciary, so name the adults who signed the lease or hold the tenancy, and name a minor only if the minor is a party to it. Whether a minor's own lease can be enforced against the minor is a question of case law; a promise made after turning 18 to pay a debt incurred as a minor can be enforced only if it is in writing and signed.

title: Fixing a Tenant's Breach Yourself
bodyText: No West Virginia statute gives a residential landlord the right to enter, fix a tenant's breach such as damage or uncleanliness, and bill the tenant for it. Your remedies are the lease's own terms, deductions from the security deposit after the tenancy ends for damage beyond reasonable wear and tear and other charges the lease provides for, a suit for damages, and the summary eviction procedure for deliberate or negligent damage. You are not required to make repairs made necessary primarily by a lack of reasonable care by the tenant, a member of the tenant's family or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent.

title: Utility Shutoffs at a Rental
bodyText: No West Virginia statute sets notice or protections aimed at tenants before a utility disconnects service at a rental, for example when a landlord who pays the bill falls behind; the Public Service Commission's rules, not reviewed here, govern disconnection by regulated utilities. A municipal water utility, a public service district or a city sewer board may, under those rules, shut off water to a delinquent user ten days after the bill becomes delinquent, which happens when it is unpaid 20 days after it is due. Water may be shut off for an unpaid stormwater fee only after at least 10 days' written notice to the user and two attempts at personal contact in the 24 hours before; those protections belong to whoever is the user, who may be a tenant. For units on direct public utility connections you must supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 through the last day of April, unless the tenant controls the installation, so keep paid any service you are responsible for.

title: Former Drug Laboratories
bodyText: If a law-enforcement agency notifies you that chemicals, equipment, supplies or precursors indicating a clandestine drug laboratory were found on your residential property, you are responsible for meeting the Department of Health's remediation standards (or you may demolish the building instead), and you must keep the property unoccupied from that notice until the Department certifies that the remediation meets its decontamination levels. The statute also directs the Department to set, by legislative rule, requirements for owners, sellers and landlords to disclose any former clandestine laboratory site or activity to any potential occupant. Those rules are not covered here: before renting a property with that history, check the current rule and give the disclosure in writing before the tenant signs. Once remediation is certified, an owner who neither knew nor should have known of the illegal use is immune from suits by later renters based on that prior use, and the same immunity applies to such an owner who completes certified remediation voluntarily before any notice. A person convicted of possessing precursors to make methamphetamine whose actions made remediation necessary is liable for its costs, including reasonable attorney's fees and court costs to collect them.

title: West Virginia Lead Abatement Rules
bodyText: West Virginia adds no lead paint disclosure of its own to the federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing. It does regulate lead abatement: only an individual holding the appropriate state lead license may carry out a lead risk assessment, inspection or abatement, and the owner of a residence where a lead abatement project is to occur must notify the state before the project starts. The homeowner exemption covers only a single-unit home occupied by the owner, not a dwelling occupied by tenants. Renovation, remodeling and repair work not intended to permanently eliminate lead hazards, and temporary interim controls, are not abatement under this law, though federal renovation rules (not covered here) may still apply. The state may order reduction or abatement of identified lead hazards when they may result in child lead poisoning.

title: Tenants After a Trustee's Sale
bodyText: When residential rental property is sold at a trustee's sale under a deed of trust, the purchaser may end the tenancy of a tenant holding an unexpired written lease that was never recorded, or was recorded after that deed of trust, by written notice: 90 days' notice, or notice given at least 30 days before the lease ends, whichever is shorter. A month-to-month or other tenancy may be ended by 30 days' written notice. These periods apply in place of the usual notice-to-quit rules. The notice must identify the property, the date of the trustee's sale, the book and page where the trustee's deed is recorded, the date the tenancy will end, and the purchaser with contact information; it is served by regular mail plus personal delivery, posting on the front door, or certified mail. The lease stays enforceable during the notice period, and if the tenant breaches it the new owner may use the summary eviction procedure. The statute does not address a lease recorded before the deed of trust. Factory-built home sites follow their own rules, and federal law may also protect tenants after foreclosure.

title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText: If you convert a residential rental building into a condominium, cooperative or other common interest community under West Virginia's Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act, you (as declarant) and any dealer offering the units must give each residential tenant and subtenant in possession notice of the conversion, setting out their rights, together with the public offering statement, at least 120 days before they must vacate, by hand delivery to the unit or prepaid mail. No tenant may be required to vacate on less than 120 days' notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste or conduct that disturbs other tenants, and the terms of the tenancy may not be changed during that period. For 60 days after the notice you must offer to sell each residential unit to the tenant who leases it; if the tenant does not buy, for the next 180 days you may not offer the unit on more favorable price or terms. Failing to give notice is a defense to an action for possession, and a lease may not be terminated in violation of its terms. These rights cannot be waived. These rules do not apply to a planned community or cooperative with 12 or fewer units and no development rights, or to a planned community whose declaration limits the average annual assessment on its residential units to $300 (adjusted for inflation), unless its declaration adopts the whole Act; and the purchase offer does not apply to a unit that will be nonresidential or whose boundaries will not substantially match the apartment.

title: West Virginia Fair Housing Act
bodyText: The West Virginia Fair Housing Act bars refusing to rent or negotiate, setting different terms or services, falsely saying a unit is unavailable, or making, printing or publishing any notice, statement or advertisement that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination, because of race, color, religion, ancestry, sex, familial status, blindness, disability or national origin. Its small-landlord exemptions are narrow: renting rooms in a rooming house you live in with no more than four rooms for rent; and, for familial status only, renting a single-family house if you own no more than three and use no broker or discriminatory advertising, or renting units in a building of up to four households where you live in one. Housing for older persons is exempt from the familial-status rule, religious organizations and private clubs have limited exemptions, reasonable occupancy limits set by law still apply, and you may refuse a person convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. Even where an exemption applies, don't advertise a preference. You may not threaten, coerce or retaliate against anyone for exercising these rights. A tenant may complain to the Human Rights Commission within one year or sue within two years; remedies include actual and punitive damages, attorney's fees and civil penalties. Federal fair housing law also applies.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: Under the West Virginia Fair Housing Act you must make reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices and services when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a home, and you must permit reasonable modifications of the premises, at the tenant's expense, that may be necessary for full enjoyment of the premises. Where reasonable, you may condition permission for a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior at move-out, reasonable wear and tear excepted. For an assistance animal you may ask for documentation from a professional treatment provider of the disability-related need, but not for medical records or detailed information about the impairment; you may not unreasonably deny it, condition it on a fee, a deposit or the terms you apply to pets, or unreasonably delay your response, and you may deny it if there is credible evidence, based on an individualized assessment of the specific animal's actual conduct, that it poses a direct threat to others' health or safety, or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property, that no other reasonable accommodation can eliminate or reduce. You need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property, but you bear the burden of proving it. Buildings of four or more units first occupied after the Act's design deadline must meet accessible design rules (every unit if the building has an elevator, otherwise the ground-floor units).

title: Applications, Questions and Ads
bodyText: West Virginia makes it unlawful to make, print or publish any notice, statement or advertisement about renting a dwelling that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, blindness, disability, familial status, ancestry or national origin, or an intention to make one. Unlike its employment law, West Virginia's housing law has no separate rule on application forms or questions, but an application or screening question about one of those traits can itself be such a statement, so leave them out. For an assistance animal request you may ask for documentation of the disability-related need, but not for medical records or detailed information about the impairment.

title: Housing Vouchers and Source of Income
bodyText: West Virginia's fair housing law does not make source of income a protected class, and no West Virginia statute requires a landlord to accept housing vouchers or other rent assistance. A provision of the municipal home rule law lets a municipality regulate activities that arise from rental use only if the regulation applies uniformly to all properties, rented or not; whether that bars a local source-of-income protection is unsettled (court decisions were not checked), so check local ordinances. A landlord who accepts a voucher must follow the program's rules and lease addendum.

title: Fee Disclosure and All-In Pricing
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires all-in rent pricing in advertisements, a first-page list of fees, or a separate fee disclosure for residential rentals. The written lease must still be clear and coherent, in everyday words and easily readable type, and organized and captioned, so list every fee and charge in the lease. A pet fee or application fee is outside the security deposit rules only if the tenant expressly agrees in writing that it is nonrefundable. A fee that is itself part of what the tenant agrees to pay (rent, reimbursement of a cost the lease makes the tenant's, or the price of an option the tenant chooses) is part of the tenant's obligation; a charge added because of a default or for collection, such as a late fee, returned-check fee, collection cost or attorney fee, needs a statute that authorizes it if West Virginia's consumer debt-collection law applies to rent, which has not been checked against court decisions.

title: Rent Statement for Senior Tax Relief
bodyText: West Virginia gives property tax relief to residents aged 65 or older, including renters, whose gross household income in the prior year was not more than $5,000, counting 12 percent of the rent they pay as rent constituting property taxes. If a tenant claiming that relief asks, you must sign a statement of the gross rent the tenant paid for the calendar year (rent for occupancy only, excluding charges for utilities, services, furniture or appliances you provide). Willfully giving a false statement, or willfully failing to give one in time for the tenant to file a timely claim, is a misdemeanor with a fine of up to $50 for each violation. Claims are filed with the State Tax Commissioner between July 1 and September 30 for the prior year. No West Virginia statute otherwise requires you to tell tenants how much of their rent goes to property taxes.

title: Required Disclosures in West Virginia
bodyText: West Virginia requires few disclosures to residential tenants. Federal lead-based paint disclosure applies to pre-1978 housing, and the Department of Health's rules govern disclosure of a former clandestine drug laboratory. The written lease must be clear and coherent, in everyday words, in easily readable type with contrasting ink, and organized and captioned by section; a violation does not void the lease, but a tenant may demand a conforming lease and sue to reform it, and cannot waive that right. Submetering or utility allocation must be provided for in the rental agreement, and a pet or application fee is nonrefundable only if agreed in writing. A real estate licensee must disclose in writing, on the Real Estate Commission's form, whom the licensee represents. A declarant converting a building must give tenants a conversion notice, and on request you must sign a rent statement for a senior tax relief claimant. No statute requires an owner-identity notice, a move-in checklist or a tenant-rights summary, but a managing agent who does not disclose the owner's name is treated as the landlord under the deposit law.

title: Which West Virginia Laws Apply
bodyText: West Virginia has no uniform residential landlord-tenant act; its rules are spread across several statutes. The general landlord-tenant article (chapter 37, article 6) covers leases of all kinds, but its habitability duties apply only to residential property. The security deposit law applies to all residential rental premises or units used as dwellings, including rooms rented to roomers and manufactured homes. Summary eviction for wrongful occupation is available for residential rental property, and older ejectment and unlawful detainer actions remain. Squatters are not governed by the landlord-tenant article. Rentals of lots in factory-built (manufactured) home rental communities follow their own articles, and residential care communities and nursing homes have their own licensing laws; both are outside this library. West Virginia's landlord-tenant and deposit articles contain no exclusion for farm housing or housing provided by an employer, and the deposit law applies to all residential rental premises or units used for dwelling purposes; whether an employee's occupancy tied to a job is a tenancy at all is a question for the courts.

title: Lease Terms West Virginia Voids
bodyText: West Virginia has no single list of forbidden lease terms; the rules are spread across several statutes. These terms in a residential lease are void or unenforceable: a term in which the tenant gives up rights under the security deposit law (if you sue to enforce one, the tenant can recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees); a term waiving the right of a deceased tenant's heir, personal representative, devisee or assignee to end the lease early, or requiring longer notice than the statute allows (leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2012; follow it for every lease); a waiver of the tenant's personal property exemptions from execution or other process; and a waiver of the tenant's right to ask for a lease rewritten in plain language. A term may not discriminate because of race, color, religion, ancestry, sex, familial status, blindness, disability or national origin. In a lease signed electronically, a party's right to refuse to do later transactions electronically cannot be waived. The habitability statute has no anti-waiver sentence, and no statute addresses a jury waiver, liability waiver or confession of judgment in an ordinary residential lease (the confession and unconscionability statutes are written for consumer credit sales, which can include a lease with an option to buy where rent is applied to the price, leases of goods and loans); whether courts enforce such terms is case law not checked here, and this library offers none of them. Under this library's reading of the Consumer Credit and Protection Act (not settled; court decisions were not checked), a charge added because of a default or for collection, such as a late fee, returned-check fee, collection costs, attorney's fees, a holdover premium or interest beyond what the statute allows, may be collected only if both the lease and a statute authorize it (statutes authorize a reasonable late charge specified in the lease and a fee of up to $25 for a check, draft or order dishonored for insufficient funds or credit), while charges that are part of what the tenant agreed to pay, such as rent, an actual cost the lease makes the tenant's, or an early-termination fee for an option the tenant chooses, are not affected. Collecting a charge the law does not allow may be a prohibited debt collection practice, which can cost the tenant's actual damages plus a $1,000 penalty per violation (adjustable for inflation).

title: Penalties for Unlawful Lease Terms
bodyText: West Virginia has no general penalty just for including an unenforceable term in a residential lease. If you bring an action to enforce a term in which the tenant waives security deposit rights, the tenant can recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. The Consumer Credit and Protection Act's debt collection rules may reach unpaid rent (the statutes do not say, and court decisions were not checked); if they do, trying to collect an incidental charge not authorized both by the lease and by a statute or regulation, or saying the debt can be increased by fees that cannot lawfully be added, can cost $1,000 per violation (adjustable for inflation) plus the tenant's actual damages, and a court can award the tenant attorney's fees. You avoid the penalty if, before being sued or notified of the error, you notify the tenant and correct it within 15 days after discovering it (60 days if it affects more than two people); for a lease term, giving the tenant a corrected copy is enough. A tenant who is refused a plain-language rewrite can sue to have the lease reformed, but the lease is not void. Under this library's reading of the Consumer Credit and Protection Act (not settled; court decisions were not checked), a charge added because of a default or for collection, such as a late fee, returned-check fee, collection costs, attorney's fees, a holdover premium or interest beyond what the statute allows, may be collected only if both the lease and a statute authorize it (statutes authorize a reasonable late charge specified in the lease and a fee of up to $25 for a check, draft or order dishonored for insufficient funds or credit), while charges that are part of what the tenant agreed to pay, such as rent, an actual cost the lease makes the tenant's, or an early-termination fee for an option the tenant chooses, are not affected.

title: Confession of Judgment
bodyText: A confession-of-judgment clause (the tenant authorizes judgment to be entered against the tenant without a contested case) is void in West Virginia consumer credit sales, consumer leases of goods, consumer loans and rent-to-own transactions. A consumer credit sale can include a lease with an option to buy the home where all or a substantial part of the rent is applied to the price. No statute addresses a confession clause in an ordinary residential lease. Once a magistrate court case is pending, a tenant may offer to confess judgment, and the magistrate takes it in writing and enters judgment for the amount confessed plus costs. Whether a confession clause written into a residential lease is enforceable is a question for case law, not checked here; this library includes no such clause.

title: Jury Trials and Jury Waivers
bodyText: West Virginia's Constitution preserves the right to a jury, if either party requires it, in suits at common law where more than $20 is in controversy. In a magistrate court eviction (wrongful occupation) case either side may elect a jury because the case involves possession of real estate, but under the magistrate court rules the election must be made in writing within 5 days after the summons and petition are served, or it is waived. No statute addresses a jury waiver written into a residential lease (the only statutory rule covers nursing home agreements); whether one is enforceable is a question for case law, not checked here. This library does not offer a jury waiver.

title: Liability Waivers
bodyText: No West Virginia statute voids, or expressly permits, a residential lease term that excuses the landlord from liability or makes the tenant indemnify the landlord. The habitability statute puts duties on every residential landlord and says nothing about waiving them, and the state Constitution guarantees every person a remedy by due course of law for an injury to person, property or reputation; how courts treat liability waivers in leases is case law not checked here. For that reason this library's West Virginia parking, storage, renter's insurance and services clauses are the versions without "Landlord is not liable" sentences.
