Laws ch. 186, § 15B(2)(b) (receipt 'at the time of receiving such security deposit'); § 15B(3)(a) ('within thirty days after such deposit is received'); § 15B(2)(c) ('upon receipt of such security deposit, or within ten days after commencement of the tenancy, whichever is later'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits or Fees
bodyText: In Massachusetts a security deposit remains the tenant's property and may be kept only for the deductions the deposit law lists, so no part of it can be made nonrefundable. Nonrefundable move-in, pet, cleaning, administrative or similar fees are also off limits at or before the start of a tenancy, because they are not on the closed list of permitted up-front payments. The only nonrefundable charge the statute contemplates is a future fee in lieu of a deposit, and only once regulations authorize it.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(e) ('A security deposit shall continue to be the property of the tenant making such deposit'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4) ('No deduction may be made from the security deposit for any purpose other than those set forth in this section'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b) (closed list of up-front payments); fee in lieu: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)(iii) ('entirely or partially non-refundable'; no regulation found, see edu-fee-in-lieu-of-deposit-ma). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposit Bank Account
bodyText: Hold every security deposit in a separate, interest-bearing account in a bank located in Massachusetts, set up so it is beyond the reach of your creditors and can transfer to a later owner. Never mix it with your own money. Within thirty days after receiving it, give the tenant a receipt naming the bank and its location, the amount and the account number. If you do not, the tenant is entitled to immediate return of the deposit. Failing to deposit it properly also forfeits your right to keep any of it and exposes you to triple damages.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(3)(a) ('held in a separate, interest-bearing account in a bank, located within the commonwealth'; 'Failure to comply with this paragraph shall entitle the tenant to immediate return of the security deposit'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(e) ('shall not be commingled with the assets of the lessor'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(6)(a), (7) ('three times the amount of such security deposit or balance thereof'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(4)(d). No small-owner or unit-count exemption; vacation rentals of 100 days or less excluded (§ 15B(9)). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposit Receipt and Records
bodyText: When you take a security deposit, give the tenant a signed receipt at that time showing the amount, who received it (and for an agent, the landlord's name), the date and a description of the unit. Keep a record for each unit of damage charged, when the tenancy ended, and any repairs with dates, costs and receipts, plus copies of receipts and condition statements, for two years after the tenancy ends. If you wrongfully fail to show these records to a tenant on request, the tenant is entitled to immediate return of the deposit.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(2)(b) ('Said receipt shall be signed by the person receiving the security deposit'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(2)(d) ('for a period of two years from the date of termination of the tenancy'; 'said tenant or prospective tenant shall be entitled to the immediate return of any amount paid in the form of a security deposit'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(4)(b). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposit Interest
bodyText: If you hold a security deposit for one year or longer from the start of the tenancy, you owe interest from the first day at five per cent a year, or the lesser rate the bank paid. At the end of each year, give the tenant a statement with the bank's name and address, the deposit amount, the account number and the interest due, and either pay the interest or tell the tenant to deduct it from the next rent. If neither arrives within thirty days, the tenant may deduct it. If the tenancy ends before an anniversary, pay accrued interest within thirty days.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(3)(b) ('for a period of one year or longer from the commencement of the term of the tenancy'; 'pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year, or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank'; 'the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(4)(c). The rate is fixed by statute and the actual bank rate, not by reference to any federal body. Interest on last month's rent: see edu-last-month-rent-interest-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A tenant cannot waive any part of the Massachusetts deposit law, and any lease term that conflicts with it is void. The cost of a bad clause is high. If you use a conflicting provision in a signed lease and try to enforce it, or try to get the tenant to waive a deposit right, you forfeit your right to keep any part of the deposit and to counterclaim for damage in the tenant's suit to recover it. Review any custom deposit language carefully.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(8) ('Any provision of a lease which conflicts with any provision of this section and any waiver by a tenant or prospective tenant of any provision of this section shall be deemed to be against public policy and therefore void and unenforceable'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(6)(c) ('attempts to obtain from the tenant or prospective tenant a waiver of any provision of this section'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(6) ('to counterclaim for any damage to the premises'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposits When You Sell
bodyText: When you transfer your interest in a rented unit, by sale or otherwise, transfer each security deposit with its accrued interest to the new owner, and credit any last month's rent with its interest. Granting a mortgage is not a transfer. You stay liable under the deposit law until the deposit has been transferred and the tenant has been told in writing of the new owner's name, business address and business telephone number, the new owner complies, or the deposit is returned to the tenant.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(5) ('the lessor shall transfer such security deposit together with any interest which has accrued thereon'; 'the granting of a mortgage on such premises shall not be a transfer of interest'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(7A) (last month's rent credited to the successor); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(4)(i). Failure to transfer: forfeiture and treble damages under § 15B(6)(d), (7). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposits When You Buy
bodyText: If you acquire a rented unit, you become liable for the tenant's security deposit and last month's rent from the transfer, even if the seller never hands the money over. Within forty-five days, notify the tenant in writing that you hold the deposit, giving the prior landlord's and your own name, business address and business telephone number, and any agent's. If the seller kept the deposit and the tenant still lives there, you may instead give free occupancy for the period the deposit would cover as rent. Cities taking tax title and certain foreclosing banks are exempt.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(5) ('within forty-five days from the date of said transfer, notify the tenant who made such security deposit that such security deposit was transferred to him'; 'assume liability for payment of the security deposit to the tenant'; 'granting the tenant free use and occupancy of the dwelling unit'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(7A) (same for last month's rent); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(4)(j) ('regardless of whether the security deposit was, in fact, transferred to him by the transferor'). Exemption covers a city or town acquiring under ch. 60 and a foreclosing mortgagee or mortgagee in possession that is a state or federally chartered financial institution. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposit Violation Penalties
bodyText: You lose the right to keep any of the deposit, and to counterclaim for damage in the tenant's suit to recover it, if you fail to bank it properly, miss the thirty-day itemized damage list, use and try to enforce a conflicting lease term, fail to handle a transfer on sale, or fail to return what is owed within thirty days. For the banking, transfer and late-return failures, the tenant also gets three times the deposit or balance owed, plus five per cent interest, court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(6) ('The lessor shall forfeit his right to retain any portion of the security deposit for any reason'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(7) ('If the lessor or his agent fails to comply with clauses (a), (d), or (e) of subsection 6'; 'three times the amount of such security deposit or balance thereof to which the tenant is entitled plus interest at the rate of five per cent'). Treble damages run from the deposit or balance owed. Separate immediate-return triggers: § 15B(3)(a) bank receipt and § 15B(2)(d) records. 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.00 does not limit § 15B(6)-(7) remedies (940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(4)). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposit Return Deadline
bodyText: Return the deposit, or its balance with interest, within thirty days. For a tenancy at will, the clock starts when occupancy ends. For a written lease, it starts at the end of the tenancy specified in the lease. If you deduct for damage, within the same thirty days give an itemized list sworn under the pains and penalties of perjury, describing the damage and repairs in precise detail, with estimates, bills, invoices or receipts. You may not deduct for damage listed in the condition statement unless you repaired it and can prove the new damage is unrelated.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4) ('within thirty days after the termination of occupancy under a tenancy-at-will or the end of the tenancy as specified in a valid written lease agreement'; 'itemizing in precise detail the nature of the damage and of the repairs necessary'; 'unless the lessor subsequently repaired or caused to be repaired said damage'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(4)(f)-(g). No tenant-demand trigger, no lease-set deadline, no pending-claim extension and no electronic-refund rule found in § 15B; a lessor may still recover from a tenant who wilfully or maliciously damages property beyond the deposit (§ 15B(4)). See planned clause security-deposit-return-ma and edu-unclaimed-deposit-refund-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule requiring you to post or disclose the standards you use to set deposit amounts. Every deposit is capped at the first month's rent, and the lease must state the amount of the deposit and the tenant's deposit rights in simple language. Fair housing law still governs how you set deposits for different applicants.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery A security-deposit-standards: posted standards for calculating deposits: 0 hits; positives passed (synthetic). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)(iii) ('a security deposit equal to the first month's rent'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(3)(b)3 ('The amount of the security deposit, if any'). Fair housing (ch. 151B) not researched here. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Separate Utility Deposit
bodyText: Do not collect a separate utility deposit from a tenant. At or before the start of a tenancy you may require only first month's rent, last month's rent, one security deposit up to the first month's rent, and a key and lock cost. After the tenancy starts, you may not demand a security deposit above the amount the law allows. Unpaid water charges billed under a lawful submetering arrangement may be deducted from the security deposit itself.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b) (closed list of up-front payments); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(d) ('or a security deposit in excess of the amount allowed by this section'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4) ('any unpaid rent or water charges which have not been validly withheld or deducted'). Deposits required by utility companies themselves are outside this rule and were not researched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Disability Modifications
bodyText: You may require consent for alterations, but you may not refuse a reasonable modification a tenant with a disability needs to fully enjoy the unit. Usually the tenant pays. In publicly assisted housing, or in multiple dwelling or contiguous housing of ten or more units, the owner pays, unless the cost would impose an undue hardship, and not for ramping an entrance of more than five steps or a wheelchair lift, or for making more than 10% of units fully wheelchair accessible. If a tenant-paid change will materially alter marketability, you may condition consent on the tenant restoring the interior or paying for restoration, reasonable wear and tear excepted. The state rule does not cover renting one unit of a two-family home whose other unit you live in, unless the home is publicly assisted housing (for example, built after 1950 with state or local funding for its purchase, construction or repair); federal law may also apply.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(7A)(1) ('reasonable modification shall be at the expense of the owner or other person having the right of ownership'; applies to 'multiple dwelling housing consisting of ten or more units, or contiguously located housing consisting of ten or more units'; 'shall not be required to pay for ramping a front entrance of more than five steps or for installing a wheelchair lift'; 'condition permission for a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore'). This goes beyond the federal Fair Housing Act cost rule. Other statutory tenant installation rights: MA battery A alterations: statutory tenant right to alter/install: 4 hits (ch. 111, § 127L repairs; lead and program rules); none general. Shared no-alterations clause is consistent (it preserves modifications law allows). Undue hardship and cap: § 4(7A) ('is not considered to be reasonable if it would impose an undue hardship'; 'Ten percent shall be the maximum number of units'). Two-family carve-out: § 4(7) ('this subsection shall not apply to the leasing of a single apartment or flat in a two family dwelling'); § 4(7A) applies 'For purposes of subsections 6 and 7' and § 4(6) (publicly assisted housing, § 1(10)) has no such carve-out. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Pest Treatment Cooperation
bodyText: Under the State Sanitary Code, a tenant must give you access, on reasonable notice and by appointment if possible, for work needed to comply with the code, including any cooperation required for pest elimination. Give at least 48 hours' notice except for emergency repairs. Before a commercial indoor pesticide application, the applicator must give occupants of all units at least 48 hours' written notice. You and the tenants must then provide access and follow the applicator's preparation instructions.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.003(E) ('any cooperation required for repairs, alterations, pest elimination, and service of utilities'; 'An owner shall provide at least 48 hours notice to the occupant, except for emergency repairs for which no notice is required'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.550(D)(1), (3) ('Adhere to all instructions provided by the pesticide applicator in preparing the common areas and units'). Bed bugs are a listed pest (105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.010). No bed-bug-specific statute searched beyond the code. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Who Pays for Pest Control
bodyText: In a building with two or more units, including a rooming house, you must keep it free from infestation and are responsible for pest elimination. In a single-unit home, the tenant must keep it pest-free and handle elimination, unless you failed to maintain the structure or other elements that keep pests out. Every tenant must keep the unit sanitary so it does not attract pests. You must also inspect each unit for pests before a new occupancy and keep records the board of health can request.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.550(A)-(B) ('The owner of a residence containing two or more dwelling units, including a homeless shelter or a rooming house, shall maintain it and its premises free from infestation'; 'The occupant shall maintain the unit free from all pest infestation'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.550(E)-(G) ('shall conduct an inspection of each unit prior to a new occupancy to identify the presence of pests'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule requiring a tenant to notify you before leaving the unit vacant in cold weather. If you want that notice, for example to protect pipes from freezing, put it in the lease as a tenant obligation, such as an extended-absence notice. Any such clause cannot shorten or waive the tenant's statutory notice and cure rights.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery A cold-weather-vacate-notice 2: notice before vacating in cold season: 2 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are recreational vehicle and public housing eligibility rules). Notice-waiver bar: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15A ('the effect of which is to waive the notices required under section eleven or twelve, shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'). See shared clause extended-absence-notice-ks. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Liens From Tenant Improvements
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute that lets a lease keep your ownership interest free of construction liens for work a tenant orders. A contractor's lien attaches to the interest of the party who contracted for the work or on whose behalf it was done. A lien for unpaid labor reaches the interest of the party who authorized or consented to the work. If your lease consents to tenant alterations, that consent may expose your interest. How far it does is unsettled. Require tenants to get your written approval for each contractor and to pay contractors in full.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 254, § 1 ('upon such interest in such real property, land, building, structure, or improvement owned by the party authorizing or consenting to said work') (labor lien). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 254, § 2 ('owned by the party with whom or on behalf of whom the contract was entered into') (contract lien). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 254, § 25 (lessee's estate: 'the lien shall bind such person's whole estate and interest in the property'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 254, § 32 bars contract terms barring lien filing ('is against public policy and is void and unenforceable'). No lease-shield provision like KRS 376.010(3): MA battery MA-B construction-lien lease shields lessor interest: 11 hits (none on point: 6C 46A, 23G 3, 23J 3, 40D 20, 40J 4A, 60 86, 106 2A-309, 175 63, 183A 6, 183A 10, 185 84); synthetic positive passed; control 0. Whether a landlord's lease consent to alterations makes the landlord a consenting owner under § 1 turns on case law. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Disclose Known Code Violations
bodyText: Before a tenancy starts, tell the prospective tenant about any condition in the unit that violates the law if you know of it or could find it by a reasonable inspection. Do not say the unit meets all legal requirements when it does not. Renting a unit that is unfit for human habitation, or that has a violation that may endanger or materially impair the occupant's health, safety or well-being, is itself an unfair or deceptive practice. A tenant's signed acknowledgment of good condition does not cure any of these.
notes: MA: 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(c) ('Fail to disclose to a prospective tenant the existence of any condition amounting to a violation of law within the dwelling unit'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(d) ('Represent to a prospective tenant that a dwelling unit meets all requirements of law when, in fact, it contains violations of law'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(a) ('is unfit for human habitation'). Last sentence: the regulation's duties do not depend on any tenant acknowledgment; that a signed acknowledgment is no defense is an inference (case law not searched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Absence Notice Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations do not require a tenant to tell you before an extended absence, and they set no penalty for not doing so. You may still ask for that notice as a lease term. It helps you tell an absence from an abandonment. That matters because one of the few times you may enter without the tenant's agreement is when the premises appear to have been abandoned by the tenant.
notes: MA: MA battery MA-B tenant notice of extended absence: 3 hits (151B 4 employee sabbath absence; 186 11A commercial lease notice; 205 Mass. Code Regs. 4.000 horse racing), none on point; synthetic positive passed; control 0. Searched General Laws, Constitution, CMR and court rules. Entry: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(a) ('if the premises appear to have been abandoned by the lessee'). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Family Child Care in Rentals
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes do not require you to let a tenant run a family child care home in a rental, and do not set lease conditions such as insurance or liability waivers for one. A separate zoning law makes family child care homes an allowable use that a city or town may not prohibit or regulate in its zoning. That limits local zoning only. It does not stop a lease from restricting the use. State licensing rules for child care providers were not reviewed.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40A, § 3 ('Family child care home and large family child care home as defined in section 1A of chapter 15D shall be an allowable use'). MA battery MA-B family child care home in rental housing: 5 hits (15D 2, 40A 3, 132B 2, 270 22, 105 Mass. Code Regs. 460.000), none a landlord-tenant rule; positive 40A 3 passed; control 0. MA battery MA-B landlord permission or bar for family child care v2: 0 hits; synthetic positives passed; control 0. EEC licensing regulations (606 Mass. Code Regs. 7.00) are not in the saved CMR corpus and were not searched. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Home Business Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations do not make a home-based business a permitted use of a rental dwelling, and they do not stop a lease from limiting one. Whether a tenant may work from home or run a business there is a matter for your lease and for local zoning. Check the city or town's zoning rules on home occupations before allowing customer visits, signs or employees.
notes: MA: MA battery MA-B home-based business permitted use: 2 hits (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40C, § 8, historic district sign exemption for a 'customary home occupation'; 540 Mass. Code Regs. 18.000, vehicle registrations), neither a permitted-use or lease rule; synthetic positives passed; control 0. Searched General Laws, Constitution, CMR and court rules. Local: city and town zoning home-occupation rules (flagged, not researched). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Co-Tenant Release After Violence
bodyText: A joint and several liability clause does not override the domestic violence termination law. A tenant or co-tenant who ends the tenancy under the domestic violence termination law (written notice within 3 months of the most recent act of domestic violence, rape, sexual assault or stalking, or while a household member is reasonably in fear of imminent serious physical harm, and moving out within 3 months of the notice) owes rent only for 30 days or 1 full rental period after the quitting date, whichever last occurs. The other co-tenants on the agreement are not released and stay fully bound. A lease term waiving these rules is void.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 24(c) ('shall be discharged from liability for rent or use and occupancy for 30 days or 1 full rental period after the quitting date, whichever last occurs'); § 24(d) ('No other tenant or co-tenant who is a party to the rental agreement shall be released'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 28 ('shall be void and unenforceable'). Co-tenant defined in Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 23 ('shares the legal obligation to pay rent'). Joint-and-several clause itself: no MA statute; case law not searched. Conditions: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 24(a) ('within 3 months of the most recent act'; 'reasonably in fear of imminent serious physical harm'), § 24(b) ('fails to quit the premises within 3 months'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Yard Work and Code Duties
bodyText: Massachusetts has no rule that yard tasks assigned to a tenant need a separate signed agreement or extra consideration. A lease may ask the tenant to mow, rake or water. The State Sanitary Code still makes the owner of any parcel of land responsible for keeping it clean, safe and sanitary, free of refuse, pests, injury hazards and standing water. Unless the code says otherwise, the owner provides the maintenance needed to comply. If the yard breaks the code, expect the board of health to look to you.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.570(A) ('The owner of any parcel of land, vacant or otherwise, shall be responsible for maintaining such parcel of land in a clean, safe, and sanitary condition'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.003(B) ('the owner is responsible for providing all maintenance, repairs, and equipment necessary to achieve compliance'). Separate-writing rule: MA battery MA-B tenant maintenance tasks need separate writing and consideration: 1 hit (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127L, two-year lease repair covenant, a different rule); positive 111 127L and synthetic passed; control 0. Last sentence is an inference from 410.570(A) and 410.003(B); case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Water and Sewer Liens
bodyText: In a city, town or district that has accepted the state water or sewer lien law, unpaid water or sewer charges become a lien on the real estate the day after they fall due. This applies whether the owner or the tenant asked for the service. The charges can then be added to the property tax. No lease term, affidavit or account name keeps the lien off your property. If you pay a tenant's charges to prevent or discharge the lien, you may sue the tenant to recover them with costs.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40, § 42A ('at the request of the owner or tenant'; 'shall be a lien upon such real estate'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40, § 42B ('Such lien shall take effect by operation of law on the day immediately following the due date'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40, § 42F ('may recover from such tenant or other person in an action of contract'). Sewer: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 83, § 16A ('at the request of the owner or tenant'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 83, § 16F (same recovery). No owner exemption: MA battery MA-B owner exemption from lien for tenant utility charges v2: 0 hits; synthetic positives passed; control 0 (v1 also 0 hits). Local: whether a city, town or district has accepted §§ 42A-42F or ch. 83 §§ 16A-16F (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Municipal Charges Lien
bodyText: A city or town may vote to make other unpaid local charges or fees, such as a trash fee, a lien on the property. A separate vote is needed for each type of charge. The lien takes effect when the list of unpaid charges is recorded at the registry of deeds, and the charge can be added to your real estate tax. Massachusetts statutes and regulations give you no way to file something that keeps a tenant's unpaid charge off your property, so watch any local account a tenant holds.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40, § 58 ('Any city or town may impose a lien on real property located within the city or town for any local charge or fee that has not been paid by the due date'; 'a separate vote at a town meeting, or by a city or town council is taken for each type of charge or fee'; 'shall forthwith add such charge or fee to the tax on the property to which it relates'). No owner exemption: MA battery MA-B owner exemption from lien for tenant utility charges v2: 0 hits; synthetic positives passed; control 0. Trash fee is an example only; which charges a town has voted to cover is local. Local: municipal votes under § 58 (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Occupancy by Floor Space
bodyText: Massachusetts sets occupancy limits by floor area, not by bedrooms, and the rule applies to every residence statewide. A dwelling unit needs at least 150 square feet of habitable floor space for its first occupant and at least 100 square feet for each additional occupant. A room slept in by one occupant needs at least 70 square feet; a shared sleeping room needs at least 50 square feet per occupant. The board of health must look into complaints from people who do not live in the unit, such as neighbors.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.420(D)(1) ('at least 150 square feet of habitable floor space for its first occupant, and at least 100 square feet of habitable floor space for each additional occupant'); 410.420(D)(3)-(4) ('at least 70 square feet of floor space'; 'at least 50 square feet of floor space for each occupant'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.003(A) ('No owner shall allow a person to occupy'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.600(B) ('received from a person who is not an occupant of that residence'). Rooming units: 410.420(D)(2). Local: stricter local occupancy or rental rules (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Children Cannot Be Excluded
bodyText: A lease term letting you end the tenancy because the tenant has or will have children living there is void. In most housing it is also unlawful to refuse to rent, or to set different terms, because a tenant has children who will live there. You may still apply state, local and federal maximum-occupancy limits. Narrow exemptions exist, such as renting one unit of a two-family home whose other unit you live in.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 16 ('if the tenant has or shall have a child or children, who shall occupy the premises'; 'shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4 ('because such person has a child or children who shall occupy the premises with such person'; 'nothing herein shall limit the applicability of any local, state, or federal restrictions regarding the maximum number of persons permitted to occupy a dwelling'; 'The leasing of a single dwelling unit in a two family dwelling, the other occupancy unit of which is occupied by the owner as his residence') (§ 4(11), with other exemptions for small dwellings with an elderly or infirm occupant and temporary owner leasing). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Acts the Code Bars Tenants From
bodyText: The State Sanitary Code puts direct limits on tenants. An occupant may not shut off or remove a required service, facility, utility or piece of equipment, except briefly for repairs with reasonable notice. No one may obstruct a means of egress. On reasonable notice, an occupant must give you access to bring the unit into compliance, including for repairs, pest control and utility service. Breaking a code provision can bring a fine of $10 to $500. Massachusetts has no tenant-specific crime for damaging rented premises.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.003(C) ('No owner or occupant shall cause any service, facility, equipment, or utility which is required to be made available'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.260(B) ('No person shall cause obstruction of any means of egress or passageway'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.003(E) ('shall give the owner thereof, or the owner's representative, access to the residence for the purpose of effecting compliance'); 105 Mass. title: Tenant Duties Under the Code
bodyText: The State Sanitary Code gives tenants their own duties. An occupant must keep the unit sanitary, use structural elements with reasonable care, and keep facilities and appliances they alone use clean and properly used. Occupants maintain equipment they own and install. In a single-unit home, the occupant keeps the unit free of pests and pays for refuse collection, unless your upkeep failures let pests in. In every residence, occupants follow local recycling rules and place refuse in the receptacles you provide.

title: No Use-Restriction Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts has no general statute that limits a tenant to the purpose stated in the lease or gives you a special remedy when the tenant uses the property for something else. A use restriction is enforced as an ordinary lease term. The one statutory remedy covers listed illegal uses, such as illegal gaming or the illegal keeping or sale of controlled substances. Those uses let you, at your election, treat the lease as void and seek possession.

title: Subletting and Short-Term Rentals
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations do not require you to approve a sublet or assignment, do not limit your reasons for refusing, and do not treat your silence as approval. Your lease controls. A lease may also forbid short-term rentals. The state short-term rental law gives no right to offer a unit as a short-term rental where a rental agreement prohibits it. A tenant who does rent rooms short-term becomes an operator subject to state registration and tax and to local licensing rules.

title: Marijuana Vaping Ban Risk
bodyText: Your lease may ban smoking marijuana, but it may not stop a tenant from consuming marijuana by means other than smoking in the home, unless allowing it would make you violate a federal law or regulation. The cannabis law does not define smoking or say whether vaping counts. The state smoke-free workplace law treats e-cigarette use as smoking, but only for tobacco products. So whether a lease may ban vaping marijuana is unsettled. Limit any vaping ban to tobacco or get legal advice.

title: No Smoke Drift Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations do not declare drifting smoke between units a nuisance, and they set no rule tying your exposure to whether the lease promises a smoke-free unit. Any claim by a neighbor bothered by smoke would rest on general nuisance or lease law. If you advertise or promise a smoke-free building, enforce the policy you promise.

title: No Duty to Forward Notices
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations do not require a tenant to tell you about, or hand over, papers in a proceeding to recover the property, and they do not void a tenant's attornment to a stranger. If you want tenants to pass along such papers, put that duty in the lease as a contract term.

title: Well and Septic Are Yours
bodyText: Under the State Sanitary Code you, not the tenant, must supply potable water sufficient in quantity and pressure for every occupant's ordinary needs. You must also keep a sanitary drainage system, which may be an on-site sewage system meeting the state environmental code. A subsurface sewage disposal system is equipment you must keep operable and free of leaks and defects. A lease cannot shift these duties. The tenant still must use the facilities with reasonable care.

title: Prior Occupant Utility Debts
bodyText: A gas or electric company may not refuse service to a new tenant who is not behind on their own account just because a previous occupant left a bill unpaid. A water company may not refuse to supply water to an owner because a prior owner owed it for past water. Unpaid municipal water and sewer charges are different: they can become a lien on the property.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 125 ('because a bill for gas or electricity remains unpaid by a previous occupant of such building or premises'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 165, § 11C ('because of the indebtedness of a prior owner to the said water company'). Liens: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40, § 42A ('shall be a lien upon such real estate') (see edu-water-sewer-lien-ma). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Shutoffs on Your Utility Account
bodyText: If gas, electricity or water to a tenant's home runs through an account in your name and you fall behind, the utility must give each affected tenant notice before shutting it off. Tenants may pay the amount due to keep service on and then deduct it from rent or recover it from you. A lease term waiving these rights is void. Failing to pay a gas or electric bill you are obliged to pay, and so exposing the tenant to loss of service, is an unfair practice.

Code Regs. 3.17(6)(g) ('To expose such occupant to the risk of loss of such service by failing to pay gas or electric bills when they become due'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Electric Submetering Regime
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations set no special interruption rules for electricity you submeter and bill to tenants. The State Sanitary Code lets a tenant pay for electricity only if it runs through a meter serving only that unit and a written rental agreement provides for tenant payment. Otherwise you must provide it. The code does not say whether a landlord-owned submeter counts. Water submetering has its own detailed rules.

title: No Self-Help Utility Cutoffs
bodyText: Do not shut off utilities in your name because a tenant failed to transfer an account. If you must furnish a utility by law or by the express or implied terms of the tenancy, wilfully failing to furnish it is a crime and makes you liable for actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater. You also may not transfer responsibility for paying a utility to the tenant without their knowledge or consent. A lease waiver of these rules is void, except for limited cases such as necessary repairs.

title: Smoke Detectors Are Your Duty
bodyText: You must provide, install and keep smoke detectors operable; the tenant does not take over maintenance. In a one- or two-family dwelling, install approved detectors on each level of habitation and the basement, on the ceiling near the base of each stairway to the floor above, and outside each separate sleeping area. In a building of three to five units, install them outside each sleeping area, plus interconnected primary power detectors in common hallways and basements. Larger buildings fall under other fire code sections. Tenants must use alarms with reasonable care.

title: Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: If a residential building has fossil-fuel burning equipment, such as a furnace, boiler, water heater or fireplace, or has enclosed parking within the structure, you must equip it with working, approved carbon monoxide alarms. You must have the alarms operating at the beginning of every rental period. After that, you maintain them and, if necessary, replace batteries or alarms each year so they keep working. Local fire officials enforce this.

Code Regs. 410.330(A). Type and placement rules (527 CMR) not saved, not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Alarm Tampering Fee Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations set no fee for a tenant who removes or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and none authorizes one. You remain responsible for keeping alarms working. Frame any charge as recovery of your actual repair or replacement cost. A landlord may not keep more than the damages the law allows or an amount the parties agreed on, so whether a flat tampering fee is enforceable is unsettled.

title: Housing After Condemnation
bodyText: If the board of health condemns and placards a unit as unfit for human habitation and the occupant is not the owner, you must provide comparable, suitable housing for the occupant. The duty is automatic; the tenant does not have to ask. It lasts for the shortest of the remaining lease or rental period, until the board finds the unit fit again, or until the occupant finds permanent housing and voluntarily ends the tenancy.

title: Appliances You Install
bodyText: If you install optional equipment such as a dishwasher, washer and dryer, garbage grinder, air conditioner, microwave or range hood, you must keep it operable and free from leaks, obstructions and defects. You may remove owner-installed optional equipment only when the unit is vacant or before a new tenancy, not mid-tenancy. A stove and oven and a refrigerator with freezer are yours to supply unless a written rental agreement requires the tenant to provide them. Tenants maintain equipment they own and install.

title: No Balcony Inspection Mandate
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and the saved regulations set no schedule of periodic engineering inspections for rental balconies or decks. You still must keep them safe. In a multi-unit residence, keep every exterior stairway, fire escape, egress balcony and bridge free of snow and ice, protect corrodible parts from rust, treat wood structural members against rot, and seal joints where they tie into the building. Missing railings or guards on a stairway, porch or balcony are treated as conditions that may endanger health or safety.

title: Rent After Condemnation
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations have no express rule barring you from collecting rent after a unit is condemned or ordered vacated. Expect little to collect anyway. If the board of health condemns and placards the unit, you must give a non-owner occupant comparable, suitable housing until the earliest of the end of the lease or rental period, the board's finding that the unit is habitable again, or the occupant's move to permanent housing and voluntary end of the tenancy. In a nonpayment eviction, a tenant may also counterclaim for the gap between the agreed rent and the fair value of use and occupation. How these rules apply to rent for a condemned unit is unsettled.

title: No Designated Repairer Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations do not let a lease name who must do repairs a tenant makes at your expense. When certified code violations go unrepaired after written notice, the tenant may repair or have the defects repaired and deduct the cost from rent, within limits. A lease term waiving those rights is void, so a clause restricting who may do the work may not be enforceable. The quality and cost of the work do bear on whether the tenant's deduction was reasonable.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: Refusing a reasonable accommodation in your rules, policies, practices or services that a person with a disability may need for equal use of a dwelling is discrimination. So is refusing a reasonable modification of the premises. The tenant usually pays for the modification. In publicly assisted housing and in buildings or contiguous developments of ten or more units, you pay unless it would impose an undue hardship. You need not pay to ramp more than five steps or install a wheelchair lift. Renting one unit of a two-family home you live in is exempt, unless the home is publicly assisted housing.

title: Restoring Tenant-Paid Modifications
bodyText: When a tenant pays for a disability modification that will materially alter the housing's marketability, you may condition permission on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior, or pay to restore it, to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. Massachusetts law does not require this condition to appear in the lease, and it sets no rule for a restoration escrow or deposit. You may not charge more rent for handicap-accessible housing than for comparable non-accessible housing.

title: Accessible Unit Vacancy Notice
bodyText: When a wheelchair accessible unit becomes or will become vacant, give timely notice to anyone who told you within the past twelve months that they need such a unit. Also give MassAbility at least fifteen days' notice of the vacancy. During that fifteen-day period you may lease the unit only to a person who needs wheelchair accessibility.

Which owners are covered follows § 4(6)-(7); case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Fire Relocation Benefit Notice
bodyText: A fire insurance policy on multi-unit residential property must include a relocation benefit of up to $750 per rental unit, with no deductible, for tenants or lawful occupants displaced by fire. It covers costs such as a hotel room, a new security deposit and first month's rent, and clothing and furniture replacement. At the beginning of the lease or tenancy you must notify each tenant or lawful occupant in writing of this benefit. A lease waiver is void.

title: No Disaster Termination Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations do not end a residential tenancy, or stop rent, when a fire, other casualty or declared disaster makes a unit unusable. Your lease and general contract law decide those questions. Code rules still apply: if the board of health condemns the unit, you must give a non-owner occupant comparable, suitable housing for the period the rule sets. Consider a lease clause on casualty and rent abatement.

title: No Double-Letting Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations have no specific rule on renting the same unit or room to two tenants for the same period, and no special rent-abatement remedy for it. If it happens, the tenant's remedies come from the lease and general contract law. Track signed leases and move-in dates carefully so you never promise the same unit twice.

title: Posted Contact and Phone Monitoring
bodyText: If you do not live in the building, post a sign with your name, street address and telephone number. If a property manager who does not live there handles the building, post the manager's details as well. Corporations, trusts and partnerships must also post the name, address and phone number of their president, managing trustee or partner. Monitor the posted owner or manager phone number regularly, and at least once every 12 hours, unless you have given occupants another contact and number for times you are temporarily away. Post the sign near the mailboxes or inside where occupants can see it.

title: Which Codes Apply
bodyText: The State Sanitary Code sets minimum housing standards, but it also requires you to follow the state building code and other specialized codes in the design, construction and maintenance of buildings and equipment. For smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms it points to the fire safety statutes, the State Building Code, the Massachusetts Comprehensive Fire Safety Code and the plumbing code. Those separate codes hold most placement and construction detail, so check them or ask the local fire department.

title: No Furnished Rental Rules
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations set no special rules for furnished rentals. The deposit cap is the same: no more than the first month's rent. You may deduct from the deposit for damage the tenant causes beyond reasonable wear and tear, which can include your furniture, but only with a sworn itemized list and written evidence of cost, and not for damage listed in the statement of condition. List furnishings in the lease and the statement of condition.

Code Regs. 461.000), none a furnished-rental rule; synthetic positive passed; control 0. Mass. Gen. title: Conditions Deemed Serious
bodyText: The State Sanitary Code lists conditions that are always treated as ones that may endanger or materially impair health or safety. They include no heat as required, water or sewage failures, shutoff or failure to restore electricity, gas or water, blocked exits, missing smoke or carbon monoxide alarms, missing railings, pest infestations, lead paint violations and serious structural defects. Any other violation becomes serious if you miss the board of health's deadline to fix it. These serious conditions trigger the tenant's strongest remedies, including repair and deduct.

Repair and deduct: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127L ('may endanger or materially impair the health, safety or well-being of a tenant'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: What a Written Agreement Can Shift
bodyText: Only specific code duties can be moved to a tenant, and each needs a written rental agreement. Electricity or gas, if metered only to the unit. Heating or hot water oil, if the unit has its own tank. The stove and oven and refrigerator. In a multi-unit building, snow and ice on egress the tenant alone uses. In a two- or three-unit building, common-area lights on the tenant's meter, starting only with a new tenancy. Water can be billed only under the submetering statute.

Code Regs. 410.210 ('The occupant is required to provide the oil under a written rental agreement'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.300(F) ('shall begin only upon commencement of a new tenancy'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.130(C) ('must be in compliance with all requirements of M.G.L. c. 186, § 22'). title: Code Violation Presumptions
bodyText: In a nonpayment or no-fault eviction, a tenant may raise defenses and counterclaims about the unit's condition. Proof that the unit violates the sanitary or building code in ways that may endanger or materially impair health or safety creates a presumption that the tenant is entitled to that defense. Proof of written notice to you of a board of health inspection creates a presumption that you knew of the conditions in the notice from the day you received it. A certified inspection report is prima facie evidence of its facts.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 8A ('shall create a presumption that conditions existed in the premises entitling the tenant or occupant to a counterclaim or defense'; 'shall create a presumption that on the date such notice was received, such person knew of the conditions'; 'shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Required Fitness Statement
bodyText: Massachusetts does not require your lease to state that you will deliver the unit fit for habitation. The duty exists anyway. Renting a unit that is unfit for human habitation, or that has a violation which may endanger or materially impair the occupant's health, safety or well-being at the start of the tenancy, is an unfair or deceptive practice. Do not write a lease statement saying the unit meets all legal requirements unless it does.

Code Regs. 410.000, condemnation), neither a private-lease statement rule; synthetic positive passed; control 0. 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(a) ('Rent a dwelling unit which, at the inception of the tenancy'; 'is unfit for human habitation'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(d) ('Represent to a prospective tenant that a dwelling unit meets all requirements of law when, in fact, it contains violations of law'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Habitability Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A lease cannot remove a sanitary code requirement or the tenant's remedies for violations. Lease terms waiving the tenant's rights to court-supervised rent payments and receivership, to repair and deduct, or to raise condition defenses in an eviction are void. The code itself lets a written rental agreement shift only who provides certain items. Only a board of health variance can vary a code provision, never the conditions deemed to endanger health or safety. One exception: a lease of two years may have the tenant make defined repairs for substantially lower rent.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127K ('to waive the benefits of any provision of section one hundred and twenty-seven C to one hundred and twenty-seven I, inclusive, shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127L ('a covenant in any lease of two years' duration not counting any renewal periods'; 'in consideration for a substantially lower rent'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 8A ('Any provision of any rental agreement purporting to waive the provisions of this section shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.700(A)(1) ('Conditions Deemed to Endanger or Materially Impair Health or Safety'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Occupants Legal Rights Notice
bodyText: Give each occupant a copy of the Department of Public Health's Notice of Occupants' Legal Rights and Responsibilities, or post it near the mailboxes or inside the residence where occupants can see it, on durable material. Tenants may ask the local board of health to inspect their unit and common areas, even anonymously and even if they never told you about the problem. The board must inspect within one business day for the most serious conditions and within five business days otherwise.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.400(C) ('a copy of the Notice of Occupants' Legal Rights and Responsibilities issued by the Department'); 410.400(D) ('on durable material not less than 20 square inches in size'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.600(A) ('regardless of whether'); 410.600(C)(1)-(2) ('within one business day after the receipt of a request'; 'within five business days after receipt of a request'). Local: board of health rules adopted under Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127A (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Heat Standards
bodyText: You must provide and maintain a heating system able to heat every habitable room and every room with a toilet, shower or bathtub. From September 15 through May 31, keep those rooms at least 68F from 7:00 A.M. to 11:00 P.M. and at least 64F overnight, and never above 78F from the heating system. A board of health may shorten the season slightly. Fireplaces, wood or pellet stoves and portable electric space heaters do not count as the heating system. Only paying for fuel can shift to a tenant, and only by written agreement with a separate meter or tank.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.160(A) ('a heating system that includes a distribution system capable of heating every habitable room'); 410.160(B) ('Portable electric space heater'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.180(A) ('from September 15th through May 31st'; 'between 7:00 A.M. and 11:00 P.M.'; 'between 11:01 P.M. and 6:59 A.M.'); 410.180(B), (D); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.210 ('Oil is provided through a separate oil tank which serves only that dwelling unit'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.200(A). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant Remedies for Bad Conditions
bodyText: If certified code violations that may endanger health or safety go unrepaired, the tenant may repair them and deduct up to four months' rent in a twelve-month period. Alternatively the tenant may treat the lease as ended, pay only fair value for use and occupation, and move out. This applies if you do not begin repairs, or contract in writing for them, within five days of written notice and substantially finish within fourteen, or within any shorter time a board of health or court orders. It does not apply to conditions the tenant, a household member, a guest or a business invitee caused, or if the tenant unreasonably denied you access to make the repairs. In a nonpayment or no-fault eviction, the tenant may counterclaim for breach of warranty, breach of the rental agreement or other violations. Wilful failure to furnish required utilities can cost the greater of actual damages or three months' rent.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127L ('failed to begin all necessary repairs or to contract in writing with a third party for such repairs within five days after such notice'; 'treat the lease or rental agreement as abrogated, pay only the fair value of their use and occupation and vacate the premises'; 'an amount greater than four months' rent in any twelve-month period'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 8A ('for breach of warranty, for a breach of any material provision of the rental agreement, or for a violation of any other law'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14 ('actual and consequential damages or three month's rent, whichever is greater'). Unfair-practice exposure: 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1). Case law (warranty of habitability, rent abatement) not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Your Repair Duty
bodyText: Unless the State Sanitary Code says otherwise, you provide all maintenance, repairs and equipment needed to meet it. Keep buildings and structural elements in good repair: weathertight, free of excess moisture and mold, pest resistant, and free of holes, cracks and loose plaster. After a leak or flood, dry all surfaces within 48 hours of notice or the end of the event, whichever is sooner. After a board of health order, make a good faith effort to fix the most serious violations within 24 hours. Fix others within the time ordered, at most 30 days.

Code Regs. 410.500(A)-(B) ('free from excess moisture or the appearance of mold'; 'within 48 hours from the time they are notified or the end of the event, whichever is sooner'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.640(A)-(B) ('make a good faith effort to correct within 24 hours of service'; 'No order shall exceed 30 calendar days'). Failing to remedy after notice: 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(b), (i). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Pest Inspection Before Move-In
bodyText: Before each new occupancy, inspect the unit for pests. Keep records of the inspection and what you did about it, including monitoring, sealing entry points, repairs, where pesticides were applied and by whom, and the date and result of any follow-up inspection. Make them available to the board of health on request. In buildings with two or more units, pest elimination is your responsibility.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.550(F) ('shall conduct an inspection of each unit prior to a new occupancy to identify the presence of pests'); 410.550(G) ('Owners shall make the documented inspection results and actions taken available upon request by the board of health'); 410.550(B) ('shall maintain it and its premises free from infestation and shall be responsible for pest elimination'). Homeless shelters excepted. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Statutory Self-Cure Right
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute letting you fix a tenant's breach and bill the cost as rent. A lease may let you enter to make repairs, and you may seek your actual cost as damages. You may not keep more than the damages the law allows or an amount the parties agreed on. Whether a lease can label repair costs as rent, so they support a nonpayment eviction, is unsettled. Deposit deductions are limited to the statutory list.

title: Screens and Building Number
bodyText: Install tight-fitting screens on openable exterior windows, and screen doors where required, in place April 1 through October 31. Post the building's street number so it is visible from the street.

Code Regs. 410.270(A) ('Every entry door of a dwelling unit shall be capable of being secured against unlawful entry'; 'shall be so designed or equipped so as to close and lock automatically'); 410.270(B) ('shall provide a key to the occupant'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.410 ('visible from the nearest street providing vehicular access'). Exceptions for lodging houses, dormitories, housing authorities and homeless shelters in 410.270(A)(3). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Apartment and Condo Pools
bodyText: A pool at an apartment house or condominium, included in what residents pay, is a semi-public pool. You need an annual board of health permit, posted near the pool, and daily operating records. Provide lifeguards if the board requires them; otherwise post the required no-lifeguard and adult-supervision warning signs. An outdoor inground pool needs a fence, generally six feet high, with self-latching gates and no openings wider than three inches, plus a life ring and rescue hook. The local building inspector must inspect it every year.

Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Repair Promises Are Binding
bodyText: Massachusetts does not require a promise to repair or improve a unit to be in writing or to carry a completion date. But once you represent to a tenant that you will make repairs, provide services or supplies, or reimburse the tenant for repairs or purchases, failing to follow through is an unfair or deceptive practice. Make repairs within a reasonable time after the tenant's notice. Reimburse within a reasonable or agreed time. Put promises in writing with dates so both sides know what was promised.
notes: MA: 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(e) ('Fail within a reasonable time after receipt of notice from the tenant to make repairs in accordance with a pre-existing representation made to the tenant'); 3.17(1)(f) ('Fail to provide services and/or supplies after the making of any representation or agreement'); 3.17(1)(g) ('Fail to reimburse the tenant within a reasonable or agreed time after notice'). No writing or completion-date rule like Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.07 was found in this read (not separately batteried). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Quiet Enjoyment by Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts makes it an offense for a landlord to directly or indirectly interfere with a tenant's quiet enjoyment, or to try to regain possession by force without going to court. Penalties include a fine of $25 to $300 or up to six months in jail. The tenant may also recover actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees, and may set them off against rent. A lease clause saying nothing you do counts as a constructive eviction is void.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14 ('directly or indirectly interferes with the quiet enjoyment of any residential premises by the occupant'; 'attempts to regain possession of such premises by force without benefit of judicial process'; 'shall be punished by a fine of not less than twenty-five dollars nor more than three hundred dollars'; 'actual and consequential damages or three month's rent, whichever is greater'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15F ('agrees that no action or failure to act by the landlord shall be construed as a constructive eviction'). What counts as interference turns on case law; case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Rent-Demand Bar
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute that bars you outright from demanding or collecting rent while a unit has code violations. The protection works through litigation instead. In a nonpayment or no-fault eviction, the tenant can raise conditions as a defense or counterclaim, and you cannot recover possession if what you are owed is no more than what the tenant is owed. In a code case, a tenant is not treated as behind on rent when the rent you claim in good faith does not exceed the tenant's good-faith counterclaim.

Foreclosing owners: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 3 (notice within 30 days stating where rent is sent). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Housing Inspector Entry
bodyText: No Massachusetts statute or regulation lets a lease authorize a housing inspector to enter so the tenant must allow it without separate consent. Inspectors act under their own authority: the board of health may enter and inspect at reasonable times and may run systematic area inspections. If anyone refuses entry, the board may seek a search warrant. Your own lease entry rights are limited to inspecting, repairing and showing the unit, so do not rely on the lease to admit inspectors.

Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Repair-Cost Termination Right
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations give you no right to end a tenancy because a needed repair would cost too much. Unless the State Sanitary Code says otherwise, you must provide all repairs needed to meet it, whatever the cost. A tenant at will can be ended by a written notice to quit for no stated reason. But a notice sent within six months after the tenant reported a code violation or sought to enforce housing law is presumed to be a reprisal.

title: No Small-Landlord Remedy Exemption
bodyText: Massachusetts has no notice that lets a small landlord opt out of tenants' repair remedies. A tenant's right to repair and deduct, or to treat the lease as ended, after certified code violations applies however few units you own. Any lease term that waives it is void, except a defined-repair covenant in a lease of two years. The only owner-occupancy carve-out found is narrow: the registered-mail unsafe-condition notice rule does not cover an owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling.

Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 19 ('A landlord or lessor of any real estate except an owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Repair Notice Triggers
bodyText: Different tenant remedies start from different notice. Repair-and-deduct, or ending the lease, needs certified code violations and written notice to you; you then have five days to begin repairs and 14 days to substantially complete them, unless an order sets a shorter time. For an unsafe condition, a tenant's written notice by registered or certified mail, or a code agency's violation notice, starts your duty to correct it within a reasonable time. In an eviction, a tenant can raise conditions you or your agent knew of before the tenant fell behind in rent; written notice is not required.

Code Regs. 3.17(1)(i) ('within a reasonable time after notice of a violation of such code or law from the tenant or agency'). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Lease Cannot Narrow Repair Notice
bodyText: Your lease may ask tenants to report repairs in writing, but it cannot take away remedies the law ties to other kinds of notice. A term that waives the tenant's eviction defense or counterclaim for bad conditions is void, and that defense needs only your knowledge of the condition. You also may not refuse a notice sent to the address where rent is customarily sent, given to the person who customarily accepts it for you, or sent to the person your rental agreement names to receive notices.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 8A ('Any provision of any rental agreement purporting to waive the provisions of this section shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'). 940 Mass. title: Locks and Keys You Must Provide
bodyText: You must provide, install and maintain locks so the building and every unit entry door can be secured against unlawful entry. In a residence with more than three units, the main entry door must close and lock automatically. Every other exterior door needs a working lock. Every openable exterior window must be securable. Egress doors must open from the inside without a key, keypad or special knowledge. Give each occupant keys to the main entry door, their unit and common areas. Lodging houses, dormitories, housing authorities and homeless shelters have exceptions.

Code Regs. 410.270(A)-(B) ('Every entry door of a dwelling unit shall be capable of being secured against unlawful entry'; 'The main entry door of a residence containing more than three dwelling units'; 'Every openable exterior window shall be capable of being secured'; 'without use of any key, keypad, or other specialized knowledge'; 'shall provide a key to the occupant'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 143, § 3R ('every apartment house having more than three apartments shall be so designed or equipped as to close and lock automatically'; fine 'of not more than five hundred dollars'). title: No Rekey or Peephole Mandate
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations do not require a peephole or door viewer, and do not require private landlords to rekey locks between tenants. Rekeying is still good practice. At or before the start of a tenancy you may charge the new tenant the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock. Local housing authorities in state-aided public housing must deliver units with re-keyed locks at initial occupancy. Separate lock-change duties apply when a tenant faces domestic violence.

title: No Senior Housing Work Card
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations do not require work cards or background checks for staff in housing for people 55 and older, or in any other rental housing. Criminal record rules for landlords cover how you may screen housing applicants, not your employees. Any staff screening you do follows general employment law.

title: No Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations do not require apartment owners to adopt a key-control policy or to run background checks on employees who have access to units. A written key-control practice is still good risk management. You must still provide locks and keys that let each unit and building be secured against unlawful entry, and your entry into a unit is limited to the purposes the law allows.

title: No Smart-Lock Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute or regulation aimed at smart locks, keypads or app-based entry in rentals. The general rules still apply whatever the technology. You must give each occupant a key to the main entry door, their unit and common areas. Egress doors must open from the inside without a key, keypad or other special knowledge. Your entry is limited to the purposes the law allows. Whether a code or app counts as the required key is not settled.

title: Limits on Utility Allowances
bodyText: Massachusetts limits utility allowance or overage plans. You must provide the electricity or gas used in a unit unless it runs through a meter serving only that unit and a written rental agreement provides for the tenant to pay. Heating or hot-water oil works the same way, with a separate tank. So you cannot bill tenants for usage above an allowance on a shared meter. Water and sewer can be billed to a tenant only under the strict submetering law, which bars any extra fee. Whether an allowance credit on a unit-only meter fits these rules is not settled.

Code Regs. 410.200(A) ('The owner shall provide the electricity or gas used in each dwelling unit unless'; 'metered through a meter which serves only the dwelling unit'; 'A written rental agreement provides for payment by the occupant'). 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.210 ('Oil is provided through a separate oil tank which serves only that dwelling unit'). Mass. Gen. title: No Ratio Utility Billing
bodyText: Massachusetts gives you no way to split a shared utility bill among tenants by a formula such as square footage or headcount. Electricity or gas on a meter serving more than one unit is yours to pay. Water and sewer can be billed only through a submeter or utility meter that measures just the tenant's unit, and the charge may not exceed the water company's calculated cost per unit of water times the unit's measured use. You also may not shift payment for any utility to a tenant without the tenant's knowledge or consent.

title: Water Submeter Certificate Copy
bodyText: If you bill a tenant separately for water or sewer through submeters, file a certificate with the board of health, signed by you under the pains and penalties of perjury, that the unit complies with the submetering law. A licensed plumber must also sign it for the submeters and ultra-low-flush toilets. Give the occupants of each unit a copy of the certificate with the written rental agreement that describes the submetering and billing arrangements. Attaching it to the lease is the simplest way.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.130(C)(3)-(4) ('Having a written rental agreement on the commencement of a new tenancy that describes the details of the water submetering and water billing arrangements'; 'The owner shall have a licensed plumber sign the certificate'; 'The owner shall also provide a copy of the certificate to the occupants of each dwelling unit with the written rental agreement'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 22(c) ('Certification by the landlord shall be provided under the penalties of perjury'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Water Submetering Conditions
bodyText: You may bill a tenant separately for water and sewer only if every condition of the submetering law is met. A unit becomes eligible only at a new tenancy: a first occupancy, or after the prior tenant left voluntarily or was evicted for nonpayment or breach. A licensed plumber installs a submeter for each unit and the common areas, and low-flow fixtures. You certify compliance to the board of health. The tenant must sign a written rental agreement that clearly and conspicuously provides for the charge. No added fees, and no water shutoff for an unpaid charge.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 22(b)-(d), (f), (j), (l) ('only upon the commencement of a new tenancy in such dwelling unit'; 'the previous tenant vacated the dwelling unit voluntarily'; 'a submeter is installed for each dwelling unit in the building and for the common areas'; 'clearly and conspicuously provides for such separate charge'; 'or other fee whatsoever, however denominated'; 'may not shut off or refuse water service to a tenant'). No type-size rule beyond 'clearly and conspicuously'; applies to any building size; public housing developments excluded (§ 22(s)). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Utility Shutoff Protections
bodyText: State law limits when a gas or electric company may shut off a home. From November 15 to March 15 it may not shut off service used for heat to a residential customer who cannot pay an overdue charge because of financial hardship. It also may not shut off service during a certified serious illness, or where a child under 12 months lives, if the customer cannot pay because of financial hardship. Households where everyone is 65 or older get added collection steps. Water companies may not shut off a home with a certified seriously ill occupant.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 124F ('between November fifteenth and March fifteenth shut off gas or electric service to any residential customer'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 124A ('during such time as there is a serious illness therein'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 124H ('domiciled a person under the age of twelve months'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 124E ('all residents are sixty-five years of age or older'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 165, § 11B ('occupied by a person who is seriously ill'). 220 Mass. Code Regs. 25.00 (DPU billing and termination rules) is not in the saved corpus. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Code Receivership Risk
bodyText: Any affected tenant, or the board of health, can petition the court over State Sanitary Code violations in any residential building, whatever its size. The court may order rent paid to the court clerk, issue injunctions, or appoint a receiver if violations will not be promptly fixed otherwise. A receiver collects the rents, makes the repairs, and gets a lien ahead of all other liens and mortgages except municipal liens. You keep your own liability and your duty to pay taxes, mortgages and repair costs. Lease terms waiving these remedies are void.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127C ('a petition may be filed by any affected tenant or by the board of health'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127I ('violations of the sanitary code will not be promptly remedied unless a receiver is appointed'; 'shall have a lien with priority over all other liens or mortgages except municipal liens'; 'The receiver shall be authorized to collect rents'; 'Nothing in this section shall be deemed to relieve the owner of property of any civil or criminal liability'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127K ('shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'). Section 127H is not in the saved corpus. Local: Boston, Worcester and Cambridge commissioners of housing inspection also petition (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Court-Ordered Rent to Clerk
bodyText: If a court finds code violations that may endanger a tenant's health or safety, it may order tenants to pay the fair value of use and occupation to the court clerk instead of to you. The tenant must be current, or willing to pay arrears into court. The clerk may release money to you for repairs, and pays you the balance once the violations are removed. In an eviction where the tenant raises bad conditions, the court can likewise require payments to the clerk, and a tenant may deposit disputed rent there voluntarily.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127F ('authorize the petitioner or any other affected tenant to pay to the clerk of the court the fair value of the use and occupation'; 'is willing to pay any arrearage into the court as ordered'; 'When the violation is removed, the court shall direct that the balance of funds'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 8A ('voluntarily deposit with the clerk any amount for rent or for use and occupation which may be in dispute'). No statute bars every eviction while payments are with the clerk; case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Subsidy Proration Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations have no special rule for reducing rent when part of a subsidized unit becomes uninhabitable. The general remedies apply to every tenant. In an eviction, a tenant may claim the difference between the agreed rent and the fair value of the use and occupation of the premises. Whether that difference is measured on the tenant's share or on the full contract rent including the subsidy is not settled. Check your subsidy contract.

Searched General Laws, Constitution, CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 8A ('the difference between the agreed upon rent and the fair value of the use and occupation of the premises'). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Cable TV Access for Tenants
bodyText: If you own or manage a multiple dwelling served by a cable TV system, you may not prevent the operator from entering to install or service cable when one or more tenants request it. You may not charge different rent or other charges to tenants who subscribe and those who do not. You may require the operator, not tenants, to pay reasonable compensation for the installation, and you may set reasonable conditions to protect the building's safety, functioning and appearance. The operator must install at no cost to you and indemnify you for damage.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 166A, § 22 ('shall prohibit or otherwise prevent an operator from entering such buildings'; 'shall discriminate in rental or other charges between tenants'; 'the owner of such real estate may require reasonable compensation in exchange for permitting the installation of CATV system equipment'; 'such reasonable conditions as are necessary to protect the safety, functioning and appearance of the premises'; 'shall do so at no cost to the landlord').
