title: Recovering Rent After Termination
bodyText: In an eviction you may claim possession and the rent and use and occupancy owed, and a judgment for possession includes any rent found due. If you leave the rent claim out, you may still sue for it later. Rent is recoverable in contract. When a lease or tenancy at will ends mid-period by surrender, a nonpayment notice to quit or a death, you may recover a proportional part of that period's rent. A tenant at sufferance owes rent for the time they stay. Contract claims generally must be brought within six years.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 2 ('Failure to claim rent and use and occupation in the action shall not bar a subsequent action therefor'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 3 ('the judgment and execution shall include the amount of the award'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 5 ('Such rent may be recovered in contract'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 8 ('a proportional part of such rent'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 3 ('shall be liable to pay rent therefor for such time as they may occupy or detain the same'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 260, § 2 ('within six years next after the cause of action accrues'). Sealed contracts and damages beyond rent: case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Holdover Liability
bodyText: A tenant who stays after the tenancy ends owes rent for the time they occupy or keep the unit. After a no-fault termination of a tenancy at will, the tenant owes rent at the same rate for any time they stay during the notice period. Massachusetts has no double-rent or other holdover multiplier. Damages you keep for a breach may not exceed what the law allows or an amount the parties agreed. Only a court can remove a holdover tenant; accepting rent after termination may create a new tenancy, a question of case law.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 3 ('Tenants at sufferance in possession of land or tenements shall be liable to pay rent therefor'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 13 ('at the same rate as theretofore payable by him while a tenant at will'). MA battery MA-C holdover double rent or holdover damages: 1 hit (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 1, summary process); positive and synthetic positives passed; control 0. Searched General Laws, Constitution, CMR and court rules. 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(6)(c). Waiver by acceptance of rent: case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Filing Before the Lease Ends
bodyText: If you expect a tenant to hold over, you may start an eviction before a written lease ends, but only if the lease was for at least six months with a specific termination date. You cannot file before the latest date the lease allows either side to give notice of renewal, or earlier than thirty days before the termination date. Notify all defendants by registered mail within twenty-four hours of filing, show substantial grounds that the tenant will stay without right, and attach a signed copy of the lease. No execution may issue before the day after the termination date.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 1A ('created for at least six months duration by a written lease in which a specific termination date is designated'; 'or in any case before thirty days before the designated termination date of the tenancy'; 'shall notify all defendants by registered mail'; 'No execution for possession may issue in any such action before the day next following the designated termination date'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Stays After No-Fault Eviction
bodyText: If you end a tenancy without fault of the tenant, other than by a nonpayment notice, the court may stay judgment and execution for up to six months in total. The limit is twelve months if a handicapped person or someone 60 or older lives there. The tenant may show they cannot find similar housing nearby despite reasonable effort and are acting in good faith, or other facts that warrant a stay. They must pay into court all unpaid rent and use and occupancy for the stay period. Lease waivers of these stays are void. Hotels and short rooming-house stays are excluded.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 9 ('a period not exceeding six months'; 'a period not exceeding twelve months or for periods not exceeding twelve months in the aggregate in the case of premises occupied by a handicapped person or an individual sixty years of age or older'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 10 ('cannot secure suitable premises for himself and his family elsewhere within the city or town'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 11 ('The deposit shall also include all rent unpaid prior to the period of the stay'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 12 ('shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: Tenants may petition the court to seal eviction records. A no-fault eviction record can be sealed any time after the case ends. A nonpayment case can be sealed four years after it ends if no eviction or tenant claim was brought in the prior four years and the tenant certifies economic hardship. A fault eviction can be sealed after seven years with a clean seven-year record. Cases dismissed or won by the tenant can be sealed any time. You get notice of most petitions and may object within 7 days. Sealed records cannot appear in tenant screening reports.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 16(b)-(e1/2), (i) ('may petition the court to seal the court record at any time after the conclusion of the action'; 'not less than 4 years before the request'; 'not less than 7 years before the request'; 'resulted in a dismissal or final judgment in favor of the defendant'; 'shall not disclose the existence of, or information regarding, an eviction record sealed under this section'). Effective date of § 16 per 2024 session law not re-verified. Application statement: edu-eviction-record-question-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: File Notice of Satisfaction
bodyText: If you obtain a judgment or agreement in an eviction case solely for nonpayment of rent, you must file a notice of satisfaction with the court within 14 days after the tenant satisfies it. If you do not, the tenant may petition to have it deemed satisfied. Once it is satisfied, the tenant may petition to seal the case record, and the court will seal it if no party objects within 7 days.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 16(k) ('not more than 14 days after satisfaction of the judgment or agreement, file with the court'; 'file a petition for the judgment or agreement to be deemed satisfied'; 'with no objection filed by a party within 7 days of filing the petition'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Statewide Just-Cause Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statewide just-cause eviction rule for ordinary private rentals. A fixed-term lease ends on its date, and a tenancy at will can be ended by proper written notice without a stated reason. Exceptions exist: an owner who took title through foreclosure needs just cause, and tenants in some publicly assisted housing are protected for a period after its affordability restrictions end. A no-fault termination also lets the court grant a stay of up to six or twelve months, and a notice soon after protected tenant activity is presumed a reprisal.
notes: MA: MA battery MA-C just cause or good cause eviction requirement: 10 hits (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, §§ 2-4; ch. 40T, § 7; ch. 121B, § 38D; public-housing and program rules in 760 CMR), none for ordinary private rentals; positive passed; control 0. Searched General Laws, Constitution, CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12 ('Estates at will may be determined by either party by three months' notice in writing'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 2 ('a foreclosing owner shall not evict a tenant except for just cause'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40T, § 7 ('except for good cause related to tenant fault'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 9. Local: just-cause ordinances (flagged, not researched). Manufactured housing (ch. 140, § 32J) not read. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Leases After Foreclosure
bodyText: When a residential property is foreclosed, a tenant under an unexpired fixed-term lease becomes a tenant at will. A tenancy at will is not ended by the foreclosure, sale or leasing of the property. A tenant whose rent is subsidized under state or federal law keeps the lease, and the foreclosing party must assume it and the subsidy contract. A mortgagee that takes possession before foreclosure, or conveys title after it, must notify all residential tenants within thirty days.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 13A ('shall be deemed a tenant at will'; 'the foreclosing entity shall assume the lease and rental subsidy contract'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 13 ('shall not be terminated by operation of law by the conveyance, transfer or leasing of the premises by the owner or landlord thereof or by foreclosure'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 244, § 15A ('notify all residential tenants of said premises'). Landlord duty to disclose a pending foreclosure: none found (battery MA-C foreclosure notice to residential tenants: 8 hits, none imposing it). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Foreclosing Owners Need Just Cause
bodyText: A lender, servicer, institutional mortgagee or Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac that takes title through foreclosure may evict a bona fide tenant only for just cause, or once a binding sale agreement with a bona fide third-party buyer is signed. Within 30 days it must post and deliver its name, address, phone and where to send rent, with a written notice of the tenant's right to a court hearing. Evictions for nonpayment, uncured breach or refusal to renew wait 30 days after that notice. Each illegal eviction carries a fine of at least $5,000.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 2 ('a foreclosing owner shall not evict a tenant except for just cause or unless a binding purchase and sale agreement has been executed'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 3 ('Within 30 days of the foreclosure'; 'a written disclosure of the tenant's right to a court hearing prior to eviction'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 4(a) ('until 30 days after the notice required by section 3 is posted and delivered'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 6 ('shall be punished by a fine of not less than $5,000'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 1 (definitions of foreclosing owner, bona fide tenancy, just cause). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Eviction Case Timeline
bodyText: An eviction (summary process) starts only after the notice to quit period has run. Use the court's required summons and complaint, have it served by an authorized officer between seven and thirty days before a Monday entry day, and file it with the notice to quit and proof of delivery. Either side may appeal within 10 days after judgment, and no execution issues until those 10 days pass. The officer must give 48 hours' written notice before removing anyone, and may not levy before 9 a.m., after 5 p.m., or on weekends or legal holidays.
notes: MA: Uniform Summary Process Rule 2(a)-(d) (court form; service 7 to 30 days before the Monday entry day under Mass. R. Civ. P. 4; file the notice to quit and proof of delivery) (court rule text read; not quotable by the checker). 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(5)(b) ('Commence summary process for possession of a dwelling unit before the time period designated in the notice to quit'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 5(a) ('within 10 days after the entry of the judgment'; 'An execution upon a judgment rendered pursuant to section 3 shall not issue until the expiration of 10 days'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 3 ('At least forty-eight hours prior to serving or levying upon an execution'; 'after five o'clock p.m. or before nine o'clock a.m., nor on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Exemption Waiver Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute letting a tenant waive, in a lease, the protections that keep property from being seized to pay a judgment, and none expressly barring it. When you collect a judgment, much of a tenant's property is exempt from seizure on execution, including necessary clothing, beds, a stove and refrigerator, household furniture up to $15,000, and money for rent up to $2,500 a month. Do not rely on a lease waiver of these exemptions; whether one is enforceable is not settled.
notes: MA: MA battery MA-C waiver of homestead or execution exemptions v2: 0 hits; synthetic positives passed; control 0. Searched General Laws, Constitution, CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 235, § 34 ('shall be exempt from seizure on execution'; 'Other household furniture necessary for the debtor and the debtor's family, not exceeding $15,000 in value'; 'not exceeding $2,500 per month, necessary to pay the rent for the dwelling unit occupied by the debtor'). Homestead estates protect owners: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 188, § 3. Enforceability of a lease waiver: case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Landlord Lien on Belongings
bodyText: Massachusetts gives a residential landlord no lien on, and no right to seize, a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. Recover possession only through the courts, and collect rent through a judgment. Holding a tenant's property or excluding the tenant to force payment risks liability for three months' rent or treble damages. Much household property is exempt from execution anyway. Innholders have a lien on guests' property for unpaid board and lodging, but that rule covers inns, not residential tenancies.
notes: MA: MA battery MA-C landlord lien or distress on tenant goods v2: 10 hits (self-storage, goods leases, innholders, manufactured housing communities, remaindermen, bailee priority, crops), none giving a residential landlord a lien on tenant goods; positive Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 140, § 14 passed; control 0. Searched General Laws, Constitution, CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 140, § 14 ('which such innholder retains by virtue of his lien thereon for the unpaid board, lodging and other charges of such guest'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 184, § 18 ('No person shall attempt to recover possession of land or tenements in any manner other than through an action'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15F ('three months' rent or three times the damages'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 235, § 34. UCC Article 9 security interests not researched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Agreed Damages for Breach
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute on liquidated damages in residential leases. The Attorney General's rule bars you from keeping, as damages for a tenant's breach, more than the damages the law allows, "or an amount which the parties have otherwise agreed as to the amount of the damages." So an agreed figure, such as an early-termination charge, is contemplated. Whether a particular figure is an unenforceable penalty turns on case law we did not research. You may not take an agreed-damages amount out of the security deposit. A late-payment penalty is barred until rent is 30 days late.
notes: MA: 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(6)(c) ('Retain as damages for a tenant's breach of lease' ... 'or an amount which the parties have otherwise agreed as to the amount of the damages'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(3)(a) ('Contains a penalty clause not in conformity with the provisions of'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4) ('No deduction may be made from the security deposit for any purpose other than those set forth in this section'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(c) ('No lease or other rental agreement shall impose any interest or penalty for failure to pay rent until thirty days after such rent shall have been due'). MA battery D liquidated-damages: liquidated damages near lease/tenant: 6 hits; positives passed (only 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.000 governs residential leases; ch. 106, § 2A-103 is goods leases). Penalty-versus-liquidated-damages test: case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Lockout for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: You may not change the locks or otherwise shut out a tenant who is behind on rent, even if the lease says you may. Massachusetts allows no one to recover possession except through a summary process (eviction) case or another proceeding authorized by law. A tenant removed or excluded without a valid court order may recover possession or end the tenancy, and recover three months' rent or three times the damages, plus costs and attorney's fees. A lease term exempting you from that liability is void. A lockout is also a crime.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 184, § 18 ('No person shall attempt to recover possession of land or tenements in any manner other than through an action brought pursuant to chapter two hundred and thirty-nine or such other proceedings authorized by law'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15F ('If a tenant is removed from the premises or excluded therefrom by the landlord or his agent except pursuant to a valid court order'; 'recover three months' rent or three times the damages sustained by him'; 'purports to exempt the landlord from any liability imposed by this section shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14 ('attempts to regain possession of such premises by force without benefit of judicial process, shall be punished by a fine'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(5)(a) ('Deprive a tenant of access to or full use of the dwelling unit or otherwise exclude him without first obtaining a valid writ of execution'). No MA opt-in lockout right exists; see edu-self-help-eviction-ban-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Never Name Minors in Eviction
bodyText: Do not name any minor as a defendant in a Massachusetts summary process (eviction) case. The statute says the defendants named in the summons and complaint "shall not include any minors," and any minor's name included must be expunged from the court record and the electronic docket. The Housing Court's standing order repeats the rule. The statute does not say what else happens to a case that names a minor. Name the adult tenants and other adult occupants you seek to remove.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 2 ('The defendant named in a summary process summons and complaint shall not include any minors, and any such minors' names so included shall be expunged from any court record and electronic docket entry'). Housing Court Standing Order 1-23 (interim, continuation of temporary modifications) also directs plaintiffs not to name minors as defendants, citing St. 2020, c. 358 (saved court-rules corpus). MA battery D minor-tenant-filing: minors as eviction defendants: 14 hits; positives passed (only ch. 239, § 2 and Standing Order 1-23 address eviction defendants). Consequence for the rest of the case (dismissal or not): not stated; case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Notice to Quit for Nonpayment
bodyText: To end a tenancy for unpaid rent, give the tenant a written fourteen days' notice to quit. Under a written lease, the tenant still keeps the tenancy by paying or tendering all rent then due, with interest and costs of suit, on or before the day the answer is due in your eviction case. A tenant at will who has not received a similar notice in the prior twelve months can stop the termination by paying the full rent due within ten days after receiving the notice. A lease term waiving these notices is void.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 11 ('fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the lease'; 'on or before the day the answer is due'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12 ('the tenancy of a tenant who has not received a similar notice from the landlord within the twelve months next preceding the receipt of such notice shall not be determined if the tenant, within ten days after the receipt thereof, pays or tenders'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15A ('the effect of which is to waive the notices required under section eleven or twelve, shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'). The written-lease cure under § 11 has no once-per-12-months limit; the tenant-at-will 10-day cure does. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Required Wording for At-Will Notices
bodyText: Every notice ending a tenancy at will for nonpayment of rent must contain this notification: "If you have not received a notice to quit for nonpayment of rent within the last twelve months, you have a right to prevent termination of your tenancy by paying or tendering to your landlord, your landlord's attorney or the person to whom you customarily pay your rent the full amount of rent due within ten days after your receipt of this notice." If it is left out, the notice stays valid, but the tenant may pay up to the answer date.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12 ('Every notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent shall contain the following notification to the tenant'; 'If you have not received a notice to quit for nonpayment of rent within the last twelve months, you have a right to prevent termination of your tenancy'; 'shall be extended to the day the answer is due in any action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises'; 'Failure to include such notice shall not otherwise affect the validity of the said notice'). Applies to tenancies at will; § 11 (written lease) prescribes no wording. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: State Form With Nonpayment Notice
bodyText: Every written notice to quit for nonpayment you give a residential tenant must be accompanied by the state form developed by the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities. It documents any repayment agreement and gives information on rental assistance, court rules and eviction restrictions. It must prominently display: "THIS NOTICE TO QUIT IS NOT AN EVICTION. YOU DO NOT NEED TO IMMEDIATELY LEAVE YOUR UNIT. YOU ARE ENTITLED TO A LEGAL PROCEEDING IN WHICH YOU CAN DEFEND AGAINST THE EVICTION. ONLY A COURT ORDER CAN FORCE YOU TO LEAVE YOUR UNIT." The court will not accept your nonpayment case without proof you delivered the form.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 31(a) ('shall be accompanied by a form'; 'documentation of any agreements between the tenant and landlord for the tenant to repay the landlord for nonpayment of rent'; 'THIS NOTICE TO QUIT IS NOT AN EVICTION. YOU DO NOT NEED TO IMMEDIATELY LEAVE YOUR UNIT.'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 31(b) ('accept for filing a writ, summons or complaint without proof of delivery of the form required under this section'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Notice to Quit Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A residential lease may not waive the notices to quit Massachusetts requires: the fourteen days' notice for nonpayment and the notice ending a tenancy at will. Any term, in any words, with that effect is void. Whether a term that only shortens a notice counts as a waiver is not stated; treat the statutory periods as minimums. Starting an eviction case before the notice period runs out is also an unfair practice. Lease waivers of the court's power to stay a no-fault eviction are void too.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15A ('by the use of any words whatsoever, the effect of which is to waive the notices required under section eleven or twelve, shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(5)(b) ('Commence summary process for possession of a dwelling unit before the time period designated in the notice to quit'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 12 ('waives the benefits of any provision of sections nine to thirteen, inclusive, shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'). Contrast Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 11A (non-dwelling leases may set their own termination terms). Whether shortening is a waiver: case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Duty to Act on Illegal Use
bodyText: It is a crime to knowingly let your property for prostitution, illegal gaming, illegal alcohol sales or the illegal keeping, sale or manufacture of controlled substances, or to knowingly permit that use. It is also a crime if, after due notice of such use, you fail to take all reasonable measures to remove the occupants as soon as it can lawfully be done. The penalty is a fine of $100 to $1,000, jail of three months to one year, or both. The same uses let you treat the lease as void and seek possession.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 139, § 20 ('Whoever knowingly lets premises owned by him'; 'or after due notice of any such use omits to take all reasonable measures to eject therefrom the persons occupying the same as soon as it can lawfully be done'; 'a fine of not less than one hundred nor more than one thousand dollars or by imprisonment for not less than three months nor more than one year, or both'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 139, § 19 ('at the election of the lessor or owner, annul and make void the lease'). See planned clause criminal-activity-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Nuisance Suits and Building Closure
bodyText: Prosecutors, the Attorney General, police chiefs, or ten legal voters of the city or town may sue to abate a building used for illegal drug or alcohol activity. The court may enjoin you as owner from permitting it and may close the building for one month to one year after repeated convictions or injunctions, but not other occupied units whose occupants were not involved. For prostitution nuisances, closure for a year can follow if you were notified and did not promptly act to end the tenancy. You may reopen early by paying costs and posting a bond.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 139, § 16A ('or by not less than ten legal voters of a town or city'; 'the owner, lessee or agent of the building, place or tenement'; 'for a period of not less than one month nor more than one year'; 'the occupants of which were not involved in said nuisance, no such closing of other occupied dwelling units shall take place'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 139, § 9 ('five or more days after notice to the record owner of the premises, and that he did not proceed forthwith to enforce his rights under section nineteen'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 139, § 11 ('If the owner of any such premises shall pay all costs of the proceedings, and file with the court a bond'). Code receivership with lien priority is under Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127I (slice C topic substandard-property-receivership). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Owner Move-In Termination Right
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no statewide rule giving you a right to end a lease so you or a relative can move in, and none regulating a lease term that reserves one. A tenancy at will can be ended without fault by written notice: three months, or if rent is paid more often, the rental interval or thirty days, whichever is longer. A fixed-term lease ends at its end date. In a no-fault eviction the court may stay the eviction up to six months, or twelve months for a disabled tenant or one aged sixty or older. Check local rules.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery D owner-move-in-reservation: owner/relative occupancy as termination ground: 0 hits; positives passed (synthetic). MA battery D owner-move-in-reservation 2: owner personal use/occupy near tenancy termination: 4 hits; positives passed (ch. 60A, § 1 excise and three CMR environmental/permit documents; none governs tenancies). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12 ('the time of such notice shall be sufficient if it is equal to the interval between the days of payment or thirty days, whichever is longer'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 9 ('for a period not exceeding six months'; 'in the case of premises occupied by a handicapped person or an individual sixty years of age or older'). Whether a mid-term reservation in a fixed-term lease is enforceable: case law not searched. Local: Boston, Cambridge, Somerville and other city ordinances (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no bond a tenant can give to deliver possession at the end of the term, enforced by a confessed judgment. Any contract term by which a party agrees to confess judgment, or authorizes someone to confess it, is void, and a judgment taken under it must be set aside on the defendant's motion. The only possession bond in the eviction statute is the bond a tenant posts to appeal a judgment for possession; it covers rent and losses during the appeal, and an indigent tenant with a non-frivolous defense can have it waived.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery D possession-bond 2: bond to deliver possession / confessed judgment: 9 hits; positives passed (hits are ch. 231, § 13A; ch. 239, §§ 5-6 appeal bonds; UCC and consumer-credit sections; 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.09). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 231, § 13A ('whereby a party thereto agrees to confess judgment in any action which may be brought thereon or authorizes or agrees to authorize another person to confess judgment as aforesaid shall be void'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 5(c) ('all rent accrued at the date of the bond, all intervening rent, and all damage and loss'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 5(e) ('has any defense which is not frivolous and is indigent'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Late Delivery of Possession
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule giving a tenant a set remedy when you cannot deliver possession on the start date. The lease and general contract law decide it. One rule applies: the Attorney General treats it as unfair or deceptive to require rent for periods when the tenant was not obligated to occupy and did not in fact occupy the unit, unless the parties agreed otherwise in writing. Write a lease term that suspends rent until possession and lets the tenant cancel and get all money back after a stated delay.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (statutory failure-to-deliver remedy). MA battery D possession-delay: failure to deliver possession at start of term: 0 hits; positives passed (synthetic). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(6)(d) ('Require payment for rent for periods during which the tenant was not obligated to occupy and did not in fact occupy the dwelling unit unless otherwise agreed to in writing by the parties'). Alternate housing after condemnation: see edu-condemnation-alt-housing-ma (105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.900(E)). MA battery D possession-delay 2: relocation or alternate housing for tenants of unfit premises: 8 hits (ch. 79A and 760 Mass. Code Regs. 27.000 public-acquisition relocation, public housing, 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.000) (supplementary only; its real positive ch. 175, § 99 did not match, recorded as failed; the absence rests on D possession-delay, whose positives passed); no other private-landlord relocation duty. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant Property After Eviction
bodyText: After you win possession, only a sheriff or constable may remove the tenant and their belongings, after at least forty-eight hours' written notice, and never before 9 a.m., after 5 p.m., or on a weekend or legal holiday. The officer stores the property with a licensed, bonded public warehouse within 20 miles, or a facility the tenant chooses in writing. You pay the cost of moving the property to storage and may recover it from the tenant. The warehouse may sell unclaimed property only after six months, and the tenant gets one free visit to retrieve personal items.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 3 ('At least forty-eight hours prior to serving or levying upon an execution'; 'shall be served or levied upon after five o'clock p.m. or before nine o'clock a.m., nor on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 4(a) ('he shall forthwith cause it to be stored for the benefit of the owners thereof'; 'within a 20 mile radius of the land or tenements from which the personal property is removed'); § 4(c) ('The plaintiff in the summary process action shall pay the costs of removing the property to the place of storage'); § 4(e) ('until it has been kept in storage for at least 6 months'); § 4(f) ('The defendant may access his stored property once, without charge'). No landlord immunity provision for writ execution found in the sections read. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Paying After a Nonpayment Judgment
bodyText: After you win a nonpayment eviction, you do not have to accept full payment of the money judgment. But if the judgment is fully paid, together with use and occupancy accrued since judgment, you may not levy the execution for possession. You must return the execution to the court as satisfied, or tell the court so no execution issues. The tenant is then a lawful tenant and can enforce that in court. Earlier, a tenant under a written lease can stop a nonpayment termination by paying all rent due, with interest and costs, by the answer date.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 3 ('has been fully satisfied, together with any use and occupancy accruing since the date of judgment, the plaintiff shall be barred from levying on any execution for possession'; 'the defendant shall be considered a lawful tenant'; 'the plaintiff shall not be required to accept full satisfaction of the money judgment'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 11 ('on or before the day the answer is due'). Partial payment and reservation wording: no MA statute (see edu-no-acceptance-waiver-statute-ma). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Pending Rental Assistance Pauses Eviction
bodyText: In a nonpayment eviction, the court must grant a continuance, and must stay execution, if the tenancy is being ended solely for nonpayment of rent, the nonpayment was due to a financial hardship, and the tenant shows a pending application for emergency rental assistance. The court may not enter judgment or issue an execution until that application is approved or denied. Emergency rental assistance means public-funded programs such as RAFT run by the state housing office, a municipality or a nonprofit on their behalf.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 15(b) ('grant a continuance for a period as the court may deem just and reasonable'; 'the non-payment of rent was due to a financial hardship'; 'a pending application for emergency rental assistance'; 'not enter a judgment or issue an execution before the application for emergency rental assistance has been approved or denied'); § 15(a) ('the residential assistance for families in transition program'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Counterclaims and Rent Paid to Court
bodyText: In a nonpayment or no-fault eviction, a tenant may raise condition and other claims as a defense or counterclaim without first paying rent into court. After hearing the case, the court may order the tenant to pay the clerk the fair value of use and occupation, less any award to the tenant, and may spend those funds on repairs. The tenant may also deposit disputed rent voluntarily. If the tenant's award equals or exceeds what you are owed, you do not get possession. If you are owed more, the tenant keeps possession by paying the balance within one week of the court's notice.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 8A ('shall be entitled to raise, by defense or counterclaim'; 'may require the tenant or occupant claiming under this section to pay to the clerk of the court the fair value of the use and occupation of the premises'; 'voluntarily deposit with the clerk any amount for rent or for use and occupation'; 'within one week after having received written notice from the court of the balance due'; 'Any provision of any rental agreement purporting to waive the provisions of this section shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'). Counterclaims are permissive, not mandatory; no prepayment condition. Appeal: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 5(e) ('pay in installments as the same becomes due, pending appeal'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: False Application Statements
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule giving you a special right to end a lease because the tenant lied on the rental application. A lease term making material false statements a breach is a contract matter, and you must still go through a court eviction. One answer is never false: an applicant with a sealed eviction record may answer "no record" to a question about that sealed record. Do not treat that answer as a misrepresentation.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery D rental-application-accuracy: false application info as lease termination/eviction ground: 1 hit; positives passed (synthetic; hit is ch. 111, § 160F, water treatment device sales). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 16(j) ('may answer 'no record' to an inquiry relative to that sealed court record'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 184, § 18 ('No person shall attempt to recover possession of land or tenements in any manner other than through an action brought pursuant to chapter two hundred and thirty-nine'). See edu-eviction-record-question-ma for the required application statement. Rescission for fraud: case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Retaliation Against Tenants
bodyText: You may not threaten or take reprisals against a tenant for reporting a suspected code or housing-law violation to a board of health or other agency, complaining in writing to you or your agent, suing to enforce housing laws, or organizing or joining a tenants' union. The tenant can recover at least one month's and up to three months' rent, or actual damages if greater, plus costs and attorney's fees. Retaliation is also a defense to eviction, and the defense also protects tenants who seek domestic violence protections or report abuse to police. Lease waivers are void.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 18 ('threatens to or takes reprisals against any tenant of residential premises'; 'reporting or complaining of such violation or suspected violation in writing to the landlord'; 'for organizing or joining a tenants' union'; 'shall not be less than one month's rent or more than three month's rent, or the actual damages sustained by the tenant, whichever is greater'; 'Any waiver of this provision in any lease or other rental agreement shall be void and unenforceable'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 2A ('It shall be a defense to an action for summary process'; 'reporting to any police officer or law enforcement professional an incident of domestic violence'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(6)(b) ('Retaliate or threaten to retaliate in any manner against a tenant'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Six-Month Retaliation Presumption
bodyText: If within six months after a tenant's protected activity you send a notice ending the tenancy (other than for nonpayment of rent), raise the rent, or substantially change the terms, the law presumes it is a reprisal. The same applies to an eviction case or notice to quit in that window. Protected activity by someone else on the tenant's behalf, or relating to the building, also starts the clock. You can rebut the presumption only by clear and convincing evidence that you had independent justification and would have acted the same way, at the same time, anyway.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 18 ('The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months'; 'or within six months after any other person has taken such action or actions on behalf of the tenant or in, or relating to, the building'; 'rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 2A ('or the sending of a notice to quit upon which the summary process action is based'). Note: § 2A's eviction presumption does not carve out nonpayment cases. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: Massachusetts bans every form of self-help eviction. You may recover possession only through a court case, ending with an execution levied by a sheriff or constable. Do not remove the tenant or their belongings, change locks, remove doors, or wilfully cut off required heat, water, electricity or other services to force a move. An excluded tenant may get back in or end the tenancy and recover three months' rent or three times the damages, plus fees. Wilful utility shutoffs and interference with quiet enjoyment separately cost the greater of actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, and are crimes.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 184, § 18 ('No person shall attempt to recover possession of land or tenements in any manner other than through an action brought pursuant to chapter two hundred and thirty-nine'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15F ('the tenant may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, in either case, recover three months' rent or three times the damages sustained by him'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14 ('who willfully or intentionally fails to furnish such water, hot water, heat, light, power, gas'; 'actual and consequential damages or three month's rent, whichever is greater'; 'shall be punished by a fine of not less than twenty-five dollars nor more than three hundred dollars, or by imprisonment for not more than six months'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(5)(a) ('without first obtaining a valid writ of execution for possession'). Related: edu-no-lockout-for-rent-ma, edu-no-utility-cutoff-ma, edu-quiet-enjoyment-statute-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Federal Servicemember Rights Extended
bodyText: Massachusetts extends the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, including its lease-termination and eviction protections, to members of the Massachusetts National Guard and state defense force ordered to active duty by the state or under federal Title 32. Guard members of other states living in Massachusetts on such orders are covered too. A servicemember may sue for actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees; a willful or knowing violation costs the greater of $5,000 or three times the damages. Before a default eviction judgment, you must file an affidavit about the tenant's military service.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 33, § 13A(b) ('shall be entitled to all rights, protections, privileges and immunities afforded under the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act'; 'all members of the armed forces of another state or territory who reside within the commonwealth'); § 13A(f) ('At least 30 days prior to filing an action pursuant to this section, a written demand for relief'); § 13A(g) ('the amount of actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater'; 'the greater of $5,000 or 3 times the amount of the damages'). Uniform Summary Process Rule 10 requires the plaintiff's affidavit that the defendant is not in military service before a default judgment (saved court rules). Federal SCRA text (50 U.S.C. 3955 lease termination) not read; the details of the federal rights are flagged NEEDS_REVIEW. MA battery D servicemember-rights 2: lease termination on military orders / SCRA analog: 6 hits; positives passed (only ch. 33, § 13A extends SCRA; no separate MA lease-termination statute). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Bias Against Service Members
bodyText: Massachusetts fair housing law bars refusing to rent to someone, or giving them different terms, conditions or privileges, because the person is a veteran or a member of the armed forces. It applies to owners, managing agents, brokers and others with the right to rent covered housing. Do not screen out applicants because they may deploy or be transferred.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(6) ('to refuse to rent or lease or sell or negotiate for sale'; 'or because such person is a veteran or member of the armed forces'). Coverage limits and exemptions (e.g. owner-occupied two-family) under ch. 151B, § 4(6)-(7): see portfolio-thresholds row. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Late Benefit Checks and Eviction
bodyText: If a tenant fell behind because a federal, state or municipal agency failed or delayed in mailing or delivering a subsistence or rental payment, check or voucher (other than a salary payment), the court must continue the eviction hearing at least seven days so the agency can be notified. If all rent due, with interest and costs, is tendered to you within that time, the court treats the tenancy as not terminated. This applies to written leases and tenancies at will. It covers benefit checks such as Social Security and rent vouchers.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 11 ('caused by a failure or delay of the federal government, the commonwealth or any municipality'; 'in the mailing or delivery of any subsistence or rental payment, check or voucher other than a salary payment'; 'continue the hearing not less than seven days'; 'treat the tenancy as not having been terminated'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12 (same rule for tenancies at will, 'in any action for possession shall continue the hearing not less than seven days'). Statute does not name Social Security; 'subsistence' payment reading is ours. Related: ch. 239, § 15 rental-assistance continuance (edu-rental-assistance-continuance-ma); ch. 239, § 17 federal-shutdown protections (corpus key GL 221 17). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: When Tenants May End Early
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes let a tenant end a lease early in only a few situations. A tenant or co-tenant may end it by written notice within three months after domestic violence, rape, sexual assault or stalking against a household member. A tenant you exclude without a court order may terminate the rental agreement. A tenant facing certified, unrepaired code violations may treat the lease as abrogated, pay only fair value, and move out. Servicemembers have federal rights, extended to state Guard duty. We found no statute ending a lease for your misrepresentation; that is case law.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 24(a) ('A tenant or co-tenant may terminate a rental agreement or tenancy and quit the premises upon written notification to the owner'; 'within 3 months of the most recent act'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15F ('the tenant may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127L ('treat the lease or rental agreement as abrogated, pay only the fair value of their use and occupation and vacate the premises within a reasonable time'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 33, § 13A(b) ('shall be entitled to all rights, protections, privileges and immunities afforded under the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act'). MA battery D statutory-early-termination 2: tenant statutory right to terminate lease: 8 hits; positives passed (others are UCC goods leases and ch. 93, § 91 consumer goods leases). No omitted-statement forfeiture rule found. Landlord-fraud rescission: case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Voucher Inspections
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule letting you refuse a subsidized tenancy because of the program's inspection, and no statute on a subsidized tenant's refusal of a program inspection. Instead, Massachusetts makes it unlawful for anyone furnishing rental accommodations to discriminate against a tenant receiving housing subsidies or rental assistance, either because of that subsidy or "because of any requirement" of the program. A unit inspection is a program requirement, so refusing a voucher holder over it risks a discrimination claim.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (inspection-specific rule). MA battery D subsidized-inspection-refusal 2: inspection refusal in subsidized tenancy: 2 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are 760 Mass. Code Regs. 38.000 DMH subsidy and 760 Mass. Code Regs. 65.000 short-term housing, neither on refusal). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(10) ('For any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against any individual'; 'who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements'; 'or because of any requirement of such public assistance, rental assistance, or housing subsidy program'). Treating an inspection as a program 'requirement' is our reading; case law not searched. Federal HCV rules not read. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: When a Lease Term Ends
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statewide good-cause rule for ending or not renewing an ordinary private lease. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date. If the tenant stays, you must still bring a court eviction; a tenant at sufferance owes rent for the time they occupy. For a written lease of at least six months, you may file up to thirty days before the end date if you can show the tenant is likely to stay, but no execution issues until after it. The court may stay a no-fault eviction. Foreclosing owners and some formerly subsidized buildings need just cause.
notes: MA: MA battery D surrender-end-of-term: just cause / good cause renewal or eviction: 24 hits; positives passed (synthetic); only Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 2, ch. 40T, § 7 and public-housing provisions require cause. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 1 ('holds possession without right after the determination of a lease by its own limitation'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 3 ('shall be liable to pay rent therefor for such time as they may occupy or detain the same'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 1A ('created for at least six months duration by a written lease'; 'or in any case before thirty days before the designated termination date'; 'No execution for possession may issue in any such action before the day next following the designated termination date'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 2 ('a foreclosing owner shall not evict a tenant except for just cause'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40T, § 7 ('shall not be evicted or involuntarily displaced from his dwelling except for good cause related to tenant fault'). Stays: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 9. Whether the § 9 stay reaches end-of-term holdovers and whether accepting rent after the term creates a tenancy at will: case law not searched. Local: just-cause or notice ordinances (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenancies at Will
bodyText: In Massachusetts, any tenancy created without a writing signed by the landlord or the landlord's attorney is a tenancy at will, whatever rent period the parties use. Either party may end it with written notice: three months, or if rent is paid more often, the rental interval or thirty days, whichever is longer. Selling, transferring or leasing the building, or a foreclosure, does not end it by operation of law. A rooming-house occupancy of three consecutive months becomes a tenancy at will. After a foreclosure sale, a tenant under an unexpired lease is deemed a tenant at will.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183, § 3 ('An estate or interest in land created without an instrument in writing signed by the grantor or by his attorney shall have the force and effect of an estate at will only'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12 ('Estates at will may be determined by either party by three months' notice in writing'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 13 ('shall not be terminated by operation of law by the conveyance, transfer or leasing of the premises by the owner or landlord thereof or by foreclosure'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 17 ('for three consecutive months shall constitute a tenancy at will'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 13A ('shall be deemed a tenant at will'). Notice details: edu-termination-notice-periods-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: You may deduct from the deposit a reasonable repair cost for damage caused by the tenant, anyone under the tenant's control, or anyone on the premises with the tenant's consent, but not reasonable wear and tear. A tenant's statutory repair-and-deduct remedy does not cover conditions caused by the tenant, a household member, or a guest or business invitee. In an eviction, a tenant's condition counterclaim fails if you show the tenant or someone under their control caused it, and a lease waiver of that counterclaim is void. Massachusetts has no casualty-termination statute.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4)(iii) ('caused to the dwelling unit by the tenant or any person under the tenant's control or on the premises with the tenant's consent, reasonable wear and tear excluded'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127L ('shall not extend to conditions or violations caused by a tenant or by a person in the family or household of a tenant or by a business invitee or guest of a tenant'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 8A ('the plaintiff does not show that such conditions were caused by the tenant or occupant or any other person acting under his control'; 'Any provision of any rental agreement purporting to waive the provisions of this section shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.510 ('Every occupant of a residence shall exercise reasonable care in the use of all building and structural elements'). No casualty statute: see edu-no-disaster-tenancy-rule-ma. Under § 8A the tenant bears the burden for violations solely in the tenant's area not reasonably attributable to the landlord. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule ending a lease when a tenant dies, letting a tenant name a contact for their property or deposit, or setting a removal procedure for a deceased tenant's belongings. If a written lease or a tenancy at will ends by the death of a party mid-period, rent is apportioned to the date it ended. Whether a written lease ends at the tenant's death is case law we did not research. This library offers no clause naming a contact for a tenant's death; if you want one, add your own term. A surviving spouse, parent or child who lived there lawfully may ask the court to stay a no-fault eviction. Check the unit for animals.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (death-termination, contact designation, property procedure). MA battery D tenant-death: death of tenant and lease/tenancy/property: 26 hits; positives passed (hits are goods leases, public and manufactured housing, homicide-defense and other off-point sections). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 8 ('or by the death of any party, the landlord or his executor or administrator may recover in contract, a proportional part of such rent'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 9 ('the surviving spouse, parent or child of a deceased tenant if such spouse, parent or child occupied said premises'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 30 (abandoned-animal inspection within 3 days of a unit being vacated). Effect of death on a written lease, and handling of a deceased tenant's property and deposit: probate and case law not searched. Rule 54: lawful option the library does not offer; the row tells the landlord it may add its own term. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Notice to End a Tenancy at Will
bodyText: Either you or the tenant may end a tenancy at will, including month-to-month and week-to-week tenancies, by written notice of three months, or, if rent is payable more often than every three months, a notice equal to the rental interval or thirty days, whichever is longer. A week-to-week tenancy therefore needs thirty days. Your notice may offer a new tenancy on different terms. After a no-fault termination you cannot sue for possession until that period has run from the tenant's receipt of written notice. A fixed-term lease needs no statutory notice to end on its date. A lease cannot waive these notices.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12 ('Estates at will may be determined by either party by three months' notice in writing'; 'the time of such notice shall be sufficient if it is equal to the interval between the days of payment or thirty days, whichever is longer'; 'Such written notice may include an offer to establish a new tenancy'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 13 ('no action to recover possession of the premises shall be brought, nor shall the tenant be dispossessed, until after the expiration of a period'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15A ('the effect of which is to waive the notices required under section eleven or twelve'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 1 ('determination of a lease by its own limitation'). Notices for nonpayment: edu-nonpayment-notice-to-quit-ma. Federal-shutdown limits on notices: ch. 239, § 17 (corpus key GL 221 17; slice A rows). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Ending a Rooming House Occupancy
bodyText: Rooming-house occupancies follow special rules. After more than thirty consecutive days but less than three months, the operator may end an occupancy by seven days' written notice; fraternity, sorority and dormitory rooms follow that rule for any length of stay. Three consecutive months of occupancy creates a tenancy at will. Even then, if rent is payable daily or weekly, seven days' written notice ends it where the occupant is causing a nuisance, substantial damage or substantial interference, and the notice must specify the problem. For a no-fault end with daily or weekly rent, you may sue seven days after written notice.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 17 ('for more than thirty consecutive days and less than three consecutive months'; 'may only be terminated by seven days' notice in writing to the occupant by the operator'; 'for three consecutive months shall constitute a tenancy at will'; 'the notice shall specify the nuisance or interference'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 13 ('in the case of a rooming house, an action to recover possession of premises occupied for dwelling purposes may be brought seven days after written notice if the rent is payable on either a weekly or daily basis'). Occupancies of 30 days or less: no statutory notice found in the sections read. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Removing People Who Never Were Tenants
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no special squatter-removal procedure. The general trespass law applies: a person who enters or remains in a dwelling without right after being forbidden by the person in lawful control may be fined, jailed up to thirty days, and arrested by police. That law does not apply to tenants or occupants who rightfully entered at the start of their tenancy or occupancy and stay after it ends or is said to end; you may remove them only through civil court proceedings. When in doubt, treat a long-term occupant as needing an eviction case.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (squatter-specific removal). MA battery D unauthorized-occupant-removal: squatter / unauthorized occupant removal outside eviction: 4 hits; positives passed (ch. 231, § 85U self-defense; three off-point CMR documents). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 266, § 120 ('Whoever, without right enters or remains in or upon the dwelling house'; 'after having been forbidden so to do by the person who has lawful control of said premises'; 'This section shall not apply to tenants or occupants of residential premises who, having rightfully entered said premises at the commencement of the tenancy or occupancy'; 'The owner or landlord of said premises may recover possession thereof only through appropriate civil proceedings'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 184, § 18. Who counts as having 'rightfully entered' (e.g., a tenant's guest): case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit
bodyText: Massachusetts zoning law says no city or town may prohibit, unreasonably restrict, or require a special permit for one accessory dwelling unit, or its rental, in a single-family zoning district. Towns may still apply reasonable rules such as site plan review, setbacks and height limits, and may restrict or ban short-term rentals of it. A town may not require you to live in either the unit or the main house. A qualifying unit is self-contained with its own entrance and no larger than half the main house or 900 square feet, whichever is smaller. A second unit needs a special permit.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40A, § 3 ('No zoning ordinance or by-law shall prohibit, unreasonably restrict or require a special permit or other discretionary zoning approval for the use of land or structures for a single accessory dwelling unit, or the rental thereof'; 'may be subject to restrictions and prohibitions on short-term rental'; 'shall not require owner occupancy of either the accessory dwelling unit or the principal dwelling'; 'For more than 1 accessory dwelling unit, or rental thereof, in a single-family residential zoning district there shall be a special permit'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40A, § 1A ('is not larger in gross floor area than 1/2 the gross floor area of the principal dwelling or 900 square feet, whichever is smaller'). Landlord-tenant law applies to an ADU tenancy as to any other dwelling. Local: municipal ADU by-laws and short-term rental rules (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Agreed Actual-Notice Rule
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no landlord-tenant rule that requires "actual notice" or lets the parties add their own method, such as a text message, for statutory notices. The notice statutes mostly just require notice in writing. Electronic delivery of ordinary lease notices works only if both parties agreed to deal electronically, but the electronic transactions law does not apply to eviction, default or right-to-cure notices under a rental agreement for a primary residence. Deliver those on paper.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery D actual-notice-method 2: actual notice / agreed notice method in tenancies: 14 hits; positives passed (hits are recording, motor vehicle, criminal and solid-waste provisions and 940 Mass. Code Regs. 10.000/38/40; none sets a tenancy notice method). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12 ('three months' notice in writing'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 110G, § 5(b) ('applies only to transactions between parties each of which has agreed to conduct transactions by electronic means'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 110G, § 3(b) ('foreclosure, or eviction, or the right to cure, under a credit agreement secured by, or a rental agreement for, a primary residence of an individual'). See planned electronic-notice-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Foreclosure Notices to Tenants
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule requiring you to tell tenants or applicants about a pending foreclosure or other claim against the property. Notice duties arise after the fact. A mortgagee that takes possession or conveys title must notify all residential tenants within thirty days. A foreclosing owner must, within thirty days, post and deliver its name, address, phone number, manager and rent address, and may evict only for just cause. A tenant's unexpired lease becomes a tenancy at will on foreclosure, but a subsidized tenant's lease and subsidy contract are assumed.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (pre-foreclosure disclosure duty). MA battery D adverse-proceeding-notice: notice to tenants of foreclosure/proceedings against property: 4 hits; positives passed (ch. 105A, § 4 self-storage; ch. 186A, §§ 1, 3-4). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 244, § 15A ('within thirty days of taking possession or conveying title, notify all residential tenants'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 3 ('Within 30 days of the foreclosure, the foreclosing owner shall post in a prominent location'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 2 ('a foreclosing owner shall not evict a tenant except for just cause'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 13A ('shall be deemed a tenant at will'; 'the foreclosing entity shall assume the lease and rental subsidy contract'). Tenant duty to forward papers: see edu-no-forward-proceedings-duty-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText: Massachusetts has no landlord-tenant statute on automatic renewal clauses, but the Attorney General's fee rule, in force since September 2, 2025, treats an automatic renewal as a "Negative Option Feature" and expressly covers dwelling units for rent. If your lease renews unless the tenant cancels, disclose clearly, conspicuously and in writing before signing that charges will recur and how to cancel; give a simple cancellation method; and for renewals longer than 31 days, send written notice 5 to 30 days before the cancellation deadline. Whether this reaches every lease renewal is untested.
notes: MA: 940 Mass. Code Regs. 38.03 ('Negative Option Feature'; 'an automatic renewal'; 'Product shall include memberships, subscriptions, and dwelling units available for rent or lease'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 38.05(2) ('For any Product with a Negative Option Feature, failing to disclose Clearly and Conspicuously and in writing, prior to the consumer's purchase of the Product'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 38.05(3) ('failing to provide a simple mechanism for a consumer to cancel the Negative Option Feature'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 38.05(4) ('For any Negative Option Feature exceeding 31 days, failing to provide the consumer written notice within no more than 30 and no fewer than five calendar days prior'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 38.09 ('shall apply to acts committed or practices in force as of September 2, 2025'). MA battery D automatic-renewal: automatic renewal / extension clauses: 10 hits; positives passed (synthetic); no landlord-tenant statute (ch. 93, § 90 is rent-to-own goods). Application to residential lease renewals and to month-to-month continuation clauses: untested; case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Other Rules Massachusetts Lacks
bodyText: Three protections found in some other states do not exist in Massachusetts statutes or regulations. (1) No ban on letting the same room or unit to two tenants at once, and no statutory remedy for it; general contract and consumer-protection law applies. (2) No rule making smoke-alarm compliance inadmissible in an injury case or barring insurers from reducing payment over it. (3) No special right to end a lease for a false rental application. By contrast, Massachusetts does ban card surcharges in sales transactions; whether that reaches rent is unsettled.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery D confirmed-absences-misc: double letting of the same room/unit: 0 hits; positives passed (synthetic). MA battery D confirmed-absences-misc 3: smoke detector compliance as evidence / insurance shield: 0 hits; positives passed (synthetic). MA battery D rental-application-accuracy: false application info as lease termination/eviction ground: 1 hit (off point); positives passed. Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Card surcharges: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 140D, § 28A ('No seller in any sales transaction may impose a surcharge on a cardholder'); see edu-credit-card-surcharge-ma. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Checked Across the Whole Code
bodyText: We searched all Massachusetts statutes, regulations and court rules, not just the landlord-tenant laws, for three things landlords ask about. (1) No squatter-specific removal procedure; general trespass law reaches only people who never rightfully entered. (2) No duty to give a receipt for ordinary monthly rent, even in cash; receipts are required only for last month's rent and the security deposit. (3) No statewide rule that a rental registration or license is a precondition to winning possession. Cities may have their own registration rules.

title: No Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule letting tenants house people displaced by a disaster despite lease guest or occupancy limits, and none limiting such stays or saying when a displaced guest becomes a tenant. Your ordinary guest and occupancy terms apply, subject to fair housing law and the sanitary code. Separately, a fire insurance policy on a multi-unit rental must carry a relocation benefit for tenants displaced by fire. Consider flexibility for displaced family members after a declared emergency.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText: Massachusetts has not moved its protection-order laws: abuse prevention orders remain in chapter 209A and harassment prevention orders in chapter 258E, which the tenant-protection statutes still cite. A 2024 law added "coercive control" to chapter 209A's definition of abuse, but the lease-termination and lock-change statutes use their own, narrower definition of domestic violence, so quote that one in leases. One stale cross-reference: the lease statutes define "owner" by citing a sanitary-code section that the 2023 revision renumbered; the definition now sits in the code's general definitions section.

title: Signing Leases Electronically
bodyText: Massachusetts has adopted the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act. If both parties agree to do business electronically, an electronic signature satisfies a law requiring a signature, and an electronic record satisfies a law requiring a writing, so a lease may be signed electronically. A tenant who agreed to one electronic transaction may refuse others, and that right cannot be waived. The act does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for a primary residence, so serve notices to quit on paper.

title: Tenants Who Call Police
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no general rule guaranteeing a tenant's right to call police or emergency services or voiding lease terms that penalize such calls. Massachusetts does protect domestic violence reports: evicting a tenant for reporting domestic violence, rape, sexual assault or stalking against a household member to police, or for seeking a protection order, is a defense to eviction, and action within six months is presumed retaliatory. Do not write lease terms that penalize calls for help.

title: No Pre-Suit Dispute Statute
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule authorizing or regulating lease clauses that require informal resolution or mediation before going to court. A written agreement to arbitrate future disputes is generally valid under the state arbitration act. But a lease term waiving the tenant's right to a jury trial is void, and so is a waiver of the tenant's right to raise defenses and counterclaims in an eviction. Keep eviction cases out of any such clause, and do not use it to delay a tenant's statutory remedies. Courts already use pre-trial mediation in eviction cases.

title: Landlord Insurance Rules
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule requiring residential landlords to carry liability insurance, except that short-term rental operators must carry it unless the booking platform does. Two insurance rules do apply. Within fifteen days of a tenant's or official's written request, you must disclose in writing the company insuring the property against fire, the amount of coverage, and who would be paid for a loss; the fine is up to $500. If you own multi-unit property, its fire policy carries a tenant relocation benefit, and you must tell each tenant in writing about that benefit at the start of the tenancy. Lease waivers of either rule are void.

title: Registration and Licensing
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no statewide registration or license for ordinary residential rentals, and no rule making registration a condition of eviction. Two kinds of rentals do need state-law licenses. A lodging house, where lodgings are let to four or more people outside the operator's close family, needs a local license; operating without one can bring a fine of $100 to $500 or jail. A short-term rental operator needs a state certificate of registration, must carry at least $1,000,000 of liability insurance unless the booking platform does, and may face local licensing. Many cities add their own rules.

title: No Crime-Free Lease Statute
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule requiring or regulating crime-free lease addenda, and no duty to give police or child-protection investigators information about tenants. The rules that do apply limit what such terms can do. You may treat a lease as void when a tenant uses the unit for listed illegal purposes such as drug dealing, and after notice of such use you must take reasonable lawful steps to remove the occupants. Evicting a tenant for reporting domestic violence to police is a defense to eviction. Eviction still requires a court case.

title: No Blank-Space Rule
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule that every blank in a lease must be filled in, or that a blank is a breach. But certain items must appear. The Attorney General treats it as unfair or deceptive to sign a written rental agreement that fails to state fully and conspicuously the owner's and any manager's names, addresses and phone numbers, the person authorized to receive notices and accept service of process, and the deposit amount with the tenant's deposit rights. Fill those in before anyone signs.

title: Give the Tenant a Signed Copy
bodyText: Within thirty days after the tenant signs a written lease or rental agreement, give the tenant a copy signed by you; failing to do so is an unfair or deceptive practice under the Attorney General's rules, which exposes you to consumer-protection claims. Where you agreed orally to sign a lease and got the tenant's signature, a separate statute also imposes a fine of up to $300 for missing that deadline, and a lease waiver of it is void. Neither rule says that a late copy makes the lease unenforceable.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule requiring a tenant to initial a lease term, such as a notice period longer than the law requires, for it to bind the tenant. The statutory notice to end a tenancy at will runs both ways, and Massachusetts says nothing about lengthening it by agreement. A lease cannot shorten or waive the statutory notices. Initials remain good practice for unusual terms.

title: Lease Length and Signatures
bodyText: Massachusetts sets no maximum lease term, but how a lease is made limits it. Any tenancy created without a writing signed by you or your attorney is only a tenancy at will, whatever term the parties intended. A lease for more than seven years binds buyers and lenders without actual notice of it only if the lease or a notice of lease is recorded at the registry of deeds. A lease of 100 years or more is treated like ownership while 50 years remain. Get every lease signed by all parties.

title: Absentee and Out-of-State Owners
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule requiring an out-of-state owner to appoint an in-state agent or broker, and none requiring tenants to withhold tax from rent paid to a nonresident. Absentee owners still have contact duties. If you do not live in the building, post a notice of at least twenty square inches near the mailboxes or inside with your name, address and phone number, plus any non-resident manager's. A separate statute fines an owner without a resident manager up to $50 a day for not posting. Your written lease must also name the person authorized to accept service of process for you.

title: Delivering Notices
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes require notices to quit to be in writing but do not say how they must be delivered or who may deliver them. Use a method you can prove, such as hand delivery by a constable or certified and first-class mail. Electronic delivery does not count for eviction, default or cure notices on a primary residence. You must accept notices from tenants sent to the address where rent is customarily sent, given to the person who customarily accepts for you, or sent to the person your lease names to receive notices.

title: Extra Terms in Quit Notices
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no required warning for a move-out notice form that adds terms not in the lease. One related rule helps you: a written notice ending a tenancy at will may include an offer of a new tenancy on different terms, and the offer does not make the notice invalid. Keep a nonpayment notice to quit to the facts, include the required wording for tenants at will, and attach the state form. Do not bury new obligations in a document the tenant signs to give notice.

title: Where Your Lease Decides
bodyText: Several Massachusetts rules depend on what a written lease says, and a silent lease takes the default against you. You pay for electricity and gas unless the unit has its own meter and a written rental agreement makes the tenant pay; heating oil works the same way with a separate tank. You supply the stove and refrigerator unless the written agreement requires the tenant to. The tenant clears snow and ice from exits in their exclusive control only if the written agreement clearly says so. Separate water charges, tax escalation and automatic rent increases each need specific written terms. A landlord attorney-fee clause automatically becomes mutual.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no general plain-language or readability law for residential leases, and no required statement listing the tenant's waivers or consumer restrictions. Narrower rules apply. A written rental agreement must state the owner and manager contacts, the person who accepts service, and the deposit amount and the tenant's deposit rights fully and conspicuously, in simple and readily understandable language. A water submetering arrangement must be disclosed in plain language. Automatic rent increase conditions must be stated clearly and conspicuously.

title: Small Landlords and Building Size
bodyText: Most Massachusetts landlord-tenant duties do not change with how many units you own, though fair housing coverage and who pays for disability modifications can turn on owning ten or more units on contiguous land. Some rules turn on the building instead. Most of the fair housing law does not apply to leasing one unit of a two-family house when you live in the other unit, but the ban on discriminating against tenants who receive public assistance or a housing subsidy still applies. If the home is publicly assisted housing, the other fair housing bans apply too, except the rule on families with children, which keeps its own two-family exemption. The duty to fix unsafe conditions after a tenant's certified-mail notice does not apply to owner-occupied two- or three-family homes. In a single-unit building the tenant handles pests and pays for trash collection; with two or more units you do. Multi-unit fire policies carry a tenant relocation benefit. A lodging house with four or more unrelated lodgers needs a license.
