title: Code Duties Follow Control
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule saying that a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage cannot let someone collect rent free of habitability duties. The sanitary code reaches the same people another way: "owner" includes anyone with legal title, anyone with care, charge or control of the residence in any capacity, including an agent or trustee, a mortgagee in possession, and a court-appointed receiver. A lease term waiving the tenant's statutory condition remedies is void.

title: Requiring Renters Insurance
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule that permits, bars or limits a lease requirement that the tenant carry renters insurance, and no required notice that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings. Requiring a policy the tenant buys directly from an insurer is not addressed. But at or before move-in you may collect only first and last month's rent, a deposit and a lock and key cost, so do not charge a premium, enrollment or administrative fee then. Renters policies may exclude claims from short-term rentals by the tenant.

title: When the Building Changes Hands
bodyText: Selling, transferring or leasing the building does not end a tenancy at will, and a buyer takes subject to it. A new owner who receives security deposits must, within forty-five days, tell each tenant in writing that it holds the deposit, with its name, business address and phone number and its agent's. The new owner is liable for deposits even if the seller never transferred them. Absentee owners must update the posted contact notice near the mailboxes, including any new manager. After a foreclosure, separate notice and just-cause rules apply to the foreclosing owner.

No MA seller-disclosure duty about tenancies found in the sections read. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Which Massachusetts Rules Apply
bodyText: Massachusetts has no single landlord-tenant act; its rules apply statewide to residential tenancies of every size. Watch the carve-outs. The security deposit law does not cover vacation or recreational rentals of 100 days or less. The utility, quiet-enjoyment and no-fault notice statutes exclude hotel rooms. Rooming houses follow special notice rules. Sites in a manufactured housing community, three or more manufactured homes on one tract, have a separate licensing and tenancy regime. The sanitary code does not apply to state-owned residences, temporary overnight shelters, licensed nursing or rest homes, or federal military bases.

title: Prescribed Texts and Forms
bodyText: Massachusetts prescribes exact wording for several landlord documents. Copy each word for word. If you take a security deposit, your statement of condition must carry the statutory notice in twelve-point bold-face type at the top of its first page. A notice ending a tenancy at will for nonpayment must contain the statutory notification of the tenant's right to cure. A nonpayment notice to quit must be accompanied by the state housing office's form. A rental application that asks about prior evictions must include the statutory "no record" statement. For a unit built before 1978, before the rental agreement is signed give the state lead notification materials and certification form, along with a copy of the most recent lead inspection report, letter of interim control, letter of compliance or abatement plan, if any exists. For every unit, give each occupant, or post, the health department's Notice of Occupants' Legal Rights and Responsibilities.

title: Protecting Tenant Personal Information
bodyText: If you keep a tenant's or applicant's name together with a Social Security number, driver's license or state ID number, or a bank account or card number, Massachusetts data-security law applies to you. You must keep a written information security program with administrative, technical and physical safeguards suited to your size. If that information is breached, you must give notice to the Attorney General, the state consumer affairs office and the affected person. Shred or destroy old records holding it; fines run up to $100 per person affected.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93H, § 1(a) ('"Personal information" a resident's first name and last name or first initial and last name in combination with any 1 or more of the following data elements'); 201 Mass. title: No Rent Ledger Duty
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes, regulations and court rules and found no duty to give a tenant a rent ledger or payment history, and no rule limiting what you may tell third parties about a tenant. Two record duties do apply. If you hold a security deposit, keep the statutory deposit record and let the tenant inspect it on request during business hours. If you sue for unpaid rent, the court's summary process complaint asks you to itemize the amount claimed or attach a rent ledger, so keep an accurate one.

title: Tenant Insurance Claims
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule on whether you may require a tenant to claim on the tenant's own renters insurance, or may claim on it yourself. Two rules limit the idea. Sanitary code repairs are your job, and a lease cannot waive them. A lease term that has the tenant indemnify you, hold you harmless or release you for your own negligence or misconduct is void. So do not make a tenant's policy pay for repairs or losses that are yours.

title: No Sunsetting Tenant Laws
bodyText: As of October 8, 2026, we found no repeal or expiration date on Massachusetts's core landlord-tenant statutes, including the security deposit, notice, eviction and retaliation laws. The only dated changes we found are amendments already in force, such as the broker-fee and up-front-payment changes effective August 1, 2025. One protection is temporary by design: the federal-shutdown protections apply only during a shutdown and a short period after it. Recheck each year, because the legislature amends these laws often.

Laws ch. 186, § 15B ('effective until August 1, 2025') and Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 112, § 87DDD1/2, plus ch. 111, § 197 letter-of-interim-control expiry; none repeals a tenant protection). Version-note scan of chs. 111, 140, 184, 186, 186A, 239, 151B: no 'effective until' note after 2026. Session laws 2023-2026 sentence scan (scratch script, not battery-logged): no repeal of tenant protections. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 17 (federal shutdown protections, time-limited by their terms; see edu-shutdown-late-fee-ma). Session laws before 2023 not saved or searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Changing Tenancy Terms
bodyText: Massachusetts has no separate notice rule for changing lease terms, and no special rule for raising a fee the lease already provides. For a tenancy at will, change any term, not just rent, the same way: give written notice ending the tenancy, three months or, if rent is paid more often, the rental interval or thirty days, whichever is longer, and offer a new tenancy on the new terms. During a fixed-term lease, terms change only as the lease allows. A substantial change in terms within six months after protected tenant activity is presumed retaliatory.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12 ('Estates at will may be determined by either party by three months' notice in writing'; 'Such written notice may include an offer to establish a new tenancy for the same premises on terms different from that of the tenancy being terminated'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 18 ('of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months'). No term-change or fee-increase notice rule found: MA battery A rent-increase-notice (logged by slice A; only manufactured housing and public housing). Fixed-term mid-lease changes are contract law; case law not searched. Up-front money and late-charge limits still bind any new fee (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)-(c)). See edu-rent-increase-notice-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no duty to translate a lease, even if you advertise or negotiate in another language, and no minimum type size for the lease itself. The one type-size rule for landlords is the statement of condition, whose statutory notice must appear in twelve-point bold-face type. Translation duties fall on government: board of health orders carry a translated warning, and the state housing office publishes the nonpayment notice form's information in the five most common languages besides English.

title: Assistance Animals Under State Law
bodyText: Massachusetts fair housing law makes it discrimination to refuse a reasonable accommodation in your rules, policies, practices or services that a person with a disability may need to use and enjoy a dwelling. A no-pets rule is such a rule. The law also separately bars discriminating in rental terms because a person has a trained dog guide due to blindness or hearing impairment. The statute does not mention emotional support animals, documentation or pet fees; those points rest on the accommodation duty and federal law. Leasing one unit of a two-family home you live in is exempt from the main rental provision.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(7A)(2) ('a refusal to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices, or services, when such accommodations may be necessary to afford a handicapped person equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 1(13) ('made generally available to the public')). title: Pet Deposits and Pet Rent
bodyText: Massachusetts has no pet-fee statute, so the general money rules decide. At or before move-in you may collect only first and last month's rent, one security deposit no larger than the first month's rent, and a lock and key cost. A refundable pet deposit is not a separate category, so treat it as part of that one capped deposit, with all deposit-law duties. After move-in you may not demand a deposit above that cap. Monthly pet rent is not addressed; if charged, collect it like rent, never in advance beyond the current month. Never charge pet fees for an assistance animal.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b) ('no lessor or agent of the lessor may require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay, to the lessor or to an agent of the lessor, any amount in excess of the following'; 'a security deposit equal to the first month's rent'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(d) ('demand rent in advance in excess of the current month's rent or a security deposit in excess of the amount allowed by this section'). Assistance animals: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(7A)(2) (accommodation duty); no-fee rule rests on federal law (not reviewed). Nonrefundable pet fees: see edu-no-nonrefundable-deposit-ma. title: Limits on Pet Rules
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute on pets in private rentals, so you may ban, limit or approve pets in the lease, subject to assistance-animal rules. Three limits apply. A lease may not let you enter to remove a pet; entry is allowed only to inspect, repair or show the unit, by court order, or if the unit appears abandoned. A lease term making the tenant indemnify you for your own negligence is void, so pet indemnities must exclude it. Within 3 days after a unit is vacated, inspect it for abandoned animals and report any to animal control or the police.

title: Dog Guide Access Penalty
bodyText: Massachusetts makes it an offense to deprive a blind, deaf or hearing-impaired, or other physically handicapped person accompanied by a dog guide of the accommodations of a place of public accommodation. The fine is up to three hundred dollars, plus damages to the person harmed. Public accommodation is defined to include the common halls of buildings and lodging for transient or permanent guests, but whether it reaches an ordinary apartment is unsettled. In housing generally, refusing a dog guide or other assistance animal is a civil fair housing violation.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 272, § 98A ('accompanied by a dog guide, shall be entitled to any and all accommodations, advantages, facilities and privileges'; 'shall be punished by a fine of not more than three hundred dollars'; 'such damages as are set forth in section five of chapter one hundred and fifty-one B'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 272, § 92A ('meeting place or hall, including the common halls of buildings'; 'resort for transient or permanent guests or patrons seeking housing or lodging'). Whether § 98A reaches residential rentals: case law not searched. Civil fair-housing basis: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(6)(b), (7)(b), (7A)(2). title: No Animal Misrepresentation Crime
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no law making it an offense to misrepresent a pet as a service or assistance animal, in housing or anywhere else, and no state rule on what documentation you may request. If you doubt a request, handle it through the reasonable accommodation process under fair housing law rather than by accusing the tenant of fraud. Do not charge a fee or penalty for a disputed assistance animal request.

title: Towing From Your Property
bodyText: You may have a vehicle towed from your private way or lot only if its driver was forbidden to park there, either directly or by a posted notice. A tenant's own car can be towed on that basis too. Before any tow without the vehicle owner's consent, notify the police chief, in Boston the police commissioner, usually in writing, with the addresses, plate number and names the statute lists. Towing and storage charges are capped at the state's police-tow rates. A tow that skips these steps must release the car free, and authorizing it carries a fine of up to one hundred dollars.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 266, § 120D ('unless the operator of such vehicle has been forbidden so to park or stand, either directly or by posted notice, by the person who has lawful control of such way or property'; 'Such notification shall be made before any such vehicle shall be removed, and shall be in writing unless otherwise specified'; 'Any person who purports to authorize the removal of a vehicle from a way or property as aforesaid without having fully complied with the provision of this section shall be punished by a fine of not more than one hundred dollars'; 'shall release such vehicle to its owner without assessing any charges for its removal or storage'). Rate caps tie to ch. 159B, § 6B; 220 CMR (DPU towing rates) is not in the saved corpus and was not read. Abandoning a vehicle on another's property is fined under Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 90, § 22B(a) ('without the permission of the owner or lessee of said property shall be fined two hundred and fifty dollars'). title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no tenant right to install electric vehicle charging equipment, and no rules for a tenant's charger in shared parking or at the end of a tenancy. Whether to allow one, and on what terms, is up to you and the lease. This library offers no charger clause; if you allow one, put your terms in your own addendum. Massachusetts does protect unit owners: a condominium or homeowners' association may not prohibit or unreasonably restrict an owner's charger in the owner's own or exclusive-use space. If you own a condominium unit, that right is yours, at your expense, installed by a licensed electrician.

title: No Residential Parking Statute
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule on parking in residential leases. Nothing requires you to provide parking, deliver parking rules before signing, use a set heading, separate parking charges from rent, or limit changes to parking rules or space assignments during the term. Parking is governed by the lease. Two general rules still apply: you may not collect a parking deposit or fee at or before move-in beyond the permitted up-front payments, and towing must follow the private-property towing statute. Check local ordinances.

title: Tenant Storage Spaces
bodyText: Massachusetts's self-service storage law covers facilities that rent storage spaces for occupants to store and remove their own property. Its lien and sale procedure is written for those facility operators, not for a storage locker that comes with an apartment, so do not rely on it to sell a tenant's stored belongings. Massachusetts gives residential landlords no lien on tenant property. Rules for a tenant's storage space, such as banning hazardous materials, come from the lease.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 105A, § 1 ('"Self-service storage facility", any real property used for renting or leasing individual storage spaces in which the occupants themselves customarily store and remove their own personal property'); Mass. Whether ch. 105A could reach storage leased with a dwelling is not addressed; case law not searched. No residential landlord lien: see edu-no-landlord-lien-ma. Fire code (527 CMR) and building code (780 CMR) are not in the saved corpus and were not searched for storage limits. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Cannabis Rules in Leases
bodyText: Massachusetts lets a property owner prohibit or regulate the consumption, display, production, processing, manufacture or sale of marijuana on property it owns or manages, so you may ban smoking and home growing. The one limit: a lease may not stop a tenant from consuming marijuana by means other than smoking at home, unless allowing it would make you violate federal law. Without a lease ban, adults 21 or older may grow up to 6 plants in their primary residence, 12 per premises. The medical marijuana statute gives patients no extra housing protection.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 94G, § 2(d)(1) ('prevent a person from prohibiting or otherwise regulating the consumption, display, production, processing, manufacture or sale of marijuana and marijuana accessories on or in property the person owns, occupies or manages'; 'a lease agreement shall not prohibit a tenant from consuming marijuana by means other than smoking'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 94G, § 7(a)(2) ('within the person's primary residence'; 'not more than 6 marijuana plants for personal use so long as not more than 12 plants are cultivated on the premises at once'). Interaction with a criminal-activity clause: state-lawful possession is not a state crime, federal status not reviewed. See edu-marijuana-vaping-limit-ma; planned cannabis-cultivation-ma. title: No Waterbed Statute
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals. Nothing gives a tenant a right to one, and nothing limits a lease term banning them or requiring consent or insurance. The lease governs. If you require the tenant to carry insurance for one, the tenant buys it directly; do not collect a premium or fee at or before move-in.

title: Flags, Signs and Religious Items
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no tenant right to display a flag, political sign or religious item that overrides a lease rule, and no limit on lease rules about displays. Your lease may regulate signs and displays. Fair housing law still applies: you may not discriminate because of religious creed in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, so apply display rules evenly and consider allowing small religious items such as a door-frame mezuzah.

title: No Candidate Access Rule
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule requiring you to let political candidates, campaign workers or voter registration volunteers into a multi-unit building, and no duty to set aside an area for voter information. Access to locked common areas for canvassing is up to you. Tenants themselves may still invite visitors to their own units.

title: Tenant Security Cameras
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule giving tenants a right to install security cameras or video doorbells, or limiting lease rules about them. The lease governs. One caution applies to anyone, landlord or tenant: Massachusetts makes it unlawful to secretly hear or secretly record a conversation with a device unless all parties consent. A camera or doorbell that records audio in hallways or common areas can create risk, so address audio recording in your rules.

MA battery E tenant-security-cameras: tenant cameras / video doorbells: 2 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits ch. 64H, § 6 tax exemptions and 400 Mass. Code Regs. 9.000 data centers, off point). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 272, § 99(B)(4) ('to secretly hear, secretly record, or aid another to secretly hear or secretly record the contents of any wire or oral communication'; 'by any person other than a person given prior authority by all parties to such communication'). How the wiretap law applies to doorbell audio: case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant Air Conditioners
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no tenant right to install a window or portable air conditioner, and no cooling standard you must meet. Your lease may allow, limit or ban tenant units. If a tenant installs their own air conditioner, the sanitary code makes the occupant responsible for installing it properly and keeping it free of leaks and defects. If you install one, you must keep it in operable condition.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (tenant cooling-device right; cooling standard). MA battery E portable-cooling-device: tenant air conditioner right: 19 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are tax, energy, zoning and equipment-maintenance provisions, none a tenant installation right). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.240(A) ('The occupant shall ensure proper installation in compliance with accepted standards'; 'all occupant owned and installed equipment'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.235 ('all owner installed equipment'). Owner-installed air conditioners are listed in 410.235(B). Local: city cooling or heat ordinances (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Solar Restriction Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts has no tenant plug-in or balcony solar statute. But a general law voids any provision in an instrument relating to the ownership or use of real property that forbids or unreasonably restricts installing or using a solar energy system. That law is written broadly enough that it might reach a lease, though no statute says so, so whether a lease ban on a tenant's solar device is enforceable is unsettled. Rather than an outright ban, use reasonable conditions on placement, safety and removal.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 184, § 23C ('Any provision in an instrument relative to the ownership or use of real property which purports to forbid or unreasonably restrict the installation or use of a solar energy system'; 'shall be void'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40A, § 1A ('"Solar energy system", a device or structural design feature'). Whether a residential lease is such an instrument, and whether a portable plug-in device qualifies: case law not searched. No tenant-specific solar statute: MA battery E portable-solar 2: solar device with tenant/landlord context (all corpora): 2 hits; positives passed (hits ch. 40A, § 3 zoning and ch. 183A, § 10 condominium energy measures, off point). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Firearms in Rentals
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule that bars or protects a private lease term restricting a tenant's lawful firearms, including firearms kept in vehicles in your parking area. The lease governs, subject to fair housing law. Separate rules let public housing authorities and certain subsidized landlords act against illegal weapon possession; those do not govern private leases.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (lease firearm restriction rule; parking-lot firearm rule). MA battery E firearms 2: firearm and tenant/lease in same sentence: 10 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are firearm licensing in ch. 140, §§ 121B-131A (renting or leasing of firearms), public and subsidized housing eviction grounds in Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 121B, § 32C ('possessed or carried a weapon in violation of section 10 of chapter 269'), and 501 Mass. Code Regs. 7.000). MA battery E firearms: firearm restrictions in leases/rentals: 28 hits (broad; same result). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Guest Rules
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule limiting lease terms on guests, setting a guest stay limit, barring guest fees, or giving guests or service providers access rights. The lease governs. Keep in mind that a guest who becomes an occupant cannot be removed without court process, that occupancy may not exceed sanitary code space limits, and that guest rules may not be applied differently because of a protected class, such as the presence of children.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (guest limits, guest fees, guest access rights). MA battery E guest-policy: tenant guests / visitors rules: 18 hits; positives passed (synthetic; landlord-relevant hits only invitee carve-outs in Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 19 and ch. 111, § 127L, condominium occupant reporting in Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 4 ('other than visitors for less than thirty days'), and public housing rules (760 Mass. Code Regs. 4.000, 6)). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(11) ('because such person has a child or children who occupy or shall occupy the premises'). See edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-ma, edu-occupancy-space-standard-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Key and Rekeying Charges
bodyText: At or before the start of a tenancy you may charge the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock, and nothing more for keys. Massachusetts sets no rule on charging a tenant who loses or fails to return keys. But the security deposit may be used only for unpaid rent or water charges, tax escalation and damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, so whether rekeying for unreturned keys can come out of the deposit is unsettled. Bill it separately instead. Different rules apply to lock changes for domestic violence victims.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b) ('the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4) ('a reasonable amount necessary to repair any damage caused to the dwelling unit by the tenant'; 'reasonable wear and tear excluded'). Whether an unreturned key is damage to the dwelling unit: case law not searched. No lost-key or rekey charge rule: see MA battery MA-C rekey locks at change of tenancy (recorded as failed: its real positive ch. 186, § 26 did not match; the broader MA-C lock change or rekey any context passed; see edu-no-rekey-peephole-rule-ma). Domestic violence lock changes: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 26 (see edu-dv-lock-change-ma). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: House Rules
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute on apartment house rules, so they bind a tenant as part of the rental agreement. A rule may not require anything unlawful; a lease term that violates any law is an unfair or deceptive practice. Changing rules mid-tenancy follows the tenancy type: for a tenancy at will, give a termination notice offering new terms; during a fixed-term lease, change rules only as the lease allows. A substantial change in terms within six months after protected tenant activity is presumed retaliatory.
notes: MA: 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(3)(a)1 ('include in any rental agreement any term which: 1. Violates any law'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12 ('Such written notice may include an offer to establish a new tenancy for the same premises on terms different from that of the tenancy being terminated'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 18 ('of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months'). No residential house-rule statute: MA battery E rules-regulations: landlord house rules enforceability: 2 hits (sports wagering, off point); MA battery E rules-regulations 2 (#346): changing rules during tenancy: 2 hits (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 140, § 32L manufactured housing communities; 760 Mass. Code Regs. 6.000 public housing); real positive § 32L passed, synthetic failed on word order. Order-independent reruns: #388 (General Laws): 2 hits, ch. 140, § 32L and ch. 93H, § 2 (off point), positives passed; #389 (General Laws, Constitution, CMR, court rules): 5 hits, adding 760 Mass. Code Regs. 6.000, 940 Mass. Code Regs. 10.00 (manufactured housing) and 105 Mass. Code Regs. 164.000 (treatment programs), none a house-rule rule for ordinary private rentals; positives passed. Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Fixed-term rule changes are contract law; case law not searched. See planned rules-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Snow and Ice on Exits
bodyText: In a single-unit home, the tenant must keep all exits free from obstruction. In a multi-unit building, you must keep common exits clear and keep every exterior stairway, fire escape, egress balcony and bridge free of snow and ice. A tenant there is responsible for snow and ice only on exits under the tenant's exclusive use and control, and only if a written rental agreement clearly identifies that duty. Shared walks and exits stay your job. Towns may also require sidewalk clearing.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.260(C) ('In a single unit residence, the occupant shall maintain free from obstruction all means of egress'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.260(D)(1)-(2) ('The owner shall maintain free from obstruction every means of egress in common areas'; 'They are maintained free of snow and ice'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.260(D)(4) ('The occupant is responsible for maintaining free of snow and ice, the means of egress under their exclusive use and control, provided there is a written rental agreement that clearly identifies the occupant's responsibility'). Whether snow is an 'obstruction' under 410.260(C) is not defined. Local: municipal sidewalk snow-removal ordinances (flagged, not researched). See edu-code-duties-written-agreement-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Bed Bug Disclosure
bodyText: Massachusetts has no bed-bug-specific disclosure. But you must tell a prospective tenant about any condition in the unit that violates the law if you know of it or could find it by a reasonable inspection, and the sanitary code counts bed bugs as pests. In a building with two or more units, a pest infestation is your code violation. You must also inspect each unit for pests before a new occupancy and keep the results. So disclose a known current infestation, and treat it before move-in.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (bed-bug-specific disclosure). MA battery E bed-bug-disclosure: bed bug disclosure/history: 1 hit; positives passed (synthetic; only 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.000). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.010 ('Insects including, but not limited to, mosquitoes, bees, flies, ants, termites, cockroaches and bed bugs'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.550(B) ('shall maintain it and its premises free from infestation and shall be responsible for pest elimination'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.550(F) ('shall conduct an inspection of each unit prior to a new occupancy to identify the presence of pests'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(c) ('Fail to disclose to a prospective tenant the existence of any condition amounting to a violation of law within the dwelling unit'). No duty found to disclose past (treated) infestations. Single-unit homes: occupant responsible unless owner failed structural upkeep (410.550(A)). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Occupancy Certificate Disclosure
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and the saved regulations and found no duty to tell a tenant whether the unit has a certificate of occupancy, or to give the tenant a copy. The State Building Code was not in our sources, and many cities and towns run their own rental inspection or certificate programs, so check local rules before renting.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (certificate of occupancy disclosure). MA battery E certificate-of-occupancy-disclosure: CO disclosure to tenants: 14 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are tax, energy, septic, waterways, housing-program and home-inspection rules; none requires disclosure to tenants). Searched General Laws, Constitution, saved CMR and court rules; the State Building Code (780 CMR) is not in the saved corpus and was not searched. Local: municipal certificate-of-fitness or rental inspection ordinances (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule requiring you to disclose defective or corrosive drywall to a tenant. If drywall causes a condition that violates the sanitary code, the general duty to disclose known code violations to a prospective tenant applies.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (defective drywall disclosure). MA battery E defective-drywall-disclosure: defective drywall: 0 hits; positives passed (synthetic). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(c) ('Fail to disclose to a prospective tenant the existence of any condition amounting to a violation of law within the dwelling unit'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Flood Disclosure
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule requiring you to tell a tenant that the property is in a flood zone, has flooded before, or lacks flood insurance. Your insurance disclosure duty is limited to fire insurance information on written request. A known flood-related condition that violates the sanitary code, such as standing water or mold, must still be disclosed to a prospective tenant.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (flood zone / flood history disclosure). MA battery E flood-disclosure: flood zone / flood history disclosure: 18 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are zoning, wetlands, waterways, septic, environmental and surveying rules; none a landlord disclosure). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 21 ('the name of the company insuring the property against loss or damage by fire'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(c) ('Fail to disclose to a prospective tenant the existence of any condition amounting to a violation of law'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Contamination Use Limitations
bodyText: Massachusetts has no general rule requiring you to tell tenants about past contamination. Two hazardous-waste cleanup rules can reach a rental, though. If the property is subject to a recorded Notice of Activity and Use Limitation, that notice must be incorporated in full or by reference into every future lease. And if a required system that protects a building from contamination, such as vapor mitigation, fails for 30 or more consecutive days, you must notify the state environmental agency and the building's non-transient occupants.
notes: MA: 310 Mass. Code Regs. 40.1074(5) ('the Notice of Activity and Use Limitation shall be incorporated either in full or by reference into all future deeds, easements, mortgages, leases, licenses, occupancy agreements or any other instrument of transfer'); 310 Mass. Code Regs. 40.1025 ('shall notify both the Department and any non-transient occupants of the building protected by such Measure'; 'lasts 30 or more consecutive days'). MA battery E hazardous-contamination-disclosure: contamination notice to tenants/lessees: 7 hits; positives passed (synthetic; landlord-relevant hits only 310 Mass. Code Regs. 40.000 and Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 21E, § 7 release notice to the agency). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. No general contamination or radioactive-material disclosure to tenants found. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Renting a Condominium Unit
bodyText: If you rent out a condominium unit, you must comply with the condominium's by-laws, rules and master deed restrictions, and the unit may not be used for a purpose the master deed prohibits. Give the condominium association in writing the names of your tenants and occupants, other than visitors staying less than thirty days. The association may charge you for expenses caused by your tenant's misconduct, as a lien on the unit. No statute requires you to give the tenant the association's documents, but a lease that makes the tenant follow them should attach or identify them.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 4(1), (3) ('No unit shall be devoted to a use prohibited in the master deed'; 'Each unit owner shall comply with the by-laws and with any administrative rules and regulations adopted pursuant thereto'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 4(6) ('Each unit owner shall provide in writing to the organization of unit owners the name or names of any tenants or occupants of the unit, other than visitors for less than thirty days'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 6 ('or by the misconduct of any unit owner, or his family members, tenants, or invitees, the organization of unit owners may assess that expense exclusively against the unit owner'). No duty to give tenants association documents: MA battery E association-obligations-disclosure: give tenant condo/HOA documents: 3 hits; positives passed (synthetic; ch. 183A, §§ 2, 6 and ch. 188, § 1, none a tenant-disclosure duty). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Recovering an association fine from the tenant is contract law and is not a security deposit deduction (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4)). Non-condominium homeowners' associations have no general statute beyond ch. 183A, § 10A; leasing restrictions in condominium documents turn on case law, not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Association Can Collect Rent
bodyText: If you own a condominium unit and fall at least twenty-five days behind on common charges, the condominium association may, after giving you a written notice and a chance to respond, direct your tenant to pay rent to it instead, up to the amount owed. You may not retaliate against a tenant who pays rent to the association, and the retaliation presumption and defense apply. A lease clause waiving these rules is void. Tell tenants in a condominium that this can happen.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 6 ('for at least twenty-five days from the date it was due'; 'collect from any tenant renting the unit any rent then or thereafter due to the owner of such unit'; 'shall give to the delinquent unit owner written notice of its intent to collect the rent owed'; 'In no event shall a unit owner take any retaliatory action against any tenant who pays rent'; 'Any waiver of the provisions of this section in any lease or rental agreement shall be void'). The statute does not state in terms that the tenant's payment discharges rent owed to the owner; case law not searched. Subject to a first mortgagee's assignment of rents. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: State Fair Housing Classes
bodyText: Massachusetts fair housing law reaches beyond federal law. Besides race, color, religious creed, national origin, sex and handicap, it protects gender identity, sexual orientation, age, genetic information, ancestry, marital status, veterans and members of the armed forces, families with children, and recipients of public assistance or housing subsidies. You may not refuse to rent, set different terms, or ask about or record these traits. Refusing to rent because a unit has lead paint is also unlawful. Exemptions are narrow: leasing one unit of a two-family home you live in is exempt from some provisions, but buildings for three or more families have no such exemption.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(6)(a), (c) ('gender identity, sexual orientation'; 'age, genetic information, ancestry, or marital status of such person or persons or because such person is a veteran or member of the armed forces'; 'to cause to be made any written or oral inquiry or record'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(10) ('who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(11) ('because such person has a child or children who shall occupy the premises'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(7) ('shall not apply to the leasing of a single apartment or flat in a two family dwelling'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 1(11) ('three or more families living independently of each other'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 199A(a) ('because such premises do or may contain paint, plaster or accessible structural materials containing dangerous levels of lead'). § 4(7) reaches 'other covered housing accommodations' only if publicly offered (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 1(13) ('made generally available to the public')); § 4(10) has no such limit. Age excludes minors and qualifying elder housing. Federal law not reviewed. Case law not searched. Local: Boston, Cambridge and other city fair housing ordinances (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Discriminatory Rental Ads
bodyText: Do not make, print or publish any notice, statement or advertisement for renting covered housing that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, national origin, genetic information, ancestry, children, marital status, public assistance recipiency or handicap. The owner-occupied two-family exemption is written into the rental provision, not the advertising ban, so whether an exempt owner may advertise a preference is unsettled. Treat the advertising ban as applying to every listing you post.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(7B) ('For any person to make print, or publish, or cause to be made, printed, or published any notice, statement or advertisement'; 'that indicates any preference, limitation, or discrimination based on race'; 'children, marital status, public assistance recipiency, or handicap'; 'except where otherwise legally permitted'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(7) ('this subsection shall not apply to the leasing of a single apartment or flat in a two family dwelling'). Whether the § 4(7) exemption or the 'except where otherwise legally permitted' proviso shelters an exempt owner's advertising: case law not searched. Federal law not reviewed. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Voucher and Subsidy Holders
bodyText: Anyone furnishing rental accommodations may not discriminate against a person who receives public assistance, or a tenant who receives federal, state or local housing subsidies such as rental assistance, because of that status or because of any requirement of the assistance or subsidy program. The text contains no exemption for small or owner-occupied properties. So you may not refuse a voucher holder, or set different terms, because of the voucher or the program's rules. Screen subsidy holders by the same lawful criteria as everyone else.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(10) ('For any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against any individual who is a recipient of federal, state, or local public assistance'; 'or who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements'; 'or because of any requirement of such public assistance, rental assistance, or housing subsidy program'). Advertising 'public assistance recipiency' preferences: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(7B). How income or screening criteria interact with § 4(10): case law not searched. See edu-no-subsidy-inspection-refusal-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Harassment and Interference
bodyText: Massachusetts fair housing law makes it unlawful for an owner, managing agent, broker, their employees or a condominium association to sexually harass a tenant, prospective tenant or buyer. It is a civil violation under that law, not a crime. It is also unlawful for anyone to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with a person exercising fair housing rights, or with someone for helping another person exercise them.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(18) ('or any organization of unit owners in a condominium or housing cooperative to sexually harass any tenant, prospective tenant, purchaser or prospective purchaser of property'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(4A) ('For any person to coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with another person in the exercise or enjoyment of any right granted or protected by this chapter'). No criminal penalty for housing sexual harassment found: MA battery E fair-housing: landlord sexual harassment of tenant penalty: 1 hit (ch. 151B, § 4 only); positives passed. General criminal laws (assault, stalking) not reviewed. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Fair Housing Case Forum
bodyText: If the Massachusetts Commission Against Discrimination finds probable cause on a housing complaint against you, it must notify both sides of their right to have the case decided in court instead of at the commission. Either the complainant or you, as respondent, may elect court by giving written notice within twenty days of receiving that notice. The commission then dismisses its case, and the claim proceeds in court.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 5 ('the commissioner shall immediately serve notice upon the complainant and respondent of their right to elect judicial determination of the complaint'; 'he shall do so in writing within twenty days of receipt of the said notice'; 'shall dismiss the complaint pending before it without prejudice'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Renting a Condominium Unit
bodyText: If you rent out a condominium unit, you must designate a person or entity to oversee maintenance and repair of the unit. At the start of any tenancy, tell the tenant and the condominium association in writing that person's name and phone number. Also tell the tenant in writing the name and phone number of the association's designee for common-area maintenance and repair. Give written notice whenever either designee changes. Separately, give the association in writing the names of your tenants and occupants, other than visitors for less than thirty days.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 10(k) ('In cases where a unit owner rents a unit to a tenant, the owner of said unit shall designate a person or entity'; 'At the commencement of any tenancy, the unit owner shall notify the tenant and the organization of unit owners in writing'; 'shall notify the tenant in writing whenever the unit owner is notified of a change'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 4 ('the name or names of any tenants or occupants of the unit, other than visitors for less than thirty days'). Applies only to units in a condominium under ch. 183A. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Condominium Rules and Tenants
bodyText: As a condominium unit owner you must follow the by-laws, the association's rules and the master deed's restrictions, and no unit may be put to a use the master deed prohibits. The association may charge you for expenses caused by your tenants' misconduct. If your common charges are at least twenty-five days late, the association may, after written notice and a statutory procedure, collect rent directly from your tenant. You may not retaliate against a tenant who pays rent to the association, and a lease waiver of this protection is void. We found no Massachusetts statute on satellite dishes or antennas.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 4 ('No unit shall be devoted to a use prohibited in the master deed'; 'Each unit owner shall comply with the by-laws and with any administrative rules and regulations'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 6 ('or by the misconduct of any unit owner, or his family members, tenants, or invitees'; 'for at least twenty-five days from the date it was due'; 'collect from any tenant renting the unit any rent then or thereafter due to the owner of such unit'; 'In no event shall a unit owner take any retaliatory action against any tenant'; 'Any waiver of the provisions of this section in any lease or rental agreement shall be void'). Satellite dishes: MA battery F hoa-compliance: satellite dish / antenna restrictions: 3 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are ch. 166A, § 22 cable access, 105 Mass. Code Regs. 122.000 radiation limits, 266 Mass. Code Regs. 6.000, all off point). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Federal over-the-air antenna rules not researched. Homeowner associations outside ch. 183A not researched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Condemned Units and Open Orders
bodyText: A unit the board of health has condemned and placarded as unfit for human habitation may not be lived in again until the board gives written approval and removes the placard. No one but the board may remove or deface the placard. Before renting any unit, you must disclose every condition violating the law that you know of or could find by a reasonable inspection, which includes conditions cited in an open inspection order. If you take a security deposit, your statement of condition must list certified or adjudicated code violations then existing. No rule requires a separate written notice of inspection orders as such.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.900(B) ('No residence or portion thereof which has been condemned and placarded as unfit for human habitation shall again be used for human habitation until written approval is secured'); 410.900(C) ('No person shall deface or remove the placard'). 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(c) ('Fail to disclose to a prospective tenant the existence of any condition amounting to a violation of law within the dwelling unit'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(2)(c) ('certified by a local board of health or building official or adjudicated by a court and then existing in the premises'). Separate order-disclosure rule: MA battery F inspection-condemnation-disclosure: condemnation/placard order disclosure to tenants: 3 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are ch. 94, § 189A and two food regulations, off point). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. That an open order's conditions fall within 3.17(1)(c) is an inference from its text. See edu-disclose-code-violations-ma, edu-statement-of-condition-ma, edu-condemnation-alt-housing-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Lead Law Deleading Duty
bodyText: If a child under six lives in a unit built before 1978 that has dangerous levels of lead in paint, plaster or other accessible structural material, you must abate or contain it. You may first get a letter of interim control, which lasts one year and can be renewed once, but full compliance is the goal. A new owner has ninety days. Repainting alone never counts. You are strictly liable for a lead-poisoned child's damages unless a letter of full compliance or interim control is in effect, and even then you must use reasonable care. Willfully ignoring a lead order or notice brings treble damages.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 189A ('"Premises", any residential premises, dwelling unit or residential property constructed prior to nineteen hundred and seventy-eight'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 197(a) ('Whenever a child under six years of age resides in any premises'; 'the new owner shall have ninety days to contain or abate'); § 197(b) ('A letter of interim control shall expire at the end of one year from the date of its issuance, and may be renewed once'); § 197(f) ('Under no circumstances shall repainting with a non-lead based paint'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 199(a) ('shall not be strictly liable under this section'; 'shall take reasonable care'); § 199(b) ('punitive damages, which shall be treble the actual damages found'). 105 Mass. Code Regs. 460.100(A) ('whether or not the residential premises have been inspected'). Exemptions: units under 250 square feet or rooming houses with no child under six, and qualifying vacation rentals of 31 days or less (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 199B). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Lead-Based Family Discrimination
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent, or offer worse terms, because a unit has or may have lead paint, because renting would trigger your deleading duties, or because a tenant uses rights under the lead law. Refusing to rent to families with children does not satisfy the lead law. Neither does refusing to renew a lease with, or evicting, a family with children; such an eviction also violates the consumer protection law and the anti-retaliation statute. A person harmed may file a discrimination complaint with the Massachusetts Commission Against Discrimination.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 199A(a) ('because such premises do or may contain paint, plaster or accessible structural materials containing dangerous levels of lead'; 'because the sale, rental or lease would trigger duties'; 'may file a complaint pursuant to section five of chapter one hundred and fifty-one B'); § 199A(b) ('Refusing to rent to families with children'); § 199A(c) ('Refusing to renew the lease of or evicting families with children shall not constitute compliance'; 'Such evictions shall also constitute a violation of section two of chapter ninety-three A and section eighteen of chapter one hundred and eighty-six'). Same exemptions as Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 199B. See edu-children-occupancy-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deleading Notice, Delay, Relocation
bodyText: Before deleading an occupied rental unit, give its occupants at least ten calendar days' notice of the start date on the state-approved form, and notify all occupants if work will touch common areas or the exterior. Generally no one may occupy the unit during deleading and until cleanup is approved; pregnant women and children under six may not be there. If no lease has been signed, you may delay the tenancy up to thirty days until you get a letter of compliance or interim control, and the prospective tenant bears living costs meanwhile. You may move a current tenant to a substitute unit on reasonable notice if you pay moving expenses and any higher occupancy charge.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 460.150(A) ('shall give a minimum of ten calendar days advance notice'; 'Notice shall be given on a form approved by the Director'; 'All other occupants of the residential premises if abatement and/or containment activities will take place in interior common areas'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 197(g) ('No person shall occupy the premises while containment or abatement'; 'pregnant women and children under the age of six are not permitted to occupy the dwelling unit during deleading activities'); § 197(h) ('provided, that no duly executed lease exists between owner and tenant'; 'no such delay shall exceed thirty days'; 'the prospective tenant shall bear any living expenses'; 'the owner pays reasonable moving expenses'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no energy-efficiency or meter conservation charge that you must disclose to new tenants or offset against rent. The general utility rules still apply. You pay for electricity or gas unless the unit has its own meter serving only that unit and a written rental agreement makes the tenant pay. Water and sewer may be billed to tenants only under the strict water submetering statute.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery F meter-conservation-charge: energy efficiency meter conservation charge: 0 hits; positives passed (synthetic). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.200(A) ('metered through a meter which serves only the dwelling unit'; 'A written rental agreement provides for payment by the occupant'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.130(C) ('If the owner intends to separately bill the occupant for water or sewer costs'). See planned utilities-responsibility-ma and water-submetering-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Meth Lab Disclosure Law
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no duty to disclose, report or clean up a former methamphetamine lab before renting, and no ban on reoccupying one. The general rule still applies: before a tenancy starts you must disclose any condition in the unit that violates the law if you know of it or could find it by a reasonable inspection. Whether leftover contamination is such a violation depends on the facts.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery F meth-disclosure: methamphetamine lab contamination: 5 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are ch. 33A, § 112A and ch. 94C, § 31 drug lists, 114.3 Mass. Code Regs. 40.000 rates, and 760 Mass. Code Regs. 38.000 and 49 subsidy eligibility bars for methamphetamine production convictions, all off point). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(c) ('Fail to disclose to a prospective tenant the existence of any condition amounting to a violation of law within the dwelling unit'). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Military Zone Disclosure
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no lease disclosure for property near a military installation or inside a military noise or accident-potential zone, and no related right for a tenant to end the lease. Massachusetts does not tie any lease disclosure to distance from a named base. Local zoning and federal rules were not researched.

Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Mold Disclosure Form
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no mold-specific disclosure form or warning for leases. But the sanitary code requires you to keep buildings watertight and free from excess moisture or the appearance of mold. An inspector who finds moisture or mold will look for sources such as leaks, structural defects and poor ventilation, and no environmental testing is needed to find a violation. A mold condition that violates the code must be disclosed to a prospective tenant if you know of it or could find it by a reasonable inspection.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (mold disclosure form). MA battery F mold-disclosure v2: mold anywhere near disclose/notify/tenant: 21 hits; positives passed (only 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.000 on point). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.500(A) ('watertight, free from excess moisture or the appearance of mold'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.620(E) ('Environmental testing shall not be required to determine the existence of excess moisture or appearance of mold'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(c) ('of which the owner had knowledge or upon reasonable inspection could have acquired such knowledge'). See edu-owner-repair-duty-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Ordnance or Demolition Notice
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no lease disclosure for a former military ordnance site nearby or for a pending permit to demolish the unit. Shared utility meters are handled by the payment rules instead of a disclosure. A tenant can be made to pay for electricity or gas only if it runs through a meter serving that unit alone and a written rental agreement says so. Electricity or gas you must pay for may run through meters serving several units. Water submetering has its own strict statute.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (ordnance and demolition disclosures). MA battery F ordnance-demolition: former ordnance / demolition permit disclosure: 12 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are environmental and munitions-investment provisions, off point). MA battery F ordnance-demolition: shared utility meter serving other units: 2 hits; positives passed (ch. 186, § 22 and 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.000). Code Regs. 410.200(A) ('metered through a meter which serves only the dwelling unit'); 410.200(B) ('may be metered through meters which serve more than one dwelling unit'). See planned utilities-responsibility-ma and water-submetering-ma. Local demolition-delay bylaws (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no state fact sheet on pets and eviction that you must give a tenant who has a dog or cat, at signing or later. Other animal rules do apply when a tenancy ends, including checking a vacated unit for abandoned animals and handling animals left behind after an eviction.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery F pet-eviction-fact-sheet: pet / animal eviction fact sheet: 17 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are tax, insurance, health facility and environmental provisions, off point). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. See edu-vacated-unit-animal-check-ma and edu-post-eviction-animals-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Statewide Well Testing Rule
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no statewide duty to test a private well or to give well test results to tenants. You must still provide a supply of potable water sufficient in quantity and pressure for every occupant's ordinary needs. The sanitary code defines potable water as water from a source approved by the Department of Environmental Protection or the board of health. Many local boards of health have their own private well rules.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (statewide well testing or disclosure). MA battery F private-well-testing v2: private well / private water supply testing near rental: 18 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are environmental, camp, food and energy regulations, off point). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.130(A) ('The owner shall provide a supply of potable water sufficient in quantity and pressure'); 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.010 ('Potable Water means water from any source that has been approved by the Department of Environmental Protection or board of health'). Local: board of health private well regulations (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Property Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no duty to tell tenants what part of their rent goes to property taxes, whether yearly or when rent changes. Taxes matter in two other ways. A lease may make a tenant pay part of a real estate tax increase only through a clause stating the tenant's proportional share, the exact percentage, and a refund of any abatement share; any other tax clause is void. And a tenant who is taxed on the real estate may keep that tax out of the rent unless you agreed otherwise.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. Code Regs. 21.000, 801 Mass. Code Regs. 51.000 and 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.000, none requiring a statement). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 59, § 12C ('he may retain out of his rent the taxes paid by him'; 'unless there is a different agreement between them'). See planned tax-escalation-ma and edu-government-charges-passthrough-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Radon Disclosure Law
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no radon disclosure, warning or testing duty for rental housing, at any floor level, and no radon-resistant construction mandate tied to rentals. The only radon references concern what home inspectors and licensed inspectors do and drinking water standards. You may choose to test and share results.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery F radon-disclosure: radon: 5 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are ch. 13, § 97 and ch. 112, § 222 home inspector provisions, 105 Mass. Code Regs. 120.000 radiation control, 266 Mass. Code Regs. 6.000 home inspection standards and 310 Mass. Code Regs. 22.000 drinking water, none on rental disclosure). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Recycling and Trash Duties
bodyText: No Massachusetts rule requires you to tell tenants where or how to recycle. But you must provide enough receptacles to store refuse and recyclables before collection, and in buildings with two or more units you pay for final collection and disposal. Tenants must follow their community's rules for separating recyclables, yard waste, food waste and bulk items, and must place refuse in the receptacles you provide. In towns with a Pay As You Throw program, tenants follow its rules and pay all its fees. A tenant may compost in the yard only with your prior written permission.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (recycling-information notice). MA battery F recycling-notice: owner must tell tenants how to recycle: 14 hits; positives passed (only 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.000 and 310 Mass. Code Regs. 19.000 bear on residences; neither requires notice). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.560(E) ('shall provide a sufficient number of receptacles'; 'for the storage of refuse and recyclables before final collection'; 'responsible for the proper placement of their refuse in the receptacles provided by the owner'; 'the occupant shall follow all municipal requirements and shall be responsible for all fees'); 410.560(A) ('the owner of any residence that contains two or more dwelling units'); 410.560(B) ('shall follow the requirements established by their community for separation of recyclables'); 410.560(F) ('the occupant obtains the prior written permission of the owner'). Local: municipal recycling ordinances (flagged, not researched). See edu-tenant-code-duties-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Rent-Law Coverage Notice
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule requiring a lease or renewal to state whether the unit is covered by a just-cause eviction or rent-increase law. Massachusetts has no such statewide law for private housing. One narrow exception: if you own publicly assisted housing whose affordability restriction will end, you must give all tenants written notice at least two years ahead and a notice of intent at least one year before termination. For three years afterward, a protected low-income tenant's rent may rise only once a year by inflation plus 3 per cent, and eviction requires good cause related to tenant fault.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (coverage notice). MA battery F required-disclosures v2: notice of just-cause or rent-regulation coverage: 25 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits include ch. 186A and ch. 140, § 32L, none requiring a coverage notice). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40T, § 2 ('all tenants and the tenant organization, if any'; 'not less than 2 years before the termination of the affordability restriction'; 'not less than 1 year before the completion of the last termination event'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40T, § 7 ('shall not be increased more than once annually by the increase in the consumer price index'; 'plus 3 per cent'; 'except for good cause related to tenant fault'). Publicly assisted housing is defined by program list in ch. 40T, § 1. See edu-rent-control-prohibited-ma. Local: municipal home-rule petitions (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Sex Offender Notice
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no duty to tell tenants about registered sex offenders living nearby or in the building, and no required registry notice in leases. If you look at registry information, do not use it to commit a crime against an offender or to engage in illegal discrimination or harassment of one. Doing so is punishable by up to two and one-half years in a house of correction, a fine of up to $1,000, or both.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (notice duty). MA battery F sex-offender v2: registry information use / housing: 6 hits; positives passed. Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 6, § 178N ('shall not be used to commit a crime against a sex offender or to engage in illegal discrimination or harassment of an offender'; 'not more than two and one-half years in a house of correction or by a fine of not more than $1,000'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Offender Occupancy Rule
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no statewide rule limiting where registered sex offenders may live, no crime of knowingly leasing a dwelling where two registered offenders live together, and no owner duty tied to an offender's distance from schools or parks. Some cities and towns have adopted their own residency rules.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery F sex-offender-occupancy: offenders residing together / near school occupancy: 0 hits; positives passed (synthetic). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Local: municipal sex offender residency bylaws (flagged, not researched). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No General Lease Font Rules
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no general font-size or first-page placement rule for leases or lease disclosures. Two specific type rules apply. The statement of condition you give with a security deposit must carry its statutory notice in twelve-point bold-face type at the top of its first page. And if you build the state lead notification and certification form into your lease, you must reproduce it unaltered, without reducing its type size.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (general font or placement rule). MA battery F sfr-occupancy-disclosure v2: point type size rules near lease/rental: 32 hits; positives passed (only ch. 186, § 15B bears on residential leases; others concern checks, sales, insurance, contractor and other contracts). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no duty to state in a lease, or tell tenants, whether the building has a sprinkler system or when it was last inspected. Where a building has one, do not shut off, disconnect, obstruct or remove any part of it without a written permit from the head of the fire department. Emergency shutoffs for necessary repairs or to prevent freezing are allowed if you notify the fire department immediately and again when it is back in service.

MA battery F sprinkler-disclosure: sprinkler notice in lease / to tenants: 6 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are ch. 25B, § 5, ch. 146, § 88A, ch. 148, § 27A and three regulations, none requiring disclosure). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 148, § 27A ('without first procuring a written permit so to do from the head of the fire department'; 'for the purpose of making necessary repairs or preventing freezing or other property damage'; 'the head of the fire department is notified immediately'). See edu-sprinkler-requirements-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule requiring you to install covers on steam radiators when a tenant asks, and no required radiator-cover lease rider or annual notice. The sanitary code's general heating standards still apply. Local codes were not researched.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery F steam-radiator-covers: radiator covers: 11 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits use the word only in definitions of heating systems or unrelated contexts). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. See edu-heat-standards-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Psychologically Impacted Property
bodyText: You do not have to tell a tenant that the property is or may be psychologically impacted. That covers a past or present occupant's HIV, AIDS or other illness very unlikely to spread through living in the home; the property having been the site of a felony, suicide or homicide; and alleged supernatural events. A tenant has no claim against you for not disclosing these facts. But you may not lie or make a false statement about them, including in answer to a direct question.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93, § 114 ('shall not be deemed to be a material fact required to be disclosed in a real estate transaction'; 'that the real property was the site of a felony, suicide or homicide'; 'No cause of action shall arise or be maintained against a seller or lessor'; 'shall not authorize a seller, lessor or real estate broker or salesman to make a misrepresentation of fact or false statement'). MA battery F stigmatized-property v2: psychologically impacted / death or crime on premises nondisclosure: 31 hits; positives passed (only ch. 93, § 114 on point). The direct-question point is an inference from the misrepresentation proviso. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Tenant Purchase Right
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no general right for tenants to buy, or receive an offer on, a rental property you plan to sell, and no statewide rent-cap or just-cause notice for leases. For publicly assisted housing, an owner may not sell before offering the state housing agency the chance to buy, and must notify all tenants in writing of the intent to sell. Tenant notices count as given when handed to the tenant or an adult household member, or mailed first class with a copy left in or under the unit door.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (general tenant purchase right and rent-law notice). MA battery F tpa-notice: tenant opportunity / right of first refusal to purchase residential rental: 3 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are tax-credit provisions recognizing tenant first-refusal rights held by agreement and 760 Mass. Code Regs. 23.000, none creating a statutory right). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40T, § 2 ('an owner shall not sell publicly-assisted housing before offering the department the opportunity to purchase'; 'notify, in writing, the parties identified in subsection (a) of the owner's intention to sell'; 'the notice is sent by first class mail and a copy is left in or under the door'). Condominium conversion rules: see conversion-notice (Not located). Local: municipal condominium conversion and tenant opportunity ordinances (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Consumer Protection Law for Rentals
bodyText: Massachusetts' consumer protection law bans unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce, and the Attorney General's landlord-tenant regulation spells out what that means for rentals. Among other things, it is unfair or deceptive to rent a unit with a violation that may endanger health or safety, to hide known violations, to put any unlawful term in a rental agreement, to leave required owner, notice and deposit information out of a written lease, or to fail to give the tenant a signed copy within thirty days. Whether the law reaches a particular small owner-occupied landlord turns on case law.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A, § 2 ('unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce are hereby declared unlawful'; 'The attorney general may make rules and regulations'). 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(1)(a) ('contains a condition which amounts to a violation of law which may endanger or materially impair the health, safety, or well-being of the occupant'); 3.17(1)(c); 3.17(3)(a) ('to include in any rental agreement any term which'; 'Violates any law'); 3.17(3)(b); 3.17(3)(c) ('fail to give the tenant an executed copy of any written rental agreement within 30 days'). No rule makes blank spaces at signing unlawful (see edu-no-blank-spaces-rule-ma). Coverage of owner-occupants and casual landlords as trade or commerce: case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Consumer Protection Remedies
bodyText: A tenant injured by an unfair or deceptive practice can sue in superior, district or housing court, or raise it as a counterclaim in an eviction. Before filing a separate suit, the tenant must send you a written demand describing the practice and the injury at least thirty days ahead; no demand is needed for a counterclaim. A reasonable written settlement offer made within thirty days of the demand can cap what you owe. Otherwise the tenant recovers actual damages or $25, whichever is greater, two to three times that if the violation was willful or knowing, plus attorney's fees and costs.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A, § 9(1) ('or in the housing court'; 'whether by way of original complaint, counterclaim'); § 9(3) ('At least thirty days prior to the filing of any such action, a written demand for relief'; 'limit any recovery to the relief tendered'; 'actual damages or twenty-five dollars, whichever is greater'; 'up to three but not less than two times such amount'; 'The demand requirements of this paragraph shall not apply if the claim is asserted by way of counterclaim'); § 9(3A) (district court); § 9(4) ('be awarded reasonable attorney's fees and costs'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Liability for Unlawful Lease Terms
bodyText: Putting a term that violates any law into a rental agreement is itself an unfair or deceptive practice, separate from trying to enforce it. The same is true of a penalty clause that does not conform to the security deposit and advance-payment statute, and of a tax escalation clause that does not meet its statute. A tenant injured by such a term may sue under the consumer protection law for actual damages or $25, whichever is greater, two to three times that if the violation was willful or knowing, plus attorney's fees. Review your lease form before using it.
notes: MA: 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(3)(a) ('to include in any rental agreement any term which'; 'Violates any law'; 'Contains a penalty clause not in conformity with the provisions of'; 'Contains a tax escalator clause not in conformity with the provisions of'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A, § 9(3) ('actual damages or twenty-five dollars, whichever is greater'; 'a willful or knowing violation of said section two'); § 9(4). MA battery F knowing-use-penalty: penalty for using a lease with prohibited terms: 5 hits; positives passed (only 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.000 governs residential leases; ch. 106, §§ 2A-103, 2A-108 are goods leases). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Whether inclusion alone causes compensable injury: case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Exculpatory Lease Clauses
bodyText: A lease term, however worded, is void if it makes the tenant indemnify you or hold you harmless, or releases you from liability to the tenant or anyone else, for injury, loss or damage caused by your own omission, fault, negligence or misconduct on the premises or in elevators, stairways, hallways or other appurtenances.
