You also cannot defend a tenant's injury claim by saying a common-area defect existed when you rented, if it violates the building code when the injury happens, and a lease waiver of that rule is void.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15 ('by the use of any words whatsoever'; 'the effect of which is to indemnify the lessor or landlord or hold the lessor or landlord harmless'; 'arising from any omission, fault, negligence or other misconduct of the lessor or landlord'; 'shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15E ('that said defect existed at the time of the letting of the property'; 'Any waiver of this provision in any lease or other rental agreement shall be void'). Including such a term is also unfair or deceptive: 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(3)(a). Clauses allocating harm the tenant causes are outside § 15's text (inference; case law not searched). See edu-casualty-clause-limits-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Jury Trial Waiver
bodyText: In a residential lease, a term by which the tenant waives the right to a jury trial in any later litigation with you is void. So is a term saying that nothing you do or fail to do counts as a constructive eviction. Leave both out of Massachusetts leases; including an unlawful term is itself an unfair or deceptive practice.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15F ('whereby the tenant agrees to waive his right to trial by jury in any subsequent litigation with the landlord'; 'shall be construed as a constructive eviction, shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'). 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(3)(a) ('Violates any law'). MA battery F jury-waiver v2: jury trial waiver provisions: 20 hits; positives passed (only ch. 186, § 15F concerns residential leases). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Confession of Judgment
bodyText: Any lease or other contract term by which the tenant agrees to confess judgment, or authorizes someone else to confess judgment for the tenant, is void, and a judgment by confession taken under it must be set aside on the tenant's motion. A term waiving service of process does not help either: a judgment entered under it will be set aside unless the tenant was served in the usual way, or you sent registered-mail notice at least seven days before entering the case and filed an affidavit saying so.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 231, § 13A ('agrees to confess judgment in any action which may be brought thereon'; 'shall be void and any judgment by confession taken in pursuance of such a stipulation shall be set aside or vacated'; 'waived or agreed to waive or authorized another person to waive or agree to waive the issue or service of process'; 'by registered mail at least seven days before the entry of such action'). MA battery F confession-of-judgment: confession / cognovit / warrant of attorney: 7 hits; positives passed (only ch. 231, § 13A applies to leases; others are negotiable instruments, consumer credit and door-to-door sales). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Lease Unconscionability Statute
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no statute letting a court strike an unconscionable apartment lease or clause. The commercial code's unconscionability rules cover sales and leases of goods, not housing. Instead, many specific lease terms are void by statute, and the Attorney General's rule makes it unfair or deceptive to include any term that violates the law. Whether the common-law unconscionability doctrine applies to a residential lease term is a case-law question we did not research.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (statute). MA battery F unconscionability: unconscionable contract or clause: 16 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are UCC goods provisions ch. 106, §§ 2-302, 2A-108, motor vehicle, timeshare, mortgage, viatical and manufactured housing rules; none governs residential real-property leases). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 106, § 2A-108 (unconscionable lease contract), which applies only to leases of goods (§ 2A-103). 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(3)(a) ('Violates any law'). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Lease Terms Massachusetts Voids
bodyText: Leave these out of a Massachusetts lease; each is void. A term that has the tenant indemnify or release you for your own negligence. A jury-trial waiver, or a clause that nothing you do is a constructive eviction. A waiver of the notice-to-quit periods. A right to end the tenancy because the tenant has children. A confession of judgment. A waiver of the tenant's deposit rights, quiet-enjoyment protections, anti-retaliation rights or reciprocal attorney's fees. A tax escalation clause that misses its statutory terms. Late interest or penalties before rent is thirty days late are barred too.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15 ('hold the lessor or landlord harmless'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15F ('waive his right to trial by jury'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15A ('to waive the notices required under section eleven or twelve'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 16 ('if the tenant has or shall have a child or children'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 231, § 13A ('agrees to confess judgment'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(8) ('any waiver by a tenant or prospective tenant of any provision of this section shall be deemed to be against public policy and therefore void'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14 ('Any waiver of this provision in any lease or other rental agreement'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 18 ('Any waiver of this provision in any lease or other rental agreement shall be void'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 20 ('Any waiver of this section shall be void as against public policy'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15C ('shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(c) ('until thirty days after such rent shall have been due'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Single Banned-Terms List
bodyText: No single Massachusetts section lists every banned lease term. Prohibitions are spread across the landlord-tenant chapter, the sanitary code, the lead law, condominium law, the Attorney General's rule and general statutes such as the confession-of-judgment ban. The Attorney General's rule works as the catch-all: putting any term that violates any law into a rental agreement is an unfair or deceptive practice. Many statutes add that a lease waiver of their protections is void, including the domestic violence, condominium rent-collection and quiet-enjoyment rules.
notes: MA: 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(3)(a) ('to include in any rental agreement any term which'; 'Violates any law'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 28 ('shall be void and unenforceable'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 6 ('Any waiver of the provisions of this section in any lease or rental agreement shall be void'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14 ('Any waiver of this provision in any lease or other rental agreement'). Home-warranty deductibles and repair fees: MA battery F prohibited-lease-terms: home warranty deductible or repair fee passed to tenant: 0 hits; positives passed (synthetic). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Owner repair duties: see edu-habitability-not-waivable-ma. Penalty money for knowing use: see edu-unlawful-lease-term-liability-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Eviction Penalty Statute
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule that specifically voids a lease clause imposing a penalty because of an eviction notice or case. Other limits reach most such clauses. You may not charge interest or a penalty for late rent until it is thirty days overdue. A penalty clause that does not conform to the deposit and advance-payment statute is an unfair or deceptive term. Damages you keep for a breach may not exceed what the law allows or an agreed amount. And if your lease lets you recover attorney's fees, the tenant gets the same right.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (eviction-specific penalty ban). MA battery F eviction-penalty-clause-ban v2: lease penalty tied to eviction notice or action: 5 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are ch. 239, §§ 4, 14, 16 storage, animal and sealing provisions and two regulations, off point). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(c) ('shall impose any interest or penalty for failure to pay rent until thirty days after such rent shall have been due'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(3)(a) ('Contains a penalty clause not in conformity with the provisions of'); 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(6)(c) ('any amount which exceeds the damages to which he is entitled under the law'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 20 ('there shall be implied in such lease a covenant by the landlord to pay to the tenant the reasonable attorneys' fees'). See edu-liquidated-damages-ma, edu-attorney-fee-reciprocity-ma. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Notices That Must Be Written
bodyText: Several Massachusetts notices must be in writing, and a lease cannot downgrade them to verbal notice. A fourteen-day notice to quit for nonpayment, under a lease or a tenancy at will, must be given in writing. A tenancy at will ends by written notice of three months, or the rent interval or thirty days if longer. A lease term waiving these notices is void. A tenant ending a tenancy because of domestic violence does so by written notification to you. Use written notices whenever a statute calls for them, even if your lease says otherwise.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 11 ('fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12 ('three months' notice in writing'; 'the interval between the days of payment or thirty days, whichever is longer'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15A ('to waive the notices required under section eleven or twelve, shall be deemed to be against public policy and void'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 24(a) ('upon written notification to the owner'). MA battery F written-notice-required v2: tenancy notices required in writing: 122 hits; positives passed (broad; landlord-tenant hits confirmed by section reading). See edu-notice-to-quit-not-waivable-ma, edu-termination-notice-periods-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Families With Children Practices
bodyText: The Massachusetts Commission Against Discrimination treats a child as anyone under 18, and protection for families with children also covers pregnant women and people in the process of getting legal custody of a child. Its examples of unlawful practices include refusing to rent to families with young children because of lead paint, refusing to let families with young children live above a certain floor, and charging families with children higher rent or a higher security deposit. State, local and federal maximum-occupancy limits still apply.
notes: MA: 804 Mass. Code Regs. 2.02(2) ('a child is any individual who has not yet attained the age of 18 years'; 'shall extend to women who are pregnant'; 'persons who are in the process of securing legal custody of a child or children'); 804 Mass. Code Regs. 2.02(3) ('Refusing to allow families with young children to live above a certain floor'; 'Charging a higher rent or security deposit to families with children'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4 ('nothing herein shall limit the applicability of any local, state, or federal restrictions regarding the maximum number of persons permitted to occupy a dwelling') (§ 4(11), with its exemptions). See edu-children-occupancy-ma, edu-lead-no-family-discrimination-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Vouchers and Public Assistance
bodyText: You may not discriminate against an applicant or tenant because they receive public assistance or a housing subsidy, such as a rental voucher or rental assistance, or because of any requirement of that assistance or subsidy program. The usual exemption for renting one unit of a two-family home you live in does not apply when the renter receives public assistance or a housing subsidy. Ads, signs and statements may not indicate a preference or limitation based on public assistance. Massachusetts does not require a lease statement about subsidies.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(10) ('who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements'; 'because of any requirement of such public assistance, rental assistance, or housing subsidy program'); § 4(7B) ('public assistance recipiency'). 804 Mass. Code Regs. 2.01(4) ('The leasing or rental of units in those two family homes in which the owner occupies one apartment'; 'The home seeker or renter is a recipient of public assistance or housing subsidy'). No lease-statement duty: MA battery F source-of-income: public assistance / rental voucher discrimination in housing: 26 hits; positives passed (only ch. 151B, § 4 and 804 Mass. Code Regs. 2.000 govern private rentals). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Whether declining specific voucher paperwork is discrimination: case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Protected-Trait Inquiries
bodyText: Separate from the ban on refusing to rent, you may not make, or have anyone make, any written or oral inquiry or record about an applicant's race, religious creed, color, national origin, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, age, genetic information, ancestry, marital status, veteran or military status, or handicap, including blindness or hearing impairment. Leave these questions off applications and screening notes. The inquiry ban does not list children or public assistance, but refusing to rent for those reasons is unlawful. The age protection does not cover minors or qualifying senior housing.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(6)(c) ('to cause to be made any written or oral inquiry or record concerning the race, religious creed, color, national origin, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation'; 'genetic information, ancestry or marital status of the person seeking to rent'; 'The word "age" as used in this subsection shall not apply to persons who are minors'); § 4(7)(c) (same for other covered housing; 'provided, however, that this subsection shall not apply to the leasing of a single apartment or flat in a two family dwelling'). 804 Mass. Code Regs. 2.01(5)(c) ('It is unlawful to cause to be made any written or oral inquiry, or record'). Children and public assistance: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(10)-(11). See edu-source-of-income-ma, edu-children-occupancy-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Immigration Status Questions
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no rule that specifically bars, or requires, asking about an applicant's immigration or citizenship status, and no law making it unlawful to rent to someone who is not lawfully present. National origin and ancestry are protected: you may not refuse to rent, offer worse terms, or make any written or oral inquiry or record concerning an applicant's national origin or ancestry. Whether immigration-status questions amount to national-origin discrimination is a case-law question we did not research.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent (immigration-status rule). MA battery F immigration-status: immigration or citizenship status in housing: 14 hits; positives passed (synthetic; only ch. 186, § 15B, which directs fee-in-lieu-of-deposit regulations to disregard immigration status, concerns private housing; others are benefits programs). MA battery F immigration-status v2: national origin / ancestry discrimination in housing: 10 hits; positives passed. Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(6) ('because of the race, religious creed, color, national origin'; 'to cause to be made any written or oral inquiry or record'). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Criminal Record Screening Limits
bodyText: You may request standard-access criminal records (CORI) to evaluate an applicant for market-rate housing, but only as the final step in the application, after the applicant signs a CORI Acknowledgment Form. Standard access shows felony convictions for 10 years, misdemeanor convictions for 5 years, and pending charges; older convictions stay visible while a later one is. Do not use standard access to screen other household members. Use CORI only to decide whether to rent, do not pass it on except as the rules allow, and keep it no longer than seven years after the later of the tenancy's end or your decision.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 6, § 172(3) ('to evaluate applicants for rental or lease of housing'; 'felony convictions or findings of not guilty by reason of insanity for 10 years'; 'misdemeanor convictions for 5 years'; 'pending criminal charges'). 803 Mass. Code Regs. 5.04 ('CORI shall only be requested for a housing applicant as the final step in the application process'; 'or for the purpose of screening other household members'); 803 Mass. Code Regs. 5.06 ('shall obtain a signed CORI Acknowledgment Form'); 803 Mass. Code Regs. 5.13 ('shall be used solely for determining whether'); 803 Mass. Code Regs. 5.08 ('shall not be retained for longer than seven years'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Criminal History Denial Steps
bodyText: Before you question an applicant about criminal history, give them a copy of any criminal record you have, from any source, and tell them its source. Before denying an application because of criminal history, notify the applicant, give them the record and its source, give your CORI policy if you have one, identify the information behind the decision, let them dispute its accuracy, give the state's information on correcting a record, and document each step. If a consumer reporting agency supplied it, also give the federal pre-adverse action disclosure. If you run five or more background checks a year, keep a written CORI policy.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 6, § 171A ('shall provide the applicant with the criminal history record in the person's possession, whether obtained from the department or any other source prior to questioning the applicant'; 'annually conducts 5 or more criminal background investigations'; 'shall maintain a written criminal offender record information policy'). 803 Mass. Code Regs. 5.10 ('before asking the applicant any questions about the criminal history'); 803 Mass. Code Regs. 5.14 ('identify the information that is the basis for the potential adverse action'; 'provide the applicant with the opportunity to dispute the accuracy of the information'; 'document all steps taken to comply'; 'A Summary of Your Rights Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act'). Section 171A does not itself bar decisions based on criminal history. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Keep Domestic Violence Proof Private
bodyText: If you obtain written proof that a household member is a victim of domestic violence, rape, sexual assault or stalking, keep the documents and the information in them confidential. Do not provide them, or allow access to them, to any other person or agency unless the victim gives written authorization, or a court order, government regulation or governmental audit requirement calls for it. Limit who in your office can see them. You also may not refuse to rent to an applicant because they ended an earlier tenancy or asked for a lock change under these protections.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 24(f) ('shall keep such documentation and the information contained in the documentation confidential'; 'shall not provide or allow access to such documentation in any way to any other person or agency'; 'unless the victim provides written authorization'; 'unless required by court order, government regulation or governmental audit requirements'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 25 ('An owner shall not refuse to enter into a rental agreement'). Limiting internal access is a recommended practice, not a statutory term. See edu-dv-proof-documents-ma, edu-dv-eviction-protections-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: No general Massachusetts rule bars you from making a tenant reimburse a government fine, but one specific rule does. If you own a large building that must report energy use to the state, a penalty for failing to report may not be assessed on or passed through to a tenant whose unit is less than 5 per cent of the building's gross floor area. Any other fine reimbursement must rest on the lease, may not exceed the damages the law allows or the agreed amount, and may not come out of the security deposit.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 25A, § 20(h) ('no such penalty shall be assessed on or passed through to a lessee of a unit within a large building that comprises less than 5 per cent of the total gross floor area'); § 20(a) ('"Large building", a building with at least 20,000 square feet of gross floor area'). 940 Mass. Code Regs. 3.17(6)(c) ('any amount which exceeds the damages to which he is entitled under the law'). Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4) ('No deduction may be made from the security deposit for any purpose other than those set forth in this section'). General pass-through ban: MA battery F governmental-fines v2: government fine charged to tenant: 8 hits (ch. 25A, § 20 and 225 Mass. Code Regs. 27.000 on point; others off point); synthetic positive for the ban wording did not match, a second synthetic passed. Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Local: Boston and Cambridge building energy ordinances (flagged, not researched). See edu-government-charges-passthrough-ma. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Foreign Ownership Limits
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no restriction on foreign nationals, foreign governments or so-called foreign adversaries owning or leasing land, and no lease-length carve-out. Massachusetts law says the opposite: aliens may take, hold, transmit and convey real property, and no title is invalid because a former owner was an alien. Residential tenancies are not limited by a tenant's citizenship. Federal rules were not researched.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery F foreign-ownership: alien / foreign adversary land ownership or leasing restriction: 2 hits; positives passed (ch. 184, § 1; ch. 23M, § 3 PACE financing, off point). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 184, § 1 ('Aliens may take, hold, transmit and convey real property'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Hot Water Temperature Range
bodyText: You must provide and maintain facilities that heat and deliver hot water in enough quantity and pressure for ordinary use. At fixtures other than a bathtub or shower, hot water must be between 110 and 130 degrees Fahrenheit. At a bathtub or shower, it must be between 110 and 120 degrees. Massachusetts has no separate rule to reset a water heater before each new tenant, but the range applies at all times. An inspector checks how the system actually performs, if possible at the times the tenant says it falls short.
notes: MA: 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.150 ('The owner shall provide and maintain in good operating condition facilities capable of heating and delivering hot water'; 'In a temperature range of not less than 110'; 'for fixtures other than a bathtub or shower'; 'for a bathtub or shower'; 'Inspection of the hot water system shall include an examination of the hot water system and its actual performance'). Upper limits (130 and 120 degrees Fahrenheit) read from the same text, whose degree symbols do not quote cleanly. MA battery F water-heater-temperature v3: hot water temperature range (degree glyph tolerant): 17 hits; positives passed (only 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.000 governs rental housing). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. Who pays for the fuel follows 105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.200-410.210. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Window Guard Rule
bodyText: We searched Massachusetts statutes and regulations and found no requirement to install window guards or window stops where children live, and no required window-guard notice or lease rider. The sanitary code's general window, screen and lock requirements still apply. Some cities may have their own rules.
notes: MA: Confirmed absent. MA battery F window-guards: window guards / window fall prevention / window stops: 3 hits; positives passed (synthetic; hits are 105 Mass. Code Regs. 150.000 and 164 health facility rules and 454 Mass. Code Regs. 22.000 deleading, off point). Searched General Laws, Constitution, full CMR and court rules. See edu-locks-screens-keys-ma. Local: municipal window-guard ordinances (flagged, not researched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Sprinkler Requirements
bodyText: Every building more than seventy feet tall must have automatic sprinklers under the state building code, including older high-rises built before 1975, except condominium buildings begun before then. In cities and towns that have accepted the local-option laws, every lodging or boarding house letting to six or more unrelated people must be sprinklered, and any building newly built or substantially rehabilitated with four or more dwelling units must have sprinklers. The sprinkler rule for buildings over 7,500 square feet does not apply to residential buildings. Never disable a system without the fire chief's written permit.
notes: MA: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 148, § 26A ('Every building or structure of more than seventy feet in height above the mean grade shall be protected with an adequate system of automatic sprinklers'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 148, § 26A½ ('constructed prior to January first, nineteen hundred and seventy-five'; 'which have been submitted to the provisions of chapter one hundred and eighty-three A'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 148, § 26H ('In any city or town which accepts the provisions of this section, every lodging house or boarding house'; 'six or more persons not within the second degree of kindred'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 148, § 26I ('containing not less than four dwelling units'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 148, § 26G ('This section shall not apply to buildings or additions used for residential purposes'); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 148, § 27A ('without first procuring a written permit'). MA battery F fire-sprinkler-duty: automatic sprinkler requirement for residential buildings: 2 hits; real positive passed, synthetic did not match (other § 26 sections read directly). Local: acceptance of §§ 26H and 26I (flagged, not researched). Building code detail not researched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Late Charge
bodyText: If Tenant does not pay Monthly Rent in full within nine days after it is due (four days after it is due in a week-to-week tenancy), Tenant will pay one late charge of {{late_fee_amount}} on that late payment. This grace period is extended by five more days for any month (or week) in which Landlord's online rental payment system prevents Tenant from paying Rent when due. Landlord will not charge a late charge on Rent paid within the grace period, and will not offer a reduced Rent for paying within it. Landlord will charge only one late charge on each late Rent payment, however long it remains unpaid. The late charge will never be more than the lesser of: (1) $5 for each day the Rent remains unpaid after the grace period ends, up to $50; or (2) 5 percent of the late Rent payment, or, if a government agency or charity pays part of the Rent, 5 percent of Tenant's share of the late payment.
notes: CT: Overrides `late-fee`, whose grace period is a variable a landlord could set below Connecticut's statutory grace period and whose amount has no cap, and whose last sentence (acceptance of a late payment does not waive any other remedy) cuts against Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-19 ('Acceptance of rent with the knowledge that such rent is overdue constitutes a waiver of the landlord's right to terminate the rental agreement for the tenant's failure to pay such rent when it was due'). Controlling text: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15a(a) (nine days, four days 'in the case of a one-week tenancy', extended 'an additional five days if a landlord's online rental payment system prevents the payment of rent when due', added by Conn. Pub. Act No. 25-1 (Nov. Sp. Sess.), § 38, effective January 1, 2026) and § 47a-15a(b) ('If a rental agreement contains a valid written agreement to pay a late charge in accordance with subsection (a) of section 47a-4 a landlord may assess a tenant such a late charge on a rent payment made subsequent to the grace period'; cap 'the lesser of (1) five dollars per day, up to a maximum of fifty dollars, or (2) five per cent of the delinquent rent payment or, in the case of a rental agreement paid in whole or in part by a governmental or charitable entity, five per cent of the tenant's share of the delinquent rent payment'; 'The landlord may not assess more than one late charge upon a delinquent rent payment, regardless of how long the rent remains unpaid'). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(8)-(9) make a term void that charges a late charge before the grace period ends, reduces rent for paying within it, or exceeds the § 47a-15a amounts (§ 47a-4(b) 'unenforceable'). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the statute does not say from which day the $5 per day runs; the clause counts days after the grace period ends, the reading whose error is cheaper (rule 79). {{late_fee_amount}} is the landlord's figure; the builder should check it against the $50 and 5 percent ceilings (§10). The grace period is statutory, so {{late_fee_grace_days}} is not used. See `edu-late-charge-limits-ct`. Read section-open from the 2026 Supplement (cga.ct.gov, § 47a-15a revised to Jan. 1, 2026) and the 2025 revision (§ 47a-4); no 2026 public act amends § 47a-15a, and Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-113 amends § 47a-4 only to add subdivision (11) from Oct. 1, 2026. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Amounts Due at Signing
bodyText: Tenant will pay Landlord the first month's Monthly Rent of {{monthly_rent}} and a Security Deposit of {{security_deposit}}, when stated here: [state when each is due]. [Optional: Tenant will also pay a deposit of [amount] for [describe the key or special equipment], refundable as stated in this Lease.] Neither Landlord nor anyone acting for Landlord will require Tenant to pay any other payment, fee or charge before or at the beginning of the tenancy, including any application, processing, administrative or pet fee (other than a fee for a tenant screening report that Connecticut law allows an applicant to be charged). Landlord will not charge a move-in or move-out fee. Any last month's Rent or other Rent paid in advance beyond the first month, and any deposit Landlord requires because of a pet, is part of the Security Deposit and counts toward its limit.
notes: CT: Overrides `due-at-signing`, whose example list includes a separate pet deposit and last month's Rent, which Connecticut's closed list of up-front money does not allow as separate charges. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4d(b), as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-68, § 59 (effective from passage; Governor's approval date recorded in log §1.2): 'No landlord, third party acting on behalf of a landlord, or third party acting on behalf of the state may demand from a prospective tenant any payment, fee or charge for the processing, review or acceptance of any rental application, or demand any other payment, fee or charge before or at the beginning of the tenancy, except a security deposit pursuant to section 47a-21, advance payment for the first month's rent or a deposit for a key or any special equipment, or a fee for a tenant screening report as provided in subsection (c) of this section. No landlord may charge a tenant a move-in or move-out fee.' Prepaid rent beyond the first month is a security deposit: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(a)(11) ('"Security deposit" means any advance rental payment ... except an advance payment for the first month's rent or a deposit for a key or any special equipment'), so it is capped and escrowed with the deposit (§ 47a-21(b), (h)). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: § 47a-21(a)(11) does not name a pet deposit; because § 47a-4d(b) bars any other charge at the start of the tenancy, the clause treats any pet deposit as part of the Security Deposit (cheaper error). The screening-report fee is paid by an applicant before the Lease (`edu-application-screening-fees-ct`), so it is not listed here. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision; Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-68 read in the enrolled act). SYNC (Claude Code, 2026-10-09): screening-report carve-out added so the promise doesn't read as barring the § 47a-4d(c) fee charged at application ('a landlord may charge a fee not exceeding fifty dollars plus an adjustment ... for a tenant screening report'), read on cga.ct.gov. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Application of Payments
bodyText: Every payment Tenant makes under this Lease will be applied first to Rent and only then to any other fee or charge, as Connecticut law requires. Nothing in this provision limits any statutory right Tenant may have to cure nonpayment of Rent.
notes: CT: Overrides `application-of-payments`, which lets the tenant direct a payment elsewhere; Connecticut's rule is mandatory. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7d(e) (Conn. Pub. Act No. 25-44, § 9): 'All payments made by a tenant pursuant to a rental agreement shall be applied first toward the payment of rent, and then toward the payment of any other fees or charges.' A landlord who violates § 47a-7d is 'liable to the tenant for a civil penalty in an amount equal to one month's rent', and the court may award reasonable attorney's fees and costs (§ 47a-7d(f)). The statute does not order rent among periods; the clause adds no order. Read section-open in the 2026 Supplement (cga.ct.gov). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If a check or other payment Tenant gives Landlord is dishonored or fails, Landlord may require Tenant to replace it with a cashier's check, certified check or money order, and Tenant will pay Landlord a service charge of [amount, not more than $20] for that payment. Landlord will charge only one service charge for each dishonored payment. Landlord will not charge a service charge if Tenant stopped payment, the check was stolen, or Tenant raises a reasonable defense about whether the underlying amount is owed. If more than two of Tenant's payments in any 12-month period are dishonored, Landlord may require future Rent to be paid by cashier's check, certified check or money order.
notes: CT: Overrides `returned-payments`, whose fee is open-ended ("not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law") and applies even when the tenant stopped payment. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-565a(i): 'in the case of a drawer who negotiates a check which is dishonored, the payee or its assignee may impose on the drawer a service charge of up to twenty dollars, provided, no such service charge may be imposed if (1) the drawer has stopped payment on the check, (2) the check was stolen, or (3) the drawer has raised a reasonable defense with respect to the validity of the underlying debt. The drawer shall not be liable under this subsection for more than one such service charge for each dishonored check.' The statutory damages in § 52-565a(a)-(c) are not available on a rent check: § 52-565a(d)(2) ('the drawer gave such check as payment for the rental of residential premises'). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: no Connecticut statute sets a fee for a failed electronic payment (whole-code search, log §17); the clause applies the check rule's $20 ceiling and exceptions to every failed payment. Requiring certified funds does not breach Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4c, which bars only requiring electronic funds transfer as the exclusive method. The fee is a hand-filled bracket, not a {{variable}} (Taylor, IN session). Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant will pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit) before occupancy. The Security Deposit remains Tenant's property, and Landlord holds it as security for Tenant's obligations. After the tenancy ends, Landlord may keep from the Security Deposit and its accrued interest only the value of damages Landlord suffers because Tenant failed to meet those obligations, which are: (1) any Rent or utility payment due Landlord; (2) Tenant's duties under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11, including not willfully or negligently damaging the property or allowing anyone else to do so; (3) the actual reasonable cost of changing the locks under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7b, if Tenant has not paid it; and (4) any remaining payments Tenant owes under a bed bug assistance repayment schedule. Landlord will not keep any part of the Security Deposit for ordinary wear and tear, or for any condition, defect or damage noted on a preoccupancy walk-through checklist signed under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7c. The Security Deposit does not relieve Tenant of paying Rent when it is due.
notes: CT: Overrides `security-deposit-use`, which lets the landlord apply the deposit to "remedy a Tenant default under this Lease" and to cleaning, wider than Connecticut's closed list of 'tenant's obligations'. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(c) ('Any security deposit paid by a tenant shall remain the property of such tenant in which the landlord shall have a security interest'); § 47a-21(a)(14) ('"Tenant's obligations" means (A) the amount of any rental or utility payment due the landlord from a tenant; (B) a tenant's obligations under the provisions of section 47a-11; and (C) the actual reasonable cost of changing the locks of the dwelling unit pursuant to section 47a-7b, if the tenant has not paid such cost'); § 47a-21(d)(1)-(2) (return less 'damages suffered by such landlord by reason of such tenant's failure to comply with such tenant's obligations'); § 47a-11(f) (tenant shall 'not wilfully or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or permit any other person to do so'). Item (4): § 47a-7a(b)(3)(B) ('At the termination of a tenancy, a landlord may deduct any remaining payments owed under a repayment schedule from a security deposit in accordance with the provisions of section 47a-21'). Walk-through: § 47a-7c(b) ('the landlord may not retain any part of the security deposit collected under chapter 831 or seek payment from the tenant for any condition, defect or damage that was noted in the preoccupancy walk-through checklist'). The cap (two months' rent; one month's rent for a tenant 62 or older) is education, not clause text (Taylor, PA session 2026-09-29): `edu-security-deposit-cap-ct`; the builder should enforce it. Read section-open in the 2026 Supplement (§ 47a-21, amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 25-145 to Jan. 1, 2026) and the 2025 revision; Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-79, § 3 (effective Oct. 1, 2026) changes only the Banking Commissioner's enforcement powers in § 47a-21(j)(1). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Security Deposit Escrow and Bank Notice
bodyText: Landlord will deposit the entire Security Deposit in an escrow account for Tenant's benefit at a financial institution located in Connecticut. The Security Deposit of {{security_deposit}} is held at: [name and address of the financial institution]. If the financial institution is not named here when Landlord receives the Security Deposit, or if Landlord later moves the Security Deposit to another financial institution or escrow account, Landlord will give Tenant a written notice stating the amount held and the name and address of the financial institution within 30 days.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(h)(1) ('Each landlord shall immediately deposit the entire amount of any security deposit received by such landlord from each tenant into one or more escrow accounts established or maintained in a financial institution for the benefit of each tenant'); § 47a-21(a)(5) ('Financial institution' ... 'that is located in this state'); § 47a-21(h)(4)(A) ('The landlord shall provide each tenant with a written notice stating the amount held for the benefit of the tenant and the name and address of the financial institution at which the tenant's security deposit is being held not later than thirty days after the landlord receives a security deposit from the tenant or the tenant's previous landlord or transfers the security deposit to another financial institution or escrow account'). Rule 46: where the landlord knows the institution at signing, the Lease itself delivers the written notice; otherwise the clause promises the separate notice the statute requires. A knowing and wilful escrow violation is a crime (§ 47a-21(k)(2), with an affirmative defense for a landlord with fewer than four deposit-paying tenants), and the Banking Commissioner may investigate and, from Oct. 1, 2026, order a civil penalty (§ 47a-21(j)(1), as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-79, § 3; compiled text pending); see `edu-security-deposit-escrow-ct`. Read section-open in the 2026 Supplement. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: When the tenancy ends, Tenant should give Landlord written notice of Tenant's forwarding address. Within 21 days after the tenancy ends, or within 15 days after Landlord receives Tenant's written forwarding address, whichever is later, Landlord will deliver to Tenant at that forwarding address either the full Security Deposit plus accrued interest, or the balance of the Security Deposit and accrued interest after lawful deductions, together with a written statement itemizing the nature and amount of each deduction.
notes: CT: Replaces the blank-states parent `security-deposit-return` for Connecticut with the state's own deadline and the forwarding-address trigger. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(d)(2): 'Upon termination of a tenancy, any tenant may notify the landlord in writing of such tenant's forwarding address. Not later than twenty-one days after termination of a tenancy or fifteen days after receiving written notification of such tenant's forwarding address, whichever is later, each landlord other than a rent receiver shall deliver to the tenant or former tenant at such forwarding address either (A) the full amount of the security deposit paid by such tenant plus accrued interest, or (B) the balance of such security deposit and accrued interest after deduction for any damages suffered by such landlord by reason of such tenant's failure to comply with such tenant's obligations, together with a written statement itemizing the nature and amount of such damages.' Penalty: 'twice the amount of any security deposit paid by such tenant' (§ 47a-21(d)(2)); see `edu-security-deposit-return-penalty-ct`. rule_type is RECOMMENDED, not the parent's REQUIRED: Connecticut requires no deposit-return text in the lease (rule 56). SERVES_LANDLORD: the written forwarding address fixes the landlord's deadline. Read section-open in the 2026 Supplement. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Condition of the Property and Walk-Through
bodyText: Before Tenant moves in, Landlord will offer Tenant a joint walk-through of the property. If Tenant asks for one, Landlord and Tenant, or their designees, will use the Connecticut Department of Housing's preoccupancy walk-through checklist, note on it any existing conditions, defects or damage, and each sign a copy and keep one. Landlord will not keep any part of the Security Deposit, or ask Tenant to pay, for any condition, defect or damage noted on that checklist. Landlord will deliver possession on the Start Date in a fit and habitable condition and no worse than recorded on any checklist, except for ordinary wear and tear.
notes: CT: Overrides `existing-condition`, whose tenant acknowledgment that the property is "in good order and repair" sits uneasily with Connecticut's statutory walk-through, the only condition record the statute protects, and with the bar on a tenant agreeing to limit the landlord's liability arising under law (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(3)). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7c(a) ('On and after January 1, 2024, upon or after the entry into a rental agreement but prior to the tenant's occupancy of a dwelling unit, a landlord shall offer such tenant the opportunity to conduct a walk-through of the dwelling unit. If the tenant requests such a walk-through, the landlord and tenant, or their designees, shall use a copy of the preoccupancy walk-through checklist prepared by the Commissioner of Housing'); § 47a-7c(b) (no retention or payment for a condition 'noted in the preoccupancy walk-through checklist'; the checklist is admissible but 'shall not be conclusive'); § 47a-7c(d) (not for rental agreements entered into before January 1, 2024). DOH checklist saved and hashed 2026-10-09 (log §1.1). Habitability: § 47a-7(a)(2). SERVES_LANDLORD: records that the statutory offer was made. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Landlord Maintenance and Repairs
bodyText: Landlord will comply with the building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety, make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the property fit and habitable, keep any common areas clean and safe, and keep in good and safe working order the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and other facilities and appliances, and any elevators, that Landlord supplies or is required to supply. If Tenant, a member of Tenant's family, or another person on the property with Tenant's consent willfully or negligently damages the property, Tenant will pay the reasonable cost of the repair. If any of them intentionally makes the property unfit or uninhabitable, repairing that condition is Tenant's responsibility. Tenant will promptly notify Landlord of any condition that needs repair, and Landlord will make required repairs within a reasonable time.
notes: CT: Overrides `landlord-maintenance`, which excuses the landlord from repairing appliances and fixtures whenever repair is needed "due to improper use by Tenant"; in Connecticut the repair duty shifts to the tenant only where the premises are 'intentionally rendered unfit or uninhabitable' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(2)), and a term limiting the landlord's liability arising under law is void (§ 47a-4(a)(3), (b)). Controlling text: § 47a-7(a)(1)-(4) (comply with chapter 368o and codes 'materially affecting health and safety'; 'make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition, except where the premises are intentionally rendered unfit or uninhabitable by the tenant, a member of his family or other person on the premises with his consent, in which case such duty shall be the responsibility of the tenant'; common areas; 'all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and other facilities and appliances and elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by him'); tenant's cost of damage: § 47a-11(f) ('not wilfully or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or permit any other person to do so'). Rule 44: § 47a-12(a) gives the tenant a termination remedy for 'material noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement' as well as with § 47a-7, so every repair promise here is a remedy trigger; the clause promises no more than § 47a-7 requires. Garbage, water, hot water and heat duties (§ 47a-7(a)(5)-(6)) are covered by `utilities-paid-by-landlord` and education rows. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Default by Tenant
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant does not pay Rent within the grace period Connecticut law provides after it is due. Tenant will also be in default if Tenant materially fails to comply with this Lease, with Landlord's rules that are valid under Connecticut law, or with Tenant's duties under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11. Before Landlord ends this Lease for a default other than nonpayment of Rent, Landlord will give Tenant any written notice and chance to cure that Connecticut law requires. Landlord need not give Tenant a chance to cure any breach, including a failure to pay Rent, where Connecticut law lets Landlord proceed without one. Tenant's failure to pay a late charge, apart from the Rent itself, will not by itself be grounds to end this Lease or evict Tenant. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may use any remedy Connecticut law allows, including ending this Lease, recovering possession through a court process, and recovering unpaid Rent and damages, less amounts kept from the Security Deposit. Landlord will make reasonable efforts to re-rent the property to reduce Landlord's damages, as Connecticut law requires. If Landlord obtains a judgment for money damages against Tenant in an action based on this Lease, Tenant will pay Landlord's reasonable attorney's fees, up to fifteen percent of the judgment. If Tenant successfully prosecutes or defends an action or counterclaim based on this Lease, Tenant may recover reasonable attorney's fees from Landlord as Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-150bb provides.
notes: CT: Overrides `default-by-tenant` on three points. (1) Rent: the shared rent limb ties default to a cure period "after receiving written notice from Landlord"; Connecticut requires no pre-suit cure notice for nonpayment, only the statutory grace period, then a notice to quit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15a(a); § 47a-23(a)(1)(D) 'nonpayment of rent within the grace period provided for residential property in section 47a-15a'), so the shared wording would add a contractual cure (rule 43). (2) Other breaches: § 47a-15 requires a written notice 'specifying the acts or omissions constituting the breach and that the rental agreement shall terminate upon a date not less than fifteen days after receipt of the notice', with a cure only where the breach 'can be remedied by repair by the tenant or payment of damages', and no notice for nonpayment, 'serious nuisance' or a violation of § 47a-11(h); the clause promises only the notice and cure Connecticut law requires, and its no-cure sentence reaches both limbs. (3) Fees: a term making the tenant pay 'the landlord's attorney's fees in excess of fifteen per cent of any judgment against the tenant in any action in which money damages are awarded' is void (§ 47a-4(a)(7), (b)); the clause allows fees only where a money judgment is awarded, capped at fifteen percent. Under § 42-150bb, a lease that gives the landlord fees gives a consumer who 'successfully prosecutes or defends an action or a counterclaim based upon the contract or lease' a fee award 'as a matter of law', sized 'as far as practicable upon the terms governing the size of the fee for the commercial party' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-150bb; lessee is a 'consumer'). Mitigation: § 47a-11a(a) and § 47a-11c ('The landlord shall be obligated to mitigate damages'). Rules: § 47a-9. Late-charge sentence kept from the shared clause (a late charge is not 'rent', § 47a-1(8) 'all periodic payments'). Case law on attorney's fees in a possession-only summary process judgment not searched; the clause does not claim them. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision and 2026 Supplement). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Keys
bodyText: At the start of the tenancy, Tenant will receive the keys specified by Landlord and will sign a receipt acknowledging the number and type of keys provided. [Optional: Tenant will pay a key deposit of [amount], which Landlord will refund when Tenant returns all keys.] Tenant may not duplicate keys without Landlord's consent. If Tenant loses a key and asks Landlord to replace it, Tenant will pay Landlord's reasonable cost of replacing it. Tenant will return all keys when the tenancy ends; if Tenant does not, Landlord may re-key the affected locks and recover the reasonable cost from Tenant as damages, to the extent Connecticut law allows. If a tenant who is protected by a court order asks Landlord to change the locks, Landlord will do so, or let the tenant do so, as Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7b requires, and will charge no more than the actual reasonable cost that law allows.
notes: CT: Overrides `keys`. Fee screen (rule 26; kickoff): Connecticut's closed list of up-front money allows 'a deposit for a key or any special equipment' and bars any other charge at the start of the tenancy and any 'move-in or move-out fee' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4d(b), as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-68, § 59); a key deposit is not a security deposit (§ 47a-21(a)(11)). A replacement charge the tenant asks for mid-tenancy is a service fee the advertising statute recognizes ('A separate fee charged for performing a service for the tenant, including, but not limited to, responding to a lockout or replacing a key', § 47a-7d(b)(5)). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: a re-key cost for keys not returned is claimed as damages, not as a move-out fee and not as a stated deposit deduction, since § 47a-21(a)(14) limits deductions to listed obligations; whether unreturned keys fall within § 47a-11(f) is unsettled (case law not searched). Protected-person lock change: § 47a-7b(a), (c) (landlord 'may charge a fee to the tenant not exceeding the actual reasonable cost of changing the locks'; unpaid cost may be recouped 'by suit against the tenant or as a deduction from the security deposit' but 'shall not be the basis for a summary process action'). Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Vehicles and Parking Rules
bodyText: Only operable, currently registered passenger vehicles may be parked at the property; commercial vehicles, recreational vehicles, trailers and oversized vehicles are not permitted without Landlord's prior written consent. Landlord may require Tenant to provide vehicle registration information and may issue parking tags, decals or access cards. Landlord will not charge Tenant for the tags, decals or cards issued at the start of the tenancy, but may charge the reasonable cost of replacing one that Tenant loses or damages. Landlord may, in accordance with applicable law, have a vehicle towed at the vehicle owner's expense if it is illegally parked, abandoned or inoperable. Vehicle repairs are not permitted at the property except minor emergency repairs necessary to move the vehicle, and vehicles may be washed only in areas Landlord designates, if any.
notes: CT: Overrides `parking-vehicle-rules`, whose "cost of which may be charged to Tenant" would let a landlord charge for tags or cards at the start of the tenancy, which Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4d(b) bars ('demand any other payment, fee or charge before or at the beginning of the tenancy'; as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-68, § 59). A replacement charge later is a service fee (§ 47a-7d(b)(5)). Towing: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 14-145(b)(1) lets an owner or lessee of private property tow 'any motor vehicle left without authorization on such private property' only with a signed written authorization form for each tow and any signage § 14-145e requires; § 14-145(b)(2) bars a private owner from issuing 'a parking citation ... to impose a monetary sanction' or using 'a wheel-locking device' (see `edu-private-towing-ct`). The clause makes inoperable, abandoned and illegally parked vehicles unauthorized and relies on "in accordance with applicable law" for the towing procedure; the shared clause's ground for "expired registration" is dropped (DRAFTING JUDGMENT: a tenant's registered-space vehicle with lapsed registration is not plainly 'left without authorization'). Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, due with each Monthly Rent payment. Landlord will not charge a separate pet fee or pet deposit at or before the start of the tenancy; any deposit Landlord requires because of a pet is part of the Security Deposit and counts toward its limit. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet, and will indemnify Landlord against claims arising from Tenant's pet, except claims arising from Landlord's own negligence or any other liability of Landlord arising under law. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or a danger to people or property, by written notice giving Tenant a reasonable time to remove it. This Section does not apply to an assistance animal, which this Lease's assistance animal terms govern.
notes: CT: Overrides `pet-policy` on three points. (1) Its separate pet deposit at signing would breach Connecticut's closed list of up-front money (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4d(b), as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-68, § 59); pet rent is periodic rent ('"Rent" means all periodic payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement', § 47a-1(8)), which the advertising statute expects ('Any fee or deposit imposed for keeping a pet', § 47a-7d(b)(2)). (2) Its indemnity reaches the landlord's own liability; a tenant may not agree 'to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law or to indemnify the landlord for that liability or the costs connected therewith' (§ 47a-4(a)(3)). (3) Its right to enter and remove a pet without the tenant's consent outside an emergency conflicts with § 47a-16(d) ('A landlord may not enter the dwelling unit without the consent of the tenant except (1) in case of emergency, (2) as permitted by section 47a-16a, (3) pursuant to a court order, or (4) if the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises'); dropped. Assistance animals: `assistance-animal-accommodation`. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Fire Sprinkler System Notice
bodyText: **FIRE SPRINKLER NOTICE: [Use if the building is required by law to be equipped with a fire sprinkler system.] The building in which the dwelling unit is located [choose one: HAS / DOES NOT HAVE] an operative fire sprinkler system. [If it has one: The fire sprinkler system was last maintained and inspected on [date].]**
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3f(b): 'When renting a dwelling unit in a building required to be equipped with a fire sprinkler system pursuant to section 29-315, the State Fire Safety Code, the State Fire Prevention Code or any other statute or regulation, the landlord of such dwelling unit shall include notice in the rental agreement as to the existence or nonexistence of an operative fire sprinkler system in such building, and such notice shall be printed in not less than twelve-point boldface type of uniform font.' § 47a-3f(c): 'If there is an operative fire sprinkler system in the building, the rental agreement shall provide further notice as to the last date of maintenance and inspection, and such notice shall be printed in not less than twelve-point boldface type of uniform font.' LAYOUT (rule 40; log §4): the builder must print this whole clause in at least 12-point boldface of one font; the asterisks mark bold for the builder (§10). The DOH model lease's checkbox describes the notice as for 'a building of more than four stories'; the statute's trigger is the sprinkler requirement, not height, and the clause follows the statute. Which buildings must have sprinklers is set by § 29-315 and the fire codes (education row `edu-sprinkler-notice-ct`). Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Common Interest Community Notice
bodyText: [Use if Landlord is the declarant or a successor declarant of the common interest community where the dwelling unit is located, or is acting on the declarant's or successor declarant's behalf.] NOTICE: The dwelling unit is located in a common interest community.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3e: 'Whenever a dwelling unit in a common interest community is rented from a declarant, successor declarant or person acting on the declarant's or successor declarant's behalf, such declarant, successor declarant or person shall, prior to entering into a rental agreement, provide the tenant with a written notice that the dwelling unit is located in a common interest community.' TIMING (rule 78): the notice must come before the rental agreement is entered into; a clause in the Lease itself arrives at signing, so `edu-cic-notice-timing-ct` tells the landlord to give the notice in writing before signing as well. The duty falls only on a declarant-side landlord; an individual unit owner who rents a condominium unit has no § 47a-3e duty (use `hoa-compliance` for association rules). Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Landlord Identification
bodyText: As Connecticut law requires, Landlord gives Tenant the name and address of: (1) the person authorized to manage the property: [name and address]; and (2) the person authorized to receive all notices, demands and service of process for Landlord: [name and address]. Landlord will keep this information current and will tell Tenant in writing of any change.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-6(a): 'It is the duty of the landlord or an agent authorized by him, or any successor landlord or such successor's agent to notify the tenant in writing, on or before the commencement of the tenancy, or in the case of a successor at the time of such succession, of the name and address of (1) the person authorized to manage the premises and (2) the person who is authorized to receive all notices, demands and service of process. Such name and address shall be kept current.' Consequence of omission: § 47a-6(b) (the person the landlord authorized to enter into the rental agreement is deemed the landlord's agent for service, for the landlord's duties under §§ 47a-7 and 47a-13 and for spending rent to perform them). Rule 46: the Lease is a writing given 'on or before the commencement of the tenancy', so this clause satisfies § 47a-6(a). The DOH Rental Terms Summary Form also asks for a point of contact (`edu-rental-terms-summary-form-ct`). Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Bed Bug Disclosure
bodyText: BED BUG DISCLOSURE. [Use for any dwelling unit other than a single-family unattached home.] Landlord discloses that the dwelling unit is not currently infested with bed bugs, and that [choose one: no / a] contiguous unit that Landlord owns, leases or subleases is currently infested with bed bugs. On request, Landlord will tell Tenant the last date on which the dwelling unit was inspected for, and found to be free of, a bed bug infestation.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7a(c): 'No landlord shall offer for rent a dwelling unit that the landlord knows or reasonably suspects is infested with bed bugs. Before renting a dwelling unit, a landlord shall disclose to a prospective tenant whether the unit the landlord is offering for rent or any contiguous unit of which the landlord is an owner, lessor or sublessor is currently infested with bed bugs. Upon request from a tenant or prospective tenant, a landlord shall disclose the last date on which the dwelling unit being rented or offered for rent was inspected for, and found to be free of, a bed bug infestation.' Scope: § 47a-7a(a)(7) ('"Dwelling unit" means a unit other than a single-family unattached unit'). Because the landlord may not offer an infested unit at all, the clause states the unit is not infested and gives a choice only for contiguous units. TIMING (rule 78): the disclosure is due 'before renting'; the DOH model lease lists it among the disclosures acknowledged at signing; `edu-bed-bug-duties-ct` tells landlords to make it before the tenant signs. Failure: the tenant may proceed under §§ 47a-12 or 47a-14h and recover 'reasonable attorneys' fees and the greater of two hundred fifty dollars or the tenant's actual damages' (§ 47a-7a(d)(1)). Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Bed Bug Reporting and Cooperation
bodyText: [Use for any dwelling unit other than a single-family unattached home.] Tenant will promptly tell Landlord, orally or in writing, if Tenant knows or reasonably suspects that the dwelling unit has bed bugs. After reasonable notice, Tenant will not unreasonably withhold access for a bed bug inspection or treatment, will comply with reasonable inspection and treatment measures, and will pay the cost of preparing the unit for them. Tenant will not remove infested furniture, clothing or other belongings from the unit until a pest control agent determines treatment is complete or Landlord approves. If Tenant is not physically able to prepare the unit, Landlord will offer reasonable assistance and will tell Tenant its cost, if any, before charging for it.
notes: CT: Restates the tenant duties in Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7a(b) (SERVES_LANDLORD): '(1) A tenant shall promptly notify a landlord orally or in writing when the tenant knows or reasonably suspects that the tenant's dwelling unit is infested with bed bugs'; '(2)(A) Upon reasonable written or oral notice to a tenant in accordance with the provisions of section 47a-16 ... a tenant shall not unreasonably withhold access to the dwelling unit'; '(B) ... such tenant shall be responsible for all costs associated with preparing a dwelling unit for such inspection and treatment'; '(C) ... such furniture, clothing, equipment or personal property shall not be removed from the dwelling unit until a pest control agent determines that a bed bug treatment has been completed, or until the landlord approves of such removal'; '(3)(A) A landlord shall offer to make reasonable assistance available to a tenant who is not physically able to comply with preparation ... The landlord shall disclose to the tenant the cost, if any'. Any assistance charge must be on a repayment schedule of up to six months and is not a ground for summary process (§ 47a-7a(b)(3)(A)-(B)); the landlord pays for inspection and treatment except as § 47a-7a provides. One subject per row: the disclosure is `bed-bug-disclosure-ct`. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Waiver of Notice to Quit at End of Term
bodyText: [Optional; use only if this Lease has a fixed Term.] TENANT GIVES UP (WAIVES) THE NOTICE TO QUIT AT THE END OF THE TERM. If this Lease ends because its Term expires and Tenant does not move out, Tenant gives up the three-day written notice to quit that Connecticut law would otherwise require before Landlord starts a court case to recover possession. This waiver applies only when this Lease ends by lapse of time at the end of the Term. It does not apply if this Lease ends early for nonpayment of Rent, a breach or any other reason, or to any month-to-month or other tenancy that follows the Term. It does not give up Tenant's right to a court hearing, any stay of execution Connecticut law allows, any notice federal law requires, or any protection Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23c gives a tenant who is 62 or older or has a disability, or who lives with a relative who is 62 or older or has a disability, in a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park. Landlord may remove Tenant only through a court eviction. Tenant's initials: ________
notes: CT: OPTIONAL CLAUSE (rule 54; Taylor 2026-10-09, log §6.2: offer it, narrowly). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-25: 'When, in any written lease of any land, building, apartment or dwelling unit, notice to quit possession has been expressly waived by the lessee in the event such lease terminates by lapse of time, the three days' notice prescribed in sections 47a-23 and 47a-23a shall not be necessary; and complaint and summons may issue in the same manner as if such notice to quit had been previously given.' The general ban on waiving statutory rights excepts a section that 'expressly states that such rights may be waived' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1)); § 47a-25 is such a section. Limits the clause states: lapse of time only (§ 47a-23(a)(1)(A)); a periodic tenancy ends by notice, not lapse of time (DRAFTING JUDGMENT: fixed Term only); the stay-of-execution rights in §§ 47a-36 to 47a-40 cannot be waived (§ 47a-41: any such provision 'is against public policy and void'); a protected tenant under § 47a-23c may not be evicted at the end of the term at all except for a listed reason (§ 47a-23c(b)(1), (3)); the CARES Act 30-day notice for covered properties is federal (`edu-cares-act-notice`). The right-to-counsel notice attaches to a notice to quit (§ 47a-75(f)(2)); with no notice to quit it still attaches to the summons and complaint. Initials line chosen to make the waiver express. Never a default. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). SYNC (Claude Code, 2026-10-09): checked against the conditions Taylor's approval carried (backlog item 22), with §§ 47a-25, 47a-23(a), 47a-23c, 47a-41, 47a-3d and 47a-75(f)(2) read on cga.ct.gov (2025 revision and 2026 Supplement): written fixed-term lease, lapse of time only, never a default, not for nonpayment, breach or a following periodic tenancy, stays and federal notices kept, initials line: all present. The § 47a-23c sentence was widened to the statute's relatives and its five-unit / mobile-home-park scope (§ 47a-23c(a)(1)); a protected tenant can't be evicted on lapse of time at all (§ 47a-23c(b)(1)), so for them the waiver has no effect. Whether accepting rent after the Term creates a new tenancy the waiver does not reach is case law not searched (§ 47a-3d: holding over alone is 'not ... evidence of any agreement for a further lease'). Missouri contrast: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.070 already needs no notice to quit for a tenancy 'whose term is to end at a certain time', so a fixed-term waiver would add nothing there; its 'special agreement' could only strip notice from periodic tenancies, which is why it was declined (Taylor, 2026-09-30) and stays declined. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Fire or Casualty
bodyText: [Optional.] If fire or other casualty not caused by Tenant's negligence or willful act damages or destroys the property so that Tenant's enjoyment of it is substantially impaired, Landlord may end this Lease by written notice to Tenant, effective on a date stated in the notice that is at least 30 days after the notice is given or, if Tenant has already moved out, on the date Tenant moved out. Rent is not owed for any period during which the impairment continues, and Rent will be accounted for as of the date of the fire or casualty. Landlord will return all security and prepaid Rent that Connecticut law allows Tenant to recover. If Tenant does not move out after this Lease ends under this Section, Landlord will recover possession only through a court process. This Section does not let Landlord end the tenancy of a tenant protected by Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23c except on a ground that statute allows, and does not limit Tenant's own rights under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14 or other Connecticut law.
notes: CT: OPTIONAL CLAUSE (rule 54: a landlord right the statute leaves to contract). Connecticut gives the tenant the casualty remedies (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14(a): unless 'caused by the tenant's negligence or wilful act', the tenant 'shall not be liable to pay rent for such period of time as such impairment continues' and may vacate and terminate on written notice within fourteen days, or stay and pay reduced rent; § 47a-14(b): 'the landlord shall return all security and prepaid rent recoverable under section 47a-21. Accounting for rent, in the event of termination or apportionment, shall be made as of the date of the fire or other casualty'). No Connecticut statute gives the landlord a casualty termination right (CT battery CASUALTY-LANDLORD, log §17); a lease may make one a ground, since a rental agreement may terminate 'by reason of any expressed stipulation therein' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a)(1)(B)). Limits: § 47a-23c(b)(1) lists the only grounds for evicting a protected tenant (62 or older, or with a disability, in a building of five or more units), and a lease stipulation is not one of them, so the clause carves those tenants out; the tenant's own § 47a-14 rights are preserved, since a waiver is void (§ 47a-4(a)(1)). Fault persons match § 47a-14 (the tenant's own negligence or wilful act) and the rent-continuation limb of `tenant-caused-damage-ct` (UT circle-back 2). The 30-day minimum is a drafting judgment, not a statutory figure. UNREAD RISK: whether a court enforces a landlord casualty termination against a tenant who stays under § 47a-14(a)(2) rests on case law not searched. Never a default. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: [Optional.] If Tenant, a member of Tenant's family, or another person on the property with Tenant's consent willfully or negligently damages the property, Tenant will pay the reasonable cost of repairing the damage. If fire or other casualty damage to the property was caused by Tenant's own negligence or willful act, Rent will continue while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues. If this Lease ends because of damage that Tenant, a member of Tenant's family, or another person on the property with Tenant's consent willfully or negligently caused, Tenant will also be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property.
notes: CT: OPTIONAL CLAUSE (rule 54, tenant-caused damage; model `tenant-caused-damage-tn`). Each limb tracks the Connecticut fault rule for the remedy it touches (rule 54 UT circle-back 1-2): REPAIR COST: the tenant shall 'not wilfully or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or permit any other person to do so' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11(f)); 'a member of his family or other person on the premises with his consent' is the statute's own phrase for the persons whose conduct defeats tenant remedies (§§ 47a-7(a)(2), 47a-12(b), 47a-13(c)(2)). RENT DURING REPAIRS: § 47a-14(a) abates rent for fire or casualty 'unless such damage or destruction is caused by the tenant's negligence or wilful act'; only the tenant's own fault is listed, so the clause continues rent only in that case, because a broader term would waive a statutory abatement right (void, § 47a-4(a)(1)). Essential-service remedies do not arise if 'the condition was caused by the wilful or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of his family or other person on the premises with his consent' (§ 47a-13(c)(2)); termination for landlord breach is barred for such a condition (§ 47a-12(b)). DAMAGES AND MITIGATION: § 47a-11c (damages 'shall include the amount of rent agreed to by the parties but unpaid by the tenant' and 'The landlord shall be obligated to mitigate damages'); § 47a-11a. The casualty clause `casualty-termination-ct` uses the same fault rule for its exclusion. No Connecticut domestic-violence exit carries a fault rule this clause would cut off (§ 47a-11e; preserved by `early-termination-ct`). UNREAD RISK: the measure of lost rent through the end of the Term rests on case law not searched. Never a default. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Serious Nuisance and Criminal Activity
bodyText: [Optional.] Tenant, members of Tenant's household and persons on the property with Tenant's consent will not commit a serious nuisance, which means: inflicting bodily harm on another tenant or Landlord, or threatening to do so with the present ability to carry out the threat and under circumstances that would lead a reasonable person to believe the threat will be carried out; substantial and willful destruction of part of the property; conduct that presents an immediate and serious danger to the safety of other tenants or Landlord; or using the property, or allowing it to be used, for prostitution or the illegal sale of drugs. A serious nuisance is a material breach of this Lease, and Landlord may end this Lease by a notice to quit without first giving Tenant a notice and chance to cure. Landlord will regain possession only through a court process. This Section does not apply to conduct of which Tenant or a member of Tenant's household is the victim, and Landlord will not treat a request for police or emergency help, or the lawful possession or consumption of cannabis that Connecticut law protects, as a violation.
notes: CT: OPTIONAL CLAUSE (rule 54, crime-free analogue). Definition follows Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15 ('"serious nuisance" means (A) inflicting bodily harm upon another tenant or the landlord or threatening to inflict such harm with the present ability to effect the harm and under circumstances which would lead a reasonable person to believe that such threat will be carried out, (B) substantial and wilful destruction of part of the dwelling unit or premises, (C) conduct which presents an immediate and serious danger to the safety of other tenants or the landlord, or (D) using the premises or allowing the premises to be used for prostitution or the illegal sale of drugs'); the housing-authority 1,500-foot limb is omitted (housing authorities only). No-cure route: § 47a-15 excepts a landlord who 'elects to proceed under sections 47a-23 to 47a-23b, inclusive, to evict based on ... conduct by the tenant which constitutes a serious nuisance'; § 47a-23(a)(1)(G) lists 'serious nuisance, as defined in section 47a-15' as a ground. Tenant's household duty: § 47a-11(g) (conduct of 'other persons on the premises with his consent'). Protected tenants: material noncompliance with the rental agreement is a listed ground (§ 47a-23c(b)(1)(D)). Cannabis carve-out: a landlord 'may not prohibit the possession of cannabis or the consumption of cannabis', except smoking or vaping (§ 47a-9a(b)). Victim carve-out: a drafting judgment consistent with § 46a-64c's protection of victims of domestic violence (log §6.3). Never a default. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Death of a Sole Occupant
bodyText: [Optional.] Tenant names the following emergency contact, whom Landlord may notify if Tenant dies: [name, mailing address and telephone number]. Tenant will tell Landlord in writing if this changes. If Tenant is the only occupant of the property and dies, Landlord may end this Lease by written notice sent to the emergency contact (if any) and to Tenant's next of kin (if known), effective on a date stated in the notice that is at least 30 days after the notice is sent. Landlord may then deal with Tenant's possessions and personal effects only as Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11d provides. Tenant's estate remains liable for Rent through the date this Lease ends and for any damage to the property.
notes: CT: OPTIONAL CLAUSE (rule 54: a procedure the statute makes available only if the lease provides for it). Conn. Gen.
