Stat. § 47a-11d(a): 'If the sole occupant of a dwelling unit subject to a monthly lease or a lease for a term has died and the landlord has complied with any provisions of any such lease permitting termination upon the death of the occupant, the landlord may elect to act in accordance with the provisions of this section.' The statute's notice goes 'to the emergency contact designated by the occupant, if any, and to the next of kin of such occupant, if known' (§ 47a-11d(a)), so the clause records the designation. The § 47a-11d procedure (60-day notice, probate affidavit, inventory, certificate deemed a summary process judgment, marshal removal) then replaces a notice to quit and summary process (§ 47a-11d(c)-(e)), and no forcible-entry action lies against a landlord who follows it (§ 47a-11d(g)); see `edu-tenant-death-ct`. The 30-day notice period and the estate-liability sentence are drafting judgments, not statutory figures. Never a default. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging Station Requests
bodyText: [Use if Tenant has a dedicated parking space at the property.] If Tenant asks in writing to install an electric vehicle charging station at Tenant's dedicated parking space, Landlord will approve the request when Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13b requires it, if the request complies with that statute and with Landlord's procedural approval process for modifications to the property. Before any work begins, Tenant will sign a written agreement with Landlord covering: installation, use, maintenance and removal of the station and its infrastructure; a complete financial analysis and scope of work; payment to Landlord of the costs of Landlord's installation, before any modification; payment of Landlord's electricity costs for the station and of the costs of damage, maintenance, repair, removal and replacement; any cooperative agreement with other tenants who will use the station; a general liability insurance policy covering the station that names Landlord as an additional insured; a surety bond equal to the cost of removal, or Landlord's right to withhold the Security Deposit for removal damages; and designation of the station as a fixture if Tenant does not remove it when this Lease ends. Landlord need not provide an additional parking space for a charging station.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13b(b) requires a landlord to approve a tenant's written request to install a charging station at a 'dedicated parking space' that meets the section and 'complies with the landlord's procedural approval process for modifications to the property', phased in by landlord size for rental agreements executed, extended or renewed on or after October 1, 2022 (250 or more units), October 1, 2023 (more than 50 but fewer than 250) and October 1, 2024 (50 or fewer). § 47a-13b(e): the request 'shall indicate such tenant's consent to enter into a written agreement with the landlord that includes, but is not limited to,' the eight listed items, which the clause lists in the statute's order; § 47a-13b(c): 'A landlord shall not be obligated to provide an additional parking space'. Exemptions (§ 47a-13b(f)): charging already provided for 10 percent or more of designated spaces; parking not provided under the rental agreement; fewer than five parking spaces; LIHTC-assisted property; housing-authority property; see `edu-ev-charging-ct`. SERVES_LANDLORD: fixes the agreement the landlord may require before work starts. The fixture and surety terms are the statute's own. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant Who Stays After the Lease Ends
bodyText: If a tenant stays after a fixed-term lease ends, the holding over is not by itself evidence that you agreed to a new lease, and an oral lease at a monthly rent with no agreed end is a lease for one month only. To remove the tenant you must serve a notice to quit through a proper officer and bring a summary process case in court (unless a valid lease waiver of the notice to quit applies). While the case is pending, the court can order the tenant to pay use and occupancy into court equal to the last agreed rent, or the fair rental value if there was no agreed rent. If you accept money after the date to quit, you can reserve your rights by including the statutory use-and-occupancy disclaimer in the notice to quit; accepting rent you know is overdue waives the right to end the tenancy for that late rent. A tenant in a building or complex of five or more units (or a mobile home park) who is 62 or older or has a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or who permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability, cannot be evicted just because the lease ended; in a condominium or other common interest community this applies only to conversion tenants or where you own five or more units in that community.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3d ('Holding over by any lessee, after the expiration of the term of his lease, shall not be evidence of any agreement for a further lease. Parol leases of lands or tenements reserving a monthly rent and in which the time of their termination is not agreed upon shall be construed to be leases for one month only'); § 47a-23(a)(1)(A) (lapse of time), (c) (service 'by a proper officer'); § 47a-25 (lease waiver of the notice to quit at lapse of time; `notice-to-quit-waiver-ct`); § 47a-26b(a) (use and occupancy 'in an amount equal to the last agreed-upon rent or, in the absence of a prior agreed-upon rent, in an amount equal to the fair rental value of the premises'); § 47a-23(e) (disclaimer 'Any payments tendered after the date specified to quit possession or occupancy, or the date of the completion of the pretermination process if that is later, will be accepted for use and occupancy only and not for rent, with full reservation of rights to continue with the eviction action.'); § 47a-19 (acceptance of overdue rent waives termination for it); § 47a-23c(b)(1) (protected tenants; lapse of time not a listed ground). The tagged shared clause `holdover-ca` (actual damages and reasonable rental value; month-to-month on accepted rent) is consistent. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision and 2026 Supplement). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Premium Holdover Charge Offered
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that sets or caps a holdover charge, so a lease could try to set a daily or premium rate for a tenant who stays after the lease ends. We do not offer one. For most of a holdover the statutes already set the measure: while an eviction case is pending the court, on your motion, orders use and occupancy payments at the last agreed rent (or at fair rental value if the tenant objects), and during a court-granted stay of execution the court may require payments at the rent the tenant was paying or another reasonable amount. A premium charge could also fall on a tenant who has a legal right to stay, such as a protected tenant 62 or older or with a disability, and an unreasonable fixed charge may be an unenforceable penalty. If you want a holdover charge anyway, have your own lawyer draft it.
notes: CT: Rule 54 option considered and declined (log §6.1). No statute sets a holdover measure (CT batteries HOLDOVER-MEASURE and the canvass holdover-rate batteries, log §§ 17 and 18). Statutory measures that apply during most holdover periods: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-26b(a) (use and occupancy 'in an amount equal to the last agreed-upon rent'); § 47a-39 (during a stay of execution the court may require payment 'for the use and occupancy of the premises for such period of the stay, at the rate to which he was liable as rent for the month immediately prior to the expiration of his term or tenancy'); § 47a-35a(a) (appeal: the defendant's portion of the last agreed rent or reasonable value). Protected tenants: § 47a-23c(b). Penalty doctrine and § 42-150u (liquidated damages acknowledgment in consumer contracts) are case-law and coverage questions not settled here (case law not searched); NEEDS_REVIEW for that reason. Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision and 2026 Supplement). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Pet Fees and Pet Deposits
bodyText: You may not charge a pet fee, or any fee other than the first month's rent, a security deposit, a key or special-equipment deposit and the capped screening-report fee, before or at the start of a tenancy. Collect any pet deposit as part of the security deposit: it counts toward the two-month limit (one month for a tenant 62 or older), must be held in escrow and earns interest. Monthly pet rent is ordinary rent and is allowed. If you advertise the unit, you may leave a pet fee or pet deposit out of the advertised rent. You may not charge any pet fee or deposit for an assistance animal.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4d(b), as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-68, § 59 (no 'other payment, fee or charge before or at the beginning of the tenancy' except a security deposit, first month's rent, a key or special-equipment deposit, or the screening-report fee); § 47a-21(a)(11), (b), (h), (i) (security deposit definition, cap, escrow, interest); § 47a-1(8) ('"Rent" means all periodic payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement'); § 47a-7d(b)(2) (advertised rent may exclude 'Any fee or deposit imposed for keeping a pet in the dwelling unit'). NEEDS_REVIEW: § 47a-21(a)(11) defines a security deposit as 'any advance rental payment'; whether a pet deposit is one, or is instead barred outright at the start of the tenancy by § 47a-4d(b), is not settled by the text, and the row takes the course that is lawful on either reading (collect it inside the capped, escrowed deposit). Assistance animals: federal Fair Housing Act and Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46a-64c reasonable accommodation (`assistance-animal-accommodation`). Read section-open (cga.ct.gov 2025 revision and 2026 Supplement). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Last Month's Rent Counts as a Deposit
bodyText: In Connecticut any rent paid in advance, other than the first month's rent, is a security deposit. Last month's rent collected at signing therefore counts toward the deposit limit of two months' rent (one month for a tenant 62 or older), must be deposited in an escrow account at a Connecticut financial institution, must be reported to the tenant with the bank's name and address within 30 days, and earns interest at the Banking Commissioner's deposit index. It is returned or applied under the security deposit rules when the tenancy ends.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(a)(11) ('"Security deposit" means any advance rental payment, or any installment payment collected pursuant to section 47a-22a, except an advance payment for the first month's rent or a deposit for a key or any special equipment'); § 47a-21(b) (cap), (h)(1), (h)(4)(A) (escrow and 30-day notice), (i) (interest), (d) (return). § 47a-4d(b) allows at the start of the tenancy only a security deposit, first month's rent, a key or special-equipment deposit and the screening fee. Clause: `due-at-signing-ct`. Read section-open in the 2026 Supplement. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: How Tenants May Pay Rent
bodyText: You may not require electronic payment (an online portal, ACH or autopay) as the only way to pay rent or the security deposit; always accept at least one paper method such as a check or money order. Connecticut's surcharge law also bars adding a fee because a person pays by a particular method, and it covers renting real property, so do not add a card or portal convenience fee to rent without legal advice. If you charge a payment-processing fee at all, it must reflect your actual cost and you must offer a fee-free way to pay, or the fee must be built into the advertised rent. Give a written receipt for every cash payment.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4c: 'For any lease or rental agreement executed on or after October 1, 2013, no landlord of residential real property shall require electronic funds transfer as the exclusive form of payment of rent or a security deposit.' Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-133ff(b): 'No person may impose a surcharge on any transaction'; § 42-133ff(a)(6) 'Surcharge' means 'any additional charge or fee that increases the total amount of a transaction for the privilege of using a particular method of payment'; § 42-133ff(a)(7)(A) 'Transaction' includes 'the lease, rental or sale by one person of any tangible or intangible personal, real or mixed property ... for a certain price in this state'; violation is a CUTPA unfair trade practice (§ 42-133ff(f)). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7d(b)(1) lets advertised rent exclude 'Any payment processing fee that reflects the actual cost of processing a payment, provided the landlord makes available to the tenant an alternative form of payment that does not require payment of any such payment processing fee'; § 47a-7d(f) civil penalty of one month's rent. NEEDS_REVIEW: whether § 42-133ff(b) reaches a rent processing fee that § 47a-7d(b)(1) contemplates is unsettled (the exclusion in § 42-133ff(a)(7)(B)(v) for a 'sum pursuant to any other provision of the general statutes' may or may not reach it); case law not searched; the row advises caution rather than resolving it. Cash receipt duty: § 47a-3a(c). Online-payment-system outage extends the nonpayment grace period five days (§ 47a-15a(a)); see late-fee rows. Shared clause acceptable-payment-methods-nj (keeps a non-EFT method, never requires EFT, no fee language) fits Connecticut as written. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Rent-Pricing Software Banned
bodyText: Since January 1, 2026, you may not use revenue management software to set rents or occupancy levels for Connecticut homes. The ban covers any software or device that runs calculations on nonpublic competitor data, such as other landlords' actual rents, occupancy or lease dates, to advise you whether to leave a unit vacant or how much rent to charge. Published reports of aggregated rental data that do not recommend rents, and tools used to set rent or income limits under an affordable housing program, are not covered. A violation is enforced under Connecticut's antitrust law.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4f(b): 'It shall be an unlawful practice in violation of chapter 624 for any person to use a revenue management device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units.' Chapter 624 is the Connecticut Antitrust Act (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 35-24); § 35-26: 'Every contract, combination, or conspiracy in restraint of any part of trade or commerce is unlawful.' § 47a-4f(a)(1) defines 'Revenue management device' as a device 'that uses one or more programmed or automated processes to perform calculations of nonpublic competitor data concerning local or state-wide rents or occupancy levels, for the purpose of advising a landlord on (A) whether to leave a unit vacant; or (B) the amount of rent that the landlord may obtain for a unit', excluding '(i) A report that publishes existing rental data in an aggregated manner but does not recommend rental rates or occupancy levels for future leases; or (ii) a product used for the purpose of establishing rent or income limits in accordance with the affordable housing program guidelines of a local, state or federal program.' § 47a-4f(a)(2) defines 'Nonpublic competitor data' (whether attributable to a competitor or anonymized). § 47a-4f(c): violations are 'subject to the investigation and enforcement provisions of chapter 624.' Added by Conn. Pub. Act No. 25-1 (Nov. Sp. Sess.), § 32, effective January 1, 2026 (2026 Supplement). Antitrust Act remedies (§§ 35-34 to 35-46) not read. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Application and Screening Fees
bodyText: You may not charge an application or processing fee. The only charge you may take from an applicant is a fee for a tenant screening report (credit, criminal background, employment or rental history), and it may not exceed $50 plus the yearly inflation adjustment the Connecticut Department of Housing sets. If you charge it, give the applicant a copy of the report (or, if you may not share it, the information needed to request it from the screening company) and a copy of the screening company's receipt or invoice. These limits also bind a property manager, screening company or other third party acting for you. You may never charge a move-in or move-out fee.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4d(b), as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-68, § 59 (effective from passage; Governor approved May 26, 2026; compiled text pending): 'No landlord, third party acting on behalf of a landlord, or third party acting on behalf of the state may demand from a prospective tenant any payment, fee or charge for the processing, review or acceptance of any rental application, or demand any other payment, fee or charge before or at the beginning of the tenancy, except a security deposit pursuant to section 47a-21, advance payment for the first month's rent or a deposit for a key or any special equipment, or a fee for a tenant screening report as provided in subsection (c) of this section. No landlord may charge a tenant a move-in or move-out fee.' § 47a-4d(c) (as amended): a fee 'not exceeding fifty dollars plus an adjustment reflecting any increase in the consumer price index for urban consumers, as determined by the Commissioner of Housing on an annual basis, for a tenant screening report concerning a prospective tenant.' § 47a-4d(d): copy of the report or information to request it, and 'a copy of the receipt or invoice from the entity conducting the tenant screening report'. § 47a-4d(a) defines 'tenant screening report'. The 2025-revision text (Conn. Pub. Act No. 23-207, § 6) covered only landlords; Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-68 adds third parties. The current CPI-adjusted dollar figure is set by DOH and is not in the loaded sources; the builder should not hard-code $50 as the cap. No statutory refund rule for an unused screening fee (the fee buys a report). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Collection Fee
bodyText: [Optional.] If Tenant does not pay an amount owed under this Lease and Landlord refers the debt to a consumer collection agency licensed in Connecticut, Tenant will pay a collection fee equal to what the agency charges Landlord for collecting it. The fee will not be more than [percentage, not more than 15]% of the total amount the agency actually collects and accepts as payment in full. This Lease expressly authorizes that fee. Court costs and attorney's fees are owed only as a court awards them and Connecticut law allows.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 36a-805(a)(11): a consumer collection agency shall not 'add any post-charge-off charge or fee for cost of collection, unless such cost is a court cost, to the amount of any claim which it receives for collection ... or knowingly accept for collection any claim to which any such charge or fee has already been added to the amount of the claim unless (A) the consumer debtor is legally liable for such charge or fee as determined by a contract or other evidence of an agreement between the consumer debtor and creditor ... and (B) the total charge or fee for cost of collection does not exceed fifteen per cent of the total amount actually collected and accepted as payment in full satisfaction of the debt.' Conn. Agencies Regs. § 36a-809-12(1) (regulation, Rule 21 flag) makes it an unfair practice for a consumer collection agency to collect 'any amount, including any interest, fee, charge or expense incidental to the principal obligation, that is not expressly authorized by the agreement creating the debt or permitted by law.' Agency definition: § 36a-800(3). A landlord collecting its own debt is a 'creditor' under § 36a-645 and may not use 'any abusive, harassing, fraudulent, deceptive or misleading representation, device or practice' (§ 36a-646). The cap in the clause is the landlord's own figure, bounded by the 15% statutory ceiling. Attorney's fees are separately capped at 15% of any money judgment by § 47a-4(a)(7) (see attorney-fees). NEEDS_REVIEW: no Connecticut landlord-tenant statute addresses a collection fee; whether a court would treat it as an unenforceable penalty is case law not searched; Creditors' Collection Practices regulations (§ 36a-647 regs) not loaded. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Advertised Rent Must Include Recurring Fees
bodyText: When you advertise, display or offer a unit, the rent you state must include every fee or cost the tenant will have to pay on a periodic basis, prorated into the rent figure. A fee charged monthly by default counts even if the tenant can opt out of it. You may leave out only: a payment-processing fee that reflects actual cost when you offer a fee-free way to pay; a pet fee or deposit; utilities that are submetered or paid directly to a utility and vary month to month; a charge for damage beyond normal wear and tear; and a separate fee for a service such as a lockout or key replacement. A violation makes you liable to the tenant for one month's rent, plus possible attorney's fees. The same total periodic rent goes on the state's Rental Terms Summary Form that must be the first page of the lease.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7d(a): 'no landlord shall advertise, display or otherwise offer a dwelling unit for rent in an amount that excludes any fee, charge or cost that the tenant of the advertised, displayed or offered dwelling unit shall be required to pay on a periodic basis. Any fee, charge or cost that the tenant shall be required to pay on a periodic basis shall be prorated and included in the advertised, displayed or offered rent. For the purposes of this subsection, any fee, charge or cost that shall be charged to the tenant, by default, on a monthly basis shall be included in the advertised, displayed or offered rent, regardless of whether the tenant may opt out of such fee, charge or cost.' § 47a-7d(b)(1)-(5) lists the exclusions (payment processing fee reflecting actual cost with a fee-free alternative; pet fee or deposit; utilities submetered under § 16-19ff or paid directly to a utility company that may vary; a fee for damage not imposed for normal wear and tear; a separate fee for performing a service such as a lockout or key replacement). § 47a-7d(f): 'Any landlord who violates the provisions of this section shall be liable to the tenant for a civil penalty in an amount equal to one month's rent, and the court may award reasonable attorney's fees and costs to the tenant.' § 47a-7d(c)-(d): Rental Terms Summary Form with 'the total periodic rent determined in accordance with the provisions of subsection (a)' as first page of written leases on and after April 1, 2026 (edu-rental-terms-summary-form-ct, slice B). Added by Conn. Pub. Act No. 25-44, § 9. Related: § 47a-4(a)(10) bars a heat or utilities surcharge when heat or utilities are included; § 47a-3a(d) ledger on request. Not searched: whether CUTPA (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-110b) reaches fees not disclosed in the lease. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Specific Rule on Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that specifically bars charging a fee for a service you do not provide. Several related rules do apply. You may not charge a heat or utilities surcharge when heat or utilities are included in the rent, and for leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, you may not charge the tenant for utilities that are not measured by a separate meter serving only the tenant's unit. You may not charge a move-in or move-out fee. Make sure every fee in your lease pays for something real.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(10) (lease may not provide that the tenant 'agrees to pay a heat or utilities surcharge if heat or utilities is included in the rental agreement'); § 47a-4(a)(11), added by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-113, § 1 (effective October 1, 2026, 'applicable to rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after said date'; compiled text pending): 'agrees to pay for utilities billed to the tenant if no separate meter is used to measure utilities delivered exclusively to such tenant's dwelling unit'; § 47a-4(b) makes such a provision unenforceable. § 47a-4d(b): 'No landlord may charge a tenant a move-in or move-out fee.' Proof of absence: CT-fee-unprovided-service-1 (statute wording "fee/charge for a service not provided/rendered/performed", all forms, with landlord/tenant context; whole corpus CGS, CGS-rev2025, CONST, RCSA, PB, PB-2027amend, ACT2026; hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-fee-unprovided-service-2 (everyday words "junk fee", "hidden fee", "bogus fee", "unearned fee"; hits 1, unrelated). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched; whether CUTPA (§ 42-110b) reaches such a fee is case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Which Charges Count as Rent
bodyText: Connecticut defines rent as all periodic payments the lease requires the tenant to make to you. A recurring charge such as monthly pet rent or a monthly parking fee is therefore rent, which means it counts for the 45-day rent-increase notice. A required periodic fee must also be built into your advertised rent and the total rent on the state's Rental Terms Summary Form, except the fees the advertising law lets you leave out, such as a pet fee or deposit, submetered or directly paid utilities, and fees for a service you perform for the tenant. One-time charges, such as a late charge, a returned-payment charge or a repair bill, are not periodic and so are not rent; calling them "additional rent" in the lease is not supported by any statute. Never base a nonpayment notice to quit on an unpaid lock-change cost or an unpaid bed bug assistance repayment; the law forbids it.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-1(8): '“Rent” means all periodic payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement.' § 47a-15a(b) treats the late charge as a separate charge on a 'rent payment made subsequent to the grace period'. § 47a-23(a)(1)(D): notice to quit for 'nonpayment of rent within the grace period provided for residential property in section 47a-15a'. § 47a-7b(c): unpaid lock-change cost 'shall not be the basis for a summary process action under chapter 832'. § 47a-7a(b)(3)(B): failure to make a bed bug assistance repayment 'shall not be the basis for a summary process action initiated pursuant to chapter 832'. § 47a-4e (45-day written notice of any rent increase) and § 47a-7d(a), (c) (periodic fees prorated into advertised rent and the summary form's total periodic rent). NEEDS_REVIEW: whether a lease can make a one-time fee "additional rent" for a nonpayment eviction turns on case law, not searched; the row's statement that the label is not supported by any statute rests on § 47a-1(8) alone. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: No Connecticut statute addresses making a tenant reimburse you for a fee a town or other government charges you, such as a rental registration or inspection fee. The library does not offer such a clause. In Connecticut any recurring payment the lease requires is rent, every recurring fee (other than a few listed exceptions, such as a pet fee or separately metered utilities, none of which covers a government fee) must be built into the rent you advertise and into the total rent on the state's Rental Terms Summary Form, and a violation costs one month's rent; a fee whose amount you don't know when you sign can't meet those rules. If you want to recover a government fee, build it into the rent, or get legal advice before adding your own clause. Check your town's rental licensing or registration rules separately.
notes: CT: No statute found authorizing or barring a pass-through of government fees. Constraints read: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-1(8) ('“Rent” means all periodic payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement'); § 47a-7d(a) (periodic fees 'shall be prorated and included in the advertised, displayed or offered rent'); § 47a-7d(c)-(d) (summary form showing 'the total periodic rent determined in accordance with the provisions of subsection (a)' as the lease's first page from April 1, 2026); § 47a-7d(f) (civil penalty of one month's rent); § 47a-4e (no rent increase effective without 45 days' written notice; 'Nothing in this section shall be construed to (1) allow a landlord to increase the rent during the term of a rental agreement'); § 47a-3 (terms 'not prohibited by law'). Proof of absence: CT-government-fee-reimbursement-1 (statute wording for rental license/registration fees and reimbursing or passing a fee/tax/assessment to a tenant; whole corpus; hits 0; synthetic positive passed), CT-government-fee-reimbursement-2 (everyday "property tax/tax increase/assessment/municipal fee/inspection fee" near "tenant"; hits 1, unrelated RCSA 8-68f-6), CT-government-fee-reimbursement-3 (municipal rental registration/licensing program wording; hits 8, none on point). Municipal rental licensing or registration ordinances flagged, not resolved. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Late Charge Limits and Grace Period
bodyText: You may charge a late charge only if the written lease provides for one, and only after the grace period ends: nine days after rent is due, or four days in a week-to-week tenancy, plus five more days for any month or week when your online payment system kept the tenant from paying. The charge may not exceed the lesser of $5 a day up to $50, or 5% of the late rent payment (5% of the tenant's share if a government agency or charity pays part of the rent). You may charge only one late charge per late payment, however long it stays unpaid, and you may not offer a discount for paying within the grace period. A lease term that charges earlier or more is unenforceable. If you knowingly accept overdue rent, you give up the right to end the tenancy for that late payment.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15a(a): 'nine days thereafter or, in the case of a one-week tenancy, within four days thereafter', 'extended an additional five days if a landlord's online rental payment system prevents the payment of rent when due' (Conn. Pub. Act No. 25-1 (Nov. Sp. Sess.), § 38, effective January 1, 2026); § 47a-15a(b): 'If a rental agreement contains a valid written agreement to pay a late charge in accordance with subsection (a) of section 47a-4 a landlord may assess a tenant such a late charge on a rent payment made subsequent to the grace period', capped at 'the lesser of (1) five dollars per day, up to a maximum of fifty dollars, or (2) five per cent of the delinquent rent payment or, in the case of a rental agreement paid in whole or in part by a governmental or charitable entity, five per cent of the tenant's share of the delinquent rent payment', and 'The landlord may not assess more than one late charge upon a delinquent rent payment, regardless of how long the rent remains unpaid.' § 47a-4(a)(8)-(9) and (b): a term requiring a late charge before the grace period ends, a reduced rent for paying within it, or a charge above § 47a-15a is unenforceable. § 47a-19: 'Acceptance of rent with the knowledge that such rent is overdue constitutes a waiver of the landlord's right to terminate the rental agreement for the tenant's failure to pay such rent when it was due.' § 47a-21(i): no deposit interest for a month the tenant is more than ten days delinquent 'unless the landlord imposes a late charge for such delinquency'. § 47a-23(a)(1)(D): no nonpayment notice to quit while the online system prevents payment within the grace period. Clause: late-fee-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no rule requiring the same rent or terms for a month-to-month tenancy and a fixed-term lease, and no cap on the rent difference between them. Unless the lease fixes a definite term, the tenancy is month to month (week to week if rent is paid weekly). Whatever the lease type, a rent increase needs written notice at least 45 days before it takes effect (for a tenancy with a term of one month or less, notice equal to one full term), and the notice rule does not let you raise rent during a fixed term unless the lease allows it.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3b: 'Unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy is month to month, except in the case of a tenant who pays weekly rent, then the tenancy is week to week.' § 47a-4e: 45 days' written notice of a rent increase (for a term of one month or less, notice equal to a full term) and 'Nothing in this section shall be construed to (1) allow a landlord to increase the rent during the term of a rental agreement'. § 47a-12(c): the tenant's termination remedy applies 'only to leases in which the term of the tenancy is more than one month'. Proof of absence: CT-lease-type-parity-1 ("more burdensome"; month-to-month near fixed/definite term; tenant/landlord context; whole corpus; hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-lease-type-parity-2 (everyday "same/different/higher rent ... lease/tenancy", "premium for short/month"; hits 0). title: No Rule on Notice Fees
bodyText: No Connecticut statute addresses charging a tenant for preparing or serving a notice, such as a notice to quit. In Connecticut a notice to quit must be served by a proper officer, such as a state marshal, and if you win a summary process (eviction) case the judgment includes your court costs. The library offers an optional clause that lets you recover only your actual cost of having a notice served, and not a second time as court costs. Any attorney's fee a lease makes the tenant pay is capped at 15% of a money judgment.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(c): 'An attested copy of such notice shall be served by a proper officer'. § 47a-26d: judgment 'that the complainant recover possession or occupancy of the premises with his costs'. § 47a-4(a)(7): no lease term making the tenant pay 'the landlord's attorney's fees in excess of fifteen per cent of any judgment against the tenant in any action in which money damages are awarded'. Proof of absence: CT-notice-service-fee-1 (fee/cost for preparing or serving a notice, notice preparation/service fee; whole corpus; hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-notice-service-fee-2 (notice to quit within 200 characters of fee/cost/charge, summary-process context; hits 1, § 47a-26d). Whether marshal fees for a notice to quit are taxable costs is not resolved (costs statutes in title 52 not read). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Notice-Service Fee
bodyText: [Optional.] If Tenant's default leads Landlord to have a state marshal or other proper officer serve Tenant with a notice to quit, Tenant will pay Landlord the officer's actual fee for serving it, up to [amount]. Landlord will not charge this fee if the notice is withdrawn because it was served in error, and will not recover the same fee again as court costs.
notes: CT: No statute authorizes or bars this fee (see edu-no-notice-fee-rule-ct and its batteries). The notice to quit must be served by 'a proper officer' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(c)); a summary process judgment for the landlord is 'with his costs' (§ 47a-26d), hence the no-double-recovery sentence. Limited to the officer's actual fee so it is not a penalty; the cap is the landlord's own figure (CONSTRAINED by actual cost). NEEDS_REVIEW: enforceability of a lease fee for a pre-suit notice is case law not searched; whether the marshal's notice-to-quit fee is already recoverable as a taxable cost was not resolved. Mirrors notice-service-fee-ut and notice-service-fee-id (offered by Taylor). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Rent Concessions
bodyText: No Connecticut statute regulates rent concessions such as a free month or a move-in discount. If you give one, state it in the lease with its amount and the rental periods it covers. Do not offer a discount for paying rent early or on time: a lease may not let a tenant pay a reduced rent for paying within the statutory grace period (nine days for monthly rent). A clause that makes the tenant repay a concession after a default may be treated by a court as a penalty, so the library does not offer one.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(8): a rental agreement shall not provide that the tenant 'agrees to pay a late charge prior to the expiration of the grace period set forth in section 47a-15a or to pay rent in a reduced amount if such rent is paid prior to the expiration of such grace period'; § 47a-4(b) makes it unenforceable. § 47a-11c: on a tenant's breach, damages 'shall include the amount of rent agreed to by the parties but unpaid by the tenant' and 'The landlord shall be obligated to mitigate damages.' title: No Rent Control, but Fair Rent Commissions
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide limit on how much you can raise rent. But every town or city with 15,000 or more people must have, or join, a fair rent commission by January 1, 2028, and smaller towns may have one. A tenant (other than in a seasonal rental of 120 days or less a year) can complain to the commission about rent, a proposed increase, or any fee you charge, and the commission can limit it if it finds it harsh and unconscionable, or suspend rent until you fix code violations. Ignoring a commission order can bring fines for each day. For protected tenants (62 or older or with a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or permanently living with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability, in a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park; in a condominium or other common interest community only for conversion tenants or where you own five or more units there), increases must be fair and equitable under the same factors. Check your town's commission and ordinance.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 7-148b(b): 'Any municipality may, and each municipality with a population of fifteen thousand or more, as determined by the most recent decennial census, shall, through its legislative body, adopt an ordinance that (1) creates a fair rent commission, (2) establishes or joins ... a joint fair rent commission ... or (3) joins ... a regional fair rent commission'; the commission acts 'in order to control and eliminate excessive rental charges'; § 7-148b(a): '“rental charge” includes any fee or charge in addition to rent'; seasonal rentals (120 days or less per year) excluded; § 7-148b(c): ordinance due 'on or before January 1, 2028' (Conn. Pub. Act No. 25-1 (Nov. Sp. Sess.), § 35, effective January 1, 2026). § 7-148c lists thirteen factors for whether a rental charge or increase is 'so excessive ... as to be harsh and unconscionable'. § 7-148d(a): commission may order rent 'limited to such an amount as it determines to be fair and equitable' and may suspend rent into escrow for health and safety violations; § 7-148d(b): cease-and-desist for retaliation. § 7-148e appeal to Superior Court; § 7-148f fines of $25-$100 per offense, each day after five a new offense. § 47a-23c(c)(1): protected tenant's rent 'may be increased only to the extent that such increase is fair and equitable, based on the criteria set forth in section 7-148c' (buildings or complexes of five or more units, mobile home parks). No statewide cap or preemption: CT-rent-control-2 (rent control/stabilization/leveling, rent increase cap/limit, regulate the amount of rent; whole corpus; hits 2, both § 7-148b; positive passed; nonsense control 0). Municipal ordinances and commission rules flagged, not resolved. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: No rent increase takes effect unless you give the tenant written notice at least 45 days before it starts; for a tenancy of one month or less, give notice equal to one full rental period. A tenant who does not answer has not agreed to the increase. The notice rule does not let you raise rent during a fixed term unless the lease allows it. You may not demand a rent increase within six months after a tenant in good faith complains to officials or a fair rent commission, asks for repairs, sues to enforce repairs, or organizes or joins a tenants' union, or after a town agency or official files a notice, complaint or order about a code violation, unless the problem was caused by the tenant's household or guests, or you became liable for a substantial increase in taxes or operating costs (not tied to fixing the complaint) at least four months before the demand and the increase does not exceed your prorated share of that net increase. In a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park, a tenant who is 62 or older or has a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or who permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability, may get only fair and equitable increases (in a condominium or other common interest community, only conversion tenants or where you own five or more units there).
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4e: 'No rent increase for a dwelling unit shall be effective unless the landlord has given the tenant of such dwelling unit written notice of the proposed increase not less than forty-five days before the day on which the increase is proposed to take effect, except in the case of a lease with a term of one month or less, such notice shall be given a number of days equivalent to the length of a full term of such lease. A tenant's failure to respond to such notice shall not constitute the tenant's agreement to such proposed increase. Nothing in this section shall be construed to (1) allow a landlord to increase the rent during the term of a rental agreement, or (2) alter any notice requirements concerning increases in rent imposed by federal law.' Applies to rental agreements entered into, renewed or extended on or after October 1, 2024 (Conn. Pub. Act No. 24-143, § 17). § 47a-20: no 'demand an increase in rent' within six months after the listed tenant acts; § 47a-20a(b): increase allowed if the condition was caused by tenant's lack of due care, or for a substantial increase in taxes or other costs incurred 'not less than four months before the demand' and the increase 'does not exceed the prorated portion of the net increase in taxes or costs'. § 47a-23c(a)(1)-(3) (protected tenants: five-plus-unit buildings or complexes and mobile manufactured home parks, qualifying relatives, common interest communities; (a)(1) cross-reference amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-11, § 15, eff. Oct. 1, 2026), (c)(1). Fair rent commissions: edu-fair-rent-commissions-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Rent Changes During the Term
bodyText: [Optional. Choose one.] [A: Monthly Rent will change during the Term as follows: [state each new amount and the date it takes effect]. Monthly Rent will not change during the Term in any other way.] [B: During the Term, Landlord may increase Monthly Rent by giving Tenant written notice at least 45 days before the increase takes effect, stating the new Monthly Rent and its effective date. Tenant may instead end this Lease, without any early termination charge, by giving Landlord written notice before the increase takes effect, effective on the last day before the increase.] Even for a change listed in this Lease, Landlord will give Tenant written notice at least 45 days before each increase takes effect. Landlord will not increase Rent to retaliate against Tenant for any complaint, request or other conduct the law protects.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3 permits terms 'not prohibited by law, including rent, term of the agreement'. § 47a-4e: 'No rent increase for a dwelling unit shall be effective unless the landlord has given the tenant of such dwelling unit written notice of the proposed increase not less than forty-five days before the day on which the increase is proposed to take effect' and 'Nothing in this section shall be construed to (1) allow a landlord to increase the rent during the term of a rental agreement' (the clause supplies the lease authority the statute says it does not give, and gives the 45-day notice even for scheduled steps, because the statute reaches every 'rent increase'). § 47a-20 (no demand for an increase within six months after protected acts) and § 47a-20a(b) (tax/cost pass-through exception). § 47a-23c(c) (protected tenants: only fair and equitable increases) and §§ 7-148b to 7-148d (fair rent commission may limit an increase) apply regardless. Scheduled amounts should match the summary form's rent terms (§ 47a-7d(c)-(d)). Option B mirrors Taylor's Indiana decision (rent-increase-midterm-ky/-wv pattern) with Connecticut's 45 days. NEEDS_REVIEW: § 47a-4e(1) signals the legislature did not itself authorize mid-term increases; whether a market-rate increase clause (Option B) is enforceable in Connecticut is case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Raising Rent During the Term
bodyText: Connecticut law does not itself let you raise rent during a fixed term; any increase during the term must come from the lease. The library's optional clause lets you either list scheduled increases or reserve a right to raise rent with the tenant free to leave instead. Either way you must give written notice at least 45 days before each increase. An increase can still be challenged before a local fair rent commission, must be fair and equitable for a tenant in a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park who is 62 or older or has a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or who permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability (in a condominium or other common interest community, only conversion tenants or where you own five or more units there), and may not be retaliatory.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4e ('Nothing in this section shall be construed to (1) allow a landlord to increase the rent during the term of a rental agreement'; 45-day written notice), § 47a-3, § 47a-20, § 47a-20a(b), § 47a-23c(a)(1)-(3) (scope; (a)(1) cross-reference amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-11, § 15, eff. Oct. 1, 2026), (c), §§ 7-148b to 7-148d. NEEDS_REVIEW: enforceability of an open-ended mid-term increase clause is case law not searched. Companion to rent-increase-midterm-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Cash Receipts and Rent Ledger
bodyText: Whenever you receive a cash payment from or for an occupant, give the person who paid a receipt showing the date, the amount and what the payment was for. If an occupant asks, you must also give them a copy of the ledger or other accounting for their unit, showing the charges, the payments and any balance owed or overpaid. Keep your records in a form you can produce on request.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3a(c): 'Upon receipt of a payment in cash from or on behalf of an occupant, a landlord shall provide the person making the payment with a receipt stating the date of the payment, the amount received and the purpose for which the payment was made.' § 47a-3a(d): 'Upon request by an occupant, the landlord shall provide such occupant with a copy of the ledger or equivalent accounting for the occupant's dwelling unit, showing charges assessed, payments made and any balance owed or surplus paid by such occupant.' (Conn. Pub. Act No. 25-146, § 3, effective July 1, 2025; 2026 Supplement). No response deadline is stated. Whether a missing receipt is an eviction defense is case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Rent Reporting Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring you to offer tenants positive rent reporting to credit bureaus, and none regulating whether you report rent payments or require a tenant to join a rent-reporting program. If you report payment data, federal credit reporting law applies. Any program fee charged before or at the start of the tenancy would run into Connecticut's ban on up-front fees other than a deposit, first month's rent, a key deposit and a screening-report fee.

title: Sales Tax and Short Stays
bodyText: Connecticut does not charge sales tax on ordinary residential rent. Its room occupancy tax applies to stays of 30 consecutive days or less in a hotel, a bed and breakfast, or a lodging house, which includes a furnished residence or similar accommodation. The rate is 15% of the rent (11% for a bed and breakfast) for the first 30 days. If you rent a furnished home for short stays, you may owe this tax; a short-term rental platform may collect it for you, and your town may require a short-term rental license.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 12-407(a)(2)(H): a taxable sale includes 'A transfer for a consideration of the occupancy of any room or rooms in a hotel, lodging house or bed and breakfast establishment for a period of thirty consecutive calendar days or less'; § 12-407 'Lodging house' means 'any building or portion of a building, other than a hotel, an apartment hotel or a bed and breakfast establishment, in which persons are lodged for hire with or without meals, including, but not limited to, any motel, motor court, motor inn, tourist court, furnished residence or similar accommodation'. § 12-408(1)(B): 'At a rate of fifteen per cent with respect to each transfer of occupancy, from the total amount of rent received by a hotel or lodging house for the first period not exceeding thirty consecutive calendar days' and eleven per cent for a bed and breakfast establishment. § 12-408h: short-term rental facilitators (furnished residence, 30 consecutive days or less) must hold a permit and are the retailer. § 7-148qq: municipalities may license short-term rentals (ordinances flagged, not resolved). NEEDS_REVIEW: tax law sits outside the landlord-tenant title; DRS guidance and regulations not loaded; the row states only the statutory text. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Put Every Fee in the Lease
bodyText: No Connecticut statute requires your lease to list every fee or bars a fee the lease does not mention. Several rules make listing them the only safe course. A late charge is allowed only under a written agreement in the lease. Every recurring fee, apart from a few listed exceptions such as pet fees and separately metered utilities, must be built into the advertised rent and the total rent on the state's Rental Terms Summary Form. Up-front charges are limited to a security deposit, first month's rent, a key or equipment deposit and a capped screening-report fee. A rule you adopt after signing that substantially changes the lease, such as a new fee, is not valid unless the tenant agrees in writing.

Pub. Act No. 26-68, § 59; up-front fee list); § 47a-9(b): 'If a rule or regulation that would result in a substantial modification of the terms of the rental agreement is adopted after the tenant enters into the rental agreement, such rule or regulation is not valid unless the tenant consents to such rule or regulation in writing.' title: No Government Shutdown Protection
bodyText: No Connecticut statute gives tenants who are government workers extra time to pay rent, or a defense to eviction, during a federal or state government shutdown. The usual nine-day grace period, late-charge limits and eviction rules apply. Agreeing to a written payment plan can avoid a costly eviction case.

title: Connecticut's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Connecticut sets these limits, whatever the lease says. Security deposit: no more than two months' rent, or one month's rent for a tenant 62 or older. Late charge: only after the grace period (nine days, four for a weekly tenancy, plus five more days when your online payment system kept the tenant from paying), no more than the lesser of $5 a day up to $50 or 5% of the late payment, and only once per late payment. Screening-report fee: $50 plus the state's yearly inflation adjustment; no other application fee, and no move-in or move-out fee. Bounced check: up to $20. Attorney's fees the lease makes the tenant pay: no more than 15% of a money judgment. Changing locks for a tenant protected by a court order: actual reasonable cost only.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(b)(1)-(2) (deposit not to exceed two months' rent, or one month's rent for a tenant sixty-two or older); § 47a-15a(b) (late charge 'may not exceed the lesser of (1) five dollars per day, up to a maximum of fifty dollars, or (2) five per cent of the delinquent rent payment'; one charge per delinquent payment); § 47a-4d(b)-(c), as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-68, § 59 ('a fee not exceeding fifty dollars plus an adjustment reflecting any increase in the consumer price index for urban consumers, as determined by the Commissioner of Housing on an annual basis'; 'No landlord may charge a tenant a move-in or move-out fee'); § 52-565a(i) ('a service charge of up to twenty dollars' per dishonored check, none for a stopped payment, stolen check or reasonable defense); § 47a-4(a)(7) (no term to pay 'the landlord's attorney's fees in excess of fifteen per cent of any judgment against the tenant in any action in which money damages are awarded'); § 47a-7b(c)(3) ('a fee to the tenant not exceeding the actual reasonable cost of changing the locks'). Detail rows: edu-security-deposit-cap-ct, edu-late-charge-limits-ct, edu-application-screening-fees-ct, returned-payments-ct, attorney-fees topic. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Late Charges When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText: If a government agency or charity pays part of the rent, any late charge is capped at 5% of the tenant's own share of the late payment (or $5 a day up to $50, if less). Connecticut law does not say whether you may charge the tenant a late charge when the tenant paid their share on time and only the agency's payment was late; the safe course is not to. Housing program rules (for example, a Housing Choice Voucher contract) may also limit late charges.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15a(b): the late charge 'may not exceed the lesser of (1) five dollars per day, up to a maximum of fifty dollars, or (2) five per cent of the delinquent rent payment or, in the case of a rental agreement paid in whole or in part by a governmental or charitable entity, five per cent of the tenant's share of the delinquent rent payment.' § 47a-4(a)(9): no term to pay a late charge exceeding § 47a-15a. NEEDS_REVIEW: whether a late charge may be assessed on the tenant when only the subsidy portion is late is not addressed by statute; case law not searched; federal program rules (HUD HAP contract) not covered (Rule 21: federal law). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Passing On Property Tax Increases
bodyText: No Connecticut statute addresses a lease clause that passes real estate tax increases on to a tenant, and the library does not offer one. Any rent increase needs 45 days' written notice (one full term for a tenancy of one month or less), and during a fixed term rent can change only as the lease allows (see the optional Rent Changes During the Term clause). Within six months after a tenant's protected complaint you may raise rent only by your prorated share of a substantial tax or operating-cost increase (not tied to fixing the complaint) that you became liable for at least four months before the demand, or where the tenant's household or guests caused the problem.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-20a(b)(2): notwithstanding § 47a-20, a landlord may increase rent if 'the landlord has become liable for a substantial increase in property taxes, or a substantial increase in other maintenance or operating costs not associated with his complying with the complaint, not less than four months before the demand for an increase in rent, and the increase in rent does not exceed the prorated portion of the net increase in taxes or costs.' § 47a-4e (45 days' written notice; does not itself allow increases during the term). Proof of absence: CT-tax-escalation-1 (property/real estate tax increase/escalation, tax escalation, increase in taxes; tenant/rent context; whole corpus; hits 2, § 47a-20a and § 21-80a; positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-tax-escalation-2 (everyday "pass on/through/along", "share of the taxes"; hits 4, unrelated). Fair rent commissions may review any increase (§ 7-148b). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: Do not charge interest on late rent: Connecticut allows only one late charge per late rent payment, and a lease may not require more. For other money a tenant owes, such as repair costs beyond the security deposit, Connecticut's legal interest rate is 8% a year unless the lease sets a different rate, and in a lawsuit a court may award interest of no more than 10% a year for money held back after it was due. The library offers an optional clause setting interest on unpaid non-rent amounts.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 37-1(a): interest 'shall, in the absence of any agreement to the contrary, be at the rate of eight per cent a year'; § 37-1(b): 'Unless otherwise provided by agreement, interest at the legal rate from the date of maturity of a debt shall accrue as an addition to the debt.' § 37-3a(a): 'interest at the rate of ten per cent a year, and no more, may be recovered and allowed in civil actions ... as damages for the detention of money after it becomes payable.' § 47a-15a(b): 'The landlord may not assess more than one late charge upon a delinquent rent payment, regardless of how long the rent remains unpaid'; § 47a-4(a)(9): no term to pay 'a late charge on rent payments made subsequent to such grace period in an amount exceeding the amounts set forth in section 47a-15a'. NEEDS_REVIEW: treating contractual interest on late rent as a barred second late charge is an inference from §§ 47a-15a(b) and 47a-4(a)(9); case law not searched. § 37-4 (12% cap) governs loans and was read only to confirm it does not set the lease rate. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts Other Than Rent
bodyText: [Optional.] Any amount other than Rent that Tenant owes under this Lease, such as the cost of repairing damage beyond what the Security Deposit covers, that is not paid within [number] days after Landlord's written demand will bear simple interest at [rate, not more than 10]% per year from the end of that period until paid. No interest or other charge will be added to late Rent beyond the one late charge this Lease allows.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 37-1(a) lets the parties agree on a rate ('in the absence of any agreement to the contrary'); the bracket stops at 10% because § 37-3a(a) caps interest recoverable as damages in a civil action at 'ten per cent a year, and no more'. Late rent is excluded because § 47a-15a(b) allows only one late charge per delinquent rent payment and § 47a-4(a)(9) makes a larger charge unenforceable. Rate is the landlord's own figure. NEEDS_REVIEW: whether a court would hold a contract rate above the legal 8% enforceable against a residential tenant, and how § 37-3a's cap interacts with a contract rate, is case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Renting to Veterans
bodyText: We found no Connecticut program that pays landlords an incentive or tax credit for renting to veterans. Connecticut's Department of Housing must give eligible veterans priority in its security deposit guarantee program, under which the state guarantees payment for tenant damage, up to two months' rent, instead of the tenant paying a cash deposit. Status as a veteran is protected under Connecticut's fair housing law, so you may not refuse to rent to, or treat differently, an applicant because they are a veteran.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 8-339(a): DOH 'may provide security deposit guarantees for use by persons who are eligible pursuant to this subsection in lieu of a security deposit on a rental dwelling unit', 'in an amount not to exceed the equivalent of two months' rent', and 'shall prioritize the provision of security deposit guarantees to eligible veterans'; § 8-339(b): written agreement 'to pay the landlord for any damages suffered by the landlord due to the tenant's failure to comply with such tenant's obligations, as defined in section 47a-21'. § 46a-64c lists 'status as a veteran' among protected characteristics (section text read for the list only; Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-77, § 27 and Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-110, § 6 amend § 46a-64c effective October 1, 2026, compiled text pending). Search: CT-veterans-incentive-1 (hits 13; property-tax exemptions for veterans' own homes, licensing preferences and appropriations are not landlord incentives). Status "Not located" rather than "Confirmed absent": incentive programs may be run by agencies without a statute; RCSA program regulations for § 8-339 (17b-802 subtitle) loaded but not separately searched for veteran rules. NEEDS_REVIEW for that boundary. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Accepting Late Rent Waives Termination
bodyText: If you accept rent knowing it is overdue, you give up the right to end the tenancy for not paying that rent on time, and a lease clause saying otherwise does not change that. If you have served a notice to quit and want to keep the eviction going, you may include in the notice the statement Connecticut law provides: "Any payments tendered after the date specified to quit possession or occupancy, or the date of the completion of the pretermination process if that is later, will be accepted for use and occupancy only and not for rent, with full reservation of rights to continue with the eviction action." The statement takes effect only after the quit date. Get legal advice before accepting money during an eviction.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-19: 'Acceptance of rent with the knowledge that such rent is overdue constitutes a waiver of the landlord's right to terminate the rental agreement for the tenant's failure to pay such rent when it was due.' § 47a-23(e): 'A use and occupancy disclaimer may be included in or combined with such notice, provided that such disclaimer does not take effect until after the date specified in the notice for the lessee or occupant to quit possession or occupancy or the date of the completion of the pretermination process, whichever is later', in 'substantially the following form' (quoted in the body; double quotes used there because the body quotes the statutory form for the landlord to copy). § 47a-4(a)(1): a lease may not waive rights under the chapter. § 47a-26b: court-ordered use and occupancy payments during the case (read for context). NEEDS_REVIEW: whether accepting payments after the quit date without the disclaimer reinstates the tenancy, and whether partial payments waive, are case law not searched. The shared `late-fee` non-waiver sentence is not used for Connecticut (late-fee-ct). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Move-In Walk-Through
bodyText: For a lease entered into on or after January 1, 2024, after the lease is signed but before the tenant moves in, you must offer the tenant a joint walk-through of the unit. If the tenant accepts, you both must use the Department of Housing's preoccupancy walk-through checklist, note every existing condition, defect or damage, and each sign and keep a copy. You may not keep any part of the security deposit, or ask the tenant to pay, for anything noted on the checklist. The checklist can be used as evidence but is not conclusive. Connecticut does not require a move-out inspection, but doing one and keeping photos helps if deductions are disputed.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7c(a): 'upon or after the entry into a rental agreement but prior to the tenant's occupancy of a dwelling unit, a landlord shall offer such tenant the opportunity to conduct a walk-through of the dwelling unit. If the tenant requests such a walk-through, the landlord and tenant, or their designees, shall use a copy of the preoccupancy walk-through checklist prepared by the Commissioner of Housing'; both 'shall sign duplicate copies of the walk-through checklist and each shall receive a copy.' § 47a-7c(b): 'the landlord may not retain any part of the security deposit ... or seek payment from the tenant for any condition, defect or damage that was noted in the preoccupancy walk-through checklist', and the checklist 'shall be admissible, subject to the rules of evidence, but shall not be conclusive'. § 47a-7c(d): not applicable to a tenancy under a rental agreement entered into before January 1, 2024. DOH checklist text at /home/claude/ct/src/agency/walk-through-checklist.docx.txt. No move-out inspection statute: CT-condition-inspection-1 (hits 2; positive passed; nonsense control 0); regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Clause: existing-condition-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Preset Deposit Charges
bodyText: Do not put a schedule of fixed cleaning, carpet or repair charges in the lease to take from the security deposit. Connecticut lets you keep only the value of damages you actually suffer because the tenant did not meet the tenant's obligations: unpaid rent or utility payments owed to you, damage or uncleanliness that breaches the tenant's legal duties, and an unpaid lock-change cost. Every deduction must be listed in an itemized written statement. You may never deduct for a condition noted on the move-in walk-through checklist, or for normal wear.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(d)(1)(A): the landlord pays back the deposit 'less the value of any damages that any person who was a landlord of such premises at any time during the tenancy of such tenant has suffered as a result of such tenant's failure to comply with such tenant's obligations'; § 47a-21(d)(2): 'a written statement itemizing the nature and amount of such damages'; § 47a-21(a)(14): 'Tenant's obligations' means '(A) the amount of any rental or utility payment due the landlord from a tenant; (B) a tenant's obligations under the provisions of section 47a-11; and (C) the actual reasonable cost of changing the locks of the dwelling unit pursuant to section 47a-7b, if the tenant has not paid such cost.' § 47a-11(b), (d), (f) (clean and safe as the premises' condition permits; no wilful or negligent damage). § 47a-7c(b) (no deduction for conditions on the walk-through checklist). Proof of absence: CT-deposit-cost-schedule-1 (cleaning/carpet/repair/replacement fee near security deposit; schedule of charges; whole corpus; hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-deposit-cost-schedule-2 (everyday "carpet", "cleaning fee"; hits 1, unrelated). NEEDS_REVIEW: "normal wear" is not a phrase in § 47a-21; the wear-and-tear statement rests on § 47a-11's standard and case law not searched. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: A deposit refund your former tenant never receives or never cashes does not become yours. Under Connecticut's unclaimed property law, money you owe someone that stays unclaimed for more than three years after it became payable is presumed abandoned. In that year, between July 1 and September 30, you must try to reach the tenant by first-class mail (if the total is $50 or more) and by email if they agreed to email notices; if they still don't claim it, you must report it and pay it to the State Treasurer by the next March 31. You may not charge a dormancy or similar fee, and the lease may not say the deposit is forfeited if unclaimed.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 3-64a: 'All property not otherwise provided for or excluded from this part ... which is held or owing in this state and has remained unclaimed by the owner for more than three years after it became due, payable or distributable, is presumed abandoned.' § 3-56a (re-enacted without change to these definitions by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-94, § 1, effective July 1, 2026; compiled text pending): 'Holder' includes any person 'who is indebted to another on an obligation subject to this part'; 'Owner' includes 'a creditor, claimant or payee in case of other choses in action'. § 3-65a(a)-(b) (as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-94, § 4, effective July 1, 2026; compiled text pending): notice 'Between July first and September thirtieth, inclusive, of the calendar year in which a presumption of abandonment is to take effect', by first-class mail if 'the cumulative value of all property belonging to the owner is fifty dollars or greater' and by email if the owner consented to electronic notices; report and delivery 'Not later than March thirty-first following the close of the calendar year in which property is presumed abandoned'. § 3-65c: no 'dormancy charge or fee, abandoned property charge or fee, unclaimed property charge or fee, escheat charge or fee, inactivity charge or fee' and no agreement 'language suggesting that the property may be subject to such a charge'. § 47a-21(c): the deposit 'shall remain the property of such tenant'. NEEDS_REVIEW: no Connecticut provision names security deposits specifically (CT-deposit-escheat-1); applying the § 3-64a catch-all is an inference; § 3-65b interest penalty and Treasurer regulations (§ 3-74a) not read. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Paying the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Connecticut gives most tenants no right to pay the security deposit in installments, so you may require it in full before move-in. You may agree to installments; if you do, put the schedule in writing, and remember every installment is part of the deposit and must go into the escrow account. Housing authorities and other state-assisted providers of public housing for older adults and people with disabilities must allow installments over at least twelve months.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-22a(b): any housing authority, community housing development corporation or other corporation approved for state financial assistance 'to provide public housing for senior citizens and disabled persons under the provisions of part VI or VII of chapter 128 shall, pursuant to a written agreement, permit the payment of a security deposit in installments that are reasonable in light of the income of the tenant'; 'Such installments shall be payable in equal amounts at approximately equal intervals not exceeding one month over a period of at least twelve months'; interest 'shall not begin to accrue until the security deposit, including all installments due if applicable, has been paid in full.' § 47a-21(a)(11): 'Security deposit' includes 'any installment payment collected pursuant to section 47a-22a'; § 47a-21(h)(1): 'immediately deposit the entire amount of any security deposit' into escrow. No general installment right: CT-deposit-installments-1 (hits 9; positive passed) and CT-deposit-installments-2 (hits 2, unrelated). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Conditions on the Deposit Refund
bodyText: You may not make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving you advance notice of moving out. Return the deposit, with interest and any itemized deductions, within 21 days after the tenancy ends, or within 15 days after you receive the tenant's written forwarding address, whichever is later. A lease term that adds conditions to the refund is unenforceable, and a late or missing return can make you liable for twice the deposit.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(d)(2): 'Upon termination of a tenancy, any tenant may notify the landlord in writing of such tenant's forwarding address. Not later than twenty-one days after termination of a tenancy or fifteen days after receiving written notification of such tenant's forwarding address, whichever is later, each landlord ... shall deliver' the deposit and interest or the balance with an itemized statement; violation: 'liable for twice the amount of any security deposit paid by such tenant'. § 47a-4(a)(1), (b): a term waiving rights under § 47a-21 is unenforceable. Proof of absence: CT-deposit-surrender-notice-1 (advance notice of surrender/intent to vacate/move-out, conditions on refund; whole corpus; hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0); CT-deposit-surrender-notice-2 (everyday "moving out", "move out", "leave" with security-deposit context; hits 2, unrelated). Clause: security-deposit-return-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposit After a Violence-Based Termination
bodyText: Connecticut has no special deposit rule when a tenant ends a lease early because of family violence or sexual assault; the normal deposit return rules apply. You may still deduct unpaid rent owed before the termination date and the cost of damage the tenant caused. If other tenants on the lease stay, they remain bound by it, and the law does not say how to split the deposit between the departing and remaining tenants; get advice before returning any part of it.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11e(c): termination 'shall not relieve (1) the tenant from liability to the landlord for any rent arrearage incurred prior to such termination of the rental agreement or from liability to the landlord for property damage caused by the tenant, or (2) any other tenant from liability to the landlord under the rental agreement.' § 47a-21(d)(2) return timing applies on 'termination of a tenancy'. Proof of absence: CT-dv-deposit-timing-1 and -2 (hits 3 each, unrelated; no deposit rule tied to § 47a-11e); no synthetic positive was run for -1 because § 47a-11e itself does not mention the deposit (section-open). NEEDS_REVIEW: deposit allocation when only one co-tenant terminates is unaddressed by statute; case law not searched. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Returning the Deposit Early
bodyText: Connecticut has no special early-return procedure for security deposits. You may return all or part of a deposit sooner than the law requires, even during the tenancy, but you must then pay the interest that has built up on the amount returned within 21 days. You may not deduct an administrative or processing fee; only damages from the tenant's failure to meet the tenant's obligations may be kept.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(h)(2)(F): escrow agent may 'disburse all or any part of the security deposit to a tenant at any time during tenancy'; § 47a-21(i): 'if the landlord or owner returns all or part of a security deposit prior to termination of the tenancy, the landlord or owner shall pay the accrued interest to the tenant or resident not later than twenty-one days after such termination or return'; § 47a-21(a)(14), (d)(1)(A) (deductions limited to damages from failure to meet 'tenant's obligations'). Proof of absence: CT-expedited-deposit-disposition-1 (early/expedited/prompt return or disposition of deposit; deposit processing/administrative/handling fee; whole corpus; hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-expedited-deposit-disposition-2 (hits 0). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Fees Instead of a Deposit
bodyText: No Connecticut statute authorizes a fee or insurance product that a tenant pays instead of a security deposit, and the library does not offer one. You may not charge any fee at or before move-in other than a security deposit, the first month's rent, a key or equipment deposit and a capped screening-report fee. A monthly fee in place of a deposit would be rent: it must be built into your advertised rent and the total rent on the state's Rental Terms Summary Form. You may accept a state security deposit guarantee from the Department of Housing in place of a cash deposit for eligible tenants; to be paid for damage, you must file a claim with repair receipts within 20 days after the tenancy ends.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4d(b) (as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-68, § 59): no 'payment, fee or charge before or at the beginning of the tenancy, except a security deposit pursuant to section 47a-21, advance payment for the first month's rent or a deposit for a key or any special equipment, or a fee for a tenant screening report'. § 47a-1(8) ('“Rent” means all periodic payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement'); § 47a-7d(a), (c)-(d). § 8-339(a): 'the commissioner may provide security deposit guarantees for use by persons who are eligible pursuant to this subsection in lieu of a security deposit on a rental dwelling unit', up to two months' rent; § 8-339(b) written agreement to pay landlord damages; § 8-339(g): 'A landlord may submit a claim for damages not later than twenty days after the date of termination of the tenancy. Payment shall be made only for a claim that includes receipts for repairs made.' Proof of absence: CT-fee-in-lieu-of-deposit-1 (hits 5; positive passed) and CT-fee-in-lieu-of-deposit-2 (hits 16, unrelated). NEEDS_REVIEW: whether a third-party deposit-alternative insurance product sold directly to the tenant (with no landlord fee) is regulated by insurance law is outside the landlord-tenant title and was not searched; RCSA 17b-802 program regulations loaded but not read for landlord terms. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Holding Fees
bodyText: Connecticut does not allow a separate fee or deposit just to hold a unit. Before or at the start of a tenancy you may collect only a security deposit, the first month's rent, a key or special-equipment deposit, and a capped screening-report fee, and the same limit applies to a property manager or anyone acting for you. If you take money to hold a unit, treat it as the security deposit or the first month's rent: a security deposit must go into an escrow account, counts toward the deposit limit and earns interest. The law does not say you may keep that money if the applicant decides not to rent, so get advice before keeping any of it.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4d(b), as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-68, § 59 (effective from passage; compiled text pending): 'No landlord, third party acting on behalf of a landlord, or third party acting on behalf of the state may demand from a prospective tenant any payment, fee or charge for the processing, review or acceptance of any rental application, or demand any other payment, fee or charge before or at the beginning of the tenancy, except a security deposit pursuant to section 47a-21, advance payment for the first month's rent or a deposit for a key or any special equipment, or a fee for a tenant screening report'. § 47a-21(a)(11) ('Security deposit' means 'any advance rental payment ... except an advance payment for the first month's rent'); § 47a-21(b) (cap), (h)(1) (immediate escrow), (i) (interest). NEEDS_REVIEW: whether money paid as a deposit by a prospective tenant who never takes possession may be kept as liquidated damages is not addressed by statute; case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits or Move-In Fees
bodyText: Connecticut has no such thing as a nonrefundable deposit.
