Any money you collect in advance, other than the first month's rent or a deposit for a key or special equipment, is a security deposit: it stays the tenant's property, goes into escrow, earns interest, counts toward the deposit limit, and may be kept only for actual damages from the tenant's breach. You may not charge a nonrefundable cleaning, pet, administrative or move-in fee at or before the start of the tenancy, and you may never charge a move-in or move-out fee.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(a)(11): 'Security deposit' means 'any advance rental payment, or any installment payment collected pursuant to section 47a-22a, except an advance payment for the first month's rent or a deposit for a key or any special equipment'; § 47a-21(c): 'Any security deposit paid by a tenant shall remain the property of such tenant in which the landlord shall have a security interest'; § 47a-21(d) (deductions only for damages from failure to meet tenant's obligations). § 47a-4d(b) (as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-68, § 59): no other 'payment, fee or charge before or at the beginning of the tenancy' and 'No landlord may charge a tenant a move-in or move-out fee.' Proof of absence: CT-nonrefundable-deposit-1 (CONST and PB-2027amend not included in that run's sources; hits 7 unrelated; synthetic positive passed) and CT-nonrefundable-deposit-2 (hits 7, none on point). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText: You may not ask for a security deposit of more than two months' rent, or more than one month's rent if the tenant is 62 or older. If a tenant turns 62 after paying a larger deposit, you must return the part above one month's rent when the tenant asks. Every advance payment except the first month's rent and a key or special-equipment deposit, including last month's rent and any pet deposit, counts toward the limit. The Banking Department enforces the limit and, starting October 1, 2026, can order civil penalties.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(b)(1): 'In the case of a tenant under sixty-two years of age, a landlord shall not demand a security deposit in an amount that exceeds two months' rent.' § 47a-21(b)(2): 'In the case of a tenant sixty-two years of age or older, a landlord shall not demand a security deposit in an amount that exceeds one month's rent. Any landlord who has received a security deposit in an amount that exceeds one month's rent from a tenant who becomes sixty-two years of age after paying such security deposit shall return the portion of such security deposit that exceeds one month's rent to the tenant upon the tenant's request.' § 47a-21(a)(11) (definition). § 47a-21(j)(1), as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-79, § 3 (effective October 1, 2026; compiled text pending): the Banking Commissioner may investigate violations of subsection (b), (d), (h) or (i) and 'order such landlord to pay a civil penalty, cease and desist from such practices and comply'. Builder should enforce the cap (Taylor's rule: caps are education rows, enforced by the builder). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Penalty Tied to the Walk-Through Offer
bodyText: Connecticut requires you to offer a move-in walk-through but sets no specific penalty, such as losing the right to make deposit deductions, for failing to offer it, and it has no move-out inspection notice rule. Skipping the offer still breaks the law and leaves you without the signed checklist, which is often your best evidence of the unit's condition at move-in. Always make and document the offer.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7c(a) ('a landlord shall offer such tenant the opportunity to conduct a walk-through'); § 47a-7c(b) (no deduction for conditions noted; checklist admissible but not conclusive). No penalty clause appears in § 47a-7c. Proof of absence: CT-inspection-notice-penalty-1 (failure to offer/give/provide a walk-through or inspection; forfeiture of deposit withholding; tenant/landlord context; whole corpus; hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-inspection-notice-penalty-2 (everyday walk-through/checklist near penalty/forfeit/liable; CGS, RCSA, ACT2026; hits 7, all unrelated). Whether a court would draw an adverse inference from a missing offer is case law not searched. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Escrow Account for Deposits
bodyText: Put the whole security deposit into an escrow account for the tenant at a bank, savings bank or savings and loan association located in Connecticut (a credit union does not qualify) as soon as you receive it; the account must be one your creditors cannot reach. Within 30 days after you receive the deposit, or move it to another institution or account, give the tenant written notice of the amount held and the name and address of the institution. Take money out only to return it, pay interest, move it to a new owner or account, keep excess interest, or keep amounts for proven damages after the tenancy ends. If the Banking Department asks about a deposit, answer within 7 days. Knowingly mishandling deposits can bring a fine of up to $500 and up to 30 days in jail per offense, unless you rented to fewer than four deposit-paying tenants.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(h)(1): 'Each landlord shall immediately deposit the entire amount of any security deposit received by such landlord from each tenant into one or more escrow accounts established or maintained in a financial institution for the benefit of each tenant.' § 47a-21(a)(3) ('Escrow account' is 'not subject to execution by the creditors of the escrow agent'), (a)(5) ('Financial institution' means a listed bank or savings institution 'that is located in this state'). § 47a-21(h)(2)(A)-(G) permitted withdrawals. § 47a-21(h)(4)(A): written notice 'stating the amount held for the benefit of the tenant and the name and address of the financial institution at which the tenant's security deposit is being held not later than thirty days after the landlord receives a security deposit ... or transfers the security deposit to another financial institution or escrow account'; (h)(4)(B): information to the commissioner 'not later than seven days after the request is made'. § 47a-21(k)(2): 'Any person who knowingly and wilfully violates the provisions of subsection (h) ... shall be subject to a fine of not more than five hundred dollars or imprisonment of not more than thirty days or both for each offense', with the affirmative defense that 'such person leased residential real property to fewer than four tenants who paid a security deposit'. § 47a-21(c) (deposit is tenant's property, exempt from landlord's creditors). Commissioner civil penalties from October 1, 2026: § 47a-21(j)(1) as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-79, § 3 (compiled text pending). Clause: security-deposit-holding-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: You must pay interest on every security deposit at no less than the rate the Banking Commissioner sets for each calendar year (the deposit index; 0.49% for 2026). On each anniversary of the tenancy, pay the interest to the tenant or credit it to the next rent. When the tenancy ends, or if you return any part of the deposit early, pay the interest that has built up within 21 days. You may skip interest only for a month in which rent was more than ten days late and you did not charge a late charge. You may not raise rent because you must pay interest, and a lease cannot make the tenant give up interest. Housing owned by a school for its students is exempt.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(i): 'On and after January 1, 2012, the rate for each calendar year shall be not less than the deposit index, as defined in section 36a-26, for that year. On the anniversary date of the tenancy and annually thereafter, such interest shall be paid to the tenant or resident or credited toward the next rental payment due'; early termination or return: 'not later than twenty-one days after such termination or return'; 'Interest shall not be paid to a tenant for any month in which the tenant has been delinquent for more than ten days in the payment of any monthly rent, unless the landlord imposes a late charge for such delinquency. No landlord shall increase the rent due from a tenant because of the requirement that the landlord pay on interest the security deposit'; exemption for 'a residential unit in any building owned or controlled by any educational institution and used by such institution for the purpose of housing students of such institution and their families'. § 36a-26: the Commissioner determines and publishes the deposit index by December 15 of the prior year. § 47a-21(d)(2): failure to deliver accrued interest: 'liable for ten dollars or twice the amount of the accrued interest, whichever is greater'; § 47a-21(k)(3): fine up to $100 per offense for knowing and wilful violation; § 47a-4(a)(4): no lease waiver of deposit interest. 2026 rate: 0.49% (Department of Banking deposit-index page, saved and hashed 2026-10-09; log §1.1); the builder should pull each year's index. Clause: security-deposit-interest-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A lease cannot make a tenant give up any right under Connecticut's security deposit law, including the right to interest on the deposit. A lease term that tries to do so is unenforceable. Also note that Connecticut deposit rules apply whatever the lease calls the payment: any advance payment other than the first month's rent or a key or special-equipment deposit is a security deposit.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a): 'A rental agreement shall not provide that the tenant: (1) Agrees to waive or forfeit rights or remedies under this chapter and sections 47a-21, ... or under any section of the general statutes or any municipal ordinance unless such section or ordinance expressly states that such rights may be waived; ... (4) agrees to waive his right to the interest on the security deposit pursuant to section 47a-21'; § 47a-4(b): 'A provision prohibited by subsection (a) of this section included in a rental agreement is unenforceable.' (From October 1, 2026, Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-113, § 1 restates § 47a-4 with gender-neutral wording; substance of (a)(1) and (a)(4) unchanged.) § 47a-21(a)(11) (definition). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: When you sell or otherwise transfer a rented property, you must take the tenants' deposits, plus the interest they have earned, out of escrow and deliver them to the new owner. The new owner takes over your rights in the deposits and must return them when each tenancy ends, even though you collected them. Give the tenant written notice of the sale: unless agreed otherwise, a seller to a good-faith buyer is released from the lease and landlord-tenant duties only for events after that notice. The new owner must give the tenant a new escrow notice within 30 days and its own name and address for notices.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(c): 'Any voluntary or involuntary transfer of a landlord's interest in residential real property to a successor shall constitute an assignment to such successor of such landlord's security interest in all security deposits paid by tenants of such transferred residential real property.' § 47a-21(h)(3)(A): the landlord 'shall withdraw from the escrow account and deliver to the successor the entire amount of security deposits paid by tenants of the property being transferred, plus any interest accrued', or a pro rata share if a commingled account is short. § 47a-21(e): 'A successor, other than a receiver, shall be liable for the claims of tenants of such property for return of any part of such security deposit which is or becomes due to such tenant during the time such successor is a landlord.' § 47a-21(d)(1)(A): the landlord at termination pays 'the amount of any security deposit that was deposited by the tenant with the person who was landlord at the time such security deposit was deposited'. § 47a-21(h)(4)(A) (30-day notice after receiving a deposit 'from the tenant or the tenant's previous landlord'). § 47a-10(a): 'Unless otherwise agreed, a landlord who conveys premises ... to a bona fide purchaser, is relieved of liability under the rental agreement and the provisions of this chapter and sections 47a-21 ... with respect to any events occurring after written notice to the tenant of the conveyance.' Successor's notice duty: § 47a-6(a) ('any successor landlord or such successor's agent to notify the tenant in writing ... at the time of such succession'). Receivers: § 47a-21(h)(3)(B), (e). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Penalties for Late or Missing Deposit Returns
bodyText: If you miss the deposit deadline (21 days after the tenancy ends, or 15 days after you get the tenant's written forwarding address, whichever is later), or fail to send the itemized statement of deductions, you can owe the tenant twice the full deposit. If the only problem is that you left out the interest, you owe $10 or twice the interest, whichever is more. Knowingly and wilfully failing to return a deposit when due can also bring a fine of up to $250, unless you honestly believed you were entitled to deduct for damages. The tenant can sue to get the deposit back, and the Banking Department can investigate complaints and, from October 1, 2026, order civil penalties, but it does not decide good-faith disputes over damages you itemized.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(d)(2): 'Any landlord who violates any provision of this subsection shall be liable for twice the amount of any security deposit paid by such tenant, except that, if the only violation is the failure to deliver the accrued interest, such landlord shall be liable for ten dollars or twice the amount of the accrued interest, whichever is greater.' § 47a-21(k)(1): 'Any person who is a landlord at the time of termination of a tenancy and who knowingly and wilfully fails to pay all or any part of a security deposit when due shall be subject to a fine of not more than two hundred fifty dollars for each offense', with an affirmative defense for a 'good faith belief that he was entitled to deduct the value of damages'. § 47a-21(g): action 'in replevin or for money damages'. § 47a-21(j)(1)-(2): Banking Commissioner jurisdiction over subsections (b), (d), (h), (i), excluding annual-interest failures and good-faith damage claims ('a claim for actual damages suffered by the landlord for which written notification of such damages has been provided to the tenant in accordance with ... subsection (d)'); civil penalty power added by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-79, § 3 (effective October 1, 2026; compiled text pending). Related penalties: § 47a-21(k)(2) (escrow; see edu-security-deposit-escrow-ct), (k)(3) (interest, up to $100). Whether 'twice the amount of any security deposit' is in addition to or inclusive of the deposit itself is case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to post or disclose the standards you use to set deposit amounts. Every deposit is still capped at two months' rent, or one month's rent for a tenant 62 or older, and fair housing law bars setting different deposit terms because of a protected characteristic such as race, familial status, lawful source of income or status as a veteran. Using written, uniform criteria is the safest practice.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(b) (cap). § 46a-64c(a)(2): discriminatory practice 'To discriminate against any person in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling ... because of race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, gender identity or expression, marital status, age, lawful source of income, familial status, status as a veteran, status as a victim of sexual assault or status as a victim of trafficking in persons' (disability in § 46a-64c(a)(6)(B)). Proof of absence: CT-security-deposit-standards-1 (standards/criteria/method for calculating or setting deposits; tenant/landlord context; whole corpus; hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-security-deposit-standards-2 (different/differing/varying deposits; hits 0). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched (RCSA 8-37ee DOH fair housing loaded). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Separate Utility Deposit
bodyText: Connecticut has no separate utility deposit for landlords. If you collect money in advance to cover utility bills the tenant owes you, it is part of the security deposit: it counts toward the two-month (or one-month for 62+) limit, goes into escrow, earns interest and must be returned under the normal deposit rules. Unpaid utility charges owed to you can already be deducted from the security deposit at the end of the tenancy.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(a)(11): 'Security deposit' means 'any advance rental payment ... except an advance payment for the first month's rent or a deposit for a key or any special equipment'; § 47a-21(a)(14)(A): 'Tenant's obligations' include 'the amount of any rental or utility payment due the landlord from a tenant'. § 47a-4d(b) (no other up-front payment). Proof of absence: CT-utility-deposit-return-1 ("utility deposit", "deposit for utilities/heat/water/electric/gas" with landlord/tenant context; whole corpus; hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-utility-deposit-return-2 (hits 1, RCSA 8-68f-2, not a utility-deposit rule). NEEDS_REVIEW not needed: classification follows the statutory definition. Utility-company customer deposits (title 16) not covered. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Alterations Tenants May Make Without Your Consent
bodyText: Your lease may require your consent before a tenant alters the unit, but Connecticut gives tenants some rights you cannot take away. A tenant may install energy conservation measures at no cost to you after sending you written notice by certified mail; the work may go ahead unless you send a written disapproval by certified mail within 20 days, and you can never block removable weatherstripping, removable interior storm windows or insulation wrap on the water heater. You must allow reasonable modifications a tenant with a disability needs, at the tenant's expense, and you may, where reasonable, require the tenant to restore the interior when they leave. A tenant with a dedicated parking space may ask to install an EV charging station under separate rules.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13a(a)-(b): a tenant 'may ... at no cost to the landlord, implement or authorize the implementation of energy conservation measures' after written notice 'by certified mail, return receipt requested'; 'Unless the landlord gives written notice of his disapproval of such implementation by certified mail, return receipt requested, within twenty days ... such energy conservation measures may be implemented, provided that ... no such disapproval shall be effective as to the installation of removable weatherstripping around doors and windows, removable interior storm windows and insulation wrap around hot water heating tanks'; § 47a-13a(c): no structural changes. § 46a-64c(a)(6)(C)(i): discrimination includes 'A refusal to permit, at the expense of a person with a physical or mental disability, reasonable modifications of existing premises ... except that, in the case of a rental, the landlord may, where it is reasonable to do so, condition permission for a modification on the renter agreeing to restore the interior of the premises to the condition that existed before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted'. § 47a-13b (EV charging; see ev-charging-ct and edu-ev-charging-ct, slice B). § 47a-7(c)-(d): written good-faith agreements for tenant-performed alterations or remodeling. Shared no-alterations carries the savings sentence "This Section does not limit any repair, installation, rekeying, or reasonable modification that applicable law entitles Tenant to perform", which preserves these rights. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Bed Bug Duties
bodyText: These rules apply to every rental unit except a single-family detached home. When a tenant reports bed bugs, you must inspect, or have a qualified inspector inspect, the unit and any connected unit you own within five business days, and if you inspect yourself, give the tenant written results within two days with local health department contact information. If bed bugs are found, begin effective treatment within five business days; if you treat without a pest control agent, vacuum first and get a qualified re-inspection within five business days. You pay for inspection and treatment; the tenant pays to prepare the unit, must allow access on reasonable notice, and is liable for extra treatments caused by knowingly and unreasonably refusing to cooperate. Offer reasonable help to a tenant who physically cannot prepare; you may charge a reasonable amount on a repayment plan of up to six months, but missed payments are not grounds for eviction (you may deduct the balance from the deposit at move-out). Failing these duties can cost you the tenant's attorney's fees and at least $250; if a tenant refuses access or cooperation, you may ask the court for an order.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7a(a)(7) ('Dwelling unit' means a unit 'other than a single-family unattached unit'); § 47a-7a(b)(1): tenant 'shall promptly notify a landlord orally or in writing'; 'Not later than five business days after receiving such notice, the landlord shall inspect or obtain an inspection by a qualified inspector'; written notice 'within two days' if the landlord inspects, with health department contact information; treatment 'not later than five business days after the date of the inspection'; self-treatment requires vacuuming and qualified re-inspection within five business days; 'the landlord shall be responsible for all costs associated with inspection for and treatment'. § 47a-7a(b)(2)(A)-(C): access on § 47a-16 notice, tenant 'shall be responsible for all costs associated with preparing a dwelling unit', liability for treatments 'arising from' the tenant's 'knowing and unreasonable failure to comply', no removal of infested property until cleared. § 47a-7a(b)(3): reasonable assistance; charge on 'a reasonable repayment schedule not to exceed six months'; nonpayment 'shall not be the basis for a summary process action'; deduction from the deposit at termination; no duty to provide alternative lodging or replace property. § 47a-7a(c) (disclosure; bed-bug-disclosure-ct, slice B). § 47a-7a(d)(1): landlord 'liable to the tenant for reasonable attorneys' fees and the greater of two hundred fifty dollars or the tenant's actual damages'; § 47a-7a(d)(2): injunctive relief under § 47a-18, small-claims entry fee, court order served 24 hours before entry. Clause: bed-bug-cooperation-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no rule requiring a tenant to tell you before leaving the unit empty in cold weather. Connecticut does require a tenant, unless the lease says otherwise, to tell you about any anticipated extended absence, and you may then enter at reasonable times to inspect or make repairs. The library's extended-absence clause covers this; it helps you protect pipes and heating while the unit is empty.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16a: 'Unless otherwise agreed, the tenant shall be required to notify the landlord of any anticipated extended absence from the premises and the landlord thereupon may enter the dwelling unit at reasonable times during such prolonged absence to inspect the premises, make necessary or agreed to repairs'. Proof of absence: CT-cold-weather-vacate-notice-1 (cold weather/winter/freezing/November/heating season near vacate/abandon/leave/absence; tenant context; whole corpus; hits 2, unrelated § 15-140c and § 49-31s; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-cold-weather-vacate-notice-2 (everyday frozen/burst pipes; hits 0). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Common-Area Lighting
bodyText: In a building with three or more households sharing halls or stairways, you must light all public halls at night, and in every building you must keep common areas clean and safe. Do not put hallway, stairway or other common-area lights on a tenant's electric meter: for leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, a tenant cannot be made to pay for utilities unless a separate meter measures what is delivered only to that tenant's unit. If common lights are on a tenant's meter now, plan to rewire them or put that service in your name.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-54d(b): 'The owner of each tenement house shall provide for the lighting of all public halls at night.' § 47a-50(1) ('tenement house' = three or more families living independently with a common right in halls, stairways or yards), (6) ('public hall'). § 47a-7(a)(3): 'keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition'. § 47a-4(a)(11), added by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-113, § 1 (effective October 1, 2026, for rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after that date; compiled text pending): a rental agreement shall not provide that the tenant 'agrees to pay for utilities billed to the tenant if no separate meter is used to measure utilities delivered exclusively to such tenant's dwelling unit'; § 47a-4(b): unenforceable. NEEDS_REVIEW: applying § 47a-4(a)(11) to a tenant-account meter that also carries common-area lights is an inference from its words ('delivered exclusively to such tenant's dwelling unit'); whether it reaches service the tenant pays directly to the utility (rather than 'billed to the tenant' by the landlord) is unsettled; title 16 utility rules (e.g., § 16-262e) not read for this point. Municipal housing codes flagged, not resolved. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Liens for Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText: In Connecticut, a contractor who works on the property under a contract with your tenant can put a mechanic's lien on the tenant's leasehold. If the work was done with your consent, the contractor may also claim a lien on your building and land. No Connecticut statute lets a lease clause block that. Before approving any tenant alteration, decide whether you want to allow it at all, require the tenant to show that contractors have been paid, and get advice on lien waivers for larger jobs.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 49-33(a): a claim for more than ten dollars for materials or services in the construction or repair of a building, 'by virtue of an agreement with or by consent of the owner of the land ... or of some person having authority from or rightfully acting for the owner', makes the building and land 'subject to the payment of the claim'. § 49-33(h): for work 'by virtue of an agreement with or by consent of the lessee', 'the leasehold interest in such real property is subject to the payment of the claim. This subsection shall not be construed to limit any of the rights or remedies available to such person under subsection (a)'. No enabling statute for a lease no-lien clause: CT-construction-liens-1 (hits 0) and CT-construction-liens-2 (positive 49-33 passed; no other on-point hits). NEEDS_REVIEW: whether a landlord's written consent to tenant alterations is 'consent of the owner' under § 49-33(a) is case law not searched. A clause making the tenant indemnify the landlord against such liens was not drafted because Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(3) bars a tenant agreeing 'to indemnify the landlord for that liability' (landlord liability arising under law); whether a lien from tenant-ordered work falls within (a)(3) is unsettled. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Family Child Care in Rentals
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to let a tenant run a family child care home in your rental, and sets no lease conditions for one. Towns may not use zoning to treat a licensed family child care home differently from any other home, and the tenant must hold a license from the Office of Early Childhood. Because the library's lease limits the unit to residential use, a tenant needs your written consent to run a child care business; if you consent, consider requiring proof of the license and of liability insurance.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 8-3j(a): 'No zoning regulation shall treat any family child care home or group child care home, located in a residence and licensed by the Office of Early Childhood pursuant to chapter 368a, in a manner different from single or multifamily dwellings.' § 19a-87b(a): no person shall maintain a family child care home 'without a license issued by the Commissioner of Early Childhood' (section read for licensing and landlord references; none found). § 19a-77 defines 'family child care home' (private family home, not more than six children with listed additions). § 47a-17: 'Unless otherwise agreed, a tenant shall occupy his dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit.' Proof of absence: CT-family-child-care-1 (hits 11, none a landlord-tenant rule; no synthetic positive run, the statutory phrase was searched directly) and CT-family-child-care-2 (hits 13, none on point). Fair housing familial-status rules unaffected. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched (Office of Early Childhood regulations not loaded). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Home Business Right
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute giving tenants a right to run a business from a rental home, so the lease decides. By law a tenant must use the unit only as a home unless you agree otherwise, and the library's lease limits use to residential purposes. If you want to allow quiet work from home or a small business, say so in writing; local zoning rules on home occupations still apply.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-17: 'Unless otherwise agreed, a tenant shall occupy his dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit.' Proof of absence: CT-home-business-1 (hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-home-business-2 (hits 2, unrelated). Municipal zoning home-occupation rules flagged, not resolved. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Water and Sewer Liens on Rental Property
bodyText: In Connecticut, unpaid municipal water and sewer charges become a lien on the property they served and a charge against the owner, collected like unpaid property taxes, even if a tenant ran up the bill. No lease clause or filing protects you from that. A private water company can lien the property only if the owner of record is the one who owes the charges. If tenants pay water or sewer directly, check the account status regularly; and in a lease signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, you cannot make a tenant pay for a utility that is not measured by a separate meter serving only that unit.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 7-239: municipal waterworks 'rates or charges ... if not paid when due, shall constitute a lien upon the premises served and a charge against the owner thereof, which lien and charge shall bear interest at the same rate as would unpaid taxes'. § 7-258: 'Any such unpaid connection or use charge shall constitute a lien upon the real estate against which such charge was levied from the date it became delinquent', collectible and continued like property tax liens. § 49-72: a private water company 'has a lien on the real estate served and a charge against the owners of such real estate ... provided the owner of such real estate when the lien is recorded is the party that owes such rates or charges'. § 47a-4(a)(11) (Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-113, § 1, effective October 1, 2026; compiled text pending). NEEDS_REVIEW: §§ 7-239 and 7-258 do not mention tenants; the statement that they apply where the tenant holds the account rests on their words ('premises served', 'charge against the owner'); case law not searched; regional water authority and special-act districts not reviewed. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Occupancy Limits
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide limit on people per bedroom for private rentals. In a building with three or more households, or a lodging or boarding house, the local health department can order a room's occupants reduced so that each person over 12 has at least 500 cubic feet of air and each child under 12 at least 300 cubic feet. The State Building Code and local housing codes may set other limits. Any occupancy limit you set must be reasonable and must not be used to turn away families with children.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-54a: 'If a room in a tenement, lodging or boarding house is overcrowded, the board of health or other enforcing agency may order the number of persons sleeping or living in such room to be so reduced that there shall not be less than five hundred cubic feet of air to each person over twelve years of age who occupies such room, and three hundred cubic feet of air to each child under twelve years of age'. § 47a-50(1)-(2) (tenement house: three or more families; lodging/boarding house: six or more persons lodged for hire). Conn. Agencies Regs. § 8-37ee-902(b) (regulation, Rule 21 flag; applies to entities under DOH fair housing regulations): 'The State Building Code shall govern maximum occupancy of a unit.' § 46a-64c(a)(1)-(2) (familial status). NEEDS_REVIEW: State Building Code occupancy provisions and local housing codes not loaded; whether a stricter landlord standard is lawful under familial-status rules is case law and federal guidance, not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Smoking, Vaping and Cannabis
bodyText: You may ban smoking and vaping of tobacco and cannabis anywhere on the property, and the library's smoking policy does so. But you may not ban a tenant from possessing cannabis or using it in other ways, such as edibles, and you may not require a tenant to take a drug test. You may not refuse to rent to, or treat differently, someone because of a past conviction for possessing a small amount of cannabis, or solely because they are a qualifying medical cannabis patient or caregiver (from October 1, 2026, including a qualifying out-of-state patient or caregiver) unless federal law or federal funding requires it. The possession, use, drug-test and conviction rules do not apply to a roomer who does not lease the whole home, a residence incidental to detention or to medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services, transitional or sober-living housing, or where federal law or a federal benefit requires a ban.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-9a(b): 'in the case of the rental of a dwelling unit, a landlord or property manager may not prohibit the possession of cannabis or the consumption of cannabis, except a landlord or property manager may prohibit smoking of cannabis or use of an electronic cannabis device or cannabis vapor product, as such terms are defined in section 19a-342a.' § 47a-9a(c): 'A landlord or property manager may not require a tenant to submit to a drug test.' § 47a-9a(a): no refusal or discrimination 'based on a past conviction for possession of a cannabis-type substance under section 21a-279a' or of four ounces or less of cannabis plant material elsewhere. § 47a-9a(d): exceptions for a roomer 'not leasing the entire residence', institutional residence, 'transitional housing or sober living facility', and where failing to prohibit 'would violate federal law or regulations or cause the landlord to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law'. § 21a-408p(b)(2): 'No landlord may refuse to rent a dwelling unit to a person or take action against a tenant solely on the basis of such person's or tenant's status as a qualifying patient' or caregiver, 'Unless required by federal law or required to obtain federal funding'; amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-8, § 39 (effective October 1, 2026; compiled text pending) to add qualifying out-of-state patients and caregivers. § 19a-342(b)(1)(H): no smoking 'in any passenger elevator'. Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-8, §§ 10-11 (effective October 1, 2026) amend the definition of 'Cannabis' in §§ 19a-342 and 19a-342a (each now defines "Cannabis" by reference to § 21a-240, as amended). Shared smoking-policy bans "Smoking of any kind, including tobacco, marijuana, and vaping" and does not ban possession or edibles, so it fits § 47a-9a(b). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant's Insurance and Your Repair Duties
bodyText: No Connecticut statute says whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's renter's insurance. Two rules limit how far a lease can go: you remain responsible for the repairs and upkeep Connecticut law puts on landlords, and a lease cannot make a tenant release you from, or pay for, liability the law places on you. Do not make a tenant's insurance claim a condition of doing repairs you owe.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(3): a rental agreement shall not provide that the tenant 'agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law or to indemnify the landlord for that liability or the costs connected therewith'; § 47a-4(b) unenforceable. § 47a-7(a) landlord repair and maintenance duties. Proof of absence: CT-tenant-insurance-claims-1 (hits 1, unrelated; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-tenant-insurance-claims-2 (hits 1, § 8-339(g), not on point). NEEDS_REVIEW: whether conditioning repairs on a tenant's claim would be an indirect exculpation under § 47a-4(a)(3) is case law not searched; insurance-law subrogation rules not searched. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Wells, Septic and Water Testing
bodyText: If the home is served by a private well or septic system, keeping it working is your job as landlord, along with supplying running water and reasonable hot water. In a single-family home you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant will handle specified maintenance tasks, but that cannot be used to dodge your duties. Whenever water testing for the property shows a contaminant above the state limit, you must send a copy of the results to every tenant within 48 hours after you receive them.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(4): 'maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and other facilities and appliances ... supplied or required to be supplied by him'; § 47a-7(a)(6): 'supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times'; § 47a-7(c): single-family residence landlord and tenant 'may agree in writing that the tenant perform the landlord's duties specified in subdivisions (5) and (6) of subsection (a) and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling, provided the transaction is entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord'. § 19a-37k: 'The owner of any residential or commercial property shall notify each tenant ... whenever any testing of the water supply for such property indicates that the water exceeds' a maximum contaminant level; 'not later than forty-eight hours after receiving notification of the results of such testing, the owner shall forward a copy of such notification to each such tenant'; Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-142, § 6 (effective October 1, 2026; compiled text pending) changes the contaminant reference to MCLs in the regulations and 'perfluoroalkyl substances and unregulated contaminants established pursuant to the provisions of section 21a-150b'. NEEDS_REVIEW: no statute names wells or septic systems in the landlord-tenant title; treating them as § 47a-7(a)(4) facilities is an inference; public health well-testing regulations (§ 19a-37 regs) not loaded. A water-testing disclosure topic may also exist in slice B. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant Duties Under Connecticut Law
bodyText: Connecticut law requires every tenant to: follow the building, housing and fire code duties that fall on tenants; keep the part of the premises they use as clean and safe as its condition allows; take garbage and waste to the place you provide; keep plumbing fixtures and appliances clean; use electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, reasonably; not deliberately or carelessly damage the property or let anyone else do so; not disturb neighbors or create a nuisance; and not let a household member who was evicted for selling drugs move back in without your consent. If a tenant materially breaks these duties in a way that materially affects other tenants' health and safety or the physical condition of the property, you must first give a written notice ending the lease at least 15 days after receipt; a breach that can be fixed by repair or paying damages is cured if the tenant does so within that time. A serious nuisance, or letting an evicted drug-selling household member back in, can go straight to a notice to quit.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11(a)-(h) (quoted in summary). § 47a-15: for 'a material noncompliance with section 47a-11 which materially affects the health and safety of the other tenants or materially affects the physical condition of the premises', written notice with a termination date 'not less than fifteen days after receipt'; remediable breaches cured within 15 days do not terminate; recurrence within six months allows termination under §§ 47a-23 to 47a-23b; serious nuisance and drug-readmission grounds go straight to a notice to quit. § 47a-23(a)(1)(F): termination for 'violation of section 47a-11'. Nuisance: § 47a-32 ('any conduct which interferes substantially with the comfort or safety of other tenants or occupants of the same or adjacent buildings or structures'); serious nuisance: § 47a-15. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Which Utilities a Tenant Can Be Made to Pay
bodyText: Make a tenant pay only for utilities measured by a meter (or billed separately) for that tenant's unit alone. By law you are responsible for electricity, gas, water and heating fuel supplied to the building unless the service is individually metered or billed for the exclusive use of one unit, and for leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, a lease term making a tenant pay for utilities without a separate meter for their unit is unenforceable. If heat or utilities are included in the rent, you may not add a surcharge for them. If a shared-meter account in your name goes unpaid, tenants who take service in their own name may deduct those payments from rent.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-262e(c): 'The owner, agent, lessor or manager of a residential dwelling shall be liable for the costs of all electricity, gas, water or heating fuel furnished ... to the building, except for any service furnished to any dwelling unit of the building on an individually metered or billed basis for the exclusive use of the occupants of that dwelling unit'; occupants on shared service may deduct 'a reasonable estimate of the cost of any portion of such service which is for the use of occupants of dwelling units other than such occupant's dwelling unit'; § 16-262e(d): payments 'deemed to be in lieu of an equal amount of rent'; § 16-262e(f): no rent increase to recoup deductions. § 47a-4(a)(10) (no heat/utilities surcharge if included); § 47a-4(a)(11), added by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-113, § 1 (effective October 1, 2026, for agreements entered into or renewed on or after that date; compiled text pending): no term that the tenant 'agrees to pay for utilities billed to the tenant if no separate meter is used to measure utilities delivered exclusively to such tenant's dwelling unit'. NEEDS_REVIEW: whether § 47a-4(a)(11) also reaches submetered billing under § 16-19ff or only unmetered allocation is not settled by its text (submetering topics in this slice). Shared utilities-responsibility says "Tenant is responsible for arranging and paying directly to the service provider for all other utilities"; it is safe only where each such utility is individually metered to the unit. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Utility Shutoffs by Landlords
bodyText: Connecticut gives you no right to cut off a tenant's electricity, gas, water or heat for nonpayment, even if you submeter or bill the tenant for it; use the court eviction process instead. Electric submetering is allowed only in limited buildings approved by the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (for example, multifamily buildings powered by renewable energy or combined heat and power), at no more than the utility's rate for that class of customer, and never for common-area use. If you fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service you are required to supply, the tenant may buy it and deduct the cost from rent, move to substitute housing with rent abated, or, if the failure is wilful, end the lease and recover up to two months' rent or double damages. Wilfully failing to furnish heat or utilities your lease requires is a crime in Connecticut, and a utility will not shut off service at your request unless the tenant signs an agreement or you swear the unit is vacant.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-19ff(a): electric distribution companies 'shall allow the installation of submeters' at listed locations including '(3) commercial, industrial, multifamily residential or multiuse buildings where the electric power or thermal energy is provided by a Class I renewable energy source ... or a combined heat and power system' or '(4) in any other location as approved by the authority'; the approved entity must charge 'a rate no greater than the rate charged to that customer class', and may not charge a submetered account for '(A) usage for any common areas ... or (B) other usage not solely for use by such account'; § 16-19ff(b)(4), (c): PURA standards protecting submetered customers against termination. § 47a-13(a)(1)-(3) (deduct, substitute housing, wilful-failure termination and damages 'not more than two months' periodic rent or double the actual damages'). Self-help: § 47a-43(a)(3)-(4) and § 47a-46 (double damages for entry and detainer); § 53a-214 (criminal lockout covers depriving a tenant of 'access' to the unit or possessions). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-109: a landlord whose lease requires furnishing heat, cooking gas, electricity, hot water or water and who 'wilfully and intentionally' fails to furnish it is guilty of a class D misdemeanor, and a utility may not terminate service at the landlord's request without 'a statement signed by the lessee agreeing to such termination or a notarized statement signed by the lessor to the effect that the premises are vacant'. Proof of absence of any landlord interruption right: CT-utility-interruption-submeter-1 (hits 1, unrelated; synthetic positive passed). NEEDS_REVIEW: whether a landlord's utility cutoff is itself an entry-and-detainer under § 47a-43 or a criminal lockout under § 53a-214 turns on case law, not searched; PURA submetering regulations not loaded. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Cutoff for Untransferred Utilities
bodyText: Connecticut has no rule letting you shut off utilities still in your name because the tenant did not move the account into their own name. Require the transfer in the lease and follow up, but if service stays in your name, keep paying or ask the utility to switch the account. If you fall behind on an account serving tenants, the utility must warn the tenants and let them take service in their own names, and they may then deduct what they pay from the rent. Wilfully failing to furnish heat or utilities your lease requires is a crime in Connecticut, and a utility will not shut off service at your request unless the tenant signs an agreement or you swear the unit is vacant.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-262e(a): before terminating for an owner's delinquent account where occupants are not the billed party, the utility must make 'a good faith effort to notify the occupants' and provide 'an opportunity, where practicable, for such occupants to receive service in their own names without any liability for the amount due while service was billed directly to the lessor ... and without the necessity for a security deposit'; § 16-262e(d)-(f): occupant payments are 'deemed to be in lieu of an equal amount of rent', and the landlord may not raise rent to recoup them. § 47a-13 (essential services remedies). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-109: a landlord whose lease requires furnishing heat, cooking gas, electricity, hot water or water and who 'wilfully and intentionally' fails to furnish it is guilty of a class D misdemeanor, and a utility may not terminate service at the landlord's request without 'a statement signed by the lessee agreeing to such termination or a notarized statement signed by the lessor to the effect that the premises are vacant'. Proof of absence: CT-utility-transfer-1 (hits 7, only occupant protections; synthetic positive passed) and CT-utility-interruption-submeter-1 (hits 1, unrelated). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched (RCSA 16-3 utility termination loaded). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: Landlord has installed the smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms that Connecticut's fire and building codes require for the property, and they were working when Tenant moved in. Tenant will not remove, disconnect, disable or tamper with any alarm or take out its batteries, and will tell Landlord promptly if an alarm is missing, beeping or not working. Landlord will repair or replace it promptly. [Optional; use only for a single-family residence: Tenant will test the alarms monthly and replace batteries as needed.]
notes: CT: Landlord code duty: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(1) ('Comply with the requirements of chapter 368o and all applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety'). Code requirement: § 29-292(a)(1) ('The code shall require ... (B) smoke detection and warning equipment in residential buildings designed to be occupied by one or more families'; carbon monoxide equipment in new one- or two-family residential buildings with a permit for new occupancy on or after October 1, 2005); Conn. Agencies Regs. § 29-292-21e, Fire Safety Code amendments 31.3.4.5.1 ('Approved single-station smoke alarms shall be installed ... outside every sleeping area in the immediate vicinity of the bedrooms and on all levels of the dwelling unit, including basements') and 9.6.2.10.2 (power source by permit date) (regulation, Rule 21 flag). Tampering: § 53a-117a(a)(2) (criminal mischief to 'damage[], tamper[] with or remove[] any tangible property owned by ... a person for ... smoke detection and alarm ... purposes'). Optional single-family sentence: § 47a-7(c) lets the landlord and tenant of a single-family residence agree in writing that the tenant perform 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks' in good faith; for other buildings § 47a-7(d)(3) bars shifting work 'necessary to cure noncompliance with subdivisions (1) and (2)', so battery and testing duties are not shifted there. NEEDS_REVIEW: the loaded RCSA 29-292 copy carries a 2015 revision stamp; the current Fire Safety Code edition and CO requirements for existing rental buildings were not verified; no Connecticut statute assigns alarm testing or batteries to tenants. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarm Rules
bodyText: Connecticut's fire code requires smoke alarms in every residential building; in existing apartments, single-station alarms must be outside each sleeping area near the bedrooms and on every level, including the basement. Newer buildings need hard-wired alarms with battery backup (buildings permitted on or after October 1, 1985). Carbon monoxide alarms are required in one- and two-family homes built under permits issued on or after October 1, 2005, and may be required elsewhere by the building and fire codes. Keeping the required alarms installed and working is your code duty; in a single-family home you may agree in writing that the tenant tests them and changes batteries. Tampering with or removing a smoke alarm is a crime. Check with your local fire marshal for your building's exact requirements.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 29-292(a)(1), (b)(1)-(2) (smoke detection in residential buildings for one or more families; CO in new one- or two-family residences permitted on or after October 1, 2005; certificates of occupancy); Conn. Agencies Regs. § 29-292-21e (Fire Safety Code CT amendments 31.3.4.5.1 and 9.6.2.10.2; regulation, Rule 21 flag); § 47a-7(a)(1), (c), (d)(3); § 47a-11(a); § 53a-117a(a)(2); § 29-453 (seller's affidavit on transfer of one- or two-family homes; not a leasing rule). Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-58, §§ 2-3 and Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-110, § 2 (effective October 1, 2026) make code-adoption timing changes and add official interpretations to §§ 29-291a and 29-292 (no change to alarm requirements found). NEEDS_REVIEW: current Fire Safety Code edition not loaded (copy stamped 2015); existing-building CO requirements unverified. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Alarm Tampering Fee Rule
bodyText: No Connecticut statute authorizes a set fee for a tenant who removes or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, so the library does not offer one. Tampering with a smoke alarm is already a crime in Connecticut. You may recover your actual cost to repair or replace an alarm the tenant damaged or removed, including from the security deposit at move-out, and repeated tampering can be a lease violation.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-117a(a)(2): criminal mischief in the fourth degree when a person intentionally or recklessly 'damages, tampers with or removes any tangible property owned by ... a person for fire alarm, smoke detection and alarm ... purposes'; class C misdemeanor. § 47a-11(f): tenant shall 'not wilfully or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises'. § 47a-21(a)(14)(B) (deposit secures § 47a-11 obligations). Proof of absence: CT-alarm-tampering-fee-1 (hits 3; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-alarm-tampering-fee-2 (hits 9, none on point). A flat fee untied to actual loss risks being an unenforceable penalty (case law not searched). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Substitute Housing and Relocation Costs
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to house a tenant elsewhere during ordinary repairs. But if you fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service you are required to provide, and the failure isn't beyond your control, the tenant may move to substitute housing after 48 hours (right away if the same failure recurs within six months); the rent stops for that period and the tenant can recover the housing cost up to the rent abated, plus attorney's fees. If a town's code enforcement forces a tenant out, the town pays relocation benefits and can bill you and place a lien on your property, unless the displacement did not result from your failure to meet your repair duties.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13(a)(2): tenant may 'procure reasonable substitute housing during the period of the landlord's noncompliance if the landlord fails to supply such service within forty-eight hours of such breach, except if the breach is the failure to provide the same service and such breach recurs within six months, the tenant may secure substitute housing immediately'; § 47a-13(b): 'rent otherwise owed to the landlord shall abate', recovery of 'actual costs of such substitute housing' not exceeding 'the amount of rent abated', and 'reasonable attorney's fees'; § 47a-13(c): reasonable notice required; no rights if the tenant caused the condition. § 8-266: Uniform Relocation Assistance Act covers persons displaced 'by building code enforcement activities'. §§ 8-268(a), 8-270(a): 'whenever any tenant in any dwelling unit is displaced as the result of the enforcement of any code ... by any town, city or borough ... the landlord of such dwelling unit shall be liable for any payments made by such town, city or borough' and the municipality or state 'may place a lien on any real property owned by such landlord', with municipal-tax priority. § 8-270a: civil action with attorney's fees; 'it shall be an affirmative defense for the landlord that the displacement was not the result of the landlord's violation of section 47a-7.' § 47a-7a(b)(3)(C) (no duty to provide alternative lodging for bed bugs). Casualty: § 47a-14 (rent abates; tenant may vacate). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Appliances You Do Not Supply
bodyText: You must keep in good and safe working order the appliances and facilities you supply, or are required by law to supply. Appliances the tenant owns are the tenant's responsibility. Be careful with appliances you leave in the unit, such as a refrigerator left by a prior tenant: if you let the tenant use it, a court may treat it as supplied by you, and a lease clause cannot excuse you from a duty the law places on you. If you don't want to maintain an item, remove it before move-in or list in writing only items the tenant owns.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(4): 'maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and other facilities and appliances and elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by him'. § 47a-4(a)(3): no term by which the tenant 'agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law'. NEEDS_REVIEW: whether an appliance left in the unit is 'supplied' by the landlord is case law, not searched. Shared appliances-included (tagged CT) lists included appliances "which Landlord will maintain as provided in this Lease and applicable law". Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Balcony Inspection Mandate
bodyText: Connecticut has no law requiring periodic engineering inspections of balconies, decks, porches or exterior stairs in rental buildings. You still must keep the premises fit and safe, keep common areas safe, and meet building and fire codes. Inspect elevated wood structures regularly and fix rot, loose railings and failing supports promptly. Buildings with three or more units get a yearly fire marshal inspection, and your town may have its own inspection rules.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(1)-(3) (codes; fit and habitable; 'keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition'). Proof of absence: CT-balcony-inspection-1 (hits 11, none on point) and CT-balcony-inspection-2 (hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0). Related: § 29-305(b) (the local fire marshal inspects buildings regulated by the Fire Safety Code at least once each calendar year, except one- and two-family homes; a fire-code inspection, not a structural inspection of balconies) and Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-100, § 60 (risk-based residential fire inspection pilot for buildings of more than two families, with an owner pre-inspection checklist; compiled number pending). Municipal ordinances flagged, not resolved. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Rent After Condemnation
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that expressly bars collecting rent after a unit is condemned or ordered vacated, but you should expect to collect little. A lease cannot let you collect rent for any period in which you are not meeting your duty to keep the unit fit and up to code, and rent stops when fire or other casualty substantially impairs the tenant's use. A fair rent commission can suspend rent until you make repairs, a court can order rent paid into court and reduced, and if the town's code enforcement forces the tenant out, you can be billed for the tenant's relocation payments.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4a: 'A rental agreement shall not permit the receipt of rent for any period during which the landlord has failed to comply with subsection (a) of section 47a-7.' § 47a-14(a): tenant 'shall not be liable to pay rent for such period of time as such impairment continues' after casualty damage substantially impairs enjoyment. § 7-148d(a): fair rent commission 'may order the suspension of further payment of rent by the tenant until such time as the landlord makes the necessary changes' for health and safety violations. § 47a-14h(h) (rent deposited with the clerk) and (e)(4) (damages 'which may include a retroactive abatement of rent'). §§ 8-268(a), 8-270(a), 8-270a (relocation chargeback and lien). § 47a-13 (substitute housing). Proof of absence: CT-condemned-premises-rent-bar-1 (hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-condemned-premises-rent-bar-2 (hits 7, none on point). NEEDS_REVIEW: whether § 47a-4a also bars collecting rent (not just lease terms permitting it) is case law not searched. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched; municipal housing codes flagged, not resolved. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenants' Repair Remedies in Connecticut
bodyText: Connecticut tenants do not have a general right to make repairs and deduct the cost from rent, or simply to withhold rent, for ordinary repair problems. Their remedies are: ending a lease longer than one month if you don't fix a material problem within 15 days of written notice; buying an essential service you failed to supply (heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas) and deducting the cost, or moving to substitute housing with rent abated; no rent while fire or other casualty substantially impairs the unit; and, after complaining to the housing code agency, paying rent into court so a judge can order repairs and reduce the rent. A lease cannot take these remedies away.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-12(a), (c) (15-day notice; 'This section shall apply only to leases in which the term of the tenancy is more than one month'); § 47a-13(a)-(c) (essential services: 'deduct the actual and reasonable cost of such service from the rent', substitute housing, wilful-failure termination and damages); § 47a-14 (casualty); § 47a-14h(a)-(b) (action after a code complaint made at least 21 days earlier; rent paid to the clerk); § 47a-4(a)(1) (no waiver). Proof of absence of general repair-and-deduct and rent withholding: CT-confirmed-absences-habitability-3 (hits 1, § 47a-13 only; both positives passed) and CT-confirmed-absences-habitability-2 (hits 0). NEEDS_REVIEW: common-law defenses (e.g., constructive eviction, implied warranty) are case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: You must make reasonable changes to your rules, policies, practices and services when a tenant or applicant with a disability needs them to have an equal chance to use and enjoy the home, such as an assigned accessible parking space or an exception to a no-pets rule for an assistance animal. You must also allow reasonable physical modifications the tenant needs, at the tenant's expense; where reasonable, you may require the tenant to restore the interior to its original condition, except for normal wear, when they leave. These rules cover learning disabilities and physical or mental disabilities. They do not apply when you rent rooms in a single-family home you live in, or a unit in a two-family home where you live in the other unit.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46a-64c(a)(6)(A)-(B) (no discrimination in rental or terms because of 'a learning disability or physical or mental disability'); § 46a-64c(a)(6)(C): discrimination includes '(i) A refusal to permit, at the expense of a person with a physical or mental disability, reasonable modifications of existing premises ... except that, in the case of a rental, the landlord may, where it is reasonable to do so, condition permission for a modification on the renter agreeing to restore the interior of the premises to the condition that existed before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted; (ii) a refusal to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services, when such accommodations may be necessary to afford such person equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling'. § 46a-64c(b)(1) exemptions (owner-occupied single-family room rental; owner-occupied two-family). Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-77, § 27 and Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-110, § 6 (effective October 1, 2026; compiled text pending) amend § 46a-64c: word-level comparison shows the criminal-penalty subsection (g) replaced by a construction clause and the design-and-construction reference changed to State Building Code accessibility provisions; no change to the accommodation or modification duties. Federal Fair Housing Act not covered (Rule 21). No Connecticut statute requires the restoration condition to appear in the lease, and none sets an interest-bearing restoration escrow (statute read; no such text). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: After a Fire or Disaster
bodyText: Connecticut has no special statute for tenancies after a declared disaster; its casualty rule applies. If fire or another casualty the tenant did not cause damages the home so much that the tenant's use is substantially impaired, no rent is owed while that lasts. The tenant may move out right away and end the lease by written notice within 14 days, or, if staying is lawful, stop using the damaged part and pay a reduced rent. If the lease ends, return the security deposit and any prepaid rent, counting rent from the date of the casualty. During a declared emergency, Connecticut also bars charging unconscionably excessive prices for items leased or rented, so avoid sharp rent increases in a declared emergency area.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14(a): 'If the dwelling unit or premises are damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty to an extent that enjoyment of the dwelling unit is substantially impaired, the tenant, unless such damage or destruction is caused by the tenant's negligence or wilful act, shall not be liable to pay rent for such period of time as such impairment continues'; tenant may '(1) immediately vacate the premises and notify the landlord in writing within fourteen days thereafter of his intention to terminate' or '(2) if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate any part of the dwelling unit rendered unusable', with proportional reduction; § 47a-14(b): return 'all security and prepaid rent recoverable under section 47a-21'; accounting 'as of the date of the fire or other casualty'. § 42-230(a)-(b): 'No vendor shall lease, rent or sell, or offer to lease, rent or sell, any item in the chain of distribution at an unconscionably excessive price at any location in an area which is the subject of any precipitating event'; CUTPA enforcement by the Attorney General (§ 42-230(c)). Proof of absence: CHK-edu-disaster-casualty-ct-1 (disaster and emergency terms with tenancy context; CGS, RCSA, 2026 acts; hits 20, none a tenancy rule other than § 42-230; synthetic positive passed). Executive orders under chapter 517 not searched. NEEDS_REVIEW: whether § 42-230's 'item in the chain of distribution' reaches residential rent is not stated and case law was not searched. Landlord's own casualty termination: casualty-termination-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute on renting the same unit or room to two tenants for the same period, and none setting a remedy when you cannot deliver possession on the start date. If it happens, the tenant who cannot move in has ordinary contract claims against you. The library's possession-delay clause sets what happens if the unit isn't ready; avoid signing a new lease until the current tenant has actually moved out or a firm move-out date is in writing.
notes: CT: Proof of absence: CT-double-letting-3 (hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0), CT-double-letting-4 (hits 0; synthetic positive passed) and CT-double-letting-2 (hits 0). Holdover by the prior tenant is handled by summary process (§ 47a-23(a)(1)(A), lapse of time). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched; case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Which Fire, Building and Housing Codes Apply
bodyText: Connecticut requires you to comply with the state's tenement and lodging house law and with every building and housing code that materially affects health and safety; if a town ordinance or a building or fire code demands more than the state landlord law, the stricter rule wins. The State Fire Safety Code, based on national model codes, applies to rental buildings other than one- and two-family private homes, though its smoke alarm rules reach those homes too, and its carbon monoxide alarm rules reach those built under a building permit for new occupancy issued on or after October 1, 2005, unless the code exempts them; the State Fire Prevention Code also regulates hazards such as fuel, gas and flammable materials. The local fire marshal inspects multifamily buildings each year and inspects one- and two-family homes for smoke alarms on a complaint or request. Ask your local building official and fire marshal which code editions apply to your building.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(1): 'Comply with the requirements of chapter 368o and all applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety of both the state or any political subdivision thereof'; § 47a-7(b): stricter 'municipal ordinance, building code or fire code ... shall take precedence'. Chapter 368o is 'TENEMENT AND LODGING HOUSES' (beginning § 19a-355; not read beyond its heading). § 29-292(a)(1) (Fire Safety Code based on nationally recognized model codes; applies 'in all buildings ... except in private dwellings occupied by one or two families'; smoke and CO equipment requirements), as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-58, § 3 (effective October 1, 2026; compiled text pending): revisions 'not later than two years' after model-code publication and 'no revisions to the Fire Safety Code shall be required after the first publication of the revisions to the 2024 model fire and life safety codes and prior to the first publication of the revisions to the 2030 model fire and life safety codes'. § 29-305(b): annual inspections 'except residential buildings designed to be occupied by one or two families which shall be inspected, upon complaint or request of an owner or occupant, only for the purpose of determining whether the requirements ... relative to smoke detection and warning equipment have been satisfied'. § 29-291a (State Fire Prevention Code; no one- and two-family exclusion), as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-58, § 2 (effective Oct. 1, 2026; compiled text pending). NEEDS_REVIEW: current code editions not loaded (RCSA 29-292 copy stamped 2015). Municipal housing codes flagged, not resolved. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Furnished Rental Rules
bodyText: Connecticut has no special rules for furnished rentals, and the security deposit limit is the same (two months' rent, or one month for a tenant 62 or older). List the furniture you provide in the lease or a signed inventory, and note its condition on the move-in walk-through checklist; you may deduct from the deposit for damage the tenant causes beyond normal use. Furnished stays of 30 days or less can be subject to the state's room occupancy tax.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(b) (cap does not vary for furnished units); § 47a-7(a)(4) (maintain facilities and appliances supplied); § 47a-11(f) (no wilful or negligent damage); § 47a-21(a)(14)(B), (d) (deductions for breach of § 47a-11); § 47a-7c(b) (no deduction for conditions on the checklist); § 7-148c(4) ('services, furniture, furnishings and equipment supplied therein' as a fair rent factor); § 12-407(a)(2)(H) and 'Lodging house' definition including a 'furnished residence' (see edu-rent-tax-ct). Proof of absence: CT-furnishings-included-1 (hits 11, none a furnished-rental rule); no synthetic positive was run because the statutory words were searched directly. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Shifting Repairs and Chores to the Tenant
bodyText: In a single-family home, you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant handles garbage removal, supplies the heat, water and hot water, and does specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, so long as the deal is made in good faith and not to escape your legal duties. In any other building, you may agree in writing only that the tenant does specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, and only if the work is not needed to bring the unit up to code or make it fit and habitable and the deal doesn't reduce what you owe other tenants. Your basic duties to meet codes and keep the home fit and habitable stay with you. List each task specifically in the lease.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(c): 'The landlord and tenant of a single-family residence may agree in writing that the tenant perform the landlord's duties specified in subdivisions (5) and (6) of subsection (a) and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling, provided the transaction is entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord.' § 47a-7(d): for 'a dwelling unit other than a single-family residence', the parties 'may agree that the tenant is to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling if (1) the agreement of the parties is entered into in good faith; (2) the agreement is in writing; (3) the work is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subdivisions (1) and (2) of subsection (a) of this section; and (4) the agreement does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises.' § 47a-1(11) defines 'Single-family residence' (direct street access, no shared heating, hot water or other essential facility, even if walls are shared). § 47a-4(a)(1), (3) (no waiver or exculpation otherwise). Applies to shared clauses landscaping-irrigation, snow-removal and tenant-maintenance. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: Connecticut law does not presume that you breached your repair duties, or took too long to fix something, in an eviction or repair case. But in an eviction a tenant may raise any legal, equitable or constitutional defense, including that you are evicting in retaliation for a complaint to housing officials or a fair rent commission. Keep records of repair requests and when you fixed each problem.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-33a: 'In any action of summary process under this chapter, the tenant may present any affirmative legal, equitable or constitutional defense that the tenant may have.' § 47a-33: affirmative defense 'that the plaintiff brought such action solely because the defendant attempted to remedy, by lawful means' a code violation, with rent or use and occupancy still owed. § 47a-20 (six-month retaliation bar). Proof of absence: CT-habitability-presumption-2 (hits 3, unrelated; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0). NEEDS_REVIEW: court-made presumptions or burdens (e.g., Practice Book housing session practice) beyond the statute were not searched beyond the Practice Book in the battery. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A Connecticut lease cannot make a tenant give up the right to a fit, code-compliant home or the remedies the law gives tenants, cannot release you from liability the law places on you, and cannot let you collect rent for any period in which you are not meeting your repair duties. Such terms are unenforceable. The only lawful way to shift work to a tenant is a written, good-faith agreement for specified tasks, and in buildings other than single-family homes that can never cover work needed to make the unit fit or code-compliant.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1) (no waiver of rights under the chapter 'or under any section of the general statutes or any municipal ordinance unless such section or ordinance expressly states that such rights may be waived'); § 47a-4(a)(3) (no exculpation or indemnity for landlord liability arising under law); § 47a-4(b) (unenforceable); § 47a-4a: 'A rental agreement shall not permit the receipt of rent for any period during which the landlord has failed to comply with subsection (a) of section 47a-7.' § 47a-7(c)-(d) (limited written reallocations; see edu-tenant-maintenance-agreements-ct). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Local Health and Housing Code Enforcement
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to hand out your local health district's rental rules, but local health and housing officials enforce minimum standards in rentals. They can order you to fix conditions that endanger life or health in a rented one- or two-family home or in a building with three or more households, and a tenant must first complain to the local housing or health agency before asking a court to have rent paid into court. When you give a tenant your written bed bug inspection results, you must include the local health department's contact information. Check your town's housing code.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-52(c): when a defect in a 'rented dwelling' (one or two families) 'constitutes a danger to life or health', the local department of health 'may order the responsible party to correct the same' and may seek injunctive relief. § 47a-53(a): board of health or enforcing agency may declare conditions in a tenement, lodging or boarding house a public nuisance and order them remedied; § 47a-53(b)-(c) (unmet orders carried out at the owner's expense plus up to a 5% service charge and 10% penalty; unpaid after 60 days, a lien if a notice of violation is recorded within 30 days). § 47a-14h(b): complaint to the municipal agency 'responsible for enforcement of the housing code or, if no housing code exists, of the public health code' at least 21 days before suit. § 47a-7a(b)(1): bed bug notice 'shall provide relevant contact information' for the local health department. Proof of absence of a duty to provide regulations: CT-health-district-rental-rules-1 (hits 1, § 19a-206 only); no synthetic positive run. NEEDS_REVIEW: Public Health Code regulations and local housing codes not loaded. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Heat and Hot Water
bodyText: You must supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat, unless the unit's heat and hot water come from equipment under the tenant's sole control or from utility service connected directly to the tenant. In a single-family home, the tenant may agree in writing to supply heat and hot water. If you fail to supply required heat or hot water, the tenant may buy it and deduct the cost from rent, move to substitute housing after 48 hours with rent abated, or, if the failure is wilful, end the lease and recover damages.
