Connecticut treats an indoor temperature below 65 degrees in an occupied home as injurious to health, and if the lease requires you to furnish heat or utilities, wilfully failing to do so is a crime. A heating oil or propane supplier serving a tenant-occupied building must keep it at 65 degrees or warn you, the state and the local health officer before stopping deliveries, and a utility will not cut service at your request without the tenant's signed agreement or your notarized statement that the unit is vacant.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(6): 'supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat except if the building which includes the dwelling unit is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose or if the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant or supplied by a direct public utility connection'. § 47a-7(c) (single-family written agreement covering (a)(5)-(6)). § 47a-13(a)-(b) (essential-service remedies). § 19a-214: suppliers of fuel oil or bottled gas to a residential building occupied by someone other than the liable party must supply 'quantities sufficient to maintain the interior of such building at sixty-five degrees Fahrenheit' unless they give 3 days' (10 days for automatic delivery) notice to the owner, the Secretary of OPM and the municipal chief health officer. § 16-262e(c) (landlord liable for heating fuel to the building except individually metered/billed service). § 19a-109: 'a temperature of less than sixty-five degrees Fahrenheit in such building or part thereof shall ... be deemed injurious to the health of the occupants'; an owner or lessor whose lease 'by its terms, express or implied, requires the furnishing of heat, cooking gas, electricity, hot water or water' and who 'wilfully and intentionally, fails to furnish such heat to the degrees herein provided' or those services, interfering with 'the comfortable or quiet enjoyment of the premises', is 'guilty of a class D misdemeanor'; no public service company or electric supplier may terminate such service at the owner's request 'unless the owner or lessor furnishes a statement signed by the lessee agreeing to such termination or a notarized statement signed by the lessor to the effect that the premises are vacant'. NEEDS_REVIEW: Public Health Code heat regulations (RCSA 19a-36) and local housing code temperature standards not loaded. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Right to Fix It and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute letting you fix a problem the tenant caused and add the cost to the rent. You may enter on reasonable notice to make necessary repairs, charge the tenant the reasonable cost of damage the tenant or their guests caused, and deduct unpaid damage costs from the security deposit when the tenancy ends. Do not label repair costs as rent: Connecticut rent means periodic payments, and an eviction for nonpayment must rest on unpaid rent. For a tenant's material breach, use the written 15-day notice to cure.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16(a) (tenant 'shall not unreasonably withhold consent' to entry 'to ... make necessary or agreed to repairs'); § 47a-16(c) (reasonable notice, reasonable times); § 47a-11(f); § 47a-15 (15-day notice; breach 'remediable by repairs or the payment of damages'); § 47a-1(8) ('Rent' means 'all periodic payments'); § 47a-21(a)(14)(B), (d) (deposit deduction). Proof of absence: CT-landlord-self-cure-2 (hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-landlord-self-cure-3 (hits 0). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Extra Standards for Buildings With Three or More Units
bodyText: If your building houses three or more households who share halls, stairways or yards (or is a lodging or boarding house), Connecticut adds specific standards: keep the building clean, in good repair and with a roof that doesn't leak; provide garbage and rubbish receptacles; light all public halls at night; provide water on every occupied floor where public water is available; provide at least one toilet for every two units of two rooms or less and one for each larger unit, on the same floor, with a window or vent; every bedroom must have an outside window (or a prescribed interior sash window); and keep interior paint free of peeling or chipping that could harm health. The local health or housing agency enforces these rules and can order repairs.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-50(1)-(2) (tenement house: 'three or more families, living independently of each other, and doing their cooking upon the premises, and having a common right in the halls, stairways or yards'; lodging/boarding house: six or more persons lodged for hire); § 47a-51(a)-(d) (clean; 'suitable receptacles' for garbage, ashes and rubbish; 'kept in good repair'; roof 'so kept as not to leak'); § 47a-54b (water on each floor); § 47a-54c(a)-(c) (toilet ratios, same floor, ventilation, light); § 47a-54d(b) ('The owner of each tenement house shall provide for the lighting of all public halls at night'); § 47a-54e (sleeping-room window or eight-square-foot sash window); § 47a-54f(b) (paint 'shall not be cracked, chipped, blistered, flaking, loose, or peeling so as to constitute a health hazard'; lead under § 19a-111c regulations); § 47a-54a (overcrowding); § 47a-52 (one- and two-family rented dwellings; dangerous defects); § 47a-53 (enforcement orders). These sections are chapter 833a; § 47a-7(a)(1) separately requires compliance with chapter 368o (tenement and lodging houses, title 19a, not read). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Terms a Connecticut Lease Cannot Contain
bodyText: A Connecticut lease may not make the tenant: give up rights under the landlord-tenant laws or any statute or town ordinance (unless that law says the right may be waived); let you get a court judgment without a hearing (confession of judgment); release you from, or pay for, liability the law places on you; give up interest on the security deposit; let you remove the tenant without a court order; let you seize the tenant's belongings for rent; pay your attorney's fees above 15% of a money judgment; pay a late charge before the grace period ends, above the legal limit, or get a discount for paying within the grace period; pay a heat or utilities surcharge when heat or utilities are included; or, for leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, pay for utilities not measured by a separate meter for the unit. A lease also cannot let you collect rent while you are not meeting your repair duties. Any such term is unenforceable.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1)-(10) (as quoted in the summary; read section-open) and § 47a-4(b): 'A provision prohibited by subsection (a) of this section included in a rental agreement is unenforceable.' § 47a-4(a)(11), added by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-113, § 1 (effective October 1, 2026, for rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after that date; compiled text pending): 'agrees to pay for utilities billed to the tenant if no separate meter is used to measure utilities delivered exclusively to such tenant's dwelling unit'. § 47a-4a: 'A rental agreement shall not permit the receipt of rent for any period during which the landlord has failed to comply with subsection (a) of section 47a-7.' Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Pools at Rental Properties
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant law has no pool fence or pool notice rule for rentals. But a pool or spa at an apartment complex or other multi-unit property counts as a public pool under state health law; only a pool used at a single-family home (and not for business) is excluded. Public pools are classified and regulated by the Department of Public Health, which reviews plans and inspects them, and local building codes govern barriers. Check with your local health department and building official before opening a pool to tenants.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-36(c)(1): '“public pool” means an artificial basin ... intended for recreational bathing, swimming, diving or therapeutic purposes ... “Public pool” does not include an artificial basin provided with a controlled water supply that is intended for use at a single-family residence, except when such basin is used for commercial or business purposes at such residence'; § 19a-36(c)(2)-(3) (DPH classification; plan review and inspection fees). NEEDS_REVIEW: Public Health Code pool regulations and State Building Code barrier provisions not loaded; whether a two-unit rental's pool is 'intended for use at a single-family residence' is unsettled. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Promises to Repair
bodyText: Connecticut has no rule that your promises to clean, repair or improve a unit be in writing or carry a completion date. Still, put any such promise in the lease or a signed addendum with a date: it then becomes a lease term you must keep, and a tenant may end a lease longer than one month if you materially fail to keep the lease and don't fix it within 15 days of written notice. You may enter on reasonable notice to make agreed repairs.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3 (parties may include terms 'not prohibited by law'); § 47a-12(a), (c) ('material noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement'; leases over one month); § 47a-16(a) (entry to 'make necessary or agreed to repairs'). Proof of absence: CT-promises-to-repair-1 (hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0); a second everyday battery was not run separately (the first included the everyday verbs clean/paint/repair). Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Respecting the Tenant's Possession
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute stating a covenant of quiet enjoyment, but courts recognize one, and several statutes protect a tenant's possession. Enter only with the tenant's consent on reasonable notice, in an emergency, under a court order, or after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit; an unlawful entry or repeated harassing demands cost at least one month's rent plus attorney's fees. Locking a tenant out or taking their belongings without a court order is a crime and can cost double damages. Wilfully failing to provide heat or utilities the lease requires is also a crime.
notes: CT: Practice Book § 10-21 (court rule, Rule 21 flag) lists 'the breach of a covenant for quiet enjoyment by the entry of the lessor' as a joinable claim; NEEDS_REVIEW: the covenant itself is common law (case law not searched). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16(c)-(d) (entry rules); § 47a-18a ('actual damages not less than an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees'); §§ 47a-43, 47a-46 (forcible entry and detainer; double damages); § 53a-214 (criminal lockout, class C misdemeanor); § 19a-109 (wilful failure to furnish heat, gas, electricity, hot water or water that 'interferes with the comfortable or quiet enjoyment of the premises' is a class D misdemeanor). Tagged landlords-access-mi covers entry. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Rental Inspections
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide rental license or inspection program, but towns may adopt housing codes for safe and sanitary housing and fine rental owners up to $2,000 per violation (violations found on the same date count as one), and many do. The local fire marshal inspects buildings with three or more units each year and may enter at reasonable hours; one- and two-family homes are inspected for smoke alarms on a complaint or request. A tenant must not unreasonably refuse you entry for inspections on reasonable notice, but no statute lets the lease itself authorize a government inspector to enter. Check your town's rental registration, licensing and inspection rules.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 7-148(c)(7)(A)(i): municipalities may 'Make rules relating to the maintenance of safe and sanitary housing and prescribe civil penalties for the violation of such rules against an owner of rental property not to exceed two thousand dollars per violation, provided if multiple violations are discovered on the same date, such violations shall be enforced as one violation'. § 29-305(b): annual inspections of occupancies under the Fire Safety or Fire Prevention Code 'except residential buildings designed to be occupied by one or two families which shall be inspected, upon complaint or request of an owner or occupant, only for the purpose of determining whether the requirements ... relative to smoke detection and warning equipment have been satisfied'; § 29-305(d): fire marshal 'shall have the right of entry at all reasonable hours'. Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-100, § 60 (risk-based residential fire inspection pilot; compiled number pending; read in context only). § 47a-16(a) (tenant not to unreasonably withhold consent to landlord's entry to inspect). NEEDS_REVIEW: municipal ordinances flagged, not resolved; proof of absence for an inspector-entry lease authorization: CHK-edu-rental-inspections-ct-1 (inspection or entry with lease consent or authorization; CGS, RCSA, 2026 acts; hits 75, none on point; synthetic positive passed). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Right to End the Lease Over Repair Costs
bodyText: Connecticut gives you no right to end a tenancy because a needed repair would cost too much. Your duty to keep the home fit and up to code applies regardless of cost. After a fire or other casualty, the tenant may end the lease, and the library offers an optional clause letting you end it too; otherwise you must repair, or end a month-to-month tenancy or let a lease expire with proper notice.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(2) ('make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition'), with no cost exception; § 47a-14 (casualty; tenant termination). Proof of absence: CT-repair-cost-termination-1 (hits 0; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0); a second everyday battery was not separately run. Optional landlord casualty termination: casualty-termination-ct. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: How Tenants Give Repair Notice
bodyText: You may ask tenants to make repair requests in writing, but Connecticut ties tenant remedies to different kinds of notice and a lease cannot take them away. A tenant who wants to end the lease for your failure to make repairs must give written notice. For heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, reasonable oral notice is enough to start the tenant's remedies. Bed bugs may be reported orally or in writing. Before suing to pay rent into court, the tenant must have complained to the local housing or health code agency at least 21 days earlier. Act on every report you receive, however it arrives.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-12(a): 'the tenant may deliver a written notice to the landlord specifying the acts and omissions constituting the breach'; § 47a-13(c): 'Rights of the tenant under this section do not arise (1) until the tenant has given reasonable written or oral notice to the landlord'; § 47a-7a(b)(1): 'A tenant shall promptly notify a landlord orally or in writing'; § 47a-14h(b): complaint to the municipal code agency 'at least twenty-one days prior to the date on which the complaint is filed'; § 47a-4(a)(1) (no waiver). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Locks and Rekeying
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring particular locks, deadbolts or door viewers in rentals, or rekeying between tenants; your town's housing code may. Rekeying at each turnover is still good practice. Connecticut does require you to change the locks, or let the tenant change them, within set deadlines when a tenant protected by a court order asks.
notes: CT: Proof of absence: CT-security-devices-1 (hits 5, none a landlord duty; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0) and CT-security-devices-2 (hits 0). § 47a-7b (lock change on request of a tenant named as a protected person; respond within six hours, change within 48 hours if the landlord does it). Municipal housing codes flagged, not resolved. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Staff Work-Card Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no law requiring work cards or background checks for maintenance or management staff in housing for older adults or in any other private rental housing. Screening staff who have keys to occupied units is still good practice; follow the state's rules on use of criminal records in employment decisions.
notes: CT: Proof of absence: CT-senior-housing-work-card-1 (hits 3, unrelated: § 8-114d resident services coordinators, § 17b-451 mandated reporters including elderly housing managers, § 17b-194 definitions; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0); a second everyday battery was not separately run. Employment criminal-record rules (e.g., § 46a-80) not read. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No State Stove or Refrigerator Requirement
bodyText: Connecticut statutes do not require you to supply a stove or refrigerator, but if you supply them you must keep them in good and safe working order. Your town's housing code may require cooking facilities, so check local rules. List the appliances you supply in the lease.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(4) (maintain appliances 'supplied or required to be supplied by him'); § 47a-1(10) ('Roomer' means a person occupying a unit that does not include 'a refrigerator, stove, kitchen sink, toilet and shower or bathtub' where one or more are shared). Proof of absence: CT-stove-refrigerator-1 (hits 30, none a supply duty); no synthetic positive run (statutory nouns searched directly). NEEDS_REVIEW: Public Health Code and municipal housing codes not loaded. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Receivership of Rents for Code Violations
bodyText: If your town has adopted Connecticut's receivership law and you don't obey a health or housing order to fix dangerous conditions, or you substantially fail your duty to keep the property fit and up to code, the town can ask the court to appoint a receiver to collect the rents and make the repairs. The town then gets a lien on the property, ahead of existing mortgages, for the receiver's costs. You or your lender can avoid a receiver by showing you can do the work promptly and posting security. Separately, an electric, gas or telephone company or a municipal utility you fail to pay can ask the court to have the rents paid to a receiver to cover service to the tenants.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-56 (municipal adoption by ordinance); § 47a-56a: application when an order under § 47a-53 or § 47a-55 is not complied with 'or whenever a landlord has not substantially complied with the provisions of section 47a-7', for a receiver to 'remove or remedy such condition and obtain a lien in favor of the municipality, having priority with respect to all existing mortgages or liens'; § 47a-56c(b)-(d) (appointment; owner or lienholder may do the work on posting security). § 16-262f (utility action for receivership of rents). § 47a-56c(c) (owner, mortgagee or lienor may do the work on showing ability and posting security); §§ 47a-56d(d), 47a-56h (municipal advances and mortgagee liens carry the § 47a-56a priority); § 47a-56i (revolving-fund lien priority); § 16-262f(a) (an electric distribution, gas or telephone company or a municipal utility may petition for a receiver of rents). NEEDS_REVIEW: Municipal adoption status flagged, not resolved. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Cable TV Access in Apartment Buildings
bodyText: If you own a building with several units, you must let a cable TV company wire the building when a tenant asks for service, as long as the company pays the full cost, indemnifies you for damage and follows state utility rules. You may not demand or accept payment for allowing cable service, except compensation the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority approves, and you may not charge different rent or provide different service to tenants who do or don't subscribe. If the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority finds a violation after a hearing, you can owe a civil penalty of up to $1,000 for each day you fail to comply after its final order. Federal rules may also protect a tenant's satellite dish in areas the tenant controls.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-333a(a): 'No owner of any multiunit residential building shall demand or accept payment, in any form, except as provided in subsection (e) of this section, in exchange for permitting community antenna television service on or within his property or premises, or discriminate in rental charges or the provision of service between tenants who receive such service and those who do not'; (b) owner 'shall permit wiring' when '(1) A tenant of such building requests' service and the company bears the cost, indemnifies and complies with PURA rules; (d) no agreement diminishing tenants' rights to use master or individual antennas; (e) PURA-approved compensation for takings; (h) also applies to trailer and mobile manufactured home parks, nursing homes, hospitals and condominium associations; (i) civil penalty 'of not more than one thousand dollars for each day' after a final order. Federal FCC over-the-air reception devices rule not covered (Rule 21: federal law). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant-Performed Repairs and Maintenance
bodyText: [Optional. Use only if Landlord and Tenant agree that Tenant will do specific work.] Landlord and Tenant agree in good faith that Tenant will perform the following specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling: [list each task specifically]. [Use only for a single-family residence, if agreed: Tenant will also arrange for removal of garbage and other waste, and will supply running water, hot water and heat, as follows: [describe].] [Use for any other dwelling: This agreement does not include any work needed to bring the property into compliance with building and housing codes or to keep it fit and habitable, and does not reduce Landlord's obligations to other tenants.] This agreement is not made to avoid Landlord's legal obligations.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(c): 'The landlord and tenant of a single-family residence may agree in writing that the tenant perform the landlord's duties specified in subdivisions (5) and (6) of subsection (a) and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling, provided the transaction is entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord.' § 47a-7(d): other dwellings — '(1) the agreement of the parties is entered into in good faith; (2) the agreement is in writing; (3) the work is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subdivisions (1) and (2) of subsection (a) of this section; and (4) the agreement does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises.' § 47a-1(11) ('Single-family residence', including attached units with direct street access and no shared heating, hot water or other essential facility). Rule 54 option: a term that exists only if the lease invokes it. Companion: edu-tenant-maintenance-agreements-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Utility Allowance Overage Charges
bodyText: If the lease includes heat or a utility in the rent, you may not charge the tenant extra when usage runs high; a lease term requiring a heat or utilities surcharge is unenforceable. For leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, you also may not make a tenant pay for any utility that is not measured by a separate meter serving only the tenant's unit. If you want the tenant to bear usage costs, put the utility in the tenant's own name on an individual meter.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(10): a rental agreement shall not provide that the tenant 'agrees to pay a heat or utilities surcharge if heat or utilities is included in the rental agreement'; § 47a-4(a)(11), added by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-113, § 1 (effective October 1, 2026, for agreements entered into or renewed on or after that date; compiled text pending); § 47a-4(b) unenforceable. § 16-262e(c) (landlord liable for non-individually-metered utilities). NEEDS_REVIEW: treating an allowance-overage charge as a 'surcharge' is an inference from the word's ordinary meaning (no statutory definition; case law not searched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Splitting of Shared Utility Bills
bodyText: Connecticut does not let you split a shared utility bill among tenants by a formula such as square footage or number of occupants. Utilities supplied to the building are your responsibility unless a meter or separate billing serves only one unit. For leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, a lease term making a tenant pay for utilities that are not measured by a separate meter for their unit is unenforceable. Build shared-utility costs into the rent instead, and remember that recurring charges must be included in the advertised rent.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-262e(c) (owner liable for all electricity, gas, water or heating fuel to the building 'except for any service furnished to any dwelling unit of the building on an individually metered or billed basis for the exclusive use of the occupants of that dwelling unit'); § 47a-4(a)(11), added by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-113, § 1 (effective October 1, 2026, for agreements entered into or renewed on or after that date; compiled text pending) ('agrees to pay for utilities billed to the tenant if no separate meter is used to measure utilities delivered exclusively to such tenant's dwelling unit'); § 16-19ff (electric submetering only in PURA-approved settings; never for common areas); § 47a-7d(a) (recurring charges in advertised rent). Proof of absence of any authorization: CT-utility-apportionment-1 (hits 1, unrelated; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0). NEEDS_REVIEW: for agreements made before October 1, 2026, whether a negotiated RUBS term was enforceable is not settled by statute (§ 16-262e(c) addresses liability to utilities, not tenant reimbursement); case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Learning of a Tenant Utility Shutoff
bodyText: Connecticut has no procedure for a tenant to authorize the utility to warn you before the tenant's own service is shut off. If you need to know, ask the tenant in the lease to show proof of payment on request, and to tell you promptly of any shutoff notice. Connecticut's utility protections run toward tenants: when an account is in your name, the utility must warn the occupants before cutting service for your nonpayment, and a utility will not cut service at your request without the tenant's signed agreement or your notarized statement that the unit is vacant.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-262e(a) (utility must make a good-faith effort to notify occupants and offer service in their names before terminating for the owner's delinquency); § 19a-109 (no termination at the owner's request 'unless the owner or lessor furnishes a statement signed by the lessee agreeing to such termination or a notarized statement signed by the lessor to the effect that the premises are vacant'). Proof of absence: CT-utility-disconnection-notice-authorization-1 (hits 2, unrelated; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0). NEEDS_REVIEW: whether a utility may lawfully share a tenant's account status with a landlord on the tenant's written consent is a utility-privacy question (§ 16-262c(e) privacy provision not read; PURA rules RCSA 16-3 loaded but not searched for consent). Tagged utility-payment-evidence covers proof of payment. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Utilities Billed in Your Name
bodyText: If an electric, gas, telephone or water company or a municipal utility bills you for service to a tenant-occupied building and you fall behind, it must try to warn the tenants (a heating oil or propane supplier instead must keep the building at 65 degrees or give advance notice to you, the state and the local health officer) and let them take service in their own names, without paying your past-due balance or a deposit; if that isn't practical, it can't shut off service but may ask a court to send the rents to a receiver to pay for service. Tenants may deduct what they pay the utility from the rent, and you may not raise the rent to get it back. You are responsible for the electricity, gas, water and heating fuel supplied to the building except service metered or billed to a single unit for its occupants alone, and wilfully failing to provide heat or utilities the lease requires is a crime.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-262e(a): utility 'shall not terminate such service for nonpayment of a delinquent account owed ... by such owner' unless it makes 'a good faith effort to notify the occupants' and provides 'an opportunity, where practicable, for such occupants to receive service in their own names without any liability for the amount due while service was billed directly to the lessor ... and without the necessity for a security deposit'; if not practicable, it 'shall not terminate service ... but may pursue the remedy provided in sections 16-262f and 16-262t'. § 16-262e(c)-(f) (owner liability for non-individually-metered service; occupant deductions 'deemed to be in lieu of an equal amount of rent'; boldface occupant notice; no rent increase to recoup). § 16-262f (receivership of rents for unpaid utility service, § 16-262f(a)); § 16-262t(a) (utility petition). § 19a-214 (a fuel oil or bottled gas supplier to a tenant-occupied residential building must maintain sixty-five degrees Fahrenheit unless it gives three days' notice, ten for automatic delivery, to the owner, the Secretary of the Office of Policy and Management and the local chief health officer). § 19a-109 (class D misdemeanor; no termination at owner's request without lessee consent or notarized vacancy statement). SYNC (Claude Code, 2026-10-09): owner-liability sentence narrowed to the utilities § 16-262e(c) names ('electricity, gas, water or heating fuel'; telephone is not among them), read on cga.ct.gov. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Utility Shutoff Protections
bodyText: Connecticut's utility shutoff rules bind utilities, not landlords, but they affect your tenants and your house accounts. Utilities may not cut service for nonpayment on a Friday, weekend, holiday or the day before one, or when their offices are closed. From November 1 through May 1, electric and gas-heat service may not be cut for a residential customer in financial hardship, and at any time service may not be cut where that would create a life-threatening situation for a household that cannot pay. A utility will not cut service to a rented unit at your request unless the tenant signs an agreement or you swear the unit is vacant, and heating oil or propane suppliers must give notice before stopping deliveries to a tenant-occupied building.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-262c(a) (no cessation 'on any Friday, Saturday, Sunday, legal holiday or day before any legal holiday', outside business hours, or within an hour of closing, with a nonresidential Friday exception); § 16-262c(b)(1): 'From November first to May first, inclusive, no electric distribution company ... shall terminate, deny or refuse to reinstate residential electric service in hardship cases'; gas companies likewise for customers who use gas for heat (with a reinstatement exception). § 16-262e (landlord-billed accounts); § 19a-109 (termination at owner's request); § 19a-214 (fuel oil and bottled gas). § 16-262c read whole, including the life-threatening-situation protection in (b)(1). NEEDS_REVIEW: PURA regulations (RCSA 16-3-100) loaded but not read. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Submetering Utilities
bodyText: Connecticut lets landlords submeter electricity only in limited situations approved by the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority, such as multifamily buildings powered by renewable energy or combined heat and power. An approved submetering entity may charge no more than the utility's rate for that class of customer and may never bill a tenant for common-area use. We found no Connecticut statute authorizing water submetering or prescribing a lease disclosure. Submetered electricity under the state program can be left out of the advertised rent, but any other recurring utility charge you bill must be in it. For leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, a tenant cannot be made to pay for a utility without a separate meter for the unit.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-19ff(a)-(c) (allowed facilities; PURA approval; rate cap; no charge for 'usage for any common areas' or 'other usage not solely for use by such account'; PURA termination protections); § 16-1 (an entity approved to submeter under § 16-19ff is treated as a utility for listed purposes; read in battery context); § 47a-7d(b)(3)(A) (advertised rent may exclude utilities 'submetered pursuant to section 16-19ff'); § 47a-4(a)(11) (Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-113, § 1, effective October 1, 2026; compiled text pending). NEEDS_REVIEW: whether a § 16-19ff submeter is "a separate meter ... used to measure utilities delivered exclusively to such tenant's dwelling unit" under § 47a-4(a)(11) (likely yes, but untested); PURA submetering regulations not loaded; water submetering absence rests on CT-utility-submetering-disclosure-1 (no synthetic positive). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Entering the Unit
bodyText: A Connecticut tenant must not unreasonably refuse to let you in to inspect, make repairs or improvements, provide services, or show the unit to buyers, lenders, new tenants or contractors. You must give reasonable written or oral notice and come at reasonable times. Without the tenant's consent you may enter only in an emergency, during a tenant's extended absence, under a court order, or after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit. If a tenant unreasonably refuses entry, you may go to court for an order or to end the tenancy and recover damages and attorney's fees. An unlawful entry, or repeated demands that harass the tenant, costs you at least one month's rent in damages plus attorney's fees.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16(a)-(d) (consent, emergency, 'reasonable written or oral notice of his intent to enter', 'may enter only at reasonable times', no abuse or harassment; non-consent entry limited to emergency, § 47a-16a, court order, abandonment or surrender); § 47a-16a (extended absence); § 47a-18 (declaratory or injunctive relief or termination, 'actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees'); § 47a-18a ('actual damages not less than an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees'). Bed bug inspections follow § 47a-16 notice (§ 47a-7a(b)(2)(A)). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Smart-Lock Statute
bodyText: Connecticut has no law aimed at smart locks, keypads or app-based entry in rentals. The usual entry rules apply whatever the technology: an electronic entry log does not replace notice and the tenant's consent. If a tenant protected by a court order asks for a lock change, you may meet the duty by reprogramming a digital or electronic lock with a new code.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7b(d): 'A landlord may reprogram a digital or electronic lock with a new entry code to comply with the provisions of this section.' § 47a-16 (entry rules). Proof of absence: CT-smart-access-1 (hits 3; synthetic positive passed; nonsense control 0); data-privacy law for biometric data (e.g., the Connecticut Data Privacy Act, §§ 42-515 et seq.) not searched. Regulations other than the loaded RCSA subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Abandonment and Property Left Behind
bodyText: The property is abandoned only if all occupants have moved out without notice to Landlord and do not intend to return, shown by their removing substantially all of their belongings and either not paying Rent for more than two months or stating that they will not occupy the property after a specified date. If Landlord believes the property is abandoned, Landlord may send each occupant a written notice, by regular mail and by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the occupant's last-known address, as Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11b requires. If the notices are returned undeliverable, or the occupant does not contact Landlord within ten days after receiving the notice, Landlord may retake possession, and this Lease will end. Landlord will inventory any belongings left behind and keep them for at least 30 days, during which the occupant may reclaim them; after that, Landlord may dispose of them. Landlord will not use this procedure if Landlord knows or reasonably should know the property has not been abandoned. Belongings left after a court eviction are handled as Connecticut law provides for summary process executions.
notes: CT: Mirrors Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11b (Taylor's PA decision: abandoned property mirrors the statute, with an education row). § 47a-11b(a) ('“abandonment” means the occupants have vacated the premises without notice to the landlord and do not intend to return, which intention may be evidenced by the removal by the occupants or their agent of substantially all of their possessions and personal effects from the premises and either (1) nonpayment of rent for more than two months or (2) an express statement by the occupants that they do not intend to occupy the premises after a specified date'); § 47a-11b(b) (notice content: belief of abandonment, intent to reenter unless contacted within ten days, intent to remove and rerent, and disposal if not reclaimed within thirty days; 'clear and simple language' with a telephone number and mailing address; reentry 'at which time any rental agreement or lease still in effect shall be deemed to be terminated'); § 47a-11b(c) (no notice to quit or summary process; not available if the landlord 'knows, or reasonably should know, that the occupant has not abandoned'); § 47a-11b(d) (inventory, keep 'for not less than thirty days', then dispose 'as he deems appropriate'); § 47a-11b(e) (no § 47a-43 action if compliant). § 47a-42 (post-judgment removal by state marshal to municipal storage; sale after fifteen days). NEEDS_REVIEW: the notice's required contents are summarized, not reproduced; the builder should generate the § 47a-11b(b) notice as a separate form. Death of a sole occupant: § 47a-11d and tenant-death-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Handling an Abandoned Unit
bodyText: Connecticut gives you a way to retake a unit all the occupants have abandoned without going to court, but only by following the statute exactly: send the notice by both regular and certified mail, wait ten days for a response, then inventory and store anything left for at least 30 days before disposing of it. If you know or should know someone still lives there, you must use the court eviction process instead. A lease cannot give you a faster or easier procedure: Connecticut voids lease terms that waive tenant rights, let you remove a tenant without a court order, or let you seize a tenant's property for rent. After a court eviction, a state marshal removes belongings to the town's storage, and the town may auction what isn't claimed within 15 days.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11b(a)-(e); § 47a-42(a)-(c); § 47a-4(a)(1) (no waiver), (5) ('agrees to permit the landlord to dispossess him without resort to court order'), (6) ('consents to the distraint of his property for rent'), (b). Lockouts: §§ 47a-43, 47a-46 (double damages), § 53a-214 (criminal lockout). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Re-Renting After a Tenant Leaves Early
bodyText: If a tenant abandons the unit before the lease ends, you must make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rent. If you don't, the law treats the lease as ended by you on the date you learned of the abandonment, which cuts off your claim for later rent. When you end a lease for the tenant's breach and sue, your damages include the rent agreed in the lease but unpaid, and you must still take reasonable steps to reduce your loss. Keep records of your advertising and showings.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11a(a): 'If the tenant abandons the dwelling unit, the landlord shall make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental in mitigation of damages'; § 47a-11a(b): 'If the landlord fails to use reasonable efforts to rent the dwelling unit at a fair rental, the rental agreement is deemed to be terminated by the landlord as of the date the landlord has notice of the abandonment.' § 47a-11c: damages 'shall include the amount of rent agreed to by the parties but unpaid by the tenant. The landlord shall be obligated to mitigate damages.' Whether mitigation reduces damages to the rent net of what could have been earned is case law not searched; the row follows the statutory words. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Attorney's Fees in Connecticut
bodyText: Your lease may make a tenant pay your attorney's fees only in a lawsuit for money damages, and then no more than 15% of the judgment. You may not collect fees for work done before a lawsuit is filed, or for a lawyer who is your salaried employee. If your lease lets you recover attorney's fees, the tenant automatically gets the same right if the tenant wins a case based on the lease. Separately, several statutes let a tenant recover attorney's fees, for example for unlawful entry, failure to supply essential services, bed bug violations or advertising rent without required fees, and let you recover fees if a tenant unlawfully refuses entry.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(7): no lease term that the tenant 'agrees to pay the landlord's attorney's fees in excess of fifteen per cent of any judgment against the tenant in any action in which money damages are awarded'. § 42-150aa(a)-(b): holder of a consumer lease with a fee provision 'shall not receive, claim or collect any payment for attorney's fees (1) for an attorney who is a salaried employee of such holder or (2) prior to the commencement of a lawsuit'; fees 'of not more than fifteen per cent of the amount of any judgment'. § 42-150bb: 'an attorney's fee shall be awarded as a matter of law to the consumer who successfully prosecutes or defends an action or a counterclaim based upon the contract or lease'. Statutory fee awards: § 47a-7a(d)(1), § 47a-7d(f), § 47a-13(b), § 47a-18 (landlord, refused entry), § 47a-18a. Clause: default-by-tenant-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText: If you convert a rental building (or mobile home park) to condominiums or another common interest community, each tenant living there before and after the conversion gets strong protections. You must hand-deliver or send by certified mail a conversion notice at least nine months before the tenant must leave, and the tenant has 90 days to buy the unit before it is offered to others on better terms. During the transition period (until nine months after the notice or the end of the lease, whichever is later) you may not raise the rent or evict except for good cause, and the tenant may end the lease on 30 days' notice. Lower-income tenants who move are entitled to a relocation payment of two months' rent or $1,000, whichever is more. A lease clause letting you cancel the lease because of a conversion is unenforceable.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47-283(4)-(5) ('conversion tenant'; 'transition period ... ending nine months after that tenant receives a conversion notice or when his existing lease ends, whichever is later'); § 47-284(a)-(c) (notice at least nine months before required to vacate; contents; hand delivery or certified mail); § 47-285(a) (90-day exclusive offer; no better terms to others for nine months); § 47-286 (tenant may terminate on 30 days' notice); § 47-287(a)-(c) (relocation payment 'two months rent or one thousand dollars, whichever is greater' for households under $21,000 (unmarried) or $25,000 (married) adjusted gross income; waivable by a one-year lease signed after notice); § 47-289 (no increase during transition; afterwards fair and equitable under § 7-148c with 60 days' notice); § 47-290 (eviction during transition only on § 47a-23c(b) grounds); § 47-291 (cancellation-on-conversion clauses unenforceable). NEEDS_REVIEW: §§ 47-288 (registration and DOH notice), 47-292 to 47-294 and the separate condominium-act provisions §§ 47-88b to 47-88d not read; RCSA 47-295 loaded but not read. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Criminal Activity and Serious Nuisance
bodyText: Connecticut lets you skip the 15-day cure notice and go straight to a notice to quit when a tenant commits a "serious nuisance": hurting or credibly threatening another tenant or you, substantial deliberate destruction, conduct posing an immediate serious danger, or using or allowing the unit to be used for prostitution or illegal drug sales. If a household member is evicted for selling drugs there, the tenant may not let that person move back without your consent. If you know your property is being used for prostitution and make no reasonable effort to stop it, you can be prosecuted yourself, and repeated arrests for listed crimes at a property can lead the state to sue to abate it as a public nuisance. Connecticut has no statute on crime-free lease addenda, so use the lease's serious-nuisance clause rather than a separate addendum.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15 (notice exception for 'conduct by the tenant which constitutes a serious nuisance'; definition (A)-(D); burden on tenant 'to show that he had no knowledge' where premises used 'for the illegal sale of drugs'); § 47a-23(a)(1)(G); § 47a-11(g)-(h); § 47a-26h(c); § 47a-31 (conviction for house of ill-fame or gaming: 'the lease ... shall thereupon be void ... notice to quit possession shall not be required'); § 53a-89(a) ('having possession or control of premises which he knows are being used for prostitution purposes, he fails to make reasonable effort to halt or abate such use'), (b) class A misdemeanor, $2,000 fine; § 19a-343(b) ('The state has the exclusive right to bring an action to abate a public nuisance', 'three or more arrests' etc. 'during the three-hundred-sixty-five-day period preceding commencement of the action'). Absence of a crime-free addendum statute: batteries CT-criminal-activity-1 and -2. §§ 19a-343a to 19a-343h (remedies) not read. Municipal nuisance or crime-free ordinances not checked (flag). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Notice Before Ending a Lease for a Breach
bodyText: For unpaid rent, you may serve a notice to quit once the nine-day grace period has passed (four days for a weekly tenancy, plus five more if your online payment system blocked the payment); no separate cure notice is needed. For other material lease or rule violations, or a tenant's breach of health and safety duties, you must first deliver a written notice describing the violation and stating the lease will end on a date at least 15 days after the tenant receives it. If the problem can be fixed by repairs or by paying for the damage and the tenant does so within those 15 days, the lease continues; if substantially the same violation happens again within six months, you can go straight to a notice to quit. A serious nuisance needs no cure notice. Every notice to quit must give at least three days, follow the statutory form and be served by a state marshal or other proper officer.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15a(a) (nine or four days; five-day extension 'if a landlord's online rental payment system prevents the payment of rent when due'); § 47a-15 ('the landlord shall deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the acts or omissions constituting the breach and that the rental agreement shall terminate upon a date not less than fifteen days after receipt of the notice'; cure 'by repair by the tenant or payment of damages'; recurrence 'within six months'; exceptions for nonpayment, serious nuisance and § 47a-11(h)); § 47a-23(a) (grounds; 'at least three days before'), (b) (form), (c) ('An attested copy of such notice shall be served by a proper officer', as amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 25-78). Nuisance: § 47a-32. Protected tenants: § 47a-23c(b). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Drug-Free Addenda and Cannabis Limits
bodyText: No Connecticut statute requires or regulates a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum; the lease's serious-nuisance clause covers illegal drug sales. Be careful with drug rules, though: you may not ban tenants from possessing or using cannabis (you may ban smoking or vaping it), and you may not require a tenant to take a drug test. Those limits do not apply to a roomer renting part of a home, transitional housing or a sober living home, or where federal law or a federal subsidy requires a ban or testing. Federally assisted housing has its own required lease addenda.
notes: CT: Absence: batteries CT-drug-free-housing-addendum-1 and -2 (and CT-criminal-activity-2). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-9a(b) ('a landlord or property manager may not prohibit the possession of cannabis or the consumption of cannabis, except ... may prohibit smoking of cannabis or use of an electronic cannabis device or cannabis vapor product'); (c) ('may not require a tenant to submit to a drug test'); (d)(1)-(4) exceptions ('transitional housing or sober living facility'; federal law or 'monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law'). § 17a-716(a) ('alcohol-free and drug-free residence'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Protections for Victims of Violence
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent to someone, or end or deny their housing, because they are a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or human trafficking, and you may not set different lease terms because someone is a victim of sexual assault or trafficking. Violations can lead to a complaint with the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities and are a criminal misdemeanor. These rules do not apply to renting rooms in a single-family home you live in, or to a two-family home where you live in the other unit. Connecticut has no special eviction defense for victims, but you should not treat violence against a tenant, or a tenant's call for help, as the tenant's lease violation.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46a-64c(a)(1) ('or otherwise make unavailable or deny, a dwelling to any person because of ... status as a victim of domestic violence, status as a victim of sexual assault or status as a victim of trafficking in persons'); (a)(2) (terms, conditions, privileges: lists 'status as a victim of sexual assault or status as a victim of trafficking in persons', not domestic violence; unchanged by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-77 § 27); (b)(1) exemptions; (g) (class D misdemeanor; deleted from October 1, 2026 by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-77, § 27, and from that date a violation is the class D misdemeanor of hate crime by discriminatory housing practice under Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-77, § 16; compiled text pending). Definitions: § 46a-51(25), (27), (28). Absence of an eviction defense: batteries CT-dv-eviction-protection-1 and -2. The last sentence is a drafting judgment that tracks the lead's criminal-activity-ct victim carve-out, not a statute. Municipal fair housing ordinances not checked (flag). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Early Termination by Victims of Violence
bodyText: A tenant who is a victim of family violence or sexual assault and reasonably fears imminent harm may end the lease early, with no penalty or liability for the rest of the term, by giving you written notice at least 30 days before the move-out date. The notice must include a sworn statement and either a police or court record dated within 90 days or a statement from the Office of Victim Services or Office of the Victim Advocate dated within 30 days. The tenant still owes rent due before the termination date and any damage they caused, and any co-tenants remain bound by the lease. Do not charge an early-termination fee in these cases. If you believe the notice does not meet the law's requirements, your remedy is to ask the housing court to block the termination.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11e(a) ('without penalty or liability for the remaining term of the rental agreement by giving written notice to the landlord at least thirty days prior'; family violence as defined in § 46b-38a; sexual assault under §§ 53a-70, 53a-70a, 53a-71, 53a-72a, 53a-72b, 53a-73a, and parent or guardian of a § 53a-70c victim); (b) (sworn statement; police or court record 'dated not more than ninety days prior'; or signed statement from the Office of Victim Services or Office of Victim Advocate 'dated not more than thirty days prior'); (c) (arrears, damage; 'any other tenant' remains liable); (d)-(e) (occupants vacate; summary process); (f) (injunctive relief 'in the housing session of the Superior Court'). § 46b-38a(1)-(2) (family or household member). "Do not charge an early-termination fee" is an inference from 'without penalty'. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Lock Changes for Tenants With Protective Orders
bodyText: If a tenant gives you a copy of a protective or restraining order that orders someone to stay away from the tenant or the tenant's home, and asks you to change the locks, you must tell the tenant within six hours whether you will change them or the tenant may. If you agree to do it, change them within 48 hours and give the tenant a new key; otherwise the tenant may change them and must give you a key within two business days. You may charge only the actual reasonable cost of the lock and locksmith, and you may collect it by suit or from the deposit at move-out, but never by eviction. If the person ordered to stay away is a co-tenant, do not give them a key or let them in without a court order; they still owe rent, and you may not charge the protected tenant extra rent or fees because of the exclusion.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7b(a) ('not later than six hours after receipt of the request'; 'not later than forty-eight hours after the date that the tenant makes such request'); (b) (tenant may change; 'similar or improved quality'; key 'not later than two business days'); (c) ('actual reasonable cost'; 'shall not be the basis for a summary process action'); (d) (digital lock reprogramming); (e) ('the landlord shall not provide a key to such tenant'; excluded tenant 'remains liable'); (f) (no additional rent, deposit or fee); (g) (immunity). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Early Termination
bodyText:
Tenant may terminate this Lease before the end of the Term by providing Landlord at least 30 days' written notice. Tenant will pay an early termination fee equal to one month's Rent ({{monthly_rent}}) or 30% of the remaining Rent due under the Term, whichever is greater, and remains responsible for Rent and other obligations up to the termination date.
I ACKNOWLEDGE THAT THIS CONTRACT CONTAINS A LIQUIDATED DAMAGES PROVISION. Tenant's initials: ________
This early-termination option and fee apply only if this Lease has a fixed Term; a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy ends on the notice that applicable law and this Lease provide, without an early termination fee. Landlord may end this Lease early only under this Lease's Tenant Default and notice provisions, any other section of this Lease that expressly lets Landlord end it, or, if Tenant abandons the property as Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11b defines abandonment, under the Abandonment section of this Lease, and will recover possession only as Connecticut law allows. Nothing in this Section limits any right either party has under applicable law, including a Tenant's right to terminate without penalty due to active military service under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, as a victim of family violence or sexual assault, due to the property becoming uninhabitable through no fault of Tenant, or any other termination right or limitation provided by applicable law.
notes: CT: Overrides `early-termination-ks` on two points (NEEDS_REVIEW). (1) Acknowledgment line: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-150u(a): 'No provision in a written contract for the purchase or lease of goods or services primarily for personal, family or household purposes that provides for the payment of liquidated damages in the event of a breach of the contract shall be enforceable unless (1) the contract contains a statement in boldface type at least twelve points in size immediately following such liquidated damages provision stating “I ACKNOWLEDGE THAT THIS CONTRACT CONTAINS A LIQUIDATED DAMAGES PROVISION”, and (2) the person against whom such provision is to be enforced signs such person's name or writes such person's initials next to such statement.' Whether a dwelling lease is a 'lease of goods or services', and whether an option fee is liquidated damages 'in the event of a breach', are unresolved; the line costs nothing if not required. Builder must render the line in bold, at least 12-point, immediately after the fee sentence. § 42-150u(a) also says it does not 'validate a clause that is a penalty clause'. Move-out fee bar: § 47a-4d(b) ('No landlord may charge a tenant a move-in or move-out fee'); the fee here is the price of the tenant's option to end a fixed Term early, not a charge for the act of moving out, so it is read as outside the bar (DRAFTING JUDGMENT; NEEDS_REVIEW, case law not searched). (2) Abandonment limb: replaces "vacates or abandons the property without notifying Landlord" with the § 47a-11b(a) definition and procedure (abandoned-property-ct); dispossession without court order is barred (§ 47a-4(a)(5)). Victim termination added to the savings sentence (§ 47a-11e). The shared clause's tenant-death limb is dropped because tenant-death-ct governs (§ 47a-11d). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Property Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText: Connecticut does not end a lease automatically when a government takes the property by eminent domain. If the taking destroys the property's value for the purpose it was leased, the court in the condemnation case may cancel the lease, end the rent and divide the award on that basis; otherwise your lease and court decisions control. If you want the lease to end on a taking, say so in the lease, and do not claim the tenant's share of any award unless the lease gives it to you. In the condemnation case, the court may value the whole property and divide the award so the tenant receives the income for the rest of the term, still subject to rent. A tenant forced to move by a state or local project is usually entitled to relocation payments and help from the acquiring agency.
notes: CT: Present in part (the id predates the round 1 check, which found the rule). No statute ends a lease automatically on a taking (batteries CT-eminent-domain-1 and -2), but the last sentence of Conn. Gen. Stat. § 48-22 lets the condemnation court end it: 'When such real estate is subject to a lease under which rent is reserved to the lessor or any other person, if the taking of or damage done to such real estate destroys its value for the purpose for which it was leased, such court may adjudge such lease to be cancelled and the obligation to pay such rent to be terminated by such taking or damage, and shall ascertain the damage to all parties in interest on the basis of such cancellation.' Earlier in § 48-22 (court may 'assess the compensation or damage for the entire title to the real estate, and order that the income during the term for which the particular estate was limited shall belong to the tenant for life or years, subject to any rent, charge or payment to which such estate for life or years was subject, and the obligation to make which still continues'). §§ 8-266 (purpose), 8-267(3) ('Displaced person'), 8-268(a) (moving expenses and payments). The third sentence is drafting advice, not a statute. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Stays After an Eviction Judgment
bodyText: Winning an eviction case does not mean immediate possession. Connecticut automatically stays execution for five days after judgment (not counting Sundays and legal holidays), and an appeal filed in that time delays it further, though the court can require the tenant to pay use and occupancy during the appeal. Except in farm-worker or employee housing, seasonal resort rentals and transient lodging, a tenant evicted for a reason other than nonpayment, nuisance, illegal or immoral use, or occupying without ever having a right to, may ask the court for up to six months to find another home; for nonpayment, the tenant can get up to three months only by paying the full arrearage to the court within five days. The court can require the tenant to keep paying use and occupancy during any stay. No lease term can waive or limit these stays.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-35(a) ('Execution shall be stayed for five days from the date judgment has been rendered, provided any Sunday or legal holiday intervening shall be excluded'), (b); § 47a-35a(a) (use-and-occupancy deposits on appeal); § 47a-36 (exclusions); § 47a-37(a) (grounds excluded; 'if within five days of the date of such judgment the defendant deposits with the clerk of the court the full arrearage'); § 47a-39 ('not exceeding six months'; 'shall not exceed three months in the aggregate if the reason for the judgment against the defendant was nonpayment of rent'; nine-month extension for conversion tenants and mobile home owners; use-and-occupancy conditions); § 47a-41 ('against public policy and void'). No winter moratorium: CT-eviction-hardship-stay-2. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: How a Connecticut Eviction Works
bodyText: You can remove a tenant only through a court "summary process" case; changing the locks, removing belongings or shutting off utilities without a court order can cost you double damages and is a crime. Start with a written notice to quit in the statutory form giving at least three days, served by a state marshal, with the court's right-to-counsel notice attached. After that date passes, a marshal serves the summons and complaint; if the tenant doesn't appear you can move for a default judgment, and if the tenant does appear you can ask the court to order use-and-occupancy payments while the case is pending. Starting January 1, 2027, in nonpayment cases you must give the tenant your latest lease with all addenda and the rent ledger by the first court date. Taking rent you know is overdue waives your right to evict for that missed payment, so accept later payments only "for use and occupancy" with the statutory disclaimer.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a)-(c), (e) (use and occupancy disclaimer: 'Any payments tendered after the date specified to quit possession or occupancy ... will be accepted for use and occupancy only and not for rent, with full reservation of rights to continue with the eviction action'); § 47a-75(f)(2) (attach right-to-counsel notice to notice to quit and to summons and complaint); § 47a-23a(a) ('returnable six days, inclusive, after service'); § 47a-26 (default); § 47a-26b(a), (d) (use and occupancy; judgment 'forthwith' for nonpayment); § 47a-26d; §§ 47a-35 to 47a-42; § 47a-19 ('Acceptance of rent with the knowledge that such rent is overdue constitutes a waiver'); §§ 47a-43, 47a-46 ('double damages'); § 53a-214 (criminal lockout, class C misdemeanor). Practice Book § 13-12B (adopted June 11, 2026, eff. Jan 1, 2027; Conn. L.J. June 23, 2026). § 47a-3a(d) ledger on request. Mediation, § 47a-26a pleading deadlines and § 47a-26c not read; rows do not describe them. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Eviction Records You Cannot Use
bodyText: When an eviction case is withdrawn, dismissed or decided for the tenant, the Judicial Branch removes it from its public website within 30 days. Once removed, no one may disclose that record for any commercial purpose, which the law defines to include tenant screening reports and any use related to screening applicants; the safe course is not to use it in your own decision about whether to rent. Cases you won are not removed and may still be considered, subject to fair housing law. Make sure any screening company you use excludes removed cases, and do not rely on old printouts or third-party copies of them.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-26j(a) ('not more than thirty days after (1) the withdrawal of such action, (2) a judgment of dismissal or nonsuit of such action upon any grounds, or (3) a final disposition of such action that includes a judgment for the defendant, the Judicial Department shall remove from its Internet web site any record or identifying information'); (b) (restoration); (c) (no bulk sale); (d) ('No person or entity shall, for any commercial purpose, disclose any record or identifying information concerning any summary process action that has been removed'; 'commercial purpose' includes '(2) the making of consumer reports containing any such record or information, (3) any use related to screening any prospective tenant'). (d) bars disclosure for a commercial purpose. NEEDS_REVIEW: the row's advice that a landlord not use removed records in its own screening reads the 'any use related to screening' definition broadly (see question). History: Conn. Pub. Act No. 23-207 § 23, applies to actions 'disposed of before or after' July 1, 2024 (revisor's history note to § 47a-26j). § 47a-26h(a) (minor's name). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Good Cause for Older and Disabled Tenants
bodyText: Connecticut has no general just-cause eviction law: you can let a lease end at its term, or end a month-to-month tenancy with a proper notice to quit, without giving a reason, as long as you are not retaliating or discriminating. There is one big exception. In a building or complex with five or more units, or a mobile home park, a tenant who is 62 or older or has a physical or mental disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or who permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or with a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent who has such a disability, can be evicted only for nonpayment, refusing a fair and equitable rent increase, serious lease, rule or health-and-safety violations, a lease made void by the tenant's conviction for keeping the unit as a house of prostitution or lewdness, or for illegal gambling there, permanently removing the unit from the rental market, or your good-faith plan to live in the unit yourself; refusing a rent increase, removal from the market and moving in yourself cannot be used during an existing lease term. In a condominium or other common interest community this applies only to conversion tenants (against whom the move-in ground is unavailable) or where you own five or more units there. Rent increases for these tenants must be fair and equitable and can be challenged before a fair rent commission or in court. You may ask a tenant claiming protection for proof, which the tenant must provide within 30 days.
notes: CT: Rule 41. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23c(a)(1) ('resides in a building or complex consisting of five or more separate dwelling units or who resides in a mobile manufactured home park'; '(A) Sixty-two years of age or older, or whose spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent is sixty-two years of age or older and permanently resides with that tenant, or (B) a person with a physical or mental disability ... or whose spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent is a person with a physical or mental disability who permanently resides with that tenant, but only if such disability can be expected to result in death or to last for a continuous period of at least twelve months'; cross-reference changed from § 46a-64b(12) to (8) by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-11, § 15, eff. Oct 1, 2026, compiled number pending); (a)(2) (common interest communities); (a)(3) ('complex' means two or more buildings on the same or contiguous parcels under the same ownership); (b)(1)(A)-(G) ('No landlord may bring an action of summary process or other action to dispossess a tenant described in subsection (a) of this section except for one or more of the following reasons'); (b)(2)-(3) ('may not be dispossessed for a reason described in subparagraph (B), (F) or (G) ... during the term of any existing rental agreement'); (c) (fair and equitable increases, § 7-148c; fair rent commission or Superior Court); (d) (proof within thirty days; physician or APRN statement for blindness or physical disability). No general just-cause rule: batteries CT-for-cause-eviction-1 to -3. Other cause limits: § 21-80, § 49-31q, § 47-290; retaliation § 47a-20 (other rows). Municipal just-cause ordinances: none known; not checked (flag). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Protected-Tenant Notice for Larger Buildings
bodyText: If your building or complex has five or more units (or you run a mobile home park with five or more homes), you must give every tenant the Department of Housing's notice of the special eviction and rent-increase protections for tenants who are 62 or older or have a long-term disability. Give it when you first rent the unit and again every time the lease is renewed, to every tenant, whether or not you think they qualify. Use the Department's one-page form (DOH Form AM-011), which is available in English and Spanish on its website. Keep a signed or dated copy with the lease as proof you delivered it.
notes: CT: Companion to edu-for-cause-eviction-ct (brief fixed id). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23c(e)(1) ('On and after January 1, 2024, whenever a dwelling unit located in a building or complex consisting of five or more separate dwelling units or in a mobile manufactured home park is rented to, or a rental agreement is entered into or renewed with, a tenant, the landlord of such dwelling unit or such landlord's agent shall provide such tenant with written notice of the provisions of subsections (b) and (c) of this section in a form as described in subdivision (2)'); (e)(2) (Commissioner of Housing's 'one-page, plain-language summary', 'in both English and Spanish', posted on the DOH website); (e)(3) (five more languages by Dec. 1, 2028). Form text read: DOH Form # AM-011 Rev. 12/1/2023 ('you MUST provide a copy of this notice to each tenant at the time of initial rental and at every renewal of the rental agreement'). Keeping proof of delivery is a drafting recommendation, not statutory. Builder: attach AM-011 (EN and ES) when unit count is 5 or more or property is a mobile manufactured home park. No statutory penalty located for failure to give it. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenants When a Rental Is Foreclosed
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to tell tenants that your lender has started a foreclosure, but your tenants keep strong rights if the foreclosure goes through. A new owner who takes the property by foreclosure generally must honor a genuine, arms-length lease for its remaining term and give at least 90 days' written notice to vacate; a month-to-month tenant also gets 90 days. The lease can end earlier only if the new owner sells to a buyer who will live there, still with 90 days' notice, and a Housing Choice Voucher tenant's lease and housing assistance contract carry over. If a foreclosing lender or buyer offers money to get a tenant to leave, the offer must be at least the deposit plus interest, two months' rent or $2,000, whichever is greatest.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-20e(a)-(b) (bona fide tenant; stay of ejectment and summary process until the earlier of the lease expiration or 60 days after title vests, or 30 days for other tenancies, except § 47a-23 or § 47a-31 grounds); § 49-31p(a) ('a notice to vacate to any bona fide tenant not less than ninety days before the effective date of such notice'; 'under any bona fide lease entered into before such date to occupy the premises until the end of the remaining term of the lease, except that a successor in interest may terminate a lease effective on the date of sale of the unit to a purchaser who will occupy the unit as a primary residence'), (b) (bona fide: not mortgagor or mortgagor's child, spouse or parent; arms-length; rent not substantially below market unless subsidized); § 49-31q(a)-(b) (voucher tenants; lease and HAP contract); § 47a-20f ('the greater of (1) the security deposit and interest ... (2) two months' rent, or (3) two thousand dollars'); § 49-22(a)-(b). Absence of a landlord disclosure duty: batteries CT-foreclosure-1 and -2. The 90-day rule applies to foreclosures on federally related mortgage loans or dwellings with return dates on or after July 13, 2011 (§ 49-31p(a)); the row simplifies to "generally". Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Lease Guarantors
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute specific to lease guarantors. A guaranty must be in writing and signed by the guarantor to be enforceable. No statute limits a guarantor to the original lease term, so whether the guarantor is bound for renewals depends on what the guaranty says; if you want coverage for renewals and month-to-month extensions, say so expressly and have the guarantor sign. Do not use a guarantor to collect more up-front money than the security deposit limit allows, since the law does not say whether a deposit taken from a guarantor counts toward that limit.
notes: CT: Absence: batteries CT-guarantor-renewal-1 and -2. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-550(a)(2) ('No civil action may be maintained ... unless the agreement, or a memorandum of the agreement, is made in writing and signed by the party, or the agent of the party, to be charged ... against any person upon any special promise to answer for the debt, default or miscarriage of another'). § 47a-21(a)(11) ('“Security deposit” means any advance rental payment'), (b)(1)-(2) (two months' rent; one month for a tenant 62 or older). The renewal and deposit advice is a drafting judgment. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Waiver of Collection Exemptions
bodyText: Do not put a clause in your lease asking the tenant to waive the homestead exemption or the exemptions that protect household goods, wages and benefits from collection. Connecticut has no law allowing such a waiver, and a lease term that gives up a tenant's statutory rights is unenforceable unless the statute itself says its rights can be waived. Connecticut also forbids lease terms that let you seize a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. If you win a money judgment, collect it through the court's ordinary execution process, subject to the exemptions.
notes: CT: Absence of a waiver authorization: batteries CT-homestead-waiver-1 and -2; Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 52-352a, 52-352b contain no waiver language (§ 52-352b(21) homestead 'to the value of two hundred fifty thousand dollars'; § 52-352a(5) 'Homestead' means owner-occupied primary residence). § 47a-4(a)(1) ('Agrees to waive or forfeit rights or remedies ... under any section of the general statutes or any municipal ordinance unless such section or ordinance expressly states that such rights may be waived'), (a)(6) ('consents to the distraint of his property for rent'), (b) ('unenforceable'). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Moving to Care or Senior Housing
bodyText: Connecticut gives tenants no statutory right to end a lease early because of age, illness, disability or a move to a nursing home, assisted living or senior housing. If a tenant with a disability asks to be released early because of that disability, treat it as a reasonable-accommodation request under fair housing law and consider it seriously. If the tenant simply leaves, you must still make reasonable efforts to re-rent the unit, which limits what you can recover. A month-to-month tenant can always end the tenancy with proper notice.
notes: CT: Absence: batteries CT-infirmity-termination-1 and -2. Reasonable accommodation: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46a-64c(a)(6)(C)(ii) ('a refusal to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services, when such accommodations may be necessary to afford such person equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling'); whether early release is a required accommodation is fact-specific and not stated by statute. Mitigation: § 47a-11a. Death: § 47a-11d (tenant-death-ct). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Landlord's Lien on Tenant Property
bodyText: Connecticut does not give residential landlords a lien on a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent, and a lease clause letting you seize or hold the tenant's property for rent is unenforceable. Keeping a tenant's belongings, or keeping the tenant from reaching them, without a court order is a crime and can make you liable for double damages. To collect unpaid rent, sue and enforce the judgment through the court, where some of the tenant's property is exempt. Belongings left in the unit are handled only through the abandonment procedure, the death-of-tenant procedure or a marshal's removal after an eviction judgment.
notes: CT: Absence: batteries CT-landlord-lien-1 and -4. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(6) ('consents to the distraint of his property for rent'), (b) ('unenforceable'); § 53a-214(a) ('deprives a tenant ... of access to his or her residential or nonresidential unit or his or her possessions'), class C misdemeanor; § 47a-43(a)(3) ('damage to or removal of or detention of the personal property of the possessor'); § 47a-46 (double damages); § 47a-42a (commercial only); §§ 47a-11b, 47a-11d, 47a-42; § 52-352b exemptions. Whether a lease may grant a UCC security interest in household goods was not resolved; the row's advice not to seize property rests on § 47a-4(a)(6) and § 53a-214. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Possession and Money Claims When a Lease Ends
bodyText: In Connecticut an eviction (summary process) case gets you possession of the unit and your court costs; to collect unpaid rent or damages for the tenant's breach, you bring an action for damages (whether it can be joined to the eviction case is a court-practice question). Those damages include the rent agreed to but unpaid, but you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent the unit to reduce your loss. While an eviction case is pending you can ask the court to order the tenant to pay use and occupancy into court each month. A lease clause making the tenant pay your attorney's fees is limited to 15 percent of any money judgment.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-26d (judgment 'that the complainant recover possession or occupancy of the premises with his costs'); § 47a-11c ('If a landlord terminates a residential or commercial tenancy on the grounds that the tenant committed a breach of the rental agreement and the landlord brings an action for damages for the breach, such damages shall include the amount of rent agreed to by the parties but unpaid by the tenant. The landlord shall be obligated to mitigate damages.'); § 47a-11a (abandonment: 'reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental in mitigation of damages'); § 47a-26b (use and occupancy deposits 'in an amount equal to the last agreed-upon rent'); § 47a-34 (other legal remedies not affected); § 47a-4(a)(7) (no term to pay 'the landlord's attorney's fees in excess of fifteen per cent of any judgment against the tenant in any action in which money damages are awarded').
