Battery CT-landlord-remedies-termination-1 (hits 1, PB § 7-10 retention table only; its known positive, § 47a-26b, falls outside the damages pattern and is read directly; synthetic positive passed) found no statute or Practice Book rule joining a rent claim to a summary process complaint; whether a money claim may be joined is a case-law/practice point, case law not searched. Small claims and civil-action limits not stated. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Agreed Damages and Early-Termination Charges
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant statutes do not address a lease term fixing in advance what a tenant owes for breaking the lease. Your damages for a breach include the agreed rent that goes unpaid, and you must try to re-rent the unit to reduce them. A separate consumer-contract law makes an agreed-damages clause in a written consumer contract for goods or services unenforceable unless the tenant signs or initials a boldface acknowledgment right after it; it is not settled whether that law covers a residential lease. A clause that works as a penalty is not enforceable either way, and you may not charge a move-out fee. Get legal advice before adding an agreed-damages or early-termination charge.
notes: CT: NEEDS_REVIEW because coverage of a residential real-property lease by Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-150u is unsettled (case law not searched). § 42-150u(a): 'No provision in a written contract for the purchase or lease of goods or services primarily for personal, family or household purposes that provides for the payment of liquidated damages in the event of a breach of the contract shall be enforceable unless (1) the contract contains a statement in boldface type at least twelve points in size immediately following such liquidated damages provision stating “I ACKNOWLEDGE THAT THIS CONTRACT CONTAINS A LIQUIDATED DAMAGES PROVISION”, and (2) the person against whom such provision is to be enforced signs such person's name or writes such person's initials next to such statement. Nothing in this section shall validate a clause that is a penalty clause or is otherwise invalid under the law of this state.' § 42-421 (early termination liability) governs consumer leases of goods, not dwellings. § 47a-11c (damages 'shall include the amount of rent agreed to by the parties but unpaid'; 'The landlord shall be obligated to mitigate damages'); § 47a-4d(b) ('No landlord may charge a tenant a move-in or move-out fee'). Batteries CT-liquidated-damages-1 (hits 12) and -2 (hits 1) found no Title 47a rule; regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: You may not change the locks, shut off access or remove a tenant's belongings because rent is unpaid, even if the lease says you may. A lease term letting you remove a tenant without a court order is unenforceable in Connecticut. Keeping a tenant out of the unit or away from their belongings without a court order is the crime of criminal lockout, and the tenant can also sue for entry and detainer and recover double damages. To regain possession, serve a notice to quit and bring a summary process (eviction) case; only a state marshal acting on a court execution may remove the tenant.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(5) (a rental agreement shall not provide that the tenant 'agrees to permit the landlord to dispossess him without resort to court order'; § 47a-4(b): 'unenforceable'); § 47a-4(a)(6) (no 'distraint of his property for rent'); § 53a-214(a) (landlord 'is guilty of criminal lockout when, without benefit of a court order, he or she deprives a tenant, as defined in section 47a-1, ... of access to his or her residential or nonresidential unit or his or her possessions'; class C misdemeanor, § 53a-214(b)); § 47a-43(a) (entry and detainer); § 47a-46 ('double damages and his costs'); § 47a-42 (removal by a state marshal under an execution). § 53a-214 is a Penal Code section, outside Title 47a (rule 21: plain statute, outside the landlord-tenant title). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Minors in Eviction Cases
bodyText: You do not need to name a tenant's minor children in a Connecticut eviction case: the judgment binds the named defendants and any minors holding under them. No statute forbids naming a minor, but if you do, the court may order the minor's name struck from the case record and removed from the Judicial Branch website. The safer practice is to name only the adult tenants and occupants.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-26h(a): 'A summary process judgment shall bind (1) the named defendants and any minors holding under them'; 'If a minor, who is or will be bound by a summary process judgment under subdivision (1) of this subsection, is named in a summary process complaint, the court, upon motion of any party or upon its own motion, may order the name of such minor to be stricken from the record of the action and the clerk shall remove or arrange for the removal of such minor's name from the record of the case maintained on the Internet web site of the Judicial Branch.' Batteries CT-minor-tenant-filing-1 (hits 4, positive passed) and -2 (hits 1) found no filing bar and no statute on a minor's capacity to lease; a minor's capacity to contract is a case-law point, case law not searched. "Safer practice" is a drafting judgment. Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Notice to Quit for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Connecticut has no separate pay-or-quit notice. If rent is still unpaid nine days after it is due (four days in a week-to-week tenancy, and five more days in a month when your online payment system kept the tenant from paying), you may end the tenancy by a written notice to quit in the statutory form, served by a state marshal, giving at least three days before the date to move out. Attach the Judicial Branch's one-page right-to-counsel notice to the notice to quit and to the eviction summons and complaint. If you knowingly accept overdue rent, you waive the right to end the tenancy for that late payment; after the notice to quit, accept money only as use and occupancy, using the statutory disclaimer.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15a(a) (nine days; 'in the case of a one-week tenancy, within four days thereafter'; 'extended an additional five days if a landlord's online rental payment system prevents the payment of rent when due'); § 47a-23(a)(1)(D) (ground: 'nonpayment of rent within the grace period ... except this subparagraph shall not apply if the owner or lessor's online rental payment system prevents such payment'); § 47a-23(a) ('at least three days before ... the time specified in the notice'); § 47a-23(b) (form); § 47a-23(c) ('An attested copy of such notice shall be served by a proper officer'); § 47a-23(d) (month-to-month/week-to-week conversion to tenancy at sufferance); § 47a-23(e) (use and occupancy disclaimer, statutory wording); § 47a-19 ('Acceptance of rent with the knowledge that such rent is overdue constitutes a waiver of the landlord's right to terminate the rental agreement for the tenant's failure to pay such rent when it was due'); § 47a-15 (no 15-day cure notice for nonpayment); § 47a-75(f)(2) (attach the right-to-counsel notice to 'a notice to quit delivered to a covered individual' and 'a summons and complaint'; covered individuals are income-eligible tenants, which the landlord cannot know in advance, so the row says attach it). The § 47a-25 waiver covers only termination by lapse of time, not nonpayment. "State marshal" paraphrases 'proper officer' (§ 47a-23(c); case law/practice on who qualifies not searched). Federal notices (CARES Act, subsidized housing) are covered by `edu-cares-act-notice`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Public Nuisance Actions Against a Rental Property
bodyText: Only the state (a state's attorney) can sue to abate a public nuisance at a Connecticut rental, and only after three or more arrests, arrest warrants showing a pattern, or listed municipal citations for listed offenses on the property within the past 365 days. Listed offenses include drug sales, prostitution, gambling, illegal liquor sales, serious assaults, firearm offenses and fire-code violations. The court can order repairs, appoint a receiver to collect the rents, or close the property, and can charge a liable owner the costs, including relocating uninvolved tenants. An owner who cooperates in good-faith efforts to abate the nuisance is exempted as a defendant, and an owner sued can defend by showing reasonable steps that did not succeed, so act promptly on criminal activity, including by eviction where the law allows.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-343(b) ('The state has the exclusive right to bring an action to abate a public nuisance ... including single or multifamily dwellings, provided there have been three or more arrests, the issuance of three or more arrest warrants indicating a pattern of criminal activity and not isolated incidents or the issuance of three or more citations for a violation of a municipal ordinance ... during the three-hundred-sixty-five-day period preceding commencement of the action'); § 19a-343(c) (offense list); § 19a-343a(f) ('the state shall exempt as a defendant any owner ... who cooperates with the state in making bona fide efforts to abate the nuisance or any tenant or resident who has been factually uninvolved'); § 19a-343a(i) (affirmative defense 'that such defendant has taken reasonable steps to abate the public nuisance, but has been unable to abate the nuisance'); § 19a-343b (repair orders, cease and desist, 'appointment of a receiver of rents'); § 19a-343d(e) (receiver may bring summary process); § 19a-343e(a) ('an order to close the real property'); § 19a-343f(a) (relocation costs of uninvolved tenants on a liable defendant). Eviction grounds: § 47a-32 (nuisance 'shall be taken to include, but shall not be limited to, any conduct which interferes substantially with the comfort or safety of other tenants or occupants'), § 47a-15 (serious nuisance), § 47a-31 (lease void on conviction for keeping a house of ill-fame or gaming), § 47a-11(g); the lead's optional clause criminal-activity-ct covers the lease side. Rule 21: Title 19a public health statutes, outside the landlord-tenant title. Municipal nuisance and blight ordinances (§ 47a-56 authorizes them) not reviewed. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Ending a Lease to Move In
bodyText: Connecticut law gives you no right to end a fixed-term lease early because you or a relative want to move in. A lease can end on a condition the lease itself states, so a clause reserving that right is not forbidden, but this library does not offer one: courts may refuse to enforce it on equitable grounds, and it cannot be used during the term against a tenant in a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park who is 62 or older or has a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or who permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability (in a condominium or other common interest community, only conversion tenants or where you own five or more units there). For those tenants, a good-faith plan to make the unit your principal residence is a ground for eviction only after the lease term ends, and never against a conversion tenant in a condominium or other common interest community. Get legal advice before adding your own clause.
notes: CT: NEEDS_REVIEW: enforceability of a reserved early-termination stipulation turns on case law (equitable defenses under § 47a-33a), case law not searched. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a)(1)(B) (lease terminates 'by reason of any expressed stipulation therein'); § 47a-3 (parties may include 'terms and conditions not prohibited by law'); § 47a-4(a) lists no ban on such a term. § 47a-23c(b)(1)(G) ('bona fide intention by the landlord to use such dwelling unit as his principal residence'), (b)(2) (not available against a conversion tenant), (b)(3) ('A tenant may not be dispossessed for a reason described in subparagraph (B), (F) or (G) ... during the term of any existing rental agreement'); § 47a-23c(a)(1) limits protection to tenants in buildings or complexes of five or more units or in mobile manufactured home parks who are 62 or older or disabled, or whose listed relative is and permanently resides with them (cross-reference amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-11, § 15, eff. Oct. 1, 2026); (a)(2) (common interest communities: conversion tenants, or where the landlord owns five or more units). § 47a-20a(a)(2) (not retaliatory if the landlord 'seeks in good faith to recover possession of the dwelling unit for immediate use as his own abode'). Municipal just-cause or fair rent rules not reviewed. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute letting a tenant give a bond to deliver possession at the end of the term, and a lease may not let you confess judgment against the tenant. If a tenant stays after the lease ends, use the notice to quit and summary process (or the end-of-term notice waiver, if the lease has one).
notes: CT: Confirmed absent. Batteries over CGS, Constitution, loaded RCSA, Practice Book and 2026 acts: CT-possession-bond-1 (statutory words "bond ... deliver/surrender/quit possession", hits 0, synthetic positive passed); CT-possession-bond-2 (confession of judgment, hits 5, positive § 47a-4 passed; only bans: § 47a-4(a)(2), § 21-83, § 42-408, Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-16, Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-113); CT-possession-bond-3 (everyday words "guarantee/surety ... vacate/move out", hits 1, § 47a-7b only). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(2) (a rental agreement shall not provide that the tenant 'authorizes the landlord to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement'). See notice-to-quit-waiver-ct (§ 47a-25). Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Late Delivery of Possession
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that says what happens if you cannot hand over the unit on the lease start date. The lease's possession-delay section governs: no rent is owed until you deliver possession, and the tenant may cancel and get back everything paid if the delay runs past 30 days. Other remedies turn on general contract law.
notes: CT: Confirmed absent. Batteries over CGS, Constitution, loaded RCSA, Practice Book and 2026 acts: CT-possession-delay-1 (statutory words "deliver/tender possession" near tenant/lessee, hits 0, synthetic positive passed) and CT-possession-delay-2 (everyday words "fail to deliver/provide possession", "unable to move in", hits 0, synthetic positive passed). Chapter 830 (§§ 47a-1 to 47a-20f) read section-open; none addresses delivery of possession. Lease term: shared clause possession-delay (tagged CT). § 47a-4(a)(3) bars a term exculpating the landlord from liability arising under law; the shared clause does not exculpate. Contract-law remedies are case law, not searched. Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant's Belongings After an Eviction
bodyText: In Connecticut only a state marshal, acting on a summary process execution after any stay ends, may remove an evicted tenant and their belongings. The marshal notifies the town's chief executive officer, serves the execution on the occupants at least 24 hours before the removal, and delivers the belongings to the town's designated storage place; you do not store them yourself. You pay the marshal for the removal and can recover that cost from the tenant. If the tenant does not reclaim the belongings and pay storage within 15 days, the town sells them at auction. A person who stays after the marshal returns and refuses to leave may be arrested for criminal trespass.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-42(a) (execution after any stay; possessions 'may be removed by a state marshal, pursuant to such execution, and delivered to the place of storage designated by the chief executive officer'); § 47a-42(b) (notice to the chief executive officer; marshal 'shall use reasonable efforts to locate and notify the defendant not less than twenty-four hours before'; execution notice of possible arrest 'for criminal trespass in the first degree, in violation of section 53a-107'); § 47a-42(c) ('The plaintiff shall pay the state marshal for such removal in accordance with the provisions of subsection (b) of section 52-261. Such removal and delivery shall be at the expense of the defendant and may be recovered by the plaintiff'; sale 'within fifteen days after such eviction'). § 47a-26h(c): no execution unless valid execution has issued against all occupants (drug-sale exception). Marshal fees: Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-80, § 3 amends § 52-261 effective October 1, 2026 (execution service fee 'not more than one hundred fifty dollars' plus mileage), uncompiled; compiled text pending; amount not stated in the row. Battery CT-post-eviction-property-1 (hits 11) found no Connecticut rule for animals left after an eviction; the row is silent on animals. Abandonment without an eviction is § 47a-11b; a deceased sole occupant's belongings are § 47a-11d. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute letting a tenant end a nonpayment eviction just by paying before judgment, but if you knowingly accept overdue rent, you give up the right to evict for that late payment. After the notice to quit, accept money only as use and occupancy, with the statutory disclaimer. After a nonpayment judgment, the tenant may deposit the full arrearage with the court clerk within five days and then ask for a stay of execution; for nonpayment, stays may total no more than three months and usually require ongoing use and occupancy payments. A lease term waiving the tenant's stay rights is void.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-37(a) ('in the case of a judgment rendered against a defendant for nonpayment of rent, if within five days of the date of such judgment the defendant deposits with the clerk of the court the full arrearage, the defendant may then apply for a stay of execution'); § 47a-39 (stay 'shall not exceed three months in the aggregate if the reason for the judgment against the defendant was nonpayment of rent'; payments for use and occupancy and 'all rent unpaid prior to the period of such stay'); § 47a-35(a) (five-day automatic stay); § 47a-19 (acceptance waiver); § 47a-23(e) (use and occupancy disclaimer); § 47a-41 (waiver of §§ 47a-36 to 47a-40 'against public policy and void'); § 47a-26i (motions to open or extend a stay). Batteries CT-redemption-1 (hits 3, positive passed) and -2 (hits 6) found no pre-judgment redemption right and no rental-assistance pause; equitable relief from forfeiture is case law, not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In a Connecticut eviction case the tenant may raise any legal, equitable or constitutional defense without first paying rent into court. Once the tenant appears, you can move for an order that the tenant deposit use and occupancy (the last agreed rent) with the court each month; if the tenant does not pay as ordered, the court can move quickly to judgment. Separately, a tenant who has complained to the housing code agency at least 21 days earlier can sue you to enforce repairs and must pay each month's rent to the court clerk; while that rent is deposited you cannot evict for nonpayment, and the court can use the money for repairs. Appeals also require use and occupancy payments.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-33a ('the tenant may present any affirmative legal, equitable or constitutional defense that the tenant may have'); § 47a-26b(a) (deposit 'in an amount equal to the last agreed-upon rent'), (d) (failure to pay: order to answer within four days, else 'judgment shall forthwith be entered for the plaintiff'); § 47a-14h(b) (complaint to the code agency 'at least twenty-one days prior'), (h) (deposit 'an amount equal to the last agreed-upon rent'; 'No landlord may maintain an action against a tenant to recover possession for nonpayment of rent if an amount equal to the rent due has been received by the clerk'), (f) (landlord counterclaim to compel tenant compliance with § 47a-11), (g) (funds for repairs); § 47a-35a and § 47a-26e (payments on appeal). Battery CT-rent-into-court-counterclaim-1 (hits 3; its known positive, § 47a-14h, falls outside the summary-process context filter and is read directly; synthetic positive passed) found no mandatory-counterclaim or deposit-to-defend rule. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Retaliation Against Tenants
bodyText: For six months after a tenant in good faith complains to a state or local official or a fair rent commission about a code violation, asks you for repairs, files a housing-code action in court, or organizes or joins a tenants' union (or after a municipal agency issues a notice or order about a violation), you may not bring an eviction, demand a rent increase or cut the tenant's services. You may still evict for nonpayment, illegal use or a lease violation, to move into the unit yourself immediately and in good faith, if the tenant willfully caused the condition, or on a periodic-tenancy termination notice given before the complaint. You may raise rent if the tenant's lack of care caused the condition, or to pass through your prorated share of a substantial tax or operating-cost increase (not tied to fixing the complaint) that you became liable for at least four months before the demand. Separately, a tenant can defend any eviction by showing you brought it solely because the tenant tried to remedy a code violation.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-20 ('A landlord shall not maintain an action or proceeding against a tenant to recover possession of a dwelling unit, demand an increase in rent from the tenant, or decrease the services to which the tenant has been entitled within six months after' the five listed events, including '(5) the tenant has organized or become a member of a tenants' union'); § 47a-20a(a) (possession exceptions: illegal use, lease violation or nonpayment; 'immediate use as his own abode'; wilful tenant-caused condition; periodic-termination notice 'given to the tenant before the tenant's complaint'), (b) (rent-increase exceptions: tenant's lack of due care; tax or operating-cost increase 'not less than four months before the demand' and not exceeding 'the prorated portion of the net increase'), (c) (§ 47a-33 defense preserved); § 47a-33 (affirmative defense where the action was brought 'solely because' the tenant attempted to remedy a violation). Municipal fair rent commissions (§ 7-148b) flagged, not reviewed. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: In Connecticut the only lawful way to remove a tenant is a notice to quit, a summary process judgment and a state marshal's execution. Changing locks, removing doors or belongings, or otherwise keeping a tenant out without a court order is criminal lockout, and the tenant can sue for entry and detainer and recover double damages and costs. If you are required to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity or gas and willfully fail to do so, the tenant may end the lease and recover up to two months' rent or double actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. Entering the unit unlawfully or to harass costs at least one month's rent in damages.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(5), (b); § 53a-214 (criminal lockout, class C misdemeanor; Penal Code, rule 21: outside Title 47a); § 47a-43(a) (entry and detainer, including entry that 'causes damage to the premises or damage to or removal of or detention of the personal property of the possessor'); § 47a-46 ('double damages and his costs'); § 47a-13(a)(3) ('if the failure to supply such service is wilful, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement and recover an amount not more than two months' periodic rent or double the actual damages sustained by him, whichever is greater'), § 47a-13(b) ('reasonable attorney's fees'); § 47a-18a (unlawful entry: 'actual damages not less than an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees'). Note: § 47a-13(a)(3) reads 'not more than two months' periodic rent or double the actual damages ... whichever is greater'; the row paraphrases as the greater of the two. Battery CT-self-help-eviction-1 (hits 1) found no separate landlord utility-shutoff statute; § 16-262e governs utility-company terminations for a landlord's unpaid bills. Companion: edu-no-lockout-ct (lockout for unpaid rent). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Servicemember Tenants
bodyText: Connecticut has no state law letting a servicemember end an apartment or house lease early; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act gives that right and its eviction protections, and the lease cannot take them away. (Connecticut's only state military termination right is for residents of mobile manufactured home parks.) Before a court enters a default judgment against a tenant who has not appeared, you must file an affidavit saying whether the tenant is in military service, and the court may appoint an attorney or stay the case. You may not refuse to rent to someone, or set different terms, because of their status as a veteran.

Batteries over CGS, Constitution, loaded RCSA, Practice Book and 2026 acts: CT-servicemember-rights-1 (statutory words "armed forces/military/national guard/servicemember/active duty" with lease or tenant context, hits 46, synthetic positive passed; none on point), CT-servicemember-rights-2 (hits 3), CT-servicemember-rights-3 (everyday words "orders ... end/break ... lease", hits 3, positive § 21-82 passed). title: No Late-Benefit Eviction Defense
bodyText: Connecticut has no special eviction defense, continuance or stay for a tenant who fell behind because a Social Security or other benefit payment arrived late. The ordinary rules apply: the nine-day grace period, the notice to quit, and, after a nonpayment judgment, a stay of up to three months if the tenant first deposits the full arrearage with the clerk.

Batteries over CGS, Constitution, loaded RCSA, Practice Book and 2026 acts: CT-social-security-defense-1 (statutory words "social security/supplemental security income/benefit/public assistance ... delayed/late/fail to mail", with summary process context, hits 2, synthetic positive passed; off-topic) and CT-social-security-defense-3 (everyday words "late/delayed check/payment/benefit", hits 2, synthetic positive passed; § 47-244 and Conn. title: When a Tenant May End the Lease Early
bodyText: Connecticut lets a tenant end a lease early, whatever the lease says, in these cases: (1) the tenant or a dependent is a victim of family violence or sexual assault and the tenant gives 30 days' written notice with the sworn statement and records the law requires; (2) in a lease of more than one month, you materially breach the lease or a health-and-safety repair duty and do not fix it within 15 days after written notice; (3) you willfully fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service you must supply; (4) fire or other casualty not caused by the tenant substantially impairs the unit, and the tenant moves out and notifies you within 14 days; or (5) you enter unlawfully or repeatedly demand entry to harass the tenant. A tenant ending the lease for family violence or sexual assault still owes rent already past due and any damage they caused.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11e(a)-(c) (family violence: 'for rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after January 1, 2011'; sexual assault: on or after January 1, 2014; 'written notice to the landlord at least thirty days prior'; notice contents in (b); (c) liability for 'any rent arrearage incurred prior to such termination' and 'property damage caused by the tenant'); § 47a-12(a) ('If the breach is not remedied within fifteen days after receipt of the notice, the rental agreement shall terminate'), (b) (not for tenant-caused conditions), (c) ('This section shall apply only to leases in which the term of the tenancy is more than one month'); § 47a-13(a)(3) (wilful failure: terminate and recover 'an amount not more than two months' periodic rent or double the actual damages sustained by him, whichever is greater'), (c) (no right if tenant-caused); § 47a-14(a) (casualty 'unless such damage or destruction is caused by the tenant's negligence or wilful act'; written notice 'within fourteen days thereafter'); § 47a-18a ('terminate the rental agreement'). Fraudulent-inducement rescission and other common-law grounds: case law not searched. Servicemembers: federal law (see edu-servicemember-rights-ct). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: When the Lease Term Ends
bodyText: A Connecticut lease can end on its last day, but if the tenant does not move out you must still serve a notice to quit (unless the lease validly waives it for the end of the term) and win a summary process case; you cannot remove the tenant or their belongings yourself. A tenant who is 62 or older or has a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death (or permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older, or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability), in a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park, cannot be evicted just because the term ended (in a condominium or other common interest community, only conversion tenants or where you own five or more units there): you need one of the reasons the good-cause law lists. A tenant staying on after the term does not by itself create a new lease.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a)(1)(A) (termination 'By lapse of time'); § 47a-25 (written-lease waiver of notice to quit on lapse of time; see notice-to-quit-waiver-ct); § 47a-23c(a)(1) (tenants 62+ or with a disability in 'a building or complex consisting of five or more separate dwelling units' or a mobile manufactured home park), (b)(1) (listed grounds only; lapse of time is not one); § 47a-3d ('Holding over by any lessee, after the expiration of the term of his lease, shall not be evidence of any agreement for a further lease'); § 47a-42 (removal only by a state marshal). Shared clause surrender-end-of-term reserves "unless applicable law entitles Tenant to remain". Its last sentence (property left "may, to the extent permitted by applicable law, be treated as abandoned") has no Connecticut statute behind it for a tenant who surrenders at the end of the term: § 47a-11b covers abandonment without notice and § 47a-42 covers eviction; see question. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenancies Without a Set Term
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant statutes do not recognize a separate residential "tenancy at will". If the rental agreement does not fix a definite term, the tenancy is month to month, or week to week if the tenant pays rent weekly, and an oral lease at a monthly rent with no agreed end date is a lease for one month. Without any agreement on rent, the tenant owes the fair rental value. To end such a tenancy you serve a notice to quit, and the good-cause rules for older and disabled tenants in larger buildings still apply.
notes: CT: Confirmed absent. Batteries over CGS, Constitution, loaded RCSA, Practice Book and 2026 acts: CT-tenancy-at-will-1 ("tenancy/tenant at will", hits 0, synthetic positive passed) and CT-tenancy-at-will-2 (everyday words "sufferance", "without a lease", "no definite term", "absence of agreement", hits 4; its known positive, § 47a-3b, falls outside the pattern and is read directly; synthetic positive passed: §§ 21-82, 47a-23(d), 47a-3c, 49-31p (foreclosure successor; 'a lease terminable at will under state law', federal-style wording)). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3b ('Unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy is month to month, except in the case of a tenant who pays weekly rent, then the tenancy is week to week'); § 47a-3d ('Parol leases of lands or tenements reserving a monthly rent and in which the time of their termination is not agreed upon shall be construed to be leases for one month only'); § 47a-3c (fair rental value absent agreement); § 47a-23 (notice to quit). Common-law tenancy at will: case law not searched. Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: When a Sole Tenant Dies
bodyText: Connecticut does not end a lease automatically when a tenant dies. If the only occupant under a monthly or fixed-term lease dies, and you have followed any lease term allowing termination on the occupant's death, you may use a special procedure instead of an eviction: mail notice (regular and certified) to the emergency contact the tenant named, if any, and to known next of kin; file an affidavit with the Probate Court; at least 30 days later inventory the belongings and file the inventory; wait 15 days before removing them, then store them securely for 15 more days. If they are not reclaimed within the 60 days, the Probate Court certificate can be filed in Superior Court, where it counts as an eviction judgment, and a state marshal removes the belongings to the town's storage. If someone applies to probate the estate within 55 days of your affidavit, you must stop. Following the procedure protects you from a lockout (entry and detainer) claim.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11d(a) ('If the sole occupant of a dwelling unit subject to a monthly lease or a lease for a term has died and the landlord has complied with any provisions of any such lease permitting termination upon the death of the occupant, the landlord may elect to act in accordance with the provisions of this section'; notice 'to the emergency contact designated by the occupant, if any, and to the next of kin of such occupant, if known, at the last-known address both by regular mail, postage prepaid, and by certified mail, return receipt requested'; four required statements; Probate Court telephone number); (b) (affidavit contents); (c) (no notice to quit or summary process needed); (d) (inventory 'On or after thirty days after the date of the filing of the affidavit'; no removal 'until fifteen days after such inventory is filed'; store 'for an additional fifteen days'; certificate 'shall be deemed a judgment of the Superior Court pursuant to chapter 832'; no filing fee; marshal removal); (e) (municipal storage, 15 days, auction, escheat); (f) (probate application 'within fifty-five days of the filing of the affidavit' stops the procedure); (g) ('No action shall be brought under section 47a-43 against a landlord who takes action in accordance with the provisions of this section'). Statute is silent on rent owed by the estate and on deposit refunds to the estate; both are estate and contract law, case law not searched. The lead's optional clause tenant-death-ct supplies the lease termination provision and the emergency-contact designation. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring 30 days' notice to end a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy. You end it by a written notice to quit in the statutory form, served by a state marshal at least three days before the date the tenant must leave, with the Judicial Branch right-to-counsel notice attached; it is safest to set the quit date at the end of a rental period. No statute says how much notice a tenant must give you, so put it in the lease. You may not end the tenancy of a tenant in a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park who is 62 or older or has a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or who permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability, except for a reason the good-cause law lists (in a condominium or other common interest community, only conversion tenants or where you own five or more units there), and for six months after a tenant's good-faith complaint to housing officials, repair request or similar protected act you may not bring an eviction unless a statutory exception applies (for example nonpayment of rent, a good-faith move into the unit as your own home, or a termination notice you gave before the complaint). A rent increase needs written notice of at least one full rental period for a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy (45 days for a longer term).
notes: CT: NEEDS_REVIEW: whether a lapse-of-time notice to quit for a periodic tenancy must name a date at the end of a rental period is case law (not searched); "safest" is a drafting judgment. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a) (notice 'at least three days before the termination of the rental agreement or lease, if any, or before the time specified in the notice'), (b) (form), (c) (service 'by a proper officer'); § 47a-3b (month to month absent a definite term); § 47a-75(f)(2) (attach right-to-counsel notice to a notice to quit); § 47a-23c(a)(1)-(3) (protected tenants; (a)(1) cross-reference amended by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-11, § 15, eff. Oct. 1, 2026), (b)(1) (listed grounds only); § 47a-20 and § 47a-20a(a)(4) (retaliation; exception where 'notice to terminate a periodic tenancy ... was given to the tenant before the tenant's complaint'); § 47a-4e ('not less than forty-five days', 'except in the case of a lease with a term of one month or less, such notice shall be given a number of days equivalent to the length of a full term of such lease'). No statute sets a tenant's notice for a periodic tenancy (chapter 830 read section-open). Municipal ordinances not reviewed. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText: If this Lease is, or continues as, a month-to-month tenancy, Tenant may end it by giving Landlord written notice at least {{m2m_notice_days}} days before the last day of a rental month, and the tenancy will end on that day. Landlord may end a month-to-month tenancy only as Connecticut law allows, by a written notice to quit served by a proper officer, such as a state marshal; when ending it for a reason other than Tenant's nonpayment or other breach, Landlord will set the date to move out at the end of a rental month at least [number of days, not less than 3] days after the notice is served. Landlord will not end the tenancy of a Tenant protected by Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23c except for a reason that statute allows. Rent is due through the date the tenancy ends.
notes: CT: CONSTRAINED_TERM: both notice periods are the landlord's own figures; Connecticut sets no periodic-tenancy notice period other than the notice to quit's 'at least three days before the termination' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a)); the tenant's period reuses the existing builder variable {{m2m_notice_days}} (rule 60); the landlord's period is a hand-filled bracket that may not be set below 3 (drafting judgment: suggest 30). § 47a-23(c) (service 'by a proper officer'; "state marshal" paraphrase); § 47a-23c(b)(1) (protected tenants: listed grounds only; § 47a-23c(a)(1) limits protection to buildings or complexes of five or more units and mobile manufactured home parks). Replaces the triaged out-of-state periodic-notice clauses, whose bases are their own statutes or which omit Connecticut's notice-to-quit and good-cause mechanics. NEEDS_REVIEW: the end-of-month quit date is a drafting judgment pending case-law review of lapse-of-time notices for periodic tenancies (case law not searched); week-to-week tenancies are not addressed (lead to decide whether to add). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Removing a Squatter or Unauthorized Occupant
bodyText: Connecticut has no fast-track for removing squatters or a tenant's guest who will not leave. Someone who never had a right to occupy the unit is removed the same way as a tenant: a notice to quit served by a state marshal (you may address an occupant whose name you do not know as 'John Doe'), then a summary process case and execution. Name and serve every occupant you know of, because an execution cannot be enforced until it has issued against all occupants. Police may treat a person who knows they have no right to be there and refuses an order to leave as a criminal trespasser, but removing anyone yourself without a court order risks a criminal lockout charge if the person turns out to be a tenant.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a)(2) (notice to quit 'when such premises, or any part thereof, is occupied by one who never had a right or privilege to occupy such premises'), (a)(3) (right or privilege terminated), (b) ('the notice for such occupant may be addressed to such occupant as “John Doe”, “Jane Doe” or some other alias'); § 47a-23a(a) (aliased occupants may be named as defendants); § 47a-26h(a) (persons bound), (c) ('no summary process execution shall be issued or enforced unless valid execution has been issued against all occupants of the premises', drug-sale exception); § 53a-107(a)(1) (criminal trespass in the first degree: 'Knowing that such person is not licensed or privileged to do so, such person enters or remains in a building ... after an order to leave or not to enter personally communicated to such person by the owner of the premises or other authorized person'); § 53a-214 (criminal lockout of a 'tenant, as defined in section 47a-1'). Rule 21: Penal Code sections outside Title 47a. Battery CT-unauthorized-occupant-removal-1 (hits 1, positive passed) found no squatter or transient-occupant removal statute. Police practice and when a guest becomes a tenant are case-law points, case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Agreed Ways to Give Notice
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant statutes have no "actual notice" rule and no provision for the parties to agree on an extra notice method such as text messages. Notice of entry may be written or oral, so long as it is reasonable. A lease may say how routine notices are given, but an agreed method can never replace the steps a statute requires, such as service of a notice to quit by a state marshal or the mailings the abandonment and deceased-tenant procedures require.

The general Uniform Electronic Transactions Act is addressed under electronic-signatures. Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Claims Against the Property
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you about a foreclosure, tax proceeding or other claim against the property, and no statute on a tenant recognizing someone else as landlord. Any such duty exists only if the lease creates it. If the property is foreclosed, a bona fide tenant keeps statutory protection against quick removal by the new owner.
notes: CT: Confirmed absent. Batteries over CGS, Constitution, loaded RCSA, Practice Book and 2026 acts: CT-adverse-proceeding-notice-1 ("attorn/attornment", hits 0; Practice Book § 4-2 heading only; synthetic positive passed) and CT-adverse-proceeding-notice-2 (everyday words: tenant shall notify/inform landlord of a proceeding, action, foreclosure or claim, hits 0, synthetic positive passed). Tenant duties (§ 47a-11) include none. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-20e(b) (foreclosure: no summary process against a 'bona fide tenant' until the lease end date or 60 days after title vests, whichever first, or 30 days for other agreements); § 47a-10 (conveyance). Landlord-side foreclosure disclosure is the foreclosure-disclosure topic. Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant statutes say nothing about lease clauses that renew automatically. Two consumer laws regulate automatic renewals in contracts for consumer goods or services, requiring conspicuous disclosure, an annual reminder (since July 1, 2026) and, for contracts longer than 180 days, a written reminder 15 to 60 days before renewal explaining how to cancel, with violations treated as unfair trade practices; it is unsettled whether either applies to a residential lease. This library offers no automatic-renewal clause; a tenant who stays after the term is simply a holdover, and any rent increase still needs 45 days' written notice. If you want an automatic renewal, make it conspicuous and send the reminder, and get legal advice.

title: Other Rules Connecticut Does Not Have
bodyText: Three rules some states have do not exist in Connecticut law. (1) No statute bans renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period or gives a special remedy for it; contract and consumer-protection law apply. (2) No statute makes smoke-alarm compliance inadmissible in an injury case or limits insurers over it. (3) No statute gives a private landlord a special right to end a lease because the rental application was false (state-assisted public housing has its own rule); the lease's application-accuracy section makes a material falsehood a breach.

title: Checked Across the Whole Code
bodyText: We searched all Connecticut statutes, the Constitution, the Practice Book, the 2026 public acts and the loaded regulations for three things landlords ask about. (1) There is no squatter-specific removal procedure; someone who never had a right to occupy is removed by notice to quit and summary process. (2) There is no statewide rental license or registration you must hold to win an eviction; a town may require a nonresident owner to file a residential address, and failing to file is an infraction, not a bar to eviction. (3) Unlike some states, Connecticut does require you to give a written receipt for every cash payment, stating the date, amount and purpose. Towns may have their own registration or licensing rules.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText: Connecticut has not moved its protective-order laws. The lock-change statute still correctly cites restraining orders (section 46b-15), civil protection orders (46b-16a), family violence protective orders (46b-38c), standing criminal protective orders (53a-40e), stalking and sexual-assault protective orders (54-1k) and registered foreign orders (46b-15a). The early-termination statute for sexual-assault victims cites a spousal sexual-assault section 'revised to January 1, 2019' because that section was repealed later that year; the reference is intentional. Quote the definitions in those statutes rather than older guidance.

title: Electronic Leases, Signatures and Notices
bodyText: Connecticut's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lets you and a tenant sign the lease and keep records electronically, but only if both of you have agreed to do business electronically, and a tenant who agrees once may refuse for other transactions. The Act does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of someone's primary residence, so give those on paper as the statutes require (a notice to quit must be served by a state marshal). An electronic record is presumed not received if you know the tenant did not receive it or could not open it.

title: Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that expressly protects a tenant's right to call the police or emergency services or bars a lease penalty for such calls. Do not penalize those calls anyway: the anti-retaliation law protects tenants who contact officials about code violations, and fair housing law forbids refusing to rent to someone because they are a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or trafficking. This library's serious-nuisance clause promises not to treat a request for police or emergency help as a violation.

title: Pre-Suit Dispute Clauses
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute authorizing or regulating lease clauses that require the parties to try informal resolution or mediation before going to court. In the Hartford, New Britain, New Haven, Bridgeport, Waterbury and Stamford-Norwalk judicial districts, housing cases go to the court's housing docket, where housing mediators screen contested cases and can recommend settlements. A lease term that makes a tenant jump through extra steps before using a statutory remedy may be unenforceable, because a lease cannot make a tenant waive rights under the landlord-tenant statutes. This library does not offer a pre-suit clause.

title: No State Insurance Mandate
bodyText: Connecticut law does not require residential landlords to carry liability insurance, and there is no state rental registration tied to insurance. Your lender, condominium association or town may require coverage. A tenant who installs an electric vehicle charging station must carry a general liability policy naming you as an additional insured.

title: Rental Registration and Local Filings
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide landlord registration or rental license. If you do not live in Connecticut, your town may require you to file your current residential address (not a post office box) with the assessor or another office; if you own through a company, the filing gives the residential address of your agent in charge and of each person with day-to-day financial or operational control. Report any change within 21 days. Failing to file is an infraction, and the town may impose civil penalties of up to $500 for a first violation and $1,000 after that; the town may serve code orders at the address on file. Towns may also license short-term rentals and, in buildings of three or more units, require a new certificate of occupancy after each vacancy, so check local ordinances.

title: No Crime-Free Lease Statute
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring or regulating crime-free lease addenda, and none requiring you to give police or child-protection investigators access or information. The rules that do apply limit such terms: eviction for criminal conduct runs through the serious-nuisance and lease-violation grounds, a lease cannot ban lawful cannabis possession (only smoking or vaping it), and fair housing law protects victims of domestic violence. Use this library's optional serious-nuisance clause rather than a separate crime-free addendum.

title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in or treating a blank as a breach. The standardized rental terms summary form that must be the first page of every written lease must be completed, though. Fill in or strike every blank before anyone signs, so the lease cannot be read against you.

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: No Connecticut statute requires you to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and not doing so is not a statutory defense to enforcing it. Several related documents are required: the completed rental terms summary form as the first page of any written lease, signed duplicate walk-through checklists if the tenant asks for a walk-through, the protected-tenant notice for buildings of five or more units, a receipt for every cash payment, and a copy of the tenant's ledger on request. Give each tenant a full signed copy of the lease anyway; it also proves the tenant had notice of your rules.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant statutes never require a tenant to initial a particular lease term, including a longer notice period. If you add an agreed-damages or early-termination charge, a consumer-contract law may require a boldface acknowledgment the tenant signs or initials (whether it covers leases is unsettled). Initials remain good evidence that the tenant saw a key term, such as a waiver of the notice to quit at the end of the term.

title: Lease Length and Formalities
bodyText: Connecticut sets no maximum length for a residential lease, but how the lease is made limits it. An oral lease at a monthly rent with no agreed end date is a lease for one month, and any tenancy without a definite term is month to month (week to week if rent is weekly). An oral lease of one year or less is enforceable once the tenant moves in; a longer lease must be in writing and signed by the party it is enforced against. A lease for more than one year, or one with a renewal or purchase option, binds a buyer or lender only if the lease or a notice of lease is executed, witnessed, acknowledged and recorded on the land records like a deed.

title: Out-of-State Landlords
bodyText: If you are not a Connecticut resident and hold a tenant's security deposit, the security deposit statute requires you to appoint the Connecticut Secretary of the State, in writing, as your attorney to receive service of process in any lawsuit against you. You do not have to name an in-state agent in the lease, and tenants do not withhold tax from rent paid to you. Like every landlord, you must tell the tenant in writing, by the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the person managing the property and the person authorized to receive notices and legal papers, and your town may require you to file your residential address.

title: Extra Terms in Move-Out Notices
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute governing a move-out notice form you ask a tenant to sign, and no required warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain. Keep such a form to the move-out date and forwarding address: a new term in it is only a proposed change the tenant must knowingly agree to, and it cannot waive any right the landlord-tenant statutes give the tenant.

title: Where Connecticut Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Several Connecticut rules depend on what the lease says, and a silent lease takes the default. (1) Rent is due at the unit, at the start of each month, unless the lease says otherwise. (2) You may charge a late charge only if the lease has a valid written late-charge term. (3) The tenant must tell you about an extended absence unless the lease says otherwise. (4) The tenant may use the unit only as a home unless you agree otherwise. (5) If you sell to a good-faith buyer and give the tenant written notice, you are released from later obligations unless the lease says otherwise. (6) A tenant may take on specified repairs only under a written good-faith agreement (in a single-family home, also trash and heat or hot water). (7) A written lease may waive the notice to quit at the end of the term. (8) The deceased-tenant procedure works best when the lease allows termination on the sole occupant's death. (9) In a converted condominium, a one-year lease signed after the conversion notice may waive the tenant's relocation payment after the transition period.

Item (8) is phrased as "works best" because whether the procedure is available absent a lease death-termination term is not settled by the text. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Rules That Depend on Size
bodyText: Connecticut has no general small-landlord exemption; each rule sets its own size test. Good-cause eviction protection for tenants 62 or older or with a disability, and the notice about it, apply in a building or complex of five or more units (a complex counts buildings on the same or adjoining lots under the same owner) or a mobile home park; in a condominium or other common interest community the protection reaches conversion tenants whatever you own, and other tenants only if you own five or more units there. A tenant's right to install an electric vehicle charger phased in by how many units you own in total, and does not apply where there are fewer than five parking spaces. Single-family residences may shift trash and heat duties to the tenant by written agreement. The bed bug statute does not cover single-family unattached units. A town may require a new certificate of occupancy after each vacancy in buildings of three or more units. Fair housing law exempts renting rooms in your own single-family home and units in an owner-occupied two-family house, and allows an owner-occupied building of up to four units to decline families with children.

title: Renter's Insurance Is Unregulated
bodyText: Connecticut neither requires renter's insurance nor limits your ability to require it in the lease, and it sets no rules on which insurer the tenant uses, proof deadlines or force-placed coverage. A lease cannot, however, make the tenant release you from liability the law places on you or indemnify you for it, so an insurance requirement cannot shift your own legal responsibilities to the tenant. Insurers, not landlords, must give renters a notice about flood coverage.

title: Selling or Changing Management of a Rented Property
bodyText: When you sell a rented Connecticut property to a good-faith buyer, you are released from lease obligations for later events only after you give the tenant written notice of the sale, unless the lease says otherwise; a manager is released for events after its management ends. The new owner must give each tenant, when it takes over, the name and address of the manager and of the person authorized to receive notices and legal papers. You must hand over the tenants' security deposits, with interest earned, to the buyer, who becomes liable for returning them; whoever holds a deposit must tell the tenant in writing, within 30 days, the amount and the name and address of the bank holding it. You may show the unit to prospective buyers on reasonable notice at reasonable times. If a lender forecloses, tenants have extra protection from quick removal.

Slice A's security-deposit-on-sale row governs deposit detail. Foreclosure successor notices (§§ 49-31p, 49-31q) are addressed under foreclosure-disclosure. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Which Rentals Connecticut Law Covers
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant chapter covers ordinary residential tenancies, but not: residence in an institution incidental to detention or medical, educational, counseling or religious services; occupancy by a buyer under a contract of sale; fraternity or similar housing; transient hotel or motel stays (under 30 days, unless the room is the occupant's primary residence from the start, and 30 to 89 days if it is not); a condominium owner living in their own unit; or a live-in personal care assistant housed by a person with a disability. An owner renting a lot in a mobile home park is governed by the separate mobile home park law; renting a mobile home itself is covered. Some duties apply only to leases signed or renewed after a set date, such as the 45-day rent-increase notice (October 1, 2024), the walk-through offer (January 1, 2024) and the unmetered-utility rule (October 1, 2026). This library's leases are not designed for any excluded arrangement.

title: Forms Connecticut Law Supplies
bodyText: Connecticut supplies these forms or required wording, which should be used as published: the notice to quit (substantially in the statutory form) and the statutory use-and-occupancy disclaimer; the Department of Housing's rental terms summary form (first page of every written lease from April 1, 2026), preoccupancy walk-through checklist and protected-tenant notice (for buildings of five or more units); the Judicial Branch right-to-counsel notice attached to notices to quit and eviction papers; and, for a lease with an option to buy, the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities fair housing disclosure signed by the tenant-buyer and (for one to four units) the residential condition report. The Department of Housing also publishes optional standardized lease forms; no statutory lease form is mandatory. Statutory wording used as required does not violate the plain-language law.

title: Tenant Portals and Online Payments
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute on tenant portals as such, but several rules limit how you use one. You may not require online or electronic payment as the only way to pay rent or a security deposit; accept at least one paper method such as a check or money order. If your online payment system keeps a tenant from paying on time, the tenant gets five extra days that month before a late charge or a notice to quit for nonpayment. A processing fee may be left out of the advertised rent only if it reflects your actual cost and you offer a no-fee way to pay. A tenant who agreed to sign or receive documents electronically may later refuse further electronic transactions, and eviction, default and cure notices cannot be given through the portal alone.

The right granted by this subsection may not be waived by agreement'); § 1-268(c)(2)(B) (eviction, default and cure notices excluded). Shared clause acceptable-payment-methods-nj (tagged) supplies the lease term; slice A covers late fees and fee transparency. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant Ledgers and Personal Information
bodyText: If a tenant or other occupant asks, you must give them a copy of the ledger (or equivalent accounting) for their unit showing charges, payments and any balance owed or overpaid; the statute sets no fee for it. Give a written receipt for every cash payment showing the date, amount and purpose. Keep applicants' and tenants' personal information, such as Social Security, driver's license and bank account numbers, safe from misuse and destroy it securely when you dispose of it. If you collect Social Security numbers in your business, you must publish or post a privacy protection policy. If computerized personal information is breached, you must notify affected Connecticut residents without unreasonable delay and within 60 days (unless an investigation reasonably shows harm is unlikely), notify the Attorney General no later than the residents, and, if Social Security or taxpayer ID numbers were exposed, offer at least two years of free identity theft prevention services.

Pub. title: Changing Rent or Other Terms
bodyText: You may raise rent only after giving the tenant written notice at least 45 days before the increase takes effect (for a lease of one month or less, notice equal to one full term), and not during a fixed lease term unless the lease itself provides for the increase (see the rent-escalation guidance). A tenant's silence is not agreement to the increase. Connecticut defines rent as all periodic payments due under the lease, so treat a new or higher recurring fee the same way. A new building rule that substantially changes the lease is not valid unless the tenant agrees in writing; other changes need the tenant's agreement. For six months after a tenant's good-faith complaint, repair request or similar protected act you may not demand a rent increase, unless the tenant's household caused the problem through lack of due care or you became liable for a substantial increase in taxes or operating costs (not tied to fixing the complaint) at least four months before the demand, and then only by your prorated share of that increase.
notes: CT: NEEDS_REVIEW: applying § 47a-4e's 45-day notice to recurring fees rests on reading 'rent' through § 47a-1(8) ('“Rent” means all periodic payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement'), which § 47a-1 makes applicable to § 47a-4e (Conn. Pub. Act No. 24-143 added § 47a-4e to the definitions' reach); case law not searched. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4e ('No rent increase for a dwelling unit shall be effective unless the landlord has given the tenant of such dwelling unit written notice of the proposed increase not less than forty-five days before the day on which the increase is proposed to take effect, except in the case of a lease with a term of one month or less, such notice shall be given a number of days equivalent to the length of a full term of such lease. A tenant's failure to respond to such notice shall not constitute the tenant's agreement to such proposed increase. Nothing in this section shall be construed to (1) allow a landlord to increase the rent during the term of a rental agreement'); applicable to agreements entered into, renewed or extended on or after Oct. 1, 2024 (history note); § 47a-9(b) ('If a rule or regulation that would result in a substantial modification of the terms of the rental agreement is adopted after the tenant enters into the rental agreement, such rule or regulation is not valid unless the tenant consents to such rule or regulation in writing'); § 47a-20 and § 47a-20a(b) (retaliation and rent-increase exceptions). § 47a-23c(c) (protected tenants: fair and equitable increases) and municipal fair rent commissions (§ 7-148b) flagged; slice A's rent-increase-notice row covers rent increases in detail. title: No Sunsetting Tenant Laws
bodyText: As of October 9, 2026, none of Connecticut's core landlord-tenant statutes, including the good-cause protection for older and disabled tenants, the security deposit law and the notice-to-quit rules, is scheduled to expire. The 2026 session amended several of them (security-deposit enforcement, screening fees, unmetered utilities and a technical fix to the good-cause law) but repealed none. Check each year's new public acts.

title: Lease Translation
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to translate a lease, even if you negotiate it in another language. The Department of Housing publishes the rental terms summary form, the protected-tenant notice and its model lease forms in English and Spanish, and must add translations of the notice and the lease forms into the five most common languages by December 1, 2028; use the version your tenant reads best. From October 1, 2026, owners of residential buildings with elevators must post the state's English-and-Spanish elevator outage sign near each elevator's call buttons.

title: Service and Assistance Animals in Connecticut
bodyText: Connecticut fair housing law requires you to make reasonable accommodations in your rules for a tenant or household member with a physical, mental or learning disability, which includes allowing a needed service or assistance animal despite a no-pet rule and without pet fees. Connecticut has no separate statute on emotional support animals or the documentation you may request; the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities posts guidance on the differences among service, emotional support and therapy animals and on how a landlord may tell them apart, so follow it. A person with a disability who visits your tenant may bring a service animal at no extra charge, though the animal's owner is liable for any damage it causes. Renting rooms in a home you live in, or a unit in a two-family house where you live in the other unit, is exempt.

title: Criminal Penalties for Refusing a Service Animal
bodyText: Refusing to let a person with a disability, or a person training a service animal, keep a service animal while visiting your tenant's home, charging them a fee other guests do not pay, or intentionally interfering with the animal's use is a crime in Connecticut (a class C misdemeanor). Separately, any violation of the state fair housing law, including refusing a reasonable accommodation for a tenant's assistance animal, is a class D misdemeanor; from October 1, 2026 that penalty is restated as the crime of hate crime by discriminatory housing practice. Owner-occupied rooms and owner-occupied two-family dwellings are exempt from both rules.

title: No Penalty for Misrepresenting an Animal
bodyText: Connecticut has no law making it a crime or civil violation to pass off a pet as a service or emotional support animal, in housing or anywhere else. Online registrations, certificates and vests prove nothing. When the need for an assistance animal is not obvious, evaluate the request as a reasonable accommodation, using the methods the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities describes.

title: Tenant Electric Vehicle Chargers
bodyText: You must approve a tenant's written request to install an electric vehicle charging station at the tenant's own dedicated parking space (an assigned space, garage, carport or exclusive-use spot) if the request meets the statute and your procedural approval process for modifications. The duty applies to leases signed, extended or renewed on or after October 1, 2022 if you own 250 or more units, October 1, 2023 if you own 51 to 249, and October 1, 2024 if you own 50 or fewer. It does not apply if chargers already serve at least 10 percent of designated spaces, parking is not part of the lease, there are fewer than five parking spaces, the property has low-income housing tax credits, or a housing authority manages it. Before work starts the tenant must sign an agreement covering installation and removal, costs, electricity, any sharing with other tenants, liability insurance naming you, a removal bond or deposit withholding, and fixture status if the station is left behind. You need not provide an extra parking space, and the installation must meet all codes, zoning and association rules.

Stat. § 47a-13b(a)(1) ('“dedicated parking space” means a parking space located within a tenant's separate interest or a parking spot that is in a common area, but subject to exclusive use rights of an individual tenant, including, but not limited to, a garage space, carport or parking space that is specifically designated for use by a particular tenant'); (b)(1)-(3) (phase-in: 'two hundred fifty dwelling units or more' Oct. 1, 2022; 'more than fifty dwelling units but less than two hundred fifty' Oct. 1, 2023; 'fifty dwelling units or less' Oct. 1, 2024; request must be one that 'complies with the landlord's procedural approval process for modifications to the property'); (c) (no additional parking space); (d) (compliance with law, zoning, covenants); (e)(1)-(8) (agreement contents, including (6) liability policy naming the landlord 'as a named additional insured' and (7) surety bond or deposit withholding under § 47a-21 and (8) fixture designation); (f)(1)-(5) (exemptions: 10 percent ratio, parking not provided, fewer than five spaces, LIHTC, housing authority under § 8-40). The lead's clause ev-charging-ct implements the agreement terms. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Giving Notice of Parking Rules
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to hand over parking rules before the lease is signed or use a particular heading. A parking rule binds the tenant only if it is reasonable, applies fairly to all tenants, is clear, and the tenant had notice of it when signing the lease or when you adopted it; a new rule that substantially changes the lease needs the tenant's written agreement. If you tow from a lot at a building of five or more units, a condominium or a common interest community, you must also post conspicuous signs at the lot listing the parking rules whose violation can lead to a tow, and you must leave a 72-hour windshield notice before towing a car only because your parking permit has expired.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-9(a) (rule enforceable only if purpose, reasonable relation, fair application, explicitness and '(5) the tenant has notice of the rule or regulation at the time he enters into the rental agreement or when the rule or regulation is adopted'), (b) (substantial modification requires written consent); § 14-145e(a)(2) ('“Residential parking facility” means a parking facility that is located at a multifamily dwelling consisting of five or more units, a condominium or a common interest community'), (g) (not applicable to a parking facility 'at a multifamily dwelling consisting of four or less units'), (c)(4) ('shall also install conspicuous signage that lists the parking rules of such facility which if violated would cause a motor vehicle to be towed'); § 14-145(c)(3) (expired residential parking permit: written notice 'at least seventy-two hours prior to towing'; temporary or visitor permits stating expiry excepted). Battery CT-parking-rules-notice-1 (hits 5) found no pre-lease delivery requirement. Rule 21: Title 14 (motor vehicles) outside Title 47a. See edu-private-towing-ct. title: Towing From Your Property
bodyText: A lease clause alone does not let you tow. In Connecticut you may have a vehicle towed from your property only if it is there without authorization, and you (or your agent) must sign the Department of Motor Vehicles written authorization form, under penalty of false statement, for each tow. At a parking lot or garage at a building of five or more units, a condominium or a common interest community (lots at buildings of four or fewer units are exempt), you must first post conspicuous towing signs at every entrance (with the tow company's contact and fees) and a sign listing the parking rules that lead to towing, at least 48 hours before towing, except for cars blocking access, a fire hydrant, a traffic aisle or an accessible space. You may not fine drivers or boot their cars. Before towing a car only for expired registration you must leave a 14-day windshield notice, and for an expired parking permit at a residential lot a 72-hour notice. You may not take any payment from the tow company, and if you tow improperly you must pay the owner's towing, storage and attorney's fees.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. title: Parking Charges and Advertised Rent

If a tenant must pay a recurring parking charge, or one that is billed monthly unless the tenant opts out, include it in the rent you advertise. A parking charge paid periodically under the lease likely counts as rent under Connecticut's definition (all periodic payments under the lease), so treat it like rent, including giving 45 days' written notice before an increase (one full term for a tenancy of one month or less).

title: Cannabis in Connecticut Rentals
bodyText: You may ban smoking or vaping cannabis anywhere on the property, but you may not ban a tenant from possessing cannabis or using it in other ways, such as edibles. You may not refuse to rent to someone, or treat them differently, because of a past conviction for possessing a small amount of cannabis, and you may not require tenants to take drug tests. These limits do not apply to a roomer renting part of a home, institutional or sober-living housing, or where following them would violate federal law or cost you a federal benefit, such as in federally assisted housing. Separately, unless federal law or federal funding requires otherwise, you may not refuse to rent to, or act against, a tenant solely because they are a qualifying medical-cannabis patient or caregiver (from October 1, 2026, including one qualifying from out of state); that rule has no roomer or sober-living exception. Connecticut lets adults and patients grow a few plants at their primary residence and gives landlords no express power to forbid it; a lease ban on home growing is unsettled.

bodyText: Connecticut has no statute letting a tenant house people displaced by a fire, storm or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none governing hotel guests displaced by a disaster. Your lease's guest terms apply, but consider consenting to temporary stays after a disaster, and apply any limit evenly so it does not fall more heavily on families with children or other protected groups.

title: Firearms and the Lease
bodyText: No Connecticut statute stops a residential lease from restricting firearms, and none protects firearms locked in a car in your parking area. This library offers no firearms clause. If you adopt a firearms rule, it must meet the general test for landlord rules, and you should get legal advice; federal and state criminal laws on carrying and storing firearms apply to tenants regardless of the lease.

title: Guests
bodyText: Connecticut does not regulate lease terms on guests or ban guest fees, apart from fair housing law and the general test for landlord rules. One specific rule: a guest with a disability (or a person training a service animal) may bring a service animal when visiting your tenant, and you may not charge them any fee you do not charge all guests. Your tenant is responsible for guests' conduct and damage, and a guest who moves in becomes an occupant under the lease's occupancy terms.

A rule limiting window units must meet the general test for landlord rules (a safety or property-protection purpose, applied fairly and stated clearly). If you supply air conditioning, you must keep it in good working order, and the tenant must use it reasonably.

title: Plug-In Solar Devices

From October 1, 2026, a small portable solar device (up to 1,200 watts, plugged into an ordinary outlet and not permanently attached) no longer needs the electric company's approval, but it must still meet building and fire codes and local rules, and that law does not override your lease or rules. title: Religious Items on the Entry Door
bodyText: If you rent out a condominium unit, you may not prohibit or interfere with your tenant attaching an object such as a mezuzah to the unit's entry door or door frame for religious reasons. The condominium's bylaws may still bar items that threaten health or safety, block the door, break the law or are obscene, and may limit items to 25 square inches on the frame and 4 square feet on the door. No Connecticut statute protects religious or cultural displays in other rentals, but a ban could raise fair housing concerns, and this library's lease rules leave room for displays the law protects.

title: When Your Rules Are Enforceable
bodyText: A building rule binds your tenant only if all of these are true: its purpose is the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protecting your property from abuse, or fairly sharing services and facilities; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies fairly to all tenants; it is clear enough to tell the tenant what to do; and the tenant had notice of it when signing the lease or when you adopted it. A rule adopted after the lease is signed that substantially changes the lease is not valid unless the tenant agrees in writing. Valid rules become part of the rental agreement, and a material violation can lead to eviction after a written 15-day notice to cure where the breach can be cured.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-9(a)(1)-(5) (enforceability conditions, quoted in substance: '(1) the purpose of the rule or regulation is to promote the convenience, safety or welfare of the tenants in the premises, preserve the landlord's property from abusive use or make a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for all the tenants generally; (2) the rule or regulation is reasonably related to the purpose for which it is adopted; (3) the rule or regulation applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner; (4) the rule or regulation is sufficiently explicit ...; and (5) the tenant has notice of the rule or regulation at the time he enters into the rental agreement or when the rule or regulation is adopted'), (b) ('not valid unless the tenant consents to such rule or regulation in writing'); § 47a-1(9) (rental agreement includes 'valid rules and regulations adopted under section 47a-9'); § 47a-15 (15-day notice; cure for breaches remediable by repair or payment); § 47a-23(a)(1)(C) (ground); § 47a-23c(b)(1)(E) (protected tenants: material noncompliance with rules is a ground).
