title: Smoke From Other Units
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute on smoke drifting between units, and a lease clause making the tenant give up claims against you over drifting smoke is unenforceable to the extent it releases liability the law places on you. Smoking is already banned in passenger elevators, and you may ban smoking (including cannabis smoking and vaping) on the property in the lease. Whether the workplace smoking ban reaches enclosed hallways where your staff work is unsettled. Use the lease's smoking policy rather than a waiver.

title: Snow and Ice
bodyText: You must keep common areas, including shared walks, stairs and parking areas, clean and safe, and you cannot shift that duty to tenants. A written lease term may make a tenant clear snow and ice from areas only that tenant uses, such as the walk and driveway of a single-family home. If your town has adopted the state sidewalk law, the owner or the person in possession and control of land next to a public sidewalk is responsible for ice and snow on it and can be sued for injuries, so say in the lease who clears the public sidewalk and check your town's ordinance for clearing deadlines.

If the rental is in a condominium or other common interest community, the association's rules must treat U.S. flag display consistently with federal law and may not ban owners' state flags or signs about candidates or ballot questions, only regulate their size, place and timing. title: Common Interest Community Notice: Timing
bodyText: If you are the developer (declarant) of a condominium or other common interest community, a successor declarant, or someone renting on the declarant's behalf, you must give the tenant written notice that the unit is in a common interest community before the rental agreement is entered into. The lease's own notice arrives only at signing, so also hand the tenant a separate written notice, and keep proof, before they sign. An individual unit owner renting out a unit has no duty to give this notice, though the association's rules still bind the tenant.

title: Certificates of Occupancy
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to tell a tenant about the unit's certificate of occupancy. But where your town requires one before a building is lived in, letting anyone occupy without it exposes you to a civil penalty of up to $20 a day per unit, for up to 200 days. Some towns also require a new certificate after every vacancy in buildings of three or more units (owner-occupied buildings of three or fewer units are exempt), and collecting rent for a unit rented without one carries the same penalty. Check your town's rules before each new tenancy.

bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to tell a tenant about flood zones or past flooding under an ordinary lease. If the lease gives the tenant an option to buy a one-to-four-unit property, you must give the state's residential condition report before signing, and it asks whether the property is in a flood hazard area. Insurers, not landlords, must tell renters' insurance customers that flood damage needs a separate flood policy. Telling tenants about known flooding is still good practice, and hiding a known defect can create liability under general law.

title: Foreclosure and Your Tenants
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to tell a prospective or current tenant that your property is in foreclosure. If a lender forecloses, a good-faith tenant keeps strong protection: the new owner takes the property subject to a bona fide lease until it ends (unless it sells to a buyer who will live there) and must give at least 90 days' written notice to vacate, eviction cannot start until the lease end date or 60 days after title passes (30 days for tenancies without a qualifying written lease), and any offer of money to leave must be at least the deposit with interest, two months' rent or $2,000, whichever is most. Voucher tenants have additional protection. The new owner also takes over the security deposits.

title: Renting Out a Condominium or CIC Unit
bodyText: If you rent out a unit in a condominium or other common interest community, the association's declaration, bylaws and rules bind your tenant. If your tenant violates them, the association may act against you and directly against the tenant: after notice and a chance to be heard it may fine you, the tenant or both, and if the violation is not fixed within 10 days after it notifies both of you, it may enforce your lease rights itself, including bringing an eviction. Association rules may restrict leasing only to meet mortgage lenders' requirements, and only if notice is recorded on the land records. If you fall behind on common charges, in the association's collection or lien-foreclosure case a court may appoint a receiver to collect the sums you owe while the case is pending.

title: Connecticut's Lead Abatement Duties
bodyText: Besides the federal lead disclosure for pre-1978 housing, Connecticut requires the owner of any dwelling with toxic levels of lead where a child under six lives to remediate it. When such a child lives in the unit, defective lead-painted surfaces (including exterior and common-area surfaces) must be abated, intact lead surfaces need a written lead management plan within 60 days of the inspection results, and you may not avoid abatement by evicting the family. If an inspection finds toxic lead, within two days you must post a warning notice on each entrance to the unit or affected common area, and give residents a summary of the inspection and the state's lead safety information. A child's elevated blood lead level triggers a health department investigation and remediation orders, and evicting a tenant who complains to the code or health agency can be retaliation. Connecticut has no lead-safe certificate you must obtain or attach to the lease, and no state lead notice due at signing or renewal.

title: Rental Terms Summary Form
bodyText: For any written lease you give a tenant on or after April 1, 2026, including a renewal, the first page must be a completed copy of the Department of Housing's Standardized Rental Terms Summary Form, in English and Spanish. The form lists the property address, every tenant, the landlord and the person signing for the landlord, the point of contact for management and maintenance, the lease start and end dates, the total periodic rent, and every other charge the tenant must pay periodically, even one the tenant can opt out of (noting any opt-out). The total rent you show must include all required periodic fees, the same way your advertised rent must. If you provide a written lease without the form, you are liable to the tenant for a civil penalty equal to one month's rent, and the court may also award the tenant reasonable attorney's fees and costs. Download the current form from the Department of Housing website; this library's lease is built to sit behind it.

Such form shall clearly summarize the key terms of a rental agreement, including, but not limited to, the term of the rental agreement, the name of the landlord, the point of contact for property management purposes, the name of each tenant and the total periodic rent determined in accordance with the provisions of subsection (a) of this section. Such summary form shall be published and provided in both English and Spanish'); (d) ('On and after April 1, 2026, no landlord shall provide a written rental agreement to any tenant unless such rental agreement includes, as the first page of such rental agreement, a completed copy of the standardized rental terms summary form'); (a) (periodic fees prorated into rent; default-monthly opt-out fees included); (f) ('liable to the tenant for a civil penalty in an amount equal to one month's rent, and the court may award reasonable attorney's fees and costs'). DOH form text (src/agency/rental-terms-summary-form.pdf.txt, read): fields Premises, Name of Tenant(s), Name of Landlord ('Owner of the property being leased, and the individual signing the lease on behalf of the landlord'), Point of Contact, Lease Term, Total periodic rent, Other Charges ('even if the tenant can opt out of the charge'); instruction 'include as the first page of any new or renewed lease', which the form ties to Conn. Pub. Act No. 25-44, § 9. "Including a renewal" rests on the DOH form's instruction; the statute says 'provide a written rental agreement' (inference that a written renewal is one). Product decision (Taylor, 2026-10-09): education row plus builder flag, not a clause. Builder: require the completed form as page 1 of every written lease and renewal. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Connecticut Disclosure Checklist
bodyText: Before the tenant signs: disclose whether the unit or a contiguous unit you own has bed bugs (not for single-family unattached homes); if you are a condominium or other community's developer, give written notice that the unit is in a common interest community; if the property has a private well, give the state's well-testing information; for pre-1978 housing, give the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet; and for a lease with an option to buy a one-to-four-unit property, give the residential condition report. In the lease: the rental terms summary form as page one, the fire sprinkler notice in 12-point bold where the building must have sprinklers (with the last maintenance and inspection date if the system is operative), any recorded environmental activity and use limitation, and the names and addresses of your manager and agent for notices (by the start of the tenancy). At signing or renewal in buildings of five or more units: the state's protected-tenant notice. After signing but before move-in: offer a walk-through using the state checklist. Within 30 days of receiving a security deposit: tell the tenant the amount and the bank holding it. If you charged a screening fee: give the applicant the report (or how to get it) and the receipt.
notes: CT: Checklist with timing (rule 78). Bed bugs: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7a(c) ('Before renting'), (a)(7) (excludes single-family unattached units). CIC: § 47a-3e ('prior to entering into a rental agreement'; declarant-side only). Well: § 19a-37(d) ('Prior to the ... rental'). Lead: federal (rule 21: 42 U.S.C. § 4852d, 40 C.F.R. part 745), tagged shared clause lead-based-paint. Lease option: § 20-327b(a), (c) (before execution of a 'lease containing a purchase option'); § 20-327h(b) also requires CHRO's fair housing form signed by the purchaser and attached 'at the time of closing' (not listed in the row; closing-stage). In the lease: § 47a-7d(d) (summary form, from April 1, 2026); § 47a-3f(b)-(c) (sprinkler notice, 12-point boldface); § 22a-133o(c)(7) (NAUL incorporation); § 47a-6(a) (names and addresses 'on or before the commencement of the tenancy'). Protected-tenant notice: § 47a-23c(e)(1) ('whenever a dwelling unit located in a building or complex consisting of five or more separate dwelling units ... is rented to, or a rental agreement is entered into or renewed with, a tenant'). Walk-through: § 47a-7c(a) ('upon or after the entry into a rental agreement but prior to the tenant's occupancy'). Deposit bank notice: § 47a-21(h)(4)(A) ('not later than thirty days after the landlord receives a security deposit'). Screening: § 47a-4d(d). Right-to-counsel notice (§ 47a-75(f)) attaches to eviction papers, not the lease. Lead clauses: landlord-identification-ct, sprinkler-notice-ct, cic-notice-ct, bed-bug-disclosure-ct; proposed here: private-well-notice-ct, activity-use-limitation-notice-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: Connecticut has no state rule requiring you to give tenants a copy of, or attach to the lease, a variance from the health or housing code. A local health or code agency that grants a variance may impose its own conditions, so follow the variance's terms.
notes: CT: Confirmed absent. Batteries over CGS, Constitution, loaded RCSA, Practice Book and 2026 acts: CT-sanitary-code-variance-1 (variance near tenant, occupant, rental, unit or lease, context health/sanitary/housing code, hits 0, synthetic positive passed) and CT-sanitary-code-variance-2 (everyday: exemption/waiver/variance from the public health, housing, sanitary or building code, hits 0, synthetic positive passed). The Public Health Code (RCSA title 19-13) was not loaded; local variance practice not reviewed. Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Basis: statute-wide search with terms and hit counts (batteries above).

title: No Sex Offender Registry Notice
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to tell tenants about the state sex offender registry or about registered offenders living nearby, and no lease notice is prescribed. If you screen applicants using registry information, apply your criteria consistently and lawfully.
notes: CT: Confirmed absent. Batteries over CGS, Constitution, loaded RCSA, Practice Book and 2026 acts: CT-sex-offender-disclosure-1 (sex/sexual offender, offender registry with tenant, landlord, lease, rental, dwelling, housing or residence context, hits 12: §§ 8-359a, 22a-66a, 53a-30, 54-253, 54-260, 54-261 and 2026 acts on background checks; none a landlord notice; synthetic positive passed) and CT-sex-offender-occupancy-2 (registered sex offender near reside/occupy/live/lease/rent/within feet, hits 4, none a landlord duty; synthetic positive passed). Screening limits are the tenant-screening topic. Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Basis: statute-wide search with terms and hit counts (batteries above).

title: No Offender Residency Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no state law limiting where registered sex offenders may live, no crime for leasing to two registered offenders who live together, and no occupancy duty for landlords near schools or child care. Any screening or occupancy policy you adopt is governed by fair housing and screening rules.
notes: CT: Confirmed absent. Batteries over CGS, Constitution, loaded RCSA, Practice Book and 2026 acts: CT-sex-offender-occupancy-2 (registered sex/sexual offender near reside/occupy/live/lease/rent or "within ... feet", hits 4: §§ 8-359a (homeless programs; identified by battery, not read), 54-253, 54-260, 54-261; synthetic positive passed) and CT-sex-offender-disclosure-1 (registry terms with housing context, hits 12; synthetic positive passed). CT-sex-offender-occupancy-1 matched "registrant" in licensing statutes (40 hits) and was not relied on. Municipal ordinances not reviewed. Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Basis: statute-wide search with terms and hit counts (batteries above).

title: Lease Layout Rules
bodyText: Connecticut has no general rule on font size or first-page placement for lease disclosures, and no single-family occupancy notice. Three layout rules do apply: the state rental terms summary form must be the first page; the fire sprinkler notice, where required, must be in at least 12-point bold type of one font; and the whole lease must meet the plain-language law's standards, including readable type and bold or otherwise prominent section headings.
notes: CT: Confirmed absent (general font/placement rule). Battery CT-sfr-occupancy-disclosure-1 (font/type "two times/twice/larger than" or "top/first page of the lease", over CGS, Constitution, loaded RCSA, Practice Book and 2026 acts; hits 6: §§ 36a-805, 22-61c, 42-103dd, 51-87a, 53-289a, Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-100; none a lease rule; synthetic positive passed); everyday battery CT-lease-completeness-1 (hits 2) found no lease form rule. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7d(d) ('as the first page of such rental agreement'); § 47a-3f(b)-(c) ('printed in not less than twelve-point boldface type of uniform font'); § 42-152(b)(5), (7) ('type of readable size'; captions 'in boldface type or which otherwise stand out significantly'), (c)(7), (10) (alternate tests: no typeface under eight points; boldface captions at least ten points). Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Lawful Source of Income Protection
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent to someone, set different terms, or advertise a preference because their income comes from a lawful source, which Connecticut defines as Social Security, SSI, housing assistance (including vouchers), child support, alimony or public or state-administered assistance. Statements like "no Section 8" are prohibited. You may deny an applicant whose total income, counting all lawful sources, is insufficient, but apply the same standard to everyone. The rule does not apply to renting rooms in a single-family home you live in or a unit in a two-family house where you live in the other unit. Violations can bring a discrimination complaint and are a crime.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46a-64c(a)(1) (refuse to rent 'because of ... lawful source of income'), (a)(2) (terms, conditions, privileges), (a)(3) (notices, statements, advertisements 'that indicates any preference, limitation, or discrimination based on ... lawful source of income'); § 46a-63(3) ('“Lawful source of income” means income derived from Social Security, supplemental security income, housing assistance, child support, alimony or public or state-administered general assistance'); § 46a-64c(b)(5) ('shall not prohibit the denial of full and equal accommodations solely on the basis of insufficient income'), (b)(1) (owner-occupied exemptions); § 46a-64c(g) (class D misdemeanor), replaced from Oct. 1, 2026 by Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-77, §§ 16, 27 (hate crime by discriminatory housing practice, class D misdemeanor; uncompiled). "Including vouchers" and the "no Section 8" example rest on 'housing assistance' in § 46a-63(3); whether refusing to sign voucher program contracts is discrimination is case law (not searched). Counting all lawful income toward an income standard is a drafting judgment consistent with (b)(5) 'solely on the basis of insufficient income'. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Which Buildings Need the Sprinkler Notice
bodyText: You must include the fire sprinkler notice in the lease if state law, the State Fire Safety Code, the State Fire Prevention Code or another regulation required your building to have a sprinkler system, whether or not one is actually working. By statute this includes any building of more than four stories built for human occupancy, and residential buildings occupied mainly by people 65 or older that have more than four stories, or more than 12 units if built or substantially renovated on or after January 1, 1997; the fire and building codes add many newer multifamily buildings. If you are not sure, ask your local fire marshal or building official, or simply include the notice, stating truthfully whether the building has an operative system and, if so, the last maintenance and inspection date, printed in at least 12-point bold type.
notes: CT: NEEDS_REVIEW: which multifamily buildings the State Fire Safety Code and Fire Prevention Code require to be sprinklered depends on the adopted model codes, whose base text is not in the corpus (only Connecticut amendments are loaded). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3f(b) ('When renting a dwelling unit in a building required to be equipped with a fire sprinkler system pursuant to section 29-315, the State Fire Safety Code, the State Fire Prevention Code or any other statute or regulation, the landlord ... shall include notice in the rental agreement as to the existence or nonexistence of an operative fire sprinkler system in such building'), (c) (last date of maintenance and inspection), 12-point boldface uniform font. § 29-315(a)(1) ('When any building is to be built having more than four stories and is to be used for human occupancy, such building shall have an automatic fire extinguishing system ... on each floor'); (d)(1) (residential buildings 'having more than four stories and occupied primarily by elderly persons', by Jan. 1, 1995; 80 percent of units with a resident 65 or older), (d)(2) (more than twelve living units occupied primarily by elderly persons, permit or substantial renovation on or after Jan. 1, 1997). The DOH model lease describes the trigger as 'a building of more than four stories', narrower than § 47a-3f (lead note on sprinkler-notice-ct). "Simply include the notice" is a drafting judgment: the statute requires a notice of existence or nonexistence, which is harmless to give where not required. Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-58, §§ 2-3 and Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-110, § 2 change fire-code adoption timing and interpretations only (Oct. 1, 2026). Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Illness on the Property
bodyText: You do not have to tell a prospective tenant that a past occupant had a reportable disease, or that the property was suspected to be the site of a death or a felony, and you cannot be sued for not disclosing it. But if a prospective tenant who is making a good-faith offer tells you or your agent in writing that knowing whether the property was the site of a suspected homicide, other felony or suicide matters to their decision, you must answer in writing through your agent, consistent with privacy laws, or have your agent state in writing that you decline to answer. Physical defects are a different matter and are not covered by this rule.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 20-329cc (nonmaterial fact: '(1) The fact that an occupant of real property is or has been infected with a disease on the list of reportable diseases ... or (2) the fact that the property was at any time suspected to have been the site of a death or felony'); § 20-329dd(a) ('not a material fact that must be disclosed in a real estate transaction'), (b) ('No cause of action shall arise against an owner of real estate, the owner's agent or any agent of the transferee for the failure to disclose'); § 20-329ee ('if a purchaser or lessee of real estate, who was in the process of making a bona fide offer, advises an owner of real estate or his or her agent, in writing, that knowledge that the property was at any time suspected to have been the site of a homicide, other felony or a suicide is important to the purchaser's decision to purchase or lease the property, the owner through his or her agent shall report any findings to the purchaser or lessee, in writing subject to and consistent with applicable laws of privacy. If the owner refuses to disclose such information, his or her agent shall so advise the purchaser or lessee in writing'); § 20-329ff. Whether § 20-329ee applies when an owner rents without an agent is not addressed (the duty runs 'through his or her agent'); the row tells the landlord to answer through an agent. Rule 21: Title 20 (real estate licensing chapter) outside Title 47a. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant Rights Statements
bodyText: Connecticut does not require private landlords to hand tenants a general statement of tenant rights. The required notices are the rental terms summary form on page one of the lease and, in buildings of five or more units, the state's protected-tenant notice. Housing authorities must also give each tenant, at the first lease signing and every year, contact information for management, the local health department and the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities, plus the Judicial Branch's guide to landlord and tenant rights.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 8-68f (housing authorities and CHFA as successor owner 'shall, for housing which it owns and operates, (1) provide each of its tenants with a written lease, (2) provide each of its tenants, at the time the tenant signs an initial lease and annually thereafter, with contact information for the management of the housing authority, the local health department and the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities, and a copy of the guidance concerning the rights and responsibilities of landlords and tenants that is posted on the Internet web site of the judicial branch'); § 47a-23c(e) (protected-tenant notice); § 47a-7d(d) (summary form). Battery CT-tenant-rights-statement-1 (statement/summary/notice of tenant rights, 'rights and responsibilities of landlords and tenants', hits 1: § 8-68f; synthetic positive passed) found no private-landlord statement. Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Condominium Conversion and Tenant Purchase Rights
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide rent cap or general just-cause eviction law, so no lease notice about one is required. If you convert a rental building into a condominium or other common interest community, though, tenants have strong rights: at least nine months' written conversion notice before they must leave, an exclusive 90-day right to buy their own unit, a bar on offering it to anyone else on better terms for the next nine months, notice of who later contracts to buy it, the right to end their lease early on 30 days' notice, and, for lower-income tenants who move, a relocation payment.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47-284(a) ('At least nine months before a conversion tenant will be required to vacate a converted unit ... a declarant shall give that tenant a conversion notice'), (b) (contents), (c) (hand delivery or certified mail); § 47-285(a) ('For the first ninety days after giving a conversion notice to a tenant, a declarant shall offer to convey the converted unit occupied by that tenant to that tenant. If a tenant fails to purchase ... the declarant may not offer to dispose of an interest in that converted unit during the following nine months at a price or on terms more favorable'), (c) (notice of the contract purchaser within one month); § 47-286 (terminate 'without penalty' on 'thirty days in advance' notice); § 47-287 (relocation payment: greater of two months' rent or $1,000 for income-qualified tenants). Conversion tenants also have § 47a-23c protections (§ 47a-23c(a)(2)). Mobile manufactured home parks: § 21-70b(a) (park owner intending to 'sell, lease or transfer land used as a mobile manufactured home park' must give written notice to each home owner 'at least forty-five days prior to the proposed sale or lease of the park'); rest of chapter 412 not reviewed. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit
bodyText: Unless your town has opted out, Connecticut zoning must allow at least one accessory apartment (called an accessory dwelling unit from October 1, 2026) as of right on each lot with a single-family home, either attached or in a separate structure. The town may not require the occupants of the main home and the accessory unit to be related or employed by each other, impose a minimum age, require separate utility billing, require more than one parking space, or require periodic permit renewals, though it may prohibit using the unit for short-term or vacation rentals. Renting the unit long term is a normal residential tenancy, subject to all the usual landlord-tenant rules; check your town's zoning regulations and opt-out status before renting.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 8-2o(a)(1) ('at least one accessory apartment shall be allowed as of right on each lot that contains a single-family dwelling'), (a)(2) (attached or detached), (a)(6)(C)-(G) (no requirement of 'more than one parking space', 'a familial, marital or employment relationship between occupants', 'a minimum age for occupants', 'separate billing of utilities', or 'periodic renewals for permits'), (a)(7)(B) (municipality may 'prohibit or limit the use of accessory apartments for short-term rentals or vacation stays'), (c)(2) (no sprinkler requirement beyond the principal dwelling's), (e)-(f) (noncompliant regulations void unless the municipality opted out). Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-7, § 2 (effective Oct. 1, 2026; uncompiled): replaces 'accessory apartment' with 'accessory dwelling unit' throughout and revises design and fee provisions (diffed word-for-word; details not stated in the row). Fair housing: an owner-occupied two-family dwelling exemption (§ 46a-64c(b)(1)(B)) may apply to an attached ADU; whether a detached ADU and main home are 'a dwelling containing living quarters occupied ... by no more than two families' is not settled (not stated in the row). Rule 21: Title 8 zoning statute outside Title 47a; municipal regulations not reviewed. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Rules Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A Connecticut lease cannot take away the tenant's statutory rights if fire or another casualty substantially impairs the unit: no rent while the impairment lasts, the right to move out and end the lease by notice within 14 days, or a proportional rent reduction for a partly usable unit (unless the tenant caused the damage). Nor can the lease relieve you of your duty to try to re-rent the unit at a fair rent when a tenant abandons it or breaches, which limits what you can collect. Lease terms that conflict with these rules are unenforceable.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1) (no term that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forfeit rights or remedies under this chapter ... unless such section or ordinance expressly states that such rights may be waived'), (b) ('unenforceable'); § 47a-14(a)-(b) (casualty: no rent liability while impaired, unless 'caused by the tenant's negligence or wilful act'; written notice 'within fourteen days'; proportional reduction); § 47a-11a (abandonment: 'shall make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental in mitigation of damages'; failure deems the agreement terminated); § 47a-11c ('The landlord shall be obligated to mitigate damages'). Neither § 47a-14 nor the mitigation statutes 'expressly states that such rights may be waived'. NEEDS_REVIEW: whether the landlord's mitigation duty is one of the tenant's 'rights or remedies' within § 47a-4(a)(1) is an inference (case law not searched); § 47a-11a's deemed termination operates regardless of the lease. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Families With Children
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent to, or set different terms for, families with children, and you may not advertise a preference against them. Your occupancy limit must be a reasonable one that applies to every occupant regardless of age and is consistent with state and local occupancy codes. Connecticut requires no lease clause about children. The familial-status rule does not apply to qualifying housing for older persons or to a building of four or fewer units where you live in one of the units.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46a-64c(a)(1)-(3) ('familial status'); (b)(4) ('The provisions of this section with respect to the prohibition of discrimination on the basis of familial status shall not apply to housing for older persons as defined in section 46a-64b or to a unit in a dwelling containing units for no more than four families living independently of each other, if the owner of such dwelling resides in one of the units'); (b)(3) (age protection 'shall not apply to minors'); (c) ('Nothing in this section limits the applicability of any reasonable state statute or municipal ordinance restricting the maximum number of persons permitted to occupy a dwelling'). Definition of familial status (§ 46a-64b) not read; the row does not define it. "Applies to every occupant regardless of age" is a drafting judgment. Lead-hazard duties for children under six: see edu-lead-abatement-ct. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Confession of Judgment
bodyText: A Connecticut lease may not include a clause letting you enter a court judgment against the tenant without a hearing (a confession of judgment or warrant of attorney). Any such clause is unenforceable; you must sue and give the tenant the chance to defend, both for possession and for money.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(2) (a rental agreement shall not provide that the tenant 'authorizes the landlord to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement'), (b) ('unenforceable'); Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-113, § 1 re-enacts § 47a-4 from Oct. 1, 2026 without changing (a)(2). Battery CT-possession-bond-2 (confession of judgment / cognovit / warrant of attorney, hits 5, positive § 47a-4 passed) found parallel bans in § 21-83 and § 42-408 (not read). Practice Book rules on confessed judgments not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act
bodyText: Connecticut's Unfair Trade Practices Act (CUTPA) covers renting and offering to rent residential property, so unfair or deceptive conduct in advertising, leasing or managing a rental can be a CUTPA violation. A tenant who loses money because of it can sue for actual damages, and the court may add punitive damages, attorney's fees and orders to stop the practice; the tenant need not show harm to the public. Some other laws that affect landlords are enforced through CUTPA, such as the rules for safeguarding tenants' Social Security numbers (enforced by the state, not by tenant lawsuits); the ban on rent-setting software is enforced separately under Connecticut's antitrust law. Using unenforceable lease terms, hiding fees or misstating tenants' rights are the kinds of practices that invite CUTPA claims.
notes: CT: NEEDS_REVIEW: CUTPA's application to particular landlord conduct, and to a landlord renting only one or two units, turns on case law (not searched); the examples in the last sentence are drafting judgments. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-110a(4) ('“Trade” and “commerce” means the advertising, the sale or rent or lease, the offering for sale or rent or lease, or the distribution of any services and any property, tangible or intangible, real, personal or mixed'); § 42-110b(a) ('No person shall engage in unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce'); § 42-110g(a) ('Any person who suffers any ascertainable loss of money or property ... may bring an action ... to recover actual damages. Proof of public interest or public injury shall not be required ... The court may, in its discretion, award punitive damages and may provide such equitable relief'); § 47a-4f(b) ('It shall be an unlawful practice in violation of chapter 624 for any person to use a revenue management device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units'); § 47a-4f(c) (enforcement under chapter 624, the Connecticut Antitrust Act, § 35-24 et seq.); § 42-471(e)(1) (violation 'shall constitute an unfair trade practice', but 'the provisions of section 42-110g shall not apply'; § 42-471(e)(2): the Department of Consumer Protection may impose a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation). Fee provisions of § 42-110g (subsection (d)) not quoted. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Protecting a Victim's Information
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring you to keep confidential the sworn statement, police or court records, or protective order a tenant gives you to end the lease early or to get the locks changed after family violence or sexual assault. Treat them as confidential anyway: share them only with staff who need them, never with the person named in the order, and store them securely. The state's address confidentiality program substitute address binds government agencies, not landlords, but honor a tenant's request to use it for mail where you can. Fair housing law forbids refusing to rent because someone is a victim of domestic violence.
notes: CT: Confirmed absent. Batteries over CGS, Constitution, loaded RCSA, Practice Book and 2026 acts: CT-dv-confidentiality-1 (address confidentiality/substitute address/confidential near victim, family violence, sexual assault or stalking, or victim ... confidential ... landlord, hits 18: §§ 46a-60, 54-192h, 54-203, 54-230, 10-221v, 10a-55m, 10a-55n, 46a-13d, 46a-13e, 46b-124a, 46b-489, 46b-490, 52-146k, 54-204, 54-228, 54-240, 54-240a, Conn. Pub. Act No. 26-15; none binds a landlord; synthetic positive passed) and CT-dv-confidentiality-2 (everyday: landlord shall not disclose / keep confidential, hits 1: § 20-325g; synthetic positive passed). Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11e(b) (notice contents); § 47a-7b(a)(3), (e) (copy of order; no key to the restrained tenant); § 54-240h(b) ('the agency shall accept and use the program address'); § 46a-64c(a)(1) ('status as a victim of domestic violence'). Confidential handling is a drafting judgment; § 42-471(a) (safeguarding personal information) may apply to identifiers in the documents. Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Employee Background-Check Mandate
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to run background checks on maintenance staff or property managers who have keys to tenants' units. Control keys carefully and give notice before entry as the law requires; careful hiring and key control also reduce your liability risk.
notes: CT: Confirmed absent. Batteries over CGS, Constitution, loaded RCSA, Practice Book and 2026 acts: CT-employee-screening-1 (background check/criminal history check near apartment, residential building, property manager, landlord or maintenance, hits 0, synthetic positive passed) and CT-employee-screening-2 (everyday: employees/staff with access, entry or keys to units or tenants, hits 0, synthetic positive passed). Entry notice: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16(c) (read section-open). Employer fair-chance hiring limits on criminal-history inquiries (§ 31-51i) were not reviewed. Negligent-hiring liability is case law, not searched. Regulations other than the loaded subtitles not searched.

title: Making the Tenant Pay Eviction Costs
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute aimed at eviction penalty clauses, but it limits what you can shift to the tenant. A lease term making the tenant pay your attorney's fees is unenforceable to the extent it exceeds 15 percent of any money judgment against the tenant. If your lease makes the tenant pay your attorney's fees, a tenant who wins a suit or counterclaim based on the lease is entitled to fees too. You recover court costs with a judgment and may recover the marshal's removal expense from the tenant, but you may not charge a move-out fee, and a flat "eviction fee" or penalty risks being an unenforceable penalty or a disguised fee. Damages for the tenant's breach are the unpaid rent and other actual losses, reduced by your efforts to re-rent.
notes: CT: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(7) (no term that the tenant 'agrees to pay the landlord's attorney's fees in excess of fifteen per cent of any judgment against the tenant in any action in which money damages are awarded'), (b); § 42-150bb ('Whenever any contract or lease entered into on or after October 1, 1979, to which a consumer is a party, provides for the attorney's fee of the commercial party to be paid by the consumer, an attorney's fee shall be awarded as a matter of law to the consumer who successfully prosecutes or defends an action or a counterclaim based upon the contract or lease'; 'commercial party' includes a lessor, 'consumer' a lessee; personal, family or household purposes only); § 47a-26d (judgment for possession 'with his costs'); § 47a-42(c) ('Such removal and delivery shall be at the expense of the defendant and may be recovered by the plaintiff'); § 47a-4d(b) ('No landlord may charge a tenant a move-in or move-out fee'); § 47a-11c (damages; mitigation). Penalty doctrine and characterization of a flat eviction fee: case law, not searched (inference). See edu-liquidated-damages-ct. Rule 21: § 42-150bb is outside Title 47a. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Waivers of Your Legal Liability
bodyText: A Connecticut lease may not say that the tenant releases you from, or limits, any liability the law places on you, or that the tenant will indemnify you for that liability or its costs. Clauses like "Landlord is not liable for any injury or damage" or "Tenant will hold Landlord harmless from all claims" are unenforceable to the extent they reach your own legal responsibility, including your negligence and your repair and code duties. A lease may still make the tenant responsible for damage the tenant or the tenant's household or guests cause.

Pub. Act No. 26-113, § 1 re-enacts § 47a-4 from Oct. 1, 2026 with (a)(3) unchanged. The quoted example clauses are illustrations (double quotes avoided because they are not library text). The lead's pet-policy-ct already narrows the shared pet indemnity for this reason. title: Connecticut Fair Housing Protected Classes
bodyText: In Connecticut you may not refuse to rent, set different terms, steer, misrepresent availability, or advertise a preference based on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, civil union or marital status, age, lawful source of income, familial status, physical, mental or learning disability, status as a veteran, or status as a victim of sexual assault or trafficking; you also may not refuse to rent to someone because they are a victim of domestic violence. Separately, you may not refuse to rent or set different terms because of an applicant's or household member's erased criminal record, unless you rent rooms in a unit you live in or live in a building of four or fewer units. You must also make reasonable accommodations and allow reasonable modifications for disability. Except for sexual orientation and civil union status, which have no owner-occupant exemption, state law exempts renting rooms in a single-family home you live in and a unit in a two-family house where you live in the other unit (and, for families with children only, owner-occupied buildings of up to four units); the federal Fair Housing Act's advertising ban still applies to those landlords. Violations can lead to a complaint with the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities, and discrimination under the main fair housing statutes is also a crime.

title: No Foreign Ownership Restriction
bodyText: Connecticut does not restrict foreign nationals, foreign companies or so-called foreign adversaries from owning or leasing residential property. State law expressly lets any alien, whether or not living in the United States, hold, acquire, lease, inherit and transfer real estate as fully as a native-born citizen. Federal rules (for example, on sanctioned persons) may still apply.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute specifically about charging tenants for fines a town or the state imposes on you. But a lease cannot make a tenant indemnify you for liability the law places on you, so you generally cannot pass on fines for your own code violations, such as failures in repairs, heat or common areas. If a tenant's own violation of the tenant duties (for example, improper trash disposal or damage) caused the fine, you may be able to recover it as damages. A condominium or homeowners association may fine a tenant directly for rule violations after notice and a hearing.

title: Immigration or Citizenship Questions
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant and fair housing statutes do not specifically forbid or require asking an applicant or tenant about immigration or citizenship status. Fair housing law does bar discrimination based on national origin and ancestry, so any such question must be applied the same way to everyone and must not be a pretext. From July 1, 2026, Connecticut's data privacy law also covers anyone who collects or uses 'sensitive data', which includes information revealing citizenship or immigration status: you may collect it only when reasonably necessary, only with the person's clear consent, and you must protect it. Unless a housing program you participate in requires immigration verification, the simplest course is not to ask.

title: Jury Trials and Jury Waivers
bodyText: In Connecticut there is no right to a jury in a summary process (eviction) case, so a lease clause waiving a jury does nothing for getting possession. In other civil cases, such as a suit for unpaid rent or damages over $250, either side may ask for a jury, and the state constitution protects that right. A Connecticut lease may not make the tenant give up rights under any state statute unless that statute expressly allows the waiver; the jury statute allows the parties to agree to a trial by the judge, but it is unsettled whether a waiver signed in a lease before any dispute counts. This library does not offer a jury waiver for Connecticut.

title: Using a Prohibited Lease Term
bodyText: Connecticut has no specific penalty for putting a prohibited term in a lease; the term is simply unenforceable. Other rules still make a sloppy lease costly. If your written lease does not start with the state's standardized rental terms summary form, or you otherwise break that statute's rules, the tenant can recover a civil penalty of one month's rent, and the court may also award attorney's fees. If your lease makes the tenant pay your attorney's fees, a tenant who wins is entitled to fees too. And trying to enforce terms the law forbids could be treated as an unfair or deceptive practice under the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act, with damages and attorney's fees.

title: Plain Language Lease Requirement
bodyText: Connecticut's plain language law covers every residential lease signed by a tenant renting for personal, family or household use, so your lease must be written in plain language. It qualifies in one of two ways. Either it substantially meets the general tests: short sentences and paragraphs, everyday words, 'you' and 'we' or the parties' names, simple active verbs, readable type, ink that contrasts with the paper, bold or prominent section captions, spacing between sections and from the page edges, and clear, coherent organization. Or it fully meets the objective tests: fewer than 22 words per sentence on average and none over 50; fewer than 75 words per paragraph on average and none over 150; fewer than 1.55 syllables per word; no type smaller than 8 points; at least 3/16 inch between paragraphs and 1/2 inch margins; printed section captions in bold of at least 10 points; and lines averaging no more than 65 characters. Wording a statute, regulation, agency or court requires or authorizes, and the legal description of the property, do not count against you. A lease that fails is still enforceable, but the tenant can recover $100 plus up to $100 in attorney's fees, unless you tried in good faith to meet the general tests. A tenant cannot waive these rights. No Connecticut law sets a separate minimum type size for the whole lease, though some notices have their own type rules, such as the fire sprinkler notice.

title: Other Lease Terms the Law Limits
bodyText: The list of banned lease terms is not the only limit on a Connecticut lease. A lease also may not: let you collect rent for a period when you are not meeting your basic repair and code duties; require rent or the security deposit to be paid only by electronic transfer; charge an application fee, move-in fee, move-out fee or any other up-front charge beyond a security deposit, the first month's rent, a key or special-equipment deposit and the capped tenant screening fee; require a security deposit above two months' rent (one month's rent for a tenant 62 or older); shift repairs to the tenant except under a written, good-faith agreement for specified tasks, which outside a single-family home cannot cover work needed to make the unit fit or code-compliant; or set terms that differ because of a protected characteristic. A liquidated damages clause may also need a signed boldface acknowledgment. No Connecticut statute specifically bars charging tenants a home-warranty deductible, but a charge for a repair that is your legal duty runs into the rule against waiving the tenant's statutory rights.

title: Questions About Protected Characteristics
bodyText: Connecticut has no separate law that forbids simply asking an applicant about a protected characteristic, but asking is risky. Fair housing law bars any notice or statement about a rental that shows a preference or limitation based on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, gender identity or expression, marital status, age, lawful source of income, familial status, disability, veteran status or victim status, and an application question can be that kind of statement or evidence of discrimination. From July 1, 2026, Connecticut's data privacy law also covers anyone who collects 'sensitive data', such as race or ethnicity, religion, health or disability, sexual orientation, citizenship or immigration status, status as a crime victim, and Social Security, driver's license and financial account numbers; you may collect it only when reasonably necessary and with the person's clear consent. Ask only what you need to apply your written criteria, such as income, rental history and references. You may ask for proof of age or disability when a law makes it relevant, for example to confirm a tenant's protection from eviction in a building converted to a condominium.

title: No State Owner-Occupancy Rental Limit
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide law limiting rentals of homes in single-family zones to owners who live on the lot. State law instead governs how towns may regulate accessory apartments, though a town may opt out of that law. Check your town's zoning regulations, which may set their own rules for accessory apartments and rentals.

bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide rule requiring you to install covers on steam radiators when a tenant asks, and no required radiator-cover lease rider or notice. title: Voucher Program Inspections
bodyText: Connecticut has no law that lets you turn down a tenant using a housing voucher or other rental assistance because the program will inspect the unit. Refusing to rent because a tenant pays with housing assistance is source-of-income discrimination under state fair housing law (unless you rent a room in your own single-family home or a unit in a two-family home where you live in the other unit); you may deny an applicant only because the applicant's income is insufficient. Treating the program's inspection or paperwork as a reason to refuse is likely to be treated as refusing because of the assistance itself.

title: Protecting Tenant and Applicant Data
bodyText: Connecticut has no landlord-specific law listing what tenant information you may not disclose, but general privacy laws apply to you. You must safeguard documents and files containing someone's personal information (such as Social Security, driver's license, account, passport or alien registration numbers) from misuse by others, and destroy or make them unreadable before you throw them away. If you collect Social Security numbers in your business, you must publish or publicly display a privacy protection policy that protects their confidentiality, prohibits unlawful disclosure and limits access. If computerized data containing a tenant's name with a Social Security, identification, account or similar number is breached, notify each affected Connecticut resident without unreasonable delay and within 60 days, notify the Attorney General, and where Social Security or taxpayer identification numbers were exposed, offer at least two years of free identity theft prevention services. From July 1, 2026, Connecticut's data privacy law also covers anyone who handles 'sensitive data', such as racial or ethnic origin, religion, health or disability, sexual orientation, citizenship or immigration status, status as a crime victim, and Social Security, driver's license, passport and financial account numbers: collect it only when reasonably necessary and with the person's clear consent, keep collection to what you need, and protect it. Share tenant information only as needed to run the tenancy or as the law requires.

title: Screening Applicants in Connecticut
bodyText: Connecticut has no single tenant-screening law, but several rules limit how you screen. Fees: the only applicant charge allowed is a capped tenant screening report fee, and you must give the applicant the report (or how to get it) and the receipt. Criminal records: you may not refuse to rent, set different terms or advertise a limitation because of an erased criminal record, which includes records erased by law, youthful offender records and criminal cases continued for more than 13 months; this does not apply to renting rooms in a unit you live in or a unit in a building of four or fewer units where you live. A person with an erased record may truthfully say the arrest never happened. You also may not refuse to rent because of a past conviction for possessing a small amount of cannabis, and generally may not require a drug test. Connecticut sets no conditional-offer or look-back rule for other convictions, so apply written criteria the same way to everyone. Income: you may turn down an applicant whose income is insufficient, but not because the income comes from housing assistance, Social Security, child support, alimony or public assistance; no statute caps the income-to-rent ratio you may use. Fair housing and data privacy rules also limit what you may ask.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant laws have no section letting a court strike an unconscionable lease term, unlike some states. Courts may still refuse to enforce a grossly unfair term under general contract law, and many one-sided terms are already unenforceable because the lease-terms statute bans them. Separately, in a town with a fair rent commission, a tenant can ask the commission to limit a rent or rent increase that is so excessive as to be harsh and unconscionable.

title: Water Heater Temperature
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide rule setting a maximum water heater temperature or requiring you to reset a unit's water heater before each new tenant moves in. You must supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, unless the hot water comes from equipment in the tenant's exclusive control or from the tenant's own utility connection, and willfully failing to furnish hot water the lease requires is a crime. Setting tank heaters at about 120 degrees Fahrenheit is a common scald-prevention practice; check your town's housing code and the Public Health Code for local standards.

title: No Window Guard Requirement
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide requirement to install window guards or window stops where children live, and no required window-guard notice or lease rider. You must still comply with the building and housing codes that apply to your property, which your town may enforce. Window stops or guards on upper-floor windows are a sensible precaution in units with young children.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Many Connecticut landlord-tenant notices must be written, and a lease cannot replace them with verbal notice. Your notices that must be in writing include: a notice to quit (in the statutory form); a notice of a lease violation that starts the cure period; a rent increase notice at least 45 days ahead (one full term for a tenancy of one month or less); the names and addresses of your manager and agent for notices; notice that you have sold the property to a good-faith buyer, if you want to end your liability for later events; the result of a bed bug inspection within two days; the notice to elderly or disabled tenants in buildings of five or more units about their eviction protections; and, for a developer renting in a common interest community, notice that the unit is in one. A tenant's notice of your failure to make repairs, and a tenant's termination notice for an unremedied breach or as a victim of family violence or sexual assault, must also be written. A tenant may report bed bugs orally or in writing, and you may give reasonable written or oral notice before entering. When in doubt, put it in writing and keep a copy.

title: Payment Methods and Convenience Fees
bodyText: Since January 1, 2025, you may not charge a tenant a convenience fee on a rent payment unless you also accept at least one way of paying rent that carries no convenience fee. So if tenants can pay by card or through a portal that adds a fee, also accept a fee-free method (for example check, money order or a no-fee bank transfer) and list it in the lease. A fee you do pass through is a fee beyond rent: disclose it in the same section of the lease as the rent, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); an undisclosed fee can be recovered by the tenant. Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to accept cash, barring you from requiring electronic payment, or banning card surcharges generally. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not. Rent is payable without demand at the time and place the lease sets; if the lease sets no place, it is payable at the dwelling unit.

Effective January 1, 2025 (R.I. Pub. L. 2024, chs. 308, 309, § 1, per the history line). 'Convenience fee' is not defined in chapter 34-18 (§ 34-18-11 read). Fee disclosure: § 34-18-15(a)(1): 'If there are fees beyond the rent that apply to the rental of a unit, the lease shall disclose those fees in the same section as the rent disclosure and shall indicate that additional fees may apply.'; § 34-18-15(a)(5) (tenant 'may recover any fees paid for the unit that were not disclosed as required'). title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on setting rents with algorithmic or revenue-management pricing software, and none on sharing rent or occupancy data with other landlords; no 2025 or 2026 act adds one. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not. Rhode Island's general antitrust act still applies: every contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade is unlawful (R.I. Gen. Laws § 6-36-4). Whether using a shared pricing tool with competing landlords amounts to such an agreement is a question for case law and federal antitrust law, which this library does not cover; take advice before adopting one.

title: No Application Fees; Background and Credit Check Costs
bodyText: Since January 1, 2024, neither you nor your broker, property manager or anyone acting for you may require or demand that a prospective tenant pay a rental application fee. You may require an official state criminal background check (from the BCI at the Department of Attorney General, the state police, or the local police department where the applicant lives) and a credit check, with these limits: if the applicant supplies a background check or credit report issued within 90 days of the application, you may not charge for one; if not, you may charge no more than the actual cost of obtaining it, and you must give the applicant a copy of any report you charged for. The section allows a charge only for those two reports, so don't charge for any other screening product (for example a private eviction-history search) or bundle a processing margin into the cost. You may always get your own report at your own expense. Rhode Island has no other application-fee rule, such as a refund rule or a fee cap formula. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.

Effective January 1, 2024 (R.I. Pub. L. 2023, chs. 319, 320, § 1). The section states no penalty of its own; remedies outside chapter 34-18 not searched. title: No Statutory Order for Applying Payments
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute fixing the order in which you apply a tenant's payments, so the lease's order controls (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). Applying each payment to rent first is the safer choice: Rhode Island's nonpayment eviction and cure rules turn on unpaid rent, not unpaid fees. Accepting a partial payment of rent does not waive the balance due. But accepting rent while knowing of a default, or accepting performance that differs from the lease, waives your right to end the tenancy for that breach unless you give the tenant written notice within ten days; you keep your other remedies for the default.

However, acceptance of partial payment of rent shall not constitute a waiver of the balance due. Acceptance does not waive the landlord’s right to seek remedies for the default.' Rent is 'the payment or consideration that a tenant pays to a landlord for the use of the premises' (§ 34-18-11(13), renumbered (16) by R.I. Pub. title: Collection Fees
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute authorizes you to add a collection-agency fee to a tenant's unpaid rent or damages (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). If you refer the debt to a collection agency, Rhode Island's debt-collection law bars the agency from collecting any interest, fee, charge or expense on top of the debt unless the agreement creating the debt expressly authorizes it or the law permits it, so without a lease term no collection fee can be collected at all. (You, collecting your own debt in your own name, and an agent who collects only for landlords are outside that law's definition of debt collector.) What the landlord-tenant act itself lets you recover: after the tenancy ends, use-and-occupation, actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees; in a nonpayment case, attorney's fees only if the tenant received a demand notice in the prior six months and the nonpayment was willful. A lease term making the tenant pay your attorney's fees beyond what the act allows is unenforceable, and knowingly using one exposes you to the tenant's actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. Take advice before adding a collection-fee term.

title: What You May Collect Before Move-In
bodyText: Rhode Island has no single list of what you may collect before a tenancy starts; several rules combine. A security deposit, however you label it (damage, pet or any other deposit, refundable or not), may not exceed one month's periodic rent in total. A furnished apartment whose furniture has a replacement value of $5,000 or more when the lease is signed may also carry a separate furniture deposit of up to one month's rent. You may not charge an application fee; you may pass on only the actual cost of an official state criminal background check or credit report the applicant doesn't supply. Any other fee beyond rent must be listed in the rent section of the lease with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it. No statute bars a move-in fee as such (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). The act treats prepaid rent separately from the security deposit, so first month's rent is not part of the deposit limit; see the last-month's-rent row before collecting more rent in advance.

(also §§ 34-18-29(a)(1), 34-18-33(b)); the definition of security deposit is a deposit 'against physical damages to the tenant’s dwelling unit' (§ 34-18-11(16), renumbered (19) by R.I. Pub. title: Disclosing Fees Beyond Rent
bodyText: If any fee beyond rent applies to renting the unit, the lease must list those fees in the same section as the rent and must say that additional fees may apply. With no written lease, give the tenant a written list of every fee beyond rent. Any change in required fees must be disclosed in writing at least 30 days before it takes effect; that sentence sits in the no-written-lease paragraph, but follow it for every tenancy. If you don't disclose a fee as required, the tenant may recover the undisclosed fees paid. The placement rule does not apply where the tenant or unit receives a state or federal subsidy that requires a different lease format. The same subsection requires the lease to say which utilities are in the rent and to state any renters-insurance requirement (covered in their own rows). Rhode Island has no all-in pricing rule for rental advertising and no first-page fee box. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.

This requirement does not apply whenever the tenant or unit are receiving state or federal subsidies that require a different lease format.' § 34-18-15(a)(2): 'If there is no written lease, the landlord shall provide to the tenant, in writing, a list of all fees beyond the rent that apply to the rental of the unit. Any change in required fees must be disclosed in writing at least thirty (30) days prior to the change becoming effective.' § 34-18-15(a)(5): 'If a landlord fails to comply with subsections (a)(1) — (a)(4) of this section, the tenant may recover any fees paid for the unit that were not disclosed as required.' title: No Specific Rule on Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute that specifically bars charging a fee for a service you don't provide (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). Related rules still apply. Every fee beyond rent must be disclosed in the rent section of the lease (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format; with no written lease, in writing), and a tenant can recover fees paid that weren't disclosed as required. If you willfully cut off or reduce heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may recover possession or end the tenancy and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. Charge only for services the lease names and you actually provide.
