title: Fees Are Not Rent
bodyText: Rhode Island defines rent as the payment or consideration a tenant pays you for the use of the premises. No statute says that late fees, utility charges or other fees are rent, and none says a lease can make a fee rent by calling it "additional rent" (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). This matters at the eviction stage: the nonpayment process (rent 15 days in arrears, then a five-day demand notice) is built on the stipulated rent, and the demand notice states the amount of rent in arrears. Put only rent in that notice and pursue fees separately. One statutory exception: if a tenant fails to fix a maintenance breach that materially affects health and safety within 20 days after your written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires), you may have the work done properly and bill its actual and reasonable cost as rent on the next rent due date, or for immediate payment if the tenancy has ended. Whether recurring charges such as pet rent or parking count as rent is for the courts; case law was not searched.
notes: RI: 'Rent' means 'the payment or consideration that a tenant pays to a landlord for the use of the premises, whether money, services, property, or produce of the land' (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-11(13), renumbered (16) by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, effective July 1, 2026). § 34-18-35(a): 'If any part of the stipulated rent is due and in arrears for fifteen (15) days, the landlord shall send a written notice, in a form substantially similar to that provided in § 34-18-56(a), specifying the amount of the rent which is fifteen (15) days in arrears'. § 34-18-39: the landlord may 'cause the work to be done in a skilled manner and submit the itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost or the fair and reasonable value thereof as rent on the next date periodic rent is due, or if the rental agreement has terminated, for immediate payment.' No other fees-as-rent rule: RI-fees-as-rent-1 (additional rent, deemed rent, considered/treated as rent, rent shall include, as rent, near tenant/landlord/lease/rental/dwelling; hits 9, OK, synthetic positives passed; §§ 34-18-15(b), 34-18-39 and payment-into-court provisions §§ 34-18-49, 34-18-52, 34-18.1-16, 34-18.1-18, which set sums 'equal to the rent', not fees). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: telling landlords to keep fees out of the § 34-18-35 demand is the cheaper error; § 34-18-56(a) form not reread for this row. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute addresses making a tenant reimburse you for a fee a government charges you (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not), such as a registration, inspection or certificate fee, and the library does not offer such a clause. State-level obligations sit with you: you must register every unit with the Department of Health's statewide rental registry (the statute sets no registration fee, but missing registration brings civil fines of at least $50 a month, or $125 a month for missing pre-1978 lead certificate information, and blocks a nonpayment eviction filing), and a $100 state fire marshal fee per inspection involving a residential use (waived if no violation is found) is payable by the property owner. In Providence and Warwick you must also register with the city clerk. If you nonetheless pass a fee on, it is a fee beyond rent: list it in the rent section of the lease (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant may recover it. Local ordinance fees were not searched.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (pass-through rule). RI-government-fee-reimbursement-1 (registration/inspection/license/certificate/permit fee, pass on/through, reimburse near tenant/landlord/lessee/dwelling unit/rental unit; hits 23, OK, synthetic positives passed; none lets or bars a residential landlord passing a government fee to a tenant). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-58(a), (b), (d), (e), (g) (registration with the department of health; civil fine 'of at least fifty dollars ($50.00) per month' for (a) information and 'at least one hundred and twenty-five dollars ($125) per month' for (b) lead information; no nonpayment eviction unless 'the landlord is in compliance with the requirements of subsections (a), (b), and (d) of this section'); no registration fee in the section. § 23-28.2-27(a), (b): an inspection fee 'of one-hundred dollars ($100.00) per inspection'; 'In the case of an inspection involving residential use, the fee shall be paid by the property owner.' § 34-18-57 (Providence and Warwick owners 'shall register their names, home addresses, including zip codes, and telephone numbers with the city clerk'). § 34-18-15(a)(1), (5) (fee disclosure and recovery). Municipal ordinances (local registration or inspection fees) not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Late Fee
bodyText: If Tenant fails to pay Monthly Rent in full within {{late_fee_grace_days}} days after it is due, a late fee of {{late_fee_amount}} will be assessed. The late fee is a fee in addition to Rent. Landlord's acceptance of a partial payment of Rent does not waive the balance due. If Landlord accepts Rent knowing that Tenant is in default, Landlord keeps the right to end this Lease for that default only if Landlord gives Tenant written notice within ten (10) days; acceptance does not waive Landlord's right to seek other remedies for the default.
notes: RI: Overrides `late-fee`, whose sentence "Acceptance of a late payment does not waive Landlord's right to require full payment of Rent on the date it is due or to pursue any other remedy available under this Lease" reads as preserving termination, which R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-41 takes away unless notice is given: 'Acceptance of rent with knowledge of a default by the tenant or acceptance of performance by him or her that varies from the terms of the rental agreement constitutes a waiver of the landlord’s right to terminate the rental agreement for that breach, unless the landlord gives written notice within ten (10) days. However, acceptance of partial payment of rent shall not constitute a waiver of the balance due. Acceptance does not waive the landlord’s right to seek remedies for the default.' A lease may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under this chapter' (§ 34-18-17(a)(1)); deliberate use of a known-prohibited provision costs actual damages plus 'an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney’s fees' (§ 34-18-17(b)). No late-fee cap or grace period for ordinary residential tenancies (see `edu-no-late-fee-limit-ri`). The late fee is a fee beyond rent, so it must also be listed in the rent section with the 'additional fees may apply' statement (§ 34-18-15(a)(1); planned `fee-disclosure-ri`). Rent is defined as payment 'for the use of the premises' (§ 34-18-11(13), renumbered (16) by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, effective July 1, 2026), so the clause calls the fee a fee in addition to Rent. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: How Late Fees Work in Rhode Island
bodyText: Rhode Island lets you charge a late fee only as the lease provides, and sets no grace period or cap for ordinary residential tenancies (see the late-fee-limit row). Three rules shape how you charge it. First, a late fee is a fee beyond rent: list it in the same section of the lease as the rent, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it. Second, it is not rent. Rhode Island defines rent as payment for the use of the premises, and the nonpayment process (rent 15 days in arrears, then the five-day demand notice) is built on rent, so leave late fees out of the demand and collect them separately. Third, accepting rent while knowing the tenant is in default waives your right to end the tenancy for that default unless you give written notice within ten days; a partial payment never waives the balance.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(1): 'If there are fees beyond the rent that apply to the rental of a unit, the lease shall disclose those fees in the same section as the rent disclosure and shall indicate that additional fees may apply.'; § 34-18-15(a)(5) (undisclosed fees recoverable). § 34-18-11(13) ('Rent' is 'the payment or consideration that a tenant pays to a landlord for the use of the premises'; renumbered (16) by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, effective July 1, 2026). § 34-18-35(a): 'If any part of the stipulated rent is due and in arrears for fifteen (15) days, the landlord shall send a written notice'. § 34-18-41 (acceptance waiver; written notice within ten days; 'acceptance of partial payment of rent shall not constitute a waiver of the balance due'). No late-fee statute for ordinary tenancies: lead batteries RI-late-fee-1 (hits 3, OK) and RI-late-fee-5 (hits 3, OK; RI-late-fee-2 to -4 recorded as failed, rerun as -5), hits only §§ 31-44-2, 31-44-7 (mobile home parks), 23-17.4-16 (assisted living) and 34-18.1-9. Penalty doctrine is case law, not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Late Fee Limit
bodyText: Rhode Island sets no maximum late fee and no grace period for ordinary residential tenancies (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not); the amount and timing are whatever the lease states. Keep the fee a reasonable estimate of what late payment costs you: a court may refuse to enforce a fee it sees as a penalty (case law, not covered here). Two kinds of housing have their own rules. A mobile and manufactured home park lease may not allow a late charge before a seven-day grace period ends or above 5% of the monthly rent due. A licensed assisted living residence may charge only reasonable late fees, under a written schedule it gave the resident at or before admission or signing.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent for ordinary residential tenancies. Lead batteries over the General Laws, Constitution, loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws and court rules: RI-late-fee-1 (late fee/charge/payment fee/penalty for late near rent/tenant/lease/landlord/dwelling; hits 3, OK, synthetic positives passed) and RI-late-fee-5 (everyday words late/delinquent/overdue ... rent; hits 3, OK, synthetic positives passed; RI-late-fee-2 to -4 recorded as failed, rerun as -5); hits only §§ 23-17.4-16, 31-44-2, 31-44-7 and 34-18.1-9 (non-URLTA possession procedure, no fee). R.I. Gen. Laws § 31-44-7(6): a park lease 'shall not contain' '(i) Any provision allowing less than a seven (7) day grace period in which to pay rent without the assessment of a late charge;' or '(ii) Any provision allowing the licensee to assess a late charge in excess of five percent (5%) of the monthly rent due;'. § 31-44-2(a)(1) (tender before the notice to quit expires, 'including a late charge of five percent (5%) of the monthly rent due after a seven (7) day grace period for the rental payment has elapsed'). § 23-17.4-16(a)(2)(xv)(B) (resident informed in writing of 'a schedule for late fee charges') and (xviii)(D) ('The provider may impose reasonable late fees for overdue payment; provided that the resident has received due notice of those charges in accordance with the residence’s policies.'). Penalty doctrine is case law, not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule requiring the same rent or terms for a month-to-month tenancy and a fixed-term lease, and no cap on the rent difference between them (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). The law still treats them differently. Unless the lease fixes a definite term, the tenancy is month to month (week to week for a roomer who pays weekly). A periodic tenancy ends by written notice in the statutory form: at least 10 days for week-to-week, 30 days for month-to-month (and any period between a month and a year), and three months before the end of the occupation year for year-to-year; a fixed term ends on its own date. A rent increase needs 60 days' written notice for every tenancy, but 120 days for a month-to-month tenant over 62 (independent living, assisted living and congregate care facilities excluded). If a tenant stays on with your consent after the term and no new term is agreed, the tenancy becomes week to week (weekly payers) or month to month.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (parity rule). RI-lease-type-parity-1 (month-to-month near fixed/definite term, or "more burdensome", near tenant/landlord/lease/rent; hits 2, OK, synthetic positives passed; only §§ 34-18-15(d), 34-18-38(c), neither a parity rule). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(d): 'Unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent, and in all other cases month to month.' § 34-18-37(a)-(c) (10 days week-to-week; 30 days 'a month-to-month tenancy or any periodic tenancy for more than a month or less than a year'; 'at least three (3) months prior to the expiration of the occupation year' for year-to-year; form § 34-18-56(c)). § 34-18-16.1(a) (60 days' written notice); (b): 'at least one hundred twenty (120) days' notice to month-to-month tenants over the age of sixty-two (62) years, before raising the rent' (both exclude 'an independent living facility, assisted living facility, or congregate care facility'). § 34-18-38(c): 'If no term is specified, the term shall be week-to-week if the tenant pays on a week-to-week basis, and in all other cases, month-to-month.' Case law and municipal ordinances not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Rule on Notice Fees
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute addresses charging a tenant for preparing or serving a notice (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not), and the library does not offer a notice-fee clause. Rhode Island's pre-eviction notices are sent by you, not served by an officer: the five-day demand for rent 15 days in arrears and the 20-day noncompliance notice are mailed, in the statutory forms. What you can recover is set by the act: in a nonpayment case, actual damages, plus reasonable attorney's fees only if the tenant got an earlier demand notice within the six months before you filed and the nonpayment was willful; a tenant who cures at the hearing pays court costs; for other breaches, attorney's fees only if the noncompliance was willful. A lease term making the tenant pay your attorney's fees beyond what the act allows is unenforceable, so don't dress a lawyer's notice-drafting charge up as a notice fee.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent. Statute-wide searches over the General Laws, Constitution, loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws and court rules: RI-notice-service-fee-1 (fee/charge/cost/expense near notice/demand/serve, or notice/demand near fee/charge, near tenant/landlord/lessee/rental agreement; hits 13, OK, synthetic positives passed; none on point: vehicle towing, mobile home park tender, § 34-18-59 application fees) and RI-notice-service-fee-2 (everyday words notice fee/service fee/cost of the notice/mailing/service, no tenancy limb; hits 58, OK, synthetic positives passed; utility, insurance, tax and court-form hits only, incl. the constable's service-fee line in the § 34-18-56 summons forms). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-35(a) (written notice after rent is 15 days in arrears; cure 'within five (5) days of the date of mailing of the notice'); (d) attorney's fee where the tenant 'had received a demand notice pursuant to subsection (a) within the six (6) months immediately preceding the filing of the action, and the tenant’s nonpayment was willful'; (e) cure at hearing 'together with court costs'. § 34-18-36(a) (written demand notice; remedy 'within twenty (20) days of mailing of the notice'); (d): 'If the tenant’s noncompliance is willful, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney’s fees.' § 34-18-17(a)(3), (b) (fee terms 'inconsistent with this chapter' unenforceable). Case law not searched. SYNC (Claude Code, 2026-10-09): read with § 34-18-35(d)-(e) on the official site. Taken literally, 'a notice pursuant to subsection (a) ... within the six (6) months immediately preceding the filing of the action' includes the demand notice for the case itself, which every nonpayment action must follow, so no tenant could ever cure at the hearing and every willful nonpayment would carry attorney's fees. DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the row reads it as an earlier notice, before the one for this case, so the hearing cure and the fee rule apply as the statute's structure suggests (case law not searched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited
bodyText: You may not raise the rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction because a tenant complained to a building or housing code agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, complained to you about your maintenance duties, organized or joined a tenants' union or similar group, or used any other lawful right or remedy. If the tenant complained within six months before your action, the court must presume it was retaliation unless you produce evidence otherwise; there is no presumption if the complaint came after you gave notice of a rent increase or service cut. A retaliating landlord faces the tenant's choice of recovering possession or ending the lease, plus up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, and attorney's fees, and the tenant has a defense to eviction. You may still evict if the tenant is behind in rent, if the tenant's own lack of care mainly caused the code violation, or if code compliance or a public taking requires work that would deprive the tenant of the unit and the city or town has met its relocation requirements. Separately, you may not evict, end the tenancy, raise rent or cut services because a tenant in good faith petitions to pay rent into court over lead hazards, or retaliate over enforcement of the lead laws, whether or not there is a written lease. While a code enforcement notice of violation, conference, hearing or appeal is pending you may not evict without just cause. The older trespass-and-possession chapter also requires judgment for a tenant whose tenancy was ended as a penalty for justified lawful acts. The rule covers every tenancy type.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-46(a): 'a landlord may not retaliate by increasing rent or decreasing services or by bringing or threatening to bring an action for possession because' (§ 34-18-46(a)) of (1) a complaint 'to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building or housing code of a violation applicable to the premises materially affecting health and safety' (§ 34-18-46(a)(1)); (2) a complaint 'to the landlord of a violation under § 34-18-22' (§ 34-18-46(a)(2)); (3) organizing or joining 'a tenants' union or similar organization' (§ 34-18-46(a)(3)); (4) having 'availed himself or herself of any other lawful rights and remedies' (§ 34-18-46(a)(4)). § 34-18-46(b): remedies of § 34-18-34 and 'a defense in any retaliatory action against him or her for possession' (§ 34-18-46(b)); 'evidence of a complaint within six (6) months before the alleged act of retaliation creates a presumption that the landlord's conduct was in retaliation' (§ 34-18-46(b)); 'The presumption does not arise if the tenant made the complaint after notice of a proposed rental increase or diminution of services' (§ 34-18-46(b)). § 34-18-34: tenant 'may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, in either case, recover an amount not more than three (3) months periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him or her, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-34). Exceptions § 34-18-46(c)(1)-(3): code violation 'caused primarily by lack of reasonable care by the tenant' (§ 34-18-46(c)(1)); 'The tenant is in default in rent' (§ 34-18-46(c)(2)); required alteration, remodeling or demolition where 'the relocation requirements have been met by the municipality' (§ 34-18-46(c)(3)); (d) no release from § 34-18-28(b) liability. Lead: § 42-128.1-14(e): 'A lessee may not be evicted, the tenancy may not be terminated, the rent may not be raised, or any services reduced, because a lessee in good faith elects to seek the remedies under this section' (§ 42-128.1-14(e)) (rent escrow in district court); § 23-24.6-23(c)(4): 'It shall be unlawful to take retaliatory actions against tenants arising from enforcement of the provisions of this chapter or chapter 128.1 of title 42; this prohibition against retaliatory actions applies whether or not the tenant has a lease' (§ 23-24.6-23(c)(4)), remedies per chapter 34-18. Fair housing: § 34-37-5.1 bars coercion or discrimination against a person who 'has made a charge, testified, or assisted' (§ 34-37-5.1) in a fair housing proceeding. Safe harbors added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026 (not yet in the compiled General Laws): § 34-18-63(f) a landlord who 'in good faith initiates an action against a remaining tenant, co-tenant, or household member' (§ 34-18-63(f)) after a survivor's termination is not subject to a retaliation claim; § 34-18-65(e) replacing a substandard tenant-installed lock 'shall be deemed not to be in retaliation' (§ 34-18-65(e)). § 34-18-46 draws no distinction by tenancy type and has no market-rate rent-increase safe harbor. Statute-wide search: RI-retaliation-1 (retaliat*/reprisal* with tenant/landlord context, hits 6, OK). § 23-24.6-23 read for (c)(4); case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open. Code enforcement: § 45-24.3-21(c)(4): 'It is unlawful for any owner, operator, or agent to evict occupants from a dwelling or dwelling unit without just cause during conferences, hearings, appeals, or when served with a notice of violation.' (§ 45-24.3-21(c)(4)). Chapter 34-20: § 34-20-10(1): judgment for the defendant where 'the alleged termination was intended as a penalty for the defendant's justified attempt to secure or enforce rights under a lease or contract, or under the laws of the state' (§ 34-20-10(1)); § 34-20-11 voids penalty rent increases; where chapter 34-20 conflicts with chapter 34-18, chapter 34-18 controls (§ 34-18-4). §§ 34-20-10, 34-20-11, 45-24.3-21 read whole. Survivor safe harbors: § 34-18-63(f), § 34-18-65(e) (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2).

title: Rent Concessions
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute regulates rent concessions such as a free month, a move-in discount or a rent credit (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). If you give one, state it in the lease (the library's rent-concession clause does this) with its amount and the rental periods it covers, so the rent and what the tenant actually owes are clear. Two statutes limit taking a concession back when a tenant leaves early. A servicemember who ends the lease under the military-orders rule can't be charged an early termination charge, and since July 1, 2026 a tenant who ends the lease because of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking owes no penalty, early-termination fee or future rent, only rent through the termination date or the move-out date, whichever is later. Clawing back a concession from either tenant risks being treated as the charge the statute forbids. Whether a general recapture-on-default term is an unenforceable penalty is a question for case law, so the library does not offer one.
notes: RI: Rent concessions: no statute. Statute-wide searches over the General Laws, Constitution, loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws and court rules: RI-rent-concession-1 (concession/free rent/rent-free/discount/rebate/reduced rent/rent credit/move-in special near tenant/landlord/lease/rental agreement/dwelling unit/lessee; hits 32, OK, synthetic positives passed; none on point: airport and park concessions, mobile home park sale notices, § 34-18-18 maintenance) and RI-rent-concession-2 (everyday words free month/first month free/move-in special/early or prompt payment discount/recapture/signing bonus, no tenancy limb; hits 22, OK, synthetic positives passed; tax-credit recapture only). Early-termination limits: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(f)(4) (servicemember): 'The lessor may not impose an early termination charge'. § 34-18-63(a) (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): a tenant may terminate 'without penalty or fees for early termination, or liability for future rent'; (d) liable only 'for rent owed through the date of termination or the date the tenant actually vacates the premises, whichever is later'. Fee disclosure: § 34-18-15(a)(1) fees beyond the rent disclosed 'in the same section as the rent disclosure'. Whether a recapture-on-default term is an unenforceable penalty is case law, not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Rent Control or Rent Cap
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statewide rent control and no limit on how much you may raise the rent, and no state statute either authorizes or forbids local rent control. We did not search city and town ordinances or charters, so check local law where the unit is. What state law does regulate is timing: you must give written notice of an increase at least 60 days before it takes effect, or 120 days for a month-to-month tenant over 62 (independent living, assisted living and congregate care facilities are excluded), and during a fixed term you can raise the rent only if the lease allows it. Two narrow rules can reach the amount. On leased land under a home owned by someone, the homeowner may send an excessive lot-rent increase to binding arbitration. And during a declared state of emergency, the price-gouging law bars unconscionably high prices for essential commodities, defined to include services; the statute doesn't say whether that reaches rent (case law was not searched), so avoid sharp increases in a declared emergency area.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (statewide rent cap and state preemption of local rent control). Statute-wide searches over the General Laws, Constitution, loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws and court rules: RI-rent-control-1 (rent control/stabilization/leveling, rent cap/limit/ceiling, limit or control the amount of rent, fair rent, rent board/review, excessive or unconscionable rent; no limb; hits 20, OK, synthetic positives passed; on point only § 34-18.2-5, leased land dwellings) and RI-rent-control-2 (ordinance/bylaw/council/municipality/city or town near rent or landlord-tenant; hits 38, OK, synthetic positive passed; none limits or preempts local rent regulation). RI-rent-control-3 (price gouging/unconscionably high price/state of emergency near rent/housing/dwelling/essential commodities; hits 1, OK): R.I. Gen. Laws § 6-13-21(a), during a declared emergency, bars selling 'essential commodities to consumers for an amount that represents an unconscionably high price'; (b)(3) 'Essential commodities' means 'any goods, services, materials, merchandise, supplies, equipment, resources, or other article of commerce'; the statute doesn't say whether rent is covered (case law not searched). § 34-18.2-5(b)-(c) (leased land dwellings only): a homeowner may arbitrate a lot rent increase that is 'excessive', meaning one 'which unreasonably exceeds the fair rental value of the property based on market conditions at the time'. § 34-18-16.1(a): notice of a rent increase 'at least sixty (60) days prior to the effective date of the increase'; (b) 120 days for month-to-month tenants over 62. Municipal ordinances and charters not searched; case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Raising Rent During the Term
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute addresses a general lease term that raises the rent during a fixed term (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not), with one exception: a term making the tenant pay an increase in real estate tax levied during the term is void unless it states the tenant's exact percentage, limits the tenant to the unit's proportionate share of the increase and refunds a proportionate share of any abatement (see the tax-escalation clause). Otherwise the act lets you and the tenant agree on rent terms that no law prohibits. Without such a term, the rent in a fixed-term lease stays the same until the term ends; the library's optional mid-term increase clause is the way to reserve one. Any increase, scheduled or not, should get written notice at least 60 days before it takes effect, or 120 days for a month-to-month tenant over 62 (the statute excludes independent living, assisted living and congregate care facilities); the statute doesn't say whether an increase already written into the lease needs a separate notice, so send one. Rhode Island's retaliation rule has no safe harbor for increases written into the lease: an increase in retaliation for the tenant complaining to a code agency or to you about repairs, joining a tenants' union or using another legal right is prohibited, and an increase within six months after such a complaint is presumed retaliatory, unless the complaint came after your notice of the increase. Raising rent in response to lead-law enforcement is also unlawful.
notes: RI: No statute addresses general escalation clauses. The exception is § 6A-2.1-222(a): 'No lease relating to residential real estate shall contain a provision which obligates a lessee to make payments to the lessor on account of an increased real estate tax levied during the term of the lease, unless such provision expressly sets forth' (§ 6A-2.1-222(a)) the unit's proportion, 'The exact percentage of any such increase which the lessee shall pay' (§ 6A-2.1-222(a)(2)) and the abatement refund; 'Any provision of a lease in violation of the provision of this section shall be deemed to be against public policy and void.' (§ 6A-2.1-222(a)); see `tax-escalation-ri`. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a): the parties 'may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by this chapter or other rule of law, including rent, term of the agreement'. § 34-18-16.1(a): 'Prior to an increase in rent being imposed by a landlord for a residential tenancy, excluding an independent living facility, assisted living facility, or congregate care facility, notice of the increase shall be given in writing to any tenant by a landlord at least sixty (60) days prior to the effective date of the increase'; (b) 120 days for 'month-to-month tenants over the age of sixty-two (62) years'. Retaliation: § 34-18-46(a) a landlord 'may not retaliate by increasing rent or decreasing services'; (b) a complaint 'within six (6) months before the alleged act of retaliation creates a presumption'; 'The presumption does not arise if the tenant made the complaint after notice of a proposed rental increase or diminution of services.' No safe harbour for increases provided in the lease. § 23-24.6-23(c)(4): retaliation guidelines cover 'arbitrary and unreasonable increase in rent' and 'It shall be unlawful to take retaliatory actions against tenants arising from enforcement of the provisions of this chapter or chapter 128.1 of title 42'. title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: Before any rent increase takes effect, give the tenant written notice at least 60 days ahead. For a month-to-month tenant over age 62, the notice must be at least 120 days. These periods apply to every kind of residential tenancy (week-to-week, month-to-month, year-to-year and fixed term), but not to independent living, assisted living or congregate care facilities. If a state or federal housing program sets a shorter notice period for the unit, the statute doesn't require more than that program's period. Keep proof of when you delivered it. During a fixed term you also need a lease term allowing the increase (see the mid-term increase clause). An increase in retaliation for the tenant complaining to a code agency or to you about repairs, joining a tenants' union or using another legal right is prohibited, and the tenant may defend an eviction and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. An increase within six months after such a complaint is presumed retaliatory, unless the tenant complained only after receiving notice of the increase.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-16.1(a): 'Prior to an increase in rent being imposed by a landlord for a residential tenancy, excluding an independent living facility, assisted living facility, or congregate care facility, notice of the increase shall be given in writing to any tenant by a landlord at least sixty (60) days prior to the effective date of the increase.' (b): 'at least one hundred twenty (120) days’ notice to month-to-month tenants over the age of sixty-two (62) years, before raising the rent.' (c): 'nothing in this section shall require a landlord to provide notice of a rent increase on a timeframe that exceeds the timeframe set forth under any other state or federal law or regulation or requirement of any applicable housing program established under state or federal law or regulation.' (Amended by P.L. 2024, chs. 243, 244, effective June 24, 2024.) § 34-18-46(a)-(b) retaliation by 'increasing rent'; presumption from a complaint 'within six (6) months before the alleged act of retaliation'. The section applies to every residential tenancy type (week-to-week, month-to-month, year-to-year, fixed term); no separate rent-increase form in § 34-18-56 (grep of the section for 'increase': none). The statute does not say whether the 60 days run from mailing or receipt. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Rent Installments and Partial Payments
bodyText: Rhode Island lets you and the tenant agree on when and where rent is paid, so a lease may split the monthly rent into scheduled installments (the library's installment clause does this). If the lease says nothing, rent is due at the unit, at the start of each term for tenancies of a month or less, and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the start of each month, and it is apportioned day by day. Partial payments are a separate thing: if the tenant pays only part of what is due, taking it doesn't waive the balance. But if you accept rent knowing of any default by the tenant, or accept performance that varies from the lease, you waive the right to end the tenancy for that breach unless you give written notice within 10 days (you keep your other remedies for the default). Each scheduled installment is rent due on its own date for the 15-day arrears rule before a nonpayment demand.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(c): 'Rent is payable without demand or notice at the time and place agreed upon by the parties. Unless otherwise agreed, rent is payable at the dwelling unit and periodic rent is payable at the beginning of any term of one month or less and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the beginning of each month. Unless otherwise agreed, rent is uniformly apportionable from day-to-day.' § 34-18-41: 'acceptance of partial payment of rent shall not constitute a waiver of the balance due'; acceptance of rent 'with knowledge of a default by the tenant' waives the right to terminate for that breach 'unless the landlord gives written notice within ten (10) days'. No statute addresses splitting rent into installments by agreement or whether a scheduled installment is a partial payment: RI-rent-installments-1 (installment/partial payment/part payment/portion of rent/split rent near rent/tenant/landlord/lessee; hits 27, OK; real positive § 34-18-15 and synthetic positive passed; on point only §§ 34-18-15(c), 34-18-41). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open. NEEDS_REVIEW: the last sentence (each installment counts separately toward the § 34-18-35(a) 15-day arrears trigger) is an inference from § 34-18-15(c) and § 34-18-35(a); no statute or case says so; case law not searched.

title: No Rent Receipt Rule
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires you to give a receipt for rent, even rent paid in cash, or to keep a rent ledger for the tenant. Giving a written receipt for every cash payment, and a statement of payments when asked, is still good practice. Tenants who claim the state's property tax relief credit for renters must give the Division of Taxation reasonable proof of rent paid and your name and address, so expect requests for a year-end statement. Records also matter to you: a nonpayment demand must state the amount of rent 15 days in arrears, and if the tenant disputes it, your payment records are your proof. Check local ordinances, which we did not search.

title: No Rent Reporting Rule
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires you to offer tenants positive rent reporting to a credit bureau, regulates whether you report rent payments, or bars you from requiring a tenant to join a rent-reporting program. If you do report payment data, federal credit reporting law applies to what you furnish, so keep it accurate and correct disputed entries; we did not review that law here. Any fee you charge the tenant for a reporting service is a fee beyond the rent, so it must be listed in the lease's rent section with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); an undisclosed fee can be recovered by the tenant.

title: Sales and Hotel Taxes on Rent
bodyText: Rhode Island taxes rent only for living quarters in hotels, rooming houses and tourist camps; no statute names an ordinary apartment or house lease as taxable, but the rooming-house definition is broad. State sales tax (7%) applies to rentals of living quarters in hotels, rooming houses and tourist camps, but only on the first 30 consecutive days of each rental, and not where the occupant has a written lease of 12 months or more. A hotel includes a house, condo or apartment used or advertised for transient lodging of 30 days or less; a home rented under a documented arrangement for more than 30 consecutive days, or for a calendar month, is outside that definition. A rooming house is any structure held out as a place where living quarters are supplied for pay to transient or permanent guests or tenants, so if you rent rooms, or rent any unit on a lease shorter than 12 months, ask the Division of Taxation whether your rentals are taxable. If you do rent short-term, the hotel taxes also apply: a 2% local hotel tax, plus either the 5% state hotel tax or, for a whole house, condo or other dwelling rented in its entirety, the 5% whole-home short-term rental tax (since January 1, 2026). Short-term and vacation rentals are outside this library; talk to the Division of Taxation before offering one.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-18-18: tax on 'charges for rentals of living quarters in hotels as defined in § 42-63.1-2, rooming houses, or tourist camps'; 'the tax imposed on charges for the rentals applies only to the first period of not exceeding thirty (30) consecutive calendar days of each rental'; rate 'seven percent (7%)'; 'Excluded from this tax are those living quarters in hotels, rooming houses, or tourist camps for which the occupant has a written lease for the living quarters which lease covers a rental period of twelve (12) months or more.' § 42-63.1-2(5): 'hotel' includes 'houses, condominiums, or other residential dwelling units, regardless of the number of rooms, which are used and/or advertised for rent for occupancy'; (6) 'Occupancy' means 'use of space for transient lodging accommodations not to exceed thirty (30) days', excluding a written lease of 'twelve (12) months or more' and any residential dwelling 'for which the occupant has a documented arrangement for the space covering a rental period of more than thirty (30) consecutive days or for one calendar month'. § 44-18-36.1 (version effective January 1, 2026, P.L. 2025, ch. 278, art. 5, § 7): (a) 5% hotel tax; (b) local hotel tax 'two percent (2%) for tax periods beginning on or after January 1, 2026'; (d) 'a whole home short-term rental tax at a rate of five percent (5%)' on occupancy of a dwelling 'rented in its entirety'. § 44-18-7.1(n)(ii): '“Rooming house” means every house, boat, vehicle, motor court, or other structure kept, used, maintained, advertised, or held out to the public to be a place where living quarters are supplied for pay to transient or permanent guests or tenants' (§ 44-18-7.1(n)(ii)); the documented-arrangement exclusion sits in the hotel definition, not in § 44-18-18, so a rooming-house rental is taxed for its first 30 days unless the written lease runs 12 months or more. The (a) whole-home exemption is 'under this subsection' only, so the (b) local tax reaches whole-home rentals. No 2026 public law amends these sections (act-text search). title: Bounced Checks and Returned Payments
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute capping a returned-payment fee you set in the lease, and none on failed electronic payments. If you charge one, it is a fee beyond rent, so state it with its amount in the lease's rent section (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); a tenant can recover a fee you didn't disclose. For a bounced check, draft or similar instrument, the dishonored-check law gives you a separate remedy: if it isn't paid within 10 days, you may send a notice of dishonor in the statutory form by certified mail, return receipt requested (or regular mail backed by an affidavit of mailing). If the tenant still hasn't paid 30 days after mailing, you may sue in district court, or under small-claims procedure, for the check amount, a $25 collection fee and three times the check amount (at least $200, at most $1,000). It is a defense that payment was stopped justifiably or the account was attached. Keep any fee separate from rent in a nonpayment demand.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 6-42-1: when a check, draft or other instrument 'has been dishonored by nonacceptance or nonpayment by any bank or other financial institution and has not been paid within ten (10) days, the holder to whom the check, draft, or other instrument was issued may send a notice of dishonor'. § 6-42-2(a) statutory form; (b) 'The notice provided for in subsection (a) shall be sent certified mail, return receipt requested, or by regular mail when such mailing is supported by an affidavit of service by mail.' § 6-42-3(a) suit in district court, at the holder's election under small-claims procedure; (b) liability for '(1) The amount of the check or other instrument; (2) A collection fee of twenty-five dollars ($25.00); (3) An amount equal to three (3) times the amount of the check or instrument, but in no case less than two hundred dollars ($200) and in no case more than one thousand dollars ($1,000).' § 6-42-4 defenses: 'a justifiable stop payment order or to the attachment of the account' or payment in full within 30 days of mailing. § 34-18-15(a)(1), (5): fees beyond the rent disclosed 'in the same section as the rent disclosure'; undisclosed fees recoverable. § 34-18-61(a): 'A landlord shall not charge a convenience fee to a tenant’s rental payment', not applicable where a fee-free method is accepted. Search: RI-returned-payments-1 (dishonor/insufficient funds/bad or worthless or returned check/stop payment/no or closed account/service charge/processing fee near check/draft/instrument/electronic transfer; hits 54, OK, synthetic positive passed): no cap on a contractual returned-payment fee and no rule on failed electronic payments; other hits are UCC articles 3-4, check cashers, DMV, tax and municipal-court fees. Criminal bad-check provisions not reviewed. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Government Shutdown Protection
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute gives tenants who are federal or state workers extra time to pay rent, protection from late fees or a defense to eviction during a government shutdown. The usual rules apply: once rent is 15 days in arrears you may send the five-day demand notice, and the tenant can cure by paying in full before you file suit (and in some cases at the hearing). Taking a partial payment doesn't waive the balance, so a written payment plan with an affected tenant can avoid the cost of an eviction without giving up your claim.

Statute-wide searches over the General Laws, Constitution, loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws and court rules: RI-shutdown-rent-1 (government/federal shutdown, lapse in appropriations, furlough, federal employees without pay, near rent/tenant/landlord/evict/lease/housing/mortgage; hits 5, OK, synthetic positive passed; prison and hospital furloughs only) and RI-shutdown-rent-2 (everyday words shutdown/furlough/federal employee or worker or contractor/unpaid government workers, 2025-2026 acts, no limb; hits 0, OK, synthetic positive passed). Ordinary rules: R.I. Gen. title: Rhode Island's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Rhode Island sets these money limits, whatever the lease says. Security deposit: no more than one month's rent, whatever you call it; for a furnished unit whose furniture is worth $5,000 or more, a separate furniture deposit of up to one more month's rent. Application fee: none; you may charge only the actual cost of a state criminal background check or credit report if the applicant hasn't supplied one issued within 90 days, and you must give them a copy. Payment method: no convenience fee on rent unless you also accept a fee-free way to pay. Attorney's fees: only as the landlord-tenant act allows. Early termination: no charge to a servicemember ending the lease under the military-orders rule, and since July 1, 2026 no fee, penalty or future rent for a tenant ending it because of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. Lock change for such a tenant: no more than the community's customary price. Rhode Island caps neither rent, rent increases (60 days' notice, 120 for month-to-month tenants over 62) nor late fees, and a returned-check fee set in the lease has no cap; the dishonored-check law adds a $25 collection fee and $200 to $1,000 in damages after its notice process.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(a) ('A landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month’s periodic rent'); (e) separate furniture deposit 'of up to one month’s periodic rent' where furniture replacement value is 'five thousand dollars ($5,000) or greater'. § 34-18-59(a) (no 'rental application fee'); (b)(2) 'not more than the actual cost of obtaining the official state background check and/or credit report' when the applicant has not provided one issued 'within ninety (90) days'. § 34-18-61(a) ('A landlord shall not charge a convenience fee to a tenant’s rental payment'); (b) exception. § 6-42-3(b) ('A collection fee of twenty-five dollars ($25.00)'; treble damages 'in no case less than two hundred dollars ($200) and in no case more than one thousand dollars ($1,000)'). § 34-18-17(a)(3) (no term to pay 'the landlord’s attorney’s fees inconsistent with this chapter'). § 34-18-15(f)(4) ('The lessor may not impose an early termination charge'). § 34-18-63(a) (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws) ('without penalty or fees for early termination, or liability for future rent'); § 34-18-65(d) ('The fee shall not exceed the reasonable price customarily charged for changing such locks in that community'). § 34-18-16.1(a)-(b) notice only. title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute bars or limits a late fee on the part of the rent a housing subsidy pays, and Rhode Island sets no late-fee cap for ordinary tenancies. Even so, charge any late fee only on the tenant's own share and only when the tenant's share is late; when a housing agency pays its share late, collect from the agency under your contract with it. Federal programs such as Housing Choice Vouchers have their own lease addenda and contract rules on fees and tenant rent, which we did not review; follow them where they apply. Units in the state's rental assistance program have their own rules: the tenant pays 30% of adjusted income, and you may end the tenancy only for serious or repeated lease violations, a violation of law or other good and substantial cause.

Statute-wide searches over the General Laws, Constitution, loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws and court rules: RI-subsidy-late-fee-1 (late fee/charge/payment, penalty for late, delinquent near subsidy/Section 8/housing voucher/housing assistance/public housing/housing authority/rental assistance/lawful source of income; hits 5, OK, synthetic positive passed; on point only § 23-17.4-16, assisted living) and RI-subsidy-late-fee-2 (everyday words voucher/subsidy/Section 8/housing assistance payment/rental assistance near rent/tenant/landlord/lease; hits 109, OK, real positive § 34-37-4 and synthetic positive passed; no late-fee rule: state rental assistance program ch. 42-11.2, Section 8 preservation ch. 34-45, fair housing § 34-37-4). title: Real Estate Tax Increases
bodyText: [Optional.] If the real estate tax on the real estate of which the property is a part increases during the Term above the tax for [the tax year in which the Term begins], Tenant will pay Landlord [__] percent of that increase, which is the proportion that the property bears to the whole of the real estate so taxed. Tenant will pay only that proportion of the increase. This payment is a fee in addition to Rent and is also listed with the Rent in this Lease's Rent section. Landlord will give Tenant written notice of each payment due under this paragraph, stating its amount, at least 60 days before it is due (at least 120 days before it is due if Tenant is then a month-to-month tenant over the age of sixty-two). If Landlord obtains an abatement of the real estate tax levied on the whole of the real estate, Landlord will refund Tenant a proportionate share of the abatement, less reasonable attorney's fees, if any.
notes: RI: Optional clause (rule 54), never a default; the percentage is the landlord's figure and must not exceed the unit's true share. R.I. Gen. Laws § 6A-2.1-222(a): 'No lease relating to residential real estate shall contain a provision which obligates a lessee to make payments to the lessor on account of an increased real estate tax levied during the term of the lease, unless such provision expressly sets forth: (1) That the lessee shall be obligated to pay only that proportion of such increased tax as the unit leased by him or her bears to the whole of the real estate so taxed; (2) The exact percentage of any such increase which the lessee shall pay; and (3) That if the lessor obtains an abatement of the real estate tax levied on the whole of the real estate of which the unit leased by the lessee is a part, a proportionate share of such abatement, less reasonable attorney’s fees, if any, shall be refunded to said lessee.' 'Any provision of a lease in violation of the provision of this section shall be deemed to be against public policy and void.' (b) excess over the unit's share returned 'plus interest calculated at the rate of five percent (5%) per year from the date of collection.' The 60-day notice sentence is Claude's drafting choice: whether a tax pass-through is an 'increase in rent' under § 34-18-16.1 is not settled by the text, and the sentence keeps the clause safe either way, including the 120-day period of § 34-18-16.1(b): 'shall give at least one hundred twenty (120) days’ notice to month-to-month tenants over the age of sixty-two (62) years, before raising the rent' (§ 34-18-16.1(b)). § 34-18-16.1(a): 'notice of the increase shall be given in writing to any tenant by a landlord at least sixty (60) days prior to the effective date of the increase'. § 34-18-15(a)(1): fees beyond the rent disclosed 'in the same section as the rent disclosure'. The section sits in the UCC leases chapter, whose scope clause (§ 6A-2.1-102(1)) reaches 'any transaction, regardless of form, that creates a lease'; its own text applies to leases 'relating to residential real estate'. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open. Rule 26: tax-escalation-ma fits in wording but rests on Mass. Gen. title: Passing On Real Estate Tax Increases
bodyText: A Rhode Island lease may make the tenant pay part of a real estate tax increase during the term, but only if the clause expressly states three things: that the tenant pays only the share of the increase that the unit bears to the whole taxed property, the exact percentage the tenant pays, and that if you win a tax abatement on the whole property you will refund the tenant a proportionate share, less reasonable attorney's fees. A clause missing any of these is void. If the percentage you set turns out to exceed the unit's true share, you must refund the excess with 5% interest a year from the date you collected it. The library's optional tax-increase clause meets these terms. Give the tenant written notice of each payment at least 60 days before it is due, since a pass-through may count as a rent increase, and list the charge in the lease's rent section with your other fees (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format).

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Damages
bodyText: No Rhode Island landlord-tenant statute sets interest on unpaid rent or damages, and the library offers no lease interest clause. You don't need one: when a court awards you money damages, such as rent or the cost of repairing damage beyond the security deposit, the clerk adds interest at 12% a year from the date your claim arose, and the judgment then carries 12% a year until paid. That automatic prejudgment interest does not apply to a contract obligation where interest is already provided, so a lease clause with a lower rate could cost you interest. A higher contract rate raises usury questions: the usury cap (the greater of 21% or prime plus 9 points) is written for loans, and the statute doesn't say whether it reaches interest under a lease (case law was not searched), so take advice before setting a high rate.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. title: Renting to Veterans
bodyText: Rhode Island has no program or tax credit that pays landlords for renting to veterans; the state's veteran property-tax exemptions apply to a veteran's own home. Veteran and servicemember status are protected under Rhode Island's fair housing law: you may not ask about an applicant's honorable-discharge veteran status or service in the armed forces, refuse to rent because of it, treat the tenant differently in the terms of the tenancy, or run an ad that indicates a preference based on it. That last rule cuts both ways, so be careful advertising a veterans-only special; the statute doesn't say whether a voluntary veteran discount is allowed (case law and Commission for Human Rights rules were not searched), so take advice first. Servicemembers also have a statutory right to end a lease on military orders.

title: Accepting Rent After a Breach
bodyText: If you accept rent knowing the tenant is in default, or accept performance that differs from the lease (for example, a payment made late or in a different way), you give up the right to end the tenancy for that breach unless you give the tenant written notice within 10 days. The notice should say you are accepting the payment without waiving the breach. Accepting a partial payment never waives the unpaid balance, and acceptance never waives your other remedies, such as damages. Don't rely on a general no-waiver sentence in the lease to do this job: the act bars lease terms that take away tenants' rights under it, so send the 10-day notice each time. Once an eviction is under way, payments a tenant makes while execution is stayed or while an appeal is pending don't waive your right to possession or reinstate the tenancy.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-41: 'Acceptance of rent with knowledge of a default by the tenant or acceptance of performance by him or her that varies from the terms of the rental agreement constitutes a waiver of the landlord’s right to terminate the rental agreement for that breach, unless the landlord gives written notice within ten (10) days. However, acceptance of partial payment of rent shall not constitute a waiver of the balance due. Acceptance does not waive the landlord’s right to seek remedies for the default.' § 34-18-49 (stay of execution) and § 34-18-52 (appeal): 'The acceptance of these sums shall not constitute a waiver of the right of the landlord to obtain possession of the premises'. § 34-18-43: after termination the landlord has a claim 'for a sum for reasonable use and occupation subsequent to the termination'. § 34-18-17(a)(1): a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under this chapter'; that a lease non-waiver clause cannot replace the § 34-18-41 written notice is an inference from § 34-18-17, not a holding. R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 282, 283 (appeals, effective January 1, 2027) read: they change appeal fees and timing, not § 34-18-52. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Move-In Inspection Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require a move-in inspection, condition checklist, inventory or move-out walk-through, and the library's existing-condition clause is all the lease needs. Document the unit's condition anyway, with a dated checklist and photos signed by you and the tenant at move-in and again at move-out. At the end of the tenancy you may deduct from the deposit only for physical damage beyond ordinary wear and tear caused by the tenant's breach of their duties (plus unpaid rent and reasonable cleaning and trash disposal), itemized in a written notice delivered with any refund within 20 days after the latest of the end of the tenancy, the tenant's delivery of possession or the tenant's giving you a forwarding address. If you withhold wrongly, the tenant can recover the amount due plus damages of twice the amount wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney's fees, and a move-in record is your best evidence of what changed.

title: No Preset Deposit Charges
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute lets a lease fix in advance the amounts you will take from the security deposit for cleaning, carpets or repairs, and the library does not offer such a schedule. What you may keep is set by statute: unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning expenses, reasonable trash disposal expenses, and the damage you actually suffered from the tenant's breach of their duties, other than ordinary wear and tear, each itemized in a written notice. A lease can't waive these limits. A preset charge is safe only if it is no more than the actual, reasonable cost when the tenancy ends, so itemize what you actually spent or would reasonably spend. Withholding more risks paying the tenant twice the amount wrongly withheld plus attorney's fees.

That a preset figure exceeding the actual reasonable cost may not be withheld is an inference from (b) and (h); case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: A security deposit refund you owe a former tenant but can't deliver, for example because the check was never cashed or the tenant can't be found, does not become yours. Rhode Island's unclaimed property act lists security deposits and refunds expressly. If you hold the money in the ordinary course of your rental business and it stays unclaimed for more than three years after it became payable, it is presumed abandoned, whether or not the tenant ever asked for it. You must then report it to the General Treasurer before November 1 each year, as of the previous June 30, and pay it over. For a refund of $50 or more, first send the tenant written notice at their last known address no more than 120 days before you file. Don't put a lease term saying an unclaimed deposit becomes yours: the deposit statute bars waivers. Keep records showing you sent the refund within 20 days.

title: Paying the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Rhode Island gives tenants no right to pay the security deposit in installments, so you may require it in full before move-in. You may agree to installments; if you do, put the schedule in writing. Every installment is part of the security deposit: the total of all installments can't exceed one month's rent, whatever you call the payments, and at the end of the tenancy the refund and 20-day itemization rules apply to everything the tenant paid toward it.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute addresses collecting the last month's rent in advance, or a tenant using the security deposit as the last month's rent. The act treats prepaid rent and the security deposit as separate things: a security deposit is money given at the start of the tenancy as a deposit against physical damage to the unit, capped at one month's rent however you label it, while prepaid rent is rent paid ahead of time. If you collect last month's rent up front, call it prepaid rent in the lease, apply it to the last month, and don't hold it back for damage; money that works as security could be counted toward the deposit cap. Prepaid rent must be returned when the tenancy ends early in the statute's listed cases: your failure to deliver possession, termination for your noncompliance, fire or casualty, unlawful ouster or cut-off of services, a servicemember's termination (within 30 days), and, since July 1, 2026, termination by a survivor of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. Nothing in the act lets a tenant skip the last month's rent because you hold a deposit.

L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1, effective July 1, 2026): 'Security deposit' means 'a sum of money given by a tenant to a landlord at the outset of the tenancy or shortly thereafter, as a deposit against physical damages to the tenant’s dwelling unit during said tenancy'. § 34-18-19(a): no security deposit 'however denominated' above 'one month’s periodic rent'. Prepaid rent kept separate: § 34-18-28(d) ('the landlord shall return all security recoverable by the tenant under § 34-18-19 and all prepaid rent' (§ 34-18-28(d))), § 34-18-33(b) ('the landlord shall return all security recoverable under § 34-18-19 and all prepaid rent' (§ 34-18-33(b))), § 34-18-29(a)(1) ('the landlord shall return all prepaid rent and security'), § 34-18-34; § 34-18-15(f)(5) servicemember: 'Rents or lease amounts paid in advance for a period after the effective date of the termination of the lease shall be refunded to the lessee' within thirty (30) days; § 34-18-63(e) (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws) refund of 'prepaid rent for any period thereafter'. Whether money labelled last month's rent but held as security counts toward the cap is not settled by the text; case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Conditions on the Deposit Refund
bodyText: Rhode Island does not let you make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out, and the deposit statute bars lease terms that waive its rules. The refund clock starts on the latest of three dates: the end of the tenancy, the tenant's delivery of possession, or the tenant's giving you a forwarding address for the refund. Within 20 days after that date, deliver the refund with a written itemized notice of any deductions. A tenant who hasn't given a forwarding address delays the deadline but doesn't lose the deposit. Failing to comply exposes you to twice the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees. A periodic tenant still owes you the statutory notice to end the tenancy, but that is a separate duty: an unpaid rent claim can be deducted, a missing notice can't forfeit the deposit.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no rule letting a lease condition the deposit refund on advance notice of surrender). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(b): the landlord 'shall deliver the notice, together with the amount of the security deposit due to the tenant, within twenty (20) days after the later of either termination of the tenancy, delivery of possession, or the tenant’s providing the landlord with a forwarding address for the purpose of receiving the security deposit'; (c) 'twice the amount wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney fees'; (h) 'No rental agreement shall contain any waiver of the provisions of this section.' The ordinary notice to end a periodic tenancy (§ 34-18-37) is a separate duty, not a refund condition. That a lease condition of this kind is void rests on § 34-18-19(h); case law not searched. title: Deposit After a Survivor Termination
bodyText: Since July 1, 2026, a tenant who ends the lease early because they or a household member were a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking (with the written verification the statute requires) gets a deposit refund under the normal deposit rules, plus any rent prepaid for the period after termination, as long as they turn over full possession without damage. The tenant must move out within 30 days of the notice unless you agree on another time, and owes rent only through the termination date or the move-out date, whichever is later; you may deduct that unpaid rent and the usual deposit items. Within 20 days after the tenancy ends, give the tenant a full and specific written statement of the basis for keeping any of the deposit or prepaid rent, with any refund. The deposit deductions don't include fees, so don't deduct a lock-change fee. If co-tenants stay, the statute doesn't say when this tenant's tenancy concludes; get advice before holding the departing tenant's share. These rights can't be waived.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-63 (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws), read in full. (c): 'The tenant who has given notice shall vacate the premises within thirty (30) days of giving notice to the landlord or at any other time as may be agreed upon by the landlord and the tenant.' (d): liable only 'for rent owed through the date of termination or the date the tenant actually vacates the premises, whichever is later.' (e): 'A tenant who terminates a lease or rental agreement pursuant to this section shall be entitled to a refund of any security deposit in compliance with § 34-18-19 or prepaid rent for any period thereafter, so long as full possession is turned over to the landlord absent any damage. The tenant shall receive a full and specific statement of the basis for retaining any of the security deposit or prepaid rent together with any refund due in compliance with § 34-18-19 and within twenty (20) days of the conclusion of the tenancy.' (f) good-faith actions against a remaining tenant are not retaliation. § 34-18-67 (same act): 'A waiver of §§ 34-18-63 through 34-18-65, shall be void and unenforceable.' § 34-18-19(b): deductions limited to 'unpaid accrued rent', 'reasonable cleaning expenses', 'reasonable trash disposal expenses' and physical damage beyond ordinary wear and tear; (c) double damages. That a § 34-18-65(d) lock-change fee cannot be deducted rests on the list in § 34-18-19(b); when 'the conclusion of the tenancy' falls where a co-tenant stays is not settled by the text. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Returning the Deposit Early
bodyText: Rhode Island has no expedited security deposit procedure. Your deadline is 20 days after the latest of the end of the tenancy, the tenant's delivery of possession, or the tenant's forwarding address, and you may always return the deposit sooner. You may not charge an administrative, processing or accounting fee for doing so, or deduct one from the deposit: the statute lists the only deductions (unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning, reasonable trash disposal and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear), and a lease can't add to them.

R.I. Gen. That an administrative fee may not be deducted rests on (b)'s list. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Fees Instead of a Deposit
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute authorizes or regulates a monthly fee, surety bond or insurance product that a tenant pays instead of a security deposit, and the library does not offer one. If you use such a program, two rules apply. Any fee the tenant pays is a fee beyond rent, so it must be listed in the rent section of the lease with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it. And money that works as security for damage, whatever you call it, can count as a security deposit, which is capped at one month's rent in total. Deposit-replacement products sold by third parties may be insurance; check that the provider is properly licensed before offering one.

title: Holding Deposits
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute addresses a holding deposit or other money taken from an applicant before the lease is signed. Two rules shape what is safe. You may not require an applicant to pay a rental application fee; you may charge only the actual cost of a state criminal background check or credit report the applicant doesn't supply. A nonrefundable payment to apply for or hold a unit risks being treated as the application fee the statute bans, so the library offers no holding-fee clause. If you take a refundable holding deposit, put in writing how long you will hold the unit and that you will refund it in full if you or the applicant don't go ahead. Once the lease is signed, money you keep as security counts toward the one-month deposit cap, and money applied to rent is rent.

title: No Inspection Notice Penalty
bodyText: Rhode Island has no inspection-notice duty, so there is no penalty, such as losing the right to deduct for damage, for not offering a move-in or move-out inspection or not telling the tenant about one. The deposit penalty that does apply is tied to the refund itself: if you don't deliver the itemized notice and any refund within 20 days after the latest of the end of the tenancy, delivery of possession or the tenant's forwarding address, or you withhold more than the law allows, the tenant can recover the amount due plus twice the amount wrongfully withheld and attorney's fees. Separately, where the unit's water service line is found to contain lead and you decline or don't respond to the tenant's request to replace it, then refuse or fail to respond within 60 days to a second request, the tenant may end the lease, and you can't withhold the deposit because the tenant used that right.

Rhode Island has no move-in or move-out inspection notice duty (see edu-no-move-in-inspection-rule-ri: RI-condition-inspection-1 (hits 20, OK) and RI-condition-inspection-3 (hits 16, OK)), so no penalty attaches to one. Gen. title: No Nonrefundable Deposits
bodyText: Rhode Island has no notice procedure for a nonrefundable deposit, because the law leaves no room for one. Any money you take as security, whatever you call it, counts toward the one-month deposit cap, and at the end of the tenancy the tenant is owed the entire amount minus only unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning, reasonable trash disposal and physical damage beyond ordinary wear and tear caused by the tenant's breach of their duties, itemized in writing within 20 days. A lease cannot waive these rules, and wrongfully keeping deposit money costs you the amount plus twice what you withheld and the tenant's attorney fees. A separately stated fee is a different thing: no statute bars a nonrefundable move-in or pet fee as such, but every fee beyond rent must be listed in the rent section of the lease with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it. You may not charge an application fee at all. Case law on disguised deposits was not searched.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no nonrefundable-deposit notice rule; the deposit rules leave no room for a nonrefundable deposit). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(a): 'A landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month’s periodic rent.' § 34-18-19(b): the deposit due is 'the entire amount given by the tenant as a security deposit, minus any amount of unpaid accrued rent, the amount due, if any, for reasonable cleaning expenses, the amount due, if any, for reasonable trash disposal expenses and the amount of physical damages to the premises, other than ordinary wear and tear, that the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant’s noncompliance with § 34-18-24', itemized and delivered 'within twenty (20) days'. § 34-18-19(c): 'damages in an amount equal to twice the amount wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney fees.' § 34-18-19(h): 'No rental agreement shall contain any waiver of the provisions of this section.' A security deposit is money given 'at the outset of the tenancy or shortly thereafter, as a deposit against physical damages to the tenant’s dwelling unit during said tenancy' (§ 34-18-11(16), renumbered (19) by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, effective July 1, 2026). Fees: § 34-18-15(a)(1) ('the lease shall disclose those fees in the same section as the rent disclosure and shall indicate that additional fees may apply'), (a)(5) undisclosed fees recoverable; § 34-18-59(a) no rental application fee. title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule requiring a separate written notice, at the time you collect a deposit, that part of it is nonrefundable. That is because no part of a Rhode Island security deposit can be made nonrefundable: whatever you call the money, it counts toward the one-month cap and must be returned within 20 days minus only the deductions the deposit law lists, and a lease cannot waive that. Don't hand a tenant a notice or receipt calling any part of a deposit nonrefundable. If you charge a separate fee, the notice that matters is in the lease itself: list every fee beyond rent in the rent section, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it. Case law was not searched.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent. No separate collection-time notice rule for a nonrefundable deposit; see `edu-no-nonrefundable-deposit-ri` for why RI allows none. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(a): 'A landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month’s periodic rent.' § 34-18-19(b) (deposit due is 'the entire amount given by the tenant as a security deposit' minus the listed deductions, within 'twenty (20) days'); (h) 'No rental agreement shall contain any waiver of the provisions of this section.' § 34-18-15(a)(1): 'the lease shall disclose those fees in the same section as the rent disclosure and shall indicate that additional fees may apply'; (a)(5) undisclosed fees recoverable. Searches over the General Laws, Constitution, loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws and court rules: RI-nonrefundable-deposit-1 (hits 2, OK) and RI-nonrefundable-deposit-2 (no context limb; hits 10, OK), synthetic positives (including a separate written notice that a portion of the deposit is nonrefundable) passed; none on point. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText: You may not ask for or accept a security deposit of more than one month's rent. The limit covers every deposit together, whatever you call it (damage, pet, key or anything else, refundable or not), and a lease cannot waive it. The cap is stated in months, not rental periods, so for a week-to-week roomer it is a month's worth of rent, not one week's. Two exceptions: if you rent a furnished unit whose furniture has a replacement value of $5,000 or more when the lease is signed, you may also take a separate furniture deposit of up to one month's rent; and a restoration escrow you negotiate with a tenant with a disability for a reasonable modification does not count toward the cap. You may not charge a tenant with a disability extra, such as a pet deposit, for a guide dog or other trained personal assistive animal (the tenant remains liable for damage it causes); other assistance animals approved as a reasonable accommodation should not carry a pet deposit either (see the assistance-animal row). When a tenant dies and an adult resident or live-in caregiver continues the tenancy for the post-death grace period, you may not require that person to pay an additional deposit. The statute does not say whether you may top up a deposit after a rent increase. Mobile home rentals by a licensed park have their own one-month limit.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(a): 'A landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month’s periodic rent.' § 34-18-19(e): a separate furniture deposit 'if the replacement value of the furniture being furnished by the landlord valued at the time the lease is executed is five thousand dollars ($5,000) or greater, in which instance the landlord may charge a separate furniture security deposit of up to one month’s periodic rent.' § 34-18-19(h): 'No rental agreement shall contain any waiver of the provisions of this section.' Restoration escrow: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-37-4(d): 'The restoration deposition shall be exempt from § 34-18-19(a) but will be subject to § 34-18-19(b) through (f) inclusive.' Assistance animals: § 34-37-4(e)(2) a person with a disability 'shall not be required to pay extra compensation for the guide dog or other personal assistive animal but shall be liable for any damage done to the premises'. Post-death grace period: § 34-18-38(d)(10): 'the landlord shall not have the right to require an additional security deposit from the grace period temporary tenant.' Mobile homes: R.I. Gen. Laws § 31-44-7.1(2): 'No deposit will be required which is more than the amount of one month’s rent.' Chapter 34-18 excludes the arrangements listed in § 34-18-8 (institutions, contract-of-sale occupancy, fraternal housing, taxed transient lodging, certain employee housing, cooperatives, ch. 34-18.1 lettings, transitional housing) unless the parties agree to it. Week-to-week reading: § 34-18-19(a) counts 'one month’s periodic rent', not one rental period; DRAFTING JUDGMENT, no conversion rule in the text. Top-up after a rent increase: not addressed (RI-deposit-cap-2 found only § 34-18-38(d)(10) and § 6-51-3 retail installment cure).
