title: Where to Keep the Deposit
bodyText: Rhode Island's landlord-tenant act does not tell you where to keep a security deposit: it requires no escrow, trust or separate account, no particular bank, and no notice to the tenant of where the money is held. What it does require is that you return the full deposit, minus the listed deductions, within 20 days, and whoever owns the property when the tenancy ends is bound by that, so keeping the money separate and traceable is the sensible course. Three narrower rules apply. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson receives the deposit, it must go into the firm's escrow account at a federally insured institution in Rhode Island, kept apart from the broker's own funds. A mobile home park licensee renting a mobile home must keep deposits in an earmarked savings account. A restoration deposit you negotiate with a tenant with a disability for a reasonable modification goes into an interest-bearing escrow account, with the interest belonging to the tenant. Since June 19, 2026 a bank account may be set up as a 'special deposit' for tenant security deposits, but this is optional.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent for ordinary residential tenancies (no holding, escrow, bank or depository-notice rule in ch. 34-18). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(b) (refund 'within twenty (20) days'); (g): 'the holder of the landlord’s interest in the premises at the time of the termination of the tenancy is bound by this section.' Brokers: § 5-20.5-26(a)(1)(i): 'All those funds paid to a salesperson or paid directly to a broker shall be segregated on the broker’s books and deposited in an account in a recognized federally insured financial institution in Rhode Island separate from any account containing funds owned by the broker.' (ch. 5-20.5 reaches leases; Department of Business Regulation escrow rules not searched). Mobile homes: § 31-44-7.1(7): 'Any security deposits received by the licensee shall be deposited in a savings account and earmarked specifically as a security deposit account'. Restoration escrow: § 34-37-4(d) ('an interest bearing escrow account'; 'The interest in the account shall accrue to the benefit of the tenant.'). Special deposits: R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 202, 203, § 1 (adds ch. 19-35, Uniform Special Deposits Act, effective on passage, enacted June 19, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): a permissible purpose includes holding funds 'As a security deposit of a tenant' (§ 19-35-2(10)(i)(B)); the chapter applies only to an account agreement that 'states the intention of the parties to establish a special deposit governed by this chapter' (§ 19-35-3(a)). Searches over the General Laws, Constitution, loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws and court rules: lead's RI-deposit-escrow-1 (hits 9, OK); RI-deposit-holding-1 (escrow/trust/separate/segregated/savings/interest-bearing/bank account, commingle, earmarked near security deposit/tenant/lessee/resident/rental/lease; hits 24, OK, real positives § 31-44-7.1 and § 34-37-4 passed); RI-deposit-holding-2 recorded as failed (real positive § 31-44-7.1 missed), rerun as RI-deposit-holding-3 (hold/keep/place the deposit in/with/at, deposits shall be held/kept/placed/deposited, no context limb; hits 17, OK, real positive § 31-44-7.1 and synthetic positives passed). Only §§ 31-44-7.1, 5-20.5-26 and 34-37-4 are on point. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (ch. 19-35 read for the definitions and scope sections only).

title: No Interest on Deposits
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to pay interest on a residential security deposit or to hold it in an interest-bearing account. At the end of the tenancy you owe back the amount the tenant gave you, minus the deductions the deposit law lists. Two exceptions. A mobile home park licensee that rents a mobile home and takes a security deposit must pay the resident 3% interest a year, annually or when the rental ends, and is liable for up to three times the interest due if it doesn't. And if you negotiate a restoration deposit with a tenant with a disability as a condition of a reasonable modification, it goes into an interest-bearing escrow account and the interest belongs to the tenant. A lease may promise interest if you choose, but nothing requires it.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent for ordinary residential tenancies. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(b): the deposit due is 'the entire amount given by the tenant as a security deposit' minus the listed deductions; no interest term in § 34-18-19. Mobile homes: § 31-44-7.1(1): 'The deposit shall accumulate interest on an annual basis at the rate of three percent (3%).' (3) 'The interest shall be paid to the resident annually or upon termination of the rental.' (6) liability 'not to exceed twice the amount of the deposit and three (3) times the amount of interest due.' Restoration escrow: § 34-37-4(d) ('an interest bearing escrow account'; 'The interest in the account shall accrue to the benefit of the tenant.'). Searches over the General Laws, Constitution, loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws and court rules: lead's RI-deposit-interest-1 (context limb tenant/landlord/lessee/lessor; hits 1, OK; cannot reach § 31-44-7.1, which says licensee/resident); RI-deposit-interest-2 recorded as failed, rerun as RI-deposit-interest-4; RI-deposit-interest-3 recorded as failed, rerun as RI-deposit-interest-4; RI-deposit-interest-4 (interest within 200 characters of security/damage/rental/tenant/restoration deposit, accumulate interest, interest-bearing escrow, no context limb; hits 5, OK, real positives § 31-44-7.1 and § 34-37-4 and synthetic positives passed; others off point: § 31-44-9.1 rent escrow, § 45-47-3 insurance proceeds, § 34-18-19 'interest in the premises'). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: No Rhode Island lease may waive any part of the security deposit law: the one-month cap, the separate furniture deposit limit, the closed list of deductions, the 20-day itemized refund, the tenant's right to twice the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney fees, and the rule that a new owner is bound. A lease term that tries is unenforceable, so terms such as "the deposit is forfeited if Tenant leaves early", "a cleaning charge of $X will be deducted in every case" or "Tenant waives the 20-day deadline" won't hold. Using such a term can also cost you: if you deliberately use a lease containing provisions you know are prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. You and a tenant can still agree after move-out on how a disputed deduction is settled.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(h): 'No rental agreement shall contain any waiver of the provisions of this section.' § 34-18-17(a)(1): a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under this chapter'; (b): 'A provision prohibited by subsection (a) included in a rental agreement is unenforceable. If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known to be prohibited, the tenant may recover, in addition to his or her actual damages, an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney’s fees.' Rights listed from § 34-18-19(a)-(g) (cap, furniture deposit, deductions, 20-day itemized refund, 'twice the amount wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney fees', transferee bound). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: that a post-tenancy settlement of a disputed deduction is not a 'rental agreement' term is an inference from § 34-18-19(h) and § 34-18-17(a) (both speak of the rental agreement); 'Rental agreement' includes all agreements 'embodying the terms and conditions concerning the use and occupancy of a dwelling unit' (§ 34-18-11(14), renumbered (17) by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, effective July 1, 2026). Example lease terms in double quotes are illustrations, not library text. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: If you transfer your interest in a rented property, whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by Rhode Island's deposit rules, so a buyer should expect to owe the full refund and 20-day itemization even if the seller never handed the money over. No statute requires the seller to transfer deposits to the buyer, so transfer them, or credit them at closing, and tell the tenant who now holds the deposit. As seller, you are released from liability under the lease and the landlord-tenant act only for events after you give the tenant written notice of a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser, never earlier than the conveyance itself. The notice must give the buyer's name, address and telephone number and certify that you complied with the housing code rule requiring outstanding violations to be corrected, or violation notices passed to the buyer and the enforcing officer, before a sale. A departing manager is released the same way after written notice naming who takes over. In a building of four or fewer units, a buyer (other than a third-party bona fide purchaser) or a successor to a mortgagor takes title with the same duties to the tenant the seller had.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(g): 'In the event the landlord transfers his or her interest in the premises, the holder of the landlord’s interest in the premises at the time of the termination of the tenancy is bound by this section.' § 34-18-23(a)(1): a landlord who conveys premises 'in a good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the rental agreement and this chapter as to events occurring after written notice to the tenant of the conveyance. In no event may the relief from liability predate the conveyance itself.' (a)(2): the notice 'must include the name(s), address, and telephone number of the person or persons purchasing the property and assuming liability' and 'must also certify compliance with § 45-24.3-17'. § 45-24.3-17(j): unlawful for an owner served with a notice of violation or order 'to sell, transfer, mortgage, lease, or dispose of the building to another until the provisions of the notice or order have been complied with or until the owner first furnishes to the grantee' a true copy and notifies the enforcing officer in writing (cross-reference checked: § 34-18-23(a)(2) points to the right section). § 34-18-23(b) (manager released after written notice naming the person assuming management); (c): 'the purchaser of property or any immediate successor in interest to a mortgagor, other than a third-party, bona fide purchaser, of a premises containing four (4) or fewer dwelling units takes title subject to the same rights and responsibilities toward the tenant that the seller or mortgagor had.' DRAFTING JUDGMENT: that the buyer owes the refund whether or not it received the money, and that a seller who gave proper notice is not liable for a refund falling due later, are readings of §§ 34-18-19(g) and 34-18-23(a)(1); case law not searched. No deposit-transfer duty: RI-deposit-on-sale-1, -2, -3 recorded as failed (real positive missed or mis-specified), rerun as RI-deposit-on-sale-4 (transfer/convey/sale of interest or premises, successor in interest, new owner, purchaser/grantee/transferee near deposit; hits 15, OK, real positive § 34-18-19 and synthetic positive passed; none on point). Foreclosing owners: §§ 34-18-38.1, 34-18-38.2 contain no deposit rule (screened by grep, not read in full for this row). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Penalty for Mishandling the Deposit
bodyText: If you don't return the deposit, minus only the deductions the law allows, with a written itemized notice within 20 days after the later of the end of the tenancy, the tenant's return of possession, or the tenant giving you a forwarding address, the tenant can sue for the amount due plus damages equal to twice the amount you wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney fees. So withholding $500 you weren't entitled to keep can cost you $1,500 plus the tenant's lawyer. The statute requires no showing of bad faith, and it can apply to a late or missing itemized notice, not only to an improper deduction. A lease term that waives any of this is unenforceable, and deliberately using a lease with terms you know are prohibited adds actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. You keep your own claims: if the damage exceeds the deposit, you may sue for the rest. Mobile home park licensees renting a mobile home face a different penalty: up to twice the deposit and three times the interest due.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(c): 'If the landlord fails to comply with subsection (b), the tenant may recover the amount due him or her, together with damages in an amount equal to twice the amount wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney fees.' § 34-18-19(b): itemized notice and refund 'within twenty (20) days after the later of either termination of the tenancy, delivery of possession, or the tenant’s providing the landlord with a forwarding address for the purpose of receiving the security deposit.' § 34-18-19(d): 'This section does not preclude the landlord or tenant from recovering other damages to which he or she may be entitled under this chapter.' § 34-18-19(h) (no waiver); § 34-18-17(b) ('an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney’s fees'). Mobile homes: § 31-44-7.1(6) ('liable for damages not to exceed twice the amount of the deposit and three (3) times the amount of interest due'). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: "no showing of bad faith" and "can apply to a late or missing itemized notice" read § 34-18-19(c) ('fails to comply with subsection (b)'); how courts measure 'the amount wrongfully withheld' where only the notice was late is case law, not searched. The $500 example is arithmetic on § 34-18-19(c), assuming the whole $500 was wrongfully withheld. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Deposit Return Deadline and Itemization
bodyText: When the tenancy ends, return the deposit with a written notice itemizing every deduction within 20 days after the latest of three dates: the end of the tenancy, the tenant's return of possession, or the tenant giving you a forwarding address for the refund. You may deduct only unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning, reasonable trash disposal, and physical damage beyond ordinary wear and tear caused by the tenant's breach of their maintenance duties. A furniture deposit is returned on the same 20-day schedule, minus reasonable cleaning and repair and damage to the furniture beyond ordinary wear and tear. Deliver the notice by hand or first-class mail to the address the tenant gave you, or their last known residence, and keep proof. Late or improper handling exposes you to twice the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney fees. Special cases: if a tenant dies and an adult resident or caregiver continues under the post-death grace period, the balance goes to that person if the grace period runs more than one month and otherwise to the tenant's estate; and from July 1, 2026, a survivor of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking who ends the lease early under the survivor-termination law must get the refund and a full and specific statement of any amount kept within 20 days of the end of the tenancy, a clock that does not wait for a forwarding address.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(b): the amount due is 'the entire amount given by the tenant as a security deposit, minus any amount of unpaid accrued rent, the amount due, if any, for reasonable cleaning expenses, the amount due, if any, for reasonable trash disposal expenses and the amount of physical damages to the premises, other than ordinary wear and tear, that the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant’s noncompliance with § 34-18-24, all as itemized by the landlord in a written notice delivered to the tenant. The landlord shall deliver the notice, together with the amount of the security deposit due to the tenant, within twenty (20) days after the later of either termination of the tenancy, delivery of possession, or the tenant’s providing the landlord with a forwarding address for the purpose of receiving the security deposit.' § 34-18-19(f) furniture deposit ('minus the amount due, if any, for reasonable cleaning expenses and repair and the amount of physical damages to the furniture, other than ordinary wear and tear'; same 20 days). § 34-18-19(c) (twice the amount wrongfully withheld and reasonable attorney fees). Delivery: § 34-18-14(b)(2): a notice is received when 'delivered in hand or sent by first class mail to him or her at a place held out by him or her as the place for receipt of the communication, or in the absence of such designation, to his or her last known place of residence.' Post-death: § 34-18-38(d)(10) ('If the duration of the post-death rental grace period exceeds one month, then the balance of the security deposit, net of damages deducted pursuant to § 34-18-19, shall be allocated to the grace period temporary tenant.'). Survivor termination: § 34-18-63(e) (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): 'The tenant shall receive a full and specific statement of the basis for retaining any of the security deposit or prepaid rent together with any refund due in compliance with § 34-18-19 and within twenty (20) days of the conclusion of the tenancy.' Two clocks (SOP rule 31): § 34-18-19(b) runs from the later of three events, § 34-18-63(e) from 'the conclusion of the tenancy'; for a survivor termination follow the shorter § 34-18-63(e) clock. See `edu-dv-deposit-timing-ri`. Tenant duties referenced: § 34-18-24(1)-(10). The base clause `security-deposit-return` (blank states) reads correctly for RI (refund "within the time period required by applicable law", itemized statement with the returned portion, forwarding address). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to post or disclose the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if you charge different tenants different deposits. Two limits still apply. Every deposit, however you label it, is capped at one month's rent (plus a separate furniture deposit of up to one month for furniture worth $5,000 or more). And Rhode Island's fair housing law bars discriminating in the terms or conditions of a rental, which includes the deposit you ask for, because of race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, lawful source of income, veteran or servicemember status, country of ancestral origin, disability, age, familial status, or a tenant's status as a victim of domestic abuse. Keep a written, neutral deposit policy and apply it the same way to everyone.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent. Searches over the General Laws, Constitution, loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws and court rules: RI-deposit-standards-1 (standards near deposit/security, post/disclose/furnish criteria/standards/policy, near tenant/landlord/lease/rental/dwelling/lessee/resident; hits 4, OK, synthetic positive passed; none on point: insurance and inmate testing) and RI-deposit-standards-2 (different/differing/varying/uniform amounts/deposits/standards/criteria, same amount for all, no context limb; hits 40, OK, synthetic positive passed; none on point: uniform-standards clauses in unrelated chapters). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(a), (e) (one-month cap; furniture deposit). Fair housing: § 34-37-4(a) bars an owner or agent from discriminating 'in the terms, conditions, or privileges of the sale, rental, or lease of any housing accommodation' on the listed bases, including 'lawful source of income' and domestic-abuse victim status; § 34-37-4(c) preserves standards and terms 'that do not discriminate'. Exemptions in ch. 34-37 (for example owner-occupied small buildings) not read for this row. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: What the Deposit Can Cover
bodyText: Rhode Island gives you a closed list of what you may keep from the deposit when the tenancy ends: unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning expenses, reasonable trash disposal expenses, and physical damage to the premises beyond ordinary wear and tear that you suffered because the tenant broke their maintenance duties. A lease cannot add to the list. Late fees, attorney's fees, utility charges and other fees are not on it, so pursue them separately rather than deducting them, unless a charge is genuinely rent for the use of the unit. Ordinary wear and tear includes deterioration caused by your own failure to prepare for expected conditions or to meet your obligations. The statute speaks only of applying the deposit when the tenancy ends; it does not provide for drawing on it, or requiring the tenant to top it up, during the tenancy. Special cases: during a post-death grace period you may deduct damage caused by the deceased tenant or the person continuing the tenancy; and if a tenant ends the lease because you refused, or failed to respond within 60 days to, a second request to replace a water service line found to contain lead, you may not withhold the deposit because of that termination.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(b): the deposit due is 'the entire amount given by the tenant as a security deposit, minus any amount of unpaid accrued rent, the amount due, if any, for reasonable cleaning expenses, the amount due, if any, for reasonable trash disposal expenses and the amount of physical damages to the premises, other than ordinary wear and tear, that the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant’s noncompliance with § 34-18-24'; (h) no waiver. 'Ordinary wear and tear' includes 'deterioration caused by the landlord’s failure to prepare for expected conditions or by the landlord’s failure to comply with his or her obligations' (§ 34-18-11(8), renumbered (11) by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, effective July 1, 2026). 'Rent' means 'the payment or consideration that a tenant pays to a landlord for the use of the premises' (§ 34-18-11(13), renumbered (16) July 1, 2026). Post-death: § 34-18-38(d)(10): 'The landlord shall have the right to deduct damages to the dwelling unit incurred by the deceased tenant or the grace period temporary tenant from a preexisting security deposit'. Lead service lines: § 23-24.6-28(o): 'Upon termination, the property owner may not withhold the tenant’s security deposit based upon the tenant’s exercise of their termination rights under this section.' Mid-tenancy use and top-up: not addressed; searches RI-deposit-use-1 recorded as failed (real positive § 34-18-38 missed), rerun as RI-deposit-use-2 (apply/use/deduct/retain/withhold within 150 characters of deposit, replenish, restore the deposit, near tenant/landlord/lease/rental/lessee/resident; hits 27, OK, real positives § 34-18-38 and § 23-24.6-28 and synthetic positive passed; on point only §§ 34-18-38, 23-24.6-28, 31-44-7.1 and § 34-18-63(e) in the 2026 acts). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: that late fees and other fees are not deductible rests on the closed list and the definition of rent; whether a recurring charge counts as rent is case law, not searched (see `edu-fees-as-rent-ri`). Renumbering checked against R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1 ((8) becomes (11); (13) becomes (16)). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Separate Utility Deposit
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule for a separate utility deposit held by a landlord, and the library offers none. Money you hold to secure the tenant's payments is a security deposit however you label it, so a "utility deposit" counts toward the one-month cap together with the security deposit. At the end of the tenancy the deposit law lets you keep only unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning, reasonable trash disposal and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear; unpaid utility charges the tenant owes you are not on that list unless they are part of the rent, so bill and collect them separately. If the tenant pays a utility company directly, any deposit the utility takes is between the tenant and the utility. Whatever the arrangement, the lease must say which utility costs are included in the rent and which the tenant pays.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no landlord-held utility deposit rule). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(a): 'A landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month’s periodic rent.' § 34-18-19(b) closed deduction list ('unpaid accrued rent', 'reasonable cleaning expenses', 'reasonable trash disposal expenses', physical damages 'other than ordinary wear and tear'). § 34-18-15(a)(3): 'In any lease agreement the landlord shall disclose which utility costs are included in the rent and which utility costs are the tenant’s responsibility.' Utility-held deposits appear only in the unclaimed property act, § 33-21.1-8 (a deposit 'made by a subscriber with a utility to secure payment'). title: Alterations Tenants May Make Without Your Consent
bodyText: Your lease may require your written consent before a tenant alters the unit, and a tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage or remove any part of the premises. But Rhode Island gives tenants some rights a lease can't take away. You may not refuse a tenant with a disability reasonable modifications, at the tenant's expense, needed for full enjoyment of the unit; where reasonable you may require restoration of the interior at move-out, and negotiate payments into an interest-bearing restoration escrow. A tenant may have repairs costing under $500 a year done and deduct the cost from rent if you fail to fix a code, habitability, facilities, trash or water and heat problem within 20 days of written notice. From July 1, 2026, if all tenants in possession (or a court order) ask you to change the locks because a tenant or adult household member reasonably believes they face an imminent threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking at the premises, and you don't within two business days, the tenant or household member may change them, in a workmanlike way with locks of similar or better quality (otherwise you may replace the lock or seek reimbursement). In a multiple dwelling, a tenant may choose their own cable, phone or internet provider, which may install its facilities at no cost to you; you can't charge tenants differently for their choice. A tenant may take on alterations or remodeling only by a signed written agreement for adequate consideration, and never work needed to cure a code violation.
notes: RI: Tenant duty: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-24(6) ('Not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair, or remove any part of the premises or knowingly permit any person to do so'). Disability: § 34-37-4(d) ('An owner may not refuse to allow a person with a disability to make, at his or her expense, reasonable modifications of existing premises occupied or to be occupied by the person if the modifications may be necessary to afford the person full enjoyment of the premises'; restoration 'reasonable wear and tear excepted'; 'an interest bearing escrow account'). Self-help: § 34-18-30(a) ('the reasonable cost of compliance is less than five hundred dollars ($500) in the aggregate per year'; landlord 'fails to comply within twenty (20) days'; covers § 34-18-22(a)(1), (2), (4), (5), (6)); (b) not for tenant-caused conditions. Locks: § 34-18-65(b), (d), (e) (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): 'within two (2) business days'; 'the tenant or household member may change the locks without the owner's permission'; locks 'of similar or better quality than the original locks'. Telecom: § 39-19-10 (a tenant 'shall have the freedom and right to select the provider of cable television, telephone, telecommunications, or information service to their living unit, without any restraints, limitations, or conditions imposed by a landlord'; provider installs 'at no cost to the landlord of the dwelling' and indemnifies; owner's compensation presumed 'one dollar ($1.00)' absent the notice process in (4)-(6); (8) unfair trade practice 'to discriminate in rental charges or other charges to tenants based on the tenants’ subscription'). Mobile home parks: § 39-19-10.1 (CATV). Written agreement: § 34-18-22(c) (tenant may 'perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, and remodeling' only by 'a writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration', not to cure § 34-18-22(a)(1) noncompliance). title: Pest Reporting and Treatment Cooperation
bodyText: [Optional.] Tenant will promptly tell Landlord if Tenant knows or reasonably suspects that the dwelling unit has bed bugs or another infestation of insects, rodents or other pests. Tenant will not unreasonably withhold consent to Landlord's entry, at reasonable times and after at least two days' notice except in an emergency, to inspect for and treat an infestation, and will follow the reasonable written preparation instructions of Landlord's pest control provider. Tenant will pay the cost of extermination when Rhode Island's housing code makes the occupant responsible for it. This section does not shift to Tenant any extermination the housing code makes Landlord's responsibility.
notes: RI: Optional; no RI bed bug statute (RI-bed-bug-1). Rests on R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-26(a) ('A tenant shall not unreasonably withhold consent to the landlord to enter into the dwelling unit in order to inspect the premises, make necessary or agreed repairs'), (c) ('at least two (2) days’ notice of his or her intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times'); § 34-18-24(1) (tenant complies with code obligations 'primarily imposed upon tenants'); § 45-24.3-6(i) (occupant responsible for extermination in a single-unit dwelling, or 'whenever his or her dwelling is the only one infected', except where infestation 'is caused by a failure of the owner to maintain a dwelling in a rodent-proof or reasonably insect-proof condition'; owner responsible 'Whenever infestation exists in two (2) or more of the dwelling units in any dwelling, or in the shared or public parts of any dwelling containing two (2) or more dwelling units'). The reporting and preparation duties are contract terms, not statutory duties. The last sentence keeps the clause from reading as a waiver (§ 34-18-17(a)(1)). Not offered as default. Local housing codes may be stricter; not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Who Handles Bed Bugs and Other Pests
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute specific to bed bugs. The state housing code divides responsibility for extermination of insects, rodents and other pests, and tenants must comply with code duties placed on them. The tenant is responsible in a single-unit dwelling, and in a multi-unit building when theirs is the only unit infested. You are responsible when two or more units, or the shared or public areas, are infested, and whenever the infestation comes from your failure to keep the building rodent-proof or reasonably insect-proof. You must also keep the premises fit and habitable, and you may not rent out a vacant unit that isn't clean and sanitary. A tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry to inspect and treat, but give at least two days' notice except in an emergency. A tenant who reports an infestation to code officials or asks you to fix it is protected from retaliation. Local codes may be stricter.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent for a bed-bug-specific statute; pest duties present in the housing code. R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-6(i): 'Every occupant of a dwelling containing a single dwelling unit and every occupant of a structure is responsible for the extermination of any insects, rodents, or other pests therein or on the premises. Every occupant of a dwelling unit, in a dwelling containing more than one dwelling unit, is responsible for this extermination whenever his or her dwelling is the only one infected. Notwithstanding the foregoing provisions of this subsection, whenever infestation is caused by a failure of the owner to maintain a dwelling in a rodent-proof or reasonably insect-proof condition, extermination is the responsibility of the owner. Whenever infestation exists in two (2) or more of the dwelling units in any dwelling, or in the shared or public parts of any dwelling containing two (2) or more dwelling units, extermination is the responsibility of the owner.' § 45-24.3-6(a): no owner shall 'let to another person, any vacant dwelling, dwelling unit, or structure unless it and the premises are clean, sanitary, fit for human occupancy'. § 45-24.3-4(a) applies the code to every dwelling portion of a building (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 327, 328 add a SAFE Units exemption; not read in full). § 34-18-24(1) (tenant complies with code obligations 'primarily imposed upon tenants'); § 34-18-22(a)(1), (2) (landlord code compliance and habitability); § 34-18-26(a), (c) (access; 'at least two (2) days’ notice'). Retaliation: § 34-18-46(a)(1)-(2) (retaliation for complaints to a code agency or to the landlord of a § 34-18-22 violation; see `edu-retaliation-ri`). Search: RI-bed-bug-1 (bed bugs/cimex/infestation/extermination/pest control/vermin/insects/rodents/roaches near tenant/landlord/lease/rental/dwelling/occupant/owner/premises; hits 31, OK, synthetic positive passed; on point only ch. 45-24.3 and § 31-44-7 for mobile home parks; others agricultural pests). Local housing codes not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (except § 34-18-46, relied on for one sentence; see edu-retaliation-ri).

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule requiring a tenant to tell you before leaving the unit empty in cold weather. What the law does allow is a lease term requiring the tenant to notify you of any anticipated absence of more than ten days, no later than the first day of the absence; the library's extended-absence clause uses it, and it protects pipes in winter as well as at any other time. During an absence of more than seven days you may enter without the tenant's consent if reasonably necessary to protect the property, for example to keep heat on or check for frozen pipes. If the tenant has actually moved out, the abandonment rules apply instead.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-27: 'The rental agreement may require that the tenant notify the landlord of any anticipated extended absence from the premises in excess of ten (10) days no later than the first day of the extended absence.' § 34-18-26(b): 'A landlord may enter the dwelling unit without consent of the tenant in case of emergency, or, during any absence of the tenant in excess of seven (7) days, if reasonably necessary for the protection of the property.' Abandonment: § 34-18-40 (not reread for this row; see the lead's ch. 34-18 read). title: Common-Area Lighting
bodyText: Rhode Island's housing code requires every dwelling unit and all public and common areas to have properly installed, working electric service, outlets and fixtures where power lines are within 300 feet, and every public hall must have at least one ceiling or wall light fixture, with switches placed so the area ahead can be lit. In a building with four or more units, every public hall and stairway must be lit, by daylight or electric light, at all times, to at least six footcandles at floor or tread level. In a building with three or fewer units, switch-controlled lighting that can be turned on when needed is enough. You must also keep all common areas clean and safe. No state statute addresses common-area lights wired to a tenant's meter, but the lease must say which utility costs are included in the rent and which the tenant pays, so disclose any such arrangement there or the tenant may recover the undisclosed charges. Local codes may be stricter.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-8(a) (no person shall 'let to another for occupancy, any dwelling or dwelling unit' that doesn't comply); (e): 'every dwelling unit, and all public and common areas, must be supplied with electric service, outlets and fixtures which are properly installed, maintained in good and safe working condition'; (e)(3) every 'public hall must contain at least one supplied ceiling, or wall, electric light fixture'; (e)(4) switches 'located so as to permit the area ahead to be lighted'; (e)(5): 'Every public hall and stairway in every multiple dwelling must be adequately lighted by natural or electric light at all times to provide in all parts at least six (6) footcandles of light at the tread or floor level. Every public hall and stairway, in structures containing not more than three (3) dwelling units, may be supplied with conveniently located light switches, controlling an adequate lighting system which may be turned on when needed, instead of full time lighting.' § 45-24.3-5(25): '“Multiple dwelling” means any dwelling containing four (4) or more dwelling units.' § 34-18-22(a)(3): 'Keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition'. § 34-18-15(a)(3) (utility disclosure), (a)(5) (undisclosed fees recoverable). Tenant-meter wiring: RI-common-lighting-2 (meter/electric service/utility service/utility bill within 150 characters of common/public/shared area/hall/part/space, no context limb; hits 1, OK, real positive § 45-24.3-8 and synthetic positive passed; no tenant-meter rule). RI-common-lighting-1 (lighting/illuminate/lamps near stairs/halls/common/public areas/entrance/exit/corridor; hits 298, OK; too broad to read, superseded by the chapter read of ch. 45-24.3 §§ 5-16 for lighting terms). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: whether a common-area electricity charge is a 'fee' under § 34-18-15(a)(1)/(5) or a utility cost under (a)(3) is not settled by the text; either way it must be disclosed. Local codes not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Liens for Tenant Work
bodyText: [Optional.] Tenant will pay in full everyone Tenant hires, or whose work or materials Tenant orders, for any construction, alteration or repair at the property, and will not allow a mechanic's lien to be filed against the property for that work. If a lien is filed because of work Tenant ordered, Tenant will have it released or discharged within [number] days after Tenant learns of it. Any consent Landlord gives to an alteration under this Lease is consent only as between Landlord and Tenant; it is not Landlord's written assent to subjecting Landlord's interest in the property to liens for that work, and Landlord gives no such assent unless it is in a separate writing signed by Landlord that says so.
notes: RI: Optional; never default. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-28-2: for work done 'by oral or written contract with or at the oral or written request of any lessee or tenant', the tenant’s interest is subject to liens, 'but not the interest or title of the landlord of such lessee or tenant, unless the consent in writing of the landlord is first obtained, assenting to the construction, erection, alteration, or reparation.' The shared `no-alterations` clause requires "the prior written consent of Landlord" for alterations, and that written consent could be read as the landlord’s assent under § 34-28-2. DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the last sentence tries to keep an alteration consent from being § 34-28-2 assent; the statute doesn't say whether a lease promise defeats assent where the consent plainly approves the construction (case law not searched), so the education row tells landlords not to rely on it alone. The tenant payment and release promises are contract terms; they are not an indemnity of the landlord for the landlord’s own liability (§ 34-18-17(a)(4)). A contractor contracting directly with a tenant can claim a lien only after giving the § 34-28-4.1 notice of possible mechanic’s lien. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Liens for Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText: In Rhode Island, when a tenant orders construction, alterations or repairs, the contractors' and suppliers' mechanic's liens reach the tenant's interest in the building and land, but not yours, unless you first gave written consent assenting to that work. That makes your written approval of a tenant's alteration risky: it may be the very consent that lets a contractor lien your property if the tenant doesn't pay. Before approving work in writing, require proof that the tenant has paid or will pay the contractor, a lien waiver, or a separate written statement that you do not assent to liens on your interest; the library's optional no-liens clause adds a lease promise along those lines, but the statute doesn't say what effect such a promise has (case law was not searched). A contractor dealing directly with a tenant must give the tenant a written notice of possible mechanic's lien before starting work, or lose its own lien right. Work you order yourself, including repairs you make on a tenant's request, can lien your interest in the ordinary way.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-28-2: the tenant’s interest 'shall stand subject to liens for all the work done by any person in the construction, erection, alteration, or reparation' ordered by a lessee or tenant, 'but not the interest or title of the landlord of such lessee or tenant, unless the consent in writing of the landlord is first obtained, assenting to the construction, erection, alteration, or reparation.' § 34-28-4.1: no direct contractor 'shall be entitled to claim a lien under this chapter unless that person shall have provided the following notice to the owner, lessee, or tenant', in the contract or 'by certified mail, return receipt requested, any time prior to commencing work'; material suppliers excepted; other claimants unaffected. DRAFTING JUDGMENT: that a lease-based written consent to alterations can be § 34-28-2 assent is a reading of the text; case law not searched. Lien procedure (§§ 34-28-1, -4 through -17) not read. Search: RI-construction-liens-1 (mechanic/construction lien, lien for work, lien against the interest of the landlord/lessor/owner, near tenant/lessee/landlord/lessor/lease; hits 10, OK, real positive § 34-28-2 and synthetic positive passed; all hits in ch. 34-28; no 2025-2026 act amends ch. 34-28). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Enforcing Against Disturbances
bodyText: Every Rhode Island tenant must behave, and make anyone on the premises with their consent behave, so as not to disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises; that duty applies whether or not the lease repeats it. The termination process below is open for a material breach of the lease, or for a breach of the statutory duty that materially affects health and safety, so keep the lease's no-disturbance term: it lets you act on a material disturbance that doesn't threaten health or safety. To enforce it, give a written demand notice in the statutory form describing the conduct and what will cure it; if the tenant doesn't cure within 20 days of mailing, the tenancy ends on the date you name, at least 21 days after mailing, and you may file for eviction the next day. If substantially the same disturbance recurs within six months of a good-faith notice, you may terminate on at least 20 days' written notice with no chance to cure. For a seasonal tenant under a written lease within the statute's summer (May 1 to October 15) or academic-year (September 1 to June 1) windows with no renewal right, who has been charged with a municipal ordinance violation or has broken a lease term on excessive noise or disturbance of the peace, you may file for eviction immediately without a notice. You may also recover actual damages and seek an injunction, plus attorney's fees if the breach is willful.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-24(7): a tenant shall 'Conduct himself or herself, and require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves, in a manner that will not disturb his or her neighbors’ peaceful enjoyment of the premises'. § 34-18-36(a)(3): 'unless the breach is remedied within twenty (20) days of mailing of the notice the rental agreement shall terminate upon a specified date, which shall not be less than twenty-one (21) days after the mailing of the notice'; (a) notice 'in a form substantially similar to that provided in § 34-18-56(b)'; (b) suit 'no earlier than the first day following the termination date'; (d) 'actual damages and obtain injunctive relief'; 'If the tenant’s noncompliance is willful, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney’s fees.'; (e): 'recurs within six (6) months, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement upon at least twenty (20) days’ written notice' and 'No allowance of time to remedy noncompliance shall be required.'; (f) seasonal tenant whose written lease 'commences no earlier than May 1st of the occupation year and expires no later than October 15th of the occupation year, or commences no earlier than September 1st and expires no later than June 1st of the next subsequent year, with no right of renewal or extension' and who 'has been charged with violating a municipal ordinance or has otherwise violated the terms of the rental agreement pertaining to legal occupancy or excessive noise or other disturbance of the peace': no notice of noncompliance required. DRAFTING JUDGMENT: § 34-18-36(a) requires a 'material noncompliance' with the lease or a § 34-18-24 noncompliance 'materially affecting health and safety'; whether a given disturbance qualifies is for the court; case law not searched. Fair housing: § 34-37-4(n) preserves eviction for § 34-18-24(7) noncompliance (read). The shared `no-disturbance` clause reads correctly for RI. Drug, drug-dealing and violent-crime breaches (§ 34-18-24(8)-(10)) are covered in `edu-nuisance-ri`. § 34-18-56(b) form not reread. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Move-In Condition and Your Repair Duties
bodyText: A tenant's signed acknowledgment that the unit is in good order is useful evidence, especially in a later deposit dispute, but in Rhode Island it cannot relieve you of your repair duties. You must comply with building and housing codes affecting health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable throughout the tenancy, and no lease may let you collect rent free of those obligations or have the tenant waive them. You may not rent out a vacant unit unless it and the premises are clean, sanitary, fit for human occupancy and code-compliant. Before signing any lease, tell the prospective tenant about any outstanding minimum housing code violations on the building, and note them in the lease's exceptions. If you are cited later, give each affected tenant a copy of the violation notice within 30 days unless you correct everything within that time. Rhode Island does not require a move-in inspection or checklist, but a dated, itemized condition record with photos is your best proof when you deduct for damage.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(a)(1), (2) (comply with codes 'affecting health and safety'; 'Make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition'). § 34-18-18: 'A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed, or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with § 34-18-22(a).' § 34-18-17(a)(1) (no waiver of chapter rights). § 45-24.3-6(a): 'No owner or operator or other person shall occupy, or let to another person, any vacant dwelling, dwelling unit, or structure unless it and the premises are clean, sanitary, fit for human occupancy, and comply with this chapter'. § 34-18-22.1(b): 'A landlord, prior to entering into any residential rental agreement, shall inform a prospective tenant of any outstanding minimum housing code violations which exist on the building that is the subject of the rental agreement.' (a): copy of a violation notice to each affected tenant 'within thirty (30) days of receipt of the notice' unless corrected. No move-in inspection rule: see `edu-no-move-in-inspection-rule-ri`. The shared `existing-condition` clause reads correctly for RI as an acknowledgment; DRAFTING JUDGMENT: it must not be read as a waiver of § 34-18-22(a), which §§ 34-18-17(a)(1) and 34-18-18 forbid. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant Absences
bodyText: Rhode Island lets your lease require a tenant to tell you about any anticipated absence of more than ten days, no later than the first day of the absence; the library's extended-absence clause does this. The statute sets no penalty if the tenant doesn't, so the lease term is enforced like any other lease breach. Separately, during any absence of more than seven days you may enter without the tenant's consent if it is reasonably necessary to protect the property, whether or not the tenant gave notice; otherwise you need the tenant's consent, which the tenant may not unreasonably withhold. Either way, give at least two days' notice unless there is an emergency or notice is impracticable, and enter only at reasonable times. An absence is not abandonment. A unit is abandoned only when the tenant has left without notice, has no intention of returning, has not paid rent for more than 15 days and has removed substantially all possessions. Even then, send a certified letter, return receipt requested, saying you will re-rent unless the tenant replies within seven days, and then make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-27: 'The rental agreement may require that the tenant notify the landlord of any anticipated extended absence from the premises in excess of ten (10) days no later than the first day of the extended absence.' No remedy for failure to notify in § 34-18-27. § 34-18-26(b): entry without consent 'during any absence of the tenant in excess of seven (7) days, if reasonably necessary for the protection of the property'; (c) 'at least two (2) days’ notice'. 'Abandonment' means 'the tenant has vacated the premises without notice to the landlord and has no intention of returning, as evidenced by nonpayment of rent for more than fifteen (15) days and removal of substantially all possessions from the premises' (§ 34-18-11, definition of 'Abandonment', number unchanged by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148). § 34-18-40: 'the landlord shall send a certified letter, return receipt requested, to the tenant’s last known address giving notice that unless a reply is received from the tenant within seven (7) days, the landlord shall re-rent the premises' and 'shall make reasonable efforts to rent the premises at a fair rental'. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Family Child Care in Rentals
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to let a tenant run a family child care home in your rental, and sets no lease conditions (such as insurance or liability terms) for one. Unless your lease says otherwise, a tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling, so whether a child care business is allowed is up to the lease; say so expressly if you want to permit or forbid it. Recent zoning changes limit what cities and towns can do to licensed family child care providers, but they don't bind you as a landlord. If you permit child care, require the tenant to keep the state license in force and to carry liability insurance that covers it, and check your own insurance. Don't refuse or condition a rental because the applicant has children: familial status is protected under fair housing law.

Laws § 34-18-27: 'Unless otherwise agreed, a tenant shall occupy his or her dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit.' Fair housing: § 34-37-4(a) ('familial status'). title: No Home Business Right
bodyText: Rhode Island gives tenants no statutory right to run a business from a rental, so the lease decides. By law a tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling unless you agree otherwise, so if you want to allow quiet home offices, remote work or a small business, or to forbid customer traffic, signage or stored inventory, say so in the lease. Zoning law treats remote work and home occupations as residential uses in many cases, but zoning rules bind towns, not your lease. Whatever you allow, the tenant still may not disturb neighbors, and you may want proof of business insurance if clients visit. Running a business can also trigger local licensing or zoning limits the tenant must meet.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no tenant right to a home business). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-27: 'Unless otherwise agreed, a tenant shall occupy his or her dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit.' § 34-18-24(7) (no disturbing neighbors). Search over the General Laws, Constitution, loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws and court rules: RI-home-business-1 (home occupation/business/home-based business, business use in a home or dwelling, remote work, working from home, commercial use near tenant/landlord/lease/rental/lessee/lessor/dwelling/residential; hits 32, OK, real positive § 45-24-37 and synthetic positive passed; on point only zoning: § 45-24-31 definition of 'Home occupation' and § 45-24-37(b)(4) remote work as a permitted residential use, read in part; other hits tax classification and building definitions). title: Co-Tenants and Joint Liability
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute sets general rules for co-tenants, so a lease term making everyone who signs jointly and severally liable is enforced as written: you may collect the full rent, or full damages, from any one of them. Several statutes change the result in specific cases. From July 1, 2026, a tenant who ends the lease under the survivor-termination law because they or a household member are a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking owes rent only through the later of the termination date or the date they actually move out, even if they were jointly liable; you can still proceed in good faith against the remaining tenants without a retaliation claim. A servicemember's lawful termination also ends any obligation of the servicemember's dependents under the lease. When a tenant dies, past-due rent is a claim against the estate, and adults who elect to stay on for the post-death grace period are jointly and severally liable for the rent during that period.

Whether the survivor's termination ends the tenancy for remaining co-tenants is not stated; § 34-18-63(f) implies they may remain. The shared `joint-liability` clause reads correctly for RI. title: Yard Work and Landscaping
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute assigns lawn, landscaping or irrigation work to either side. Grounds and areas held out for tenants generally are part of the premises, and you must keep all common areas clean and safe, so in a multi-unit building shared yards stay your responsibility. You may have a tenant take on yard work, but Rhode Island allows a tenant to perform specified maintenance tasks only under a writing signed by both of you, made in good faith and supported by adequate consideration; the work may not be something needed to bring the property into code compliance, and the arrangement may not reduce what you owe other tenants. Put the tasks in the signed lease or a signed addendum, list them specifically, and make the consideration clear (for example, that the rent reflects the tenant's yard work). Report leaks and watering problems promptly so you can meet your own repair duties.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(c): 'The landlord and tenant of a dwelling unit may agree in writing that the tenant perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, and remodeling but only if: (1) The agreement of the parties is entered into in good faith and set forth in a writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration; (2) The work is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subsection (a)(1); and (3) The agreement does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises.' § 34-18-22(a)(3): 'Keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition'. 'Premises' means 'a dwelling unit and the structure of which it is a part and facilities and appurtenances therein and grounds, areas, and facilities held out for the use of tenants generally, or the use of which is promised to the tenant' (§ 34-18-11(12), renumbered (15) by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, effective July 1, 2026). Unlike some states, § 34-18-22(c) makes no single-family exception. title: Tenant Water Bills Can Become a Lien
bodyText: In Rhode Island, you as owner are liable for the water rates set by a city, town, fire district or water district for water furnished to your building, whether the owner or a tenant used it, and unpaid charges are a lien on the property collected the same way as real estate taxes. No statute lets a lease clause or a notice to the water supplier shift that liability to the tenant or keep the lien off your property. So if the tenant pays the water bill, watch for nonpayment (ask for proof of payment or arrange for the supplier to copy you on delinquency notices), and say in the lease that the tenant must pay the bill and reimburse you for any amount charged to you. Sewer, refuse and other district charges are often set by local or special acts with their own lien rules; check with your municipality. The lease must still disclose which utilities the tenant pays.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 39-15-12: 'The owner of any house, building, tenement, or estate shall be liable for the payment of the price or rent or rates fixed by any town, city, or incorporated fire district or water district for the use of water furnished by such town, city, fire district, or water district to the owner or occupant of the house, building, tenement, or estate; and the price, rent, or rates shall be a lien upon the house, building, tenement, and estate in the same way and manner as taxes assessed on real estate are liens'; Cranston (12%) and Woonsocket (18%) interest provisos. Special acts repeat the rule for individual districts (e.g. § 45-48-5 Nasonville water district; R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 272, 273, North Tiverton Fire District, read only for the water-rate lien lines). § 34-18-15(a)(3) (utility disclosure). title: Occupancy Limits and Listing Occupants
bodyText: Your lease may list who will live in the unit and require the tenant to tell you about new occupants. Two sets of rules limit what you can do. The state housing code caps occupancy by floor space: at least 150 square feet of habitable room space for the first occupant and 130 for each additional one; each bedroom needs 70 square feet for the first sleeper and 50 for each additional one; usable closet space counts too. It also bars more than one family plus two unrelated occupants (guests and domestic employees aside), or one household of unrelated people, without a rooming house permit. You may not rent a unit for more occupants than the code allows. Fair housing law bars limits based on familial status or other protected traits, so set any occupancy limit by space and safety, apply it to everyone, and don't use it to exclude families with children. Since July 1, 2026, a person living with the tenant as an authorized occupant is a household member with rights under the survivor-protection laws, so keep your occupant list current.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-11: 'No person shall occupy, or let to be occupied, a dwelling or dwelling unit, for the purpose of living, unless there is compliance with the requirements of this section.' (1) 'at least one hundred fifty (150) square feet of floor space for the first occupant, and at least one hundred thirty (130) square feet of floor space for every additional occupant'; (2)(i) sleeping rooms 'at least seventy (70) square feet of floor space for the first occupant, and at least fifty (50) square feet of floor space for each additional occupant'; (3) closet deficiency subtracted; (4): 'A dwelling unit must not be occupied by more than one family plus two (2) occupants unrelated to the family, except for guests or domestic employees or by not more than one household if the occupants are unrelated, unless a permit for a rooming house has been granted by the appropriate authority.' Fair housing: § 34-37-4(a) ('familial status'), (c) (standards and terms 'that do not discriminate'). Household member: R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1, adding § 34-18-11(9) (effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): 'a person residing with a tenant as an authorized occupant of the premises.' Seasonal leases: § 34-18-36(f) (breach of terms 'pertaining to legal occupancy'), see `edu-disturbance-ri`. Local occupancy ordinances may be stricter; not searched. The shared `permitted-occupants` clause reads correctly for RI. Federal occupancy guidance not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Acts the Law Bars Tenants From
bodyText: Rhode Island's landlord-tenant act lists what every tenant must refrain from, whether or not the lease repeats it. A tenant may not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly let anyone else do so; may not disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment, or let people there with the tenant's consent do so; may not use any part of the premises in a way that maintains a narcotics nuisance; may not use the premises or adjacent public property to manufacture, sell or deliver a controlled substance, or possess one there with intent to do so (schedule I or II); and may not commit a crime of violence on the premises or adjacent public property. For damage or disturbance you must generally give a 20-day cure notice before ending the tenancy, but a repeat of substantially the same breach within six months of that notice lets you terminate on 20 days' notice without a chance to cure, and for a seasonal tenant under the statute's summer or academic-year lease, an ordinance charge or a breach of the lease's occupancy or noise terms lets you file without notice. For the drug and violent-crime breaches, cure doesn't save the tenancy and you may file for eviction without a notice of noncompliance. You may also recover actual damages and, for willful breaches, attorney's fees.

Laws § 34-18-24(6): 'Not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair, or remove any part of the premises or knowingly permit any person to do so'; (7) not disturb 'his or her neighbors’ peaceful enjoyment of the premises'; (8) 'Refrain from using any part of the premises in a manner such as would constitute the maintaining of a narcotics nuisance under the provisions of § 21-28-4.06'; (9) 'Refrain from using any part of the premises or any public property adjacent thereto for the manufacture, sale, or delivery of a controlled substance or from possessing on the premises or any public property adjacent thereto with the intent to manufacture, sell, or deliver a controlled substance classified in schedule I or schedule II of chapter 28 of title 21'; (10) 'Refrain from any crime of violence on the premises or on any public property adjacent to said premises', with the listed crimes. § 21-28-4.06(a) (places 'used for the unlawful sale, use, or keeping of a controlled substance shall be deemed a common nuisance'; cross-reference checked). Enforcement: § 34-18-36(a) (20-day cure); (b) cure ineffective for § 34-18-24(8), (9), (10); (f) no notice of noncompliance required for those breaches; (d) actual damages, injunction, attorney's fees if willful. title: No Special Remedy for Misuse of the Unit
bodyText: Rhode Island has no general statute giving you a special remedy when a tenant uses the property for a purpose other than the one the lease states (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). Two old criminal-law sections are exceptions: a lease of a place used as a gambling house is void, and the occupant can be ejected after a demand for possession (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-19-23); and a tenant's use of the premises for a purpose the nuisance chapter lists (such as lewdness, assignation or prostitution, a house of ill fame, illegal gaming, or unlicensed liquor sales) annuls the lease and lets the owner re-enter without process of law (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-30-6; see the nuisance row). Take advice before relying on either, since the landlord-tenant act bars self-help and its eviction procedure may still apply. The act's default rule is that, unless you agree otherwise, a tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling, and a lease use restriction is enforced like any other term. If the misuse is a material breach of the lease, give the statutory 20-day cure notice; if the tenant doesn't stop, the tenancy ends on the date you name (at least 21 days after mailing) and you may file for eviction. A repeat of substantially the same breach within six months needs only 20 days' notice with no cure. Drug dealing, a narcotics nuisance or a crime of violence on the premises is different: those breaches can't be cured and you may file without a noncompliance notice. You may also recover actual damages and seek an injunction.

(§ 11-19-23). And § 11-30-6: if a tenant 'shall use the premises or any part for any of the purposes enumerated in §§ 11-30-1 and 11-30-2, that use shall annul the lease or other title under which the occupant holds' and 'the owner may make immediate entry on it and repossess himself or herself of the premises without process of law' (§ 11-30-6); see `edu-nuisance-ri`. How §§ 11-19-23 and 11-30-6 interact with chapter 34-18's eviction procedure and its self-help bar (§ 34-18-44) the statutes don't say; case law not searched (drafting judgment to advise caution). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-27: 'Unless otherwise agreed, a tenant shall occupy his or her dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit.' § 34-18-36(a) (written demand notice; 20 days to remedy; termination 'shall not be less than twenty-one (21) days after the mailing of the notice'), (b), (d) ('actual damages and obtain injunctive relief'), (e) (repeat within six months: 'at least twenty (20) days’ written notice'), (f) (no notice for § 34-18-24(8)-(10)). title: Smoking, Vaping and Cannabis Rules
bodyText: Your lease may ban smoking and vaping of tobacco and cannabis anywhere on the property, and Rhode Island law already bans smoking, including electronic cigarettes, in lobbies, hallways and other common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums and other multi-unit residential buildings with more than four units; those buildings must post "No smoking" signs. The units themselves, as private residences, are not covered by the smoke-free law, so a ban inside units comes only from your lease. Cannabis has two limits. You may not prohibit a tenant from consuming cannabis by means other than smoking or vaping (edibles, for example), or from transferring cannabis without payment, as long as the tenant stays within the legal possession and transfer limits. And you may not refuse to rent to, or penalize, a medical marijuana cardholder solely for being a cardholder, although you may decline to lease, or to continue leasing, to a cardholder who cultivates, manufactures, processes, smokes or vaporizes medical marijuana in the unit.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-20.10-3: 'Smoking shall be prohibited in all enclosed public places within the state of Rhode Island, including, but not limited to, the following places:' ... '(10) Lobbies, hallways and other common areas in apartment buildings, condominiums, trailer parks, retirement facilities, nursing homes and other multiple unit residential facilities with more than four (4) units'. § 23-20.10-2 ('Smoking' includes 'the use of electronic cigarettes, electronic cigars, electronic pipes, electronic nicotine delivery system products'; renumbered (20) in the version effective January 1, 2027 under R.I. Pub. L. 2025, chs. 444, 445; definition text unchanged in the part read). § 23-20.10-6(a)(1) exempts 'Private residences, except when used as a licensed childcare, adult daycare, or healthcare facility'. § 23-20.10-7(a) signs posted 'by the owner, operator, manager or other person in control of that place'. Cannabis: § 21-28.11-29(h): 'in the case of the rental of a residential dwelling unit governed by chapter 18 of title 34, a landlord may not prohibit the consumption of cannabis by non-smoked or non-vaporized means, or the transfer without compensation of cannabis by the tenant as defined in § 34-18-11, provided the tenant is in compliance with the possession and transfer limits and other requirements set forth in this chapter.' (g) otherwise no duty to allow consumption or transfer. Medical: § 21-28.6-4(d): 'No school or landlord may refuse to enroll, or lease to, or otherwise penalize, a person solely for his or her status as a cardholder. Provided, however, due to the safety and welfare concern for other tenants, the property, and the public, as a whole, a landlord may have the discretion not to lease, or continue to lease, to a cardholder who cultivates, manufactures, processes, smokes, or vaporizes medical marijuana in the leased premises.' Penalties in § 23-20.10-10 are framed against an 'employer'; how they apply to a residential owner not resolved. title: Subletting and Assignment
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on residential subletting or assignment, so the lease decides: you may require your prior written consent, in your sole discretion, and treat an unauthorized sublease as a breach, enforced through the usual 20-day cure notice. No statute requires you to be reasonable or to answer a sublet request within a set time. A tenant who does sublet becomes a landlord under the act toward the subtenant, with all of a landlord's duties, and stays liable to you unless you release them. Short-term rentals add a state rule: no one may list a residence on a hosting platform for stays of up to 30 nights without the property's current state registration number, and the registration records whether the registrant owns or rents. A tenant who lists your unit without your consent breaches a lease ban, but the registration rule doesn't itself require your permission, so keep the lease ban explicit.

'Landlord' means 'the owner, lessor, or sublessor of the dwelling unit or the building of which it is a part' (§ 34-18-11(7), renumbered (10) by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, effective July 1, 2026). Breach enforcement: § 34-18-36(a) (written demand; 20 days to remedy). title: No Statutory Duty to Forward Legal Papers
bodyText: Rhode Island law does not require a tenant to tell you about, or hand over, papers in a lawsuit or other proceeding to recover the property, and it has no rule on a tenant attorning to (recognizing as landlord) someone who claims the property. If you want tenants to pass such papers along promptly, the duty has to come from the lease; the library's notice-of-proceedings clause does this. Keep your own address current with tenants (the act requires you to disclose who manages the property and who receives notices for you), so papers reach you directly, and watch for foreclosure postings at your buildings.

title: Tenant's Insurance and Your Repair Duties
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute says whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's renters insurance. You may require renters insurance, but only if the lease states the requirement (or, without a written lease, you tell the tenant in writing). Two rules limit how far you can go. Your repair and habitability duties stay with you: no lease may let you collect rent free of them, so you can't make a tenant's insurance claim a condition of repairs you owe. And a lease may not make the tenant indemnify you, or limit your liability, for liability that arises under law, so a clause shifting your own losses to the tenant's insurer through the tenant is unenforceable, and using a term you know is prohibited can cost up to three months' rent plus attorney's fees. For damage the tenant caused, you may recover your actual damages from the tenant, whom their insurer may then cover.

title: Shifting Repairs and Chores to the Tenant
bodyText: Every tenant must keep the unit clean and safe and use its facilities reasonably, but the repair and habitability duties are yours. Rhode Island lets you and a tenant agree that the tenant will do specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling only if the agreement is made in good faith, is in a writing signed by both of you, and is supported by adequate consideration; the work must not be something needed to bring the property up to the building and housing codes, and the deal must not reduce what you owe other tenants. There is no single-family exception. List the tasks specifically and state what the tenant gets for them. If a tenant breaches their own maintenance duties in a way that materially affects health and safety and doesn't fix it within 20 days after your written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires), you may enter, have the work done properly and bill the actual and reasonable cost as rent on the next rent due date, or for immediate payment if the tenancy has ended.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(c): 'The landlord and tenant of a dwelling unit may agree in writing that the tenant perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, and remodeling but only if: (1) The agreement of the parties is entered into in good faith and set forth in a writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration; (2) The work is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subsection (a)(1); and (3) The agreement does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises.' § 34-18-22(a)(1), (2) (code compliance; fit and habitable). § 34-18-24(2), (5) (tenant keeps occupied part 'as clean and safe as the condition of the premises permit'; reasonable use of facilities and appliances). § 34-18-39: if a § 34-18-24 noncompliance 'materially affecting health and safety' is not remedied 'as promptly as conditions require in case of emergency or within twenty (20) days after written notice by the landlord', the landlord 'may enter the dwelling unit and cause the work to be done in a skilled manner and submit the itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost or the fair and reasonable value thereof as rent on the next date periodic rent is due, or if the rental agreement has terminated, for immediate payment.' § 34-18-18 (no rent free of § 34-18-22(a)). The shared `tenant-maintenance` clause (general care, excepting conditions the law requires Landlord to repair) reads correctly for RI; it does not assign 'specified repairs'.
