title: Tenant Duties Set by Law
bodyText: Rhode Island puts these duties on every tenant, whether or not the lease repeats them: comply with building and housing code obligations primarily imposed on tenants that materially affect health and safety; keep the part of the premises the tenant occupies and uses as clean and safe as its condition permits; dispose of ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste cleanly and safely; keep plumbing fixtures as clean as their condition permits; and use electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, reasonably. The state housing code adds occupant duties, including: furnishing garbage containers in one- to three-family buildings (you supply them in buildings of four or more units); maintaining and replacing screens and storm doors and windows once installed for the season, unless you agree otherwise; replacing shades or other privacy devices you first installed; and extermination when the tenant's unit is the only one infested and you didn't cause it. Tenants must also not unreasonably refuse you access and, unless agreed otherwise, use the unit only as a dwelling. The acts a tenant must refrain from are covered separately.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-24: 'A tenant shall: (1) Comply with all obligations primarily imposed upon tenants by applicable provisions of building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety; (2) Keep that part of the premises that he or she occupies and uses as clean and safe as the condition of the premises permit; (3) Dispose from his or her dwelling unit all ashes, garbage, rubbish, and other waste in a clean and safe manner; (4) Keep all plumbing fixtures in the dwelling unit or used by the tenant as clean as their condition permits; (5) Use in a reasonable manner all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, in the premises'. Housing code occupant duties: § 45-24.3-6(c) (clean and sanitary the parts the occupant 'occupies and controls'), (d), (e) (rubbish and garbage), (f) ('In the case of single, two (2) or three (3) family dwellings and structures it is the responsibility of the occupant to furnish those facilities or refuse containers'; owner supplies in dwellings of 'four (4) or more dwelling units'), (g) ('In the absence of an agreement, maintenance or replacement of screens, and storm doors and windows, once installed in any one season, become the responsibility of the occupant.'), (h) ('Once installed in any one rental by the owner, replacements become the responsibility of the occupant.'), (i) extermination, (j) plumbing fixtures. Access: § 34-18-26(a). Use: § 34-18-27. Prohibited acts (§ 34-18-24(6)-(10)): see `edu-tenant-prohibited-acts-ri`. Remedies: § 34-18-36 (cure notice), § 34-18-39 (repair and bill). Local codes may add duties; not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Who Pays Which Utilities
bodyText: Every Rhode Island lease must say which utility costs are included in the rent and which are the tenant's responsibility; with no written lease, give the tenant that information in writing. If you don't, the tenant can recover fees paid that weren't properly disclosed. Whoever pays, you must supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, and reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1, as the housing code requires, unless the building isn't required to have them or the heat or hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control with a direct utility connection. If you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service that the lease or the law makes yours, the tenant may, after notice, buy the service and deduct the cost from rent, recover damages for reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing rent-free (and recover its cost up to one rental period's rent), plus attorney's fees. These remedies don't apply if the tenant or their household or guests caused the problem.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(3): 'In any lease agreement the landlord shall disclose which utility costs are included in the rent and which utility costs are the tenant’s responsibility. If there is no written lease, the landlord shall provide this information to the tenant in writing.' (a)(5): 'the tenant may recover any fees paid for the unit that were not disclosed as required.' § 34-18-22(a)(6): 'Supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times as required by § 45-24.3-7 ... and reasonable heat as required by § 45-24.3-9 ... between October 1 and May 1, except where the building that includes the dwelling unit is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant and supplied by a direct public utility connection'. § 34-18-31(a): if 'the landlord willfully or negligently fails to supply heat, running water, hot water, electric, gas, or other essential service', the tenant may (1) secure the service and 'deduct their actual and reasonable costs from the periodic rent', (2) recover diminution damages, or (3) 'Procure reasonable substitute housing' and be excused from rent; (b) substitute housing cost 'not in excess of an amount equal to the periodic rent' and 'reasonable attorney’s fees'; (d) notice required; not if caused by the tenant, family or guests. Housing code standards §§ 45-24.3-7, 45-24.3-9 not read for this row. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Utility Cutoffs for Submetered Service
bodyText: Rhode Island has no special rules letting a landlord who submeters or bills tenants for electricity, gas or water interrupt the service for nonpayment. The general rules control: you may not interrupt, or cause the interruption of, heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or any other essential service, whether to recover possession or to collect a charge; a tenant whose service you willfully cut off may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. If a tenant doesn't pay a utility charge you bill under the lease, pursue it as a debt or a lease breach, not by shutting anything off. Two other rules matter if you meter electricity yourself: apartment buildings with more than ten units whose construction began after July 1, 1977 may not use master meters for electricity, and each unit must have its own meter (publicly financed elderly or disabled housing may elect a single meter). And the lease must say which utilities are included in rent and which the tenant pays.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no submeter interruption regime). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-44: 'A landlord may not recover or take possession of the dwelling unit by action or otherwise, including willful diminution of services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of heat, running water, hot water, electric, gas, or other essential service to the tenant, except in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted in this chapter.' § 34-18-34: 'If a landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises or willfully diminishes services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of heat, running water, hot water, electric, gas, or other essential service, the tenant may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, in either case, recover an amount not more than three (3) months periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him or her, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney’s fees.' (§ 34-18-34); it is not limited to recovering possession, so a shutoff to collect a billed charge is reached (see `edu-self-help-eviction-ri`). Master meters: § 39-3-7.1: 'The use of “master-meters,” so-called, in apartment or tenement houses containing more than ten (10) apartments or dwelling units is hereby prohibited; provided, however, that this section shall only apply to apartment houses, construction of which is commenced after July 1, 1977. Each apartment or dwelling unit shall have a measuring device or meter for the purpose of measuring the electricity used only by that apartment.' Elderly/disabled exception in the same section. Mobile home parks: § 31-44-3 bars a licensee reselling electricity, gas or water to residents for more than the utility charged (read in part). Disclosure: § 34-18-15(a)(3). Public Utilities Commission rules not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (§§ 34-18-44, 39-3-7.1, 34-18-15).

title: Keeping Utilities On
bodyText: Neither side may cut off essential services as a pressure tactic. You may not interrupt, or cause the interruption of, heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential service to get a tenant out, and if you willfully or negligently fail to supply a service the lease or the law makes yours, the tenant may, after notice, buy it and deduct the cost from rent, recover damages, or move to substitute housing rent-free, plus attorney's fees. If Woonsocket (under its ordinance) or the Narragansett Bay Commission shuts off, or is about to shut off, water for unpaid sewer fees, a tenant may pay those charges and deduct them from rent by giving you the receipt. A lease term making the tenant keep the services in their name on and paid is a contract term you can enforce as a lease breach. When service is in the tenant's name, the utility's own shutoff rules protect some households: a regulated electric, gas or water utility must follow Public Utilities Commission rules before terminating a household where all adults are 65 or older, or where a resident is disabled or seriously ill, and some low-income households have added protection. A utility may not refuse service to a new occupant because the previous occupant left without paying, unless the service benefits that previous occupant.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-44 (no recovery of possession by 'interrupting or causing the interruption of heat, running water, hot water, electric, gas, or other essential service'). § 34-18-31(a), (b), (d) (tenant remedies after notice for willful or negligent failure to supply; not if tenant-caused). § 39-1.1-1(a): no public utility supplying electricity, gas or water 'shall terminate service to any household in which all adult residents are sixty-five (65) years of age or older, or where any resident is disabled or seriously ill, for failure to pay an outstanding indebtedness for service, without first complying with all rules and regulations for such terminations issued by the commission.' (b) LIHEAP households ('three hundred dollars ($300) or less and not more than two (2) months in arrears'; Block Island Power Company and Pascoag Utility District excluded). § 39-2-1.1: 'No public utility shall refuse to furnish services to new occupants at any premises on the grounds that the previous occupant has vacated the premises without paying the public utility for services furnished, provided that the service is not for the use or benefit of the previous occupant.' No statute found requiring a utility to notify tenants or let them take over service when a landlord's account is terminated: RI-utility-continuity-1 recorded as failed (real positive § 39-2-1.1 missed), rerun as RI-utility-continuity-2 (terminate/shut off/discontinue/disconnect/cut off/interrupt/refuse to furnish near service/utility/electric/gas/water/heat near tenant/occupant/landlord/lessee/resident; hits 25, OK, real positives §§ 34-18-44 and 39-2-1.1 passed); RI-utility-continuity-3 (landlord/owner fails to pay utility bills; utility account of owner and tenants, no context limb; hits 1, OK, synthetic positive passed; only § 23-24.6-28). One qualifier: for water shut off for an owner's unpaid sewer charges, R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-6-9(c) (Woonsocket ordinance): 'When service is provided to a residence occupied by a tenant, the tenant may, after paying the fees, charges and assessments in order to restore or prevent termination of service, deduct the amount paid from the rent due the landlord. The tenant shall provide the landlord with a copy of the receipt from the city when making a deduction from the rent.' (§ 45-6-9(c)); § 46-25-22.1(d) (Narragansett Bay Commission), same text with 'a copy of the receipt from the commission' (§ 46-25-22.1(d)); both were hits of RI-utility-continuity-2. The shared `utility-service-continuity` clause reads correctly for RI. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: Rhode Island's smoke and carbon monoxide alarm rules live in the state Fire Safety Code, which adopts the national Fire Code (NFPA 1) and Life Safety Code (NFPA 101) as amended by the state Fire Safety Code Board's regulations, not in the landlord-tenant act. The statute itself says the code must set standards for smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in one-, two- and three-family homes and that three-family dwellings must have both; larger residential buildings are covered by the code's full requirements, including approved fire alarm systems where the code requires them. Through the landlord-tenant act, you must comply with these codes as they affect health and safety, and tenants must meet any code duties placed on occupants. Local fire officials review and inspect alarm installations and issue smoke and carbon monoxide detector certificates, which are valid for at least 120 days. Check the current Fire Safety Code regulations, or ask your local fire marshal, for placement, power and testing rules; the library does not restate them.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-28.1-2(a) (NFPA 1 and NFPA 101, 'with annexes, except as updated, amended, altered, or deleted, and by the addition of certain provisions, as indicated in the rules and regulations adopted by the fire safety code board, is hereby adopted as the “Rhode Island fire safety code.”'); (b)(2)(i): minimum requirements 'except in private dwellings occupied by one, two (2), or three (3) families' but 'this code shall provide reasonable standards for the installation of smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms in private dwellings occupied by one, two (2), and three (3) families; provided, further, that three-family (3) dwellings shall be equipped with smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms'; (b)(2)(ii) local plan review and inspection fees ($75/$125/$175). § 23-28.25-1: covered buildings 'shall be equipped with an approved fire alarm system installed and maintained in accordance with this chapter'. § 23-28.1-6(a) (code applies to all structures unless exempted). § 23-28.1-10: 'smoke detector and carbon monoxide detector certificates issued by any state or local authority shall be valid for such period as the issuing authority may specify, but in no event for less than a period of one hundred twenty (120) days from the date of issuance.' Landlord-tenant link: § 34-18-22(a)(1) (codes affecting health and safety); 'Building and housing codes' include 'any law, ordinance, or governmental regulation concerning fitness for habitation' (§ 34-18-11(3), renumbered (4) by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, effective July 1, 2026); § 34-18-24(1). NEEDS_REVIEW: the operative alarm rules are in the Fire Safety Code Board's regulations and the adopted NFPA editions, which are not in the corpus and were not read; no RI landlord-tenant statute on alarms. title: No Alarm Tampering Fee Rule
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute authorizes or caps a set fee for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, so the library does not offer one. The only tampering crime found covers public fire alarm apparatus, not alarms inside a home. A lease may forbid tampering and make the tenant responsible for the actual cost of repairing or replacing an alarm the tenant damaged or removed, and a tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage or remove any part of the premises. Keep the remedy to actual cost: a fixed penalty beyond your real loss risks being unenforceable, and any fee beyond rent must be listed in the rent section of the lease (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format). Your own duty to keep alarms code-compliant doesn't shift to the tenant.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent. Search over the General Laws, Constitution, loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws and court rules: RI-alarm-tampering-1 (tamper/disable/remove/disconnect/interfere/impair within 100 characters of smoke/carbon monoxide/fire alarm/detector/detection, either order, no context limb; hits 1, OK, real positive § 11-4-10 and synthetic positive passed). R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-4-10 reaches only one who 'tampers with, interferes with or in any way impairs any public fire alarm apparatus, wire or associated equipment'. § 34-18-24(6) (tenant shall 'Not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair, or remove any part of the premises'). § 34-18-15(a)(1), (5) (fees beyond rent disclosed in the rent section; undisclosed fees recoverable). § 34-18-22(a)(1) (landlord code compliance). title: Substitute Housing
bodyText: Rhode Island does not make you house a tenant elsewhere during ordinary repairs, after a fire, or during lead hazard work. Three rules still cost you money. If you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service the lease or the law makes yours, the tenant may, after notice, move to reasonable substitute housing for the period of your noncompliance, owes no rent for that period, and may recover its actual and reasonable cost up to one rental period's rent, plus attorney's fees (not if the tenant's household or guests caused the problem). If fire or casualty substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may vacate and end the lease by written notice within 14 days, or stay in the usable part and pay reduced rent; you return the deposit and prepaid rent if the lease ends. And during lead hazard reduction you must make all reasonable efforts to keep occupants out, are not responsible for providing alternative housing, but must reduce the rent pro rata if occupants have to leave for three days or more.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-31(a)(3): the tenant may 'Procure reasonable substitute housing during the period of the landlord’s noncompliance, in which case the tenant is excused from paying rent for the period of the landlord’s noncompliance.' (b): 'the tenant may recover the actual and reasonable cost or fair and reasonable value of the substitute housing not in excess of an amount equal to the periodic rent, and in any case under subsection (a) of this section, may recover reasonable attorney’s fees.' (d) notice; tenant-caused exception. § 34-18-33(a)(1) ('notify the landlord in writing within fourteen (14) days thereafter'), (a)(2) (rent 'reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value'), (b) ('the landlord shall return all security recoverable under § 34-18-19 and all prepaid rent'). Lead: § 23-24.6-17(a)(3): regulations shall 'Require owners to make all reasonable efforts to ensure that occupants are not present during the lead hazard reduction; variances may be granted according to regulations; provided, that the owners are not responsible for providing alternative housing.' and 'If the occupants are required to vacate the premises for a three (3) day period or longer, there shall be a pro-rata adjustment or abatement of the rent during the period of lead hazard reduction'. Not in body: § 34-45-11 (relocation assistance owed by owners of federally assisted developments to designated households on mortgage prepayment or § 8 non-renewal; read in part). title: Appliances Not Supplied by Landlord
bodyText: [Optional.] The following appliances at the property are not supplied by Landlord, and Landlord is not responsible for maintaining or repairing them: [list each appliance, for example a washer owned by Tenant or an air conditioner left by a prior occupant, or state 'None']. [Include only if Tenant will supply them: Tenant will provide a cooking stove and a refrigerator, properly installed with all necessary connections for safe, sanitary and efficient operation, when Tenant moves in, and will maintain them; Landlord has provided sufficient space and adequate connections for them.] This Section does not relieve Landlord of any duty to supply or maintain any other facility or appliance that Landlord supplies or that the law requires Landlord to supply.
notes: RI: Optional; never default. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(a)(4): the landlord must 'Maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord'. So an appliance the landlord neither supplies nor must supply can be left to the tenant. § 45-24.3-7(1)(iii) requires 'A stove, or similar device, for cooking food, and a refrigerator, or similar device' 'properly installed with all necessary connections for safe, sanitary, and efficient operation; provided, that the stove, refrigerator, and/or similar devices, need not be installed when a dwelling unit is not occupied and when the occupant is expected to provide these on occupancy, and that sufficient space and adequate connections for the safe and efficient installation and operation of the stove, refrigerator, and/or similar devices is provided.' The bracketed stove/refrigerator sentence uses that proviso. § 34-18-18 bars rent free of § 34-18-22(a), so the last sentence keeps the clause from reading as a waiver. No RI presumption that appliances present are landlord-supplied (RI-appliances-1). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Appliances You Do Not Supply
bodyText: You must keep in good and safe working order every electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facility and appliance you supply or are required by law to supply. Appliances you don't supply, such as a tenant's own washer, are the tenant's responsibility. Rhode Island has no rule presuming that an appliance left in the unit is yours, so say clearly in the lease which appliances you supply and which you don't; an appliance you list as included is one you must maintain. The housing code requires every unit to have a working stove and refrigerator, among other basic kitchen and bathroom facilities, but a stove and refrigerator need not be installed while the unit is vacant if the incoming tenant is expected to provide them, as long as you provide the space and connections for them. A lease cannot excuse you from code-required facilities or let you collect rent free of your repair duties.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(a)(4): 'Maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord'. § 45-24.3-7(1)(iii) (stove and refrigerator; proviso 'need not be installed when a dwelling unit is not occupied and when the occupant is expected to provide these on occupancy'); § 45-24.3-7(1)-(3) (kitchen sink, storage, toilet, lavatory, tub or shower). § 34-18-18 (no rent free of § 34-18-22(a)); § 34-18-17(a)(1). Local codes may be stricter; not searched. The shared `appliances-included` clause reads correctly for RI. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Furniture Provided by Landlord
bodyText: [Optional. Use only where Landlord provides furniture.] Landlord provides, and Tenant may use, the following furniture owned by Landlord: [list each item of furniture]. [Include only if Landlord takes a furniture security deposit: The replacement value of this furniture on the date this Lease is signed is $[replacement value; must be $5,000 or more]. Tenant will pay Landlord a separate furniture security deposit of $[amount]. At the end of the tenancy Landlord will return the furniture security deposit, less any reasonable cleaning and repair expenses for the furniture and the amount of physical damage to the furniture beyond ordinary wear and tear, together with a written notice itemizing any deductions, within 20 days after the latest of the end of the tenancy, Tenant's delivery of possession, or Tenant's giving Landlord a forwarding address for that purpose.] Tenant will keep the furniture in the property, will not remove or dispose of any item, and will return it at the end of the tenancy in the same condition as at the start, less ordinary wear and tear. Tenant will report damage to the furniture promptly.
notes: RI: Optional; never default. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(e): 'This section does not preclude any landlord who rents a furnished apartment from demanding or receiving a furniture security deposit if the replacement value of the furniture being furnished by the landlord valued at the time the lease is executed is five thousand dollars ($5,000) or greater, in which instance the landlord may charge a separate furniture security deposit of up to one month’s periodic rent.' So the clause records the replacement value at signing (the fact that makes the deposit lawful) and the landlord's own deposit figure; the builder must keep [amount] at or below one month's periodic rent and must not offer the deposit sentence if the stated value is under $5,000. § 34-18-19(f): the furniture deposit due is 'the entire amount given by the tenant as a furniture security deposit, minus the amount due, if any, for reasonable cleaning expenses and repair and the amount of physical damages to the furniture, other than ordinary wear and tear', delivered with 'the notice' 'within twenty (20) days after the later of either termination of the tenancy, delivery of possession, or the tenant’s providing the landlord with a forwarding address for the purpose of receiving the furniture security deposit.' The clause tracks those deductions and that deadline. § 34-18-19(h): 'No rental agreement shall contain any waiver of the provisions of this section.' The ordinary security deposit stays capped at one month under § 34-18-19(a) ('however denominated'), so furniture money beyond the (e) deposit cannot be taken as extra security. The return-of-condition sentences follow the shared Kansas furnished-unit clause (`furnishings-included-ks`), with its maintenance promise dropped because § 34-18-22(a)(4) speaks of 'facilities and appliances' and furniture is left to the lease. title: Heat Requirements
bodyText: Between October 1 and May 1 you must supply reasonable heat as the state housing code requires, or as a stricter local code requires. The code requires heating facilities, properly installed and kept in safe working condition, able to heat every habitable room, bathroom and toilet room to at least 68°F, measured 18 inches above the floor, under average winter conditions. Unvented flame space heaters are banned, except listed unvented portable oil (such as kerosene) heaters that meet the statute's labeling and safety standards; approved portable electric heaters are acceptable. The heat-supply duty does not apply where the building is not legally required to be equipped for heat, or where the unit's heat comes from equipment in the tenant's exclusive control supplied by a direct public utility connection. Even then you must keep heating equipment you supply in good and safe working order, and no agreement can make the tenant responsible for bringing heat up to code. Say in the lease who pays for heating fuel. If you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, the tenant may, after notice, buy reasonable heat and deduct the cost from rent, recover the drop in rental value, or move to substitute housing and pay no rent meanwhile (recovering its cost up to one period's rent), plus attorney's fees, unless the tenant's household or guests caused the problem. Willfully cutting off heat lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(a)(6): the landlord shall supply 'reasonable heat as required by § 45-24.3-9, or applicable local codes if more restrictive, between October 1 and May 1, except where the building that includes the dwelling unit is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant and supplied by a direct public utility connection'. § 45-24.3-9(1): 'Every dwelling must have heating facilities properly installed and maintained in safe and working condition, and capable of safely and adequately heating all habitable rooms, bathrooms, and water closet compartments in every dwelling unit located at a distance of eighteen inches (18") above the floor level under average winter conditions to a temperature of at least sixty-eight degrees (68 °) fahrenheit.' § 45-24.3-9(2): 'Unvented flame space heaters are prohibited in any dwelling or dwelling unit except as provided in § 45-24.3-9.2.' and 'Portable electric heaters, approved under the appropriate local or state electrical and/or fire prevention code, are acceptable where they meet the above provisions of this section.' § 45-24.3-9.2(a), (d), (e) (listed oil-fueled portable heaters; labeling, tip-over shut-off, carbon monoxide and sleeping-area warning rules). § 34-18-22(a)(4) (maintain heating facilities 'supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord'); § 34-18-22(b) (the code duty in (a)(1) governs where greater); § 34-18-22(c)(2) (tenant work agreement only if 'The work is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subsection (a)(1)'). § 34-18-15(a)(3): 'In any lease agreement the landlord shall disclose which utility costs are included in the rent and which utility costs are the tenant’s responsibility.' Remedies: § 34-18-31(a)(1)-(3), (b), (d) (on willful or negligent failure to supply heat 'contrary to the rental agreement or § 34-18-22', after notice: secure heat and deduct, diminution damages, or substitute housing with rent excused and its cost recoverable 'not in excess of an amount equal to the periodic rent', and 'reasonable attorney’s fees'; not where tenant-caused). § 34-18-34 (willful interruption of heat: 'an amount not more than three (3) months periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him or her, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney’s fees'). The 2026 SAFE Unit amendment to § 45-24.3-4 (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 327, 328, § 6) concerns temporary shelter structures, not leased dwellings. title: Your Repair and Habitability Duties
bodyText: Rhode Island puts the repair and habitability duties on you for every residential tenancy, with no single-family exception. You must comply with the building and housing codes affecting health and safety; make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the unit fit and habitable; keep common areas clean and safe; keep in good and safe working order the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facilities and appliances (including elevators) that you supply or must supply; provide trash receptacles as the housing code requires and arrange for removal; and supply running water and reasonable hot water at all times (the code's heated water is at least 120°F) and reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1. Where the code demands more than these general duties, the code controls. You may not let a vacant unit unless it is clean, sanitary, fit for occupancy and code-compliant. No lease, assignment, deed or mortgage can let anyone collect rent free of these duties, and a lease term waiving them is unenforceable (knowingly using one exposes you to up to three months' rent plus fees). The only way to have a tenant do specified repairs is a good-faith written agreement signed by both of you (in the lease or an addendum) for adequate consideration, which can't cover work needed for code compliance or reduce what you owe other tenants. Tenants who aren't at fault have repair, rent and termination remedies if you fall short.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(a)(1)-(6) (quoted in part): '(1) Comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes affecting health and safety; (2) Make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition; (3) Keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition;' (4) facilities and appliances 'supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord'; (5) receptacles 'as required by § 45-24.3-6, or applicable local codes if more restrictive, and arrange for their removal'; (6) 'running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times' and reasonable heat 'between October 1 and May 1' (exceptions in edu-heating-ri). § 34-18-22(b): 'If the duty imposed by subsection (a)(1) is greater than any duty imposed by any other paragraph of subsection (a) of this section, the landlord’s duty shall be determined by reference to subsection (a)(1).' § 45-24.3-5(19): '“Heated water” means water heated to a temperature of not less than one hundred twenty degrees (120 °) fahrenheit.' § 45-24.3-6(a): no owner shall 'let to another person, any vacant dwelling, dwelling unit, or structure unless it and the premises are clean, sanitary, fit for human occupancy, and comply with this chapter'. Receptacles: § 45-24.3-6(f) (owner of a dwelling of four or more units supplies them; 'In the case of single, two (2) or three (3) family dwellings and structures it is the responsibility of the occupant to furnish those facilities or refuse containers'), so in 1-3 family buildings the code assigns containers to the occupant while § 34-18-22(a)(5) still says the landlord will 'arrange for their removal'; body states the duty generally. § 34-18-18: 'A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed, or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with § 34-18-22(a).' § 34-18-17(a)(1), (b) (no waiver; 'an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney’s fees' for deliberate use of known-prohibited terms). § 34-18-22(c) (tenant work agreements; edu-tenant-maintenance-agreement-ri). Remedies: §§ 34-18-28, -30, -31, -32 (edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ri). No single-family or exempt-property carve-out in § 34-18-22 (read whole); chapter exclusions in § 34-18-8 not reopened here. (a)(7) insurance is covered by `edu-landlord-liability-insurance-ri`. Local codes may be stricter (not searched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Rent Suspended Under a Code Repair Order
bodyText: If a city or town code officer designates your unit unfit for human habitation under the state housing code and orders it repaired, the tenant's duty to pay you rent is suspended, whatever the lease says, and the rent is paid instead into the city or town's housing revolving fund, which pays for code repairs. Where a city or town has adopted a minimum housing ordinance under the separate minimum housing standards chapter, the same happens when its code officer orders repairs because the dwelling is a serious hazard or imminent peril to the occupants: rent goes into an escrow account the officer sets up, is used to pay for the repairs, and any balance is paid to you when the work is done. While the tenant pays into that escrow you cannot sue for rent or for possession; if the tenant stops paying into it, you may sue, subject to the tenant's defenses. Separately, you may not evict without just cause while you have been served with a code notice of violation or while code conferences, hearings or appeals are pending. No lease term can change these rules. Ask the local code office which procedure and account your city or town uses.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-19(f): 'Notwithstanding any lease or other agreement, if the enforcing officer of any corporate unit has ordered the repair, alteration, or improvement of a dwelling in that the officer designates the dwelling to be an unfit dwelling, as provided for in this section, then the obligation of rent to the landlord is suspended and the rent shall be paid into the revolving fund as established in subsection (e) of this section.' (§ 45-24.3-19(f) was added by P.L. 2022, chs. 198, 199, effective June 27, 2022, per the section history; it does not say whether fund money reaches the landlord or bar a rent suit, so the body does not say so.) Unfit designation: § 45-24.3-19(b)(1). R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.2-11: 'Notwithstanding any lease or other agreement, if the enforcing officer of any city or town, which has adopted the provisions of this chapter, has ordered the repair, alteration, or improvement of a dwelling in that the officer has disclosed the dwelling to be a serious hazard or imminent peril to the health, safety, or welfare of the occupants, then the obligations of paying the rent to the landlord are suspended, and the rent shall be paid into an escrow account established by the enforcing officer' ... 'and no action shall be maintained by the landlord against the tenant for the rent or for possession. Sums paid into the escrow fund in excess of those necessary to make repairs shall be paid to the landlord on completion. If the tenant fails to make payments to the enforcing officer then an action for rent or possession may be maintained, subject to any defenses that the tenant may have under the lease or agreement.' Chapter 45-24.2 is enabling law for local minimum housing ordinances (§ 45-24.2-3(a)), so § 45-24.2-11 applies only where the city or town 'has adopted the provisions of this chapter'; which cities have done so was not searched (municipal ordinances not loaded). § 45-24.3-21(c)(4): 'It is unlawful for any owner, operator, or agent to evict occupants from a dwelling or dwelling unit without just cause during conferences, hearings, appeals, or when served with a notice of violation.' RI-repair-escrow-1 recorded as failed (missed § 34-18-32 'pay into court'), rerun as RI-repair-escrow-2 (escrow/pay rent into court/paid into/deposit rent with clerk/rent withholding or abatement/withhold rent near tenant/landlord/lessee/lessor/rental/dwelling unit, window 400; hits 9, OK, real positives §§ 34-18-32, 34-37-4, 45-24.2-11 and three synthetic positives passed); RI-condemned-1 (unfit for habitation/placard/condemn/order to vacate/rent suspended near rent/tenant/lessee/lease/moving/relocate, window 1500; hits 52, OK, real positives §§ 45-24.3-19, 45-24.2-11, 45-24.2-12 passed): no other rent bar for residential tenancies (§ 34-18.1-8 is for commercial and other estates, excluding chapter 34-18 tenancies, § 34-18.1-1). Lead-based rent escrow is separate (§ 42-128.1-14, edu-rent-into-court-ri). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Unfit or Placarded Units
bodyText: If a code officer finds your unit damaged, dilapidated, unsanitary, unsafe or vermin-infested, lacking light, ventilation or required heat and sanitary facilities, or in an unsafe location, and that the condition endangers the occupants or the public, the officer must designate it unfit for human habitation, placard it and, if occupied, order it vacated within no more than 30 days. Nobody may live there again until the officer approves in writing and removes the placard, and no one may deface or remove the placard. The officer may not vacate the building until the occupants have been offered decent, safe and sanitary housing; if the city or town relocates them, the cost is a debt you owe. If you are cited for minimum housing violations and the tenant has to move because the local code agency declares the property unfit, you owe the tenant's reasonable moving expenses unless it is determined you did not cause the violations. If you created an apartment by alterations you knew or should have known broke zoning or housing laws, you pay tenants' moving costs to a place in the same city or town. Once you have been served with a notice of violation or order, you may not lease the unit until you comply, unless you first give the new tenant a true copy and notify the code officer in writing. Rent is suspended while an unfit unit is under a repair order, and you may not evict without just cause during the code process. You may contest a designation before the code officer and the housing board of review.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-19(b)(1) (unfit 'when any of the following defects or conditions are found, and when, in the opinion of the enforcing officer, these defects create a hazard to the health, safety, or welfare of the occupants or of the public'; (i)-(iii) list the conditions). § 45-24.3-19(b)(2): 'the enforcing officer shall placard the dwelling, dwelling unit, or rooming unit, or structure, indicating that it is unfit for human habitation, and, if occupied, shall order the dwelling, dwelling unit, rooming unit, or structure vacated within a reasonable time, that time to be not more than thirty (30) days.' (b)(3) (no reuse 'until written approval is secured from the enforcing officer and the placard removed by the enforcing officer'), (b)(5) (placard), (b)(6) (hearing under § 45-24.3-21). § 45-24.3-19(d): 'no dwelling shall be vacated or demolished by the enforcing officer, under the powers granted to him or her by the provisions of this chapter, until persons occupying the dwelling at the time the compliance order is issued have been offered housing accommodations in a decent, safe, and sanitary dwelling which meets the requirements of this chapter. Should a municipality relocate occupants, the cost of relocation shall constitute a debt in favor of the corporate unit against the owner'. § 45-24.2-12(a): 'If any property owner is cited for minimum housing violations, causing a tenant to vacate the subject property as a result of the property being declared unfit for habitation by the local code enforcement agency vested with the authority, the owner is liable to the tenant for all reasonable moving expenses incurred by the tenant. The owner is not responsible for this expense if it is determined that the owner was not the cause of the violations'; (b) excludes a secured party taking title by enforcing its interest. § 34-18-22.2 (moving costs for apartments created in knowing or should-have-known violation of zoning or housing codes; 'only to a place within the same city or town'). § 45-24.3-17(j): 'It is unlawful for the owner of any residential or non-residential building upon whom a notice of violation or order has been served to sell, transfer, mortgage, lease, or dispose of the building to another until the provisions of the notice or order have been complied with or until the owner first furnishes to the grantee, lessee, or mortgagee prior to the transfer, lease, or mortgage, a true copy of any notice or order issued by the enforcing officer, and, at the same time, notify the enforcing officer, in writing'. Rent suspension (§ 45-24.3-19(f); § 45-24.2-11) and § 45-24.3-21(c)(4): edu-rent-suspension-code-order-ri. Contest: § 45-24.3-21(a), (b) (reconsideration and housing board of review petitions within 10 days). No statute bars accepting a deposit after condemnation as such; RI-condemned-1 (hits 52, OK; see edu-rent-suspension-code-order-ri for terms). § 34-18.1-8 (tenant may quit after condemnation) applies only to commercial and other estates (§ 34-18.1-1). Fire or casualty: § 34-18-33 (edu-alt-housing-ri). Local ordinances not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Don't Repair
bodyText: If you breach the lease, or breach your maintenance duties in a way that materially affects health and safety, a Rhode Island tenant has several remedies. Termination: the tenant may give written notice naming the breach and a termination date at least 30 days after you receive it; the lease ends then unless you fix the breach within 20 days. If substantially the same breach recurs within six months, the tenant may end the lease on 14 days' written notice. You return the deposit and prepaid rent. Damages: the tenant may sue for actual damages and an injunction for any breach of the lease or your maintenance duties, plus attorney's fees if your breach was willful. Repair and deduct: for code, habitability, facility, trash or water and heat failures costing less than $500 in total per year to fix, the tenant may have the work done skillfully and to code and deduct the reasonable cost from rent after telling you in writing they intend to do so, if you don't fix it within 20 days or show ongoing good-faith efforts (in an emergency, if you can't be reached or don't act promptly), and must give you an itemized statement. Essential services: separate remedies apply when heat, water, hot water, electricity or gas fail. The tenant can also counterclaim in a rent or eviction case, and rent is suspended if a code officer orders an unfit unit repaired. The termination, repair-and-deduct and essential-services remedies don't apply to a condition the tenant, their family or their guests caused deliberately or negligently.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-28(a): 'if there is a noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement or a noncompliance with § 34-18-22 materially affecting health and safety, the tenant may deliver a written notice to the landlord specifying the acts and omissions constituting the breach and that the rental agreement will terminate upon a date not less than thirty (30) days after receipt of the notice if the breach is not remedied in twenty (20) days'. § 34-18-28(a)(1) (no termination if 'the landlord adequately remedies the breach before the date specified in the notice'; the body follows the 20-day remedy period stated in the notice language), (a)(2) ('within six (6) months, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement upon at least fourteen (14) days’ written notice'), (a)(3) (not for a condition caused by 'the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of his or her family, or other person on the premises with his or her consent'), (b) ('actual damages and obtain injunctive relief'; 'If the landlord’s noncompliance is willful, the tenant may recover reasonable attorney’s fees.'), (d) (return of security and 'all prepaid rent'). § 34-18-30(a): 'If the landlord fails to comply with § 34-18-22(a)(1), (2), (4), (5), or (6), and the reasonable cost of compliance is less than five hundred dollars ($500) in the aggregate per year, the tenant may cause repairs to be done in a skilled manner, in compliance with applicable state and local codes, and deduct from the tenant’s rent the actual and reasonable cost or the fair and reasonable value of the repairs if:' (1) notice of 'the tenant’s intention to correct the condition at the landlord’s expense'; (2) the landlord 'fails to comply within twenty (20) days, or fails to demonstrate ongoing, good faith efforts to comply, after being notified by the tenant in writing'; emergency branch; (3) 'an itemized statement'. § 34-18-30(b) (tenant-caused conditions excluded). The $500 figure is from R.I. Pub. L. 2023, chs. 286, 287 (effective January 1, 2024), per the section history. § 34-18-31 (essential services; edu-heating-ri, edu-utility-service-continuity-ri, edu-alt-housing-ri); § 34-18-31(c) (electing § 34-18-31 bars §§ 34-18-28 and 34-18-30 'as to that breach'). § 34-18-32 (counterclaim and rent into court; edu-rent-into-court-ri). Code-order rent suspension (§§ 45-24.3-19(f), 45-24.2-11): edu-rent-suspension-code-order-ri; lead rent escrow (§ 42-128.1-14): edu-rent-into-court-ri. Retaliation protection: edu-retaliation-ri. Case law (for example on the implied warranty) not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Small-Landlord Remedy Exemption
bodyText: Rhode Island has no notice or other procedure that lets a landlord with only a few units opt out of tenants' repair remedies. The tenant's rights to end the lease, recover damages, repair and deduct, use the essential-services remedies and counterclaim in a rent or eviction case, and the rent suspension under a code repair order, apply however many units you own, and a lease cannot waive them. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's exclusions turn on the kind of occupancy, not portfolio size: residence in an institution incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services; a buyer occupying under a contract of sale; members in a fraternal or social organization's building; taxable transient hotel or motel stays; employees housed on condition of working on premises of more than 11 units; cooperative proprietary lessees; commercial lettings; and transitional housing. Even those arrangements come under the Act if the parties expressly agree. Do not add a small-landlord exemption notice to a Rhode Island lease.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-8: 'Unless the parties expressly agree to be governed by the provisions of this chapter, the following arrangements are not governed by this chapter:' (1)-(8), including '(5) Occupancy by a paid employee of a landlord, whose right to occupancy is conditional upon employment substantially for services, maintenance, or repair of premises containing more than eleven (11) units;' and '(8) Residence at a transitional housing facility.' No unit-count or notice exemption in §§ 34-18-28, -30, -31, -32 (read whole). § 34-18-17(a)(1) (no waiver of chapter remedies). Statute-wide search with terms and hit counts: RI-repair-escrow-exemption-1 (number words with (n) or fewer/less/more, fewer/less/more than (n), not more than (n) units, (n) to (n) units near tenant/landlord/rental agreement/lessee/lessor/dwelling unit, window 600; hits 154, OK, real positives §§ 34-18-38.1, 34-18-8 and three synthetic positives passed; chapter 34-18 hits are periodic-rent multiples, definitions and the foreclosure 'four (4) or fewer dwelling units' definition in § 34-18-38.1(6), none exempting a landlord from tenant remedies); RI-repair-escrow-exemption-2 (everyday words: small landlord/owner, owner-occupied, exempt from this chapter/section, does not apply to a landlord/owner, opt out/in near tenant/rental agreement/lessee/dwelling unit/rent, window 400; hits 71, OK, four synthetic positives passed; landlord-tenant hits only § 34-18-61 (convenience fees) and foreclosure and zoning sections). Corpus: Rhode Island General Laws, Constitution, three RICR parts and 2025-2026 public laws; case law and municipal ordinances not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A Rhode Island lease cannot remove or water down your habitability duties. A term in which the tenant waives rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, or excuses or limits your liability under the law, is unenforceable, and knowingly using a lease with such a term lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' rent and attorney's fees. No lease, assignment, deed or mortgage may let anyone collect rent free of the repair duties. What you can do is have the tenant perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, and only by a good-faith agreement in a writing you both sign, supported by adequate consideration (something of value for the tenant, such as reduced rent), that does not cover work needed to meet the building and housing codes and does not reduce what you owe other tenants. The duty itself stays yours: if the tenant doesn't do the agreed work and the unit falls below code, you are still answerable. The housing code itself lets a written owner-occupant agreement assign who puts up screens and storm doors and windows. A settlement in which a tenant gives up a claim can be refused enforcement if a court finds it unconscionable.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a): 'A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant: (1) Agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under this chapter;' and '(4) Agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law'. § 34-18-17(b): 'A provision prohibited by subsection (a) included in a rental agreement is unenforceable. If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known to be prohibited, the tenant may recover, in addition to his or her actual damages, an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney’s fees.' § 34-18-18: 'A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed, or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with § 34-18-22(a).' The qualifier that allows reassignment is § 34-18-22(c) only: 'The landlord and tenant of a dwelling unit may agree in writing that the tenant perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, and remodeling but only if: (1) The agreement of the parties is entered into in good faith and set forth in a writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration; (2) The work is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subsection (a)(1); and (3) The agreement does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises.' It reassigns performance of tasks; no sentence lets an agreement remove a § 34-18-22(a) duty. The (a)(6) heat and hot water exception turns on how the unit is built ('an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant'), not on agreement. Housing code: § 45-24.3-6(g) (owner provides and hangs screens and storm doors and windows 'except where there is a written agreement between the owner and occupant'; once installed in a season, maintenance or replacement falls to the occupant absent agreement). § 34-18-13(a)(2) (unconscionable settlement waiving a claim or right under the chapter). The DRAFTING JUDGMENT that the landlord stays answerable if the tenant fails the agreed work rests on § 34-18-22(c)(2) and § 34-18-18; case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: Rhode Island statutes create no presumption that you breached your habitability duties because of a code violation or a missing facility, and none presuming that you had notice or took too long to repair. A tenant who claims a breach must prove it, and the tenant-fault exceptions still apply. The one landlord-tenant presumption in the Act concerns retaliation: if a tenant complained to a code agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, or complained to you about your repair duties, within six months before you raised rent, cut services or sued or threatened to sue for possession, the court presumes you retaliated unless evidence supports the opposite finding (not if the complaint came after notice of the increase or cut). Retaliation for joining a tenants' union or using other lawful remedies is also prohibited, but without the presumption. Keep records of repair requests and responses, since they decide both kinds of dispute. Case law on the burden of proof was not searched.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no habitability-breach or notice presumption). Statute-wide search with terms and hit counts: RI-habitability-presumption-1 (presum*/prima facie near habitab/housing code/minimum housing/code violation/unfit/fit for/repair/noncompliance by the landlord/§ 34-18-22, window 600; hits 13, OK, three synthetic positives passed; only landlord-tenant hit § 34-18-46, retaliation; others motor vehicle, bedding, lead presumptive-compliance certificates in § 42-128.1-4); RI-habitability-presumption-2 (everyday words: rebuttable/shall be deemed/shall be considered/shall be evidence/burden of proof near habitab/housing code/code violation/unfit/fit for human/repair, window 600; hits 37, OK, three synthetic positives passed; no landlord-tenant hit). § 34-18-46(b): 'In an action by or against the tenant, evidence of a complaint within six (6) months before the alleged act of retaliation creates a presumption that the landlord’s conduct was in retaliation. The presumption does not arise if the tenant made the complaint after notice of a proposed rental increase or diminution of services.' and '“Presumption” means that the trier of fact must find the existence of the fact presumed unless and until evidence is introduced which would support a finding of its nonexistence.' § 34-18-46(a)(1)-(4) (protected acts). Retaliation detail is in edu-retaliation-ri. Corpus: General Laws, Constitution, three RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws, court rules; case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Required Fitness Statement
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require your lease to state that you will deliver the unit fit for habitation. The duty exists anyway: at the start of the term you must deliver possession in compliance with the lease and with your repair and code duties, and throughout the tenancy you must keep the unit fit and habitable and up to the building and housing codes. You also may not let a vacant unit unless it is clean, sanitary, fit for human occupancy and code-compliant. A lease sentence promising a habitable unit is harmless, but a sentence saying the tenant accepts the unit as is, or that you make no promise about its condition, cannot excuse these duties and is unenforceable to that extent. The lease does have to carry other required disclosures, such as fees, included utilities, any renters-insurance requirement and your insurance declaration page.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no required lease statement of fitness). § 34-18-21: 'At the commencement of the term a landlord shall deliver possession of the premises to the tenant in compliance with the rental agreement and § 34-18-22.' § 34-18-22(a)(1), (2) (codes; 'put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition'). § 45-24.3-6(a) (no letting a vacant unit 'unless it and the premises are clean, sanitary, fit for human occupancy, and comply with this chapter'). § 34-18-17(a)(1), (4), (b) (waiver and exculpation terms unenforceable); § 34-18-18. Required lease contents that do exist: § 34-18-15(a)(1), (3), (4); § 34-18-22(a)(7). Statute-wide search with terms and hit counts: RI-habitability-statement-1 recorded as failed (real positive § 34-18-15 has no fitness term in the context window), rerun as RI-habitability-statement-3 (lease/rental agreement ... shall/must state/contain/include/provide/set forth/disclose/specify/recite near habitab/fit for/fitness/condition of the premises/repair/warrant, window 600; hits 4, OK, two synthetic positives passed; only landlord-tenant hit § 34-18-22(a)(7) insurance page); RI-habitability-statement-2 (everyday words: warranty of habitability or fitness, fit for or to live, habitable condition, livable, condition permitting habitation near lease/rental agreement/tenancy/landlord/lessor, window 600; hits 7, OK, real positive § 34-18-22 and three synthetic positives passed; others § 34-18-56 statutory answer form, § 45-24.2-3, UCC lease warranties). Case law (implied warranty) not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Landlord May Fix Tenant-Caused Conditions
bodyText: [Optional.] If Tenant fails to comply with Tenant's maintenance duties under Rhode Island law in a way that materially affects health and safety and that can be remedied by repair, replacement of a damaged item or cleaning, and Tenant does not remedy it as promptly as conditions require in an emergency, or within 20 days after Landlord gives Tenant written notice specifying the breach and requesting that Tenant remedy it within that time, Landlord may enter the property, as this Lease's Access & Entry terms and Rhode Island law permit, and have the work done in a skilled manner. Landlord will give Tenant an itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost, or the fair and reasonable value, of the work, and Tenant will pay it as Rent on the next date Rent is due, or immediately if this Lease has ended.
notes: RI: Optional; never default. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-39: 'If there is noncompliance by tenant with § 34-18-24 materially affecting health and safety that can be remedied by repair, replacement of a damaged item, or cleaning, and the tenant fails to comply as promptly as conditions require in case of emergency or within twenty (20) days after written notice by the landlord specifying the breach and requesting that the tenant remedy it within that period of time, the landlord may enter the dwelling unit and cause the work to be done in a skilled manner and submit the itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost or the fair and reasonable value thereof as rent on the next date periodic rent is due, or if the rental agreement has terminated, for immediate payment.' The clause tracks every condition (20 days, not the 14 or 7 days of the TN, IA and NM versions). Tenant duties it reaches: § 34-18-24(1)-(6) (codes, cleanliness, waste, plumbing fixtures, reasonable use of facilities, no damage). Entry: § 34-18-26 (two days' notice except emergency or impracticability; see planned `landlords-access-ri`), so the clause routes entry through the Access & Entry terms because § 34-18-26(c) requires two days' notice except in emergency or where impracticable (drafting judgment, cheaper error), although § 34-18-26(d)(2) lists entry 'As permitted by § 34-18-39' as its own access ground. The statute works without a clause; the clause gives notice of the remedy and the billing-as-rent rule. It does not reach conditions the landlord must fix under § 34-18-22, and does not let the landlord charge more than actual reasonable cost or fair value (§ 34-18-17(a)(3), (4) not engaged). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Quiet Possession
bodyText: Rhode Island's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act contains no general covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession for tenants; its only 'peaceful enjoyment' language is the tenant's duty not to disturb the neighbors. The protections such a covenant gives come from specific sections instead. At the start of the term you must deliver possession in line with the lease and your repair duties. You may not take back possession yourself, by lockout, removal, or willfully interrupting heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, except after abandonment or surrender or as the Act allows. If you unlawfully remove or exclude the tenant or willfully cut such a service, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. You may enter only on at least two days' notice and at reasonable times (except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable) and may not use entry to harass; an unlawful, unreasonable or harassing entry lets the tenant get an injunction or end the lease, with damages, costs and attorney's fees. The common-law covenant of quiet enjoyment in Rhode Island case law was not searched.

title: No Double-Letting Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute aimed specifically at renting the same unit or room to two tenants. The failure-to-deliver-possession rules cover it. If you don't deliver possession at the start of the term, the tenant owes no rent until you do and may either end the lease on at least five days' written notice (you then return all prepaid rent and the deposit) or demand performance and sue you for possession. You may sue anyone wrongfully in possession. If a failure to deliver possession is willful and not in good faith, the person harmed may recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees, so knowingly signing two leases for the same unit is costly.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no double-letting statute). § 34-18-29(a): 'If the landlord fails to deliver possession of the dwelling unit to the tenant as provided in § 34-18-21, rent abates until possession is delivered and the tenant may: (1) Terminate the rental agreement upon at least five (5) days’ written notice to the landlord, and, upon termination, the landlord shall return all prepaid rent and security; or (2) Demand performance of the rental agreement by the landlord and, if the tenant elects, bring action for possession of the dwelling unit against the landlord.' § 34-18-29(b): 'If a person’s failure to deliver possession is willful and not in good faith, an aggrieved person may recover from that person an amount not more than three (3) months’ periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney’s fees.' § 34-18-21 ('The landlord may bring an action for possession against any person wrongfully in possession'). title: How Tenants Must Give Repair Notice
bodyText: How a tenant tells you about a repair problem decides which remedies the tenant can use. To end the lease for your breach, the tenant must give you written notice naming the breach. To repair and deduct, the tenant must tell you they intend to fix the condition at your expense, and the 20-day period runs from written notice (in an emergency, the tenant may act if you can't be reached or don't act promptly). For heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant need only give you reasonable notice specifying the breach; the Act does not require it in writing. A repair complaint made to you in any form is protected against retaliation. Under the Act you have notice of a fact you actually know, were notified of, or have reason to know from the circumstances, and a notice reaches you when it comes to your attention or is handed to you or sent first-class mail to the address you hold out for notices. Your lease may ask tenants to report ordinary repairs in writing or through a portal, but that term cannot take away a remedy the Act grants on oral or reasonable notice, or excuse a condition you already know about, because lease terms waiving tenant remedies are unenforceable.
notes: RI: § 34-18-28(a) ('the tenant may deliver a written notice to the landlord specifying the acts and omissions constituting the breach'). § 34-18-30(a)(1) ('The tenant notifies the landlord of the tenant’s intention to correct the condition at the landlord’s expense'), (a)(2) ('fails to comply within twenty (20) days, or fails to demonstrate ongoing, good faith efforts to comply, after being notified by the tenant in writing; or, in the case of emergency, the landlord either cannot be reached by the tenant, or the landlord fails to comply as promptly as conditions require'). § 34-18-31(a) ('the tenant may give reasonable notice to the landlord specifying the breach'), (d) (rights 'do not arise until he or she has given notice to the landlord'). § 34-18-46(a)(2) ('The tenant has complained to the landlord of a violation under § 34-18-22'). § 34-18-14(a)(1): 'A person has notice of a fact if: (i) He or she has actual knowledge of it; (ii) He or she has received a notice or notification of it; or (iii) From all the facts and circumstances known to him or her at the time in question he or she has reason to know that it exists.' § 34-18-14(b)(1), (2) (receipt: 'It comes to his or her attention' or delivered in hand or 'sent by first class mail to him or her at a place held out by him or her as the place for receipt of the communication'). § 34-18-17(a)(1), (b) (waiver of remedies unenforceable). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: a lease term requiring written repair requests is a lawful records term but cannot narrow § 34-18-31 or § 34-18-46(a)(2), which do not require writing. Whether a lease that invites oral repair reports waives the landlord's right to the written notices in §§ 34-18-28 and 34-18-30 is not answered by statute; case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Designated-Repairer Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute that lets you name, in the lease, who must do repairs a tenant makes at your expense. The tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy (for problems costing under $500 a year to fix, after notice and 20 days) requires only that the work be done in a skilled manner and in compliance with state and local codes, and the tenant may deduct only the actual and reasonable cost or fair value. A lease clause forcing the tenant to use your contractor for that remedy would narrow a right the Act gives, so it risks being an unenforceable waiver, and knowingly using a prohibited term can cost up to three months' rent plus attorney's fees. You may list preferred vendors and an emergency repair number and ask the tenant to call them first, as long as the lease does not make that a condition of the remedy. When you do work after a tenant's own breach, it too must be done in a skilled manner.

title: No Repair-Cost Termination
bodyText: Rhode Island gives you no right to end a lease because a repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value, and a lease cannot create one by cutting back the tenant's rights. Your repair duties run for the whole tenancy; to end a periodic tenancy you give the ordinary termination notice, and a fixed-term lease runs to its end. After a fire or casualty that substantially impairs the unit, the statute gives the choice to the tenant: vacate and end the lease by written notice within 14 days, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stay in the usable part at reduced rent. If the lease ends you return the deposit and prepaid rent, and you may sue a tenant who caused the fire negligently or deliberately. The Act gives you no matching right to terminate after a casualty, so any landlord option to do so must come from the lease and must leave the tenant's own choices intact. Cost-against-value tests appear only in code enforcement: a code officer may make repairs at your expense when they cost no more than half the structure's fair market value, and may order an unfit, placarded and vacated building demolished if it does not warrant repair.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no landlord termination for uneconomical repairs). § 34-18-33(a): 'If the dwelling unit or premises are damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty to an extent that enjoyment of the dwelling unit is substantially impaired, the tenant may: (1) Immediately vacate the premises and notify the landlord in writing within fourteen (14) days thereafter of his or her intention to terminate the rental agreement, in which case the rental agreement terminates as of the date of vacating; or (2) If continued occupancy is lawful, vacate any part of the dwelling unit rendered unusable by the fire or casualty, in which case the tenants’ liability for rent is reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value of the dwelling unit.' § 34-18-33(b), (c) (return of security and prepaid rent; landlord's tort action). § 34-18-17(a)(1). title: Promised Repairs
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule that your promises to clean, repair or improve a unit must be in writing, carry a completion date, or be made before the lease is signed. Promises you make still bind you. The rental agreement includes all agreements, written or oral, so an agreed repair or improvement is part of the lease; you must deliver possession in compliance with it, and if you don't keep the promise the tenant may recover damages and an injunction (with attorney's fees if your breach is willful), and may give you written notice ending the lease on a date at least 30 days after you receive it unless you fix the breach within 20 days. The tenant must allow reasonable access for agreed repairs. Put every promised repair or improvement in the lease or a signed addendum with a target date, so both sides know what was agreed and an entire-agreement clause doesn't leave a dispute about oral promises.

title: No Balcony Inspection Law
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to inspect balconies, decks, porches or other elevated exterior structures on a schedule, or to report on them. Your general duties still cover them: you must comply with the building and housing codes, keep the premises fit and habitable and keep common areas clean and safe, and the housing code requires floors, walls and other parts of the building to be kept in sound condition and good repair, exterior wood to be protected from decay, accessory structures to be structurally sound and in good repair, and all ways and means of egress to meet fire protection laws. Local building officials may run periodic inspections of existing buildings, and minimum housing ordinances may set standards for the condition and repair of stairs and porches, so check your city or town's code. A failing balcony or railing is the kind of condition that can lead to code orders, an unfit designation and tenant remedies, so inspect wooden balconies and railings yourself, especially in multi-unit buildings.

title: No Emergency Number Requirement
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule requiring a dedicated emergency repair phone number or on-call contact. What the law does require is that, at or before the start of the tenancy, you give the tenant in writing the name, address and number of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or agent authorized to accept service of process and notices, and keep that information current; a manager who fails to disclose becomes your agent for notices and for performing your duties under the lease and the Act. Give a number that works around the clock anyway: in an emergency a tenant may make limited repairs at your expense if you cannot be reached, and may use the essential-services remedies after giving you notice.

title: Tenant Choice of Cable and Internet Provider
bodyText: A tenant in a multiple dwelling may choose their own cable television, telephone, telecommunications or information service provider, free of restraints or conditions you impose. A provider may install facilities to serve a tenant's unit at no cost to you, must indemnify you for installation damage, may not interfere with the building's safety, functioning, appearance or use or with your reasonable rules (including reasonable access rules for soliciting), must review its plans with you first (you may waive that in writing), must honor reasonable installation requests, and maintains its own equipment. The provider has your consent once it delivers a copy of the statute and a signed statement agreeing to be bound. You may charge only a nominal $1 for permitting installation unless you notify the provider by certified mail within 20 days of learning of the planned installation, then state your claim in writing within 30 days and, if it is refused, sue in superior court within six months; you must show a specific alternative use of the space or a loss of rental or resale value. It is an unfair trade practice to charge tenants different rent or other charges based on their choice of service, or to take payment for installation outside this process. You and a provider may not agree to interfere with tenants' use of a master or individual antenna. Mobile home parks have a parallel rule.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. (2) (no agreement or act that would 'diminish or interfere with the rights of any tenant to use a master or individual antenna system'). (3)(i), (ii) (consent by delivery of the section and a signed statement; plans review, 'The owner may waive, in writing, the prior presentation of the plans and specifications'; provider maintains equipment). (8): 'It shall be an unfair trade practice under chapter 13.1 of title 6 for any person owning, leasing, or managing any multiple dwelling unit served by a CATV system or other telephone, telecommunications, or information service provider to discriminate in rental charges or other charges to tenants based on the tenants’ subscription to a CATV, telephone, telecommunications, or information service from and after June 25, 1986'; contracts on or before June 25, 1986 excepted. title: No Utility Allowance Rules
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on utility allowances, caps on the utilities you pay, or how you may pass utility costs through to tenants in ordinary residential rentals (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). Mobile home parks that resell electricity, gas or water may not charge residents more than the utility's rate, plus a return on metering costs. A lease may set the split, but two disclosure rules apply: the lease must say which utility costs are included in rent and which are the tenant's, and any fee beyond rent, such as an overage charge above a utility allowance, must be listed in the same section as the rent with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); an undisclosed fee can be recovered by the tenant. Separately, apartment buildings with more than ten units whose construction began after July 1, 1977 may not use an electric master meter: each unit must have its own electric meter (publicly financed elderly or disabled housing may elect a single meter). Whatever you bill, you may not cut off a utility to collect it.

Each apartment or dwelling unit shall have a measuring device or meter for the purpose of measuring the electricity used only by that apartment.' (elderly/disabled public-financing exception). No shutoff: § 34-18-44 (see edu-no-submeter-interruption-ri). title: No Required Security Devices
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring particular security devices in rental units, such as deadbolts, door viewers, window latches or keyless locks, and no duty to rekey between tenants. Your general duties still apply: comply with building and housing codes, keep the premises fit and habitable and keep common areas safe, and local codes may require more. From July 1, 2026 there is one lock rule you must follow. If all tenants in possession ask, or a court order is furnished, because a tenant or adult household member reasonably believes they face an imminent threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking at the premises, you must within two business days make a good-faith effort to change the unit's locks (and give the requester a key) or allow the tenant to change them. You may ask in good faith for written verification and charge no more than the reasonable price customarily charged for changing such locks in that community. If you don't act in time, the tenant may change the locks with locks of similar or better quality and must try to give you a key within two business days. Blocking a lawful change or failing to try to provide a key can cost two months' rent plus costs and attorney's fees, unless a court finds you acted in good faith. Rekeying at turnover is good practice, not a legal requirement.

(a) household member is 18 or older or an emancipated minor; (c) perpetrator who is a tenant or household member may be denied a key on a protective or court order; (f) no liability for refusing a key to a reasonably believed perpetrator.
