title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: You may not refuse reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices or services when they may be necessary to give an occupant with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, such as a reserved accessible parking space, a change in rent-payment method or an exception to a no-pets rule for an assistance animal. You also may not refuse to let a person with a disability make, at their own expense, reasonable modifications to the premises that may be necessary for full enjoyment of them. For a rental, where it is reasonable you may condition permission on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. If needed to make sure restoration money will be there at the end of the tenancy, you may negotiate payments over a reasonable period into an interest-bearing escrow account, not exceeding the restoration cost; the interest belongs to the tenant. That restoration deposit does not count toward the one-month deposit cap, but the deposit return rules (itemized refund within 20 days, double damages for wrongful withholding) apply to it. Rhode Island does not require the lease itself to state your restoration right; put any restoration agreement in a separate signed writing. You need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property, and a disability does not shield a tenant from eviction for disturbing neighbors.

title: Receivership for Abandoned Buildings
bodyText: Rhode Island's receivership law targets abandoned buildings that have become public nuisances. A court infers abandonment from serious code violations posing a health or safety hazard together with facts such as vacancy, unmaintained grounds, an unsound interior, unrepaired vandalism and whether the owner has been collecting rents. If such a building is dangerous or violates the building codes or minimum housing standards, the city or town, a neighboring landowner within 200 feet, or a qualifying housing nonprofit may ask the court for an injunction ordering repairs. If the owner, given a reasonable chance, does not begin correcting a public nuisance, the court first offers the work to mortgagees and lienholders and may then appoint a receiver, a court-certified lawyer, who can take possession, manage the property, collect rents, lease units, evict tenants, make repairs and borrow against the property with a first-priority lien. Separately, after a second Department of Health notice of violation for unmet lead hazard reduction in a rental occupied by a pregnant woman or a child under six, the unit may be treated as abandoned and a public nuisance, and the department, the attorney general, a nonprofit or the city or town may ask for a receiver. 2026 amendments narrowed when property counts as abandoned and let owners cure listed conditions. A landlord who keeps an occupied building maintained and answers code notices is outside this law; ignoring repeated code orders is what brings it on.

title: Code Inspections of Rental Units
bodyText: City and town housing code officers may inspect rental units under an adopted inspection plan (including systematic inspection of designated neighborhoods), in response to a complaint, or when they have valid reason to believe the code is being violated. They may enter between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., or at another time by appointment. For a plan inspection, the owner or occupant in charge must give entry and free access once the officer shows proper identification, a copy of the relevant inspection plan and a schedule of the areas and facilities to be inspected; if entry is refused, the officer may get a court order on a showing of probable cause, and disobeying it is contempt. Information unrelated to the code that the officer learns is confidential. When an officer is repairing at your expense after a second violation notice, refusing or obstructing entry carries a $25 civil penalty each time. A lease cannot itself authorize an inspector to enter: your own right of entry is limited to the reasons the Act lists, with at least two days' notice except in emergencies, so arrange inspections with the tenant or through the officer's own powers. The statewide rental registry does not involve inspections. Some cities have their own rental licensing or inspection ordinances, which were not searched.

title: Pools at Rental Properties
bodyText: If you maintain a swimming, wading or therapeutic pool for your tenants, it is a regulated pool unless it is an individual's own household pool used without charge and not in connection with a business run for profit. You need a Department of Health license before operating it (seasonal, June 1 to September 30, or year-round, expiring December 31); the department inspects before licensing and at least once a year, and its rules govern design, equipment, condition, maintenance and water testing. No lifeguard is required unless a swim club or a group of unsupervised children who may have access uses the pool. When no lifeguard is on duty you must limit access to guests and members by an attendant or a mechanical system, have a person trained in first aid in close proximity, post the required signs (NO LIFEGUARD ON DUTY — SWIM AT YOUR OWN RISK in red letters at least 4 inches high; no one under 18 unless accompanied by an adult; adults should not swim alone; pool hours; no glass; no running or rough housing; no diving; no animals or pets), and for an outdoor pool surround the pool area with a fence at least six feet high with a lockable gate or door. Condominium projects of 45 units or fewer need no lifeguard, but minors may use the pool only with a parent or other responsible adult. Whether a private pool at a single-family rental needs a license is not clear from the statute; ask the department.

title: Which Fire Code Applies
bodyText: When Rhode Island law refers to fire safety requirements, it means the Rhode Island Fire Safety Code: the National Fire Protection Association's Fire Code (NFPA 1) and Life Safety Code (NFPA 101), with annexes, as amended and added to by rules of the Fire Safety Code Board of Appeal and Review. The code sets minimum fire safety requirements for new and existing buildings, but not for private dwellings occupied by one, two or three families, except that it sets smoke alarm and carbon monoxide alarm standards for those dwellings, and three-family dwellings must be equipped with both. For existing buildings, the local fire authority applies the parts of the codes written for existing structures, subject to board rules, variances and written modifications. Cities and towns may adopt stricter fire ordinances only with the board's approval, and may not set their own fire alarm requirements. These rules are part of your repair duty: you must comply with building and housing codes affecting health and safety, which the Act defines to include any law, ordinance or regulation on a building's construction, maintenance, operation or occupancy, and the housing code requires egress, construction and equipment to meet fire protection laws. The board's rules, which fix the edition of each NFPA code in force, are regulations not reproduced in the General Laws; check them, and your local fire marshal, for a specific building.

title: After a Disaster
bodyText: Rhode Island has no special rules for tenancies after a declared disaster or an evacuation order: a disaster does not by itself end the lease, and no statute sets debris-removal or hazard-cleanup deadlines for landlords. The fire-or-casualty rule covers storm, flood and other disaster damage. If the damage substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may vacate immediately and end the lease by written notice to you within 14 days (the lease ends as of the date they left), or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stay and vacate only the unusable part, paying rent reduced in proportion to the drop in fair rental value. Rent is accounted for as of the date of the casualty, and if the lease ends you return the deposit and prepaid rent. Your repair and code duties continue for any tenant who stays, including essential services, and if a code officer designates the unit unfit, rent is suspended under a repair order and the unit may be placarded and vacated. A lease cannot take these rights away. The rule for commercial and other estates that lets an occupant quit after destruction or condemnation does not apply to residential tenancies.

title: No Health-District Rental Rules
bodyText: Rhode Island has no local health districts with their own rental-unit regulations, and no rule requiring you to give tenants health-department rental rules on request or to post a notice of occupants' rights. Rental health and safety is handled in two other ways. Each city or town's housing code officer enforces the state Housing Maintenance and Occupancy Code (and any local minimum housing ordinance), inspecting on complaint or under an inspection plan; the code's health officer is the state director of health. The state Department of Health runs the lead poisoning prevention rules and the statewide rental registry. You may not retaliate against a tenant who complains to a code enforcement agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, and a rent increase, service cut, or eviction filing or threat within six months after such a complaint is presumed retaliatory (unless the complaint came after your notice of the increase or cut). You may still sue for possession if the tenant is in default in rent, if the code violation was caused primarily by lack of reasonable care by the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent, or if code compliance or other public action requires work that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit and the municipality has met its relocation requirements. Treat any such complaint as a repair request and respond in writing.

title: Facilities the Housing Code Requires
bodyText: Beyond the general repair duty, Rhode Island's housing code requires specific facilities in every rental, and you must keep in good and safe working order every facility and appliance you supply or must supply. Required items include: a kitchen with a sink with hot and cold running water, food-storage cabinets or shelves, a counter or table, and (unless the incoming tenant is to provide them) a stove and a refrigerator; a toilet and washbasin in a separate room and a bathtub or shower in a room affording privacy; heated water of at least 120°F; at least one window or skylight in every habitable room, sized at 10% of floor area with at least half openable, or approved ventilation; electric service with at least two outlets per habitable room (one per 60 square feet) and a light fixture in each bathroom, kitchen, laundry, furnace room and public hall; lighted public halls and stairways; dual egress for units above the first floor; screens on doors and ventilation windows during insect season, with self-closing outside screen doors; and rodent-proofing. You must provide and hang screens and storm doors and windows where the code requires them, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise in writing (once installed for a season the tenant maintains them), and shades on bedroom and bathroom windows (replacements are the tenant's). In buildings of four or more units you supply trash containers; in one- to three-family buildings the occupant does.

title: No Subsidy Proration Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule on prorating rent for a subsidized tenant when part of the unit becomes unusable. The general fire-or-casualty rule applies to every tenancy: if continued occupancy is lawful, the tenant may vacate the unusable part and the tenant's liability for rent is reduced in proportion to the drop in the unit's fair rental value, or the tenant may vacate and end the lease by written notice within 14 days. The statute does not say how a reduction is split between the tenant's share and the subsidy payment. For public, federally subsidized or regulated housing, the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies except where federal law preempts the subject or federal rights and duties directly conflict with it, in which case the federal rules control, so follow your housing assistance payments contract and program rules on abatement and inspections. Separately, if you set a minimum-income standard, it must be applied only to the tenant's portion of the rent, counting any rental assistance.

title: Habitability Rules Rhode Island Lacks
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no Rhode Island counterpart. (1) No statutory list of imminently dangerous conditions: whether a condition is a serious hazard or imminent peril is decided case by case by local code officers, whose findings can lead to repair orders, an unfit designation, placarding and rent suspension. (2) Air conditioning is not named as an essential service. If you supply air conditioning you must keep it in good and safe working order, and the essential-services remedies cover heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas and other essential service without defining the last term. (3) No presumption that a code violation proves a breach, no required lease statement of fitness, no small-landlord exemption from tenant remedies, no landlord right to terminate instead of making a costly repair, no designated-repairer rule and no rule that repair promises be written. Each of these has its own explanation in the library. Case law was not searched, and local codes may add requirements.

title: No Rule on Splitting Shared Utility Bills
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on splitting a shared utility bill among tenants. No law bans it, sets a formula (square footage, number of occupants or a ratio), makes a lease term charging for a utility that isn't separately metered unenforceable, or prescribes a disclosure form or lease attachment for it. If you split a shared bill, the general lease rules apply: the lease must say which utility costs are included in the rent and which are the tenant's (with no written lease, tell the tenant in writing), and any charge beyond rent must be listed in the same section as the rent with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format). A tenant can recover fees you didn't disclose that way. Electricity has one hard limit: an apartment house with more than ten units whose construction began after July 1, 1977 may not use a master meter, and each unit must have its own electric meter (publicly financed housing for elderly or disabled residents may elect a single meter). City, town and district water charges stay your liability, and a lien on the property, whoever uses the water. You may not cut off service to collect a tenant's share. Utility commission rules, local ordinances and case law were not searched.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no utility apportionment rule). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(3): 'In any lease agreement the landlord shall disclose which utility costs are included in the rent and which utility costs are the tenant's responsibility. If there is no written lease, the landlord shall provide this information to the tenant in writing.' (§ 34-18-15(a)(3)); § 34-18-15(a)(1): 'If there are fees beyond the rent that apply to the rental of a unit, the lease shall disclose those fees in the same section as the rent disclosure and shall indicate that additional fees may apply.' (§ 34-18-15(a)(1)); § 34-18-15(a)(5): 'the tenant may recover any fees paid for the unit that were not disclosed as required' (§ 34-18-15(a)(5)). Master meters: § 39-3-7.1: 'The use of "master-meters," so-called, in apartment or tenement houses containing more than ten (10) apartments or dwelling units is hereby prohibited; provided, however, that this section shall only apply to apartment houses, construction of which is commenced after July 1, 1977.' title: Learning of a Tenant Utility Shutoff
bodyText: Rhode Island has no procedure for a tenant to authorize the utility to warn you before the tenant's own service is shut off, and no statute requiring a utility to copy a landlord on a tenant's shutoff notice. The general rule is that a public utility supplying heat, light, water or power may not shut off service for nonpayment without written notice at least 10 days before the shutoff date, to the user of the service or the building owner as recorded with the utility; when the account is the tenant's, expect the notice to go to the tenant. If you need to know, the lease may require the tenant to keep the services in the tenant's name on and paid, to show proof of payment on request, and to tell you promptly of any shutoff notice. You may also ask the utility whether it will copy you with the tenant's written consent; its own rules decide that. City, town and district water charges remain your liability and a lien on the property even when the tenant holds the account. Utility commission rules were not searched.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no tenant authorization of shutoff notices to the landlord). R.I. Gen. Laws § 39-2-1(a): no public utility providing heat, light, water, or power 'shall terminate the service or deprive any home or building, or whatsoever, of service if the reason therefor is nonpayment of the service without first notifying the user of the service, or the owner, or owners, of the building as recorded with the utility of the impending service termination by written notice at least ten (10) days prior to the effective date of the proposed termination of service.' (§ 39-2-1(a)). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the 'or' does not on its face require notice to both user and owner (§ 39-2-1(a)), so the body does not promise the landlord a copy. Water lien: § 39-15-12 (owner liable for water furnished 'to the owner or occupant'; § 39-15-12). Lease-term suggestions rest on § 34-18-15(a) (terms 'not prohibited by this chapter or other rule of law'; § 34-18-15(a)); the shared utility-payment-evidence clause covers proof of payment. title: When the Utility Account Is Yours
bodyText: When a utility account serving your tenants is in your name, the risk of nonpayment is yours. A public utility supplying heat, light, water or power must give written notice at least 10 days before a shutoff for nonpayment, to the user or to the building owner as recorded with the utility. No Rhode Island statute requires it to warn each tenant or let tenants take over your account (at least one water district's own act requires mailed notice to occupants before it shuts off water for charges more than 60 days overdue). If the lease or the law makes a service yours (running water and reasonable hot water at all times; reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1, unless the building isn't required by law to be equipped for them or the heat or hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control on a direct utility connection) and you willfully or negligently fail to supply it, the tenant may, after giving you reasonable notice, buy the service and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent, recover damages for lost rental value, or move to substitute housing, owe no rent meanwhile and recover its reasonable cost up to the amount of one period's rent, plus reasonable attorney's fees. These remedies do not apply if the tenant, a member of the tenant's family or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent deliberately or negligently caused the condition. If you willfully let service be cut off, the tenant may also recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. Water charges billed to the building are also a lien on your property.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 39-2-1(a): no public utility providing heat, light, water, or power shall terminate for nonpayment 'without first notifying the user of the service, or the owner, or owners, of the building as recorded with the utility of the impending service termination by written notice at least ten (10) days prior to the effective date of the proposed termination of service.' (§ 39-2-1(a)). Landlord supply duty: § 34-18-22(a)(6) ('Supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times' and 'reasonable heat ... between October 1 and May 1', except where 'heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant and supplied by a direct public utility connection'; § 34-18-22(a)(6)). Remedies: § 34-18-31(a): 'If, contrary to the rental agreement or § 34-18-22, the landlord willfully or negligently fails to supply heat, running water, hot water, electric, gas, or other essential service, the tenant may give reasonable notice to the landlord specifying the breach' (§ 34-18-31(a)), then deduct 'actual and reasonable costs from the periodic rent' (§ 34-18-31(a)(1)), damages (a)(2), or substitute housing (a)(3); (b) substitute housing cost 'not in excess of an amount equal to the periodic rent' and 'reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-31(b)); (d) notice first; no remedy if tenant-caused. § 34-18-34: if the landlord 'willfully diminishes services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of heat, running water, hot water, electric, gas, or other essential service', the tenant may recover possession or terminate and recover 'an amount not more than three (3) months periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him or her, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-34); see § 34-18-44. Water-district occupant notice: § 45-48.1-6(3) (after charges 'remain unpaid for a period of more than sixty (60) days', notice to the owner 'and to occupants of said premises by mail' before the district may 'shut off the supply of water'; § 45-48.1-6(3)); other district and municipal water acts not surveyed. title: Utility Shutoff Protections
bodyText: Rhode Island's shutoff rules bind utilities, not landlords, but they protect your tenants and govern your own house accounts. A public utility supplying heat, light, water or power must give written notice at least 10 days before shutting off service for nonpayment. State law fixes the winter moratorium period for residential electric and gas shutoffs at November 1 through May 1 (the Public Utilities Commission may extend it); who it protects is set by commission rules, which were not searched. All year: a utility must follow commission rules before shutting off electric, gas or water service to a household where every adult is 65 or older or anyone is disabled or seriously ill (a doctor's certification of serious illness puts the shutoff date at least three weeks out); a gas or electric company may not shut off a home where a child under two lives if the customer can't pay because of financial hardship and service wasn't shut off for nonpayment before the child's birth; and the main gas and electric companies may not shut off a household eligible for federal heating assistance (LIHEAP) that owes $300 or less and is no more than two months behind; the same subsection separately says service may not be terminated unless two termination notices have been sent. None of this cancels the debt. You may never cause a tenant's service to be cut off.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 39-2-1(a): no public utility providing heat, light, water, or power shall terminate for nonpayment 'without first notifying the user of the service, or the owner, or owners, of the building as recorded with the utility of the impending service termination by written notice at least ten (10) days prior to the effective date of the proposed termination of service.' (§ 39-2-1(a)); (b) commission rules on 'winter moratorium and medical emergency protections' apply to electric distributors (§ 39-2-1(b)); (d)(2) LIHEAP arrearage forgiveness plan. § 39-1-63(a): the commission shall amend 810-RICR-10-00-1 'in order that the utility termination moratorium period shall mean the period of time between 12:01 a.m. on November 1 and 11:59 p.m. on May 1 of each year.' (§ 39-1-63(a)); proviso preserving emergency suspensions under chapter 15 of title 30; (b) discretion to extend. § 39-1.1-1(a): no utility supplying electric, gas or water service 'shall terminate service to any household in which all adult residents are sixty-five (65) years of age or older, or where any resident is disabled or seriously ill, for failure to pay an outstanding indebtedness for service, without first complying with all rules and regulations for such terminations issued by the commission.' (§ 39-1.1-1(a)); § 39-1.1-1(b): gas and electric distribution companies other than 'the Block Island Power Company or the Pascoag Utility District' (§ 39-1.1-1(b)) 'shall not shut off service to a household eligible for LIHEAP if the customer's outstanding bill is three hundred dollars ($300) or less and not more than two (2) months in arrears. Service may not be terminated unless two (2) notices of termination have been sent.' (§ 39-1.1-1(b)). § 39-1.1-2(b)(1): termination date 'not less than three (3) weeks from receipt by the public utility of the written certification' (§ 39-1.1-2(b)(1)); (b)(3): 'Nontermination for any reason does not, in any way, relieve the customer of liability incurred for utility services.' (§ 39-1.1-2(b)(3)). § 39-1.1-2.1 (no gas or electric termination where 'a person under the age of two (2) years' is domiciled, 'the customer's service has not been previously shut off for nonpayment before the birth of the child' and 'the customer cannot afford to pay any overdue bill because of financial hardship'; § 39-1.1-2.1). § 39-1.1-3 (reasonable debt-collection methods first), § 39-1.1-4 (winter rules preserved). Landlord: § 34-18-44, § 34-18-34. No 2026 act amends these sections: RI-utility-shutoff-statute-1 (cites to § 39-1-63, § 39-2-1, chapter 39-1.1 and winter-moratorium words, no context limb; hits 24, OK; real positives § 39-1-63 and § 39-1.1-4 passed; 2026 hits are thermal-energy acts citing § 39-2-1.2 only). title: No Cutoff for Untransferred Utilities
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule letting you shut off utilities still in your name because the tenant didn't move the account into their own name. The lease may require the tenant to put named utilities in the tenant's name by a set date and to pay them, and failing to do so is a lease breach you can pursue (after a 20-day notice to cure for a material breach, or by charging the tenant what you paid if the lease says so). But don't let the service lapse: if you willfully interrupt, or cause the interruption of, heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees, and you must return the deposit and prepaid rent. Heat from October 1 to May 1, running water and hot water are yours to supply anyway, unless the building isn't required by law to be equipped for them or the heat or hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control on a direct utility connection. A utility may not refuse a tenant service because a previous occupant left without paying, unless the service would benefit that occupant.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no cutoff for an untransferred account). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-34: 'If a landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises or willfully diminishes services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of heat, running water, hot water, electric, gas, or other essential service, the tenant may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, in either case, recover an amount not more than three (3) months periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him or her, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees. If the rental agreement is terminated the landlord shall return all security recoverable under § 34-18-19 and all prepaid rent.' (§ 34-18-34). § 34-18-44 (no recovery of possession by 'willful diminution of services'; § 34-18-44). Supply duty: § 34-18-22(a)(6) ('reasonable heat' between October 1 and May 1 and running and hot water, except an installation 'within the exclusive control of the tenant and supplied by a direct public utility connection'; § 34-18-22(a)(6)). Lease term: § 34-18-15(a) (terms 'not prohibited by this chapter or other rule of law'; § 34-18-15(a)); utility disclosure § 34-18-15(a)(3). Breach: § 34-18-36 20-day cure notice (see edu-termination-notice-ri and related rows; § 34-18-36 read whole). New occupants: § 39-2-1.1: 'No public utility shall refuse to furnish services to new occupants at any premises on the grounds that the previous occupant has vacated the premises without paying the public utility for services furnished, provided that the service is not for the use or benefit of the previous occupant.' (§ 39-2-1.1). Statute-wide search over the RI corpus (General Laws with all dated versions, Constitution, three loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws, court rules), no context limb: RI-utility-transfer-1 recorded as failed (a synthetic positive missed), rerun as RI-utility-transfer-3 (transfer/place/put/change/switch/establish/open a utility, account or service into the tenant's, occupant's, lessee's or resident's own name; hits 3, OK; three synthetic positives passed; § 39-26.4-2 net-metering only); RI-utility-transfer-2 (everyday words: put the utilities in their name, switch the electric over, new account for the tenant, start service; hits 0, OK; three synthetic positives passed). title: Survivor Lock Changes
bodyText: Since July 1, 2026, if all tenants in possession ask, or someone gives you a court order, because a tenant or household member (an authorized occupant 18 or older, or an emancipated minor) reasonably believes they face an imminent threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking at the premises, you must, within two business days, make a good faith effort to change the unit's locks or let them change the locks in a workmanlike manner. If you change them, try to get the requester a key within the same two business days. You may ask in good faith for the written verification the survivor early-termination law accepts. If the threat comes from a tenant or household member, you may change the locks and refuse that person a key once the request comes with a valid protective order against them or another court order requiring the change. Your fee is capped at the reasonable price customarily charged locally for that lock change. If you don't act in two business days, the tenant may change the locks with locks of similar or better quality and must try to give you a key within two business days. Blocking the change, or not trying to give a key, costs two months' rent plus costs and attorneys' fees, unless a court finds you acted in good faith. A lease cannot waive these rules.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-65 (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws), act read in full: (a) for this section 'household member' means 'a person residing with the tenant or co-tenant as an authorized occupant of the premises, and who is eighteen (18) years of age or older or an emancipated minor' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2), narrower than the new chapter definition '(9) "Household member" means a person residing with a tenant as an authorized occupant of the premises' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1); (b) a lessor or owner 'shall, upon the request of all tenants in possession, or furnishing of a court order, change the locks of the individual dwelling unit in which the tenant or household member lives if the tenant or household member reasonably believes that the tenant or household member is under an imminent threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking at the premises' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2), and may 'request, in good faith, written verification of the status as a victim' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2) as provided in § 34-18-63; (c) where the threat is posed by a tenant or household member, the lessor or owner 'may change the locks and deny a key to the alleged perpetrator upon receipt of a request to change the locks; provided, however, that such request shall be accompanied by a copy of a valid protective order issued against a tenant or household member or other court order requiring change of locks' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); (d) 'within two (2) business days, make a good faith effort to change the locks or give the tenant or household member permission to change the locks in a workman-like manner' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2), key 'within the same two (2) business day period' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); 'The fee shall not exceed the reasonable price customarily charged for changing such locks in that community.' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); (e) tenant self-help 'with locks of similar or better quality than the original locks' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2), key to the owner within two business days, owner may replace or seek reimbursement, 'deemed not to be in retaliation' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); (f) tenant may not give the perpetrator a key; owner refusing a key on reasonable belief 'shall not be liable for such refusal' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); (g) liability 'for the amount of two (2) months' rent and the costs of the action, including reasonable attorneys' fees' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2), usable as setoff or recoupment; 'Damages shall not be imposed if the court determines that the lessor or owner acted in good faith.' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2). § 34-18-64: no refusal of a rental agreement 'based upon an applicant having requested a change of locks under § 34-18-65' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2). § 34-18-66 district court equity jurisdiction. § 34-18-67: 'A waiver of §§ 34-18-63 through 34-18-65, shall be void and unenforceable.' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); its heading reads 'Waivers of §§ 34-18-63 through 34-18-64 void and unenforceable' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2), so the heading and text differ (flagged, not resolved; the body follows the text). title: Entering the Unit in Rhode Island
bodyText: Rhode Island's entry rule is consent-based. A tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or show the unit to prospective or actual buyers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors. Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give at least two days' notice of your intent to enter, and enter only at reasonable times. Without consent you may enter only in an emergency, or during a tenant absence of more than seven days if reasonably necessary to protect the property. You have no other right of access except under a court order, to do repair, replacement or cleaning work to fix a tenant's breach of the tenant's statutory duties that materially affects health and safety, after the tenant fails to fix it within 20 days of your written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires), or after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit. Never abuse access or use it to harass. If the tenant refuses lawful access, you may get a court order compelling access or terminate the rental agreement; if you enter unlawfully, enter in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated harassing demands, the tenant may get an injunction or terminate. Either way the winner may recover actual damages and must be awarded costs and reasonable attorney's fees. A lease term waiving these rules is unenforceable.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-26(a): 'A tenant shall not unreasonably withhold consent to the landlord to enter into the dwelling unit in order to inspect the premises, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers, or contractors.' (§ 34-18-26(a)); (b): 'A landlord may enter the dwelling unit without consent of the tenant in case of emergency, or, during any absence of the tenant in excess of seven (7) days, if reasonably necessary for the protection of the property.' (§ 34-18-26(b)); (c): 'A landlord shall not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant. Except in case of emergency or unless it is impracticable to do so, the landlord shall give the tenant at least two (2) days’ notice of his or her intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times.' (§ 34-18-26(c)); (d): 'A landlord has no other right of access except' by court order, 'As permitted by § 34-18-39', or abandonment or surrender (§ 34-18-26(d)). § 34-18-39 (entry to cure a § 34-18-24 health-and-safety noncompliance after 'twenty (20) days after written notice' or promptly in an emergency; § 34-18-39). § 34-18-45(a)-(c): refused access: 'injunctive relief to compel access, or terminate the rental agreement' (§ 34-18-45(a)); unlawful or unreasonable entry or harassing demands: tenant injunction or termination (§ 34-18-45(b)); 'the prevailing party may recover actual damages and shall be awarded costs and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-45(c)). Waiver: § 34-18-17(a)(1), (b) (a term that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under this chapter' is unenforceable; § 34-18-17(a)(1)). Notice form: the statute does not say written; see edu-notice-delivery-methods-ri. Other entry rules: § 23-33-25 lets owners enter leased premises to bring the building into compliance with the elevator chapter, 'interfering with the lessee no more than may be necessary' (§ 23-33-25); housing code entry under §§ 45-24.3-15, 45-24.3-19 runs to the enforcing officer, not the landlord (battery excerpts only). Foreclosure just-cause grounds include refusal of access (§§ 34-18-38.1, 34-18-38.2; not reread here). No statute treats a repair request as consent to entry, lets a separate notice dispense with the two-day notice, or provides landlord-initiated temporary relocation: RI-landlord-entry-1 (owner/landlord/lessor/operator near enter/entry/access near dwelling/unit/premises, or occupant/tenant giving/refusing access; no context limb; hits 18, OK; real positives §§ 34-18-26 and 34-18-45 passed; other hits are inspector-entry, condominium/time-share access, elevator and drug-nuisance sections); RI-landlord-entry-2 (maintenance/repair/service/work request or order near consent/entry, temporary relocation/housing/lodging near tenant/landlord; hits 1, OK; two synthetic positives passed; § 42-128.1-4 lead-hazard temporary-housing definition only). title: No No-Notice Service Entry
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule letting a lease authorize entry without notice for regularly scheduled services such as pest control, filter changes or smoke alarm checks. Supplying necessary or agreed services is one of the purposes for which a tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry, but the general notice rule still applies: except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, give at least two days' notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times. A lease term waiving that notice is unenforceable. If you run a recurring service, give the tenant a written schedule with the dates at least two days before each visit, and a fresh notice if a date changes; no statute says a schedule printed in the lease is enough on its own. Entry without consent is limited to emergencies and tenant absences of more than seven days where reasonably necessary to protect the property. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws, three loaded regulation parts and the court rules were searched; case law and ordinances were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no scheduled-services entry exception). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-26(a) (consent may not be unreasonably withheld to 'supply necessary or agreed services'; § 34-18-26(a)); (c): 'Except in case of emergency or unless it is impracticable to do so, the landlord shall give the tenant at least two (2) days’ notice of his or her intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times.' (§ 34-18-26(c)); (b) no-consent entry 'in case of emergency, or, during any absence of the tenant in excess of seven (7) days, if reasonably necessary for the protection of the property' (§ 34-18-26(b)). Waiver: § 34-18-17(a)(1), (b). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the statute requires notice of 'intent to enter' (§ 34-18-26(c)) and does not say whether one advance schedule can serve as notice of each entry, so the body recommends a written schedule delivered at least two days before each visit; no case law searched. title: No Smart-Lock Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute aimed at smart locks, keypads, key fobs or app-based entry in residential rentals, and no rule requiring you to offer a physical key instead. The ordinary rules apply whatever the technology. Unlocking a unit remotely, or letting a vendor in with a code, is an entry: it needs the tenant's consent (which may not be unreasonably withheld for the listed purposes) and at least two days' notice except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, and you may not use access, or entry data, to harass the tenant. If a tenant or adult household member facing an imminent threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking asks under the survivor lock-change law, treat resetting codes and deleting the other person's credentials as changing the locks, within the same two business days. Any charge for fobs, cards or code resets is a fee beyond rent that must be listed in the lease's rent section (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format). Rhode Island's General Laws, 2025-2026 public laws, three loaded regulation parts and court rules were searched; general data-privacy law, case law and ordinances were not.

Laws § 34-18-26(a) (consent 'shall not unreasonably' be withheld; § 34-18-26(a)), (c) ('A landlord shall not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.' § 34-18-26(c)) and the two-day notice in § 34-18-26(c). L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): 'change the locks of the individual dwelling unit' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2) within 'two (2) business days' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2). title: No Procedure for Belongings Left Behind
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on storing, selling or disposing of belongings a tenant leaves behind after moving out or abandoning the unit: no notice form, no storage period and no value threshold. The law defines abandonment (the tenant left without notice and does not intend to return, shown by rent unpaid for more than 15 days and removal of substantially all possessions) and lets you retake an abandoned or surrendered unit without going to court, but you have no lien on the tenant's household goods and may not seize them for rent. So belongings left behind stay the tenant's until a court or general property law says otherwise. Before disposing of anything, send written notice to the tenant's forwarding or last known address describing the items and giving a reasonable date to collect them, and keep records; the library's optional abandoned-property clause sets that procedure in the lease. A lease term excusing you from liability for the property is unenforceable. After an eviction, property removed under the execution is released to the tenant only after the tenant pays the moving costs and any prepaid storage charges. Case law (conversion, bailment) and local ordinances were not searched.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no procedure for property left behind). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-11(1): '"Abandonment" means the tenant has vacated the premises without notice to the landlord and has no intention of returning, as evidenced by nonpayment of rent for more than fifteen (15) days and removal of substantially all possessions from the premises' (§ 34-18-11(1); still (1) after R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1). Retaking possession: § 34-18-44 (no self-help 'except in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted in this chapter'; § 34-18-44); § 34-18-26(d)(3). Liens: § 34-18-42(a): 'A lien or security interest on behalf of the landlord in the tenant's household goods is not enforceable unless perfected before the effective date of this chapter, except as provided in § 34-18-50.' (§ 34-18-42(a)); (b): 'Distraint for rent is abolished.' (§ 34-18-42(b)). § 34-18-40 (re-renting procedure; addresses the unit, not belongings). Exculpation: § 34-18-17(a)(4), (b) (a term limiting 'any liability of the landlord arising under law' is unenforceable; § 34-18-17(a)(4)). After execution: § 34-18-50 (tenant pays moving and prepaid storage costs before release, reimbursed to the landlord; see edu-post-eviction-property-ri). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the notice-and-wait advice is a cautious practice, not a statutory rule. title: Property Left Behind
bodyText: [Optional.] When this Lease ends or Tenant gives up possession, Tenant will remove all of Tenant's personal property from the property. If Tenant has moved out and given up possession, or has abandoned the property, and has left personal property behind, Landlord will send Tenant a written notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, to Tenant's forwarding address (or, if Tenant has not given one, Tenant's last known address), describing the property and stating where and by what date Tenant may collect it. That date will be at least [number] days after the notice is sent. If Tenant does not collect the property by that date, Landlord may dispose of it. Landlord need not store garbage, perishable items or anything hazardous. Landlord has no lien on Tenant's household goods and will not hold any property to secure Rent or other charges. Property removed under a court execution will be handled as the court and Rhode Island law direct. While Tenant remains in possession, Landlord will not remove Tenant's property, change the locks or interrupt essential services to force Tenant out. This Section does not apply to motor vehicles.
notes: RI: Optional; never default. No Rhode Island statute sets a procedure for property left behind (see edu-no-abandoned-property-procedure-ri, with batteries RI-abandoned-property-1 and -2), so this is a contract procedure that serves the landlord by fixing notice and a collection date before disposal. Abandonment as defined in R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-11(1) (see that row). The no-lien sentence tracks § 34-18-42: 'A lien or security interest on behalf of the landlord in the tenant's household goods is not enforceable unless perfected before the effective date of this chapter, except as provided in § 34-18-50.' (§ 34-18-42(a)); 'Distraint for rent is abolished.' (§ 34-18-42(b)). The last sentence on self-help tracks § 34-18-44. Executions: § 34-18-50. DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the clause deliberately omits the "without liability" language some states' clauses use, because § 34-18-17(a)(4) bars a term providing that the tenant 'Agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law' (§ 34-18-17(a)(4)); the bracketed day count has no statutory minimum, and a reasonable period (we suggest at least 14 days) lowers conversion risk; case law not searched. Certified mail mirrors the § 34-18-40 abandonment letter ('a certified letter, return receipt requested, to the tenant's last known address'; § 34-18-40). Motor vehicles: towing rules (see edu-towing-ri). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Abandonment and Re-Renting
bodyText: A unit is abandoned in Rhode Island when the tenant has left without notice and does not intend to return, shown by rent unpaid for more than 15 days and removal of substantially all possessions. When that happens, send a certified letter, return receipt requested, to the tenant's last known address saying that unless you hear from the tenant within seven days you will re-rent. If the letter comes back undeliverable or the tenant doesn't contact you within seven days, you must make reasonable efforts to rent the unit at a fair rental. If you re-rent for a term starting before the old lease would have ended, the old tenancy ends when the new one starts. If you don't make reasonable efforts to re-rent, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the lease is treated as ended by you on the date you learned of the abandonment, so expect no rent claim after that date. More broadly, the act puts a duty to mitigate damages on any party claiming them, so a lease term making the tenant owe the rest of the term's rent whether or not you re-rent will not override it. After termination you may claim reasonable use and occupation, actual damages for the breach and reasonable attorney's fees. Unless the unit meets the abandonment test, don't retake it without a court order.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-40: 'If the tenant abandons the dwelling unit, the landlord shall send a certified letter, return receipt requested, to the tenant's last known address giving notice that unless a reply is received from the tenant within seven (7) days, the landlord shall re-rent the premises. If the notice is returned as undeliverable, or the tenant fails to contact the landlord within seven (7) days, the landlord shall make reasonable efforts to rent the premises at a fair rental. If the landlord rents the dwelling unit for a term beginning before the expiration of the rental agreement, the tenancy terminates as of the date of the new tenancy. If the landlord fails to use reasonable efforts to rent the dwelling unit at fair rental, or if the landlord accepts the abandonment as a surrender, the rental agreement is deemed to be terminated by the landlord as of the date the landlord has notice of the abandonment.' (§ 34-18-40). Abandonment: § 34-18-11(1) ('nonpayment of rent for more than fifteen (15) days and removal of substantially all possessions from the premises'; § 34-18-11(1), unchanged by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1). Mitigation: § 34-18-5(a): 'The aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages.' (§ 34-18-5(a)). Waiver: § 34-18-17(a)(1), (b). After termination: § 34-18-43 ('a claim for possession, for a sum for reasonable use and occupation subsequent to the termination, and for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement and reasonable attorney's fees'; § 34-18-43). Self-help: § 34-18-44. DRAFTING JUDGMENT: 'deemed to be terminated by the landlord' (§ 34-18-40) is read as cutting off rent after the notice date; whether other breach damages survive is a case-law question not searched. Other searches: RI-abandonment-and-mitigation-1 (mitigate, re-rent, relet, reletting, fair rental, acceleration of rent, with tenant/landlord/lessee/lessor/dwelling unit/rental agreement/lease within 1,500 characters; hits 41, OK; real positive § 34-18-40 passed; § 34-18-5 found; other hits are lead and radon mitigation, insurance and eminent-domain sections; no acceleration rule for residential leases); RI-abandonment-and-mitigation-2 recorded as failed (a synthetic positive missed), rerun as RI-abandonment-and-mitigation-3 (everyday words: find or look for a new tenant, rest/remainder/balance of the lease or term, break the lease, skip out; no context limb; hits 29, OK; three synthetic positives passed; hits are vacancy terms of office and UCC goods leases). title: Attorney's Fees in Rhode Island
bodyText: A Rhode Island lease may not make the tenant agree to pay your attorney's fees in a way inconsistent with the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; such a term is unenforceable, and knowingly using it lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. Your fee rights come from the act. You may recover reasonable attorney's fees in a nonpayment eviction only if the tenant received a five-day demand notice in the six months before you filed and the nonpayment was willful; for willful lease noncompliance; for a willful, bad-faith holdover; when the tenant's defense or counterclaim is frivolous; and, in an access dispute, as the winning party (the court must award them). The act also lists attorney's fees among your claims after a lease is terminated; for unpaid rent, assume the narrower nonpayment rule controls. Tenants recover fees for wrongful deposit withholding, your willful noncompliance, willful failure to deliver possession, failure to supply essential services, lockouts and service shutoffs, retaliation, access abuse, and blocked survivor lock changes. Outside the act, a court may award fees to the winner of a contract suit only after a default judgment or where the loser raised no justiciable issue. No statute makes a fee clause reciprocal.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a)(3): a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to pay the landlord's attorney's fees inconsistent with this chapter' (§ 34-18-17(a)(3)); (b): 'A provision prohibited by subsection (a) included in a rental agreement is unenforceable. If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known to be prohibited, the tenant may recover, in addition to his or her actual damages, an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees.' (§ 34-18-17(b)). Landlord awards: § 34-18-35(d): 'In cases where the tenant had received a demand notice pursuant to subsection (a) within the six (6) months immediately preceding the filing of the action, and the tenant's nonpayment was willful, the landlord may also recover a reasonable attorney's fee.' (§ 34-18-35(d)); § 34-18-36(d): 'If the tenant's noncompliance is willful, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney's fees.' (§ 34-18-36(d)); § 34-18-38(c) (holdover 'willful and not in good faith'; § 34-18-38(c)); § 34-18-32(a): 'If the defense or counterclaim by the tenant is frivolous or without any basis in fact, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney's fees.' (§ 34-18-32(a)); § 34-18-45(c): 'the prevailing party may recover actual damages and shall be awarded costs and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-45(c)); § 34-18-43: after termination 'a claim for possession, for a sum for reasonable use and occupation subsequent to the termination, and for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-43). TWO PROVISIONS (SOP rule 31): § 34-18-43 lists fees without conditions, while § 34-18-35(d) conditions fees in nonpayment evictions on a prior demand notice and willfulness; landlords should assume § 34-18-35(d) governs nonpayment claims (flag for legal watch). Tenant awards: §§ 34-18-19(c), 34-18-28(b), 34-18-29(b), 34-18-31(b), 34-18-34, 34-18-45(c), 34-18-46(b) (by reference to § 34-18-34); § 34-18-65(g) (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws). General: § 9-1-45: 'The court may award a reasonable attorney's fee to the prevailing party in any civil action arising from a breach of contract in which the court: (1) Finds that there was a complete absence of a justiciable issue of either law or fact raised by the losing party; or (2) Renders a default judgment against the losing party.' (§ 9-1-45). No reciprocity statute: RI-attorney-fees-1 (attorney's/counsel/legal fees with tenant/landlord/lessee/lessor/rental agreement/lease/dwelling unit/eviction within 600 characters; hits 28, OK; real positives §§ 34-18-17, 34-18-45, 34-18-43 passed; every chapter 34-18 award listed above found); RI-attorney-fees-2 and RI-attorney-fees-3 recorded as failed (synthetic positives missed), rerun as RI-attorney-fees-4 (reciprocal near attorney/counsel fees, prevailing party near attorney/counsel, justiciable issue; no context limb; hits 26, OK; real positive § 34-18-45 and three synthetic positives passed; § 9-1-45 found; no residential-lease reciprocity rule). title: After a Fire or Casualty
bodyText: If fire or another casualty damages the unit or premises so that the tenant's enjoyment of the unit is substantially impaired, the tenant may either (1) move out immediately and, within 14 days after leaving, notify you in writing of the intent to end the lease, which then ends on the date of vacating, and you must return the security deposit (less lawful deductions) and all prepaid rent; or (2) if continued occupancy is lawful, stop using the part of the unit made unusable and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost fair rental value. Either way, rent is accounted as of the date of the fire or casualty. These options apply whatever caused the damage; if the tenant caused it negligently or deliberately, your remedy is a damages lawsuit. The act gives you no right of your own to end the lease after a casualty and sets no repair deadline or belongings-retrieval rule; a landlord termination option exists only if the lease provides one (the library's optional casualty-termination clause), and the lease cannot cut down the tenant's options. The fire-and-storm surrender statute in the commercial leasing chapter does not apply to residential tenancies under the act. For a tenant who stays, your duty to repair and keep the unit fit and habitable continues.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-33(a): 'If the dwelling unit or premises are damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty to an extent that enjoyment of the dwelling unit is substantially impaired, the tenant may: (1) Immediately vacate the premises and notify the landlord in writing within fourteen (14) days thereafter of his or her intention to terminate the rental agreement, in which case the rental agreement terminates as of the date of vacating; or (2) If continued occupancy is lawful, vacate any part of the dwelling unit rendered unusable by the fire or casualty, in which case the tenants’ liability for rent is reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value of the dwelling unit.' (§ 34-18-33(a)); (b): 'If the rental agreement is terminated the landlord shall return all security recoverable under § 34-18-19 and all prepaid rent. Accounting for rent in the event of termination or apportionment shall be made as of the date of the fire or casualty.' (§ 34-18-33(b)); (c): the section does not limit 'the right of the landlord to recover in an action in tort damages resulting from a fire or other casualty damage caused either negligently or deliberately by the tenant' (§ 34-18-33(c)). No tenant-fault exception in (a), unlike §§ 34-18-28(a)(3) and 34-18-31(d). Waiver: § 34-18-17(a)(1), (b). Repair duty: § 34-18-22(a)(1)-(2). Commercial chapter: § 34-18.1-1: 'This chapter shall apply to all commercial properties and other estates, excluding residential properties governed by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, chapter 18 of this title.' (§ 34-18.1-1), so § 34-18.1-8 (fire or storm surrender, fault-limited) does not reach act tenancies. § 45-24-37(c) (zoning: an owner may temporarily place manufactured homes for displaced occupants for up to 12 months after a fire or flood) read only for subsection (c) and not relied on. No landlord casualty-termination, repair-deadline or retrieval statute: RI-casualty-termination-1 (fire/casualty/destroyed/damaged/untenantable/unfit for occupancy within 250 characters of terminate/cancel/abate/surrender/retrieve/removal of belongings, with tenant/landlord/lessee/lessor/lease/rental agreement/tenancy within 1,500 characters; hits 7, OK; real positive § 34-18-33 and two synthetic positives passed; § 34-18.1-8 found); RI-casualty-termination-2 (everyday words: burned down, burnt out, flooded out, house or apartment fire, storm damage, roof collapsed, uninhabitable; no context limb; hits 18, OK; three synthetic positives passed; zoning, tax-abatement and coastal sections).
