title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText: If you, as declarant, or anyone in the business of selling real estate for its own account will offer units in a condominium that includes a building now rented to residential tenants, each residential tenant and subtenant in possession must get notice of the conversion, with the public offering statement, at least 120 days before they must move out; a tenant who has lived in the unit 10 years or more or is 62 or older gets one year. Hand-deliver the notice to the unit or mail it prepaid to the unit or another address the tenant gave, and describe the tenants' rights. During the notice period rent may not rise, the tenancy terms may not change, and no one may be made to leave on less notice except for nonpayment, waste or disturbing other tenants. Conversion never lets you end a lease early. For 60 days after the notice (180 days for the long-term or 62-plus tenants) you must offer each residential unit to its tenant; if the tenant doesn't buy, you may not offer it to others on better terms for the next 180 days. A tenant current on lease obligations may cancel the lease without penalty. Pay reasonable moving costs within 50 miles for tenants who are disabled or 62 or older. Missing notice is a defense to eviction. No statement about conversion is required in the lease itself. Time-share conversions follow nearly the same rules, except that the notice need not come with a public offering statement and the moving-cost duty covers only tenants 62 or older, not disabled tenants under 62.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-36.1-4.12(a): notice of the conversion and the public offering statement 'no later than one hundred twenty (120) days before the tenants and any subtenant in possession are required to vacate. Rents shall not be increased during the notice period.' (§ 34-36.1-4.12(a)); notice 'shall be hand delivered to the unit or mailed by prepaid United States mail to the tenant and subtenant at the address of the unit or any other mailing address provided by a tenant' (§ 34-36.1-4.12(a)); 'No tenant or subtenant may be required to vacate upon less than one hundred twenty (120) days’ notice, except by reason of nonpayment of rent, waste, or conduct that disturbs other tenants’ peaceful enjoyment of the premises, and the terms of the tenancy may not be altered during that period. Failure to give notice as required by this section is a defense to an action for possession.' (§ 34-36.1-4.12(a)); (b) 60-day offer, cancellation 'as long as all obligations of the lease have been met', 180-day no-better-terms period, exception for nonresidential or nonconforming units (§ 34-36.1-4.12(b)); (c) bona fide purchaser; (d) a conforming notice 'also constitutes a notice to vacate specified by that statute' (§ 34-36.1-4.12(d)); (e)(1) one-year notice and 180 days to buy for a tenant 'who has continuously resided in the unit for ten (10) years or more or any tenant who has attained the age of sixty-two (62)' (§ 34-36.1-4.12(e)(1)); (e)(2) moving costs 'to any tenant who is disabled or has attained the age of sixty-two (62), within a fifty (50) mile radius' (§ 34-36.1-4.12(e)(2)); (f) 'Nothing in this section permits termination of a lease by a declarant in violation of its terms.' (§ 34-36.1-4.12(f)). Which statute governs: § 34-36.1-1.02(a)(1) (chapter applies to condominiums created after July 1, 1982) and (b): 'The provisions of the Condominium Ownership Act, chapter 36 of this title, do not apply to condominiums created after July 1, 1982' (§ 34-36.1-1.02(b)); so a new conversion is governed by § 34-36.1-4.12, and the older § 34-36-37 (120 days, one year for 62+, 120-day no-better-terms period, moving costs for 62+ only) reaches only pre-1982 condominiums. Time-share: § 34-41-4.10 (same structure; moving costs for 62+ only; § 34-41-4.10(e)(2)). No lease-text requirement and no other conversion regime: RI-conversion-notice-1 (convert/conversion within 200 characters of condominium/cooperative/ownership/change of use/nonresidential, either order, with tenant/lessee/resident/occupant/rental within 1,500 characters; hits 15, OK; real positives §§ 34-36.1-4.12 and 34-36-37 and a synthetic positive passed; other hits: § 34-41-4.10, mobile home park resident organizations (§ 31-44-1), § 34-45-10 assisted housing, zoning definitions). Federally assisted developments: see edu-tenant-purchase-rights-ri. Municipal ordinances and case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Drug and Violent Crime
bodyText: [Optional.] Tenant will not, and will not allow any person on the premises with Tenant's consent to: (1) use any part of the premises in a way that maintains a narcotics nuisance; (2) use any part of the premises, or any public property next to them, to manufacture, sell or deliver a controlled substance, or possess there with intent to manufacture, sell or deliver a controlled substance in schedule I or II of Rhode Island's controlled substances act; or (3) commit, or attempt, a crime of violence on the premises or on public property next to them, meaning murder, manslaughter, arson, rape, sexual assault, mayhem, kidnapping, assault with a dangerous weapon, assault or battery involving grave bodily injury, or a felony assault with intent to commit any offense. This Section does not restrict consumption of cannabis by non-smoked or non-vaporized means, or transfer of cannabis without compensation, within the limits Rhode Island law allows. If Tenant violates (1), (2) or (3), Landlord may file for eviction without first giving a notice and an opportunity to cure, as Rhode Island law permits. A violation by another person on the premises with Tenant's consent is a material noncompliance with this Lease, for which Landlord will give the notice Rhode Island law requires. Landlord will not treat a tenant's or household member's status as a victim of domestic abuse as a violation of this Section.
notes: RI: Optional; never default. Restates tenant duties for the landlord's benefit. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-24(8)-(10): a tenant shall '(8) Refrain from using any part of the premises in a manner such as would constitute the maintaining of a narcotics nuisance under the provisions of § 21-28-4.06' (§ 34-18-24(8)); '(9) Refrain from using any part of the premises or any public property adjacent thereto for the manufacture, sale, or delivery of a controlled substance or from possessing on the premises or any public property adjacent thereto with the intent to manufacture, sell, or deliver a controlled substance classified in schedule I or schedule II of chapter 28 of title 21' (§ 34-18-24(9)); '(10) Refrain from any crime of violence on the premises or on any public property adjacent to said premises' (§ 34-18-24(10)), with the statutory list of crimes and attempts (§ 34-18-24(10)). No cure: § 34-18-36(b) ('Unless it is a violation of § 34-18-24(8), (9), or (10)'; § 34-18-36(b)) and (f) (landlord 'shall not be required to send a notice of noncompliance to the tenant and may immediately file a complaint for eviction'; § 34-18-36(f)). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: §§ 34-18-24(8)-(10) and 34-18-36(f) speak of the tenant's own acts, so the no-cure sentence is limited to Tenant, and conduct by others with Tenant's consent is treated as an ordinary material noncompliance under § 34-18-36(a) (20-day notice). Cannabis carve-out: § 21-28.11-29(h): 'a landlord may not prohibit the consumption of cannabis by non-smoked or non-vaporized means, or the transfer without compensation of cannabis by the tenant as defined in § 34-18-11, provided the tenant is in compliance with the possession and transfer limits and other requirements set forth in this chapter' (§ 21-28.11-29(h)). Victim sentence: § 34-37-4(a) bars discrimination in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental 'on the basis that a tenant or applicant or a member of the household is, or has been, or is threatened with being the victim of domestic abuse' (§ 34-37-4(a)). Narcotics nuisance: § 21-28-4.06(a). Related education: edu-tenant-prohibited-acts-ri, edu-nuisance-ri. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Notice and Cure Before Eviction
bodyText: Rhode Island has two notice-and-cure tracks. Unpaid rent: once any part of the rent is 15 days in arrears, mail the statutory five-day demand; you may file no earlier than the sixth day after mailing. The tenant may cure by paying the full rent owed before you file, and may also cure at the hearing by paying all arrears plus court costs, unless the tenant received an earlier demand notice (before the one for this case) in the six months before you filed. Other breaches: for a material noncompliance with the lease, or a breach of the tenant's statutory duties that materially affects health and safety, deliver a written notice in the statutory form stating the breach, what will remedy it (acts, repairs or payment of damages), and that the lease will end on a date at least 21 days after mailing unless the tenant remedies it within 20 days of mailing. If the tenant remedies it in time, the lease continues; if not, you may file the day after the termination date. There is no cure and no notice for maintaining a narcotics nuisance, drug manufacture or dealing, or a crime of violence, or for a qualifying seasonal tenant charged with an ordinance violation or breaching occupancy or noise terms. If substantially the same breach recurs within six months of a good-faith notice, you may end the lease on 20 days' written notice with no chance to cure. Your lease cannot shorten any of this.
notes: RI: Present. Nonpayment: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-35(a) (rent 'due and in arrears for fifteen (15) days', written notice in the § 34-18-56(a) form, cure 'within five (5) days of the date of mailing of the notice'; § 34-18-35(a)); (b) suit 'no earlier than the sixth (6th) day after mailing of the written demand notice' (§ 34-18-35(b)); (e): 'The tenant shall have the right to cure his or her failure to pay rent by tendering the full amount of rent prior to commencement of suit. If the tenant has not received a notice pursuant to subsection (a) of this section within the six (6) months immediately preceding the filing of the action, the tenant shall have the right to cure his or her failure to pay rent after commencement of suit by tendering the full amount of rent in arrears, together with court costs, at the time of hearing.' (§ 34-18-35(e)). Noncompliance: § 34-18-36(a) ('a material noncompliance by the tenant with the rental agreement or a noncompliance with § 34-18-24 materially affecting health and safety'; notice 'in a form substantially similar to that provided in § 34-18-56(b)' specifying the breach, the remedy, and 'That unless the breach is remedied within twenty (20) days of mailing of the notice the rental agreement shall terminate upon a specified date, which shall not be less than twenty-one (21) days after the mailing of the notice'; § 34-18-36(a)); (b) cure saves the tenancy 'Unless it is a violation of § 34-18-24(8), (9), or (10)' and filing 'no earlier than the first day following the termination date' (§ 34-18-36(b)); (e) recurrence 'within six (6) months': 'at least twenty (20) days' written notice' with 'No allowance of time to remedy noncompliance' (§ 34-18-36(e)); (f) no notice for § 34-18-24(8)-(10) or seasonal tenants (leases running May 1-October 15 or September 1-June 1 with no renewal) charged with an ordinance violation or breaching occupancy or noise terms (§ 34-18-36(f)). Waiver: § 34-18-17(a)(1), (b). Related rows: edu-nonpayment-notice-ri, edu-notice-to-quit-waiver-ri, edu-redemption-ri; edu-tenant-prohibited-acts-ri. Delivery methods: edu-notice-delivery-methods-ri. Forms in § 34-18-56 not reread here. SYNC (Claude Code, 2026-10-09): read with § 34-18-35(d)-(e) on the official site. Taken literally, 'a notice pursuant to subsection (a) ... within the six (6) months immediately preceding the filing of the action' includes the demand notice for the case itself, which every nonpayment action must follow, so no tenant could ever cure at the hearing and every willful nonpayment would carry attorney's fees. DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the row reads it as an earlier notice, before the one for this case, so the hearing cure and the fee rule apply as the statute's structure suggests (case law not searched). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Drug-Free and Crime-Free Addenda
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires, authorizes or regulates a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum, so one is an ordinary lease term (a federally assisted property may have its own program addendum). The law already supplies the core: a tenant must not maintain a narcotics nuisance, manufacture, sell or deliver controlled substances on or next to the premises, possess schedule I or II drugs there with intent to sell, or commit a crime of violence there, and for those breaches you may file for eviction without a cure notice. The library's optional criminal-activity clause states those duties. Two limits matter for any addendum: you may not prohibit a tenant's consumption of cannabis by non-smoked or non-vaporized means, or transfer of cannabis without payment, within the legal limits (you may ban smoking and vaping); and you may not treat a tenant as in breach because they or a household member are a victim of domestic abuse. If you run a recovery residence (sober home), it must be registered with the state behavioral health department and follow the national recovery-residence certification process from January 1, 2027, and zoning must treat a certified recovery residence as a residential use. Case law and ordinances were not searched.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no drug-free or crime-free addendum statute). Tenant duties: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-24(8)-(10); no cure: § 34-18-36(b), (f) (see criminal-activity-ri and edu-tenant-prohibited-acts-ri). Cannabis: § 21-28.11-29(h): 'a landlord may not prohibit the consumption of cannabis by non-smoked or non-vaporized means, or the transfer without compensation of cannabis by the tenant as defined in § 34-18-11' (§ 21-28.11-29(h)); smoking and vaping may be prohibited (see edu-cannabis-ri). Fair housing: § 34-37-4(a). Recovery housing: § 40.1-1-13(18): 'As of January 1, 2027, all recovery housing facilities shall be registered with the department and shall adhere to the NARR certification process.' (§ 40.1-1-13(18)); § 45-24-33.1 (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 242, 244, § 1, effective on passage; not yet in the compiled General Laws): zoning 'Shall treat a NARR-certified recovery residence as a residential use of property' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 242, 244, § 1). Statute-wide search with terms and hit counts over the RI corpus (General Laws with all dated versions, Constitution, three loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws, court rules), no context limb: RI-drug-free-housing-addendum-1 (drug/alcohol/crime/substance-free housing, lease, addendum, program, residence, premises, home or zone; lease addendum; addendum to the lease or rental agreement; hits 1, OK; three synthetic positives passed; § 42-109-4 community prevention program only); RI-drug-free-housing-addendum-2 (everyday words and sober-home regimes: sober home/house/living, recovery residence/housing/home, no drugs allowed, zero tolerance; hits 17, OK; three synthetic positives passed; found § 40.1-1-13(18) and the 2026 recovery-house act; others are school, rideshare and zoning occupancy sections); RI-dv-eviction-protection-2 (crime-free; hits 0, OK). Federal HUD program addenda not reviewed. Rule 15: written section-open (§ 40.1-1-13 read with long items truncated in display).

title: Protections for Domestic Abuse Victims
bodyText: Rhode Island's fair housing law protects tenants and applicants who are, have been or are threatened with being victims of domestic abuse, and those who have sought or obtained a court restraining order for protection from domestic abuse, and the protection covers household members' status too. You may not ask about that status, refuse to rent because of it, or treat the tenant differently in the terms, conditions or privileges of the tenancy, which includes ending or refusing to renew a tenancy because of it. The law keeps one exception: you may still evict a tenant who fails to conduct themselves, and to make others on the premises with their consent conduct themselves, so as not to disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment. Since July 1, 2026, you also may not refuse to rent to an applicant because they ended a lease under the survivor early-termination law or asked for a survivor lock change (nor may a housing subsidy provider deny assistance on that basis), and if a survivor ends their lease you may, in good faith, bring an action against a remaining tenant, co-tenant or household member without facing a retaliation claim. No statute creates a separate eviction defense for victims or a special procedure to remove only the abuser, though a court protective order may itself order the abuser to vacate the household unless the abuser holds sole legal interest in it; use the ordinary eviction process against the person in breach.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-37-4(a): no owner shall 'make any written or oral inquiry concerning whether a tenant or applicant or a member of the household is, or has been, or is threatened with being the victim of domestic abuse, or whether a tenant or applicant has obtained, or sought, or is seeking relief from any court in the form of a restraining order for protection from domestic abuse' (§ 34-37-4(a)), nor 'discriminate against any individual' on that basis 'in the terms, conditions, or privileges of the sale, rental, or lease of any housing accommodation' (§ 34-37-4(a)). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the refusal-to-rent sentence of § 34-37-4(a) is garbled where the domestic-abuse clause is spliced in ('or shall, or on the basis that a tenant or applicant, or a member of the household, is or has been, or is threatened with being, the victim of domestic abuse'; § 34-37-4(a)); the body reads it, with § 34-37-2 and § 34-37-1(c), as barring refusal to rent on that basis, and treats termination or nonrenewal because of victim status as discrimination in terms, conditions or privileges; case law not searched. Exception: § 34-37-4(n): 'Nothing in this section shall prevent a landlord from proceeding with eviction action against a tenant who fails to comply with § 34-18-24(7).' (§ 34-37-4(n)); same proviso in § 34-37-2; § 34-18-24(7) (not disturbing neighbors' peaceful enjoyment). Definitions: § 34-37-3(6) ('domestic abuse' has the meaning in § 15-15-1 'and include all forms of domestic violence as set forth in § 12-29-2'; § 34-37-3(6)); (16): 'The term "victim" means a family or household member and all other persons contained within the definition of those terms as defined in § 12-29-2.' (§ 34-37-3(16)), so the protected status is abuse within family or household relationships; §§ 15-15-1 and 12-29-2 not reread. Survivor act: § 34-18-64 (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): 'A lessor or owner shall not refuse to enter into a rental agreement, nor shall a housing subsidy provider deny assistance, based on an applicant having terminated a rental agreement under § 34-18-63 or based upon an applicant having requested a change of locks under § 34-18-65.' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); § 34-18-63(f): 'A landlord who in good faith initiates an action against a remaining tenant, co-tenant, or household member, or takes any other action under this section, shall not be subject to a claim of retaliation or any other claim under this chapter.' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); § 34-18-67 (no waiver). No victim eviction defense or perpetrator-only removal procedure: RI-dv-eviction-protection-1 and RI-dv-eviction-protection-3 and -4 recorded as failed (real positives missed), rerun as RI-dv-eviction-protection-5 (victim/survivor/domestic abuse/domestic violence/restraining or protective order within 300 characters across sentences of evict/terminate/nonrenew/refuse to renew/action for possession/recover possession/action against, or the reverse with victim and an abuse word, with tenant/landlord/lease/rental/lessee/lessor/housing within 1,500 characters; hits 5, OK; real positives R.I. Pub. L. 2026, ch. 147 and § 34-37-2 and two synthetic positives passed; hits are §§ 34-37-1, 34-37-2, the 2026 survivor act and a District Court form title); RI-dv-eviction-protection-2 (everyday words: attacked or hurt by a partner, police calls leading to eviction, crime-free; hits 0, OK; three synthetic positives passed). Corpus: General Laws (all dated versions), Constitution, three loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws, court rules. Rule 15: written section-open. § 8-8.1-3(a)(2): 'Ordering the defendant to vacate the household forthwith, unless the defendant holds sole legal interest in the household' (§ 8-8.1-3(a)(2)); § 8-8.1-3 read for (a)(1)-(4) only; chapter 15-15 not read.

title: Survivor Early Lease Termination
bodyText: Since July 1, 2026, a tenant may end a lease early, with no penalty, early-termination fee or liability for future rent, if the tenant or a household member was a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking within the last 150 days, or if within the last 150 days an event tied to past abuse makes the victim fear for their safety. The tenant must give you written verification (see the qualifying-documents row) and must move out within 30 days of giving notice, or at another time you both agree. A tenant liable for rent under the lease owes it only through the termination date or the move-out date, whichever is later. If full possession is returned without damage, the tenant gets the deposit under the normal deposit rules and any rent prepaid for later periods, with a full and specific written statement within 20 days after the tenancy ends. The statute does not say whether co-tenants who stay remain bound; you may, in good faith, act against a remaining tenant, co-tenant or household member without a retaliation claim. Keep the verification and the household's personal information strictly confidential. Domestic violence here includes, without being limited to, listed crimes between family or household members; abuse is any act or failure to act that presents an imminent risk of serious harm to someone, whoever commits it, and includes listed crimes such as sexual assault, stalking and trafficking, whether or not reported to police. You may not refuse to rent to someone for having used this right, and a lease cannot waive it.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-63 (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws), act read in full: (a) 'A tenant may terminate their lease or rental agreement without penalty or fees for early termination, or liability for future rent when: (1) The tenant or household member within the most recent one hundred fifty (150) days has been a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking; or (2) Within the most recent one hundred fifty (150) days, an event occurs relative to the victim of past abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, that, in conjunction with the past abuse, causes a victim lessee or victim household member to fear for their safety.' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); (a)(3) written verification conditions (see edu-dv-qualifying-documents-ri); (b) strict confidence; (c): 'The tenant who has given notice shall vacate the premises within thirty (30) days of giving notice to the landlord or at any other time as may be agreed upon by the landlord and the tenant.' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); (d) rent 'only liable, if solely or jointly liable for purposes of the lease or rental agreement, for rent owed through the date of termination or the date the tenant actually vacates the premises, whichever is later' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); (e) deposit and prepaid rent 'so long as full possession is turned over to the landlord absent any damage', statement 'within twenty (20) days of the conclusion of the tenancy' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); (f) good-faith action against 'a remaining tenant, co-tenant, or household member' not retaliation (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2). § 34-18-64 (no refusal to rent), § 34-18-66 (equity jurisdiction), § 34-18-67 ('A waiver of §§ 34-18-63 through 34-18-65, shall be void and unenforceable.'; R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2). Definitions (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1, amending § 34-18-11): '(2) "Abuse" means an act or failure to act that presents an imminent risk of serious harm to an individual' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1), including listed crimes 'regardless of whether these acts or threats have been reported to law enforcement officers' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1); '(5) "Domestic violence"' covers listed crimes 'when committed by one family or household member against another' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1); '(9) "Household member" means a person residing with a tenant as an authorized occupant of the premises.' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1). The act does not define 'sexual assault' or 'stalking' separately, and does not define 'family or household member' (DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the § 12-29-2 meaning is likely; not reread). Effective date: act § 3; no transition rule for leases signed before July 1, 2026, so the body applies it to all tenancies from that date. Notice form and method: the act requires only written verification and 'notice' (§ 34-18-63(c)); see edu-statutory-early-termination-ri for how this sits with the other early-exit rights, and edu-dv-deposit-timing-ri on deposit timing. Rule 15: written section-open (ch. 148 identical to ch. 147).

title: Survivor Verification Documents
bodyText: To use Rhode Island's survivor early-termination right (from July 1, 2026), the tenant or the household member who is the victim gives you written verification of one of these: (1) that they have obtained a valid protective order against the perpetrator; (2) that they have started a legal action for a protective order; (3) that they reported the abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking to a law enforcement agency; or (4) a written statement from a law enforcement official, attorney, healthcare provider, social worker, mental health counselor, therapist, domestic violence advocate, sexual assault advocate, child abuse advocate, or other victim's advocate at a nonprofit, college, university or state agency, that the tenant or household member is a victim. Any one is enough; the statute prescribes no form and does not let you demand more. For a survivor lock change you may ask, in good faith, for the same verification; if the threat comes from a tenant or household member and you are to deny that person a key, the request must come with a copy of a valid protective order against them or another court order requiring the lock change. Keep the verification, the fact of victim status and the household's personal details (address, Social Security number, email, phone, birthdate) strictly confidential, disclosing them only with the victim's written consent or as law requires.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-63(a)(3) (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): termination is 'conditioned on: (i) The tenant or household member of a tenant who is the victim provides the lessor or owner with written verification that the tenant or household member of a tenant has obtained a valid protective order against the perpetrator' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); or (ii) the victim '(A) Initiates legal action to obtain a protective order and provides written verification thereof to the lessor or owner; or (B) Reports the abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking to a law enforcement agency and provides written verification thereof to the lessor or owner; or (C) Provides written verification from a law enforcement official, attorney,' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2) healthcare provider, social worker, mental health counselor, therapist, domestic violence advocate, sexual assault advocate, child abuse advocate, 'or other victim's advocate at a nonprofit organization, college, university, or state agency' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2). (b): verification 'shall be maintained in strict confidence' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2); personal information '(such as address, social security number, email, phone number, birthdate)' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2) disclosed only if '(1) Requested and consented to in writing by the tenant or household member of the tenant who is the victim' or '(2) Otherwise required by applicable law' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2). Lock change: § 34-18-65(b) (owner may 'request, in good faith, written verification of the status as a victim'; R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2) and (c) ('a copy of a valid protective order issued against a tenant or household member or other court order requiring change of locks'; R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: (a)(3) lists alternatives joined by 'or', so any one suffices and the body does not let the landlord require more; the act does not say what a 'written verification' of (A) or (B) must contain. Waiver: § 34-18-67. Rule 15: written section-open (act read in full).

title: Early Termination
bodyText: Tenant may terminate this Lease before the end of the Term by providing Landlord at least 30 days' written notice. Tenant will pay an early termination fee equal to one month's Rent ({{monthly_rent}}) or 30% of the remaining Rent due under the Term, whichever is greater, and remains responsible for Rent and other obligations up to the termination date. This fee is also listed with the Rent in the Rent section of this Lease. This early-termination option and fee apply only if this Lease has a fixed Term; a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy ends on the notice that Rhode Island law and this Lease provide, without an early termination fee. Landlord may end this Lease early only under this Lease's Tenant Default and notice provisions, any other section of this Lease that expressly lets Landlord end it, or, if Tenant abandons the property as Rhode Island law defines abandonment, after Landlord sends the certified-letter notice Rhode Island law requires, and Landlord will recover possession only as Rhode Island law allows. No early termination fee applies when Tenant ends this Lease under a right Rhode Island or federal law gives, including as a servicemember, as a tenant 65 or older entering assisted living, a nursing facility or elderly housing, as a survivor of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, after a fire or casualty, or because of Landlord's noncompliance. Nothing in this Section limits any right either party has under applicable law.
notes: RI: Overrides `early-termination-ks` on three points (NEEDS_REVIEW: penalty and liquidated-damages case law not searched). (1) Abandonment limb: replaces "vacates or abandons the property without notifying Landlord", because R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-11(1) defines abandonment as vacating 'without notice to the landlord' with 'no intention of returning, as evidenced by nonpayment of rent for more than fifteen (15) days and removal of substantially all possessions from the premises' (§ 34-18-11(1)), § 34-18-40 requires 'a certified letter, return receipt requested, to the tenant's last known address' (§ 34-18-40) before re-renting, and § 34-18-44 bars self-help except 'in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted in this chapter' (§ 34-18-44); a tenant who leaves without notice but pays rent has not abandoned. (2) Fee placement: § 34-18-15(a)(1): 'If there are fees beyond the rent that apply to the rental of a unit, the lease shall disclose those fees in the same section as the rent disclosure and shall indicate that additional fees may apply.' (§ 34-18-15(a)(1)); (a)(5) undisclosed fees recoverable. BUILDER: the fee must also appear in the rent section (planned fee-disclosure-ri). (3) Statutory exits without fee: servicemember § 34-18-15(f)(4) ('The lessor may not impose an early termination charge'; § 34-18-15(f)(4)); 65 or older § 34-18-15(e); survivor § 34-18-63(a) ('without penalty or fees for early termination, or liability for future rent'; R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws); casualty § 34-18-33(a); landlord noncompliance § 34-18-28(a). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: § 34-18-15(e) does not itself bar a fee, but charging one would burden a statutory right a lease may not waive (§ 34-18-17(a)(1)), so the clause waives the fee there too. The fee formula is unchanged: no Rhode Island statute caps an agreed early-termination fee or regulates liquidated damages in residential leases (see edu-no-liquidated-damages-rule-ri; RI-liquidated-damages-1 and -2). Mitigation: § 34-18-5(a) applies to damages claims, not to the agreed price of the tenant's option (DRAFTING JUDGMENT). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Property Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute saying what happens to a lease, or to the rent, when the government takes all or part of the property by eminent domain, and none lets the condemnation court cancel a lease. Your lease and court decisions control, so if you want the lease to end, or the rent to drop, on a taking, say so in the lease and say how any award is split. In proceedings by a housing authority, a person with an estate or interest in the property, which can include a tenant, counts as an owner for valuing the taking. Displaced tenants may be entitled to relocation payments from the acquiring agency under the state and municipal relocation laws, which bind the agency, not you. If a taking or other public action requires work that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit, you may bring an eviction action even within the retaliation window, but only once the municipality's relocation requirements have been met. Case law on leases and condemnation was not searched.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no statute on a lease or rent after a taking). R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-29-32(f): 'The term "owner", as used in this section, includes a person having an estate, interest, or easement in the property to be acquired or a lien, charge, or encumbrance on the property.' (§ 45-29-32(f)), in proceedings 'for property taken or to be taken by eminent domain for an authority' (§ 45-29-32); (a) lease rent admissible as evidence of value. Relocation: § 45-31.2-5 (replacement-housing payment by a relocation agency to a displaced person from a dwelling 'actually and lawfully occupied by the displaced person for not less than ninety (90) days prior to the initiation of negotiations for acquisition' (§ 45-31.2-5)); state relocation chapter 37-6.1 (battery excerpts only, not relied on). Retaliation exception: § 34-18-46(c)(3): a landlord may bring an action for possession if 'Compliance with the applicable building or housing code or other public action such as eminent domain, requires alteration, remodeling, or demolition which would effectively deprive the tenant of use of the dwelling unit, and the relocation requirements have been met by the municipality.' (§ 34-18-46(c)(3)). Statute-wide search over the RI corpus (General Laws with all dated versions, Constitution, three loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws, court rules): RI-eminent-domain-1 (eminent domain, condemnation, taking for public use, condemned land or property, with tenant/lessee/lease/leasehold/tenancy/occupant/rent within 600 characters; hits 35, OK; two synthetic positives passed; hits are agency acquisition powers, rights-of-first-refusal carve-outs, § 34-18-46 and § 45-29-32; no lease-termination, rent-abatement or award-apportionment rule for leaseholds); RI-eminent-domain-2 (relocation assistance, payments or benefits, displaced persons, tenants, residents or occupants; no context limb; hits 34, OK; two synthetic positives passed; relocation chapters 37-6.1 and 45-31.2, mobile home park § 31-44-3.2). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination
bodyText: Rhode Island gives you no statutory right to end a lease because a sudden environmental or public health event, or a government order, makes occupancy impossible or unlawful, and no statute lets a lease create one with special effect. What the law does provide runs mostly to the tenant: after fire or other casualty that substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease or stay in the usable part at reduced rent, and the housing code's rules on condemned or unfit premises and rent suspension apply when a code officer acts. If you want the lease to end when the unit can't lawfully be occupied, say so in the lease, and still recover possession only through the courts or after a surrender; you may never lock out the tenant or cut services to force them out. A lease term cannot reduce the tenant's own casualty rights. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws, three loaded regulation parts and court rules were searched; case law (frustration, impossibility) and local ordinances were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no environmental-event termination right). Casualty: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-33(a) (tenant options after fire 'or casualty' substantially impairing enjoyment; § 34-18-33(a)); see edu-casualty-termination-ri. Self-help: § 34-18-44 ('A landlord may not recover or take possession of the dwelling unit by action or otherwise, including willful diminution of services' except 'in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted in this chapter'; § 34-18-44). Waiver: § 34-18-17(a)(1). Code orders: § 45-24.3-19(f) and § 45-24.2-11 (rent suspension/escrow; see edu-condemned-premises-ri and edu-rent-suspension-code-order-ri; not reread). title: No Hardship Stay Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute giving an evicted tenant a hardship stay, such as extra months to move because of age, disability, children, winter or difficulty finding housing, and no criteria for one. After a judgment for possession, no execution may issue for five days, and if no appeal is claimed and the judgment is unpaid it issues on the sixth day after judgment. A court may still stay execution in its discretion (for example while a motion to vacate the judgment is pending, or on motion for cause shown), and an appeal stops execution. But any stay, by court order or by law, must be conditioned on the tenant paying you amounts equal to the rent, when rent would be due; taking those payments does not waive your right to possession or reinstate the tenancy, and missed payments let you ask for the execution. Court-ordered stays depend on the judge and the case; case law and court practice were not searched.

The acceptance of these sums shall not constitute a waiver of the right of the landlord to obtain possession of the premises, nor shall the receipt thereof be deemed to reinstate the tenancy.' title: How a Rhode Island Eviction Works
bodyText: You may recover a Rhode Island rental only through a court eviction (or after abandonment or surrender). Start with the right notice: the five-day demand for unpaid rent, the 20-day cure notice for other breaches, or the periodic termination notice; a fixed term that has ended needs none. To file for nonpayment you must show the court that you are registered with the Department of Health rental registry (with a lead certificate of conformance or exemption for a pre-1978 unit). Nonpayment cases get a hearing date on the summons; other cases give the tenant 20 days to answer. In a nonpayment case the tenant may counterclaim, and the court may order rent paid into court; if discovery delays the hearing, the court may order interim rent. After judgment no execution issues for five days; if there is no appeal and the judgment is unpaid, it issues on the sixth day to a sheriff or certified constable and lasts one year. Either side may appeal to the superior court within five days; from January 1, 2027 that period counts weekends and holidays and the appellant pays a $75 filing fee instead of costs and a $50 attorney's fee. During a stay or appeal the tenant must keep paying amounts equal to the rent, or you may move for the execution. A tenant may later move to seal a resolved case.

title: Sealing Eviction Records
bodyText: Since January 1, 2024, any party to a Rhode Island eviction case for nonpayment, lease noncompliance or holdover may ask the court to seal the case file, by motion filed at least 30 days after the appeal period has run following the end of the case. The court must grant it if the case was dismissed on a motion to dismiss, was resolved by a stipulation whose terms both sides have satisfied, ended with any money judgment against the moving party paid in full, or was dismissed for lack of prosecution after five years, and if the moving party notified every other party of the motion and has made no other sealing request in the previous five years. Each party may ask once every five years. Expect to receive notice of a tenant's motion; you may respond, but the statute leaves the court no discretion once those findings are made. The statute does not say how a sealed record may be used in tenant screening, and no Rhode Island law requires automatic removal of eviction records from public indexes; the Supreme Court's public-access rules do not list eviction cases. Case law was not searched.

(§ 34-18-60(a)); (b): 'the court shall grant the motion and seal the record of the civil action upon a finding that the underlying civil action was dismissed as a result of a motion to dismiss, the action was resolved by stipulation and the terms of the stipulation have been satisfied by the parties, any monetary judgment against the moving party has been satisfied in full, or the action has been dismissed for lack of prosecution after a five-year (5) period' (§ 34-18-60(b)), plus findings of notice to all parties and that the motion 'is the only request made under this section by the moving party within the previous five (5) years' (§ 34-18-60(b)); (c) 'limited to one request every five (5) years' (§ 34-18-60(c)). title: Who Can Be Served With Eviction Papers
bodyText: Rhode Island does not provide for a lease naming someone to accept eviction papers for the tenant, and for nonpayment cases a lease designation would not help. In a nonpayment eviction the statute fixes service: on filing day you mail the summons, complaint and a blank answer to the tenant by first-class mail, and a sheriff or constable serves them by handing them to the tenant, leaving them at the unit with a person of suitable age and discretion living there, or, if no one is found, posting them on the unit door, at least five days before the hearing. In noncompliance and holdover evictions the statutory summons form lets the officer serve an agent authorized by appointment or by law to receive service, as the court's service rule also allows, so a tenant's own written appointment could be used there; the rule doesn't say whether a lease clause signed at move-in counts as that appointment (case law was not searched). A tenant who is not a Rhode Island resident may designate an in-state agent for service in a writing filed with the secretary of state; if none is designated, service may be made on the secretary of state with a copy mailed by registered or certified mail. The library offers no clause naming an agent.

title: Evictions for Drug or Violent Crime
bodyText: Rhode Island has no fast-track court procedure for evictions based on drug or violent crime, and no statute lets a tenant organization, prosecutor, neighbor or the Attorney General bring an eviction against your tenant. What the law does give you is a shortcut at the notice stage: if the tenant maintains a narcotics nuisance, manufactures, sells or delivers controlled substances (or possesses schedule I or II drugs with intent to do so) on the premises or adjacent public property, or commits a crime of violence there, you need not send a noncompliance notice or allow a cure, and may immediately file a complaint for eviction for reason other than nonpayment. The tenant still has the usual 20 days after service to answer, and the case is heard under the court's ordinary rules. Separately, it is a crime to knowingly let property you own or control be used as a drug nuisance (a place used for the unlawful sale, use or keeping of controlled substances), and the older common-nuisance laws (prostitution, illegal gaming, disorderly houses, unlicensed liquor) make it a crime to let premises for those uses or knowingly permit them, let the Attorney General or a citizen sue to abate them, and say that such use annuls the lease; even then, recover possession through the eviction process, not self-help.

(§ 34-18-36(c)). Breaches: § 34-18-24(8)-(10). title: When Rhode Island Requires a Reason to Evict
bodyText: Rhode Island has no general just-cause eviction law. You may let a fixed-term lease end, or end a periodic tenancy with the statutory notice, without giving a reason, as long as the real reason is not retaliation or discrimination (including against a victim of domestic abuse). Cause is required only in these settings. (1) A foreclosing lender or other foreclosing owner of a building with four or fewer units may evict a bona fide tenant only for the statute's just causes, unless the owner is exempt (see the foreclosure row). The other grounds are a signed purchase-and-sale agreement with a bona fide third-party buyer whom the owner has told it may have to evict the occupants, and, in FHA-insured housing, HUD's denial of a tenant's request for an occupied conveyance or the tenant's failure to request continued occupancy by the deadline in the owner's notice of pending acquisition. (2) While housing-code conferences, hearings or appeals are pending, or once you have been served with a notice of violation, you may not evict occupants without just cause. (3) During a condominium or time-share conversion, no tenant may be made to leave on less than 120 days' notice (one year for a tenant of 10 years or aged 62 or older) except for nonpayment, waste or disturbing other tenants. (4) A mobile or manufactured home park owner may end a lot tenancy only for listed reasons (nonpayment, law or park-rule violations after notice and a chance to comply, damage, repeated disturbance, or condemnation or change of use) and on at least 60 days' written notice (30 days for nonpayment). No statute ties cause to how long a tenant has lived there. Public housing authority and assisted living tenancies have their own rules, not covered here.

(2) Code notices: § 45-24.3-21(c)(4): 'It is unlawful for any owner, operator, or agent to evict occupants from a dwelling or dwelling unit without just cause during conferences, hearings, appeals, or when served with a notice of violation.' (§ 45-24.3-21(c)(4)). (3) Conversion: § 34-36.1-4.12(a), (e)(1); § 34-41-4.10(a), (e)(1) (see edu-condo-conversion-ri). (4) Mobile home parks: § 31-44-2(a) (termination 'subject to one or more of the following reasons and limitations which shall take precedence over any conflicting state statute or local ordinance'; § 31-44-2(a)), reasons (1)-(6) including cure of nonpayment by tender 'including a late charge of five percent (5%) of the monthly rent due after a seven (7) day grace period' (§ 31-44-2(a)(1)); (b) 'not less than sixty (60) days; provided that upon grounds of nonpayment of rent, a tenancy may be terminated upon giving thirty (30) days notice' (§ 31-44-2(b)). title: Tenants and Foreclosure
bodyText: If your mortgage is 120 days delinquent, you must tell your tenants that the property may be foreclosed; they must keep paying you rent until a foreclosure happens. Before a foreclosure sale, your lender must mail each bona fide tenant (it may address it to "Occupant") a notice of the sale date, time and place, telling them to keep paying rent and that it is not an eviction notice. After foreclosure of a building with four or fewer units, a foreclosing lender, servicer, institutional mortgagee, Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac (unless exempt as a Rhode Island-headquartered full-service lender or one with fewer than 15 Rhode Island foreclosures the prior year) may evict a bona fide tenant only for just cause: unpaid rent after written notice of the amount and payee, an uncured material breach, nuisance or substantial damage, illegal use, refusing a like renewal or reasonable access, or code-driven board-up, demolition or repair. It may also evict once a bona fide third-party buyer has signed a binding purchase-and-sale agreement and been told it may have to evict the occupants, or, in FHA-insured housing, once HUD denies a tenant's request for an occupied conveyance or the tenant fails to request continued occupancy by the deadline in the notice of pending acquisition. Within 30 days it must post and deliver a notice giving its contacts, where to pay rent and a continued-occupancy form to return within 30 days. A tenancy is bona fide only if the tenant isn't the borrower or the borrower's child, spouse or parent, it was at arm's length, and the rent is near market or subsidized. A tenant may knowingly waive these protections for consideration.

title: Lease Guarantors
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute specific to lease guaranties or co-signers. A guarantor's promise to answer for the tenant's debt is enforceable only if it, or a note of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor or someone the guarantor authorized. No statute limits a guarantor to the original term, or requires a guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, so whether a guarantor stays liable after a renewal, an extension, a switch to month-to-month or a rent increase depends on what the guaranty says and on contract law; say it expressly in the guaranty. If a guarantor gives you money to secure the tenant's obligations, treat it as part of the security deposit, which may not exceed one month's periodic rent however it is labeled. If you require a guarantor because an applicant's income falls below your minimum, the income standard must be based only on the tenant's share of the rent after any rental assistance or subsidy. title: No Premium Holdover Charge Offered
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute that sets or caps a holdover rate, so a lease could try to set a daily or premium charge for a tenant who stays after the lease ends. The library does not offer one. The law already gives you a strong remedy: if the holdover is willful and not in good faith, you may recover, besides possession, not more than three months' periodic rent or three times your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees; and after the lease ends you may claim a reasonable sum for use and occupation plus actual damages. A fixed premium rate risks being treated as an unenforceable penalty (case law not searched), and any agreed holdover charge would be a fee beyond rent that the lease must list in the rent section (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format). If you consent to a tenant staying on without agreeing a new term, the tenancy becomes week-to-week if the tenant pays weekly and otherwise month-to-month; the statute doesn't say whether accepting rent counts as that consent, but payments equal to rent that you accept while execution of an eviction judgment is stayed do not reinstate the tenancy. Separately, accepting rent with knowledge of a tenant's default waives your right to terminate for that breach unless you give written notice within 10 days; if you take money from a tenant who stays after the lease ends, reserve your rights in writing within 10 days. A landlord may add a holdover-rate clause of its own after taking advice.

If the landlord consents to the tenant's occupancy, the parties may agree to a definite term. If no term is specified, the term shall be week-to-week if the tenant pays on a week-to-week basis, and in all other cases, month-to-month.' title: No Waiver of Collection Exemptions
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute letting a tenant waive, in a lease, the protections that keep property from being taken to pay a judgment, and none expressly barring such a waiver; the library offers no waiver clause, and you should not add one. When you collect a judgment for rent or damages, the tenant keeps the statutory exemptions, including household furniture, clothing and family stores (with beds and bedding) up to $9,600 in value, and other exempt property and benefits. A homestead estate of up to $500,000 protects a debtor's principal residence, including a home the person possesses by lease (for example a manufactured home on a rented lot), subject to listed exceptions. Separately, the landlord-tenant act gives you no lien on a tenant's household goods and abolishes distraint for rent, so a lease cannot make the tenant's belongings security for the rent, and an unenforceable lease term you knowingly use can cost up to three months' rent plus damages and fees. Case law on exemption waivers was not searched.

(§ 9-26-4(3)); the section lists other exempt property (tools, books, wages, retirement accounts, vehicles to $12,000, jewelry to $2,000, deposits to $500) and has no waiver provision. Homestead: § 9-26-4.1(a) ('an estate of homestead to the extent of five hundred thousand dollars ($500,000) in the land and buildings, or personal property that the owner uses as a residence, may be acquired pursuant to this section by an owner of a home or an individual who rightfully possesses the premises by lease' (§ 9-26-4.1(a)), automatic by operation of law, exceptions (1)-(7)). Liens: § 34-18-42(a), (b) ('Distraint for rent is abolished.'; § 34-18-42(b)). Prohibited terms: § 34-18-17(a), (b). Court rule: R.I. Dist. Ct. R. Civ. P. (supplementary proceedings) states that a debtor's failure to object 'shall not be deemed as a waiver of any statutory exemption' (battery excerpt only; not relied on). title: Seniors Moving to Care or Elderly Housing
bodyText: A Rhode Island tenant who is 65 or older, or who will turn 65 during the lease, may end the lease early to move into a residential care and assisted living facility, a nursing facility, or a unit in a private or public housing complex the federal government designates as housing for the elderly. The tenant gives written notice to the person who usually receives the rent, with documentation of admission or pending admission. The termination takes effect no earlier than 45 days after the first rent due date following delivery of the notice, and rent is owed until then. The statute sets no termination fee, and a lease cannot waive this right. Rhode Island gives no comparable right to a younger tenant who must move because of illness, disability or a need for care, and none tied to a co-tenant's death; those tenants are bound by the lease unless another statutory exit applies (for example the survivor early-termination right). A periodic tenant can always end the tenancy with the ordinary statutory notice.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(e): 'A tenant who is sixty-five (65) years of age or older or who will turn sixty-five (65) during the term of a rental agreement for a dwelling unit may terminate such a rental agreement in order to enter a residential care and assisted living facility, as defined in § 23-17.4-2, a nursing facility, or a unit in a private or public housing complex designated by the federal government as housing for the elderly. The tenant may terminate the rental agreement by notice given in writing to the usual person to whom rental payments are made. The notice shall be accompanied by documentation of admission or pending admission to a facility or housing complex described in this section. Termination of the rental agreement shall be effective no earlier than forty-five (45) days after the first rental payment due date following delivery of written notice of termination.' (§ 34-18-15(e)). Waiver: § 34-18-17(a)(1), (b). title: No Landlord Lien on Belongings
bodyText: Rhode Island gives a residential landlord no lien on, and no right to seize or hold, a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. Distraint for rent is abolished, and a lien or security interest in the tenant's household goods is unenforceable (the only exceptions are interests perfected before the 1986 act took effect, and the rule that a tenant whose property was moved under a court execution must pay the moving and storage costs before release, which are reimbursed to you). A lease clause making the tenant's belongings security for the rent, or letting you keep them until the tenant pays, is unenforceable, and knowingly using one can cost up to three months' rent plus damages and attorney's fees. Seizing property or locking the tenant out also breaks the self-help ban. Collect unpaid rent through the eviction case or a court judgment, subject to the statutory exemptions from attachment. A self-storage operator's lien does not apply to a dwelling.

Laws § 34-18-42(a): 'A lien or security interest on behalf of the landlord in the tenant's household goods is not enforceable unless perfected before the effective date of this chapter, except as provided in § 34-18-50.' (§ 34-18-42(a)); (b): 'Distraint for rent is abolished.' (§ 34-18-42(b)). § 34-18-50 (moving and prepaid storage costs paid before release 'shall be paid to the landlord as reimbursement for the costs of removing the personal property'; § 34-18-50). Effective date: chapter 34-18 enacted by P.L. 1986, ch. 200, § 2 (history line). Prohibited terms: § 34-18-17(a)(1), (b). Self-help: § 34-18-44; remedies § 34-18-34. Exemptions: § 9-26-4 (see edu-no-exemption-waiver-ri). Self-storage liens: § 34-42-3 (self-service storage facilities only; battery excerpt). title: Your Remedies for Tenant Breach
bodyText: Rhode Island's act sets your money and possession remedies. In a nonpayment eviction you may recover possession and actual damages (unpaid rent), plus a reasonable attorney's fee only if the tenant received a five-day demand in the six months before you filed and the nonpayment was willful. For other lease or statutory breaches you may recover possession, actual damages and an injunction, with attorney's fees if the breach was willful; you need not end the lease to sue for damages or an injunction. After the lease is terminated you have a claim for possession, a reasonable sum for use and occupation after termination, actual damages for the breach and reasonable attorney's fees. Every claim is subject to your duty to mitigate damages. For a willful, bad-faith holdover you may recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater. Accepting rent knowing of a default waives termination for that breach unless you give written notice within 10 days, though partial payment never waives the balance. A tenant who counterclaims in a nonpayment case may be ordered to pay rent into court. You have no lien on the tenant's belongings, and recover possession only through the court.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-35(d): 'Except as provided in this chapter, the landlord may recover possession and actual damages.' (§ 34-18-35(d)); fee condition (§ 34-18-35(d)). § 34-18-36(d): 'Except as provided in this chapter, the landlord may recover possession, actual damages and obtain injunctive relief for noncompliance by the tenant with the rental agreement or § 34-18-24. If the tenant's noncompliance is willful, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney's fees.' (§ 34-18-36(d)). § 34-18-43: 'If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord has a claim for possession, for a sum for reasonable use and occupation subsequent to the termination, and for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement and reasonable attorney's fees.' (§ 34-18-43). Mitigation: § 34-18-5(a) ('The aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages.'; § 34-18-5(a)). Holdover: § 34-18-38(c). Waiver by acceptance: § 34-18-41 ('unless the landlord gives written notice within ten (10) days'; 'acceptance of partial payment of rent shall not constitute a waiver of the balance due'; § 34-18-41). Counterclaim: § 34-18-32(a). Liens: § 34-18-42. Self-help: § 34-18-44. Fee interplay: see edu-attorney-fees-ri on § 34-18-43 versus § 34-18-35(d). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the body reads § 34-18-36(d) as allowing a damages or injunction suit without termination (its remedies are listed for 'noncompliance', not conditioned on termination); case law not searched. title: Agreed Damages for Breach
bodyText: Rhode Island's landlord-tenant act and its other statutes do not address a residential lease term fixing in advance what a tenant owes for a breach (liquidated damages), and no regulation permits or bars one. Your statutory damages are actual damages for the breach, reasonable use and occupation after termination, and, for a willful bad-faith holdover, up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages; every damages claim is subject to your duty to mitigate. The security deposit is not liquidated damages: at move-out you may keep only unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning and trash-disposal costs and physical damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, itemized in writing. A fixed charge that is out of proportion to likely harm risks being struck as a penalty under general contract law (case law not searched), and any agreed charge is a fee beyond rent that must be listed in the lease's rent section (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format). An agreed fee for the tenant's option to end a fixed term early is treated differently, as the price of that option; see the library's early-termination clause.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (no residential liquidated-damages statute). Damages: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-36(d) (actual damages); § 34-18-43 ('a sum for reasonable use and occupation subsequent to the termination, and for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement'; § 34-18-43); § 34-18-38(c) holdover; § 34-18-5(a) ('The aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages.'; § 34-18-5(a)). Deposit: § 34-18-19(b) (deductions limited to 'unpaid accrued rent, the amount due, if any, for reasonable cleaning expenses, the amount due, if any, for reasonable trash disposal expenses and the amount of physical damages to the premises, other than ordinary wear and tear'; § 34-18-19(b)), (h) no waiver. Fee disclosure: § 34-18-15(a)(1), (5). title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Rhode Island does not allow a lockout for unpaid rent, and a lease term that gives you one is unenforceable. You may not recover or take possession of the unit by any action of your own, such as changing the locks or willfully interrupting heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, except after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit or as the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act allows. For unpaid rent the act's route is: once rent is 15 days in arrears, mail the five-day demand notice and, if the tenant does not pay, file an eviction for nonpayment no earlier than the sixth day after mailing. A tenant who is locked out may recover possession or end the lease, and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees; if the lease ends, you must return the security deposit and all prepaid rent. Distraint for rent is abolished, so you may not hold the tenant's belongings for rent either. Deliberately using a lease with a term you know is prohibited adds up to three months' periodic rent and fees.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-44: 'A landlord may not recover or take possession of the dwelling unit by action or otherwise, including willful diminution of services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of heat, running water, hot water, electric, gas, or other essential service to the tenant, except in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted in this chapter.' § 34-18-34: the tenant 'may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, in either case, recover an amount not more than three (3) months periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him or her, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-34); 'If the rental agreement is terminated the landlord shall return all security recoverable under § 34-18-19 and all prepaid rent' (§ 34-18-34). § 34-18-42(b): 'Distraint for rent is abolished.' § 34-18-17(a)(1): a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under this chapter' (§ 34-18-17(a)(1)); (b): such a provision 'is unenforceable' (§ 34-18-17(b)) and deliberate use adds 'an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-17(b)). Nonpayment route: § 34-18-35(a) (rent 'due and in arrears for fifteen (15) days' (§ 34-18-35(a)), written demand in the § 34-18-56(a) form), (b) (filed 'no earlier than the sixth (6th) day after mailing of the written demand notice' (§ 34-18-35(b))). Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2), none permitting one. Mobile home park chapter 31-44 not addressed here. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Minors in Eviction Cases
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute or court rule that bars naming a tenant's minor child in an eviction case, or that requires it. Rhode Island's age of majority is 18. The District Court civil rules govern eviction cases, and two of them matter if a minor is a party: a minor without a guardian or other representative may defend only through a guardian ad litem, whom the court must appoint, and no default judgment may be entered against a minor unless a guardian, guardian ad litem or other representative has appeared for the minor (the clerk may not enter a default judgment against a minor at all). In practice, name the adults who signed the lease or hold the tenancy. Rhode Island's General Laws, Constitution, the District Court civil rules, the Supreme Court access rules and the 2025-2026 public laws were searched; case law was not.

title: Five-Day Demand Before a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: Before you can evict for unpaid rent, Rhode Island requires a written five-day demand. Once any part of the rent has been due and unpaid for 15 days, mail the tenant a notice substantially in the statutory 'Five-Day Demand Notice for Nonpayment of Rent' form, stating the amount 15 days in arrears, demanding it, and saying that unless the tenant pays within five days of the mailing date the rental agreement will terminate and you will file an eviction. The form ends with your certificate that you mailed it by first-class mail. If the tenant does not pay, file a 'Complaint for Eviction for Nonpayment of Rent' with the notice attached, no earlier than the sixth day after mailing. The tenant may cure by paying the full arrears any time before you file; a tenant who has not received an earlier demand notice (before the one for this case) in the six months before you file may also cure at the hearing by paying all arrears plus court costs. You recover attorney's fees only if the tenant received an earlier demand notice in those six months and the nonpayment was willful. You may not file a nonpayment eviction unless your Department of Health rental registry filing is current, and you must show the court proof when you file. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies, and a lease cannot waive it.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-35(a): 'If any part of the stipulated rent is due and in arrears for fifteen (15) days, the landlord shall send a written notice, in a form substantially similar to that provided in § 34-18-56(a), specifying the amount of the rent which is fifteen (15) days in arrears, making demand for the rent, and notifying the tenant that unless he or she cures the breach within five (5) days of the date of mailing of the notice, the rental agreement shall terminate, and the landlord shall commence an eviction action in the appropriate district court or housing court.' § 34-18-35(b): action 'shall be filed no earlier than the sixth (6th) day after mailing of the written demand notice' (§ 34-18-35(b)), by a 'Complaint for Eviction for Nonpayment of Rent' in the § 34-18-56(d) form. § 34-18-35(d): fees only where 'the tenant had received a demand notice pursuant to subsection (a) within the six (6) months immediately preceding the filing of the action, and the tenant's nonpayment was willful' (§ 34-18-35(d)). § 34-18-35(e): cure 'by tendering the full amount of rent prior to commencement of suit' (§ 34-18-35(e)); and at the hearing, 'together with court costs' (§ 34-18-35(e)), if no notice within the prior six months. § 34-18-56(a) form (heading 'FIVE-DAY DEMAND NOTICE FOR NONPAYMENT OF RENT', with the certificate 'I certify that I placed in regular U.S. mail, first class postage prepaid, a copy of this Notice, addressed to the tenant' (§ 34-18-56(a))); § 34-18-56(d) complaint para. 3: 'a copy of that notice is attached to this complaint' (§ 34-18-56(d)). Registry precondition: § 34-18-58(g): 'a landlord or any agent of a landlord may not commence an action to evict for nonpayment of rent in any court of competent jurisdiction, unless, at the time the action is commenced, the landlord is in compliance with the requirements of subsections (a), (b), and (d) of this section' (§ 34-18-58(g)); subsection (b) adds a lead certificate of conformance (or proof of exemption) for pre-1978 units. No waiver: § 34-18-17(a)(1). Notice and receipt by first-class mail: § 34-18-14(b)(2). § 34-18-35 draws no distinction by tenancy type. No 2026 public law amends § 34-18-35 (lead's currency screen). SYNC (Claude Code, 2026-10-09): read with § 34-18-35(d)-(e) on the official site. Taken literally, 'a notice pursuant to subsection (a) ... within the six (6) months immediately preceding the filing of the action' includes the demand notice for the case itself, which every nonpayment action must follow, so no tenant could ever cure at the hearing and every willful nonpayment would carry attorney's fees. DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the row reads it as an earlier notice, before the one for this case, so the hearing cure and the fee rule apply as the statute's structure suggests (case law not searched). title: Notices to End a Tenancy Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Your lease may not waive or shorten the notices Rhode Island requires before you end a tenancy: the five-day demand for unpaid rent, the 20-day notice to cure a breach (termination no sooner than 21 days after mailing), and the notice ending a periodic tenancy (10 days for week-to-week; 30 days for month-to-month or any period between a month and a year; three months before the end of the occupation year for year-to-year). A lease term giving up rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is unenforceable, and deliberately using a lease with a term you know is prohibited lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. Some steps need no notice by statute, so there is nothing to waive: when a fixed term expires you may file for possession the next day; and for drug, drug-dealing or violent-crime breaches, or a qualifying seasonal tenant charged with an ordinance violation or breaching the lease's occupancy or noise terms, you may file without a noncompliance notice. You may agree to give longer notice than the statute requires.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a)(1): a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under this chapter' (§ 34-18-17(a)(1)); (b) such a provision 'included in a rental agreement is unenforceable' (§ 34-18-17(b)); deliberate use: 'in addition to his or her actual damages, an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-17(b)). Notices: § 34-18-35(a) (five-day demand); § 34-18-36(a)(3) ('unless the breach is remedied within twenty (20) days of mailing of the notice the rental agreement shall terminate upon a specified date, which shall not be less than twenty-one (21) days after the mailing of the notice' (§ 34-18-36(a)(3))); § 34-18-37(a)-(c) ('at least ten (10) days' (§ 34-18-37(a)); 'at least thirty (30) days' (§ 34-18-37(b)); 'at least three (3) months prior to the expiration of the occupation year' (§ 34-18-37(c))). None of these sections lets the parties agree otherwise. No notice at end of a fixed term: § 34-18-38(a) (action 'may be filed no earlier than the first day following the expiration or termination of the tenancy' (§ 34-18-38(a))). No noncompliance notice: § 34-18-36(f) (§ 34-18-24(8)-(10) breaches; seasonal leases running May 1-Oct. 15 or Sept. 1-June 1 with no renewal right, where the tenant 'has been charged with violating a municipal ordinance or has otherwise violated the terms of the rental agreement pertaining to legal occupancy or excessive noise or other disturbance of the peace' (§ 34-18-36(f))). Longer notice: DRAFTING JUDGMENT — the chapter sets minimums ('at least'); a longer landlord notice waives no tenant right. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Nuisance Laws and Rental Property
bodyText: Rhode Island's nuisance laws reach a landlord whose rental is used for crime. A place used for prostitution or lewdness, illegal gaming or unlicensed liquor sales, or where disorderly persons habitually gather, is a common nuisance. For those places it is a crime to let a building for those purposes, to knowingly permit that use, or to fail, after five days' notice from an officer or magistrate, to take all reasonable measures to remove the tenant as soon as lawfully possible ($100-$1,000 fine or 60 days to a year in prison), and the attorney general or any citizen may sue in superior court to abate the nuisance and enjoin everyone with an interest in the place; the court may close it for a year, and an owner can lift the closure only by paying costs, posting a bond and proving it neither knew nor could reasonably have learned of the nuisance. An old criminal statute says that use annuls the lease and lets the owner re-enter without court process, but the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act bars self-help. Separately, any place used for the unlawful sale, use or keeping of a controlled substance is a drug nuisance, and knowingly permitting one in a place you own or control carries up to 15 years and $20,000. Use the eviction route: drug nuisance, drug dealing and violent crime on the premises let you file without a cure notice.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-30-1(1) (common nuisance includes places where 'lewdness, assignation, or prostitution is conducted, permitted, continued, or exists' (§ 11-30-1(1)), places used 'for illegal gaming, or where intemperate, idle, dissolute, noisy, or disorderly persons are in the habit of resorting' (§ 11-30-1(1))); § 11-30-2(a) (unlicensed liquor). § 11-30-7: liability for one who lets premises for those purposes, 'or who shall knowingly permit any building, tenement, or part of one to be so used while under his or her control, or who shall after five (5) days notice from any officer or magistrate of that use of the building or tenement omit to take all reasonable measures to eject the tenant or occupant from the premises as soon as it may lawfully be done' (§ 11-30-7); penalty 'fined not less than one hundred dollars ($100) nor more than one thousand dollars ($1,000) or be imprisoned in the adult correctional institutions not less than sixty (60) days nor more than one year' (§ 11-30-7). Drugs: § 21-28-4.06(a) ('used for the unlawful sale, use, or keeping of a controlled substance shall be deemed a common nuisance' (§ 21-28-4.06(a))), (b)(2) (knowingly permitting: 'imprisoned for not more than fifteen (15) years, and fined not more than twenty thousand dollars ($20,000), or both' (§ 21-28-4.06(b)(2))). title: No Owner Move-In Termination Right
bodyText: Rhode Island has no general just-cause eviction law for ordinary tenancies, and no statute giving you a right to end a lease early so you or a relative can move in, or regulating a lease term that reserves one. Without such a term, a fixed-term lease runs to its end date, and you end a periodic tenancy with the statutory notice: 10 days (week-to-week), 30 days (month-to-month or any period between a month and a year) or three months before the end of the occupation year (year-to-year). Rhode Island's just-cause rules are narrow: they cover tenants of a foreclosing lender-owner of a building with four or fewer units (owner move-in is not one of its grounds), and any tenant while housing-code conferences, hearings or appeals are pending or after you are served with a notice of violation; see the for-cause eviction row. This library does not offer a move-in reservation clause; a landlord who wants one should take advice and add it as their own term. Rhode Island's General Laws, Constitution, loaded regulations, court rules and 2025-2026 public laws were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute letting a tenant give a bond to deliver possession at the end of the term, and a lease may not authorize anyone to confess judgment against the tenant on a claim arising from the rental agreement. Such a term is unenforceable, and deliberately using a lease with a term you know is prohibited lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. If a tenant stays after the lease ends, file an eviction for holding over, which you may do from the first day after the term expires; a willful, bad-faith holdover lets you recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus fees. Money taken to secure the tenant's performance counts toward the one-month security deposit cap, however it is labelled. Rhode Island's General Laws, Constitution, loaded regulations, court rules and 2025-2026 public laws were searched; case law was not.
