title: If You Can't Deliver Possession on Time
bodyText: At the start of the term you must deliver possession of the unit as the lease and Rhode Island's maintenance duties require. If you do not, rent abates until you do, and the tenant may either end the lease on at least five days' written notice (you must then return all prepaid rent and the security deposit) or insist that you perform and sue you for possession. If your failure is willful and not in good faith, the tenant may also recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees. If a holdover tenant or anyone else is wrongfully in possession, you may sue that person for possession and the same holdover damages. Rhode Island has no general duty to provide alternate housing, but if you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, a tenant who has given notice may move to reasonable substitute housing, owe no rent for that period, and recover its cost up to one period's rent.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-21: 'At the commencement of the term a landlord shall deliver possession of the premises to the tenant in compliance with the rental agreement and § 34-18-22. The landlord may bring an action for possession against any person wrongfully in possession and may recover the damages provided in § 34-18-38(c).' § 34-18-29(a): 'rent abates until possession is delivered and the tenant may' (§ 34-18-29(a)) '(1) Terminate the rental agreement upon at least five (5) days' written notice to the landlord, and, upon termination, the landlord shall return all prepaid rent and security' (§ 34-18-29(a)(1)), or '(2) Demand performance of the rental agreement by the landlord and, if the tenant elects, bring action for possession of the dwelling unit against the landlord' (§ 34-18-29(a)(2)). § 34-18-29(b): willful bad faith: 'an amount not more than three (3) months' periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-29(b)). Substitute housing: § 34-18-31(a)(3) ('Procure reasonable substitute housing during the period of the landlord's noncompliance, in which case the tenant is excused from paying rent for the period of the landlord's noncompliance' (§ 34-18-31(a)(3))); (b) cost 'not in excess of an amount equal to the periodic rent' (§ 34-18-31(b)); (d) notice first; not if tenant-caused. title: Tenant Belongings After an Eviction
bodyText: After a Rhode Island eviction judgment, only a sheriff or certified constable acting on an execution removes the tenant and the tenant's belongings. If no appeal is claimed and the judgment is unpaid, the execution issues on the sixth day after judgment and stays in force for one year. The officer may put the belongings out on the street and then have them removed and stored for the owner; whoever stores them has a lien for reasonable storage and moving fees but may not sell them until they have been in storage at least 30 days. If the tenant is present and claims the items when they are put out, the officer does not store them. The tenant must pay the whole moving cost and any prepaid storage charges before the property is released, and that amount is paid to you as reimbursement; the officer's costs, including reasonable moving costs, may also be added to the execution with the court's approval. Otherwise you have no lien on the tenant's household goods. Rhode Island has no statute on animals left at an eviction and none aimed at a tenant who returns after one (general trespass law not reviewed).
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-48: 'If no appeal is claimed, and if the judgment has not been satisfied, execution shall be issued on the sixth (6th) day following judgment. Executions shall be issued to the division of sheriffs or certified constable.' (§ 34-18-48); 'shall continue in full force and effect for one year after the date thereof' (§ 34-18-48); 'All costs, including reasonable moving costs, incurred by the division of sheriffs or certified constable in carrying out the mandates of the execution may be added to the execution by the clerk upon approval of the court upon presentment of evidence of the costs.' (§ 34-18-48). § 34-18-50: 'the tenant shall pay the entire amount of the cost of moving the personal property and any prepaid storage charges' (§ 34-18-50) before release; 'This amount shall be paid to the landlord as reimbursement for the costs of removing the personal property.' (§ 34-18-50). § 34-18-42(a) (no landlord lien on household goods 'except as provided in § 34-18-50' (§ 34-18-42(a))). D.C.R. 62(a) (court rule): 'In residential landlord/tenant matters, no execution shall issue upon a judgment until the expiration of five (5) days after its entry.' (D.C.R. 62(a)), consistent with the sixth-day rule. title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: A Rhode Island tenant behind on rent can stop a nonpayment eviction by paying in full at two points. Before you file, the tenant may cure by tendering all the rent owed, and you must take it. After you file, the tenant may cure at the hearing by paying all rent in arrears plus court costs, but only if the tenant had not received an earlier five-day demand notice from you (before the one for this case) in the six months before you filed, so in practice this right comes round no more than once every six months. After judgment there is no statutory right to redeem by paying; a stay of execution, or an appeal, keeps the tenant in place only while the tenant keeps paying amounts equal to the rent as it falls due, and missed payments let you ask the court to issue the execution. Accepting partial rent does not waive the balance, but accepting rent knowing of a default waives your right to end the tenancy for that breach unless you give written notice within 10 days.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-35(e): 'The tenant shall have the right to cure his or her failure to pay rent by tendering the full amount of rent prior to commencement of suit. If the tenant has not received a notice pursuant to subsection (a) of this section within the six (6) months immediately preceding the filing of the action, the tenant shall have the right to cure his or her failure to pay rent after commencement of suit by tendering the full amount of rent in arrears, together with court costs, at the time of hearing.' Post-judgment: § 34-18-49 (stay 'conditioned upon the payment by tenant to the landlord of sums of money equal to the rent for the premises' (§ 34-18-49); acceptance 'shall not constitute a waiver of the right of the landlord to obtain possession of the premises, nor shall the receipt thereof be deemed to reinstate the tenancy' (§ 34-18-49)); § 34-18-51 (execution on nonpayment, no appeal); § 34-18-52 and § 34-18-53 (same during appeal). § 34-18-41: acceptance of rent with knowledge of a default 'constitutes a waiver of the landlord's right to terminate the rental agreement for that breach, unless the landlord gives written notice within ten (10) days. However, acceptance of partial payment of rent shall not constitute a waiver of the balance due.' (§ 34-18-41). No post-judgment redemption: RI-redemption-1 (recorded as failed, rerun as RI-redemption-3); RI-redemption-3 (pay/tender/satisfy/redeem near judgment/execution, or redeem the tenancy / right of redemption, with tenancy context, hits 15, OK; § 34-18-48 positive and three synthetics passed; landlord-tenant hits are §§ 34-18-48, -49, -51, -53, none a redemption right); RI-redemption-2 (everyday words: catch up / pay back rent / bring current, hits 0, OK; synthetic passed). Case law not searched. SYNC (Claude Code, 2026-10-09): read with § 34-18-35(d)-(e) on the official site. Taken literally, 'a notice pursuant to subsection (a) ... within the six (6) months immediately preceding the filing of the action' includes the demand notice for the case itself, which every nonpayment action must follow, so no tenant could ever cure at the hearing and every willful nonpayment would carry attorney's fees. DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the row reads it as an earlier notice, before the one for this case, so the hearing cure and the fee rule apply as the statute's structure suggests (case law not searched). title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In a nonpayment eviction, or a suit for rent while the tenant still lives in the unit, a Rhode Island tenant may counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, such as damages for your failure to maintain the unit. The tenant does not have to pay rent into court first, but once a counterclaim is filed the court may order the tenant to pay into court all or part of the rent accrued and accruing. The court nets the claims: whoever is owed a net amount is paid first from the money in court, and if no rent remains due, the tenant wins the possession case. If the counterclaim is frivolous or has no basis in fact, you may recover reasonable attorney's fees. A tenant who has moved out may counterclaim without paying anything into court. Counterclaims are never compulsory in residential landlord-tenant cases. Separately, a tenant of a unit that is not lead-safe compliant (for example, no valid lead certificate of conformance) may petition the district court to pay rent into the court's registry instead of to you, whatever the lease says, until you comply.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-32(a): 'In an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent or in an action for rent when the tenant is in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for any amount he or she may recover under the rental agreement or this chapter. In that event, the court, from time to time, may order the tenant to pay into court all or part of the rent accrued and thereafter accruing, and shall determine the amount due to each party.' (§ 34-18-32(a)); 'If no rent remains due after application of this section, judgment shall be entered for the tenant in the action for possession. If the defense or counterclaim by the tenant is frivolous or without any basis in fact, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney's fees.' (§ 34-18-32(a)); (b) tenant not in possession 'is not required to pay any rent into court' (§ 34-18-32(b)). Court rule: D.C.R. 13(a): 'Except in residential landlord/tenant actions, a pleading shall state as a counterclaim' (D.C.R. 13(a)). § 34-18-35(d) (interim rent may be ordered on a discovery continuance). Lead escrow: § 42-128.1-14(a): 'Notwithstanding any general law, public law, special law, or any agreement, whether written or oral, a tenant may file a petition to deposit the tenant's rent in an escrow account in the district court' (§ 42-128.1-14(a)) where the property 'is not compliant with the risk reduction provisions of this chapter' (§ 42-128.1-14(a)); release on compliance (c); tenant's compliance costs (d); no retaliation (e). title: False Applications: No Special Remedy
bodyText: Rhode Island gives you no special statutory right to end a lease because the tenant's application was false. This library's application-accuracy clause makes a materially false answer a breach of the lease, so you would use the ordinary noncompliance route: a 20-day notice to remedy, with termination at least 21 days after mailing, then an eviction if the breach is not cured. The clause does not reach questions you may not ask. Rhode Island bars any written or oral inquiry about an applicant's race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, lawful source of income, veteran or servicemember status, country of ancestral origin, disability, age or familial status, or about domestic-abuse victim status or protective orders (you may ask whether the applicant is 18 or older and confirm the source, amount and expected duration of lawful income), and since July 2, 2025 any inquiry about immigration or citizenship status (identity and financial verification remain allowed). Rhode Island has no rule letting an applicant deny a sealed eviction record.

Inquiry bans: § 34-37-4(a) (no owner or agent shall 'make, or cause to be made, any written or oral inquiry concerning the race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, lawful source of income' (§ 34-37-4(a)) and the other listed classes; exception: 'whether the prospective purchaser or tenant is eighteen (18) years of age or older, or to confirm the source, amount, and expected duration of the lawful source of income' (§ 34-37-4(a))). § 34-18-62(a)(1) (no inquiry 'regarding or based on the immigration or citizenship status of a tenant, prospective tenant, occupant, or prospective occupant' (§ 34-18-62(a)(1))); (c)(2) financial and identity verification allowed; effective July 2, 2025. title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: In Rhode Island you may take back a rental unit only through the court eviction process, or after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered it. You may not change the locks, remove the tenant or the tenant's belongings, or willfully interrupt (or cause the interruption of) heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or any other essential service to force the tenant out. A tenant who is unlawfully removed, locked out or deprived of an essential service may recover possession or end the lease, and in either case recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees; if the lease ends you must return the security deposit and all prepaid rent. The state housing code also bars an owner from shutting off a required service or utility to an occupied unit except for a temporary interruption during actual repairs or an approved emergency. A lease cannot waive these rules. One narrow exception from July 1, 2026: on a tenant's lock-change request accompanied by a protective order against another tenant or household member, you may change the locks and refuse that person a key. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-44: 'A landlord may not recover or take possession of the dwelling unit by action or otherwise, including willful diminution of services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of heat, running water, hot water, electric, gas, or other essential service to the tenant, except in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted in this chapter' (§ 34-18-44). § 34-18-34: 'If a landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises or willfully diminishes services to the tenant' (§ 34-18-34), the tenant 'may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, in either case, recover an amount not more than three (3) months periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him or her, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-34); on termination 'the landlord shall return all security recoverable under § 34-18-19 and all prepaid rent' (§ 34-18-34). Housing code: § 45-24.3-10(19): 'No owner, operator, or occupant shall cause any service, facility, equipment, or utility, required under this chapter, to be removed from, or shut off from, or discontinued for any occupied dwelling or dwelling unit let or occupied by him or her, except for a temporary interruption that may be necessary while actual repairs or alterations are in process, or during temporary emergencies when discontinuance of service is approved by the appropriate authority' (§ 45-24.3-10(19)). No waiver: § 34-18-17(a)(1). Exception: § 34-18-65(c) (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): 'the lessor or owner may change the locks and deny a key to the alleged perpetrator upon receipt of a request to change the locks; provided, however, that such request shall be accompanied by a copy of a valid protective order issued against a tenant or household member or other court order requiring change of locks' (§ 34-18-65(c)); § 34-18-65(f) no liability for refusing a key on a reasonable belief. Lawful removal after judgment is by execution served by a sheriff or constable (§ 34-18-48; see edu-post-eviction-property-ri). Chapter 34-19 (forcible entry and detainer, superior court jury procedure, § 34-19-1) is a separate remedy against anyone who forcibly enters or detains land; not relied on for the body. title: Servicemember Lease Termination
bodyText: Rhode Island gives servicemembers a state-law right to end a lease, alongside the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. A lease of a home occupied (or to be occupied) by a servicemember or dependents may be ended early if the tenant enters military service after signing, or signed while in service and then receives orders for a permanent change of station or a deployment of 90 days or more. The tenant must give you or your agent written notice and a copy of the orders. For a lease with monthly rent, termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date following the notice; for any other lease, on the last day of the month after the month of notice. You may not charge an early termination fee. The tenant owes prorated rent up to the termination date and any other obligations due under the lease, including reasonable excess-wear charges; refund rent paid for any later period within 30 days. Termination also ends any obligation of the servicemember's dependents under the lease. Rhode Island National Guard members on state active duty for more than 90 days get the federal Act's protections, including protection from eviction and the right to end a lease. You also may not ask about, or refuse to rent because of, an applicant's servicemember or veteran status.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(f)(1): 'A lease of premises occupied, or intended to be occupied, by a servicemember or a servicemember's dependents may be unilaterally terminated if' (§ 34-18-15(f)(1)): (i) 'The lease is executed by or on behalf of a person who, thereafter, and during the term of the lease, enters military service' (§ 34-18-15(f)(1)(i)); or (ii) the servicemember 'receives military orders for a change of permanent station or to deploy with a military unit, or as an individual in support of a military operation, for a period of not less than ninety (90) days' (§ 34-18-15(f)(1)(ii)); and (iii) delivers 'written notice of the termination, and a copy of the servicemember's military orders' (§ 34-18-15(f)(1)(iii)). Effective date: monthly rent: 'effective thirty (30) days after the first date on which the next rental payment is due and payable after the date on which the notice is delivered' (§ 34-18-15(f)(2)); any other lease: 'effective on the last day of the month following the month in which the notice is delivered' (§ 34-18-15(f)(3)). § 34-18-15(f)(4): 'The lessor may not impose an early termination charge' (§ 34-18-15(f)(4)), but obligations due under the lease 'including reasonable charges to the lessee for excess wear' (§ 34-18-15(f)(4)) remain payable. § 34-18-15(f)(5): advance rent refunded 'within thirty (30) days of the effective date of the termination of the lease' (§ 34-18-15(f)(5)); (f)(6) dependents released. Added by P.L. 2024, chs. 308, 309, § 2, effective January 1, 2025. Chapter 34-18 does not define 'servicemember' or 'military service' (§ 34-18-11 checked); the terms track the federal Act (50 U.S.C. § 3955, not read). Guard: § 30-7-10: 'All national guard members on state active duty for a continuous period exceeding ninety (90) days shall be entitled to the rights, protections, privileges, and immunities afforded under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act' (§ 30-7-10), including 'protection from eviction as well as the right to terminate a lease due to military service' (§ 30-7-10); superior court has exclusive jurisdiction. title: No Late-Benefit Eviction Defense
bodyText: Rhode Island has no special eviction defense, continuance or stay for a tenant who fell behind because a Social Security, public assistance, rental voucher or other government benefit payment arrived late. The ordinary nonpayment rules apply. You must mail the five-day demand once rent is 15 days in arrears and wait until the sixth day after mailing to file. The tenant may cure by paying all the arrears before you file, and a tenant who has not received an earlier demand notice (before the one for this case) in the six months before you file may also cure at the hearing by paying all arrears plus court costs. A court may continue the hearing for discovery on good cause and order interim rent, but that is not tied to benefit delays. Rhode Island's General Laws, Constitution, the 2025-2026 public laws and the District Court civil rules were searched; case law and federal program rules for subsidized tenancies were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (late-benefit eviction defense, continuance or stay). Batteries over the RI corpus (General Laws, Constitution, three loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws, District Court civil rules, Supreme Court public-access and e-filing rules): RI-social-security-defense-1 (social security/supplemental security/subsistence/public assistance/benefit payment/rental assistance/voucher/housing assistance payment/furlough/government shutdown/delay in mailing near evict, nonpayment, arrears, possession, continuance, stay; hits 15, OK; synthetic positive passed; all hits are child support, public assistance administration or insurance, none an eviction defense); RI-social-security-defense-2 (everyday words: late/delayed/not received near check, payment or benefit and eviction or nonpayment; hits 3, OK; synthetic positive passed; none relevant). Ordinary rules: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-35(e): 'The tenant shall have the right to cure his or her failure to pay rent by tendering the full amount of rent prior to commencement of suit' (§ 34-18-35(e)); a tenant without a notice in the prior six months may cure 'by tendering the full amount of rent in arrears, together with court costs, at the time of hearing' (§ 34-18-35(e)). § 34-18-35(d): the court 'may continue the hearing to allow a reasonable time for the completion of discovery' (§ 34-18-35(d)) and 'may, in its discretion, order interim rent' (§ 34-18-35(d)). Demand timing: § 34-18-35(a), (b). Case law and federal subsidy program rules not searched. SYNC (Claude Code, 2026-10-09): read with § 34-18-35(d)-(e) on the official site. Taken literally, 'a notice pursuant to subsection (a) ... within the six (6) months immediately preceding the filing of the action' includes the demand notice for the case itself, which every nonpayment action must follow, so no tenant could ever cure at the hearing and every willful nonpayment would carry attorney's fees. DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the row reads it as an earlier notice, before the one for this case, so the hearing cure and the fee rule apply as the statute's structure suggests (case law not searched). title: When a Tenant May End the Lease Early
bodyText: Rhode Island lets a tenant end a lease early, whatever the lease says, in these cases. (1) A tenant who is 65 or older (or turns 65 during the lease) and is entering assisted living, a nursing facility or federally designated elderly housing: written notice with proof of admission, effective no earlier than 45 days after the next rent due date. (2) A servicemember entering service or receiving qualifying orders (see the servicemember row). (3) From July 1, 2026, a tenant who is, or whose household member is, a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking within the last 150 days, with written verification; the tenant must vacate within 30 days and owes rent only through termination or move-out, with no termination fee. (4) Your noncompliance with the lease, or with your maintenance duties in a way that materially affects health and safety, if you don't fix it within 20 days of written notice (termination at least 30 days after notice; 14 days for a repeat within six months), unless the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent caused the condition. (5) Your failure to deliver possession (five days' notice). (6) Fire or casualty substantially impairing the unit (notice within 14 days of vacating). (7) Lockout or willful essential-service shutoff. (8) Unlawful or harassing entry. (9) Conversion to condominiums (cancellation without penalty if lease obligations are met). In cases (4)-(7) you must return the security deposit and prepaid rent.
notes: RI: (1) R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(e): tenant 65 or older 'may terminate such a rental agreement in order to enter a residential care and assisted living facility, as defined in § 23-17.4-2, a nursing facility, or a unit in a private or public housing complex designated by the federal government as housing for the elderly' (§ 34-18-15(e)); 'Termination of the rental agreement shall be effective no earlier than forty-five (45) days after the first rental payment due date following delivery of written notice of termination' (§ 34-18-15(e)). (2) § 34-18-15(f) (see edu-servicemember-rights-ri). (3) § 34-18-63 (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): 'A tenant may terminate their lease or rental agreement without penalty or fees for early termination, or liability for future rent' (§ 34-18-63(a)) where the tenant or household member 'within the most recent one hundred fifty (150) days has been a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking' (§ 34-18-63(a)(1)), conditioned on written verification (§ 34-18-63(a)(3)); vacate 'within thirty (30) days of giving notice' (§ 34-18-63(c)); rent through 'the date of termination or the date the tenant actually vacates the premises, whichever is later' (§ 34-18-63(d)); waiver void (§ 34-18-67, same act). Detail belongs to the dv-lease-termination topic. (4) § 34-18-28(a): termination 'upon a date not less than thirty (30) days after receipt of the notice if the breach is not remedied in twenty (20) days' (§ 34-18-28(a)); repeat within six months: 'at least fourteen (14) days' written notice' (§ 34-18-28(a)(2)); not for tenant-caused conditions (§ 34-18-28(a)(3)); (d) return of security and prepaid rent. (5) § 34-18-29(a)(1): 'upon at least five (5) days' written notice' (§ 34-18-29(a)(1)). (6) § 34-18-33(a)(1): vacate and notify 'in writing within fourteen (14) days thereafter' (§ 34-18-33(a)(1)); (b) return of security and prepaid rent. (7) § 34-18-34. (8) § 34-18-45(b): unlawful, unreasonable or harassing entry: tenant 'may obtain injunctive relief to prevent the recurrence of the conduct or terminate the rental agreement' (§ 34-18-45(b)). § 34-18-31 (essential services) gives substitute housing and rent remedies, not termination. (9) § 34-36.1-4.12(b): 'Tenants shall have the right to cancel their lease and receive no penalties for the cancellation as long as all obligations of the lease have been met' (§ 34-36.1-4.12(b)) during the 60-day purchase offer after the conversion notice. Non-waivable: § 34-18-17(a)(1). title: When the Lease Term Ends
bodyText: A Rhode Island lease for a fixed term ends on its last day without any notice from you. If the tenant stays without your consent, you may file an eviction for holding over as early as the next day, and if the holdover is willful and not in good faith you may also recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. You may not remove the tenant or the tenant's belongings yourself. If you consent to the tenant staying without agreeing a new term, the tenancy becomes week-to-week (if rent is paid weekly) or month-to-month, and it then ends only on written notice: 10 days for week-to-week, 30 days for month-to-month. A periodic tenancy (no fixed term) never simply expires; it ends on the statutory notice. If you acquired a building of four or fewer units through foreclosure as a foreclosing owner, you may evict tenants only for just cause unless an exemption applies. You have no lien on the tenant's household goods. Rhode Island has no statute on disposing of belongings a tenant leaves behind after moving out, so get advice before discarding anything of value.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-38(a): 'If the tenant remains in possession without the landlord's consent after expiration of the term of the rental agreement or after the termination of a periodic tenancy, the landlord may commence an eviction action, which may be filed no earlier than the first day following the expiration or termination of the tenancy' (§ 34-18-38(a)). § 34-18-38(c): willful bad-faith holdover: 'an amount not more than three (3) months' periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by the landlord, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-38(c)); 'If no term is specified, the term shall be week-to-week if the tenant pays on a week-to-week basis, and in all other cases, month-to-month' (§ 34-18-38(c)). Periodic notice: § 34-18-37(a)-(c) (10 days, 30 days, three months before the end of the occupation year). Self-help ban: § 34-18-44 (see edu-self-help-eviction-ri). Foreclosure: § 34-18-38.2(a): 'a foreclosing owner shall not evict a tenant except for just cause' (§ 34-18-38.2(a)), with the third-party purchase and FHA exceptions in (a) and the (h) exemptions (Rhode Island-headquartered full-service mortgage operations; fewer than 15 Rhode Island foreclosures the prior year); 'Housing accommodation' is 'a building or structure containing four (4) or fewer dwelling units' (§ 34-18-38.1(6)); just cause includes refusal of 'a written extension or renewal thereof for a further term of like duration' (§ 34-18-38.1(9)(v)). No lien: § 34-18-42(a); 'Distraint for rent is abolished' (§ 34-18-42(b)). Condition at move-out: § 34-18-24(6) (no deliberate or negligent damage); deductions under § 34-18-19. No statute on disposal of property left behind: lead's RI-abandoned-prop-3. Shared clause surrender-end-of-term reads correctly: "unless applicable law entitles Tenant to remain" covers § 34-18-38.2, and "to the extent permitted by applicable law" covers the absence of a disposal statute. §§ 34-18-38.1 and 34-18-38.2 read for the cited subsections; some long subsections (§ 34-18-38.2(d)(3)) were truncated in reading. Case law (abandoned property, bailment) not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenancies Without a Set Term
bodyText: Rhode Island's residential landlord-tenant law does not recognize a separate "tenancy at will" for homes and apartments. A rental agreement may be written or oral, and if it does not fix a definite term the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer who pays rent weekly and month-to-month in every other case. Either you or the tenant ends it by written notice in the statutory form: at least 10 days before the termination date for week-to-week, at least 30 days for month-to-month. The same applies when a tenant stays on with your consent after a lease expires and no new term is agreed. Rhode Island's older rules letting a landlord end a tenancy at will or by sufferance on a written notice naming the day apply only to commercial property and other estates outside the residential act, such as transient hotel stays, institutional residence and transitional housing, unless the parties agree to be covered by the residential act.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (residential tenancy at will). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(d): 'Unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent, and in all other cases month to month' (§ 34-18-15(d)). 'Rental agreement' means 'all agreements, written or oral' (§ 34-18-11(14), renumbered (17) by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1, effective July 1, 2026). Notice: § 34-18-37(a) ('at least ten (10) days before the termination date specified in the notice' (§ 34-18-37(a))) and (b) ('at least thirty (30) days before the date specified in the notice' (§ 34-18-37(b))), each in the § 34-18-56(c) form. Holdover with consent: § 34-18-38(c). Chapter 34-18.1: § 34-18.1-1: 'This chapter shall apply to all commercial properties and other estates, excluding residential properties governed by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, chapter 18 of this title' (§ 34-18.1-1); § 34-18.1-2: tenants 'at will or by sufferance covered by this chapter shall quit upon notice in writing from the landlord at the day named therein' (§ 34-18.1-2); §§ 34-18.1-3, -6. § 34-18-8 exclusions (institutional residence, contract-of-sale occupancy, fraternal housing, transient lodging, certain employee occupancy, cooperatives, 'Commercial letting and any other estate governed by chapter 18.1 of this title' (§ 34-18-8(7)), transitional housing), 'Unless the parties expressly agree to be governed by the provisions of this chapter' (§ 34-18-8). Searches over the RI corpus: RI-tenancy-at-will-1 (at will/at sufferance/by sufferance near tenant, lease, landlord, rent; hits 74, OK; synthetic positive passed; landlord-tenant hits only chapter 34-18.1 and the words 'tenants at will' in the lead retaliation rule, § 23-24.6-23(c)(4)); RI-tenancy-at-will-2 (everyday words: without a lease/no written lease/oral lease/by parol/no definite term near tenant, occupant, rent; hits 14, OK; real positive § 34-18-15 passed). title: When the Tenant Causes Damage
bodyText: A Rhode Island tenant must not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly let anyone else do so. Where the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent caused a condition, the tenant cannot use it to end the lease for your noncompliance, repair and deduct at your expense, or claim the essential-service remedies, and you may evict despite a recent code complaint if the tenant's lack of reasonable care mainly caused the violation. Your remedies: for damage affecting health and safety that can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, give written notice; if the tenant does not fix it within 20 days (or promptly in an emergency) you may do the work and bill the reasonable cost as rent on the next due date. You may also serve a 20-day noncompliance notice, sue for actual damages (with attorney's fees if the breach is willful), and deduct damage beyond ordinary wear and tear from the security deposit at move-out. One gap: after a fire or casualty that substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may vacate and end the lease even if the tenant caused it; your remedy is a lawsuit for the damage, not a lease term blocking termination.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-24(6): tenant shall 'Not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair, or remove any part of the premises or knowingly permit any person to do so' (§ 34-18-24(6)). Tenant-fault exclusions: § 34-18-28(a)(3): 'The tenant may not terminate for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of his or her family, or other person on the premises with his or her consent' (§ 34-18-28(a)(3)); § 34-18-30(b) (repair and deduct); § 34-18-31(d) (essential services: does not apply 'if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant' (§ 34-18-31(d))); § 34-18-46(c)(1) (retaliation: violation 'caused primarily by lack of reasonable care by the tenant' (§ 34-18-46(c)(1))). Landlord remedies: § 34-18-39: after 'twenty (20) days after written notice by the landlord specifying the breach' (§ 34-18-39), the landlord 'may enter the dwelling unit and cause the work to be done in a skilled manner and submit the itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost or the fair and reasonable value thereof as rent on the next date periodic rent is due' (§ 34-18-39); § 34-18-36(a) 20-day notice and (d) actual damages, injunctive relief, fees if willful; § 34-18-19(b) deposit deduction for 'physical damages to the premises, other than ordinary wear and tear, that the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with § 34-18-24' (§ 34-18-19(b)). Casualty: § 34-18-33(a) termination and pro-rating rights contain no tenant-fault exception; § 34-18-33(c): 'This section shall not be construed to limit the right of the landlord to recover in an action in tort damages resulting from a fire or other casualty damage caused either negligently or deliberately by the tenant' (§ 34-18-33(c)); a lease term removing the § 34-18-33 rights would be a waiver (§ 34-18-17(a)(1)). Whether a landlord may recover lost rent as tort damages after a tenant-caused fire is case law, not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: If a tenant dies during the lease and no other person who signed it still lives in the unit, Rhode Island lets the deceased's live-in caregiver, or anyone 18 or older living there, continue the lease for a post-death grace period: three months or the rest of the term, whichever is shorter (longer if you agree), starting on the date of death. A resident who stays more than seven days after the death is treated as having chosen to continue. The grace-period tenant pays the agreed rent (prorated for part months), takes on the other lease obligations, may end the grace period at any time, and is not liable for the deceased's past-due rent, which stays with the estate. If you dispute that the person lived there, they must prove it (for example with a voter registration, ID, utility bill or affidavit), and you may rebut. You may deduct damage from the existing deposit but may not demand a new deposit; the balance goes to the grace-period tenant if the grace period lasts more than a month, otherwise to the estate. Several residents who elect are jointly liable. A pending noncompliance eviction may continue as to the grace-period tenant's own breaches of the lease. Rhode Island has no statute ending the lease at death, giving the estate a special right to end it, or setting how to handle a deceased tenant's belongings; get advice before entering or removing property.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-38(d) (P.L. 2024, chs. 409, 410, § 1, effective June 28, 2024): 'If a tenant dies during the term of the rental agreement, leaving no remaining signatories to the rental agreement living within the dwelling unit, the deceased's live-in caregiver or any other person of at least eighteen (18) years of age residing in the dwelling unit shall be permitted to continue the rental agreement for a period of time known as the post-death rental grace period' (§ 34-18-38(d)). (d)(1) pay 'the agreed rent set forth in the rental agreement and assume all other obligations' (§ 34-18-38(d)(1)); (d)(2) burden of proving residence, list of evidence (A)-(M), landlord may rebut ((d)(2)(ii)); (d)(3) may terminate the grace period at any time; (d)(4): 'three (3) months or the remaining term of the rental agreement, whichever is shorter' (§ 34-18-38(d)(4)), commencing 'upon the death of the leaseholder' (§ 34-18-38(d)(4)); (d)(5) prorated rent; (d)(8): 'Any past due rent left unpaid by the deceased tenant shall remain an obligation of the estate of the deceased tenant' (§ 34-18-38(d)(8)); (d)(10): 'the landlord shall not have the right to require an additional security deposit from the grace period temporary tenant' (§ 34-18-38(d)(10)); balance to the grace-period tenant if over one month, otherwise to the estate; (d)(11) joint and several; (d)(12): 'more than seven (7) days after the death of the deceased tenant, they shall be assumed to have elected to become a grace period temporary tenant' (§ 34-18-38(d)(12)); (d)(13) a § 34-18-36 eviction may continue. No waiver: § 34-18-17(a)(1). Searches over the RI corpus: RI-tenant-death-1 (death of the tenant/deceased tenant/tenant dies/post-death/estate of deceased near rent, lease, dwelling; hits 5, OK; real positive § 34-18-38 passed; only § 34-18-38(d) is a residential rule); RI-tenant-death-2 (everyday words: dies/died/passes away/decedent near rental agreement, lease, landlord, dwelling unit, apartment; hits 72, OK; real and synthetic positives passed; many false hits from 'remedies'; no estate termination right or property procedure found). § 34-18.1-11 (executors, arrears of rent) applies only to chapter 34-18.1 estates. Probate law and case law on the estate's continuing lease liability not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Ending a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: In Rhode Island either you or the tenant may end a periodic tenancy without giving a reason, by written notice delivered at least: 10 days before the termination date for a week-to-week tenancy; 30 days before it for a month-to-month tenancy or any period longer than a month and shorter than a year; and three months before the end of the occupation year for a year-to-year tenancy. Use the statutory 'Notice of Termination of Tenancy' form or language substantially like it. The form tells the tenant to vacate on the first day after the end of the current rental period, says rent must be paid until then, and ends with your certificate of first-class mailing; so pick a date that is the day after a rental period ends and at least the required number of days after delivery. A fixed-term lease needs no termination notice: it ends on its last day. If the lease does not fix a term, the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer paying weekly and otherwise month-to-month. Your lease may give longer notice but may not shorten these periods. Separate rules apply to foreclosing owners of buildings with four or fewer units (just cause required), to a tenant's breach (20-day cure notice) and to unpaid rent (five-day demand).
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-37(a): week-to-week, written notice 'delivered to the other at least ten (10) days before the termination date specified in the notice' (§ 34-18-37(a)); (b) 'a month-to-month tenancy or any periodic tenancy for more than a month or less than a year' (§ 34-18-37(b)), 'at least thirty (30) days before the date specified in the notice' (§ 34-18-37(b)); (c) year-to-year 'at least three (3) months prior to the expiration of the occupation year' (§ 34-18-37(c)); each 'in a form substantially similar to that provided in § 34-18-56(c)' (§ 34-18-37(a)). Form, § 34-18-56(c): 'NOTICE OF TERMINATION OF TENANCY' with the date to 'deliver control of the premises to the landlord/owner on the first day after the end of your current rental period' (§ 34-18-56(c)); 'You must continue to pay rent as it becomes due until the date indicated above' (§ 34-18-56(c)); certificate of mailing 'in regular U.S. mail, first class postage prepaid' (§ 34-18-56(c)). Two figures (SOP rule 31): § 34-18-37 counts only days before 'the date specified', while the form names the day after the end of a rental period; following the form with at least the statutory lead time satisfies both. Delivery: § 34-18-14(b)(2) (received when 'delivered in hand or sent by first class mail' (§ 34-18-14(b)(2))). Fixed term: § 34-18-38(a) (filing 'no earlier than the first day following the expiration or termination of the tenancy' (§ 34-18-38(a))). Default tenancy: § 34-18-15(d). No waiver: § 34-18-17(a)(1). Foreclosing owners: § 34-18-38.2 (see edu-surrender-end-of-term-ri). No 2026 public law amends § 34-18-37 or § 34-18-56 (lead's currency screen). § 34-18-56 read for subsection (c) (the other subsections are the other statutory forms). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Removing a Squatter or Unauthorized Occupant
bodyText: Rhode Island has no special fast-track for removing squatters, and no procedure for police to remove a person on an owner's affidavit. Two routes exist. First, criminal trespass: anyone who, with no legitimate purpose, stays on the premises of a home after being told to leave by the owner, the owner's authorized agent or the person entitled to possession commits willful trespass (up to a $1,000 fine or a year in jail), which the police may enforce. But that law does not apply to tenants or occupants who rightfully entered the premises when their tenancy or occupancy began and stayed after it ended or was said to have ended; against them you may recover possession only through a civil court case. So a tenant's guest who moved in with the tenant's permission, or a former tenant, must be removed through the courts, not the police. Second, the civil route: you may bring an action for possession against any person wrongfully in possession and, if the holdover is willful and in bad faith, recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. Never change the locks or remove the person or belongings yourself.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-44-26(a): 'Every person who willfully trespasses or, having no legitimate purpose for his or her presence, remains upon the land of another or upon the premises or curtilage of the domicile of any person legally entitled to the possession of that domicile, after having been forbidden to do so by the owner of the land or the owner's duly authorized agent or a person legally entitled to the possession of the premises' (§ 11-44-26(a)) is punished by 'a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars ($1,000), or imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or both' (§ 11-44-26(a)). § 11-44-26(b): 'This section shall not apply to tenants or occupants of residential premises who, having rightfully entered the premises at the commencement of the tenancy or occupancy, remain after that tenancy or occupancy has been or is alleged to have been terminated. The owner or landlord of the premises may recover possession only through appropriate civil proceedings' (§ 11-44-26(b)). Civil: § 34-18-21: 'The landlord may bring an action for possession against any person wrongfully in possession and may recover the damages provided in § 34-18-38(c)' (§ 34-18-21); § 34-18-38(c) damages; self-help ban § 34-18-44. Chapter 34-18.1 (§ 34-18.1-9 trespass and action for possession) applies only to non-residential estates. Searches over the RI corpus: RI-unauthorized-occupant-removal-1 (squat/unauthorized occupant/unlawful occupancy/trespass/intruder near dwelling, residence, premises, tenant, owner; hits 37, OK; synthetic positive passed; no squatter-removal statute, only § 11-44-26 and unrelated trespass sections); RI-unauthorized-occupant-removal-2 (everyday words: overstay/houseguest/police or sheriff may remove/removal of the person/refuses to leave; hits 16, OK; synthetic positive passed; nothing relevant beyond § 34-18.1-20 tourist camps). Whether a tenant's guest is an 'occupant' who 'rightfully entered' under § 11-44-26(b) is case law, not searched; the body takes the cautious reading. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Agreed Ways to Give Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no special "actual notice" rule and no provision letting you and the tenant agree on an extra method, such as text messages, that counts as notice. The act's general rule: a person has notice of a fact if they actually know it, have received a notice of it, or have reason to know it from the circumstances; you give notice by taking steps reasonably calculated to inform the tenant in the ordinary course; and the tenant receives it when it comes to their attention or when it is delivered by hand or sent by first-class mail to the address they gave for notices (or, if none, their last known residence). The two days' notice before entry has no prescribed method. Where a statute or statutory form calls for first-class mail (the five-day demand, the 20-day noncompliance notice, the termination notice), use it. E-mail or text works only if both sides have agreed to deal electronically, either may later refuse further electronic dealings, and it cannot replace a mailing method a statute requires unless that statute allows it. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (agreed actual-notice method). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-14(a)(1): a person has notice if 'He or she has actual knowledge of it' (§ 34-18-14(a)(1)(i)), has received it, or 'has reason to know that it exists' (§ 34-18-14(a)(1)(iii)); (b): notifies 'by taking steps reasonably calculated to inform the other in ordinary course whether or not the other actually comes to know of it' (§ 34-18-14(b)); receives when '(1) It comes to his or her attention' (§ 34-18-14(b)(1)) or '(2) It is delivered in hand or sent by first class mail to him or her at a place held out by him or her as the place for receipt of the communication, or in the absence of such designation, to his or her last known place of residence' (§ 34-18-14(b)(2)). Entry: § 34-18-26(c) 'at least two (2) days' notice of his or her intent to enter' (§ 34-18-26(c)), no method stated. First-class mailing certificates appear in the § 34-18-56(a)-(c) forms (see edu-termination-notice-ri, edu-nonpayment-notice-ri). title: No Statutory Addendum Precedence
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring a separate addendum that overrides the lease, and no rule on which lease document wins when they conflict, so the lease's own precedence clause governs. Two limits apply. First, the lead disclosure acknowledgment must be either a stand-alone document that includes the property address or its own separate page within a written lease, and it is required for every lease of pre-1978 housing covered by the lead rules, including oral leases. Second, no addendum or precedence clause can take away a tenant's rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act: a term waiving them is unenforceable, and knowingly using a prohibited term exposes you to actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. In public or federally subsidized housing, federal rules that directly conflict with the act control. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the three loaded health and housing regulations were searched; case law was not.

title: Telling Tenants About a Possible Foreclosure
bodyText: If you fall 120 days behind on a mortgage on the property where the unit is located, Rhode Island requires you to notify your tenant that the property may be subject to foreclosure. Until a foreclosure actually occurs, the tenant must keep paying rent to you under the lease. The statute sets no form or method for this notice; give it in writing and keep a copy. Separately, the lender foreclosing the mortgage must mail each bona fide tenant (not the borrower or the borrower's child, spouse or parent, in an arm's-length tenancy at roughly market rent) a notice of the scheduled sale telling them to keep paying rent and that it is not an eviction notice. After a foreclosure, a foreclosing owner of a building with four or fewer units, unless exempt, must post and mail its contact details and the address for rent within 30 days and may evict only for just cause or after a binding sale contract with a bona fide buyer (see the foreclosure row). Rhode Island has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you about a foreclosure, tax proceeding or other claim against the property; if you want that, it must come from the lease.

No form, method or remedy stated. title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute regulates automatic renewal clauses in residential leases: there is no required notice, type size or reminder before a lease renews itself. Rhode Island's automatic-renewal notice law (45 to 90 days' written notice, or the renewal is voidable by the lessee) applies only to written leases of personal property, such as equipment, with a term of a year or more, not to apartments or houses. A residential lease may therefore include a renewal or extension term the parties agree to, subject to the general rule that it cannot waive the tenant's rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Without a renewal clause, a fixed-term lease ends on its last day, and if the tenant stays with your consent and no new term is agreed, the tenancy becomes week-to-week (weekly rent) or month-to-month, ended on 10 or 30 days' written notice. Good practice: remind the tenant in writing before a renewal date. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law, municipal ordinances and Attorney General rules were not.

title: Other Rules Rhode Island Does Not Have
bodyText: Three rules some states have do not exist in Rhode Island law. (1) No statute bans renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period or gives a special remedy for it; general contract law applies, and if you can't deliver possession to a tenant at the start of the term, rent abates and the tenant may end the lease on five days' notice. (2) No statute makes smoke-alarm compliance inadmissible in an injury case or limits what an insurer may do because of it; the fire and housing codes still require the alarms. (3) No statute gives you a special right to end a lease because the rental application was false; the lease's application-accuracy section makes a material falsehood a breach handled through the 20-day noncompliance notice, and general fraud and misrepresentation law still applies. By contrast, Rhode Island does have a payment-method rule: you may not charge a convenience fee on a rent payment unless you also accept a form of payment that carries no fee. Rhode Island's General Laws, Constitution, the 2025-2026 public laws, the loaded regulations and court rules were searched; case law and municipal ordinances were not.

title: Checked Across the Whole Code
bodyText: We searched all of Rhode Island's General Laws, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 public laws, the loaded regulations and the court rules, not just the landlord-tenant act, for three things landlords ask about. (1) There is no squatter-specific removal procedure. Willful trespass is a crime, but it does not reach tenants or occupants who rightfully entered and stayed after their occupancy ended; you remove them through a civil eviction case. (2) There is no duty to give a receipt for rent paid in cash; give one anyway, as it is your proof of payment too. (3) Unlike many states, Rhode Island does make registration a precondition to one kind of eviction: you may not file a nonpayment-of-rent eviction unless your statewide rental registry filing with the Department of Health is current (with a lead certificate of conformance or proof of exemption for covered pre-1978 units), and you must show the court proof when you file. The rule does not apply to holdover or lease-violation evictions. Separately, a state statute requires everyone who owns and leases property in Providence or Warwick to register their name, home address and telephone number with that city's clerk, and cities may have their own ordinances.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText: Rhode Island has not moved its protective-order laws. Orders still issue under the divorce statute's restraining-order section, the family court's Domestic Abuse Prevention Act (chapter 15-15), the district court's protective-order chapter (chapter 8-8.1) and the criminal no-contact order section (§ 12-29-4), and the new survivor-protection definitions cite them correctly. From July 1, 2026, the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act defines "abuse", "domestic violence" and "household member" for the first time and renumbers every other definition in its definitions section; cite those definitions by term, not number, in leases and notices. "Domestic violence" there includes, without being limited to, listed crimes (from simple assault and trespass to stalking, cyberstalking, violating a protective order and abuse) committed by one family or household member against another, whether or not reported to police. The lock-change and early-termination sections refer to a "valid protective order" without citing a chapter, and the fair housing ban on asking about domestic abuse refers to court restraining orders generally, so neither depends on a section number.

title: Electronic Leases, Signatures and Notices
bodyText: Rhode Island's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lets you and a tenant sign the lease and keep records electronically, but only if both of you have agreed to do business electronically (agreement can be shown by the circumstances and conduct). An electronic record satisfies a law requiring a writing, and an electronic signature satisfies a law requiring a signature, so a lease and the required written disclosures may be signed electronically. A tenant who agreed to one electronic transaction may refuse to do others electronically, and the lease cannot take that right away. An electronic record does not count as a written notice if you send it in a way that stops the tenant from printing or storing it, and then it is not enforceable against the tenant. Unlike Connecticut and Massachusetts, Rhode Island's Act does not exclude eviction, default or cure notices; but where a statute or statutory form calls for first-class mail (the five-day demand, the noncompliance notice, the termination notice), you must still mail it, because e-mail can replace a required mailing method only if that statute allows it.

The right granted by this subsection may not be waived by agreement' (§ 42-127.1-5(c)). § 42-127.1-7(c): 'If a law requires a record to be in writing, an electronic record satisfies the law' (§ 42-127.1-7(c)); (d): 'If a law requires a signature, an electronic signature satisfies the law' (§ 42-127.1-7(d)). § 42-127.1-8(a): 'An electronic record is not capable of retention by the recipient if the sender or its information processing system inhibits the ability of the recipient to print or store the electronic record' (§ 42-127.1-8(a)); (c) 'the electronic record is not enforceable against the recipient' (§ 42-127.1-8(c)); (b)(2)(ii) record 'must be sent, communicated, or transmitted by the method specified in the other law' (§ 42-127.1-8(b)); (d)(2) mail requirement 'may be varied by agreement to the extent permitted by the other law' (§ 42-127.1-8(d)). Chapter 34-18 does not permit varying its mailing method (§§ 34-18-35(a), 34-18-36(a), 34-18-56(a)-(c)). Shared clause electronic-signatures reads correctly for RI (mutual consent to electronic execution). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute that expressly protects a tenant's right to call the police or emergency services, bars a lease penalty for such calls, or limits nuisance or crime-free programs that count calls for service. Don't penalize those calls anyway. Rhode Island's retaliation law bars raising rent, cutting services, or bringing or threatening an eviction because a tenant used any lawful right or remedy, and a complaint in the six months before your action creates a presumption of retaliation. Fair housing law bars refusing to rent to, or setting different terms for, a tenant or applicant because they or a household member are or have been a victim of domestic abuse or have sought a restraining order, and bars asking about it. From July 1, 2026, you also may not refuse to rent to an applicant because they ended an earlier lease as a survivor of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or asked for a lock change. This library's Rhode Island clauses contain no call-penalty term; do not add one. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.

title: Changing the Lease After Signing
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute letting you amend existing leases by written notice to comply with new laws, so a clause requiring signed written amendments gives up no statutory right. New laws that apply to existing tenancies operate on their own terms. Three narrower changes are possible without a signed amendment. (1) Rules: you may adopt a rule about the tenant's use and occupancy, but it is enforceable only if it promotes the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protects the property from abusive use or fairly shares services; is reasonably related to that purpose; is clear enough to tell the tenant what to do; applies fairly to all tenants; does not evade your own obligations; and the tenant had notice of it when the lease was signed or when the rule was adopted. A rule adopted later that substantially modifies the tenant's bargain is not valid without the tenant's written consent. (2) Fees: if there is no written lease, give the tenant a written list of fees and disclose any change at least 30 days before it takes effect. (3) Rent: give written notice of an increase at least 60 days before it takes effect (120 days for month-to-month tenants over 62), subject to any fixed rent in the lease.

'Rental agreement' includes 'valid rules and regulations adopted under § 34-18-25' (§ 34-18-11(14), renumbered (17) on July 1, 2026). title: Pre-Suit Dispute Clauses
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute authorizing or regulating lease clauses that require you and the tenant to try informal resolution or mediation before going to court, and no statute requiring mediation in landlord-tenant cases. Rhode Island's arbitration act makes a clearly written agreement in a written contract to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable on ordinary contract grounds. But a lease may not make a tenant waive or give up any right or remedy under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; such a term is unenforceable, and knowingly using one exposes you to actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. So if you use a pre-suit or mediation clause, keep it voluntary in effect: it must not delay or condition the five-day demand, the 20-day cure notice, the termination notices, an eviction, or the tenant's own remedies such as repair and deduct, rent abatement or a retaliation defense. Whether a residential arbitration clause can cover eviction or chapter 34-18 claims is a question for case law, which was not searched; get advice before adding one.

title: You Must Carry Liability Insurance
bodyText: Rhode Island requires every residential landlord to obtain and keep in force a general liability insurance policy of at least $100,000 covering people injured on the premises because of your negligence. You must give the tenant a copy of the carrier's declaration page showing the policy with the written lease at the beginning of the tenancy, and a new copy each time the policy renews. The duty is part of your statutory maintenance obligations, so it applies to every tenancy type and building size and cannot be waived in the lease; a lease term limiting your liability or making the tenant indemnify you for it is also unenforceable. If you don't comply, the tenant may recover actual damages and get a court order, with attorney's fees if the failure is willful, and a tenant who complains to you about it is protected from retaliation. The statute names a written lease; for an oral tenancy, hand over the declaration page at move-in anyway. The library's insurance-disclosure clause records delivery of the page.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(a)(7): a landlord shall 'Obtain and have in full force and effect a general liability insurance policy of at least one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) for those persons injured on the premises due to the negligence of the landlord' (§ 34-18-22(a)(7)); 'The landlord shall provide a copy of the declaration page from the carrier showing the policy to the tenant with the written lease at the beginning of the tenancy and shall provide a new copy with each policy renewal to the tenant' (§ 34-18-22(a)(7)). Added by P.L. 2021, chs. 210, 323, § 1, effective January 1, 2022. Remedy: § 34-18-28(b): 'the tenant may recover actual damages and obtain injunctive relief for noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement or § 34-18-22. If the landlord's noncompliance is willful, the tenant may recover reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-28(b)). Retaliation: § 34-18-46(a)(2) (complaint 'to the landlord of a violation under § 34-18-22' (§ 34-18-46(a)(2))). Lease limits: § 34-18-17(a)(1) waiver; (a)(4) 'exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law or to indemnify the landlord for that liability' (§ 34-18-17(a)(4)). Whether § 34-18-28(a) termination is available turns on 'materially affecting health and safety' (§ 34-18-28(a)); not stated in the body. Oral-tenancy delivery is a recommendation, not a statutory rule. title: Statewide Rental Registry
bodyText: Every Rhode Island residential landlord must register with the Department of Health: the names of the individual landlords or business entity, an active mailing address, e-mail address and telephone number, any property manager, management company or agent (with the same contact details), and information identifying each dwelling unit. If you lease a unit in a building built before 1978 that is not exempt from the lead hazard mitigation law, you must also file a valid lead certificate of conformance for each unit, or evidence that it is exempt. Register within 30 days after you acquire a rental property or begin leasing to a new tenant, whichever is earlier, and re-register or confirm your information by October 1 every year. Failing to register costs at least $50 a month ($125 a month for missing lead information), with further penalties for repeated failures. Most importantly, you may not file an eviction for nonpayment of rent unless your registration is current when you file, and you must give the court evidence of compliance; holdover and lease-violation evictions are not affected. Short-term rentals of 30 nights or fewer listed on hosting platforms register separately with the Department of Business Regulation.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-58(a): 'All landlords shall register the following information with the department of health' (§ 34-18-58(a)), items (1)-(6). (b) pre-1978 non-exempt units: 'provide the department of health with a valid certificate of conformance in accordance with chapter 128.1 of title 42' (§ 34-18-58(b)) or exemption evidence. (d) timing: a landlord who acquires or begins leasing after September 1, 2024 'shall register the information required by subsections (a) and (b) of this section within thirty (30) days after the acquisition or lease to a tenant, whichever date is earlier' (§ 34-18-58(d)); 're-register by October 1 of each year' (§ 34-18-58(d)). (e) fines: 'at least fifty dollars ($50.00) per month' (§ 34-18-58(e)) and 'at least one hundred and twenty-five dollars ($125) per month' (§ 34-18-58(e)) for (b) information. (g): 'a landlord or any agent of a landlord may not commence an action to evict for nonpayment of rent in any court of competent jurisdiction, unless, at the time the action is commenced, the landlord is in compliance with the requirements of subsections (a), (b), and (d) of this section' (§ 34-18-58(g)). (h) Department of Health injunction and up to $50 per violation for repeated (a) failures; attorney general up to $1,000 per violation for repeated (b) failures. Added by P.L. 2023, chs. 156, 157, § 1, effective June 20, 2023. Short-term rentals: § 42-63.1-14(b): 'Any short-term rental property listed for rent on the website of any third-party hosting platform that conducts business in Rhode Island shall be registered with the department of business regulation' (§ 42-63.1-14(b)), short-term rental meaning 'not to exceed thirty (30) nights at a time' (§ 42-63.1-14(b)); § 42-63.1-14 read for (a)-(e) only. Nonresident agent filing (§ 34-18-22.3) is a separate row under nonresident-owner-agent. Municipal registration ordinances not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Providence and Warwick Owner Registration
bodyText: If you own and lease property in the city of Providence or the city of Warwick, a state statute requires you, whether you are an individual or an entity, to register your name, home address (including zip code) and telephone number with the city clerk of the city where the property is located. This applies only to property in those two cities; it is in addition to the statewide Department of Health rental registry, which applies everywhere in Rhode Island. The statute does not set a deadline, fee or penalty itself; check with the city clerk, because each city's own ordinance may add requirements. Other cities and towns may have their own registration ordinances, which this library does not track.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-57 (Providence and Warwick Absentee Landlord Enforcement Act): 'All persons, corporations, organizations, associations or other legal entities owning and leasing property in the cities of Providence or Warwick shall register their names, home addresses, including zip codes, and telephone numbers with the city clerk in the city where such property is located' (§ 34-18-57). State statute limited to two cities; the section states no deadline, fee or penalty. Municipal ordinances (Providence, Warwick and others) not searched; flagged, not resolved (SOP rule 3). Statewide registry: § 34-18-58 (see edu-rental-registry-ri). RI-landlord-registration-1 (hits 24, OK; real positive § 34-18-57 passed). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in before signing, or treating a blank as a breach (a fill-every-term rule exists only for mobile home leases in the town of Exeter). Fill in or strike every blank anyway, because several Rhode Island rules turn on what the written lease says: any fees beyond rent must be disclosed in the same section as the rent, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); the lease must say which utilities are included in the rent and which the tenant pays; any renters-insurance requirement must be stated in the lease; and a tenant may recover any fee that was not disclosed as required. A court that finds a rental agreement or any term unconscionable when made may refuse to enforce it, strike the term or limit it. A blank filled in after signing invites a dispute over what was agreed. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (blank-space rule for residential leases). Searches over the RI corpus (General Laws, Constitution, three loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws, court rules): RI-lease-completeness-1 (blank space/line, left blank, filled in, fill in every blank, completed in full near lease, rental agreement, tenant, landlord; hits 3, OK; synthetic positive passed; only § 31-44-7.2, mobile home and lot leases in the town of Exeter, which 'shall not be executed unless each term of it either shall have been completed in full or shall contain a statement that the terms may not be applicable' (§ 31-44-7.2)); RI-lease-completeness-2 (everyday words: incomplete/unfinished/left empty/missing terms near lease or rental agreement; hits 3, OK; synthetic positive passed; none relevant); RI-lease-completeness-3 (unconscionability near rental agreement, lease, tenant; hits 5, OK; real positive § 34-18-13 passed). See planned fee-disclosure-ri and utilities-responsibility-ri. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: Apart from mobile home leases in the town of Exeter, no Rhode Island statute requires you to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease by a deadline, and not giving one is not a statutory defense when you enforce the lease. Give every tenant a fully signed copy at signing anyway: you will need it to prove the terms, and several Rhode Island rules depend on what the written lease says. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson handles the lease for you, the licensee must furnish a copy to everyone who signed it at the time it is signed, or risk license discipline and an administrative penalty of up to $2,000. Mobile home park leases have their own rules: the park must show the prospective resident a copy of the written lease before move-in and may not rent until a written lease is signed, and in the town of Exeter the lease must be executed in duplicate originals with one given to the lessee within 30 days of signing. Rules you adopt bind the tenant only if the tenant has notice of them when the rental agreement is made or when they are adopted, so hand over your written rules with the lease. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws, the loaded regulations and court rules were searched; case law was not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (landlord duty to deliver a copy of the signed residential lease, apart from the Exeter mobile home rule below; lease-copy defense). title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires a tenant to initial a particular lease term for that term to bind the tenant; the tenant's signature on the lease is enough as far as the statutes go. That does not make every term lawful: the statutory notice to end a periodic tenancy belongs to the tenant as well as to you, so a term requiring the tenant to give more notice than the statute requires risks being an unenforceable waiver (case law not searched). The statutory notice to end a periodic tenancy runs both ways: at least 10 days for a week-to-week tenancy, at least 30 days for a month-to-month tenancy (or any period between a month and a year), and at least three months before the end of the occupation year for a year-to-year tenancy, each in writing in a form substantially like the statutory form. A lease term in which the tenant gives up a right under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is unenforceable, and knowingly using one exposes you to actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. Having the tenant initial an unusual term is still good evidence the tenant saw it, but it cannot rescue a prohibited term. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (initials or separate-acknowledgment requirement for a lease term, including a lengthened notice period). Waiver: R.I. Gen. title: Lease Length and Signatures
bodyText: Rhode Island sets no maximum length for a residential lease, but how the lease is made can limit it. If you sign and deliver a written lease and the tenant never signs it, the tenant's taking possession and paying rent without reservation makes it binding as if signed; if the tenant signs and delivers it and you never sign, your accepting rent without reservation does the same. A lease given effect this way that provides for a term longer than one year is effective for only one year. A lease of one year or less is valid even if oral, but a lease for a longer term is void against buyers, lenders and others without notice of it unless it is in writing, signed, acknowledged, delivered and recorded in the city or town land records (a memorandum of lease may be recorded instead). If no definite term is fixed, the tenancy is month to month (week to week for a roomer paying weekly). Mobile home park leases have a one-year minimum unless the resident asks in writing for a shorter term. Have every tenant and every landlord sign before move-in.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-16(a): 'If the landlord does not sign and deliver a written rental agreement signed and delivered to him or her by the tenant, acceptance of rent without reservation by the landlord gives the rental agreement the same effect as if it had been signed and delivered by the landlord' (§ 34-18-16(a)); (b) 'acceptance of possession and payment of rent without reservation gives the rental agreement the same effect as if it had been signed and delivered by the tenant' (§ 34-18-16(b)); (c): 'If a rental agreement given effect by the operation of this section provides for a term longer than one year, it is effective for only one year' (§ 34-18-16(c)). Writing and recording: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-11-1: every conveyance 'for any term longer than one year' 'shall be void unless made in writing duly signed, acknowledged as hereinafter provided, delivered, and recorded in the records of land evidence in the town or city where the lands, tenements or hereditaments are situated' but, if delivered, is 'valid and binding though not acknowledged or recorded' between the parties and against those having notice (§ 34-11-1); 'A lease for the term of one year or less shall be valid although made by parol' (§ 34-11-1); 'Leases for terms of more than one year may be recorded with a memorandum of lease in writing rather than the original lease' (§ 34-11-1). Default term: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(d): 'Unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent, and in all other cases month to month' (§ 34-18-15(d)). Mobile homes: R.I. Gen. Laws § 31-44-8: 'The term of the lease shall not be less than one year unless the resident requests, in writing, a term for less than one year, or requests in writing that he or she does not desire a written lease' (§ 31-44-8). No maximum term for residential leases: RI-lease-term-limitation-1 (lease/tenancy/term for more than, longer than, exceeding, not to exceed, up to N years; maximum term; near tenant/landlord/lease; hits 16, OK; real positive § 34-18-16 and synthetic positive passed; only state, port and coastal-council leases (§§ 37-7-9, 46-5-10, 46-23-6) carry term caps); RI-lease-term-limitation-2 (everyday words: length, duration, minimum or maximum term of a lease or tenancy; may not last longer; hits 2, OK; synthetic positives passed; none relevant).
