title: Out-of-State Landlords Must Name a Rhode Island Agent
bodyText: If you are not a Rhode Island resident, you must designate, and keep in place for as long as you rent, an agent in Rhode Island who can be served with any legal process, notice or demand, including notices of minimum housing code violations. The agent must be a Rhode Island resident or a corporation authorized to do business here. The designation must be in writing, give the agent's name and address and the street address of each property assigned to the agent, and be filed with both the secretary of state and the clerk of the city or town where the unit is. The fine for not complying is $100 a month, up to $1,200 in a calendar year, or one month's rent for the year if your monthly rent is more than $1,200, payable to the municipality. The minimum housing code separately requires a nonresident owner to keep a registered agent on file with the city or town clerk, with a $100 fine; one filing that meets the landlord-tenant statute covers both. The lease does not have to name the agent, but you must still give every tenant, in writing, the name, address and number of the manager and of an owner or agent for service of notices. Rhode Island does not require tenants to withhold tax from rent paid to you.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22.3: 'A landlord who is not a resident of this state shall designate and continuously maintain an agent upon whom service may be made of any process, notice, or demand required or permitted by law to be served, including, but not limited to, notices of minimum housing code violations' (§ 34-18-22.3); 'The agent shall be a resident of this state or a corporation authorized to do business in this state' (§ 34-18-22.3); the designation 'shall be in writing, shall include the name and address of the agent, shall include the street address of each property designated to the agent, and shall be filed with the secretary of state and with the clerk of the city or town wherein the dwelling unit is located' (§ 34-18-22.3); penalty: 'a civil fine of one hundred dollars ($100) per month up to a maximum of one thousand two hundred dollars ($1,200) in a calendar year or if the monthly rent exceeds one thousand two hundred dollars ($1,200), the civil fine shall be one month's rent for the calendar year, payable to the municipality' (§ 34-18-22.3). Enacted twice (SOP rule 31): R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-17(b) (minimum housing code): a nonresident owner 'shall have and continuously maintain with the city or town clerk where the property is located a registered agent' (§ 45-24.3-17(b)); 'Any person who fails to maintain a registered agent shall be subject to a fine of one hundred dollars ($100)' (§ 45-24.3-17(b)). The two differ on where to file (secretary of state and clerk vs. clerk only) and the fine; the row tells landlords to meet § 34-18-22.3, which satisfies both. Voluntary designation for process under the Act: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-10(c): a nonresident landlord or tenant 'may designate an agent upon whom service of process may be made in this state'; failing designation, 'process may be served upon the secretary of state' (§ 34-18-10(c)). Tenant disclosure: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-20(a)(2): disclose 'An owner of the premises or a person authorized to act for and on behalf of the owner for the purpose of service of process and receiving and receipting for notices and demands' (§ 34-18-20(a)(2)). Searches over the RI corpus (General Laws, Constitution, three loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws, court rules): RI-nonresident-owner-agent-1 (nonresident, out-of-state, not a resident of this state, absentee, near landlord/owner/lessor/tenant/rental; hits 52, OK; real positives §§ 34-18-22.3, 34-18-57 passed; relevant hits §§ 34-18-10, 34-18-22.3, 34-18-57, 45-24.3-17 only); RI-nonresident-owner-agent-2 (withholding near rent, for nonresident-owner tax withholding; hits 2, OK; synthetic positive passed; none relevant). No 2026 public law amends these sections. Municipal ordinances not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: How to Deliver Rhode Island Notices
bodyText: Rhode Island sets the delivery method notice by notice, and your lease cannot change a method a statute requires. Mail the five-day demand for unpaid rent and the 20-day noncompliance notice by regular first-class mail: both deadlines run from the date of mailing, and the statutory forms end with your signed certificate that you mailed them first class, postage prepaid. The termination notice for a periodic tenancy must be delivered at least 10 days, 30 days or three months ahead; its statutory form also ends with a first-class mailing certificate, so mail it and allow time for delivery. If a tenant abandons the unit, send a certified letter, return receipt requested, to the last known address. Rent increase notices and the written notice that keeps your right to terminate after accepting rent must be in writing, with no set method; use one you can prove. A foreclosing owner of a building with four or fewer units must post its notice in the building, mail it first class to each unit and slide it under each door. No statute requires a sheriff or constable to deliver your notices, but once you file an eviction you must mail the summons and complaint to the tenant that day, and a deputy sheriff or constable serves them by hand, with a suitable adult at the unit, or by posting on the door.
notes: RI: Nonpayment: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-35(a): 'the landlord shall send a written notice, in a form substantially similar to that provided in § 34-18-56(a)' and the tenant may cure 'within five (5) days of the date of mailing of the notice' (§ 34-18-35(a)); suit 'shall be filed no earlier than the sixth (6th) day after mailing of the written demand notice' (§ 34-18-35(b)). Noncompliance: § 34-18-36(a): 'the landlord shall deliver a written demand notice to the tenant, in a form substantially similar to that provided in § 34-18-56(b)', with a cure period running 'within twenty (20) days of mailing of the notice' (§ 34-18-36(a)(3)); repeat breach: 'upon at least twenty (20) days' written notice, specifying the breach and the date of termination of the rental agreement' (§ 34-18-36(e)). Periodic termination: § 34-18-37(b): 'by a written notice, in a form substantially similar to that provided in § 34-18-56(c), delivered to the other at least thirty (30) days before the date specified in the notice' (§ 34-18-37(b)). Forms: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-56(a), (b) and (c) each end: 'I certify that I placed in regular U.S. mail, first class postage prepaid, a copy of this Notice, addressed to the tenant' (§ 34-18-56(a)-(c)). Abandonment: § 34-18-40: 'the landlord shall send a certified letter, return receipt requested, to the tenant's last known address' (§ 34-18-40). title: Extra Terms in Move-Out Notices
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute governing a move-out notice form you ask a tenant to sign, and no required warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain. Keep such a form to what the tenant's notice needs: the tenant's written notice ending a periodic tenancy must be delivered at least 10 days ahead (week-to-week), 30 days ahead (month-to-month) or three months before the end of the occupation year (year-to-year), in a form substantially like the statutory termination notice. Any added term in which the tenant gives up a right under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (for example, agreeing to a deposit deduction the statute does not allow) is unenforceable, and knowingly using one exposes you to actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. A new rule adopted during the tenancy that substantially changes the bargain is valid only if the tenant consents in writing. Put any genuine new agreement, such as an agreed early move-out date, in a separate signed amendment. title: Where Rhode Island Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Several Rhode Island rules depend on what the lease says, and a silent lease takes the statutory default. (1) Rent is due without demand at the agreed time and place; if the lease is silent, it is payable at the unit, at the start of each period of a month or less (otherwise monthly in advance), and is apportioned day by day. (2) Without a definite term, the tenancy is month to month (week to week for a roomer paying weekly). (3) Unless otherwise agreed, the tenant may use the unit only as a dwelling. (4) Only if the lease requires it must the tenant tell you of an absence longer than ten days, by the first day of the absence. (5) The tenant does repairs or maintenance only under a separate good-faith writing signed by both of you, for adequate consideration, never to cure a housing code violation. (6) A renters-insurance requirement, any fees beyond rent (stated in the rent section unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format) and the utility split must be in the lease, or in writing if there is no written lease; otherwise the tenant can recover undisclosed fees. (7) A seasonal lease within the statutory dates lets you skip the cure notice for occupancy or noise breaches.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(c): 'Rent is payable without demand or notice at the time and place agreed upon by the parties. Unless otherwise agreed, rent is payable at the dwelling unit and periodic rent is payable at the beginning of any term of one month or less and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the beginning of each month. Unless otherwise agreed, rent is uniformly apportionable from day-to-day' (§ 34-18-15(c)); (d): 'Unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent, and in all other cases month to month' (§ 34-18-15(d)); (a)(4): 'If a tenant is required to obtain renters insurance, this requirement must be stated in the lease or if there is no written lease the landlord shall provide this information to the tenant in writing' (§ 34-18-15(a)(4)); (a)(5): 'the tenant may recover any fees paid for the unit that were not disclosed as required' (§ 34-18-15(a)(5)). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-27: 'Unless otherwise agreed, a tenant shall occupy his or her dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit. The rental agreement may require that the tenant notify the landlord of any anticipated extended absence from the premises in excess of ten (10) days no later than the first day of the extended absence' (§ 34-18-27). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(c): the parties 'may agree in writing that the tenant perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, and remodeling but only if' the agreement is 'entered into in good faith and set forth in a writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration' (§ 34-18-22(c)(1)) and 'The work is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subsection (a)(1)' (§ 34-18-22(c)(2)). title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Rhode Island has no plain-language or readability law for residential leases, no readability test, and no required statement listing the rights a tenant gives up under the lease. Plain-language rules exist only for other kinds of contracts. What limits a Rhode Island lease instead is the list of prohibited provisions: a lease may not have the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, authorize anyone to confess judgment, agree to pay your attorney's fees except as the Act allows, or excuse or limit your legal liability or make the tenant indemnify you for it. Such a provision is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease containing one, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. Write the lease clearly anyway: required disclosures (fees in the rent section, the utility split, any renters-insurance requirement) must be understandable to do their job. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.

title: Rules That Depend on Building Size
bodyText: Rhode Island's landlord-tenant duties do not change with how many units you own, and there is no general small-landlord exemption; a few rules turn on the size of the building instead. If you buy a building of four or fewer units at foreclosure as a foreclosing owner, you may evict only for just cause, unless you are headquartered and fully operating in Rhode Island or conducted fewer than 15 Rhode Island foreclosures in the prior calendar year. Anyone other than a bona fide third-party purchaser who takes a building of four or fewer units from a seller or mortgagor takes it subject to the existing tenants' rights. Fair housing law lets an owner decline to rent to a family with children only in a two-unit building the owner lives in, or a building of four or fewer units the owner lives in where a senior or infirm occupant would suffer demonstrated hardship (or qualifying elderly housing). An owner living in a building of three or fewer units may refuse a tenant based on lawful source of income. A building employee's housing falls outside the Act only if the premises have more than eleven units. Federal fair housing law has its own tests and was not read.
notes: RI: Foreclosure: R.I. Gen. title: Requiring Renter's Insurance
bodyText: You may require a Rhode Island tenant to carry renter's insurance, but only if the requirement is stated in the lease; if there is no written lease, you must give the tenant the requirement in writing. If you charge any fee connected with insurance (for example, for a program you arrange), disclose it in the rent section of the lease with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it. No Rhode Island statute regulates which insurer the tenant uses, how soon the tenant must show proof, force-placed coverage, or a notice that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings, so those are contract terms. An insurance requirement cannot shift your own legal duties: a lease term excusing or limiting your liability, or making the tenant indemnify you for it, is unenforceable, and you still must make repairs and keep the premises fit. Separately, you must carry your own general liability policy of at least $100,000 and give the tenant the declaration page with the lease. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; insurance department regulations and case law were not.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
bodyText: When you sell a rented Rhode Island property in good faith to a bona fide buyer, you are released from liability under the lease and the landlord-tenant act only for events after you give the tenant written notice of the sale, and never for anything before the sale itself. The notice must give the buyer's names, address and telephone number and must certify that you complied with the housing-code rule on transfers: if the building has an outstanding violation notice, you may not sell or lease it until the violation is corrected, or until you give the buyer a copy of every notice and tell the code officer in writing of the intended sale. A manager who leaves is released after written notice to the tenant naming the new manager or the person in Rhode Island responsible for the property. Keep your written owner and manager disclosure current; it binds every successor. A family member or other successor who is not a bona fide third-party buyer of a building of four or fewer units takes it subject to the tenant's existing rights. No sale or mortgage can let anyone collect rent without the repair duties. Tenants may not unreasonably refuse showings to buyers or lenders, on two days' notice at reasonable times. For deposits on a sale, see the deposit-transfer row.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-23(a)(1): 'A landlord who conveys premises that include a dwelling unit subject to a rental agreement in a good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the rental agreement and this chapter as to events occurring after written notice to the tenant of the conveyance. In no event may the relief from liability predate the conveyance itself' (§ 34-18-23(a)(1)); (a)(2): the notice 'must include the name(s), address, and telephone number of the person or persons purchasing the property and assuming liability' and 'must also certify compliance with § 45-24.3-17' (§ 34-18-23(a)(2)); (b): the manager's notice 'must include the name(s), address, and telephone number of the person or persons assuming management and/or the person or persons within the state exercising ownership or responsibility over the property' (§ 34-18-23(b)); (c): 'the purchaser of property or any immediate successor in interest to a mortgagor, other than a third-party, bona fide purchaser, of a premises containing four (4) or fewer dwelling units takes title subject to the same rights and responsibilities toward the tenant that the seller or mortgagor had' (§ 34-18-23(c)). Housing code: R.I. Gen. Disclosure: § 34-18-20(b): 'The information required to be furnished by this section shall be kept current. This section extends to and is enforceable against any successor landlord, owner, or manager' (§ 34-18-20(b)). § 34-18-18: 'A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed, or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with § 34-18-22(a)' (§ 34-18-18). title: What the Rhode Island Act Covers
bodyText: Rhode Island's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies statewide to every rental agreement for a dwelling unit in Rhode Island, wherever the lease was signed; a dwelling unit is any structure or part of one designed or intended as a home, residence or sleeping place. Unless you and the occupant expressly agree to be governed by the Act, it does not cover: residence in an institution incidental to detention, medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services; a buyer occupying under a contract of sale; fraternal or social organization housing; transient stays in a hotel, motel or other lodging subject to sales or lodging tax; a paid employee whose housing depends on working on premises of more than eleven units; a cooperative shareholder's proprietary lease; commercial lettings; and transitional housing. Mobile home park lots have their own act, which uses the Act's eviction procedure but limits the grounds and requires at least 60 days' written notice (30 days for nonpayment). Homes on leased land and commercial leases have separate chapters. This library's Rhode Island rows cover Act tenancies only. One state statute (absentee landlord registration) applies only in Providence and Warwick, and city ordinances are not covered.

title: Severability Cannot Cure Banned Terms
bodyText: Rhode Island strikes bad lease terms one at a time, so a severability clause works as intended: a provision the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act prohibits is unenforceable, and a court that finds a term unconscionable when made may enforce the rest of the lease without it or limit the term. But a severability clause is no safety net. If a court finds the agreement unconscionable as a whole, it may refuse to enforce any of it. And if you deliberately use a lease containing terms you know are prohibited (a waiver of the tenant's rights under the Act, a confession of judgment, attorney's fees the Act does not allow, or an exculpation or indemnity for your own liability), the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees, whatever the severability clause says.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(b): 'A provision prohibited by subsection (a) included in a rental agreement is unenforceable. If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known to be prohibited, the tenant may recover, in addition to his or her actual damages, an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-17(b)). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-13(a)(1): if 'A rental agreement or any provision thereof was unconscionable when made, the court may refuse to enforce the agreement, enforce the remainder of the agreement without the unconscionable provision, or limit the application of any unconscionable provision to avoid an unconscionable result' (§ 34-18-13(a)(1)). No search battery needed: the topic asks how the Act treats invalid terms, answered by the two sections read whole. Supports tagging the shared severability clause for RI. Case law not searched. title: Leases Longer Than One Year Must Be in Writing
bodyText: In Rhode Island a lease for longer than one year cannot be enforced against a party unless the lease, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by that party or someone lawfully authorized by them. A lease of one year or less is valid even if oral, and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act protects oral tenants too. A lease for more than one year is also a conveyance: between you and the tenant it binds once signed and delivered, but to bind a buyer or lender without notice of it, it must be acknowledged and recorded in the city or town land records (a memorandum naming the parties, the property and the duration, including renewal and purchase options, may be recorded instead). If you promise a lease longer than a year to get someone to move in and then refuse to give it, you may have to repay the cost of improvements they made with your approval, unless rent was reserved for a definite letting or they occupy under a signed writing. Sign every lease, and record any lease longer than a year.

title: Forms Rhode Island Law Supplies
bodyText: Rhode Island prescribes no form for a residential lease, but its landlord-tenant act supplies the forms for the three notices that matter most, and the statute requires your notice to be in a form substantially similar to them: the Five-Day Demand Notice for Nonpayment of Rent, the Notice of Noncompliance (20 days to remedy a breach) and the Notice of Termination of Tenancy. Each form has a date of mailing and ends with your signed certificate that you mailed a copy by regular first-class mail, postage prepaid. The same section supplies the Complaint for Eviction for Nonpayment of Rent (with the five-day notice attached), the Complaint for Eviction for Reason Other Than Nonpayment of Rent (with the noncompliance or termination notice attached), a landlord-tenant complaint for other claims, the court summonses and the tenant's blank answer form, which lists defenses such as no required notice and retaliation. Copy the statutory wording rather than drafting your own. Mobile home park leases must print the park-tenancy notice word for word. The Executive Office of Housing publishes a landlord-tenant guide in English and Spanish; you are not required to give it to tenants. The lead disclosure documents have their own required content (see the lead rows).

title: Tenant Portals and Online Payments
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on tenant portals as such, but two rules limit how you use one. First, you may not charge a convenience fee on a tenant's rent payment (such as a portal or card-processing fee) unless you also accept a way of paying rent that carries no convenience fee; offer at least one free method. Second, Rhode Island's electronic-transactions law applies only when both you and the tenant have agreed to deal electronically, nothing in it requires anyone to use electronic records or signatures, and a tenant who agreed to one electronic transaction may refuse to conduct others electronically; that right cannot be waived in the lease. So you may offer a portal for payments, maintenance requests and signatures, but a lease term making the portal the only way to sign or receive documents will not bind a tenant who later declines. Notices the statutes require by first-class or certified mail still go by mail. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.

title: Tenant Ledgers and Personal Information
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to give a tenant a rent ledger or payment history, though keeping one is the best proof in a nonpayment case. If you collect or keep an applicant's or tenant's name together with a Social Security number, driver's license or state ID number, a bank or card number with its access code, medical or health insurance information, or an e-mail address with its password, Rhode Island's Identity Theft Protection Act applies to you, whatever your size. You must keep a risk-based information security program with reasonable safeguards for the size of your business and the information; keep the data no longer than reasonably needed or than your written retention policy or the law requires; destroy it securely (shredding, erasure and the like); and require by written contract that any outside company you share it with protects it. If a breach poses a significant risk of identity theft, notify each affected Rhode Island resident within 45 days after confirming it, and notify the attorney general and the credit reporting agencies if more than 500 residents are affected. Penalties run up to $100 per record for reckless violations and $200 per record for knowing ones.

title: No Sunsetting Tenant Laws
bodyText: As of October 9, 2026, none of Rhode Island's landlord-tenant statutes, including the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's deposit, notice, eviction, retaliation and fee rules, the fair housing act and the foreclosure just-cause law, carries a repeal or expiration date. The dated changes run the other way: the domestic-violence survivor protections (early lease termination, no refusal to rent for having used it, lock changes on request within two business days) took effect July 1, 2026, and the written shoreline-access disclosure for shoreline property takes effect January 1, 2027. Plan for the current rules to stay in force until the General Assembly changes them, and watch each year's new public laws, since Rhode Island amends this area most sessions. title: No Translation Duty
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to translate a lease or any landlord notice into the tenant's language, even if you advertised or negotiated in another language, and it sets no minimum type size for residential lease text. Once you file an eviction, the District Court rules require the court's Language Assistance Notice, which tells the tenant of the right to a free interpreter, to be served with the summons and complaint. The state's Executive Office of Housing must publish its landlord-tenant guide in both English and Spanish on its website, which you can point tenants to. If you negotiate in a language other than English, giving the tenant a translation (and keeping the English lease as the controlling text) reduces later disputes about what was agreed; federal fair housing and language-access rules for subsidized housing were not reviewed. title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Many Rhode Island landlord notices must be written, and a lease cannot downgrade them to verbal notice, because a lease term waiving a tenant's rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is unenforceable. In writing: the names, addresses and numbers of the manager and of an owner or agent for notices, at or before move-in; where there is no written lease, the list of fees, any fee change (30 days ahead), the utility split and any renters-insurance requirement; a rent increase (60 days ahead, or 120 days for month-to-month tenants over 62); the itemized deposit deductions with the refund, within 20 days; notice that you have sold the property or that a manager has left; the five-day demand for unpaid rent, the 20-day noncompliance notice, the repeat-breach notice and the notice ending a periodic tenancy; the certified letter after abandonment; and, if you accept rent knowing of a default, the notice within 10 days that keeps your right to terminate. The two days' notice before entering is not required to be written, but a written or texted notice is the easiest to prove.

title: Assistance Animals in Rhode Island
bodyText: Rhode Island's fair housing law requires you to make reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices and services when needed to give a tenant or occupant with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the home; waiving a no-pet rule or pet fees for an assistance animal is the usual example. Two Rhode Island statutes go further for a guide dog or other personal assistive animal (one specifically trained by a certified animal training program to help a person with a disability with independent living tasks): the person is entitled to full and equal access to housing and may not be charged extra for the animal, but is liable for any damage it does. Rhode Island statutes do not mention emotional support animals or say what documentation you may request; untrained support animals are handled as reasonable-accommodation requests, and federal fair housing guidance (not reviewed here) governs documentation. You need not accommodate a tenancy that would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property. Violations are unlawful housing practices enforced by the Commission for Human Rights.

Laws § 34-37-4(e)(1): 'An owner may not refuse to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices, or services when those accommodations may be necessary to afford an occupant with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling' (§ 34-37-4(e)(1)); (e)(2): every person with a disability who has 'a guide dog or other personal assistive animal' 'shall be entitled to full and equal access to all housing accommodations provided for in this section and shall not be required to pay extra compensation for the guide dog or other personal assistive animal but shall be liable for any damage done to the premises by a guide dog or other personal assistive animal' and 'a “personal assistive animal” is an animal specifically trained by a certified animal training program to assist a person with a disability to perform independent living tasks' (§ 34-37-4(e)(2)); (j): 'Nothing in this section requires that a dwelling be made available to an individual whose tenancy would constitute a direct threat to the health or safety of other individuals or whose tenancy would result in substantial physical damage to the property of others' (§ 34-37-4(j)). Enacted twice (SOP rule 31): R.I. Gen. title: Penalties for Refusing an Assistance Animal
bodyText: Refusing to rent to, or to accommodate, a tenant with a disability who needs a guide dog, a trained assistive animal or another assistance animal is an unlawful housing practice under Rhode Island's fair housing law, and so is charging extra for a guide dog or trained assistive animal. A tenant may file a charge with the Commission for Human Rights within one year. If the Commission finds a violation, it may order you to stop, take corrective action, pay the tenant's damages and reasonable attorney's fees, and pay a civil penalty of up to $10,000 for a first violation, up to $25,000 if you were found to have committed another discriminatory housing practice in the prior five years, and up to $50,000 for two or more in the prior seven years; the case can also move to superior court with a jury. Rhode Island's separate service-animal law makes denying access a misdemeanor (up to six months in jail or a fine of at least $100, plus actual and punitive damages), but it covers streets, public buildings, transportation, schools, hotels, restaurants and other places open to the public, not ordinary rental homes. Treat common areas open to the public with care.

title: Misrepresentation Penalty Does Not Reach Housing
bodyText: Rhode Island's service-animal misrepresentation law does not reach rental housing. It makes it a civil violation, punishable by up to 30 hours of community service for an organization serving people with disabilities, for someone to claim a pet is a service animal to get into or stay in a public area where pets are not allowed, when they knew or should have known it was not one. A public area is the part of a public place listed in the service-animal chapter (streets, public buildings, transportation, schools, hotels, restaurants and similar places) that is open to the general public, and a service animal there means a specially trained dog. No Rhode Island statute penalizes a tenant who misrepresents an emotional support or other assistance animal to a landlord. If you doubt a request, handle it through the reasonable-accommodation process rather than accusing the tenant of fraud; a lease term making a false accommodation request a default is your own contract term, not a statutory penalty.

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Rent and Pet Fees
bodyText: In Rhode Island a refundable pet deposit is a security deposit, whatever you call it, so it counts toward the one-month limit on all deposits: the pet deposit plus the general deposit together may not exceed one month's periodic rent (a separate furniture deposit is allowed only for furniture worth $5,000 or more). At move-out you may deduct pet damage only as physical damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, itemized in writing with the refund within 20 days. Monthly pet rent or a nonrefundable pet fee is not prohibited, but every fee beyond rent must be stated in the same section of the lease as the rent, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); if it is not, the tenant can recover what was paid. You may not charge anything extra for a guide dog or trained assistive animal, and assistance animals approved as a reasonable accommodation should not carry pet fees. Mobile home parks may charge a pet fee only for special pet facilities or services they actually provide, reasonably related to the cost.

title: Pet Rules in Rhode Island
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to allow pets in an ordinary rental, and no statute gives older tenants or public housing residents a right to keep one, so your lease may ban pets or limit their number, kind and size, apart from assistance animals. A pet rule adopted after the lease is signed binds the tenant only if it meets the statute's tests for rules and the tenant had notice of it; a new rule that substantially changes the tenant's bargain, such as banning a pet you already allowed, needs the tenant's written consent. To deal with a pet problem, enter only for the purposes the statute allows (inspection, repairs, services, showings) with two days' notice at reasonable times, or without consent in an emergency or during an absence of more than seven days if reasonably necessary to protect the property; otherwise you may enter only by court order, after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit, or, where pet damage or mess breaches the tenant's statutory duties in a way that affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, to do the work yourself after the tenant fails to fix it within 20 days of your written notice, billing the reasonable cost as rent. You may not seize or hold a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent, or lock a tenant out, so enforce pet violations through the 20-day noncompliance notice. A clause making the tenant answer for damage and injuries the tenant's pet causes is fine, but not one that excuses or limits any liability the law places on you, or makes the tenant indemnify you for it. Mobile home parks cannot apply a new no-pet rule to a pet already there that met the old rules, and the resident may replace that pet if it dies.

title: No Tenant EV-Charging Right
bodyText: Rhode Island gives tenants no statutory right to install or use an electric vehicle charger at a rental, and sets no rules for how you approve, price or remove one, so charging is a matter for your lease and your own consent. title: Towing From Your Rental Property
bodyText: As the owner or person in control of a Rhode Island property, you may have a vehicle that is parked there without your consent towed without going to court, but only by hiring, in writing, a tow company holding a state certificate (a certificated tower). The tower must keep your written direction, take the vehicle to its own impound lot within 10 miles, and keep the lot open to release vehicles during the same hours it receives them. The vehicle's owner pays the towing and storage charges in the tower's published tariff; but if the owner later proves in court that the vehicle was not trespassing, you must pay those charges. A vehicle left on your property without consent for more than three days counts as abandoned, and you may also order an abandoned or unattended vehicle removed. State law sets no sign-posting requirement, though a city ordinance may. Because the statute covers vehicles present without consent, be cautious about towing a tenant's own car for breaking a parking rule: enforce parking rules through the lease (a noncompliance notice) unless the lease clearly withdraws consent to park in that place.

title: Giving Notice of Parking Rules
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to hand over parking or towing rules before the lease is signed, use a particular heading, or limit what vehicle information you collect. Parking rules are treated like your other building rules: one is enforceable against a tenant only if it serves the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protects the property or fairly shares facilities; is reasonably related to that purpose; is clear enough to tell the tenant what to do; applies fairly to all tenants; does not evade your own obligations; and the tenant had notice of it when signing the lease or when you adopted it. A parking rule adopted later that substantially changes the tenant's bargain, such as taking away a space the tenant was promised, is valid only with the tenant's written consent. Give tenants the parking rules in writing at signing and whenever they change.

title: Cannabis in Rhode Island Rentals
bodyText: Rhode Island's adult-use cannabis law limits what your lease can ban. You may not prohibit a tenant from consuming cannabis by means other than smoking or vaping (for example edibles), or from giving cannabis to another adult without payment, as long as the tenant stays within the legal possession and transfer limits. You may prohibit smoking and vaping cannabis in the unit and on the property; the smoking-policy clause covers this. Adults 21 and over may legally grow, for personal use within a residence, up to three mature and three immature plants per dwelling unit, however many people live there, if they meet the Cannabis Control Commission's security requirements; the statute does not say whether a lease may ban home growing, so take advice before relying on a cultivation ban against an adult-use tenant. Under the medical marijuana law you may not refuse to rent to, or penalize, someone solely because they hold a medical marijuana card, but you may decline to lease, or to continue leasing, to a cardholder who grows, manufactures, processes, smokes or vaporizes medical marijuana in the unit. Federal law and HUD rules for subsidized housing, which still treat marijuana as illegal, were not reviewed.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 21-28.11-29(h): 'Except as provided in this section, in the case of the rental of a residential dwelling unit governed by chapter 18 of title 34, a landlord may not prohibit the consumption of cannabis by non-smoked or non-vaporized means, or the transfer without compensation of cannabis by the tenant as defined in § 34-18-11, provided the tenant is in compliance with the possession and transfer limits and other requirements set forth in this chapter' (§ 21-28.11-29(h)); (g): 'Except as provided in this section, the provisions of this chapter do not require any person, corporation, state department or any other entity that occupies, owns, or controls a property to allow the consumption, or transfer of marijuana on or in that property' (§ 21-28.11-29(g)). Cultivation: § 21-28.11-22(a)(2): 'Within any residence, possessing, cultivating or processing not more than a total of three (3) mature cannabis plants and up to a total of three (3) immature cannabis plants per dwelling unit for personal use' (§ 21-28.11-22(a)(2)); 'These limits shall apply no matter how many persons reside at the premises' (§ 21-28.11-22(a)(2)). § 21-28.11-29(g) names only 'consumption, or transfer', not cultivation, and § 21-28.11-22(b) protects a person allowing property they own or manage to be used lawfully; the statute doesn't say whether a lease may ban adult-use cultivation (case law not searched). Medical: R.I. Gen. Laws § 21-28.6-4(d): 'No school or landlord may refuse to enroll, or lease to, or otherwise penalize, a person solely for his or her status as a cardholder. Provided, however, due to the safety and welfare concern for other tenants, the property, and the public, as a whole, a landlord may have the discretion not to lease, or continue to lease, to a cardholder who cultivates, manufactures, processes, smokes, or vaporizes medical marijuana in the leased premises' (§ 21-28.6-4(d)). §§ 21-28.6-4, 21-28.11-29 and 21-28.11-22 were read whole; § 21-28.6-4 touches landlords only in (d) and in (r) (medical growers grow at one registered premises, no more than 24 tagged mature plants per dwelling unit). title: Religious Items on the Entry Door
bodyText: Rhode Island bars a landlord from prohibiting a tenant from displaying or affixing religious items on the entry to the tenant's unit when the display is motivated by the tenant's sincere religious belief (a mezuzah is a common example). You may still limit an item that threatens public health or safety, violates fair housing or other law, sits anywhere other than the entry door or door frame or extends past the frame's outer edge, or that, with the other religious items on the door or frame, totals more than 25 square inches. The rule does not let the tenant repaint or alter the door or frame against your rules. The protection covers religious items only; Rhode Island has no statute protecting purely cultural displays. Apart from this, Rhode Island has no statute on tenant displays, signs, waterbeds or fastening items in a rental, so the lease's common-area and use rules are contract terms, subject to the statute's tests for rules.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-37-5.5(a): a landlord or owner 'may not enforce or adopt a restrictive covenant or otherwise prohibit a unit owner or tenant from displaying or affixing on the entry to the unit owner's or tenant's dwelling one or more religious items, the display of which is motivated by the unit owner's or tenant's sincere religious belief' (§ 34-37-5.5(a)); (b) permitted limits: an item that 'Threatens the public health or safety' (§ 34-37-5.5(b)(1)), violates housing-discrimination or other law, 'Is in a location other than the entry door or door frame or extends past the outer edge of the door frame' (§ 34-37-5.5(b)(3)), or has 'a total size of greater than twenty-five (25) square inches' (§ 34-37-5.5(b)(4)); (c) no right to alter the door or frame; (d) removal by an association. The section cites § 34-18-11 for 'landlord' and 'owner'; those definitions were renumbered by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1, effective July 1, 2026 (cite by term; SOP rule 77). title: No Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute letting a tenant house people displaced by a fire, storm or other disaster in spite of the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none limiting what you may charge or require when they stay. Your lease's guest terms apply, subject to the housing code's occupancy limits; if a tenant asks to house displaced family or friends, a written temporary consent with an end date avoids later disputes. The state's disaster laws give the governor and cities and towns powers to arrange temporary housing for disaster victims and provide relocation payments when government action displaces people, but they do not change private leases. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; executive orders issued in an emergency were not.

title: Guests in Rhode Island Rentals
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute limits how long a tenant's guests may stay or gives guests any right to stay, so a lease guest limit is a contract term you enforce like any other (the 20-day noncompliance notice, not a lockout). The tenant must require anyone on the premises with the tenant's consent to behave so as not to disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment, and answers for a guest who damages the premises with the tenant's knowledge. The state minimum housing code limits a unit to one family plus two unrelated occupants, or one household of unrelated people, unless a rooming-house permit has been granted; guests and domestic employees are not counted, but a 'guest' who has in fact moved in may be. Apply guest limits the same way to every household: limits that fall harder on families with children or on a domestic-abuse survivor's household can raise fair housing problems. Mobile home parks must make reasonable rules for guest parking.
notes: RI: Tenant duty: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-24(7): a tenant shall 'Conduct himself or herself, and require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves, in a manner that will not disturb his or her neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises' (§ 34-18-24(7)); (6) not 'knowingly permit any person to do so' (damage) (§ 34-18-24(6)). Occupancy: R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-11(4): 'A dwelling unit must not be occupied by more than one family plus two (2) occupants unrelated to the family, except for guests or domestic employees or by not more than one household if the occupants are unrelated, unless a permit for a rooming house has been granted by the appropriate authority' (§ 45-24.3-11(4)). Mobile homes: § 31-44-7(1)(xiii): 'Make reasonable rules for guest parking which shall be clearly stated in the rules of the park' (§ 31-44-7(1)(xiii)). title: No Firearms Lease Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on firearms in residential leases. No state law stops you from restricting a tenant's lawful possession of firearms in the unit or common areas, and none requires you to allow them, so any firearms term is a contract term. Before adding one, consider that Rhode Island's criminal firearms laws, not your lease, govern who may possess and carry, that a restriction must be clear and applied evenly to be enforced, and that public housing and federally assisted housing raise separate federal questions not reviewed here. A tenant's crime of violence on the premises or on adjacent public property, including assault with a dangerous weapon, already breaches the tenant's statutory duties, and you may file for eviction for it without first sending a noncompliance notice. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.

title: No Guest or Visitor Rights Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute guaranteeing tenants the right to have guests, visitors, caregivers, tradespeople or delivery people, and no statute bars a guest fee, so lease terms on guests and visitors are contract terms. A guest fee is a fee beyond rent: list it in the same section of the lease as the rent, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or, with no written lease, in a written fee list, or the tenant may recover it. Two state rules still shape them. The state minimum housing code treats a person who shares a unit in a nonpermanent status for not more than 30 days as a guest, and guests are not counted as occupants for the code's occupancy limits; someone who stays longer may be counted. And a guest rule must be applied the same way to every household, because fair housing law protects familial status, disability and domestic-abuse victim status, among others. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.

Laws § 45-24.3-5(16): '"Guest" means any person who shares a dwelling unit in a nonpermanent status for not more than thirty (30) days.' (§ 45-24.3-5(16)); § 45-24.3-5(26): 'except that in dwelling units a guest will not be considered an occupant' (§ 45-24.3-5(26)). title: Routine Inspections in Rhode Island
bodyText: Inspecting the premises is one of the purposes for which a Rhode Island tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry. Give at least two days' notice of your intent to enter, except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, and enter only at reasonable times. No statute sets how often you may inspect, but you may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant: if you enter unlawfully, enter in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated demands for entry that unreasonably harass the tenant, the tenant may get a court order or terminate the lease. If the tenant refuses lawful access, you may get a court order compelling it or terminate the lease. Either way the winner recovers actual damages and must be awarded costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Apart from emergencies, absences over seven days (to protect the property), a court order, a repair after an ignored 20-day notice, or an abandoned or surrendered unit, you have no other right of entry.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-26(a): 'A tenant shall not unreasonably withhold consent to the landlord to enter into the dwelling unit in order to inspect the premises' (§ 34-18-26(a)); (b) entry without consent 'in case of emergency, or, during any absence of the tenant in excess of seven (7) days, if reasonably necessary for the protection of the property' (§ 34-18-26(b)); (c) 'A landlord shall not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant. Except in case of emergency or unless it is impracticable to do so, the landlord shall give the tenant at least two (2) days' notice of his or her intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times.' (§ 34-18-26(c)); (d) 'A landlord has no other right of access except' by court order, as permitted by § 34-18-39 (entry to remedy a tenant's § 34-18-24 noncompliance materially affecting health and safety after 20 days' written notice, or promptly in an emergency), or 'Unless the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises' (§ 34-18-26(d)(3)). Remedies: § 34-18-45(a) 'If the tenant refuses to allow lawful access, the landlord may obtain injunctive relief to compel access, or terminate the rental agreement.'; (b) unlawful entry, entry 'in an unreasonable manner' or 'repeated demands for entry otherwise lawful but which have the effect of unreasonably harassing the tenant' (§ 34-18-45(b)); (c) 'the prevailing party may recover actual damages and shall be awarded costs and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 34-18-45(c)). No statute on inspection frequency or move-out walk-throughs (see edu-no-move-in-inspection-rule-ri). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Keys and Lock Changes in Rhode Island
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on how many keys you issue, key receipts, lost-key charges or rekeying between tenants, so those are lease terms. Two money rules apply. A refundable key deposit is part of the security deposit, which may not exceed one month's periodic rent in total, whatever you call it. And a lost-key or rekey charge is a fee beyond rent, so it must be listed in the lease's rent section with a statement that additional fees may apply (or, with no written lease, in a written fee list), unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format. In a rooming house, each rooming unit door must have an operating lock. Since July 1, 2026, if all tenants in possession ask (or a court order is furnished) because a tenant or adult household member reasonably believes they face an imminent threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, you must, within two business days, make a good faith effort to change the unit's locks (and get them a key) or let them change the locks; you may charge no more than the customary local price. Blocking the change or failing to try to give them a key costs two months' rent plus fees unless you acted in good faith. A lease cannot waive these rules.
notes: RI: Deposit cap: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(a): 'A landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent.' (§ 34-18-19(a)); definition § 34-18-11(16) (renumbered (19) by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1, effective July 1, 2026): a deposit 'against physical damages to the tenant's dwelling unit'. DRAFTING JUDGMENT: a key deposit is treated as within the cap (cheaper error; consistent with edu-due-at-signing-ri). Fee disclosure for lost-key or rekey charges: § 34-18-15(a)(1) (see edu-fee-disclosure-ri). Rooming houses: R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-12(c)(7): 'That rooming unit doors have operating locks to insure privacy.' (§ 45-24.3-12(c)(7)). Survivor lock change: § 34-18-65 (added by R.I. Pub. title: No Candidate Access Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to let political candidates, campaign workers or voter-registration volunteers into an apartment building to reach tenants' doors, and no duty to set aside an area for campaign or voter literature. Whether outsiders may canvass in locked hallways and other common areas is up to your building rules, which must be reasonable and applied evenly. Your tenants themselves may invite whomever they like to their own unit, subject to the lease's guest and conduct terms. Two related protections apply: you may not retaliate against tenants for organizing or joining a tenants' union, and in a mobile home park, park rules may not stop residents from meeting in the common areas or stop a home owner from canvassing other owners about association matters, at reasonable times and in a reasonable manner. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.

title: Flags and Political Signs
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute gives a tenant a right to display the U.S. flag, another flag, a banner or a political sign against your lease rules, and none limits a condominium or homeowners' association's display rules for occupants, so the lease's sign and display terms govern. Write them as neutral rules on size, placement, attachment and damage, and apply them evenly: a rule aimed at one tenant's message or at a protected group's displays can raise fair housing or retaliation problems. The one display right Rhode Island does protect is for religious items on the unit's entry door or door frame (see the religious display row). Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances, association documents and case law were not.

title: No Window Unit Right
bodyText: Rhode Island gives tenants no statutory right to install a window or portable air conditioner, and the lease need not say anything about it. Your lease may allow, limit or ban tenant-owned units, for example by requiring your approval, proper brackets and no blocking of a window needed as a fire exit. A rule adopted after the lease starts must meet the statute's tests for rules. No state law requires you to provide cooling. If you do supply air conditioning, you must keep it in good and safe working order, and the tenant must use it in a reasonable manner and must not damage the premises, which includes damage from installing a window unit. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (tenant right to a portable or window cooling device; cooling standard). Landlord duty if supplied: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(a)(4): 'Maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord' (§ 34-18-22(a)(4)). title: No Plug-In Solar Right
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute giving tenants a right to install a plug-in, balcony or other portable solar device, and no law that voids lease or covenant restrictions on solar equipment. Treat a tenant's request under the lease's alterations and appliance terms: you may allow it, set conditions (safe mounting, no damage, approved equipment, removal at move-out) or refuse. The tenant must not damage the premises in installing or removing it. Rhode Island's solar easement law only lets property owners grant recorded easements protecting a solar system's sun exposure, and its solar consumer-protection law covers companies selling or leasing solar systems to homeowners; neither gives tenants rights against you. title: Recycling
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires you to tell tenants where and how to recycle, or to provide a recycling service, so the lease need not say anything about it. In a building of four or more units you must supply containers for the sanitary storage and disposal of rubbish and garbage; in a one-, two- or three-family house the state housing code makes the occupant furnish them, unless a stricter local code says otherwise, and in either case you must arrange for waste removal. The tenant must dispose of all waste from the unit in a clean and safe manner. Rhode Island's cities and towns run their own curbside and recycling programs and may require residents or building owners to separate recyclables; check the local ordinance and, if it applies, describe the recycling setup in your rules. title: Smoke From Other Units
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on smoke drifting between units and no statute letting a tenant waive smoke-drift claims. Don't use a lease term that makes the tenant give up or limit claims against you over drifting smoke: a rental agreement may not have the tenant agree to excuse or limit any liability the law places on you, or to indemnify you for it. Such a term is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease with prohibited terms the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. A plain statement that smoking is allowed in other units, with no release, is not prohibited by statute. State law already bans smoking, including e-cigarettes, in lobbies, hallways and other common areas of apartment buildings and other residential buildings with more than four units; units themselves are exempt as private residences. In smaller buildings, the separate workplace smoking ban may reach enclosed hallways and stairs your employees work in. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.

If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known to be prohibited, the tenant may recover, in addition to his or her actual damages, an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees.' title: Snow and Ice
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute says who clears snow and ice at a rental. You must keep all common areas clean and safe, including shared walks, steps, driveways and parking areas, and you cannot shift that duty for shared areas to one tenant in a way that reduces what you owe the other tenants. You may have a tenant clear snow and ice from areas only that tenant uses, such as the walk and driveway of a single-family home, but only under a writing signed by both of you, made in good faith and supported by adequate consideration; the task can't be something needed to bring the property up to code. Put the duty in the signed lease, list the areas, and state the consideration (for example, that the rent reflects the tenant's snow work). Cities and towns may set their own sidewalk snow-clearing rules by ordinance, and an ordinance may make the property owner responsible whatever the lease says. title: Tenant Cameras and Video Doorbells
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute says whether a tenant may install a security camera or video doorbell, so the lease controls: its alterations terms for anything drilled or wired in, and your building rules, which must be reasonable, clear and applied fairly to all tenants. The tenant must not damage the premises in installing or removing a device. Consider allowing devices that mount without damage and aim only at the tenant's own door or unit. Audio is a separate question: Rhode Island makes it a crime to willfully intercept a wire, electronic or oral communication, but a private person who is a party to the conversation, or has one party's prior consent, may record it unless the purpose is criminal, tortious or otherwise injurious, so a doorbell that records strangers' conversations in a hallway can raise legal problems. Never place or allow a camera that views inside a tenant's home or private areas: apart from privacy claims, using an imaging device to view intimate areas or the inside of an occupied dwelling for a sexual purpose is the crime of video voyeurism (up to three years and/or $5,000). Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.

title: Waterbeds
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on waterbeds or other water-filled furniture in rentals. Nothing gives a tenant a right to one, and nothing limits a lease term that bans them, requires your written consent, or conditions them on proof of insurance and a safe installation. A rule on water-filled furniture adopted after the lease is signed must meet the statute's tests for rules and, if it substantially changes the tenant's bargain, needs the tenant's written consent. Whatever the lease says, the tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises, and remains liable for water damage the tenant causes. title: Renting a Condominium Unit
bodyText: If you rent out a Rhode Island condominium unit, the association enforces the condominium's declaration, bylaws and rules against you. In a condominium under the older Condominium Ownership Act (one created before July 1, 1982 that has not accepted the 1982 Condominium Law), the statute itself makes tenants subject to the declaration and bylaws; under the 1982 Condominium Law no statute binds the tenant directly, so the tenant's duty to follow them rests on your lease. After notice and a chance for a hearing the association may fine the unit owner, up to $100 a day for continuing violations or $500 per other fine in a residential condominium, and the fines, the hearing costs and any reasonable attorney's fees awarded (when the prevailing side has a Rhode Island lawyer) become a lien on your unit. The lease's association-compliance clause lets you pass those consequences to the tenant. If your common-expense assessments go unpaid for 60 days while a tenant lives in the unit, the association may demand that the tenant pay the overdue amount and later monthly assessments directly to it; whatever the tenant pays the association counts as rent paid to you, so a demand can cut off your rent until the arrears are cleared. This direct-demand rule applies to condominiums under the 1982 Condominium Law (created after July 1, 1982, or that opted in). No state statute addresses association rules on satellite dishes or antennas. As landlord, though, you may not agree to or do anything that would interfere with a tenant's use of a master or individual antenna system in a building served by cable television (see the telecommunications-access row). Federal rules were not reviewed.

title: Association Rules on Renting
bodyText: Rhode Island's condominium laws do not cap fees an association charges to approve a lease, regulate deposits an association collects from tenants, limit what tenant information it may ask for, or say whether a new rental restriction binds owners who bought before it was adopted. Those questions are answered by the condominium's declaration, bylaws and rules, so read them before you sign a lease and build any approval step into your timeline. In a condominium under the 1982 Condominium Law (created after July 1, 1982, or one that accepted that law), two statutory rules matter: if your assessments are 60 days overdue, the association may collect them directly from your tenant, and the tenant's payments count against rent owed to you; and if the declaration gives lessees the vote on specified matters, your tenant votes on them instead of you and gets meeting notices and records access for them. Rhode Island has no general homeowners' association statute for planned communities, so their covenants govern. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; association documents and case law were not.

title: No Association Document Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require a lease for a condominium or other association unit to describe the association's obligations, and no statute requires you to hand the tenant the declaration, bylaws or rules. Give them anyway. Your tenant will be expected to follow them, the association can fine you for the tenant's violations, and your lease can pass those fines on only if the tenant knew the rules: a rule you rely on binds a tenant only if the tenant had notice of it when signing the lease or when it was adopted. Attach the association's current rules to the lease, or list where the tenant can read them, and send changes when the association adopts them. title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to disclose a unit's bed bug or pest history or setting a treatment timeline. Three general rules still apply. You may not rent out a vacant unit unless it and the premises are clean, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, so treat a known infestation before a new tenant moves in. Before signing any lease you must tell the prospective tenant about any outstanding minimum housing code violations on the building, which includes an infestation an inspector has cited, and within 30 days of a citation you must give every affected tenant a copy unless you have corrected it. And the housing code decides who pays for extermination (see the pest treatment row). Disclosing a recent, treated infestation voluntarily is lawful and reduces later disputes. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; local housing codes and case law were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (bed bug or pest-history disclosure; treatment timeline). Vacant units: R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-6(a): 'No owner or operator or other person shall occupy, or let to another person, any vacant dwelling, dwelling unit, or structure unless it and the premises are clean, sanitary, fit for human occupancy' (§ 45-24.3-6(a)). Code violations: § 34-18-22.1(b): 'A landlord, prior to entering into any residential rental agreement, shall inform a prospective tenant of any outstanding minimum housing code violations which exist on the building that is the subject of the rental agreement.' title: Certificates of Occupancy
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to tell a tenant whether the unit has a certificate of occupancy, or to give the tenant a copy. But a newly built building may not be used or occupied until the local building official issues a certificate of use and occupancy, which is issued only after the work meets the building and fire codes and, for a property on a private well, after you document the required drinking water testing. Don't lease a unit that needs a certificate and lacks one. If an inspector has cited the building for an outstanding minimum housing code violation, you must tell a prospective tenant before signing. Your city or town may require more, such as a rental permit or inspection; local rules were not searched. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (certificate of occupancy disclosure). Building code: R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-27.3-120.1: 'No building or structure hereafter erected shall be used or occupied in whole or in part until a certificate of use and occupancy shall have been issued by the building official.' ... 'the certificate shall not be issued for any property serviced by a private well until the property owner has submitted documentation to the building official which demonstrates compliance with the drinking water testing requirements' (§ 23-27.3-120.1). Changes of use and alterations of existing buildings fall under other sections of chapter 23-27.3, not read here. Code violations: § 34-18-22.1(b) 'prior to entering into any residential rental agreement, shall inform a prospective tenant of any outstanding minimum housing code violations' (§ 34-18-22.1(b)). title: No Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to disclose defective, corrosive or sulfur-emitting drywall, or a crumbling foundation, to a tenant. If such a condition affects health or safety, it falls under your general duties to comply with building and housing codes and to make all repairs needed to keep the premises fit and habitable, and if an inspector has cited it as an outstanding minimum housing code violation you must tell a prospective tenant before signing the lease. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law (including misrepresentation claims for hiding a known defect) was not.

title: Submetered Electricity
bodyText: Rhode Island has no lease disclosure rule specific to submetered electricity. The general rule covers it: the lease must say which utility costs are included in the rent and which are the tenant's, so if you bill the tenant for electricity measured by your own meter, say so in the lease, or the tenant may recover undisclosed fees. In an apartment house of more than ten units whose construction began after July 1, 1977, you may not use a master meter for electricity: each unit must have its own meter (publicly financed housing for elderly or disabled residents may elect a single meter). Anyone who charges for electricity furnished to a building must show on each bill the kilowatt hours used and the separate charges (base rate, adjustments, conservation costs, credits, taxes and any other fees), so use that format if you bill tenants for electricity. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; Public Utilities Commission rules and case law were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (submetering-specific lease disclosure). Utility disclosure: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(3): 'In any lease agreement the landlord shall disclose which utility costs are included in the rent and which utility costs are the tenant's responsibility.' (§ 34-18-15(a)(3)); (a)(5) recovery of undisclosed fees. Master meters: § 39-3-7.1: 'The use of "master-meters," so-called, in apartment or tenement houses containing more than ten (10) apartments or dwelling units is hereby prohibited; provided, however, that this section shall only apply to apartment houses, construction of which is commenced after July 1, 1977.' (§ 39-3-7.1). title: No Flood Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to tell a tenant whether the property is in a flood zone, has flooded before, or carries flood insurance. The state's property-condition disclosure, which asks about flood plains and flood insurance, applies when real estate is sold, not when it is rented. Consider telling tenants anyway if a unit, especially a basement unit, has a known flooding history, and remind them that renters insurance often excludes flood. If a flooding problem has been cited as an outstanding housing code violation, you must tell a prospective tenant before signing. From January 1, 2027, rentals of shoreline property also need a written shoreline access disclosure, a separate rule covered in its own row. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.

Laws § 5-20.8-2(a): 'the seller of the real estate shall deliver a written disclosure to the buyer' before 'signing any agreement to transfer real estate' (§ 5-20.8-2(a)); the form for one-to-four-unit buildings includes a Flood Plain (Flood Insurance) item (§ 5-20.8-2(b)(3)); § 5-20.8-3 lists exempt transfers and says nothing of leases. title: No Good Cause Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no general good-cause eviction law and no notice you must give tenants about one. You may end a periodic tenancy with the statutory notice, or decline to renew a fixed term, without stating a reason, as long as the reason is not retaliatory or discriminatory. Just cause is required only in narrow cases. A foreclosing lender or other foreclosing owner of a building with four or fewer units (unless exempt as a Rhode Island-based full-service lender or one with fewer than 15 Rhode Island foreclosures the prior year) may evict a bona fide tenant only for just cause (or after a disclosed binding sale contract with a bona fide buyer, and in some FHA-insured cases; a tenant may knowingly waive the protection for consideration), and within 30 days after the foreclosure must post and mail a notice giving its contact details, the address for rent and a continued-occupancy form. And no owner may evict occupants without just cause while housing-code conferences, hearings or appeals are pending or after being served with a notice of violation (see the code-order row). A mobile home park may end a lot tenancy only for the reasons in the mobile home statute, and public housing authorities must have just-cause rules. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (general good-cause law and coverage notice). Foreclosed properties: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-38.2(a): 'a foreclosing owner shall not evict a tenant except for just cause' (§ 34-18-38.2(a)); (b) 'Within thirty (30) days of the foreclosure, the foreclosing owner shall post in a prominent location in the building in which the rental housing unit is located, a written notice stating' contact details, 'The address to which rent charges shall be sent' (§ 34-18-38.2(b)(2)) and the continued-occupancy form requirement, satisfied by posting, first-class mail to each unit and sliding a notice under each door (§ 34-18-38.2(b)); (h) exemptions: a foreclosing owner 'headquartered in Rhode Island' with full-service mortgage operations, or one that 'conducted fewer than fifteen (15) foreclosures in Rhode Island during the prior calendar year' (§ 34-18-38.2(h)). Definitions: § 34-18-38.1(4) 'Foreclosing owner', (6) 'Housing accommodation' means 'a building or structure containing four (4) or fewer dwelling units' (§ 34-18-38.1(6)), (9) just-cause grounds, (12) 'Tenant' (bona fide tenancy at foreclosure). Housing code: § 45-24.3-21(c)(4) unlawful 'to evict occupants from a dwelling or dwelling unit without just cause during conferences, hearings, appeals, or when served with a notice of violation' (§ 45-24.3-21(c)(4)); section read whole on the independent check; the sentence is printed under subsection (c), headed 'Emergencies', but is general in wording; DRAFTING JUDGMENT: read as general, which is the cheaper error (see edu-rent-suspension-code-order-ri). Other just-cause regimes: § 31-44-2(a): a mobile home park tenancy may be terminated 'subject to one or more of the following reasons and limitations which shall take precedence over any conflicting state statute or local ordinance' (§ 31-44-2(a)); § 45-25-18.1(a)(3): housing authority rules must establish 'Just cause for the termination of the right of use and occupation, so that a tenant may be clearly apprised of the precise reasons for a termination.' (§ 45-25-18.1(a)(3)). Foreclosure exceptions: § 34-18-38.2(a) 'or unless a binding purchase-and-sale agreement has been executed for a bona fide third party to purchase the housing accommodation from a foreclosing owner' (§ 34-18-38.2(a)); (g): 'Nothing herein shall be deemed to limit the right of any tenant to knowingly waive the provisions of this section for consideration acceptable to such tenant.' (§ 34-18-38.2(g)). Retaliation and fair housing limits: edu-retaliation-ri, § 34-37-4.
