title: No Contamination Disclosure Statute
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires you to tell a residential tenant that the property is or was contaminated with hazardous materials, is on a federal Superfund list, or is subject to a recorded environmental land usage restriction. If your property has a recorded environmental land usage restriction from a state-supervised cleanup, read it and the Department of Environmental Management's remediation rules before leasing: such restrictions typically limit how the land can be used, and the rules (not reviewed here) may require you to give notice to, or bind, tenants. Separate rules cover lead, radon and private wells; see those rows. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; DEM regulations, recorded restrictions and case law were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent in the General Laws (contamination, Superfund or land-use-restriction disclosure to tenants). Remediation act: R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-19.14-7(2)(iv) exempts from liability a tenant who certifies, among other things, that it 'will comply with, and will not impede the effectiveness or integrity of, any institutional controls at a facility' (§ 23-19.14-7(2)(iv)(F)); seen through a --grep excerpt, not read in full. The statement that use restrictions typically limit land use is general background, not a cited rule. NOT SEARCHED: DEM Rules and Regulations for the Investigation and Remediation of Hazardous Material Releases (not loaded); recorded restrictions. NEEDS_REVIEW for that boundary. Statute-wide search with terms and hit counts over the RI corpus (General Laws, Constitution, three loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws, court rules): RI-contamination-disclosure-1 (hazardous materials/substances/wastes, contamination, environmental land usage or use restrictions, activity and use limitations, Superfund, brownfields, remediation, radioactive, petroleum releases, underground storage tanks within 800 characters of tenant/lessee/lease/rental agreement/landlord/lessor/renter/occupants; hits 15, OK; synthetic positive passed; hits are the remediation act, medical-waste, lead-law, radon, self-storage, mobile home park closure and housing-code provisions; no tenant disclosure); RI-contamination-disclosure-2 (everyday words: toxic, pollution, chemicals, oil spill or tank, vapor intrusion, dump site, contaminated soil/land/site/groundwater within 300 characters of tenant/renter/apartment/landlord/lease/rental; hits 10, OK; synthetic positive passed; no tenant disclosure). Case law not searched.

title: Disclosing Housing Code Violations
bodyText: Before you sign any lease, tell the prospective tenant about every outstanding minimum housing code violation on the building. If an enforcing officer has served you with a notice of violation or order that you have not yet complied with, the housing code adds two steps before you lease: give the new tenant a true copy of each notice or order, and at the same time notify the enforcing officer in writing that you intend to lease, with the tenant's name and address, either by hand delivery for a receipt or by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested. Leasing without these steps is unlawful under the housing code. During the tenancy, if you are cited, deliver a copy of the violation notice to each tenant of the affected building within 30 days unless you correct every violation to the agency's satisfaction within that time. Keep proof of each disclosure. If a unit has been designated unfit, see the condemned-premises row.
notes: RI: Landlord-tenant act: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22.1(b): 'A landlord, prior to entering into any residential rental agreement, shall inform a prospective tenant of any outstanding minimum housing code violations which exist on the building that is the subject of the rental agreement.' (§ 34-18-22.1(b)); (a) 'within thirty (30) days of receipt of the notice, deliver a copy of the notice of violation to each residential tenant of the building affected by said violation, unless within said thirty (30) day period the landlord has corrected all violations' (§ 34-18-22.1(a)). Housing code: § 45-24.3-17(j): 'It is unlawful for the owner of any residential or non-residential building upon whom a notice of violation or order has been served to sell, transfer, mortgage, lease, or dispose of the building to another until the provisions of the notice or order have been complied with or until the owner first furnishes to the grantee, lessee, or mortgagee prior to the transfer, lease, or mortgage, a true copy of any notice or order issued by the enforcing officer, and, at the same time, notify the enforcing officer, in writing, of the intent to transfer, lease, or mortgage' (§ 45-24.3-17(j)); 'A transferee, lessee, or mortgagee who has received actual or constructive notice of the existence of a notice or order is bound by the notice or order' (§ 45-24.3-17(j)). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: (j) speaks of leasing 'the building'; the body applies it to leasing a unit in the building (cheaper error; case law not searched). Recorded second notices bind later transferees and lapse after three years absent renewal (§ 45-24.3-17(i), (k)). Unfit designation and reoccupancy: see edu-condemned-premises-ri. Local housing codes not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Rhode Island Lead Disclosure
bodyText: For housing built before 1978, Rhode Island adds to the federal lead disclosure. Before the tenant is bound by any lease, including an oral one: give the EPA pamphlet Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home with the insert What You Should Know about the Rhode Island Lead Law; include a lead warning statement and a signed disclosure acknowledgment; and disclose, for the address and unit, everything you know about lead-based paint or lead hazards, a copy of each current lead certificate for the unit and common areas, a dated list of all lead inspection reports and certificates, how to get copies (you must deliver them free within 7 days of a request), basic information about the state lead rules and how they apply, and the name and contact details of the owner, registered agent or person responsible for maintaining the property. The acknowledgment must be a stand-alone document with the property address, or its own separate page of a written lease. Keep the signed copy for 3 years or the whole tenancy, whichever is longer. Exempt: housing built after January 1, 1978; units with a lead-free or full lead-safe certificate given to the tenant; renewals where you fully complied before and kept proof; zero-bedroom units and elderly or disability housing where no child lives; and leases of 100 days or less that cannot be renewed. Tell occupants of any inspection results within 7 days. The Department of Health may fine up to $5,000 per violation per day.
notes: RI: 216-RICR-50-15-3.5.1: the state requirements 'are in addition to, not in lieu of, Federal requirements' (24 C.F.R. Part 35, Subpart A; 40 C.F.R. Part 745, Subpart F; not read). 3.5.3(A): 'Non-exempt sellers and lessors shall meet all of the following requirements before a purchaser or lessee is obligated under any contract to purchase or lease target housing' (216-RICR-50-15-3.5.3(A)); (A)(1) pamphlet 'containing the insert What You Should Know about the Rhode Island Lead Law' (216-RICR-50-15-3.5.3(A)(1)); (A)(2) 'include in each contract for the sale or lease of any residential dwelling, including oral leases, a lead warning statement and a written disclosure acknowledgment' (216-RICR-50-15-3.5.3(A)(2)); (A)(3)(c)(1)-(4) address and unit, 'A copy of any current lead certificate(s) for the dwelling or dwelling unit and common areas', chronological listing, copies 'within seven (7) days of the request and at no charge'; (A)(3)(d) rental additions: 'Basic information about this Part and its applicability to the subject property' and owner, registered agent or designee contact; (A)(3)(e) 'The disclosure acknowledgment must be a stand-alone document, which includes the property address, or its own separate page when included in a written lease.' (216-RICR-50-15-3.5.3(A)(3)(e)); (A)(3)(f) retain 'for a minimum of three (3) years or the term of the tenancy, whichever period is longer' (216-RICR-50-15-3.5.3(A)(3)(f)). Exemptions: 3.2.1(A)(4)(a)(1)-(5) ('Sales and leases of any residential dwelling constructed after January 1, 1978'; lead-safe premises 'provided that a Certification of Lead-Free Status or Full Lead-Safe Certificate (Form PBLC-21) is provided to the purchaser(s) or lessee(s)'; renewals 'if proof of disclosure is retained for at least three (3) years or the term of tenancy, whichever period is longer'; zero-bedroom or elderly/disability housing 'in which no child resides'; 'Short-term leases of one hundred (100) days or less where no lease renewal or extension can occur'). Inspection results: 3.5.6(G) 'notify the occupants of the results within seven (7) days of receiving those results' (216-RICR-50-15-3.5.6(G)); § 23-24.6-15(b)(1) gives 'five (5) business days' for comprehensive environmental lead inspections (see edu-lead-tenant-notices-ri; follow the shorter). Enforcement: 3.6.2(A)(3) 'Failure to comply with the lead disclosure requirements'; 3.6.5(A)(1) fine 'of up to five thousand dollars ($5,000.00) per violation per day' (216-RICR-50-15-3.6.5(A)(1)). CROSS-REFERENCE FLAG: 3.2.1(A)(3)(a) says lessors are subject to the disclosure requirements 'in § 3.8 of this Part', but § 3.8 is Interpretation and Severability; the disclosure rules are § 3.5 (SOP rule 77; flagged, not resolved). Read in full: §§ 3.2 and 3.5 of the Part and §§ 3.6.2, 3.6.5(A); definition 3.3(A)(65): '“Target housing” means any pre-1978 residential dwelling, except housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities or zero (0) bedroom units in which no child resides.' (216-RICR-50-15-3.3(A)(65)); the rest of the Part was not read. Rule 15: written section-open (subsections stated).

title: Lead Certificates for Pre-1978 Rentals
bodyText: If your rental unit was built before 1978, Rhode Island requires a valid lead certificate for every non-exempt unit, obtained by hiring a licensed lead inspector, and you must keep the property lead-safe. Give the tenant a copy of each current lead certificate for the unit and common areas as part of the pre-lease lead disclosure. Until a pre-1978 rental dwelling has been made lead safe or lead hazard abated, you (or someone you designate) must take a lead hazard awareness seminar, have the unit and premises evaluated, correct lead hazards and keep them corrected, and give tenants basic information about lead hazard control, a copy of the independent clearance inspection and instructions for reporting deteriorating conditions. These mitigation duties apply from the first change of ownership or tenancy after November 1, 2005, and do not let you make a tenant who has stayed continuously since January 1, 2004 move out, even temporarily, unless a child under six or pregnant occupant asks and agrees. If a tenant in a unit where a child under six or a pregnant woman has lived for at least 30 days reports a hazard, correct it within 30 days. A new owner of a unit with such an occupant, where the previous owner had not met the requirements, gets up to 60 days, if it is visually inspected within 30 business days of the purchase. Lead-safe or lead-free units, temporary housing, elderly housing and condominium association common areas are outside these duties. Such a household may sue to compel compliance, and whoever prevails recovers costs and reasonable attorney's fees; a court may also award double or treble damages. The registry row explains the rental registry's lead certificate information and its effect on eviction filings.
notes: RI: Regulation: 216-RICR-50-15-3.5.6(A) 'Owners of regulated facilities shall maintain their properties in a lead-safe condition, free from lead hazards.'; (B) 'Owners of pre-1978 residential rental units shall obtain a valid lead certificate for all non-exempt rental units by hiring a licensed Lead Inspector to perform a lead inspection.' (216-RICR-50-15-3.5.6(B)); disclosure copy: 3.5.3(A)(3)(c)(2) 'A copy of any current lead certificate(s) for the dwelling or dwelling unit and common areas'; enforcement 3.6.2(A)(2) 'Failure of a non-exempt residential rental unit or child care facility to have an appropriate lead certificate' (216-RICR-50-15-3.6.2(A)(2)). Statute: R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-128.1-8(a): owners of 'pre-1978 rental dwellings, which have not been made lead safe or have not been lead hazard abated' must (1) take 'a lead hazard awareness seminar, themself or through a designated person'; (2) evaluate; (3) 'Correct identified lead hazards by meeting and maintaining the lead hazard mitigation standard' (§ 42-128.1-8(a)(3)); (4) 'Provide tenants: (i) Basic information about lead hazard control; (ii) A copy of the independent clearance inspection; and (iii) Information about how to give notice of deteriorating conditions' (§ 42-128.1-8(a)(4)); (5) 'Correct lead hazards within thirty (30) days after notification from the tenant of a dwelling unit with an at-risk occupant, or as provided for by § 34-18-22' (§ 42-128.1-8(a)); (b) new owners 'up to sixty (60) days' with a visual inspection 'within thirty (30) business days after assuming ownership'; (e) exemptions: condominium association common areas and units that are 'Lead-safe or lead free', 'Temporary housing' or 'Elderly housing' (§ 42-128.1-8(e)). 'At-risk occupant' is defined in § 42-128.1-4(1) as 'a person under six (6) years of age, or a pregnant woman, who has been a legal inhabitant in a dwelling unit for at least thirty (30) days' (§ 42-128.1-4(1)); guests excluded: 'a guest of any age shall not be considered an occupant for the purposes of this chapter' (§ 42-128.1-4(1)). Trigger: § 42-128.1-8(c): 'The requirements for lead hazard mitigation shall apply to the first change in ownership or tenancy after November 1, 2005; provided further, that unless requested and agreed to by an at-risk occupant, meeting the lead hazard mitigation standard shall not be construed to authorize a property owner to compel or cause a person, who is in tenancy on January 1, 2004, and remains in tenancy continuously thereafter, to vacate a rental unit temporarily or otherwise.' (§ 42-128.1-8(c)). Remedies: § 42-128.1-10(b) injunctive relief for 'households that include an at-risk occupant', prevailing party 'entitled to an award of the costs of the litigation and reasonable attorneys' fees'; § 42-128.1-11(c) 'damages, which may include double or treble the actual damages found, as well as reasonable attorneys' fees' (§ 42-128.1-11(c)). title: Rhode Island Lead Notices to Tenants
bodyText: Rhode Island's lead notices go beyond the federal disclosure and continue during the tenancy. At signing, for pre-1978 housing: the EPA pamphlet with the state insert, basic information about the state lead rules, and the certificates and report list described in the lead disclosure row; and, until the unit has been made lead safe, basic information about lead hazard control, a copy of the independent clearance inspection, and instructions for reporting deteriorating paint. After a comprehensive environmental lead inspection, tell current occupants the results within five business days after you receive them, and tell every prospective occupant before a lease is signed (or before move-in without a lease) while a significant lead hazard remains; this duty ends once the unit reaches at least lead-safe level. Missing these notices costs $100 to $500 per violation. For other lead inspections, notify occupants within 7 days and give a full report copy on request. If your water supplier finds a lead service line, you must inform your tenants; and if you refuse or ignore a tenant's second request to replace a lead service line for 60 days, the tenant may end the lease and you may not withhold the deposit for that.

Laws § 42-128.1-8(a)(4): 'Provide tenants: (i) Basic information about lead hazard control; (ii) A copy of the independent clearance inspection; and (iii) Information about how to give notice of deteriorating conditions' (§ 42-128.1-8(a)(4)), for 'pre-1978 rental dwellings, which have not been made lead safe or have not been lead hazard abated' (§ 42-128.1-8(a)). Inspection results: § 23-24.6-15(b)(1) occupants 'shall be notified of the results within five (5) business days after the owner receives the results'; (b)(2) prospective occupants 'shall be notified of the inspection results if a significant lead hazard exists, before any lease is signed or before occupancy begins in cases where no lease is signed'; (b)(3) the duty 'terminates with the performance of the necessary lead reduction actions required to reach at least the “lead safe” level'; (c) civil penalty 'of not less than one hundred dollars ($100) nor more than five hundred dollars ($500) for each violation' (§ 23-24.6-15(c)). 216-RICR-50-15-3.5.6(G): 'notify the occupants of the results within seven (7) days of receiving those results and provide a complete copy of the lead inspection report upon request' (216-RICR-50-15-3.5.6(G)); SOP rule 31: for comprehensive environmental lead inspections the statute's five business days controls; the 7-day rule covers other lead inspections. If the property owner refuses or fails to respond within sixty (60) days, the tenant shall have the option to terminate the lease. Upon termination, the property owner may not withhold the tenant's security deposit based upon the tenant's exercise of their termination rights under this section.' (§ 23-24.6-28(o)). R.I. Pub. title: No Meter Conservation Charge Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no meter conservation charge, on-bill energy-efficiency loan or similar meter-tied charge that you must disclose to a new tenant or deduct from rent. Electric bills show a conservation-cost line, but that is part of every customer's utility bill, not a charge you need to disclose. If the tenant pays utilities, the lease must still say which utility costs are included in rent and which are the tenant's. title: No Meth Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to disclose that a rental was used to make methamphetamine or other drugs, to report a suspected drug lab, or to decontaminate before re-renting, and no law bars occupying such a property. Your general duties still apply: the unit must be fit and habitable and code-compliant when rented, and a contamination hazard that a code officer cites must be disclosed to a prospective tenant before signing. A tenant must not use the premises to maintain a narcotics nuisance or to manufacture, sell or deliver controlled substances, and for those breaches you may file for eviction without giving a chance to cure. title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to tell a prospective tenant about a former military ordnance site nearby, a demolition permit you have applied for, or a gas or electric meter that also serves other units or common areas. Two general rules still matter. If the tenant pays a utility, the lease must say which utility costs are included in rent and which are the tenant's, so a tenant-paid meter that also carries hallway lights or another unit's usage should be disclosed and the arrangement stated, or the tenant may recover the undisclosed charges. And if you plan to demolish, remember that a fixed-term lease runs to its end and a periodic tenancy needs the statutory notice to end it. title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to disclose mold to a tenant or setting mold-specific duties. Mold falls under your general obligations: comply with the building and housing codes affecting health and safety, make all repairs needed to keep the premises fit and habitable, and, before signing any lease, tell the prospective tenant about any outstanding minimum housing code violations on the building, which would include a cited moisture or mold condition. The tenant must keep the unit as clean and safe as its condition permits and use facilities such as ventilation reasonably. Fixing leaks promptly and documenting the unit's condition at move-in is the practical protection. title: Owner and Manager Disclosure
bodyText: At or before the start of every tenancy, give the tenant in writing the name, address and number of (1) the person authorized to manage the premises and (2) an owner, or a person authorized to act for the owner, for service of legal papers and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands. Keep the information current, for example after a sale or a change of manager; the duty binds every successor landlord, owner or manager. Whoever fails to make the disclosure becomes the landlord's agent for service of process and notices, and for performing the landlord's obligations under the law and the lease and applying the rent collected to them; a manager who doesn't disclose is treated as the landlord. The lease is a convenient place for the disclosure. Failing to disclose does not by itself block an eviction, but separate rules do: a landlord not in compliance with the state rental registry may not file a nonpayment eviction (see the registry row), and nonresident landlords must keep an in-state agent (see that row).

title: Private Well Test Results
bodyText: If the rental is served by a private well, give the tenant the results of any previous well water testing before the lease is signed. Rhode Island's law directs the Department of Health to require property owners to disclose those results before a sale or lease of the property, so treat it as a pre-lease disclosure and keep proof you made it. State law does not require you to test the well before leasing (testing is required before a sale, and before a newly built building is first occupied), but a well you supply is part of the plumbing and water supply you must keep in working order and safe. Check the Department of Health's private well regulations for the exact form and timing, which were not reviewed here. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched.

title: No Pest Control Notice Rule
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires you to tell tenants about a pest control contract or to give advance notice before pesticides are applied in a rental building, and the lease need not say anything about it. If treatment requires entering a unit, the ordinary access rules apply: at least two days' notice, entry only at reasonable times, except in an emergency. One special case: if a tenant runs a family day care home or other child care program in the unit, only a certified or licensed commercial applicator may apply pesticides there during regular business hours, enrolled children may not enter a treated area until the label says it is safe, and the parents of enrolled children must get notice at least 24 hours before any application (gels, baits in tamper-resistant containers, disinfectants and similar products are excluded); coordinate with the provider before any treatment. Telling all tenants in advance about building-wide treatments is good practice. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; Department of Environmental Management pesticide regulations and case law were not.

bodyText: California's Proposition 65 warnings do not apply in Rhode Island, and Rhode Island has no similar law requiring landlords to warn tenants about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm on rental property. title: No Property Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to tell tenants what part of their rent goes to property taxes, whether annually or when rent changes. A tenant who is 65 or older or disabled, and was domiciled in Rhode Island for the whole year, may claim the state property tax relief credit if their household income qualifies; the statute counts 20% of the gross rent they paid for the year as the property tax they bore (none if the unit is legally exempt from property tax), so no landlord figure is needed. The tenant must give the Division of Taxation reasonable proof of rent paid and your name and address (or your managing agent's). You are not required by statute to sign a rent certificate or issue receipts, but providing a year-end rent statement on request helps older and disabled tenants claim the credit and costs you little. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; Division of Taxation forms and rules were not.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to test a rental for radon or to disclose radon results to tenants, and the rule does not vary by floor level. Mandatory radon testing and mitigation apply to public buildings and 'high priority' buildings: schools and licensed child care facilities caring for five or more unrelated children. If such a child care facility operates in your building, ask the Department of Health whether the testing duty reaches you as owner. Sales are different: for purchase and sale agreements signed on or after June 1, 2027, selling a residential property, including a multi-family home or apartment complex, will require a radon test within a year before closing, with results shared with the buyer and lender and mitigation of levels above 4.0 pCi/L, unless an exemption applies. If you know of high radon results in a rental, telling tenants is good practice. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded radon regulation were searched; case law was not.

title: Rhode Island Required Disclosures
bodyText: Rhode Island's required disclosures, by timing. At or before the tenancy starts, in writing: the name, address and number of the manager and of the owner or owner's agent for legal papers and notices. In the lease: any fees beyond rent, listed in the rent section with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); which utilities rent includes and which the tenant pays; and any renters-insurance requirement (without a written lease, give these in writing). With the written lease: a copy of your liability insurance declaration page, and a new copy at each renewal. Before signing: any outstanding minimum housing code violations, plus a true copy of any unresolved violation notice or order with written notice to the enforcing officer; for pre-1978 housing, the state lead disclosure on its own page; for a private well, prior test results. From January 1, 2027, for shoreline property: the written shoreline access disclosure. During the tenancy: 60 days' written notice of a rent increase (120 days for month-to-month tenants over 62; neither applies in independent living, assisted living or congregate care facilities); 30 days' written notice before a required fee changes; copies of new code violation notices within 30 days; lead inspection results; and notice once you are 120 days behind on the mortgage. Undisclosed fees can be recovered. No state form must open the lease, and no just-cause coverage notice is required.

title: No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no state rule requiring you to give tenants a copy of, or attach to the lease, a variance or extension granted from the housing code. Local housing boards of review can modify an enforcing officer's order, extend the time to comply or grant a variance, and none of those decisions carries a statutory tenant-notice duty. But a violation that a variance or extension leaves uncorrected is still an outstanding violation: tell a prospective tenant about it before signing, and give current tenants a copy of a new violation notice within 30 days unless you correct it. Sharing the board's decision with affected tenants is good practice. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and local board rules were not.

Laws § 45-24.2-5(c)(4) majority vote needed 'to reverse or modify any order or decision of the enforcing officer and to authorize a variance or modification in the application of any provisions of any ordinance, rule, or regulation' (§ 45-24.2-5(c)(4)); § 45-24.3-21(b)(6) the housing board of review 'may grant an extension of time, for the performance of any act required, of not more than three (3) additional months' and may find 'that a variance is in harmony with the general purpose' of the chapter (§ 45-24.3-21(b)(6)); both sections read whole on the independent check. Disclosure of outstanding violations: § 34-18-22.1(a), (b) (read in full). title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require a lease notice about the sex offender registry, does not require you to tell tenants that a registered offender lives in or near the building, and has no statute barring landlords from considering registry information. The state's public registry website warns that its information must not be used to unlawfully injure or harass anyone named in it, so never share or act on it in a way that does. Residency limits apply to the registrant, not to you: a registered offender may not knowingly live within 300 feet of a school, or within 1,000 feet for a level-three offender. If you screen applicants for criminal history, apply one written policy to everyone; fair housing and other screening laws were not reviewed for this row. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.

Laws § 11-37.1-10(c): a registrant 'who knowingly resides within three hundred feet (300′) of any school as defined in § 11-37.1-2' commits a felony (except level-three offenders, covered by (d)); (d) a 'level-three (3) sex offender who knowingly resides within one thousand feet (1,000′) of any school' (§ 11-37.1-10(d)). Website warning: § 11-37.1-12(4) website content '(C) A warning that the information contained on the website should not be used to unlawfully injure, harass, or commit a crime against any individual named in the registry or residing or working at any reported addresses' (seen through --grep; § 11-37.1-12 not read in full; the body paraphrases it only). Shelters: § 42-11.2-11 limits beds for registrants in small homeless shelters (battery excerpt; not a landlord-tenant rule). title: Registered Sex Offenders
bodyText: Rhode Island limits where registered sex offenders may live, but the duty is the offender's, not yours. A person required to register who knowingly lives within 300 feet of a school commits a felony; for a level-three offender the distance is 1,000 feet. A school here means the buildings and land of a public or private kindergarten, elementary, middle or secondary school, and the distance runs from the nearest boundary line of the residence's property to the nearest boundary line of the school's property. No Rhode Island statute requires you to check the registry, bars you from renting to a registrant, makes it a crime to lease to two registrants who live together, or requires you to disclose nearby registrants. If you screen applicants for registration status, apply the same written standard to everyone. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.
notes: RI: Present (offender residency limit near schools; no landlord duty). R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-37.1-10(c): 'Except in the case of a level-three (3) sex offender, any person who is required to register or verify his or her address, who knowingly resides within three hundred feet (300′) of any school as defined in § 11-37.1-2' (§ 11-37.1-10(c)) is guilty of a felony (up to five years, $5,000, or both); § 11-37.1-10(d): 'Any level-three (3) sex offender who knowingly resides within one thousand feet (1,000′) of any school as defined in § 11-37.1-2' (§ 11-37.1-10(d)); distance 'measured from the nearest boundary line of the real property supporting the residence of the person to the nearest boundary line of the real property that supports or upon which there exists a school' (§ 11-37.1-10(c)). The offense is the registrant's; no section names a landlord, owner or lessor. § 42-11.2-11(c) caps beds for registrants in homeless shelters on state property (seen in battery hit; not a tenancy rule). title: Lease Layout Rules
bodyText: Rhode Island sets no font size, type size or first-page placement for a residential lease or any lease disclosure, and has no single-family residence occupancy notice. Two placement rules do apply. If any fee beyond rent applies to the unit, the lease must list it in the same section as the rent and say that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy program requires a different lease format); a tenant may recover any fee that was not disclosed this way. And for target housing (generally pre-1978), the lead disclosure acknowledgment must be a stand-alone document that includes the property address, or its own separate page if it is part of a written lease. Otherwise you choose the layout; a readable type size and clear headings still help show the tenant saw each required term. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.

title: Source of Income and Housing Vouchers
bodyText: Rhode Island fair housing law protects a renter's lawful source of income: child support, alimony, Social Security, SSI, any other public assistance (including medical or veterans assistance), and any federal, state or local rental assistance or housing subsidy, including Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers, together with any requirement that comes with the program. You may not refuse to rent, set different terms, misrepresent availability, delay an application or advertise a preference because of it. You may not ask about it, except to confirm the source, amount and expected duration of income to check that the applicant meets your nondiscriminatory standards. If you use a minimum-income test, apply it only to the tenant's share of the rent after any rental assistance or subsidy. Because program requirements are part of the protected source, refusing because of a voucher program's requirements is unlawful too. One exemption: if the building has three units or fewer and you live in one of them, you may refuse based on source of income. No lease statement is required.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-37-3(18): 'The term “lawful source of income” means and includes any income, benefit, or subsidy derived from child support; alimony; Social Security; Supplemental Security Income; any other federal, state, or local public assistance program, including, but not limited to, medical or veterans assistance; any federal, state, or local rental assistance or housing subsidy program, including Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers as authorized by 42 U.S.C. § 1437; and any requirement associated with such public assistance, rental assistance, or housing subsidy program.' (§ 34-37-3(18)). Prohibited acts (inquiry, refusal, advertising, terms and conditions, misrepresenting availability, delaying applications): § 34-37-4(a). Allowed inquiry: 'Nothing in this section shall be construed to prohibit any oral or written inquiry as to whether the prospective purchaser or tenant is eighteen (18) years of age or older, or to confirm the source, amount, and expected duration of the lawful source of income of the prospective purchaser or tenant' (§ 34-37-4(a)). Income standard: 'If a landlord requires that a prospective or current tenant have a certain minimum level of income, the standard for assessing eligibility shall be based only on the portion of the rent to be paid by the tenant, taking into account the value of any federal, state, or local rental assistance or housing subsidy.' (§ 34-37-4(c)). Exemption: 'Nothing in this chapter shall prohibit an owner of a housing accommodation from refusing to rent to a person based on their lawful source of income if the housing accommodation is three (3) units or less, one of which is occupied by the owner.' (§ 34-37-4.6). Effective April 15, 2021 (R.I. Pub. L. 2021, chs. 3, 4). title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Rhode Island has no law requiring you to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, whether the building has a fire sprinkler system or when it was last inspected. Whether a building must have sprinklers is a building and fire code question: the state Fire Safety Code applies to all structures unless specifically exempted, and for existing buildings the local fire official enforces it as the Uniform Fire Code (NFPA 1) and Life Safety Code (NFPA 101) apply to existing structures. Those code regulations were not part of this search, so ask your local fire official what your building needs. If you mention sprinklers in a listing or the lease, describe them accurately. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; the fire and building code regulations, municipal ordinances and case law were not.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Rentals
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires you to install or retrofit fire sprinklers in an existing rental home or apartment building; the sprinkler mandates written into the General Laws cover places of assembly such as nightclubs. Sprinkler requirements for housing come instead from the state Fire Safety Code, which applies to all structures unless specifically exempted and, for existing buildings, is enforced as NFPA 1 and NFPA 101 apply to existing structures, and from the building codes. If you change a building's use or type of occupancy (for example, converting a single-family house or commercial space into apartments), the building must meet the rehabilitation building and fire code for existing buildings, or new-construction rules where that code does not apply, which can bring sprinkler requirements with it. The code regulations were not part of this search: confirm your building's requirements with the local fire official before buying, converting or adding units. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; the code regulations, municipal ordinances and case law were not.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Illness at the Property
bodyText: Rhode Island's rule on psychologically impacted property is written for sales. For land and buildings of one to four units, the fact or suspicion that a property is psychologically impacted is not a material fact requiring disclosure, and no claim arises against a seller or agent for not telling a buyer. Psychologically impacted includes an occupant who has or had, or is suspected of having, HIV, AIDS or another disease medical evidence shows is highly unlikely to spread through living in a home, and a property suspected at any time of being the site of a homicide, other felony or suicide. The statute names sellers and buyers, and no statute says whether you must tell a prospective tenant, so don't treat the sales rule as protection in a rental. The statute also never authorizes a false statement: if an applicant asks, answer truthfully or decline to answer, but never mislead. If a licensed broker handles your rental of a building with four or fewer units, the broker treats such facts as confidential information. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.
notes: RI: Present (sales-only rule; no landlord-to-tenant rule). R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-20.8-6(a): 'The fact or suspicion that real property may be or is psychologically impacted is not a material fact requiring disclosure in any real estate transaction.' (§ 5-20.8-6(a)); impacts listed in § 5-20.8-6(a)(1) (HIV, AIDS or 'any other disease that has been determined by medical evidence to be highly unlikely to be transmitted through the occupying of a dwelling place' (§ 5-20.8-6(a)(1))) and (a)(2) ('That the real property was or has been, at any time, suspected of being the site of a homicide, other felony, or suicide.' (§ 5-20.8-6(a)(2))). § 5-20.8-6(b)(1): 'No cause of action shall arise against the seller of the real property or his or her agent for failure to disclose to the buyer that the real property was psychologically impacted as defined in this chapter.' (§ 5-20.8-6(b)(1)); § 5-20.8-6(b)(2): 'Under no circumstances shall this provision be interpreted as or used as authorization for an agent or seller to make any misrepresentation of fact or false statement.' (§ 5-20.8-6(b)(2)). Chapter scope: § 5-20.8-1(7) real estate is 'vacant land or real property and improvements consisting of a house or building containing one to four (4) dwelling units' (§ 5-20.8-1(7)); 'Transfer' means 'the sale or conveyance, exchange of, or option to purchase any real estate' (§ 5-20.8-1(10)); no lease or tenant term. Whether 'any real estate transaction' in (a) reaches a lease is not settled by the text: DRAFTING JUDGMENT, the row treats the rule as sales-only and tells landlords not to rely on it. title: No Required Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to give tenants a state-prepared statement, summary or bill of tenant rights, or to attach one to the lease. (Owners of federally insured or assisted developments must include a summary of tenants' rights in the notices and offers that law requires before prepaying the mortgage, not renewing a Section 8 contract or selling the development; those are event notices, not lease documents.) The Executive Office of Housing must publish a written guide to landlords' and tenants' rights and duties under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, in English and Spanish, update it at least every two years and post it on its website, but no law makes you hand it out. Giving tenants the link is a good practice, not a duty. The one state-prepared document you must hand over at the start of a tenancy is lead information: for target housing (generally pre-1978), before the tenant is bound, give the EPA pamphlet Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home with the Rhode Island insert What You Should Know about the Rhode Island Lead Law. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.

title: Condominium Conversion and Tenant Purchase Rights
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statewide rent cap or just-cause law, so no notice about one belongs in your lease. Tenants do get notice and purchase rights in two situations. Condominium conversion: if units in your building will be sold as condominiums, each residential tenant and subtenant must get notice of the conversion, with the public offering statement, at least 120 days before having to vacate, or one year for a tenant aged 62 or older or one who has lived in the unit continuously for 10 years or more. During the notice period rent may not rise, the terms of the tenancy may not change, and the tenant cannot be made to leave except for nonpayment of rent, waste or disturbing other tenants; a lease also may not be ended against its own terms. A tenant may cancel the lease without penalty if all lease obligations have been met. Each tenant gets the first chance to buy the unit (60 days, or 180 days for the protected tenants), and if the tenant does not buy, for the next 180 days you may not offer the unit to anyone else at a better price or on better terms (the purchase right does not apply to a unit that will be used only for nonresidential purposes or whose converted boundaries do not substantially match the rented unit). You must pay reasonable moving costs within 50 miles to a tenant who is disabled or 62 or older. Missing the notice is a defense to an action for possession. These rules come from the Condominium Act; the older Condominium Ownership Act's conversion rules apply only to condominiums created before July 1, 1982. Federally assisted housing: an owner ending a Section 8 contract must give two years' notice to Rhode Island Housing, copy the tenant association and post it, and must first offer the development for sale, in this order, to the tenant association, Rhode Island Housing, the local housing authority and the city or town before a sale, lease, prepayment or condominium conversion that ends the assistance or its use restrictions. At least 90 days before prepaying the mortgage or not renewing a Section 8 contract, the owner must also give each assisted household a written notice of intent summarizing its rights, pay move-in help (up to $500) and relocation costs (up to $450), and offer a household in good standing at least a one-year lease extension (two years for certain households with a disabled or senior member or a child under 10) at a tenant share of no more than 30% of income, unless the owner records a covenant keeping the income restrictions. Case law was not searched.

Rents shall not be increased during the notice period.' (§ 34-36.1-4.12(a)); 'Failure to give notice as required by this section is a defense to an action for possession.' (§ 34-36.1-4.12(a)); § 34-36.1-4.12(b) 60-day offer to the tenant; 'Tenants shall have the right to cancel their lease and receive no penalties for the cancellation as long as all obligations of the lease have been met.' (§ 34-36.1-4.12(b)); no more favorable offer for 180 days (§ 34-36.1-4.12(b)); § 34-36.1-4.12(e): tenants of ten years or more or aged 62 get one year's notice and 180 days to buy, and 'The owner or developer shall pay reasonable moving expenses and costs, to any tenant who is disabled or has attained the age of sixty-two (62), within a fifty (50) mile radius.' title: No Exemption Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no law requiring a lease or notice telling tenants that a property is exempt from rent limits, just-cause eviction rules or tenant purchase rights, because the state has no general rent cap or just-cause law to be exempt from. The narrower rules that do exist (just cause after a foreclosure of a building with four or fewer units, and tenant notice and purchase rights on condominium conversion or on sale of federally assisted housing) carry no exemption notice either. Don't add a statement borrowed from another state's lease, such as California's 'not subject to the rent limits' notice: it cites law that does not apply in Rhode Island. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (statutory notice telling tenants a property is exempt from a rent-cap, just-cause or tenant-purchase regime). Rhode Island has no statewide rent cap or general just-cause regime (edu-no-rent-control-ri, edu-no-good-cause-notice-ri); the foreclosure just-cause rule (§§ 34-18-38.1, 34-18-38.2) has exemptions but no exemption notice; the conversion and assisted-housing purchase rights (edu-tenant-purchase-rights-ri) have no exemption notice. title: No Truth-in-Renting Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no truth-in-renting law: no statute requires your lease to carry a notice that it must comply with state law, warns tenants about unenforceable clauses, or delivers a state truth-in-renting statement. What Rhode Island does require is specific content. A written lease must list any fees beyond rent in the same section as the rent and say additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), say which utilities are included in rent and which the tenant pays, and state any renters-insurance requirement. If the lease passes real estate tax increases on to the tenant, the clause is void unless it limits the tenant to the unit's proportionate share, states the exact percentage, and promises a proportionate refund of any abatement. You must give the tenant your liability insurance declaration page with the written lease, disclose in writing who manages the property and who accepts notices for the owner, and for target housing include the lead warning statement and acknowledgment. A lease may not waive the security deposit rules or include the provisions the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act prohibits. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit
bodyText: Rhode Island zoning law makes it easier to build and rent an accessory dwelling unit (ADU): a separate, complete living unit on the same lot as a legally established single-family or multi-family home, such as a detached cottage, a unit over a garage or an addition. One ADU per lot is allowed by right, through an administrative building permit only, if it is on an owner-occupied property as a reasonable accommodation for family members with disabilities, on a residential lot of at least 20,000 square feet, or inside the existing footprint of the home or an existing accessory structure. A city or town may not limit who rents the ADU by family relationship or age (unless a federal affordability subsidy requires it), require low- or moderate-income tenants outside inclusionary or comprehensive-permit projects, or revoke a legal ADU when the property or the occupancy changes hands. Condominium or homeowners association rules that conflict with these protections are void. One limit binds you: an ADU may not be offered or rented for tourist or transient use or through a hosting platform, so rent it as a regular residential tenancy, not a short-term rental. Local ordinances and case law were not searched.
notes: RI: Present (state zoning rules for ADUs, including rental limits). R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24-31(2): an ADU is 'A residential living unit on the same lot where the principal use is a legally established single-family dwelling unit or multi-family dwelling unit. An ADU provides complete independent living facilities for one or more persons.' (§ 45-24-31(2), read as a subsection only). § 45-24-37(e) (version effective January 1, 2026): an ADU meeting §§ 45-24-31 and 45-24-73(a) 'shall be a permitted use in all residential zoning districts' and 'shall be permitted through an administrative building permit process only' (§ 45-24-37(e)). § 45-24-73(a): 'one accessory dwelling unit (ADU) per lot shall be allowed by right' (§ 45-24-73(a)) on an owner-occupied property as a reasonable accommodation for family members with disabilities, on a residential lot of 20,000 sq. ft. or more, or within an existing footprint (§ 45-24-73(a)(1)-(3)). A municipality may not 'Restrict tenants based on familial relationships or age unless such restriction is necessary to comply with the terms of the federal subsidy related to affordability' (§ 45-24-73(b)(2)(i)), require low- or moderate-income occupancy outside inclusionary zoning or comprehensive permits (§ 45-24-73(b)(2)(xi)), or 'Revoke the permitted status or otherwise require the disassembly of a legally established ADU upon transfer of title or occupancy' (§ 45-24-73(b)(2)(xii)). Conflicting condominium or homeowners association restrictions 'shall be void as against public policy' (§ 45-24-73(b)(6)). title: Casualty and Mitigation Rules Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Your lease cannot take away the tenant's fire and casualty rights or your duty to re-rent after abandonment, because both are in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and a lease may not make the tenant waive any right or remedy under that Act. If fire or another casualty substantially impairs the tenant's use of the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease by written notice within 14 days, getting back prepaid rent and the security deposit less the deductions the deposit statute allows, or, if staying is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value, counted from the date of the fire. The section has no exception for a fire the tenant caused, so plan on these rights applying either way; your remedy then is a damages claim against a tenant who caused it negligently or deliberately. If a tenant abandons the unit, you must send the certified-letter notice and then make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental; if you don't, the lease is treated as ended when you learned of the abandonment. A waiver clause is unenforceable, and knowingly using one exposes you to actual damages plus up to three months' rent and attorney's fees. Case law was not searched.
notes: RI: Present (both rules are in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and cannot be waived). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a): 'A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant: (1) Agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under this chapter' (§ 34-18-17(a)(1)); § 34-18-17(b): 'A provision prohibited by subsection (a) included in a rental agreement is unenforceable. If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known to be prohibited, the tenant may recover, in addition to his or her actual damages, an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney’s fees.' (§ 34-18-17(b)). Casualty: § 34-18-33(a): if the unit or premises are 'damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty to an extent that enjoyment of the dwelling unit is substantially impaired' (§ 34-18-33(a)), the tenant may vacate and give written notice 'within fourteen (14) days thereafter' (§ 34-18-33(a)(1)) or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part with rent 'reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value of the dwelling unit' (§ 34-18-33(a)(2)); (b) return of security and prepaid rent, accounting 'as of the date of the fire or casualty' (§ 34-18-33(b)); (c) landlord's tort action for fire 'caused either negligently or deliberately by the tenant' (§ 34-18-33(c)) is preserved; the section has no tenant-fault exception to the tenant's options and no landlord termination right. Mitigation: § 34-18-40: after abandonment, certified letter, seven days, then 'the landlord shall make reasonable efforts to rent the premises at a fair rental' (§ 34-18-40); 'If the landlord fails to use reasonable efforts to rent the dwelling unit at fair rental, or if the landlord accepts the abandonment as a surrender, the rental agreement is deemed to be terminated by the landlord as of the date the landlord has notice of the abandonment.' (§ 34-18-40). Related planned clauses: casualty-termination-ri (landlord option preserving § 34-18-33), tenant-caused-damage-ri (damages only). Case law on casualty or mitigation waivers not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Families With Children
bodyText: Rhode Island fair housing law protects families with children: anyone under 18 living with a parent, a legal custodian or the custodian's written designee, and anyone who is pregnant or securing custody of a child. You may not refuse to rent, ask about familial status, set different terms or fees, misrepresent availability or advertise a preference because a household has children. Exemptions are narrow: a two-unit building where you live in the other unit; an owner-occupied building of four units or fewer where a unit is already occupied by a senior or infirm person for whom children would be a demonstrated hardship; housing under a state or federal elderly program; housing solely for people 62 or older; and qualifying 55-or-older housing. You may apply reasonable occupancy limits set by state or local codes, by space and safety, to every household alike. No statute requires your lease to address children. Lead law adds a rule: you may not retaliate against a tenant, with or without a lease, for seeking lead-safe housing, including for a pregnant woman or a child under six. Municipal ordinances and case law were not searched.
notes: RI: Present (familial status protection; no required lease term on children). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-37-3(7)(i): '“Familial status” means one or more individuals who have not attained the age of eighteen (18) years being domiciled with' (§ 34-37-3(7)(i)) a parent or legal custodian, or a designee with written permission (a non-relative designee only after six months' domicile); § 34-37-3(7)(ii): 'The protections afforded against discrimination on the basis of familial status shall apply to any person who is pregnant or is in the process of securing legal custody of any individual who has not attained the age of eighteen (18) years.' (§ 34-37-3(7)(ii)). Inquiry, refusal, different terms, advertising, misrepresenting availability: § 34-37-4(a). Exemptions, R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-37-4.1(a): 'Nothing in this chapter requires an owner of a housing accommodation to rent to a family with children if: (1) The housing accommodation is two (2) units, one of which is occupied by the owner' (§ 34-37-4.1(a)(1)); (a)(2) four units or less, owner-occupied, where a unit is 'already occupied by a senior citizen or infirm person for whom the presence of children would constitute a demonstrated hardship' (§ 34-37-4.1(a)(2)); (a)(3) state or federal elderly housing programs; (a)(4) housing solely occupied by persons 62 or older; (a)(5) 55-or-older housing (80% occupancy, facilities and services, published policies); (b)(2) age inquiries allowed for qualifying housing. Occupancy limits: 'Nothing in this chapter limits the applicability of any reasonable local, state, or federal restrictions regarding the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling.' (§ 34-37-4.2(b)); see edu-occupancy-limits-ri. Lead retaliation: § 23-24.6-23(c)(4): 'It shall be unlawful to take retaliatory actions against tenants arising from enforcement of the provisions of this chapter or chapter 128.1 of title 42; this prohibition against retaliatory actions applies whether or not the tenant has a lease.' (§ 23-24.6-23(c)(4)); guidelines cover action 'based on the presence of a pregnant woman or child under age six (6) who in any manner seeks to enforce their right to housing in which lead hazards have been corrected' (§ 23-24.6-23(c)(4)); remedies 'as provided for in chapter 18 of title 34' (§ 23-24.6-23(c)(4)). title: No Confession of Judgment
bodyText: Your lease may not authorize anyone, including you or your attorney, to confess judgment against the tenant on any claim arising out of the rental agreement, meaning a clause letting a court judgment be entered against the tenant without a contested case. Such a clause is unenforceable. If you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. Rhode Island court rules provide no confessed-judgment or confessed-ejectment procedure for residential tenancies, so a claim for unpaid rent or possession must go through the ordinary District Court process. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws, the loaded regulations and the court rules were searched; case law was not.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a): 'A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant:' (§ 34-18-17(a)) ... '(2) Authorizes any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement' (§ 34-18-17(a)(2)); § 34-18-17(b): 'A provision prohibited by subsection (a) included in a rental agreement is unenforceable. If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known to be prohibited, the tenant may recover, in addition to his or her actual damages, an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney’s fees.' (§ 34-18-17(b)). Search for any other route: RI-confession-of-judgment-1 (confess judgment, confession of judgment, cognovit, warrant of attorney, judgment by confession, consent/agreed judgment, confessed ejectment, no context limb; hits 15, OK; real positive § 34-18-17 and synthetic positives passed; other hits are lender, small-loan, debt-management, structured-settlement and rental-purchase bans (§§ 19-14.1-1, 19-14.2-2, 19-14.8-28, 27-9.3-7, 6-44-4), the statutory power of attorney § 18-16-9, UCC § 6A-3-104 and pension consent judgments; no court rule provides for confessed judgment or confessed ejectment in landlord-tenant cases). title: Deceptive Trade Practices Act and Rentals
bodyText: Rhode Island's Deceptive Trade Practices Act makes unfair or deceptive acts or practices in trade or commerce unlawful, including any act that is unfair or deceptive to the consumer and any practice that misleads the public in a material respect. Trade and commerce covers advertising, offering, selling or distributing services and real or personal property, and a consumer who leases goods or services for household purposes and loses money may sue for actual damages or $500, whichever is greater, with possible triple damages and attorney's fees. The statute does not say expressly whether renting an apartment is covered, and we did not search case law, so assume the Act may apply to your advertising, fees and dealings with tenants. Since January 1, 2026, short-term lodging prices must be advertised as the federal junk-fee rule requires. The Act has no rule about blank spaces in a lease or giving the tenant a copy at signing. Plainly, don't misstate rent, fees, amenities or the condition of a unit. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.
notes: RI: Present (Deceptive Trade Practices Act exists; its reach to residential leases is not settled by the text). R.I. Gen. Laws § 6-13.1-2: 'Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce are declared unlawful.' (§ 6-13.1-2). § 6-13.1-1(5) (version effective March 31, 2026): '“Trade” and “commerce” mean the advertising, offering for sale, sale, or distribution of any services and any property, tangible or intangible, real, personal, or mixed' (§ 6-13.1-1(5)); the definition does not say 'lease' or 'rent'. Listed practices include 'Engaging in any act or practice that is unfair or deceptive to the consumer' (§ 6-13.1-1(6)(xiii)) and 'Advertising, displaying, or offering a price for live-event tickets or short-term lodging in violation of 16 C.F.R. Part 464' (§ 6-13.1-1(6)(xxi), added by R.I. Pub. L. 2025, chs. 371, 372, effective January 1, 2026). Private action: § 6-13.1-5.2(a): 'Any person who purchases or leases goods or services primarily for personal, family, or household purposes and thereby suffers any ascertainable loss of money or property, real or personal' (§ 6-13.1-5.2(a)) may sue in superior court 'to recover actual damages or five hundred dollars ($500), whichever is greater' (§ 6-13.1-5.2(a)); treble damages discretionary; attorney's fees (§ 6-13.1-5.2(d)). FTC interpretations given 'great weight' (§ 6-13.1-3). Exemption for 'actions or transactions permitted under laws administered by the department of business regulation or other regulatory body or officer acting under statutory authority of this state or the United States' (§ 6-13.1-4(a)). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: whether a residential rental is 'trade or commerce' (§ 6-13.1-2) and whether a tenant 'leases goods or services' (§ 6-13.1-5.2(a)) is a case-law question; case law was not searched, so the row says the Act may apply. title: Keeping Survivor Information Confidential
bodyText: Since July 1, 2026, if a tenant or household member gives you written verification to end a lease early as a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, you must keep that verification, the fact that the person is a victim, and their personal identifying information (such as address, Social Security number, email, phone number and birthdate) in strict confidence. Don't disclose any of it to any other person or entity unless the victim asks for and consents to the disclosure in writing, or another law requires it. You also may not refuse to rent to an applicant because they ended a lease this way or asked for a lock change, and a lease cannot waive these rules. Even before any termination, fair housing law bars asking applicants or tenants whether anyone in the household is or has been a domestic abuse victim. If a tenant is in the Secretary of State's Address Confidentiality Program, knowingly obtaining or disclosing their actual address without authority carries a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per disclosure. The District Court can order you to stop a violation. Case law was not searched.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-63(b) (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): 'The written verification provided to the lessor or owner, including the fact that an individual is a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, shall be maintained in strict confidence. The lessor or owner shall keep this information and any further personally-identifiable information of the tenant and tenant's household members (such as address, social security number, email, phone number, birthdate) confidential and shall not disclose this information to any other entity, party, or individual, except to the extent that such disclosure is: (1) Requested and consented to in writing by the tenant or household member of the tenant who is the victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking; or (2) Otherwise required by applicable law.' (§ 34-18-63(b), act text with markup removed). Verification types in § 34-18-63(a)(3). No refusal to rent for having terminated under § 34-18-63 or requested a lock change under § 34-18-65 (§ 34-18-64); district court equity jurisdiction (§ 34-18-66); 'A waiver of §§ 34-18-63 through 34-18-65, shall be void and unenforceable.' (§ 34-18-67; heading says '§§ 34-18-63 through 34-18-64', text says through 34-18-65: flagged, not resolved). Inquiry ban: § 34-37-4(a) bars any written or oral inquiry 'concerning whether a tenant or applicant or a member of the household is, or has been, or is threatened with being the victim of domestic abuse' (§ 34-37-4(a)). A person who violates this section shall be assessed a civil penalty of not more than five thousand dollars ($5,000).' (§ 42-164-10); agencies must accept the substitute address (§ 42-164-5, seen in excerpt; binds state and local agencies only). Pub. L. 2026, ch. 147 and synthetic positive passed; other hits bind courts, agencies, employers (§ 28-57-11), insurers (§ 27-60.1-4) and the program; no other landlord duty). title: No Employee Background-Check Mandate
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to run background checks on maintenance workers, property managers or other employees who have keys to or enter tenants' units. If you choose to screen, Rhode Island employment law (not landlord-tenant law) governs how and when an employer may ask about criminal records, and that law was not reviewed for this row. What landlord-tenant law does control is entry: whoever enters for you must follow the two-day notice and reasonable-time rules, and you remain responsible for how your staff use keys. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; employment-law details, municipal ordinances and case law were not.

title: No Eviction Penalty Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute written specifically against lease clauses that penalize a tenant because you served an eviction notice or filed an eviction case. Such a clause is still limited by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. A lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Act or agree to pay your attorney's fees in a way the Act does not allow, and the Act allows fees in a nonpayment case only if the tenant received a five-day demand notice in the prior six months and the nonpayment was willful. A clause that does either is unenforceable, and knowingly using it lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. A court may also refuse to enforce an unconscionable term. So don't add an eviction fee, notice fee or flat penalty for being sued; recover only what the Act and the court award. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws, the loaded regulations and court rules were searched; case law was not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (statute aimed at lease clauses that impose a penalty because of an eviction notice or action). The general limits that reach such clauses: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a): a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under this chapter' (§ 34-18-17(a)(1)) or 'Agrees to pay the landlord’s attorney’s fees inconsistent with this chapter' (§ 34-18-17(a)(3)); § 34-18-17(b): such a provision 'is unenforceable' and deliberate use of known-prohibited provisions lets the tenant recover actual damages plus 'an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney’s fees' (§ 34-18-17(b)). The Act's own fee and cost rules (nonpayment fees only after a demand notice in the prior six months and willful nonpayment, § 34-18-35; § 34-18-43 after termination) are explained in edu-attorney-fees-ri and edu-no-notice-fee-rule-ri; unconscionability (§ 34-18-13) in edu-severability-limits-ri. title: No Liability Waivers or Indemnity for Your Liability
bodyText: Your lease may not excuse or limit any liability the law places on you as landlord, or make the tenant indemnify you for that liability or its costs. That covers clauses saying you are not responsible for injuries, property damage, repairs, security or acts of your employees, and hold-harmless or indemnity clauses that shift your own legal liability to the tenant. Such a clause is unenforceable, and knowingly using one lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. What a lease may still do: hold the tenant responsible for damage the tenant, household or guests cause, require renters insurance if the lease says so, and leave you free to sue a tenant who negligently or deliberately causes a fire. Write those terms as the tenant's own responsibilities, not as a release of yours. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; case law was not.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a): a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant '(4) Agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law or to indemnify the landlord for that liability or the costs connected with the liability.' (§ 34-18-17(a)(4)); § 34-18-17(b): 'A provision prohibited by subsection (a) included in a rental agreement is unenforceable.' (§ 34-18-17(b)); deliberate use of known-prohibited provisions: actual damages plus 'an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney’s fees' (§ 34-18-17(b)). The tenant's own statutory duty not to damage the premises (§ 34-18-24(6), printed in full) and the landlord's tort claim for tenant-caused fire (§ 34-18-33(c)) remain. No general contract statute voiding exculpatory clauses found. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (§§ 34-18-17, 34-18-24, 34-18-33).

title: Fair Housing in Rhode Island
bodyText: Rhode Island's Fair Housing Practices Act protects more groups than federal law: race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, lawful source of income (including housing vouchers), veterans with an honorable or general discharge, servicemembers, country of ancestral origin, disability, age (adults 18 and over), familial status, and victims of domestic abuse or people who have sought a protective order. Treat homelessness (housing status) as protected too; it appears in the Act's definitions. You may not ask about these traits, refuse to rent, set different terms, misrepresent availability, delay an application, advertise a preference or retaliate against anyone who complains. Exemptions are narrow and class-by-class: families with children (owner-occupied two-unit buildings and senior housing), source of income (owner-occupied buildings of three units or fewer), religious organizations and private clubs, and choosing a roommate of a particular gender for a unit you will share. There is no general small-landlord exemption and none for advertising. A tenant may file with the Commission for Human Rights within one year; penalties reach $10,000 for a first violation and $50,000 for repeats, plus damages and attorney's fees, and either side may move the case to Superior Court, where a jury and punitive damages are available. Case law was not searched.
notes: RI: Present. Rhode Island Fair Housing Practices Act, chapter 34-37. Protected classes in R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-37-4(a): race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, lawful source of income, 'military status as a veteran with an honorable discharge or an honorable or general administrative discharge, servicemember in the armed forces' (§ 34-37-4(a)), country of ancestral origin, disability, age (§ 34-37-3(1): '“Age” means anyone over the age of eighteen (18).'), familial status, and status as a victim of domestic abuse or as someone who has sought a restraining order (§ 34-37-4(a)). Housing status appears in the definition of 'Discriminate' (§ 34-37-3(5)) and the policy section (§ 34-37-1, seen in hit) but not in the operative lists of § 34-37-4(a): DRAFTING JUDGMENT, the row tells landlords to treat it as protected (cheaper error); flagged. Prohibited: inquiries, refusal, terms and services, advertising preference, misrepresenting availability, delaying applications (§ 34-37-4(a)); aiding or coercing (§ 34-37-4(l)); retaliation (§ 34-37-4(m), § 34-37-5.1). Exemptions are class-specific: familial status (§ 34-37-4.1), religious organizations and private clubs (§ 34-37-4.2(a)), lawful source of income in owner-occupied buildings of three units or less (§ 34-37-4.6), same- or opposite-gender roommate selection for a unit the owner, lessee, sublessee or assignee will share (§ 34-37-4(k)); no general owner-occupied small-building exemption and no advertising carve-out. Enforcement: charge to the Commission for Human Rights within one year (§ 34-37-5(b)); commission may order damages, costs and attorney's fees and civil penalties 'not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000)' for a first practice, up to $25,000 and $50,000 for repeat practices (§ 34-37-5(h)(2)); right to sue after 120 days (§ 34-37-5(l)); 'The complainant or the respondent may elect, within twenty (20) days after receipt of a finding of probable cause, to terminate by written notice to the commission all proceedings before the commission and have the case heard in the superior court.' (§ 34-37-5(n)); jury trial and punitive damages (§ 34-37-5(l), (o)(3)); judicial review (§ 34-37-6). Constitution: R.I. Const. art. I, § 2: 'No otherwise qualified person shall, solely by reason of race, gender or handicap be subject to discrimination by the state, its agents or any person or entity doing business with the state.' (R.I. Const. art. I, § 2); it reaches private landlords only as persons doing business with the state. title: No Foreign-Ownership Restriction
bodyText: Rhode Island has no law restricting foreign governments, foreign adversaries or noncitizens from buying, owning or leasing real estate, and no lease-length rule tied to a tenant's nationality. State law says the opposite: aliens may take, hold, transfer and convey real estate and sue to recover possession on the same terms as U.S. citizens. So nothing in state law stops you from renting to, or buying from, a foreign national or foreign-owned company. Separately, you may not ask applicants or tenants about immigration or citizenship status (see the immigration-status rules). Federal law on foreign investment near sensitive sites was not reviewed. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; federal law and case law were not.

Laws § 34-2-1: 'Aliens may take, hold, transmit, and convey real estate, and may sue for and recover possession of real estate in the same way and with the same effect as if they were citizens of the United States, and no title to real estate shall be invalid on account of the alienage of a former owner' (§ 34-2-1); no 2025-2026 act amends it. title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute written specifically about charging tenants for fines a city, town or the state imposes on you. But your lease may not make the tenant indemnify you for liability the law places on you, or the costs of that liability, and a fine for breaking your own legal duties (housing-code repairs, registration, smoke alarms, permits) is that kind of liability. A clause making the tenant reimburse such fines is unenforceable, and knowingly using it exposes you to actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. Where the tenant caused the problem, for example by breaking the tenant's own housing-code duties or damaging the unit, you may recover your loss as damages for the tenant's breach, so write the lease in those terms. Some code citations, such as fire-code citations, can be issued to an occupant directly. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (statute specifically on passing government fines to tenants). Limits that apply: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a)(4): a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law or to indemnify the landlord for that liability or the costs connected with the liability.' (§ 34-18-17(a)(4)); unenforceable, with damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and fees for knowing use (§ 34-18-17(b)). Tenant's own code duty: § 34-18-24(1): a tenant shall 'Comply with all obligations primarily imposed upon tenants by applicable provisions of building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety' (§ 34-18-24(1)); (6) no damage to the premises. Fire-code citations can name an occupant directly (§ 23-28.2-14(e), seen in battery hit, not read). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: a fine imposed on the landlord for the landlord's own duty is a 'liability of the landlord arising under law', so a clause making the tenant reimburse it is an indemnity the Act bars; reimbursement for a condition the tenant caused can be framed as the tenant's damages for breach of § 34-18-24.
