Municipal ordinances not searched. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (§§ 34-18-17, 34-18-24).

title: No Immigration or Citizenship Inquiries
bodyText: Since July 2, 2025, you and anyone acting for you may not make any inquiry about, or prompted by, the immigration or citizenship status of a tenant, applicant or occupant of residential rental property, and may not require anyone to make a statement, representation or certification about their status. Don't base rental decisions on status either: you can't lawfully learn it by asking, and country of ancestral origin is a fair housing protected class. Remove citizenship, Social Security-only and immigration questions from applications and leases. You may still ask for information or documents needed to verify an applicant's income and financial qualifications, or to verify the identity of an applicant or occupant, and you may comply with any obligation under federal law (for example, a federal housing program's rules). Accept identity documents without treating them as proof of status: a Rhode Island driver privilege card or state ID may not be used as evidence of citizenship or immigration status. No city, town or housing agency may require you to collect or report status, and no Rhode Island law bars renting to someone because of their status. Case law was not searched.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-62(a) (R.I. Pub. L. 2025, chs. 395, 396, effective July 2, 2025): 'No landlord or any agent of the landlord shall: (1) Make any inquiry regarding or based on the immigration or citizenship status of a tenant, prospective tenant, occupant, or prospective occupant of residential rental property; or (2) Require that any tenant, prospective tenant, occupant, or prospective occupant of the rental property make any statement, representation, or certification concerning their immigration or citizenship status.' (§ 34-18-62(a)); (b) no municipality or housing agency may compel a landlord to inquire, report or refuse to rent based on status; (c) 'Nothing in this section shall prohibit a landlord from: (1) Complying with any legal obligation under federal law; or (2) Requesting information or documentation necessary to determine or verify the financial qualifications of a prospective tenant, or to determine or verify the identity of a prospective tenant or prospective occupant.' (§ 34-18-62(c)). The section states no separate penalty; tenant remedies would come from the Act generally (not analysed here). Related: country of ancestral origin is a fair housing class (§ 34-37-4(a)); a driver privilege card 'shall not be used as evidence of the holder’s citizenship or immigration status' (§ 31-10.4-2(h), seen in excerpt), and likewise a state identification card (§ 31-10.4-2.1(d), seen in excerpt). No statute makes renting to an unlawfully present person unlawful: RI-immigration-status-1 (immigration or citizenship status, unlawfully present, illegal alien/immigrant, undocumented, harboring, lawful presence within 1,500 characters of landlord/tenant/lease/rent/dwelling/housing/occupant/shelter; hits 65, OK; real positive § 34-18-62 and synthetic positive passed; other hits are criminal harboring of fugitives and child molesters, animal "harbors", harbors and ports, ID-card sections, student aid and data-privacy definitions; no rental-to-unlawfully-present rule). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (§ 34-18-62; §§ 31-10.4-2, 31-10.4-2.1 seen in excerpt).

title: Jury Waivers Not Offered
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute addresses a jury-trial waiver in a residential lease, and the library does not offer one. The state constitution keeps the right of trial by jury inviolate. An eviction or other landlord-tenant case starts in District Court, and any party may appeal within five days after judgment to Superior Court for a new trial on all questions of law and fact; there, a party must claim a jury under the court rules or the right is treated as waived. The Act's ban on waiving rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not plainly reach the jury right, which comes from the constitution, and whether a court would enforce a lease jury waiver signed before any dispute is a case-law question we did not research. If you want one, get legal advice and draft your own. From January 1, 2027, the five days expressly include weekends and holidays, and the party appealing pays a $75 filing fee instead of the old $50 attorney's fee and minimum costs. Case law was not searched.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (statute allowing, limiting or voiding a jury waiver in a residential lease). R.I. Const. art. I, § 15: 'The right of trial by jury shall remain inviolate.' (R.I. Const. art. I, § 15). R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-11-7: in an action 'originally brought in the superior court or removed to the superior court on appeal from a district court, if neither party claims a jury trial in accordance with applicable procedural rules, then jury trial as of right shall be deemed to be waived' (§ 9-11-7). Landlord-tenant appeals: § 9-12-10.1 (as amended by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 282, 283, § 1, effective January 1, 2027): 'In any civil action pursuant to chapter 18 of title 34, in the district court or other appropriate court, any party may cause the case to be removed for trial on all questions of law and fact to the superior court' (§ 9-12-10.1, act text with markup removed), by written claim 'within five (5) days after the judgment is entered' (§ 9-12-10.1) (from January 1, 2027, "inclusive of Saturdays, Sundays, or legal holidays", added by the act); from January 1, 2027 the appellant pays a $75 filing fee and no longer the $50 attorney's fee and minimum costs (struck by the act). § 34-18-17(a)(1) bars waiving rights 'under this chapter'; the jury right comes from the Constitution and court rules, not chapter 34-18, so that bar does not plainly reach a jury waiver. Search: RI-jury-waiver-1 (jury trial, trial by jury, right to a jury, waiver of jury within 1,500 characters of tenant/landlord/lease/rental/eviction/possession/district court/housing; hits 11, OK; real positive § 34-37-5 and synthetic positive passed; hits are criminal and juvenile procedure, eminent domain (§ 45-29-28 lets parties waive by agreement), debt-management (§ 19-14.8-19) and rental-purchase (§ 5-55-4) bans on limiting jury rights, § 9-11-7 and fair housing § 34-37-5; no lease rule). Case law on pre-dispute jury waivers not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (R.I. Const. art. I, § 15; § 9-11-7; § 9-12-10.1 in the 2026 act).

title: No Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require apartment owners, at any size of complex, to adopt a key-control policy, keep a key log or background-check employees who can get into units. A written practice is still sensible risk management: limit who holds master keys, record who checks keys out, and rekey when keys are lost or staff leave. Two rules already shape how keys are used. Anyone entering for you must follow the entry rules (consent not unreasonably withheld, at least two days' notice except in an emergency or where impracticable, at reasonable times). And since July 1, 2026, on a qualifying request from a tenant or household member facing a threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, you must within two business days make a good-faith effort to change the locks or let the tenant do so. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.

title: Penalty for Using Prohibited Lease Terms
bodyText: If you deliberately use a lease containing terms you know Rhode Island prohibits, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees, on top of the term being unenforceable. The prohibited terms are those that make the tenant waive or give up rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, authorize a confession of judgment, make the tenant pay your attorney's fees in a way the Act does not allow, or excuse, limit or make the tenant indemnify you for liability the law places on you. Because the first category covers any right in the Act, a clause waiving deposit rules, casualty rights, entry notice or termination notice also counts. A real estate tax pass-through that leaves out the required statements is void but outside this penalty. A waiver of the survivor protections in effect since July 1, 2026 is void under its own section and, because those protections are part of the Act, is also a prohibited waiver that carries the penalty. Use the library's state-specific clauses instead of an out-of-state form. Case law was not searched.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(b): 'A provision prohibited by subsection (a) included in a rental agreement is unenforceable. If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known to be prohibited, the tenant may recover, in addition to his or her actual damages, an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney’s fees.' (§ 34-18-17(b)). The penalty attaches to the four prohibited provisions in § 34-18-17(a) (waiver of rights or remedies under chapter 34-18, confession of judgment, landlord's attorney's fees inconsistent with the chapter, exculpation or indemnity). Because (a)(1) bars any waiver of chapter 34-18 rights, a clause waiving another chapter right (for example the § 34-18-19 deposit rules or § 34-18-33 casualty rights) is within (a)(1). Section 6A-2.1-222(a) carries no § 34-18-17(b) penalty: real estate tax pass-through terms that omit the required statements are 'against public policy and void' (§ 6A-2.1-222(a)). § 34-18-67 (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): 'A waiver of §§ 34-18-63 through 34-18-65, shall be void and unenforceable.' (§ 34-18-67); its voidness overlaps (a)(1), since §§ 34-18-63 to 34-18-65 are in chapter 34-18 ('Chapter 34-18 of the General Laws entitled "Residential Landlord and Tenant Act" is hereby amended by adding thereto the following sections' (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, ch. 147, § 2)), so knowing use of such a waiver carries the § 34-18-17(b) penalty; DRAFTING JUDGMENT: the statute doesn't say whether § 34-18-67's own voidness rule displaces § 34-18-17(b), and the row reads the two together. No battery needed: the topic asks for the penalty, answered by the section read whole. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (§§ 34-18-17, 6A-2.1-222; § 34-18-67 in the act text).

title: No Crime-Free Lease Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring or regulating crime-free lease addenda, and no law requiring you to give police or child-protection investigators information about tenants or access to a unit. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act already gives you remedies for serious criminal conduct at the premises, and some cities and towns run their own nuisance or crime-free programs, which were not searched. One reporting duty applies only to short-term rentals: since January 1, 2026, every operator of a residential unit offered for tourist or transient use through a hosting platform must complete human trafficking awareness training within 180 days of first listing and every year after, and must adopt procedures for reporting suspected human trafficking to the National Human Trafficking Hotline or local police. For ordinary tenancies, respond to a warrant or subpoena as the law requires, and get advice before sharing tenant information informally. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (crime-free lease statute; landlord duty to give police or child-protection investigators information or access). One related duty, for short-term rentals only: R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-14.1-3(b) (effective January 1, 2026): 'Every operator of a hotel or short-term rental property in this state shall implement procedures and adopt policies for the reporting of suspected human trafficking to the National Human Trafficking Hotline or to a local law enforcement agency.' (§ 5-14.1-3(b)); (a) annual human-trafficking awareness training for every operator of a short-term rental property; § 5-14.1-1(5): '“Short-term rental property” means a residential unit used or offered for tourist or transient use through a hosting platform, as such terms are defined in § 42-63.1-2.' (§ 5-14.1-1(5)) (R.I. Pub. L. 2025, chs. 175, 176). title: What a Rhode Island Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Rhode Island has no single list of terms every lease must contain, does not require a written lease, and has no statute requiring you to hand the tenant a signed copy (do it anyway). What it does require is specific content. In a written lease: any fees beyond rent, listed in the same section as the rent with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a subsidy program requires a different format); which utilities are included in rent and which the tenant pays; and any renters-insurance requirement. With an oral tenancy, give the fee list, the utility split and any insurance requirement in writing, and give 30 days' written notice before changing fees. A tenant may recover any fee you did not disclose this way. At or before the start of every tenancy, disclose in writing the name, address and number of the manager and of the owner or owner's agent for notices, and keep it current; give a copy of your liability insurance declaration page with the written lease. For target housing, include the lead warning statement and acknowledgment, even in oral leases. Any agreement for the tenant to do repairs must be in a signed writing. If the lease passes real estate tax increases on to the tenant, the clause must state the tenant's proportionate share, the exact percentage and a proportionate refund of any abatement, or it is void. From January 1, 2027, shoreline property needs a written shoreline access disclosure. Case law was not searched.
notes: RI: Present (no single list of required lease contents; specific items must be in the lease or in writing). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a): parties 'may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by this chapter or other rule of law' (§ 34-18-15(a)); (a)(1) fees beyond rent 'in the same section as the rent disclosure' (§ 34-18-15(a)(1)), except where a subsidy program requires a different lease format; (a)(2) 'If there is no written lease, the landlord shall provide to the tenant, in writing, a list of all fees beyond the rent that apply to the rental of the unit. Any change in required fees must be disclosed in writing at least thirty (30) days prior to the change becoming effective.' (§ 34-18-15(a)(2)); (a)(3) 'In any lease agreement the landlord shall disclose which utility costs are included in the rent and which utility costs are the tenant’s responsibility. If there is no written lease, the landlord shall provide this information to the tenant in writing.' (§ 34-18-15(a)(3)); (a)(4) renters-insurance requirement 'must be stated in the lease' (§ 34-18-15(a)(4)); (a)(5) undisclosed fees recoverable. § 34-18-20(a): owner and manager names, addresses and numbers 'in writing, at or before the commencement of the tenancy' (§ 34-18-20(a)); kept current (§ 34-18-20(b)). § 34-18-22(a)(7): declaration page of the landlord's liability policy 'to the tenant with the written lease at the beginning of the tenancy' (§ 34-18-22(a)(7)). § 34-18-22(c): tenant repair agreements only in 'a writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration' (§ 34-18-22(c)(1)). 216-RICR-50-15-3.5.3(A)(2): lead warning statement and acknowledgment 'in each contract for the sale or lease of any residential dwelling, including oral leases' (216-RICR-50-15-3.5.3(A)(2)). title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island sets no minimum type size for a residential lease, and no court rule or statute bars you from relying on a lease, or part of one, because the print is small. Type-size rules in Rhode Island law apply to other contracts, such as car-rental agreements, insurance premium finance agreements and home-solicitation and retail installment contracts. Print your lease clearly anyway: a tenant who can read the terms is less likely to dispute them, and the lease's required disclosures (fees in the rent section, the utility split, any renters-insurance requirement, the lead acknowledgment) only protect you if the tenant can see them. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws, the loaded regulations and the court rules were searched; case law was not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (minimum type size or legibility rule for a printed residential lease, with or without an evidentiary sanction). Statute-wide search with terms and hit counts over the RI corpus (General Laws, Constitution, three loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws, District Court civil rules, Supreme Court rules): RI-lease-type-size-1 (illegible, legible, small print, fine print, printed clearly or legibly, type at least / of not less than / no smaller than, eight- or ten-point, within 1,500 characters of lease/rental agreement/tenant/lessee/contract; hits 21, OK; synthetic positives passed; type-size rules only for insurance premium finance agreements (§ 19-14.6-1), food labels, surplus lines notices, motor-vehicle rental agreements (§§ 31-34-4, 31-34-7), contest disclosures, social referral, foreclosure-rescue, home-solicitation and retail installment contracts; none for residential leases and no evidence rule); RI-sfr-occupancy-disclosure-1 (hits 106, OK) and RI-sfr-occupancy-disclosure-2 (hits 16, OK), see edu-no-lease-font-rules-ri. title: Terms a Rhode Island Lease Cannot Contain
bodyText: The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's list of prohibited provisions is not the only limit on a Rhode Island lease. A lease may not: make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Act; authorize a confession of judgment; make the tenant pay your attorney's fees beyond what the Act allows; excuse or limit your legal liability or make the tenant indemnify you for it; let you collect rent free of your repair and code duties; waive the security deposit rules; waive the survivor early-termination, no-refusal and lock-change protections in effect since July 1, 2026; give you a lien on the tenant's household goods or a right to seize property for rent; charge a convenience fee on rent unless you also accept a fee-free payment method; require a statement of immigration or citizenship status; pass on real estate tax increases without stating the tenant's proportional share, the exact percentage and a refund of any abatement; ban using cannabis by non-smoked, non-vaporized means; bar a small religious item on the entry door; or charge a tenant with a disability extra for a guide dog or other trained personal assistive animal (the tenant remains liable for damage it causes). Tenant repair or maintenance duties need a good-faith writing signed by both parties and adequate consideration, can never cover code compliance, and cannot reduce your duties to other tenants. Knowingly using a term the Act prohibits costs actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees, and a court may refuse to enforce any unconscionable term. Case law was not searched.

title: Questions You May Not Ask Applicants
bodyText: Rhode Island bars more than discrimination: you and your agents may not ask, in writing or orally, about an applicant's or tenant's race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, lawful source of income, veteran or servicemember status, country of ancestral origin, disability, age or familial status, or whether anyone in the household is or has been a domestic abuse victim or has sought a protective order. Since July 2, 2025, you also may not ask about immigration or citizenship status or require a statement about it. Questions you may ask: whether the applicant is 18 or older; questions confirming the source, amount and expected duration of income to apply your nondiscriminatory standards; questions verifying identity and financial qualifications; and age questions if the housing qualifies as 62-or-older or 55-or-older housing. Review application forms, screening scripts and online portals: a question about marital status, children, disability, benefits type or national origin can itself be a violation, even if you never use the answer. Case law was not searched.
notes: RI: Present. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-37-4(a): no owner or agent 'shall, directly or indirectly, make, or cause to be made, any written or oral inquiry concerning the race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, lawful source of income, military status as a veteran with an honorable discharge or an honorable or general administrative discharge, servicemember in the armed forces, country of ancestral origin, or disability, age, familial status' (§ 34-37-4(a)) nor any inquiry 'concerning whether a tenant or applicant or a member of the household is, or has been, or is threatened with being the victim of domestic abuse, or whether a tenant or applicant has obtained, or sought, or is seeking relief from any court in the form of a restraining order for protection from domestic abuse' (§ 34-37-4(a)), of any prospective purchaser, occupant or tenant. Allowed: 'Nothing in this section shall be construed to prohibit any oral or written inquiry as to whether the prospective purchaser or tenant is eighteen (18) years of age or older, or to confirm the source, amount, and expected duration of the lawful source of income of the prospective purchaser or tenant' (§ 34-37-4(a)); age questions for qualifying 62-or-older or 55-or-older housing (§ 34-37-4.1(b)(2)). Separate inquiry ban for immigration or citizenship status (§ 34-18-62(a), effective July 2, 2025), with identity and financial verification allowed (§ 34-18-62(c)). No separate ban on keeping records of protected traits: the text bars inquiries, not records (the list-style section was read whole, so no battery needed). Remedies: § 34-37-5 (see edu-fair-housing-ri). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: No Senior Housing Staff Work Card
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require work cards or background checks for maintenance or management staff in private housing for people 55 or older, or in any other private rental housing. Rules that do require criminal records checks cover licensed health-care settings, such as long-term-care hospitals and personal care aides, and public housing authorities' elderly housing, not a private landlord's employees. If your community qualifies as 55-or-older or 62-or-older housing under fair housing law, that status turns on occupancy, facilities and published policies, not on staff screening. Screening staff who have keys to units of older residents is still prudent, following Rhode Island employment law (not reviewed here). Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; employment-law details and case law were not.

title: No State Owner-Occupancy Rental Limit
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statewide law limiting the rental of homes in single-family zones to owners who live on the lot. State zoning law points the other way: households are a permitted use in every residential zoning district, and one accessory dwelling unit per lot is allowed by right in three situations, only one of which (an ADU built as a reasonable accommodation for family members with disabilities) requires the property to be owner-occupied. A city or town may not revoke a legally established ADU when the title or occupancy changes. Local zoning ordinances, which were not searched, still govern use, density and short-term rentals, so check the town's rules before converting or renting a property. Separately, a 2025 state tax on certain non-owner-occupied residential property may apply to rented homes; it was not reviewed for this row. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; local ordinances and case law were not.

Laws § 45-24-37(b) (version effective January 1, 2026): 'Notwithstanding any other provision of this chapter, the following uses are permitted uses within all residential zoning use districts of a municipality' (§ 45-24-37(b)), including '(1) Households' (§ 45-24-37(b)(1)); ADUs: § 45-24-73(a) (one ADU by right on an owner-occupied property as a reasonable accommodation for family members with disabilities, on residential lots of 20,000 sq. ft. or more, or within an existing footprint; only the first route turns on owner occupancy) and § 45-24-73(b)(2)(xii) (no revocation on 'transfer of title or occupancy'). title: Hot Water Temperature
bodyText: Rhode Island sets a minimum, not a maximum, for hot water. The state housing code defines heated water as water heated to at least 120 degrees Fahrenheit, and every unit's kitchen sink, bathroom sink and tub or shower must supply an adequate amount of heated and unheated running water under pressure at all times; you may not rent a unit that falls short. Your landlord-tenant duty matches it: supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, unless the building isn't required by law to be equipped for it or the hot water comes from equipment in the tenant's exclusive control on the tenant's own utility connection. No statute requires you to set a water heater no higher than a stated temperature or to reset it before each new tenant. Set it at or a little above 120 degrees: too low breaks the code, and much higher risks scalding. Local codes may be stricter. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; plumbing and building code regulations, municipal codes and case law were not.
notes: RI: Present (minimum heated-water temperature; no maximum or reset rule). R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-5(19): '“Heated water” means water heated to a temperature of not less than one hundred twenty degrees (120 °) fahrenheit.' (§ 45-24.3-5(19)). § 45-24.3-7: 'No person shall occupy as owner or occupant, or let to another for occupancy, any dwelling or dwelling unit' (§ 45-24.3-7) without a kitchen sink, lavatory and tub or shower that provide 'an adequate amount of heated and unheated running water under pressure' (§ 45-24.3-7(1)(i)). § 34-18-22(a)(6): landlord shall 'Supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times as required by § 45-24.3-7, or applicable local codes if more restrictive' (§ 34-18-22(a)(6)), except where hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection.
