title: No Radiator Cover Requirement
bodyText: Rhode Island has no law requiring you to install radiator covers when a tenant asks, or to attach a radiator-cover rider or notice to the lease. Your general duties still cover steam and hot-water heat: keep heating facilities in good and safe working order, and supply reasonable heat between October 1 and May 1 as the housing code requires. A hot, exposed radiator in a home with young children is a foreseeable injury risk, so consider offering covers on request. Local codes may say more. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal codes and case law were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (radiator covers on request; radiator-cover lease rider or notice). Statute-wide search over the RI corpus (General Laws, Constitution, three loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws, court rules): RI-steam-radiator-covers-1 (radiator, steam heat/pipes/risers, heating pipe/element/unit covers or guards, radiator covers/guards/shields, no context limb; hits 3, OK; synthetic positives passed; only motor-vehicle warranty parts (§ 31-5.4-2) and fixtures in property-law and tax definitions (§§ 34-17-1, 44-4-3)). Heating duties: § 34-18-22(a)(4), (6) (maintain heating facilities in good and safe working order; reasonable heat between October 1 and May 1). Municipal codes not searched. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (§ 34-18-22).

title: No Window Guard Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring window guards, window stops or other window-fall protection in rental housing, and no window-guard notice in the lease. The state housing code's window rules are about light, ventilation and screens: every habitable room needs a window or skylight to the outdoors, part of it openable, and screens are required in insect season. Window-opening limits for new construction may come from the building code, which was not searched. If young children live in an upper-floor unit, installing window stops or guards on request is a sensible safety step, as long as they don't block a required emergency exit. Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; building code regulations, municipal codes and case law were not.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (window guards, window stops or other window-fall prevention in rentals; window-guard lease notice). Statute-wide search over the RI corpus (General Laws, Constitution, three loaded RICR parts, 2025-2026 public laws, court rules): RI-window-guards-1 (window guards/stops/falls/bars/limiters/opening control devices, fall prevention or protection devices, children falling from windows, no context limb; hits 0, OK; all positives synthetic and passed). Housing-code window rules that do exist cover light, ventilation, openable area and screens (§§ 45-24.3-8, 45-24.3-10, seen in excerpt), not fall protection. Building code regulations and municipal codes not searched. Case law not searched. Rule 15: no section relied on beyond the battery.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: Rhode Island protects tenants who organize: you may not raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction because a tenant organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization. If you act within six months after a protected complaint, the law presumes retaliation unless you produce evidence otherwise, and a tenant who proves retaliation gets the Act's retaliation remedies and a defense to eviction. You may still evict for unpaid rent or for a code violation the tenant's household caused. State law gives ordinary tenants no separate right to hold meetings in common areas, distribute literature door to door or invite organizers into the building, so apply your building rules on common areas and solicitation evenly and never single out organizing. In federally assisted developments, a tenant association that represents a majority of tenants receives notices and a first chance to buy the property before a sale or conversion that ends the assistance. Municipal ordinances and case law were not searched.
notes: RI: Present (protection from retaliation only; no affirmative organizing or meeting right for ordinary tenancies). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-46(a): a landlord may not retaliate by increasing rent, decreasing services or bringing or threatening an action for possession because '(3) The tenant has organized or become a member of a tenants’ union or similar organization' (§ 34-18-46(a)(3)); § 34-18-46(b): remedies under § 34-18-34 and a defense to possession; 'evidence of a complaint within six (6) months before the alleged act of retaliation creates a presumption that the landlord’s conduct was in retaliation' (§ 34-18-46(b)); exceptions in (c) (tenant-caused code violation, rent default, code or eminent-domain alterations with relocation met). Federally assisted developments: tenant associations receive notices and a first opportunity to purchase (§§ 34-45-4(9), 34-45-5(d), 34-45-7; see edu-tenant-purchase-rights-ri). Search: RI-tenant-right-to-organize-1 (tenant union/association/organization/council, resident association, organize tenants, right to organize/assemble/meet, distribute literature/leaflets/flyers, door-to-door, meeting rooms, common areas for meetings, within 1,500 characters of landlord/lessor/owner/licensee/tenant/resident/dwelling/housing/park; hits 20, OK; real positive § 34-18-46 and synthetic positive passed; other hits are nursing-home family councils (§ 23-17.5-30), mobile-home park resident associations (chapter 31-44), chapter 34-45 tenant associations, public-employee organizing and door-to-door sales; no right to meet in common areas or distribute literature in ordinary rentals). Retaliation remedies detailed in edu-retaliation-ri. Municipal ordinances not searched. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (§§ 34-18-46, 34-45-4, 34-45-5, 34-45-7).

title: Voucher Program Inspections
bodyText: You may not turn down an applicant who pays with a Housing Choice Voucher or other rental assistance because the program will inspect the unit, require a lease addendum or impose other program paperwork. Rhode Island defines a protected lawful source of income to include any federal, state or local rental assistance or housing subsidy, including Section 8 vouchers, and any requirement associated with the program, so refusing because of the inspection is treated as refusing because of the voucher. The one exemption: a building of three units or fewer where you live in one unit. Rhode Island has no statute on a tenant who refuses a subsidized-housing inspection; any such rule comes from the federal program and your program contract, and you still need to follow the state entry rules (consent not unreasonably withheld, at least two days' notice except in an emergency). If a unit fails inspection, the program's repair and payment rules apply; federal program rules were not reviewed here. Case law was not searched.
notes: RI: Present (refusing a voucher tenancy because of the program's inspection is source-of-income discrimination; no statute on tenant refusal of subsidized-housing inspections). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-37-3(18): lawful source of income includes 'any federal, state, or local rental assistance or housing subsidy program, including Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers as authorized by 42 U.S.C. § 1437; and any requirement associated with such public assistance, rental assistance, or housing subsidy program.' (§ 34-37-3(18)); refusal, different terms and delaying applications because of lawful source of income barred (§ 34-37-4(a)); exemption for buildings of three units or less, one owner-occupied (§ 34-37-4.6). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: a program's unit inspection is a 'requirement associated with' the program, so refusing because of it is refusing because of the protected source; no case law searched. Search: RI-subsidized-inspection-refusal-1 (inspect* within 600 characters of Section 8, housing voucher, housing subsidy, rental assistance, subsidized housing, housing authority, federally insured or assisted; hits 2, OK; synthetic positive passed; only a dairy compact and the HUD lead-inspection finding § 42-128.1-2; no state rule on subsidized-housing inspections or tenant refusals). Entry for inspections generally: § 34-18-26 (see landlords-access-ri, edu-landlord-entry-ri). Federal program rules (HUD Housing Quality Standards / NSPIRE) not searched. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (§§ 34-37-3, 34-37-4, 34-37-4.6).

title: Keeping Tenant Information Confidential
bodyText: Rhode Island has no general law listing what a landlord may not disclose about tenants or applicants, but several specific rules apply. Since July 1, 2026, if a tenant gives you verification to end a lease as a survivor of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, you must keep it, the victim status and the household's personal identifying information (address, Social Security number, email, phone, birthdate) strictly confidential, disclosing only on the victim's written request and consent or where the law requires. Knowingly obtaining or disclosing the actual address of someone in the state's Address Confidentiality Program without authority carries a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per disclosure. A real estate licensee working for you treats a client's finances, offers and motivations as confidential information. And if you keep Social Security, driver's license, financial account or health information, the state's Identity Theft Protection Act requires security, retention limits, secure destruction and breach notices (see the tenant-records rules). Outside these rules, share tenant information only as needed to run the tenancy, such as with a screening company, a collection agency or a court. Case law was not searched.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (general statute barring a landlord from disclosing tenants' or applicants' information); specific rules present. Survivors: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-63(b) (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws): the lessor or owner 'shall not disclose this information to any other entity, party, or individual, except to the extent that such disclosure is' (§ 34-18-63(b)) requested and consented to in writing by the victim or otherwise required by law (see edu-dv-confidentiality-ri). Address Confidentiality Program: § 42-164-10: 'No person shall knowingly and intentionally obtain or disclose a program participant’s actual address knowing that they were not authorized to do so.' (§ 42-164-10); civil penalty up to $5,000 per disclosure. Brokers: § 5-20.6-2(6) defines 'Confidential information' (§ 5-20.6-2(6)) to include a tenant's willingness to pay more, prior offers, motivating factors and 'Any information about a party’s assets, liabilities, income, or expenses.' (§ 5-20.6-2(6)(viii)); licensees owe a duty to protect a client's confidential information (§ 5-20.6-5(a)(3), seen in excerpt). Data security and breach notice under the Identity Theft Protection Act (chapter 11-49.3) are explained in edu-tenant-records-ri (not reread here). Search: RI-tenant-confidential-information-4 (disclose/release/reveal/share/sell/provide personal, confidential, private, identifying or personally identifiable information/data/records, either order, within 600 characters of tenant/applicant/lessee/landlord/lessor/household member; hits 7, OK; real positive R.I. Pub. L. 2026, ch. 147 and synthetic positives passed; other hits are firearms applications, insurer abuse information, human services records, broker relationship disclosures and racing commission applicants; no general landlord disclosure ban). RI-tenant-confidential-information-1, -2 and -3 recorded as failed (the act's markup splits 'personally-' / 'identifiable' at a line break), rerun as 4. Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (§§ 34-18-63 in the act, 42-164-10, 5-20.6-2).

title: Screening Applicants in Rhode Island
bodyText: Rhode Island has no single tenant-screening act, but several rules shape screening. You may not charge an application fee. You may require an official state criminal background check and a credit check; if the applicant supplies one issued within 90 days you may not charge for it, and otherwise you may charge only the actual cost and must give the applicant a copy. A minimum-income test may count only the share of rent the tenant will pay after any voucher or subsidy. You may not ask about fair housing traits, domestic-abuse status or immigration status. Since July 1, 2026, you may not refuse an applicant because they ended an earlier lease as a survivor of abuse or asked a landlord to change locks. An applicant whose conviction was expunged may lawfully answer that they were never convicted. Rhode Island has no conditional-offer or look-back rule for criminal history, but if you deny housing to a holder of a certificate of recovery and re-entry based on a criminal records check, the law bars claims against you for that denial. Use one written standard for everyone, applied the same way. Federal credit-reporting law and case law were not searched.
notes: RI: Present (no dedicated screening-fairness act; specific rules). Screening costs: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-59(a): no landlord, broker, property manager or designee may 'require or demand any prospective tenant to pay for a rental application fee' (§ 34-18-59(a)); official state criminal background checks and credit checks allowed, at no charge if the applicant supplies one issued within 90 days, otherwise at 'not more than the actual cost' with a copy to the applicant (§ 34-18-59(b)(1)-(2)) (see edu-application-fees-ri). Income test: § 34-37-4(c): 'the standard for assessing eligibility shall be based only on the portion of the rent to be paid by the tenant, taking into account the value of any federal, state, or local rental assistance or housing subsidy' (§ 34-37-4(c)). Inquiries: § 34-37-4(a); § 34-18-62. Survivors: § 34-18-64 (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026): 'A lessor or owner shall not refuse to enter into a rental agreement, nor shall a housing subsidy provider deny assistance, based on an applicant having terminated a rental agreement under § 34-18-63 or based upon an applicant having requested a change of locks under § 34-18-65.' (§ 34-18-64). Expunged convictions: § 12-1.3-4(b): in 'any application for employment, license, or other civil right or privilege' a person whose conviction was expunged 'may state that he or she has never been convicted of the crime' (§ 12-1.3-4(b)); custodians may not disclose expunged records (§ 12-1.3-4(c)); R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 171, 172 amend §§ 12-1.3-1 to -3 only. Certificate holders: § 13-8.2-8: 'An individual or entity that denies employment, professional licensing, housing or other benefits or opportunities to a holder of a certificate of recovery & re-entry on the basis of a criminal records check shall not be liable for civil damages or subject to any claim, demand, cause of action, or proceeding of any nature as a result of such denial.' (§ 13-8.2-8). Credit-report notice statute § 6-13.1-21 applies to applications 'for credit, employment, or insurance' (§ 6-13.1-21(a)), not rentals by its terms; federal FCRA not searched. Eviction-record sealing: § 34-18-60 (edu-eviction-record-sealing-ri). Search: RI-tenant-screening-1 (criminal records/history/convictions/background, convicted, arrest records, expunged, sealed records, conditional offer, look-back, negligent rental/leasing within 300 characters of rent/lease/tenant/housing/landlord/lessor; hits 190, OK; real positive § 34-18-59 and synthetic positive passed; hits are criminal penalty clauses, expungement (§ 12-1.3-4), the certificate of recovery and re-entry (chapter 13-8.2) and § 34-18-59; no conditional-offer, look-back or negligent-renting rule). Case law not searched. Rule 15: written section-open (§§ 34-18-59, 34-37-4, 34-18-62, 12-1.3-4, 13-8.2-8, 6-13.1-21; § 34-18-64 in the act). DRAFTING JUDGMENT: a rental application is treated as an application for an other civil right or privilege under § 12-1.3-4(b); no case law searched.

title: Landlord's Right of Entry
bodyText: Tenant will not unreasonably withhold consent to Landlord's entry into the property to inspect it, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or show it to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors. Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable to do so, Landlord will give Tenant at least two days' notice of Landlord's intent to enter, and will enter only at reasonable times. Landlord may enter without Tenant's consent in an emergency, or during any absence of Tenant of more than seven days if entry is reasonably necessary to protect the property. Landlord will not abuse this right of access or use it to harass Tenant.
notes: RI: Overrides `landlords-access`, whose "right of reasonable access" does not fit Rhode Island's consent-based rule. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-26(a): 'A tenant shall not unreasonably withhold consent to the landlord to enter into the dwelling unit in order to inspect the premises, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers, or contractors.' (§ 34-18-26(a)); (b): 'A landlord may enter the dwelling unit without consent of the tenant in case of emergency, or, during any absence of the tenant in excess of seven (7) days, if reasonably necessary for the protection of the property.' (§ 34-18-26(b)); (c): 'Except in case of emergency or unless it is impracticable to do so, the landlord shall give the tenant at least two (2) days' notice of his or her intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times.' (§ 34-18-26(c)). The statute does not say the two-day notice must be written; the clause leaves the form open. Other access grounds (court order, § 34-18-39 repairs, abandonment or surrender, § 34-18-26(d)) need no lease text. Remedies for refused or abusive access: § 34-18-45. The dormant `landlords-access-hi-ky-ri-dc` (48 hours) is left switched off (RI log §5). See `edu-landlord-entry-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Notice of Extended Absence
bodyText: Tenant will occupy the property only as a dwelling unit unless Landlord and Tenant agree otherwise in writing. If Tenant anticipates being away from the property for more than 10 consecutive days, Tenant will notify Landlord no later than the first day of the absence.
notes: RI: Overrides `extended-absence-notice-ks`, whose seven-day trigger is shorter than the absence Rhode Island lets a lease cover. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-27: 'Unless otherwise agreed, a tenant shall occupy his or her dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit. The rental agreement may require that the tenant notify the landlord of any anticipated extended absence from the premises in excess of ten (10) days no later than the first day of the extended absence.' (§ 34-18-27). The KS clause's damages sentence is dropped: Rhode Island sets no damages rule for a missed notice, so the ordinary remedies for breach apply. The landlord's separate entry right during an absence of more than seven days (§ 34-18-26(b)) is in `landlords-access-ri`. See `edu-extended-absence-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Keys
bodyText: At the start of the Term, Tenant will receive the keys specified by Landlord and will sign a receipt acknowledging the number and type of keys provided. Tenant will return all keys to Landlord at the end of the Term. If Tenant fails to return all keys or loses a key, Landlord may re-key the applicable locks and charge Tenant the reasonable cost, which is listed with the Rent in this Lease's Rent section. Tenant may not duplicate keys or change the locks without Landlord's consent, except as Rhode Island law allows a tenant or household member who reasonably believes they are under an imminent threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking to have the locks changed. For a lock change Landlord makes on that request, Landlord's charge will not exceed the reasonable price customarily charged for changing such locks in the community.
notes: RI: Overrides `keys` (fee screen, rules 26 and 53). From July 1, 2026, R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-65 (added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 2, effective July 1, 2026; not yet in the compiled General Laws) requires the landlord, within two business days of a request by all tenants in possession or a court order, to make a good faith effort to change the locks or give permission to change them, where a tenant or household member reasonably believes they are under imminent threat, and caps the fee: 'A lessor or owner may charge a fee for the expense of changing the locks. The fee shall not exceed the reasonable price customarily charged for changing such locks in that community.' (§ 34-18-65(d)); if the landlord does not act, the tenant or household member 'may change the locks without the owner's permission' (§ 34-18-65(e)), and a waiver is void (§ 34-18-67). The shared clause's uncapped "charge the cost" and its flat ban on lock changes would read wrongly for those requests. The lost-key charge is a fee beyond rent, so R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(1) requires it in the rent section: 'If there are fees beyond the rent that apply to the rental of a unit, the lease shall disclose those fees in the same section as the rent disclosure and shall indicate that additional fees may apply.' (§ 34-18-15(a)(1)); see `fee-disclosure-ri`. A key deposit would be part of the security deposit (§ 34-18-19(a), 'however denominated'). Read in the act text (PL2026-ch147, chs. 147 and 148 identical apart from sponsor lines). See `edu-keys-ri`, `edu-dv-lockchange-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Use of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit) prior to occupancy. Any other deposit Landlord requires, however it is described (including any pet, key or damage deposit), is part of the Security Deposit, except a separate furniture security deposit that this Lease states for furnished property. When the tenancy ends, Landlord may deduct from the Security Deposit only unpaid accrued Rent, reasonable cleaning expenses, reasonable trash disposal expenses, and the cost of physical damage to the property, other than ordinary wear and tear, that Landlord suffers because Tenant did not meet Tenant's maintenance duties. Landlord will not deduct late fees or other fees. Landlord will itemize any deductions in a written notice to Tenant and deliver it with the balance of the Security Deposit as Rhode Island law requires. The Security Deposit will not relieve Tenant of any obligation to pay Rent due before this Lease ends.
notes: RI: Overrides `security-deposit-use`, which lets Landlord apply the deposit "to remedy a Tenant default" (late fees, other charges); Rhode Island's list is closed. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(b): 'the amount of security deposit due to the tenant shall be the entire amount given by the tenant as a security deposit, minus any amount of unpaid accrued rent, the amount due, if any, for reasonable cleaning expenses, the amount due, if any, for reasonable trash disposal expenses and the amount of physical damages to the premises, other than ordinary wear and tear, that the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with § 34-18-24, all as itemized by the landlord in a written notice delivered to the tenant.' (§ 34-18-19(b)); (a): 'A landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent.' (§ 34-18-19(a)); (e) separate furniture deposit; (h) 'No rental agreement shall contain any waiver of the provisions of this section.' (§ 34-18-19(h)). The clause states the landlord's figure; the one-month limit is education (rule 55; `edu-security-deposit-cap-ri`). Return timing and the double-damages penalty: `edu-security-deposit-return-ri`. A restoration escrow for a disability modification is outside the cap (§ 34-37-4(d)). 'Ordinary wear and tear' is § 34-18-11(8), renumbered (11) on July 1, 2026 (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 147, 148, § 1). See `edu-security-deposit-use-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Amounts Due at Signing
bodyText: Tenant will pay Landlord the first month's Monthly Rent of {{monthly_rent}} and a Security Deposit of {{security_deposit}}, when stated here: [state when each is due]. [Other amounts due at signing, each of which is also listed with the Rent in this Lease's Rent section: [list each, or state "none"].] Any deposit Landlord requires because of a pet, a key or anything else is part of the Security Deposit, except a separate furniture security deposit of up to one month's Monthly Rent that this Lease states for furniture Landlord provides with a replacement value, when this Lease is signed, of $5,000 or more. Neither Landlord nor anyone acting for Landlord has required or will require Tenant to pay a rental application fee.
notes: RI: Overrides `due-at-signing`, whose bracketed example lists a pet deposit beside the security deposit and "last month's Monthly Rent" as extra money at signing. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(a): 'A landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent.' (§ 34-18-19(a)), so every refundable deposit counts toward one cap, except the separate furniture security deposit that § 34-18-19(e) allows for a furnished apartment whose furniture has a replacement value of $5,000 or more (`furnishings-included-ri`). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-59(a): 'shall not be allowed to require or demand any prospective tenant to pay for a rental application fee' (§ 34-18-59(a)); only the actual cost of an official state criminal background check or credit report the applicant does not supply may be charged (§ 34-18-59(b)), which is paid at application, not at signing. Other amounts beyond rent must also appear in the rent section (§ 34-18-15(a)(1); `fee-disclosure-ri`). Last month's rent is left out of the example on purpose: whether prepaid rent beyond the first month counts as security 'however denominated' is not settled in the statute (case law not searched); see `edu-last-month-rent-ri`. See `edu-due-at-signing-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Utilities Included in Rent and Utilities Paid by Tenant
bodyText: Utility costs included in Monthly Rent (Landlord arranges and pays for these): [list each utility or service included in Monthly Rent, for example water, sewer, trash removal, heat, hot water or electricity, or state "none"]. Utility costs that are Tenant's responsibility (Tenant arranges and pays the provider directly unless this Lease states otherwise): [list each, for example electricity, gas, telephone, cable or internet]. A utility not listed in either place is not included in Monthly Rent, and Landlord will not charge Tenant for it unless this Lease is amended in writing.
notes: RI: Overrides `utilities-responsibility`, whose catch-all ("all other utilities ... as applicable") does not say which costs are in the rent. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(3): 'In any lease agreement the landlord shall disclose which utility costs are included in the rent and which utility costs are the tenant's responsibility.' (§ 34-18-15(a)(3)); (5) 'If a landlord fails to comply with subsections (a)(1) — (a)(4) of this section, the tenant may recover any fees paid for the unit that were not disclosed as required.' (§ 34-18-15(a)(5)). This row carries both lists, so `utilities-paid-by-landlord` is not tagged RI (one curated answer; the two could contradict each other; RI log §2.2). Rule 44: a listed utility becomes a term of the rental agreement, and § 34-18-28(a) gives remedies for 'noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement'; heat, water, hot water, electric and gas are essential services under § 34-18-31. The landlord must supply running and hot water at all times and reasonable heat October 1 to May 1, except where the building is not required by law to be so equipped or 'the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant and supplied by a direct public utility connection' (§ 34-18-22(a)(6)), and a rental agreement 'may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with § 34-18-22(a)' (§ 34-18-18). The statute doesn't say whether a lease may make the tenant buy delivered heating oil or propane, which is not a public utility connection, so "heating fuel" is left out of the tenant-paid example; list heat or heating fuel as Tenant's only where the exception plainly applies (drafting judgment). Anyone who bills for electricity must itemize the bill (§ 39-3-37.2). See `edu-utilities-responsibility-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Lead-Based Paint Disclosure (Rhode Island)
bodyText: [Use for housing built before 1978, except a zero-bedroom unit in which no child resides, or housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities in which no child resides and no child under 6 is expected to reside. Print this disclosure and acknowledgment on its own separate page of this Lease, or as a stand-alone document that includes the property address.] LEAD WARNING STATEMENT. Housing built before 1978 may contain lead-based paint. Lead from paint, paint chips, and dust can pose health hazards if not managed properly. Lead exposure is especially harmful to young children and pregnant women. Before renting pre-1978 housing, lessors must disclose the presence of known lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards in the dwelling. Lessees must also receive a federally approved pamphlet on lead poisoning prevention. Property: {{property_address}}, unit [unit number, if any]. Landlord's disclosure: [state either that Landlord has no knowledge of lead-based paint or lead hazards at the property, or describe all known lead-based paint and lead hazards]. Lead certificates: [attach a copy of each current lead certificate for the dwelling unit and the common areas, or state that there is none]. Records and reports: [list in date order all available records and reports pertaining to lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards at the property, including every lead inspection report and lead certificate, and confirm they have been provided to Tenant, or state that Landlord has none]. Tenant may obtain a further copy of any report or certificate listed by asking [name and contact information]; Landlord will deliver it within 7 days of the request at no charge. Rhode Island lead law: [state basic information about Rhode Island's lead poisoning prevention rules and how they apply to this property, for example whether it has a lead certificate of conformance or is exempt]. Person responsible for maintaining the property: [name and contact information of the owner, registered agent or designated person]. Tenant acknowledges receipt of the information above and of the pamphlet Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home with the insert What You Should Know about the Rhode Island Lead Law. Landlord and Tenant each certify, to the best of their knowledge, that the information they have provided is true and accurate.
notes: RI: Overrides `lead-based-paint` (federal text only) for Rhode Island's additions. 216-RICR-50-15-3.5.3(A): 'Non-exempt sellers and lessors shall meet all of the following requirements before a purchaser or lessee is obligated under any contract to purchase or lease target housing'; (A)(1) 'The seller or lessor shall provide the purchaser or lessee with the EPA pamphlet Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home containing the insert What You Should Know about the Rhode Island Lead Law'; (A)(2) a lead warning statement and written disclosure acknowledgment in each lease 'including oral leases'; (A)(3)(c) the property address and unit, a copy of any current lead certificate(s) for the unit and common areas, a chronological listing of all available lead inspection reports and certificates, and instructions for obtaining copies, 'Delivery to the requesting purchaser or lessee must be made within seven (7) days of the request and at no charge.'; (A)(3)(d) for rentals, basic information about the Part and its applicability, and the name and contact information of the owner, registered agent and/or designated person responsible for maintaining the property; (A)(3)(e) 'The disclosure acknowledgment must be a stand-alone document, which includes the property address, or its own separate page when included in a written lease.' (216-RICR-50-15-3.5.3); (A)(3)(f) keep the signed copy three years or the tenancy, whichever is longer. 'Target housing' (216-RICR-50-15-3.3): 'any pre-1978 residential dwelling, except housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities or zero (0) bedroom units in which no child resides'. The use-bracket keeps the elderly or disability exemption only where no child resides and no child under 6 is expected to reside, reading 'in which no child resides' as attaching to both exceptions and adding the federal definition (40 C.F.R. § 745.103, not in the corpus), which exempts such housing only where no child under 6 resides or is expected to reside (drafting judgment). 'The requirements in § 3.5 of this Part are in addition to, not in lieu of, Federal requirements for disclosure of lead-based paint and/or environmental lead hazards in housing (24 C.F.R. Part 35, Subpart A and 40 C.F.R. Part 745, Subpart F).' (216-RICR-50-15-3.5.1), so the records line keeps the federal duty to provide the tenant all available records and reports (40 C.F.R. § 745.107(a)(4), not in the corpus) alongside the Rhode Island listing. The federal warning statement is verbatim from 40 C.F.R. § 745.113(b)(1) as in the shared row. Placement (rule 40): own page; builder flag in RI log §10. Read 216-RICR-50-15-3.2, 3.3 (target housing), 3.5 in full; the Part's § 3.2.1(A)(3)(a) cross-reference to '§ 3.8' for disclosure is stale (flagged, RI log §10). Lead certificate of conformance and registry: ch. 42-128.1, 860-RICR-00-00-2, § 34-18-58(b). See `edu-lead-disclosure-ri`, `edu-lead-certificate-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant Default
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and does not cure the failure within the time period specified by applicable law after receiving written notice from Landlord. Tenant will also be in default if Tenant fails to comply with any other obligation under this Lease and does not cure the failure after receiving written notice. Landlord need not give Tenant an opportunity to cure any breach, including a failure to pay Rent, where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without one. Except as required by applicable law, Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise all rights and remedies available under applicable law, including terminating this Lease, regaining possession of the property, and recovering unpaid Rent, late fees, actual damages and court costs as Rhode Island law allows, less amounts obtained from the Security Deposit. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to mitigate damages resulting from Tenant's default to the extent required by applicable law. If Landlord accepts Rent knowing that Tenant is in default, Landlord may end this Lease for that default only by giving Tenant written notice within 10 days; accepting a partial payment of Rent does not waive the balance due. Landlord may recover attorneys' fees from Tenant only where Rhode Island's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act allows them, and Tenant may recover attorneys' fees from Landlord where applicable law allows them.
notes: RI: Overrides `default-by-tenant` on two points. (1) Fees: its sentence "To the extent permitted under applicable law, the prevailing party may recover from the other party court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees" and "reasonable costs and expenses" risk a term that 'Agrees to pay the landlord's attorney's fees inconsistent with this chapter' (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a)(3)), and § 34-18-17(b): 'If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known to be prohibited, the tenant may recover, in addition to his or her actual damages, an amount up to three (3) months periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees.' (§ 34-18-17(b)), so rule 47 rules out relying on self-limiting wording. The chapter's own fee grants: §§ 34-18-35(d) (nonpayment, only after a demand notice in the prior six months and willful nonpayment), 34-18-36(d) (willful noncompliance), 34-18-38(c) (willful bad-faith holdover), 34-18-43, 34-18-45(c), 34-18-32(a) (frivolous counterclaim). (2) Waiver: § 34-18-41: 'Acceptance of rent with knowledge of a default by the tenant or acceptance of performance by him or her that varies from the terms of the rental agreement constitutes a waiver of the landlord's right to terminate the rental agreement for that breach, unless the landlord gives written notice within ten (10) days. However, acceptance of partial payment of rent shall not constitute a waiver of the balance due.' (§ 34-18-41). Cure (rule 43): nonpayment cure by tender before suit, and at the hearing if no demand notice in the prior six months (§ 34-18-35(e)), is left to applicable law; no-cure grounds §§ 34-18-24(8)-(10), 34-18-36(e)-(f). Mitigation: § 34-18-5(a). See `edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-ri`, `edu-attorney-fees-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord: [list approved pets, or state that no pets are permitted]. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, due with each Monthly Rent payment and also listed with the Rent in this Lease's Rent section. Any deposit Landlord requires because of a pet is part of the Security Deposit. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet, and will indemnify Landlord against claims arising from Tenant's pet, except claims arising from Landlord's own negligence or any other liability of Landlord arising under law. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or a danger to people or property, by written notice giving Tenant a reasonable time to remove it. Landlord will enter the property because of a pet only as this Lease's Access & Entry terms and Rhode Island law allow. This Section does not apply to an assistance animal, which this Lease's assistance animal terms govern.
notes: RI: Overrides `pet-policy` on three points. (1) Its indemnity "from claims arising from Tenant's pet(s)" could reach the landlord's own liability, which § 34-18-17(a)(4) bars: 'Agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law or to indemnify the landlord for that liability or the costs connected with the liability.' (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a)(4)). (2) Its power to "enter the property and remove a pet, without liability to Tenant" meets § 34-18-26(d): 'A landlord has no other right of access except:' (§ 34-18-26(d)), and the exculpation bar; entry stays within `landlords-access-ri` (emergency entry, § 34-18-26(b)). (3) Pet rent is a fee beyond rent that must be in the rent section (§ 34-18-15(a)(1); `fee-disclosure-ri`), and a pet deposit is part of the one-month cap (§ 34-18-19(a), 'however denominated'). Modeled on `pet-policy-ct`. Assistance animals: no extra compensation, liability for damage (§ 34-37-4(e)(2)). See `edu-pet-policy-ri`, `edu-pet-fees-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If a check or other payment Tenant gives Landlord is dishonored or fails, Landlord may require Tenant to replace it with a cashier's check, certified check or money order, and Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount] for that payment, which is also listed with the Rent in this Lease's Rent section. Landlord will charge only one returned-payment fee for each dishonored or failed payment. If more than two of Tenant's payments in any 12-month period are dishonored or fail, Landlord may require future Rent to be paid by cashier's check, certified check or money order.
notes: RI: Overrides `returned-payments`, whose "fee ... not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law" states no amount; R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(1) requires every fee beyond rent to be disclosed in the rent section ('the lease shall disclose those fees in the same section as the rent disclosure'), and an undisclosed fee is recoverable (§ 34-18-15(a)(5)); see `fee-disclosure-ri`. No Rhode Island statute caps a lease's returned-payment fee; chapter 6-42 gives the holder of a dishonored check separate statutory remedies after notice (`edu-returned-payments-ri`). The fee is the landlord's figure, so it is a bracket, not a statutory cap. Requiring certified funds does not charge a convenience fee (§ 34-18-61). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Vehicles and Parking Rules
bodyText: Only operable, currently registered passenger vehicles may be parked at the property; commercial vehicles, recreational vehicles, trailers and oversized vehicles are not permitted without Landlord's prior written consent. Landlord may require Tenant to provide vehicle registration information and may issue parking tags, decals or access cards. Landlord will not charge Tenant for the tags, decals or cards issued at the start of the tenancy, but may charge the reasonable cost of replacing one that Tenant loses or damages, which is also listed with the Rent in this Lease's Rent section. A vehicle parked anywhere at the property other than where this Lease or Landlord's parking rules allow is parked without Landlord's consent. Landlord may have a vehicle that is parked without Landlord's consent or abandoned at the property removed at the vehicle owner's expense only as Rhode Island law permits. Vehicle repairs are not permitted at the property except minor emergency repairs necessary to move the vehicle, and vehicles may be washed only in areas Landlord designates, if any.
notes: RI: Overrides `parking-vehicle-rules`. Towing: R.I. Gen. Laws § 39-12.1-12 reaches vehicles trespassing on private property without the consent of the owner or person in control, and the owner who orders a tow bears the cost if the vehicle was not trespassing (read section-open); the shared clause's grounds "inoperable, or has expired registration" would let Landlord tow a tenant's car parked with consent. The clause defines parking outside permitted areas as parking without consent and otherwise defers to Rhode Island law (case law not searched). Tag and decal charges: fee beyond rent, so listed in the rent section (§ 34-18-15(a)(1); `fee-disclosure-ri`). Modeled on `parking-vehicle-rules-ct`. See `edu-towing-ri`, `edu-parking-rules-notice-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Landscaping & Irrigation
bodyText: Unless Landlord provides landscaping service, Tenant will perform these landscaping tasks: [list each task, for example mowing the lawn and raking leaves]; in a building with more than one dwelling unit, this applies only to areas Tenant alone uses. If Landlord has set an irrigation schedule, Tenant will not modify it, and will promptly inform Landlord of any irrigation or landscaping issue, such as a leak or watering deficiency. Tenant agrees in good faith to perform these tasks as part of the bargain reflected in the Monthly Rent. They do not include any work needed to bring the property into compliance with building and housing codes, and they do not reduce Landlord's duties to other tenants.
notes: RI: Overrides `landscaping-irrigation` to meet R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(c). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(c): 'The landlord and tenant of a dwelling unit may agree in writing that the tenant perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, and remodeling but only if:' (1) 'The agreement of the parties is entered into in good faith and set forth in a writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration;' (2) 'The work is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subsection (a)(1); and' (3) 'The agreement does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises.' (§ 34-18-22(c)). Rhode Island has no single-family split and does not require a separate writing (rule 48's settled branches don't fit), so the signed Lease is the writing, and the tasks are listed one by one because (c) reaches only 'specified' tasks; the added sentence states the good faith, the consideration and conditions (2)-(3). Whether a court would require consideration beyond the Lease bargain is case law, not searched. In a multi-unit building the task is limited to areas the tenant alone uses, since common areas are the landlord's duty (§ 34-18-22(a)(3)). See `edu-landscaping-ri`, `edu-tenant-maintenance-agreement-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Snow Removal
bodyText: Unless Landlord provides snow removal, Tenant will promptly remove snow and ice from the areas of the property Tenant uses for walking, parking and access. This does not include areas shared with other residents. Tenant agrees in good faith to perform these tasks as part of the bargain reflected in the Monthly Rent. They do not include any work needed to bring the property into compliance with building and housing codes, and they do not reduce Landlord's duties to other tenants.
notes: RI: Overrides `snow-removal` to meet R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(c). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(c): 'The landlord and tenant of a dwelling unit may agree in writing that the tenant perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, and remodeling but only if:' (1) 'The agreement of the parties is entered into in good faith and set forth in a writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration;' (2) 'The work is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subsection (a)(1); and' (3) 'The agreement does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises.' (§ 34-18-22(c)). Rhode Island has no single-family split and does not require a separate writing (rule 48's settled branches don't fit), so the signed Lease is the writing; the added sentence states the good faith, the consideration and conditions (2)-(3). Whether a court would require consideration beyond the Lease bargain is case law, not searched. Shared areas stay excluded, keeping § 34-18-22(c)(3). See `edu-snow-removal-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Fees in Addition to Rent
bodyText: [Place this text in the same section of the Lease as the Monthly Rent; if the tenant or unit receives a state or federal subsidy that requires a different lease format, follow that format instead.] In addition to Monthly Rent, the following fees apply to the rental of the property: [list each fee this Lease provides for, with its amount or how it is calculated and when it is charged, for example the late fee, returned-payment fee, pet rent, parking or storage fee, key or lock replacement charge, and any early termination fee, or state "none"]. Additional fees may apply. Landlord will give Tenant written notice at least 30 days before any change in a required fee takes effect.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(1): 'If there are fees beyond the rent that apply to the rental of a unit, the lease shall disclose those fees in the same section as the rent disclosure and shall indicate that additional fees may apply. This requirement does not apply whenever the tenant or unit are receiving state or federal subsidies that require a different lease format.' (§ 34-18-15(a)(1)); (2) 'Any change in required fees must be disclosed in writing at least thirty (30) days prior to the change becoming effective.' (§ 34-18-15(a)(2)), a sentence in the no-written-lease paragraph that the clause adopts for every tenancy (drafting judgment, cheaper error); (5) undisclosed fees are recoverable. 'Additional fees may apply' is the statute's required indication. Placement (rule 40): inside the rent section; the use bracket tells a landlord bound by a subsidy program's required lease format to follow that format (drafting judgment: the clause wording is lawful either way, so only the placement instruction changes); builder flag in RI log §10 (fill the list from the fee clauses the landlord selects). See `edu-fee-disclosure-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Landlord's Liability Insurance
bodyText: Landlord has obtained, and will keep in force, a general liability insurance policy with coverage of [coverage amount] for persons injured on the premises due to Landlord's negligence. A copy of the declaration page from the insurance carrier showing the policy is attached to this Lease, and Landlord will give Tenant a new copy each time the policy is renewed.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(a)(7): 'Obtain and have in full force and effect a general liability insurance policy of at least one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) for those persons injured on the premises due to the negligence of the landlord. The landlord shall provide a copy of the declaration page from the carrier showing the policy to the tenant with the written lease at the beginning of the tenancy and shall provide a new copy with each policy renewal to the tenant.' (§ 34-18-22(a)(7); P.L. 2021, chs. 210, 323, effective January 1, 2022). The written lease is the statute's vehicle for the declaration page, so the clause records the attachment. The coverage is the landlord's figure (a bracket); the $100,000 minimum is in `edu-landlord-liability-insurance-ri` (rule 55). Builder flag (RI log §10): attachment prompt. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Owner and Manager Information
bodyText: The person authorized to manage the property is: [name, address and telephone number]. The owner of the property, or the person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands, is: [name, address and telephone number; if Landlord does not live in Rhode Island, this is Landlord's designated Rhode Island agent]. Landlord will keep this information current and will tell Tenant in writing of any change.
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-20(a): 'A landlord or any person authorized to enter into a rental agreement on his or her behalf shall disclose to the tenant in writing, at or before the commencement of the tenancy, the name, address and number of:' (1) 'The person authorized to manage the premises; and' (2) 'An owner of the premises or a person authorized to act for and on behalf of the owner for the purpose of service of process and receiving and receipting for notices and demands.' (§ 34-18-20(a)); (b) 'The information required to be furnished by this section shall be kept current.'; (c) a person who fails to disclose becomes the landlord's agent. The lease is a writing given at commencement, so it can carry the disclosure. A nonresident landlord must keep an in-state agent filed with the secretary of state and the city or town clerk (§ 34-18-22.3). From January 1, 2027, § 34-18-20(e) adds the shoreline disclosure (`shoreline-access-disclosure-ri`). See `edu-owner-manager-disclosure-ri`, `edu-nonresident-landlord-agent-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: [Use only if the dwelling unit is shoreline property, meaning real estate that abuts the shore. Required for tenancies beginning on or after January 1, 2027.] SHORELINE ACCESS DISCLOSURE. Shoreline Access – Members of the public shall have the right to access shoreline property as defined in § 5-20.8-1. The public's rights and privileges of the shore may be exercised, where shore exists, on wet sand or dry sand or rocky beach, up to ten feet (10') landward of the recognizable high tide line, subject to the restrictions governed by § 46-23-26 and any general laws to the contrary. Public rights-of-way on the property known to Landlord: [describe each, or state that Landlord knows of none]. On request, Landlord will give Tenant a copy of any documentation in Landlord's possession evidencing those rights-of-way or conditions of public access. Tenant is advised to contact the coastal resources management council, the municipality, or applicable nonprofit organizations to determine whether any public rights-of-way exist.
notes: RI: New § 34-18-20(e), added by R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 165, 166, § 1, effective January 1, 2027 (not yet in the compiled General Laws): 'For any dwelling unit that constitutes shoreline property as defined in § 5-20.8-1, the landlord shall provide the tenant, prior to the commencement of the tenancy, with a written shoreline access disclosure, which shall include the following information:' (i) the shoreline access text (quoted verbatim in the clause from (e)(1)(i)); (ii) 'The landlord is required to notify the tenant of any public rights-of-way on the real estate that are known to the landlord.' and copies on request; (iii) the advice to contact the council, municipality or nonprofits; (e)(2) 'The disclosure required by this subsection may be satisfied by incorporating it into any written rental agreement'. R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-20.8-1(9): '"Shoreline property" means any real estate that abuts the shore as governed by § 46-23-26.' Chapters 165 and 166 are identical after markup is removed (checked by script). Effective-date clause read: 'This act shall take effect on January 1, 2027.' The statute ties the duty to providing the disclosure 'prior to the commencement of the tenancy' from that date; for a tenancy that began earlier the statute is silent (rule 37), so use it on every new lease or renewal from January 1, 2027. Flag for the legal watch (changeover date). New topic key. Short-term rentals: § 42-63.1-14(l). Rule 15: written section-open.
lease_clause_basis: REQUIRED_DISCLOSURE: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-20(e) (R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 165, 166, § 1)

title: Housing Code Violations
bodyText: Before Tenant signed this Lease, Landlord informed Tenant of the following outstanding minimum housing code violations on the building: [list each outstanding violation, or state that there are none]. [If any notice of violation or order served on Landlord has not been complied with: Before Tenant signed this Lease, Landlord gave Tenant a true copy of each such notice or order, which is attached, and notified the enforcing officer in writing as Rhode Island law requires.]
notes: RI: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22.1(b): 'A landlord, prior to entering into any residential rental agreement, shall inform a prospective tenant of any outstanding minimum housing code violations which exist on the building that is the subject of the rental agreement.' (§ 34-18-22.1(b)). R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-17(j) adds, where a notice of violation or order has been served and not complied with, that the owner may not lease until it 'first furnishes to the grantee, lessee, or mortgagee prior to the transfer, lease, or mortgage, a true copy of any notice or order' and notifies the enforcing officer in writing (read section-open). Neither section makes the lease the vehicle or requires writing for § 34-18-22.1(b), so this is a record of the pre-signing disclosure (rule 78: the disclosure must come before signing; the clause records it), basis SERVES_LANDLORD. Whether the 'lease ... the building' wording of § 45-24.3-17(j) reaches a single-unit lease is applied as written (drafting judgment). See `edu-code-violation-disclosure-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Seasonal Tenancy
bodyText: [Optional. Use only for a written seasonal lease whose Term begins no earlier than May 1 and ends no later than October 15 of the same year, or begins no earlier than September 1 and ends no later than June 1 of the next year.] This Lease is a seasonal lease. It ends at the end of the Term, and Tenant has no right to renew or extend it beyond that date. Tenant will not allow more persons to occupy the property than this Lease and the law allow, and will not make or allow excessive noise or other disturbance of the peace. If Tenant is charged with violating a municipal ordinance, or violates this Lease's terms on legal occupancy or on excessive noise or other disturbance of the peace, Landlord may file an eviction action without first giving Tenant a notice of noncompliance or an opportunity to cure, as Rhode Island law allows for seasonal tenants.
notes: RI: Optional (rule 54: a right that exists only if the lease sets it up). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-36(f): 'is a seasonal tenant occupying the premises pursuant to a written lease agreement which commences no earlier than May 1st of the occupation year and expires no later than October 15th of the occupation year, or commences no earlier than September 1st and expires no later than June 1st of the next subsequent year, with no right of renewal or extension beyond the above dates; and (ii) has been charged with violating a municipal ordinance or has otherwise violated the terms of the rental agreement pertaining to legal occupancy or excessive noise or other disturbance of the peace, the landlord shall not be required to send a notice of noncompliance to the tenant and may immediately file a complaint for eviction' (§ 34-18-36(f)). The route needs a written lease with the statutory dates, no renewal right, and lease terms on occupancy and noise, which this clause supplies; the builder's Term dates must fall inside a window (builder flag, RI log §10). Holdover after the term follows § 34-18-38. Municipal occupancy or noise ordinances not searched (rule 3). New topic key. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Rent Changes During the Term
bodyText: [Optional. Choose one.] [A: Monthly Rent will change during the Term as follows: [state each new amount and the date it takes effect]. Monthly Rent will not change during the Term in any other way.] [B: During the Term, Landlord may increase Monthly Rent by giving Tenant written notice at least 60 days before the increase takes effect, stating the new Monthly Rent and its effective date. Tenant may instead end this Lease, without any early termination charge, by giving Landlord written notice before the increase takes effect, effective on the last day before the increase.] Even for a change listed in this Lease, Landlord will give Tenant written notice at least 60 days before each increase takes effect, or at least 120 days if Tenant is over 62 and the tenancy is month to month. Landlord will not increase Rent to retaliate against Tenant for any complaint, request or other conduct the law protects.
notes: RI: Optional (rule 54; Taylor's IN decision, 2026-09-30, and `rent-increase-midterm-ct` pattern). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-16.1(a): 'notice of the increase shall be given in writing to any tenant by a landlord at least sixty (60) days prior to the effective date of the increase.' (§ 34-18-16.1(a)); (b) 'shall give at least one hundred twenty (120) days' notice to month-to-month tenants over the age of sixty-two (62) years, before raising the rent.' (§ 34-18-16.1(b)); both exclude independent living, assisted living and congregate care facilities. The statute does not say whether an increase already scheduled in a signed lease needs notice; the clause gives it anyway (cheaper error). Rent terms not prohibited by the chapter may be agreed (§ 34-18-15(a)). Retaliation: § 34-18-46 (presumption within six months of a complaint). Option B's exit is a drafting choice that keeps the term from being one-sided (case law on unilateral mid-term increases not searched). See `edu-rent-escalation-ri`, `edu-rent-increase-notice-ri`. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Landlord's Option to End the Lease After a Fire or Casualty
bodyText: [Optional.] If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty so that Tenant's enjoyment of it is substantially impaired, and the fire or casualty was not caused by Landlord's deliberate or negligent act, Landlord may end this Lease by written notice to Tenant, effective on a date stated in the notice that is at least 14 days after the notice is given or, if Tenant has already moved out, on the date Tenant moved out. Rent will be accounted for as of the date of the fire or casualty, and Landlord will return the Security Deposit as this Lease and Rhode Island law provide and all prepaid Rent. This Section is in addition to Tenant's rights under Rhode Island law after a fire or casualty, including Tenant's right to move out immediately and end this Lease by written notice within 14 days, or to stop using any part of the property made unusable and pay reduced Rent, and it does not limit them.
notes: RI: Optional landlord casualty termination (rule 54: a landlord right the statute leaves to contract). R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-33(a) gives only the tenant rights: 'Immediately vacate the premises and notify the landlord in writing within fourteen (14) days thereafter of his or her intention to terminate the rental agreement, in which case the rental agreement terminates as of the date of vacating; or' (§ 34-18-33(a)(1)) or pro rata abatement ((a)(2)); (b) 'If the rental agreement is terminated the landlord shall return all security recoverable under § 34-18-19 and all prepaid rent. Accounting for rent in the event of termination or apportionment shall be made as of the date of the fire or casualty.' (§ 34-18-33(b)). The tenant's options have no tenant-fault exception, so the clause preserves them in full (§ 34-18-17(a)(1)). The 14-day minimum notice is a drafting judgment matching the statute's tenant notice window; possession after termination is recovered only by court action (§ 34-18-44). Modeled on the AL, SC and KS landlord-option rows. See `edu-casualty-termination-ri`, `edu-tenant-caused-damage-ri` (no tenant-caused-damage clause offered: the lease cannot remove the § 34-18-33 options and tort damages need no clause). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Automatic Renewal
bodyText: [Optional.] This Lease will renew automatically for a further term of [state the renewal term] on the same terms, except for any change made as this Lease and Rhode Island law allow, unless either party gives the other written notice of non-renewal at least [state the notice period] before the end of the then-current Term. Landlord will remind Tenant in writing of this automatic renewal provision at least 30 days before the last day for giving that notice. A rent increase on renewal requires the written notice Rhode Island law requires before it takes effect.
notes: RI: Optional (triage candidate from `auto-renewal-ny`, rule 54). No Rhode Island statute regulates automatic renewal of residential leases (`edu-no-automatic-renewal-rule-ri`; RI-automatic-renewal-1, hits 7, and RI-automatic-renewal-3, hits 4, both OK, statute-wide; the only statute requiring notice of an automatic lease renewal, § 6-13-14, is limited to 'a written lease of personal property' (§ 6-13-14(a)); RI-automatic-renewal-2 is recorded as FAILED and was rerun as -3). The parties may agree the term (§ 34-18-15(a), 'term of the agreement'). Without renewal, a holdover with consent becomes week-to-week or month-to-month (§ 34-18-38(c)). The reminder is a drafting judgment that protects enforceability (case law not searched); a renewal rent increase needs 60 days' written notice (§ 34-18-16.1(a)). No statute sets the non-renewal notice period for a fixed term, so the landlord's figure goes in the bracket; the § 34-18-37 periods apply only once a tenancy is periodic. Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Asbestos in the Building
bodyText: Rhode Island has no asbestos disclosure rule for leases, but the state asbestos law applies to rental buildings. If your building has friable (crumbling or easily damaged) asbestos, you must not let anyone be exposed to it where the exposure breaks the asbestos law, a Department of Health asbestos regulation, or an abatement plan the Department approved. Any occupant, including a tenant or the parent of a child living there, may ask the Department of Health in writing to inspect the building for friable asbestos or to enforce an abatement plan; the Department must answer within 45 days, and the complainant's name stays confidential. Removal or repair of friable asbestos is regulated work that follows the Department's rules and licensing. Before renovating, or if a tenant reports damaged pipe insulation, ceiling or floor material, have it assessed.
notes: RI: Found by the landlord-scenario screen (battery RI-scen-asbestos-1; the sales disclosure in § 5-20.8-2 lists 'Hazardous Waste — (Asbestos and Other Contaminants)' for sales only, and no landlord-tenant or housing code section mentions asbestos). R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-24.5-5(a): 'No owner of a structure with friable asbestos or with friable asbestiform materials or any person or entity owning or controlling asbestos or asbestiform products in a friable state shall allow any person to be exposed to asbestos or asbestiform materials in a friable condition when the exposed condition is a violation of a provision this chapter, of a regulation issued pursuant to the authority of this chapter, or of an abatement plan approved by the director.' (§ 23-24.5-5(a); R.I. Pub. L. 2026, chs. 44 and 45 (companion acts, effective on passage), § 1, only insert 'of' after 'provision'). § 23-24.5-11(a): 'An occupant of any building or the parent or guardian of any minor who is an occupant of a building' may request an inspection 'for the purpose of detecting friable asbestos, of demanding enforcement of an abatement plan' (§ 23-24.5-11(a)); (b) answer 'within forty-five (45) days' (§ 23-24.5-11(b)); (d) 'The name of the complainant shall remain confidential.' (§ 23-24.5-11(d)). The anti-retaliation protection in § 23-24.5-11(e) covers only public employees and beneficiaries of public funds, so the row does not state a tenant retaliation rule. Abatement plans, orders and fines: §§ 23-24.5-6, -12. The same acts also amend §§ 23-24.5-2, -6, -8, -12 to -14 and -25 (licensing and abatement detail, not read for this row). Rule 15: written section-open.

title: Tenant Bankruptcy
bodyText: Rhode Island's landlord-tenant law has no rule of its own on what happens when a tenant files for bankruptcy; a search of the Rhode Island General Laws and the 2025 and 2026 public laws found none. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act says general principles of law, including bankruptcy, supplement it, so federal bankruptcy law decides whether you can continue an eviction, collect past-due rent or enforce a lease term that ends the lease because of the bankruptcy. If a tenant tells you they have filed, stop collection and eviction steps and get advice on federal bankruptcy law before going further.
notes: RI: Confirmed absent (state rule on tenant bankruptcy), found by the landlord-scenario screen. Battery RI-scen-bankruptcy-1 (bankrupt*/insolven* within 300 characters of tenant, lessee, rental agreement or lease, over the General Laws and the 2025-2026 acts) hit 11 units: none governs residential tenancies (UCC Article 2A goods leases in ch. 6A-2.1, dealer franchises § 5-55-4, exemptions § 6-16-1, a public hub § 23-99-5 and its 2025 acts) except R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-3(a): 'Unless displaced by the provisions of this chapter, the principles of law and equity, including the law relating to capacity to contract, mutuality of obligations, principal and agent, real property, public health, safety, and fire prevention, estoppel, fraud, misrepresentation, duress, coercion, mistake, bankruptcy, or other validating or invalidating cause supplements its provisions.' (§ 34-18-3(a)). The federal rules (automatic stay, ipso facto clauses) are outside this state pass and were not checked; the row only points the landlord to them. Rule 15: written section-open.
